question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Social Protection for an overview of the Budget 2027 supports for pensioners.
reply:
Over €13 billion was allocated to State Pensions in Budget 2027, which is an increase of almost €1 billion compared with Budget 2026.
There will be a €10 increase in the maximum weekly rate of all State Pensions from January 2027. This means the State Pension (Contributory) will exceed €300 per week for the first time at a maximum rate of €309.30. The State Pension (Non-Contributory) will increase to a maximum weekly rate of €298. There will be proportionate increases for qualified adults and people getting a reduced rate of pension.
The Living Alone Increase is increasing to €25 per week from January, the first increase to the payment in five years. This payment has increased by nearly 178% since 2019, when it was just €9 per week.
Budget 2027 also provides for a €5 increase in Fuel Allowance, from €38 to €43 per week. This represents an additional €140 over the fuel season and will bring the total annual value of the payment to over €1,200. Budget 2027 also improves access to Fuel Allowance for older people by increasing the means threshold for single pensioners. The income limit for a single person aged 66 or over will increase from 50% to 60% of the corresponding limit for a couple.
In addition, from July 2027 the upper income threshold for the Increase for a Qualified Adult in relation to the State Pension (Contributory) and other social insurance schemes will increase from €310 to €340 per week.

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Social Protection the measures being taken by his department to improve awareness and uptake of the Household Benefits Package among eligible people, particularly those aged 70 and over; and whether an automatic enrolment of eligible recipients would be considered.
reply:
The Household Benefits package is available to those aged 70 or over regardless of means and household composition, however there is no automatic entitlement to the payment and similar to many other Social Welfare benefits a person aged over 70 must submit an application form to determine entitlement.
To qualify for the Household Benefits Package applicants aged over 70 must be legally resident in the State and no other person in their household can be in receipt of the allowance. An applicant must also be the registered consumer of electricity/gas if she or he is applying for an Electricity Allowance or Natural Gas Allowance and must also register for the Public Services Card when requested to do so by the department.
Taking the above into consideration, the introduction of automatic enrolment of eligible recipients would not be practical and therefore cannot be considered at this time.
With regards to improving awareness and uptake of the Household Benefits Package, information regarding the Household Benefits Package is widely available in Department of Social Protection and Citizen’s Information offices, and online through the Gov.ie and Citizen Information websites.
To further increase awareness of the scheme my Department launched a public information campaign to promote the Household Benefit Package. This was launched on 12th October and advertisements feature across regional radio and social media channels until 15th November.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Social Protection whether consideration is being given to extending eligibility for domiciliary care allowance from 16 to age 18 years-of-age; the rationale for the current age limit; and the review undertaken or planned in this regard.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 77 and 94 together.
Domiciliary Care Allowance is a payment to a parent or guardian in respect of a child under 16 who has a severe disability and requires continuous care and attention, substantially more than is typically required by a child of the same age.
From January 2026, the monthly rate of Domiciliary Care Allowance increased from €360 to €380. Over 66,600 families receive Domiciliary Care Allowance in respect of approximately 76,400 children, with estimated expenditure of almost €359 million in 2026.
Domiciliary Care Allowance stops being paid when a child turns 16 years of age. A young person whose disability significantly impacts their daily living activities may then apply for Disability Allowance in their own right, which is currently payable at a maximum personal rate of €254 per week. To help avoid a gap in support, an application for Disability Allowance can be made up to three months before the young person’s 16th birthday.
Where the young person's carer is also receiving Carer's Allowance or Carer's Benefit, those payments may continue for as long as the relevant qualifying conditions continue to be met. The carer may also continue to qualify for the annual Carer's Support Grant of €2,000 where the qualifying conditions are met.
There are no plans to extend Domiciliary Care Allowance from age 16 to 18 years at this time.

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Social Protection the steps he will take to ensure that seasonal workers, including those who work in schools, who lose working family payment during holiday time, do not have to wait six or eight weeks when employment resumes to get their WFP back in payment.
reply:
Working Family Payment (WFP), formerly Family Income Supplement, is a weekly in-work support which provides an income top-up for employees on low earnings with children. To qualify for Working Family Payment the customer must be working a minimum of 38 hours per fortnight in ongoing insurable employment and have at least 1 qualified child who normally resides with them.
The Department is committed to providing a quality service to all its customers. This includes ensuring that applications are processed as quickly as possible, currently within 4 weeks.
Working Family Payment (WFP) new claim applications have increased by 27% in 2026, with 58,764 customers currently in receipt of the payment compared to 51,323 at the beginning of the year. The number of WFP claims for Educational Sector Workers requiring reinstatement during the same period has also increased significantly. Despite this increased workload, processing times have remained in line with the 2025 levels, and all outstanding ESW cases were cleared by mid to late October 2026.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Social Protection for an update on the rate of rejected domiciliary care allowance applications subsequently overturned on appeal; and the average length of time taken to process an appeal.
reply:
There is no direct correlation between the number and percentage of Domiciliary Care Allowance decisions and the number of appeals registered during a particular time period. Timing differences will always apply. This is particularly the case since the Appeal Regulations which came into effect from April 2025 increased the number of days a person has to make an appeal from 21 days to 60 days. Accordingly appeals received in January 2026 may refer to decisions made in November 2025.
However, as an indication of the appeal rate, 4,864 Domiciliary Care Allowance applications were rejected up to end of Quarter 3 2026. The number of Domiciliary Care Allowance appellants who received a favourable decision on their appeal in the same period of time was 1,918. This indicates that 39% of those who appealed received a favourable decision.
Where an appeal is successful it does not always indicate that the original decision was incorrect. In many cases, an appellant submits additional information or evidence during the review or appeals process that was not available to the Deciding Officer when the original decision was determined. This can result in a different decision being made on review or appeal.
The average timeframe to process all appeals up to end of Quarter 3 2026 was 10.7 weeks. The average timeframe to process Domiciliary Care Allowance appeals for the same period was 9 weeks.

question: Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Social Protection to report on the findings of the nutritional review and survey on hot school meals.
reply:
The key finding in the Nutrition Review report was there is a wide variety of healthy meals on offer. 82% of meal options reviewed did not contain foods considered to be high in fat, salt or sugar such as chicken goujons, sausages or fried potato products. However, when data on meals ordered was analysed, it is evident that high, fat ,salt and sugar foods are chosen over healthier options when available on the menu.
There was a total of 18 recommendations. The Government has already accepted these recommendations, and work has commenced to implement them over the next 12 months.
These include increasing the provision of fruit, vegetables and wholegrain foods, improving some recipes that are higher in fat and salt than desirable, strengthening nutritional provision in vegetarian and vegan meals, ensuring age-appropriate portion sizes and enhancing menu options for children with special dietary requirements.
Nutrition Standards for Hot School Meals have been in place since the inception of the scheme and were strengthened in 2025 through the removal of foods high in fat, salt and sugar from menus. Following the nutritional review, the standards have been revised and consolidated to remove ambiguity and further support compliance with national healthy eating guidelines.

This includes where the applicant received a revised decision from my Department or where the claim was allowed or partially allowed by an Appeals Officer.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Social Protection for an overview of the Budget 2027 supports for carers.
reply:

As part of Budget 2027, I announced a number of measures to support carers, these include:

Even with an income of €156,000 a couple could still receive a partial Carer’s Allowance payment. question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Social Protection his plans to review the means test for the qualified adult payment for pensions.
reply:
My Department provides State Pension payments through the State Pension (Contributory), which is based on a person's social insurance record, and the State Pension (Non-Contributory), which is means-tested social assistance payment.
A State Pension (Contributory) recipient can claim an increase on their pension in respect of a qualified adult subject to a means test and where the eligibility conditions are satisfied. Only the means of the spouse or partner of the claimant are assessed. Where savings, property or other assets are held jointly, the spouse or partner's means is taken to be half of the total amount.
Article 7 of SI 142 of 2007, the Social Welfare (Consolidated Claims, Payments and Control) Regulations, as amended, sets out the income limit for the payment of an Increase for a Qualified Adult across a range of schemes, not solely in respect of the State Pension (Contributory) scheme.
An Increase for Qualified Adult is payable at the maximum rate of payment where the means of the qualified adult are not more than €100 per week.
Currently, reduced rates are payable where means are over €100 and not more than €310 per week. However, as I announced in Budget 2027, from July next year the upper threshold for qualified adults will increase to €340 for a number of schemes, thus enabling more pensioners to qualify for an increased payment in respect of their spouse or partner.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will review the rules governing receipt of carer's allowance and carer's benefit with a view to increasing the maximum number of hours carers may engage in employment, self-employment, education or training outside the home, which is currently limited to 18.5 hours per week.
reply:
My Department provides a comprehensive package of income supports for carers, including Carer’s Allowance, Carer’s Benefit, Domiciliary Care Allowance and the Carer’s Support Grant. Combined expenditure on these schemes in 2026 is expected to exceed €2.2 billion.
The primary objective of carers payments is to provide an income support to carers whose earning capacity is substantially reduced because of their full-time caring responsibilities.
A primary qualifying condition for Carer's Allowance and Carer's Benefit is that the applicant must be providing full-time care and attention. A person is regarded as providing full time care where they provide at least 35 hours of care per week, over any five days in a seven day period.
While carer income support payments are based on the provision of full-time care and attention, they also provide flexibility in terms of supporting carers to engage in work, training or education for up to 18.5 hours per week. During this time, adequate provision must be made for the care of the relevant person.
There are no plans to amend this condition at this time. In setting the relevant threshold, it is essential to balance the needs of the carer and the needs of the person receiving care. question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of people in receipt of carer's allowance for the years 2022-2026 inclusive; and the way in which the income disregards for carer's allowance have made a difference to carers during this time.
reply:
Carer’s Allowance is the main income support for carers in the community, with at an estimated cost of over €1.4 billion this year.
- At the end of 2022 there were 92,175 recipients.
- At the end of 2023 there were 95,787 recipients.
- At the end of 2024 there were 97,985 recipients.
- At the end of 2025 there were 104,522 recipients.
- At the end of October 2026 there were some 113,085 recipients of the payment.
Over the period the number of Carer’s Allowance recipients has increased by 23%.
Budget 2027 is the Government’s second Budget. Since 2025 we have increased the income disregard for single carers by €525 and by €1,050 for a carer in a working age couple household, an increase of 84%.
From July this year, the weekly disregard increased from €625 to €1,000 for a single carer and from €1,250 to €2,000 for a carer in a couple household.
This means that a carer in a two-adult working-age household with an income of €110,000 can retain their full Carer’s Allowance payment and receive a partial payment with a household income up to €139,000.
Some 2,700 carers received an increase payment in July as a result of this measure and virtually all Carer’s Allowance recipients are now receiving their maximum weekly payment. There are 570 carers being paid Carer’s Allowance at a reduced rate due to means, representing approximately 0.5% of the total customer base.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Social Protection if his attention has been drawn to concerns related to the quality and nutritional value of some of the food provided under the Hot School Meals Programme; if he proposes to create guidelines regarding standards and nutritional requirements for service providers.
reply:
I am aware that concerns have been raised by some parents, schools and public representatives regarding the quality and nutritional value of certain meals provided under the Hot School Meals Scheme.
To assess these concerns and identify opportunities for improvement, I commissioned a comprehensive nutritional review of the scheme, led by a CORU-registered School Meals Dietitian under the clinical supervision of the Department of Health. In parallel, an extensive survey of principals, teachers, parents, children and meal suppliers was undertaken by IPSOS/Behaviour and Attitudes.
The findings of both exercises were generally positive. The nutritional review found that there is a wide variety of nutritious and well-balanced meals available under the scheme and that 82% of meals examined did not contain foods considered to be high in fat, salt or sugar. Feedback from schools was also largely positive, with 78% of teachers rating the nutritional value of meals as acceptable, good or excellent and 79% rating meal quality positively.
The survey findings similarly demonstrated strong support for the programme. 85% of children reported that they liked their lunch, while 76% stated that they eat all, most or some of their meal. The survey also found that the programme is now deeply embedded in participating schools and widely recognised for its benefits.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Social Protection the average wait time for medical review for those on domiciliary, disability and invalidity in each of the past five years.
reply:
The assessment of medical-related schemes like Domiciliary Care Allowance, Disability Allowance and Invalidity Pension involves a medical assessment as part of the decision process encompassing all qualifying criteria for the relevant scheme.
In medical review process, my department’s Medical Assessors consider the medical reports, customers’ statement on the impact of their daily activities, care provided, and any relevant information submitted by the customer or their treating physicians against the qualifying criteria of the scheme applied for. The medical opinions are recorded for consideration before a decision is made on the eligibility by a Deciding Officer having examined the non-medical qualifying criteria for the relevant scheme.
The Deputy’s question on average wait time for medical review per se is not available but average weeks to awards on claims for these schemes in the past few years are as follow: -
Domiciliary Care Allowance
From 2019, the average weeks to award was 10 weeks, down to 7 weeks in 2025.
Disability Allowance
From 2019, the average weeks to award was 13 weeks, down to 6 weeks in 2025.
Invalidity Pension
From 2019, the average weeks to award was 9 weeks, down to 6 weeks in 2025.
In all these schemes the reduction in waiting time is between 30%- 54% in the intervening years.
I hope this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

reply:

Budget 2027 provides for €30 billion in social protection expenditure, a €2 billion increase on 2026. Social welfare payment rates will increase by €10, at a cost of some €755 million and will assist in mitigating the prices increase for both pension and working age recipients.
ESRI analysis of Budget 2027 shows that the increases announced in core weekly rates of Social Protection supports are again ahead of inflation, as they were in Budget 2026 and Budget 2025. The analysis shows that changes to direct tax and welfare measures and childcare supports announced as part of Budget 2027 are, on average, ahead of forecast price growth of 3% and broadly in line with forecast wage growth of 4.1% for 2027. question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Social Protection to provide an update on the introduction of a pay-related carer’s benefit for family carers.
reply:
Carer’s Benefit is a payment made to insured people who are required to leave the workforce or reduce their working hours to care for a person in need of full-time care. The scheme has, since January 2025, been extended to the self-employed.
There are currently over 5,000 people receiving Carer's Benefit and expenditure in 2026 is estimated to exceed €76 million.
The Government acknowledges the valuable role that family carers play and is fully committed to supporting carers in that role. This is recognised in the Programme for Government, which includes a number of commitments in relation to carers, including the commitment to examine the introduction of a Pay Related Carer’s Benefit for individuals who have to give up work suddenly in order to provide full-time care to a loved one.
The Jobseeker's Pay-Related Benefit scheme started in March of last year. While it is a relatively new payment our experience in operating it will help to inform future decisions regarding pay-related schemes, including, potentially, Carer's Benefit. I also intend to consult in the coming months on the further extension of pay-related schemes, which will be useful to inform thinking on this approach.

reply:

reply:

Under Treatment Benefit, unlike other social welfare schemes, the amount of social insurance contributions required depends on the person's age, taking into account their opportunity to have accumulated contributions.
For those aged under 21, the only requirement is to have at least 39 contributions paid at any time.

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Social Protection the rationale for excluding children under 16 in receipt of the Domiciliary Care Allowance from the new €500 annual Cost of Disability Payment announced in Budget 2027; and whether consideration will be given to reviewing their eligibility as part of the future development of the scheme.

question: Deputy Liam Quaide asked the Minister for Social Protection if his Department will commit to a review of the excessive paperwork and administrative burdens surrounding the wage subsidy scheme and the work and access scheme which employers and disabled jobseekers report acts as a barrier to employment.
reply:
The Government is committed to improving the employment position of disabled people, and I am determined that we will do that. My Department offers a range of employment supports in pursuit of this goal and we want these schemes to be accessible and easy to use.
My Department reviewed the Work and Access scheme guidelines earlier this year after feedback was received from disabled people and employers. Revised operational guidelines and application forms were published in April. The guidelines have been shortened and application forms were simplified and we hope that this will reduce the administrative burden and applicants will find them easier to navigate and understand.
In 2023, a review of the Wage Subsidy Scheme took place and was published in 2024. The report found that out of employers who had used the scheme before, 79% of them approved of the application process and 89% approved of the payments system. It found that "The scheme’s ongoing administrative procedures were widely approved."

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Social Protection if he has plans to review the means test for the State pension (non-contributory) or the disability allowance.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 54 and 69 together.
The system of social assistance supports provides payments based on an income need. The means test plays a critical role in determining whether or not an income need arises as a consequence of a particular contingency – such as disability, unemployment or caring. This ensures that each recipient has a verifiable income need and that resources are targeted to those who need them most.
Social welfare legislation provides that means tests take account of the income and assets of the person (and their spouse or partner) applying for the relevant scheme. The means assessment includes income from sources such as employment, self-employment, and occupational pensions. It also includes property owned, other than the family home, and capital such as savings, shares, and other investments.
However, specific disregards apply for certain sources of income or amounts of capital. In the case of the State Pension (Non-Contributory) the first €20,000 of capital is disregarded entirely, meaning no assessment is applied to this portion. For the next €10,000 above this threshold, an assessment of €1 per €1,000 is applied. The subsequent €10,000 is assessed at a rate of €2 per €1,000. Any remaining balance above these amounts is assessed at €4 per €1,000. This ensures a progressive approach to capital means assessment. question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Social Protection for an overview of the Budget 2027 supports for families and children.
reply:
In recognition of the financial pressures facing families and children, Budget 2027 builds on the significant supports provided in recent Budgets, and includes a range of measures to provide additional support to families and children.
Budget 2027 provides for a €6 increase in the weekly Child Support Payment, bringing the weekly rate to €64 for children under 12 and €84 for children aged 12 and over from January 2027. The Child Support Payment is included with most social welfare payments in respect of qualified children and provides targeted assistance to families on low incomes.
Budget 2027 also provides for a €10 weekly increase in most social welfare core payments from January 2027, providing additional support to families receiving these payments.
The weekly income thresholds for the Working Family Payment will increase in 2027 by €30 for all families. The Working Family Payment provides an income top-up to employees on low earnings with children and supports low-income working families.
In addition, the employment earnings disregard for One-Parent Family Payment and Jobseeker's Transitional Payment will increase by €10 per week, from €165 to €175, from July 2027.
The weekly rate of Fuel Allowance will also increase by €5, from €38 to €43 in January, providing additional support to eligible low-income households.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will review his decision to continue means testing for the carers allowance and make a provision for this in the Social Welfare Bill that is currently being debated in Dáil Eireann; and to make a statement on the matter.
reply:

From July 2026, I increased the weekly income disregard from €625 to €1,000 for a single person, and from €1,250 to €2,000 for a carer in a couple household.
These changes mean that a carer in a two-adult working-age household with an income of €110,000 can retain their full Carer’s Allowance payment and receive a partial payment with a household income up to €139,000.

This will mean that a working-age couple household will be able to earn more than €126,000 annually and retain a full Carer's Allowance payment. question: Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Social Protection when he expects to bring forward proposals to introduce a pay related parent's benefit, as committed to in the Programme for Government.
reply:
The Programme for Government commits to introducing Pay-Related Parent's Benefit and exploring other payments where a similar model could be applied.
Parent’s Benefit provides nine weeks paid leave to parents during the first two years of a child’s life or following adoption. Parent’s Benefit is currently paid at €299 per week, increasing to €309 from January 2027. Government has provided over €123m for the scheme in 2026.
My Department will draw on the learnings from the Jobseeker's Pay-Related Benefit scheme introduced last year, to inform options for pay-related Parent’s Benefit. I also intend to issue a public consultation document on a pay-related approach to Parents' Benefit over the coming months.

reply:
This issue relates to a group of former workers who left the service of Waterford Crystal between 1990 and 1992 under a redundancy arrangement. At the time of the redundancy, the workers received a refund of their pension contributions relating to their service in the relevant company pension schemes up to that time. As a result, they then ceased to be members of the pension scheme and no longer had any rights or entitlements under the schemes.
Separately, in 2010, a legal action was taken by a group of former Waterford Crystal workers against the State following the insolvency of the Waterford Crystal Factory and Staff pension schemes. In 2015, a mediated settlement was reached between the parties to that legal action. The mediated settlement applied to all persons who were members of the Waterford Crystal Staff and Factory pension schemes on the date of wind-up of the schemes (31st March 2009). In total, 1,774 scheme members are covered by the agreement. The total costs to the Exchequer arising from the mediated agreement were estimated at €253 million.

question: Deputy Rose Conway-Walsh asked the Minister for Social Protection whether he will consider extending the wage subsidy scheme to disabled entrepreneurs.
reply:
The Wage Subsidy Scheme is a financial incentive to employers to hire disabled people. The key aim of the scheme is to encourage employers to provide substantial and sustainable work to disabled people. It is open to employers in the private, commercial semi-state, and non-profit sectors.
The scheme is available to disabled entrepreneurs when hiring staff for their business; however, the subsidy is not available to a person as incentive for their own self-employment, given the fundamentally different nature of that form of employment.
A review of the scheme in 2024 resulted in many changes to the scheme including expanding eligibility for both employers and employees. Budget 2027 brought changes to the scheme such as reducing the minimum hours from 15 to 8 and increasing the Employee Assistance Officer grant by €15,000. Any further changes to the scheme could only be considered in a budgetary context.
However, there are other supports available to disabled entrepreneurs such as the Work and Access scheme and the Enterprise Support Grant.
Work and Access offers seven supports to improve access in the workplace for disabled people. Funding is available for communication supports, work equipment, workplace adaptations and training. question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Social Protection for a progress update on his plans to remove the means-test for the carer's allowance.
reply:
Carer’s Allowance is the main income support for carers in the community, with 113,000 people receiving the payment, at an estimated cost of over €1.4 billion this year.
The Programme for Government commits to significantly increasing the income disregards for Carer’s Allowance, with a view to phasing out the means test during the lifetime of this Government. We are well on our way to achieve this commitment whereby I have significantly increased the rate of disregard by 84% over the last two budgets.
From July 2026, I increased the weekly income disregard from €625 to €1,000 for a single person, and from €1,250 to €2,000 for a carer in a couple household.
These changes mean that a carer in a two-adult working-age household with an income of €110,000 can retain their full Carer’s Allowance payment and receive a partial payment with a household income up to €139,000.
Some 2,700 carers received an increase in their payment because of this measure. Almost everyone on the scheme is now being paid at their maximum weekly rate.
As part of Budget 2027, I announced that the disregard will increase by a further €150 to €1,150 for a single carer and by €300 to €2,300 for a carer in a couple household. This will mean that a working-age couple household can earn more than €126,000 annually and retain a full Carer's Allowance payment. Even with an income more than €156,000 a couple will receive a partial Carer's Allowance payment.

question: Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will review the means-testing arrangements for jobseeker's allowance in the case of cohabiting couples, given that the income of a cohabiting partner is assessed for social welfare purposes while such couples are not afforded the same treatment as married couples for taxation purposes, including the ability to be jointly assessed by the Revenue Commissioners.
reply:
The purpose of the means test for certain social welfare payments is to ensure that State resources are targeted towards those with the greatest need for income supports.
The social welfare and tax systems have evolved over time and in response to a variety of factors, including Constitutional imperatives as interpreted by the Courts, changing social trends and European Union legislation.
A Supreme Court case (Hyland v Minister for Social Welfare, 1989) led to the current treatment of non-married cohabiting couples in the social welfare code. The Court ruled that it was unconstitutional for the total income a married couple received in social welfare benefits to be less than the couple would have received if they were unmarried and cohabiting. This means that for social assistance means-tested schemes such as Jobseeker’s Allowance, married couples, civil partners and cohabiting couples are treated in the same manner.
Under Schedule 3 of the Social Welfare (Consolidation) Act 2005, as amended, all income and assets belonging to a claimant and, where applicable, their spouse, civil partner or cohabitant are taken into account when assessing eligibility for means?tested social assistance schemes.
Where a claimant’s spouse, civil partner or cohabitant is in employment, their earnings are assessed in accordance with the legislation governing the relevant means?tested scheme.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will provide additional financial supports to healthcare workers suffering with long-Covid.
reply:
In November 2023, my Department published a report on the inclusion of long COVID in the Occupational Injuries Benefit Regulations.
The report concluded that COVID-19 does not satisfy the statutory criteria for recognition as an occupational illness or accident at work. Specifically, it found that presumptions about workplace transmission would not be sustainable as it is not possible to establish with confidence that the disease has been contracted through a person’s occupation and not through community transmission. This is because data show that community transmission was the primary means of transmission.
It is important to note that, even if Ireland did recognise COVID-19 as an occupational disease, this would not encompass long COVID and would only apply to new claims for new cases of COVID-19. As such, it would not benefit those who contracted COVID-19 during the pandemic.
With specific reference to workers in the health services, the report found that the Temporary Scheme of Paid Leave for Public Health Service Employees was the appropriate channel through which a targeted sectoral support should be considered. This Temporary Scheme was a matter for the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, who extended it a number of times. McGuinness asked the Minister for Social Protection whether there are statutory or administrative time limits on the recovery of historic social welfare overpayments, particularly those arising during the Covid-19 pandemic; and whether consideration is given to the passage of time and the circumstances in which such overpayments occurred.
reply:
Overpayments of social welfare payments arise when a person receives a payment to which they were not entitled. Social welfare legislation provides that where any person receives a social welfare payment or a portion of a payment they were not entitled to, the sum which was overpaid is recoverable from the person who received the payment.
A Deciding Officer will determine, based on the facts and evidence of each case, if a person had an entitlement to a payment and if an overpayment should be assessed. The principles of natural justice are applied and the customer may provide any further information in advance of a final decision. This final decision can be reviewed and/or appealed to the Social Welfare Appeals Office. This ensures fairness and transparency in the decision making process and in the overpayments that are assessed.
An overpayment will remain on a persons record and can be pursued up to future pension entitlements and following death, where an estate remains. The provisions in respect of recovery of debts outstanding are covered by Section 338 of the Social Welfare Consolidation Act.
A structured debt management policy in line with normal good practice in recovery of overpayments operates within my Department, including yearly statements issued to customers of outstanding overpayments.
My Department is satisfied that the current procedures for raising overpayments and recovery of overpayments are fair, consistent and equitable for all customers.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Social Protection to provide an update on the extension of illness benefit to the self-employed.
reply:
Illness Benefit is the primary short term income support provided by the Department of Social Protection to those who are unable to work due to illness of any type and who are covered by social insurance. Eligibility for Illness Benefit depends on the person’s PRSI record and class.
The person must have made the required number of contributions under class A, E, H or P to qualify. In general, self-employed people make PRSI contributions at class S.
Self-employed contributors pay class S PRSI at a rate of 4.35%. This is 11.40 percentage points lower than the combined employer and employee contribution of 15.75% made in respect of employed contributors. However, self-employed contributors do have access to over 90% of benefits available to employed contributors.
The only benefits that class S PRSI does not provide access to are Health and Safety Benefit, Illness Benefit and Occupational Injuries Benefits. Self-employed contributors who are ill may qualify for Invalidity Pension which is also based on a person’s PRSI record.
In circumstances where people are ill but do not qualify for a contributory payment, my Department provides means tested supports under the Disability Allowance scheme and the Supplementary Welfare Allowance scheme. An Additional Needs Payment may also be available to people who have expenses that they cannot pay from their weekly income.

question: Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Social Protection if his Department will review the eligibility requirements for the bereaved partners pension.
reply:
Bereaved Partner's (Contributory) Pension (BPCP) is a weekly social insurance payment for a person whose spouse, civil partner or qualified cohabitant has died.
To qualify for the payment, a person must:
• be a widow, widower, surviving civil partner or surviving qualified cohabitant;
• not be cohabiting with another person; and,
• satisfy the relevant social insurance contribution conditions.
Entitlement may be based on either the claimant's own social insurance record or that of their deceased partner, subject to the scheme conditions. The two contribution records cannot be combined.
From 21 July 2025, eligibility for the payment was extended to surviving qualified cohabitants. Prior to this change, the scheme was available only to surviving spouses and civil partners.
For the purposes of the scheme, a person is regarded as a qualified cohabitant where the couple had lived together as a couple for a continuous period of at least two years where there are children of the relationship, or five years where there are no children of the relationship.
The Bereaved Partner's (Contributory) Pension is not payable where a person remarries, enters into a civil partnership or cohabits with another person. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if facilities which have received funding under the Community Centres Investment Fund, including facilities developed on school grounds, are required to demonstrate that the completed facility is being operated and made accessible for the benefit of the wider community.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 406, 407, 408 and 409 together.
Since becoming Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht, I have prioritised investment in community infrastructure.
The Community Centre Investment Fund (CCIF) was introduced to provide high-quality community facilities that are available to community groups in both urban and rural communities. Through the CCIF, some €118 million has been allocated for the enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres and the construction of new centres where such a need has been identified.
The 2026 CCIF guidelines state that schools, sports clubs or other single purpose organisations can apply where they can clearly show that they have a facility which is already open to and used by the wider community for defined eligible activities to a good extent. The information provided in this regard is considered as part of the application appraisal process.
It is expected that such access would continue to be provided following provision of the grant.
My department does not have a role in the management structure of community centres or in the ranges of services provided.
The designation of community infrastructure under other schemes would be a matter for each individual scheme.
Should the Deputy have a query in relation to a specific facility, I would be happy to arrange for my officials to examine any such query further.

reply:

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the rationale for requiring a married student under 23 years-of-age who is living independently of their parents to be assessed as a dependent student for SUSI grant purposes; and whether consideration is being given to providing an exemption in such circumstances.
reply:
The decision on eligibility for a student grant is a matter, in the first instance, for the centralised student grant awarding authority SUSI (Student Universal Support Ireland) to determine.
It is important to note that currently under the Student Grant Scheme, a student can only be assessed as independent if they were 23 years of age or older on 1 January of the year they first entered higher education and were not living with their parents. Unfortunately, if a student does not meet these conditions, they will be assessed as a dependent student, meaning parental income will be considered when assessing eligibility for a student grant.
It is also important to point out that SUSI provide an appeals process for students who are unhappy with the outcome of a grant application. The appeal must be received by SUSI within 30 days of an original grant decision.
Subsequently, where an appeal has been turned down in writing by an appeals officer in SUSI and the student remains of the view that the scheme has not been interpreted correctly, an appeal may be lodged with the independent Student Grants Appeals Board within the required timeframe. Such appeals can be made online via www.studentgrantappeals.ie.

reply:

reply:
The HSE remains responsible for managing recruitment and workforce planning, including the assessment and prioritisation of posts through its national and regional structures. Where additional recruitment controls apply, proposals require HSE approval and prioritisation before being submitted to the Department of Health for financial sanction. These arrangements do not transfer responsibility for managing recruitment or running health services to the Department.
The controls do not constitute a recruitment freeze. Recruitment can continue within approved pay allocations, subject to the necessary approvals. question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of cases of overpayment currently with his Department; the overall number of cases; the overall amount involved; and the highest amount of overpayment in a single case.
reply:
People who have received an overpayment from the Department of Social Protection have a liability under law to refund the overpayment. They have received money to which they were not entitled. The Department has a responsibility to ensure that all overpayments are refunded in full.
Social Welfare overpayments in any given year represent less than 0.5% of total expenditure. In general, the majority of overpayments are a result of customer error, where information that affects entitlement to payments is not provided in a timely manner resulting in small overpayments.
The Department can recover an overpayment by deducting instalments from on-going weekly payments or entering into a repayment plan where a person is no longer receiving a social welfare payment. Where a person does not engage with the Department to agree a repayment plan, the Department has powers of attachments to a person’s earnings or to funds held in financial institutions to recover an overpayment. Debt holders are made aware that a social welfare debt will remain on their records until it is fully recovered.
At the end of 2025 the closing debt balance stood at €597m for just over 222,350 overpayments, it is important to note that a person may have a number of overpayments. The highest value overpayment raised in 2025 was for €268,145.

question: Deputy Marie Sherlock asked the Minister for Health to set out in specific detail the dataset, methodology and the weighting applied in the “data driven scientific approach” to the application process for the social deprivation practice grant.
reply:
The 2019 GP GMS Agreement introduced a social deprivation grant to support GMS GPs in socially deprived urban areas to provide additional services.
In late 2025, the HSE, Department of Health, GP representatives and representatives of GPs working in areas of deprivation reached agreement to improve the targeting of the social deprivation grant for GPs.
It had always been intended that the grant allocation process would use a data analysis approach. However, work to identify those practices was delayed by the Covid Pandemic. Grants were therefore allocated in the years 2020 to 2024 on the basis of applications received from GPs.
The HSE National Contracts Office collaborated with the National Health Intelligence Unit (NHIU) to apply a data analysis approach to the grant allocation process. The current grant allocation process is based on GEO coding of patients’ places of residence and referencing those to their GP practices to identify the most socially deprived GP panels held by GMS GPs across the country.
GPs receive the grant each year on a three-year basis, providing funding security for the practice. After the three-year period, it is envisioned that GEO coding analysis will re-identify the most socially deprived GMS panels whose GP will receive the grant over the next term.

reply:

The Household Benefits Package is available to those aged 70 or over regardless of means and household composition. It is also available as a supplementary allowance to those in receipt of various social welfare payments.
With regards to targeted measures, the Department provides support to households who are most vulnerable to energy poverty via the Fuel Allowance payment. The Fuel Allowance payment is a means tested payment which is targeted towards households that are at a higher risk of poverty.
Fuel Allowance eligibility encompasses 22 qualifying schemes, with approximately 26% of all households nationwide qualifying for the payment demonstrating the comprehensive nature of the support. In addition to these qualifying schemes, people over 66 do not need to be in receipt of a payment from this Department to qualify for Fuel Allowance, subject to satisfying a means test.

Of these, 466,723 households are eligible for the Fuel Allowance scheme, representing approximately 26% of all households nationwide. reply:

Officials from this Department has worked with officials in the Department of Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht and compiled a list of supports available to local communities, including meals on wheels services, who may wish to expand their operation into the school meals area. I would note that consideration of any proposed changes to Ireland’s screening programmes will be facilitated through established evidence-driven protocols.
The National Screening Advisory Committee (NSAC) is the expert group that considers proposed changes to Ireland’s screening programmes. NSAC assesses the evidence in a robust and transparent manner and against internationally accepted criteria, before making recommendations to myself as Minister.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Social Protection if he is aware of the growing concerns that the €10 core social welfare increase is not sufficient to match the pace of inflation; the measures he will take to address this.
reply:
On Budget day, I announced an increase the weekly rates of payment for working age recipients under 66 years of age and pensioners by €10 per week, with proportionate increases for qualified adults and those on reduced rates.
This increase is estimated to cost €750 million in 2027 and will benefit over 1.5 million recipients, with over 600,000 recipients on means-tested payments. Over 700,000 pensioners will benefit from this increase, along with over 40,000 qualified adults.
In the case of the State Pension (Contributory), the €10 increase represents a 3.3% increase on the 2026 weekly rate, which will be higher than 3.0% inflation rate forecast by the Economic and Fiscal Outlook for 2027.
Other increases announced in Budget 2027 include increased Fuel Allowance payment from €38 to €43 per week, a 13% increase. Coupled with the Fuel Allowance weekly rate increase is improvements in the Fuel Allowance means test for single pensioners. The income limit for a single person aged 66 or over will increase to 60% of the limit for a couple. The Living Alone Allowance also increased by €3, to €25 per week.
Thresholds for Working Family Payment will increase by €30 in 2027. This measure builds on increases applied in recent budgets: as a result, income thresholds for all family sizes will have increased by €274 per week since Budget 2020.

question: Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Social Protection if he is aware of the hardship the provision in the bereaved partner's pension Bill to exclude divorced and separated partners has had, particularly in the instance of lone parents; and if he will consider extending supports to this small group.
reply:
As the Deputy is aware, the Social Welfare (Bereaved Partner's Pension and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2025 was enacted on 21 July 2025.
The provisions of the Act which introduced the Bereaved Partner's (Contributory) Pension were as a result of the Supreme Court decision on the entitlement of an unmarried cohabitant to a Widower's Contributory Pension. In simple terms, the Court found that section 124 of the Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005 (as amended) was inconsistent with the Constitution insofar as it excluded the claimant from the category of persons entitled to a Widower's Contributory Pension. The Supreme Court recognised that legislation was necessary in order to give effect to its decision.
In developing the legislative response, the basis upon which earlier rules for the scheme were framed, including (a) the entitlement of divorced partners, at the time when divorce was first introduced, and, (b) rates of payment based on an earlier marriage, had to be considered in light of new rights to the payment created for surviving qualifying cohabitants.
In this regard, the new legislation underpinning the Bereaved Partner's (Contributory) Pension sets the qualifying criteria for ongoing relationships equally on a marriage, civil partnership or a relationship of qualified cohabitation that has not ended via divorce or broken down for more than two years at the date of death.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine further to Parliamentary Question No. 68013/26, the way in which he reconciles this response with the repeated, documented use of “snare”, “snares” and “snaring” by NPWS and DAFM officials in 2015, 2018, 2023 and 2024, including selective retention of that terminology by a person (details supplied) in his substantive 2024 reply.
reply:
As noted in the previous reply to PQ 68013/26 a stopped body restraint has erroneously been referred to as a snare by many stakeholders. The Wildlife Act 1976 (Approved Traps, Snares and Nets) Regulations 2003 provides for the methods by which wildlife may be captured subject to a licence in accordance with the provisions of the Wildlife Act 1976, as amended. Badgers are captured using 'stopped body restraints' as defined under regulation 3(d) of the above Regulations.
The “substantive reply” you refer to was a reply to an email received by my Department. The phrase referred to in the Deputy’s question was in fact the language used by the person who posed the question to my Department. My Department responded to the question in the email as it was posed in that email. My Department supplied numerical data to answer the question and correctly used the legal defined term stopped body restraint to describe the device used to capture badgers in the reply.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Social Protection for an update on the work and access employment programme.
reply:
Work and Access offers seven supports to help reduce or remove barriers in the workplace for disabled people. The supports include funding for a workplace needs assessment, workplace adaptations and communication/ Irish Sign Language support.
Work and Access is open to all non-public sector employers, including the self-employed and people working in the community and voluntary sector. Supports are available for both business premises and remote workplaces.
My Department reviewed the scheme guidelines this year and revised operational guidelines and application forms were published in April. The guidelines have been shortened and we hope that applicants will find them easier to navigate and understand.
The application procedure for Communication Support/Irish Sign Language interpreting has been simplified following input from a Deaf Disabled Persons Organisation. Eligibility for 90% funding for Disability Equality and Inclusion Training has been extended.
Applications for Workplace Needs Assessments and In-Work Support are now made by employers to reduce the administrative burden on disabled customers and the application process has been simplified. The application forms have also been updated to simplify the process of applying for the scheme. The changes have been made in response to feedback from employers and disabled people.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if his Department will support engagement between Kerry County Council and relevant stakeholders to examine the management and operational model at Fenit Marina, including its annual berth-fee income, long-term tenancy arrangements with the RNLI and commercial operators, and its ability to operate on a self-funding basis; if his Department has undertaken or commissioned any assessment of successful marina management models in Ireland; and if similar models will be supported at smaller coastal locations such as Knightstown.
reply:
The Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine is responsible for the operation and maintenance six designated State-owned Fishery Harbour Centres, located at Castletownbere, Dingle, Dunmore East, Howth, Killybegs and Ros An Mhíl under statute.
The responsibility for the development, operation and maintenance of local authority owned piers, harbours and slipways rests with each local authority in the first instance and their parent Department, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage thereafter.
The management and operational arrangements at Fenit Marina, including any berth-fee income, tenancy arrangements with the users and commercial operators, and the assessment of its financial sustainability, are matters for Kerry County Council as the relevant harbour authority.
This Department has not undertaken or commissioned an assessment of any local authority marina management models in Ireland. Such an assessment would fall primarily within the remit of the relevant local authority, in conjunction with their parent Department.

reply:

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as the State's lead authority for cyber security and the management of major cyber incidents, continues to monitor developments in AI-enabled cyber threats and works closely with EU and international partners to address emerging risks.

question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an update on establishing a child maintenance service.
reply:

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will provide an update on improvements to the hot school meals programme this school year.
reply:
The School Meals Programme continues to be a key priority for Government, supporting children to access nutritious food during the school day while also reducing household costs for families. All 3,200 primary schools and 550,000 children are eligible for hot school meals. Across all meal types there some 3,700 schools and 682,000 children are eligible for support. This equates to the distribution of up to 3.4 million school meals per week.
In order to obtain an up-to-date assessment of the Hot School Meals Scheme following it's expansion I commissioned a comprehensive nutritional review of the scheme, led by a CORU-registered School Meals Dietitian under the clinical supervision of the Department of Health. In parallel, an extensive survey of principals, teachers, parents, children and meal suppliers was undertaken by IPSOS/Behaviour and Attitudes. Both of these reports were published in September 2026.
The findings of both exercises were generally positive. The nutritional review found that there is a wide variety of nutritious and well-balanced meals available under the scheme and that 82% of meals examined did not contain foods considered to be high in fat, salt or sugar. Feedback from schools was also largely positive, with 78% of teachers rating the nutritional value of meals as acceptable, good or excellent and 79% rating meal quality positively.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of applications for naturalisation received by his Department in each month to date in 2026.
reply:
All applications for a certificate of naturalisation are assessed individually based on the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended.
Applicants are required to have 5 years reckonable residence in the State prior to making an application, except for spouses of Irish nationals where the requirement is 3 years. In all cases, the final 12 months must be continuous residence in the State with up to 70 days allowed to facilitate foreign travel for business family or holiday purposes.
The Programme for Government contains a commitment to continue to implement a firmer and more sustainable migration system which protects the integrity of the State's immigration framework. reply:
It is a central priority for me that Ireland's immigration system is robust and rules based. Effective enforcement of our immigration laws, including the implementation of deportation orders, is essential to maintaining confidence in the integrity of the system and ensuring that our legislation is applied consistently.
The removal of individuals involved in criminality, and those who pose a danger to society, is a priority for me as Minister. My Department works closely with An Garda Síochána and the Irish Prison Service to ensure that high-risk individuals are prioritised for removal from Ireland.
I can advise the Deputy that a total of 130 people were removed from the State in 2025 due to criminality, of which 56 were removed under an EU Removal Order and 74 under a deportation order. Up to 30 October this year, 241 people have been removed due to criminality, of which 149 were removed under an EU Removal and 92 under a deportation order.
The Chișinău Declaration was finalised and adopted by the Committee of Ministers on 15th May 2026 at the 135th Session of the Committee of Ministers in Chișinău .
The Declaration first reaffirms Member States’ deep and abiding commitment to the Convention, and their support for the independence of the European Court of Human Rights. question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of an appeal lodged with the International Protection Appeals Tribunal by a person (details supplied) following a negative recommendation from the International Protection Office in January 2026; when the person can expect to be scheduled for an oral hearing, given that they have been waiting for most of 2026 without a date or any update.
reply:
As the Deputy may be aware, my Department is unable to publish any information that would identify any person as being an international protection applicant. This is a separate matter to the law dealing with data protection matters more generally.
My officials and I are legally obliged, under Section 26 of the International Protection Act 2015, to ensure that the identity of any person who applies for international protection is kept confidential. Section 26(1) sets out that:
“the Minister and the Tribunal and their respective officers shall take all practicable steps to ensure that the identity of applicants is kept confidential”.
As I am sure you will appreciate, these confidentiality requirements are especially important for an asylum-seeker, whose claim inherently supposes a fear of persecution by the authorities of their home country and whose situation, or that of their family or friends still living in the country from which they have sought protection, can be jeopardised if the protection of their personal information is not ensured.
An applicant for such protection status, or their legal representative, should contact either the International Protection Office (IPO) or the International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) directly, as appropriate if they wish to receive an update on the status of their case.
Contact information for The International Protection Office can be found at www.ipo.irishimmigration.ie/contact-us/.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the steps his Department is taking to support public bodies and local authorities in implementing the new Code of Practice for the operation of CCTV under the recent Act.
reply:
CCTV in public places can play an important role in supporting community safety and providing reassurance to the public. While the use of CCTV by An Garda Síochána and local authorities can bring significant benefits, its operation must be carefully managed to ensure that it is lawful, necessary and proportionate and complies with data protection requirements.
Part 5 of the Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) Act 2023 was commenced on 14 October 2026. The commencement of Part 5, together with related transitional arrangements and the publication of the Garda CCTV Code of Practice, establishes a new statutory framework for the authorisation and operation of public CCTV schemes, repealing section 38 of the Garda Síochána Act 2005. The Code of Practice and supporting guidance are publicly available.
Under the new framework, only local authorities or An Garda Síochána may be authorised to operate public CCTV schemes. Existing CCTV schemes authorised under section 38 of the 2005 Act may continue to operate for a period of up to four years from commencement, or until their authorisation is revoked by the Garda Commissioner, whichever occurs first. Applications submitted before 2 April 2025 on which a decision remains pending will continue to be processed under the previous legislative framework.
Community groups that identify a need for CCTV in public places may engage with their local authority or An Garda Síochána. Local Community Safety Partnerships, established under the Policin

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Social Protection the total number of habitual residence condition (HRC1) assessments conducted in the past 24-months; the specific percentage of applicants who failed the initial assessment; and the number of those failed assessments that were subsequently overturned on appeal to the social welfare appeals office.
reply:
The Habitual Residence Condition is a key eligibility requirement for many of the schemes operated by my Department. It applies to all exchequer-funded schemes, and requires that the applicant has a proven, close link to Ireland. A person has to have been in the State for some time, and they must demonstrate their intention to stay here for the foreseeable future.
To satisfy the Habitual Residence Condition, a person must have the legal right to reside in Ireland, and they must have the legal right to claim social protection benefits. The Habitual Residence Condition is assessed against the five grounds set out in legislation:
• Length and continuity of residence in Ireland.
• Length and purpose of any absence from Ireland.
• Nature and pattern of employment.
• The applicant's main centre of interest.
• Future intentions to live in Ireland as it appears from the evidence provided.
The Habitual Residency Condition and visa requirements work together to ensure the State's resources are targeted to people with a long-term interest in Ireland, and not those here on a temporary or short-term basis.
As most of my department's means-tested payments, as well as Child Benefit, have habitual residence as an eligibility condition, habitual residence assessments are carried out for all such claims. To date in 2026, this means that 106,000 Habitual Residency Condition assessments have been carried out across new Jobseeker’s Allowance applications alone; a further 29,000 on Disability Allo

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of members of the Reserve Defence Force insured at PRSI Class M in each of the past five years; the number of paid days of reserve service in respect of which no PRSI contributions were credited; and whether he will review Schedule C, paragraph 4 of S.I. 312 of 1996.
reply:
The Department doesn't hold sufficient data to identify the number of the Reserve Defence Forces insured at PRSI class M nor able to provide the number of paid days of which no PRSI contributions were credited. The employer, in this case the Department of Defence, would hold such data to provide these statistics.
Schedule C, paragraph 4 of S.I. 312 of 1996 was introduced by S.I. 26 of 1970 which provided for the exception from insurance under the Social Welfare Acts of employment for short periods as members of An Fórsa Cosanta Áitiúil or An Slua Muirí, now the Reserve Defence Force.
It is my understanding that the Reserve Defence Force is a part-time, volunteer organisation. Members are free to determine their own level of participation in Reserve activities and may resign from the Reserve at any time. Their service is provided entirely on a voluntary basis with no compulsion to attend.
Consequently, service as a member of the Reserve Defence Force for a period not exceeding 21 consecutive days is not considered insurable employment for social insurance purposes as this employment is considered to be subsidiary employment only and not the principal means of livelihood. PRSI Class M applies in these cases and therefore no PRSI is liable.
For those who undertake more than 21 consecutive days service, they and their employer are liable to pay PRSI under Class H.
There are no plans to review this arrangement by my Department. Any such review would be a matter for my colleague th

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Social Protection further to Parliamentary Question No. 71226/26, if correct legislation has been applied to the case taking into account the additional information (details supplied).
reply:
Legislation was introduced in 2009 which restricted the refund of PRSI on both compulsory PRSI and Voluntary PRSI.
A refund application has to be made within 4 years of the end of the contribution year in respect of which the contributions concerned were paid.
The legislation is contained in Section 38A, Chapter 6 of Part 2 of the Social Welfare Consolidation Act, 2005.
Section 38A(2) makes an exception to the 4-year time limit for applications received on or before 31 Dec 2009, so the legislation is not applied retrospectively.
Therefore, if the voluntary contributions were paid more than four years prior to the date of the refund application, where the application is made after 01 January 2010, no refund is due.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Social Protection whether, in the context of forthcoming proposals on surrogacy leave, he will also consider additional income and financial supports for intended parents who have undertaken surrogacy arrangements and incurred significant associated costs.
reply:
The Minister for Health leads on the Health (Assisted Human Reproduction) Act 2024, which includes provisions in relation to surrogacy which have implications for the introduction of surrogacy leave, while policy on parentage is a matter for the Minister for Justice. The implementation of this legislation is a prerequisite for the introduction of surrogacy leave by the Department of Children, Disability and Equality and the payment by my Department of an associated benefit.
My Department will work closely with the Department of Children, Disability and Equality, once the necessary legislation is in place, to progress proposals around surrogacy leave.
In the intervening period, my Department currently provides a number of key supports to new parents, including the monthly Child Benefit payment and the Newborn Baby Grant.
Both intended parents of a child born through surrogacy may be entitled to claim Parent’s Leave and Benefit, depending on their circumstances. Parent’s Benefit is available for up to nine weeks and is paid at €299 per week, increasing to €309 from January 2027.
The biological father of a child born through surrogacy may also qualify for Paternity Leave and Benefit. The leave entitlement is for two weeks, to be taken within six months of the child's birth. Paternity Benefit is paid at €299 per week, increasing to €309 from January 2027.
I trust this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of social welfare claims held by non-Irish nationals that were the subject of a control review or investigation in each of the years from 2020 to 2025 and to date in 2026; the number that resulted in a payment cessation or reduction; and the total value of overpayments assessed in respect of those claims.
reply:
My Department is committed to ensuring that only those people who are eligible, receive payments and other social protection entitlements. Achieving this requires that robust safeguards are in place that secure payment systems, detect possible fraud and error, and prevent possible fraudulent claiming. All schemes operated by my Department are subject to on-going control reviews and eligibility checks.
The Department’s Compliance and Anti-fraud Strategy comprises four pillars: “Prevent”, “Deter”, “Detect” and “Account”, which are leveraged to ensure that suspected fraud and non-compliance in our welfare system is kept to a minimum.
It is not the department’s policy to profile individuals based on nationality or place of birth.
My Department measures the underlying incidence rate of suspected fraud via control surveys. The surveys examine all relevant eligibility criteria, including both the means test and the Habitual Residence Condition, where applicable. Tests for statistically significant associations of overpayments relating to fraud and error and have consistently found that there is no difference in the likelihood of overpayments between Irish and non-Irish customers.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Social Protection further to his commitment that the programme for Government undertaking to phase out the means test for carer's allowance will be delivered during the lifetime of this Government, the further measures planned to advance this objective; and the timeframe envisaged for the full abolition of the means test.

question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of persons currently awaiting a decision on a disability allowance application for more than 12 weeks; the longest waiting period recorded; and the actions being taken to address the backlog.
reply:
Processing times are kept under constant review. It is important to ensure people receive an accurate decision on their claim application in as timely manner as possible. This is why claim processing is monitored, and targets are set out each year in the Revised Estimates and Volumes for the Public Services. The exact statistics requested by the Deputy are not available, but I can confirm that in October 2026, the average time for a Disability Allowance claim to be awarded was 6 weeks, and 93% of Disability Allowance claims were awarded within 10 weeks.
There has been a sustained improvement in the time taken to process Disability Allowance claims. In 2016 the average time to award a Disability Allowance claim was 12 weeks, for example; current processing times are half that. In order to expedite the claim decision process, I would encourage persons applying to supply all the relevant material with their initial application where possible. If the Deputy has a specific case in mind, officials in my Department will be happy to look into the matter.

question: Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Social Protection if his Department will consider introducing a structured mechanism to enable representatives of pensioner members of occupational pension schemes to participate in ongoing engagement with scheme trustees, including being informed of and contributing to discussions on proposals and decisions affecting members already in receipt of benefits; if consideration has been given to models operating in the Netherlands and Austria, recognising that, while trade unions often play an important role in scheme governance, representatives of pensioner members have no formal channel of collective communication.
reply:
Pension scheme trustees have duties and responsibilities under the Pension Act 1990, as amended, under trust law and under other relevant legislation. The duties of pension scheme trustees include administering the scheme in accordance with the law and the terms of the trust deed and scheme rules as well as ensuring compliance with the requirements that apply to these schemes.
Trustees must act in the best financial interests of all scheme members, whether active, deferred or retired, and must serve all beneficiaries of the scheme impartially. If there is a conflict of interest, then a person's duty as a trustee must take precedence over interests.
Under section 62 of the Pensions Act 1990, as amended, members (active and pensioner) of relevant schemes have a statutory right to participate in member trustee selection procedures, where the scheme is subject to the member participation provisions of Part VI of that Act and the regulations made thereunder, namely, the Occupational Pension Schemes (Member Participation in the Selection of Persons for Appointment as Trustees) Regulations 1996. Those regulations define 'relevant scheme' as meaning occupational pension schemes established under trust with a total of 50 or more qualified members and certain smaller schemes.
