question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Social Protection if persons with a medically certified disability who are not in receipt of disability allowance, invalidity pension, blind pension or partial capacity benefit may qualify for the cost of disability payment under any discretionary, exceptional or hardship provision; and if applications will be considered on an individual basis in such cases.
reply:
In Budget 2027, the Government provided for the first ever Cost of Disability payment. This will be paid as a lump sum payment of €500, in the week beginning 15 February 2027, to people receiving a long-term working age disability payment, specifically Blind Pension, Disability Allowance, Invalidity Pension, and Partial Capacity Benefit. There are no discretionary, exceptional or hardship provisions for people with medically certified disabilities who are not in receipt of one of these four working age long term schemes. The payment will be made to approximately 240,000 people at an estimated cost of €119 million in 2027.
Over 1,100 submissions were received in the public consultation process earlier this year. In addition the contributions at the Strategic Focus Network Summit I hosted in the Aviva Stadium in May, and the discussions I've had with disabled people and their advocates at several engagements in recent months have all informed the approach that we, across Government, have taken in Budget 2027.
Reflecting these inputs we want to involve, as far as possible, disabled people and their advocates in a co-design of the payment. This was the main agenda item at my Department’s quarterly Disability Consultative Forum on November 2nd. This co-design process will build on the detailed consultation process that has already taken place and the information that has already been gathered in that process. I intend to bring recommendations to Government arising from this proces

question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Social Protection the progress made to date in implementing the commitments contained in the Roadmap for Social Inclusion 2026-2030; and the number of actions scheduled for delivery in 2026 that have been completed.
reply:
The Roadmap for Social Inclusion 2026-2030, published in May 2026, is the whole-of-Government strategy to reduce poverty and improve social inclusion over the next five years.
Its overarching priorities are to reduce consistent poverty to 2 per cent or less by the end of 2030, to reduce income inequality, and to make Ireland one of the most socially inclusive countries in the European Union.
To help deliver these ambitions, the Roadmap sets out 63 cross-Government actions, recognising that poverty is multi-dimensional and must be addressed across a broad range of policy areas.
These actions span income support, employment, housing, education, health, transport, childcare and community supports.
Progress will be measured against 25 high-level indicators and reported on annually in Progress Reports brought to Government and subsequently published. A mid-term review will also be carried out in 2028.
Oversight in delivering the Roadmap is being provided through a Steering Group chaired by me, as Minister for Social Protection, with representation from Government Departments and the community and voluntary sector. The first meeting of this Steering Group takes place later this month, where updates on progress in delivering the actions will be examined in detail. Until this process takes place, it is not feasible to provide full updates on progress in delivering actions scheduled for delivery in 2026.
However my priority, working with Government colleagues, is to ensure that these,

question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Social Protection if the Government will implement further reforms to support family carers; whether consideration is being given to increasing the carer's support grant and earnings disregard.
reply:
The main income supports to carers provided by my Department are Carer’s Allowance, Carer’s Benefit, Domiciliary Care Allowance and the Carer’s Support Grant. Spending on these payments is expected to amount to over €2.2 billion in 2026.
The Government acknowledges the valuable role that carers play and is fully committed to supporting them in their role. As part of Budget 2027, I have recently announced a number of measures to support carers, these include:
• From January 2027 there will be a €10 increase in the maximum rate of Carer's Allowance and Carer's Benefit.
• From next July, there will be a further increase in the Carer's Allowance income disregard to €1,150 for a single person and €2,300 for a couple. This will mean that a working-age couple household can earn €126,000 annually and retain a full Carer’s Allowance payment. Even with an income of €156,000 a couple could still receive a partial Carer’s Allowance payment. Over the last two Budgets the income disregards have increased for single carers by a total of €525 and by €1,050 for carers who are part of a couple. These changes represent increases of 84%.
• The earnings limit for Carer’s Benefit will also increase next year to €1,150, after tax.
• Some 27,000 Carer’s Allowance recipients will benefit from the increase to the Fuel Allowance payment of €5 per week.
• For carers with children the weekly rates of the Child Support Payment will increase from €78 to €84 for children aged 12 and over, and from €58 to €6

question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Social Protection if he is satisfied that current rates of social welfare payments are keeping pace with inflation and rising housing, energy and food costs.
reply:
On Budget day, I announced an increase the weekly rates of payment for working age recipients under 66 years of age and pensioners by €10 per week, with proportionate increases for qualified adults and those on reduced rates. This increase is estimated to cost €750 million in 2027 and will benefit over 1.5 million recipients.
In the case of the State Pension (Contributory), the €10 increase represents a 3.3% increase on the 2026 weekly rate, which will be higher than 3.0% inflation rate forecast by the Economic and Fiscal Outlook for 2027.
Other increases announced in Budget 2027 include increased Fuel Allowance payment from €38 to €43 per week, a 13% increase. I also provided an increase to the limit for single pensioners in the Fuel Allowance means test. The income limit for a single person aged 66 or over will increase to 60% of the limit for a couple. The Living Alone Allowance also increased by €3, to €25 per week, a 12% increase.
Thresholds for Working Family Payment will increase by €30 in 2027. This measure builds on increases applied in recent budgets: as a result, income thresholds for all family sizes will have increased by €274 per week since Budget 2020.
There will be almost €31 billion spent on social protection schemes and services next year. The increases in core rates and targeted supports announced as part of Budget 2027 will continue to assist in mitigating the impact of price increases for social protection recipients.

question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of persons that have been refused the fuel allowance in each of the past three years due to the operation of the means test; and whether a review of the qualifying criteria is planned.
reply:
Fuel Allowance is paid, in conjunction with a wide range of qualifying primary schemes. We do not collate data on disallowed fuel allowance applications, therefore, this information cannot be provided to the Deputy.
Fuel Allowance operates as part of an overall system of social protection supports which provides assistance payments based on a system of means testing. The means test ensures that the recipient has a verifiable income need and that resources are targeted to those who need them most.
It is the nature of means-tested schemes that above a certain level of means, a person is not entitled to any payment as their means are deemed to be sufficient to provide for their needs. This approach reflects the policy of ensuring that those with no means or modest amounts receive the most available support from the State.
Fuel Allowance eligibility encompasses 22 qualifying schemes, demonstrating the comprehensive nature of the support available to eligible households. In addition to these qualifying schemes, people over 66 do not need to be in receipt of a payment from this Department to qualify for Fuel Allowance, subject to satisfying a means test. According to the latest CSO data, there are just over 1.8 million households in Ireland. Of these over 471,000 households are eligible for the Fuel Allowance scheme, representing approximately 26% of all households nationwide.
I trust that this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

As a result of Budget 2027, over €30 billion will be spent on social welfare in 2027, including almost €1.15 billion in new measures. A number of these measures provide targeted support to disabled people, including those who rely on social welfare payments as their primary or sole source of income.
In particular, in Budget 2027, the Government provided for the first ever Cost of Disability payment. This will be paid as a lump sum payment of €500 in the week beginning 15 February 2027 to people in receipt of a long-term working age disability payment from my Department, specifically Blind Pension, Disability Allowance, Invalidity Pension, Partial Capacity Benefit. Approximately 240,000 people are expected to benefit, at an estimated cost of €119 million in 2027. Further consultation with disabled people and their advocates in relation to the development of the payment for future years has begun.

question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Social Protection the actions being taken to improve turnaround times when a submission in respect of a disallowed application is submitted to the appeals office.
reply:
As of end of Q3 2026, the average processing time for an appeal made to the Social Welfare Appeals Office is 10.7 weeks. This is a reduction from 12 weeks at the end of Q2 2026 and from 21.2 weeks at the end of 2025.
An Appeals Modernisation Project was completed in 2025. The project streamlined and enhanced the end-to-end appeals process for the customer. It also added functionality to MyWelfare so that a customer can now make an appeal online. This has resulted in a secure, comprehensive, online appeals service for customers. question: Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Social Protection if he is aware of delays that are being caused for persons appealing a finding of the deciding officer due to the paperwork not being sent by the deciding officer; if there is a timeframe in which this information should be communicated; and if not, if he is considering bringing in a time limit.
reply:
The Social Welfare (Appeals) Regulations 2024 (S.I. No. 744 of 2024) came into effect in 28th April 2025. The regulations set out timelines for the appeals process.
Under the regulations the Chief Appeals Officer, within 14 days of receiving an appeal against the decision of a Deciding Officer, shall cause notice of the appeal together with the grounds submitted to be sent to the relevant section of my Department. My Department may then revise the original decision in favour of the appellant and advise the Chief Appeals Officer accordingly as soon as may be, but not later than 21 days thereafter.
If the decision is not revised, my Department makes available to the Chief Appeals Officer all claim forms and relevant documents, including reports of any assessors or inspectors, considered by the Deciding Officer, when making the decision that is being appealed.
The date fixed for the scheme area to furnish the information requested to the Appeals Office may be extended on application, subject to a valid reason being submitted by the Department, and at the discretion of the Chief Appeals Officer. Extensions to timeframes may be permitted where further investigation is required, for example in relation to means or medical issues. This process can ensure that full consideration is given to the appeal contentions and any additional information provided on appeal at the earliest stage in the appeals process.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage when he will announce if there will be an increase in the overall number of city and county councillors nationally; and the criteria to be used in determining where those councillors will be allocated.
reply:
Section 23 of the Local Government Act 2001 empowers the Minister to divide a local authority administrative area into local electoral areas by order and to determine the municipal districts within the administrative area by order. Each municipal district must consist of one or more than one local electoral area. The section also empowers the Minister to amend those orders. In advance of deciding to make an order under section 23 of the 2001 Act, the Minister must, in accordance with section 32(2) of the Local Government Act 1991, request An Coimisiún Toghcháin to prepare a report having regard to such matters as may be specified by the Minister.
Before making a request to An Coimisiún, section 61 of the Electoral Reform Act 2022 provides that the Minister shall lay a draft of the request before each House of the Oireachtas for approval by resolution by each House. Following the completion of a review, the Minister must publish the report of An Coimisiún and must have regard to the report in deciding whether to make an order in relation to any amendment to local electoral area boundaries or municipal districts.
The current configuration of local electoral areas has applied since the 2019 local elections, and followed a review of local electoral area boundaries conducted in two parts, both published in 2018. question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if, on foot on the findings of Census 2027, he intends to request An Coimisiún Toghcháin to review the electoral boundaries for the next Dáil, European and local elections; and if so, the timeframe he envisions for such reviews.
reply:
The Electoral Reform Act 2022 provides for a Dáil and European Parliament constituency review to be conducted following each census of population, assigns responsibility to An Coimisiún Toghcháin and sets out the terms of reference for such reviews.
More specifically, section 56(1) of the Act provides that An Coimisiún shall conduct a review of Dáil and European Parliament constituencies following the publication, by the Central Statistics Office, of the preliminary result of a census of population, i.e. the publication of preliminary census results will automatically trigger a review of Dáil and European Parliament constituencies. The Act requires that the Report of an Coimisiún Toghcháin on the review of Dáil and European Parliament constituencies be published within three months of the publication of final Census results. While the holding of a census is a matter for the Central Statistics Office, that Office has signalled that the 2027 census date will be Sunday, 9 May 2027.
In relation to local electoral areas, section 23 of the Local Government Act 2001 empowers the Minister to divide a local authority administrative area into local electoral areas by order. However, in advance of deciding to make an order under section 23 of the 2001 Act, the Minister must, in accordance with section 32(2) of the Local Government Act 1991, request An Coimisiún Toghcháin to prepare a report having regard to such matters as may be specified by the Minister.

reply:

question: Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Social Protection to provide an update on the current and projected levels of surplus in the Social Insurance Fund.
reply:
The current cumulative surplus in the Social Insurance Fund is approximately €17.5 billion. This is estimated to reach approximately €20 billion by the end of 2026.
The Department does not have updated projections beyond 2026. The most recent projections were published in the latest Actuarial Review of the Social Insurance Fund, which was published in 2023. However, these figures are now considered outdated as the projections are based on 2022 real price terms, do not account for the legislated PRSI roadmap rate increases, and did not anticipate the exceptionally high levels of employment activity experienced in recent years.

question: Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the rationale for charging public services, for example primary schools, for water.
reply:
The basis of charging for water is set out in Section 21 of the Water Services (No 2) Act 2013 as amended by Section 15 of the Water Services Act 2017. The legislation provides that Uisce Éireann shall charge each customer for the provision of water services.
However, the legislation exempts dwellings (a premises occupied by a person as his or her place of private residence (whether or not as his or her principal private residence)) and water services provided to a fire authority within the meaning of the Fire Services Act 1981. Therefore, as set out in legislation all public bodies including schools are required to pay water charges.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Social Protection to confirm the changes made to social protection payments in budget 2027 to support older people and carer's; and the timeframe for these changes to take effect.
reply:
Next year we will spend almost €31 billion on social protection, a €2 billion increase on 2026. Over half of all social welfare expenditure will be directed towards pensioners and carers.
In respect of supporting older people, I have focused on protecting core rates as part of Budget 2027 by increasing social welfare payments by €10 from January.
This increase is in line with inflation and means that the contributory state pension will exceed €300 per week for the first time, reaching €309.30.
The Government is mindful of the uncertainty surrounding fuel and the rising costs for people heating their homes. Therefore, I am increasing the rate of the Fuel Allowance payment by €5 per week from January, bringing it from €38 to €43. This will mean a payment of over €1,200 for Fuel Allowance recipients in 2027.
The Fuel Allowance means test for single people over 66 is also being improved. From January 2027, the limit for a single person will increase to 60% of a couple. Up to now, this limit for a single person has been half of a couple.
For the first time in five years, I am increasing the rate of payment of the Living Alone Allowance by €3, from €22 to €25 per week from January. Together with the increase to core social welfare rates and Fuel Allowance, this means an annual increase of €816 for pensioners and disabled people living alone.

question: Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Social Protection further to Parliamentary Question Nos. 47658/26 and 67576/26, the assistance he will provide to those who face financial barriers to accessing social welfare payments, such as the cost of a GP visit or doctor's note where these are essential criteria for the payment in question.
reply:
My Department is committed to reducing any administrative, financial and other barriers that may prevent people from accessing their social welfare entitlements.
Eligibility for the Department's schemes is generally based on either on an applicant's PRSI contribution record of in respect of Social Insurance schemes or by applying a means test in the case of Social Assistance schemes. Other conditions may apply as appropriate to the relevant scheme.
In respect of contributory schemes, the Government has broadened access and entitlements in recent years through the introduction of new schemes such as Jobseekers Pay-Related Benefit; the expansion of access to existing schemes, such as provision of access to Carer's Benefit for the Self Employed and the extension of the duration of schemes, such as Parent's Benefit.
In respect of means-tested Social Assistance schemes, significant adjustments have been made in income disregards, which have enabled more people to qualify for schemes such as Carer's Allowance, Fuel Allowance and Disability Allowance in recent years.
I would like to make it clear that the Department does not require applicants to obtain private assessments or specialist medical reports in order to submit an application for a social welfare payment. All available evidence submitted as part of the application or appeal process is considered.

question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Education and Youth to clarify if a formal diagnosis, professional report or assessment of need is required for children who need to access a SET, SNA or special class in a mainstream setting; and if this has been communicated to schools.
reply:
Ensuring that children and young people can access the educational provision and supports they need in an equitable, timely and appropriate manner is a priority for this Government. It is also a key priority for me, my department and for the National Council for Special Education (NCSE).
My department is committed to an education-based, needs-led approach to accessing education services. Children and young people in the education system have never required an Assessment of Need (AON) in order to access education supports.
Since 2017, children and young people in mainstream schools have not required a diagnosis to access supports from the 15,200 special education teachers (SET) in our school system. My department has also removed the need for health-related information for special education teaching allocations, transitions between primary and post-primary special classes, assistive technology supports, and additional Special Needs Assistant (SNA) requirements.
A diagnosis is currently still required for access to a special school or special class place.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to her Department's updated June 2024 procedures on the use of school property and sports facilities outside of school hours, whether her Department has engaged with the Department of Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht, regarding schools which have received public funding for the development of community sports facilities and Community Centre Investment funds.
reply:
Officials from my department have had engagement with colleagues in the Department of Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht in relation to a specific school that had received funding previously. Queries relating to legal arrangements for the school are being progressed with the relevant stakeholders.
The department has had communication with the Department of Culture, Communication and Sport in relation to the Community Sports Facilities Fund that launched in October, officials from my department were briefed on the changes to the process compared to previous funding applications.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her Department considers that the 2024 procedures provide an appropriate framework for ensuring that facilities developed with public community funding are made available to communities; if her Department has issued guidance on the arrangements required to ensure that such facilities remain accessible to the wider community, particularly in circumstances where schools have previously restricted external use of their premises on insurance or liability grounds.
reply:
The procedures on the use of school property and school sports facilities outside of school hours provide important information and guidance to school communities when engaging with community groups and other third-party operators. The procedures cover the required legal arrangements between the parties to have use of the premises and sets out the relevant insurances needed to operate on the premises or use the facilities.
The Department of Education and Youth encourage all schools to allow the use of school's facilities for community use where feasible. The patron and school management are responsible for the management of the school and engaging with local community groups if access is requested to utilise school facilities, however the school's priority is the provision of education and any requests received should not negatively impact this provision.

question: Deputy Marie Sherlock asked the Minister for Education and Youth In light of the upcoming bicentenary of the national school system in 2031 the steps her Department is taking to identify the old national schools in existence; and the plans she has to commemorate this important milestone.
reply:
The national school system in Ireland was established following the issue of the Stanley Letter in 1831. The bicentenary of this significant milestone will occur in 2031 and will provide an opportunity to reflect on the development and contribution of the national school system to education and society over the past two centuries.
While supportive of ideas around commemorating this milestone, no specific programme of commemorative events has yet been finalised.
There have been some proposals and I wrote to my colleague the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport earlier this year in relation to the possibility of the National Archives collecting school registers and school roll-books from the early years of the National School system as a commemorative activity.
My Department will continue to engage with relevant Government Departments, agencies and cultural institutions regarding opportunities to acknowledge and preserve the history and heritage of the national school system.

reply:

question: Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Social Protection for a report on his campaign to raise awareness on eligibility and how to apply for the household benefits package.
reply:
The Household Benefits Package comprises of an electricity or gas allowance, and a Free Television Licence. Only one Household Benefits Package is payable per household. The Household Benefit Package is generally available to applicants aged 66 years or over, who are in receipt of a social welfare type payment, or who satisfy a means test. The package is also available to applicants under age 66 who are in receipt of certain social welfare payments. For applicants aged 70 or over, there is no requirement to be in receipt of a qualifying payment or to satisfy a means test.
The Department of Social Protection launched a public information campaign to raise awareness of the Household Benefits Package and encourage people to check their eligibility for the scheme.
The campaign commenced with a press release on 16 September, which outlined a number of ways people could check their eligibility and access further information:
• By contacting the Department directly.
• By visiting the scheme page on gov.ie
• By visiting the Department's stand at the National Ploughing Championships and speaking with staff.
This initial awareness activity was followed by a paid advertising campaign, which commenced on 12 October and will run until 15 November. Advertising has been placed across regional radio, digital audio and social media platforms. question: Deputy Aisling Dempsey asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of pupils enrolled in special schools who were eligible for the Summer Programme in 2026; the number and percentage who subsequently availed of the programme; the number of special schools that provided an in-school Summer Programme.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 256 and 257 together.
The Summer Programme is an educational programme which is run during the summer months. It is a vital and targeted intervention that is specifically designed for children with special educational needs or those at risk of educational disadvantage.
All schools are offered the opportunity to run a school-based programme for the children who need it the most. These children can continue to be supported, nurtured and encouraged to engage in a fun and inclusive educational setting. age.
My department does not collect data on the number of pupils enrolled in mainstream schools who were eligible for the Summer Programme in 2026. Eligibility decisions are made at school level and are not reported centrally. In addition, participation in the Summer Programme is dependent on schools and their staff choosing to participate on a voluntary basis which may also influence the level of pupil participation.
Accordingly, the total number of pupils that may be eligible for the scheme in mainstream schools is not available. All pupils in special schools would, however, be eligible for the programme.
Final participation figures for the 2026 Summer Programme will only be available after all claims have been submitted and processed.

reply:

Information Note TC/IN 0001/2026, which was published by my Department in September, provides for an extension of this temporary arrangement for the 2026/27 school year. As stated in the Information Note, this temporary arrangement is due to cease at the end of the 2026/27 school year.
As provided for under Section 24 of the Education Act, the terms and conditions of employment of teachers and other staff of a recognised school shall be determined from time to time by the Minister for Education and Youth, with the concurrence of the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation.

The Council is comprised of representatives from the Teacher Unions, the School Management Bodies, the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Ref

question: Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Education and Youth the amounts paid by primary schools in water charges in each of the years since 2020.
reply:
My Department collates available data from school authorities as part of broader efforts to support an efficient and effective education system.
Officials of my Department currently analyse financial data relating to primary, voluntary secondary, and community and comprehensive schools. This information is derived from the annual financial returns submitted by schools to the Financial Support Services Unit (FSSU), a subset of which is subsequently provided to inform financial analysis and strategic decision-making. These data are subject to significant data quality limitations and do not include fee-charging or Education and Training Board schools.
The Financial Support Services Unit (FSSU) split the combined code 5610 (Water Rates and Refuse Expense) into two distinct nominal codes from the 2021/2022 school year. The updated structure separated them as follows:
5610: Refuse Expense
5611: Water Rates Expense
Therefore, for the 2020/2021 school year, it is not possible to isolate water rates expenditure. While it is possible to collate expenditure reported by many schools from the 2021/2022 school year onwards, a significant minority of schools have not reported water rates expenditure accurately to the FSSU. Consequently, it is not possible to confirm the cost of water charges across the primary school network for the years requested.
I am committed to improving the quality of these data, and officials of my Department are working with stakeholders to increase their accuracy.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he has had any communication from an organisation (details supplied) concerning the future of their shops in Ireland; and if any measures can be put in place to help secure the employment of those working in those shops.
reply:
I am aware of media reports that the UK parent of the company referenced has filed notice of its intention to appoint an administrator to the company in the UK. I appreciate this is an uncertain time for all involved and I do not want to speculate on these media reports, given this is an evolving situation.
My Department has not received a collective redundancy notification from the company referenced.
In the circumstances where an employer does becomes insolvent, there are robust protections in place for affected workers. In such cases, employees’ entitlements are protected under the Redundancy Payments Scheme and Insolvency Payments Scheme. These schemes guarantee employees’ statutory redundancy payments and certain wage-related entitlements, such as arrears of wages and minimum notice.
In such circumstances, normal collective redundancy rules must still be complied with, either by the employer or a responsible person such as a liquidator or receiver.
Where job losses occur, the Intreo service of the Department of Social Protection can also assist with income supports and employment and training opportunities where needed.
My Department has published an Information Handbook on Collective Redundancies, which provides clear and accessible information on employees’ rights and remedies, particularly in cases of company insolvency. A plain language summary of the Handbook is available in eight languages. This is available on my Department's website at: enterprise.gov.ie/en/publi

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to provide funding to carryout urgent coastal protection works adjacent to the Lower Road, Valentia, County Kerry.
reply:
Local coastal erosion and flooding issues are a matter, in the first instance, for each local authority to investigate and address and a local authority may carry out mitigation works using its own resources.
Minor Works Scheme
Local authorities may apply to the OPW for funding for flood mitigation and coastal protection works under the OPW Minor Flood Mitigation Works and Coastal Protection Scheme. Since its introduction in 2009, some €70 million has been approved under the Scheme for 930 local authority led projects that are delivering flood mitigation and coastal protection for some 8,000 properties.
Since 2009, the OPW has approved some €4.2 million funding to Kerry County Council (KCC) for 40 projects. Some €2.9m of this approved funding relates to coastal erosion works or studies. Under the Minor Works Scheme, it is the responsibility of the local authority to advance the works, once approved by the OPW. This includes all environmental assessments, planning consents, health and safety requirements and landowner agreements.
In May this year, I was pleased to announce the details of the revised criteria for the Minor Flood Mitigation Works and Coastal Protection Scheme, which greatly increase the scope of the Scheme and provide local authorities with a greater opportunity to address localised flood and coastal erosion risks within their administrative areas. question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation his views on the requirement imposed by a company (details supplied) that players purchase a minimum of two lines when entering the National Lottery Lotto draw; whether consideration has been given to permitting single-line entries; and if he is satisfied that the current arrangement provides adequate consumer choice within a State-licensed monopoly.
reply:
I wish to inform the Deputy that responsibility for the operation of the National Lottery and implementation of changes to the Lotto game lies with the Operator (Premier Lotteries Ireland DAC).
The requirement that National Lottery ('Lotto') players purchase a minimum of two Lotto lines has been part of the Lotto game rules for over 30 years.
Changes to the Lotto game have been introduced periodically over the years following a review of the game by the Operator (An Post National Lottery Company or Premier Lotteries Ireland DAC) and approval through the appropriate regulatory process in place at the time (now the Regulator for the National Lottery) as being compliant with the legal framework. Changes have included, for example: guaranteed minimum jackpots, an additional draw day, additional prize tiers, additional balls, and ticket price increases. Each time, the aim is to support the long-term sustainability of Lotto while continuing to provide players with an engaging game experience.
The most recent changes to Lotto, in September, are the first significant changes in ten years. They follow a detailed review of the game by the Operator, included research into Lotto players’ preferences. The changes include, for the first time, the removal of two number balls from the game to improve the odds of winning a prize at each tier, including the jackpot. Ticket prices per line are unchanged.
The changes to the Lotto game structure were approved by the Regulator prior to their launc

question: Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Social Protection for an update on the evaluation of the hot school meals programme; and the progress of the remuneration of 98 schools for the instances in which they were overcharged by €786,000, as detailed in the 2025 Comptroller and Auditor General's report.
reply:
The market research agency IPSOS Behaviour and Attitudes was engaged to carry out an Evaluation Of Service Review of the Hot School Meals Scheme. The survey was conducted during the period 29 May 2026 to 7 July 2026 by way on online quantitative surveys amongst primary school principals, teachers, children and their parents/guardians and suppliers of school meals. The survey was completed by 512 principals/teaching principals, 1,908 teachers, 6,884 children, 86,637 parents/guardians and 47 suppliers.
The survey found the Hot School Meals Scheme is now deeply embedded in participating primary schools, with strong reach among children and broad recognition of its benefits. 88% of children who try their lunch like it. 84% of parents felt that children should have the option of a hot or cold lunch.
The survey showed that food waste is a challenge and that this was also the case prior to the introduction of the hot school meals scheme with parents reporting that 48% of their children brought home uneaten food.
The main challenges now identified by the survey are not around access to meals but rather meal acceptability, menu choice and to include both hot and cold options.
I also commissioned a comprehensive nutritional review of the scheme, led by a CORU-registered School Meals Dietitian under the clinical supervision of the Department of Health. The findings of both exercises were generally positive. The nutritional review found that there is a wide variety of nutritious and well

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he will consider issuing a new circular providing special leave without pay, with a right to return, for civil servants who are members of the Reserve Defence Force while on Supplemental Military Service or service outside the State, separate from Circular 51/1979 on training leave.
reply:
The Civil Service is currently a leading employer in the field of flexible working arrangements for employees. Civil servants can avail of a number of flexible working arrangements and a range of paid and unpaid leave types, depending on the circumstances of each request.
I have responsibility for setting the terms and conditions for various leave types for civil servants only. There are currently no plans at this time to expand the provisions of what is already provided for in Circular 51/1979 (www.circulars.gov.ie/pdf/circular/finance/1979/51.pdf) in relation to paid training leave for civil servants who are members of the Reserve Defence Forces. My department keeps all leave provisions under review in line with operational requirements and Civil Service priorities.
Under the current arrangements, eligible officers are entitled to specific periods of paid leave to attend basic, annual and or specialist training, which represents a longstanding and supportive measure recognising the contribution of civil servants to the Reserve Defence Force.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if any help-to-buy payments have been recovered from recipients who subsequently ceased to occupy the property as their principal private residence due to the loss or refusal of immigration permission; the number of such cases; and the amounts recovered, in tabular form.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 242, 243, 244, 245, 246, 247 and 248 together.
The Help to Buy (HTB) incentive, is a tax-based scheme to assist first-time purchasers with the deposit they need to buy or build a new house or apartment. It also aims to encourage additional supply of new houses by supporting demand. Based on the latest available data (30 September 2026), the scheme has supported over 70,000 individuals or couples to buy or build their own home.
HTB provides a refund of Income Tax and Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) paid in Ireland over the previous four years, subject to limits outlined in the legislation.
The level of support available to first time buyers under the HTB scheme, is whichever is the lesser of:
• €35,000 (from 07 October 2026); or
• 10 per cent of the purchase price of the new property; or
• the amount of Income Tax and DIRT paid in the four years before application for the relief.
The relief available to a qualifying applicant will be limited to the amount of Irish Income Tax and DIRT paid by the applicant over the four years prior to the making of his/ her HTB application. If the applicant has paid no Irish Income Tax or has paid no DIRT in the four years prior to making the application, then there is no amount available to be refunded under the scheme.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if the introduction of the Outbound Payments Defensive Measures (OPDM) has satisfied the relevant milestone under Ireland's Recovery and Resilience Plan; if there is any continuing obligation under the plan or any requirement of the European Commission to retain these measures following completion of that milestone; if he has sought or received clarification from the European Commission on the implications of amending or abolishing the measures for receipt of the final Recovery and Resilience Facility payment; and if his Department has concluded its review of the interaction bet.
reply:
Ireland has been allocated approximately €1.15 billion under the EU’s Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), of which €928 million has been drawn down to date. This consists of the first payment of €324 million in July 2024, the second payment of €115 million in June 2025, the third payment of €240 million in November 2025 and the fourth payment of €249m in May 2026. In total Ireland has received approximately 80% of its RRF allocation while achieving 80% of its milestones and targets.
The RRF is a performance-based instrument with payment contingent on evidenced completion of agreed milestones and targets. The Outbound Payments Defensive Measures (OPDM) is just one reform milestone included as part of Ireland’s recovery and resilience plan which includes 19 investment streams and 11 reforms in total. RRF projects are pre-funded through the Estimates processes and the National Development Plan, with the RRF allocated funding being recouped from the EU after the milestones and targets have been achieved.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will review the exclusion of development land from the capital gains tax (CGT) reductions introduced in Budget 2027; if he will examine the potential anomaly where the disposal of a derelict building for housing qualifies for a 31% rate while a vacant site for the same purpose remains at 33%; if a Committee Stage amendment to the Finance Bill will be considered to extend the 31% rate specifically to land brought forward for genuine residential development.
reply:
Section 28 of the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997 (‘TCA’) sets the rate of Capital Gains Tax (CGT) which applies to chargeable gains arising on the disposal of assets, subject to certain exceptions. In Budget 2027, I reduced the standard rate of CGT by 2% to 31%. To mitigate market distortions, the reduction was given immediate temporary legal effect by way of a financial resolution passed on Budget Night, 6 October last, pending full enactment of the current Finance Bill (No 2) 2026. The reduced rate therefore applies for disposals of assets made on or after 7 October 2026.
Development land is defined in Section 648 of the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997 (TCA 1997) as land or shares deriving their value from land, where the market value at the time of the disposal exceeds the current use value at the time of the disposal. Current use value is defined as the market value of the land if no development (other than minor development) could be carried out.
The standard rate of CGT does not apply to development land. Section 649A sets out the rate of CGT in relation to development land, by reference to the date of the relevant disposal. The CGT rate on the disposal of development land made on or after 6 December 2012 is 33%.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance further to Parliamentary Question Nos. 143 and 144 of 6 October 2026, if credit servicing firms are considered the legal owners of mortgages; and if so, the reason for considering a credit servicing firm the legal owners when they are not the beneficial owner.
reply:
The role of legal owner of a mortgage is distinct from that of beneficial owner. The legal owner of a mortgage can be the same entity as the beneficial owner or a different entity.
Similarly to banks and retail credit firms, credit servicing firms can hold the legal title to mortgages.
The Consumer Protection (Regulation of Credit Servicing Firms) Act 2015 introduced a new Central Bank authorisation and regulatory regime in respect of credit servicing. Under this Act, any entity carrying out that activity (such as through collecting payments, communicating with the borrower and dealing with complaints) is, unless already subject to Central Bank authorisation, required to be authorised as a credit-servicing firm. In addition, any entity which holds the legal title to the rights of the creditor (and is not itself an authorised entity) must appoint an authorised credit-servicing firm to manage the agreement.
The Consumer Protection (Regulation of Credit Servicing Firms) Act 2018 expanded the scope of credit-servicing firms and provides that any entity which holds the legal title to the rights of a creditor must be subject to Central Bank regulation. This is irrespective of whether a credit-servicing firm has already been appointed.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Transport the steps his Department and the RSA are taking to address concerns regarding excessive glare from modern vehicle headlights and the associated potential road safety risk.
reply:
As Minister of State for International & Road Transport, Logistics, Rail & Ports, I wish to advise that light emitting diode (LED) and high intensity discharge (HID) headlights are known to provide greater brightness, improved colour rendering, increase efficiency and, in the case of LED in particular, longer performance life.
I am aware that concern has been expressed in some quarters in relation to the use of LED and HID headlights. It is worth noting that the use of these headlights in the EU is regulated by the European type-approval system. Type-approval requires the vehicle or component to meet specific safety standards in order to be placed on the European market and used in any Member State. Accordingly, if a headlight has been type-approved and entered into service, it is considered safe to use within the EU.
During national roadworthiness testing, a vehicle's lighting system is tested to ensure it is in full working order and correctly aligned for the safe performance of the vehicle. Factors which can contribute to headlamp glare include misaligned aim, dirty or damaged headlamps or the use of incorrect bulbs or unapproved components.
As outlined, the standards for these lights are regulated at EU level. However, as with any concerns over vehicle safety, I am willing to consider evidence-based policy reviews in relation to their use.

question: Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Transport if he will review the policy of the National Car Testing Service under which purchasers of used vehicles inherit missed NCT test schedules from previous owners, resulting in certificates of significantly less than 12 months' duration despite the vehicle passing the test; if he considers this fair to new owners who were not responsible for the missed test dates; and if he will consider providing a full 12-month certificate from the test date following a change of ownership.
reply:
Under EU law, Ireland, like other Member States, is obliged to adhere to the requirements on periodic roadworthiness tests for motor vehicles. The National Car Test operates in Ireland in line with EU Directive 2014/45/EU. This is given effect in Irish law by means of the Road Traffic (NCT) Regulations 2017 (S.I. No. 41 of 2017), as amended.
Under the Regulations, the initial test due date for a vehicle is determined using the date of registration of that vehicle and subsequent test due dates fall on anniversaries of that date. All test due dates are predetermined based on the date of registration of a vehicle.
Any NCT certificate issued for a vehicle is only ever valid up to the test due date that falls after that certificate was issued and does not automatically apply for 12 months, or 24 months as the case may be, from the date of testing. Issuing a NCT certificate for a period of validity greater than the next due date would be in breach of EU law.

question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Transport if he will reintroduce and expand the electric vehicle scrappage scheme which was piloted earlier in 2026.
reply:
The ICE2EV Pilot Scheme, which launched on 1 July, has committed the full €17 million available in funding, comprising of €10 million for the scrappage grant and €7 million for the EV purchase grant.
Approximately 2,000 successful applications were processed within 75 minutes of the scheme opening, supporting the replacement of around 2,000 internal combustion engine vehicles with electric vehicles. While strong demand was anticipated, the level of interest exceeded expectations.
The high level of interest demonstrated in the scheme is welcome and reflects growing consumer engagement with the transition to electric vehicles. This momentum supports Ireland’s Climate Action ambitions, including the target for 30% of the national vehicle fleet to be electric by 2030.
The policy purpose of this capped initiative was to test the effectiveness of scrappage as a tool to stimulate EV uptake among those who may not otherwise transition in the near term, with the ultimate goal of delivering additional emissions reductions necessary for our climate targets.
While the pilot scheme has closed for new applications, validation and payment processing remain ongoing. Dealers are given a period of time to complete the sale and provide the necessary documentation. Once the scheme has concluded and the relevant information is available, a post-completion evaluation will be undertaken to assess its effectiveness, emissions impact and overall value for money, and to inform future policy decisions

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Defence further Parliamentary Question No. 76831/26, to specify if a birth certificate and a valid passport are required as proof of identify or if it is the case that a birth certificate alone may suffice, or a passport alone may suffice; and if she will also confirm that security vetting involves An Garda Síochána checking police records in the persons stated country of origin.
reply:
As Minister for Defence, I am fully committed to strengthening recruitment to and supporting the retention of personnel in the Defence Forces.
It was positive to see the growth in numbers last year, with 790 inductions and I have set a target of over 800 inductions for 2026. Interest in a career in the Defence Forces continues to grow, with a total of 16,510 applications received in 2025 and more than 15,700 received to end of September 2026.
In relation to the specific matter raised by the Deputy, the military authorities advise me that each candidate for entry is required to furnish proof of his/her identity and produce his/her Certificate of Registration, birth certificate, national passport together with visa stamps, work permits and ID Card as applicable.
The vetting process is a matter for An Garda Síochána, who conduct the vetting process on behalf of the Defence Forces. A vetting disclosure shall include particulars of the criminal record (if any) relating to the person, and a statement of the specified information (if any) relating to the person or a statement that there is no criminal record or specified information, in relation to the person. Any information furnished to the Defence Forces by an Garda Síochána on foot of the outcome of the vetting process are considered by the Defence Forces in determining the suitability or otherwise of each candidate.
I must further reiterate that all applicants to the Defence Forces must meet all eligibility criteria for service

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment If he would designate as critical infrastructure all pipelines and structures required to bring onshore energy generated by offshore wind.
reply:
The Critical Infrastructure Act 2026 (Act No. 16 of 2026) was developed by the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation and was signed into law on 25 June 2026. It provides for the designation of certain infrastructure projects developed by or on behalf of the State as being of critical national importance, mandating all public bodies to do everything within their power to accelerate any decision-making processes associated with these projects.
The first projects to be designated under the Act included three energy-related projects: the North South 400 kV Interconnector; the Moneypoint 400 kV Series Capacitator Project; and the Letterkenny 110 kV Redevelopment Project. At the moment no structures related to offshore wind have been designated as critical infrastructure.
There are currently 5 Phase One projects intended for the East Coast that are progressing through the planning system, with a further Phase Two project in the South Coast DMAP having been auctioned in late 2025. My Department will continue to monitor these projects, and the associated grid infrastructure build out and will engage with EirGrid and other relevant stakeholders to identify which projects would benefit from a designation as critical infrastructure in the coming years, in accordance with the legislation and relevant guidance.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of additional people in Kildare who are qualifying for the carer’s allowance since July 2026.
reply:

There are a number of qualifying conditions for Carer’s Allowance. These include conditions relating to the care recipient’s need for full-time care and attention, the provision of that care by the applicant, the applicant’s employment or education circumstances, residency requirements and satisfaction of the means test.

The weekly income disregard increased by 60%, from €625 to €1,000 for a single person and from €1,250 to €2,000 for carers who are part of a couple. Following the increase in the income disregard in July 2026, approximately 2,700 Carer's Allowance recipients benefited from an increase in their weekly rate of payment.

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the assessment his Department has made of the increase in recycling of in-scope bottles and cans since the introduction of the deposit return scheme; the estimated overall recycling rate now being achieved; and the way in which this compares with the position before the scheme was introduced.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 217 and 218 together.
The Deposit Return Scheme (DRS), operated by Re-turn, plays an important role in supporting Ireland’s transition to a circular economy by ensuring the separate collection of high-quality plastic bottles and drinks cans for recycling.
Since its introduction in February 2024, more than 3.6 billion containers have been returned. The high-quality PET material collected through the scheme can provide an important feedstock for food-grade recycled PET (rPET), supporting bottle-to-bottle recycling and helping meet EU recycled content requirements. The potential therefore exists for bottles returned by consumers in Ireland to be recycled and reused in new drinks packaging, thereby supporting a more circular and resource-efficient economy within the State.

This could help keep material in higher-value use, move Ireland further up the rPET value chain, retain more economic value domestically, support high-value green jobs and skills, and reduce reliance on overseas processing and external supply risks.

question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the way in which the 1 January 2027 target for the introduction of the renewable heat obligation scheme will be met as the legislation has not yet been published.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 214 to 216, inclusive, together.
Decisions made in relation to the Renewable Heat Obligation (RHO) scheme design, including initial obligation rates and the level of increases as the scheme progresses, were based on a full examination of the scale of obligation required to meet Ireland’s renewable heat targets, and encompassed extensive engagement with key industry stakeholders, including the liquid fuel sector.
The scheme is considered appropriate and effective to support market participation and achievement of our energy and climate targets. question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Social Protection if the Government still commits to allowing older people in receipt of the State pension and carer’s allowance to receive a full-rate carer’s allowance, rather than the current half rate.
reply:
Generally, social welfare payments are made in respect of a defined contingency that compromises a person's ability to earn an income from employment. Accordingly, when a person incurs two or more contingencies, for example unemployment and disability, they receive just one payment - the higher of the available payments - as the loss of the opportunity of employment does not double up.
However, in recognition of the important contribution made by carers, an exception applies where a person who is receiving a primary social welfare payment and who is also providing full-time care and attention may receive a Half-rate Carer's Allowance in addition to their main payment. This arrangement applies to almost all weekly social welfare payments, including the State Pension.
There are currently more than 113,000 people in receipt of Carer’s Allowance, at an estimated cost of more than €1.4 billion in 2026. Of that total, 52,786 are receiving their full primary social welfare payment together with a half-rate Carer's Allowance payment. Currently, there are 17,918 people receiving a State Pension together with a half-rate Carer's Allowance payment.
Carer’s Allowance recipients who qualify for the full State Pension (Contributory) can receive a combined weekly payment of €453.30 on reaching age 66, compared to a payment of €270 on Carer’s Allowance before reaching pension age. reply:

However, my Department will continue to monitor developments in the EV charging market, including pricing trends and impacts on users who rely on public charging, as part of its ongoing engagement with stakeholders and its wider work on the delivery of a fair, accessible and reliable EV charging network.
The National EV Charging Infrastructure Strategy 2026-2028, published 4th November 2026, outlines the requirements for publicly accessible charging, and for installing EV Infrastructure that can meet future demand and user needs. It also sets out plans for a regulatory review to commence in 2027, one focus area of which will include pricing, including AFIR compliance around disclosure.
While this question relates to the price of public EV charging, it should be noted that the price of home EV charging remains significantly cheaper than charging on the public charging network, meaning that the price of running an EV is significantly cheaper than petrol or diesel for those who have access to home charging. The Department of Transport encourages overnight home charging whenever possible and estimates that over 80% of charging will take place at home. The SEAI provides grants to support the installation of domestic EV chargers.

question: Deputy Rose Conway-Walsh asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will examine the feasibility of introducing a targeted employer PRSI rebate scheme for small and medium-sized enterprises to help alleviate the rising cost of doing business.
reply:
In general, the issue of targeted supports for businesses, including the scale of any such supports and eligibility terms is a matter for the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment.
With respect to a mechanism for delivery of supports I can confirm that at this time there are no proposals nor are there plans to examine the feasibility of introducing an employer PRSI rebate for small and medium sized enterprises. In saying this I have to stress that the purpose of the social insurance system is to provide funding for vital social benefits including pension and disability payments. Given the well known demographic pressures that will arise in coming years it is important to protect the social insurance fund so that current and future generations of workers can rely on these supports.
In doing so we do look to ensure that PRSI thresholds are aligned with labour cost changes. Accordingly, it was agreed to increase the employer PRSI threshold from €552 to €600 per week, effective from 1 January 2027.
Raising the threshold to €600 per week ensures that employers with employees on the National Minimum Wage qualify for the lower PRSI rate. Additionally, this creates a buffer allowing businesses to pay the lower employer PRSI rate for all employees earning under €600 a week, regardless of whether they earn the National Minimum Wage.

As the Deputies are already aware, the National Transport Authority (NTA) is the independent transport regulator of the SPSV sector, and I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of that sector.
SPSV licence holders are independent business owners who are free to decide on their own business model, including their hours of work and area of operation. An SPSV driver licence entitles the holder to operate taxis, hackneys and limousines. SPSV driver licences can be operated anywhere in Ireland on a pre-booked basis (e.g. booking by app), but the ability to stand and ply for hire on the street as a taxi is restricted to the county in which the driver is licensed to operate. SPSV drivers can apply to operate in as many counties as they wish.
In relation to barriers to entry, quantitative restrictions which led to an undersupply of SPSVs in the past, have been removed from the SPSV sector and there are no barriers to entry to this industry in Ireland other than the obligation to use a wheelchair accessible vehicle (WAV). In order to fulfil the WAV requirement, significant WAV and eSPSV grants have been provided to SPSV operators to enable them to upgrade their vehicles. As of 30 September 2026, the number of licensed SPSV drivers was 28,588, while the number of licensed vehicles was 21,490.

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Transport if he or his Department have recently undertaken a review of the updated scrambler, e-bike and e-scooter regulations that have been implemented since January 2026.
reply:
Government has moved to addressed road safety concerns around scramblers and e-scooters this year. A range of measures have been introduced since January 2026 that include:
• Regulations to make helmets and high-visibility clothing mandatory for e-scooter users came into effect on Friday 4th September 2026.
• New regulations come into effect on the 2nd of October raising the age limit for e-scooter users from 16 to 18 years of age.
• From 18th November, fees for detention and storage of seized e-scooters will double, increasing fixed charge notices to €100 for e-scooter offences and the new fixed charge notice offence of €100 for not wearing a helmet or high visibility clothing will be introduced.
In addition, new regulations, known as Grace's Law in memory of Grace Lynch, were signed into law in April 2026. The regulations implement an explicit ban on scrambler use in any public place and strengthen existing provisions and powers of enforcement by An Garda Síochána.
The Department is considering potential options with regards to registration, licensing and insurance of e-scooters and will bring proposals to the Oireachtas as required. These are necessary and proportionate road safety measures and they are designed to address the number of serious injuries and fatalities among young e-scooter users.

reply:

The payment will be made to approximately 240,000 people at an estimated cost of €119 million in 2027.
Many of the factors identified as giving rise to additional costs for disabled people also apply in the case of pensioners. For example, costs related to spending more time at home with an increased need for lighting and heating, additional costs related to transport, and additional health related costs. As a result of Budget 2027, the maximum rate of Non-contributory State Pension will increase to €298, and the Contributory State Pension will increase to €309.30 from January 2027. This compares to €264 and €269.50 per week for recipients of Disability Allowance and Invalidity Pension respectively. question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Transport if his Department will both future-fund and retrospectively-reimburse the boards of State-owned airports who have had to significantly invest in their security systems (within their terminals and along their perimeter boundaries).
reply:

The primary objective of funding under this programme is to target aviation safety and security activities and operations to ensure regulatory compliance in these areas. Since the publication of the NAP in 2015, over €183 million has been allocated to Irish airports under various regional airport programmes.
While the State owned airports at Dublin, Cork and Shannon are established as commercial State companies and as such are expected to operate without recourse to Exchequer funding, in recognition of the very difficult circumstances faced by regional State airports during COVID-19 and beyond as connectivity recovered, over €81 million of this funding was provided to Cork (€38 million) and Shannon (€43 million ) airports since 2020.

question: Deputy Martin Kenny asked the Minister for Transport if he will provide details of representations that he or his Department made to Irish Rail prior to the licensing of a greenway on the former railway track between Claremorris and Collooney which make up part of the Western Rail Corridor.
reply:
As outlined in my meeting with the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Transport on 22 October, the Government has decided to proceed with the development of a greenway utilising the disused railway alignment between Claremorris and Collooney. This decision was taken in the absence of any plans to reinstate the railway along this section until at least 2050 under existing plans as set out in the 2024 All-Island Strategic Rail Review, which was prepared by my Department in conjunction with the Department for Infrastructure in Northern Ireland.
My officials have engaged with Iarnród Éireann on the licensing of lands to facilitate the development of a greenway on the alignment. The development of the greenway in the coming years will deliver a socially and economically useful active travel asset in the west, but does not preclude the possibility of developing a railway at some point in the future. Moreover, I note that this Government is committed to the development of rail infrastructure in the west. Early work is underway on the reinstatement of the railway between Athenry and Claremorris and funding is in place under the National Development Plan for construction to commence in the coming years.
The All-Island Strategic Rail Review will be reviewed and updated once a decade, offering the opportunity to reconsider a potential extension of the Western Rail Corridor further north, taking account of future population and settlement development patterns and other relevant factors.

question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Transport if, as part of the ongoing interdepartmental consideration of horse-drawn vehicles on public roads, he will examine the introduction of a statutory minimum age for persons driving or otherwise in control of such vehicles; and if he has concerns regarding children or young persons being in control of horses and horse-drawn vehicles on public roads from both an animal welfare and public safety perspective.
reply:
The use of horse-drawn vehicles on public roads is a cross-government issue involving consideration of road safety, enforcement and animal welfare, and this issue involves my Department, the Department of Justice and the Department of Agriculture. There are existing provisions addressing this issue under road traffic legislation, the Roads Act 1993, the Animal Health and Welfare Act 2013 and the Control of Horses Act 1996.
All road users, including the drivers of horse-drawn vehicles, are required to comply with road traffic legislation and to behave in a safe manner paying due care to other road users. The enforcement of road traffic legislation is first and foremost a matter for An Garda Síochána, and legislation and measures to protect the safety of all road users are kept under constant review.
Animal welfare issues are a matter for my colleague the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine. I understand that the Control of Horses Act 1996 includes provisions in relation to the minimum age to obtain a horse licence, and the selling of a horse to a person under the age of 16 years.
Senior officials from the three departments are engaging on this issue to consider if improvements can be made to existing legislation and I will consider any requests for additional enforcement powers under road traffic legislation from An Garda Síochána or local authorities. In this context, my Department is considering amendments to Section 74 of the Roads Act 1993 in the next Road Traffi

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Social Protection if he has engaged with public transport operators in relation to these operators charging free travel pass holders booking fees for free travel journeys.
reply:
The Free Travel scheme is available to persons aged 66 years and over, and to people in receipt of certain social welfare payments, or those medically certified as unfit to drive for a period of at least 12 months, who are over 17 and under 66 years. Free Travel recipients must be permanently resident in the State. The scheme permits travel for free on most CIÉ public transport services, Luas, and a range of transport services offered by private transport operators countrywide. Free travel is also available on cross border journeys to and from Northern Ireland, and for those over aged 66 or over, within Northern Ireland.
Under the Free Travel scheme, there is no requirement or impediment for transport operators to provide additional services such as a seat booking service. Some travel operators provide an online booking services for customers who wish to guarantee their seat on a particular service. This is entirely a matter for the transport operator concerned.
Importantly, Free Travel customers are not required to reserve a seat in advance to avail of their Free Travel entitlement. Eligible customers can continue to present on their preferred day of travel and avail of Free Travel using their Free Travel Public Services Card.
It is open to any Free Travel customer, who wants to be guaranteed a seat on a particular service, to book their seat in advance, where a pre-booking facility exists but there may be a seat booking cost.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy

question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Transport if he is aware that taxi and hackney unavailability is causing huge challenges for the night-time economy, particularly in rural areas; and if he will take urgent action to tackle this problem.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 145, 153, 155 and 188 together.
As the Deputies are already aware, the National Transport Authority (NTA) is the independent transport regulator of the SPSV sector, and I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of that sector.
SPSV licence holders are independent business owners who are free to decide on their own business model, including their hours of work and area of operation. An SPSV driver licence entitles the holder to operate taxis, hackneys and limousines. SPSV driver licences can be operated anywhere in Ireland on a pre-booked basis (e.g. booking by app), but the ability to stand and ply for hire on the street as a taxi is restricted to the county in which the driver is licensed to operate. SPSV drivers can apply to operate in as many counties as they wish.
In relation to barriers to entry, quantitative restrictions which led to an undersupply of SPSVs in the past, have been removed from the SPSV sector and there are no barriers to entry to this industry in Ireland other than the obligation to use a wheelchair accessible vehicle (WAV). In order to fulfil the WAV requirement, significant WAV and eSPSV grants have been provided to SPSV operators to enable them to upgrade their vehicles. As of 30 September 2026, the number of licensed SPSV drivers was 28,588, while the number of licensed vehicles was 21,490.
In line with the Programme for Government 2025 commitment to 'extend the ten-year vehicle limit for taxis registered in 2015

reply:
The Department of Transport has been tasked with developing a new Vehicle Adaptation Scheme (VAS), to provide financial assistance towards the cost of adapting vehicles for drivers and passengers who require assistance to enter, exit, or operate a vehicle. The VAS is being developed as a standalone scheme and does not replace the Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme, which is under the remit of the Department of Finance.

Through extensive stakeholder engagement and consultation, the Department has established the key principles and parameters underpinning the Scheme. Subject to timely completion of the necessary preparatory work, it is possible that the VAS will open for applications in Q1 2027.

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Transport to clarify the reason it is taking so long to re-establish the Dublin to Derry air link; and the reason the target date of October 2026 has now been missed.
reply:
I wish to assure the Deputy that this Government is fully committed to establishing a new Public Service Obligation (PSO) air service between Dublin Airport and City of Derry Airport. This will deliver the Programme for Government commitment to establish air connectivity between the two cities.
As City of Derry Airport is outside of the European Union, the PSO air service will operate outside of Regulation (EC) 1008/2008, which provides for the common rules for the operation of air services in the Community.
My Department has had extensive engagement with the Chief State Solicitors Office (CSSO) and the Office of the Attorney General (AGO) in recent months, in relation to the appropriate legal framework to underpin the procurement of this new service. Detailed work has been undertaken to ensure that the Request for Tenders (RfT) which is currently being finalised, is compliant with the appropriate procurement Regulation as well as EU State aid rules.
It is anticipated that the Department will be in a position to finalise and publish the RfT shortly. Following the completion of the procurement process, it is expected that a contract will be awarded to enable services to commence on the route as soon as operationally feasible by the successful operator in the New Year.
The detailed work undertaken, together with comprehensive stakeholder engagement throughout the process, has been critical to ensure a service on this route can be established as soon as possible.
