question: Deputy Martin Daly asked the Minister for Transport the plans in place to expand the provision of publicly accessible electric vehicle charging points, particularly fast and rapid charging facilities, in rural towns and communities across Roscommon and East Galway; whether additional funding will be made available to local authorities to address gaps in charging infrastructure in towns such as Boyle, Castlerea, Ballaghaderreen, Ballygar and Roscommon town.
reply:
The Government is fully committed to supporting the expansion and modernisation of Ireland’s electric vehicle (EV) charging network. A comprehensive and reliable charging network is essential to support the continued uptake of EVs and Ireland’s transition to sustainable transport.
To meet Ireland’s obligations under the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR), it is estimated that between 3,200 and 6,210 publicly accessible charge points will be required nationally by 2030, depending on the power output of the charging infrastructure installed. AFIR requires Member States to provide 1.3kW of publicly accessible charging capacity per battery electric vehicle (BEV) and 0.8kW per plug-in hybrid electric vehicle (PHEV).
The National EV Charging Infrastructure Strategy 2026-2028, published 4th November 2026, sets out the requirements for publicly accessible charging infrastructure and the actions needed to meet future demand.
Ireland has made significant progress in EV charging roll-out in recent years. While most EV charging is expected to take place at home, supported through the Home Charger Grant and Apartment Charging schemes, a strong public charging network is required to support longer journeys and drivers who do not have access to private off-street parking.
Support has been allocated through the Light Duty Vehicle (LDV) National Road Grant Schemes, which provide funding towards the installation of more than 500 high-powered recharging points on the national ro

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Social Protection the key budget social protection measures to support rural communities in 2027.
reply:
As a Minister who also holds a portfolio in rural development, I recognise the important contribution that rural communities make to our country, and I want our social welfare system to do more to meet their particular needs.
Budget 2027 includes €2 billion of social protection measures. This investment will protect core rates and delivers a number of targeted measures that support those living in rural households, farmers, self-employed fishermen and women, and island communities.
We are also continuing to support rural employment and community participation through schemes such as the Rural Social Scheme, Community Employments and Tús. An increase in the weekly top-up for these schemes brings it to €35 per week. This is in addition to the €10 general increase and will support participants who make such a valuable contribution to local services and community organisations.
People who are engaged in farming and fishing and in receipt of certain social welfare payments can move to the Rural Social Scheme, which provides a supplementary income for low-income farmers and fishers aged 25 years or over. Participants work 19.5 hours per week providing services that benefit rural communities and receive a top-up on their social welfare payment.
As part of the Budget Bill, I intend to put Fish Assist on a statutory basis.
To provide more opportunities for people in rural communities, the Rural Dweller Pilot will be expanded to 500 places. I am also doubling the disregard for seaweed

reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and exchequer funding in relation to the National Roads Programme. As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport; however, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of public transport.

reply:
The Government is fully committed to supporting a significant expansion and modernisation of the EV charging network over the coming years and reaching climate targets.
Rural motorists are often in an advantageous position to make the switch to an electric vehicle, due to the large number of dwellings in rural Ireland that have access to off-street parking and are therefore suitable for home EV charging. However, there is also a need for a seamless public charging network to provide for situations or instances where home charging is not possible.
The National EV Charging Infrastructure Strategy 2026-2028, published in November 2026, outlines the requirements for publicly accessible charging and installing EV Infrastructure that is capable of meeting user needs.
The Regional and Local EV Charging Network Plan, which focuses on neighbourhood and destination charging locations, will be led by Local Authorities in partnership with both public and private sectors. Donegal has been identified as Regional Lead for Region 7 under this plan.
Local authorities are being supported by ZEVI to develop regional and local EV charging network strategies and implementation plans. This work will identify charging requirements at local level, including neighbourhood charging solutions for residents without access to private off-street parking.

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Transport for an update on the recently announced new vehicle adaptation scheme to open in early 2027, including the number of applications envisioned; and the number and location of pre-approved suppliers.
reply:
The Department of Transport has been tasked with developing a new Vehicle Adaptation Scheme (VAS) to provide financial assistance towards the cost of adapting vehicles for people with disabilities.
Over the past twelve months, the Department has made significant progress towards the implementation of the VAS. In line with the proposals set out by the Transport Working Group of the National Disability Inclusion Strategy and the Senior Officials Group on Disability, as well as further engagement and consultation, the core principles and parameters of the Scheme have been established. This, in turn, has enabled the Department to develop a high-level framework for its operation.
Unlike schemes which link eligibility to specific medical criteria or disability categories, the VAS is intended to support a much broader cohort of people whose mobility needs may require vehicle adaptations. The number of potential beneficiaries, however, will depend on a range of factors, including the final design of the Scheme and levels of uptake. There may also be a degree of pent-up demand arising from the absence of this type of support scheme to date. Any estimate at this stage would be subject to a significant degree of uncertainty.
The Department is working with stakeholders to develop eligibility criteria for inclusion on the supplier register. Further information on the framework and application process will be provided in due course.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Transport to report on progress to meet his commitments under the national human rights strategy for disabled people; the measures taken since the strategy was introduced; the key metrics identified to measure progress; if he is satisfied with the progress that has been made.
reply:
I am fully committed to improving accessibility across our public transport system, in line with the National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People 2025–2030.
With its overarching whole-of-government approach, delivery on the actions and commitments under the Strategy’s five pillars are being led by several Government departments and public bodies as befits their remits. My Department is the Pillar Lead for Pillar 5 'Transport and Mobility.'
In terms of metrics, the First Programme Plan of Action 2025-2026 sets out how the priority actions under each commitment will be delivered by various lead government departments and public bodies, the timeframe for delivery, and the success indicators by which performance will be measured. The first set of bi-annual reports were reviewed by the Delivery and Monitoring Committee, chaired by the Taoiseach, in July and were published afterwards. The second set of bi-annual reports are currently being drafted.
I can advise the Deputy that good progress overall is being made in relation to the 'open' public transport actions under Pillar 5. For example, we are maintaining funding under the Accessibility Retrofit Programme at €25m which is a 67% increase compared to 2024, prior to the publication of the Strategy. In relation to Action 22.1, the Expert Technical Group, under its independent chair Ann Frye, has met three times since July with another meeting planned next month.
Other examples of progress include the success of the Smart Dema

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Transport his plans to further amend scrambler, e-bikes and e-scooters regulations, following the introduction of new measures in 2026.
reply:
Government has moved to addressed road safety concerns around scramblers and e-scooters this year. A range of measures have been introduced since January 2026 that include: -
• Regulations to make helmets and high-visibility clothing mandatory for e-scooter users came into effect on Friday 4th September 2026.
• New regulations come into effect on the 2nd of October raising the age limit for e-scooter users from 16 to 18 years of age.
• From 18th November, fees for detention and storage of seized e-scooters will double, increasing fixed charge notices to €100 for e-scooter offences and the new fixed charge notice offence of €100 for not wearing a helmet or high visibility clothing will be introduced.
In addition, new regulations, known as Grace's Law in memory of Grace Lynch, were signed into law in April 2026. The regulations implement an explicit ban on scrambler use in any public place and strengthen existing provisions and powers of enforcement by An Garda Síochána.
These are necessary and proportionate road safety measures and they are designed to address the number of serious injuries and fatalities among young e-scooter users.
The Department is considering potential options with regards to registration, licensing and insurance and will bring proposals to the Oireachtas in due course as required.
An outright ban on e-scooters remains under consideration and the situation will be actively monitored by Government. Further protections will be provided to members of An Garda

question: Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Transport if he will consider introducing a statutory indemnity or other legal protection for members of An Garda Síochána who, acting lawfully and in good faith, engage in pursuit of persons using scramblers, e-bikes, e-scooters and other vehicles.
reply:
Members of An Garda Síochána, as well as members of ambulance and fire services, enjoy exemptions from a number of road traffic provisions in order to address emergencies. So, for example, they may exceed the speed limit, or drive through red lights, when an emergency situation requires.
However, neither the Garda nor the other emergency services have exemptions from careless or dangerous driving offences, nor from intoxicated driving offences.
There is general agreement, including from the Garda, that public safety must always come first. However, there is room for consideration of what dangerous driving means in a Garda context, whether it is rushing to an emergency or engaging in a pursuit.
Concerns in this area carry a potential risk that Garda members, if in doubt, may hesitate to pursue suspects when it might actually be safe to do so and this matter was raised by the Garda with my colleague, the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration.
As the legislation in question lies within the remit of my Department, the issue was referred to my Department, and we have been examining whether the legislation may be amended in a way which would provide more certainty to the Garda as to what is permitted, while continuing to prioritise public safety.
What would be of assistance to the Garda would be greater legislative clarity on the manner in which cases of potential dangerous driving by a Garda member are to be judged.

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Transport the status of Local Link services for the east Cork area as provided for in Budget 2027.
reply:
As Minister of State at the Department of Transport with special responsibility for Rural Transport I recognise the vital role that enhanced connectivity plays in supporting communities across rural Ireland, including in Cork.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Transport the immediate measures being taken to address persistent overcrowding on DART services, particularly during peak hours on the Malahide to Bray route; whether additional carriages and services will be introduced; and for an update on DART+ Coastal North, including the expected timeline for delivering increased passenger capacity.
reply:
This Government has invested significantly in public transport infrastructure and services, with record numbers using public transport services each year. With this increased demand, however, overcrowding has become an issue on some rail services, particularly during peak times. I can assure the deputy, however, that every available train is being used for passenger operations to mitigate these issues to the greatest extent possible.
To fundamentally address the overcrowding issue, the capacity of out rail system must expand to meet demand. Additional capacity will be provided from the second quarter of next year, when the first of the 95 new DART+ electric and battery-electric carriages starts entering service on the Northern line from Dublin to Drogheda.
The second order of 90 carriages is planned to start entering service in 2028 and will enable the extension of the DART to Wicklow in 2029. The entry into service of these first two orders will allow for the cascade of existing Intercity and Commuter trains to other busy sections of the rail network.
I am also happy to say that €93 million in Shared Island Initiative funding was announced in June, which will allow for the accelerated delivery of DART+ Coastal North. This funding will provide a signalling upgrade as well as a turn-back at Malahide Station and a passing loop at Clongriffin Station. question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding work ongoing within his Department to encourage the use of, or research the benefits of, HVO fuel as a direct alternative to diesel across a variety of sectors including transport, agriculture and industry with a view to reducing emissions in these sectors.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 111 and 113 together.
Hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) is a bioliquid which can be used as a renewable energy source and which, in a transport context, is classified as a biofuel. HVO is currently available for consumers to purchase for use in transport and other sectors.
The Minister recently published the Hierarchy of Use of Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil (HVO) Across Transport and Other Sectors Report. The Report examines the growing demand for HVO, and optimal focus for intervention to best promote efficient use of this renewable energy within and outside the transport sector both in the short-term and beyond 2030. The report addresses concerns raised by the Climate Change Advisory Council in its 2025 Annual Review of Transport, which recommends a coherent plan for the most efficient use of sustainable biofuels across all sectors to be developed by the Department of Transport and the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment. The Report confirms a hierarchy of use of HVO which aligns with several existing policies and measures, including the Sustainable Aviation Fuel Taskforce Report, the Road Haulage Strategy, the Renewable Transport Fuel Policy, the Ports Policy, and the design of the Renewable Heating Obligation. The Report will inform the continued development and implementation of Departmental policy and plans.

question: Deputy Keira Keogh asked the Minister for Transport the measures his Department is considering for rail infrastructure serving County Mayo and the western region, to improve service reliability, journey times and passenger capacity.
reply:
My Department is currently delivering several rail infrastructure projects in the West and in County Mayo. question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Education and Youth if consideration will be given to a review being undertaken of a school bus route (details supplied) following the first term of the school 2026-2027 school year in order to ascertain if there are any seats which have not been taken up by pupils, and which may be allocated to a pupil.
reply:
Bus Éireann is responsible for the planning, timetabling of school transport routes and issuing of tickets on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
Where a child is eligible for transport and the application and payment process has been completed on time, they will get a seat on a school bus service, where a service is available.
Where a child is not eligible for school transport, but the application and payment process has been completed on time, they will be considered for any spare seats available after eligible children have been accommodated. These seats were previously known as concessionary seats.
Because of the nature of transport for non-eligible children and the priority of providing places for eligible children, there may be an excess of demand over supply for non-eligible pupils. In these cases, Bus Éireann will allocate tickets for spare seats using an agreed selection process.
It is important to note that all seats on a given route are ticketed. There can be instances where tickets are not utilised every day, which is a decision of the ticket holder that can give the impression that a bus is operating with vacant seats.
In the first instance, it is the responsibility of ticket holders to utilise their tickets. While there is no obligation, families are welcome to return their tickets at any stage in cases where they are not using the service as originally intended. question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment in the context of public sector industrial action, the expected surplus on the payroll budgets and or an unexpended budget and or appropriation in respect of one, two, and three days of full strike action; if he will outline what happens to excess funds; if his accounting officer has or will seek permission to reappropriate those funds; and if he will outline the purpose to which they will be reappropriated or if they will carry over into the next accounting year.
reply:
My Department continues to manage its pay budget and overall expenditure in the normal manner, having regard to operational requirements and established public financial management arrangements.
The Department is currently working with its payroll service provider, the National Shared Services Office (NSSO), to ensure that any pay adjustments arising from the day of industrial action on the 14th October are administered correctly and in line with applicable rules and procedures. As the industrial relations situation continues to evolve, it would be premature to comment on the potential financial implications of any future days of industrial action.
At this stage, the Department expects to utilise its full approved pay allocation over the course of the remainder of the year.
As with all expenditure programmes, the management of any year-end budget position will be considered in the context of the overall Estimates process and in accordance with the relevant public financial procedures.

reply:
The Health and Safety Authority (HSA) has confirmed that it has no record of observations or inspections relating to the storage of firearms, ammunition, flares and fireworks in a shipping container at Garda Headquarters in the Phoenix Park.
Any inspection relating to such a matter is potentially within the remit of the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, which is the competent authority for Class 1 dangerous goods (explosives).

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to provide an update on the rollout of the AI regulatory sandboxes planned under the EU AI Act.
reply:
Ireland's AI Regulatory Sandbox is currently under development and is on schedule to be launched by 2 August 2027. The Sandbox will support safe innovation, increase legal certainty, and strengthen regulatory preparedness for SMEs, start-ups and public sector organisations.
The development of the Sandbox will take into account specific provisions under the implementing acts for sandboxes, setting out principles around application processes and procedures, participant selection criteria and MSA engagement.
In addition, as prescribed under the EU AI Act, SMEs, start-ups and public sector organisations will be given priority access for Sandbox participation.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment for an update on the implementation date for the next increase in the MAR Thresholds; if his Department has engaged with the nursing home sector on this implementation date.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 92 and 93 together.
The employment permits system is grounded in legislation that sets clear and objective criteria for minimum annual remuneration (MAR) thresholds, qualifications, and the eligibility of occupations. The MAR represents the minimum salary that must be paid to a non-EEA national for an employment permit to be issued or renewed.
The Employment Permits: Minimum Annual Remuneration – Outcome of the Roadmap Review 2025 published at the end of last year sets out the policy rationale, evidence basis and revised, phased roadmap for implementation of the thresholds applicable across the employment permits system.
The review was informed by a public consultation process and undertaken in response to a range of structural changes in the labour market since MAR thresholds were last comprehensively updated. This consultation included engagement with sectoral representative bodies, including organisations representing the nursing home sector and independent nursing homes. The review included consideration of issues such as sustained inflationary pressures, increases in average earnings, rising costs of living, and changing labour market dynamics. Under this roadmap, the first increases took effect on 1 March 2026.
I can confirm that increases to MAR thresholds for 2027 will not be implemented in January 2027. In line with the approach taken for the 2026 increases, changes to the thresholds will be implemented with sufficient lead-in to allo

question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to address the long delays facing local authorities recruiting new staff through the Public Jobs provider process.
reply:

It is responsible for the sourcing, assessment and delivery of quality candidates to public service clients. The activities are primarily focused on the sourcing of candidates for roles in the Civil Service; the most senior roles in Local Authorities; trainee Garda, and some promotional campaigns for An Garda Síochána; and a range of management, executive and specialist roles across the civil and public service. Publicjobs also has a key role in the identification of suitable members for State Boards.
Recruitment to the civil service and a range of other public bodies operates under the provisions of the Public Service Management (Recruitment and Appointments) Acts, 2004 to 2013. Publicjobs operates under licence from the Commission for Public Service Appointments (CPSA) and is independent in its operations. In carrying out its recruitment and selection processes, it complies with the Codes of Practice published by the CPSA, which ensure that fair and open processes are in place.
For competitions which are run for specific clients, Publicjobs agrees the competition timeline with the client at the outset of the process, however, situations can occur which impact on Publicjobs’ capacity to meet the agreed delivery dates. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he is satisfied that Ireland meets all its commitments to the Brussels Declaration of 13 June 2025 and the Brussels Declaration of 14 December 2020 and the Rome Declaration of June 2020 and the commitments made in the Hague in May 2019 with respect to the transposition of EU Directive 2019/1937.
reply:
EU Directive 2019/1937 on the protection of persons who report breaches of Union law was adopted on 23 October 2019 and sets minimum standards for the protection of whistleblowers across the EU.
The Directive requires Member States to ensure that:
• whistleblowers have at their disposal effective channels to report breaches of EU rules confidentially, both internally (within an organisation) and externally (to a competent authority),
• whistleblowers’ reports are properly investigated and acted upon by the organisations and competent authorities,
• whistleblowers are protected from retaliation.
The Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 2022 fully transposed this Directive into Irish legislation.
The EU Commission is currently carrying out a review of the transposition of this Directive. This review consists of the following elements:
• An assessment of the completeness of the measures i.e. if all the requirements of the Directive have been transposed.
• An assessment of the conformity of the notified measures with the Directive i.e. if all the transposition measures are correct.
As the Deputy is aware, two infringement cases were opened against Ireland in 2022 for failing to meet the deadline for transposition of the Directive. Both these infringement cases were closed in 2023 following commencement of the Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 2022.

reply: In relation to the public sector industrial action, arrangements are in place to deduct the appropriate amount from officers who participate in a strike. The financial amount in respect of the last strike action day on 14 October is being compiled and checked. Currently the Department has no plans to seek permission to reallocate any surplus payroll funds resulting for this industrial action. question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation in the context of public sector industrial action, the expected surplus on the payroll budgets and or an unexpended budget and or appropriation in respect of one, two, and three days of full strike action; if he will outline what happens to excess funds; if his accounting officer has or will seek permission to reappropriate those funds; and if he will outline the purpose to which they will be reappropriated or if they will carry over into the next accounting year.
reply:
I wish to advise the Deputy that this reply relates solely to my Department, as the Department would not have the necessary information in respect of all public bodies.
The impact of the strike action on 14 October, 2026 on the payroll budget of my Department is not yet known. Data in respect of deductions from payroll due to strike action is collected and sent to the National Shared Services Office (NSSO), which provides payroll services to my Department. The NSSO will process the payroll deductions for relevant staff in this regard and it is only on conclusion of this process that a final figure will be available.

More broadly, I welcome the proposed agreement reached earlier today at the Workplace Relations Commission, which underlines the value of collective bargaining and constructive engagement in resolving complex issues and delivering balanced outcomes for public servants, public services and taxpayers.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if the Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 2022 necessarily prohibits full or any disclosure to a whistleblower as to the outcome, or confirmation of completion, of an investigation on foot of their open disclosure, or disclosure of information forming the basis of a report on that investigation, where the information pertains to them.
reply:
The purpose of the Protected Disclosures Act 2014, as amended, is to promote the reporting of relevant wrongdoing in the workplace, to provide protection for reporting persons against penalisation and other adverse consequences arising from making a protected disclosure, and to provide mechanisms of redress where such penalisation occurs.
While not specifically prohibited, the legislation does not create a general entitlement for reporting persons to receive full investigation reports or all information that may have been generated during a follow-up process.
The Act requires that a reporting person be provided with some feedback. This includes information on the actions taken or envisaged and the reasons for such follow-up. The Act also requires that, subject to legal constraints, the reporting person be informed of the final outcome of any investigation triggered by the report.
To be clear to the Deputy, the legislation does not require the disclosure of the full investigation report, nor does it require a reporting person to be kept fully informed of all aspects of an investigation. The extent of the information that may be provided will depend on the circumstances of the particular case and on the obligations imposed by the Act and other applicable law.
In practice, disclosures may give rise to disciplinary processes, further investigations, employment disputes or court proceedings. In such circumstances, the disclosure of detailed findings, evidence, witness statements o

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the estimated annual loss to the Exchequer arising from the sale of solid fuels on which applicable taxes have not been paid.
reply:
I am advised by Revenue that while it does not estimate the annual tax loss arising from illegal or non-compliant solid fuel trading, Revenue assures me that combatting the risk of potential Solid Fuel Carbon Tax (SFCT) and VAT evasion in the solid fuel sector is a priority for Revenue.
Revenue has measures to ensure that it appropriately tackles SFCT and VAT evasion in the solid fuel sector.
Revenue operates a multi tax compliance framework - SFCT and VAT checks in the solid fuel sector are integrated into Revenue’s broader, risk?based and intelligence?driven compliance programme. Compliance interventions, particularly those conducted in the border counties, have enhanced Revenue’s understanding of the solid fuel supply chain and have generated important sectoral intelligence to support the development of targeted compliance strategies. This intelligence is further enhanced by cooperation and collaboration with HM Revenue and Customs in Northern Ireland.
Revenue’s outdoor and uniformed staff integrate SFCT and VAT checks into their wider field operations, and visits to fuel retailers. SFCT and VAT issues may be examined as part of cross tax head checks. Where under declaration or non-payment is suspected, Revenue fully investigates and seeks to collect unpaid tax, interest, and penalties.
Revenue continuously reviews the deployment of its compliance and enforcement resources across all sectors, including the solid fuel sector, in line with emerging risks and intelligence.

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance in the context of public sector industrial action, the expected surplus on the payroll budgets and-or an unexpended budget and-or appropriation in respect of one, two and three days of full strike action; if he will outline what happens to excess funds; if his Accounting Officer has or will seek permission to reappropriate those funds; and if he will outline the purpose to which they will be reappropriated or if they will carry over into the next accounting year.
reply:
I wish to inform the Deputy that it is not possible to provide an estimate of the potential reduction in payroll expenditure arising from one, two or three days of strike action. Any reduction in payroll expenditure would depend on a range of factors, including the number of staff participating, their grades and their individual rates of remuneration in line with the relevant salary scales.
Any savings arising from pay withheld in respect of strike action will be retained within the Department's pay subhead and will contribute to the Department's overall pay provision for the year. Such savings do not give rise to a separate fund available for expenditure or reallocation to other purposes. Any resulting underspend will be managed in accordance with the annual Appropriation Act, Public Financial Procedures and the requirements of the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation. At year-end, any unspent funding will form part of the Department's surplus for surrender and will be surrendered to the Exchequer in accordance with established public financial procedures.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to provide an update on the revised disabled drivers and disabled passengers scheme; if it will be replaced entirely by a new grant-based scheme led by the Department of Transport.
reply:
My Department and I share concerns that the Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme or DDS is no longer fit-for-purpose. The Government has now agreed to commence from early 2027 the Department of Transport’s Vehicle Adaptation Scheme (VAS). The VAS will provide direct financial assistance to all individuals with qualifying vehicle adaptation needs to meet the costs of those adaptations. The VAS will improve individuals’ functional mobility that in turn can contribute to better social and economic opportunities.
The Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme (DDS) remains with the Department of Finance and will be kept under review. Learning from the commencement and initial operation of the VAS will further inform reform options for the DDS.
As the Deputy will be aware, when this government took office, we committed to a step change in the delivery of supports and services for people with disability and their families.
Budget 2027 delivers significant progress for disabled children and adults, bringing the budget to over €4 billion for the first time.
This funding will be vital in delivering the National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People. The commitment to develop a new scheme by the Department of Transport, and in this context review the Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme, are strong commitments in this strategy.

question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance for an update on his Department’s consideration of proposed amendments previously submitted to his Department by industry to update the Irish Collective Asset-management Vehicles Act 2015 and company law to support tokenisation in the funds industry.
reply:
Work is ongoing in relation to the development of an appropriate legislative approach, and I hope to be able to provide greater clarity on timelines in the near future.
Last week, the Central Bank published the feedback statement to its discussion paper on Distributive Ledger Technology (DLT) and tokenisation in financial services. Responses reflected significant industry interest in the potential of DLT and tokenisation to enhance market efficiency and streamline financial services operations. Stakeholders emphasised that broader adoption will require the right enabling environment – which includes legal and regulatory clarity, interoperable market infrastructure, on-chain settlement assets, alongside robust risk management frameworks. Overall, the findings support a coordinated approach to enabling innovation with targeted adaptations to the existing legal and regulatory framework, while ensuring financial stability and market integrity.
Funds tokenisation is emerging as a potentially significant innovation in global capital markets, with the potential to transform how investment funds are issued, administered, traded and settled. Tokenisation, the process whereby an underlying asset or pool of assets, tangible or intangible, is converted into digital “tokens” that act as its proxy – could fundamentally reform how capital markets operate, enabling real-time trades; increasing transparency and liquidity; expediting clearing and ultimately providing for atomic settlement.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade to outline Ireland’s relationship with the Nordic-Baltic group; and if she has plans for Ireland to join the group.
reply:
The Nordic Baltic 8 group or NB8, is a regional cooperation format which, since 1992, has brought together the five Nordic and the three Baltic states (Finland, Sweden, Norway, Iceland, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania) to discuss current issues of regional and international importance in an informal setting. It has no permanent separate structure or organisation. NB8's day-to-day work is coordinated each year by one of the eight partner countries, which sets the priorities and draws up the work programme for its year in the chair. As of 1 January 2027, Norway will take over the chair of NB8 from the current holder, Estonia.
I took the opportunity in September to visit two of the NB8 member states (Estonia and Latvia) and I have the opportunity to meet most of my Nordic-Baltic counterparts regularly at the monthly EU Foreign Affairs Council. I was particularly delighted to welcome colleagues from all the NB8 states to the Gymnich meeting of foreign ministers held in Co. Wicklow in early September. NB8 leaders have just attended the European Political Community meeting in Dublin on 12th November. question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Transport the steps being taken to ensure that public electric vehicle or EV charging remains affordable for motorists, particularly those without access to home charging.
reply:

It also sets out plans for a regulatory review to commence in 2027, one focus area of which will include pricing, including AFIR compliance around disclosure.
Home charging remains the most cost-effective method of charging. The Department of Transport encourages overnight home charging whenever possible and estimates that over 80% of charging will take place at home. The SEAI provides grants to support the installation of domestic EV chargers.
In the context of those who do not have access to off-street parking, cross pavement charging is not yet regulated in Ireland and there is no consenting or permitting scheme in place.
The Department of Transport has established a cross-sectoral, targeted working group to consider the development and testing of a licensing regime for cross pavement charging. This group has agreed on the need for a robust licensing regime, to be administered at Local Authority level, for robust but affordable solutions that are pragmatic and consistent across the country.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Transport if a licensed haulier (details supplied), that failed to apply for the road transporters support scheme due to medical emergency at the time, can now apply retrospectively or seek an appeal on those grounds.
reply:
The Road Transporters Support Scheme (RTSS) opened at 12 noon on Wednesday 20 May and closed at 12 noon Friday 12 June 2026. During this window, my Department received over 4,400 applications in respect of approximately 31,500 vehicles.
Despite the large number of applications received, my Department was aware that situations could arise where eligible operators were unable to apply for the Scheme due to reasons outside of their reasonable control. Therefore, a second ‘request to submit a late application window’ was opened at 12 noon Monday 20 July and closed at 12 noon Friday 24 July 2026. Approximately 120 further applicants made a request during this time, and approximately 100 late applications were permitted. The remainder of applications related to operators who had already submitted an application during the original application window but had not yet received an assessment outcome, or operators that submitted more than one request.
While Budget 2027 approved further payments in respect of September and October, this was on the same criteria as previously. Consequently, it is not possible for operators that did not submit an application during the original application window or during the window to submit a late application request, to do so now.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her Department’s views on the high levels of reported sexual and gender-based violence in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo; the steps her Department is taking to support international organisations within the DRC to combat reported violence against women and girls; and the steps her Department is taking to ensure that resources for healthcare and justice for victims-survivors are received by verified organisations via Irish Aid.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 3, 4 and 6 together.
The Government remains deeply concerned by the security situation and humanitarian crisis in the eastern part of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
Since January 2025, the offensive by M23 militia in eastern DRC has seen thousands killed and hundreds of thousands displaced. In response to the escalation of violence, the UN Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 2773 in February 2025. In March 2025, the EU adopted additional sanctions in respect of the situation in DRC.
Alongside these international responses, there are a number of peace processes, facilitated by the United States, Qatar, and the African Union. While the diplomatic progress made is welcome, the violence continues and the humanitarian situation remains appalling. There are reports of widespread violence, forced displacement and mistreatment of civilians by all sides to the conflict.
Sexual and gender-based violence and sexual violence are widespread and represent a severe crisis driven by the conflict, mass displacement, weak justice systems, and deep-rooted gender inequality. For Ireland, the elimination of gender-based violence and conflict-related sexual violence is a precondition to achieving gender equality and is a core tenet of our foreign policy. We will continue to advocate for gender equality and speak out against sexual and gender based-violence in international fora, including during our membership of the United Nations Human Ri

question: Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Transport if he will ensure that local authorities are given more discretion to decide on their road works programme and not have a sizeable portion of their overall financial allocation assigned by his Department to particular projects.
reply:
In accordance with Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993, as amended, the improvement and maintenance of regional and local roads is the statutory responsibility of each local authority. Work on such roads is funded from Councils' own resources, supplemented by State road grants. The initial selection and prioritisation of work to be funded is a matter for local authorities.
Within the budget available for the Regional and Local Roads Grant Programme, which provides for the maintenance of regional and local roads, the objective is to allocate supplemental funding to eligible local authorities on as equitable a basis as possible, taking the length of the road network into account. The main focus of the grants is the protection and renewal of the regional and local roads network.
Owing to budgetary circumstances or external events, there have been occasions where funding outside of initial allocations have been provided. In the past this has been carried out through the provision of supplemental grants, readjustments to account for project over and under spends, and, in the recent case of Storm Chandra, the provision of additional exceptional funding.
Funding provided through my Department's Regional and Local Roads Grant Programme serves to supplement that of the local authorities, provide them additional support that might be required when available, and provide for targeted subvention to projects.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the steps her Department is taking at UN and EU levels to demonstrate that diplomatic condemnation and sanctions against states that perpetrate violence against their own populations or engage in ethnic targeting must be followed by genuine consequences; and the steps Ireland is taking to call out business-as-usual economic relationships with countries where state militaries and militias engage in human rights violations against civilians.
reply:
The protection and promotion of human rights is a core tenet of Ireland's foreign policy and our bilateral and multilateral engagement. We have a strong record of consistent engagement on human rights and accountability at the United Nations Human Rights Council and the General Assembly, including the sponsorship of resolutions condemning States who commit serious human rights abuses, including violence and ethnic targeting.
Ireland has recently been elected as a member of the Human Rights Council for a three-year term from January 2027 and this provides an important opportunity to continue to call attention to situations of concern and pursue accountability.
Ireland applies sanctions adopted by the UN Security Council or by the European Union against states who perpetrate human rights violations. The EU Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime (EUGHRSR) was established in December 2020 as a universal human rights sanctions framework to address serious human rights violations and abuses.
The human rights sanctions framework provides a legal basis for the EU to target individuals, entities and bodies – including state and non-state actors – responsible for, involved in or associated with serious human rights violations and abuses worldwide, no matter where they occur. The sanctions consist of travel bans for individuals, asset freezes for individuals and entities, and a prohibition on making funds or economic resources available to those listed. Derogations from the sanctions are

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Transport if he will consider and respond to correspondence (details supplied) regarding the digital driving licence.
reply:
Irish driver licensing operates within a framework of EU law, which sets out the driver licensing legislation with which all member sates must comply. Licence formats, vehicle categories and driving test standards are all set at EU level. As all member states test drivers to the same standards, there can be mutual recognition of driving licences.
Article 5 of Directive (EU) 2025/2205 establishes the EU framework for mobile driving licences. The deadline for implementation of the mobile driving licence, as per Article 3(4) of the Directive, is currently set at 54 months from the date of adoption of the first implementing act on mobile licences, as referred to in Article 5(7). This implementing act was adopted on 16 July 2026. Accordingly, the current deadline for introducing the mobile licence is January 2031.
However, Article 24(3) provides that the Commission may assess whether the 54-month deadline, for mobile licences to become the default format, can be brought forward and it will provide a report on its findings before 26 November 2026. Accordingly, the current deadline for implementation could be brought forward following this process.
Department officials are currently engaging with relevant stakeholders, including the European Commission, other member sates and the relevant Government departments, to meet the deadline for implementation of the mobile driving licence as set out in the Directive.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Transport if he is aware of the recent ESB price hike that electric cars are more expensive to refuel than petrol or diesel; who regulates the price that is charged; to outline where regulations are accessed.
reply:
Price setting by charge point operators (CPOs) is a commercial and operational matter for the companies concerned. Each such company has its own approach to pricing decisions over time, in accordance with factors such as developments in their cost base.
With over 20 commercial CPOs operating in Ireland, there are no current plans to introduce regulation of charging costs within the public EV charging sector. The Department of Transport will continue to monitor developments in the EV charging market, including pricing trends and impacts on users who rely on public charging.
The National EV Charging Infrastructure Strategy 2026-2028, published 4th November 2026, outlines the requirements for publicly accessible charging, and for installing EV Infrastructure that can meet future demand and user needs. It also sets out plans for a regulatory review to commence in 2027, one focus area of which will include pricing, including AFIR compliance around disclosure.
While this question relates to the price of public EV charging at ESB's eCars chargers, it should be noted that the price of home EV charging remains significantly cheaper than charging on the public charging network, meaning that the price of running an EV is significantly cheaper than petrol or diesel for those who have access to home charging.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Transport when the successor scheme to the disabled driver and passenger scheme will be introduced; if this will be in addition to the disabled driver and passenger scheme or if it will replace it entirely; to report on engagement with stakeholders on the successor scheme; if the disabled drivers and disabled passengers scheme will be wound down.
reply:
The Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme (DDS), which falls under the remit of the Minister for Finance, provides a range of tax reliefs to assist with the purchase and use of adapted vehicles by drivers and passengers with qualifying disabilities. Eligibility for the DDS is determined by assessment against six prescribed medical criteria. As a result, individuals who do not meet at least one of these criteria are not eligible to access the scheme. There has been sustained feedback from stakeholders highlighting that many people who require vehicle adaptations are unable to avail of State support under the existing arrangements.
The VAS is being developed as a separate scheme, to address this gap and to provide support for individuals who require vehicle adaptations but who may not qualify for assistance under the DDS. While the detailed eligibility criteria are still under consideration, it is not currently envisaged that individuals who are eligible for, or in receipt of, support under the DDS would also be eligible for the VAS.
A number of important aspects of the Scheme, including the level of financial support available and elements of its administration, have yet to be finalised. To inform these decisions, the Department has sought the views of Disabled Persons Organisations (DPOs), interested parties and potential beneficiaries on the design and operation of the Scheme. Subject to timely Government approval and the completion of the necessary preparatory wor

reply:

In response to the escalation of violence, the UN Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 2773 in February 2025. In March 2025, the EU adopted additional sanctions in respect of the situation in DRC.

reply:

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Transport if funding from the Climate Action Fund will be allocated in 2027 to support the continuation or expansion of the ICE2EV scheme, given the success of the pilot programme in 2026.
reply:

question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Transport when the Government intends to publish its proposed reform and implementation plan for the Road Safety Authority; and the changes envisaged to its governance, operational structures and enforcement functions.
reply:

reply: My Department has a total payroll budget of €24.2 million for 2026, with the processing of payroll completed on our behalf by the National Shared Services Office (NSSO). For the recent day of strike action, held on 14 October 2026, the NSSO have been requested to process payroll deductions for relevant staff amounting to approximately €56,000, exclusive of employers PRSI. We would expect any additional days to result in a similar deduction, with the exact amount depending on the number of staff who take part in the action. The timing of payroll deductions will depend on processing by the NSSO and could result in the saving accruing to 2026 or 2027 payroll. The current expected level of saving is very small compared to the overall payroll budget, and it is not currently envisaged that the funds would be re-appropriated for another purpose. Furthermore, in general, movement of funds from payroll to programme purposes are not facilitated, and any saving on the payroll budget would therefore be returned to the Exchequer.

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health to respond to matters raised in correspondence related to the reimbursement of CPAP treatment under the drugs payment scheme (details supplied); if the HSE has any plans to streamline the process; and if so, the status of this work.
reply:
The Drugs Payment Scheme (DPS) ensures that expenditure on approved prescribed medicines or medical appliances does not exceed a named threshold in any calendar month. The DPS is not means tested and is available to anyone ordinarily resident in Ireland.
Currently, the DPS threshold is €80, so no individual or family pays more than that a month on approved prescribed medicines or medical appliances. The DPS significantly reduces the cost burden for people with ongoing expenditure on medicines.
The Health Service Executive (HSE) has electronic claiming processes in place which enable pharmacies to submit claims in relation to services provided to patients whose family monthly medicines requirements exceed the DPS monthly threshold (currently €80).
In such circumstances the family pays the first €80 of the claim and the pharmacy submits the entire DPS record to the HSE at month end and the HSE pays the balance of the claim to the pharmacy based on the prices approved for medicines on the list of reimbursable items and the fees set out in legislation. DPS refund applications do not arise in such circumstances.
Patients registered under the DPS can apply for a refund where they opted to use more than one pharmacy to supply their family medicines needs or where they received items from their community pharmacy and other approved services provided by a supplier other than a community pharmacy (e.g. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or Oxygen treatment), and have paid in ex

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health further to Parliamentary Question No. 250 of 13 May 2026, to provide an update on the strategic review of the eligibility framework; and if the phase one report has been published (details supplied).
reply:
The Strategic Review of the Eligibility Framework is a multi-annual programme of work intended to support the consideration of a progressive coherent, equitable and sustainable framework for access to publicly funded healthcare, consistent with the objectives of Sláintecare and Universal Health Coverage.
The substantive work underpinning Phase 1 of the Review had been completed and the report is being finalised. Phase 1 has examined existing eligibility arrangements for health services, with a particular focus on primary and community care, including how eligibility operates from the legislative and policy framework through to its practical application.
The draft Phase 1 report and its findings are now entering an internal validation and consultation phase within my Department. question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Health if she will examine the inclusion of medical reports required for the renewal of driving licences under the medical card and GP visit card schemes, given that applicants who are required to submit a medical report as part of the driving licence renewal process must typically pay their GP a fee of between €65 and €75 for the completion of the report, notwithstanding that there is no charge for the renewal of the driving licence itself.
reply:
GPs are private practitioners. Most GPs hold contract(s) with the HSE for the provision of certain health services without charge, such as for the provision of GP care to medical card and GP visit card holders under the GMS contract.
Under the terms of the current GMS contract, GPs are required to provide eligible patients, persons who hold a medical card or GP visit card, with ''all proper and necessary treatment of a kind usually undertaken by a general practitioner and not requiring special skill or experience of a degree or kind which general practitioners cannot reasonably be expected to possess". Eligible persons are not subject to any co-payments or other charges in respect of such services including GP consultations.
The HSE reimburses GPs for services provided under the GMS contract to medical and GP visit card holders. The contract stipulates that fees in respect of certain medical certificates which may be required, for example, "under the Social Welfare Acts or for the purposes of insurance or assurance policies or for the issue of driving licences" are not covered by the contract.
Any fees charged by GPs for services provided outside the terms of the GMS contract are a matter of private contract between the GP and their patient.

reply:
The National Children’s Hospital Ireland (NCHI) is a much-needed investment in healthcare services for our children and young people which is now in the final stages of construction.
Once NCHI is open and fully operational, the three existing children’s hospitals at Temple Street, Crumlin and the paediatric inpatient unit at Tallaght will close. question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Transport the timeframe for a decision on an appeal for the fuel support scheme for a person (details supplied).
reply:
Applicants to the Road Transporters Support Scheme (RTSS) were permitted to submit an appeal if they considered that the Department had made an error by refusing to provide support for one or more vehicles.
It is important to note that support was only provided for vehicles that were in an operator’s fleet as of 01 March 2026 and remained in their ownership for the duration of the Scheme. Vehicles that were sold or acquired during 01 March – 31 May 2026 are not eligible for support.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Health who is responsible for reviewing cases where a woman is excluded from publicly funded assisted human reproduction treatment despite having an established clinical pathway; the reason no formal appeals or exceptional circumstances process exists; and whether she will consider introducing such a mechanism to ensure individual circumstances can be fairly assessed.
reply:
The Model of Care for Fertility was developed by the Department of Health in conjunction with the HSE’s National Women & Infants Health Programme to ensure that fertility-related issues are addressed through the public health system at the lowest level of clinical intervention necessary.
Under the Model of Care for Fertility, referrals for publicly-funded, privately-provided assisted human reproduction (AHR) treatment are subject to patients meeting the access criteria agreed by the Department and the HSE.
The access criteria were agreed following consultation with experts in the field of reproductive medicine and include limits in respect of the age of the intending birth mother, body mass index (BMI) and the number of previous AHR treatment cycles couples had already undertaken.
Patients, following consultations in primary care, are referred by their GP to their designated Regional Fertility Hub for assessment and investigation. Before making a referral, the GP will provide appropriate advice and information on lifestyle factors, carry out relevant tests and examinations, and undertake any necessary initial interventions. The GP must also be satisfied that the couple has been trying to conceive naturally for an adequate period of time. The specific access criteria to avail of services provided at a Hub are less stringent than those required to be met in order to qualify for free AHR treatment.

reply:
My Department does not currently have an estimate of any potential surplus on payroll budgets, unexpended budget, or appropriation that may arise in the event of one, two or three days of full strike action across the public service.
Any pay savings arising from industrial action would form part of the overall management of the Defence Vote. Where industrial action results in pay deductions, any consequential savings would, in the first instance, be reflected through the normal expenditure monitoring process and, subject to the relevant financial procedures, would form part of any surplus surrendered to the Exchequer. Any decision regarding the retention or reallocation of such savings to address spending pressures elsewhere within the Vote Group would be considered in accordance with Government accounting procedures and the relevant public financial management rules and procedures, including engagement with the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation. As industrial action is ongoing, no decision has been taken regarding the treatment of any savings that may arise.

question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Defence if she is aware of concerns raised by descendants of members of the Portlaoise volunteers regarding discrepancies in the State's roll of honour for participants in the 1916 Rising; and if her Department has examined claims that a number of volunteers who undertook service comparable to comrades who received official recognition were excluded from the roll of honour and other forms of recognition.
reply:
I am aware that, from time to time, concerns have been raised by, or on behalf of, descendants and representative groups regarding individuals whom they believe should have received recognition equivalent to that afforded to other participants in the struggle for independence, including individuals from Portlaoise.
The Roll of Honour is a closed historical document held by the National Museum of Ireland.
The award of 1916 medals is based on long-established criteria, and on evidence that can be corroborated by official Department of Defence records.
The process by which applications and petitions or appeals under the Military Service Pensions Acts were made, investigated and verified concluded in 1958, and there is no statutory or other mechanism available now by which service can be investigated or verified.
You will appreciate with the passage of over 100 years since the events of the 1916 Rising and some 60 years since the winding up of the investigation process, it is no longer possible, in the absence of official Departmental records, to obtain the level of verification required for the posthumous award of 1916 medals or other recognition.
Furthermore, there is no provision under the relevant legislation for the Department to retrospectively revisit or alter the determinations made by the statutory bodies responsible for assessing qualifying military service.
I wish to emphasise that accounts of involvement by individuals in the 1916 Rising are not disputed by my Departm

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Defence the reason the triple lock was not applied to the Government's decision to participate in military training of the Ukrainian army, when she has stated that it would apply to participation in the military training strand of the proposed new EU mission to Lebanon.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 19 and 20 together.
The EU’s Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine (EUMAM Ukraine) was established in 2022 in response to Ukraine’s request for assistance. The Government approved the Defence Forces’ participation in the mission in February 2023.
EUMAM Ukraine is, first and foremost, a non-executive training mission. Training activities are conducted on the territory of participating EU Member States and Defence Forces personnel are not deployed to Ukraine as part of the mission.
EUMAM Ukraine aims to enhance the military capability of the Ukrainian Armed Forces through the provision of individual, collective and specialised training delivered by the participating Member States.
Since its establishment, EUMAM Ukraine has trained almost 100,000 Ukrainian Armed Forces personnel and is the European Union's largest military training mission under the Common Security and Defence Policy (CSDP).
The participation of members of the Defence Forces in EUMAM Ukraine, including the provision of training activities under the mission, takes place under Section 3 of the Defence (Amendment) Act 2006 governing the despatch of contingent or member of the Permanent Defence Force for external service for purposes other than service with International United Nations Force. Section 3 (1)(b) of the Act provides that a contingent or member of the Permanent Defence Force may, with the prior approval of and on the authority of the Government, be despatched

reply: Developing and maintaining foreign language skills in our Embassies is important in building key relationships and enabling officers to integrate more deeply. A wide range of skills are required to carry out the functions of an Embassy and, to that end, the staffing profile of our Embassies include both posted staff and locally-hired staff. question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the research his Department has funded, commissioned or carried out on Mycoplasma bovis in cattle in the past five years, including on infection in dairy-bred calves sold into beef rearing herds; the findings of that research; the further research planned.
reply:
Mycoplasma bovis is an endemic pathogen. The disease is well understood from international and domestic research; the primary challenge lies in the practical application of this knowledge on farms.
The pathogen frequently co-occurs with viral infections, and control is centred on excellent animal husbandry.
My Department’s Veterinary Laboratory Service, alongside partners in Northern Ireland, prepared a 2024 All-Island Animal Disease Surveillance Report.
This included extensive investigations into Bovine Respiratory Disease (BRD), the leading cause of mortality in cattle over one month of age and caused by Mycoplasma bovis. Key findings included:
• Detection: It was detected in 9.5% of post-mortem BRD cases nationally, proving a top respiratory pathogen in both dairy and beef sectors.
• Age Impact: It disproportionately affects younger stock, accounting for 12% of respiratory diagnoses in calves aged 1–6 months (including dairy-bred calves sold into beef rearing herds) and 9.3% in weanlings.
• Pathology: Investigations confirmed a strong association with chronic bronchopneumonia and severe ill-thrift in animals under one year old.
In addition, experts from my Department have actively collaborated on peer-reviewed research:
• Herd Seroprevalence (2022): Collaborative research (McAloon et al., J. Dairy Sci.) established the seroprevalence of M. bovis in bulk milk samples and identified herd-level risk factors.
• Diagnostic Precision (2024): Research (McAloon et al., J. Dairy Sc

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether his Department has considered measures to reduce losses from Mycoplasma bovis in calves bought in from dairy herds, including awareness work with Animal Health Ireland and support for vaccinating calves on the farm of origin before sale.
reply:
Mycoplasma bovis is an endemic pathogen and is not a notifiable disease. The disease is well understood from international and domestic research; the primary challenge lies in the practical application of this knowledge on farms. Farmers are advised to discuss control of this disease with their private veterinary practitioner.
Animal Health Ireland have recently launched their 2026-2030 strategy titled: "Healthier Animals, Stronger Sector" which includes a strong focus on the principles of biosecurity and disease prevention in protecting animal health in Ireland, including in calves.

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the number of aquaculture licence determinations issued by his Department since June 2026.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 166, 167, 168, 169 and 170 together.
Applications for aquaculture and foreshore licences are considered by my Department in accordance with the provisions of the Fisheries (Amendment) Act 1997, the Foreshore Act 1933 (as amended) and applicable national and EU legislation. The licensing process is complex and involves consultation with a wide range of scientific and technical advisors, in addition to various Statutory Consultees. The legislation also provides for a period of public consultation.
The length of time taken to process an aquaculture licence application varies depending on a number of factors including location, species, scale and intensity of production, statutory status of sites and potential visual impact. My Department also takes full account of all scientific and technical advice, in addition to all issues identified during the public and statutory consultation phases.
Further factors that can impact the time taken to process an application can include; the requirement for an Appropriate Assessment and whether the application is required to be accompanied by an Environmental Impact Assessment Report; the need for additional underwater or archaeological assessments, etc. Decisions in respect of aquaculture licence applications are only taken following the fullest consideration of all consultations and public interest elements of each application, including environmental considerations.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the amount raised through the return for children initiative since its establishment; the amount distributed to each participating charity; and the oversight involved in the transfer of these funds to charities.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 14 and 17 together.
The Deposit Return Scheme, operated by Re-turn, was introduced in February 2024 to encourage more people to recycle plastic bottles and cans and to deliver on our ambitious EU targets for the recycling of those products.
In June 2024, Re-turn launched its own charity initiative, Return for Children, which supports six major children’s charities: Barnardo’s Ireland, Barretstown, Childline, The Jack & Jill Children’s Foundation, LauraLynn Ireland’s Children’s Hospice, and Make A Wish Ireland. I am advised that it has raised over €780,000 to date. Funds raised through the initiative are divided equally between the six participating charities.
Through Return for Children, members of the public can donate the deposits from eligible bottles and cans at participating events and through participating organisations. The funds support the work of the six charities in providing services to vulnerable and seriously ill children and their families. question: Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will allow payments to be made for lands (details supplied).
reply:
My Department publishes Terms and Conditions annually to help support applicants making claims under the Basic Income Support for Sustainability (BISS) and other Area Based Schemes. This document along with the Guide to Land Eligibility sets out the criteria used to determine the eligibility of lands for payment. Non-agricultural areas are ineligible for payment, which includes waterbodies such as streams, lakes, and ponds greater than 0.2 ha.
As part of the application process an applicant or their advisor can look to adjust the eligibility of their lands as a result of changes on the ground. In circumstances where applicants look to restore the eligibility of their lands they may be asked to provide supporting evidence where this change is not obvious from the imagery available to my Department.

These are important screening processes, designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to his revised reply of 2 November 2026 to Parliamentary Question No. 574 of 13 October 2026, the number of investigations into protected disclosures made within An Garda Síochána opened before 1 January 2025 that remain open, broken down by the year in which each investigation was opened; the date on which the longest running of these investigations was opened.
reply:
An Garda Síochána fully complies with the Statutory Guidance for public bodies and the protected disclosures reporting requirements established by the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation.
The Statutory Guidance details the timeframes in relation to protected disclosures assessments. The Statutory Guidance also details the information which Annual reports on protected disclosures should contain. An Garda Síochána publish Annual Reports on Protected Disclosures can be accessed at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/publications/annual%20reports/an-garda-siochana-annual-reports/.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether measures are in place to prevent the importation and sale of illegal or non-compliant solid fuels entering the State; and whether additional enforcement measures are under consideration.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 15 and 16 together.
My Department sets the policy and legislative framework within which environmental regulators, such as the EPA and local authorities, operate.
Local Authorities are responsible for the enforcement of the solid fuel regulations, identifying unauthorised fuels placed on the market, and taking measures to counteract any illegal trade. They are also responsible for ensuring that they can fulfil their air quality enforcement obligations.
The Air Pollution (Amendment) Act 2026, published earlier this year along with forthcoming secondary legislation, will ensure enhanced enforcement tools are available to the sector and will strengthen the labelling, registration and advertising of solid fuels. However, prosecution for breaches of the legislation by local authorities will remain as the main avenue for dealing with any breaches of solid fuel.
Over €1m has been made available to Local Authorities to directly support action in this area since the introduction of the new solid fuel regulations in 2022. In 2026 €300,000 was allocated to support local authorities with the highest levels of air pollution to put in place air quality roadmaps to improve air quality in those areas.
Financial allocation of budgets for individual programmes for 2027 will be finalised by end of year. Detailed allocations at programme and subhead level will be set out in the Revised Estimates Volume (REV) in December.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will report on the closure of the 'Horses of Hope' equine unit at Castlerea Prison; the exact operational or financial reasons behind the decision; and if there are any active plans or assessments underway to reinstate the Equine Programme or a similar rehabilitation project at Castlerea Prison in the near future.
reply:
I am advised by the Irish Prison Service that the ‘Horses of Hope’ programme at Castlerea Prison has been paused due to resourcing challenges.
A key factor affecting the programme’s ability to operate at full capacity has been the difficulty in recruiting a suitably qualified an Equine Work Training Officer.
Despite several recruitment efforts, including expressions of interest and consideration of alternative staffing arrangements, it has not been possible to secure a suitable candidate.
The Irish Prison Service is undertaking a feasibility assessment of alternative operating models for the facility. This includes consideration of potential arrangements involving community-based organisations to support former prisoners and other vulnerable or marginalised groups. Any future arrangements will be informed by the outcome of this assessment and the staffing, operational and governance requirements identified.
The Irish Prison Service recognises the potential contribution of animal-assisted programmes to rehabilitation. Its consideration of future options will take account of the need for a safe, sustainable and appropriately resourced service.

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Social Protection in the context of public sector industrial action, the expected surplus on the payroll budgets and or an unexpended budget and or appropriation in respect of one, two, and three days of full strike action; if he will outline what happens to excess funds; if his accounting officer has or will seek permission to reappropriate those funds; and if he will outline the purpose to which they will be reappropriated or if they will carry over into the next accounting year.
reply:
The salary deductions for staff members who engaged in the public sector industrial action on Wednesday the 14th October are currently being complied and will be processed by the NSSO, on behalf of my Department, over the coming weeks. The final total amount deducted from pay in respect of this day and any future strike action will largely depend on the number of staff who participate in industrial action on the day, as well as a number of other factors such as leave arrangements and worksharing patterns that apply on the specific day.
