question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Social Protection if retained firefighters are disadvantaged in accessing working family payment due to the requirement to demonstrate a minimum of 38 hours' employment per fortnight, given that their hours are dependent on emergency call-outs and are not guaranteed by employers; whether any flexibility exists in the assessment process for such workers.
reply:
The Working Family Payment is a weekly, tax-free payment available to low-income employees with children. It provides extra financial support to families with children with rates of payment based on household income and family size. There are over 57,000 families with some 114,000 children currently in receipt of the Working Family Payment.
To qualify for the Working Family Payment, a person must be in paid employment working for a minimum of 38 hours per fortnight. Applicants, including retained fire-fighters, may qualify for Working Family Payment by combining their working hours with those from additional part-time employment. An applicant may also combine their employment hours with those of a spouse, civil partner or cohabitant to meet the 38-hour fortnightly requirement.
Retained fire-fighters who are otherwise unemployed are entitled to apply for Jobseeker's Benefit or Jobseeker's Allowance, subject to the normal qualifying conditions for a jobseeker's payment. This includes satisfying the statutory requirements for a jobseeker's payment of being available for full-time work and genuinely seeking work. However, taking account of the unusual circumstances of retained fire-fighters, the rules of these schemes provide that retained fire-fighters can be considered to satisfy the availability requirement even where they are on call.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection whether his Department has assessed the need for non-halal meat options within the State-funded school meals programme, to accommodate parents and children who object on religious, philosophical or conscientious grounds to consuming halal-certified meat.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 146, 147, 148, 149 and 150 together.
My Department provides the funding for the School Meals Programme directly to schools. My Department does not select or approve suppliers. All schools as independent contracting authorities are responsible for choosing their school meals supplier on the open market, in a fair and transparent manner in accordance with public procurement rules. These rules clearly define the successful tenders responsibilities and obligations.
The Department's role is to ensure compliance with the nutritional standards of the School Meals Programme. Provided that meals on the submitted approved food business operator menu meet the required nutritional standards, decisions regarding specific food products and sourcing arrangements are matters for the supplier and the school to address through their contractual relationship.
As the contracting authority, the school has responsibility for managing its contract with the supplier and may discuss available menu options directly with the supplier. Where concerns or preferences arise regarding the type of meat provided, including requests for non-halal chicken or other suitable alternatives, the school is best placed to engage with the supplier to explore the options available and determine whether these can be accommodated within the terms of the contract and the programme's nutritional standards.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the funding allocated to local authorities for enforcement of solid fuel regulations in 2026 and proposed for 2027; the number of staff assigned to those enforcement activities.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 15 and 16 together.
My Department sets the policy and legislative framework within which environmental regulators, such as the EPA and local authorities, operate.
Local Authorities are responsible for the enforcement of the solid fuel regulations, identifying unauthorised fuels placed on the market, and taking measures to counteract any illegal trade. They are also responsible for ensuring that they can fulfil their air quality enforcement obligations.
The Air Pollution (Amendment) Act 2026, published earlier this year along with forthcoming secondary legislation, will ensure enhanced enforcement tools are available to the sector and will strengthen the labelling, registration and advertising of solid fuels. However, prosecution for breaches of the legislation by local authorities will remain as the main avenue for dealing with any breaches of solid fuel.
Over €1m has been made available to Local Authorities to directly support action in this area since the introduction of the new solid fuel regulations in 2022. In 2026 €300,000 was allocated to support local authorities with the highest levels of air pollution to put in place air quality roadmaps to improve air quality in those areas.
Financial allocation of budgets for individual programmes for 2027 will be finalised by end of year. Detailed allocations at programme and subhead level will be set out in the Revised Estimates Volume (REV) in December.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Social Protection if consideration has been given in budget 2027 to recognising those who are living with a disability and who previously were in receipt of a long-term disability payment but have since transitioned to the State pension.
reply:
The Government recognises the additional costs that disabled people can face in their daily lives and is committed to improving outcomes for disabled people. My Department provides a range of income support payments for disabled people of working age and a different suite of payments for those aged 66 or over.
In keeping with this, the new Cost of Disability Payment will be made to people who are in receipt of one of those working age disability payments.
This means that, in Quarter 1, 2027, this will be paid as a lump sum payment of €500 to working-age people in receipt of a long-term disability payment from my Department, specifically Blind Pension, Disability Allowance, Invalidity Pension, and Partial Capacity Benefit. The new payment will be made to approximately 240,000 people at an estimated cost of €119 million.
Further consultation with disabled people and their advocates in relation to the development of the payment for future years has begun. This was the main agenda item at my Department’s quarterly Disability Consultative Forum on November 2nd. A range of requests have been received regarding the final payment’s eligibility criteria. These are all being considered in the co-creation process and having the 2027 budget line in place will aid in how the process will develop.
This co-creation process should build on the detailed consultation process that has already taken place and the information that has already been gathered in that process.

reply:
My Department engages with the National Shared Services Office (NSSO) regarding the processing of payroll. Instructions regarding the processing of payroll deductions for staff members who engaged in industrial action on 14 October 2026 are currently being examined and the exact deductions for this or any future strike action days will be dependent on a number of factors. The calculations are incomplete at this stage.
In accordance with Public Financial Procedures, payroll budgets cannot be carried forward to the next accounting year. My Department will engage with the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation as part of the normal year-end expenditure management process.

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if his Department will examine whether targeted legislative amendments are required to ensure that genuine house shares remain a viable source of affordable accommodation.

Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if the impact of the March 2026 residential tenancy reforms on individual-room house shares was specifically assessed, particularly their importance to people on low and modest incomes.
reply:
In line with a commitment in Housing for All, a review of the Private Rental Market was undertaken by my Department and published in July 2024, which included significant consultation with stakeholders. It set out an overview of the rental market in Ireland, including the composition of the market and trends in rent levels, set out suggested policy objectives and considered a range of potential avenues for policy change to support these objectives.
Following on from this review, the Housing Agency was commissioned to undertake a comprehensive review of the Rent Pressure Zones (RPZs) rent control system. The key focus of the review was to assess the operation of RPZs since their introduction and consider their impact on the market and relevant stakeholders, including the retention of landlords and new investment. It considered whether RPZs should continue without change, or be removed, modified or replaced. The review, which was extensive and detailed, also included options and recommendations in relation to potential amendments to rent control.
The review, published on the Housing Agency website, involved engagement with a wide variety of stakeholders, including investors, representatives of landlord and tenant advocacy groups, academics and the RTB. The Housing Agency submitted its report to my Department at the end of April 2025 and advised that its preferred recommendation was to modify the current RPZ rent controls.

question: Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the plans his Department has to develop and protect the neighbourhood character of Dublin's urban villages (details supplied).
reply:
The local authority Development Plan is the principal planning strategy document which sets out the relevant policies and objectives to guide the physical development of each city and county over the development plan period. Responsibility for the making of a development plan rests with the relevant local authority in accordance with Part 3 of the Planning and Development Act 2024, and under section 30 of the Planning and Development Act 2000, the Minister shall not exercise any power or control in relation to any particular case with which a planning authority or the Commission is or may be concerned. Local authorities are independent in their functions under the Local Government Act.
All current development plans across the country were adopted under the Planning and Development Act 2000. Part 3, Chapter 5 (Development Plans) of the Planning and Development Act 2024 commenced on 31st December 2025. Sections 44 to 51 of the Act of 2024 require planning authorities to include various strategies and objectives in preparing development plans made under the 2024 Act, including in relation to the sustainable development of their functional area. Section 52 of the Act enables local authorities to provide settlement-specific objectives for parts of a city areas including objectives related to sustainable placemaking, renewal and growth of the settlement concerned, having regard to the physical, socio-economic, cultural and environmental context of the settlement.

question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of units currently subject to a croí cónaithe cities application in each of the cities included in the scheme, by units under construction and by units not yet commenced; the number of units completed to date in each of the cities under the scheme where funding is paid out, by the amount paid to date; and if he plans to extend the scheme to other areas.
reply:
The Croí Cónaithe (Cities) Scheme supports the building of apartments for sale to owner-occupiers in our five cities. Since the inception of the Scheme, support for the delivery of 2,863 apartments has been approved across 27 developments. This represents a funding commitment of approximately €339m. Six of these approvals, for 681 units in total, are for developments in Cork. The remaining twenty-one approvals, delivering 2,182 units, relate to developments in Dublin.
2,497 of the total of approved units are currently under construction (1,914 in Dublin and 583 in Cork). 366 of the total of approved units have been completed (268 in Dublin and 98 in Cork). Details of the contracted schemes are available on the Housing Agency website: www.housingagency.ie/CroiConaitheCities.
The amount of Croí Cónaithe (Cities) subvention provided to successful applications is dependent on the final open market selling price of each home. This open market price, along with the open book delivery cost determines the final subsidy amount. The maximum subsidy available for each apartment is €120,000 in Dublin, and €144,000 in the other regional cities, where the viability gap is greater. Accordingly, it is only possible to determine the final Croí Cónaithe (Cities) subsidy payable when apartment sales have closed. Funding of €11,187,832 has been paid out in respect of 211 units in Dublin and funding of €13,623,160 has been paid out in respect of 95 units in Cork.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the number of schools, sports clubs, charities and community groups that have participated in fundraising activities through the deposit return scheme; and the total funds generated by those organisations.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 14 and 17 together.
The Deposit Return Scheme, operated by Re-turn, was introduced in February 2024 to encourage more people to recycle plastic bottles and cans and to deliver on our ambitious EU targets for the recycling of those products.
In June 2024, Re-turn launched its own charity initiative, Return for Children, which supports six major children’s charities: Barnardo’s Ireland, Barretstown, Childline, The Jack & Jill Children’s Foundation, LauraLynn Ireland’s Children’s Hospice, and Make A Wish Ireland. I am advised that it has raised over €780,000 to date. Funds raised through the initiative are divided equally between the six participating charities.
Through Return for Children, members of the public can donate the deposits from eligible bottles and cans at participating events and through participating organisations. The funds support the work of the six charities in providing services to vulnerable and seriously ill children and their families. More information about the initiative is available on Re-turn's website at re-turn.ie/returnforchildrencampaign/ and in the Annual Report for 2025 at media.re-turn.ie/wp-content/uploads/2025-Annual-Report.pdf.

question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to provide an update on the environmental assessment process for the proposed planning changes to one-off rural housing; and the expected timeframe for this process to be completed.
reply:
The Government agreed a proposed policy direction for rural and Gaeltacht housing on 30 June 2026, enabling a proposed Draft National Planning Statement (NPS) on Sustainable Rural and Gaeltacht Housing to proceed to assessment for the purposes of Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) and Appropriate Assessment (AA), which is required to be undertaken prior to its final approval by Government.
The proposed new policy approach seeks to provide more clarity and consistency across the planning system, by setting out standardised criteria for assessing local rural housing need for new single housing in rural areas and new guidance on language criteria for housing in Gaeltacht areas.
The draft Sustainable Rural and Gaeltacht Housing National Planning Statement (NPS) is currently undergoing environmental assessment under the relevant EU Directives.
In accordance with Section 26(4) of the Planning and Development Act 2024, the draft NPS and the associated environmental documentation will be published for public consultation, and submissions will be invited before the Statement is finalised for Government approval and subsequent issuance by the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage under Section 25 of the Planning and Development Act of 2024.

question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will amend the eligibility criteria for the above-the-shop grant to allow applications from limited companies in addition to individuals, in order to facilitate the refurbishment and conversion of vacant upper-floor premises into residential accommodation.
reply:
Addressing vacancy and dereliction is a key priority for this Government, as reflected in the Housing Plan, Delivering Homes, Building Communities. The Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant, funded under the Croí Cónaithe Towns Fund, has been a key measure in addressing vacancy and dereliction across the country.
The Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant provides a grant of up to €50,000 to support the refurbishment of vacant properties for occupation as a principal private residence and for properties which will be made available for rent. A top-up grant of up to €20,000 is available where the property is confirmed to be derelict, bringing the total grant available for a derelict property up to a maximum of €70,000. In order to qualify for the grant, the property must be vacant for two years or more at the time of application.
To the end of Q3 2026, almost 20,000 Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant applications have been received, of which 15,300 have been approved, 747 rejected and over 7,100 grant paid out following completion of works, totalling almost €397 million.
Under the Housing Plan, a commitment was given to provide additional support for the refurbishment and conversion of above the shop vacant space for use as homes. The Vacant Above the Shop Grant was launched in April 2026, with a package of up to €140,000 being made available where vacant above the shop space is being converted/refurbished for residential use and the commercial element is remaining. question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he engaged with the DCB Stakeholder Forum in 2026, regarding the ongoing difficulties experienced by homeowners in obtaining mortgage finance, insurance cover and completing property transactions; if he will provide an update on the recommendations made by the forum; whether he accepts that the effective operation of the defective concrete blocks grant scheme, based on the most up-to-date scientific and technical evidence and delivering genuine 100% redress, is fundamental to restoring confidence in the housing market.
reply:
My Department has had a number of engagements with the Banking and Payments Federation (BPFI) on specific issues raised by Defective Concrete Blocks (DCB) homeowners. In addition, my Department attended the Quarter 3 DCB Stakeholder Forum meeting on 25 September 2025, which was chaired by the BPFI, and I have indicated that attendance at future meetings will continue to be considered where appropriate.
More recently, on 25 February 2026, my Department met with representatives of Insurance Ireland to discuss aspects of the Scheme.
An Implementation Steering Group for the Scheme has been in place since 2023, and a sub-group of this Steering Group was established to consider and discuss financial aspects of the scheme. Similarly, Insurance Ireland confirmed that, properties once remediated and certified, will be assessed, underwritten and insured as normal.

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of Irish language officers at each pay grade, in each of the local authorities, in tabular form.
reply: Under Section 159 of the Local Government Act 2001, each Chief Executive is responsible for the staffing and organisational arrangements necessary for carrying out the functions of the local authority for which he/she is responsible. My Department oversees strategic workforce planning for the local government sector, including the monitoring of local government sector employment levels. To this end, my Department gathers aggregate quarterly data on staff numbers in each local authority on a whole time equivalent basis. However, granular data, in terms of the number and grades of staff assigned to specific work areas in each local authority, is not collected and consequently is not available in my Department. The information sought would be available from each local authority.

question: Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the plans to provide an extension of Shannon navigation to Dowra, County Cavan.
reply:
Waterways Ireland is a North South Implementation Body established under the British Irish Agreement of 10 April 1998. It is funded by my Department and the Department for Infrastructure in Northern Ireland.
The detailed information requested in relation to the proposal to extend the Shannon Navigation from Lough Allen to Dowra is not held in my Department. However, arrangements have been put in place by all bodies under the aegis of my Department to facilitate the provision of information directly to members of the Oireachtas. This provides a speedy, efficient and cost-effective system to address queries directly to the relevant bodies. The contact email address for Waterways Ireland is oireachtas@waterwaysireland.org.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the timeframe in which the NPWS plans to carry out dredging on the canal at Ross Castle, Killarney, County Kerry.
reply:
The eastern end of the Ross Castle Canal is maintained as part of an ongoing maintenance programme at Killarney National Park, with additional works planned for 2027. As with the timing of many conservation projects, this is subject to suitable weather conditions and lake levels.
Planning for the large scale removal of accumulated silt from the mooring areas along the canal is currently at a preliminary stage. Subject to the availability of funding, it is expected that a tender process will commence in 2027 for a proposed canal de-sludging and sediment management project, including the necessary inputs for any licence applications. It is not yet possible to provide a timeframe for the commencement of dredging works.

question: Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to urgently look at increasing the HAP rates, because since the change in legislation for rented accommodation and the sudden large increase in rents, the HAP rates need to be dramatically increased so renters, especially single adults and young families, can afford to rent.
reply:
The HAP scheme plays a vital role in housing eligible families and individuals. At the end of Q2 2026, over 134,700 HAP tenancies had been set up since the scheme commenced, of which there were 47,166 households actively in receipt of HAP support nationally.
Maximum rent limits for HAP were set for each housing authority area in 2016 in conjunction with the Department of Social Protection (DSP). Since 11 July 2022, each local authority has statutory discretion to agree to a HAP payment up to 35% above the prescribed maximum rent limit. Discretion can be increased up to 50% above the prescribed maximum rent limits for Homeless HAP tenancies in Dublin. Local authorities also have additional flexibility to apply a couple HAP rate to single-person households where required. This additional measure recognises the challenges experienced by single-person households, and the fact that both single and couple households have a one-bed need.
It is a matter for the local authority to determine if the application of the discretion is warranted on a case-by-case basis and also the level of additional discretion applied in each case. question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh den Aire Cultúir, Cumarsáide agus Spóirt cén fath nach bhfuil an staidéar indéantachta ar stáisiún raidió Gaeilge a bhunú a bheadh dírithe ar an aos óg, a choimisiúnaigh Coimisiún na Meán agus atá faoi bhráid na Roinne, foilsithe go fóill; an bhfoilseoidh sé go luath é; agus nár chóir go mbeadh an taighde sin ar fáil don phobal agus iad ag glacadh páirt sa chomhairliúcháin maidir leis an Straitéis um Sheirbhísí Craolacháin atá le críochnú ar an 9ú Samhain 2026, go háirithe i gcomhthéacs na Prionsabail agus Treoir maidir le Comhairliúchán (2016) a d’fhoilsigh an Roinn Caiteachais Phoiblí agus Athchóirithe do chomhlachtaí poiblí.
reply:
Our language is a cornerstone of our heritage and national identity, and it is a priority of this Government to ensure the continued and increased support of the Irish language across all media platforms. Government recognises the value in young people having access to vibrant, relevant Irish language content. Coimisúin na Meán, the media regulator, administers funding and support for high-quality Irish language content via a range of media fund schemes which are funded from the Exchequer via the annual budgetary process.
Coimisúin na Meán commissioned a piece of research to explore the feasibility of an Irish language radio service aimed at young listeners, which the Deputy has mentioned. In parallel, Coimisúin na Meán commissioned an extensive review of the current provision of Irish language media, as recommended by the Report of the Future of Media Commission. Both of these pieces of research, along with other work, are informing An Coimisiún’s Action Plan for the Development & Promotion of the Irish Language in Media, which is being developed by An Coimisiún’s new Irish Language unit. An Coimisiún is currently consulting with stakeholders on the draft plan, which will be sent to me once finalised. Coimisiún na Meán has indicated its intention to publish its commissioned research when it publishes the Action Plan.

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport in the context of public sector industrial action, the expected surplus on the payroll budgets and/or an unexpended budget and/or appropriation in respect of one, two, and three days of full strike action; if he will outline what happens to excess funds; if his accounting officer has or will seek permission to reappropriate those funds; and if he will outline the purpose to which they will be reappropriated or if they will carry over into the next accounting year.
reply:
Any such estimate of the impacts referred in the question depend on factors such as the number of staff involved in any strike action along with their rate of pay as determined by the relevant salary scales.
Any pay underspend arising from strike action remains within the Department's subhead allocation for pay and does not give rise to a reappropriation for other purposes.
At year-end, any funding underspend will form part of the Department's surplus for surrender and will be surrendered to the Exchequer.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the engagement his Department has had with a company (details supplied) regarding the proposed development of Ireland's first rPET recycling facility; and the anticipated timeline for completion of the site.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 12 and 13 together.
Re-turn has stated its ambition to support long-term circular economy infrastructure through the development of an rPET recycling facility in Ireland. In this regard, Re-turn has provided preliminary briefing to me and the Department on its plans.

In due course, the procurement process will provide greater certainty in relation to costs, timelines and technical requirements, informing the final business case and any subsequent decision on whether to proceed.

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Education and Youth in the context of public sector industrial action, the expected surplus on the payroll budgets and or an unexpended budget and or appropriation in respect of one, two, and three days of full strike action; if she will outline what happens to excess funds; if her accounting officer has or will seek permission to reappropriate those funds; and if she will outline the purpose to which they will be reappropriated or if they will carry over into the next accounting year.
reply:
The financial impact of any industrial action on the Department's payroll expenditure would depend on a range of factors, including the duration of the industrial action, the number and categories of staff participating, and the application of relevant public service pay deduction arrangements. Therefore, while the Department has an overall pay allocation of €8.9 billion in 2026 and this equates to over €20 million per day, it is not possible to provide a precise estimate of any potential underspend associated with one, two or three days of strike action.
Any unspent Exchequer funding at year-end does not automatically carry forward into the following year and, subject to the relevant financial procedures, forms part of the surplus surrendered to the Exchequer. While there is standard procedure that allows for the carryover of unspent capital expenditure, this is not the case for current expenditure that includes pay related costs.
Where industrial action results in pay deductions, any consequential savings would in the first instance be subject to surrender back to the central Exchequer and would be reported through the normal expenditure monitoring process. Any alternative decision regarding the reallocation of potential savings would be considered in the context of the overall management of the Department's Vote and in line with the relevant public financial management rules and procedures.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Education and Youth when she expects to announce the next tranche of school building projects under the National Development Plan, following the first tranche of 105 projects identified for progression to tender and/or construction in 2026 and 2027; whether a date has been set for the release of the next tranche.
reply:
A total capital allocation of €7.55 billion for the Department of Education and Youth was confirmed for the period 2026-2030 under the National Development Plan.
As part of this NDP allocation my department is placing a strong emphasis on provision for children with special educational needs, with a particular focus on meeting annual school place needs. Optimising the capacity of the existing school estate continues to be a key priority, so that capital investment can be directed to where it is most needed.
Our sectoral NDP implementation plan set out a first tranche of 105 projects identified to progress to tender or construction during 2026 and 2027. 56 of these projects have now been completed, commenced construction or received approval to commence construction. Further modular and smaller scale additional accommodation projects continued to be progressed to meet annual September needs.
It is expected that the next tranche of projects to proceed to tender will be published in 2027. Prioritisation will continue over the coming months to identify this next tranche of projects. This will be informed by latest available demographic and capacity data, the department’s energy and condition inventory (the validation of which is due to be completed by early 2027), opportunities for phased development to prioritise the most urgent accommodation needs and consultation with patrons and management bodies.

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of schools in Kildare that have applied for emergency works scheme in the past 12 months; and the status of each request, in tabular form.
reply:
As the Deputy may be aware, the purpose of the Emergency Works Scheme (EWS) is to provide funding specifically for unforeseen emergencies, or to provide funding to facilitate inclusion and access for pupils with special needs. It does so by ensuring the availability of funding for urgent works to those schools that are in need of resources as a result of an emergency situation.
An emergency is deemed to be a situation which poses an immediate risk to health, life, property or the environment, which is sudden, unforeseen and requires immediate action, and in the case of a school, if not corrected would prevent the school or part thereof from opening.
The EWS operates on the basis of a minimal scope works to address the emergency situation. The EWS is intended to remedy an emergency situation and usually provides only an interim measure until a permanent solution can be delivered under the Summer Works Scheme (SWS) which deals with upgrade works to the school.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether an independent assessment has been undertaken of the reduction in bottle and can litter attributable to the deposit return scheme.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 10 and 11 together.
The Deposit Return Scheme (DRS) was introduced in February 2024 to encourage more people to recycle plastic bottles and cans and to deliver on our ambitious EU targets for the recycling of those products, and had an immediate effect on the number of these items being discarded as litter.
In January 2025, Irish Business Against Litter (IBAL) reported a near 50% fall in the prevalence of plastic bottles and cans in litter in the more than 500 sites monitored since the DRS was introduced. The IBAL Anti-Litter League surveys are conducted by An Taisce on behalf of IBAL.
The subsequent IBAL report published in 2026 stated that these items are now 60% less common in litter than when the scheme was first introduced.
To date, over 3.6 billion bottles and cans have been returned through the DRS. The Scheme's return rate has continued to increase since its introduction, from 66% in 2024 to 76.4% in 2025. At end September 2026, the return rate is running at 80% for 2026, in line with Re-turn's projections towards the EU target rate of 90% separate collection by 2029. When material collected through mixed dry recycling is also taken into account, the overall recycling rate for in-scope bottles and cans is estimated to already be above 90%.
The DRS is also providing a high-quality, separately collected stream of PET material, supporting Ireland's ability to meet EU recycled content requirements by increasing the availability of material

Where a child is eligible for transport and the application and payment process has been completed on time, they will get a seat on a school bus service, where a service is available.
Where a child is not eligible for school transport, but the application and payment process has been completed on time, they will be considered for any spare seats available after eligible children have been accommodated. These seats were previously known as concessionary seats.
Because of the nature of transport for non-eligible children and the priority of providing places for eligible children, there may be an excess of demand over supply for non-eligible pupils. In these cases, Bus Éireann will allocate tickets for spare seats using an agreed selection process.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the extent to which the deposit return scheme has contributed towards Ireland meeting EU recycled content and separate collection targets under the EU single-use plastics directive.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 10 and 11 together.
The Deposit Return Scheme (DRS) was introduced in February 2024 to encourage more people to recycle plastic bottles and cans and to deliver on our ambitious EU targets for the recycling of those products, and had an immediate effect on the number of these items being discarded as litter.
In January 2025, Irish Business Against Litter (IBAL) reported a near 50% fall in the prevalence of plastic bottles and cans in litter in the more than 500 sites monitored since the DRS was introduced. The IBAL Anti-Litter League surveys are conducted by An Taisce on behalf of IBAL.
The subsequent IBAL report published in 2026 stated that these items are now 60% less common in litter than when the scheme was first introduced.
To date, over 3.6 billion bottles and cans have been returned through the DRS. The Scheme's return rate has continued to increase since its introduction, from 66% in 2024 to 76.4% in 2025. At end September 2026, the return rate is running at 80% for 2026, in line with Re-turn's projections towards the EU target rate of 90% separate collection by 2029. When material collected through mixed dry recycling is also taken into account, the overall recycling rate for in-scope bottles and cans is estimated to already be above 90%.
The DRS is also providing a high-quality, separately collected stream of PET material, supporting Ireland's ability to meet EU recycled content requirements by increasing the availability of material

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Taoiseach in the context of public sector industrial action, the expected surplus on the payroll budgets and-or an unexpended budget and-or appropriation in respect of one, two and three days of full strike action; if he will outline what happens to excess funds; if his accounting officer has sought or will seek permission to reappropriate those funds; and if he will outline the purpose to which they will be reappropriated or if they will carry over into the next accounting year.
reply:
It is not possible, in the time available to respond to the Deputy's question, to provide an estimate of the potential reduction in the Department of the Taoiseach's payroll expenditure arising from strike action.
Any such reduction in payroll expenditure would depend on a range of factors, including the number of staff participating, their grades and their individual rates of remuneration.
Any savings arising from pay withheld in respect of strike action will be retained within the Department's pay subhead and will contribute to the Department's overall pay provision for the year. Such savings do not give rise to a separate fund available for expenditure or reallocation to other purposes. Any resulting underspend will be managed in accordance with the annual Appropriation Act, Public Financial Procedures and the requirements of the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation. At year-end, any unspent funding will form part of the Department's surplus for surrender and will be surrendered to the Exchequer in accordance with established public financial procedures.

Growing tourism from new and high-growth markets is a central objective of the Government's tourism strategy, A New Era for Irish Tourism, which targets overseas tourism revenue of €9 billion and domestic tourism revenue of €5.8 billion by 2031. A key priority within the strategy is market diversification, ensuring the tourism sector remains competitive, resilient and less dependent on any single source market.
To support this objective, the Government has provided additional funding for Tourism Ireland's marketing activity in new and high-growth markets. reply:

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will outline Ireland's position at recent meetings of the EU REACH Committee regarding restrictions on use of lead ammunition.
reply:
The regulation for the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (known as the REACH regulation) was created for the purpose of protecting human health and the environment from the most dangerous chemicals. As part of the process of restricting dangerous chemicals, the European Commission set up the REACH Committee. Every EU Member State, including Ireland, is represented on the REACH Committee. All restrictions proposed by the European Chemicals Agency and the European Commission are discussed and voted on by all EU Member States. Ireland is typically represented at the REACH Committee by the Health and Safety Authority, for matters within the remit of the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment.
In recent years, restrictions under REACH have expanded into areas beyond my Department’s remit, such as the proposal for a restriction on lead in ammunition. As such, my Department has no policy responsibility for lead ammunition or the matters addressed by the proposed restriction. Policy responsibility for environmental protection, wildlife, hunting and firearms rests with other Government Departments and Agencies, and national implementation measures arising from the adopted EU restriction does not rest with my Department.
REACH Committee proceedings and Member States' individual positions are confidential until the European Commission publishes the overall voting outcome through the Comitology Register in accordance with the applicable proced

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health the guidance the HSE will issue before 13 December 2026 to people with medical conditions, or on medication, who have been advised by their doctor to monitor or limit their folic acid intake, so that they can identify foods made with fortified flour, including unwrapped bread and bakery products.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 942, 944, 947, 948 and 949 together.
Ireland has a high incidence of babies who are born with neural tube defects compared to many other countries. Folic acid intake has been recognised as playing a key role in helping to prevent the occurrence of neural tube defects. Increasing folic acid intake among women of childbearing age continues to be a public health priority.
The Department of Health is currently considering policy options to increase folic acid intake in Ireland through on-going discussions by relevant experts at the 'Folic Acid Steering Group' and associated working groups relating to the areas of surveillance, food fortification, supplementation, and promotion/awareness.
The Department is considering mandatory fortification of flour as one possible policy option to reduce the incidence babies who are born with neural tube defects. Mandatory fortification of flour with folic acid has been introduced in several countries internationally and has been shown to help reduce the incidence of neural tube defects in these countries. The Steering Group is considering the available evidence and policy options associated with this proposal and has not yet made a recommendation for mandatory fortification of flour with folic acid.
Recognising the importance of public and stakeholder engagement, the Department conducted a public consultation on mandatory fortification of non-wholemeal flour with folic acid which was open for submissions between

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if his Department has conducted an analysis at to whether its Enterprise Strategy in relation to data centres is compatible with available renewable energy and Ireland's decarbonisation targets.
reply:
This Government is successfully delivering on both the digital and green transitions in parallel. The past 10 years have seen significant growth in data centres on our electricity system, and over the same period electricity system emissions have reduced substantially.
As the Deputy will be aware, Government policy has placed an emphasis on aligning data centre growth with overarching national energy and decarbonisation objectives. This has been a consistent, longstanding pillar of national enterprise strategy and associated policy development. It was reflected in the 2022 Government Statement on the Role of Data Centres in Ireland’s Enterprise Strategy, which highlights the need to prioritise projects primarily powered by renewables and efficient use of electricity grid infrastructure.
More recently, my Department published the independent report, The Value of Data Centres to Ireland, prepared by KPMG. The report assessed the economic contribution and strategic importance of data centres to Ireland. It identified substantial economic benefits arising from data-centre construction and operation and from the wider economic activity enabled by data-centre infrastructure. It also highlighted the need to ensure that future development is consistent with Ireland’s climate, energy and wider infrastructure objectives.
This alignment with climate and energy policy objectives is reflected in the Large Energy Users Connection Policy, published by the Commission for Regulation of Utilit

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Health if her Department plans to introduce lower maximum permitted levels for vitamins and minerals in food supplements.
reply:
Dear Deputy Farrell
The Department of Health is aware of the ongoing work by the European Commission to establish Maximum Amounts (MAs) for vitamins and minerals in food supplements and fortified foods.
Vitamins and minerals are essential micronutrients that play an important role in maintaining health and wellbeing. While they are necessary for normal bodily functions, excessive intake of some vitamins and minerals can result in adverse health effects. For this reason, scientific bodies such as the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) have established Tolerable Upper Intake Levels (ULs), which indicate the maximum amount of a nutrient that can be consumed daily without posing a risk to health.
Maximum Amounts are limits on the levels of vitamins and minerals that may be present in food supplements and fortified foods. Their purpose is to protect consumers by ensuring that products placed on the market do not contribute to unsafe levels of nutrient intake. The proposed approach being developed by the European Commission is based on scientific risk assessment and takes account of the most up-to-date evidence, dietary intake data and established safety thresholds.
The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) Scientific Committee previously gave advice with regards to setting maximum amounts www.fsai.ie/publications/the-safety-of-vitamins-and-minerals-in-food-supple.

reply:
I fully acknowledge the distress and inconvenience for patients and their families when hospital appointments are cancelled, particularly in the case of clinically urgent procedures.
While every effort is made to avoid cancellation or postponement of planned procedures, the Health Service Executive (HSE) has advised that planned procedures and operations can be postponed or cancelled for a variety of reasons including capacity issues due to increased unscheduled care demand.
Patient safety remains at the centre of all hospital activity and elective care scheduling. To ensure services are provided in a safe, clinically aligned and prioritised way, hospitals follow HSE clinical guidelines and protocols.
Cancelled hospital procedures/appointments are, where appropriate, rescheduled as early as possible with priority given to patients requiring time-sensitive and urgent treatment. Patients that are cancelled are rescheduled with the next available appointment based on their clinical prioritisation, with urgent patients prioritised for access.
In relation to the particular query raised, as this is a service matter, I have asked the HSE to respond to the Deputy directly, as soon as possible.

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Health if she or her Department have considered expanding the national bowel screening programme for those over 71 years-of-age.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 854, 873, 909 and 930 together.
As Minister for Health, I am committed to supporting our cancer screening programmes, which are a vital component of our health services. They enable early treatment and care for many people, thereby improving the overall health of our community.
BowelScreen, the national bowel screening programme, invites men and women aged 57–71 to take a free at-home screening test. The Programme for Government commits to extend the BowelScreen cancer screening programme.
In terms of progress, BowelScreen has been successfully extended to five additional age cohorts since 2023, with the most recent extension being completed in April 2026 (to include those aged 57 and 71).
Additionally, in April 2026, I approved a recommendation from the National Screening Advisory Committee (NSAC), the expert group that considers proposed changes to Ireland’s screening programmes, on the proposed extension of BowelScreen to those aged 50–54.
The full extension of BowelScreen to those aged 50-74 remains a key ambition of mine. However, this will take a number of years to complete, in order to ensure that there is sufficient capacity in the health system to diagnose and treat those who receive a positive screening result in a timely manner.
Finally, it should be emphasised that population-based screening programmes are for people without symptoms. If anyone becomes aware of symptoms, or if they have concerns or worries, they should contact a me

Tourism has a unique role to play in fostering stronger links between communities, supporting regional development and enhancing the visitor experience.
The Programme for Government commits to supporting Tourism Ireland in promoting and developing tourism offerings on an all-island basis. This complements ongoing work with Fáilte Ireland to encourage the sustainable growth of tourism throughout the country and to further develop Ireland’s tourism experience brands.
The Government’s tourism policy, A New Era for Irish Tourism, highlights the importance of Shared Island collaboration and recognises the significant opportunities that cross-border tourism presents. The Government recognises that the cost of doing business, including labour, energy and overall utility costs, has been a significant issue for businesses in recent years, driven by wider inflationary pressures. The Government continues to actively monitor cost developments across all sectors of the economy including SMEs, nationally and regionally.
In August 2026, I welcomed the publication of the Final Report of the Cost of Business Advisory Forum, which examined non-pay cost drivers affecting enterprise, including energy, insurance, legal services, water and wastewater services, infrastructure and planning, tax administration and regulatory compliance, and banking and financial services. It contains 63 recommendations aimed at reducing costs, strengthening competitiveness, improving price transparency, simplifying regulation, and addressing bottlenecks that impact businesses, particularly SMEs.
Addressing these actions will require sustained engagement across Government Departments, Agencies, and Regulators to advance the short, medium and long-term recommendations. To maintain momentum, I have written to the Departments, Agencies and Regulators with responsibility for recommendations under their remit, seeking a progress update, together with any anticipated timelines or next steps.
The Department has also committed to monitoring and tracking progress on the implementation of all recommendations. The work of the Forum is already informing Government policy development. Fo

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Health the additional funding provided for 2027 to improve HSE pathfinder services; and the 2026 budget allocation for pathfinder services.
reply:
Budget 2027 provides a significant increase of €1.6 billion (6.2%) in current funding and €160 million (10.3%) in capital funding for the health service in 2027. While there is no specific ringfenced allocation for HSE pathfinder services arising from the Budget, the overall additional funding will support the continued delivery and development of services across hospital and community care settings.
Following the Budget, the Department issued the annual Letter of Determination to the HSE, setting out the overall funding available and the key priorities to be delivered in 2027. Consistent with the health service reforms underway, funding is allocated at Health Region and national service level rather than being centrally ringfenced for individual programmes. Health Regions will be responsible for managing their allocations and prioritising expenditure to meet population needs and deliver agreed national priorities.
The HSE will set out its detailed plans for service delivery, including priorities and resource allocations, in the National Service Plan for 2027. Within that framework, decisions regarding the level and configuration of HSE pathfinder services will be a matter for the HSE and the relevant Health Regions.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Health if the shingles vaccination programme for persons aged over 65 years-of-age will be free of charge with effect from January 2027 from GPs and pharmacies.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 907, 908 and 914 together.
Ireland’s immunisation programme is informed by the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). NIAC considers the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland as well as international best practice in relation to immunisation when developing its advice.
The current NIAC guidelines state that the shingles vaccine may be considered for those aged 65 years and older, due to the greater burden and severity of disease in this age group and in those aged 18 years and older at increased risk of shingles.
I can confirm that I have approved the introduction of a Shingles Vaccination Programme, in line with NIAC advice, to be implemented on a phased basis over 5 years, for immuno-compromised groups and persons aged 65 and over.
The programme is expected to commence in 2027, initially offering shingles vaccines to immuno-compromised groups. This will be followed by the 80 years and older cohort. The programme will conclude with the 65–69-year-old cohort.
It is expected that the vaccine will be administered in the main by GPs and Pharmacists. Further programme details will become available in due course.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Health her views on expanding bowel screening from age 59-69 to 50-74 to help detect bowel cancer early and prevent unnecessary deaths from the disease.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 854, 873, 909 and 930 together.
As Minister for Health, I am committed to supporting our cancer screening programmes, which are a vital component of our health services. They enable early treatment and care for many people, thereby improving the overall health of our community.
BowelScreen, the national bowel screening programme, invites men and women aged 57–71 to take a free at-home screening test. The Programme for Government commits to extend the BowelScreen cancer screening programme.
In terms of progress, BowelScreen has been successfully extended to five additional age cohorts since 2023, with the most recent extension being completed in April 2026 (to include those aged 57 and 71).
Additionally, in April 2026, I approved a recommendation from the National Screening Advisory Committee (NSAC), the expert group that considers proposed changes to Ireland’s screening programmes, on the proposed extension of BowelScreen to those aged 50–54.
The full extension of BowelScreen to those aged 50-74 remains a key ambition of mine. However, this will take a number of years to complete, in order to ensure that there is sufficient capacity in the health system to diagnose and treat those who receive a positive screening result in a timely manner.

question: Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Health the way in which patients that will be receiving maternity care services will be consulted as part of the new National Maternity Strategy.
reply:

Since 2016, €28 million in development funding has been invested through the Strategy, supporting the recruitment of more than 567 additional whole-time equivalent staff, including 44 consultants and over 390 nurses and midwives.
Over €130 million of capital investment has been directed into maternity services over the lifetime of the strategy. This has modernised facilities, delivering refurbishments to wards, and home-from-home birthing rooms across the country.

question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the action he is taking to help businesses invest, innovate and reduce costs.
reply:
Supporting businesses to invest, innovate and reduce their costs is a key priority for my Department. By investing in innovation, companies develop new products and services that improves their ability to compete in global markets while also improving their productivity, thereby reducing their costs.
Research conducted by Knowledge Transfer Ireland in 2024 found that firms availing of Enterprise Ireland’s research and innovation (R&I) supports had, on average, 1.3 times more domestic sales, 2.5 times higher turnover, and 4.7 times greater exports than competitors not investing in RD&I – as well as an average 2.5% productivity increase per person employed.
In addition to being the bedrock of numerous strategies, such the Government’s Action Plan on Competitiveness and Productivity, as well as the White Paper on Enterprise 2022-2030, my Department and agencies offer a comprehensive suite of RD&I supports.
SMEs can avail of multiple Innovation Vouchers, each worth up to €10,000, enabling collaboration with a third-level institution or research body on an industry challenge.
The RD&I Fund provides direct grants, through the enterprise agencies, designed to help Irish businesses grow their sales and employment by addressing key challenges in engaging in R&I.
Enterprise Ireland administers the Technology Centres who work in partnership with businesses to drive innovation adoption, increase efficiencies and achieve higher levels of productivity across a range of sectors.

reply:
The Government has provided funding to support the implementation of the Public Only Consultant Contract (POCC) and the associated reduction in private income available to public hospitals (Including Maternity Hospitals). Budget 2026 included provision of €100 million to address the impact of reduced private income in public hospitals.
Budget 2027 provides a further €151 million for this purpose. The transition to the POCC is expected to support increased public patient activity and improved utilisation of hospital capacity, including during evenings and weekends.
Detailed allocations by Health Region and care group will be set out in the Department's Letter of Determination and the HSE National Service Plan for 2027.

question: Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to provide details of the number of Irish SMEs which have been taken over in ownership by US-run private equity companies in the past three years.
reply:
Irish-owned exporting companies make a huge contribution to the Irish economy. They compete internationally, generate revenues in overseas markets and return that value to Ireland through employment, wages, investment, innovation and expenditure with Irish suppliers. In 2025, Enterprise Ireland (EI) client companies spent a record €43.73 billion in the Irish economy, an increase of 57.4 % since 2018. That equates to almost €120 million every day and more than €840 million every week through payroll, material and services spend.
My Department does not track data to the granular detail as outlined in the question, however, Enterprise Ireland tracks the number of client companies that are acquired and this equates to approximately 120 companies from the start of 2024 to date in 2026. This information is not broken down by the nature of the acquirer nor its jurisdiction. In broad terms, Enterprise Ireland has advised that there does appear to be an increasing trend of their more mature clients being acquired. This differs from earlier periods, when a greater proportion of exits involved earlier-stage, equity-backed companies being sold through trade sales.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Health whether her Department or State agencies under its aegis have a policy regarding the use of artificial intelligence to produce artwork for social media, public information campaigns, and graphic design.
reply:
The Department of Health has an approved policy governing the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI), based on recommendations contained in the National Cyber Security Centre’s Cyber Security Guidance on Generative AI for Public Sector Bodies and the Department of Public Expenditure, NDP Delivery and Reform’s Interim Guidelines for Use of AI in the Public Service.
The Department of Health does not use AI to create imagery, artwork or graphics for social media. The Department works transparently to produce and source original graphic design, social media imagery photography, and videography for use across its social media channels and creative campaigns.
Information on bodies under the aegis of the Department of Health is an operational matter for each body. The Deputy should contact the relevant Director/CEO/Registrar directly.

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Health if her Department will reconsider funding a dedicated stem-cell transplant unit in Cork to serve the south of the country.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the Government is committed to improving cancer care, ensuring better prevention, maintaining improvements in cancer survival rates, and facilitating timely access to treatments. This includes through the increased provision of access to advanced cellular therapies. Advanced cellular therapies are highly specialised treatments used in the management of a range of malignant and non-malignant diseases.
These therapies require specialist multidisciplinary teams, dedicated laboratory facilities, tissue establishment infrastructure, specialised inpatient facilities and robust regulatory and accreditation arrangements. Cellular therapies currently available to patients in Ireland include autologous stem cell transplantation, allogeneic stem cell transplantation and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. Adult Autologous Stem cell transplantation services are currently provided in St James's Hospital, University Hospital Galway and St Vincent's University Hospital. Adult allogeneic stem cell transplantation is currently provided through St James's Hospital.
The Government continues to progress the expansion of advanced cellular therapies nationally. In 2026, Beaumont Hospital was designated as an additional autologous stem cell transplantation and CAR-T Centre, working towards commencement of services in 2027.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Health her Department's plans to bring complaints against private hospitals and private consultants under the remit of the Ombudsman; and the timeline for when this will be enacted (details supplied).
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 881 and 882 together.
My Department has been engaged in early scoping work for the development of a policy in relation to the areas of Patient Safety, Complaints and Advocacy.
A national patient complaints and patient safety incidents policy covering both public and private health services is being considered through a number of work streams. A comprehensive stakeholder engagement process has been done to gather information from health and social care services, advocacy groups, the Office of the Ombudsman and the regulators. My Department continues to collaborate closely with all relevant stakeholders.
My Department also commissioned several independent research projects regarding clinical complaints and patient safety incidents, including looking at international comparisons. My Officials are currently taking stock and analysing all work previously undertaken.
While this policy work is being fully considered and progressed, it is not currently possible to provide an expected date of completion.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health the date on which clinical activity at the HSE south-west surgical hub at Cork University Hospital was paused following additional commissioning checks; the number of patients whose procedures or appointments at the hub were cancelled or postponed between 29 September and 12 October 2026 as a result; and the number of those patients who have since been rescheduled or treated.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 859, 860, 864, 866, 867, 868 and 869 together.
The HSE South West Surgical Hub in Cork includes two theatres (with two additional theatres to open in 2027), two minor procedure rooms and a number of outpatient rooms. The Hub was scheduled to initially commence operations on a limited activity basis, allowing the service to become established in a safe and controlled manner with the necessary processes embedded, ensuring a safe, sustainable and effective expansion of operations. In this regard, patients were scheduled over five days between 29 September and 9 October.
Following established commissioning processes and the ongoing air sampling that is routine in theatres and procedure rooms, on 29 September air sampling results for one theatre and one minor procedure room returned results above acceptable levels. As a precautionary measure, both areas were unavailable for clinical use while further deep cleaning and resampling occurred.
In order to protect patient confidentiality, it is not possible to provide a figure for the number of patients treated at the Hub before temporary closure as the number involved could allow potential patient identification. However, low clinical risk has been confirmed and appropriate patient follow up has been carried out. Other patients who were due to be treated on the day were accommodated at an alternative facility. The patients scheduled for procedures in Theatre in the following weeks have been rescheduled.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Health the immediate steps being taken to stabilise the supply of lenzetto in pharmacies; and the protocols being introduced to ensure that when critical shortages occur, alternative options such imported stocks are fully available and accessible without compromising patient care.
reply:
The Department is aware of the stress that medicine shortages can cause for patients and healthcare professionals. Managing and mitigating medicine shortages is a priority for the Department of Health and is the subject of several workstreams across the Department and the wider health service.
Under European and national medicines legislation, pharmaceutical companies and wholesalers are required to ensure an appropriate and continuous supply of the medicines they place on the market. Companies are also required to notify the Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA) of actual or anticipated shortages affecting the Irish market. The HPRA maintains a publicly available list of current and resolved medicine shortages and works closely with suppliers to minimise the duration and impact of shortages on patients.
All shortages, including persistent shortages, are managed via the national Medicines Shortages Framework (MSF), which is coordinated by the HPRA. The MSF involves a multi-stakeholder approach to handling shortages of human medicinal products. Where required, the HPRA engages with all relevant stakeholders to support continuity of care until sufficient supply of the medicinal product is available to meet demand.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health the number of persons aged 70 years and over holding a full medical card whose assessed gross weekly income is within €10 of the income or €1,050 for a couple, in view €10 weekly increase in the State Pension in Budget 2027 and the fact that the limits have not changed since 1 November 2020; and whether her Department has assessed the impact of the Budget 2027 pension increases on eligibility.
reply:
Medical Card provision is primarily based on financial assessment. In accordance with the Health Act 1970 (as amended), eligibility for a medical card is determined by the HSE, which assesses each application on a qualifying financial threshold. This is the amount of money that an individual can earn a week and still qualify for a card. It is specific to the individual’s own financial circumstances.
Persons aged 69 and under are assessed under the general means tested medical card thresholds which are based on an applicant’s household income after tax and the deduction of PRSI and the Universal Social Charge. Certain expenses are also taken into account. Detailed guidelines are available at: www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/medical-cards/applying/assessment/
Persons aged 70 or older are assessed under medical card income thresholds which are based on gross income. However, it should be noted that those aged over 70 can also be assessed under the general means tested scheme where there are particularly high medical costs. Details are available at: Medical card for over 70s www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/medical-cards/other-types-of-medical-card/over-70s/.
In response to the Deputy’s query regarding the impact of State pension payment increase on medical card eligibility, it is important to note that where a person's sole household income is derived from a social protection payment, he/she will be awarded a medical card.

question: Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Health when the last healthcare inspection by HIQUA was carried out at Tallaght University Hospital; the key findings from this inspection that were identified as requiring corrective action in preparation for winter flu season; and whether these actions have been implemented and when the next inspection is due to take place.
reply:
HIQA is an independent statutory body established to promote safety and quality in the provision of health and social care services. Under the Health Act 2007, HIQA has a statutory role to set, and monitor compliance with, standards for the quality and safety of health and social care services in Ireland.
Inspections of hospitals by HIQA are not conducted to a set timetable. HIQA is a risk-based regulator and conducts inspections as needed on the basis of risk. As some of HIQA’s inspections are unannounced, and because it must remain dynamic in addressing risk issues as they emerge, HIQA does not release its inspection schedule.
In the main, however, HIQA typically aims to conduct two inspections in a three-year cycle, one announced and one unannounced inspection. Inspections will occur more often if risk issues arise. Alongside its onsite inspection activity, HIQA also continuously takes account of notifications, solicited and unsolicited information, as well as key performance data, in fulfilling its responsibilities in monitoring hospitals against the National Standards for Safer Better Healthcare.
The most recent inspection of Tallaght University Hospital took place on the 10th and 11th of March 2026. The report from the inspection was published on the 15th of September 2026. As the implementation of actions arising from the report are a service matter, I have asked the HSE to respond to the Deputy directly, as soon as possible.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health further to Parliamentary Question No. 73153/26, the reply to which from the Health Service Executive dated 21 October 2026 did not address whether a requirement will be introduced for documentary evidence from foreign healthcare providers of compliance with local child protection legislation or Hague Convention obligation treatment abroad scheme applications involving children, if she will now state, as a matter of Departmental policy, whether such a requirement will be introduced; if not, the reasons; whether the Department has assessed the need for such a requirement since 2020.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the HSE operates the EU Treatment Abroad Scheme (TAS), for persons entitled under EU Regulation 883/04 and has a dedicated office for that purpose. The TAS is a consultant led scheme and allows for a public consultant based in Ireland to refer a public patient who is normally resident in Ireland for treatment in the public healthcare system of another EU member state, the UK or Switzerland, subject to the EU Regulations and Guidelines. The HSE TAS application requires the patient's referring public consultant, following clinical assessment, to certify, among other things, that the treatment is medically necessary, will meet the patient’s needs, is provided in a recognised public hospital or other institution that will accept EU/EEA form S2 (IE) and is under the control of a registered medical practitioner. The treatment must not be available within the State or not available within a time normally necessary for obtaining it. Once a patient is discharged from a specific episode of care abroad, their care immediately reverts to their referring public consultant based in Ireland.
As the detailed operation of the Treatment Abroad Scheme, including detailed operational requirements in relation to the HSE TAS application, is an operational matter for the HSE rather than the Department of Health, I have referred the Deputy’s question to the HSE for direct response.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Health if she is aware of ongoing shortages of rapamune 1mg medication affecting transplant recipients; if she is aware of the case of a heart transplant patient who was forced to travel from Mayo to Dublin to secure an emergency supply after being unable to source the medication locally; and the urgent measures being taken to protect patients who depend on this life-sustaining medication.
reply:
The Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA) is the competent authority for the regulation of medicines in Ireland.
Sirolimus (Rapamune®) is an authorised medicinal product in Ireland. The Marketing Authorisation Holder, Pfizer, has confirmed that Rapamune is currently available for supply to Irish patients across all marketed presentations, including 1 mg tablets, and that no shortages are anticipated or ongoing.
Rapamune 1 mg remains authorised in Ireland and is listed as an authorised medicinal product on the HPRA Authorised Medicines database.
In relation to the specific case raised, the Department has engaged with the HSE and the relevant transplant centre and understands that this appears to have been an isolated issue involving the patient and their community pharmacy, which has since been resolved. No other supply issues have been reported and no supplier shortage has been identified.
