question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the national plan that is in place to ensure that adults with intellectual disabilities completing specialist training programmes have timely access to appropriate adult day services; whether the HSE maintains a national register of individuals expected to require day-service placements in each of the next five years; the way in which future demand is assessed and incorporated into annual budgets; and the arrangements that exist to ensure that funding is approved before individuals complete their training programmes.
reply:
HSE-funded day programmes for people with intellectual disabilities, autism, or complex physical disabilities include a range of centre-based and community-based activities. Access to services is based on an individual’s needs rather than on their diagnosis. The focus is on supporting people to participate in the mainstream activities and in the life of their community, in line with their wishes and needs.
Day services are a vital support for adult with disabilities to participate in the life of their community and to realise their own ambitions and desires. The majority of young people due to leave school in a given year that require a HSE funded day service have been profiled by the end of the previous year to establish their support needs. Once needs are identified, referrals are made to the service provider of choice, funding is committed and negotiations are concluded with providers by end of May to confirm placements to young people and their families. In many instances young people due to leave school at end of June are introduced to their day services for trialling purposes during April, May and June so there is a natural transition into day services in September.
As this question refers to service matters, I have asked the Health Service Executive (HSE) to respond to the Deputy directly, as soon as possible.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether the HSE has a policy governing interim day-service provision for adults with intellectual disabilities who have completed training programmes but are awaiting approval of funding for an adult day-service placement; whether she is aware that, in the case of an individual seeking a placement with an organisation (details supplied), only an informal arrangement of three days per week has been offered pending full funding approval; and the safeguards in place to ensure that such interim arrangements are not withdrawn while funding remains outstanding.
reply:
HSE-funded day programmes for people with intellectual disabilities, autism, or complex physical disabilities include a range of centre-based and community-based activities. Access to services is based on an individual’s needs rather than on their diagnosis. The focus is on supporting people to participate in the mainstream activities and in the life of their community, in line with their wishes and needs.
Day services are a vital support for adult with disabilities to participate in the life of their community and to realise their own ambitions and desires. The majority of young people due to leave school in a given year that require a HSE funded day service have been profiled by the end of the previous year to establish their support needs. Once needs are identified, referrals are made to the service provider of choice, funding is committed and negotiations are concluded with providers by end of May to confirm placements to young people and their families. In many instances young people due to leave school at end of June are introduced to their day services for trialling purposes during April, May and June so there is a natural transition into day services in September.
As this question refers to service matters, I have asked the Health Service Executive (HSE) to respond to the Deputy directly, as soon as possible.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether her Department or State agencies under its aegis have a policy regarding the use of artificial intelligence to produce artwork for social media, public information campaigns, and graphic design.
reply:
The Department has adopted the Guidelines for the Responsible Use of AI in the Public Service and is developing a Department-specific AI Framework. A suite of supporting documents, including an AI Policy, staff guidance and a Training and Awareness Plan has been prepared and is progressing through the Department’s approval process. The framework is intended to align AI use with the EU AI Act and relevant public-service, data protection and cybersecurity requirements.
The Department has an AI governance group in place to oversee the Department’s approach. Governance arrangements include an AI Register and a proportionate use-case assessment process to ensure that proposed uses are assessed, recorded and subject to appropriate safeguards.
AI is used as a general productivity and administrative support tool. Microsoft Copilot Chat is available to staff through Teams and staff have also been provided with practical guidance on the appropriate use of AI, including clear do’s and don’ts. AI is not used to make decisions or issue replies independently. Any material produced with AI assistance must be checked, validated and approved by the responsible officials, with the final response remaining the responsibility of the Department in line with human oversight.
The Department will continue to develop its governance, policy, guidance and training arrangements to support the safe, responsible and proportionate use of AI, with human oversight remaining central.

reply:

They are central to delivering high-quality services, and play a crucial role in bringing about the changes necessary to realising the vision for early childhood.
Pay is one of a number of challenges impacting the early learning and care and school-age childcare workforce. The level of pay for early years educators and school-age childcare practitioners does not reflect the value of their work for children, families, society and the economy. Although the Government is the primary funder of the sector, it is not the employer and cannot directly set wages or conditions for any staff in the sector. The Joint Labour Committee (JLC) is the formal mechanism established by which employer and employee representatives can negotiate minimum pay rates, which are set down in Employment Regulation Orders (EROs), and is independent in its functions.
Through the work of the JLC and successive EROs, minimum pay rates have now risen three times in four years, delivering an average 15% increase in minimum rates of pay. question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether additional deer population management measures are under consideration in light of concerns regarding road safety and agricultural impacts.
reply:
My Department, along with the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage established the Irish Deer Management Strategy group to develop a strategy for the sustainable management of deer in Ireland. The Group comprised representatives from my Department, National Parks & Wildlife Service (NPWS) and Coillte. A report was published into “Developing a Sustainable Deer Management Strategy for Ireland” in December 2023.
The report listed 16 Actions, 8 of which are recommended in the short term and 8 of which are recommended in the medium term. These recommended actions address a wide range of issues from hunter training and forest design to land use management and the venison market. The report concluded that a formal structure was required to manage deer in Ireland, which involved the appointment of a Programme Manager to implement the recommendations of the report and the establishment of local deer management units in known hotspot areas.
My Department is committed to progressing the implementation of the actions identified by the Irish Deer Management Strategy Group (IDMSG) in this report. The Programme Manager works closely with the IDMSG, my Department and the National Parks and Wildlife Service in prioritising and implementation of the short term recommendations identified in the report.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on the future of the rapid build houses for Ukrainians once they are no longer in use (details supplied).
reply:

The modular units delivered under the Rapid Build Programme, were developed following a Government decision to proceed in June 2022.
In total, 654 homes were built across 11 locations, including 66 homes at the site identified by the Deputy accommodating 264 people. A total of 2,640 people are being accommodated across all 11 sites. Each adult occupant signs a license agreement, and a weekly contribution is payable at a rate of 16% of household income plus a fee of €40 for utilities.
The OPW developed an exemplar single-storey modular design for the programme, with a specification to ensure Building Regulation compliance. The design is also aligned with the Department of Housing’s equivalent space standards to allow the units to be potentially utilised for social housing at a future date. question: Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide the exact operational or financial reasons behind the decision to shut down the "Horses of Hope" Equine Unit at Castlerea Prison (details supplied); and if there are any active plans or assessments underway to reinstate the equine program or a similar rehabilitation project at Castlerea in the near future.
reply:
I am advised by the Irish Prison Service that the ‘Horses of Hope’ programme at Castlerea Prison has been paused due to resourcing challenges. A key factor affecting the programme’s ability to operate at full capacity has been the difficulty in recruiting a suitably qualified equine work training officer. Despite several recruitment efforts, including expressions of interest and consideration of alternative staffing arrangements, it has not been possible to secure a suitable candidate.
The Irish Prison Service is undertaking a feasibility assessment of alternative operating models for the facility. This includes consideration of potential arrangements involving community-based organisations to support former prisoners and other vulnerable or marginalised groups. Any future arrangements will be informed by the outcome of this assessment and the staffing, operational and governance requirements identified.
The Irish Prison Service recognises the potential contribution of animal-assisted programmes to rehabilitation. I am advised that consideration of future options will take account of the need for a safe, sustainable and appropriately resourced service.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of private companies currently receiving payments under the International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS), the amount paid to each company in each of the past five years and to date in 2026, in tabular form.
reply:

The State is currently accommodating over 31,000 people seeking international protection in 293 International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centres around the country.
The Department treats accommodation centres' contractual details as commercially sensitive, and does not publish details of contractual information on the basis that it could place the State at a disadvantage in ongoing commercial negotiations.
However, there is full transparency from the Department in terms of providers receiving payments, with details of all payments over €20,000 and the recipients published quarterly online at Gov.ie.
Details of payments while the IPAS accommodation was provided through the Department of Children, Disability, and Equality (DCDE) are available here: Purchase Orders for €20,000 or above. www.gov.ie/en/collection/dfdadb-department-of-children-and-youth-affairs-purchase-orders-for-20000-o/
Details of payments since transfer to this Department are available here: Department of Justice Purchase Orders Issued over €20,000 in value www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/collections/department-of-justice-purchase-orders-issued-over-20000-in-value/

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to outline with regards to IPAS accommodation for each contract, the procurement or tender process used, including whether the contract was publicly tendered, awarded through an existing framework, or awarded by another mechanism.
reply:
The Department ensures that there is ongoing focus on good procurement practice in the award of contracts and that procedures are in place to ensure compliance with all relevant guidelines.
In the case of IPAS accommodation contracts, the Deputy will be aware of an unprecedented increase in applications for international protection from 2022-2024, creating a requirement to procure accommodation for applicants at an accelerated rate and leading to a growth of almost 400% in capacity in a very short period.
In that period, which has been the subject of detailed analysis by the Comptroller and Auditor General (C&AG) in their September 2025 report, today’s standards of pre-contract assessments and negotiations could not be applied to all the accommodation that had to be sourced at pace.
In order to meet statutory obligations during a period of unprecedented demand for accommodation, the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration, and Youth (DCEDIY) was required to utilise both competitive tendering processes and emergency accommodation procurement measures where sufficient capacity was not available through existing procurement mechanisms.
DCEDIY initially sought to secure accommodation through a Request for Tender process launched on 18 January 2022. The procurement process was re-advertised in November 2022. However, as the capacity required could not be met through the RFT process, emergency accommodation procurement through direct sourcing and direct award cont

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position Ireland has taken, including during its Presidency of the Council of the European Union, on the European Commission's January 2026 proposal to revise the EU Cybersecurity Act and phase out equipment from high-risk suppliers in critical infrastructure; and whether Ireland supports making that phase out mandatory across all Member States.
reply: The Proposal for a revised Cybersecurity Act, known as the Cybersecurity Act 2 (CSA2), was published on 20 January 2026. It is now under active discussion by the Council of the European Union through the work of the Horizontal Working Party on Cyber Issues. As Ireland now holds the Presidency of the Council of the European Union, we must set aside our national position and chair the discussions on this file in the Council in a neutral manner. I am not therefore able to comment on Ireland's position on this file at the moment.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to outline the homelessness and housing services that exist for an individual (details supplied).
reply:
I understand that Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection are not eligible to apply for Local Authority Social Housing, Homeless Services or the Housing Assistance Payment (HAP). Further to a Government Decision in May of 2026, Ireland is progressing a phased withdrawal of State-supported accommodation for Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection who arrived in Ireland prior to 14 March 2024. It is important to note that all State contracted commercial accommodation will cease in the coming months. Residents in State accommodation affected by the withdrawal are given not less than three months’ notice of the ending of their accommodation.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if an assessment has been undertaken of the DBS Update Service and the Teaching Council’s disclosure-sharing arrangements as potential models for wider Irish vetting reform; and the conclusions reached.
reply:
The primary purpose of vetting carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau is to ensure the safety of children and vulnerable adults. Clearly, this requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust.
The Government is aware of ongoing concerns regarding certain aspects of the vetting process and I have listened carefully to the views of affected sectors. I believe that the vetting system should be updated to ensure that the burden of seeking vetting disclosures, particularly on volunteers and organisations working in their communities, is minimised to the greatest extent possible, while maintaining the high standards that are necessary.
The Teaching Council conducts vetting of all teachers at the point of initial registration and re-registration. The effect of this is that teachers are vetted to work as teachers in this jurisdiction and do not require additional vetting by their employers as they move through their career. This model is one that facilitates portability within sectors and is suitable for regulated professions where a single regulator or registrar is in a position to carry out vetting as part of its role.

reply:

All visa applicants are advised that the responsibility is on them to provide as much information in support of their applications as they feel is necessary. question: Deputy Seán Crowe asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to intercede to prevent the transfer of a family (details supplied) that is being moved from a Dublin IPAS centre, given the move will severely impact medical treatment being received by a member of the family.
reply:
The International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) is responsible for the accommodation of people who have applied for international protection in Ireland while their applications are being processed.
Accommodation provided by IPAS is, by its nature, temporary, and it is necessary for a range of operational reasons to relocate residents from one centre to another to manage the overall capacity of the system.
While I cannot comment on any individual family, I assure the Deputy that my officials are aware of this case and are in direct contact with the family concerned.
IPAS acknowledges that relocating can be disruptive for people and families. Where appropriate, IPAS can work with colleagues in the National Social Inclusion Office in the HSE and the Tusla Education Support Service to assist with transfer of medical services or education in the new area. Where persons are required to continue to attend a particular hospital or medical facility for their treatment, transport if required to those appointments, will be arranged by centre managers.
Due to the high demand for accommodation, IPAS can only consider transfer requests for international protection applicants that involve a medical priority, or otherwise exceptional cases. To submit a transfer request on medical grounds, individuals and families are required to submit a referral form in accordance with: assets.gov.ie/static/documents/7027f7e8/IPAS_Medical_Transfer_Request_2026.pdf

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his plans to increase the availability of free civil legal aid in cases where a family home is at risk of repossession, especially where the family is not eligible for legal support from Abhaile.
reply:
The Legal Aid Board is the statutory, independent body responsible for the provision of civil legal aid and advice to qualifying individuals. Eligibility for the Civil Legal Aid Scheme is determined by reference to a financial assessment and the merits of the case being taken. Civil legal aid and advice is provided primarily through a network of law centres by solicitors employed by the Board. The Board operates a total of 34 full-time law centres and dedicated units along with three part-time centres, and three specialist legal offices.
The Board also operates 19 family mediation centres with a number of law centres and family mediation offices co-located. In addition, the Board engages private solicitors to supplement the services provided by Board solicitors in certain areas of law on a case-by-case basis. These areas include District Court family law matters, Circuit Court judicial separation and divorce cases, international protection cases, and cases arising under the Abhaile scheme.
The Abhaile Mortgage Arrears Resolution Service which was established in 2016, ensures that borrowers at risk of losing their homes due to mortgage arrears can access free, independent and expert financial and legal advice with the aim of finding solutions that will, wherever possible, allow people to stay in their homes. Abhaile, which is jointly administered by my Department and the Department of Social Protection, provides a number of aids to those experiencing problems with debt.

question: Deputy Danny Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his plans to open new IPAS centres in Kerry in 2027 (details supplied).
reply:
On 26 May 2026, the Government agreed to commence a phased withdrawal of state-contracted commercial accommodation for people fleeing the war in Ukraine with Temporary Protection status who arrived in Ireland prior to 14 March 2024. This forms part of a wider transition program to support people towards greater independence, while ensuring continued support for those who remain in need of state accommodation.
The phased withdrawal of some commercial accommodation is being implemented on a region-by-region basis. These providers will receive notice of termination in due course, if they have not yet already.
A list of all properties whose contracts are being terminated is available on: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/news/accommodation-centres-returning-to-original-or-alternative-use/
The contract of the property referred to by the Deputy is ending on 31 January 2027.
My Department is not considering the property referred to, or any other property in Co. Kerry, for future use as international protection accommodation.
Where contracts between my Department and accommodation providers for those fleeing the war in Ukraine come to an end, the future use of the property is a commercial decision for the provider. My Department does not determine the future use of these properties.

question: Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he would make available the number of Garda checkpoints that took place in the Roscommon / Mayo / Longford Division on the weekend of 23 to the 26 of October 2026; if this list could identify the number of checkpoints undertaken in each county; the locations; and any results.
reply:
Road traffic legislation is enforced by members of An Garda Síochána as part of their day-to-day duties and through a programme of high-visibility road safety and enforcement operations conducted in partnership with other State agencies and GoSafe. These operations are designed to improve road safety and reduce the incidence of road traffic collisions.
I have been informed by the Garda authorities that a total of 145 checkpoints were conducted in the Roscommon/Mayo/Longford Division during the period from 23 October 2026 to 26 October 2026. This figure includes both mandatory intoxicant testing checkpoints and other high-visibility policing checkpoints. The information provided is based on operational data from the PULSE system as available on 9 November 2026 and is therefore subject to change.
The Garda authorities have further advised that the information is recorded and reported in line with Garda administrative divisional boundaries. Accordingly, a county-by-county breakdown is not available.
The Deputy may be interested to note that a nationwide Garda roads policing operation took place throughout the October bank holiday weekend from Thursday, 22 October to Tuesday, 27 October 2026. During this operation, a total of 218 people were arrested for driving under the influence of an intoxicant (alcohol and drugs) and just over 4,840 drivers were detected for speeding offences. 500 drivers were detected holding a mobile phone or not wearing a seatbelt.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his Department or State agencies under its aegis have a policy regarding the use of artificial intelligence to produce artwork for social media, public information campaigns, and graphic design.
reply:
My Department complies with the "Guidelines for the Responsible Use of AI in the Public Service" issued by the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, and with guidance issued by the National Cyber Security Centre in relation to cyber security.
My Department is currently finalising a formal policy on the use of artificial intelligence. In the interim, guidance has been issued to staff on the responsible, secure and appropriate use of AI tools, including requirements relating to data protection, confidentiality, information security and human oversight.
With regards to the use of artificial intelligence tools to produce artwork for social media, public information campaigns and graphic design in agencies under the aegis of my Department, I can confirm that no AI tools are currently in use for this purpose.
I am informed that no specific policy has been developed in relation to these use cases. Any future adoption of artificial intelligence tools for such purposes would be subject to appropriate governance processes, including risk assessment, and would be required to comply with relevant Government guidance and legal obligations.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of applications of Ukrainians who claimed temporary protection in Ireland were rejected on the grounds of inability to provide military documents/proofs of “satisfaction of military obligations” or “authorised leave of Ukraine according to law” since new rules for obtaining temporary protection were adopted on 4 of August 2026.
reply:
Following the introduction of Council Implementing Decision 2026/1912, Temporary Protection can only be granted to individuals who can provide proof to Member State authorities that they are in compliance with their military obligations.
I can confirm that 173 applicants for Temporary Protection in Ireland have been refused permission on this basis since 5 August 2026.

My Department is not considering the property referred to for future use as international protection accommodation.
Where contracts between my Department and accommodation providers for those fleeing the war in Ukraine come to an end, the future use of the property is a commercial decision for the provider. My Department does not determine the future use of these properties.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current legislative and regulatory framework governing the online sale and home delivery of alcohol; the obligations placed on retailers and third-party delivery platforms regarding the quantity of alcohol delivered and deliveries to intoxicated persons; and whether consideration has been given to introducing additional safeguards, including purchase limits or voluntary exclusion arrangements.
reply:
It is important to note that, under existing legislation, where alcohol is purchased online, the same restrictions on the sale and supply of intoxicating liquor apply as they do to onsite purchases. Under section 17(3) of the Intoxicating Liquor Act 2003, it is an offence for a licensee, with intent to evade the conditions of the licence, to take intoxicating liquor from the licensed premises for the purpose of its being sold on the account, or for the benefit or profit of, the licensee, or to permit any other person to do so. The penalty on conviction is a fine of up to €1,500 for a first offence and up to €2,000 for a second or subsequent offence.
The Programme for Government commits to updating our licensing laws. The Autumn Legislative Programme, published on 16 September, sets out the 32 Bills that have been prioritised for publication, and a further 32 Bills prioritised for drafting in the current Dáil session.
Other legislative projects, including work on updating our licensing laws, will be taken forward in subsequent iterations of the legislative programme, to be determined by Government in due course. In that regard, the points raised in respect of regulations around alcohol delivery have been shared with relevant officials in my Department and will be considered as part of this work.

question: Deputy Niall Collins asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will respond to correspondence (details supplied).
reply:
I can advise the Minister that, in response to the correspondence received regarding the State's migration system, I remain committed to ensuring that Ireland's international protection and immigration systems are robust, rules-based and that the integrity of all processes is maintained.
Legal migration plays an essential and very positive role in Ireland's society, as immigrants bring essential skills and experience that are much needed in the current labour market and are vital to addressing labour shortages.
Additionally, the right to claim asylum is an important principle of international law that dates back to the Geneva Convention in 1951 and the Government takes its obligations and commitments under international and EU asylum law seriously.
There has been investment in international protection application processing to speed up decisions, as well as a move away from commercial accommodation provision to more State-owned accommodation. These reforms will help to drive down pressure and costs as well as to curtail the growth seen over recent years in the accommodation and asylum system.
The number of applications for international protection has decreased compared to the same period last year. So far, for the period of 1 January 2026 to 6 November 2026, there have been a total of 9,458 international protection applications, as compared to the total of 11,043 applications during the same period in 2025.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of requests for information received by An Garda Síochána from housing authorities under section 15 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1997 in 2023, 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026, by Garda division, with a separate figure for the Cork city division; and the average time taken to respond.
reply:
The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 34 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. This includes all operational matters such as the process for local authorities to obtain criminal record checks for local authority housing applicants.
I have contacted the Garda authorities and have been advised that this process remains decentralised and these requests are processed by the Superintendent in Charge of the District wherein the subject of the request resides in accordance with Section 15 of the Housing Miscellaneous Provisions Act 1997. As such, records are not held centrally and the information requested is not available.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will clarify whether the probation service maintains a list or record of approved places of worship with respect to those who may have been convicted of offences related to religious or ideological extremism.
reply:
As the Deputy is aware, the Probation Service has a central statutory role in the management of risk and rehabilitation of individuals who are subject to court ordered supervision. Probation Service supervision is supported by the conditions attached to a specific Court Order.
While neither I nor the Probation Service can comment on individual cases or on arrangements relating to particular individuals, I can say that, more generally, decisions concerning a person’s supervision, risk management and engagement with external organisations are made on a case-by-case basis, having regard to the relevant assessment, identified risks and court ordered conditions.
I am advised that, where relevant to an individual’s risk-management plan and conditions of court ordered supervision, engagement with community, cultural or faith-based supports may be part of structured supervision.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of unannounced inspections carried out by his Department and or An Garda Síochána and GNIB on English language education providers participating in the Interim List of Eligible Programmes in each of the years from 2020 to 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 644 to 646, inclusive, together.
The majority of English language schools in Ireland operate under the Interim List of Eligible Programmes (ILEP), which was introduced in 2015. The ILEP is a restrictive list of full-time education programmes eligible for international student visas and Stamp 2 immigration permissions.
Education providers must remain compliant with the relevant criteria in order to retain their listing on the ILEP. My Department monitors compliance, and any education provider may be subject to unannounced inspections, online monitoring or random spot checks to ensure compliance with ILEP requirements. This includes the maintenance of records and reports, which may be requested by my Department at any time. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the removal of a provider from the ILEP.
To retain a listing on the ILEP, providers are required to keep within the criteria laid down in the 'Arrangements applying to English Language Programmes, Higher Education Programmes and Foundation Programmes from 1 October 2015 (updated 21 March 2025)' . Any education provider who does not adhere to ILEP criteria, or whose programme(s) no longer meet the criteria, may be removed from the ILEP.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 75235/26, whether the notarised declaration of personal circumstances provided by IPAS accommodation providers is verified against any independent source, including the Register of Beneficial Ownership or Courts Service records; the number of such declarations found to be inaccurate since 1 January 2025; and whether the Minister will require checks with An Garda Síochána or the Criminal Assets Bureau on the directors and beneficial owners of providers before contracts are awarded or renewed.
reply:
Since assuming responsibility for this service in 2025, my Department has taken action across all aspects of the international protection accommodation system to improve value for money, strengthen governance and compliance, and renegotiate contracts with providers.
As the Deputy will be aware from previous responses, each new or renewing provider of accommodation services must provide a declaration of their personal circumstances.
This declaration, which must be notarised, is not checked against other sources, but requires the provider to provide a declaration, verified by a notary, that they are tax compliant, free of any convictions for corruption, fraud or being a member of a criminal organisation.
They must also confirm that they are solvent and have no history of failing to meet terms of public service contracts, among other requirements. The data requested in relation to declarations found to be inaccurate is not available for publication. All providers are checked again CRO records and tax compliance is verified at invoicing stage through a tax clearance cert.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 75235/26, of the 46 IPAS accommodation contracts terminated since 2025, the number terminated on each of the grounds set out in that reply, namely compliance concerns, failure to meet contractual requirements, health and safety, fire safety, planning, other regulatory non-compliance, non-agreement of commercial terms and termination at the request of the provider, in tabular form.
reply:
The Department is taking action across all aspects of the international protection accommodation system to improve value for money, strengthen governance and compliance, and renegotiate contracts with providers.
Details of individual contractual arrangements and processes are treated as confidential, so the information requested by the Deputy is not available for publication. As noted by the Deputy, however, reasons for not renewing or ending a contract may include compliance concerns, including failure to meet contractual requirements, health and safety concerns, fire safety issues, planning issues, or other regulatory non-compliance, or non-agreement of commercial terms. Contracts may also be terminated at the request of the provider within the terms of the contract.
In line with the Programme for Government, the State is working to develop more State-owned international protection accommodation and reduce reliance on commercially contracted accommodation.
The new International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the measures of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and has passed into law. The new rules came into effect on 12 June. Reforming and speeding up processing of applications should also serve over time to reduce the scale of the demand for international protection accommodation.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Social Protection when the Household Benefits Package was last increased; and his plans to review the value of the package in light of significant increases in electricity, gas and other household utility costs in recent years.
reply:
The Household Benefits Package comprises the electricity or gas allowance, and the free television license. The Department of Social Protection will spend approximately €317 million this year on the Household Benefits Package.
There has been no increase to the gas/electricity element of the Household Benefits Package since the gas/electricity element was changed from a unit-based allowance to a monthly cash allowance in January 2013. Given the many competing demands for the limited funding available to the Department, recent Budget spending increases have been targeted to ensure that it goes to those people who need help the most. The Household Benefits Package is available to those aged 70 or over regardless of means and household composition. It is also available as a supplementary allowance to those in receipt of various social welfare payments.
With regards to targeted measures, the Department provides support to households who are most vulnerable to energy poverty via the Fuel Allowance payment. The Fuel Allowance payment is a means tested payment which is targeted towards households that are at a higher risk of poverty.
Fuel Allowance eligibility encompasses 22 qualifying schemes, demonstrating the comprehensive nature of the support available to eligible households. In addition to these qualifying schemes, people over 66 do not need to be in receipt of a payment from this Department to qualify for Fuel Allowance, subject to satisfying a means test. reply:

In 2025, the latest period for which comparable statistics are available, Ireland's long-term unemployment rate was 1.1%. This compares favourably to the EU average of 1.9%, and the Eurozone average of 2.1%.
Jobseeker's Pay-Related Benefit is payable for a maximum duration of 9 months; accordingly, the figures below all refer to Jobseeker's Allowance. The official measure of unemployment, including long term unemployment, is the responsibility of the Central Statistics Office.
It is important to set out the limitations of the below statistics, which are derived from administrative data. These statistics are based off the durations of current Jobseeker's Allowance claims and excludes jobseekers who are currently in casual employment. Over the time periods requested, it is possible that many of these jobseekers had, at prior points in time, been engaged in casual employment and maintained their Jobseeker's Allowance claim over that time. The durations are calculated from the initial registration date of the claim, where the claim is currently in an Awarded and Paying status. These claims may have had periods where payments were suspended or otherwise did not issue, but the claim remained open and was later put into an Awarded and Paying status.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of persons who have had a penalty rate applied to their payment due to failure to engage with employment activation services in 2025 and to date in 2026.
reply:
A Jobseeker payment is conditional on the recipient being available for, capable of and genuinely seeking work. This reflects the concept of ‘rights and responsibilities’ whereby people who are unemployed have the right to an income support from the State and a right to be supported in their efforts to secure employment but also have a responsibility to seek employment and to engage with the employment services offered by the State.
Jobseekers who do not engage with Intreo, the Public Employment Service or who fail to participate in appropriate employment interventions can have their jobseeker’s payment reduced and subsequently be disqualified from their payment for up to 9 weeks. They may also have their entitlement to a Jobseeker's payment reviewed based on a failure to genuinely seek work.
A reduced rate aims to encourage a jobseeker to fully engage and avail of the employment supports on offer. Once a jobseeker resumes engagement with the employment support service, the reduced rate is lifted immediately.
The following table sets out the number of persons who had a reduced rate applied to their payment due to failure to engage with employment activation services in 2025 and to date in 2026. It should be noted that a person may have multiple reduced rates applied throughout the course of the year.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Social Protection the current cumulative value of the surplus in the Social Insurance Fund; and the projected overall cumulative surplus in 2026, 2027, 2028, 2029 and 2030.
reply:
The current cumulative surplus in the Social Insurance Fund is approximately €17.5 billion. This is estimated to reach approximately €20 billion by the end of 2026.
The Department does not have updated projections for the 2027–2030 period. The most recent projections were published in the latest Actuarial Review of the Social Insurance Fund, which was published in 2023. However, these figures are now considered outdated as the projections are based on 2022 real price terms, do not account for the legislated PRSI roadmap rate increases, and did not anticipate the exceptionally high levels of employment activity experienced in recent years.
The Department will be undertaking the next Actuarial Review of the Fund in early 2027. This review will include projections out to and including 2081.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of persons currently in receipt of jobseeker's payments for longer than one year.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 623, 632, 633 and 634 together.
In 2025, the latest period for which comparable statistics are available, Ireland's long-term unemployment rate was 1.1%. This compares favourably to the EU average of 1.9%, and the Eurozone average of 2.1%.
Jobseeker's Pay-Related Benefit is payable for a maximum duration of 9 months; accordingly, the figures below all refer to Jobseeker's Allowance. The official measure of unemployment, including long term unemployment, is the responsibility of the Central Statistics Office.
It is important to set out the limitations of the below statistics, which are derived from administrative data. These statistics are based off the durations of current Jobseeker's Allowance claims and excludes jobseekers who are currently in casual employment. Over the time periods requested, it is possible that many of these jobseekers had, at prior points in time, been engaged in casual employment and maintained their Jobseeker's Allowance claim over that time. The durations are calculated from the initial registration date of the claim, where the claim is currently in an Awarded and Paying status. These claims may have had periods where payments were suspended or otherwise did not issue, but the claim remained open and was later put into an Awarded and Paying status.

question: Deputy Ged Nash asked the Minister for Social Protection if he plans to review social welfare policy to take account of the circumstances of a person (details supplied).
reply:
The social welfare and tax systems have evolved over time and in response to a variety of factors, including Constitutional imperatives as interpreted by the Courts, changing social trends and European Union legislation.
A Supreme Court case (Hyland v Minister for Social Welfare, 1989) led to the current treatment of non-married cohabiting couples in the social welfare code. The Court ruled that it was unconstitutional for the total income a married couple received in social welfare benefits to be less than the couple would have received if they were unmarried and cohabiting. This means that for social assistance means tested schemes such as Jobseeker’s Allowance, married couples, civil partners and cohabiting couples are treated in the same manner.
The purpose of the means test for social assistance payments is to ensure that State resources are targeted towards those with the greatest need for income supports. Under Schedule 3 of the Social Welfare (Consolidation) Act 2005, as amended, all income and assets belonging to a claimant and, where applicable, their spouse, civil partner or cohabitant are taken into account when assessing eligibility for means?tested social assistance schemes.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Social Protection his views on the concern of families of persons with lifelong disabilities, that inheritances left by parents for the future care and security of their disabled child, may result in a reduction or loss of disability allowance and associated supports (details supplied); and if he will examine measures to exempt such inheritances from means testing.
reply:
Disability Allowance is my Department’s primary disability-related social assistance scheme. It is a means-tested payment for people with a disability aged between 16 and 66. To qualify, a person must have a disability that has continued, or is expected to continue, for at least one year and, as a result of that disability, be substantially restricted in undertaking work that would otherwise be suitable having regard to their age, experience and qualifications. Eligibility is also subject to satisfying the habitual residence condition.
Social welfare legislation provides that, for means-tested social assistance schemes, all income and assets belonging to the claimant, and their spouse or partner, where applicable, is assessable. This recognises the fact that couples operate as a single household and can share living expenses in a manner not available to a single person. The means test takes account of the income a person or couple has in terms of cash, property – other than the family home – and capital.
Where an adult with a disability resides with their parents or other family members, the income of their parents or other family members is not assessed when applying for Disability Allowance, only income and assets belonging to the claimant are assessed.
The purpose of a means test is to ensure that scarce resources are directed to those with the greatest need and it supports an economically sustainable and socially equitable allocation of scarce resources.

reply:

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Social Protection for an update on the work his Department is doing to ensure those in receipt of Bereaved Partner's (Contributory) Pension can access illness benefit into the future.
reply:
Illness Benefit is the primary short term income support provided by my Department to those who are unable to work due to illness of any type and who are covered by social insurance. Eligibility for Illness Benefit depends on the person’s PRSI record and class. People must have made the required number of contributions under PRSI classes A, E, H or P to qualify.
The Widow’s/Widower’s/Surviving Civil Partner’s Pension was renamed the Bereaved Partner’s Pension on 21 July 2025, the date of enactment of the Social Welfare (Bereaved Partner’s Pension and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2025. This Act extends eligibility to a qualified cohabitant of the deceased person. The pension is a weekly payment to those who have lost their spouse, civil partner or qualified cohabitant and who satisfy the qualifying conditions.
There is a general principle of one person, one payment, which applies across the social welfare system. Given the contingency-based nature of this system, it can happen that a person may experience more than one contingency at the same time but, generally, they can receive only one payment. Illness Benefit and the Bereaved Partner's Pension are, generally, not payable concurrently.
However, if a person is getting a reduced rate of Bereaved Partner’s (Contributory) Pension, they may also get a reduced rate of Illness Benefit, so that the combined amount of both payments reaches the maximum rate of Illness Benefit to which they would otherwise be entitled.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Social Protection if his Department will review access to pathways to employment, training and upskilling for those in receipt of bereaved partner's (contributory) pension and bereaved partner's (non-contributory) pension as compares to those on the one-parent family payment for example.
reply:
Bereaved Partners (Contributory) Pension (BPCP) is a weekly payment to the widow, widower, surviving civil partner or surviving qualified cohabitant of a deceased person. The pension remains payable unless the person cohabits with another person, marries or enter into a new civil partnership. The payment is not means tested. As a result, a person can be in receipt of BPCP and earn income from employment or self-employment. Recipients of this payment can also receive the Working Family Payment provided they meet the criteria.
The Bereaved Partners (Non-Contributory) Pension (BNCP) is a weekly payment to a widow, widower, surviving civil partner or surviving qualified cohabitant of a deceased person who does not meet the social insurance contributions required for the BPCP, and who satisfy a means-test. It is only available to those aged 65 and under. Cash income from employment is assessed as part of the means test, however, there is an earnings disregard of €100 per week for a person in insurable employment.
Recipients of Bereaved Partner's Pension (Contributory) and Bereaved Partner's Pension (Non-Contributory) are not regarded as jobseekers and are therefore not subject to the activation, availability-for-work or genuine job-seeking conditions that apply to jobseeker payments. Recipients can choose to avail of employment and training supports, but participation is voluntary and is not a condition of entitlement to either pension.

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Social Protection if a late paternity benefit application for a person (details supplied) will be awarded given the force majeure reasons.
reply:
Under legislation a person must take paternity leave within six months of the birth of the child, there is no exceptions to this, including ‘force majeure.’ Section 8(1) of the Paternity Benefit Leave and Benefit Act 2016 states:
“Subject to this section, section 10 and sections 12 to 14, the period of paternity leave shall commence on such day as the relevant parent selects in his or her notification given in accordance with subsection (2) or (5) of section 7, being not earlier than the date of confinement or day of placement, as the case may be, and not later than 26 weeks after such date or day.”
Unfortunately, the legislation does not allow for any discretion.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Máire Devine asked the Minister for Social Protection when the treatment of Reserve Defence Forces service as subsidiary employment under schedule C, paragraph 4 of S.I. 312 of 1996, first introduced by S.I. 26 of 1970, was last reviewed.
reply:
Statutory Instrument 26 of 1970 provided for the exception from insurance under the Social Welfare Acts of employment for short periods as members of An Fórsa Cosanta Áitiúil or An Slua Muirí, now the Reserve Defence Force.
It is my understanding that the Reserve Defence Force is a part-time, volunteer organisation. Members are free to determine their own level of participation in Reserve activities and may resign from the Reserve at any time. Their service is provided entirely on a voluntary basis with no compulsion to attend.
Consequently, service as a member of the Reserve Defence Force for a period not exceeding 21 consecutive days is not considered insurable employment for social insurance purposes as this employment is considered to be subsidiary employment only and not the principal means of livelihood. PRSI Class M applies in these cases and therefore no PRSI is liable.
For those who undertake more than 21 consecutive days service, they and their employer are liable to pay PRSI under Class H.
No review of this arrangement has been undertaken by my Department. Any such review would be a matter for my colleague the Minister for Defence who is responsible for the terms and conditions of service in the Reserve Defence Force.
I trust this clarifies the matter.

question: Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Social Protection will examine increasing the income threshold for people seeking the back-to-school clothing and footwear allowance; in particular if he will examine payments based assessed on a net income basis as opposed to a parent or guardian's gross income.
reply:
The Back-to-School Clothing and Footwear Allowance scheme provides a once-off payment to eligible families to assist with the costs of clothing and footwear when children start or return to school each autumn. The scheme operates from June to September each year.
In order to target those families most in need of assistance, the allowance is payable in respect of eligible children between the ages of 2 and 17 in respect of whom a qualified child allowance is being paid, and eligible children between the ages of 18 and 22 who are in full-time second level education and in respect of whom a qualified child allowance is being paid.
To qualify for the allowance a person must meet a number of conditions namely:
• The child must meet the age criteria,
• The applicant must be in receipt of a qualifying payment and getting an increase in that payment for the qualified child (except in certain circumstances) in the period 1 June to 30 September,
• The assessable income for the household must be within prescribed limits,
• The applicant and the child (or children) in respect of whom the allowance is claimed must be resident in the State.
Income thresholds for Back-to-School Clothing and Footwear Allowance are increased each year in line with increases in the rates of State Pension Contributory. question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Social Protection to review correspondence (details supplied).
reply:
The person concerned is in receipt of an increase for a qualified adult (IQA) on their spouse’s state pension contributory.
Where a qualified adult has weekly means of up to €100, the maximum rate of IQA is payable. Where weekly means exceed €100 but are not more than €310, a reduced rate of IQA is payable on a tapered basis. Where weekly means exceed €310, there is no entitlement to an IQA.
A review of the IQA entitlement was undertaken on 11 June 2026. Based on the information provided, the qualified adult's means were assessed at €175.39 per week.
This assessment included weekly means of €36.31 from self-employment. This figure was derived from the 2025 financial accounts submitted, which showed profits from a taxi business. In line with the means assessment provisions, the annual profit was converted to a weekly amount and divided equally between the spouses. The documentation provided indicates that the business was operated on a partnership basis. If the partnership has ceased, it is open to the spouse of the person concerned to submit documentary evidence confirming the date the partnership ended. On receipt of this, their entitlement will be reviewed.
On 27 October the spouse of the person concerned was advised that the rate of IQA payable would be reduced from €259.00 to €193.20 with effect from 25 September 2026. They were also notified of their right to appeal the decision to the Social Welfare Appeals Office.
I trust this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Social Protection the actions that have been taken by his Department to recognise the labour of children who were 'boarded out' in the 20th century in their pension and other entitlements.
reply:
My Department administers the State pension system, including State Pension (Contributory) and State Pension (Non-contributory), in accordance with the qualifying conditions set out in social welfare legislation.
Entitlement to State Pension (Contributory) is determined under social welfare legislation by reference to a person’s social insurance record. This includes paid, credited and voluntary contributions, together with any relevant caring periods that may be taken into account.
There is no specific provision within the State Pension (Contributory) scheme to award social insurance contributions retrospectively in respect of work undertaken by children who were boarded out where that work did not give rise to an insurable employment record. Pension entitlement under the scheme is based on a person’s social insurance record and cannot be awarded on the basis of particular historical experiences. Providing retrospective contributions in these circumstances would represent a significant departure from the contributory basis of the scheme.
A person who does not qualify for a State Pension (Contributory), or who only qualifies for a reduced rate contributory pension based on their social insurance record, may qualify for State Pension (Non-contributory). This is a means-tested payment funded from general taxation and provides an important pension safety net for people with limited means. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection further to Parliamentary Question No.75386/26, the procedure for restoring a payment that was suspended following a committal where the person is released on bail, acquitted, granted temporary release or released at the end of a sentence; whether arrears are paid where a person on remand is subsequently released without conviction; the average time taken to restore a payment on release.
reply:
My Department receives information from the Irish Prison Service for people who are committed to prison. Payments will be suspended as soon as possible after the person is imprisoned to minimise overpayments. A Deciding Officer, on review of the information may subsequently terminate the payment depending on the individual circumstances of the case. Overpayments are assessed for periods of ineligibility and the recovery of same is followed up by the relevant section of the Department.
In cases where a person is committed to prison and a Social Welfare payment is suspended or terminated on foot of that committal, the scheme may be reinstated on release depending on the duration of imprisonment, the provision of release papers and whether the person satisfies the eligibility conditions for the scheme. Arrears are not payable in cases where a person is released without conviction.
Where the payment can be reinstated it will be, however in some cases the person may need to reapply or apply for the payment most appropriate to their circumstances. My Department officials work closely with the Care and Rehabilitation Directorate of the Irish Prison Service and with TOSU, to strengthen supports available at the point of release.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Social Protection whether his Department or State agencies under its aegis have a policy regarding the use of artificial intelligence to produce artwork for social media, public information campaigns, and graphic design.
reply:
Use of artificial intelligence (AI) in my Department is governed by the national and EU public service strategies and guidelines including the National Digital and AI Strategy, Digital Ireland – Connecting our People Securing our Future, the Guidelines for the Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Public Service, and the Cyber Security Guidance on Generative AI for Public Sector Bodies. These provide a framework for the responsible, ethical and transparent use of artificial intelligence across the public service.
An Artificial Intelligence Policy on the use of AI in my Department is currently being developed, which will incorporate the principles set out in the relevant National and EU AI strategies.
My Department has established an Innovation Hub to assess and evaluate the potential future use of AI technologies to support the work of the Department in a safe and secure manner.
Any use of AI tools by the Department must be consistent with Government guidance and with relevant legal and regulatory requirements, including those relating to data protection, information security, transparency, copyright, accessibility and procurement.
I can confirm that my Department’s Communications Unit does not currently use artificial intelligence tools to generate artwork for social media, public information campaigns or graphic design. The Department will continue to assess the suitability of AI technologies on a case-by-case basis and in line with Government guidance.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Social Protection if his Department have considered broadening the eligibility criteria for the Living Alone Allowance.
reply:
It is acknowledged that people who live alone and are in receipt of certain payments from my Department can face higher per-person household costs than those who share household expenses with another adult. It is for this reason that the Living Alone Increase is available to recipients of qualifying payments from my Department.
The Living Alone Increase is a supplementary payment to those who are aged over 66, living alone and in receipt of a State Pension (Contributory), State Pension (Non-Contributory), Bereaved Partner’s (Contributory) Pension, Bereaved Partner's Pension under the Occupational Injuries Benefit Scheme, an Incapacity Supplement under the Occupational Injuries Benefit Scheme or a Deserted Wife's Benefit. It is also paid to people aged under 66 who live alone and are in receipt of a Disability Allowance, Invalidity Pension, Incapacity Supplement or Blind Pension.
The Living Alone Increase is not a standalone payment and for this reason it is only available to those who are living alone and in receipt of one of those specified payments. In total about 260,000 people receive the payment on a weekly basis.
As part of Budget 2027, the LAI is increasing to €25 per week from next January. This payment has increased by nearly 178% since 2019, when it was just €9 per week.
There are currently no plans to broaden the eligibility criteria for the Living Alone Increase. Any future changes would have to be considered in the context of overall social welfare policy priorit

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection whether suppliers under the School Meals Programme are required to notify his Department of, or seek approval for, changes to their menus or to the sourcing or certification of meat and poultry after a school's application has been approved; and whether his Department was notified by any supplier of a change in 2026 to supply only halal friendly chicken and turkey.
reply:
My department provides the funding for the meals directly to the school. The school is required to submit their chosen supplier menu with their funding application each year. The primary relationship is between the school and the food business operator. It is the responsibility of each school board to select a food business operator on the open market, in a fair and transparent manner in accordance with public procurement rules. These rules clearly define the successful tenderer’s responsibilities and obligations, including in relation to compliance with Nutrition Standards for School Meals.
The Department's role is to ensure compliance with the nutritional standards of the School Meals Programme. Provided that meals on the submitted approved food business operator menu meet the required nutritional standards, decisions regarding specific food products and sourcing arrangements are matters for the supplier and the school to address through their contractual relationship.
As the contracting authority, the school has responsibility for managing its contract with the supplier and may discuss available menu options directly with the supplier. Where concerns or preferences arise regarding the type of meat provided, including requests for non-halal chicken or other suitable alternatives, the school is best placed to engage with the supplier to explore the options available and determine whether these can be accommodated within the terms of the contract and the programme's nutrition

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will assist a family resource centre (details supplied) to access ESF+ food credits for a project.
reply:
The European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) Food and Basic Material Assistance programme in Ireland provides food assistance to the most deprived.
The ESF+ Managing Authority is the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science, they have overall responsibility for implementation of the Employment, Inclusion, Skills and Training programme.
The specific objective of addressing material deprivation through food and basic material assistance is managed by my department on behalf of Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science.
The programme seeks to help people take their first steps out of poverty and social exclusion by addressing their most basic needs i.e. food and or basic materials.
The aim with this programme, is to have a geographical spread of charities and nationwide availability of ESF+ product. Aid under this programme is targeted for those on the margins of society and in need of essential supports.
The programme is delivered by my Department in partnership with over 160 charitable organisations throughout the country.
Brill Family Resource Centre has indicated its interest in participating in the programme. A formal application form has been provided, and my Department are awaiting its completed return.
I hope this clarifies the matter.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Social Protection the position regarding any review of paid paternity benefit that would encourage more fathers to take additional time with their families following the birth of their children.
reply:
Paternity Benefit is paid for two weeks at €299 per week increasing to €309 from January 2027, and is payable to relevant parents who meet the qualifying Pay-Related Social Insurance (PRSI) contribution conditions while on Paternity Leave from their employment. Government has provided over €17.3 million for the scheme in 2026.
While the Department of Social Protection has responsibility for the administration of Paternity Benefit, the legal and policy responsibility for the periods of leave rests with the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality.
The Programme for Government commits to introducing Pay-Related Parent's Benefit and exploring other payments where a similar model could be applied.
My Department will draw on the learnings from the Jobseeker's Pay-Related Benefit scheme introduced last year, to inform options for pay-related Parent’s Benefit. To progress this commitment, I intend to issue a public consultation document on a pay-related approach to Parents' Benefit over the coming months, which will help inform decisions about other family benefits.
I trust this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Social Protection to clarify the decision to withdraw the free travel entitlement of a person (details supplied).
reply:
Under the Make Work Pay initiative, a person is entitled to retain their entitlement to Free Travel for a period of 5 years after their entitlement to Disability Allowance ceases due to taking up employment. The entitlement of the person concerned to Free Travel was linked to their Disability Allowance payment, which is a qualifying payment for Free Travel.
When the Disability Allowance ended in October 2025 as the person concerned returned to work, their Free Travel was extended for 5 years under the "Make Work Pay" Initiative. One of the conditions for this extension is that the customer remains in employment.
As the person concerned has ceased employment and is now in receipt of Jobseeker's Pay Related Benefit, their entitlement to Free Travel has ceased. The person concerned was notified of this in writing in October 2026. This letter also advised about Free Travel for those medically certified as unfit to drive.
For your information, persons aged over 17 and under 66 who are medically certified as being unfit to drive may also qualify for Free Travel. To qualify, a person must:
• have never been medically fit to drive due to a disability; or
• be deemed medically unfit to drive for a period of at least one year.
There is no requirement to satisfy a means test or to be in receipt of a Social Protection payment to qualify for Free Travel for those medically unfit to drive.
I trust this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Social Protection the policies in place to prevent third party VR headsets to be used by members of staff at the Department of Social Protection or their contractors, given the reports online (details supplied).
reply:
It is vitally important to maintain this Department’s good record in relation to safeguarding confidential data and the confidence of the public across all our customers interactions with the Department - be they be in-person at Intreo Offices, on-line, by phone or through written correspondence. To this end, my Department has a number of policies in relation to the use of digital devices and data protection
The Management Board of my Department recently agreed a revised and amalgamated ‘Digital Systems and Internet Use Policy’ which applies to all staff - replacing a number of pre-existing policies. This updated policy prohibits the use of personal devices such as smart glasses, smart audio or other wearable devices capable of recording or transmitting audio, images or video, by staff when conducting official business with customers.
In addition, all staff are required to read and sign the Department's Data Protection Policy on an annual basis. This sets out their responsibilities as regards protection personal data.
Any substantiated breach of these policies may be followed-up under the provisions of the Civil Service Code of Conduct.
In relation to the specific compliant referenced by the Deputy - it is not appropriate for me to comment on individual cases.
I trust this clarifies matters for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to respond to the findings regarding Ireland in the European Court of Auditors (ECA) Special Report 25/2026, which highlighted that managing authorities could not provide requested information for 10 of the 15 Irish marine protected areas examined; if he will outline the specific reasons for these critical information gaps; and the measures his Department will take to address them.
reply:

In order to assess the implementation of EU legislation and the effectiveness of marine protected areas management, the auditors selected three Member States for close examination: Ireland, France and Sweden.

The audit team's fieldwork comprised a series of detailed meetings with officials, together with site visits to a number of protected marine sites.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the position regarding the review of Part V processes obligations.
reply:
Part V of the Planning and Development Act 2000 applies to applicable developments of houses on any land that is zoned residential (either exclusively or mixed use) or is granted planning permission for houses as a material contravention of the development plan. Part V captures a portion of the increase in the land value when a local authority grants planning permission for residential development. It allows a local authority purchase a percentage of the land at less than the enhanced market value. Alternatively, it can also allow for a transfer of units built in lieu of the relevant portion of land.
Recognising the importance of this mechanism for the delivery of social housing, my Department is currently examining the potential scope of a review of the current Part V arrangements.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to give an update on the next call for proposals under the cost rental equity loan scheme.
reply:
The Cost Rental Equity Loan (CREL) funding scheme is available to Approved Housing Bodies (AHBs) to provide affordable rented accommodation to those who meet the income eligibility requirements for cost rental homes. The most recent call for proposals to AHBs closed on 31st July and I have recently approved 12 proposals delivering more than 1,200 cost rental homes out to 2028.
In order to further drive the delivery of affordable housing under the new plan, local authorities are currently preparing new Housing Delivery Action Plans (HDAPs), for review by my Department, setting out how the Starter Homes Programme will be implemented within their area. These plans are expected to be completed and published by the local authorities later this year. In preparing their HDAP, each local authority is required to ensure the right mix of homes to respond to local needs and priorities and to collaborate closely with the delivery partners who operate within their area, or may do so in future, including the Land Development Agency, the Approved Housing Bodies and the development sector.
Future calls under the CREL will be informed by the outcome of HDAP exercise.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the position regarding the review of affordable housing schemes; and his plans if any to consolidate AHF, STAR and CREL.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 573 and 576 together.
The 2025 Programme for Government commits to supporting the delivery of additional Cost Rental homes through the Approved Housing Body sector, Local Authorities, and the Land Development Agency, embedding cost rental as a category of tenure on a permanent basis. More than 6,600 Cost Rental homes were delivered from the enactment of the Affordable Housing Act in 2021 to the end of Q1 2026.
My Department currently operates three funding schemes which support the delivery of new Cost Rental homes, and approximately €2.25 billion in Exchequer funding has so far been approved.
The Cost Rental Equity Loan (CREL) scheme supports delivery by Approved Housing Bodies;
The Secure Tenancy Affordable Rental (STAR) investment scheme supports delivery by the Land Development Agency and may also support participation by private providers; and
The Affordable Housing Fund (AHF) supports delivery by Local Authorities.
The principle of the Cost Rental model is that rents are set to recover the costs of the development, financing, management and maintenance of the homes over a multi-decade timeframe. This cost-covering approach underpins the model's long-term financial sustainability. Cost Rental developments are already assessed, costed and financed at the overall project level, which allows for a degree of flexibility in setting rents across different unit types within a development. question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to give an update on his Departments engagement with the European Construction Strategy particularly with regard to modern methods of construction.
reply:
The EU Affordable Housing Plan commits that, in order to support the construction industry in stepping up to the challenge of supplying affordable housing, the Commission will, in close coordination with industry, promote innovation in construction and renovation materials and methods and support a shift to more circularity and digital processes through a new European Strategy for Housing Construction presented together with the plan.
The strategy identifies offsite construction as one of the solutions that offer the clearest potential for ramping up housing supply rapidly.
Initiated by the Commission and managed by DG GROW, the High Level Construction Forum (HLCF) co-creates and monitors the green, digital and resilient transition pathways for the EU construction industry ecosystem. The HLCF is leading a Task Force on offsite construction.
There are close links between the work of the Task Force and ongoing Commission initiatives, including the Competitiveness Coordination Tool pilot, the European Affordable Housing Plan and work of the Housing Task Force. The outputs of the Task Force are expected to contribute directly to these wider policy processes.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to give an update on the implementation of the Approved Housing Bodies Strategic Forum Report, including the amalgamation and consolidation of the AHBs and sector sustainability fund.
reply:

Its report, published in November 2025, sets out a 10-year strategic vision for a sector that is strategically consolidated, financially sustainable, and capable of delivering both at scale and for specialised needs.
The report outlines the evidence base that must be built to underpin the advancement of eight interlinked policy development reforms that will support the realisation of that vision.
