question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to give an update on the Housing Infrastructure Investment Fund; the timelines for the next call under the fund and future calls.
reply:
On 21 January 2026, the Government launched the €1 billion Housing Infrastructure Investment Fund (HIIF) to support investment in housing-enabling public infrastructure. The Fund is managed by the Housing Activation Office (HAO) in my Department.
Under the first call for applications under the HIIF, 138 applications were received from 30 local authorities and the Land Development Agency. Following assessment of the applications received, 82 infrastructure projects were accepted onto the HIIF programme in June 2026.
These projects relate to sites where infrastructure deficits have been identified as barriers to housing delivery. The approved projects span transport, water, wastewater, electricity and other housing-enabling infrastructure and will support the activation of housing sites at both a local level and a number of strategically important locations.
The HAO team is working directly with local authorities and the Land Development Agency to progress the 82 projects and with critical utilities such as Uisce Éireann and ESB Networks to ensure complementary investment in water and energy in tandem with the delivery of these projects.
Of the 82 approved projects, seven are in construction or are expected to commence construction in 2026. Five projects are expected to be completed by the end of Quarter 1 2027, directly unlocking lands capable of supporting approximately 4,000 new homes.

question: Deputy Holly Cairns asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to outline the policy relating to specific acquisitions of housing to meet the housing needs of disabled persons with very urgent, specific and complex needs that cannot be met through general housing stock; if this policy has been altered over the past 12 to 24 months; and the number of properties purchased by Cork County Council for the provision of housing to people meeting these criteria in each of the years 2022 to 2025, and to date in 2026.
reply:
The provision of social homes for social housing qualified households, including for Persons with Disabilities, should be provided, in the first instance, via suitable new build local authority and Approved Housing Body homes, casual vacancies arising in existing local authority or AHB social homes, or social housing supported tenancies in private rented accommodation. This policy has not changed.
Thereafter, my Department's Social Housing Second Hand Acquisitions Programme is available as a policy tool to local authorities and AHBs for urgent priority cases, including for Persons with a Disabilities and other specialist needs, where no alternative suitable social housing solution can be found.
To this end, some €50 million has been ringfenced for AHBs to progress urgent acquisitions for Persons with Disabilities, Older Persons and Care Leavers in the 2026 Programme. Furthermore, local authorities can also progress acquisitions for Persons with Disabilities from the €173 million available for Local Authority Priority Acquisitions.
Ultimately, it is a matter for each local authority to determine how it meets the needs in individual social housing qualified households. question: Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether his Department has considered introducing targeted transitional protection or security-of-tenure measures for existing tenants of institutional landlords, corporate bodies or landlords owning four or more residential tenancies whose tenancies commenced prior to 11 June 2022.
reply:
The Residential Tenancies Act 2004 to 2026 (the RTA) regulates the landlord-tenant relationship in the residential rental sector and sets out the rights and obligations of landlords and tenants. The Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) was established as an independent statutory body under the RTA to operate a national tenancy registration system and to facilitate the resolution of disputes between landlords and tenants.
The Residential Tenancies (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 came into effect on 1 March 2026. The policy measures, including modifications to rent controls, were introduced to boost investment in the supply of homes available for rent and keep existing landlords in the market. The legislative changes also provide significantly stronger tenancy protections; finely balancing the interests of tenants with the need for greater private investment in the rental market across the country, taking account of stakeholder engagement.
More favourable rent controls for investors are balanced with stronger tenancy protections. The Government is satisfied that it is not legally feasible to retrospectively apply legislation, as the Question suggests, to tenancies that were entered before 11 June 2022 on the basis of a landlord having a right to terminate a 6 year Part 4 tenancy/further Part 4 tenancy upon the expiry of its term, irrespective of the number of tenancies to which a landlord is party.

question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if tenants of a local authority dwelling can apply for solar panels privately through the medically vulnerable scheme, or are local authority tenants obliged to wait for such works to be completed by the local authority.
reply:
The Solar PV for Medically Vulnerable Customers Scheme is administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) and is intended to support eligible households where a person is registered under the life support category of their electricity supplier's Priority Services Register.
In the case of local authority social homes, the property is owned by the local authority, and any alteration to the fabric of the building, including the installation of Solar PV panels, requires the consent of the local authority.
Local authorities continue to undertake energy retrofit works to their housing stock through the national Energy Efficiency Retrofit Programme. Where a medically vulnerable tenant considers that solar PV would be beneficial, they should engage with their local authority in the first instance to discuss the options available in their particular circumstances.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the status of the review of housing assistance payment rent limits commissioned in November 2025; whether the review has been completed; when its findings will be published; the number of HAP tenancies where the tenant is aged 65 or over, broken down into single person and couple households.
reply:
The HAP scheme plays a vital role in housing eligible families and individuals. At the end of Q2 2026, over 134,700 HAP tenancies had been set up since the scheme commenced, of which there were 47,166 households actively in receipt of HAP support nationally.
Maximum rent limits for HAP were set for each housing authority area in 2016 in conjunction with the Department of Social Protection. Since 11 July 2022, each local authority has statutory discretion to agree to a HAP payment up to 35% above the prescribed maximum rent limit. Discretion can be increased up to 50% above the prescribed maximum rent limits for Homeless HAP tenancies in Dublin. Local authorities also have additional flexibility to apply a couple HAP rate to single-person households.
I gave my approval for a review of the current HAP rent limits to be undertaken to ensure there is sufficient support under the HAP scheme to assist eligible households in accessing accommodation in the private rental sector.
As part of this review, the Housing Agency carried out an analysis of the rental market and produced a report. This has helped inform my Department’s review of the HAP rent limits, which has now concluded. I am currently considering its findings before setting out the next steps.

reply:
The Housing Assistance Payment (HAP) is a form of social housing support available for people who have a long-term housing need. Once a household has been deemed eligible for social housing support, it is a matter for the local authority to examine the suite of social housing supports available, including the HAP scheme, to determine the most appropriate form of social housing support for that household in the administrative area of that local authority.
The day-to-day operation of the social housing system is a matter for the relevant local authority, and ultimately, it is the responsibility of the local authority, to make a decision in each individual case.
The Office of the Ombudsman completed an investigation into the administration of the HAP scheme to look at ways to improve the operation of the current scheme and highlight good practice in this area. My Department continues to engage with the Office of the Ombudsman in relation to these recommendations and is working with all the relevant stakeholders regarding their implementation. My Department is committed to making any viable changes to ensure that the HAP scheme continues to provide a vital social housing support which assists those with a long-term housing need to access accommodation in the private rental market.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the exact date for the publication of the child and family homelessness action plan; the reasons for its repeated delays through 2026; and the specific ring-fenced budgetary allocations assigned to fund its implementation in budget 2027.
reply:
The Government's national housing plan, ‘Delivering Homes, Building Communities: An Action Plan on Housing Supply and Targeting Homelessness’ is an integrated housing and homelessness plan. The new plan is based on two key pillars: activating the supply of 300,000 more homes; and supporting people to have a home of their own.
Our housing plan recognises that homelessness is the single most pressing social issue that we face and introduces a number of key measures to address homelessness. It is anticipated that the Child and Family Homelessness Action Plan will be published this year.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of households prevented from entering emergency accommodation via the Social Housing Second-Hand Acquisitions programme in each local authority area for Q1 and Q2 2026; and the way in which this compares to Q1 and Q2 in 2025.
reply:
My Department’s role in relation to homelessness involves the provision of a national framework of policy, legislation and funding to underpin the role of local authorities in addressing homelessness at local level. Statutory responsibility in relation to the provision of accommodation and related services for homeless persons rests with individual local authorities.
The Social Housing Second-Hand Acquisitions Programme is a policy tool available to local authorities to support social housing qualified households in the most challenging and precarious housing situations. The programme is there to help prevent these households from falling into homelessness.
My Department publishes quarterly progress reports which are based on quarterly performance reports submitted by the nine regional lead authorities responsible for the administration of homeless services at local level. These quarterly reports include details of the numbers of individuals and households who were prevented from entering homelessness through tenant in situ acquisitions.
Progress and performance reports are available on my Department’s website at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-housing-local-government-and-heritage/collections/homelessness-data/.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the reason the collation of monthly homelessness figures has not been prioritised by his Department during the work-to-rule industrial action.
reply:
The administration of homeless services is organised across nine administrative regions, with a lead authority in place for each region. The lead authority in each of the regions have overall responsibility for submitting data to my Department.
My Department gathers and publishes data on a monthly basis on the number of homeless persons accommodated in homeless emergency accommodation funded and overseen by local authorities. These reports are based on data provided by local authorities, produced through the Pathway Accommodation & Support System (PASS). The reports are collated on a regional basis and are published by my Department, typically on the last Friday of the following month.
The most recently published data is in respect of August 2026. The reports are available on my Department’s website at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-housing-local-government-and-heritage/collections/homelessness-data/ and are also published to the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation's open data portal: https://data.gov.ie/.
Due to the current industrial relations action, my Department has not received returns from all regional lead authorities. With incomplete data, my Department is not in a position to publish the report for September.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number and percentage of active HAP tenancies requiring a discretionary uplift, including localized breakdowns for the 35% standard and 50% homeless discretion rates in Dublin, in tabular form.
reply:
The HAP scheme plays a vital role in housing eligible families and individuals. At the end of Q2 2026, over 134,700 HAP tenancies had been set up since the scheme commenced, of which there were 47,166 households actively in receipt of HAP support nationally.
Maximum rent limits for HAP were set for each housing authority area in 2016 in conjunction with the Department of Social Protection. Since 11 July 2022, each local authority has statutory discretion to agree to a HAP payment up to 35% above the prescribed maximum rent limit. Discretion can be increased up to 50% above the prescribed maximum rent limits for Homeless HAP tenancies in Dublin. Local authorities also have additional flexibility to apply a couple HAP rate to single-person households.
It is a matter for the local authority to determine if the application of the discretion is warranted on a case-by-case basis and, also the level of additional discretion applied in each case.
From available data, at the end of Q2 2026, 34,023 households (72.4%) of the total number of households being supported by HAP were benefiting from the additional flexibility, at an average rate of discretion of 30.8% above the relevant limit. When the additional discretion available to homeless households in the Dublin Region is removed, 25,292 (70.6%) of households nationally were benefitting from the additional flexibility. In those cases, the average rate of discretionary payment being used was 26.0% above the relevant limit.

reply:

Applicants approved will follow the existing eight stages of pyrite remediation, with an additional assessment step. The Housing Agency will oversee assessment and testing on behalf of the PRB.
I have approved the establishment of a Working Group to assist the PRB in the wind-down process of the Scheme, including technical aspects associated with the potential for additional pyrite cases into the future, following the Scheme closing for applications.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the actions he is taking to support small businesses that are facing increased council rates.
reply:
Local authorities are under a statutory obligation to levy rates on any property used for commercial purposes in accordance with the details entered in the valuation lists prepared by Tailte Éireann under the Valuation Act 2001, as amended. Tailte Éireann has responsibility for valuation matters, including the revaluation of properties. Tailte Éireann is independent in the performance of its functions under the Valuation Act.
The amount of rates liable on a property is determined by multiplying the valuation of the property set by Tailte Éireann by the Annual Rate on Valuation (ARV) set by the local authority. The ARV is decided by the elected members of each local authority in their annual budget and its determination is a reserved function of a local authority. I have no role in this regard.
Commercial rates income makes a significant and stable contribution to the funding of local government, providing between 13% and 41% of total funding for local services at individual local authority level, averaging 24% nationally. Rates income is a very important contribution to the cost of services provided by local authorities such as roads, footpaths, the public realm, litter management, public lighting, development control, parks and open spaces; all essential elements to create the environment in which businesses can prosper.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether his Department or State agencies under its aegis have a policy regarding the use of artificial intelligence to produce artwork for social media, public information campaigns, and graphic design.
reply:

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the estimated deer population in County Offaly and Laois, Westmeath, and Longford; the measures currently being undertaken by the National Parks and Wildlife Service to manage deer numbers in those counties.
reply:
The matter of deer management lies with the Department of Agriculture, Food and Marine. The National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) of my Department has no general policy, operational or regulatory function in relation to the management of the national deer population, other than the management of deer on lands owned or managed by the Department.
In respect of those lands owned or managed by the NPWS deer populations are monitored as necessary and localised deer management measures may be undertaken where required to meet conservation objectives, protect habitats and species, or prevent damage to designated sites. In addition, the NPWS administers the statutory deer hunting licensing system and may issue permits in accordance with the provisions of the Wildlife Act.
While the NPWS licenses the hunting of deer, it does not own the deer population and is not responsible for their control on private lands or in the wider countryside. In the case of deer on private property, landowners may apply to my Department for permission under section 42 of the Wildlife Acts to cull deer where this is necessary outside the annual open seasons. These permissions offer a facility whereby a person can obtain a permit, on a case by case basis, to prevent serious damage caused by individual deer on specific lands. Permissions are issued where there is evidence of such damage.

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the way in which the Housing and Residential Tenancies (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 will impact local authorities in allocating their housing stock.
reply:
Applications for social housing are assessed by the relevant local authority, in accordance with the eligibility and need criteria set down in section 20 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2009 and the associated Social Housing Assessment Regulations 2011, as amended. Decisions on the qualification of households for social housing support, the most appropriate form of such support, and the allocation of that support are a matter solely for the local authority concerned
The Housing and Residential Tenancies (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026, signed by the President on 22 July 2026, does not alter the fundamental role of local authorities in the allocation of social housing. The Act puts existing policy in relation to residency requirements on a statutory footing and introduces a new habitual residency requirement. These criteria will be part of the eligibility assessment. A household deemed eligible and in need of social housing support in accordance with the legislation and associated regulations, will qualify for social housing support and will be placed on the social housing waiting list.
My Department is currently finalising the arrangements necessary for commencement of the new statutory arrangements, including detailed guidance for local authority decision makers.

question: Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage when he expects to publish the Apartment and Duplex Defects Remediation Scheme Bill 2024; when second stage is expected to commence.
reply:
Drafting of the Apartment and Duplex Defects Remediation Scheme Bill is at an advanced stage and it is listed for publication this session. Subject to the legislative process, the statutory scheme will be in place as soon as possible following its passage through the Dáil.
The statutory scheme will provide supports for the remediation of relevant fire safety, structural safety and water ingress defects in apartment buildings, including duplexes, constructed between 1991 and 2013. It is envisaged that 100% of eligible remediation costs will be funded.

reply:
The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) is the statutory body responsible for the provision of special education and allocating supports for students with special educational needs. Parents and schools can contact the NCSE directly using the details available on the NCSE's ncse.ie/seno-contact-information
Local special educational needs organisers (SENOs) are available to offer advice, support and guidance as required to ensure students with special educational needs are supported to achieve their full potential.
At present, there are four special schools, and fourteen special classes attached to mainstream schools to support students with a specific learning disability such as severe dyslexia. I want to acknowledge the excellent work they do. It is important to note they were established at a time when there were much fewer additional supports in schools.
In pursuit of a more inclusive education system it is important, as far as possible to support students to attend their local mainstream schools. This means that children and young people can be educated with their peers and are not required to travel long distances to attend special schools or classes.

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which local specialist music retailers can become approved suppliers to schools; whether a central supplier application process exists; the guidance that is provided to businesses registered on eTenders; and whether she will review procurement arrangements to ensure fair access for small specialist suppliers and value for money where approved intermediaries charge more for identical products.
reply: There is no central approved supplier scheme operated by my Department for musical instruments or related equipment. Individual schools are responsible for their own purchasing and must comply with public procurement requirements appropriate to the value of the purchase. Suppliers may register on eTenders, where guidance and support materials are available. Schools are expected to seek value for money in all purchasing decisions, whether through framework agreements or other procurement processes undertaken in accordance with national procurement rules.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Education and Youth her plans to address the lack of secondary Gaelcholáiste in Swords, County Dublin.
reply:
I recognise the importance that many parents place on access to Irish-medium education and I remain committed to supporting the continued development of Gaelscoileanna and Gaelcholáistí, in line with parental demand and demographic need.
My department has a robust school planning process to ensure that sufficient school places are available to meet current and future demand. This process involves the preparation of detailed demographic profiles and school place demand projections using a range of data sources, including school enrolment trends, Census data, child benefit records, geocoded pupil enrolment data, population estimates and projections, residential development activity, housing completion data, planning permissions, local authority development plans and information on planned housing delivery. These datasets enable the Department to assess the current and projected population of school-age children and young people at both school planning area and settlement level and to identify where additional school capacity may be required.
Where demographic data indicates that additional provision is required, my department examines a range of options, including utilising existing spare capacity, expanding existing schools or, where necessary, establishing a new school. In line with the objectives of Project Ireland 2040, my department's preference, where feasible, is to meet additional demand through the expansion of existing schools.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to Parliamentary Question No. 75893/26, whether she considers that the wording in her response that the right to opt out under Section 30 of the Education Act 1998 is "expected to be upheld" accurately reflects the statutory provision; whether she accepts that the legislation establishes a legal protection rather than a discretionary expectation; and if she will clarify the legal status of this right.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 486 and 489 together.
Section 30(e) of the Education Act 1998 provides that schools “shall not require any student to attend instruction in any subject which is contrary to the conscience of the parent of the student or in the case of a student who has reached the age of 18 years, the student.”
The Education Act, 1998 sets out the legal framework for schools, their boards and their patrons. The act provides that the Board of Management is the body charged with the direct governance of a school on behalf of the Patron.
It is the responsibility of each individual school managerial authority to arrange for appropriate supervision of its pupils when pupils are on the school premises, during school time and/or school activities, taking into account the school's particular circumstances. The manner in which any school ensures that the right to opt out of classes is upheld is a matter for the school concerned.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether a school can lawfully refuse to facilitate a parent's request under Section 30(2)(e) of the Education Act 1998 on the grounds of insufficient space, staffing, supervision capacity or classroom organisation; if so, to identify the specific statutory provision permitting such a refusal; and if not, the reason these considerations were presented as relevant in her previous response.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 484, 487 and 488 together.
Under the provisions of the Education Act 1998, where schools provide religious instruction, parents or in the case of a student who has reached the age of 18 years, the student, can request that the student attend the school without attending religious instruction in the school. It is expected that this right will be upheld by schools on foot of a parental request.
The manner in which a school ensures that this right is upheld is a matter for the school concerned. Each school must determine the particular arrangements which are most appropriate in its individual circumstances having regard to local issues such as available space, supervision requirements and how the school concerned organises classes etc.
Guidance for good practice is available to schools in the follow-up paper to the Report of the Forum on Patronage and Pluralism in the Primary Sector which was published in 2014. The paper provides an overview of different types of arrangements that schools can put in place to facilitate parents who do not wish for their children to attend religious instruction. The paper encourages school authorities to consider their policies and practices and to review whether they are taking the steps necessary to welcome all pupils and make them feel included.

question: Deputy Niall Collins asked the Minister for Education and Youth her views on correspondence (details supplied).
reply:
In 2012 a public service-wide review of allowances was carried out by the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform. As a result of the review, qualification allowances were abolished with effect from 1st February 2012. Department Circular 0008/2013 outlines the effect of this decision on teachers.
In common with a number of job-role based allowances, sanction for payment to new beneficiaries of the Special Education Needs (SEN) allowance was withdrawn from 1st February 2012 under the terms of the Circular.
Section 15 of Circular 0008/2013 states that “Where a teacher has an entitlement to a qualification allowance prior to 05 December 2011 and has failed to claim this allowance, an application should be made for the allowance within a period of 3 months from the date of this circular”.
This teacher is not being paid on the payroll operated by the Department. As she is an employee of Cork Education and Training Board (CETB) she should address any queries in relation to her pay and allowances to CETB.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to Parliamentary Question No. 75044/26, the specific activities, outputs and staff costs funded by the €600,000 core funding allocated to an organisation (details supplied) in 2026; and whether any performance indicator or target is attached to that core funding under the service level agreement.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 422, 423, 424, 425, 426, 427, 428, 429, 430, 431 and 481 together.
The functions of a parents’ association are set out under Section 26 of the Education Act 1998. The National Parents Council (NPC) is the only national association of parents recognised by the Minister for Education and Youth under Section 2 of the Education Act 1998 and represents parents of children in primary and post-primary education.
Under the Education Act, parents’ associations affiliated with the NPC must conduct their affairs in accordance with the following guidelines: Working Effectively as a Parent Association.
My department provides funding to the National Parents Council (NPC) on an annual basis. This funding is provided on a year-to-year basis, subject to the availability of Exchequer funds. I have previously provided Service Level Agreements to the Deputy.
The Deputy will note that the annual audited accounts of the NPC must be provided to my department as a condition of their annual funding. My officials review this documentation upon receipt. May I also draw the deputy’s attention to the fact that these figures are also published in the NPC’s annual reports, which are publicly available to view on their website. The reports also contain the details of the Directors of the NPC.

reply:
Ensuring that children and young people can access the educational provision and supports they need in an equitable, timely and appropriate manner is a priority for this Government. It is also a key priority for me, my department and for the National Council for Special Education (NCSE).
Together with Minister Naughton, I secured a record budget of €3.8 billion for special education in 2027, enabling us to build on the significant progress already made across the system. I regularly hear from families, parents and schools about the importance of ensuring that supports are available when they are needed, and I am committed to addressing barriers that may delay or impede access to appropriate educational provision.
Working to enhance our education system further my department is building on a series of significant reforms that have already moved the system towards a needs-based approach. These include the introduction in 2017 of a needs-based model for the allocation of special education teaching supports in mainstream schools, as well as subsequent reforms to arrangements for Special Needs Assistant supports and summer programmes. These changes have strengthened access to support for many children and young people.
At the same time, I recognise that a diagnosis continues to play an important role for many children, young people and their families, including in accessing services and understanding individual needs.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide an update on the backlog in processing assistive technology applications; whether staffing levels or administrative processes are contributing to delays; the additional resources and measures being introduced to address the backlog; and the target date for clearing it.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 468, 472, 473, 474, 475 and 476 together.
Under the Assistive Technology Scheme, as set out in my Department’s Circular 0010/2013, funding is provided to schools towards the cost of computers and specialist equipment which are required for educational purposes.
All equipment provided under this scheme supports children with more complex disabilities who, in order to access the school curriculum, require essential specialist equipment. It must be clear that the existing IT equipment in the school is insufficient to meet the child's needs.
While schools are awaiting a decision on an assistive technology application, schools should review their existing assistive technology resources to determine whether equipment not currently assigned to another student can be used. Where necessary, schools may also purchase additional equipment or software from their existing resources to support the student’s needs.
These interim arrangements are intended to help ensure that students can continue to access and participate in the curriculum while the school’s application is being processed.
As applications for assistive technology are submitted by schools, schools may contact the relevant section of the Department to obtain an update on the status of an application.

An emergency is deemed to be a situation which poses an immediate risk to health, life, property or the environment, which is sudden, unforeseen and requires immediate action, and in the case of a school, if not corrected would prevent the school or part thereof from opening.
The EWS operates on the basis of a minimal scope works to address the emergency situation. question: Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of post-primary schools whose admission policies include a parent or grandparent criterion under section 62(10)(b) of the Education Act 1998, as inserted by the Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018; the number of first-year places allocated under that criterion in the 2025/2026 and 2026/2027 admission years; the findings of her Department’s review of the provision.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 440 and 451 together.
The overall objective of the Education (Admission to schools) Act 2018 is to provide a framework for school enrolment that is designed to ensure that every child is treated fairly and that the way in which schools decide on applications for admission is structured fair and transparent. The Act creates confidence for parents that the admission criteria laid down by schools and the procedures used by them are visible, legitimate, reasonable, and fair. The legislation is part of a suite of measures taken to take greater account of the needs of parents and students in the school system.
Parents have the right to choose which school to apply to and where the school has places available for the relevant year, the student should be admitted. However, in schools where there are more applicants than places available, a selection process will be necessary. This selection process and the enrolment policy on which it is based must be non-discriminatory and must be applied fairly in respect of all applicants. However, this may result in some students not obtaining a place in the school of their first choice.
In accordance with the provisions of the Act, schools are required to clearly set out their selection criteria in their admission policies. question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Education and Youth to rectify an issue in relation to outstanding payments (details supplied).
reply:
The Summer Programme is an educational programme for children with complex special educational needs which is run during school summer holidays. All primary, post primary and special schools are given an opportunity to run a programme for those children who need it the most. These children can continue to be supported, nurtured and encouraged to engage in a fun and inclusive educational setting.
The main priority of the Summer Programme is to ensure that those children with the most complex special educational needs, especially in special schools, should have access to a school-based summer programme.
However, the department recognises that not all schools are in a position to provide a school-based programme. Where is school-based programme is not being run or a place on the programme is not available, the home-based programme will be available for children with complex special educational needs.
Under the Home-based Summer programme, grant funding is made available so that parents/legal guardians can engage the services of a teacher or a SNA to provide tuition or care support as appropriate in the child’s home. The allocation of hours which can be provided to an eligible child on a one-to-one basis is strictly 10 hours per week, for up to 4 weeks, with the maximum of the 5 hours per day being allowable.
In the case referred to by the Deputy, the timetable submitted shows that more than 10 hours were completed per week and that the hours were delivered over a 2 week period.

reply:

The Act creates confidence for parents that the admission criteria laid down by schools and the procedures used by them are visible, legitimate, reasonable, and fair. question: Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the projected demand for and supply of first-year post-primary places in the school planning areas covering Dublin Rathdown from 2027-2028 to 2030-2031.
reply:
While my department is aware of demand pressures and oversubscription in some individual schools within the Rathdown constituency area, current demographic analysis does not indicate a requirement for additional post-primary capacity beyond that already planned.
Analysis undertaken by my department indicates that demand for first-year post-primary places in the Rathdown area is expected to remain broadly stable over the period 2027/28 to 2030/31.
In September 2025, there were approximately 1,457 post-primary school-aged children residing in the Rathdown area. Based on a zero-migration demographic scenario, this population is projected to decline to approximately 1,347 by 2027 and to 1,322 by 2030. However, residential development is expected to influence future demand. Taking account of projected housing delivery of approximately 1,000 each year between 2025 and 2030, the population of children likely to require a first-year post-primary place is projected at approximately 1,410 in 2027 and 1,479 in 2030, representing a slight increase of 22 pupils, or 1.5%, relative to 2025 levels.
On the basis of current projections, my department does not anticipate a requirement for significant additional post-primary capacity beyond that already planned and in development. Existing accommodation, together with capacity being delivered through projects at Goatstown ETSS and Stepaside ETSS and developments in adjoining areas, is expected to be sufficient to meet projected demand for first-

question: Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Education and Youth the actions that have been taken by her Department to pursue religious orders for financial compensation for the mistreatment of survivors of institutions when they were interred.
reply:
The 18 religious congregations involved in the management of most of the residential institutions covered by the Residential Institutions Redress Scheme have made contributions towards the costs incurred by the State in responding to the issue of abuse in residential institutions under two rounds: the legally binding 2002 Indemnity Agreement and the voluntary offers made in 2009 in the aftermath of the publication of the report of the Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse (the “Ryan Report”).
Some €125 million of the €128 million provided for under the 2002 Indemnity Agreement has been contributed, with the transfer of two properties remaining to be fully completed, although both properties are in use by the intended State recipient.
Following the publication of the Ryan Report in 2009 there was further detailed engagement with the congregations concerned to seek further contributions. This gave rise to further voluntary offers including cash, properties and contributions in kind, valued by the congregations at €352.6 million. To date, contributions amounting to approximately €124 million have been received. When account is taken of offers not accepted, changes in the valuation of the properties offered and the value of properties offered but not being reckoned as a contribution, the total value of the voluntary offers achievable may be lower than the amount offered.

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to the publication of Circular Number 0076/2026, whether increased funding for the UBU your place your space scheme to provide youth services for young people attending schools participating in the DEIS plus scheme will come from DEIS plus funding or youth affairs funding; the increases being made the funding.
reply:
The Department of Education and Youth is committed to enhancing the delivery and development of youth work services and opportunities for young people across the country.
UBU Your Place Your Space (UBU) is the Department's largest youth services scheme and supports young people aged 10 to 24 who are identified as marginalised, vulnerable and at risk of not flourishing. In 2026, over €54 million has been allocated to the scheme, supporting 258 targeted youth services across the 16 Education and Training Board (ETB) areas.
As part of the DEIS Plus plan, funding will be provided to expand UBU provision near DEIS Plus schools. Work is ongoing to develop a scheme for distribution to ETBs with DEIS Plus schools. This work will take into account school enrolment, proximity and size of nearby UBUs and other factors. Engagement with relevant ETBs will be an important part of the process before any decisions are made on funding distribution.
As the Deputy may be aware, in line with standard practice, the annual allocation of funding for each Vote is initially set out in the Revised Estimates Volume (REV). Further details on the 2027 allocations for my Department will be available after the 2027 REV process, which is due to be completed and published later this year. This will inform the overall level of 2027 funding being made available for the UBU your place your space scheme, including for youth services for young people attending schools participating in the DEIS Plus scheme.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 422, 423, 424, 425, 426, 427, 428, 429, 430, 431 and 481 together.
The functions of a parents’ association are set out under Section 26 of the Education Act 1998. The National Parents Council (NPC) is the only national association of parents recognised by the Minister for Education and Youth under Section 2 of the Education Act 1998 and represents parents of children in primary and post-primary education.
Under the Education Act, parents’ associations affiliated with the NPC must conduct their affairs in accordance with the following guidelines: Working Effectively as a Parent Association.
My department provides funding to the National Parents Council (NPC) on an annual basis. This funding is provided on a year-to-year basis, subject to the availability of Exchequer funds. I have previously provided Service Level Agreements to the Deputy.
The Deputy will note that the annual audited accounts of the NPC must be provided to my department as a condition of their annual funding. My officials review this documentation upon receipt. May I also draw the deputy’s attention to the fact that these figures are also published in the NPC’s annual reports, which are publicly available to view on their website. The reports also contain the details of the Directors of the NPC.

reply:

Under the Education Act, parents’ associations affiliated with the NPC must conduct their affairs in accordance with the following guidelines: Working Effectively as a Parent Association.

The reports also contain the details of the Directors of the NPC.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether her Department or State agencies under its aegis have a policy regarding the use of artificial intelligence to produce artwork for social media, public information campaigns, and graphic design.
reply:
My Department has an Acceptable Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems Policy, which provides a framework for the safe and responsible use of AI within the Department. This policy permits the use of approved AI tools to generate images or visual content for illustrative or design purposes, where appropriate.
Where AI tools are used, all AI-generated or AI-assisted content is subject to appropriate human review, validation, and approval by authorised personnel before use or publication.
The Department’s Communications unit currently does not use AI to create imagery, artwork or graphics for social media or campaigns.
My Department will continue to assess opportunities to use AI where it can support the effective delivery of public services, subject to appropriate safeguards, governance, and human oversight.

All school building projects, as they progress through the pipeline, must undergo the necessary due diligence outlined in the Infrastructure Guidelines and Capital Works Management Framework.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if his Department is considering the introduction of statutory bereavement leave as various bereavement entitlements currently exist in different area of the public and private sector.
reply:
There is currently no form of statutory bereavement leave in Ireland. Bereavement leave is normally addressed through employment contracts and can be negotiated between employers and employees when entering into contracts of employment. Employers may also grant bereavement leave at their discretion if their employees suffer the bereavement of close family members.
The introduction of any new form of broad-based employment rights or leave entitlements require careful consideration to ensure that the needs of employees are adequately met and to assess impacts for employers. There is currently no commitment in the Programme for Government to introduce bereavement leave for the loss of a family member.

question: Deputy Fionntán Ó Súilleabháin asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the dual-use products exported licences granted for ICT hardware, software, cybersecurity and data-storage products destined for Israel since October 2023, at a cost of €97 million worth of Irish technology exported during an active conflict; and the assurance he will give that Irish-made technology has not contributed in any way to military operations.
reply:
My Department’s responsibilities centre around the control of exports of dual-use and military items under EU and national legislation. Controls on the export of dual-use items are administered by my Department, in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2021/821 of the European Parliament and of the Council setting up a Union regime for the control of exports, brokering, technical assistance, transit and transfer of dual-use items.
The bulk of licensed dual-use exports from Ireland, including those destined for Israel, comprise mainstream commercial ICT hardware and software products. They are categorised as dual-use items as a consequence of the fact that they incorporate strong encryption for ICT security purposes.
All export licence applications are considered by my officials in accordance with criteria set out within the relevant dual-use and military EU and National Regulations and with Ireland’s international obligations and responsibilities as members of non-proliferation regimes and export control arrangements. Each application is assessed individually, considering the nature of the items, the destination country, the identity of the end-user, and the intended end-use. Ireland’s decisions are guided by the EU Common Position and its eight criteria, which include respect for human rights, international obligations, regional stability and risk of diversion to another end use or end user.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment for an update on the steps his Department has taken specifically to provide relief to entities currently reporting under Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive wave 1 reporters, based on the ‘quick fix’ delegated act signed on 11 July 2025 by the European Commission, that extended certain phase-in provisions that were previously only available to companies with less than 750 employees to all wave 1 companies for FY2025 and FY2026; and if there are any further measures under consideration for companies in Wave 1; and the timeframe for future steps, if any.
reply:
The European Commission adopted a delegated act on 11 July 2025 amending certain provisions of the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) applicable under the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD). The measure extended a number of transitional disclosure reliefs for financial years 2025 and 2026 to companies already reporting under CSRD, including certain phase-in provisions that had previously been available only to undertakings with fewer than 750 employees.
As this measure was adopted by way of a Commission delegated regulation amending the ESRS, it applies directly across all Member States and does not require national transposition. Accordingly, no legislative action was required at national level to give effect to these reliefs.
Ireland has implemented the EU sustainability reporting framework in a timely manner, having transposed the CSRD and subsequently implemented the requirements arising from the Directive postponing certain sustainability reporting obligations within the applicable timelines.
In relation to further measures affecting companies within the current Wave 1 cohort, the Department is progressing work on the transposition of the CSRD-related elements of the Omnibus I Directive in advance of the 19 March 2027 transposition deadline. The Companies Act 2014 provides a modern and comprehensive framework for the incorporation, governance and regulation of companies in Ireland. The framework is updated where appropriate to ensure it remains aligned with international developments, most recently through the Companies (Corporate Governance, Enforcement and Regulatory Provisions) Act 2024.
Ireland's business and regulatory environment is internationally recognised for its quality and competitiveness. The Institute for Management Development (IMD)'s World Competitiveness Ranking ranks Ireland as the most competitive country in the euro area and the seventh most competitive economy globally. Ireland also ranks second globally for Business Legislation, reflecting the strength of its legal and regulatory framework for enterprise.

My officials are therefore actively engaged in the drafting process, which is expected to conclude by the end of this year.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment his views on the use of AI overview by dominant search engines such as a search engine (details supplied) that take work from news organisations without payment, consent or attribution and use it for their own products; the impact this is having on the viability of news media organisations who are deprived of clicks through to the website and advertising and subscriber revenue; and if he will take steps to address the matter.
reply:

With regard to competition policy, Article 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) prohibits abusive conduct by companies that have a dominant position in a particular market. Investigations relating to any potential abusive behaviour are matters for the European Commission or for National Competition Agencies depending on the circumstances involved. My Department has no role in relation to such matters.
With regard to copyright, the European Commission is currently reviewing the operation of the 2019 Copyright in the Digital Single Market (DSM) Directive. The review of the Directive will include the Text and Data Mining (TDM) exception under Article 4 and Article 15 on protection of press publications concerning online uses. Emerging case law from the Court of Justice of the EU will also inform this review.
In parallel, the European Commission is considering future measures to strengthen the position of creators and creative industries in the online and AI environment as part of a suite of measures on copyright expected in mid-2027. The aim is to ensure that creators can better control the use of their works and enforce their rights, while supporting innovation and the development of AI technologies. The European Commission is currently gathering feedback from stakeholders through a targeted consultation open until 10 November 2026 on challenges and options to address them.

question: Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment for an update on his engagement with the relevant stakeholders in the Childcare sector regarding the “50:50 rule” in the Employment Permits Act 2024; and if a review of the policy is being carried out by his Department which will consider risks of viability in the sector due to staffing shortages.
reply:
The Employment Permits Act 2024 requires that, in order for an employment permit to be granted, at least 50% of the employees of an employer are Irish/EEA/UK/Swiss nationals. The mandatory application of the 50:50 rule underpins the Government's employment creation strategy by requiring employers in the State to hire in a balanced manner from domestic and EEA labour markets. Under this rule, an employment permit will not issue unless, at the time of application, at least 50% of the employees of the employer are EEA, UK or Swiss nationals.
Officials of my Department conducted a review of Ireland's use of the 50:50 rule, the outcome of which recommended amending the Employment Permits Act 2024 to address critical recruitment difficulties in key health and social care services sectors through the creation of new sector-specific and sector-wide regulation-making powers.
Following the review, Government approval was secured to prepare the General Scheme of a Bill to amend the relevant legislation. The immediate focus is now progressing the amendments as set out in the General Scheme, and working with the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel to draft the Bill.
My Department remains committed to progressing the proposed legislative changes to the 50:50 rule and will continue to provide updates as the legislation advances. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the means by which an Irish songwriter, composer or performer can establish whether their work has been used to train a general purpose artificial intelligence model; whether his Department considers the existing transparency obligations on providers of such models adequate for that purpose; and the role of the AI office of Ireland in assisting Irish rights holders in this regard.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the EU AI Act provides an important framework for transparency and copyright compliance by providers of general-purpose AI models. The general-purpose AI obligations applied from 2 August 2025 and providers of models placed on the market before that date have until 2 August 2027 to comply.
Under Article 53 of the Act, providers must put in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright and related rights. They must also must draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used to train their models, using the template provided by the EU AI Office. Furthermore, the Act mandates providers to maintain technical documentation and provide information to downstream providers integrating their models into AI systems. The Act provides for penalties in the event of breach, including fines and remedial actions.
The EU Commission has prepared a General-Purpose AI Code of Practice to provide practical support for compliance for businesses. This voluntary code which has been endorsed by large number of frontier GPAI providers, is a practical compliance tool that helps providers demonstrate adherence to their transparency obligations under the EU AI Act, giving them a standardised way to document model capabilities, training data, and limitations for downstream providers and regulators, while offering greater legal certainty for all stakeholders.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the position regarding any proposed engagement with the nursing homes sector in relation to the impact that increases in the minimum annual remuneration thresholds will have on this sector.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 378, 379, 380 and 381 together.
The employment permits system is grounded in legislation that sets clear and objective criteria for minimum annual remuneration (MAR) thresholds, qualifications, and the eligibility of occupations. The MAR represents the minimum salary that must be paid to a non-EEA national for an employment permit to be issued or renewed.
The Employment Permits: Minimum Annual Remuneration – Outcome of the Roadmap Review 2025 published at the end of last year sets out the policy rationale, evidence basis and revised, phased roadmap for implementation of the thresholds applicable across the employment permits system.
The review was informed by a public consultation process and undertaken in response to a range of structural changes in the labour market since MAR thresholds were last comprehensively updated. This consultation included engagement with sector representative bodies, organisations representing the nursing home sector and independent nursing homes. The review included consideration of issues such as sustained inflationary pressures, increases in average earnings, rising costs of living, and changing labour market dynamics. Under this roadmap, the first increases took effect on 1 March 2026.
I can confirm that increases to MAR thresholds for 2027 will not be implemented in January 2027. In line with the approach taken for the 2026 increases, changes to the thresholds will be implemented with sufficient lead-in to allo

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the actions he is taking to support small businesses that are struggling with increased costs related to staffing.
reply:
The Government recognises that rising business costs, including labour costs, have placed significant pressure on firms, particularly SMEs, in recent years. The Government continues to closely monitor cost trends across the economy.
Government is taking significant action to tackle the cost of doing business, including on labour costs. As part of measures designed to bolster business resilience and competitiveness, this year the Government decided to remove the timeline for the transition to a living wage. This decision reflected the challenges faced by the enterprise sector in recent years and is intended to provide certainty to businesses, particularly SMEs where a significant majority of minimum wage workers are employed. The Government also made changes to Employers PRSI which serve to mitigate the increase in the National Minimum Wage in 2027.
The Government has also delivered on several Programme for Government commitments relating to this issue, including through the establishment of the Cost of Business Advisory Forum and the publication and continued implementation of the Action Plan on Competitiveness and Productivity.
The publication of the Cost of Business Advisory Forum report in August represents a notable step forward in this regard. The report is the product of nine meetings held with public and private sector stakeholders, with discussions encompassing a wide range of cost drivers, including energy and insurance costs, planning and infrastructure regulations,

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether, as part of the review of remote work legislation, commuting time, congestion, commuting costs and the environmental impact of travelling to work will be recognised as legitimate factors when an employer considers a flexible or remote working request, particularly where the role can be carried out effectively on a hybrid or remote basis.
reply:
The right to request a remote working arrangement for all employees was commenced through the Work Life Balance and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2023.
As required by Section 29 of the Act, my Department recently concluded a review of the operation of the right to request remote working legislation. The purpose of the review was to fulfil the legislative requirement of the Act. The final report has been published and was laid before the Houses of the Oireachtas in March 2026.
The objectives of the statutory review were to assess the effectiveness of the legislation in providing the new entitlements, to evaluate the clarity of the legislation, and to identify any unintended consequences of the legislation.
The review found that the legislation is highly effective in practice when used, with almost all of those using their right to request remote work being approved either fully or partially.
However, the report highlights that public awareness of the legislative right remains low, with fewer than half of employees aware of their right to request remote work. Awareness is particularly low in rural areas, and knowledge of the Code of Practice on the right to request remote work is lower still.
Recommendations from the report to further improve the effectiveness and uptake of the legislation, including greater awareness and guidance, will now be put in place to underpin the Government’s continued support for a balanced approach to remote working which benefits employees, employers

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he is aware of delays in his Department relating to the appeals process for work permits; the number of applicants awaiting a decision on an appeal in each month of the years 2023, 2023, 2025, and to date in 2026; the reason for these delays; and his plans to address them.
reply:
Ireland operates a managed employment permits system which seeks to maximise the benefits of economic migration while minimising disruption to Ireland's labour market. The system is demand-led, with the volume of applications received reflecting labour market demand.
The processing times for employment permit appeals have come under pressure due to a combination of increased application volumes and the growing complexity of appeals received.
The Employment Permits Unit has experienced a significant increase in the volume of applications received in 2026. From 01/01/2026 to 31/10/2026 the Department received 41,386 employment permit applications, representing a 30% increase on the number of applications received for the same period in the previous year (31,941).
The Unit received 1,660 appeals during the first ten months of 2026, compared with 1,091 during the corresponding period in 2025, an increase of 52%.
At the same time, the Employment Permits Unit has experienced an increase in the complexity of appeals received, a growing number of which involve detailed legal submissions requiring careful and through examination. This has placed additional demands on processing resources and contributed to longer processing times.
My department has allocated additional staff resources to the processing of employment permit appeals and continues to examine ways to improve the efficiency of the appeals process.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether his Department or State agencies under its aegis have a policy regarding the use of artificial intelligence to produce artwork for social media, public information campaigns, and graphic design.
reply:
My Department first issued a policy document on the use of Generative AI to all staff in July 2023. That policy highlighted some of the potential areas where Generative AI can deliver efficiencies but also set out the risks of using such technologies and the mitigations that staff in the Department must adopt to avoid those risks. This was based on guidance received from the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC).
The Department's original Generative AI Policy was reviewed in April 2025, and an updated version was issued to all staff which encourages and fosters greater use of Generative AI. The general principle of the Departments Generative AI Policy is that the technology can be used in most situations where it can improve the efficiency of the work and functions of the Department. General use cases include research, creating initial drafts or layouts for documents and supporting decision making. However, Department staff have been advised that they must make their own value judgments and be transparent and vigilant about any significant use of Generative AI. Where appropriate approval processes are put in place to ensure that all generated content is reviewed by multiple officials before it is published.

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether workplace injuries have occurred on Irish data centre campuses, including during construction, in each of the past ten years; and the nature of these injuries, in tabular form.
reply:
Ireland maintains a robust occupational safety and health regulatory framework designed to protect workers. Employers have legal obligations to safeguard the safety, health and welfare of their employees. We also maintain a comprehensive body of employment rights legislation that safeguards workers and promotes fair treatment in the workplace. This legislation applies horizontally across all sectors to all employees employed in the State.
The Health and Safety Authority (HSA) is the national body responsible for promoting and enforcing workplace safety and health in Ireland. Its functions are set out in the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005.
Under the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work (General Application) Regulations 2016 all employers and self-employed persons are legally obliged to report the injury of an employee as a result of an accident while at work. Injuries must be reported if an employee is unable to carry out their normal work for more than three consecutive days, excluding the day of the accident.
Accident notifications are submitted to the HSA by construction companies and other employers, some of which operate across multiple sites, including data centres. However, the information reported does not allow notifications relating specifically to data centre sites to be readily determined.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the current status of the new €1.3 million water sports and outdoor activities facility at Fenit, County Kerry; the reasons the facility has not yet opened to the public despite being substantially complete; whether his Department has been informed of any outstanding commissioning, technical or operational issues; the expected date for the facility to open to the public; whether he will engage with Fáilte Ireland and Kerry County Council to ensure that the facility is opened without further delay.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 368 and 369 together.
The Fenit Water Sports and Outdoor Activities Facility is a best-in-class outdoor tourism amenity designed to enhance the visitor experience and serve as a central hub for water-based activities in the region.
The project is one of several developments being delivered under Fáilte Ireland’s €32 million Platforms for Growth 2 capital investment programme, which is focused on creating high-quality infrastructure to support outdoor and water-based tourism across Ireland. These facilities are designed to provide a focal point for local communities and visitors alike, supporting a range of water sports operators while offering modern amenities including changing facilities, hot showers, lockers and toilets. Fáilte Ireland has awarded funding of €1.39M for the Fenit Water Sports and Outdoor Activities Facility.
The appointed contractor commenced construction works on 24 March 2025, with an initial programme duration of 52 weeks, which indicated an anticipated completion date in March 2026. During construction, a number of unforeseen issues arose, including the diversion of underground services by third parties, additional foundation works required due to ground conditions encountered on site, and delays relating to the manufacture and delivery of bespoke materials. These factors impacted the overall project timeline.
A Certificate of Practical Completion was issued in June 2026, with the commissioning phase commencing in July 2

question: Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the specific negotiating position Ireland coordinated on behalf of the EU at the World Intellectual Property Organisation Standing Committee meeting regarding AI and copyright; if the position included calls for global transparency standards regarding music data scraping.
reply:
Ireland generally assumes the EU position at the WIPO Standing Committee on Copyright and Related Rights (SCCR). The EU position is agreed at Council Working Party level. The European Commission and EU Member States attend the SCCR and the European Commission generally speaks on behalf of the EU and its Member States.
Copyright and AI is not a formal agenda item at the SCCR. However, the 49th session in November-December 2026 will include a presentation on the Scoping Study on AI Training and Copyright and an information sharing session on copyright and generative AI.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether his Department plans to remove or amend the 50/50 non-EEA staffing rule (details supplied).
reply:
The Employment Permits Act 2024 requires that, in order for an employment permit to be granted, at least 50% of the employees of an employer are Irish/EEA/UK/Swiss nationals. The mandatory application of the 50:50 rule underpins the Government's employment creation strategy by requiring employers in the State to hire in a balanced manner from domestic and EEA labour markets. Under this rule, an employment permit will not issue unless, at the time of application, at least 50% of the employees of the employer are EEA, UK or Swiss nationals.
Officials of my Department conducted a review of Ireland's use of the 50:50 rule, the outcome of which recommended amending the Employment Permits Act 2024 to address critical recruitment difficulties in key health and social care services sectors through the creation of new sector-specific and sector-wide regulation-making powers.
The immediate focus is now progressing the amendments as set out in the General Scheme, and working with the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel to draft the Bill.
My Department remains committed to progressing the proposed legislative changes to the 50:50 rule and will continue to provide updates as the legislation advances. These policy developments are intended to ensure that the employment permits system remains responsive to evolving labour market needs while continuing to support key national priorities.

question: Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the steps he is taking to ensure that representatives from the Irish music industry, including IMRO, RAAP and the Screen Composers Guild of Ireland are legally mandated to hold board seats or advisory positions within the upcoming AI Office of Ireland.
reply:
The Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Act 2026 establishes the AI Office of Ireland as an independent statutory body with a Board appointed in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The Act does not provide for any organisation, sector or representative body, including music industry organisations such as IMRO, RAAP or the Screen Composers Guild of Ireland, to hold reserved or legally mandated Board seats or advisory positions.
Board appointments are to be made through the statutory appointments process set out in the Act, including a selection process undertaken by the Public Appointments Service, with members selected having regard to the experience, training and expertise required to support the Office in carrying out its functions.
While there are no plans to provide for mandated representation for specific stakeholder groups on the Board, the AI Office has begun engaging with a broad range of stakeholders, and will continue that work, including with representatives of the creative sectors, as part of its ongoing work to support the effective implementation and oversight of the EU AI Act in Ireland.

question: Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment in light of evidence that over 120 songs by an Irish band were scraped by AI developers without notice or compensation, the compliance checks or audit frameworks the national competent authorities will enforce on generative AI firms headquartered in Ireland to ensure they compile and publish comprehensive summaries of their training datasets.
reply:
I would like to thank the Deputy for raising this important question. Ireland’s legislative approach to copyright and AI and digital regulation is closely aligned with developments at European Union level.
Ireland is committed to ensuring that AI technologies are developed and used in a manner that is trustworthy, transparent, and compliant with national, EU, and international law. The EU AI Act provides a comprehensive regulatory framework that enables us to build on our existing legislative foundations and harness the benefits of AI while addressing associated risks. The obligations placed on providers and deployers of AI systems vary depending on an AI system’s purpose, use, and risk classification.
Under the EU AI Act providers of general-purpose AI models must maintain technical documentation about their models and provide this information to the EU AI Office or national competent authorities when requested. They must also make certain information available to businesses that use their models to develop AI systems. In addition, providers must have a policy to comply with EU copyright law and publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used to train their models.
For the obligations that apply to general-purpose AI models, as well as AI systems constituting or integrated into very large online platforms (VLOPs) or very large online search engines (VLOSEs) designated under the Digital Services Act (DSA), the EU AI Office is the primary supervisory and enforcemen

question: Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether the average grant rates approved by IDA Ireland for research, development and innovation projects have decreased following the decision in 2025 to increase the research and development tax credit to 35%; and if so, whether this reflects an explicit policy, guidance or established practice of his Department or IDA Ireland to reduce research and development grant rates when the research and development tax credit increases; and the average grant rate for 2023, 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form.
reply:

The strategy includes a target to secure €7bn in new client investment in RD&I over the five-year period to 2029. Progress towards this target has been strong, with client investments in RD&I reaching record levels in volume and value in 2025 and remaining robust in the first half of 2026. In the first year of the strategy, client RD&I investment commitments totalled €2.5bn, 36% of the five-year target.
Multinational companies within IDA Ireland’s client portfolio are undertaking larger and more complex RD&I projects in Ireland, in line with the strategic focus in national enterprise policy and IDA Ireland’s 2025–29 strategy to increase the scale and scope of RD&I. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the procedure that applies where a civil servant or other person working in a Government department wishes to make a complaint of bullying, harassment or sexual harassment against a Minister or Minister of State; the person or body responsible for receiving and investigating such a complaint; whether such conduct falls within the scope of the Code of Conduct for Office Holders; and whether he is informed when such a complaint is made.
reply:
The Code of Conduct for Office Holders was issued by the Government in July 2003 under the Standards in Public Office Act 2001. It covers the standards and behaviours expected of, inter alia, Government Ministers and Ministers of State.
While the Code does not explicitly refer to the matters mentioned in the Deputy’s question, it does provide that office holders should “at all times observe the highest standards of behaviour and act in good faith with transparency, fairness and impartiality to promote the common good in the performance of their official functions.”
In respect of the matters raised by the Deputy, very broadly, under the 2001 Act, a complaint can be made to the Standards in Public Office Commission (SIPO) in respect of an act that is inconsistent with the proper performance by an office holder of his or her functions, or with the maintenance of confidence in such performance by the general public, where the matter is one of significant public importance. SIPO is empowered to investigate such a complaint, taking account of relevant provisions of the Code of Conduct for Office Holders. Where SIPO believes that an offence may have been committed, it must refer the matter to the Director of Public Prosecutions.
On foot of a determination by SIPO that an office holder has committed such an act, the report of the investigation must be submitted to the Committee on Members’ Interests of the relevant House of the Oireachtas. Taking account of the gravity of the matters
