question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he has further considered designating large scale geological energy storage projects under the critical infrastructure act process.
reply:
The Critical Infrastructure Act 2026 allows the Government to designate certain infrastructure projects by or on behalf of the State as being of critical national importance. This provides a statutory basis for accelerating decision making in respect of designated projects and programmes.
The Act establishes a framework through which projects and programmes of strategic national importance can be considered by Government on a rolling basis. To date, the Government has designated nine projects as critical infrastructure and these projects are being prioritised through the consenting and approval processes. Further designation orders will be brought forward at regular intervals to ensure continued progress on nationally important infrastructure projects. My intention is to bring further recommendations to Government for designation under the Act before the end of the year.
Any future recommendations will be assessed having regard to the criteria set out in the Act, including the importance of the project or programme to the State, the potential economic or social consequences of delay, and its contribution to national strategic objectives.
Any decision to designate a project remains a matter for Government.

question: Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation his plans to extend the Freedom of Information Act 2014 an organisation (details supplied).
reply:
I would like to thank the Deputy for his question.
The Freedom of Information Act 2014 uses a criteria-based system to determine which bodies are subject to FOI. These criteria are set out in Section 6 of the Act, and include factors such as being a Department of State, an entity established by or under any enactment (other than the Companies Acts), or a higher education institute in receipt of public funding. In comparison to the previous list-based approach, this criteria-based system has enabled a record number of bodies to be brought within scope of the Act.
The legislation recognises that some bodies, particularly public bodies which operate mostly or entirely within the private commercial market, ought to be treated somewhat differently. The Deputy may be familiar with the bodies that attract only partial inclusions or full exemptions from FOI, as per Schedule 1 of the Act. Part 1 of the Schedule lists bodies that are partially included within the FOI regime, including Iarnród Éireann and EirGrid plc., among others. Part 2 of the Schedule lists the bodies which have been made fully exempt from FOI, which includes Dublin Airport Authority plc.
As is apparent from the Oireachtas debates at the time of the Bill's passage, the rationale behind the partial or full exemption of such bodies from FOI is to restrict the release of commercially sensitive information, in support of the competitiveness of the market as a whole, and in the public interest.

reply:

There are currently no plans at this time to amend the provisions of Circular 51/1979 in relation to paid training leave for civil servants who are members of the RDF. My department keeps all leave provisions under review in line with operational requirements and Civil Service priorities.
Under the current arrangements, eligible officers are entitled to specific periods of paid leave to attend basic, annual and or specialist training, which represents a longstanding and supportive measure recognising the contribution of civil servants to the Reserve Defence Force.
The introduction or amendment of various leave types in the wider public sector are a matter for the relevant employing bodies in the first instance, with my consent and that of the relevant Minister.

question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he will consider making changes to the occupational supplementary pension (OSP) to allow a retiree to take up some employment without the OSP being impacted, to allow the retiree to still contribute to society and earn some extra income.
reply:
Occupational Supplementary Pensions (OSP) are a feature of pre-existing public service pension schemes, where member benefits are integrated with social insurance benefits. The purpose of an OSP is to ensure that the overall pension package (occupational pension, and social insurance benefits) of the individual is no less than the pension they would have received, had their pension been calculated on a non-integrated basis, where an individual is not in employment. It should be noted that the payment of an OSP is not automatic, and is subject to the individual meeting the relevant eligibility criteria.
The purpose of the OSP is to provide a payment to individuals who retire before State Pension Age and are not in employment, thus individuals are not eligible for an OSP if they take up employment post-retirement.
Prior to the release of Circular 12/2024 "Arrangement for Occupational Supplementary Pensions (OSP)", an OSP was not payable where an individual availed of any form of paid employment. Following extensive review of OSP policy and engagement with various stakeholders, this criteria was amended under Circular 12/2024, to allow for the payment of a partial OSP on a pro-rata basis, where the individual is engaged in part-time employment. There are no plans to review this policy further.

The HSE notifies Revenue of amounts that have become due for collection and supplies the contact details of the relevant accountable persons. Revenue then acts based on the information supplied by the HSE, in line with the legislative provisions.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the number of pensioners in receipt of both the State Pension (Contributory) and an occupational pension who are liable for income tax and USC; and whether he has examined the impact of State Pension increases on the tax position of such pensioners.
reply:
I am advised by Revenue that, in relation to self-assessed taxpayers who file a Form 11 tax return, those in receipt of a State Pension do not separately declare that income source, but rather they declare that income source along with a wide range of other possible incomes received from the Department of Social Protection, in a single aggregated field on the Form 11 return.
In addition to this, occupational pensions cannot be readily and precisely identified in Revenue data. Occupational pensions are operated through payroll in the same manner as employment income and are therefore not separately identified.
Therefore, I am advised by Revenue that it is not possible from Revenue data sources to provide the information requested.
However, turning to the Deputy’s question regarding increases to the State Pension rates and its impact on the tax position of pensioners, it should be noted that the current tax arrangements for persons aged 65 or older compare favourably with the tax treatment of the generality of taxpayers. The age tax credit (€245/€490 for single and married persons respectively) or the age exemption limits and marginal relief are available to persons aged 65 or over. Reduced rates of USC also apply for persons aged 70 or older where their total income is €60,000 or less per annum. Furthermore, the State Contributory Pension and the State Non-Contributory Pension are not chargeable to USC or Pay Related Social Insurance.

question: Deputy Ged Nash asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he can provide an update on Ireland's position in the ongoing negotiations on the UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation; Ireland's key negotiating priorities in relation to each of the three workstreams; the officials leading Ireland's participation in the negotiations; and the specific interdepartmental cooperation taking place in preparing Ireland's negotiating positions.
reply:
The United Nations General Assembly established an Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee (INC) to draft a United Nations Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation in 2025. This work will culminate in a vote of the UN General Assembly in the latter half of 2027. Five sessions of the INC have taken place to date and intersessional meetings are ongoing, on the following three workstreams:
• Framework Convention (Workstream I)
• Early Protocol on the taxation of income derived from the provision of cross-border services in an increasingly digitalised and globalised economy (Workstream II)
• Early Protocol on the prevention and resolution of tax disputes (Workstream III)
The sixth session of the INC is scheduled to take place in Nairobi from 30 November to 10 December 2026.
Senior officials from the business and international tax division of the Department of Finance and from the tax treaty branch of the Revenue Commissioners are actively participating in the INC plenary sessions and have been engaging constructively in the process, in collaboration with colleagues from the Department of Foreign Affairs at home and in New York. In addition to the plenary meetings, Irish officials have also taken part in inter-sessional virtual meetings and have been providing written feedback to the UN Secretariat and the Co-Leads of the workstreams. These submissions are available on the United Nations website.

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the rationale for restricting the help to buy scheme to newly built homes; whether consideration has been given to extending the scheme to second-hand or previously owned homes; and if he recognises that many first-time buyers, particularly in rural areas, are purchasing existing properties due to the limited availability and affordability of new builds.
reply:
The Help to Buy (HTB) incentive, is a tax-based scheme to assist first-time purchasers with the deposit they need to buy or build a new house or apartment. It also aims to encourage additional supply of new houses by supporting demand.
HTB provides a refund of Income Tax and Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) paid in Ireland over the previous four years, subject to limits outlined in the legislation.
The level of support available to first time buyers under the HTB scheme, is whichever is the lesser of:
• €35,000 (from 07 October 2026); or
• 10 per cent of the purchase price of the new property; or
• the amount of Income Tax and DIRT paid in the four years before application for the relief.
For a property to qualify for the HTB scheme, it must be new or converted for use as a dwelling, having not previously been used as a dwelling. Additionally, the purchase value/approved valuation of the property must not exceed €500,000.
Based on the latest available data (30 September 2026), the scheme has supported over 70,000 individuals or couples to buy or build their own home.
In relation to second-hand properties, an increase in the supply of new housing remains a priority aim of Government policy. The HTB scheme is specifically designed to support the demand for affordable new build homes so as to encourage the construction of an additional supply of such properties.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he is considering reforming and increasing the widowed parent tax credit which currently has not changed since 2011.
reply:
Section 463 of the Taxes Consolidation Act (“TCA”) 1997 provides for the widowed parent tax credit. The tax credit is available for widowed parents and surviving civil partners, with a qualifying child or children, following the death of a spouse or a civil partner.
The tax credit, which applies for the five years following the year in which the person is bereaved, is as follows:
• €3,600 in the first year after bereavement,
• €3,150 in the second year after bereavement,
• €2,700 in the third year after bereavement,
• €2,250 in the fourth year after bereavement and
• €1,800 in the fifth year after bereavement.
In order to qualify for the tax credit, the widowed person must not have remarried by the start of the year, not be cohabiting and must have a qualifying child residing with him or her for all or part of the year.
For the purposes of section 463 TCA 1997, a “qualifying child” has the same meaning as it has in section 462B TCA 1997. A qualifying child is a child:
• who is born in the year of assessment, or
• who is under 18 years of age at the beginning of the year of assessment, or
• who, if over 18 at the beginning of the year of assessment:
• is receiving full-time instruction at an educational establishment, or
• is permanently incapacitated by reason of mental or physical infirmity from maintaining himself/herself and had become so incapacitated before the age of 21 or while receiving full-time instruction at an educational establishment.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if there are active plans to extend the "right to be forgotten" legislation beyond mortgage protection to include standard, standalone life insurance policies for cancer survivors; the timeline for any such expansion.
reply:
The Insurance (Disregard of Certain Medical History and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026, commonly known as the “Right to Be Forgotten” legislation was signed into law by the President on 15th July 2026. From 15 October 2026, insurers are required to disregard an applicant’s cancer-related medical history when considering an application for mortgage protection insurance, where the statutory criteria are met.
The Act replaces Insurance Ireland's Voluntary Code of Practice with a statutory framework that provides certainty, consistency, and protection for cancer survivors seeking mortgage protection insurance. Insurers will now be legally required to disregard an applicant’s cancer-related medical history when considering an application for mortgage protection insurance, where the statutory criteria are met.
The legislation significantly strengthens the protections available to cancer survivors by reducing both the period since the completion of active treatment and the required period of complete remission to five years, regardless of the applicant’s age at diagnosis. The legislation also increases the cover threshold from €500,000 to €650,000, with normal underwriting applying above that threshold.

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance given the insurance compensation fund levy will reduce to 0% at the beginning of 2027, if he has considered replacing it with a levy to fund protection for household unable to access home flood insurance.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 325 and 326 together.
Government policy in relation to flood insurance coverage is focused on the development of a sustainable, planned, and risk-based approach to managing flooding. Preventing flooding remains the best approach to reducing flood risk and increasing flood insurance capacity.
In terms of flood insurance, the Central Bank of Ireland has undertaken extensive research into the nature and scale of the flood insurance protection gap in Ireland. They found that 1 in 20 buildings have limited access to flood insurance; and that 54% of this gap is concentrated in Dublin, Cork, Louth, Clare, and Kildare.
Building on the work of the Central Bank of Ireland, Government recognises that the availability and affordability of flood insurance is a significant issue for groups and communities in high-risk areas and has therefore prioritised reform in this area under the Action Plan for Insurance Reform 2025 – 2029. This is a multi-faceted policy area that cuts across the remit of a number of Departments and Agencies. A coordinated response is therefore required to assess the most appropriate solutions to address the nature of the flood insurance protection gap in Ireland.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance in respect of an apartment development which is excluded from the Government's interim remediation scheme for fire safety defects in apartments and duplexes on the grounds that it is not a new build (details supplied), but whose owners paid VAT at the new build rate at the time of purchase; and whether Revenue should refund the VAT to resolve the discrepancy.
reply:
The VAT rating of goods and services is subject to EU VAT law, with which Irish VAT law is obliged to comply. In general, the VAT Directive provides that all goods and services are liable to VAT at the standard rate unless they fall within the categories listed in Annex III of the Directive, in respect of which Member States may apply a lower rate. The “supply of housing, as part of a social policy” is listed in Annex III. The Directive also allows for a Member State’s historic VAT treatment to be maintained under certain strict conditions.
On this basis, Ireland has for many years continued to apply its reduced rate, currently 13.5%, to the supply of new residential property. Ireland also applies its second reduced rate, currently 9%, to the supply and the construction of certain new apartments, as part of a social policy which will run until 31 December 2030.
The VAT rates above are set by reference to the VAT Directive, which also limits the extent to which VAT can be refunded. Generally, VAT may only be reclaimed by a VAT-registered business making taxable supplies of goods or services. The VAT Directive does not permit the refund of VAT paid by purchasers on the supply of these apartments as a remedy for their exclusion from the Government's interim remediation scheme for fire safety defects.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether any compensation paid to a person arising from the compulsory acquisition of that person's principal private residence by way of a compulsory purchase order is subject to taxation; if so, to specify which elements of such compensation are taxable, including compensation for the property itself, disturbance, severance, injurious affection, accommodation loss or other associated payments; the tax heads under which such compensation is taxed, including capital gains tax, income tax or any other tax; and the applicable rates of taxation.
reply:
I am informed by Revenue that the acquisition of a property by way of compulsory purchase order (CPO) comprises the disposal of that property for the purposes of Capital Gains Tax (CGT). Any chargeable gain arising on such a disposal is subject to CGT at 31%. The first €1,270 of total chargeable gains in respect of an individual in any year of assessment is exempt from CGT.
It is the amount of the chargeable gain, if any, arising on the disposal of an asset which is subject to CGT. In these circumstances, the chargeable gain is calculated as the difference between the proceeds received in respect of the property by way of CPO and the price paid for the property (or in certain circumstances, the market value at the time of acquisition). A deduction may be claimed for certain costs incurred in acquiring and disposing of the property such as stamp duty, legal fees, auctioneers’ fees.
For CGT purposes, the chargeable gain, if any, arising on the disposal of a property by way of CPO is deemed to accrue on the day on which the payment of the compensation amount is received by the person making the disposal. Any CGT liability arising in respect of such a disposal will be payable by reference to that date.
If the property acquired by way of CPO was occupied by the owner as his or her principal private residence (PPR), then full or partial relief from CGT will be available where a chargeable gain arises on the disposal of that property.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance further to Parliamentary Question No. 75249/26, the change in median net wealth of households by housing status, that is owners outright, owners with a mortgage and tenants, between 2015 and 2025, with reference to the Distributional Wealth Accounts; and the share of total household net wealth held by tenant households in 2015 and in 2025.
reply:
Between 2015 and 2025, Ireland experienced significant economic and employment growth. Together with rising household incomes and asset values, this contributed to substantial household wealth creation. As set out in the Department of Finance’s recently published Beyond GDP analysis, total household net wealth more than doubled over the decade and now stands at over €1.45 trillion.
Housing assets constitute around 60 per cent of total household assets and, as such, rising property values contributed significantly to this increase in household net wealth. This is reflected in the Distributional Wealth Accounts, which indicate that the average net wealth of homeowner households more than doubled between 2015 and 2025.
The average net wealth of households classified as tenants, or as occupying their accommodation free of charge, also increased over the period, rising by approximately 40 per cent. It is important to note that the Distributional Wealth Accounts report these statistics as an average, rather than median, meaning the figures may be influenced by households with particularly high levels of assets.
The share of total household net wealth held by tenant households declined marginally over the period, from 5 per cent in 2015 to just under 4 per cent in 2025. This reflects in part the younger age profile of renters and the fact that homeowners account for around two-thirds of households.
The Distributional Wealth Accounts do not provide a separate breakdown for homeowners

question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Transport the status of the proposal for a transport support scheme to replace the mobility allowance and motorised transport grant, which was raised in the 2022 National Disability Inclusion Strategy Action 104 Transport Working Group Final Report; the steps being taken to advance the scheme.
reply:
I wish to advise that the Motorised Transport Grant was a means-tested Health Service Executive (HSE) payment for people with disabilities. The Deputy will be aware that the Department of Health announced in 2013 that the Motorised Transport Grant scheme was closed to new applicants. The development of an alternative scheme to replace the Motorised Transport Grant falls within the remit of my colleague the Minister for Health.
I can confirm that in recent months my officials have made significant progress in the development of the Vehicle Adaptation Scheme (VAS). Guided by the proposals set out by the Transport Working Group of the National Disability Inclusion Strategy and the Senior Officials Group on Disability, as well as further engagement and consultation, the Department has established the key principles and parameters underpinning the Scheme. This has facilitated the development of a high-level framework for its operation. However, some elements of the Scheme, including aspects of its administration and delivery, remain under development and have yet to be finalised. Full details of the Scheme will be published once these arrangements have been agreed.

question: Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Transport for an update on the National Aviation Policy; and if updates to the policy are planned.
reply:
The 2015 National Aviation Policy (‘NAP’) established a policy framework for the development of the aviation sector in Ireland. It was designed to create an environment that encouraged the sector to enhance Ireland's connectivity, to foster the growth of aviation enterprise and maximise the contribution of aviation to Ireland's sustainable economic growth and development.
Whilst the principal goals of the 2015 NAP remain valid, and it continues to guide decision-making, my Department has commenced preparatory work on revising the NAP. My Department is working towards the publication of a call for evidence in early 2027 to enable stakeholders to inform the development of the revised NAP.
The revised NAP will update existing policy in response to developments in the aviation sector since 2015.

question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Transport when the new vehicle adaptation scheme will open for applications; the eligibility criteria, grant levels and application procedures that will apply; and the provision that has been made to ensure timely processing of applications.
reply:
I can confirm that in recent months my officials have made significant progress in the development of the Vehicle Adaptation Scheme (VAS). Guided by the proposals set out by the Transport Working Group of the National Disability Inclusion Strategy and the Senior Officials Group on Disability, as well as further engagement and consultation, the Department has established the key principles and parameters underpinning the Scheme.
In line with the social model of disability, the VAS will be based on an individual's needs, not characteristics. Accordingly, eligibility will extend to drivers and passengers who require assistance to enter, exit, or operate a vehicle, rather than being linked to any particular medical condition or disability. The Scheme will be simple to access, use, and receive payments through. It will not be means tested and applicants needing adaptations will not be required to pay upfront themselves.
In light of the funding secured through Budget 2027
(www.gov.ie/en/department-of-transport/press-releases/budget-2027-securing-sustainable-accessible-and-safe-transport-and-extending-opportunities/), the Department is now in a position to proceed to implementation of the Scheme. Subject to timely completion of the necessary preparatory work, it is expected that the VAS will open for applications in Q1 2027.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Transport the number of cattle grids located on national, regional and local public roads, insofar as this information is available; if his Department, Transport Infrastructure Ireland or local authorities have undertaken any assessment of compliance with the requirement in TII Standard Construction Detail CC-SCD-02755 that ramps to aid the escape of small animals be provided within cattle-grid pits; and whether consideration has been given to surveying and retrofitting older cattle grids which do not contain such wildlife escape measures.
reply:
In accordance with Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993, as amended, the improvement and maintenance of regional and local roads is the statutory responsibility of each local authority. Work on such roads is funded from Councils' own resources, supplemented by State road grants.
Cattle grids on roads is a matter for Local Authorities or where they are on private land, the land owner. The only exception is in the Curragh, which is under the control of the Department of Defence. As Minister for Transport I have no role in their use.
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and exchequer funding in relation to the National Roads Programme. Under the Roads Acts 1993-2015 and in line with the National Development Plan (NDP), the operation and management of individual national roads is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned. This is also subject to the Infrastructure Guidelines and the necessary statutory approvals. In this context, TII is best placed to advise you in relation to the relevant TII standards.

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Transport the reasons for the increased waiting time to take a category B driving test at Gorey Driving Test Centre, County Wexford; the reason for these increases; if he is aware drivers from the local fire service are awaiting testing for many months; and the measures being taken to reduce the waiting time.
reply:
Under the Road Safety Authority Act 2006, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) has statutory responsibility for all aspects of the National Driver Testing Service. Given the RSA's responsibility in this matter, I have referred the Deputy's question to the Authority for direct response. Please contact my office if a reply is not received within ten days.
Pending this response, the latest information provided to me by the RSA indicates that, as of 31 October, the average waiting time for an invitation to book a driving test at the Gorey test centre was 15 weeks. I am assured by the RSA that work is continuing to reduce waiting times in line with the target 10-week service level agreement.
I am pleased that as of end June, the full sanctioned complement of 200 driver testers are employed by the RSA, which is a significant increase on the 151 testers available at the beginning of 2025 and a doubling of permanent posts since June 2022.
I would encourage learner drivers awaiting a test to monitor the driver testing booking system which makes available cancelled test slots for candidates to take up at short notice across the service.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Transport whether he has engaged with Insurance Ireland and motor insurance providers on reports that disabled vehicle owners are being refused insurance renewals because they do not possess a driver number; and the steps he is taking to ensure that disabled persons are not unfairly excluded from insurance cover.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 231, 232, 233, 292, 297 and 298 together.
The legislative changes to which the Deputy refers are set out in Section 56A(1)(d)(ii) of the Road Traffic Act 1961 (as inserted by the Road Traffic and Roads Act 2023). The legislation provides that only drivers named in Particular 6 of the Certificate of Insurance are required to provide their driver number.
The approach adopted for open driving policies is a matter for the insurer concerned. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Transport whether RSA or statutory licensing requirement provides that a person must have held a category B licence for two years before obtaining or holding a full category D licence; whether previous category B entitlement obtained in another EU member state is recognised following an exchange for an Irish licence; and if he will clarify the requirements.
reply:
Irish driver licensing law operates within a framework of EU law, which sets out the driver licensing legislation with which all Member States must comply. The format of driving licences, categories of vehicles, and the standards to be met in driving tests to qualify for a licence, are all set at EU level. Therefore, all EU issued licences are recognised in Member States.
Regulation 19(2)(a) of the Road Traffic (Licensing of Drivers) Regulations 2006 requires an applicant to hold a category B driving licence issued by Ireland or another EU member state before applying for a category D learner permit. There is no restriction with regards to the period of time that a person must hold a category B driving licence prior to applying for a category D learner permit.

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Transport if, in view of the barrier created to families with children, soon to start learning to drive, moving to electric vehicles, he will provide a simpler route to a licence for manual vehicles for current holders of licences to drive automatic vehicles, such as a specified number of approved lessons, without the need to pass a driving test in a manual vehicle.
reply:
If a person wishes to obtain a driving licence to operate a vehicle with a manual transmission, they must pass a driving test in a manual transmission vehicle.
If a person passes their driving test in an automatic transmission vehicle, the driving licence issued restricts the driver to driving automatic transmission cars only and this is indicated by a code on the licence. A person with such a licence cannot drive a manual transmission car legally as they have not displayed in the driving test that they possess sufficient ability to safely drive a manual car on a public road.
A holder of a licence restricted to driving cars with an automatic transmission only can remove this restriction by passing a test in a car with a manual transmission. Details can be found on the National Driver Licence Service (NDLS) website here: www.ndls.ie/about/upgrade-an-automatic-car-licence-to-manual-licence.html.
For reasons of road safety, I have no plans to change the rules to allow a person who holds a driving licence for an automatic transmission car to drive a manual transmission car.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Transport the arrangements under which driving licences issued by Ukraine have been exchanged for Irish driving licences since 2022; whether category C and D entitlements are included in those exchanges; the verification checks applied to such licences; and the number of exchanges that included bus categories to date.
reply:
Following the outbreak of war in Ukraine and the subsequent arrival in Ireland of Ukrainian nationals seeking protection, the Government introduced the Road Traffic (Recognition of Foreign Driving Licences)(Ukraine) Order, SI 192/2022, in April 2022 which permitted Ukrainian category B driving licences to be exchanged for Irish licences. It was not permitted to exchange category C or D driving licences under this order.
SI 192/2022 was a short-term response and was revoked following the introduction of Regulation (EU) 2022/1280 in July 2022, which allowed for the recognition of all categories of Ukrainian licences where their holders are in receipt of temporary protection in any EU member state, without the need for exchange.
Under Regulation (EU) 2022/1280, a person who is in Ireland under the EU Temporary Protection Directive and section 60 of the International Protection Act 2015 shall have their driving licence recognised in any category issued, subject to any relevant conditions. Such licences are recognised for the period of temporary protection.
A person with category C or D on their Ukrainian licence (trucks and buses) must have a driver certificate of professional competence (CPC) to drive a truck or bus professionally in Ireland. The EU Regulation allows for the recognition of Ukrainian CPCs, subject to the holder undergoing additional compulsory training.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Transport whether his Department holds estimates on the number of disabled people who own vehicles but do not hold driving licences and rely on others to drive on their behalf; whether the impact of recent legislative or insurance changes on this cohort has been assessed.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 235 and 296 together.
The legislative changes to which the Deputy refers are set out in Section 56A(1)(d)(ii) of the Road Traffic Act 1961 (as inserted by the Road Traffic and Roads Act 2023). The legislation provides that only drivers named in Particular 6 of the Certificate of Insurance are required to provide their driver number. The data that the Deputy has requested is not held by the Department of Transport.
The approach adopted for open driving policies is a matter for the insurer concerned. However, it is the Department’s understanding that a driver number is not required where a driver is not specifically named in Particular 6 of the Certificate of Insurance under such policies, which typically provide cover for drivers aged between 25 and 70 who hold a full driving licence and have the policyholder’s consent.
Department officials have raised the issue with Insurance Ireland and await their response.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Transport the additional toll revenue expected to be generated in 2027 as a result of the toll increases approved by Transport Infrastructure Ireland from 1 January 2027, broken down by each of the ten toll roads on the national road network, including the M8 Fermoy toll; and if he will request this information from TII where it is not held by the Department.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 222, 223, 228 and 229 together.
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and funding in relation to the national roads programme. Under the Roads Acts 1993-2015, the operation and management of individual national roads is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned.
Therefore, matters relating to the day to day operations regarding national roads, including toll roads are within the remit of TII. More specifically, the statutory power to levy tolls, to make toll bye-laws and to enter into agreements with private investors are vested in TII under Part V of the Roads Act 1993 (as amended). Moreover, the contracts for the privately-operated toll schemes are commercial agreements between TII and the Public Private Partnership (PPP) concessionaires concerned.
Noting the above position, I have referred these questions regarding tolls to TII for a direct reply. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 working days.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he has considered expanding Action 15 of the National Hydrogen Programme Implementation Plan working group on the legal and regulatory structure needed to encompass enabling long duration energy storage for natural gas and bio-methane gas as well as hydrogen under the groups work and green energy transition.
reply:
Government recognises the role that renewable hydrogen is anticipated to play in our future energy system and as a key component of our zero-carbon economy. It will be extremely challenging for Ireland to achieve our legally binding target of net zero emissions by 2050 without decarbonised gases like renewable hydrogen. It is the strongest contender to displace fossil fuels in dispatchable power generation, which is essential for a reliable power system and is especially important during periods of low renewable generation (i.e. dunkelflaute). Renewable hydrogen can also enhance our security of supply as it can be produced in Ireland with our abundant wind and solar energy resources, and it provides long-term, inter-seasonal storage of renewables.
The National Hydrogen Programme Taskforce was launched in September 2025 to oversee the delivery of the actions and wider strategic ambitions set out in the National Hydrogen Strategy. The Taskforce works across Government Departments and State Agencies, working with key stakeholders to remove barriers to early hydrogen project development and lay the ground to enable the development of the hydrogen sector in Ireland.
The National Hydrogen Programme Taskforce is making good progress on a number of key strands to deliver the actions set out in the National Hydrogen Strategy. The next meeting of the National Hydrogen Programme Taskforce is scheduled for Q4 2026. More details on the progress of the Taskforce to date will be made availa

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he has further considered long-term energy storage projects (details supplied) to complement the floating storage regassification unit.
reply:
My Department currently has no plans to use the Ballycotton fields for gas storage. My officials are aware of interest by a number of parties in potentially developing natural gas and hydrogen storage in the Ballycotton area. Progressing any such projects would be a matter for the project promoters concerned, including obtaining any necessary consents and permits.
The primary focus of this Government in relation to gas storage is the Strategic Gas Emergency Reserve. As part of the review of Energy Security published in November 2023, my Department completed an assessment of gas storage that concluded a floating storage and regassification unit known as an FSRU would be the most appropriate gas storage approach. The Strategic Gas Emergency Reserve is not intended for commercial use and will be divested when no longer required to secure the Irish energy system.
Regarding hydrogen, a number of key work strands are being progressed over the next two years which will build the evidence base for informed policymaking on hydrogen storage in Ireland. Under action 10 of the National Hydrogen Strategy, my Department is working to develop the necessary legislative and regulatory frameworks required for the development and operation of geological hydrogen storage facilities.

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to provide an update on the transposition of Article 12 of the EU Energy Efficiency Directive, which establishes mandatory energy and sustainability performance reporting obligations for data centres.
reply:
Article 12 of the Energy Efficiency Directive establishes the legislative framework for the annual monitoring, reporting and publication of information on key metrics on energy and sustainability performance of data centres above a specified size threshold. My Department has nearly finalised the secondary legislation to effect the transposition of the relevant provisions which includes assignment of compliance oversight to the SEAI, confidentiality safeguards, and penalties for non-compliance.
While Article 12 must be transposed by Member States, that framework is supplemented and implemented by the directly applicable Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364. The Delegated Regulation operationalises the reporting regime established under the EED by detailing the information, key performance indicators (KPIs) and reporting methodology required for compliance with Article 12, including the public disclosure and reporting of that information to the European database for data centres established and operated by the European Commission.
Data centres in Ireland are actively reporting to this European database, as overseen by my Department, with publication of the data by the Commission in an aggregated manner in accordance with the Delegated Regulation.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the actions he is taking to support small businesses with increasing costs of energy.
reply:
In June last year, my Department established the National Energy Affordability Taskforce (NEAT), which I chair, to identify, assess and implement measures that will enhance energy affordability for households and businesses while delivering key renewables commitments, and protecting security of supply and economic stability.
The NEAT continues to work intensively on an Energy Affordability Action Plan to be submitted to Government in the coming weeks. Publication of the Action Plan will follow approval by Government. This Action Plan is focused on short, medium and longer term measures to support households and businesses in meeting their energy costs and will be built around 4 key pillars:
• addressing the price of energy;
• sustainable demand and enhancing flexibility;
• addressing energy poverty and customer protections; and
• energy affordability for businesses.
To facilitate this robust and coordinated cross-Government response, a number of NEAT subgroups, including one on energy affordability for business, have been established. The business subgroup brings together officials from a wide range of Government Departments and Agencies. A period of intensive engagement to refine options for consideration by the Taskforce has concluded with each of the subgroups meeting intensively over the past months.
This work has been supported by structured engagement with relevant external stakeholders. This included a targeted stakeholder consultation session with business representat

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to provide an update on the commitment in the Programme for Government to prioritise a review and reform of the legislation underpinning the Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU); to outline which legislation is being reviewed and the basis; and to provide a timeframe for completion of this reform and review.
reply:
The Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) is an independent regulator, accountable to a Committee of the Oireachtas and not to the Minister for the performance of its functions. The CRU was assigned responsibility for the regulation of the Irish electricity and gas retail markets under the Electricity Regulation Act 1999 and Gas (Interim) (Regulation) Act, 2002 and its statutory remit has subsequently expanded to include energy safety and water.
The Programme for Government 2025 makes a commitment to "prioritise a review and reform of the legislation underpinning the Commission for the Regulation of Utilities (CRU)" and to "emphasise that low costs for households and businesses are a central tenet in the updated mandate of the CRU".
Comprehensive work has been carried out by my Department, working with the CRU, to undertake a review of its leadership structures, resourcing requirements, functions, and accountability mechanisms, as committed to under Actions 21 and 26 of the Energy Security Package. The objective of the review is to ensure that Ireland has a best-in-class energy regulator that is structured and equipped to deal with current and future demands, and to ensure decarbonisation is achieved in a secure and cost-effective manner while protecting consumers. My officials will continue to engage with the CRU and relevant stakeholders as work progresses on the review and reform of the legislative framework underpinning the regulator.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the number of bottles and cans returned through the deposit return scheme since its launch in February 2024; the current return rate; and the progress being made towards the 90% separate-collection target for 2029.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 189 and 190 together.
The Deposit Return Scheme was introduced in February 2024 to encourage more people to recycle plastic bottles and cans and to deliver on our ambitious EU targets for the recycling of those products.
To date, over 3.6 billion bottles and cans have been returned through the deposit and return scheme, representing more than €618 million in deposits. The Scheme's return rate has continued to increase since its introduction, from 66% in 2024 to 76.4% in 2025. At end September 2026, it is running at 80% for 2026, in line with Re-turn's projections.
Re-turn have advised that they currently have 5,958 community groups registered to use the Deposit Return Scheme as a means of fundraising. These include schools, sports clubs, charities and other community organisations across the country.
As individual groups raise and retain funds for their own purposes, Re-turn does not hold information on the total amount raised collectively by all registered groups.
Re-turn’s own charity initiative, Return for Children which supports six major children’s charities, has raised over €650,000 to date.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the current timeline for the draft and final National DMAP; when the west coast areas will go to public consultation.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 186 to 188, inclusive, together.
The National Designated Maritime Area Plan for Offshore Renewable Energy (National DMAP for ORE) will deliver a strategic long-term plan for ORE development. The DMAP will identify suitable areas for ORE within our entire maritime area and is not focused on one specific regional location.
Potentially suitable areas for offshore wind (called Emerging Renewable Energy Areas) have been identified using a multi criteria spatial optimisation methodology, underpinned by policy direction and stakeholder feedback. These areas represent locations where fixed-bottom offshore wind, floating offshore wind, or a potential future combination of both technologies could be considered.
The project team continues to develop the draft plan and further refine these Emerging Renewable Energy Areas into Draft Renewable Energy Areas (DREAs). This work is being informed by the iterative environmental and social and economic impact assessments along with local knowledge and feedback shared through extensive stakeholder engagement.
The spatial policy framework of the National DMAP for ORE will support the principle of demonstrator floating offshore wind projects being located in suitable sites within DREAs only, subject to Government policy.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether his Department or State agencies under its aegis have a policy regarding the use of artificial intelligence to produce artwork for social media, public information campaigns, and graphic design.
reply:
My Department has an approved policy for the use of Artificial Intelligence which is in line with the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Reform and Digitalisation's Guidelines for the Responsible Use of AI in the Public Service (2025) and the National Cyber Security Centre’s (NCSC) Securing AI Adoption in the Public Sector Cyber Security Guidelines for AI Deployments (2026).
This policy establishes the principles, governance framework and oversight arrangements for the responsible use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within the Department to enable innovation and efficiency while protecting public trust, personal data, security and legal compliance.
This policy aligns with the EU Artificial Intelligence Act including the transparency requirements of Article 50, and prohibits the deceptive, manipulative, or non-transparent use of AI Systems, including the failure to clearly identify AI-generated content where appropriate.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she has raised or will raise the ongoing imprisonment of the pro-democracy activist (details supplied) with the Chinese authorities.
reply:
Ireland has continuously raised concerns about the human rights situation in Hong Kong, as well as concerns about the erosion of democracy and fundamental freedoms since the introduction of the National Security Law in June 2020.
Officials at the Consulate General of Ireland in Hong Kong, along with our EU counterparts, have been monitoring the case of Joshua Wong with concern. Since 2020, Mr. Wong has been held in custody and was expected to be released next year. However, this month he was sentenced to a further ten years' imprisonment.
Ireland supports the statement by the European External Action Service on 5 November 2026, which referred to the sentencing of the pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong as politically motivated and called for his immediate release.
While I have not yet had a bilateral meeting with my Chinese counterpart since my appointment as Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade, Ireland has repeatedly raised human rights issues bilaterally with Chinese interlocutors. The Taoiseach raised human rights issues with the Chinese leadership when he visited earlier this year.
Ireland regularly raises human rights in China at multilateral fora. Ireland’s recent national statement at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly made explicit reference to our concerns with the repressive use of the National Security Law in Hong Kong. question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade following on from her leadership on commencing a strategic dialogue with the life science industry under the Irish EU Presidency, her plans post this meeting to have her Department advance the strategic dialogue concept with the life sciences sector and formulate an EU Pharma Taskforce.
reply:
The life sciences sectors, encompassing pharmaceuticals and medtech and biotech, are absolutely essential for our global competitiveness, accounting for almost 10% of European GDP.
To ensure this crucial ecosystem remains vibrant and resilient, I convened a strategic dialogue on life sciences on the margins of the informal meeting of the Foreign Affairs Council on Trade or FAC (Trade), which I hosted in Dublin on 22 and 23 October. Bringing together the European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security, Maroš Šefčovič, trade ministers from a number of EU Member States with significant pharmaceutical and medical devices sectors and key industry representatives from the sector allowed us to foster an open dialogue and facilitated a vital exchange of ideas. As trade ministers we bring a particular perspective to the issue, not least against the background of the changed international trading environment in recent times.
My ambition is that this strategic dialogue on life sciences will mark the beginning of a more structured, ongoing engagement both among policy makers and between policymakers and industry leaders. By working closely together, we can ensure that Europe's life sciences sector continues to innovate and deliver effectively for our citizens, communities, companies and jobs across the continent. I am in ongoing discussion with my trade minister counterparts on the next steps in achieving this ambition.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade in respect of long-stay study visa applications by Palestinian nationals in Gaza in each of the years 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026, the number and percentage of applications in which officials of her Department, Embassy staff or persons acting on their behalf sought further information or documentation before a first-instance decision; the nature of the information or documentation sought; and whether such requests were made on the Department’s own initiative or at the request of the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 169, 174, 175, 176 and 177 together.
As the Deputy will be aware, since the start of the Gaza crisis, my Department has facilitated nearly 400 people to exit Gaza and travel to Ireland, including students taking up studies in Ireland’s Higher Education Institutions, some of whom won places on the Ireland-Palestine Scholarship Programme.
These operations require close coordination between my Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science, and Irish Higher Education Institutions.
The Deputy will appreciate that any individual seeking assistance to leave Gaza must first be in possession of a valid visa to travel to Ireland. Visa policy is a matter for the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, which assesses each visa application on its own merits.
Any movement from Gaza is also dependent on receipt of several permissions from the relevant authorities, including the Israeli authorities, which set the date for all exits from Gaza, as well as the number of individuals permitted to leave. While every effort is made to secure these permissions, the decision to grant or deny them rests outside the control of the Government of Ireland.
On the matter raised by the Deputy, under delegated sanction from the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, my Department, through the Irish Embassy in Tel Aviv, is responsible for deciding on visa applications f

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the legal basis under the Treaty on European Union for the Council decision establishing the EU mission to support the Lebanese Armed Forces; the position taken by Ireland at Council when the mission was approved; and whether the Council decision refers to a UN Security Council resolution.
reply:
The EU Support Mission in Lebanon (EUSM Lebanon), was established at the Foreign Affairs Council on 12 October 2026 by Council Decision (CFSP) 2026/2296, which was adopted with regard to the Treaty on European Union, and in particular Articles 42(4) and Article 43(2) thereof.
Ireland was an early proponent of the need for and potential added value of a CSDP mission in Lebanon, and I was particularly pleased that agreement was reached on establishing the new EU Support Mission at the October Foreign Affairs Council, as this has been a priority of our EU Presidency.
EUSM Lebanon is a non-executive Training Mission and has been established as an EU Common Security and Defence Policy mission focused primarily on capacity building, training, mentoring and strategic advice. The mission is intended to support Lebanese state institutions, particularly the Lebanese Armed Forces and other Lebanese security bodies, in strengthening their ability to exercise effective control over Lebanese territory, improve border security, enhance maritime security, counter illicit trafficking and smuggling, and improve command, planning and operational capabilities.
The Council decision refers to United Nations Security Council Resolution (UNSCR) 1701(2006). It states that EUSM Lebanon shall contribute to lasting stability and peace throughout Lebanon, in line with UNSCR 1701(2006), by supporting the strengthening of the capabilities of the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) and the Internal Security Forces

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade whether she intends to bring forward amendments to the Israeli Settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (Prohibition of Importation of Goods) Act 2026 to include services in its provisions.
reply:
The Israeli Settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (Prohibition of Importation of Goods) Act 2026, commenced on 15 September, fulfils the Programme for Government commitment to progress legislation prohibiting the importation of goods from Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territory.
The importation of goods from Israeli settlements is now an offence under section 14 of the Customs Act 2015.
The Act positively contributes towards Ireland’s compliance with its international legal obligations as identified in the 2024 ICJ Advisory Opinion, including the obligation on states to take steps to prevent trade or investment relations that assist in maintaining the illegal situation created by Israel in the occupied Palestinian territory.
Regarding services, there are two principal reasons we are pursuing prohibition of trade in services at the EU rather than national level: the lack of a clear legal basis available under EU law for a Member State to act at the national level, and the practical challenges relating to implementation and enforcement.
In the case of goods, a public policy exception exists in the EU regulation which controls the import of goods. This allows Member States to adopt prohibitions on the import of goods for public policy reasons. There is no equivalent or similar broad public policy exception relating to external trade in services.
The Government must ensure that measures adopted are not only politically meaningful, but also legally defens

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she plans to have an Ireland House Model in Bangkok.
reply:
There is an Embassy of Ireland in Bangkok, Thailand's capital city.
Ireland Houses involve the co-location of Irish diplomatic missions and State Agencies working together under one roof, sharing services and facilities and adopting collaborative work practices.
While State Agencies such as Bord Bia, Enterprise Ireland, IDA Ireland and Tourism Ireland have offices in different cities around Asia, some of which they share with Irish diplomatic missions in an Ireland House format, none of these State Agencies have offices in Bangkok.
There are therefore no plans at present to open an Ireland House in Bangkok.
There are currently twenty Ireland Houses overseas shared by Embassies or Consulate Generals and State Agencies, and these are located in Atlanta, Austin, Beijing, Chicago, Kuala Lumpur, Los Angeles, Madrid, Mumbai, New York, Prague, Riyadh, San Francisco, São Paulo, Seoul, Shanghai, Singapore, Stockholm, Sydney, Tokyo and Warsaw.
New Ireland House property projects are underway in London and Toronto with both expected to be completed by the end of 2027.

question: Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she will provide a list of diaspora groups and organisations that benefitted from funding from the Emigrant Support Programme during 2025 and 2026.
reply:
The Government’s third Diaspora Strategy was launched on 30 April 2026 at the Global Irish Civic Forum in Croke Park.
The strategy was drafted following a year of consultations with the Irish diaspora and reflects the commitment of the Government to work with the diaspora on a new and unprecedented chapter in diaspora relations.
The Emigrant Support Programme (ESP) remains central to the delivery of the Diaspora Strategy to deepen the ties with the diaspora and support Irish communities abroad. The programme supports organisations across the world to work with the vulnerable and under-represented, and deliver projects and initiatives that strengthen networks and nurture Ireland’s cultural heritage abroad amongst the diaspora.
In 2025, the Government allocated €16.495m to support our diaspora and €17.5m for 2026.
A breakdown of organisations/projects that received funding under the Emigrant Support Programme in 2025 is set out on the programme’s website: www.ireland.ie/en/irish-diaspora/emigrant-support-programme/previous-funding/.
Details of our 2026 funding will be published in late December.
In Budget 2027, the Government allocated €19.5 million to support our diaspora next year, by far the highest to date. Applications for the 2027/2028 Emigrant Support Programme funding round will open on 9 December 2026 and remain open until 14 January 2027. Further details can be found on www.ireland.ie/en/irish-diaspora/emigrant-support-programme/.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade whether her Department or State agencies under its aegis have a policy regarding the use of artificial intelligence to produce artwork for social media, public information campaigns, and graphic design.
reply:
My Department has made available to staff its Policy for the Appropriate Use of Artificial Intelligence, which is aligned with the Guidelines for the Responsible Use of AI in the Public Service. The Policy makes clear that any content produced with the assistance of artificial intelligence must be reviewed, validated and approved by an appropriately authorised staff member before use. It further provides that material intended for public dissemination should not be generated or published without appropriate human oversight, review and accountability.
All official outputs remain the responsibility of the relevant officials and are subject to established quality assurance, clearance and approval processes. The Policy also provides guidance on the appropriate use of AI tools, data protection considerations, information security requirements and the importance of maintaining human oversight and professional judgement.
In addition, my Department's Communications Unit has issued supplementary guidance for staff regarding the use of AI in communications activities. This guidance advises that AI-generated imagery should not be used in external communications.
The Department has no State agencies under its aegis.

We welcome the participation of these organisations, and believe that they may contribute to the richness of the conversation.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Taoiseach the timeline for the formal establishment of the proposed public body to examine the models and challenges of Irish unification; the intended staffing and recruitment structure for research and policy roles within this body.
reply:
The principle of consent and the possibility of change in the constitutional status of Northern Ireland are fundamental elements of the Good Friday Agreement, endorsed by the people of this island, North and South.
The Government respects and upholds everyone’s right on this island to make the case for the constitutional future for Northern Ireland they wish to see, and to work for.
The Government intends to establish a body to oversee a programme of research and consultation on a range of future constitutional scenarios. It is proposed that the terms of reference for such a body will be published by the Government before the end of the year.
The overall objective will be to foster a more informed, inclusive and comprehensive public discourse and expert analysis over time.
The Good Friday Agreement is the blueprint for unlocking the full potential of our island, and the Government is committed to implementing the Good Friday Agreement in full. The Government will continue to prioritise the essential work of building understanding and consensus across all communities and political traditions around a shared future for all who live on the island.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Taoiseach whether his Department or State agencies under its aegis have a policy regarding the use of artificial intelligence to produce artwork for social media, public information campaigns, and graphic design.
reply:
In its Statement of Strategy 2025 - 2028, the Department of the Taoiseach commits to the judicious deployment of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology with a view to enhancing its capacity to deliver its strategic and operational objectives.
The Department has an AI Governance Board which oversees the ongoing development and iteration of its AI strategy and policy in line with the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation's Guidelines for the Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Public Service and the National Cyber Security Centre's Guidelines on "Securing AI Adoption in the Public Sector".
The Department employs specialist communications staff with design and videography skills. While some of the design and video editing software programmes used by the Department include generative AI tools, the Department has not used these features to produce artwork for social media, public information campaigns, or graphic design of published reports and documents.
The National Economic and Social Development Office (NESDO) is the only body under the aegis of the Department of the Taoiseach. NESDO does not use any AI tools for any graphic design or similar work in place of artists, designers or videographers.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Taoiseach the number of complaints of bullying, harassment or sexual harassment made against a Minister or Minister of State by a civil servant or other person working in a Government Department that have been received by or notified to his Department in each of the years 2020 to 2025 and to date in 2026; and the number of such complaints investigated and the number upheld in each year; noting that no information identifying any individual is sought; in tabular form.
reply:
The Department of the Taoiseach is committed to protecting dignity and respect in the workplace and is guided by Circular 12/2026 on Dignity at Work and the Civil Service Code of Standards and Behaviour in this regard.
No complaint of bullying, harassment or sexual harassment against any office holder was received by, or notified to, the Department's Personnel Officer in the period specified by the Deputy.

question: Deputy George Lawlor asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will commit to engagement with both the Minister for Finance and outside groups in pursuing and promoting the concept of employee ownership trusts.
reply:
An Employee Ownership Trust is a form of employee ownership structure wherein a trust acquires a significant stake in the company on behalf of the workers. In effect, this structure allows for collective ownership of the company by its employees without requiring workers to purchase shares individually. I appreciate that an EOT structure could represent a new partnership approach, within an Irish context, and believe that it would be worthwhile examining the potential for an EOT structure in this light.
It is my understanding that a number of countries have either recently introduced, or are currently examining the introduction of an EOT structure. Furthermore, I understand that EOTs have seen significant growth in the UK since relevant changes to tax law were introduced there in 2014. It is my Department’s present understanding that the promotion of an EOT structure in Ireland does not require changes to company law and that the promotion of an EOT structure is primarily concerned with changes to tax law.
Ultimately, matters of tax policy are a consideration for the Minister for Finance as part of the annual budgetary process. In this context, any changes to tax law would need to be carefully considered.

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if his attention has been drawn to a paper (details supplied); and the consideration his Department has given to the recommendations therein.
reply:
I welcome all contributions to the ongoing policy debate on promoting quality employment and good jobs, including, of course, ICTU's Quality Employment and Good Jobs Paper, published by the Nevin Economic Research Institute - or NERI.
Our Government recognises that economic success is measured not only by growth and investment, but also by the availability of quality employment that provides security, opportunity, fair reward and pathways for career development.
To this end, the Government has taken significant steps to promote quality employment, including increasing the National Minimum Wage, introducing statutory sick leave and remote-working rights, strengthening protections on tips and working conditions, extending working-time protections and strengthening employees’ right to remain at work until State pension age.
Moreover, a key focus of discussions during Ireland's Presidency of the Council of the European Union is how best to create and sustain high-quality jobs in a rapidly changing labour market, ensuring that workers and employers alike can benefit from opportunities within and beyond the Single Market. The Presidency has actively supported the development of the European Commission's proposed Quality Jobs Act, an initiative under the Quality Jobs Roadmap. This Act is intended to strengthen worker protections while supporting productivity, competitiveness and labour market resilience. It will complement a range of existing EU initiatives, including the Competitiv

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the position regarding any Department-led initiative in relation to future proof employment legislation in the ever-changing jobs market due to AI technology changes.
reply:
Ireland has a robust suite of employment rights legislation which applies regardless of whether AI or other advanced technologies are used in the workplace. While there are currently no plans for AI-specific employment legislation, the Government keeps the suite of employment rights legislation under ongoing review to ensure it remains effective and fit for purpose in a changing labour market. This work is informed by the Employment Law Review Group (ELRG), which monitors, reviews and advises on all aspects of employment and redundancy law.
The Government also recognises that AI has the potential to reshape labour markets, skills demand and work practices. Accordingly, my Department continues to monitor developments in this area through research and analysis undertaken by the Expert Group on Future Skills Needs (EGFSN), including its recent reports The Irish Labour Market and AI in 2026 and Skills for Digital Specialists: An Assessment of the Future Skills Needs of Ireland's Digital Specialists to 2030.
More broadly, the National Digital and AI Strategy, Digital Ireland: Connecting Our People, Securing Our Future, sets out measures to support the responsible adoption of AI while ensuring workers can adapt to technological change.
The Government will continue to keep both labour market developments and the adequacy of employment protections under review as AI technologies evolve.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to report on the recent AI summit organised by his Department, including its final cost; and the rationale behind the selection of speakers.
reply:
My Department hosted the International AI Summit 2026 on 14 October at the Royal Dublin Society, or RDS. This was a flagship event of Ireland's 2026 Presidency of the Council of the European Union. The Summit brought together government representatives, EU institutions, industry leaders, investors, researchers and academics. Discussions focused on how artificial intelligence can support competitiveness, innovation and economic growth across Europe.
Speakers were nominated with the Department’s stakeholders in IDA and EI across a number of key areas relevant to the Summit's focus on artificial intelligence, competitiveness, innovation and economic growth. The agenda reflected the range of expertise needed to inform discussion of these themes.
Speakers were aligned with the Summit's three strategic themes: Applied AI and Sectoral Value Creation; Infrastructure: Building Europe's AI Capacity; and The AI Opportunity Ahead. Speakers were selected for expertise relevant to the practical application of AI across sectors, the infrastructure needed to build Europe's AI capacity, and the opportunities for AI to support future innovation and competitiveness.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to outline the assessment his Department has undertaken of the potential advantages and disadvantages for Irish companies of operating under the proposed EU Inc. framework rather than existing Irish corporate structures.
reply:
The proposed new corporate form, EU Inc., will be an optional, digital-by-default European corporate framework intended to make it easier for businesses to start, operate and grow across the EU.
From a domestic perspective, Ireland already benefits from a modern and well-regarded company law regime. In future, Irish companies who convert to an EU Inc., or new companies that incorporate directly as an EU Inc., will benefit from a single corporate form recognised across the EU, facilitating cross-border operations and potentially improving access to finance. The particular advantages of EU Inc. will depend on a company’s business model and growth ambitions and are likely to be most significant for those companies seeking to scale or operate in cross-border activity.
It is important to emphasise that negotiations have not been completed on the EU Inc. file. Under the Irish Presidency, agreement was secured in October on a Council negotiating mandate. However, the European Parliament has yet to adopt a position. A final agreement on EU Inc. will depend on forthcoming trilogue negotiations.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment his plans to amend employment legislation to improve employment rights and job security of film workers.
reply:
As Minister for Employment, Small Business and Retail, I have responsibility for a robust suite of employment rights legislation that protects all workers, including those employed in the film and audiovisual industry. It is important to note that all employers, regardless of sector, are responsible for ensuring that their employees receive the protections afforded to them under employment legislation.
There is no exemption or separate category under Irish employment law for individuals working in the film sector. Employment rights legislation, including the National Minimum Wage, Payment of Wages, Organisation of Working Time, Employment Equality Acts, Health and Safety, Terms of Employment (Information) Act and Unfair Dismissals Act (in certain circumstances), apply horizontally across all sectors.
The Deputy will be aware that work in the film sector is often project based. As such, workers are often hired on fixed-term contracts for the duration of a project.
The Protection of Employees (Fixed-Term Workers) Act 2003 provides for the improvement of the quality of fixed-term work by ensuring the application of the principle of non discrimination (i.e. fixed-term workers may not be treated less favourably than comparable permanent workers). The Act transposes EU Directive 1999/70/EC concerning the Framework Agreement on Fixed-term Work into Irish law.
The Act also provides for the establishment of a framework to prevent abuse arising from the use of successive fixed-term emp

question: Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the assessment his Department has made of the impact of high public liability and employer liability insurance premiums on SMEs, hospitality businesses and community organisations; to confirm the details of any such assessment.
reply:
While my Department has not undertaken a specific assessment of the impact of public liability and employer liability insurance premiums on SMEs, hospitality businesses and community organisations, I am aware that insurance costs continue to be identified by enterprises as a significant input cost component of doing business.
The issue of insurance costs was considered by the Cost of Business Advisory Forum, established under a commitment in the Programme for Government to examine the factors contributing to the cost of doing business in Ireland. The Forum's Final Report, published in August 2026, identified insurance as one of a number of important non-pay cost drivers affecting enterprises. In its Final Report, the Forum made recommendations aimed at improving competitiveness, increasing transparency and reducing business costs. This report is published on the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment website.
More generally, my Department regularly engages with businesses and representative organisations, including SME and hospitality sector stakeholders, which have highlighted concerns regarding the affordability and availability of insurance cover and the impact of insurance costs on business operations and growth.
