question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment given the economic reliance on multinational corporations engaged in artificial intelligence, the way in which the market volatility of these companies affect the Government’s National Digital and AI Strategy decisions.
reply:
The National Digital and AI Strategy - Digital Ireland provides the long-term framework for Ireland's approach to harnessing the opportunities of artificial intelligence across the economy and society. The Strategy is focused on supporting innovation and enterprise, investment in digital infrastructure, developing AI and digital skills, enhancing public services, and promoting responsible AI adoption to ensure Ireland remains internationally competitive in an increasingly digital economy. The Strategy is being implemented through a broad range of actions across Government and its agencies.
While multinational technology companies continue to make an important contribution to Ireland's digital economy, Digital Ireland is focused on ensuring that the benefits of AI are shared across the wider economy, reflecting the fact that long-term competitiveness and resilience also depend on a strong and innovative domestic enterprise base. In particular, a central pillar of Digital Ireland is to accelerate AI adoption among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), enabling them to enhance productivity, drive innovation, improve competitiveness and access new opportunities for growth.
Through targeted supports delivered by Enterprise Ireland and other agencies, the Strategy includes measures such as targeted funding for SMEs, building AI awareness and advisory supports. question: Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment for a report on his work on the Red Tape Challenge initiative.
reply:
Regulation, and the extent of any regulatory or administrative burden, has recently become a greater focus both at European Union level and nationally as a means to enhance competitiveness. question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the funding allocated in Budget 2027 to develop Next Generation Strategic Sites.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he is considering a review of policy on dual-use exports and to ban exports to countries in breach of international law.
reply:
Controls on the export of dual-use items are administered by my Department, in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2021/821 of the European Parliament and of the Council setting up a Union regime for the control of exports, brokering, technical assistance, transit and transfer of dual-use items.
The bulk of dual-use exports from Ireland are mainstream business ICT products, both hardware and software. They are categorised as dual-use items as a consequence of the fact that they incorporate strong encryption for ICT security purposes.
All export licence applications are considered by my officials in accordance with criteria set out within the relevant dual-use and military EU and National Regulations and with Ireland’s international obligations and responsibilities as members of non-proliferation regimes and export control arrangements. Each application is considered on its own merits, taking account of the nature of the items concerned, the destination, the end-user and the stated end-use. Decisions are guided by the EU Common Position and its eight criteria, which include respect for human rights, international obligations, regional stability and risk of diversion to another end use or end user.

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will consider putting in place additional measures to ensure that financially viable multi-national companies that close or move their operations for strategic reasons provide an increased level of support and redundancy provision in line with their financial situation to alleviate the impact of a strategic decision on the devastated staff and communities left in their wake.
reply:
The Redundancy Payments Act 1967, as amended, provides for a minimum statutory redundancy payment to eligible employees who are made redundant.
In order to be eligible for a statutory redundancy payment, an employee must have at least two years’ continuous service with an employer, excluding any period of employment with that employer before the age of 16 years, and be in employment which is insurable under the Social Welfare Acts.
An eligible employee is entitled to two weeks' pay for every year of service plus one additional week's pay, with weekly pay capped at €600 per week. It is the employer’s responsibility to pay statutory redundancy to eligible employees. This entitlement applies equally to all eligible employees being made redundant, regardless of the reason underpinning the redundancies.
In certain circumstances, an employer may offer a redundancy payment which is over and above the statutory amount. This is sometimes referred to as enhanced redundancy.
Negotiations on enhanced redundancy packages, over and above the statutory amount set out in law, are entirely a matter for negotiation and agreement between employers and employees and the State has no role in this matter.
The State’s independent industrial relations dispute settlement mechanisms, the Workplace Relations Commission and the Labour Court, can support parties where needed in their efforts to resolve their differences.

question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the plans in place for the expansion of the growth and sustainability loan scheme.
reply:
On 12 October 2026, I announced a significant expansion of the Growth and Sustainability Loan Scheme. The expansion doubles the Scheme's lending capacity from €500 million to €1 billion and extends its availability until 30 June 2029.

It provides access to competitively priced, longer-term finance for eligible businesses and primary producers to support investment in growth, innovation, productivity, resilience and sustainability. Loans are available from €25,000 to €3 million, for terms of up to 10 years, with loans of up to €500,000 available without a collateral requirement. The expanded Scheme is available through participating finance providers.

• Embracing research, innovation and skills
• Boosting FDI and exports and influencing at an EU level
• Creating and scaling more SMEs
• Regulating for growth and controlling costs
• Increasing the State’s capacity to deliver infrastructure
• Growing sustainable Irish businesses and boosting regional development

question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will undertake a further review of the critical skills occupations list in light of the increasing difficulties being experienced by Irish graduates in securing employment; and if he is satisfied that the occupations currently included on the list reflect the actual skills shortages in the labour market.
reply:
The employment permits system is designed to address clearly evidenced labour and skills shortages that can not be met from within the domestic or wider EEA labour market.
The Critical Skills Occupations List and the Ineligible Occupations List are reviewed periodically to ensure that the employment permits system remains aligned with current labour market intelligence. The review process includes public and stakeholder consultation, providing an opportunity for stakeholders to present sector-specific evidence of labour and skills shortages or surpluses.
During periods of economic expansion, the range of eligible occupations can be broadened to address labour and skills shortages. During periods of economic contraction, eligible occupation categories can be narrowed and additional restrictions applied.
The review process is informed by analysis from the Expert Group on Future Skills Needs (EGFSN) and the Skills and Labour Market Research Unit (SLMRU) of SOLAS, and is overseen by the Economic Migration Policy Interdepartmental Group (IDG). The reviews assess where adjustments are appropriate based on the available evidence and the observations of relevant Government Departments and the IDG.

The tables presented at the end of this response set out the number of inspections by year and by sector.
HSA Inspectors carry out inspections across all work sectors and work activities which come under the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 and the Chemicals Act 2008. Whereas some workplaces are pre-selected for inspection based on risk and previous history, most inspections are targeted at high-risk sectors such as construction, agriculture, forestry, manufacturing, mines, quarries, transport of dangerous goods by road, or the chemical sectors. Other inspections can be part of a campaign. Approximately 5% of all visits are due to accident and/or complaint investigations.
HSA inspectors, following an inspection may give advice either verbally or in writing, on how a duty holder can make improvements on health and safety in their workplace. The inspector may also take action if the inspector finds a duty holder is breaking the law or the inspector may stop work which is dangerous.
Enforcement actions may include:
• A Report of Inspection setting out areas for improvement and advice about health and safety at work.
• An Improvement Notice or a Contravention Notice for breach

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will report on the findings of the Driving Cost Savings for Business Through Industrial Decarbonisation report.
reply:
As Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, I am committed to enhancing the long-term competitiveness and resilience of our manufacturing industries by supporting their decarbonisation ambitions. On the 19th of October, I published the report Driving Cost Savings for Business Through Industrial Decarbonisation, in collaboration with the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment. The report outlines how Irish-based manufacturers are being supported by Enterprise Ireland, IDA Ireland and the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland to invest in decarbonisation.
The report highlights how Ireland’s industrial emissions are now decoupled from economic and population growth. The drive to electrify industry, encourage the uptake of renewable fuels, and focus on energy efficiency measures has reduced Ireland’s industrial emissions by 15.9% on 2018 levels to date. This is ahead of the Environmental Protection Agency’s With Additional Measures (WAM) estimate of an 11.8% decrease between 2018 and 2030.
The report identifies my Department's Environmental Aid fund as a key enabler of industrial decarbonisation, helping firms invest in technologies that improve energy efficiency, reduce operating costs and strengthen long-term competitiveness. question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will outline his proposals and considerations regarding Ireland's employment permit system.

The system is vacancy-led and managed through the Critical Skills Occupations List and the Ineligible Occupations List, which are reviewed periodically to ensure they remain aligned with labour market needs and Government policy objectives.
In framing economic migration policy and employment permits legislation, my Department takes an evidence-based approach, informed by labour market data, stakeholder engagement and consultation across Government, but also more directly with relevant Government Departments through the Interdepartmental Group on Economic Migration Policy.

question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will review the operation of the employment permit system, particularly the requirement for employers to demonstrate that they have made reasonable efforts to recruit suitable candidates from within Ireland and the European Economic Area before seeking to employ workers from outside the EEA.
reply:
The employment permits system is grounded in legislation that sets clear and objective criteria applied to the grant of an employment permit including minimum salary thresholds, availability of skills in the domestic labour market, and the eligibility of occupations. These criteria ensure that permits are issued only where there is a demonstrable shortage and that the system remains fair, transparent, and responsive to Ireland’s labour market needs.
A key mechanism supporting these objectives is the Labour Market Needs Test (LMNT), which requires employers seeking to recruit a non-EEA national under certain permit types to demonstrate that genuine efforts have been made to recruit from within Ireland and the wider EEA before an employment permit application can be considered.
The Employment Permits Act 2024 updated the LMNT requirement by removing the need for vacancies to be advertised in hard copy newspapers. The revised LMNT process now allows employers to advertise the vacancy on at least one online platform in addition to the Department of Social Protection’s JobsIreland and EURES online employment services. Suitable platforms include those that are accessible to the general public, the principal purpose of which is to publish offers of employment including for example online newspaper publications and employment websites.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he has engaged with Irish data centre construction companies in relation to an investigation finding them in gross breach of workers' rights across Europe (details supplied); if he has concerns that similar abuses may occur or be occurring on data centre construction sites in this country.

The development of data centre infrastructure must not come at the expense of workers’ safety or employment rights. These principles apply equally to Irish businesses operating internationally. Those businesses must comply with the applicable employment and occupational safety and health requirements in the jurisdictions in which they operate.

Employers have legal obligations to safeguard the safety, health and welfare of their employees. We also maintain a comprehensive body of employment rights legislation that safeguards workers and promotes fair treatment in the workplace. question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht to provide a chronology of all actions taken by his Department since 2009 with a view to commencing the financial reporting provisions of the Charities Act 2009, including any consultations with the Charities Regulator.
reply:
The Charities Regulatory Authority (the ‘Charities Regulator’) was established in October 2014 pursuant to the Charities Act 2009. The Charities Regulator is the State's independent statutory agency responsible for registering and regulating Ireland’s charities, with the mandate to promote good governance practice.
The Charities Act 2009 is fully commenced with the exception of sections 89 and 93-98.
Section 89 was repealed and replaced by section 6A of the Charities (Amendment) Act 2024. Section 6A was commenced in January 2025.
Further sections of the Charities (Amendment) Act 2024 were commenced on 30 October 2026, including section 17 which amended section 48 of the 2009 Act, allowing for the introduction of regulations that prescribe the form and content of financial statements to be prepared by charitable organisations.
The timing of the introduction of regulations, and the commencement of the remaining sections of the Act, will take into account the operational impacts on the Charities Regulator and the charity sector respectively.
At present, each registered charity is legally obliged under section 52 of the Charities Act 2009 to submit an annual report to the Charities Regulator within 10 months of their financial year end. That information is publicly available for each charity on the public Register.

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Sinéad Gibney den Aire Forbartha Tuaithe agus Pobail, agus Gaeltachta cén uair a fhoilseofar na caighdeáin teanga chríochnaithe; agus an ndéanfaidh sé ráiteas ina thaobh.
reply:
Bhí ríméad orm fógra a dhéanamh ag Oireachtas na Samhna le déanaí go bhfuil dréacht de na Caighdeáin Teanga glanta agam le seoladh chuig an gCoiste Comhairleach um Sheirbhísí Gaeilge mar chéad chéim den phróiseas comhairliúcháin orthu. Tá an dréacht seo de na Caighdeáin dírithe ar eagraíochtaí ar leith a thagann faoi scáth Acht na dTeangacha Oifigiúla, is iad sin - Ranna agus Oifigí Rialtais, Údaráis Áitiúla agus Comhlachtaí Fóntais Phoiblí.
Déanfaidh an Coiste Comhairleach scrúdú ar an dréacht agus ansin tabharfar faoi na céimeanna eile den phróiseas comhairliúcháin mar atá leagtha amach san Acht:
• Comhairliúchán leis na Ranna Rialtais;
• Comhairliúchán leis na hOifigí Rialtais, Údaráis Áitiúla agus comhlachtaí fóntais phoiblí atá luaite sna Caighdeáin; agus
• Comhairliúchán leis an bpobal i gcoitinne.
Cé nach bhfuil aon amscála don phróiseas iomlán leagtha síos san Acht, meastar go dtógfaidh sé thart ar ocht mí ó thús go deireadh. Foilseofar cóip de na dréacht-Chaighdeáin mar chuid den chomhairliúchán poiblí a dhéanfar orthu. Tar éis den phróiseas comhairliúcháin a bheith curtha i gcrích an bhliain seo chugainn, déanfar na heagraíochtaí poiblí cuí a fhorordú chun críche na gCaighdeán cuí.
Tá mé an-dóchasach faoin dea-thionchar a bheidh ag na Caighdeáin Teanga, atá bunaithe ar an gcóras rathúil atá i bhfeidhm sa Bhreatain Bheag agus a chuirfidh dualgais bhreise, dhearfacha ar eagraíochtaí poiblí maidir le seirbhísí poiblí Gaeilge a sholáthar.
Tógfar sna Caighdeáin chomh mai

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht whether his Department or State agencies under its aegis have a policy regarding the use of artificial intelligence to produce artwork for social media, public information campaigns, and graphic design.
reply:

question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if changes in visa application processes are having a negative impact on Ireland's reputation and attractiveness to international students.
reply:
I am aware of the concerns being raised in the higher education sector regarding visa processing. These concerns have been raised directly with me, and I have met with representative bodies to hear their views.
I have also directed my officials to engage with colleagues in the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration on these matters. However, ultimately responsibility for visa processing rests with that department and my department has no role in such matters.
While concerns have been raised by stakeholders, I am not aware of any evidence that these issues have materially affected Ireland's overall attractiveness as a destination for international students.
My department will continue to engage with the sector and monitor developments closely.
Ireland remains committed to ensuring that we are a destination of choice for high-calibre international students, researchers and innovators, in line with the objectives of Global Citizens 2030.
Despite increased competition globally, Ireland's higher education system continues to enjoy a strong international reputation based on the quality of its education and research, the breadth of programmes available, and the global recognition of Irish qualifications.

question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to address concerns among HEI's that the significant surplus in the National Training Fund is not being used to meet higher education and research critical funding needs.
reply:

Established under the National Training Fund Act 2000, the NTF is a dedicated funding mechanism that supports lifelong learning and workforce development. It invests in raising the skills of people in employment, provides training opportunities for those seeking to enter or re-enter the labour market, and supports the identification of skills needs across the economy to ensure Ireland remains competitive and responsive to emerging challenges.
Over the past decade, the NTF has grown significantly in both scale and impact. Expenditure has risen from €360 million in 2017 to over €1.15 billion allocated in 2026, reflecting a substantial expansion in investment in education, training and skills development.

question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the engagements his Department had with TUD regarding their ongoing financial difficulties, as highlighted by the Comptroller and Auditor General in September 2025.
reply:
The Higher Education Authority (HEA), which has statutory responsibility for oversight of publicly funded higher education institutions, has been engaged with Technological University Dublin (TU Dublin) through a Section 64 review process since 2024.
TU Dublin was subsequently requested to prepare a recovery plan to address concerns identified by the HEA, including the timeliness and accuracy of financial reporting and forecasting and the University's financial position.
TU Dublin continues to implement a recovery programme arising from the Section 64 review. The HEA requires quarterly reports on progress in implementing the associated Action Plan.
Representatives of TU Dublin's Governing Body and the HEA met most recently on 16 September 2026 to discuss the University's Plan for Financial Stability. TU Dublin advised that implementation of the Plan has commenced and that both the Governing Body and Executive are fully committed to eliminating the University's deficit.
My Department remains in close engagement with the HEA regarding TU Dublin's financial position and recovery programme and will continue to monitor developments.

question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the financial supports that are available to students completing their Erasmus in the United States.
reply:

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the statutory powers available to Quality and Qualifications Ireland in respect of private providers operating in the State that offer programmes leading to awards from non-Irish awarding bodies, including powers to require that learners are given accurate information on professional recognition and to protect learners where that information proves misleading; whether he will bring forward legislative change to close the regulatory gap.
reply:

QQI has responsibility for oversight of providers operating within the National Framework of Qualifications (NFQ), including matters relating to access, transfer and progression arrangements for learners.

reply:

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if his attention has been drawn to a skills certification barrier to the rapid mobilisation of international utility crews for emergency storm restoration where certain activities require a specific construction certification, which has the potential to affect any critical infrastructure operator that is required to rapidly mobilise crews from outside the State; if he is aware that ESB Networks are meeting with SOLAS to resolve this issue; and if his Department engaged with either or both parties to see if a rapid resolution can be achieved.
reply:
SOLAS is engaging with ESB Networks on this matter, and further discussions are being arranged. The engagement is focused on how SOLAS, ESB Networks and the relevant Departments can work together to support the timely recognition of international qualifications and occupational competence for emergency mobilisation, while continuing to maintain the necessary statutory, safety and competency requirements.
There is an existing EU framework for the recognition of professional qualifications, under Directive 2005/36/EC which facilitates the mobility of appropriately qualified workers within the EU/EEA. This also provides a mechanism to fast-track the recognition of competent persons from countries covered by the Directive for both temporary and occasional entry into the State to carry out their profession. In the period January to October 2026, SOLAS approved 287 temporary applications.
This mechanism is not available to persons coming into the State from third countries. In these cases, SOLAS must have regard to the provisions of the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 and the Regulations prescribed under that Act. The Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 is under the remit of the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment.

GRETB’s proposal aims to provide a state-of-the-art purpose-built College building, on a site owned by GRETB located adjacent to the existing Training Centre in Mervue. The development will provide a modern, sustainable, and highly visible education campus, consolidating GRETB’s FET provision within the city into a single, fit-for-purpose location. This new development will facilitate the expansion of services in the city with additional full-time and part-time offerings including additional traineeships, apprenticeships, and programmes for enterprise provided on the campus.

This framework has been evaluated and is now in place for all ETB’s who are ready to draw down services.

question: Deputy Niall Collins asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if he can assist a person (details supplied).

The Deputy will be aware that Higher Education Institutions are autonomous bodies with statutory responsibility for their own governance and operational affairs, including matters relating to tuition fees. Decisions regarding the fees charged to individual students, the determination of fee status and the assessment of eligibility for the Free Fees Initiative are matters for the institution concerned, having regard to its statutory autonomy.
In relation to the Free Fees Initiative, first-time undergraduate students attending an approved full-time course may be eligible to have their tuition fees paid on their behalf, subject to meeting all of the scheme's eligibility criteria. question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Health if she will outline the reasons for rejecting calls from families affected by the scoliosis and spina bifida controversy for a Public Tribunal of Inquiry.
reply:
I published the independent report of the Children's Health Ireland Inquiry into Spina Bifida and Complex Scoliosis Scoping Exercise on 28 September following engagement with patients and families. Mr Farrell, the independent facilitator of the scoping exercise, recommended a Commission of Investigation covering four defined modules; waiting lists, spinal surgery, hip dysplasia and the cohort of children who were not transferred to Temple Street post 2008.
Mr Farrell’s recommendation for a Commission of Investigation was based on the view that a Commission can deliver the same core statutory powers as a Tribunal while being better suited to the specific subject matter of the inquiry, namely the medical treatment of children. A Commission can compel witnesses and the production of documents and would publish a final report. Mr Farrell is of the view that as the issues deal with the personal and medical information of children who have specific legal protections and given the relatively finite number of children, there is a significant risk that children may be identifiable.
A Commission, by default is conducted in private which alleviates those concerns compared to a Tribunal which by default is conducted in private. I am aware that there is a view among some parents that it should be entirely in public. A Commission has a more flexible framework which could allow an element of the proceedings to occur in public.

reply:
Sexual health is a priority for this Government. The National Sexual Health Strategy, 2025-35 was published last year, and an HIV Action Plan is in preparation. The national HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) programme commenced in 2019, following a HIQA HTA, which concluded that its introduction would be safe, effective, and cost saving.
The HIV Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis scheme is available to people ordinarily resident in Ireland who are deemed at risk of HIV and likely to benefit clinically from its prevention. PrEP can be accessed through 14 public PrEP clinics or through 50 approved private PrEP providers; more details are available on the HSE website: www2.hse.ie/conditions/hiv/about-prep/.
Appointments at the public PrEP services are free of charge, however, the private providers charge for consultations. PrEP medications are free of charge. The population has grown significantly in recent years, and clinical criteria for PrEP eligibility have been widened, increasing the number of people eligible for PrEP. While the PrEP service continues to grow, many PrEP services had reached capacity and service users are reporting challenges accessing appointments.
In order to expand PrEP services and provide additional supports to our rapidly growing population, we allocated additional funding of €550,000, and 7 WTE through Budget 2025, and an additional €100,000 in 2026, to further support delivery of the PrEP scheme. question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment his plans to ensure that workers working for Irish construction companies at data centre construction sites domestically and abroad are operating within the framework of labour legislation.
reply:
I am deeply concerned by the matters outlined in the media report about working conditions in some datacentres in the European Union. All workers should be able to carry out their work safely and raise concerns about their working conditions without intimidation.
The development of data centre infrastructure must not come at the expense of workers’ safety or employment rights. These principles apply equally to Irish businesses operating internationally. Those businesses must comply with the applicable employment and occupational safety and health requirements in the jurisdictions in which they operate.
Ireland maintains a robust occupational safety and health regulatory framework designed to protect workers. Employers have legal obligations to safeguard the safety, health and welfare of their employees.
We also maintain a comprehensive body of employment rights legislation that safeguards workers and promotes fair treatment in the workplace. This legislation applies horizontally across all sectors to all employees employed in the State.
It is important to distinguish allegations concerning particular companies from findings made by the competent authorities. question: Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Health whether the HSE is discontinuing toshai blister packs or removing associated machines from pharmacies; the reasons, timeline, and consultation undertaken; whether changes will be paused pending assessment of patient safety and accessibility; the alternatives for patients unable to use standard blister packs; the supports for blister-packing costs, including for long-term illness scheme patients.
reply:
My Department has not placed any requirements on operational aspects for blister-packing practices in community pharmacies, nor does it specify any particular automation aspects.
Regarding supports for blister-packing costs, in March 2026 I announced the introduction of a new patient-centred medicines optimisation support service (MOSS) framework which commenced on 1 June 2026.
This framework is designed to strengthen supports for medical card holders in vulnerable patient groups, including those with diagnosed cognitive impairment or dementia, intellectual disability, physical impairment or those patients at risk of medication misuse. The reform ensures that resources are targeted towards those who genuinely need them. These patients will be supported where appropriate with a range of tailored supports including:
• adjustments to facilitate use of original packaging.
• medication reminder systems.
• administration charts.
• instalment dispensing; and
• blister packs where clinically necessary.
Blister packs remain a last resort in line with the international evidence due to associated risks including reduced patient autonomy and potential safety concerns. It is also important to note that not all medicines are suitable for blister packs. Pharmacists will consider relevant medicine-specific factors to assess if all the patient’s individual medicines are suitable for supply in a blister pack. As Minister for Health, I am dedicated to enhancing Ireland’s population screening programmes, which are a vital component of our health services. They enable early treatment and care for many people, thereby enhancing the overall health of our community.
I would note that consideration of any proposed changes to Ireland’s screening programmes will be facilitated through established evidence-driven protocols.
The National Screening Advisory Committee (NSAC) is the expert group that considers proposed changes to Ireland’s screening programmes. NSAC assesses the evidence in a robust and transparent manner and against internationally accepted criteria, before making recommendations to myself as Minister.
It is important that we have rigorous processes in place to ensure our screening programmes are effective, quality assured, validated and operating to safe standards, and that the benefits of screening outweigh the harms.
NSAC holds annual Calls for Submissions, which invite all stakeholders, including members of the public, HSE and other medical professionals, to propose changes to Ireland’s screening programmes. As part of its 2025 Call for Submissions, NSAC received a proposal related to bone health screening, referencing the increased risk of osteoporosis amongst post-menopausal women.

question: Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Health if her Department has begun evaluating the previous National Maternity Strategy; and if work on a new revision is underway.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 993 and 1000 together.
Maternity care in Ireland is provided in line with the National Maternity Strategy (NMS), Creating a Better Future Together, 2016 - 2026, which is in its final year. The Strategy has delivered significant reform, with the majority of actions now completed or well underway.
Since 2016, €28 million in development funding has been invested through the Strategy, supporting the recruitment of more than 567 additional whole-time equivalent staff, including 44 consultants and over 390 nurses and midwives.
Over €130 million of capital investment has been directed into maternity services over the lifetime of the strategy. This has modernised facilities, delivering refurbishments to wards, and home-from-home birthing rooms across the country.
More than €20 million capital funding has also advanced our information sharing infrastructure, with the Maternal and Neonatal Clinical Management System now live in Cork, Kerry, Limerick, the Rotunda, the National Maternity Hospital, and the Coombe.
The Government remains committed to the continued improvement of maternity services, including the development of a successor National Maternity Strategy, as set out in the Programme for Government.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether, building on the childcare fee reductions announced in Budget 2027, consideration will be given to further supports for families on 50-hour contracts, particularly where providers do not offer shorter options.
reply:
For a place for 50 or more hours per week, from September 2027 the maximum fee for a Core Funding Partner Service will be lowered from €336 per week to €300 per week. When combined with the increase in the Universal National Childcare Scheme subsidy, a family being charged the maximum fee for 50 or more hours (a “Band F” fee) and receiving 45 hours of subsidy, will save more than €52 per week, or more than €2,500 over 48 weeks.
The Government is committed to reduce parental fees to a maximum of €200 per month over the lifetime of the Government. Measures that will come into effect in September 2027 include both a lowering of fee caps for Core Funding Partner Services and increased National Childcare Scheme subsidies. As a result, many parents will see reductions in the amount they pay for early learning and childcare.
Later this year I will publish Shaping the Future Phase 2 which will set out the roadmap for how the €200 commitment will be achieved.
From September 2027, the maximum fees that early learning and childcare providers in receipt of Core Funding can charge will be reduced across all fee bands. All services with fees below the new caps will continue to be subject to existing fee controls.
Over €80 million is being allocated to support providers in adhering to this change to fee management conditions. The total allocation for year 6 of the scheme, commencing in September, is projected to exceed €650 million. This represents a 35% increase over year 5.

It follows the increase in the membership of the Programme in 2025 by five members, and in 2026 by a further ten members, bringing overall membership to its current 136 members. The most recent national application and assessment process for the Programme was undertaken in 2025. It was led by Tusla and independently chaired by a representative of the University of Limerick. Decisions on the successful services were made by an assessment panel.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if she will support extending paid paternity leave.
reply:
There have been significant developments in entitlements for parents of working families in recent years. The Government is committed to supporting workers, including by extending paid leave for parents to allow them to spend more time with their child during their earliest years.
The Paternity Leave and Benefit Act 2016 provides the relevant parent (other than the mother of the child) with 2 weeks paid Paternity Leave Ireland's statutory Paternity Leave arrangements are fully aligned with the requirements of the EU Work-Life Balance Directive, which introduced a minimum standard for Paternity Leave across EU Member States.
Under the Parent’s Leave and Benefit Act 2019, working parents are also entitled to nine weeks of paid Parent's Leave for each relevant parent, to be taken in the first two years after the birth or adoptive placement of a child. Parent's Leave is an individual separate entitlement and is non-transferable between parents.
Under the Parental Leave (Amendment) Act 2019, an employee who is a relevant parent in respect of a child under the age 12 is entitled to 26 weeks’ unpaid Parental Leave for each child. Where a child has a disability or long-term illness, the entitlement can continue until the child is 16. A relevant parent is a parent, an adoptive parent, or a person acting in ‘loco parentis’. Both parents have an equal, separate entitlement to Parental Leave.

question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the way in which she and her Department are engaging in the cross-government network for the child poverty and well-being programme.
reply:

reply:

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to provide an update on the childcare providers who have received proposed commercial rates valuations that threaten the viability of their services.
reply:
The majority of early learning and childcare providers operating on a for-profit basis are liable for commercial rates, as they do not qualify for the not-for-profit exemption under Schedule 4 of the Valuation (Amendment) Act 2015.
Paragraph 22 of the Schedule provides that early childhood care and education facilities that are established and operated on a not-for-profit basis are exempt from rates; it does not provide a general exemption from rates for all childcare or childminding facilities operating on a for-profit basis. To avoid ambiguity, if an early childhood care and education facility is established and operated on a for-profit basis, then it does not fulfil the criteria for exemption under Paragraph 22.
The Department, and others, have previously advised the sector that ECCE-only services are exempt from paying commercial rates under Paragraph 10, Schedule 4 of the Valuation Act 2001. However, I am aware that a number of ECCE-only services have been receiving rates-payable notifications from their Local Authorities.
Given the importance of early learning and childcare for children, families and communities across the country, I am giving this matter my full attention.
I have engaged with my cabinet colleague, Minister Browne, on this matter, and I am hopeful that a satisfactory conclusion can be reached.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he, or his senior officials, have had meetings with the national waste collection permit office since March 2025.

This study, which has been shared with the Department, examines what changes could be made to the permitting system for waste collectors to fully incentivise waste prevention and improve source segregation practices by their customers to minimise their waste collection bills.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the actions her Department is taking to strengthen the rights of non-binary people.
reply:
As Minister for Children, Disability and Equality, responsibility for gender recognition does not come within my remit. question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if his Department is tracking or monitoring the projected fines or financial penalties Ireland could face if we fail to meet our emissions targets.
reply:
It is the preference of the Government to meet our EU climate and energy targets through domestic action and investment, but there are a variety of compliance options available to Member States across the respective instruments.
For example, under the revised Effort Sharing Regulations (ESR), Ireland’s target to reduce emissions is set at 42% compared to 2005 levels by 2030. Within the ESR framework, Member States are encouraged to meet their targets through direct emissions reductions. It should be noted that the ESR framework does not provide for the imposition of direct fines or penalties. However, there are certain other additional compliance measures. This includes the purchase of surplus allowances from Member States who have overperformed on their national targets.
My Department is keenly aware that, as there is no fixed price or price cap per allowance for inter-Member State trading, significant costs may arise for Member States in the event that the purchasing of allowances becomes necessary. Furthermore, no market currently exists for purchasing allowances. The first compliance check only begins in Q2, 2027. It is only then that the supply and demand picture will become clearer.
Estimating these costs requires working with significant data limitations, this was acknowledged by the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council (IFAC) in their multiple reports on the matter.

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the steps being taken to ensure that data centres reduce energy and water consumption.
reply:
Data centres are central to Ireland’s economic and digital future. Unlike many other European countries, Ireland does not have a heavy industrial base. For that reason, the digital economy and its infrastructure is very visible in our electricity demand profile.
According to the Central Statistics Office, the percentage share of metered electricity consumption used by data centres in 2025 was 23%. Uisce Éireann have advised that data centres are not a major driver of demand on the public water supply network, accounting for less than 0.3% of the water supplied by them. Due to advances in cooling technology, modern data centres use relatively small volumes of water. Government is committed to supporting a balanced and plan-led approach to the sustainable growth of data centres and achieving the twin objective of decarbonisation and digitalisation including through stricter and targeted connections criteria, renewable matching and flexibility, alongside coordinated infrastructure development, grid investment, green energy parks and additional renewable generation.

question: Deputy Tony McCormack asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the measures being taken to reduce delays in securing electricity grid connections for new businesses, housing developments and renewable energy projects.
reply:
The management of, and matters related to, connections to the electricity grid are matters for ESB Networks and EirGrid under rules determined by the Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU). ESB Networks, EirGrid and the CRU are independent of me, as Minister, in the exercise of their functions.
The pathway to connect to the electricity grid is dependent on the nature and scale of the project seeking connection. Recent measures to reduce connection times include streamlining permitting processes and developing grid infrastructure.
The CRU’s Electricity Connections Policy – Generation & System Services (ECP-GSS), introduced in 2025, has streamlined the permitting process for onshore renewable energy projects, allowing for the parallel processing of grid connection and planning applications. question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he is aware of the recently published report from the SEAI; to report on the likelihood of reaching 2030 targets based on this data; the measures he is taking to address this.
reply:
Ireland is subject to ambitious EU climate and energy targets up to 2030. Ireland has made substantial progress in the development of renewable electricity capacity in recent years, doubling our wind capacity and establishing a thriving solar industry in the last ten years.
Two cross-Government taskforces, the Accelerating Renewable Electricity Taskforce (ARET) for onshore renewables and the Offshore Wind Delivery Taskforce (OWDT), continue to develop effective policies designed to deliver an accelerated and increased level of renewable generation capacity and related infrastructure.
The Renewable Electricity Support Scheme (RESS), including onshore and offshore wind and solar auctions, is pivotal to the achievement of Ireland’s 2030 target. The sixth onshore auction is underway with final results due to be published in December.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the assessment that has been made of Ireland’s capacity to produce HVO from indigenous feedstocks, including the need for imports and their carbon and sustainability implications; and if any studies have been undertaken in this regard.
reply:
Hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) is a bioliquid which can be used as a renewable energy source for heating and which, in a transport context, is classified as a biofuel. HVO is currently available for consumers to purchase for use in both transport and heating. The Climate Action Plan includes a range of measures to address the use of fossil fuels in heating systems in buildings, with the National Heat Study (2021) published by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland containing the detailed analysis that is informing the development of options to decarbonise the heating and cooling sectors in the period to 2050.
The National Heat Study considered a number of potential decarbonisation options for a wide range of dwellings and business premises. These included the use of liquid biofuels such as HVO, solid biomass, biogases, as well as heat pumps and district heating networks. The recommendation of the National Heat Study is that heat pumps are the optimal decarbonisation path for heating systems, with district heating also being an option that can be widely deployed. However, the National Heat Study also recognised the potential role for sustainable bioenergy for buildings that require alternative routes to decarbonisation, which is being considered as part of a suite of measures to decarbonise heat. question: Deputy Brian Stanley asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will make grants available to persons who can avail of plug-in solar panels, as they currently do not qualify.
reply:

Budget 2027 provided a record €654 million for residential and community energy upgrade schemes. This investment will support more households in improving the energy performance of their homes, lowering energy consumption, reducing bills and improving comfort, while decreasing reliance on imported fossil fuels. question: Deputy Joe Cooney asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if recipients of the SEAI medically vulnerable solar PV scheme are eligible to have their existing systems upgraded with the enhanced scheme announced under budget 2027.
reply:
The Solar PV for the Medically Vulnerable Scheme is a targeted scheme for the installation of solar photovoltaic (PV) panels for customers/households who are registered on the life support category of the Priority Services Register. These homes have a dependence on electrically powered equipment, including medical equipment, life protecting devices and assistive technologies such as dialysis machines and respirators. As such, these households may have a higher energy demand than the average user and this scheme is designed to go some way towards helping to reduce those energy costs.
The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) in conjunction with energy suppliers and is open to all suppliers who wish to participate, with each energy supplier contacting their own eligible customers directly, in line with the work plans for their solar PV installers.
The scheme is kept under ongoing review by my Department and the SEAI, with the SEAI meeting regularly with the energy suppliers, with a focus on continuous improvement of the scheme.
I have recently announced a package of enhanced renewable energy and retrofit grants designed to help households and businesses reduce energy costs, lower dependence on fossil fuels and strengthen Ireland’s energy security.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment in view of the serious funding crisis facing the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) and the risk to completion of its Seventh Assessment Report, whether Ireland will make an immediate additional financial contribution to the IPCC Trust Fund; the amount and date of any contribution planned for 2026; and the steps he is taking at EU and international level to secure sustainable, multi-year funding for the IPCC.
reply:
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) provides the scientific information that is the bedrock of the international climate process. Ensuring that the IPCC is supported to deliver its work and that it can continue to provide the best available science to the UNFCCC process is a key priority of Ireland's international climate diplomacy.
It is deeply regrettable that it was not possible to reach agreement on the timeline for the IPCC's Seventh Assessment Repot (AR7) or the IPCC budget for its work in 2027 at the recent 65th Plenary Meeting in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Ireland stands ready to work with global colleagues in an effort to address this impasse and ensure that the IPCC is ready and able to continue its work on the AR7.
Ireland has long been a supporter of the work of the IPCC and has provided financial support to the IPCC for its work in recent years. Ireland provided €115,000 to the IPCC Trust Fund in both 2024 and 2025, with an additional €150,000 provided in 2025, earmarked for the work AR7's Working Group III, which focuses on mitigation of climate change, in light of the funding challenges facing the IPCC during its AR7 period. Consideration is currently being given to a contribution to the IPCC Trust Fund for 2026.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment following the UK’s decision to permit plug-in solar panels, whether he will introduce a safe, simplified route for households in Ireland to use plug-in solar systems and compatible batteries; and when he expects to publish the necessary technical standards and registration rules.
reply:
Plug-in solar is an emerging low-carbon technology that has seen rapid adoption in countries such as Germany and was recently permitted in the UK. It is the Government’s intention to accelerate the introduction of plug-in solar in Ireland. Once enabled, it could present a cost-effective and accessible option for customers to become more active participants in our energy transition, with benefits including lower electricity bills, greater demand flexibility and supporting our renewable energy and climate ambitions.
At my request, ESB Networks established a plug-in solar working group in May of this year to identify and assess potential pathways for the safe, standardised and scalable deployment of plug-in solar in Ireland. The working group has convened nine times to date.
The working group recently submitted an options report for my Department’s consideration including recommendations on the proposed installation approach, product specification pathway, customer guidance and more.
While the focus has been on plug-in solar, in alignment with the sequence of development of these emerging technologies, plug-in batteries have also been considered and detailed work will take place on this in due course.

Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment his plans to assist families and individuals who are in arrears with their energy bills.

The over-90-day figures provide a better indication of how many households are struggling with their bills and are in longer term debt.
It is important to note that the number of domestic disconnections remains significantly lower than the number of customers in arrears, reflecting the extensive protections and engagement measures that are in place. The CRU report notes that 234 domestic electricity customers and 237 domestic gas customers were disconnected due to non-payment of account in July.
Addressing energy affordability is a priority for this Government. Budget 2027 delivered a package of measures to help households and businesses with the cost of energy. question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to respond to the 'extreme disappointment' expressed by the Climate Change Advisory Council that new partially fossil fuel powered data centres are to be permitted, that this 'threatens Ireland's decarbonisation and climate targets',.
reply:
The Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) is an independent regulator, accountable to a Committee of the Oireachtas. Section 34 of the Electricity Regulation Act 1999 provides that the CRU has the power to issue Directions to the Electricity System Operators in relation to the terms and conditions offered to parties seeking to connect to and use the electricity system.
While the concerns expressed by the Climate Change Advisory Council are noted with respect to the CRU Large Energy Users Connection Policy, it is important to recognise that the CRU Connection Policy was expressly designed to address concerns regarding sustainable data centre demand growth, grid constraints, security of supply and decarbonisation, while supporting renewable energy targets and minimising impacts on national carbon emissions.
The idea that current policy permits unconstrained growth does not reflect or recognise the Government's Large Energy User Action Plan (LEAP) or the CRU's connection framework and the strategic plan-led approach being taken that aligns future development with available grid capacity, network investment and renewable energy resources. There is no automatic entitlement to a connection with applications subject to detailed and substantial requirements against grid capacity and system constraints.

question: Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether his Department has assessed the extent to which the cost of remedial works, including electrical rewiring, upgrades to existing electrical systems and other preparatory works required before grant-aided energy efficiency upgrades can proceed, acts as a barrier to households seeking to avail of Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) grants; and if he is considering expanding grant supports to cover such remedial works.
reply:
The Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) provides a range of supports to help households improve energy efficiency and adopt renewable energy technologies. Under the Microgeneration Support Scheme, grants of up to €1,800 are available for household solar PV installations, and more than 128,000 homes have been supported since the scheme was introduced in 2018.
Earlier this year, and again in advance of Budget 2027, the Government introduced enhanced retrofit and renewable energy supports through the work of the National Energy Affordability Taskforce, including new supports for solar PV and batteries and expanded eligibility for existing schemes.
While preparatory electrical works can add to project costs, they are generally specific to the condition of an individual property and remain the responsibility of the homeowner. An exception applies under the fully funded Warmer Homes Scheme, where necessary meter tail upgrades may be completed at no cost to the homeowner.
Separately, the Housing Aid for Older People Scheme is available to assist older people living in poor housing conditions to have necessary repairs or improvements carried out. The scheme is administered by Local Authorities. Details are available at: www.gov.ie/en/service/1ca60-housing-aid-for-older-people-grant/.

question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment for an update on the work of the National Energy Affordability Taskforce.
reply:
Addressing energy affordability is a key priority for this Government. That is why in June of last year, I established the National Energy Affordability Taskforce (NEAT) to identify, assess and implement measures that will enhance energy affordability for households and businesses while delivering key renewables commitments, and protecting security of supply and economic stability.
The first report of the Taskforce, which included measures for consideration in Budget 2026, was published last November.
The work of the Taskforce has also informed measures announced in Budget 2027. In this year's Budget, the Government delivered a package of measures to help households and businesses with the cost of energy, with a particular focus on those most vulnerable to volatility in the price of imported fossil fuels. This included targeted social welfare supports, energy efficiency and retrofit supports, and measures to protect consumers most exposed to energy costs.
A range of improvements to the retrofit schemes administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland, launched in October, was also developed through the work of the NEAT. This will make it easier and more affordable for households and businesses to improve energy efficiency, install renewable energy technologies and switch to cleaner heating systems. A particular focus of this package is ensuring that households most exposed to high energy costs can benefit from the energy transition.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether funding allocated by his Department to the SEAI in Budget 2027 will be sufficient to match the rate of inflation.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 42 and 53 together.
Budget 2027 includes a record capital allocation of over €650 million for the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland’s (SEAI) home energy upgrade schemes. This means that more funding than ever will be available to make homes warmer, healthier, more comfortable, less expensive to heat and less reliant on fossil fuels. The allocation is expected to be further supplemented with additional funding, such as an allocation from the European Regional Development Fund. Further details will be published as part of the Revised Estimates 2027 later this year.
Accordingly, Government has in place record funding as well as a package of supports to make it easier and more affordable for homeowners to undertake energy upgrades for warmer, healthier homes with lower energy bills. This includes the SEAI’s part-funded schemes, as well as fully funded energy upgrades for people at risk of energy poverty through the Warmer Homes Scheme.
Capital expenditure of over €2 billion has delivered over 296,000 home energy upgrades from 2019 to end September 2026, including over 40,800 fully funded upgrades for households at risk of energy poverty under the Warmer Homes Scheme.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the measures in place to ensure transparency regarding electricity costs for data centres in Ireland; whether the cost per unit of electricity paid by data centres is lower than that paid by domestic and commercial consumers; and the actions being taken to ensure that energy costs are allocated fairly across all electricity users.
reply:
Electricity network tariffs provide essential funding required to operate, maintain and expand Ireland’s electricity grid to meet growing demand and ensure safe, secure and reliable supplies of electricity for every customer in Ireland.
Responsibility for the regulation of electricity network tariffs is a matter for the Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) which is an independent regulator, accountable to a Committee of the Oireachtas.
Network costs are recouped through a mix of energy, capacity and standing charges.
Extra-large energy users have contributed significantly to the recovery of costs associated with maintaining system security in recent years. Between 2020 and 2025, the typical extra-large energy user saw an estimated 175% increase in network costs, compared to an estimated 45% increase for domestic customers.
The CRU is currently undertaking a multi-annual review of electricity network tariffs which seeks to put in place a framework to ensure tariffs are fit-for-purpose and reflective of the costs attributable to different customer groups, including extra-large energy users such as data centres.
The review will also take account of current EU proposals to future-proof electricity bills through the establishment of a system-friendly network design.
Both the Large Energy User Action Plan and ongoing work under the National Energy Affordability Taskforce identify the importance of reviewing network tariffs to support effective grid operation and investment.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the measures his Department is taking to improve energy affordability.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 51 and 62 together.
The conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East have caused significant disruption to international energy markets. This has resulted in higher energy prices for households and businesses across Europe, including in Ireland. In response, the Government has taken a range of measures to help support consumers with energy costs.
The Government established the National Energy Affordability Taskforce (NEAT) to examine energy affordability challenges and identify practical measures to support households and businesses. The work of the Taskforce helped to inform key aspects of Budget 2027, with a particular focus on those most vulnerable to high energy costs.
A central element of the Government's approach is reducing energy bills through improved energy efficiency and increased deployment of solar PV. Budget 2027 provided a record €654 million for residential and community energy upgrade schemes. This investment will support more households in improving the energy performance of their homes, lowering energy consumption, reducing bills and improving comfort, while decreasing reliance on imported fossil fuels. The Government also continues to support fully funded energy upgrades for eligible low-income households.

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will report on the recent EU Energy Council in Dublin on the 28 and 29 September 2026.
reply:
I recently chaired the informal meeting of EU Energy Ministers at Dublin Castle. The meeting brought together Ministers from Member States, representatives of the European Commission and invited partner countries, as well as a number of Third Countries. The meeting offered Ministers and Heads of Delegation an opportunity to exchange perspectives on energy challenges impacting all Member States across the European Union, and beyond. The meeting also provided an opportunity for informal and forward-looking discussions.
The agenda for the meeting included three main sessions:
Session 1: Energy Affordability.
Session 2: A panel discussion which focussed on innovation and market disruption.
Session 3: European Energy Security and Cooperation. EU Ministers were joined in this session by the Energy Ministers and Heads of Delegation of Moldova, the United Kingdom and Ukraine.
The meeting provided an opportunity to consider how Europe can build a future that is more competitive, more secure and more sustainable. This is a shared challenge facing all Member States in terms of how to strengthen Europe's economy and resilience, while remaining true to the values and environmental ambition that underpin our Union.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht when the awards for the Community Centre Investment Fund will be announced.
reply:
The Community Centre Investment Fund (CCIF) was introduced to provide high quality community facilities that are available to community groups in both urban and rural communities. Through the CCIF, some €112 million has been allocated for the enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres and the construction of new centres where such a need has been identified.
I launched the latest round of funding under CCIF 2026 on the 26th of March for enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres. The fund will be delivered across 2 categories with maximum funding levels of €25,000 and €100,000 respectively. The closing date for the CCIF 2026 has now passed.
Applications are currently being assessed and I look forward to shortly announcing the successful projects under category 1, which provides funding of up to €25,000. Approvals under category 2, which provides funding of up to €100,000, will be announced before year-end.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht when the awards for the TVRS grant will be announced; and whether consideration will be given to an application (details supplied).
reply:
The Town and Village Renewal Scheme (TVRS) was introduced in 2016 and is one of a number of measures designed to rejuvenate rural towns and villages throughout Ireland. Over €217 million has been allocated to almost 2,000 projects since the launch of the scheme.
In December 2025, funding of over €26.2 million was announced for a total of 116 projects for the Main Scheme and Project Development Measure under the 2025 Call for Proposals. Of this over €497,000 was allocated to Cork City Council for four successful projects, including almost €160,000 for a project which is being implemented by the group referenced by the Deputy.
The 2026 TVRS Call for Proposals was issued to local authorities on the 16 September last. This Call also has two funding streams for project applications, the Main Scheme and the Project Development Measure. Project proposals that will be submitted for application are selected by local authorities in consultation with local communities. The closing date for the submission of applications to the Department is 22 January 2027 and at this point no applications have been received.
The TVRS funding call is always heavily subscribed, and applications received are assessed on a competitive basis for suitability against scheme criteria and objectives. Other factors such as the geographical spread of projects, the quality of the proposed projects, and the available budget will also be considered to maximise the impact of funding allocated.

reply:
The main support available to students is the statutory based Student Grant Scheme which is administered by SUSI (Student Universal Support Ireland). Under the terms of the Student Grant Scheme, grant assistance is awarded to students attending an approved course in an approved institution who meet the prescribed conditions of funding, including those relating to nationality, residency, previous academic attainment and means.
The decision on eligibility for a student grant is a matter, in the first instance, for the awarding authority, SUSI to determine.
An official in my Department has advised that the student referred to by the Deputy submitted an application to SUSI and that the applicant was awarded the 50% rate of Student Contribution. SUSI advised the applicant of the award decision by letter dated 16 July 2026.
I understand from SUSI that the applicant in question subsequently appealed the decision to SUSI but was advised by the SUSI Appeals Officer that their appeal was unsuccessful.
If the applicant remains of the view that the scheme has not been interpreted correctly in their case, an appeal may be submitted to the independent Student Grants Appeals Board (SGAB) within the required timeframe (i.e. not later than 30 days after the notification of the determination of the appeals officer to the applicant). Such appeals can be made by the applicant on-line via www.studentgrantappeals.ie.

question: Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the number of applicants currently awaiting a Youthreach placement in County Westmeath; the current capacity of Youthreach provision in this country; and if he will outline the plans to expand Youthreach capacity in County Westmeath.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 493 and 494 together.
Youthreach provides an alternative education and training pathway for young people who leave school with limited qualifications. The two-year programme combines accredited learning, vocational skills development, work experience and learner supports to help participants progress to further or higher education, training or employment.
My Department has been advised by Longford and Westmeath Education and Training Board (LWETB) that there are currently no applicants awaiting a Youthreach placement in County Westmeath. LWETB has also advised that it has no current plans to increase Youthreach capacity in the county. However, it continues to monitor local demand and learner needs.
SOLAS has advised my Department that the total national capacity of Youthreach provision in 2025, across both Youthreach Centres and Community Training Centres, was 5,163 places. 215 of these places are in Longford and Westmeath ETB.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science his plans to ensure advertising for third level courses that lead to teaching council registration are correct .
reply:
The Teaching Council is the regulator of the teaching profession in Ireland. Its role is to protect the public by promoting and regulating professional standards in teaching. A list of all programmes of initial teacher education that have been accredited by the Teaching Council is available on the Teaching Council website.
Education and training providers in Ireland have a statutory obligation for accurate information provision to learners as outlined in Section 67 of the Quality and Qualifications (Education and Training) Act 2012 as amended, and in the Policy and Criteria for Access, Transfer and Progression in Relation to Learners for Providers of Further and Higher Education and Training.
In cases where issues are signalled in relation to the accuracy in advertising for courses, QQI will engage with relevant parties and may review relevant communications to identify opportunities for improvement of clarity and accuracy of the information provided to learners. QQI will continue to monitor compliance with the Act to ensure that programme information is clear and accurate for learners.
Programmes leading to an award on the NFQ and published in the Irish Register of Qualifications highlight to learners that the provider or awarding body is subject to the quality assurance arrangements of QQI. These statutory oversights should provide trust and confidence to learners in the standards of education they will receive from providers.

question: Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if his Department will consider allowing domiciliary care allowance recipients to be eligible for the Springboard+ initiative.
reply:
Springboard+ is a targeted initiative which began in 2011 as part of the Government’s Jobs Initiative. Its aim is to provide free and heavily subsidised upskilling and reskilling opportunities through higher education in areas where there is an identified skills need.
A particular emphasis of the Springboard+ programme is to provide upskilling supports for people who are unemployed. Under the Unemployed Category for Springboard+ applications, an individual may apply for a fully subsidised course if they are not currently working, are available for work, are actively seeking employment, and are receiving a qualifying social welfare payment (such as Jobseeker's Benefit, Jobseeker's Allowance, Disability Allowance, or Carer’s Allowance).
The Domiciliary Care Allowance is classified as a financial support for a child's care needs, not an adult employment or income support payment, and it is therefore not one of the qualifying Department of Social Protection (DSP) payments under this category.
Further Education and Training (FET) in Ireland offers a vast and diverse range of part time and full-time options for learners which are designed to provide practical skills for employment or pathways to higher education. Further information on the range of courses on offer is available at: www.fetchcourses.ie/courses

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment following the submission of the ESB networks plug-in solar working group report to his Department on 1 October 2026, when the report and its recommendations will be published; the actions that are now required to permit the safe use of plug-in solar systems up to 800 watts; and whether he will provide a firm timeline for their introduction in Ireland.
reply:

The group has met nine times to date. The working group recently submitted an options report to my Department, setting out recommendations on matters including installation approaches, product specifications and customer guidance. It is the Working Group’s intention that this report will be published as soon as is possible. Timelines will depend on stakeholders' internal review processes and public accessibility requirements before the document can be made available online.
In parallel, my Department is working with stakeholders to progress elements of the regulatory framework. Planned next steps include an Ireland-specific safety assessment, a legislative review, development of a product specification, publication of detailed customer guidance, and the establishment of an online product registration portal.
Further work is required to ensure the technology can be deployed safely, is supported by an appropriate regulatory framework, and that any legal barriers are addressed. My Department is currently progressing the safety assessment and legislative review, both of which are expected to conclude next year.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Health if she will consider extending the timeframe of the proposed CHI Commission of Investigation beyond 2019, given that concerns relating to paediatric orthopaedic surgeries may pre-date the establishment of CHI.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 474 and 486 together.
The independent report of the Children's Health Ireland Inquiry into spina bifida and complex scoliosis scoping exercise was published by the Minister for Health on 28 September following engagement with patients and families
In his report, Mr Farrell notes that inquiries work best when they have a defined scope and time. Any inquiry that's absolutely open-ended or has very broad terms of reference can go on for so long. Mr Farrell recommends the period 2019 to 2025 inclusive with 2019 being the establishment of CHI.
In Mr Farrell's view, this is a six-year period that deals with before COVID-19 affected services, during COVID-19 and after allowing assessment of the pandemic’s impact on waiting lists and focussing on events relevant to CHI as an organisation.
Although waiting list challenges existed before 2019, he has made the recommendation to put constraints on the Commission.
Officials in my Department will work in close consultation with the Office of the Attorney General on the Terms of Reference (ToR) and there will be a call for input from Advocacy Groups on the ToR also. The final ToR will be submitted to Government for approval.

question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Health the plans that are in place to expand access to continuous glucose monitoring for people living with Type 2 diabetes; the work being undertaken by the Department of Health and the HSE to assess potential eligibility criteria; and when a decision on wider access can be expected.
reply:
