question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Health to consider extending the timeline for investigation for the Inquiry into CHI spina bifida and complex scoliosis services to include cases before the establishment of CHI in 2019.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 474 and 486 together.
The independent report of the Children's Health Ireland Inquiry into spina bifida and complex scoliosis scoping exercise was published by the Minister for Health on 28 September following engagement with patients and families
In his report, Mr Farrell notes that inquiries work best when they have a defined scope and time. Any inquiry that's absolutely open-ended or has very broad terms of reference can go on for so long. Mr Farrell recommends the period 2019 to 2025 inclusive with 2019 being the establishment of CHI.
In Mr Farrell's view, this is a six-year period that deals with before COVID-19 affected services, during COVID-19 and after allowing assessment of the pandemic’s impact on waiting lists and focussing on events relevant to CHI as an organisation.
Although waiting list challenges existed before 2019, he has made the recommendation to put constraints on the Commission.
Officials in my Department will work in close consultation with the Office of the Attorney General on the Terms of Reference (ToR) and there will be a call for input from Advocacy Groups on the ToR also. The final ToR will be submitted to Government for approval.

reply:

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health to outline in detail the reason the south west surgical hub was closed temporarily (details supplied); the length of time it was closed; the manner in which the issues which lead to its closure were identified; the date these issues were identified; and the number of patients seen in the new hub between its opening and temporary closure.
reply:
The HSE South West Surgical Hub in Cork includes two theatres, two minor procedure rooms and a number of outpatient rooms. The Hub was scheduled to initially commence operations on a limited activity basis, allowing the service to become established in a safe and controlled manner with the necessary processes embedded, ensuring a safe, sustainable and effective expansion of operations. In this regard, patients were scheduled over five days between 29 September and 9 October.
Following established commissioning processes and the ongoing air sampling that is routine in theatres and procedure rooms, on 29 September air sampling results for one theatre and one minor procedure room returned results above acceptable levels. As a precautionary measure, both areas were unavailable for clinical use while further deep cleaning and resampling occurred.
In order to protect patient confidentiality, it is not possible to provide a figure for the number of patients treated at the Hub before temporary closure as the number involved could allow potential patient identification. However, low clinical risk has been confirmed and appropriate patient follow up has been carried out. Other patients who were due to be treated on the day were accommodated at an alternative facility. The patients scheduled for procedures in Theatre in the following weeks have been rescheduled.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment for an update on the technical process and timeline for the approval for sale and use of plug-in photovoltaic (PIPV) solar panels in Ireland.
reply:
Plug-in solar is an emerging low-carbon technology, and the Government is committed to accelerating its introduction in Ireland. Once enabled, it can provide a cost-effective and accessible way for customers to participate more actively in the energy transition, with potential benefits including lower electricity bills, greater demand flexibility, and support for Ireland’s renewable energy and climate objectives.
At my request, ESB Networks established a plug-in solar working group in May 2026 to examine pathways for the safe, standardised and scalable deployment of the technology. The group has met nine times to date.
The working group recently submitted an options report to my Department, setting out recommendations on matters including installation approaches, product specifications and customer guidance. In parallel, my Department is working with stakeholders to progress elements of the regulatory framework. Planned next steps include an Ireland-specific safety assessment, a legislative review, development of a product specification, publication of detailed customer guidance, and the establishment of an online product registration portal.
Further work is required to ensure the technology can be deployed safely, is supported by an appropriate regulatory framework, and that any legal barriers are addressed. My Department is currently progressing the safety assessment and legislative review, both of which are expected to conclude next year.

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health the status of the Patient Safety (Licensing) Bill; and the timeline for publication.
reply:
On 24 June 2025, I brought a Memorandum to Government seeking approval to recommence drafting of the Patient Safety (Licensing) Bill 2025. Approval was granted.
Legislative priority had previously been given to the Patient Safety (Notifiable Incidents and Open Disclosure) Act 2023 which was commenced in September 2024 (other than Section 68).
The Patient Safety (Notifiable Incidents and Open Disclosure) Act 2023 includes provisions for the establishment of a legislative framework for mandatory open disclosure and reporting of designated serious patient safety incidents and, the provision of certain legislative protections for the conduct of clinical audit against explicit clinical standards on a national basis. The Patient Safety (Notifiable Incidents and Open Disclosure) Act 2023 also provides the legislative framework for the extension of the Health Information Quality Authority's regulatory remit to private hospitals. The Patient Safety (Licensing) Bill is the next important step in this suite of legislation.
The Patient Safety (Licensing) Bill is being developed to facilitate the creation of a comprehensive system of regulation to oversee all hospitals in the State, both public and private. It will also provide the Minister for Health with the authority to designate certain activities that take place outside of a hospital setting as carrying a sufficiently high risk to warrant their providers to also come within the scope of the new regime.

reply:

The Minister has no power to set prices in a private competitive market.
The National Waste Collection Permit Office (NWCPO) has conducted a study on incentivised charging structures in the waste collection market. This study also considers mechanisms for supports in relation to households disposing of medical incontinence products based on international practice.
Recommendations will be considered in conjunction with outcomes from the feasibility study into transitioning our national waste collection from its current competitive licensing system to a franchise model which has recently been completed. Both will inform the development of the next iteration of the Waste Action Plan for a Circular Economy (WAPCE).
The Department has previously engaged with relevant public bodies, including the HSE, the Department of Social Protection, and representative organisations with respect to the waste disposal costs for incontinence wear, and further engagement will be undertaken in the context of updating the WAPCE in the coming months.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the progress his Department is making in developing battery energy storage facilities to support the delivery of Ireland's clean energy objectives.
reply:
In line with the Electricity Storage Policy Framework for Ireland and the 10 Government actions contained within it, my Department is focused on removing the barriers for electricity storage projects and their incorporation to the Irish grid system.
Action 6 of the Policy Framework supports the immediate procurement of 1GW of demand flexibility and long duration electricity storage to meet specific network needs on the distribution and transmissions systems respectively.
In line with action 6, ESB Networks have completed the first iteration of their route to market for Demand Flexibility Products on to the Distribution system. First contracts for 42 MW were awarded in Q2 2026. Likewise, EirGrid, in conjunction with the CRU, are developing a route to market for Long Duration Energy Storage (LDES). The first LDES contracts are expected to be signed in 2028.
Actions 7 and 8, as well as Actions 9 and 10 (if required), of the Policy Framework will provide a glidepath for electricity storage out to 2040.
Action 7, a quantitative consultation to identify the minimum storage requirements between 2030 and 2040 for the electricity grid, is underway and outputs are expected by the end of 2028.
Also underway is Action 8, a ‘Financial analysis’ to determine if the available market mechanisms due between 2025-2028 will provide sufficient revenue certainty to industry and financial institutions to deliver the minimum amount of electricity storage identified by Action 7.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment his views on whether sufficient steps have been taken to implement adaptation measures in Ireland to date.
reply:
The Government is committed to protecting Ireland’s present and future generations with a whole of government approach to Climate Adaptation underpinned by the 2024 National Adaptation Framework (NAF).
In November Sectoral Adaptation Plans (SAPs) covering 13 key sectors under the remit of 8 Government Departments were approved by Government and published. All SAPs were underpinned by data from Ireland's first National Climate Change Risk Assessment (NCCRA) undertaken by the EPA and climate projection data from Met Éireann. Sectors are now implementing their SAPs. The preparation and implementation of SAPs is the responsibility of each responsible line Minister.
The Climate Change Advisory Council (CCAC) published their latest annual review on adaptation in September 2026.
Last year, in order to tackle system wide barriers to adaptation, I established a Climate Adaptation Taskforce (CAT) to provide for senior-level oversight and greater consideration of cross cutting issues to improve capacity across Government to deliver effective adaptation measures over time.
In 2024, 31 Local Authority Climate Action Plans (LACAPs) were published which include adaptation actions to build resilience against the impacts of climate change in our communities. Since 2022, approximately €19m has been paid to local authorities by my Department to develop and implement their LACAPs.

question: Deputy Martin Kenny asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the number of bovines and ovines that have contracted Bluetongue including fatalities and recoveries from the disease to date.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 398 and 400 together.
My Department continues to undertake nationwide surveillance for bluetongue and publishes updated information on confirmed detections; including their geographical distribution and species at: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-agriculture-food-and-the-marine/publications/bluetongue-virus/#bluetongue-updates each week.
As of 2 November 2026, there have been 70 confirmed cases of bluetongue virus serotype 3 (BTV-3) across 15 counties in Ireland, comprising 66 affected bovine herds and four ovine flocks. These figures refer to affected herds and flocks rather than the total number of individual animals infected.
My Department’s surveillance programme is primarily concerned with monitoring the geographical spread of the virus and informing stakeholders of developments. While information on individual animal fatalities may arise through surveillance activities, comprehensive data on fatalities and recoveries attributable to bluetongue are not routinely collated.
According to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), both cattle and sheep are susceptible to bluetongue. Cattle often have higher rates of infection, while sheep generally experience more severe clinical disease. The severity of infection can also vary depending on the virus strain.
Farmers who suspect infection in their animals should consult their private veterinary practitioner.

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the timeline and the budget available for the SEAI free solar PV scheme for the medically vulnerable; when eligible customers will be contacted about the scheme; and the number of customers who have already availed of the scheme.
reply:
The Solar PV for the Medically Vulnerable Scheme is a targeted scheme for the installation of solar photovoltaic (PV) panels for customers/households who are registered on the life support category of the Priority Services Register. These homes have a dependence on electrically powered equipment including medical equipment, life protecting devices and assistive technologies such as dialysis machines and respirators. As such, these households may have a higher energy demand than the average user and this scheme is designed to go some way towards helping to reduce those energy costs.
The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) in conjunction with energy suppliers and is open to all suppliers who wish to participate. The scheme is energy supplier-led, meaning each energy supplier is responsible for contacting their own eligible customers directly. Government, through the SEAI, funds each energy supplier for the installations they provide to their eligible customers. It is important to note that suppliers, who manage the administrative aspects of the scheme, issue offers to eligible homeowners and contact eligible households in batches, based on their operational capacity.

question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the type of grants and government entitlements sheep owners are entitled to; the criteria for such entitlements; and the way in which these are funded.
reply:
In Budget 2027, I secured an allocation of €131m for the livestock sector, including schemes worth €42m to sheep farmers in 2027. This is a continuation of the supports currently available in 2026.
These consist of €20m for the multi-annual CSP Sheep Improvement Scheme (SIS) and €22m for the annual National Sheep Welfare Scheme (NSWS).
The SIS is the principal dedicated support for the sector with an allocation of €100m over the duration of the current CAP Strategic Plan (CSP). This multi-annual scheme will operate until 2027 and provides financial support to upland and lowland farmers who undertake additional measures to improve the welfare of their flocks. The targeted welfare measures include lameness control, parasite control, flystrike control, mineral supplementation and meal feeding, management of pregnant ewes, as well as the purchase and use of a genotyped ram.
The objective of the 2026 National Sheep Welfare Scheme (2026 NSWS) is to further enhance animal health and welfare on sheep farms. Scheme applicants must complete two mandatory actions from a menu of three - shearing, body condition scoring of ewes and vaccination of ewes which can be carried out against Clostridial diseases or Bluetongue disease. Scheme applicants may also undertake an additional voluntary action from a choice of two – footbathing or plunge dipping to control external parasites.
It is important to note that all supports must be justified on the basis of the costs incurred and income foregone

question: Deputy Marie Sherlock asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he supports the specific recommendations within the Garda Training Review Group for the delivery of a suitable Garda training facility in the greater Dublin area; and if he accepts the findings of the review group that this should be “an early priority”.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 393, 394 and 396 together.
The Garda Training Review Group was established to identify delivery options that would increase the scale and capacity of high-quality education, training and continuous professional development within An Garda Síochána. This will help ensure that the organisation's skills needs are met over the next decade.
The Group comprised officials from the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science, the Office of Public Works, the Higher Education Authority and An Garda Síochána.
The Group's report made 21 recommendations across three thematic areas:
Strategic and Operational Planning (including workforce planning and capital development);
Planning for Future Flexibility; and
Future Focus for Education and Training Development.
My officials are currently considering the recommendations contained in the report, and I have spoken with the Garda Commissioner regarding support for the implementation of the recommendations.
Representatives from An Garda Síochána, my Department and the Office of Public Works currently meet on a monthly basis to discuss matters relating to Garda estates, this will include any recommendations arising from this report.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of a citizenship application (details supplied) in view that it is 46 months since the application was submitted; whether any further documentation or information is required, clarification as to the cause of the delay in view that it was previously indicated in March 2026 that a decision would be reached in 12 weeks.
reply:
The naturalisation application referred to by the Deputy continues to be processed by my Department.
I understand that extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants. I want to assure anyone who has an application for naturalisation submitted that the Citizenship Division of my Department is doing everything possible to progress applications as quickly as possible.
It is important to note, however, that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process.
I can clarify to the Deputy that my Department cited that a decision would be reached in 12 weeks once the final checks were completed and were returned. The checks required in this case have not yet been completed and my Department is therefore not yet in a position to make a final decision on the application.
Given the importance of citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place on each application. Unfortunately, some checks, such as international checks, can take a considerable amount of time and these are largely outside of the control of the Immigration Service.
For that reason, while, I expect that going forward, that most applicants will receive a decision within one year, this cannot be guaranteed in the case of applications made in any specific year.
Citizenship Division have taken a significant number of steps to improve the process for applicants. These included introducing an online digital application, online payments, and the introduction of eVetting

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he can outline what the proceeds for CAB are used for; and if he will consider putting some of this funding going forward into projects like the drive project.
reply:
CAB is a multi-agency statutory body established under the Criminal Assets Bureau Act, 1996. I am advised that all monies seized by CAB are remitted to the Central Fund of the Exchequer after the appropriate statutory time frame under the Proceeds of Crime Acts.
Figures relating to asset recovery under the Proceeds of Crime Acts by CAB are available publicly in the annual reports published on the Bureau's website: www.cab.ie/annual-reports/
The disbursement of monies collected by the Criminal Assets Bureau is controlled by the Central Exchequer. The Community Safety Fund is a means of re-directing the proceeds of crime, seized by the Criminal Assets Bureau (CAB) and An Garda Síochána, back into communities in order to fund innovative local projects aimed at building stronger, safer communities.
In September, I announced the allocation of a record €4.84 million through the Community Safety Fund to support 56 community safety projects nationwide. This is a 10% increase on the €4.4 million awarded in 2025, and a 146%, or €2.84 million increase on the funding allocated to the first Community Safety Fund in 2022.
This year’s successful projects will deliver community initiatives across a broad range of priorities, including community safety & local engagement; support, inclusion & integration of minority and marginalised groups; domestic, sexual & gender-based violence (DSGBV); and youth focused community safety.

Improving the energy efficiency of our homes through schemes like the Warmer Homes Scheme is a key pathway to addressing energy affordability and reducing household exposure to energy price changes.
In 2026 the scheme has delivered 34% more property upgrades,158% more upgrades to Building Energy Rating of B, and 328% more heat pump installations than the same period in 2025. Over 34,000 homes were upgraded under the scheme from 2022 to date.
To help maximise delivery and continue to improve waiting times, Budget 2026 has provided €340 million for the Warmer Homes Scheme, with a target of 11,500 fully funded home upgrades for 2026.
This record level of funding underlines the Government’s commitment to addressing energy poverty and means that more funding than ever will be available to make homes warmer, healthier, more comfortable and less expensive to heat.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment for an update on the Hydrogen Strategy.
reply:
My Department established the National Hydrogen Programme Taskforce to oversee the delivery of the actions and wider strategic ambitions set out in the National Hydrogen Strategy. The Taskforce works across government departments and state agencies, engaging with key stakeholders, to remove barriers to early hydrogen project development and lay the groundwork to enable the development of the hydrogen sector in Ireland.
The twenty-one actions from the Strategy have been developed into a multi-year work programme and assigned to working groups across three pillar areas: Working Group 1 on safety and regulation, Working Group 2 on infrastructure and systems, and Working Group 3 on markets and commercialisation. The National Hydrogen Programme Implementation Plan, which is available on the gov.ie website (https://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/0a80ed16/National_Hydrogen_Programme_Implementation_Plan.pdf), sets out the details of this work programme.
Significant progress has been made on actions to develop the necessary legislative and regulatory frameworks for hydrogen, to develop a fund for hydrogen demonstration projects, and to further build a solid evidence base to inform policymaking. The Taskforce is due to meet before the end of the year to approve the publication of an update report that will provide stakeholders with more details on the Taskforce’s progress to date in implementing the National Hydrogen Strategy.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of single people, families and minor children currently living in IPAS accommodation with an active deportation order, in tabular form.
reply:
The number of people resident in the International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centres who have been refused permission to remain in the State is a small proportion of our total resident population of nearly 32,000 people.
Currently, there are over 900 people subject to deportation orders residing in IPAS accommodation. This number fluctuates regularly as people leave Ireland under the relevant return pathways and as new orders are made.
The breakdown of data requested in terms of resident family status is not routinely collated and available for publication.
Some people subject to deportation orders may have the enforcement of their order suspended due to legal proceedings or due to personal circumstances such as health grounds. Others will be in the process of arranging to leave the State as directed.
My Department works closely with the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB) to arrange for the removal of persons subject to deportation orders.
The enforcement of deportation orders is an operational matter for GNIB, and my Department works closely with the GNIB to progress arrangements for the removal of people subject to deportation orders. If a person issued with a deportation order does not leave the State independently then they are required to present to the GNIB in accordance with the conditions of their deportation order.

question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when a visa application arrives to the relevant office, is the nationality of the applicant flagged as or before it is forwarded.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 370, 371 and 372 together.
I can advise the Deputy that an applicant’s nationality has no bearing on how a visa application is processed. All applications are treated on an equal basis and an applicant’s nationality is not a factor in determining the initial processing route.
Visa applications are submitted online through the Automated Visa Application and Tracking System (AVATS), which is available at www.visas.inis.gov.ie. Applicants are generally required to apply from their country of nationality or from a country in which they are lawfully resident.
Once an application has been completed online, the applicant must submit it electronically and print the summary application form generated by the system. This form contains details of the application and provides instructions on the submission of supporting documentation. These instructions vary depending on the location in which the application is made.
In many jurisdictions, supporting documentation and biometric information are submitted through the Department’s contracted service provider, VFS Global. In other locations, applications are submitted directly to an Irish Embassy, Consulate or Visa Office. The method of submission is determined by local operational arrangements and not by the applicant’s nationality. question: Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether the additional funding provided in Budget 2027 for the SEAI warmer homes scheme will reduce waiting times for applicants, the current waiting time for homeowners in County Louth is approximately 15 months before being contacted for a home survey due to high demand; the further average waiting time between survey completion and commencement of works.
reply:
The Warmer Homes Scheme aims to improve the energy efficiency and warmth of homes owned by people at risk of energy poverty by providing fully funded retrofits. The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) on behalf of my Department and is funded through the carbon tax revenues and the European Regional Development Fund.
The scheme targets support to those on the lowest incomes who are living in the least efficient homes so that the resources available can have the greatest impact in addressing energy poverty. Over 8,100 homes were upgraded last year, 109% of the annual target.
This year, there have been over 8,000 upgrades completed under the scheme to end September, an increase of 34.5% on the same period last year. The current wait time from application to survey completed is not routinely collated on a county-by-county basis. However, for the first half of the year the average waiting time in all counties from application to contractor allocation under the scheme was 15 months. The overall waiting time from application to works completed was 23 months.
A range of measures have been introduced by my Department and the SEAI to reduce overall waiting times, including the establishment of a new €1.2 billion contractor panel this year with additional contractors. This will support continued growth with a focus on scale, quality and output under the scheme.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will expedite refuse visa appeals by students from Palestine who are challenging the decision made by his Department to refuse their visas.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 368, 369 and 392 together.

It is important to note that visa applications are part of a screening process, designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel, and all such applications undergo this process. question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Social Protection the reason a person with a lifelong severe disability who transitions from disability allowance to the State Pension (Contributory) upon reaching the age of 66 is excluded from disability-specific supports and once-off disability payments, including the recently announced cost of disability payment; if his attention has been drawn to concerns that the additional costs associated with a permanent disability continue beyond pension age; and whether his Department has considered extending such supports to pensioners with lifelong disabilities.
reply:
The Government recognises the additional costs that disabled people can face in their daily lives and is committed to improving outcomes for disabled people. My Department provides a range of income support payments for disabled people of working age and a different suite of payments for those aged 66 or over.
In keeping with this, the new Cost of Disability Payment will be made to people who are in receipt of one of those working age disability payments.
This means that, in Quarter 1, 2027, this will be paid as a lump sum payment of €500 to working-age people in receipt of a long-term disability payment from my Department, specifically Blind Pension, Disability Allowance, Invalidity Pension, and Partial Capacity Benefit. The new payment will be made to approximately 240,000 people at an estimated cost of €119 million. Building on the detailed consultation already undertaken, there will be further engagement with disabled people and their representatives in relation to the shape of the payment in future years.
As a result of Budget 2027, over €30 billion will be spent on social welfare in 2027, including almost €1.15 billion of new measures. I recognise that disabled people of any age can incur additional costs. The Budget package includes a range of measures to support people in receipt of a State Pension as well as disabled people.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Social Protection whether the Citizens Information Board is taking any action or otherwise addressing the prevalence of incorrect and outdated information being promoted by AI Overviews and attributed to the Board; and if so, the actions being taken.
reply:
The Citizens Information Board (CIB) is the statutory body, under the aegis of my Department, that is responsible for supporting the provision of information, advice (including money and budgeting advice) and advocacy services on a wide range of public and social services.
AI tools typically draw on a number of different sources when generating responses to queries. AI summaries that are generated independently by third-party technology companies are outside the control of CIB, including in how they reference or attribute information.
However, CIB is fully aware that many people choose to get answers from AI tools rather than directly from sources like the citizensinformation.ie website. Content remains at the core of a good answer, whether direct from the citizensinformation.ie website or from an AI tool.
Within this context, CIB has developed its own AI tool, AskCI (askci.ie), which takes content only from the citizensinformation.ie website and where the underlying database is updated at least daily.
AskCI also allows CIB to explore how its content can be structured and presented for use in an increasingly AI-driven information environment.
Alongside AskCI, CIB continues to provide accurate information to people who visit citizensinformation.ie and through its publications. CIB respond to queries and clarify information through our social media channels.
CIB also fund and support the Citizens Information Phone Service, available from 9am to 8pm, Monday to Friday, on 0818 07

reply:

My Department will work closely with the Department of Children, Disability and Equality, once the Health (Assisted Human Reproduction) Act 2024, has commenced, to progress proposals for surrogacy leave.

Both intended parents of a child born through surrogacy may be entitled to claim Parent’s Leave and Benefit, depending on their circumstances. Parent’s Benefit is currently paid at €299 per week, increasing to €309 from January 2027.
The father of a child born through surrogacy can also qualify for Paternity Leave and Benefit if he is the biological father of the child and declared to be the father of the child. The leave entitlement is for two weeks, to be taken within six months of the child's birth. Paternity Benefit is paid at €299 per week, increasing to €309 from January 2027.
Under the Supplementary Welfare Allowance scheme, the Department may make Additional Needs Payments for those whose resources are insufficient to meet their needs. The payment is available to anyone who needs it and qualifies, whether the person is currently receiving a social welfare payment or working on a low income.

question: Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will provide clarification regarding the unique obligations in respect of eligible recipients of maternity benefit from his Department who are partaking in a scheme (details supplied); if their receipt of maternity benefit continues to allow them to attend or vote at monthly meetings of their local authority without impacting their payment.
reply:
The Local Government (Maternity Protection and Other Measures for Members of Local Authorities) Act 2022 makes Maternity Leave entitlement, as provided for under the Maternity Protection Act 1994, available to members of local authorities.
This legislation provides for a temporary absence where the member takes leave in accordance with the Maternity Protection Act 1994 and can seek to have a temporary substitute during the absence.
Maternity Benefit is a payment for employed and self-employed persons, who are on Maternity Leave from work and who satisfy certain PRSI contribution conditions. It is currently paid at €299 per week, increasing to €309 from January 2027, for up to 26 weeks.
The legislation provides that a person may be disqualified from receiving maternity benefit where they engage in insurable employment or self-employment. This could include a local authority member who is receiving renumeration to attend Local Authority meetings.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether he has assessed the risk that payments to households for exporting surplus solar electricity will fall or cease in future; and what measures he proposes to protect households that invested on the expectation of export income, including support for battery storage to increase their use of the electricity they generate.
reply:
The Domestic Solar PV Grant Scheme, delivered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) under the Micro-generation Support Scheme (MSS), has supported more than 25,500 homes this year (end September 2026) with applications up 66% compared to end September 2025. This strong uptake shows householders continue to recognise the benefits of solar PV.
The Clean Export Guarantee (CEG) provides for micro and small-scale generators to receive payment from electricity suppliers for excess electricity exported to the grid.
The Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) has statutory responsibility for regulating the electricity market, including with regard to the CEG. In June 2024, the CRU published its decision paper Clean Export Guarantee: Enduring Arrangements to Remunerate Customers for Microgeneration Exports. The CRU confirmed in that paper that the competitive approach, whereby suppliers set their own export tariffs, has functioned well and will continue.
My Department is aware there has been some concern that tariffs may diminish but has no information that suggests this is the case. Notwithstanding this, as part of our energy transformation, it is important for businesses and households to have maximum flexibility and control in how they consume electricity.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Social Protection to confirm the status of a person's application (details supplied) for the household benefits package; and when a decision is likely to be reached in this case.
reply:
The Household Benefits Package comprises of an Electricity Allowance or Gas Allowance, and a Free Television Licence. Only one Household Benefits Package is payable per household.
The person concerned is in receipt of the Household Benefits Package with effect from 11 April 2016, including an Electricity Allowance and a Free Television Licence.
The Electricity Allowance is paid at the rate of €1.15 per day (approximately €35 per month), to their nominated bank account, on the first Tuesday of each month.
The Free Television Licence is valued at €160 per year.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Social Protection if his Department plans to run a new recruitment campaign for Community Welfare Officers within the Department early in the year.
reply:
Community Welfare Officers (CWOS) are employed in my Department at the Civil Service generalist Higher Executive Officer (HEO) grade. As such, the Department do not hold specific recruitment competitions for these roles.
Recruitment and assignment of HEOs, including CWOs, is through recruitment and promotion competitions run by Publicjobs, the civil service mobility scheme, internal assignments and internal promotion competitions.
Publicjobs are currently recruiting for HEOs through a nationwide open competition. There is also an internal HEOS promotional panel in place in my Department, as well as plans for a further competition in 2027. CWO posts will continue to be filled through these recruitment avenues, as well as through internal and civil service wide mobility schemes over the coming months.
I trust this information is of use to the Deputy.

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Social Protection further to Parliamentary Question No. 1983 of 28 of July, the progress and latest engagements he has had with the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality on the Programme for Government commitment to introduce paid surrogacy leave since June 2026.
reply:
My colleague the Minister for Health leads on the Health (Assisted Human Reproduction) Act 2024, which includes provisions in relation to surrogacy which have implications for the introduction of surrogacy leave, while policy on parentage is a matter for the Minister for Justice. It is not possible to finalise provisions in relation to surrogacy leave in advance of the commencement of that Act as it will determine who is to be recognised as a parent when a child is born through a surrogacy arrangement.
My Department will work closely with the Department of Children, Disability and Equality, once the 2024 Act has commenced, to progress proposals for surrogacy leave. The latest engagement of officials from my Department with officials from the Department of Children, Disability and Equality on this matter was in June 2026.
I trust this clarifies the matter.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Social Protection the financial supports, if any, that are available to families with minor children who have received a final negative decision on their international protection application, or a deportation order or return order.
reply:

The current weekly rates of payment are €38.80 per adult and €29.80 per child. A payment rate of €113.80 per week applies where a person is unaccommodated and is on a waiting list for the International Protection Accommodation Service.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the plans in place to provide and expedite offshore windfarms, off the coast of Ireland.
reply:
Five Phase 1 offshore wind projects are currently in development off our East coast, with planned capacity of 3.8 gigawatts. All five have submitted planning applications and first determinations from An Coimisiún Pleanála are anticipated in the first half of 2027. Subject to planning approval, I anticipate that some of these projects will be in construction by 2030 and operational in the early 2030s.
The 900 megawatt Tonn Nua project, off the coast of Waterford, is progressing well since approval in 2025 and I expect it to be energised by 2033. Tonn Nua was the first of four sites to be brought to auction from the South Coast DMAP. My Department is making preparations to develop the remaining three South Coast DMAP sites over the coming years.
Separately, my Department is advancing the National DMAP process which will designate sufficient additional renewable energy areas around our coast to facilitate our longer term target of 20 gigawatts.
The international market situation for offshore wind has changed much since Ireland's first offshore wind auction in 2023. As prices in the supply chain have increased, many offshore wind developers have rationalised their operations and now have a more risk averse investment outlook, and many jurisdictions have seen failed auctions for various reasons. reply:

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether funding provided to local authorities in respect of national public service pay agreements includes the consequent increase in the cost of pensions in payment arising from pay parity; if not, whether his Department has estimated that cost to local authorities; and the estimated cost in each of the years 2021 to 2025.
reply:

The funding system that applies to local authorities in Ireland is complex, as they derive their income from a variety of sources including commercial rates, charges for goods and services and funding from central government, including my Department and other government departments and state bodies.
Regarding the impact of national public sector pay agreements, the table below indicates the allocations made to individual local authorities in each of the years 2021 to 2026. question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he shares concerns that the absence of a central EU mechanism for packaging producer responsibility compliance is creating significant red tape for Irish businesses trading across the single market; whether he has raised the issue with his European counterparts; and the actions he is taking to ensure that companies are not subject to multiple reporting systems and payment arrangements for the same packaging obligations across different Member States.
reply:
The new EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) applies generally from 12 August 2026. We are currently in the introductory phase, with only a limited number of provisions applying at present and further requirements being introduced on a phased basis over the coming years.
The PPWR was introduced to address very significant environmental challenges associated with packaging waste. Packaging waste generation has grown by some 20% over the 10 years to 2023 so that packaging now accounts for approximately 40% of virgin plastic and 50% of paper used in the EU. As a directly applicable EU Regulation, it was also intended to harmonise the approach to packaging across the Single Market, and there is little discretion for Member States to diverge from its requirements.
Since its introduction in August, however, there has been widespread concern about its impact on small businesses across Europe, particularly in terms of the burden of meeting Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) obligations. In this regard, after extensive discussion among Member States facilitated by the Irish Presidency, the European Council agreed its position on 21 October on a proposal to suspend the application of certain EPR obligations under the PPWR.
This proposal is subject to further negotiations with the European Parliament. As Ireland holds the Presidency of the European Council at present, our role is to represent the collective position of the Member States in those negotiations. Ireland h

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the statutory methodology that approved housing bodies (AHBs) must use when assessing variable income for cost rental applicants; if AHBs must average all payslips provided within the assessment period of three months; if periods of payroll processing lag (details supplied) should be legally recognised as periods of active employment and included in the averaging division.
reply:
Cost Rental forms a key part of the Government's plans to deliver more affordable rental housing, under the Delivering Homes, Building Communities, 2025-2030 strategy. Cost Rental homes are intended to provide secure, long-term rental accommodation for households whose incomes are above the threshold for social housing support, but who may face affordability challenges in the private rental market and previously had no option of State-supported housing. The primary eligibility condition for accessing Cost Rental housing is a maximum net annual household income of €66,000 for homes in Dublin and €59,000 elsewhere.
It is important to note that Cost Rental is not social housing. It is not an entitlement to State support based on need, but rather a more affordable rental option within the overall housing system. When someone applies for a Cost Rental tenancy, the Local Authority does not automatically assess their net income as a statutory duty, as it does for social housing applicants. It is the Cost Rental landlord which must satisfy itself that a prospective tenant has a net income within the relevant limit, in order to comply with the legislation, and also that they are in a position to reasonably afford the rent over the long term.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport which Night-Time Economy Taskforce recommendations and Programme for Government commitments concerning nightclubs, dance venues and club culture remain outstanding; the action that has been taken to address concerns raised by an organisation (details supplied) regarding the slow pace of implementation; and whether a definitive timeline for delivering these commitments will be provided.
reply:

Following the publication of the Night-Time Economy Task Force Report in 2021, a high-level Night-Time Economy (NTE) Implementation Group was established by my department. question: Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport for an update on the development of a new National Velodrome and Badminton Centre.
reply:
On 3 September 2025, the Government approved funding of €99.6 million and the appointment of Walls Construction as principal contractor for the National Velodrome and Badminton Centre (NVBC). Construction commenced in February of this year and I am pleased to inform the Deputy that the project is progressing well and is expected to be delivered on time and within budget.
Since the commencement of construction, significant progress has been made on the development of the groundworks and the erection of the steel frame for the building. In parallel with the main construction works, the design team for the project continues to progress plans for the timely fit-out to the facility, with a view to it being fully operational and in use by Q2 2028.
The Project will deliver a 250-metre cycling track, the standard required length for hosting major international events. It will also deliver up to 12 badminton courts in the in-track area, seating for 1,000 spectators and ancillary facilities.
When operational, the NVBC will address the need to provide world-class track cycling facilities for our athletes as well as providing the sport of badminton with integrated training, gym and medical facilities. This state of the art facility will afford our track cycling athletes the opportunity to train in Ireland and should have a positive effect on future international performance levels in both sports.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the actions that are being taken to increase the maximum level of renewable electricity that can be accommodated on the grid, given the high levels of dispatch down in 2026.
reply:
The Government recognises that renewable dispatch down is an increasingly important issue as Ireland continues to increase levels of renewable electricity generation and works towards its climate and energy objectives.
At present, my focus is on delivering a holistic and enduring approach to addressing dispatch down and facilitating greater levels of dispatchable demand across the electricity system. A comprehensive strategic and operational assessment document is currently being prepared which will set out the full range of measures being progressed across Government, regulators, network operators and industry to address renewable dispatch down and maximise the utilisation of renewable electricity generation. This work encompasses a wide range of measures, including demand response, storage, network reinforcement, smart technologies and other flexibility solutions, and is being progressed through established policy, regulatory and system planning processes.
By improving the efficiency with which renewable energy is utilised, these measures aim to support lower system costs, reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels and contribute to a more affordable energy transition, delivering benefits for all consumers, including households vulnerable to energy poverty.
Regarding timelines, it is expected that the document under development will be completed by year end, while the actions within the document span across future years with many already commenced.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the measures he intends to take to ensure that households, farmers and small businesses investing in solar panels receive a fair and sustainable payment for electricity exported to the national grid.
reply:
The matter referred to in the Question, is not within my remit as Minister.
The electricity and gas retail markets in Ireland operate within a European Union regulatory regime wherein electricity and gas markets are commercial, liberalised, and competitive. Operating within this overall EU framework, responsibility for the regulation of the electricity and gas markets is solely a matter for the Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) which was assigned responsibility for the regulation of the Irish electricity and gas markets following the enactment of the Electricity Regulation Act, 1999.
CRU provides a dedicated email address for Oireachtas members, which enables them to raise questions on general energy regulatory matters to the CRU at oireachtas@cru.ie for timely direct reply.
In line with long standing policy on deregulating price setting, the CRU ended its regulation of retail prices in the electricity market in 2011, and in the gas market in 2014. Price setting by electricity suppliers, including renumeration for microgeneration is a commercial and operational matter for the companies concerned. The CRU published a decision on an interim enabling framework for the Clean Export Guarantee (CEG) on 1 December 2021. This decision outlined the interim arrangements for the implementation of the CEG, including eligibility criteria and a remuneration methodology. I regularly hear from families, parents and schools about the importance of ensuring that supports are available when they are needed, and I am committed to addressing barriers that may delay or impede access to appropriate educational provision.

These changes have strengthened access to support for many children and young people.

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of school days missed at primary and post-primary respectively in Cork in September 2026, September 2024 and September 2022.
reply:
Tusla Education Support Service (TESS) is under the remit of my Department, and operates under the Education (Welfare) Act, 2000, a piece of legislation that emphasises the promotion of school attendance, participation and retention.
Section 21(6) of the Act provides that all recognised primary and post primary schools, including special schools, submit an Annual Attendance Report (AAR) to TESS on student non-attendance at an aggregated level, within six weeks of the end of the school year. The AAR provides four pieces of data in respect of all students enrolled in the school;
- total days lost by all students,
- total students absent for 20 or more days,
- total students suspended,
- total students expelled at the school level.
In accordance with Section 21(4) of the Act, Student Absence Reports (SARs) are submitted to TESS by recognised schools and provide data only on those students aged over 6 years and under 16 years, who are absent for a cumulative total of 20 or more days in the school year, by the recorded reason for their absence. The recorded absence reasons are; illness, urgent, holiday, suspension or other.
The reports for the 2022/23 and 2024/25 school years are available on Tusla's website at the following link: www.tusla.ie/services/educational-welfare-services/publications/research-and-statistics.

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of teaching posts unfilled in Cork currently.
reply:

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of SNA posts unfilled in Cork currently.
reply:

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will provide an update on an application for assistive technology (details supplied).
reply:
Under the Assistive Technology Scheme, as set out in my Department’s Circular 0010/2013, funding is provided to schools towards the cost of computers and specialist equipment which are required for educational purposes.
All equipment provided under this scheme supports children with more complex disabilities who, in order to access the school curriculum, require essential specialist equipment. It must be clear that the existing IT equipment in the school is insufficient to meet the child's needs. Where necessary, schools may also purchase new or additional equipment or software for students from normal school resources or funds.
In the case referred to by the Deputy, Department officials have confirmed that a decision letter in relation to the Assistive Technology application was issued to the school on the 2nd of November 2026.

question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Education and Youth to investigate with urgency the claim for an unpaid increment for a person (details supplied); if this can be resolved with urgency and the back pay owed to this person be paid in full.
reply:
The criteria required to have incremental credit awarded to qualified Special Needs Assistants (SNA) is set out in Circular 0139/2006 and was agreed with the union representing Special Needs Assistants, School Management Representatives, the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform, and the Department of Education and Youth.
To qualify for an award of incremental credit an SNA and their prior work experience being claimed must satisfy the eligibility criteria set out in the relevant circular. An award of incremental credit cannot be made where the eligibility criteria are not satisfied.
In relation to the SNA referred to, the Department notes that an application for incremental credit was received on 8 August 2022, with supporting documentation received on 21 September 2022.
On 20 December 2022, an outcome letter was issued to the applicant. The prior service claimed did not meet the eligibility requirements of the circular. Under Section 4.3(b) of Circular 0139/2006, "Incremental credit shall not be awarded in respect of work undertaken in a clerical/administrative capacity."
Please note that the position of Clerical Officer with the Department of Social Protection is an administrative role and, therefore, does not meet the agreed criteria set out in Section 4.3(b) of Circular 0139/2006.
As the applicant did not demonstrate that they met the relevant eligibility criteria, their application for incremental credit was refused.

question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to remove the condition to qualify for the solar PV and battery grants that homes must be built and occupied before 2025.
reply:
My Department funds a number of grant schemes, administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI), to support homeowners in improving the energy efficiency of their existing properties.
The schemes, along with the eligibility rules, are kept under review by my Department and the SEAI with a view to delivering energy savings for the widest range of homeowners possible, while also making the most efficient use of Exchequer funding.
Last January, and later in the run-up to Budget 2027, I expanded and reformed retrofitting schemes to ensure that more homeowners can receive grants. The new measures included increased insulation supports, an increased grant for heat pumps, expanded eligibility for solar PV and solar thermal grants for homes built and occupied prior to 2025 (pre-2021 previously).
Increasing and expanding the grant offerings is paying dividends with clear evidence of growth in both demand and output. This year, to end September 2026, over 40,000 applications have been received for solar PV, an almost 66% increase over 2025.
Targeting the grant scheme at older homes makes the most efficient use of limited Exchequer funding for the scheme. The cost of installing solar PV systems during the new build process is significantly lower than for existing homes. There are no plans at present to further amend the building year requirement but grant eligibility is kept under review.

question: Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she is aware that there is no Gaelcholáiste in Laois, Offaly or Westmeath; if her Department has assessed the demand for one in Offaly, given the number of pupils attending Gaelscoileanna in Birr and Tullamore; and the steps she will take to establish one.

My Department has a robust school planning process to ensure that sufficient school places are available to meet current and future demand. This process involves the preparation of detailed demographic profiles and school place demand projections using a range of data sources, including school enrolment trends, Census data, child benefit records, geocoded pupil enrolment data, population estimates and projections, residential development activity, housing completion data, planning permissions, local authority development plans and information on planned housing delivery. question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Education and Youth to rectify the outstanding summer provision payment for a person (details supplied).
reply:
The Summer Programme is an educational programme for children with complex special educational needs which is run during school summer holidays. All primary, post primary and special schools are given an opportunity to run a programme for those children who need it the most. These children can continue to be supported, nurtured and encouraged to engage in a fun and inclusive educational setting.
The main priority of the Summer Programme is to ensure that those children with the most complex special educational needs, especially in special schools, should have access to a school-based summer programme.
However, the department recognises that not all schools are in a position to provide a school-based programme. Where is school-based programme is not being run or a place on the programme is not available, the home-based programme will be available for children with complex special educational needs.
Under the Home-based Summer programme, grant funding is made available so that parents/legal guardians can engage the services of a teacher or a SNA to provide tuition or care support as appropriate in the child’s home. The allocation of hours which can be provided to an eligible child on a one-to-one basis is strictly 10 hours per week, for up to 4 weeks, with the maximum of the 5 hours per day being allowable.
In the case referred to by the Deputy, the timetable submitted shows that more than 10 hours were completed per week and that the hours were delivered over a 2 week period.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether the Health and Safety Authority has ongoing initiatives to combat online disinformation related to their remit for disseminating public information; and if so, the expenditure associated with any such initiative.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 293 and 297 together.
The Health and Safety Authority (HSA) is aware that AI tools may produce reports or summaries that draw on information that is available online, including information that has been superseded or is now out of date. The use of AI in this context is outside of the HSA’s control, and any AI-generated output may not always reflect current HSA guidance or information.
The HSA keeps under continuous review the public information and guidance published through its own official channels, including its website and social media.
The HSA does not operate a dedicated initiative to combat online disinformation. The HSA is responsible for the information it publishes through its official channels; it has no control over potentially inaccurate information independently generated by third parties, AI tools, or other sources.
The HSA is focused on providing clear, accurate and up-to-date public information and guidance related to its mandates through official channels, including its website and social media.
Duty holders and members of the public who are seeking information on any matters related to its mandates are encouraged to refer to its website, and other official publications, for factual and up-to-date information.
Where any inaccurate information is found to be in the public domain, this can be brought to the HSA’s attention for review, and appropriate action where necessary.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment his views on allegations of electrocutions, ‘mental terror’ and withheld wages among the exploited workers building Europe’s data centres including several Irish firms (details supplied).
reply:
The allegations referred to by the Deputy are deeply concerning. All workers should be able to carry out their work safely, receive the pay to which they are entitled and raise concerns about their working conditions without intimidation. The development of data centre infrastructure must not come at the expense of workers’ safety or employment rights.
These principles apply equally to Irish businesses operating internationally. Those businesses must comply with the applicable employment and occupational safety and health requirements in the jurisdictions in which they operate.
Ireland maintains a robust occupational safety and health regulatory framework designed to protect workers. Employers have legal obligations to safeguard the safety, health and welfare of their employees. We also maintain a comprehensive body of employment rights legislation that safeguards workers and promotes fair treatment in the workplace. This legislation applies horizontally across all sectors to all employees employed in the State.
It is important to distinguish allegations concerning particular companies from findings made by the competent authorities. Responsibility for investigating incidents and enforcing the relevant law rests with the authorities with jurisdiction over the workplace and employment arrangements concerned. Where work takes place outside Ireland, the authorities in the country concerned have responsibility for enforcement.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment for an update on guidelines for the development of battery energy storage facilities; and a timeframe for same.
reply:

In July 2024, my Department published the Electricity Storage Policy Framework for Ireland. Chapter 4 of the Policy Framework provides an overview of the regime in place for grid scale electricity storage systems, outlining the roles and remits of the relevant Government Departments, State bodies and public authorities.

The current planning system provides a robust policy and legislative framework to facilitate the proper planning and sustainable development of such systems, which are considered on a case-by-case basis in accordance with the relevant County Development Plan and Government Policy as applicable.

reply:
As Minister, I do not review or reconsider individual support decisions made by Enterprise Ireland in respect of specific companies. The provision and administration of such supports are matters for Enterprise Ireland in the exercise of its statutory functions.
Enterprise Ireland supports Irish owned companies to develop their capabilities, expand internationally and grow exports and employment in Ireland. In the high-tech construction sector, this support includes market intelligence, business development advice, introductions to potential customers and partners, and assistance through Enterprise Ireland's international office network.
Enterprise Ireland is not involved in the day-to-day operational decisions of the companies it supports, including the management of their overseas operations or subcontractors. The Enterprise Ireland material referred to by the Deputy highlighted the international activities and technical expertise of Irish companies operating in Sweden's data centre sector. It was not an assessment or endorsement by Enterprise Ireland of the workplace practices of individual companies.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the way in which the Government intends to interpret and apply the definition of a digital labour platform under Directive (EU) 2024/2831; whether the definition adopted in Irish legislation will align directly with that set out in Article 2 of the Directive; whether the Government intends to broaden the scope of this definition as part of the transposition process.
reply:
The Improving Working Conditions in Platform Work Directive entered into force on 1 December 2024. EU Member States have until 2 December 2026 to transpose the Directive into national law.
The Directive is technically complex and wide-ranging. It seeks to ensure that people working through digital labour platforms have the correct legal employment status that corresponds to their actual working arrangements, enabling them to benefit from the employment rights to which they are entitled.
The approach currently being taken by my Department in transposing Article 2 of the Directive is to adopt a definition of ‘digital labour platform’ in Irish legislation that is directly aligned with that contained in the Directive.
Under Article 2 of the Directive, a digital labour platform is a service provided, (i) remotely via electronic means, (ii) at the request of the service recipient, (iii) which involves organising work performed by individuals for payment irrespective of whether that work is performed online or in a certain location, and (iv) which uses automated monitoring or decision-making systems.
To qualify as a digital labour platform, a service provider must meet all of the criteria listed in the definition. These criteria are cumulative, meaning that if any single one is not met, the provider does not qualify as a digital labour platform.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether the Government remains on track to fully transpose the EU Platform Work Directive by the deadline of 2 December 2026; whether the Directive will be transposed through primary or secondary legislation, or a combination of both; whether the Government intends to introduce any additional requirements that go beyond those set out in the Directive.
reply:
The Improving Working Conditions in Platform Work Directive entered into force on 1 December 2024 and EU Member States have until 2 December 2026 to transpose the Directive into national law.
The Directive is technically complex and wide-ranging. It seeks to ensure that people working through digital labour platforms have the correct legal employment status corresponding to their actual working arrangements, enabling them to benefit from the employment rights to which they are entitled.
Work on the transposition of the Platform Work Directive remains ongoing, and officials in my Department continue to progress the legislative and administrative measures required for its transposition. Officials continue to work with a view to completing the transposition process by the deadline of 2 December 2026.
The current approach is to transpose the Directive through secondary legislation, by way of regulations made under section 3 of the European Communities Act 1972. Officials in my Department continue to engage with the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel and other relevant stakeholders on the preparation of the necessary transposing measures.
It is currently intended that the transposing measures will give effect to Ireland's obligations under the Directive, and, at present, no additional policy measures beyond those necessary for that purpose are proposed.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the measures being taken to protect Irish songwriters, composers and performers from the unauthorised use of their copyrighted works in the training of artificial intelligence systems; whether he supports requirements for transparency, consent, licensing and fair remuneration where copyrighted music is used for AI training purposes.
reply:
Ireland’s legislative approach to copyright, AI and digital regulation, is closely aligned with developments at the European Union level. To this end, my Department is actively engaging in discussions at EU level in these areas, and in particular at present as Ireland has assumed the Presidency of the Council of the EU.
The AI Act requires providers of generative AI services available in the EU put in a place a policy to demonstrate compliance with EU copyright law, specifically Article 4(3) of the Copyright in the DSM Directive (the Text and Data Mining (TDM) exception) and providers are required to complete a ‘Transparency Template’ providing a high-level overview of data used to train models. The general-purpose AI (GPAI) Code of Practice developed under the AI Act helps industry comply with the legal obligations on copyright. From the 2 August 2026, Article 50 of the AI Act imposed mandatory transparency obligations on providers and deployers of AI systems, which have a number of applications, including for copyright.
