question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if Dignity at Work, Circular 12/2026, which took effect on 31 March 2026, applies where the person complained of by a civil servant is a minister or minister of State rather than a civil servant; if not, the procedure that applies to such complaints; whether the question of complaints against office holders was considered during the development of the circular.
reply:
Circular 12/2026, Dignity at Work, An Anti-Bullying, Harassment and Sexual Harassment Policy for the Civil Service was developed as a Civil Service HR policy and applies to civil servants and other categories of workers falling within the policy scope.
Ministers and Ministers of State are Office Holders and are subject to the governance, accountability and ethics arrangements applicable to their role. Accordingly, where a complaint concerns a Minister or Minister of State, it would be considered under those arrangements. Depending on the circumstances, this may include consideration under the relevant ethics and accountability framework applicable to Office Holders, and where appropriate, under relevant statutory provisions including the Employment Equality Acts and the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the progress made towards the State’s 2030 biomethane targets; whether biomethane is expected to be prioritised for industrial or domestic heat; and the economic viability and route to market for biomethane.
reply:
Delivery of the Government's target of up to 5.7 TWh of indigenous biomethane per annum by 2030 and its use within our energy system will have multiple cross-sectoral benefits for Ireland’s economy, energy security and emissions profile. As such, development of this industry is being advanced through a collaborative approach to policy implementation across all sectors including energy, agriculture and enterprise.
The Biomethane Implementation Group has been established to oversee implementation of the National Biomethane Strategy and delivery of the 25 key strategic actions to ensure the necessary infrastructure and supports are in place to support development of an indigenous biomethane industry of scale.
Biomethane will play a critical role in sectors where no alternative decarbonisation options exist, such as high temperature heat processes. In addition to high temperature heat processes, biomethane will play an important role in the transport, electricity and built environment sectors.
Biomethane production is not being prioritised for exclusive allocation to either industrial or domestic heating sectors. The sector that pays the highest premium for biomethane will ultimately secure the resource. Also, Government policy is for the residential heat sector to be decarbonised using heat pumps and district heating.
Ireland’s biomethane sector is gaining significant momentum. Seven anaerobic digestion plants are currently under construction or have just completed construction,

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if the records and statistics of formal complaints which departments are required to keep under paragraph 56 of Dignity at Work, Circular 12/2026, or under the previous 2015 policy, are collected centrally; the total number of formal complaints of bullying, harassment and sexual harassment recorded across the civil service in each of the years 2021 to 2025 and to date in 2026; the number of those in which the person complained of was not a civil servant.
reply:
Circular 12/2026 Dignity at Work, An Anti-Bullying, Harassment and Sexual Harassment Policy for the Civil Service provides that ‘Civil Service Departments and/or Offices should keep records and statistics of formal complaints of bullying, harassment and sexual harassment in order to assist them in taking corrective action in the implementation of this policy’.
Civil Service Departments and Offices in their capacity as employers, are responsible for managing formal complaints of bullying, harassment and sexual harassment in line with the provisions of Circular 12/2026.
In this context, my Department does not maintain central statistics on formal complaints of bullying, harassment and sexual harassment across the Civil Service and does not hold the figures requested for the years 2021 to 2026, including the number of cases where the person complained of was not a civil servant.
Each Civil Service Department or Office should have information available on the number of complaints recorded within their respective organisations for the time period specified.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the total pension contributions remitted by local authorities in respect of members of the single public service pension scheme in each year since 2013, in tabular form; the status and expected publication date of the actuarial review of public service occupational pension liabilities as at 31 December 2024; and whether that review will set out the accrued liability attributable to local authorities.
reply:
The total Single Public Service Pension Scheme pension contributions remitted by Local Authorities are provided in tabular form below.
The actuarial review of public service occupational pension liabilities, as at 31 December 2024, is in progress and will be finalised by year end 2026 in line with EU reporting deadlines. It is proposed to publish a report on the actuarial review thereafter.
The actuarial review is being carried out on behalf of the Central Statistics Office (the “C.S.O.”) who are required to compile a supplementary table showing the accrued liabilities of all funded and unfunded Irish pension schemes as part of the National Accounts, under Regulation (EU) No. 549 / 2013. This review is being carried out every three years.
The review places an actuarial value on the accrued pension entitlements of all current and former public service employees as at valuation date.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation whether his Department has received any proposal or engaged with the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage since 1 January 2022 regarding the transfer of local authority pension liabilities to the Exchequer or Exchequer funding of local authority pension costs; and the status of any such engagement.
reply: Local Government superannuation matters are, in the first instance, a policy matter for the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage. I have been informed by the Minister's Department that the County and City Management Association (CCMA) are preparing a paper on the Local Authority Pension Liability issue to submit to the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage. When the paper has been considered by the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, they will engage, in due course, with the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation.

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he will designate the TEN-T Priority Improvement Project Donegal as a critical infrastructure project, as requested by Donegal County Council.
reply:
The Critical Infrastructure Act 2026 allows the Government to designate certain infrastructure projects developed by or on behalf of the State as being of critical national importance. This provides a statutory basis for accelerating decision making in respect of designated projects and programmes.
The Act establishes an ongoing framework through which projects and programmes of strategic national importance can be considered by Government on a rolling basis. To date, the Government has designated nine projects as critical infrastructure and these projects are being prioritised through the consenting and approval processes. Further designation orders will be brought forward at regular intervals to ensure continued progress on nationally important infrastructure projects. My intention is to bring further recommendations to Government for designation under the Act before the end of the year.
Any future recommendations will be assessed having regard to the criteria set out in the Act, including the importance of the project or programme to the State, the potential economic or social consequences of delay, and its contribution to national strategic objectives.
Any decision to designate a project remains a matter for Government.

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the amount that has been paid by the Revenue Commissioners for the first three quarters of 2026 in corporation tax credits under Section 481 film tax credit to fil, TV companies and visual media production companies.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 269, 270, 271 and 272 together.
Section 481 provides relief in the form of a corporation tax credit related to the cost of production of certain films. The scheme is intended to act as a stimulus to the creation of an indigenous film industry in the State, creating quality employment opportunities and supporting the expression of Irish culture.
The scheme provides relief in the form of a corporation tax credit related to the cost of production of certain films. The credit is granted at a rate of 32% of the lowest of:
- eligible expenditure.
- 80% of the total cost of production of the film.
- €125 million.
The Section 481 tax credit is reviewed regularly under the Department of Finance’s Tax Expenditure Guidelines. The most recent Cost-Benefit Analysis was completed in 2022 and published in the Department’s “Budget 2023, Report on Tax Expenditures 2022”. It is envisaged that a further Cost Benefit Analysis will be undertaken in 2027 and preparatory work on this project has already commenced.
I am advised by Revenue that the value of payments made by Revenue from 1 January to 30 September 2026 in relation to the section 481 film corporation tax credit is approximately €147 million.
Producer companies may claim the film tax credit in two instalments, the first instalment being up to 90% of the expected credit based on budgeted expenditure and the second instalment being the balancing payment claimed on completion of the production. Alternatively

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment for an update on the Hydrogen Strategy.
reply:
My Department established the National Hydrogen Programme Taskforce to oversee the delivery of the actions and wider strategic ambitions set out in the National Hydrogen Strategy. The Taskforce works across government departments and state agencies, engaging with key stakeholders, to remove barriers to early hydrogen project development and lay the groundwork to enable the development of the hydrogen sector in Ireland.
The twenty-one actions from the Strategy have been developed into a multi-year work programme and assigned to working group areas across three pillar areas: Working Group 1 on safety and regulation, Working Group 2 on infrastructure and systems, and Working Group 3 on markets and commercialisation. The National Hydrogen Programme Implementation Plan, which is available on the gov.ie websitehttps://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/0a80ed16/National_Hydrogen_Programme_Implementation_Plan.pdf sets out the details of this work programme.
Significant progress has been made on actions to develop the necessary legislative and regulatory frameworks for hydrogen, to develop a fund for hydrogen demonstration projects, and to further build a solid evidence base to inform policymaking. The Taskforce is due to meet before the end of the year to approve the publication of an update report that will provide stakeholders with more details on the Taskforce’s progress to date in implementing the National Hydrogen Strategy.

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to provide an estimate of the additional revenue that could be raised through each 1% increase in the 30 per cent effective rate of income tax that must be paid by individuals subject to the high income earner restriction.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 267 and 268 together.
The Deputy may wish to note that the high-income individuals’ restriction (“HIIR”) works by limiting the total amount of specified reliefs that can be used by a high-income individual to a maximum amount each year. The maximum amount is set by reference to a specific figure or to a maximum percentage of income for the year. Relief that is disallowed for a tax year is added-back to the individual’s taxable income for the year to give a recalculated taxable income figure. The recalculated taxable income amount is then taxed in accordance with normal income tax rates and the individual is entitled to normal tax credits against the tax due. Changes introduced by Finance Act 2010, with effect from 1 January 2010, ensured that individuals who are fully subject to the restriction, pay an effective rate of income tax of approximately 30 per cent.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether the Future Ireland Fund is intended to contribute towards the cost of public service occupational pensions, including pensions arising from service in local authorities.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the Future Ireland Fund (FIF) was established in 2024, following the commencement of the Future Ireland Fund and Infrastructure, Climate and Nature Fund Act 2024 (“the Act”).
The establishment of this fund is a key pillar of the Government’s fiscal risk management strategy and an important move for inter-generational equity.
The FIF will be maintained over the longer term with the return on the Fund used to support government expenditure for future generations. This will help to deal with future recognised expenditure pressures including ageing, climate, digitalisation and other fiscal and economic challenges.
The FIF will support, in a consistent and sustainable manner, State expenditure from 2041 onwards. Decisions in relation to that expenditure will be a matter for the Government of the day and the Act does not limit the areas to which drawn down funding may be allocated.

question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Transport if he intends to reintroduce the ICE2EV scrappage scheme given the success of the recent pilot scheme and broader Government commitments to reduce carbon emissions by 50% by 2030.
reply:
The ICE2EV Pilot Scheme, which launched on July 1st, has committed the full €17M available in funding, comprising of €10M for the scrappage grant and €7M for the EV purchase grant.
Approximately 2,000 successful applications were processed within 75 minutes of the scheme opening, supporting the replacement of around 2,000 internal combustion engine vehicles with electric vehicles. While strong demand was anticipated, the level of interest exceeded expectations.
The high level of interest demonstrated in the scheme is welcome and reflects growing consumer engagement with the transition to electric vehicles. This momentum supports Ireland’s Climate Action ambitions, including the target for 30% of the national vehicle fleet to be electric by 2030.
The policy purpose of this capped initiative was to test the effectiveness of scrappage as a tool to stimulate EV uptake among those who may not otherwise transition in the near term, with the ultimate goal of delivering additional emissions reductions necessary for our climate targets.
While the pilot scheme has closed for new applications, the final stages of validation and payment processing remain ongoing. Dealers have a period of up to 4 months to complete the sale and submit the documentation. A post-completion evaluation of the scheme is underway and will be completed once all documentation has been collected, to assess its effectiveness, emissions impact and overall value for money, and to inform future policy decisions in thi

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Transport to expedite works on the South Kerry Greenway; and to provide a detailed progress report on this tourism project for the county, including commencement and completion dates for the remaining sections.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and exchequer funding in relation to Greenways. I note that there has been significant investment in Greenway schemes in County Kerry, with €9,950,000 allocated in 2026.
Under the Roads Act 1993, the planning, design, and construction of individual Greenways is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned.
Noting the above position, I have referred your question, on this occasion, to TII for a direct reply. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 working days.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Transport to give a detailed progress report on agreements reached, accommodation works carried out and payments made to date to landowners adjacent to the South Kerry Greenway; if he will ensure that all outstanding agreements are reached and finalised as soon as possible; if he will introduce a sustainability payment similar to the new Code of Practice 1 payment for all landowners adjacent to the South Kerry Greenway; and if he will ensure that this tourism project is completed at the earliest possible date.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and exchequer funding in relation to Greenways. To date, there has been a significant amount of investment for Greenway schemes in County Kerry, with €9,950,000 allocated in 2026 alone.
In relation to the South Kerry Greenway, 28% of landowners had been paid to end June 2026. It is expected that further claims will be settled by the end of 2026. Kerry County Council continue to work with landowners to advance and finalise the settlement of claims.
The Code of Practice for National and Regional Greenways includes information on the acquisition of private lands for developing Greenways and eligibility criteria for sustainability payments. The Code acknowledges the important role of farmers and landowners in the process. It outlines the procedures to ensure that they are treated fairly and equitably. TII are tasked with maintaining the Code of Best Practice for National and Regional Greenways.
Landowners on some greenway schemes are not eligible for Early Sign-on Payment part A of the Greenway Sustainability as the statutory consents granted preceded the introduction of the Code in January 2022. Additional proposals have been brought forward (by some landowners, farming organisations, and elected members) regarding providing a financial support similar to the ‘Early Sign-On Payment’ to these landowners.
While these fall outside the current Code of Best Practice, I am positively disposed to examining them further

reply:
Irish driver licensing operates within a framework of EU law, which sets out the driver licensing legislation with which all member states must comply. The vehicles which may be driven under each licence category are set out in European Directive 2006/126/EC.
It is important to distinguish between the entitlement to drive a vehicle and the professional qualification required to drive that vehicle commercially. To drive a truck or bus professionally in Ireland, drivers must have a valid driving licence in the relevant category and a valid driver certificate of professional competence (CPC).
The driver CPC process is based on European Union Directive 2022/2561, on the initial qualifications and periodic training of drivers of vehicles carrying goods or passengers. The European Communities (Vehicle Drivers Certificate of Professional Competence) Regulations 2008, as amended, transpose these requirements into Irish law. Regulation 7 transposes article 5 of the Directive and specifies that the minimum age for completing an initial CPC test for categories D, DE, D1 and D1E is 21.
Regulation 9 of the Road Traffic (Licensing of Drivers) Regulations 2006 (SI 537 of 2006), as amended, sets out the minimum age at which a person may drive a particular category of vehicle. This Regulation states that the minimum age for applying for a driving licence in category D1 and D1E is 21 and the minimum age for applying for a D or DE licence is 24. However, if an individual holds a CPC, the minimu

Noting the NTA's responsibility in the matter, I have referred the Deputy's question to the NTA for a more detailed reply. Please contact my private office, if you do not receive a reply within 10 working days.

In terms of infrastructure, the programme will provide for a total of 11 Sustainable Transport Corridors, delivering approximately 90km of bus lane and bus priority measures to improve bus system efficiency, as well as 95km of cycle lanes. BusConnects Cork will also see the implementation of a new, redesigned bus network across Cork City and its suburbs increasing bus services by over 50%, with the first phases planned for 2027, subject to funding and operational readiness.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Transport if he will stop the planned increase in the price of tolls from January 2027.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and funding in relation to the national roads programme. Under the Roads Acts 1993-2015, the operation and management of individual national roads is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned.
Therefore, matters relating to the day to day operations regarding national roads, including toll roads are within the remit of TII. More specifically, the statutory power to levy tolls, to make toll bye-laws and to enter into agreements with private investors are vested in TII under Part V of the Roads Act 1993 (as amended). Moreover, the contracts for the privately-operated toll schemes are commercial agreements between TII and the Public Private Partnership (PPP) concessionaires concerned.
Toll revenues received by TII contribute to the funding of essential services on the national primary and secondary road network including general day to day maintenance and operation of the network e.g., pavement repair and renewal, road safety improvements, incident and emergency response, winter gritting and safety barrier repair and renewal. These essential services are necessary to ensure the national road network is managed and maintained and TII relies upon tolling revenue along with funding from the exchequer to fund this work.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Transport the number of rest stops on the motorway network that are closed.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and exchequer funding in relation to the National Roads Programme. Under the Roads Acts 1993-2015 and in line with the National Development Plan (NDP), the operation and management of individual national roads is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned. This is also subject to the Infrastructure Guidelines and the necessary statutory approvals. In this context, TII is best placed to advise you in relation to the number of lay-bys that are closed on motorways.
Noting the above position, I have referred your question to TII for a direct reply. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 working days.

question: Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Transport if he will provide an update on the status of the Dublin Port 3FM infrastructure project.
reply:
My Department maintains a strong and constructive relationship with the State-owned commercial ports and I am kept informed of all significant matters, including the progression of major infrastructure strategies such as Dublin Port Company's (DPC's) Masterplan 2040.
DPC's third and final Masterplan project, known as the 3FM Project, comprises the redevelopment of port lands on the Poolbeg Peninsula and the construction of a new bridge across the River Liffey to provide a Southern Port Access Route for port-related heavy goods vehicle traffic. The project will also make a significant contribution to active travel infrastructure in the area through the provision of a new Maritime Village, enhanced public and community amenities, and approximately 5.5 kilometres of pedestrian and cycling routes across the Poolbeg Peninsula. The project is of strategic national importance, providing essential infrastructure to support Ireland's international trade and economic competitiveness.
DPC submitted its planning application for the 3FM Project to An Coimisiún Pleanála on 22 July 2024 and a final decision on the application is awaited.
On 6 August 2026, DPC received a second Further Information Request from An Coimisiún Pleanála as part of the planning application process comprising 17 items to be addressed, primarily relating to environmental matters. reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport.
Under the Dublin Transport Authority Act 2008 and the Public Transport Regulation Act 2009, the Oireachtas assigned statutory responsibility to the National Transport Authority (NTA) for promoting the development of an integrated, accessible public transport network and public transport infrastructure. question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment when he will finalise the review and approval for the sale and use of plug-in photovoltaic (PIPV) solar panels in Ireland.
reply:
Plug-in solar is an emerging low-carbon technology, and the Government is committed to accelerating its introduction in Ireland. Once enabled, it can provide a cost-effective and accessible way for customers to participate more actively in the energy transition, with potential benefits including lower electricity bills, greater demand flexibility, and support for Ireland’s renewable energy and climate objectives.
At my request, ESB Networks established a plug-in solar working group in May 2026 to examine pathways for the safe, standardised and scalable deployment of the technology. The group has met nine times to date.
The working group recently submitted an options report to my Department, setting out recommendations on matters including installation approaches, product specifications and customer guidance. In parallel, my Department is working with stakeholders to progress elements of the regulatory framework. Planned next steps include an Ireland-specific safety assessment, a legislative review, development of a product specification, publication of detailed customer guidance, and the establishment of an online product registration portal.
Further work is required to ensure the technology can be deployed safely, is supported by an appropriate regulatory framework, and that any legal barriers are addressed. My Department is currently progressing the safety assessment and legislative review, both of which are expected to conclude next year.

question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Transport if a school (details supplied) in County Kildare is eligible for the Safe Routes to School programme; and if he will outline the way in which a school applies for the programme.
reply:
The Safe Routes to School (SRTS) Programme was launched in March 2021 with the aim of supporting walking, scooting, and cycling to primary and post-primary schools, and creating safer walking and cycling routes within communities, through the provision of infrastructure interventions including, in some cases, School Zones.
These projects should help alleviate congestion at school gates and increase the number of students who walk or cycle to school. The Safe Routes to School Programme is funded by the Department of Transport through the National Transport Authority (NTA) and An Taisce's Green Schools is co-ordinating the programme.
Invitations to express interest were sent to all primary and secondary schools in the country, and 932 applications were received from schools across every county in Ireland. Schools are processed in tranches, with five rounds having been announced to date. It should be noted that all schools that applied to the original call for applications were accepted into the programme, and if not selected in the initial rounds will be selected at a later date.
It is my understanding that the school in question, Suncroft National School, did not apply to the SRTS programme. Given the pipeline of projects due for completion, there are no plans for an additional call for schools to join the SRTS programme currently.

question: Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Transport to provide an update on the potential return of the Greystones/Bray coach to Dublin Airport; if options have been explored to add stops in these places to existing routes from places such as Wexford.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport; however, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of public transport. The National Transport Authority (NTA) has statutory responsibility for securing the provision of public passenger transport services nationally and is responsible for the licensing of public bus passenger services under the provisions of the Public Transport Regulation Act 2009.
While most public transport in Ireland comprises the bus and rail services funded through the NTA’s public service obligation (PSO) programme, there is part of the national public transport system that comprises non-subvented bus services, which are run on a commercial basis by bus and coach businesses of varying sizes throughout the country. As a commercial operator, any decisions taken by Aircoach regarding routes, scheduling and timetabling are a matter for the company, the NTA has no powers to refuse an application from an operator to reduce or withdraw services on a commercial route.
In light of the NTA’s responsibility as licencing authority, I have forwarded the Deputy's question to the NTA for direct reply. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a response within ten working days.

question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Defence whether her Department has a role in the maintenance of the Curragh; and if so, if she will outline these responsibilities.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 239 to 243, inclusive, together.
Grazing of sheep on the Curragh Plains was initially permitted under the Curragh of Kildare Act of 1870. Sheep are allowed to graze on all Curragh lands with the exception of the Defence Forces Training Centre (Curragh Camp) and other enclosed lands such as the Curragh Racecourse. “Claims” in this regard were awarded to various landowners in townlands surrounding the Curragh of Kildare. I am advised that the Department of Defence does not charge any fees for claims or grazing rights. My Department requests farmers to complete forms annually to identify the numbers of sheep claims they are using and in order to ensure that “rights of pasture” can be verified. I am advised that the current available number of sheep claims is 5,995.
Given the open nature of the Plains, sheep wandering is a regular occurrence , the management of the animals is the responsibility of the owners. In addition, the Department has no role in the installation, repair or maintenance of livestock control measures on public roads in the area. Responsibility for such measures lies with the local authority Kildare County Council.

question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment for an update on the work of the National Energy Affordability Taskforce.
reply:
Addressing energy affordability is a key priority for this Government. That is why in June of last year, I established the National Energy Affordability Taskforce (NEAT) to identify, assess and implement measures that will enhance energy affordability for households and businesses while delivering key renewables commitments, and protecting security of supply and economic stability.
The first report of the Taskforce, which included measures for consideration in Budget 2026, was published last November.
The work of the Taskforce has also informed measures announced in Budget 2027. In this year's Budget, the Government delivered a package of measures to help households and businesses with the cost of energy, with a particular focus on those most vulnerable to volatility in the price of imported fossil fuels. This included targeted social welfare supports, energy efficiency and retrofit supports as well as measures to protect consumers most exposed to energy costs.
A range of improvements to the retrofit schemes administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland, launched in October, was also developed through the work of the NEAT. This will make it easier and more affordable for households and businesses to improve energy efficiency, install renewable energy technologies and switch to cleaner heating systems. A particular focus of this package is ensuring that households most exposed to high energy costs can benefit from the energy transition.

question: Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Defence if she has spoken formally with the UK Secretary of Defence in the past three months.
reply:
On 17 September this year, I had a virtual meeting with my UK counterpart, Secretary of State for Defence, Wes Streeting, to discuss a range of issues of mutual interest. Our discussion included the recently refreshed Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), signed earlier this year with Secretary Streeting's predecessor, John Healey. The refreshed MoU, originally signed in 2015, provides a framework for developing and furthering bilateral co-operation between the Department of Defence and the UK Ministry of Defence and places particular emphasis on areas such as maritime co-operation, including the protection of critical undersea infrastructure, cyber defence and security, air domain information-sharing, support for Ukraine, training and education exchanges, and the exploration of potential joint procurement initiatives.
We also exchanged views on maritime security, which was timely, following my launch of Ireland's first National Maritime Security Strategy in February, and the actions arising from that Strategy.
The meeting also provided an opportunity to discuss the Defence Attaché network, under which London was selected as one of the locations for a newly established Defence Attaché post. I highlighted the importance of this posting in supporting our growing defence relationship with the United Kingdom, particularly in areas such as maritime security and the protection of critical infrastructure. The post will also enable Ireland to engage more effectively with the extensive d

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will work with the DSO and TSO to accelerate the timeline for implementation of hybrid grid connections for battery, wind and solar projects.
reply:
The Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) is responsible for grid connection policy including hybrid connections. The CRU is an independent regulator, accountable to a Committee of the Oireachtas and not to me as Minister.
Under Climate Action Plan 23 the CRU is tasked with ensuring that hybrid technology grid connections are facilitated. Work on this action is progressing. In April 2026, the CRU published a decision paper on the Sharing of Maximum Export Capacity. The decision allows for multiple generation assets to share a single grid connection point. This work follows their January 2024 decision paper on removing the Installed Capacity Cap.
As part of the CRU decision paper on Sharing of Maximum Export Capacity (MEC), the System Operators, EirGrid and ESBN Networks, were tasked with developing a roadmap outlining the steps required to implement MEC sharing. This implementation roadmap was published in June, and work is ongoing to deliver on its programme of activities. The System Operators are responsible for implementing the CRU decision and, in this regard, operate independently of me as Minister in the exercise of their respective functions.
My Department engages with the CRU and System Operators on a continuous basis and receives updates on the status of their hybrid connections policy through the Connections Working Group. The group provides coordination and support to the development of connection policy and reports to the Accelerating Renewable Energy Taskf

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether Ireland has designated renewables acceleration areas in accordance with Article 15c of Directive (EU) 2023/2413; whether the plans and strategic environmental assessment required by that Article have been adopted; and the date on which the coordinated mapping required by Article 15b was completed.
reply:
Article 15b of the recast Renewable Energy Directive 2023/2413 (REDIII) requires EU Member States to carry-out national territory mapping, to identify the domestic potential and the available areas that are necessary for the installation of renewable energy plants and their related infrastructure as required, to meet Ireland’s national contributions towards the overall EU renewable energy target for 2030.
Additionally, the Directive requires Member States to ensure that competent authorities identity at least one Renewable Acceleration Area (RAA) (under Article 15c) which must be a “sub-set” of areas identified under the national territory mapping exercise.
The coordinated mapping and public consultation report in relation to Article 15b were finalised in July this year and submitted to the European Commission in September.
My Department has been begun the preparation of a draft plan for the designation of a Renewable Acceleration Area, as per Article 15c of REDIII. Further statutory Public Consultation on a draft plan for the designation of any Renewable Acceleration Area and the establishment of appropriate rules on effective mitigation measures will take place at a later date and in accordance with the requirements of Article 15d of REDIII.
The purpose of the Public Consultation is also to invite any key considerations from the public, in preparing a draft plan for the designation of at least one Renewable Acceleration Area, as required under Article 15c of REDIII.

question: Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the mechanisms in place through QQI and the national quality assurance framework to ensure that programme curricula remain responsive to technological developments, enterprise opportunities and evolving consumer trends.
reply:
Quality and Qualifications Ireland (QQI) is the State agency responsible for the external quality assurance of Ireland's further and higher education sectors. In this role, QQI monitors that each provider has the necessary internal quality assurance procedures in place to ensure that programmes and their content are reviewed at regular intervals and that feedback is obtained from learners and stakeholders which is, where relevant, used to further develop each programme’s curriculum. This would include engagement with industry bodies to ensure programmes remain responsive to technological developments, enterprise opportunities and evolving consumer trends.
Under the Universities Act 1997 and the Technological Universities Act 2018, higher education institutions are autonomous bodies, retaining responsibility for their day-to-day management and academic affairs. The curriculum content of programmes is therefore a matter for the institutions themselves and does not fall under the remit of the Minister or Department.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the number of additional student accommodation bed spaces planned for Galway under the National Student Accommodation Strategy 2026–2035; the proposals currently being considered in respect of University of Galway and Atlantic Technological University; the anticipated delivery timelines; and the measures being taken to ensure that new accommodation is affordable for students.

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the work being undertaken by his Department to encourage more students from the North to attend HEIs in the South as part of cross-border student mobility; whether work is being carried out to examine the effect of the technical misalignment of A-Levels and the Leaving Certificate which means Northern students have to sit four A-Levels in order to achieve maximum CAO points.
reply:
My Department continues to engage with higher education stakeholders to explore what further measures could be taken to facilitate Northern Irish students wishing to study in this jurisdiction. There has been extensive engagement on the issue of alignment between points awarded on the CAO system to students from Northern Ireland and the rest of the UK.
Changes to the conversion criteria for A-Level applicants to Irish higher education, via the CAO, were announced in December 2023, following a review led by Universities Ireland. The resulting changes were adopted by all individual universities for new entrants to higher education in the 2025/26 academic year.
These changes mean that students from Northern Ireland no longer have to sit four A-levels to score maximum CAO points. They are now able to combine thee A-Levels with either a fourth A-Level, an AS Level or an Extended Project Qualification and, with top grades, attain 600 points in the CAO or 625 points if one of the A-Levels is maths. These changes are a positive contribution to increasing student mobility.
Measures have also been undertaken to increase information to Northern Irish students considering studying in Ireland, including a dedicated page on the CAO website to advise those with A-Levels of the application process. CAO representatives also participate in the annual conferences of Northern Irish Career Advisers.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science for guidance to higher education institutions to stop the number of universities paying for invasive animal experiments abroad.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, regulatory responsibility with regard to the use of animal's in research activities does not rest with my Department. This legislation is implemented by the Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA), the competent authority in Ireland responsible for the protection of animals used for scientific purposes.
The agency aims to improve the welfare of animals used for scientific purposes and to promote the principles of the 3Rs - Replacement, Reduction and Refinement. Applicants are expected to adhere to the general principles and best practice outlined in the guidance provided by the HPRA.
Research Ireland’s policy in this area, setting out the requirements that must be met where research it is funding involves the use of animals, is available on its website. I would in particular note the following:
• The Research Body and Principal Investigator must ensure that all necessary ethical, legal and regulatory requirements in order to conduct the research are met, and all necessary licences and approvals have been obtained.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the steps being taken to ensure apprenticeship, further education and skills programmes are responding to the impact of AI and automation on the labour market; and whether new or expanded training programmes are planned for sectors facing significant skills shortages.
reply:
We know that we are in a period of rapid change, as artificial intelligence and automation change work practices, role profiles and our daily lives.
Recognising this, I was delighted to announce a multinational €150 million National Training Fund package, €50 million annually over three years, for AI Skills Resilience.
This builds on our current strong digital and AI skills levels and responds directly to recommendations of the National Skills Council to strengthen Ireland’s capacity to anticipate and respond to technological, economic and labour market change.
The package will support curriculum renewal, educator capability, specialist and emerging skills needs, technology adoption, and lifelong learning opportunities across the economy. It will also expand AIReady.ie, the gateway portal for AI skills, and support further development of upskilling and reskilling initiatives, flexible learning pathways including micro-credentials, and sector-specific workforce development.
Budget 2027 also provides an additional €35 million for apprenticeship, bringing overall apprenticeship funding to a record €446 million. There are now nearly 90 apprenticeship programmes nationally, including 11 launched in 2026. These programmes are developed with industry to meet skills needs in a rapidly evolving labour market. question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science for an update on the planned new funding model for students of graduate entry medicine.
reply:
I recognise the significant financial commitment involved in undertaking Graduate Entry Medicine (GEM), and I am committed to ensuring that financial barriers do not prevent suitably qualified students from pursuing a medical career. Expanding the supply of doctors remains a key Government priority, and Graduate Entry Medicine plays an important role in achieving that objective.
Graduate Entry Medicine students are in a distinct position within the higher education system. As students undertaking a second degree, they are generally not eligible for many of the supports available to first-time undergraduate students, including the Free Fees Initiative and associated fee supports. At the same time, GEM programmes involve substantial tuition fee costs for students.
The Programme for Government contains a commitment to improve affordability for Graduate Entry Medicine students. In that context, my Department is working closely with the Department of Health and the Department of Finance to examine options to support students undertaking these programmes.
This work is considering a range of possible approaches, including tuition fee supports and other financing arrangements that could assist students with the cost of participation. No final decisions have been taken at this stage and the detailed design of any future support mechanism remains under consideration.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science his plans for further decreases to the student contribution charge.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 208 and 222 together.
The Programme for Government takes a balanced approach to reducing the cost of higher education by combining universal measures with targeted supports, while ensuring these commitments are delivered in a financially sustainable manner. Commitments include reducing student contribution fees, enhancing SUSI supports, providing additional assistance for specific groups of students, and expanding pathways into and through higher education.
Ahead of Budget 2027, I engaged with students and key stakeholders and published Funding the Future: An Annual Options Paper on Reducing the Cost of Education to inform decision-making on measures that could most effectively reduce education costs. I remain acutely aware of the financial pressures facing students and families and the need to address cost as a barrier to participation.
Budget 2026 delivered a permanent €500 reduction in the Student Contribution Fee, while Budget 2027 builds on this with a further permanent reduction of €150. Taken together, these measures reduce the standard Student Contribution Fee from €3,000 to €2,350, providing a lasting benefit for students and families.
Budget 2027 also introduces new and enhanced SUSI student contribution grant supports for households with two or more dependant family members in tertiary education. From September 2027, these measures are expected to benefit approximately 11,000 students from households with incomes of up to €150,000.

Delivering greater numbers of qualified workers to address key national challenges. The new strategy will support growing annual apprentice registrations from 9,400 in 2025 to 12,500 by 2030 with two-thirds of those registrations in craft and construction-related disciplines.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he remains committed to the promised waiver for waste collection for households where a person has incontinence and therefore, bigger waste collection charges.
reply:
The waste collection market is serviced by competing private companies, where prices charged are matters between those companies and their customers, subject to compliance with all applicable legislation. This includes contract, consumer and competition legislation. The Minister has no power to set prices in a private competitive market.
The National Waste Collection Permit Office (NWCPO) has conducted a study on incentivised charging structures in the waste collection market. This study also considers mechanisms for supports in relation to households disposing of medical incontinence products based on international practice.
Recommendations will be considered in conjunction with outcomes from the feasibility study into transitioning our national waste collection from its current competitive licensing system to a franchise model which has recently been completed. Both will inform the development of the next iteration of the Waste Action Plan for a Circular Economy (WAPCE).
The Department has previously engaged with relevant public bodies, including the Department of Social Protection, and representative organisations with respect to the waste disposal costs for incontinence wear, and further engagement will be undertaken in the context of updating the WAPCE in the coming months.

question: Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to outline the importance of Ireland’s first Tertiary Education Strategy, which he recently launched; and the way in which it will create better pathways for learners while meeting Ireland’s future skills needs.
reply:
On 17 September 2026, I launched Ireland’s first Tertiary Education Strategy 2026-2031.
This is the first Strategy bringing together further education and training, higher education, and research and innovation under a single national framework.
The strategy has been developed at a time of profound change, including the growth of artificial intelligence, climate transition, demographic change and evolving workforce needs. Its central purpose is to ensure that Ireland’s education and research system can respond in a coordinated way to these challenges while supporting economic competitiveness, social inclusion and lifelong learning.
In delivering this strategy we will make it easier for learners to access flexible pathways across further and higher education, and help employers meet current and future skills needs in areas including construction, healthcare, AI and renewable energy.
We will increase pathways by expanding the part-time fee scheme which is supporting students who are balancing study with work, health, and caring responsibilities to pursue a degree.
We will continue to grow tertiary pathways in areas of priority skills needs. Nursing, primary education, social care and occupational therapy are now offered through tertiary degree programmes. Tertiary pathways allow learners to start their education in further education and complete their studies with a higher education degree. question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the engagement he and his Department has had with the Department of Health and the HSE regarding employment opportunities for nursing and physiotherapy graduates.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 189 and 218 together.
My Department engages on an ongoing basis with the Department of Health, the Health Service Executive (HSE), the Higher Education Authority (HEA) and higher education institutions to support alignment between healthcare education provision and the workforce requirements of the health service, including in nursing, physiotherapy and other priority health and social care professions.
Responsibility for health workforce planning rests primarily with the Department of Health and the HSE. In December 2025, the Department of Health published Ireland's Future Health and Social Care Workforce, which forms part of its long-term workforce planning programme. The report highlights the need to significantly increase the domestic supply of health and social care professionals over the coming years and notes that expanding higher education and training capacity across a range of healthcare disciplines will be required to meet projected workforce demand.
My Department works closely with the Department of Health and the HSE to ensure that higher education planning and student capacity expansion are informed by these workforce projections. Engagement takes place on a continuous basis regarding workforce requirements, priority disciplines, clinical placement capacity, programme development and future student number requirements.

reply:
Budget 2027 delivers a significant package of measures designed to reduce the cost of higher education for students and families, strengthen workforce skills, and ensure Ireland is well positioned to thrive in an increasingly AI-driven economy.
A key element of the Budget is a €159 million investment in pay and pensions across the higher and further education sector. This funding will support public sector pay commitments, address university pay gaps, and provide additional resources to meet pension-related obligations across universities and technological universities. This investment will help ensure that institutions can continue to attract and retain the staff needed to deliver high-quality education and training.
I've also secured a major new €150 million investment over three years from the National Training Fund to build skills resilience across the economy and society. This funding will support learners, workers, educators and employers in developing the capabilities required to adapt to technological change, while helping Ireland seize the opportunities presented by artificial intelligence and emerging technologies. It represents a significant investment in future-proofing the workforce and strengthening national competitiveness.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science whether any targeted measures are planned to support the development of the specialist technical skills required for offshore wind deployment.
reply:
My Department is leading a multi-faceted approach to build the skills needed to support the development of Ireland's offshore wind sector. The Offshore Wind Skills Action Plan (2024) identified skills shortages across 33 roles required for offshore wind deployment and sets out the measures needed to address these gaps.
Key measures being progressed under the Plan are intended to strengthen the pipeline of skilled workers and support the specialist technical skills required across the industry. These measures include the development of a more coordinated approach to skills provision and training.
This is being progressed in phases, with the next step, an online platform, being launched later this month. Coordinating training provision will support industry engagement across the sector, and so contribute to building a sustainable skills pipeline.
In terms of current provision, Ireland's tertiary education sector offers a range of programmes relevant to offshore wind development, including apprenticeships in wind turbine maintenance, offshore safety training, and academic programmes in marine engineering, supply chain management and logistics.
In addition, through Skillnet Ireland, my Department has supported the establishment of the Skillnet Offshore Wind Academy (SOWA), which helps experienced professionals with transferable skills transition into the offshore wind sector. question: Deputy Tony McCormack asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the measures being considered to make it easier for small businesses to employ and train apprentices; and if additional supports for SMEs participating in the apprenticeship system are being examined.
reply:
Apprenticeships are fundamentally different from other forms of education and training because they are built on an employment relationship. A priority for me is to continue growing and strengthening our apprenticeship system, and in particular supporting employers, including SMEs, to participate.
There is a suite of financial supports available to employers and SMEs, including employer grants for consortia-led programmes, craft apprenticeship allowances and targeted grants supporting inclusion objectives. If a business employs an apprentice on one of the 50+ consortia apprenticeships they are eligible for a €2000 grant payment for each apprentice. The grant windows are May & November each year and businesses can apply via the Apprenticeship.ie Online platform.
SOLAS's One More Job initiative also provides practical, one-to-one support specifically to help micro and small businesses become apprenticeship employers.
These measures are supporting strong growth in employer participation. Annual apprentice registrations have risen from 5,326 in 2020 to 9,461 in 2025, and the number of people employed on apprenticeship programmes has grown from 19,600 in 2020 to 31,000 today.
In line with the Programme for Government, we are growing the apprenticeship system further, towards 12,500 registrations annually by 2030.

question: Deputy George Lawlor asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science for a full update on the plans for the Wexford campus of the South East Technological University.
reply:

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the way in which budget 2027 will deliver for Ireland's skills, especially those needed for the digital and green transitions.
reply:
The digitalisation of the economy and society, the adoption of AI and the green transition are reshaping our country. They are changing the skills needed for both current and future workers. Whilst they are both distinct skills areas, there are also areas of overlap, for example, in the installation and maintenance of solar panels, and so they are more correctly viewed as twin transitions.
Budget 2027 outlines the Government’s commitment to responding to evolving skills needs arising from this transition journey, with a dedicated AI Skills resilience package.
Through the National Training Fund, this will see €150 million invested over three years, starting with €50 million in 2027.
The package will deliver a national skills programme to enhance workforce skills with flexible learning opportunities. It will support further capacity building across the tertiary sector, the development of flexible learning pathways, including micro-credentials, continued investment in further and higher education, and sector-specific workforce development initiatives.
For instance, the package will fund initiatives such as the expansion of AIReady.ie, the national portal for accessing AI training, and support the growth of training and opportunities in emerging areas such as offshore wind.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the annual cost of the student contribution charge for third level education in 2024 to 2027, inclusive.
reply:
The cost of the student contribution charge for higher education students has reduced significantly in recent years, reflecting the Government’s commitment to easing the financial burden on students and families while maintaining a sustainable funding model for the higher education sector.
Under the Free Fees Initiative, the State meets the tuition fee costs of eligible Irish and EU undergraduate students undertaking approved full-time undergraduate courses in approved higher education institutions. In addition, the SUSI scheme provides support towards student contribution charges for eligible students. In the last academic year, more than 71,000 students received fee grant assistance through SUSI, including almost 49,000 students whose student contribution charge was paid in full.
For the 2024/25 academic year, the standard student contribution charge was €3,000. However, in that year a temporary once-off measure was introduced that provided a €1,000 reduction on the student contribution fee for qualifying students.
In Budget 2026, I secured a permanent reduction of €500 in the student contribution charge. This reduced the standard charge for the 2025/26 academic year from €3,000 to €2,500. Importantly, this reduction was backdated to September 2025 to ensure that students and families benefited immediately from the measure.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to provide an update on college fees.
reply:
Under the Free Fees Initiative (FFI), the State provides funding toward the tuition fee costs of eligible Irish and EU undergraduate higher education students who are pursuing approved full-time undergraduate courses of study in an approved higher education institution.
The State pays the student contribution, in full or part, on behalf of students who qualify under the Student Grant Scheme operated by SUSI. In this regard, over 71,000 students received fee grant supports from SUSI last year with almost 49,000 students having their fees fully paid.
As part of Budget 2027, I am introducing new and enhanced student contribution grant supports for households with two or more dependant family members in tertiary education, targeted at reducing student contribution costs for eligible undergraduate students from September 2027. Approximately 11,000 students from households with incomes of up to €150,000 are expected to benefit.
The Programme for Government commits to reducing the student contribution fee in a financially sustainable manner over the lifetime of this Government. Budget 2026 provided my first opportunity, as Minister, to deliver on that commitment through a permanent €500 reduction in the student contribution fee. I am pleased to announce a further permanent reduction of €150, bringing the fee down from its original level of €3,000 to €2,350. Combined, these measures represent a reduction of €650, providing meaningful and lasting support to students and their families

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the measures being taken to ensure students with disabilities and additional needs can access appropriate supports when moving from second-level to further and higher education; and whether gaps in supports during this transition have been identified.
reply:
Making sure disabled students can access the supports they need as they move into and through further and higher education is a key priority for me, my Department, and this Government.
The main support available is the Fund for Students with Disabilities (FSD). This fund helps colleges provide a wide range of supports to both full-time and part-time disabled students. It supports students with conditions such as dyslexia, autism, and mild general learning difficulties, as well as many other disabilities.
Each year, over €10.5 million is provided through the FSD in higher education, helping around 21,500 students access the supports they need to succeed in their studies.
The funding can be used for a range of practical supports, including:
• Assistive technology, equipment and software, along with training on how to use it
• Personal supports such as note-takers or personal assistants
• Academic and learning support services
• Supports for students who are deaf or hard of hearing, including sign language interpreters and SpeedText services
• Transport assistance.
These supports can make a real difference in helping students participate fully in college life and achieve their potential.
The fund is also available to students taking PLC courses in further education, with €5.7m provided each year.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science for an update on the INSPIRE Research Infrastructure Programme; the investment being made available to higher-education institutions; and how the programme will support Irish research, regional development and economic competitiveness.
reply:
I launched the INSPIRE Research Infrastructure Programme - a €750 million research infrastructure investment package - last year.
As well as supporting Ireland’s High-Performance Computing capability and Tyndall National Institute, at least €500 million will be invested in two funding streams.
Firstly, it will fund local institutional infrastructure, i.e. research equipment that is used routinely within a higher education institution for both teaching and research purposes and, secondly, shared advanced infrastructures, i.e. bigger-ticket equipment that is appropriately shared across a number of institutions and, critically, with external users. A central access portal will be built to maximise accessibility and utilisation, having particular regard to enterprise of all sizes across Ireland and, by extension, our economic competitiveness.
While funding research equipment, INSPIRE is a strategic investment in Ireland’s talent and innovation. Its mission is therefore broadly two-fold:
To accelerate the delivery of institutional strategies - across talent development, research performance, industry collaboration, research commercialisation and international connectivity.
In realising this goal, to advance national priorities having particular regard to economic competitiveness and resilience, as well as to wider important national policy objectives, for example, in relation to regional development, climate action, life sciences and digitalisation.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to provide a detailed up-to-date report on the Pretty Polly site in Killarney which is earmarked for development as a training college for the hospitality industry; if this important project for Killarney and County Kerry will be expedited.
reply:
Kerry ETB are currently progressing their proposal for a purpose-built Further Education and Training college in Killarney under my department’s FET College Major Capital Programme. KETB’s proposal aims to transform FET provision in Killarney through the development of a modern, state of the art campus with a strong focus on hospitality skills development.
The former Pretty Polly site was identified by Kerry ETB as their preferred site option for this project. At the end of last year, I provided approval to KETB to agree a purchase price for the site with Kerry County Council and to proceed with relevant legal and site due diligence requirements.
I understand that this work is at an advanced stage, and the acquisition of the site is targeted for completion by year end, subject to the satisfactory conclusion of the due diligence requirements.

reply:

The Government also continues to support fully funded energy upgrades for eligible low-income households. Homeowners can save up to €1,120 per year when they carryout a whole home upgrade.

reply:

question: Deputy Martin Daly asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the measures that have taken effect in the 2026 academic year, and the new supports in Budget 2027 to reduce the cost of further and higher education for students and families.
reply:
I know that the cost of going to college for students and families can be difficult. I have spoken to many families across the country who find the cost of college a strain.
Last year in my first budget, I reduced the student contribution charge permanently by €500, increased all SUSI non-adjacent maintenance grant rates by between €200 - €430 and increased the threshold for the €500 student contribution grant to €120,000 for the current academic year.
This year, in Budget 2027, I secured a €34 million student support package that is enabling me to make further enhancements to respond to needs of students and families.
This package will see SUSI grant improvements which include a 4.5% increase to all maintenance grant rates - adjacent and non-adjacent - benefitting 54,000 students, as well as both new and enhanced student contribution grant supports for families with more than one dependent student in tertiary education.
The maintenance grant improvements will come into effect on a pro rata basis from January 2027.
The Budget also recognises affordability challenges for those currently not in receipt of grants. A further €150 reduction in the student contribution charge will provide direct assistance to students and families who do not qualify for full SUSI support. Over 110,000 students in higher education and 16,000 apprentices will benefit.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science his views on the merits of creating a student finance model that would provide interest free loans to students that do not qualify for SUSI grants, to support the associated costs of attending third level education.
reply:
I am firmly committed to ensuring that financial circumstances do not act as a barrier to accessing higher and further education. I have consistently prioritised reducing the cost of higher education for students and families, recognising that access to education should be based on ability and ambition rather than financial means.
Budget 2027 further strengthened the Government's commitment to reducing the cost of higher education through a €34 million package of student supports. Measures include a 4.5% increase in SUSI maintenance grants for approximately 54,000 students, enhanced student contribution grant supports for around 11,000 students from families with two or more dependent learners in tertiary education, expanded eligibility thresholds, and targeted cost-of-attendance supports. question: Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will outline the programme of investment that will be undertaken to upgrade the electricity network. .
reply:
The System Operators, EirGrid and ESB Networks have primary responsibility for upgrading our electricity system including planning and constructing new investments in the grid. They are accountable to the Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) for this responsibility.
The CRU has approved the PR6 grid investment programme, which is unprecedented in scale and will see an investment of up to €18.9 billion in over 500 capital investment projects over the period 2026-2030. These include 29 priority transmission infrastructure projects and 32 priority distribution substations. By the end of September, construction had started on 10 priority transmission and 3 priority distribution projects, while one other priority distribution project - the Blacklone Substation in Laois - is already completed and energised.
Investing in and ensuring a fit for purpose electricity grid is a key priority for Government and I regularly meet with EirGrid and ESB Networks to monitor the progress of the PR6 grid investment programme. In July I was delighted to open ESB Networks new Bracklone 110kV Substation in Laois.
Also, in July the Government designated three grid projects as Critical Infrastructure under the Critical Infrastructure Act. reply:

Responsibility for health workforce planning rests primarily with the Department of Health and the HSE. The report highlights the need to significantly increase the domestic supply of health and social care professionals over the coming years and notes that expanding higher education and training capacity across a range of healthcare disciplines will be required to meet projected workforce demand.
My Department works closely with the Department of Health and the HSE to ensure that higher education planning and student capacity expansion are informed by these workforce projections. Engagement takes place on a continuous basis regarding workforce requirements, priority disciplines, clinical placement capacity, programme development and future student number requirements.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if his Department has ever commissioned a study on the number of third level students who intend to emigrate when they graduate.
reply:
My department has not commissioned a specific study on the number of third level students who intend to emigrate when they graduate. However, the Higher Education Authority, as an agency of my department conducts a national Graduate Outcomes Survey distributed to all graduates of HEIs, approximately nine months after graduation. The survey collects information on graduates' employment and further study outcomes, including where they are located following graduation.
The outputs of this nationwide survey highlight the current constraints or demands on new graduates, and give a picture of what graduates are doing in their early-stage careers. This includes detailed outcome for undergraduates and postgraduates, as well as international graduates. Earnings analyses are also provided and each report contains a particular focus on an area of topical interest.
Furthermore, detailed information provides a detailed analysis into the Graduate Outcomes Survey dataset, demonstrating the breadth of insight the Survey provides, for example into trends of women in STEM, barriers to employment or further study and a range of other areas. These survey outcomes are all publicly available on the HEA's website.
While these data provide valuable information on what graduates do after completing their studies, they do not collect information on students' intentions to emigrate while they are undertaking their studies.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science whether his Department has assessed the impact of artificial intelligence on higher education provision, including the likely demand for new AI-related courses and skills.
reply:
My Department, the HEA and other bodies are actively assessing how artificial intelligence will affect higher education provision, particularly the skills required to meet changing labour market needs. This work is informing both our future skills policy and the higher education system.

We also funded an Expert Group on Future Skills Needs report on Ireland’s digital specialist skills needs to 2030. question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the way in which Ireland intends to position itself to benefit from the development of a more integrated European education and skills market.
reply:
I am committed to strengthening Ireland’s engagement and influence in European education, training, research and skills policy. Through initiatives such as Erasmus+, the European Education Area, the European Universities Alliances and the Union of Skills agenda, Ireland works closely with European partners to ensure that learners, graduates, workers and employers can benefit from a more integrated European education and skills market.
This engagement is reflected in a range of initiatives being advanced at both European and national level.
Through Ireland’s Presidency of the Council of the European Union, we are leading discussions on the future of Erasmus+ and advancing Council Conclusions on STEM education and training and on skills and competences for engaging with Artificial Intelligence. question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the measures being taken to increase the number of apprenticeship places available nationally and in County Galway; whether new apprenticeship programmes are planned in areas experiencing skills shortages; and the steps being taken to encourage more employers, particularly SMEs, to take on apprentices.

The SOLAS-led One More Job initiative also provides practical support to help micro and small businesses take on one or more apprentices.
With these supports in place, demand from employers, including SMEs, for apprenticeships is growing. Annual apprentice registrations increased by 78%, from 5,326 in 2020 to 9,461 in 2025.

Since my Department was established, 34 new apprenticeship programmes have been launched. question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to outline the measures that have taken effect in the 2026 academic year; and what new supports will be introduced to support students following budget 2027 to reduce the cost of further and higher education for students and families.
reply:

The Budget also recognises affordability challenges for those currently not in receipt of grants. A further €150 reduction in the student contribution charge will provide direct assistance to students and families who do not qualify for full SUSI support. question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the number of apprentices currently awaiting access to an off-the-job training phase, by apprenticeship programme and education and training board; the average waiting time for such training; the additional training capacity to be provided in 2027.
reply:
