Since my Department was established, investment to grow apprenticeship has more than doubled, to €446 million in 2027, including €35 million investment in Budget 2027.
COVID-19-related workshop closures led to significant delays in Phase 2 training, particularly during 2023 and 2024. However, substantial Government investment in additional training capacity has largely resolved these delays. The number of apprentices waiting six months or longer to commence Phase 2 training has fallen by 62%, from 5,319 in October 2023 to 1,924 in June 2026.
Apprenticeships operate on a national basis, with apprentices entering and progressing through the system throughout the year. Apprentices are scheduled for training based on eligibility dates and, when not attending off-the-job training, continue their on-the-job training with employers. As a result, apprenticeship pipelines are managed nationally and cannot be attributed to individual ETBs.
Craft apprenticeships take a minimum of four years, or 208 weeks to complete. SOLAS data shows that median completion times fell from 239 weeks in 2024 to 227 weeks in 2025, indicating that apprentices are largely completing their training within expected timeframes. question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if any of the additional €30 million allocated to apprenticeships in the budget will be used to fund additional cost of living supports for apprentices.
reply:

The Minister and I have introduced a permanent reduction in the Student Contribution Charge for undergraduate students from €3,000 to €2,350 between Budget 2026 and Budget 2027. This will support the further expansion in capacity across key areas. Currently there 89 different apprenticeships now on offer. question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if he believes the measures included in budget 2027 are sufficient to address the crisis in student accommodation across the country.
reply:

question: Deputy Joe Cooney asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if he will consider the development of a national certified traineeship in boat-building skills, particularly in locations such as Kilrush, County Clare, where successful maritime traineeships are being delivered and significant expertise already exists.

The appropriate pathway depends on the occupational and workforce need.

question: Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment for consideration of the measures available under the SEAI Traditional Homes Pilot to be made available through the warmer homes scheme and the individual energy upgrades given the current pilot’s one stop shop approach being unaffordable for many owners of older and traditionally built homes.
reply:
The Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland's (SEAI) processes regarding energy upgrades, including with regard to old stone houses, are determined by the Building Regulations, incorporating NSAI S.R.54: 2014 Code of Practice for the energy efficient retrofit of dwellings.
As such, wall insulation is not recommended on dwellings built before 1940 which are constructed in stone, single-leaf masonry or composite wall construction. The retrofit of traditional buildings is a complex issue that requires careful consideration. The materials and techniques used in energy efficiency upgrades of such buildings must be suitable for the buildings in question including for use with vapour permeable construction where applicable. This is to ensure that upgrade works don't create issues such as damp or mould.
Under the Warmer Homes Scheme all eligible homes are assessed and where they comprise stone, the SEAI will not insulate the stone walls, but will assess, for example, a post-1940 extension if present, which based on the determination of the surveyor, may be deemed appropriate for insulation.
The SEAI launched a pilot scheme for the retrofit of traditionally built homes in September 2024. question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the reason individual applicants in some areas, particularly rural areas, continue to face significant delays before they can avail of the solar PV for the medically vulnerable scheme.
reply:
The Solar PV for the Medically Vulnerable Scheme is a targeted scheme for the installation of solar photovoltaic (PV) panels for households who are registered under the life support category of the Priority Services Register with their energy supplier.
The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) in conjunction with energy suppliers and is open to all suppliers who wish to participate. The scheme is energy supplier-led, meaning each energy supplier is responsible for contacting their own eligible customers directly. Government, through the SEAI, funds each energy supplier for the installations they provide to their eligible customers. It is important to note that suppliers, who manage the administrative aspects of the scheme, issue offers to eligible homeowners and contact eligible households in batches, based on their operational capacity.
The SEAI report that 137 systems were installed in 2024 with expenditure of €1.78 million, 473 systems were installed last year with expenditure of €2.8 million, and 352 systems were installed this year to end September with expenditure of €2.36 million.
I have recently announced a package of enhanced renewable energy and retrofit grants, including that eligible households under this scheme can now avail of a fully funded solar PV system of up to 4kWp and a 5kWh battery, covering survey/design, supply, installation, and the post works BER. question: Deputy Aisling Dempsey asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the additional supports she can provide to an organisation (details supplied) in view of the important advocacy and work they do.
reply:
Foster carers play a vital and valued role in the care of the most vulnerable children in our society. Foster care is the preferred option for children who cannot live with their family of origin, and foster carers provide a safe, secure and stable home environment for these vulnerable children and young people.
I have met with a number of foster care stakeholder bodies since becoming Minister for Children, including the association referenced by the Deputy, and I am keenly aware of the current challenges facing the sector.
The Irish Foster Care Association [IFCA] receives its funding primarily from Tusla, and requests for additional funding are considered within the overall context of Tusla's allocation. In Budget 2027, the allocation for Tusla stands at €1.404 billion, representing a 5% increase on Budget 2026. This will ensure that Tusla can continue to support tens of thousands of children and families, as well as the many organisations which provide vital services for vulnerable children, families and carers. The referenced organisation has also received additional funding in recent years from this Department in order to fund its annual conference.
I fully intend to prioritise foster care and ensure that we build upon the suite of supports of which foster carers can avail in future.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the steps being taken to improve the coordination of transition between children's disability services and adult services.
reply:
Transitioning from children to adult services can be a particularly challenging period for young people with disabilities and their families, especially where a young person has complex health, disability and support needs and is receiving services from multiple providers. Effective transition therefore requires early planning, clear communication and coordination across children’s and adult services, with the young person and their family appropriately involved throughout.
As part of the development of the Service Improvement Plan for Children and Young Adults, specific actions are being identified to improve transition planning and build on existing processes and pathways. This work will seek to strengthen the interface between children’s and adult services, support earlier planning and improve continuity for young people as they move between services.
This is particularly important for young people with complex disabilities and multiple health needs, where transition may involve not only disability services but Primary Care, acute hospitals, specialist clinical services, mental health services and other supports. The objective is to ensure, as far as possible, that transition is person centred, planned and coordinated across the relevant services rather than experienced by the young person and family as a series of separate service transfers. question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality her plans to extend paid paternity leave to eight weeks.
reply:
There have been significant developments in entitlements for parents of working families in recent years. The Government is committed to supporting workers, including by extending paid leave for parents to allow them to spend more time with their child during their earliest years.
The Paternity Leave and Benefit Act 2016 provides the relevant parent (other than the mother of the child) with 2 weeks paid Paternity Leave. Ireland's statutory Paternity Leave arrangements are fully aligned with the requirements of the EU Work-Life Balance Directive, which introduced a minimum standard for Paternity Leave across EU Member States.
Under the Parent’s Leave and Benefit Act 2019, working parents are also entitled to nine weeks of paid Parent's Leave for each relevant parent, to be taken in the first two years after the birth or adoptive placement of a child. Parent's Leave is an individual separate entitlement and is non-transferable between parents.
Under the Parental Leave (Amendment) Act 2019, an employee who is a relevant parent in respect of a child under the age 12 is entitled to 26 weeks’ unpaid Parental Leave for each child. Where a child has a disability or long-term illness, the entitlement can continue until the child is 16. A relevant parent is a parent, an adoptive parent, or a person acting in ‘loco parentis’. Both parents have an equal, separate entitlement to Parental Leave.

question: Deputy Aisling Dempsey asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality for an update on her work on the Early Learning and Childcare Planning Matters Working Group regarding a review of the 2001 planning guidelines for local authorities on early learning and childcare settings.
reply:

question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the way in which measures under Budget 2027 will reduce childcare costs for families.
reply:
The Government is committed to reduce parental fees to a maximum of €200 per month over the lifetime of the Government. A number of steps have already been taken in 2025 and 2026 to reduce the costs of early learning and childcare for parents, with further measures announced in Budget 2027.
Measures that will come into effect in September 2027 include both a lowering of fee caps for Core Funding Partner Services and increased National Childcare Scheme subsidies. As a result, many parents will see further reductions in the amount they pay for early learning and childcare.
Later this year I will publish Shaping the Future Phase 2 which will set out the roadmap for how the €200 commitment will be achieved.
From September 2027, the maximum fees that providers in receipt of Core Funding can charge will be reduced across all fee bands. All services with fees below the new caps will continue to be subject to existing fee controls.
At the same time, from September 2027, the universal subsidy for children up to and including senior infants will rise to €2.50 per hour (or €112.50 for 45 hours per week), while changes will also be made to Income-Assessed subsidies.
The universal rate of €2.14 per hour (or €96.30 for 45 hours per week) will continue to be available to all children from 1st class up to the age of 15 years. People with Temporary Protection who wish to transition to the new permission must meet the eligibility criteria, including a minimum earnings requirement of €29,432 per year, have independent accommodation, and be resident in Ireland for a period of one year as a beneficiary of Temporary Protection prior to the opening of the new permission application process. The earnings threshold applies to all applicants seeking to avail of this alternative immigration permission.
Full details of the scheme and eligibility criteria are outlined in the Scheme Policy Document and FAQ document available online at www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/collections/a-new-permission-en/.

The alternative permission is not intended to replace Temporary Protection, but to provide an alternative permission for those who are eligible and who wish to remain in Ireland beyond its protection. Persons who do not apply or are unable to satisfy the eligibility criteria will continue to be entitled to and benefit from the Temporary Protection Status while the Temporary Protection Directive remains in effect.

Any policy proposals developed will need to ensure the privacy of parties involved continues. question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on citizenship applications for persons (details supplied); and for a timeframe on a decision to be communicated.
reply:
The naturalisation applications referred to by the Deputy continue to be processed by my Department.
These applications are based on Section 16 'Irish Association', which can take longer to process than applications based upon residency.
Section 15 of the Act sets out the statutory conditions that must be fulfilled for a certificate of naturalisation to be granted. Section 16 of the Act gives discretion to waive the statutory conditions (including the 5 year residency requirement) in certain circumstances. This includes where the applicant is a direct descendant of someone who is or was an Irish citizen (for example, a grandparent), has a family connection to an Irish citizen (including by blood, adoption, or civil partnership), or is related by affinity, meaning a close relationship through a spouse’s family.
Last year my Department published new guidelines for applications on the basis of Irish Associations under Section 16(1)(a) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. They set out the factors that may be considered when deciding whether to waive the statutory conditions in certain circumstances, including where the applicant is of Irish descent or Irish associations. Details of the guidelines are available on my Department’s website at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-an-irish-citizen-guide/
As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireach

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Social Protection if it is possible for a person (details supplied), regarding any American pension entitlement, to use a portion of their Irish credits to make up the shortfall for the six quarters under the bilateral agreement; whether this would affect his Irish entitlements.
reply:
The person concerned was awarded state pension contributory from their 66th birthday based on their Irish social insurance record.
The state pension contributory is currently in payment at the weekly rate of €293.50 which equates to 98% of the maximum personal rate.
Under the Bilateral Social Security Agreement between Ireland and the United States of America, insurance periods completed in one country may be taken into account by the other country for the purpose of establishing entitlement to certain social security benefits. Entitlement is determined separately by each country in accordance with its own legislation.
This process does not involve any transfer of social insurance contributions from one country to the other. Coverage in one country may be used to give entitlement to a pro rata pension in the other country. As a person's state pension contributory entitlement is based solely on their Irish social insurance record, any pension entitlement they may have from any other jurisdiction does not affect their rate of payment.
The agreement with the United States provides that where a person has completed at least six quarters of coverage under U.S. laws, but does not have sufficient coverage to qualify for a benefit from there, periods of coverage in Ireland could be used to establish entitlement. question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Social Protection if an oral hearing and a date for same will be expedited in respect of an application for the State Pension (details supplied).
reply:
The person concerned was in receipt of payment as a qualified adult on their spouse's State pension contributory from 12 November 2015 to 7 May 2026.
An Increase for Qualified Adult (IQA) is a means-tested allowance which may be paid where a claimant's spouse, civil partner or cohabitant is being wholly or mainly maintained by them and where the qualified adult's means do not exceed the prescribed limits.
Where a qualified adult has weekly means of up to €100, the maximum rate of IQA is payable. A reduced rate is payable where weekly means exceed €100 but do not exceed €310. Where weekly means exceed €310, there is no entitlement to an IQA payment. Where property or assets are held jointly, the qualified adult's means are assessed as half of the total amount. The family home is not included in the means assessment.
As part of the Department's ongoing programme of review to ensure that customers are receiving their correct entitlement, a review questionnaire issued to the spouse of the person concerned on 21 October 2025 seeking details on the means of the qualified adult.
Following examination of the information provided, it was established that the person concerned had weekly means of €735.78, arising primarily from capital held in joint bank accounts. As the means exceed the statutory limit for the IQA, a decision issued on 30 April 2026 advising that the IQA payment was being terminated.
There is no record of an appeal having been received by my Department or the Social We

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Social Protection his currents plans to address the issue of parents who are transgender not being recognised as the parents of their children.
reply:
The legislation governing the registering of a birth is set out in the Civil Registration Act (2004). The required particulars of the parent(s) of a child to be recorded in the birth registration include the sex of the parent.
Where the gender of the person who gives birth to the child is female, that person can select "mother" or "parent" as their label on the child's birth certificate.
Where the gender of the person who gives birth to the child is male, that person can only select "parent" as their label on the child's birth certificate.
Where the gender of the other parent is female, that person can only select "parent" as their label on the child's birth certificate.
Where the gender of the other parent is male, that person can select "father" or "parent" as their label on the child's birth certificate.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Social Protection whether his Department has undertaken a review of how fibromyalgia is considered in the assessment of applications for disability-related payments and supports; and the measures in place to ensure that the functional limitations associated with fibromyalgia, including chronic pain, fatigue, cognitive impairment and reduced capacity for employment, are fully reflected in assessment processes.
reply:
Fibromyalgia is a recognised medical condition under World Health Organisation, International Classification of Diseases. As with all disability-related applications, the eligibility is assessed based on functional capacity or lack of, and in conjunction with corroborative medical evidence provided.
My Department’s Medical Assessors are required to complete mandatory hours of continuous professional development annually. This includes participation in medical conferences, study days and journal clubs.
Relevant and current areas of clinical focus, including chronic pain, fibromyalgia, endometriosis and neurodiversity, to name a few feature in these professional development activities. These ongoing programmes allow Medical Assessors keep abreast with the development of clinical practice and maintain up-to-date medical knowledge relevant to the assessment of disability-related applications.
In the example of Fibromyalgia, myofascial pain, fatigue, poor sleep and resulting cognitive difficulties are well-recognised symptoms. Its effect on work capacity is often driven by the fluctuating nature of these symptoms. Hence, each Fibromyalgia customer is likely to present with varying level of limitations at different times.
In the process of assessing the disability-related payments, all information provided by the applicant and all supporting medical evidence are considered and measured against the qualifying criteria of the scheme applied for.
I hope this clarifies for the Deputy.

reply:
The Remediation of Dwellings Damaged by the use of Defective Concrete Blocks Act 2022 as amended by the Act of 2025 sets out the framework under which the Grant Scheme which provides grant funding to people whose homes have been affected by Defective Concrete Blocks (DCB) operates.
A number of amendments contained in the 2025 Act came into operation on 25 February 2026 and, more recently, further provisions commenced on 27 May 2026.
The detailed operation of the Scheme is a matter for the designated local authorities in the first instance and their role is set out clearly in the 2022 Act.
Local authorities have responsibility for the administration of the scheme. This includes the initial validation of applications, notifying homeowners of the Housing Agency's determinations on damage threshold, the appropriate remediation option and grant amount, determination of the grant payable for alternative accommodation and storage costs and immediate repair works and the subsequent payment of grants to successful applicants.
My Department engages regularly with the local authority teams responsible for the operation and administration of the Scheme. Representatives from the designated local authorities attend meetings of the Implementation Steering Group, which provides a forum for the ongoing monitoring of the operation and implementation of the Defective Concrete Blocks Grant Scheme.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to outline the entitlement of an individual to apply for social or affordable housing where they are currently living in a private home but where they are going through separation or divorce proceedings and have to share the home with their current spouse.
reply:
In relation to Starter Homes, the Fresh Start principle forms a key element in the Government’s housing policy and is applied across a number of schemes of my Department that support buying a home.
The Fresh Start principle, as defined in Section 10 of the Affordable Housing Act 2021, allows certain purchasers to be treated as First Time Buyers and be eligible to apply for the purchase of an affordable home. All other eligibility criteria will apply. In order to be eligible under the Fresh Start principle, under the Affordable Housing Act 2021 (as amended), one of the following provisions must be met:
• A person has been divorced, legally separated or their civil partnership or relationship has ended, and they are no longer living in and have no financial interest in the previous family home.
• A person has been divested of a home through personal insolvency or bankruptcy proceedings.
• A person previously owned, was beneficially entitled to, or had an interest in a dwelling in the State and that this dwelling, because of its size, is not suited to the current accommodation needs of their household, that person is still eligible to apply if they own or are beneficially entitled to an estate or interest in the dwelling at the time at which they apply for an affordable dwelling.

reply:
None of the business energy support schemes administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) on behalf of my Department currently allow for vessel electrification.
The SEAI recently received several queries in relation to funding support for vessel decarbonisation, but such projects are likely not eligible under current programme rules. Communities do this by bringing together groups of buildings under the same retrofit initiative to facilitate community-wide energy improvements more efficiently and cost effectively than might otherwise be possible.
The CEG Programme is intended to support comprehensive energy retrofit projects rather than standalone renewable energy installations. Consistent with the scheme's fabric-first approach, solar PV is supported where it forms part of a wider building upgrade project. Single-measure solar projects are not a primary focus of the programme.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which a teacher (details supplied) can appeal an incorrect pension scheme classification and incomplete service record where their former school has closed and successive amalgamations and changes in roll numbers have complicated verification of their service; and the alternative evidence that can be accepted.
reply:
In cases as described by the Deputy, the Department has a process in place which requires teachers to make every reasonable effort to obtain independent verification of their service. This may include seeking confirmation from the school's patron body, a successor school established following an amalgamation, a former principal or colleague, or other available sources such as records held by the Revenue Commissioners or the Department of Social Protection.
Where a school has closed, amalgamated or otherwise ceased to exist and employment records are no longer available, the teacher may provide an explanation of the circumstances together with any supporting documentation available to them and arrange for the completion of an affidavit form.
Any affidavit submitted must be witnessed by a Commissioner for Oaths or practising solicitor and is considered together with any supporting evidence provided. The Department then assesses all of the information available and determines whether the service can be accepted for pension purposes. An affidavit does not in itself establish entitlement. It is one element of the evidential process used by the Department where original records are unavailable.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will review the refusal of school transport applications for children (details supplied); if she will consider making an exception to the nearest-school requirement under the primary school transport scheme in light of the closure, and the parish and community ties of the families concerned; and if she will engage with Bus Éireann to explore the provision of a transport service for the pupils affected.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
The purpose of my Department's School Transport Scheme is, having regard to available resources, to support the transport to and from school of children who reside remote from their nearest school.
Children are eligible for school transport at primary level where they reside not less than 3.2 kilometres from and are attending their nearest national school, and at post primary level where they reside not less than 4.8 kilometres from and are attending their nearest post primary school/education centre, as determined by the department/Bus Éireann, having regard to ethos and language.
Officials from the School Transport Section of my Department are looking into the matter raised by the Deputy and are currently engaging with Bus Éireann and will reply directly to the Deputy as soon as the information is available.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Education and Youth the procedures used by her Department in determining if a new educational technological product can by trialled in schools; and the supports given to the trialling of such products.
reply:
As the deputy is aware, it is the responsibility of each individual school to select the digital resources, if any, that it will use to support its implementation of the curriculum. The Digital Strategy for Schools to 2027 does not mandate or prescribe the use of any particular devices or technologies in teaching and learning, rather it advocates for the deeper embedding of digital technologies in teaching and learning to develop digital literacy and competence, critical thinking and collaborative practice. It is not merely focused on using digital devices as an alternative to physical textbooks or resources.
Through the digital strategy, schools are directly funded for ICT and have autonomy to determine which infrastructure and devices (including tablets or laptops) are implemented, in line with their Digital Learning Plans. Schools must also have acceptable usage policies in place and may use ICT funding to support new curricula and assessment.

question: Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if there have been discussions on whether emissions from crematoria should become a licensable activity with enforcement mechanisms under the Air Pollution Act (1987), given the increasing number in the country; if this matter will be examined further given the lack of legislation surrounding crematoria and the lack of a direct and specific role for a Government department and Minister in regulating the industry.
reply:
My Department has no function in relation to the regulation of the human cremation process. The power to make regulations in relation to this process rests with the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage under planning legislation and Section 47 the Local Government (Sanitary Services) Act.
In relation to the Deputy's specific query, I understand that there are currently no plans to introduce new regulations in this area.
In general, regarding Crematoria, the establishment and operation of any such activity is subject, where applicable, to the provisions of legislation dealing with planning and development.
I also understand there are professional bodies for these activities with their own codes and standards, but my Department has no role in this regard.

Enterprise Ireland (EI) then ensures that companies of all sizes in the manufacturing and internationally traded services sectors are assisted on their development journey, maximising their growth and job creation potential.
In recognition of those businesses that have grown beyond micro-enterprise scale (up to 10 Employees), my Department introduced the over 10 Framework in 2023. The framework extended the LEO mandate to allow for the provision of all LEO grant supports, including Business Expansion and Feasibility Grants for growth and expansion, to small businesses in the Manufacturing and Internationally Traded sector with up to 50 employees.
To ensure a smooth transition between the enterprise development agencies, EI and the LEOs together undertake an evaluation of those companies employing more than 10 seeking financial assistance to determine the organisation best placed for their developmental needs. Firms that already export or are ready to enter new markets will be eligible to access Enterprise Ireland assistance. question: Deputy Denise Mitchell asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will outline details of upcoming changes to the minimum annual remuneration (MAR) for 2027; the implementation guidelines for same.
reply:
The employment permits system is grounded in legislation that sets clear and objective criteria for minimum annual remuneration (MAR) thresholds, qualifications, and the eligibility of occupations. The MAR represents the minimum salary that must be paid to a non-EEA national for an employment permit to be issued or renewed.
The Employment Permits: Minimum Annual Remuneration – Outcome of the Roadmap Review 2025 published at the end of last year sets out the policy rationale, evidence basis and revised (phased) roadmap for implementation of the thresholds applicable across the employment permits system.
The review was informed by a public consultation process and undertaken in response to a range of structural changes in the labour market since MAR thresholds were last comprehensively updated. This included consideration of issues such as sustained inflationary pressures, increases in average earnings, rising costs of living, and changing labour market dynamics. Under this roadmap, the first increases took effect on 1 March 2026.
In line with the approach taken for the 2026 increases, the next phase of increases to MAR thresholds for 2027 will be implemented with sufficient lead-in to allow sectors time to prepare for the changes.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the reasons liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) has been excluded from the carbon tax relief announced for kerosene and natural gas in Budget 2027; whether he has assessed the impact of this differential treatment on households and businesses relying on LPG, particularly in rural areas without access to the natural gas network; and whether he will extend the relief to LPG through the Finance Bill 2026, taking account of its carbon emissions relative to kerosene.
reply:
As per the most recent CSO Energy Use Survey (2024), around three in every five households use home natural gas or heating oil (kerosene) as their main home heating fuel. Around 1 per cent of households identified as using Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) as their main heating fuel according to this survey.
The Natural Gas Carbon Tax and the carbon component of Mineral Oil Tax on kerosene used other than as a propellant has been reduced to €48.50 per tonne of CO2 emitted. For kerosene used other than as a propellant, this equates to €122.83 per 1,000 litres.
These reductions were targeted to provide a cost reduction on the two predominant home heating fuels in the country, taking into account the extraordinary, market driven, price increases to kerosene since March and an anticipated increase in natural gas price inflation arising from recent increases in unit rates by major suppliers. Reductions were not extended across all fuels.
Home heating oil and LPG are used predominately by households who do not have access to natural gas infrastructure; these are generally households in more rural areas.
LPG used other than as a propellant does not attract the non-carbon component of Mineral Oil Tax. Only the carbon component of Mineral Oil Tax (i.e. carbon tax) applies.
The carbon tax on LPG is currently paused at €63.50 per tonne of CO2 emitted. This equates to €103.66 per 1,000 litres. This is the same rate that has applied since 1 May 2025.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he plans to review the investment regulations for credit unions in order that they may provide funding to tier 1 & 2 approved housing bodies for social housing, or to lend to them directly.
reply:
The Government recognises the potential role that credit unions can play in supporting housing delivery. The current legislative and regulatory framework provides for investment by credit unions to Approved Housing Bodies (AHBs).
Investment in AHBs is permitted under credit union regulations, introduced by the Central Bank of Ireland in March 2018. Under Regulation 25(1)(f) of the Credit Union Act 1997 (Regulatory Requirements) Regulations 2016, credit unions may invest through regulated investment vehicles where the underlying investments of the regulated investment vehicle are investments in Permitted Approved Housing Bodies, as defined in the Regulations. Under these Regulations, over €1.6 billion may be invested by credit unions in AHB's. This is estimated on the concentration limits set out in Regulation 27(5) of the 2016 Regulations.
There is one such fund established under these Regulations, the Credit Union AHB Fund ("the Fund"), who on-lend investment monies received to AHBs for the purpose of delivery of social housing units. Further information on the Fund, including updates on its lending, is available on the Credit Union AHB Fund website. The most recent update indicates that the Fund has issued total loans of approximately €44 million and have supported the delivery of 175 homes.

question: Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance for an update on plans and timelines for a review of the section 110 regime under the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997.
reply:
The section 110 regime was designed to offer a tax neutral regime for certain securitisation transactions and to improve Ireland’s offering as a location for the conduct of financial services activities.
A broad review of the section 110 regime is being carried out by my Department in conjunction with a major domestic project to reform Ireland’s taxation regime for interest. Many of the broader questions on interest deductibility that are being considered as part of the interest review are relevant to a review of the section 110 regime. Draft legislation for fundamental reform of the interest regime will be published this year for stakeholder consultation to inform proposals for legislative changes to the interest regime in Finance Bill 2027. These proposals will inform the review of the section 110 regime.
In addition, provisional political agreement on the revision of the EU securitisation framework was announced on Wednesday 21 October. Technical work remains ongoing on the package and following completion of this work, formal approval of the agreement will be sought from both the European Council and European Parliament. My officials will monitor any changes relevant to our securitisation regime as part of the above review.

question: Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether potential amendments to section 626B of the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997, relating to the substantial shareholding exemption, will be considered as part of any upcoming tax reviews.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 36 and 37 together.
Section 626B TCA 1997, Substantial Shareholding Exemption, introduced in 2004, provides for an exemption from capital gains tax on certain disposals of subsidiary shareholdings, subject to conditions including shareholding, residence and trading requirements.
There have been a number of requests through parliamentary questions and submissions to consider the alignment of the regime with the Participation Exemption regime which was introduced in 2024.
The Participation Exemption, which applies to qualifying foreign dividend income, simplifies the double tax relief system and enhances Ireland’s attractiveness for multinational businesses. The exemption is available, subject to conditions, in respect of distributions received from qualifying subsidiaries in EEA and treaty partner jurisdictions and jurisdictions that have imposed a non-refundable withholding tax on the distribution.
With regard to the proposal to align both regimes, it is worth noting that the two provisions apply to different taxes, dividend income and gains on disposals, and were designed with different policy objectives in mind. The nature and extent of each exemption reflect these fundamental differences. Any proposed amendments to the Substantial Shareholding exemption therefore require consideration of the core policy objectives of the exemptions.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Transport whether Class 5 passenger vessels operating tourism and sightseeing services are classified as commercial vessels for the purposes of Government grant, energy-efficiency and decarbonisation schemes; whether any regulatory barriers exist to the conversion of such vessels to electric propulsion systems.
reply:
It is understood that this matter refers to a Class V Passenger Ship carrying more than 12 passengers. The issuing of grants, energy-efficiency supports or decarbonisation schemes for commercial vessels is not within the remit of the Department of Transport. The eligibility for any such scheme is accordingly a matter for the appropriate body responsible for administering the relevant scheme.
In relation to the conversion of such vessels to an electric propulsion system, any changes in a vessel's propulsion system would constitute as a significant modification and would accordingly be subject to further approval by the Marine Survey Office of my Department on safety grounds. Any safety regulatory matters should be addressed to the Marine Survey Office who will be able to assist in relation to any proposed conversion of a passenger vessel.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if the withdrawal of overseas aid funding by the United States through USAID has had specific impacts on any projects in which Ireland is a partner.
reply:
The OECD has reported that, globally, Official Development Assistance fell by 23.1% between 2024 and 2025, with assistance from the United States falling by 56.9%. Since the closure of USAID in early 2025 much of their functions have passed to the State Department which has launched a new Bureau of Disaster and Humanitarian Response, while support to agriculture and food security is now primarily administered through the US Department of Agriculture.
Despite these changes, the US continues to provide substantial development and humanitarian assistance. Since December 2025, the US has announced US$3.8 billion in support of the Humanitarian Reset being led by the UN, with most of this funding directed towards life-saving assistance and protection activities in priority humanitarian crises. However, some areas, including Afghanistan, Yemen and Somalia were excluded from this. This US humanitarian funding is a welcome contribution at a time of growing global humanitarian need.
One area particularly affected by aid reductions by the US and some other major states has been maternal and child health, where the US had been the single largest contributor to initiatives and partners working in the area. There has been a significant impact on supply chains of essential medicines and life-saving reproductive health and family planning commodities. question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport whether he has engaged with the Dublin Airport Authority in relation to its practice of paying the tax liabilities of benefits provided to directors on the company's board; and whether this practice will be extended to the benefits accrued by its new CEO.
reply:
In accordance with the Code of Practice for the Governance of State Bodies, daa's annual financial statements disclose details of the benefits and expenses paid to members of the Board in respect of their services as directors. As also required under the Code, these are also reported to me annually in the Chairperson's Comprehensive Report.
I am advised by daa that the benefits and expenses provided to employees (including the CEO) and Board members are taxed and reported in accordance with applicable legislation, including section 118 of the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997, and Revenue guidance. question: Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Transport if the shared island sports club EV charging scheme is reopen for clubs to apply; if not, will it reopen; and the number of clubs who availed of the scheme when it was open.
reply:
The Shared Island Sports Club EV Charging Infrastructure Scheme is a €15 million all-island initiative supporting the installation of publicly accessible EV chargers in sports clubs. The aim of the scheme is to install a network of publicly accessible EV chargers in communities throughout the country, through their local sports clubs. Progress is being made on the Scheme which is closed for initial applications and there are no current plans to reopen.
Over 220 clubs across the island reached the eligibility criteria. To date, 135 clubs have formally entered the scheme and selected a Charge Point Operator (CPO). Three sites are live and operational and a further 12 are in various stages of construction.
The first launch of a Shared Island Sports Club EV charging scheme site will take place at Cobh Golf Club on 6th November.
Electric vehicle and charging supports are continually reviewed. It should be noted that decisions on financial incentives must be taken in the context of overall financial sustainability.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Transport if he will engage with the National Transport Authority regarding a temporary extension to the maximum permissible age of taxis that remain roadworthy, well maintained and compliant with all safety and suitability requirements; whether the economic circumstances facing SPSV operators will be considered.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 17 and 20 together.
The regulation of the small public service vehicle (SPSV) industry, including vehicle age limits for SPSVs, is a matter for the independent transport regulator, the National Transport Authority (NTA), under the provisions of the Consolidated Taxi Regulation Acts 2013 and 2016. I have no role in the day-to-day operations of the SPSV sector.
The NTA extended vehicle age limits during Covid-19, but this was a temporary measure, aimed at ensuring that no operator would be required to change their vehicle while passenger demand remained low due to the pandemic. Programme for Government 2025 (PfG) contained a commitment to 'extend the ten-year vehicle limit for taxis registered in 2015, offering another year of service.' To address this PfG commitment, the NTA made a new Regulation in April 2015 which permitted an extension to the final operation date of taxis in the fleet that were first registered in 2015, and due to reach their final operation date between 1st January 2025 and 31st December 2025. For those operators with licenced vehicles that met this description, licences could be renewed from April 1st 2025 until its new final operation date in 2026. From Jan 1st, 2028, all vehicle age extensions provided for due to the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic on the sector, will have ended.

question: Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the frequency with which agricultural course curricula are updated to reflect emerging market trends and opportunities, including diversification, direct-to-consumer sales, agri-tourism and evolving consumer demands to meet this rapidly changing sector.
reply:
Under the Universities Act 1997 and the Technological Universities Act 2018, higher education institutions are autonomous bodies, retaining responsibility for their day-to-day management and academic affairs. The curriculum content of programmes is therefore a matter for the institutions themselves and does not fall under the remit of the Minister or Department.
Quality and Qualifications Ireland (QQI) is the State agency responsible for the external quality assurance of Ireland's further and higher education sectors. In this role, QQI monitors that each provider has the necessary internal quality assurance procedures in place to ensure that programmes and their content are reviewed at regular intervals and that feedback is obtained from learners and stakeholders which is, where relevant, used to further develop each programme’s curriculum. This would include engagement with industry bodies to ensure programmes remain responsive to emerging trends and opportunities, such as those outlined by the deputy.

Under this model, funding is provided to institutions as a block grant which supports teaching, research and other institutional activities. The allocation is determined on a formula basis, taking account of weighted eligible EU student numbers, research activity and a range of other factors, including access and research metrics. Additional weightings apply in respect of postgraduate and research students.

question: Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Health when the shingles vaccination programme will be made available free of charge through the HSE to people aged 65 and over; the proposed timeline for each phase of the rollout; and the eligibility criteria that will apply to each age group.
reply:
Ireland’s immunisation programme is informed by the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). NIAC considers the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland as well as international best practice in relation to immunisation when developing its advice.
The current NIAC guidelines state that the shingles vaccine may be considered for those aged 65 years and older, due to the greater burden and severity of disease in this age group and in those aged 18 years and older at increased risk of shingles.
I can confirm that I have approved the introduction of a Shingles Vaccination Programme, in line with NIAC advice, to be implemented on a phased basis over 5 years, for immuno-compromised groups and persons aged 65 and over.
The programme is expected to commence in 2027, initially offering shingles vaccines to immuno-compromised groups. This will be followed by the 80 years and older cohort. The programme will conclude with the 65–69-year-old cohort.
It is expected that the vaccine will be administered in the main by GPs and Pharmacists. Further programme details will become available in due course.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Health the role of telehealth in delivering health services in Ireland; and if her Department has a strategy to develop it further.
reply:
Telehealth has an increasingly important role in the delivery of health services in Ireland, enabling patients, where clinically appropriate, to access healthcare remotely through video, telephone and other digitally enabled consultations. It forms part of the wider approach to Virtual Care, alongside remote monitoring, Virtual Wards and other technology-enabled models of care.
The objective of Virtual Care is not to replace traditional face-to-face services, but to complement them by improving access, supporting greater patient choice and enabling more care to be delivered in people's homes and communities.
A range of Virtual Care initiatives are already operating within the health service. Virtual Wards focused on Early Discharge, which support suitable patients to leave hospital earlier while continuing to receive care and monitoring at home, have been in operation June 2024 and there is now at least one of these Virtual Wards in active in each of the HSE Health Regions. These Virtual Wards have collected seen over 5,300 patients and delivered over 49,000 bed days since launch, freeing up resources in hospitals for those who require more traditional forms of care.
There are also a number of Hospital Avoidance Virtual Wards in operation, which support patients, including older people and those living with chronic conditions, to receive proactive care in the community and help avoid unnecessary hospital attendance or admission.

question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Health if the cost of a nurse employed directly is €25 per hour while the cost of an agency nurse is €120 per hour; the costs, if these are not correct; her views on whether this is value for taxpayers money; and the steps she will take to address this unjustified expenditure from the public purse.
reply:
There is no single national hourly rate applicable to all directly employed nurses or agency nurses. The cost of directly employed nursing staff includes salary and associated employer costs, while agency expenditure varies depending on the grade of nurse, location, specialty requirements, duration of the placement and the terms of the relevant procurement framework.
Agency staffing is used only where necessary to maintain safe services and support continuity of patient care when permanent or other directly employed staff are not available. Significant measures have been taken in recent years to reduce reliance on agency staffing, including increased recruitment to permanent and fixed-term posts and strengthened controls on agency usage.
The Minister recognises the importance of ensuring value for money in the use of public resources. The HSE is continuing to implement measures to reduce agency expenditure and increase direct employment across the health service, while ensuring that patient safety and service delivery are maintained.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Health to outline the extent of the rollout of AI-assisted diagnostics across the health service; and the policies that are in place underpinning its use.
reply:
The Minister for Health launched AI for Care – The Artificial Intelligence Strategy for Healthcare in Ireland 2026–2030 on 11 March 2026. It provides the national strategic framework for the safe, responsible and effective adoption of artificial intelligence across health and social care and sets out how AI can improve care across four key areas: clinical care, operations, research and innovation, and public health.
Implementation of AI for Care is already under way across the health service. This includes the deployment of AI solutions in medical imaging to support faster diagnosis and improved clinical decision-making. The Strategy identifies the potential for certified AI solutions to support radiologists in reading X-rays, CT scans and MRIs faster and in detecting strokes, cancers and fractures earlier.
The National Screening Service is also assessing the potential application of AI across its screening programmes. BreastCheck has been identified as the lead programme to explore the use of AI, with research into potential applications for other screening programmes continuing. The National Screening Service is developing a four-year AI implementation strategy for 2026–2029 to support this work.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health further to Parliamentary Question No. 52802/26, her views on whether the position stated by Children's Health Ireland in its reply, that it does not intend to provide an itemised list of the criteria used to determine readiness for the opening of the National Children's Hospital; whether her Department holds a copy of those criteria; whether she will direct that the list be provided to Dáil Éireann.
reply:
I understand the Deputy has been advised by Children’s Health Ireland that the readiness for opening the National Children's Hospital Ireland (NCHI) is assessed through a cumulative process which takes account of a range of clinical, operational, governance, and patient safety considerations. These considerations are assessed collectively by the relevant teams and inform the overall assessment of readiness. The assessment is an integrated process with individual considerations evaluated in the context of the wider operational requirements for opening.
Overall progress on the NCHI Project and Programme, including operational readiness, is overseen and monitored by the National Oversight Group (NOG), chaired by the Secretary General with membership including the HSE CEO. The NOG is supported by the HSE Lead Director, who in 2024 commissioned an assurance review of CHI’s operational readiness to commission and commence operations at the NCHI.
This external review contained 13 recommendations, with 45 actions identified by CHI in its implementation plan of which 43 have been completed. The remaining two have transitioned and continue to be implemented and monitored as part of ongoing work within CHI's operational, commissioning, governance, and clinical integration workstreams to open the new hospital.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Health to ensure that the proposed scoliosis and spina bifida enquiry be a public tribunal of enquiry as families want and deserve an open, inclusive and transparent process.
reply:
I published the independent report of the Children's Health Ireland Inquiry into Spina Bifida and Complex Scoliosis Scoping Exercise on 28 September following engagement with patients and families. Mr Farrell, the independent facilitator of the scoping exercise, recommended a Commission of Investigation covering four defined modules; waiting lists, spinal surgery, hip dysplasia and the cohort of children who were not transferred to Temple Street post 2008.
Mr Farrell’s recommendation for a Commission of Investigation was based on the view that a Commission can deliver the same core statutory powers as a Tribunal while being better suited to the specific subject matter of the inquiry, namely the medical treatment of children. A Commission can compel witnesses and the production of documents and would publish a final report. Mr Farrell is of the view that as the issues deal with the personal and medical information of children who have specific legal protections and given the relatively finite number of children, there is a significant risk that children may be identifiable.
A Commission, by default is conducted in private which alleviates those concerns compared to a Tribunal which by default is conducted in private. I am aware that there is a view among some parents that it should be entirely in public. A Commission has a more flexible framework which could allow an element of the proceedings to occur in public.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Defence if she will publish, in full, the updated memorandum of understanding between Ireland and the UK on the enhancement of bilateral engagement on certain aspects of defence and security; if the agreement commits Ireland to explore participation with British Joint Expeditionary Force activities; and if so, if she will confirm the nature of that exploration.
reply:
As Minister for Defence, I outlined in this House on 16 September last, the refreshed Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between Ireland and the United Kingdom on Defence and Security Co-operation (signed on 11 March of this year) which was laid before both Houses of the Oireachtas in June 2026.
The MoU is a refresh of the 2015 agreement and provides a framework for developing and furthering bilateral co-operation between the Department of Defence and the UK Ministry of Defence. It places particular emphasis on areas such as maritime co-operation, including the protection of critical undersea infrastructure, cyber defence and security, air domain information-sharing, support for Ukraine, training and education exchanges, and the exploration of potential joint procurement initiatives.
The MoU is a voluntary, non-binding arrangement which fully respects the differing policy positions and security arrangements of both countries.
The MoU does not reference Irish participation in the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) or JEF+, which remains voluntary. Rather, it focuses on bilateral co-operation between Ireland and the United Kingdom in the areas outlined above.
A copy of the MoU is publicly available through the Oireachtas Library.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health whether any assessment has been carried out by her Department or the HSE of the risk that further restrictions on the number or location of licensed retailers of nicotine inhaling products would displace sales to unlicensed retailers, online sellers and the illicit market; whether her Department has engaged with the Revenue Commissioners on that risk.
reply:
The Public Health (Tobacco Products and Nicotine Inhaling Products) Act 2023 introduced a licensing system for the retail sale of tobacco products and nicotine inhaling products, including online. The licensing system came into operation for all retailers on 2 August 2026. Retailers wishing to sell these products must apply for a licence, pay the required fee and renew that licence annually for each premises or website. Selling tobacco or nicotine inhaling products without a licence is an offence under the Act. Enforcement of the Act is a matter for the National Environmental Health Service in the HSE.
Other than that licences will not be granted to temporary or moveable premises, such as those at festivals, the Act does not restrict the number or location of licensed retail outlets.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health the status of the review of Tobacco Free Ireland; the expected date of publication of a successor policy; whether a prohibition on the retail sale of nicotine inhaling products or nicotine pouches is under consideration as part of that review.
reply: The Tobacco Free Ireland policy review is currently at an advanced stage, with a view to publish a new strategy in Q1 2027. It will consider all available options to provide a pathway to eliminate the harm caused by tobacco use by preventing initiation and increasing cessation, and to prevent children and young people from using nicotine products.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine for an update on conservation and management plans for the North Irish Sea razor clam fishery, including Dundalk Bay; the changes being considered; and the way in which local fishermen will be consulted before decisions are made.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 116, 117, 118 and 120 together.
The razor clam fishery in Dundalk Bay and the wider North Irish Sea is an important inshore fishery on the east coast.
The Marine Institute assesses razor clam stocks through annual research surveys. My Department has recently received the Institute’s latest scientific advice on the North Irish Sea razor clam stock, which is currently under consideration. Trends in the fishery are reported in the Institute’s annual Shellfish Stocks and Fisheries Review, available at https://oar.marine.ie/.
My Department, together with the marine agencies, is examining a proposal brought forward by the North East Regional Inshore Fisheries Forum (RIFF) on the future management of the fishery, including Dundalk Bay. Fishing effort is being considered as part of the examination of this proposal and of potential management measures.
I can assure the Deputy that local fishers will be consulted before any changes are made to the management of the fishery, and my Department intends to engage further with the North East RIFF and other stakeholders as a priority.
There are a number of regulations in place to give legal effect to the current management measures for the sustainable fishing of razor clam, including:
• S.I. No. 160 of 2018: establishes a minimum conservation reference size of 125 mm for razor clams fished in the North Irish Sea,
• S.I. No. 588 of 2015: reduces the weekly landing limit for razor clam for vessels in the North

question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of student visa appeals for all nationalities that were successful in each of the past five-year to date in 2026.
reply:
Visa and preclearance applications provide legal avenues for people moving to Ireland and to facilitate visitors who wish to travel for business and/or tourism. These are important screening processes, designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel. Verifying an application is an important part of our immigration system. Each visa application is assessed on its own merits, taking all relevant information into consideration at that time.
All visa applicants are advised that it is their responsibility to provide as much supporting information as they consider necessary in support of their application. Guidance in this regard is available on my Department's website. Applicants who carefully follow this guidance are more likely to submit a complete application that can be fully assessed.
Where a visa application is refused, the reasons for the refusal are clearly set out in the decision letter issued to the applicant. Applicants may avail of the visa appeals process, under which an appeal is examined by a Visa Appeals Officer following a full consideration of all information and supporting documentation submitted. Where appropriate, individuals may also choose to submit a new visa application, taking account of the reasons for the original refusal.

question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to respond to correspondence (details supplied) regarding the new temporary protection transition scheme.
reply:
The Temporary Protection Transition Scheme was launched on 30 September 2026, in line with the EU Council recommendation for a co-ordinated approach to transition people from Temporary Protection across the EU.
People with Temporary Protection who wish to transition to the new permission must meet the eligibility criterion, including being in employment or self-employment for six months on or before 30 September 2026 with a minimum earnings requirement of €29,432 per year, have independent accommodation, and be resident in Ireland for a period of one year as a beneficiary of Temporary Protection prior to the opening of the new permission application process.
In accordance with S3(5) of the Scheme Policy, time spent as an International Protection applicant will be disregarded and the period of time spent as a beneficiary of Temporary Protection, both before and after the time spent as an International Protection applicant, will count towards the one-year residency requirement. question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will publish a fossil fuel phaseout plan as part of the 2026 Climate Action Plan.
reply:
This Government is committed to delivering on Ireland’s responsibility to address the climate crisis and work remains ongoing across Government to implement climate mitigation measures every day. We have a robust climate delivery framework and detailed plans in place across all sectors. The priority is driving implementation, particularly of high impact measures with multiple societal and economic benefits.
The EPA's latest provisional greenhouse gas emissions inventory, published in July, shows that this is working. Ireland recorded overall emissions reductions for a fourth consecutive year. All main sectors saw reductions in 2025 and we have the lowest level of emissions in 36 years, which is notable given a concurrent population increase of approximately 1.5 million people, more than one million new homes and over one million extra vehicles on our roads.
By changing how we heat our homes, power our transport and drive our industrial processes from fossil-based sources to electricity generated from clean energy technologies like solar and wind, we can decarbonise our economy and further protect households and businesses from price volatility linked to the importation of increasingly erratic fossil fuels. In 2025, we ended the use of coal in Moneypoint power station, marking a significant milestone in our progressive transition away from fossil fuels.

reply:

At the same time, those who seek the assistance of the courts in resolving their family justice disputes need to be assured that their privacy, and that of their children, will be maintained at what can be a very difficult time. Any policy proposals developed will need to ensure the privacy of parties involved continues. question: Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide details of the engagement between his Department and an organisation(details supplied) concerning its recent consent awareness video; who initiated this engagement; whether he personally authorised or directed officials to contact the organisation; and the specific requests that were made.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 101, 102, 103 and 104 together.
The Dublin Rape Crisis Centre's We Consent programme is funded by Cuan, the Domestic, Sexual and Gender-Based Violence Agency, and seeks to inform, educate and engage society on the issue of consent.
Following public concern regarding a recent video produced as part of that programme, officials in my Department engaged with the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre regarding the matter. I am of the view that the content of the video was not an effective means of communicating the important message around consent and that it did not reflect the Government's views. This does not detract from the importance of the wider We Consent programme, nor from the valuable work undertaken by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre and other organisations funded through Cuan.
The Department's engagement focused on conveying those concerns. No issues relating to the Centre's funding arrangements or its ongoing relationship with the Department were raised. The Dublin Rape Crisis Centre subsequently decided to remove the video and review the content. That decision was a matter for the organisation itself.
My Department and Cuan fund a range of independent organisations to deliver specialist services, supports, and advocacy activities. Such funding arrangements do not diminish the operational independence of those organisations who remain responsible for their own programmes, communications, and operational decisions.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Taoiseach if there have been any allocations for environmental projects from the Shared Island Fund; if so, the project; and the amount contributed.
reply:

reply:

question: Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport to provide a breakdown of the local authorities that have availed of funding under the artist workspaces scheme; the amount of funding that has been awarded to each; the number of projects; and the way in which the funding was used in each instance.
reply:
My Department launched the €6 million pilot Artist Workspaces Scheme in June 2024. Under this scheme, local authorities outside Dublin City Council are invited to propose projects which enable them to provide additional artist workspaces in their regions on a sustainable basis and produce fit for purpose workspaces. Funding of up to €300,000 is available for densely populated local authority areas and €150,000 for other local authorities. The scheme to date has allocated over €1.58 million, funding 9 local authorities, providing support for 10 projects and 30 artist workspaces. My Department welcomes applications under this Scheme and I encourage any local authority that has not yet applied to consider an application to develop artist workspaces in their area. Full details including guidelines and the application form are available at Creative Arts: Grants and Funding (www.gov.ie/en/department-of-culture-communications-and-sport/publications/creative-arts-grants-and-funding/#artist-workspaces-capital-scheme)

Separately, in Dublin City, my Department has allocated a specific €3 million in funding to 'Space to Create', an initiative that aims to provide up to sixty artist workspaces in Dublin City, and these projects are currently being progressed in partnership with Dublin City Council.

question: Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he will provide funding to Coimisiún na Meán to offset the €1.04 million increase in the 2026 radio broadcasting levy, in order that the increase is not borne by radio stations.
reply:
There is a long-standing principle that costs of regulation are met by regulated sectors themselves, and therefore, the Broadcasting Act provides for the imposition by Coimisiún na Meán of levies to meet the costs of its full range of statutory functions and duties.
Furthermore, the Act vests authority and responsibility for such a levy in Coimisiún na Meán. The Minister does not have a role in approving the proposed income or expenditure of Coimisiún na Meán, or importantly in the setting of the annual levy for any category of regulated entities, including that of sound broadcasting.
In formulating its annual levies, Coimisiún na Meán is required to ensure that the levies are such an amount so as to meet all expenses properly incurred in the period, and is also required to ensure proportionality in attribution of expenses and application of levies across relevant categories of regulated service providers or entities. An Coimisiún must also have regard to a number of factors in setting the levy including the financing of a service provider and the nature and scale of its services.
In relation to potential Exchequer funding of any of Coimisiún na Mean’s activities, other than in cases where the imposition of a levy is either not permitted or not feasible, it is not intended to replace An Coimisiún’s existing levy income with direct Exchequer funding. question: Deputy Brian Stanley asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he will indicate when fibre optic broadband services will be made available to the property located at R32 K2E2, County Laois, given that access to reliable high-speed broadband is required for employment purposes.
reply:
The National Broadband Plan (NBP) is the Government's initiative to deliver high speed broadband services to all premises in Ireland.
The Government identified a need to deliver broadband services where commercial operators would not operate. As part of the NBP, the Government appointed National Broadband Ireland to deliver wholesale broadband services to those parts of the country, not served by commercial operators. The Department defines high-speed broadband as a connection with minimum speeds of 30 Mbps download and 6 Mbps upload.
The premises in question is in the BLUE area on the broadband map which is available on www.gov.ie/en/publication/5634d-national-broadband-plan-map/ and is currently capable of receiving in excess of 30 Mbps from open eir’s local high-speed broadband to the cabinet per information available at www.openeir.ie/fibre/broadband-checker.
The BLUE area represents those areas where commercial providers are either currently delivering or have plans to deliver high-speed broadband services.
The activities of commercial operators delivering high-speed broadband within BLUE areas are not planned or funded by the State and the Department has no statutory authority to intervene in that regard.
There may be a choice of operators offering this service in any given area. Further information in this regard is available at www.comreg.ie/compare/#/services.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he has had any consultation with an organisation (details supplied) since the Ireland versus Israel fixtures on their handling of the matter.
reply:
National Governing Bodies of sport (NGBs), such as the Football Association of Ireland (FAI), are independent, autonomous bodies responsible for the governance of their own sports, including the organisation of sporting fixtures, whether in domestic or international competitions. Neither the Government, my Department nor Sport Ireland have a role in determining or supporting the organisation of such fixtures.
The Government has consistently recognised and respected the right of the FAI to decide how to fulfil these fixtures in accordance with its obligations as a member of UEFA.
I have not engaged with the FAI in relation to this matter since the playing of the fixtures.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport whether contracts recorded in his Department's internal contract register can be linked to their corresponding contract award notices published on eTenders, where applicable; whether his Department records the relevant eTenders notice reference, URL or other identifier; and if not, the reasons that prevent this information from being recorded.
reply:
My Department operates a number of controls and procedures in relation to procurement and contracts largely informed by Public Procurement Guidelines published by the OGP which performs a key role in helping the State to save money when buying goods and services.
Contracts in excess of €50,000 (ex VAT) are advertised through the eTenders website. Such contracts are subject to Government Circular 05/2023 which provides for greater use of existing OGP frameworks, as well as EU Directives 2014/23, 2014/24, and 2014/25.
By way of additional internal controls in my Department, all contracts in excess of €25,000 (ex VAT), and contracts of a consultancy nature regardless of value, are subject to approval by my Department’s Management Board before any competitive or selection process commences. This is followed up by a formal process which underlines the final value and expiry date of the contract, the latter being monitored on an ongoing basis. In addition, a quarterly report issues to all staff showing vendors paid over €25,000 (ex VAT), for sign off and agreement at senior official level. There are also area-specific monthly transaction reports issued for similar sign off. Purchase orders in excess of €20,000 (inc. VAT) are submitted to the Management Board and published quarterly online.
