question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the total cost to date for the renovation works on the Dead Zoo since it closed for renovation in 2024; the full and detailed breakdown of those costs; the timeline for when the works will be completed; and the estimated cost for the entire project.
reply:
The conservation and refurbishment of the National Museum of Ireland (NMI)- Natural History Museum is being progressed as part of the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport’s capital investment programme under the National Development Plan, and delivered in partnership with the Office of Public Works (OPW).
The project is currently at Stage 2a of the Capital Works Management Framework which is focused on design development, cost optimisation, statutory approvals (Planning Permission, Fire Safety Certificates, and Disability Access Certificates), and development of a procurement strategy.
Following approval of the Preliminary Business Case and appointment of integrated design team, the museum closed its doors in September 2024 to facilitate a full decant of its extensive and sensitive collections. Some of the most popular exhibits from the natural history collection, as well as some specimens that haven’t been on display for many years, are now accessible to the public at the Dead Zoo Lab opened in August 2025 at the NMI Collins Barracks site.
The project is funded by the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport (D/CCS). In line with the Governance and Operational Arrangements agreed between the Department (the Approving Authority), the National Museum of Ireland (the Sponsoring Agency) and the Office of Public Works (the Contracting Authority), a pre-funding mechanism has been put in place allowing for periodic advancement of funds to cover OPW and NMI’s forec

The overarching aim is to support increased participation in cultural life among young people in Ireland, encouraging engagement with arts and creative industries at a critical developmental stage. This remains an important priority.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport to provide an update on the planned introduction of core and development funding for organisations (details supplied), either through the Department or the Arts Council.
reply:
This Department recently launched the Arts Capital Investment Fund, a €6 million pilot scheme delivering on a Programme for Government commitment. Along with supporting arts and culture organisations with construction works and equipment, Category 3 of the scheme will also support community and voluntary groups with funding for equipment to increase participation in arts and culture. This is a new category of funding offered by my Department and provides much needed investment for groups, such as amateur drama and musical societies, with limited access to resources until now.
Under the Arts Act 2003, the Arts Council has primary responsibility for the development of the arts in Ireland. I have asked the Arts Council to make direct contact with the Deputy in relation to the question. Please contact my private office if you do not hear from the Council within the next ten working days.

question: Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport for an update on the proposed culture card which was promised in advance of Budget 2027; and if consideration can now be given to expand this to cover sporting activities for children.
reply:
The Programme for Government committed to “examine the introduction of a Culture Card for 16 and 17-year-olds to access theatre, music and art events”. The delivery of a youth Culture Card was always subject to budget allocation, and while Budget 2027 has not provided funding to being the roll-out of the programme in the coming year, the Department will continue to explore the development of the Culture Card for our young people, in line with the Programme for Government commitment.
Our overarching aim here is to support increased participation in cultural life among young people in Ireland, encouraging engagement with arts and creative industries at a critical developmental stage. This remains an important priority.
Options for the development, operation, scope and funding structure for Culture Cards are currently being explored further. Anticipated benefits would include stimulating lifelong creative engagement, improving wellbeing outcomes, and providing direct economic stimulus for the cultural and creative sectors.
The proposed Culture Card is just one way to increase young people's cultural engagement. question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport to outline the statutory or regulatory requirements that apply to telecoms operators regarding the maintenance of duct and pole networks to ensure resilience during severe weather events such as Storm Éowyn; whether any such requirements are under review; whether his Department has examined comparable regimes in other EU Member States; and whether similar measures are being considered for introduction in Ireland.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 922 and 923 together.
Since Storm Éowyn impacted the State in 2025, my Department has had significant engagement with industry in the development of resilience and emergency response, primarily via the establishment of the Telecommunications Response and Resilience Group (T-RRG). Cooperation and coordination between industry and Government via the T-RRG to improve sectoral preparedness for, and response to severe weather incidents, is ongoing.
On Friday, 30 October, my Department chaired Exercise Lugh. Held in partnership with the telecommunications industry and designed to test and enhance the sector’s response capability to severe weather events, Lugh is the Department's inaugural terrestrial emergency planning exercise. Exercise Lugh was a tabletop exercise simulating a severe winter storm on the scale of Storm Éowyn and was the first to be held by the Department as part of the workplan of the T-RRG.
While I do not have a statutory remit to compel network operators to carry out maintenance to their pole infrastructure, they are obliged to take appropriate and proportionate measures to ensure the security of their networks under the Communications Regulation and Digital Hub Development Agency (Amendment) Act 2023.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the way in which his Department is building cyber resilience; and the strategy in place to address cyber attacks.
reply:
My Department is aware of the resilience requirements arising under the forthcoming NIS2 Directive and is taking the necessary preparatory steps to ensure compliance. This approach is informed by guidance from the National Cyber Security Centre and relevant national and EU cyber security requirements, which are designed to strengthen cyber resilience, risk management and incident response capabilities across the public sector.
The Department also has arrangements in place to respond to and manage cyber security incidents as they arise. However it is not considered appropriate to disclose detailed information relating to the Department's cyber security approaches or contingency planning. The disclosure of such information could compromise the Department's security posture by assisting malicious actors to identify potential vulnerabilities.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if his Department or public bodies under the aegis of his Department have tested their ability to transfer essential data and services from their principal cloud-service provider to an alternative provider or State-controlled infrastructure; the number possessing a fully costed and tested cloud exit plan; the number of critical public services that could not presently be migrated within six months; whether vendor-concentration risk is recorded centrally; and if he will publish an anonymised aggregate assessment of that risk.
reply:
My Department is aware of the resilience considerations arising under the forthcoming NIS2 requirements and is taking the necessary preparatory steps to ensure compliance with those requirements. This includes consideration of supplier-dependency management and other measures designed to strengthen the resilience and portability of critical ICT services as part of the Department's commitment to meet its NIS2 obligations. However, for operational and security reasons, my Department does not publicly disclose detailed information relating to its ICT systems, infrastructure, cloud service arrangements or contingency planning.
However, I can confirm that my Department has successfully undertaken a number of migrations involving the transfer of data and associated ICT services between different organisational environments. These exercises have demonstrated the Department's capability to transfer data and services while maintaining service continuity and operational effectiveness. My Department incorporates data portability, service continuity and migration planning within its ICT governance and service management arrangements. It also considers supplier and service risks as part of its ongoing procurement and service management processes.
The information sought in relation to agencies and bodies under the aegis of my Department is not held centrally by the Department and is an operational matter for the individual bodies concerned.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport for an update on the procurement process for the emergency call answering service contract; whether a preferred bidder has been selected; and when a final contract award decision is expected.
reply:
The procurement process for the Emergency Call Answering Service (ECAS) remains ongoing. The procurement process is at an advanced stage and is being progressed in accordance with the requirements of the competition and applicable public procurement rules.
No contract award decision has been made at this time and, accordingly, no preferred bidder has been selected.
Given the live nature of the procurement process, it would not be appropriate to comment further on detailed aspects of the evaluation or commercially sensitive matters.
The Department's priority remains the delivery of a robust and resilient ECAS while ensuring compliance with public procurement requirements. A contract award decision will be made following completion of the procurement process and the necessary governance and approval arrangements. The Department anticipates that these processes will conclude, and a contract award decision can be made, by the end of November 2026.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the reason for the delay in concluding the emergency call answering service (ECAS) procurement process; the arrangements in place to ensure continuity of the 999/112 service pending its completion; and the protections that will apply to existing ECAS staff in the event of a change of service provider.
reply:
The duration of the procurement process reflects the complexity and strategic importance of the ECAS service, together with the requirement to ensure a thorough and legally compliant procurement process. The current competition is the second procurement process undertaken. The original procurement, which commenced in January 2024, had progressed to an advanced stage before it was cancelled as a result of all remaining tenderers withdrawing from the process for reasons outside of DCCS’s control. A new procurement process was therefore required which is now in the final stage and due to conclude by end of November.
The current ECAS contract includes exit management provisions, while the new contract will contain comprehensive mobilisation and transition arrangements. The Department will oversee and manage these contractual provisions to ensure that any transition is delivered in a controlled manner.
Any new service provider appointed to provide the ECAS service will be required to comply with all relevant employment legislation including the European Communities (Protection of Employees on Transfer of Undertakings) Regulations 2003, where the Regulations apply, together with any other applicable contractual obligations. These arrangements are intended to protect the employment rights of existing ECAS staff in the event of a transition to a new service provider together with supporting continuity of service and minimising disruption in the delivery of the ECAS services.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport his Department's position regarding the protection of artistic intellectual property in the era of artificial intelligence.
reply:

DETE is leading on the implementation of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act and has policy responsibility for copyright law in Ireland.
As recommended by the 2025 report of the National AI Advisory Council "The Impact of AI on Ireland’s Creative Sector", the overarching objective must be to protect creatives and ensure meaningful artistic freedom while fostering innovation and potential of AI for the Creative and Cultural Sector. question: Deputy Fionntán Ó Súilleabháin asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the public information and awareness measures planned ahead of the roll-out of IE Alert; whether a national information campaign will be undertaken before the system becomes operational; if advance notice will be given prior to any testing; the plans to educate the public, schools, community groups and vulnerable persons on the system's purpose and operation; and the steps being taken to ensure alerts do not cause unnecessary alarm or distress when introduced.
reply:
My Department is working with the Department of the Taoiseach and the Department of Defence to establish “IE-Alert”. This inter-departmental initiative aims to develop the technology, expertise, operational processes and public awareness necessary to create a comprehensive public warning system capable of effectively alerting the public of threats during emergency situations.
Cell broadcast Public Warning System (CB-PWS) is an effective technology for distributing public warning messages. The CB-PWS will be part of the existing emergency communications structures that are in place, such as TV, radio and social media. In the appropriate circumstances, it will be an additional channel available to provide information to the public.
The role of my Department in the IE-Alert initiative is to lead on the procurement of the CB-PWS equipment and services. I expect procurement of the CB-PWS to begin this year. Based on current planning, a public launch is anticipated in 2029.
Responsibility for operation and management of the system will transfer to the Department of Defence, through the Office of Emergency Planning, once the system becomes operational. Protocols and procedures for the use of the CB-PWS, along with appropriate public awareness campaigns will be established through the IE-Alert inter-departmental initiative, by the relevant Departments.

question: Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the criteria used by his Department to determine whether a premises is included in the National Broadband Plan intervention area.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 899 and 901 to 903, inclusive, together.
Ireland's Digital Connectivity Strategy published in December 2022, sets out a number of targets including that all Irish households and businesses will be covered by a Gigabit network no later than 2028.
The National Broadband Plan (NBP) is the Government's initiative to deliver high-speed broadband services to all premises in Ireland. The Government identified a need to deliver broadband services where commercial operators would not operate such as in parts of rural Ireland. The Department defines high-speed broadband (HSBB) as a connection with minimum speeds of 30Mbps download and 6Mbps upload, which was the threshold used to determine eligibility for inclusion in the NBP intervention area as part of the mapping consultation conducted in 2019.

question: Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport to publish his Department's plan for the future of television; the way in which the shutdown of satellite broadcasting will be managed, ensuring no one is left behind and audiences can continue to have access to television programming.
reply:
Ensuring ongoing access to free-to-air television content, and in particular that produced by our public service media providers, is a key objective of my Department.
The Broadcasting Act 2009, as amended, places an obligation on RTÉ to establish, maintain, and operate national multiplexes, which are to provide for the broadcast of our public service broadcasting services, any other public service television services designated by order, or television services with public service obligations under licence.
The Saorview service remains a widely accessible and important platform for viewers to access free-to-air broadcast content. Viewers are, however, increasingly accessing broadcast media online and shifting away from traditional TV platforms such as Saorview and those operated by satellite or other commercial providers.
Broadcasters, including our public service media providers, are responding to these changes by making their content available across multiple TV distribution platforms. In this regard, the Broadcasting Act also provides that both RTÉ and TG4 must make available their broadcasting services, in so far as reasonably practicable, by any and all means of transmission, whether by terrestrial, cable or satellite networks, or other electronic means such as the Internet.

question: Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of National Educational Psychological Service (NEPS) psychologists currently allocated to primary schools in Dublin mid-west; the number of primary schools operating without access to a dedicated NEPS psychologist; the average waiting time for a NEPS assessment of a child with suspected dyslexia or other specific learning difficulties; and the measures being taken to improve early identification and assessment of children with reading and literacy difficulties.
reply:
I would like to take this opportunity to outline the work of NEPS. All schools have access to:
• General support and advice from an educational psychologist in NEPS, either through the school’s assigned psychologist or through the NEPS Advisory Support Service.
• Support from an educational psychologist in NEPS in the event of a Critical Incident.
• National and Regional Support and Development service for school staff.
• Individual casework where a priority need is established to either an educational psychologist in NEPS or a private educational psychologist on the Scheme for Commissioning Psychological Assessments (SCPA) panel.
NEPS does not operate waiting lists. In common with other psychological services and best international practice, NEPS operates on a consultative model of service with assessments only one aspect of the NEPS service.
Schools are encouraged to support children and young people using the Continuum of Support, whereby school staff use a problem-solving, evidence-based approach to intervention for children and young people experiencing difficulties in the school context, including those experiencing literacy difficulties. This process includes initial screening at school level. Response-to-intervention is monitored and recorded in the Student Support File. The teachers, parents and children or young people are all involved in this process.

question: Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Education and Youth the steps being taken to improve initial teacher education and continuing professional development in relation to dyslexia, literacy difficulties and specific learning disabilities; and the extent to which teachers are trained to identify children who may require assessment or intervention.
reply:
The Department is committed to ensuring that teachers are equipped, through both Initial Teacher Education (ITE) and Continuing Professional Development (CPD), to support students with dyslexia, literacy difficulties and specific learning disabilities.
All ITE programmes are accredited under Céim: Standards for Initial Teacher Education (2020), which sets out the requirements programmes must meet to gain accreditation. The standards require all programmes to incorporate seven core elements, including Inclusive Education, Literacy and Numeracy, and Digital Skills.
The Literacy and Numeracy element requires student teachers to demonstrate competence in teaching and assessing literacy and numeracy appropriate to their curricular or subject area. This supports the development of teacher capacity to identify and respond to literacy difficulties, including dyslexia and specific learning disabilities, through evidence-informed approaches to teaching, assessment and early intervention.
Inclusive Education, as defined in Céim, aims to strengthen teachers' capacity to respond to the diverse needs of learners, remove barriers to participation and learning, and ensure that all learners can derive maximum benefit from education. Through the accreditation process, Higher Education Institutions demonstrate that programmes incorporate appropriate content, inclusive pedagogical approaches and school placement experiences.

reply:
This government is fully committed to supporting students with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this objective.
At present, there are four special schools, and fourteen special classes attached to mainstream schools to support students with a specific learning disability such as severe dyslexia. I want to acknowledge the excellent work they do. It is important to note they were established at a time when there were much fewer additional supports in schools.
In pursuit of a more inclusive education system it is important, as far as possible to support students to attend their local mainstream schools. This means that children and young people can be educated with their peers and are not required to travel long distances to attend special schools or classes.
15,000 special education teachers have been provided to enable schools to achieve this objective. In practical terms this means schools get a substantial additional teaching allocation to support students with special education needs who are in mainstream classes.
The additional resources are intended to support students with the greatest level of need, including those with a specific learning disability such as dyslexia, dyscalculia or dysgraphia.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of vacancies that exist in each school completion programme across the country, in tabular form.
reply:
The School Completion Programme (SCP) is a central element of the Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools (DEIS) strategy and operates under Tusla Education Support Service (TESS), as a commissioned service under section 56 of the Child and Family Agency Act 2013. SCP provides vital support to children and young people at risk of early school leaving across over 800 schools, delivered through 121 individual projects.
While TESS holds operational responsibility for the programme, projects are managed locally by voluntary Local Management Committees (LMC’S) who generally act as employer for SCP staff. LMCs are responsible for local programme oversight, staff employment, resource management and accountability for public funds.
Information on staffing levels within the 121 SCP projects, including current vacancies, is not held centrally by my department. The relevant information is maintained at local level by the individual LMCs.
A programme of reform is underway which will see the establishment of a new employment and governance framework for the SCP under the education and training board (ETB) sector. Work to develop this framework is progressing steadily, with the first wave of transfers scheduled to take place on 30 November 2026, with full rollout expected to be completed during 2027. Where students with more complex needs require additional supports, special class and special school places are provided. This is in keeping with policy on an inclusive education, which promotes that students will be supported to receive an education in the most inclusive setting possible.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of annual school accounts submitted to the financial support services unit that required amendment, correction, clarification or resubmission following review in each school year from 2019-20 to date; and the most common reasons such follow-up was required.
reply:
The Financial Support Services Unit (FSSU), funded by the department, is an important source of advice and support to schools on financial matters, including budgeting and cashflow management.
In line with Circulars www.assets.gov.ie/static/documents/86fe1745-00602017-.pdf and www.assets.gov.ie/static/documents/86fe1745-00602017-.pdf,
the FSSU acts as a central repository for annual school accounts prepared for the school by an external accountant/auditor registered with a recognised accountancy body in the State.
In collating annual school accounts and financial data submitted to the FSSU, queries may arise which require engagement with a school and/or its external accountant/auditor where submission is late, or the school is selected for review or audit.
The FSSU does not currently record under the categories specified in this question, namely amendment, correction, clarification or resubmission, on a school-year basis.
The FSSU provides ongoing guidance and support to schools and their external accountants/auditors in relation to the preparation and submission of annual accounts and the application of the prescribed FSSU accounting and reporting requirements.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether the financial support services unit records instances where annual school accounts are deemed non-compliant with its financial reporting requirements; and, if so, the number of schools concerned in each school year from 2019-20 to date.
reply:
The Financial Support Services Unit (FSSU), funded by the department, is an important source of advice and support to schools on financial matters, including budgeting and cashflow management.
In line with Circulars [0060/2017] www.assets.gov.ie/static/documents/86fe1745-00602017-.pdf
and 0002/2018 www.assets.gov.ie/static/documents/becccdb8-00022018-.pdf,
the FSSU acts as a central repository for annual school accounts prepared for the school by an external accountant/auditor registered with a recognised accountancy body in the State.
Annual school accounts are required to be prepared in the prescribed FSSU format and submitted annually to the FSSU by the 28th of February following the end of the preceding school year.
Compliance with the annual accounts requirements is primarily monitored by reference to whether the required annual accounts have been submitted to the FSSU in the prescribed format and within the required timeframe.
The FSSU provides ongoing guidance and support to schools and their external accountants/auditors in relation to the preparation and submission of annual accounts and the application of the prescribed FSSU accounting and reporting requirements.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Taoiseach when the Cabinet Committee on Artificial Intelligence will meet.
reply:
As part of the Government’s response to AI, a new Cabinet Committee on AI has been established.
This reflects the Government’s ambition on AI, as set out in Digital Ireland, and the significant potential of AI technologies to bring profound and transformative changes across the economy and society.
The Cabinet Committee will focus on whole-of-society impacts of AI, including impacts on the economy and the labour market, wider societal impacts and regulation, and AI deployment in the public service.
It is intended that this Cabinet Committee will meet on the 16 November.

question: Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Education and Youth the escalation procedure where a post-primary pupil has an NCSE letter of eligibility and professional recommendations for a special class but remains without a suitable placement following repeated refusals arising from oversubscription or admissions criteria; the body responsible for coordinating and securing a placement; the applicable timelines; and the circumstances in which the section 67 or section 37A powers cited in her previous reply are considered and used.
reply:
Enabling students with special educational needs to receive an education that meets their needs is a priority for this Government. It is also a key priority for me, my department and for the National Council for Special Education (NCSE).
Local SENOs remain available to assist and advise the parents of children with special educational needs. I would urge families to engage with their local SENO for support with specialist places.
The vast majority of students with special educational needs are supported to attend mainstream classes with their peers. Where students with more complex needs require additional supports, special class and special school places are provided. This is in keeping with policy on an inclusive education, which advocates that students will be supported to receive an education in the most inclusive setting possible.
I am satisfied that I have the necessary statutory powers under Section 37A of the Education Act 1998 to compel schools to make provision for children and young people with special education needs, if necessary. In addition, the NCSE also has the power to direct schools to admit individual children and young people with special education needs.
Under Section 67 of the Education Act, the NCSE may designate a school place for a child with special educational needs. The NCSE are required to carry out this function in accordance with the provisions set out in primary legislation.
It is the responsibility of the managerial authorities of all schools

question: Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of post-primary pupils with an NCSE letter of eligibility who remain without their recommended special class placement, nationally and in County Waterford, broken down by school year, length of time awaiting placement and whether they are on a reduced timetable, in tabular form; where these data are not collected, the way in which her Department and the NCSE identify and monitor this unmet need; and whether she will arrange for these data to be collected.
reply:
This government is fully committed to supporting students with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this objective.
The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) is, in the first instance, the primary body responsible for the matter the Deputy has raised. I will arrange for your query to be forwarded to the NCSE for their attention and direct reply. Deputies are also welcome to raise such queries with the NCSE directly through their dedicated Oireachtas email address.
My department and the NCSE have sanctioned 587 new special classes for the school year 2026/27, including 70 inclusive special classes. This is one of many ways my department is actively engaging to meet the increased demand. This brings the total number of special classes sanctioned to date to over 4,300. Forward planning has already commenced ahead of the 2027/28 school year.
It is the responsibility of the managerial authorities of all schools to implement an admissions policy in accordance with the Education Act, 1998 and the Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018.
Under the provisions of this act, all schools are required to have admissions policies which have been approved by the patron following consultation with staff and parents of students who are attending the school. It is a key requirement of the act that all school admission policies are fair and transparent.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which a revised eligibility framework will align with the inclusive, strengths-based, relational and child-centred approaches currently promoted by the National Council for Special Education (NCSE); and the way in which schools will be supported to implement both objectives consistently.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 858, 859, 862 and 883 to 885, inclusive, together.
At the outset, my priority, and that of my department, is to ensure that children and young people can access the educational provision and supports they need in an equitable, timely and appropriate manner. Together with Minister Naughton, I have secured a record budget of €3.8 billion for special education in 2027, enabling us to build on the significant progress already made across the system. I regularly hear from families, parents and schools about the importance of ensuring that supports are available when they are needed, and I am committed to addressing barriers that may delay or impede access to appropriate educational provision.
In considering future improvements, the department is building on a series of significant reforms that have already moved the system towards a needs-based approach. These include the introduction in 2017 of a needs-based model for the allocation of special education teaching supports in mainstream schools, as well as subsequent reforms to arrangements for Special Needs Assistant supports and summer programmes.
These changes have strengthened access to support for many children and young people. At the same time, I recognise that a diagnosis continues to play an important role for many children, young people and their families, including in accessing services and understanding individual needs.

reply:

question: Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Taoiseach when the Cabinet Committee on EU and International Affairs will next meet.
reply:
The Programme for Government 2025, Securing Ireland’s Future, recognises the importance of Cabinet Committees to the policy development and oversight work of Government.
The Cabinet Committee on EU and International Affairs was established by the Government on 18 February 2025. It last met on Monday 2 November 2026.
Its role is to oversee implementation of Programme for Government commitments in relation to the European Union, including Ireland’s 2026 EU Presidency, and international issues.
The Cabinet Committee is scheduled to next meet on 23 November in advance of the Special meeting of the European Council due to take place on 26-27 November.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether the Department will review the need for a new post-primary school in Newcastle, County Dublin, in light of the recent variation to the South Dublin County Development Plan and the additional residential development envisaged for the area; and to outline the next steps in assessing future school provision.
reply:

In this regard, my department has been actively engaged with South Dublin County Council in relation to the preparation and variation of the South Dublin County Development Plan, including Variation No. 2, which provides for revised housing targets and associated population growth.
My department maintains a close working relationship with the planning section of South Dublin County Council and continually assesses current and future school place requirements across the County. Consequently, there are currently no plans to establish a new post-primary school in Newcastle.

question: Deputy Johnny Mythen asked the Minister for Education and Youth the completion date for the evaluation of the pilots currently underway; and if she will commit to ensuring that there is an appropriate space for every child on the school transport scheme.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth that has expanded significantly over the past six years. In that time, the numbers of children and young people using the service have grown from under 120,000 pupils in 2018 to over 181,000 pupils including over 24,000 pupils with Special Educational Needs in 2025 which equates to an increase of over 50%. Since 2018, investment in the scheme has more than doubled, from €200 million to €537 million.
The School Transport 2030 report was published in early 2024. The recommended changes to the schemes include expansion of the current eligibility criteria, addressing current operational challenges and moving towards better integration with public transport to ensure the best value for money to the Exchequer.
It was outlined at the time the Review was published that the proposed changes to the eligibility criteria would further increase demand for the scheme. Therefore, it was considered prudent to implement the changes on a phased basis.

reply:

The majority of newer developments in the Citywest area are located within the Newcastle-Rathcoole School Planning Area, while other parts are served by schools in the Tallaght School Planning Area. Accordingly, the primary school-going population of Citywest is accommodated through a network of schools across both planning areas, and demographic analysis of current and future demand takes account of enrolment patterns and population growth across these areas.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which teaching hours for non-new entrant EAL students (criteria B) are assessed, in tabular form, by number of students.
reply:

All schools are advised in the first instance to review whether the needs of newly enrolled pupils can be met from within existing allocations. Language supports are also included through the Special Education Teaching (SET) which encompasses an element of language support allocation. Under this SET model, schools are frontloaded with resources to provide support immediately to those pupils who need it without delay.
My Department's policies enable flexible resource allocation to ensure that the resources follow pupils in the event of them changing schools. question: Deputy Niamh Smyth asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will review correspondence and address the concerns raised regarding transport for pupils attending a school and accessing after-school services (details supplied); and if she will advise whether a transport solution will be provided.
reply:
School transport is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department and Youth.
The School Transport Schemes are designed to provide transport for children travelling between home and school during normal school opening and closing times. Transport to or from alternative addresses is not a standard feature of the scheme.
Bus Éireann endeavours to provide a reasonable level of transport service for all eligible children. The safety and wellbeing of pupils travelling on school transport services is of paramount importance to both the Department and Bus Éireann. In some cases, specialised transport services, including the provision of a bus escort, may be necessary where a child's care or safety needs warrant this level of support.
Requests for transport to an alternative address may be considered for an eligible child, provided that a number of conditions are met. These include:
• An existing school transport service is already in place.
• The request does not require any change to the current route or timetable.
• The arrangement is consistent and regular (the same address and times each day: Monday to Friday.
• No inconvenience is caused to other children using the service.
• No health and safety concerns arise.
• There is no additional cost to the State.
Each application is considered on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the conditions outlined above.
The request submitted by the Deputy has been forwarded to Bus Éireann who will liaise direc

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Taoiseach if he will report on engagements his Department has had with German Chancellor Merz during his visit to Ireland in July.
reply:
I met with the Chancellor of Germany, Friedrich Merz, on 28 July at Farmleigh House in the context of Ireland’s Presidency of the Council of the European Union which began on 1 July.
We discussed Ireland’s Presidency priorities, including competitiveness, enlargement, and advancing agreement on the EU’s next long-term budget, the Multiannual Financial Framework.
We also discussed the economic challenges facing all EU countries, including the impacts of rising energy prices on our citizens and enterprises, security, and global issues, including the situation in the Middle East and Ukraine.
I took the opportunity to express the solidarity of the Irish people with the victims of the horrific attack on the Pride parade in Berlin, which took place just before his visit to Ireland.
Ireland and Germany will continue to work constructively together on the full range of issues on the EU agenda.

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of primary schools that have lost a mainstream classroom teacher following the reassessment of pupil enrolments on 30 September 2026; the number that have had their teacher allocations reduced as a result of this reassessment; the average pupil-to-teacher ratio in these classrooms following the loss of a teacher; the number of classrooms now that have 30 or more pupils, 35 or more pupils, and the maximum number of pupils in any one classroom; and whether she is satisfied that these class sizes allow teachers to adequately support pupils, particularly those with needs.
reply:
The Department's Primary Staffing Schedule is a long-established element of the primary school staffing allocation system and is designed to ensure fairness, transparency and consistency in the allocation of mainstream teaching posts across all primary schools.
The principal factor in determining the number of mainstream teaching posts allocated to a school is its recognised enrolment, as recorded on 30 September of the previous school year.
Class sizes are influenced by a range of factors, including enrolment trends and the accommodation available within a school. Responsibility for the organisation of classes and the deployment of teachers rests with individual schools, as they are best placed to assess and respond to their particular circumstances.
The Department's guidance is that class sizes should be kept as low as possible, having regard to the school's particular context and available resources. School authorities are also encouraged, where feasible, to use the flexibility available under the staffing schedule to provide smaller class sizes in the junior classes.
In recognition of expected enrolment growth, 154 schools were provisionally sanctioned for an additional temporary mainstream teaching post for the 2026/27 school year under the projected enrolment and retention on increased enrolment processes. The allocation was conditional on each school attaining a specified minimum enrolment threshold by 30 September 2026.

Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of NEPS assessments available to each school in Dublin Mid-West; and the number of NEPS psychologists available to each school in Dublin Mid-West.
reply:
I would like to take this opportunity to outline the work of NEPS. All schools have access to:
• General support and advice from an educational psychologist in NEPS, either through the school’s assigned psychologist or through the NEPS Advisory Support Service.
• Support from an educational psychologist in NEPS in the event of a Critical Incident.
• National and Regional Support and Development service for school staff.
• Individual casework where a priority need is established to either an educational psychologist in NEPS or a private educational psychologist on the Scheme for Commissioning Psychological Assessments (SCPA) panel.
NEPS does not operate waiting lists. In common with other psychological services and best international practice, NEPS operates on a consultative model of service with assessments only one aspect of the NEPS service.
The focus of the NEPS Casework Service is to use a consultative, problem-solving approach to promote better understanding of the child or young person’s strengths and needs, to suggest interventions that may be helpful to include in the Student Support Plan, and to assist schools to implement, monitor and review those interventions. The Student Support Plan is developed collaboratively and may involve the child's teacher, parents or guardians, the child themselves, and other relevant professionals.
NEPS encourages schools to implement a Continuum of Support Framework with each school taking responsibility for providing universal and pre

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether additional capacity for NEPS assessments will be contracted in from outside the existing services to provide additional support to schools.
reply:
Each year, NEPS staffing levels are evaluated and capacity to serve schools is established. There is currently a nationwide shortage of educational psychologists which has resulted in vacancies in NEPS. Due to this shortage, it is not possible for all schools to have an assigned NEPS psychologist.
Where a school temporarily does not have an assigned psychologist due to a vacancy, it continues to have access to a range of NEPS services including:
• The NEPS Advisory Support Service.
Through this service schools have the opportunity to access responsive support and advice from a NEPS educational psychologist. Schools can contact the service as needed throughout the school year. The educational psychologist can provide advice and support and, where a priority need is established, can sanction an assessment through the Scheme for the Commissioning of Psychological Assessments (SCPA).
• The NEPS National and Regional Support and Development Service.
This service covers areas such as trauma informed practice, cluster group support for post-primary special education teachers and special class teachers and training for Student Support Teams.
Support from a NEPS psychologist in the event of a Critical Incident.
The Scheme for the Commissioning of Psychological Assessments (SCPA) may be of particular interest to the deputy as it represents an interim measure intended to supplement the NEPS service and meet current urgent needs for psychological assessment of children and young people.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which demand for Irish-medium primary and post-primary education in County Louth is assessed; the unmet demand that has been identified, by school planning area; and the measures that are planned to meet that demand.
reply:
New schools are established in areas of demographic growth, as the resources available for school infrastructure have to be prioritised to ensure that every child has a school place.
My department has a robust school planning process to ensure that sufficient school places are available to meet current and future demand. This process involves the preparation of detailed demographic profiles and school place demand projections using a range of data sources, including school enrolment trends, census data, child benefit records, geocoded pupil enrolment data, population estimates and projections, residential development activity, housing completion data, planning permissions, local authority development plans and information on planned housing delivery. These datasets enable the department to assess the current and projected population of school-age children and young people at both school planning area and settlement level and to identify where additional school capacity may be required.
Though there are no Irish medium or English medium schools planned currently (other than new special schools) this position is kept under constant review by my department. However, it is worth noting that Gaelcholáiste Dhún Dealgain satellite school is in operation and is accepting new enrolments. It currently offers a wide range of post-primary subjects through the medium of Irish.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Education and Youth for the SEC to provide clarity to a student (details supplied) regarding completing the 2027-28 junior certificate examinations cycle.
reply:
The Constitution acknowledges the family as the primary and natural educator of the child and sets out the rights and duties of the State in the matter of education. The Constitution makes explicit that the State does not oblige parents to send their children to any particular type of school. Parents are free to provide education in their homes, in private schools, or in schools recognised or established by the State.
Tusla’s Alternative Education Assessment and Registration Service (AEARS) is under the remit of my department. AEARS is responsible for the regulation of provision for education in places other than recognised schools, including children who are home schooled or who are enrolled in a non-recognised independent school.
Parents who wish to educate their child in a place other than a recognised school are required to make an application to AEARS to have their child included on the Section 14 Statutory Register. AEARS will then carry out an assessment of the educational provision to determine if the child is eligible to be placed on the register. Assessments are carried out by an authorised person in line with the ‘Guidelines on the Assessment of Education in Places Other Than Recognised Schools' (www.tusla.ie/uploads/content/Guidelines_on_Assessment_of_Education.pdf) issued by my department.

reply:
I wish to advise the Deputy that my department has no current record of receiving an application for funding to develop an outdoor sensory garden from the school in question.
Sensory gardens form part of the accommodation brief for Special Education Classroom accommodation for new school buildings and major extension projects (if there is not already one at the school). The overall accommodation suite for students with special education needs also generally includes ancillary accommodation such as a Central Activities Space, a Multi Activity Room and Quiet Spaces as well as an outdoor Secure Play Area.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Education and Youth the emergency capital funding options or discretionary grants available to small primary schools with limited financial reserves that face immediate health and safety infrastructure crises but cannot afford the upfront costs of hiring independent consultant engineers required in order to apply for the emergency works scheme.
reply:
As the Deputy maybe aware, the purpose of the Emergency Works Scheme (EWS) is to provide funding specifically for unforeseen emergencies, or to provide funding to facilitate inclusion and access for pupils with special needs. It does so by ensuring the availability of funding for urgent works to those schools that are in need of resources as a result of an emergency situation.
An emergency is deemed to be a situation which poses an immediate risk to health, life, property or the environment, which is sudden, unforeseen and requires immediate action, and in the case of a school, if not corrected would prevent the school or part thereof from opening.
The EWS operates on the basis of a minimal scope works to address the emergency situation. The EWS is intended to remedy an emergency situation and usually provides only an interim measure until a permanent solution can be delivered under the Summer Works Scheme (SWS) which deals with upgrade works to the school.
The EWS is open to primary and post primary schools with permanent recognition and in non-rented accommodation.
To make an application schools must complete the online Emergency Works Application Form available through the Esinet system. It should be noted that as per Circular Letter 0068/2020, the appointment of a consultant to complete the application form is a matter for the school authority and any fees arising must be borne by the school.

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Taoiseach if he will report on the work of the Climate Action Unit of his Department.
reply:
The Climate Action Unit in my Department supports the Government in responding to the climate crisis and advancing Ireland’s climate, energy and environmental objectives.
The Unit provides secretariat support to the Cabinet Committees on Climate Action, Environment and Energy, and on Water Quality, as well as associated Senior Officials Groups and the Offshore Wind Energy Clearing House.
The Unit monitors the implementation of Ireland’s national and international climate commitments and prepares progress reports on the delivery by Government Departments of actions under the Climate Action Plan.
The Unit engages with and supports Departments in the design, implementation and monitoring of climate, energy and environmental policy, providing analysis and advice on cross-cutting issues.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Education and Youth for an update on matters raised in correspondence (details supplied).
reply:
The key factor for determining the level of staffing resources provided at individual school level is the staffing schedule for the relevant school year and pupil enrolments on the previous 30 September. The staffing schedule operates in a clear and transparent manner and treats all similar types of schools equally.
The staffing arrangements include a staffing appeals process whereby schools may appeal their staffing allocation to an independent Appeals Board. The school referred to by the Deputy was successful in its appeal considered at the June meeting of the Primary Staffing Appeals Board and was allocated an appeal post, having advised of an expected enrolment of 642 pupils. The school was advised that to retain the post, the enrolment on 30 September must meet the retention figure of 639, set out in the staffing schedule. As the school's enrolment was 626 on 30 September, the post will not be retained for the remainder of the year. The school appealed again to the October meeting of the Primary Staffing Appeals Board. The appeal was unsuccessful. The Primary Staffing Appeals Board operates independently of the Department and its decision is final.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Education and Youth the projected demand for primary and post-primary school places in Kildare north over the next five years; and the measures being taken to ensure sufficient capacity is available.
reply:
My department’s demographic analysis indicates that school place demand across North Kildare will vary by school planning area over the coming years.
At primary level, the school-going population in the Newbridge, Kilcock, Celbridge, Prosperous-Clane and Maynooth school planning areas is projected to remain broadly stable to 2030, while growth is projected in the Naas and Leixlip school planning areas over the same period.
At post-primary level, the school-going population in the Newbridge, Celbridge and Prosperous-Clane school planning areas is projected to remain broadly stable, while demand is projected to increase in the Naas, Kilcock, Leixlip and Maynooth school planning areas to 2033.
My department is taking a range of measures to ensure that sufficient capacity is available to meet this demand. These measures include the delivery of new school buildings, extensions to existing schools, the provision of additional accommodation where required and, where demographic growth warrants it, the establishment of new schools. In line with the objectives of Project Ireland 2040, My department seeks, where possible, to meet emerging demand through the expansion of existing schools, thereby maximising available capacity within the existing school estate.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her Department will urgently review the case of a school (details supplied) in County Monaghan, where the deteriorating condition of the student facilities poses an immediate health and safety concern; and if an inspector from her Department can be deployed to assess the site to bypass the costly consultant report requirement.
reply:
As the Deputy may be aware, the purpose of the Emergency Works Scheme (EWS) is to provide funding specifically for unforeseen emergencies, or to provide funding to facilitate inclusion and access for pupils with special needs. It does so by ensuring the availability of funding for urgent works to those schools that are in need of resources as a result of an emergency situation.
An emergency is deemed to be a situation which poses an immediate risk to health, life, property or the environment, which is sudden, unforeseen and requires immediate action, and in the case of a school, if not corrected would prevent the school or part thereof from opening.
The EWS operates on the basis of a minimal scope works to address the emergency situation. The EWS is intended to remedy an emergency situation and usually provides only an interim measure until a permanent solution can be delivered under the Summer Works Scheme (SWS) which deals with upgrade works to the school.
The EWS is open to primary and post primary schools with permanent recognition and in non-rented accommodation.
The school in question has yet to make an application for emergency works funding. To make an application schools must complete the online Emergency Works Application Form available through the Esinet system. question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which reforms will support community organisations providing a range of youth and family services; the way in which universal youth work will be supported alongside targeted services.
reply:
The department provides funding to thirty-five national youth organisations under the Youth Services Grant Scheme (YSGS). Just over €16.7m has been allocated under the YSGS in 2026, including funding for National Youth Council of Ireland programmes which support the overall youth sector (for example, NYCI's child protection and youth health programmes).
The Youth Services Grant Scheme has been in existence for four decades and its reform is a commitment under Opportunities for Youth, the national strategy for youth work and related services.
Opportunities for Youth commits the department to delivering a reformed YSGS that is more responsive to the current needs of young people, facilitates youth organisations to more effectively deliver services to young people, and enhances the governance and oversight structures for the scheme.
As part of this process of reform the scheme was opened to applications from new youth organisations in 2024. Five new organisations were successful in their application to the scheme under that pilot process.
Given the considerable variety in scale and activities among the national youth organisations currently funded under the YSGS, the factors to be considered in reforming the scheme are very complex. While the process of reform is ongoing, national youth organisations continue to receive funding under the existing scheme.
National youth organisations funded under the YSGS play a crucial role in supporting universal, primarily volunteer-led youth

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether youth service funding will take greater account of population growth and increasing demand in counties such as Louth.
reply:
The department is dedicated to enhancing the delivery and development of youth work services and opportunities for young people across the country.
Funding for the provision of targeted youth services is administered on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth by ETBs, which allocate funding via applications to the UBU Your Place Your Space (UBU) scheme. This scheme is aimed at young people between the ages of 10 and 24 who are, or are at risk, of becoming disadvantaged, marginalised or vulnerable.
Over €54 million has been allocated to UBU in 2026. The scheme provides funding to 258 targeted youth services across the 16 ETBs which coordinate delivery of funding to the services in their areas.
Key to achieving the aims of the scheme is the development of the Area Profile and Needs Assessment Tool. The purpose of this tool is to allow each ETB to avail of quantitative and qualitative information to objectively identify the needs of young people within their functional area. This analysis leads to the development of a Service Requirement which is then used as the basis for discussion between ETBs and service providers in terms of service delivery to meet the needs of young people in the area. The approach ensures that the department can target funding and supports to the young people most in need of intervention and that funding is allocated based on evidence-informed need. ETBs have recently updated their Area Profiles and Service Requirements as preparation for Cycle 3

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the practical supports that will be provided to help youth organisations recruit and retain staff and meet their governance and compliance requirements.
reply:
I wish to acknowledge the outstanding work carried out by the approximately 2,000 youth workers and 40,000 volunteers who support young people in communities across the country. Their dedication is central to the delivery of high-quality youth work services and to the positive outcomes achieved for young people every day.
In 2026, current funding of over €90 million supports existing youth services. Building on this, Budget 2027 increases current funding for youth work services by €7 million, bringing total current funding to over €97 million. This represents an increase of almost 8% on 2026 levels. More broadly, funding for youth services has increased by over €34 million since 2020.
This additional investment will help strengthen the capacity and sustainability of youth services, supporting organisations in meeting growing demand, maintaining service provision and continuing to recruit, retain and support the staff and volunteers who deliver services to young people.
It is important to note that the department does not employ or fund posts directly. Rather, the department provides funding to youth services and youth organisations to deliver youth work services. These organisations are responsible for determining their staffing requirements and deploying resources in a manner that best meets the needs of the young people who use their services.
Support for youth workers emerged as a strong theme in the consultation with the youth work sector as part of the development for Op

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which local youth organisations, youth workers and young people will be involved in shaping reforms and the review of the Youth Work Act 2001.
reply:
Opportunities for Youth: National Strategy for Youth Work and Related Services is the strategic framework for the youth work sector, published in September 2024. The strategy aims to build awareness of and strengthen youth services and ensure that youth services remain accessible and of value to young people across Ireland.
It is intended that, informed by progress to date, further actions for delivery in 2027 and 2028 will be identified after the first phase of delivery. It is anticipated that actions during the second phase will include a review of the Youth Work Act, 2001. The implementation of Opportunities for Youth, including any legislative reviews, will be supported through a new National Youth Sector Reference Group (NYSRG), as well as a group comprising representatives from departments and agencies that provide funding to or interact with the youth sector.
The establishment of the NYSRG will include representatives from across the youth sector, including youth workers, academics and young people. This will support a balanced and transparent input from across the wider youth sector into national decision-making. A key pillar of this will be the representation of the views of young people, including young people of diverse backgrounds, so that they can influence decision-making in respect of youth work services. The department is working in partnership with the National Youth Council of Ireland (NYCI) on the membership and establishment of this group.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Education and Youth when the UBU review will be completed; the changes that are planned to reduce paperwork and duplicated reporting for youth organisations.
reply:
The department is dedicated to enhancing the delivery and development of youth work services and opportunities for young people across the country.
The UBU scheme is a youth funding scheme that targets young people aged between 10 to 24 who are identified as marginalised, vulnerable and at risk of not flourishing. The UBU scheme now provides funding to 258 targeted youth services across the 16 education and training boards (ETBs) that coordinate delivery of funding to the services in their local ETB areas.
There is a commitment to review the UBU Your Place Your Space (UBU) scheme under Action 8 of the national strategy for youth work and related services, Opportunities for Youth (OfY), which was published in September 2024.
The purpose of the review is to assess the extent to which the UBU scheme is achieving its policy objectives and to determine whether changes to its operational arrangements are required to ensure that it continues to meet the needs of its target groups.
During the consultation phase of OfY and in feedback received by the Department, the cumbersome nature of the processes involved in UBU administration was a strong theme from stakeholders. Accordingly, an initial exercise is focussing on procedure.
The department's Youth Affairs Unit has been working closely with the Business Process Improvement (BPI) Unit to undertake a comprehensive scoping exercise of the scheme’s operating processes.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether youth service funding will cover the full costs of staffing, premises and activities; whether multiannual funding will be introduced to reduce reliance on fundraising.
reply:
In 2026, current funding of over €90 million supports existing youth services. Building on the progress achieved in 2026, Budget 2027 increases current funding for youth work services by a further €7million, bringing total current funding to over €97 million. This represents an increase of almost 8% on 2026 levels and brings the overall increase in youth funding since 2020 to more than €34million.
Further, youth capital funding of €4.0 million will be available annually to support the youth sector from 2026 to 2030.
The allocation of this additional funding across the range of youth funding schemes and programmes administered by the department is currently under consideration. As these decisions have not yet been finalised, it is not currently possible to provide a detailed breakdown of how the additional funding will be distributed.
However, I can assure the Deputy that the funding will be targeted towards strengthening youth work provision and supporting increased participation opportunities for young people across the country. This additional investment will support the sustainability of youth services, enhance capacity across the sector, and help ensure that young people continue to have access to high-quality youth work opportunities in their communities.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth the measures she is taking to encourage schools to allow their playing pitches and sports facilities to be used 'out-of-hours' by local sports groups; if she has analysed barriers to same; and if she has plans to address these barriers.
reply:
The Programme for Government commits to expand the provision of after-school, childcare and sports use in school buildings and campuses, in tandem with the school building programme, to provide better access for parents and communities.
While the primary role of my department is the provision of primary and post primary school education, my department encourages the use of school facilities for a wider community use, where appropriate.
In June 2024 my department published revised “Procedures on the use of School Buildings and School Sports Facilities outside of School Hours” which cater for a wide range of local level arrangements, including early learning and childcare, use by sports club, recreational use, community use and other services on school property where circumstances permit.
In general, my department recognises that the use of school premises for community or after-school purposes is managed at local level and school authorities have a considerable degree of autonomy in relation to how their respective premises are managed and utilised. A school must obtain the permission of their patron and the property owner before permitting the use of the school premises for after school activities.

question: Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her Department is developing proposals to establish centralised or regional panels for the allocation of special class places for the 2027/28 school year; whether these proposals would alter the statutory admissions responsibilities of boards of management; and if she will publish the proposals in full.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 795 and 796 together.
At the outset, my priority, and that of my department, is to ensure that children and young people can access the educational provision and supports they need in an equitable, timely and appropriate manner. Together with Minister Naughton, I have secured a record budget of €3.8 billion for special education in 2027, enabling us to build on the significant progress already made across the system. I regularly hear from families, parents and schools about the importance of ensuring that supports are available when they are needed, and I am committed to addressing barriers that may delay or impede access to appropriate educational provision.
In considering future improvements, the department is building on a series of significant reforms that have already moved the system towards a needs-based approach. These include the introduction in 2017 of a needs-based model for the allocation of special education teaching supports in mainstream schools, as well as subsequent reforms to arrangements for Special Needs Assistant supports and summer programmes.
These changes have strengthened access to support for many children and young people. At the same time, I recognise that a diagnosis continues to play an important role for many children, young people and their families, including in accessing services and understanding individual needs.
I want to be clear that no decisions have been made regarding any future changes to eligibility

reply:

Practically all schools have outdoor play areas and many schools use adjacent local facilities, including community halls, public parks, playing fields and swimming pools. The provision of outdoor play areas form part of the accommodation brief for all new school buildings or where a major building or refurbishment project is being delivered for an existing school. question: Deputy Niall Collins asked the Minister for Education and Youth If an additional school bus will be supplied to accommodate 28 school children that have been left with no school transport in 2026 (details supplied).
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
The purpose of my Department's School Transport Scheme is, having regard to available resources, to support the transport to and from school of children who reside remote from their nearest school.
Children are eligible for school transport at primary level where they reside not less than 3.2 kilometres from and are attending their nearest national school, and at post primary level where they reside not less than 4.8 kilometres from and are attending their nearest post primary school/education centre, as determined by the department/Bus Éireann, having regard to ethos and language.
Where a child is not attending their closest school or resides under the distance criteria, they are considered to be ineligible for school transport under the terms of the Scheme.
A minimum number of 10 eligible children living in a distinct locality, as determined by Bus Éireann, is required before consideration may be given to the establishment or retention of school transport services, provided this can be done within reasonable cost limits.
All eligible children who complete the application process and pay or enter their medical card details on time are prioritised for a seat/ticket, if a service is available.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Education and Youth the reason qualified teaching experience gained in overseas post-primary schools may be excluded from incremental credit while certain forms of relevant non-teaching professional experience may qualify for such credit.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 776, 777 and 787 together.
The criteria for the award of incremental credit are set out in the Department of Education’s Circular 10/2001 for Primary teachers, and Circulars 29/2007 and 29/2010 for post-primary teachers. These circulars provide for the award of incremental credit in respect of prior teaching service, including overseas teaching service, both within and outside the EU and/or relevant non-teaching service.
Teaching service given outside the Republic of Ireland as per paragraph 6 a) of circular 29/2007 for post-primary teachers and paragraph 4 of circular 10/2001 for primary teachers, which is equivalent to a primary or post primary school in the Republic of Ireland, may qualify for the award of incremental credit.
Where the service/school satisfies the criteria set out in the circulars to have service at that school recognised for incremental credit, an award of incremental credit can be made.
Common reasons for why applications for incremental credit for teaching service outside of the EU can be refused are that:
• the school is not in receipt of any state funding,
• the school does not offer the range of studies which incorporates all of the courses prescribed on the national curriculum of the State in which the school is located,
• the length of time the school has been in existence,
• the service at the school has not been deemed to be satisfactory,
• the applicant was not a qualified teacher at the time the service was prov

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether purchase orders issued by her Department under procurement contracts can be linked to the corresponding contracts held in its internal contract register; whether a contract reference or other unique identifier is maintained to enable this linkage; and if not, the way her Department monitors cumulative expenditure against the approved value of each contract.

reply:

reply:

question: Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Education and Youth the reason a school (details supplied) does not have access to a NEPS psychologist; the measures which are in place to ensure families with children in the school can access NEPS referrals; and if this school will be provided with access to a NEPS psychologist.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 778, 779 and 782 together.
Each year, NEPS staffing levels are evaluated and capacity to serve schools is established. There is currently a nationwide shortage of educational psychologists which has resulted in vacancies in NEPS. Due to this shortage, it is not possible for all schools to have an assigned NEPS psychologist.
Where a school temporarily does not have an assigned psychologist due to a vacancy, it continues to have access to a range of NEPS services including:
• The NEPS Advisory Support Service.
• Through this service schools have the opportunity to access responsive support and advice from a NEPS educational psychologist. Schools can contact the service as needed throughout the school year. The educational psychologist can provide advice and support and, where a priority need is established, can sanction an assessment through the Scheme for the Commissioning of Psychological Assessments (SCPA).
• The NEPS National and Regional Support and Development Service.
• This service covers areas such as trauma informed practice, cluster group support for post-primary special education teachers and special class teachers, training for Student Support Teams and supporting reluctant school attendance/school avoidance behaviour.
• Support from a NEPS psychologist in the event of a Critical Incident.
NEPS encourages schools to support children and young people using the Continuum of Support, whereby school staff use a problem-solving approach,

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she is aware that a new school building (details supplied), will be too small based on recent and projected local demand; if there are plans to extend the school to accommodate this demand; and if she will provide the timeline for same.
reply:
The major building project for the school referred to by the Deputy is part of my Departments' Employer Led Design construction programme and will be delivered as part of a campus project with Coláiste Rioga.
The campus project will provide a new 8 classroom primary school and accommodation including 2 classrooms for children with special educational needs and a new 1,000 pupil post-primary school and accommodation including 6 classrooms, for children with special educational needs.
In order to plan for school provision and analyse the relevant demographic data, my Department divides the country into 314 school planning areas and uses a Geographical Information System, using data from a range of sources, including CSO Census data, Child Benefit and school enrolment data, to identify where the pressure for school places across the country will arise and where additional school accommodation is needed at primary and post-primary level.
