question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to Parliamentary Question No. 75111/26, to clarify whether a person (details supplied) remains enrolled at a school; and if not, when and the basis on which has this enrolment ended; and the reason her Department was advised that the individual was no longer seeking transport, despite the NCSE’s written confirmation on the 7 October, 2026 that it was seeking the Department’s position on reinstating transport.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
The National Council for Special Education acts in an advisory role to the Department of Education and Youth on the suitability of placements for children with special educational needs.
Under the terms of the School Transport Scheme for Children with Special Educational Needs, the Department will consider the report of the Special Education Needs Organiser (SENO). School transport is provided to children with special educational needs who are attending the nearest school to their place of residence that is or can be resourced to meet their educational needs, as identified by the SENO.

The NCSE has advised that the pupil is currently without a school placement and they are currently working with the parent regarding seeking an alternative school placement for this pupil.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Education and Youth the reason teaching service in private international schools outside the European Union may be recognised for incremental credit purposes for primary teachers but not for post-primary teachers; and if she will outline the policy rationale underpinning this distinction.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 776, 777 and 787 together.
The criteria for the award of incremental credit are set out in the Department of Education’s Circular 10/2001 for Primary teachers, and Circulars 29/2007 and 29/2010 for post-primary teachers. These circulars provide for the award of incremental credit in respect of prior teaching service, including overseas teaching service, both within and outside the EU and/or relevant non-teaching service.
Teaching service given outside the Republic of Ireland as per paragraph 6 a) of circular 29/2007 for post-primary teachers and paragraph 4 of circular 10/2001 for primary teachers, which is equivalent to a primary or post primary school in the Republic of Ireland, may qualify for the award of incremental credit.
Where the service/school satisfies the criteria set out in the circulars to have service at that school recognised for incremental credit, an award of incremental credit can be made.
Common reasons for why applications for incremental credit for teaching service outside of the EU can be refused are that:
• the school is not in receipt of any state funding,
• the school does not offer the range of studies which incorporates all of the courses prescribed on the national curriculum of the State in which the school is located,
• the length of time the school has been in existence,
• the service at the school has not been deemed to be satisfactory,
• the applicant was not a qualified teacher at the time the service was prov

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether her Department is working to provide greater transparency on the number of qualified teachers on supplementary panels; the waiting times of teachers on these panels; and the statistics on the appointment outcomes for teachers on these panels.
reply:
The core purpose of the redeployment arrangements is to facilitate the redeployment of surplus permanent and CID-holding teachers to schools with approved teaching vacancies.
At primary level, schools are required, under the panel arrangements, to fill permanent teaching vacancies from the Main Redeployment Panel. Once all teachers on the Main Panel have been redeployed, any remaining permanent vacancies are made available to teachers on the Supplementary Redeployment Panel, which is comprised of eligible fixed-term (temporary/substitute) and part-time teachers.
The current eligibility criteria for the Supplementary Panel, as agreed with the education partners, are set out in Circular 74/2025. To gain access to the Supplementary Panel, teachers must hold the appropriate Teaching Council registration, have reached the required point on the salary scale and satisfy the relevant earnings threshold. These arrangements are reviewed annually in consultation with the education stakeholders, including the teacher unions.
My Department publishes the number of teachers admitted to Supplementary Panels each year on its website.
Teachers may remove themselves from the Supplementary Panel at any stage for a variety of reasons, including accepting a teaching position, taking a career break or travelling abroad. Withdrawal from the Supplementary Panel in any given year does not affect a teacher's eligibility to apply again in subsequent years.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether substitute-teaching arrangements, including sub seeker, can better support teachers seeking sustained and predictable employment.
reply:
This Government is committed to ensuring that every child has a positive school experience, with access to qualified and engaged teachers who are dedicated to supporting their learning.
The recruitment and appointment of?teachers to fill teaching posts is a matter for individual school authorities, subject to procedures agreed under Section 24 of the Education Act 1998 (as amended by the Education (Amendment) Act 2012). In that regard, there are more than 3,700 individual employers (boards of management of primary schools and post-primary schools, as well as ETBs).
As school authorities are the employer of teachers, a central facility for teacher recruitment has not been provided. However, following on from the Department’s Action Plan on Teacher Supply, the Irish Primary Principals’ Network (IPPN) operates an online portal for the recruitment of teachers to long-term teaching positions. The portal was developed in conjunction with the National Association of Principal and Deputy Principals (NAPD). The portal facilitates the matching of demand and supply and provides an efficient and user-friendly recruitment process for both schools and teachers, including teachers working abroad who wish to apply for posts here.
SubSeeker is a service that operates within the IPPN portal to facilitate the short-term recruitment of Teaching Council-registered teachers in both primary and post primary schools.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her Department is working on providing clearer requirements on schools to provide recruitment feedback, access to individual interview scores and explanations of appointment outcomes to candidates who applied for a teaching position.
reply:
The recruitment and appointment of teachers to fill teaching posts is a matter for the individual school authority, subject to procedures agreed under Section 24 of the Education Act 1998 (as amended by the Education (Amendment) Act 2012). In that regard, there are more than 3,700 individual employers (boards of management of primary schools and post-primary schools, as well as Education and Training Boards).
Chapter 2 of Circular 0044/2019 outlines the recruitment and appointment procedures for teachers. 13.10 of chapter 2 advises that an applicant’s own marking sheets should be made available on request after the recruitment process is complete.
The circular does not provide for schools to provide any further feedback to an applicant. Therefore, this would be a matter for the individual school authority.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether her Department will review the way in which accumulated teaching service and experience are recognised in recruitment processes for teaching positions.
reply:
The recruitment and appointment of teachers to fill teaching posts is a matter for the individual school authority, subject to procedures agreed under Section 24(3) of the Education Act 1998 (as amended by the Education (Amendment) Act 2012).
In accordance with Department Circular 44/2019 and Circular 31/2011, which are available on the Department’s website under gov.ie - Department of Education (www.gov.ie), schools are required to employ appropriately qualified and registered teachers and ensure that unemployed teachers are offered employment in preference to those who have retired. These measures were taken in an effort to increase employment opportunities for unemployed teachers.
In particular, Circular 44/2019 requires that teaching experience and other relevant experience be taken into account in establishing the criteria for the assessment of applicantions.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which her Department is aware that current CID requirements are achieving the objective of providing employment stability given it is not collecting the information necessary to measure the outcomes for teachers who remain outside the CID permanent system.
reply:
Department Circulars 20/2026 and 21/2026 sets out the revised criteria for the award of a CID in Primary Schools and in Post Primary Schools. The revised circulars reduced the period of service for the award of a CID from a period of 2 years continuous service to a period of 1 year of continuous service. The amended period of service applies to all teachers who satisfy the criteria set out in the circulars. The criteria include that the school has a viable post available and that the post does not solely relate to temporary cover.
Where a teacher is not awarded a CID and they believe that they were entitled to a CID, the circular provide that a teacher may submit an appeal in relation to the decision of the school not to award a CID to the teacher.
It is the responsibility of each school/ETB to ensure that they comply with all relevant employment legislation and to ensure that they comply with the provisions of all relevant recruitment and appointment circulars issued by the Department of Education and Youth.
Teachers are free to pursue statutory relief where they believe that their employer has not complied with their obligations.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide an update on the ongoing review of the Education for Persons with Special Educational Needs (EPSEN) Act 2004, targeting the way in which the State plans to eliminate the financial barriers to literacy support.
reply:
I wish to thank the Deputy for their question.
My department undertook a comprehensive review of the Education for Persons with Special Educational Needs (EPSEN) Act 2004 to ensure that the legislation reflects current policy, practice and the experiences of children, families and education stakeholders. The final review report, containing 51 recommendations across 16 themes, was published in June 2025, followed by the publication of an implementation plan in July 2026.
Work is now underway on 149 actions arising from the review, including policy and legislative changes to strengthen inclusive education and support students with special educational needs. The implementation plan provides the framework for delivering these reforms on a phased basis with ongoing oversight, stakeholder engagement and progress reporting. Implementation of the review recommendations is scheduled to continue through to the end of 2029.
The review was informed by an extensive consultation process, including over 28,000 survey responses, focus groups and direct engagement with children and young people.
A number of actions are relevant to literacy provision and access to supports. question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Education and Youth if arrangements will be put in place whereby parents can pay for school transport on an instalment basis for their children (details supplied).
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
Families are required to register their details on the Bus Éireann Family Portal to have their eligibility for transport assessed and to make applications under the scheme: https://buseireann.ie/schooltransport/.
Once the Bus Éireann Family Portal opens for applications and payments each year, families have the ability to pay into this family portal in instalments, allowing them to spread the total cost of a school bus ticket over a number of months. Provided a full payment is made by the closing date, families will be deemed to have paid on time, and their application will be assessed.
It is important to note that eligible children holding valid medical cards and eligible children with special educational needs are exempt from paying the annual charge.

question: Deputy Denise Mitchell asked the Minister for Education and Youth the provision being put in place to ensure that young people currently receiving support from a school (details supplied) and the CAMHS Day Hospital are supported to return to or re-engage with education and to manage their mental health positively when the adolescent school closes in November 2026.
reply:
Enabling students with special educational needs to receive an education that meets their needs is a priority for this Government.?It is also a key priority for me, my department and for the National Council for Special Education (NCSE).
My department’s focus in recent years has been on expanding special school provision for the growing numbers of children and young people with additional needs. Closing any special school is not a position my department normally finds itself in. However, given the decision of the HSE to restructure its CAMHs services it means that there are no longer inpatients and ultimately students on the St Vincents Hospital / St Josephs Adolescent School site. The timeline relating to the HSE decision has provided very limited time to consider the future education provision previously provided by staff at St Josephs at a second outreach site to day patients.
My department reiterates its commitment to finding a solution to allow education provision to continue at that second outreach site as long as health services for young adults continue to be provided there.
My department is actively working with stakeholders on this matter.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Education and Youth to confirm if her Department is contacting patrons of schools to change the way children access a special class or a special school (details supplied).
reply:
At the outset, my priority, and that of my department, is to ensure that children and young people can access the educational provision and supports they need in an equitable, timely and appropriate manner. Together with Minister Naughton, I have secured a record budget of €3.8 billion for special education in 2027, enabling us to build on the significant progress already made across the system. I regularly hear from families, parents and schools about the importance of ensuring that supports are available when they are needed, and I am committed to addressing barriers that may delay or impede access to appropriate educational provision.
In considering future improvements, the department is building on a series of significant reforms that have already moved the system towards a needs-based approach. These include the introduction in 2017 of a needs-based model for the allocation of special education teaching supports in mainstream schools, as well as subsequent reforms to arrangements for Special Needs Assistant supports and summer programmes.
These changes have strengthened access to support for many children and young people. At the same time, I recognise that a diagnosis continues to play an important role for many children, young people and their families, including in accessing services and understanding individual needs.

reply:

• High-quality Irish-medium education will be available to all, in inclusive and multicultural educational settings
• A particular affinity with and love for the Irish language and culture will be fostered in children and young people so that they will continue to use the language competently and with pride throughout their lives

Foraois provides access to a wide range of clubs and programmes that foster the use of Irish as a social language.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth the total cost to her Department of conducting, commissioning or administering the recent survey of primary schools, including the costs of external consultants, survey providers, administration and analysis, where applicable.
reply:
The development and operation of the Primary School Survey was funded within my department's existing resources. The survey instrument was developed in-house and is based on the Geographical Information System (GIS) which my department uses as part of its forward planning function. As my department was already using GIS, no additional cost arose from running the survey on this system.
Any external costs were to support the communications strategy and were also managed within existing resources. My department's communications strategy was aimed at increasing awareness of the survey to ensure as high a response rate as possible.
The survey was delivered at a very low cost, representing excellent value for money for a national, school-specific survey.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Education and Youth to confirm the steps being taken by her Department to resolve an issue regarding school transport for a student (details supplied).
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
Bus Éireann manages the procurement tender process and contract management arrangements to include services provided by private contractors. They are required to tender services in line with procurement guidelines and are responsible for the allocating and vetting of contractors and this process can sometimes take several weeks. They have advised that the start date for this pupil's service is 02 November 2026.
Both the Department and Bus Éireann are very conscious of the challenges faced by parents awaiting transport for children with special educational needs. Families of children who are eligible for these services may therefore receive an interim Special Transport Grant (STG). This is a once off payment, paid retrospectively to families once the School Transport service is in place and is intended to assist with the cost of private transport arrangements the family had put in place until the service starts or recommences. If the family wishes to claim the grant they should contact CorkSchoolTransport@education.gov.ie and officials in my Department will be happy to assist.

It is important that schools are given the time and space to reflect carefully on their results and to engage fully with parents and their wider school communities.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide a breakdown of the total revenue collected by the State Examinations Commission from Junior Cycle, Leaving Certificate and Leaving Certificate Applied examination entry fees in each of the years 2022 to 2025; the number of candidates who paid fees in each year; the number of candidates who received exemptions on the basis of a full medical card.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 758, 759, 760 and 761 together.
Examination entry fees were not charged in the years 2022-2025. Entry fees were applied for the 2026 State exams at the rate of €116 for Leaving Certificate candidates and €109 for Junior Cycle candidates, for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic. These rates are unchanged since 2012. Protections are in place so that any student with a full medical card, or covered under a parent or guardian’s card, continues to be fully exempt. This approach strikes a fair balance, maintaining support for those who need it most while restoring a long-standing contribution towards the cost of running the examinations system, the majority of which is funded by the State.
The Department of Health has advised that the Medical Card provision is primarily based on financial assessment. In accordance with the Health Act 1970 (as amended), eligibility for a medical card is determined by the HSE, which assesses each application on a qualifying financial threshold.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she can provide a breakdown of the additional €7 million in current funding for youth services in Budget 2027; and the way in which the funding will be broken into existing services and programmes, and new measures.
reply:
In 2026, current funding of over €90 million supports existing youth services. Building on the progress achieved in 2026, Budget 2027 increases current funding for youth work services by a further €7million, bringing total current funding to over €97 million. This represents an increase of almost 8% on 2026 levels and brings the overall increase in youth funding since 2020 to more than €34million.

Furthermore, youth capital funding of €4.0 million will be available annually to support the youth sector from 2026 to 2030.

The allocation of this additional funding across the range of youth funding schemes and programmes administered by the department is currently under consideration. As these decisions have not yet been finalised, it is not currently possible to provide a detailed breakdown of how the additional funding will be distributed.

However, I can assure the Deputy that the funding will be targeted towards strengthening youth work provision and supporting increased participation opportunities for young people across the country. This additional investment will support the sustainability of youth services, enhance capacity across the sector, and help ensure that young people continue to have access to high-quality youth work opportunities in their communities.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth given the Budget 2027 announcement by the Department of Social Protection to make the pilot Holiday Hunger Programme permanent, if she intends to do the same with the scheme for youth services.
reply:
The Holiday Meals Pilot Programme was developed as part of the Government's wider commitment to addressing child poverty and wellbeing. In the youth sector, the programme is delivered through UBU Your Place Your Space (UBU) youth services and targets young people aged 10 to 18 who may be at risk of not having access to a hot or substantial meal during school holiday periods.

The pilot was launched in June 2025, with 41 UBU youth services across the 16 ETBs participating. An initial budget of €500,000 was allocated to the programme. Following the success of the pilot, the department provided funding of €600,000 to support the delivery of a further Summer Holiday Meals Pilot Programme in 2026.

An end-to-end evaluation of the 2025 pilot programme was undertaken by an external evaluator procured by ETBI. The evaluation found that over 5,000 young people benefited from the programme and identified a high and widespread level of need for holiday food provision. The findings highlighted positive impacts on nutrition, wellbeing, youth engagement and family support. The evaluation also recommended that consideration be given to moving from a pilot initiative to a permanent programme.

The findings of the evaluation, along with feedback on the 2026 pilot, will inform future decisions regarding the development of the programme. While I note the recent decision by the Department of Social Protection to place its Holiday Hunger Programme on a permanent footing, no decision has been made

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth the funding that has been made available as part of the DEIS plus scheme to expand UBU provision near DEIS Plus schools; and the number of additional UBU schemes that are likely to be provided.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 750, 751 and 752 together.
The Department of Education and Youth is committed to enhancing the delivery and development of youth work services and opportunities for young people across the country.

UBU Your Place Your Space (UBU) is the Department's largest youth services scheme and supports young people aged 10 to 24 who are identified as marginalised, vulnerable and at risk of not flourishing. In 2026, over €54 million has been allocated to the scheme, supporting 258 targeted youth services across the 16 Education and Training Board (ETB) areas.

As part of the DEIS Plus plan, funding will be provided to expand UBU provision near DEIS Plus schools. Work is ongoing to develop a scheme for distribution to ETBs with DEIS Plus schools. This work will take into account school enrolment, proximity and size of nearby UBUs and other factors. Earlier this year the department asked ETBs to provide details on waiting lists for UBU projects in their functional areas as part of this work.

Final decisions regarding the allocation of funding and the number of additional services to be supported have not yet been made. However, the information gathered for this exercise, which will be completed this year, will help to inform this targeted expansion of youth services in communities where demand is greatest and where additional supports can contribute to improved outcomes for disadvantaged young people, focusing on youth services in areas with post-primary

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Taoiseach for a report on the work of the Child Poverty and Well-Being Programme Office in his Department.
Deputy Johnny Guirke asked the Minister for Education and Youth the DEIS schools in Meath that have an application in but were refused or are awaiting approval.
reply:
Addressing educational disadvantage in all schools is a key priority for me as Minister for Education and Youth.

The DEIS programme is targeted at schools with the highest levels of concentrated disadvantage. Schools that were included in the most recent expansion of the programme in 2022 were those with the highest levels of concentrated disadvantage as identified through the refined DEIS identification model. Schools were not required to apply for inclusion in the DEIS programme, and the model was applied fairly and equally to all schools. A detailed paper on the refined DEIS identification model is available on gov.ie.

The DEIS Strategy to 2035 sets out a long-term plan to address educational disadvantage in all schools and work to ensure that any child or young person experiencing educational disadvantage is supported through their education journey.

The DEIS Strategy implementation plan 2026-2028, under the strategic objective 2.2, sets out to develop an agile resource allocation model to support children and young people at risk of educational disadvantage in all primary and post-primary schools.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Education and Youth her Department's plans to provide additional post-primary school places in the Rathdown area, given population growth and the consequent recurrence of oversubscribed schools within the constituency.
reply:
I can assure the Deputy that the provision of sufficient school places to meet the needs of children and young people remains a priority for my department.

While my department is aware of demand pressures and oversubscription in some individual schools within the Rathdown constituency area, current demographic analysis does not indicate a requirement for additional post-primary capacity beyond that already planned.

Analysis undertaken by my department indicates that the underlying demographic profile of the Rathdown area points to a gradual decline in the population of school-going children. There are approximately 11% fewer children in fifth and sixth class than in first to third year at post-primary level, while the number of children in junior and senior infants is approximately 8% lower than the fifth and sixth class cohort. In turn, the pre-school population is approximately 8% lower than the junior and senior infant cohort. These trends indicate a declining underlying demographic profile, although future internal migration arising from new housing developments may alter this picture.

My department’s analysis also indicates that there are currently more pupils enrolled in the 33 primary schools serving the area than there are primary school-aged children residing within the area. question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide a statement on discrimination against students that do not come from preferred feeder primary schools when applying to a school that is oversubscribed (details supplied).
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 745, 746 and 747 together.
The overall objective of the Education (Admission to schools) Act 2018 is to provide a framework for school enrolment that is designed to ensure that every child is treated fairly and that the way in which schools decide on applications for admission is structured fair and transparent. The Act creates confidence for parents that the admission criteria laid down by schools and the procedures used by them are visible, legitimate, reasonable, and fair. The legislation is part of a suite of measures taken to take greater account of the needs of parents and students in the school system.

Parents have the right to choose which school to apply to and where the school has places available for the relevant year, the student should be admitted. However, in schools where there are more applicants than places available, a selection process will be necessary. question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Education and Youth who will be invited to the National Forum on Inclusive Education for Students with Special Educational Needs.
reply:
This government is fully committed to supporting students with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this objective.

On the 8 July 2026, it was announced that Minister Naughton and I had secured Government approval to establish a new Forum on Inclusive Education for Students with Special Educational Needs. The Forum will bring together key stakeholders to develop a shared national vision for inclusive education and identify practical actions to support children and young people with special educational needs across the education system.

Professor Noel Purdy, Director of Research and Scholarship at Stranmillis University College, was announced as chair for the Forum.

Membership will include representatives from disabled persons’ organisations, advocacy groups, education stakeholders, senior officials from relevant Government departments and external experts.

My department and the NCSE are committed to delivering an education system that is of the highest quality and where every child and young person feels valued and is actively supported and nurtured to achieve their full potential.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of children currently in receipt of the home tuition grant at primary and post-primary, broken down by country, in tabular form.
reply:

The Home Tuition Grant Scheme (Special Education Component) provides support for:
(a) pre-school children with autism who meet the scheme's eligibility criteria;
(b) children seeking a Special School or Special Class placement;
(c) students enrolled in schools who have a significant medical condition which has caused, and is likely to continue to cause, major disruption to their attendance at school; and

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Education and Youth the reason cycle to work scheme applications are closed until 2027; and if there any way people can avail of the cycle to work scheme this year.
reply:
As per the Cycle to Work scheme Circular Letter 0056/2020:” The total cost of the bicycle and/or bicycle safety equipment as stated on the invoice from the supplier will be deducted from salary and the employee will not pay income tax, PRSI, or Universal Social Charge on the remuneration sacrificed.”
Input of a salary deduction concerning the Cycle to Work scheme, on the payroll system; results in the application of tax relief referenced above as per the Cycle to Work scheme circular.
The salary deduction option selected on the Application Form, and number of pay dates remaining to avail of the Cycle to Work scheme in the current year; determines the salary deduction amount per pay date.
The Cycle to Work Applications timeframe was chosen as it is operable from a resources point of view and with consideration to the financial year end. Circular Letter 0056/2020 stipulates “All salary deductions must be completed by the last payroll in October of the calendar year in which they commence.”
It would not be administratively possible for the department to provide the Cycle to Work application window all year round.
The department appreciates that this can be inconvenient for some applicants, however the window provided for is a significant portion of a given year. The approach chosen enables the payroll to function efficiently, ensuring that the needs of schools and teachers are met in a structured, consistent manner throughout the full academic year.

The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
Bus Éireann manages the procurement tender process and contract management arrangements to include services provided by private contractors. They are required to tender services in line with procurement guidelines and are responsible for the allocating and vetting of contractors and this process can sometimes take several weeks. They have advised that the services for both pupils referenced, have now commenced, on 02 November and 23 October respectively.
Both the Department and Bus Éireann are very conscious of the challenges faced by parents awaiting transport for children with special educational needs. Families of children who are eligible for these services may therefore receive an interim Special Transport Grant (STG). This is a once off payment, paid retrospectively to families once the School Transport service is in place and is intended to assist with the cost of private transport arrangements the family had put in place until the service starts or recommences. School Transport section will contact the families with information on this grant.
The information on SEN routes in Galway is currently being collated by Bus Éireann and they will provide this directly to the Deputy.

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Shane Moynihan den Aire Oideachais agus Óige an mbunófar grúpa saineolaithe gan mhoill chun Polasaí don Ghaeilge sa chóras oideachais, ón luath-oideachas go dtí an tríú leibhéal, a fhorbairt agus a ailíniú go hiomlán leis an bhFráma Tagartha Comónta Eorpach.
reply:
Tá cur chuige céimniúil, seicheamhach á leanúint ag mo roinn maidir le forbairt bheartais don Ghaeilge sa chóras oideachais. Maidir le cúraim mo roinne, tá trí shnáithe leis an obair seo: an Polasaí don Oideachas Gaeltachta; an Polasaí don Oideachas Lán-Ghaeilge lasmuigh den Ghaeltacht agus an Plean Gnímh don Ghaeilge i Scoileanna Meán-Bhéarla. Le chéile, is céimeanna tábhachtacha iad na polasaithe agus na tionscnaimh seo i dtreo polasaí cuimsitheach don Ghaeilge sa chóras oideachais a sholáthar.
I gcomhthreo leis an obair atá ar bun ag mo roinn, tá obair ar an nGaeilge idir láimhe ag an Aire Leanaí, Míchumais agus Comhionannais agus an Aire Breisoideachais agus Ardoideachais, Taighde, Nuálaíochta agus Eolaíochta. Tá ár ranna ag obair go dlúth le chéile chun a chinntiú go bhfuil an beartas ag teacht le chéile.
Tá gealltanas sa Chlár Rialtais oibriú i dtreo ailíniú a dhéanamh ar churaclaim scoile ag leibhéil éagsúla leis an gComhchreat Tagartha na hEorpa um Theangacha (CEFR). Ag teacht leis an ngealltanas seo, áirítear sa Phlean Gnímh nua don Ghaeilge i Scoileanna Meán-Bhéarla gníomh chun curaclaim na Gaeilge, mar aon le tacaíochtaí teagaisc agus socruithe measúnaithe a bhaineann leo, a ailíniú leis an CEFR, d’fhonn feabhas a chur ar an nGaeilge labhartha sna scoileanna.
Tá tús curtha ag an CNCM le próiseas chun an Ghaeilge san Ardteistiméireacht a ailíniú leis an CEFR. Tá an obair seo ar siúl mar chuid den chlár atá ar bun faoi láthair chun an tSraith Shinsearach a athfhorbai

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Shane Moynihan den Aire Oideachais agus Óige an bhfuil machnamh déanta ar mholtaí an Ollaimh Emeritus Pádraig Uí Dhuibhir sa cháipéis Ó Dhíolúine go hIonchuimsiú: Tuarascáil Taighde ar Dhíolúintí ó Staidéar na Gaeilge i gcomhthéacs an mhéadaithe shuntasaigh atá tagtha ar líon na ndíolúintí ó staidéar na Gaeilge san iar-bhunoideachas, ó 33,476 in 2017 go 60,946 in 2024, agus an réamh-mheastacháin go sroichfidh an líon sin 22.5% de dhaltaí faoi 2030.
reply:
Cuireadh an tuarascáil a rinne an Teachta Dála tagairt di isteach chuig an Roinn le déanaí agus déanfar athbhreithniú uirthi.
Tá an Roinn Oideachais agus Óige tiomanta ar son an Gaeilge a bhunú mar ghné lárnach den churaclam scoile. Is cuid ríthábhachtach dár bhféiniúlacht náisiúnta agus dár n-oidhreacht oideachais í an Ghaeilge, agus fanann a cur chun cinn mar phríomhthosaíocht dúinn.
Tá prionsabail na hionchuimsitheachta agus na foghlama difreáilte mar bhonn le sonraíochtaí curaclaim bunscoile agus iar-bhunscoile. Baineann siad le rannpháirtíocht daltaí agus scoláirí i ngach ábhar, an Ghaeilge ina measc. Dá réir sin, moltar do scoileanna deiseanna a sholáthar do gach dalta agus scoláire páirt a ghlacadh i ngníomhaíochtaí teanga agus cultúrtha Gaeilge. Ba cheart é seo a dhéanamh a mhéid is féidir agus ar bhealach atá tairbheach, ba cheart é a dhéanamh ar leibhéal atá oiriúnach dá riachtanais foghlama agus chun leibhéal inniúlachta pearsanta a bhaint amach atá oiriúnach dá gcumas. I gcúinsí áirithe, féadfar díolúine ó staidéar na Gaeilge a dheonú do dhalta bunscoile nó do scoláire iar-bhunscoile. Tá an t-údarás ag bainistíocht na scoile díolúine a dheonú de réir na gcritéar atá leagtha amach i gCiorcláin 0054/2022 (Bunscoil) agus 0055/2022 (Iar-bhunscoil).
Tugadh faoi phróiseas fairsing comhairliúcháin phoiblí in 2018 a bhí mar bhonn eolais ag na ciorcláin reatha. Léirigh aiseolas na bpáirtithe leasmhara a bailíodh i gcomhthéacs an athbhreithnithe seo ar chiorcláin na 1990idí

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her Department and each agency and public body under her aegis maintain a supplier register or equivalent electronic record in which suppliers are assigned unique identifiers; the identifier types held by each body, including CRO registration numbers, VAT numbers and internally generated supplier IDs; whether these identifiers are recorded against individual purchase orders, contracts and payments; and, where no such identifier is maintained, the way in which suppliers are uniquely identified within the body's financial and procurement systems, in tabular form.
reply:
My department maintains a record of each supplier through our Financial Management System (FMS).
When a supplier is set up on our FMS, a unique supplier number is assigned by the system. Tax Registration Numbers are also recorded with the supplier information on our FMS where applicable. This unique supplier number is recorded against any purchase order or payment linked to that supplier number.
Our suite of reporting tools enables us to generate reports of payments based on a range of parameters including supplier name, supplier number, purchase order numbers, payment amounts and dates.
The information in respect of state bodies under the aegis of my department that fall within the scope of the Deputy’s question, is not held by my department. The relevant state bodies have been provided with the question and have been advised to respond directly to the Deputy.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Education and Youth her Departments plans for lands adjacent to a school (details supplied).
reply:
My department has determined that the Minister-owned site at Hollywoodrath will be the permanent location of Ériu Community College.
The school building on that site is currently occupied by two primary schools while refurbishment works are being carried out on their permanent school buildings. Once these schools return to their refurbished accommodation, the vacated building at the Hollywoodrath site will provide part of the permanent accommodation required for pupils attending Ériu Community College. This is not expected to occur before September 2028.
My department will keep the school authority and patron body informed of progress in relation to this project.
In relation to the balance of the lands at the site and the potential for future school development. This is being kept under review, my department is aware of planned residential development across North County Dublin. My department will continue to liaise with the local authority and monitor these developments to ensure that school infrastructure planning keeps pace with demographic change.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Education and Youth when a letter of intent will be issued for a school building project (details supplied), given the impending expiry of planning permission for that project.

Dublin.
The original invitation to tender issued in Q1 2025 and tenders were returned to the Design Team. However, following the Design Teams due diligence review of tenders received, the successful tenderer identified at that time withdrew from the award process. question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth to detail the membership of the National Forum on Inclusive Education for Students with Special Educational Needs; the number of times this group has met to date; and the recommendations the group has made at this stage.
reply:
This government is fully committed to supporting students with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this objective.
On 8 July 2026, it was announced that Minister Naughton and I had secured Government approval to establish a new Forum on Inclusive Education for Students with Special Educational Needs.
The Forum will bring together key stakeholders to develop a shared national vision for inclusive education and identify practical actions to support children and young people with special educational needs across the education system.
Professor Noel Purdy, Director of Research and Scholarship at Stranmillis University College, was announced as chair for the Forum.
Membership will include representatives from disabled persons’ organisations, advocacy groups, education stakeholders, senior officials from relevant Government departments and external experts.
My department and the NCSE are committed to delivering an education system that is of the highest quality and where every child and young person feels valued and is actively supported and nurtured to achieve their full potential.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth to clarify whether her Department has the authority to direct a primary school Board of Management to review or remove a designated liaison person where concerns have been formally substantiated regarding inaccurate information provided to Tusla in connection with a mandated report; and the procedures that are in place to address such matters while ensuring fair procedures for all involved.
reply:
Tusla is the agency of the State with the statutory responsibility to assess all reports of child welfare and protection concerns and as such my Department does not have powers to investigate child protection concerns.
My Department has no role in employer/employee matters. The Education Act, 1998 sets out the legal framework for schools and their patrons. The act provides that the board of management is the body charged with the direct governance of a school on behalf of the patron and is the employer of school staff. In the case of schools established or maintained by an ETB the ETB in the employer of school staff. Any actions in relation to the school employee, in relation to employment matters, are exclusively a matter for the employer.
My Department's Child Protection Procedures for Schools set out the reporting requirements for school personnel, including the Designated Liaison Person. Where any member of school personnel fails to report a matter to Tusla where advised by Tusla to do so, or otherwise fails to comply with the procedures, this is to be reported to and dealt with separately by the employer in accordance with the relevant disciplinary procedures. The procedures are available on the gov.ie website: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-education/policy-information/child-protection-procedures-in-schools/

question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Education and Youth to outline the process by which a qualified teacher from a non-EEA country may apply for a teaching post in Ireland; the requirements that apply in respect of teaching council registration; and if registration can be completed in advance, before moving to Ireland.
reply:
The Teaching Council is the body with the statutory authority and responsibility for the regulation of the teaching profession in Ireland including the registration of teachers in the State.
The Teaching Council register teachers under the Teaching Council Act 2001-2015 and in line with the Teaching Council Registration Regulations 2025. As set out in the Schedule of the Regulations, the Council registers teachers under five routes of registration: Route 1 - Primary, Route 2 - Post-primary, Route 3 - Further Education, Route 4 - Other and Route 5 - Student Teacher. The qualification requirements for each route are set out in the Schedule of the Regulations.
As the independent regulator of the teaching profession in Ireland, the Teaching Council’s role is to protect the public by promoting and regulating professional standards in teaching. This is carried out through the statutory registration of teachers, ensuring a highly qualified teaching profession whose members meet and uphold high standards of professional competence and conduct.
Teachers who have qualified as teachers outside of the Republic of Ireland and who are eligible to teach in the country in which they obtained their qualification can apply for recognition as a teacher with the Teaching Council.

question: Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Education and Youth the steps being taken to ensure that children with complex physical, medical and additional educational needs attending mainstream schools have access to appropriate staffing, equipment, facilities and care supports; and whether her Department has assessed the adequacy of current provision in this regard.
reply:
Enabling students with special educational needs to receive an education that meets their needs is a priority for this Government.?It is also a key priority for me, my department and for the National Council for Special Education (NCSE).
The vast majority of students with special educational needs are supported to attend mainstream classes with their peers. Where students with more complex needs require additional supports, special class and special school places are provided. This is in keeping with policy on an inclusive education, which promotes that students will be supported to receive an education in the most inclusive setting possible.
In 2027, the Government has prioritised ensuring that schools have the necessary resources to support children with special educational needs in the setting that best meets their needs. Since 2020, over 2,400 new special classes have been provided and there are now more than 4,300 special classes available in our primary and post-primary schools. Since 2020, 20 new special schools have been opened.
Budget 2027 will increase our special education teachers by 1,353 and 2,339 special needs assistants (SNAs) will be funded to support children across mainstream and specialist settings. This brings the total number of SNAs to over 28,000 by the end of 2027, which is the highest ever number of SNAs allocated to our education system. This is in recognition of the growing needs of children across all settings.

question: Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Education and Youth the current plans in place to modernise ageing primary school buildings, improve energy efficiency, address overcrowding and provide appropriate facilities for pupils and staff; and the level of funding allocated for these purposes over the next five years.
reply:
The Department of Education and Youth continues to invest significantly in school infrastructure through a range of programmes to modernise and upgrade school buildings, improve energy efficiency, and to address accommodation needs arising from demographic growth. Since 2020 in the region of €3.4 billion in capital funding has been invested in Primary schools across the country.
The Department of Education and Youth has an approved capital allocation of €7.55 billion over 2026-2030 NDP period and continues to optimise outputs with a strong focus on maximising existing school capacity, progressing priority projects where local capacity across schools in the area is insufficient, and ensuring delivery that is affordable, offers value for money, and meets functional needs. Our priorities are:

• Projects for special schools
• Projects for schools fully in interim accommodation and that have an urgent need for permanent accommodation due to demographic pressures or condition issues
• Projects delivering significant special class capacity
• Projects addressing major condition issues
• Projects providing additional capacity where required to cater for demographic growth

This prioritisation framework is applied across the school building pipeline as projects progress through the various stages of delivery.

The wellbeing of our school staff, including teachers and principals, is vital to our education system.
The Programme for Government commits to the preparation of a school workforce development plan. Research and consultation processes in support of this objective are currently underway. One major output of this work is the recent publication of the findings of a research project investigating issues associated with teacher shortages. This project, led by UNESCO and supported by the EU Commission, has published recommendations for addressing the main factors affecting teacher supply in Ireland. The project report, which was launched on 7th September 2026, can be accessed online at the following link <https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000399288.locale=en>
As part of this broader work which is looking at the sustainability and attractiveness of the teaching profession, teacher workload and wellbeing will be carefully considered. My department is aware of the issues raised in relation to workload and will be commissioning research into the area of school workforce workload and work intensity. The scope will include primary, post-primary, and special schools.

question: Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Education and Youth the measures being taken to ensure that primary schools have adequate classroom resources, materials and staffing supports so that teachers are not required to personally fund educational resources for their pupils; and whether her Department has assessed the extent to which teachers are using personal income to subsidise classroom provision.
reply:

The Programme for Government contains a commitment to “provide free schoolbooks to all children in the Free Education Scheme and introduce changes as needed to the operation of this scheme”.
The previous Programme for Government in 2020 contained a commitment to commence a free schoolbooks scheme pilot in September 2020 and, pending a successful review of the pilot, expand the scheme to schools nationwide, as resources allow. From 2020 to 2022, a three-year free schoolbooks scheme pilot was introduced in 102 DEIS primary schools.
Budget 2023 announced funding of over €50 million to provide free schoolbooks, workbooks and copybooks, to all children and young people enrolled in recognised primary schools, including special schools. The per capita rate was reduced to €80 for the 2024/25 school year to take account of schools having purchased stocks of books for the 2023/24 school year that can be reused in subsequent school years. The per capita rate of €80 has been maintained for the 2025/26 and the 2026/27 school years.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether special needs assistants employed in schools will be covered in full by any new public service pay agreement arising from the talks now under way at the Workplace Relations Commission, including any retrospective pay increases.
reply:

It is a matter for each individual union to decide to ballot its members on any matter, including the agreed outcomes of local bargaining negotiations. reply:

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which her Department is building cyber resilience; and the strategy in place to address cyber attacks.
reply:
My department takes the issue of cyber security very seriously and is committed to maintaining and strengthening its cyber resilience.
An organisation-wide approach is adopted to protect departmental information, data and ICT systems, supported where appropriate by specialist ICT security providers. This approach includes staff awareness and training initiatives to promote good cyber security practices and hygiene.
Robust arrangements are in place to help prevent, detect and respond to cyber security threats and incidents. These arrangements are regularly reviewed and updated to address emerging threats and reflect evolving best practice. At a national level, the Government's recently published National Cyber Security Strategy 2030 sets out a framework for strengthening cyber defence capabilities and enhancing resilience to cyber security threats.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the State's primary cyber security authority, provides a range of services and supports across Government. My department works closely with the NCSC and benefits from its threat intelligence, alerts, guidance and incident response support, including support from the national Computer Security Incident Response Team (CSIRT).

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will provide an update in respect of the timeline for the Strand 2 announcement.
reply:
Under the National Development Plan (NDP), youth capital funding of €4.0 million per annum will be available to support the youth sector from 2026 to 2030. The 2026 allocation represents a significant increase of €3.5 million on the 2025 allocation and a substantial enhancement of annual youth capital funding available to the sector in recent years. For the first time, the NDP provides a dedicated multi-annual capital funding stream for the youth sector from 2026 to 2030, supporting strategic investment and long-term planning.
To date, over €500,000 has been allocated to national youth organisations, while a further €1.6 million has been allocated to Education and Training Boards (ETBs) under Strand I of the UBU Youth Service Capital Funding Scheme 2026.
Strand II of the scheme supports larger-scale capital projects, with a value exceeding €20,000, that will enhance the quality, accessibility, safety and sustainability of existing UBU-funded youth services.
I am pleased to advise the Deputy that the department is at a very advanced stage of its internal approval process for Strand II allocations. Subject to the completion of the remaining approval requirements, the department expects to notify ETBs of the outcome of the process very shortly, enabling successful projects and purchases to proceed as soon as possible.

reply:
The school to which the Deputy refers has been granted capital funding for 2 x special education classrooms plus ancillary accommodation under my Department’s SEN Reconfiguration and Modular Accommodation Programme.
This Programme involves the use of Project Management supports which is designed to enable the accommodation to be provided as quickly as possible and help ease the administrative workload for school authorities in relation to the management and delivery of projects.
Kerrigan Sheanon Newman (KSN) has been appointed, from my Department’s Framework to design and tender this school's project. This is a collaborative process between the Project Manager, School Authority and the Department.
The project started on site in July 2026 and is earmarked for occupation by the end of November 2026.
My Department is fully aware of the urgency in respect of this accommodation and will be working closely with the Project Managers and School Authority to keep the school updated on overall project delivery and timelines.

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Education and Youth for an update on the school building project for a school (details supplied).
reply:
The school to which the Deputy refers remains at Stage 2b (Post-Planning). The Stage 2b report was submitted to the Department in January 2026 and is presently being assessed from both a technical and cost perspective.
All school building projects, as they progress through the pipeline, must undergo the necessary due diligence outlined in the Infrastructure Guidelines and Capital Works Management Framework.
The timing of a project moving from one stage to the next requires careful planning and takes account of factors such as compliance with all scope, design and cost requirements; timing of affordability; and the prioritisation necessary for the school building programme to remain within agreed annual funding allocations.
It is expected that the next tranche of projects to proceed to tender will be published in 2027. Prioritisation will continue over the coming months to identify this next tranche of projects. This will be informed by latest available demographic and capacity data, the department’s energy and condition inventory (the validation of which is due to be completed by late 2026/early 2027), opportunities for phased development to prioritise the most urgent accommodation needs and consultation with patrons and management bodies.
The project at this school will be considered as part of the prioritisation process, along with all other projects at the required stage of readiness.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will consider providing interim teaching support to a school (details supplied), following the loss of a teaching post which will leave one class with 35 pupils, including a high number of pupils with additional educational needs; the supports that are available to schools in such circumstances.
reply:
The key factor for determining the level of staffing resources provided at individual school level is the staffing schedule for the relevant school year and pupil enrolments on the previous 30 September. The staffing schedule operates in a clear and transparent manner and treats all similar types of schools equally.
The staffing arrangements include a provision whereby schools experiencing rapid increases in enrolment can apply for additional permanent mainstream posts, using projected enrolment. The school referred to by the Deputy was allocated a post on this basis, having advised of an expected enrolment of 207 pupils. The school was advised that to retain the post, an enrolment of 199 was required on 30 September. As the school's enrolment was 191 on 30 September, the post will not be retained for the remainder of the year.
Class sizes in schools are affected by a variety of factors including enrolment fluctuations and available accommodation. Schools are best placed to determine the appropriate numbers in any class and so the configuration of classes and the deployment of classroom teachers are done at local school level. The Department's guidance to schools is that the number of pupils in any class is kept as low as possible taking all relevant contextual factors into account.

This allows my department to keep a strong focus on the provision of additional capacity to cater for demographics, new housing developments and the roll-out of additional special classes for children with additional needs. In this regard, there will continue to be a strong emphasis on maximising existing capacity across the school estate and also ensuring that school admissions policies and processes are targeted at meeting local mainstream and special class requirements.

reply:

reply:

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether, under the Education Act, a school may require a child to remain in class during SPHE/RSE lessons covering sexuality, gender identity or transgender-related topics where a parent has requested withdrawal on grounds of conscience; if not, what national guidance governs the child's removal and alternative supervision; and if she will issue specific guidance to ensure a consistent approach across schools.
reply:
In accordance with Section 30 of the Education Act, 1998, parents have a right to have their children opt out of classes which are contrary to the conscience of the parent if they so wish. It is expected that this right be upheld by schools on foot of a parental request.
The manner in which any school ensures that the right to opt out of classes is upheld is a matter for the school concerned. The school must determine the particular arrangements which are most appropriate in its individual circumstances having regard to local issues such as available space, supervision requirements and how the school concerned organises classes etc.
Under the provisions of the Education Act 1998, the board of management is the body charged with the direct governance of a school. It is the responsibility of each individual school managerial authority to arrange for appropriate supervision of its pupils when pupils are on the school premises, during school time and/or school activities.
The Department of Education and Youth has not issued specific guidelines on requirements for supervision of pupils and acknowledges that the degree of supervision in any given school will depend on the school's particular circumstances and on factors such as the age of pupils and the nature and layout of the accommodation. Therefore, queries regarding supervision are matters for each individual school managerial authority.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to Parliamentary Question No. 74451/26, if she is aware that 199 students would be a ratio of 25:1 and not 23:1 as set out in Circular 0025-2026.
reply:
The key factor in determining the level of mainstream teaching staff allocated to an individual primary school is the school's recognised enrolment as recorded on 30 September of the previous school year.
Staffing allocations for individual schools are determined in accordance with the enrolment bands set out in the staffing schedule. The 23:1 allocation ratio is not a ratio for class size in schools. It is a general average used to allocate classroom teaching posts to schools. Class sizes can vary from school to school and are determined by the number of pupils enrolled divided by the number of classroom teachers in the school.
The average class size nationally is 21.9 while the EU average class size is 20. The latest figures in relation to pupil: teacher ratio (commonly referred to as PTR) show the ratio of pupils to teachers as 12.6: 1 at primary level; with the EU average pupil teacher ratio is 15:1.
The configuration of classes and the deployment of classroom teachers are done at local school level. The Department's guidance to schools is that the number of pupils in any class is kept as low as possible taking all relevant contextual factors into account (e.g. classroom accommodation, fluctuating enrolment etc.). School authorities are also requested, where possible, to use their autonomy under the staffing schedule to implement smaller class sizes for junior classes. If a school has a large class, it generally also has a small class.

question: Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Education and Youth for an update on the status of DEIS Plus applications submitted by schools (details supplied), which are located in the same town as schools that have already been included in the DEIS Plus programme; the criteria used in assessing these applications; and whether consideration will be given to providing additional DEIS Plus funding and supports to all eligible schools in Longford town.
reply:
Addressing educational disadvantage and ensuring that every child and young person can reach their full potential is a key priority for me as Minister for Education and Youth and for the Government. The DEIS Plus scheme, launched as part of the DEIS Strategy to 2035, represents the most significant expansion of targeted supports since the establishment of DEIS. DEIS Plus is designed to provide enhanced, evidence-based supports to a cohort of schools with the highest concentrations of children and young people at risk of educational disadvantage, identified through a refined data-based model drawing on a range of indicators associated with persistent and intergenerational disadvantage.
Schools were identified for inclusion in the DEIS Plus scheme using the DEIS Plus identification model, an objective and data-based approach that applies nationally available indicators consistently across all schools. The identification model is underpinned by a range of administrative data on every child and young person enrolled in primary and post-primary schools. This data includes:
• The Pobal HP Deprivation Index for the small area in which the child or young person lives, based on address data provided by schools through the Primary Online Database (POD) and the Post-Primary Online Database (PPOD).
• The child’s or young person’s ethnicity, where provided by schools on POD or PPOD.
• Whether the child’s or young person’s address matches an address of State-funded homeless accommodation.

Language supports are also included through the Special Education Teaching (SET) which encompasses an element of language support allocation. Under this SET model, schools are frontloaded with resources to provide support immediately to those pupils who need it without delay.
My Department's policies enable flexible resource allocation to ensure that the resources follow pupils in the event of them changing schools. These supports to schools, based on an application process, are provided for new-entrant pupils (i.e., pupils arrived in the country in the last 2 years with an EAL requirement). Similar to previous years, supports may also be provided for schools with a high concentration of pupils that are not classified as new-entrant pupils, but who have an EAL need i.e., those pupils with less than 3 years EAL support and register less than B1 in an English proficiency test.

reply:
The key factor for determining the level of staffing resources provided at individual school level is the staffing schedule for the relevant school year and pupil enrolments on the previous 30 September. The staffing schedule operates in a clear and transparent manner and treats all similar types of schools equally.
The staffing arrangements include a provision whereby schools experiencing rapid increases in enrolment can apply for additional permanent mainstream posts, using projected enrolment. The school referred to by the Deputy was allocated a post on this basis, having advised of an expected enrolment of 207 pupils. The school was advised that to retain the post, an enrolment of 199 was required on 30 September. As the school's enrolment was 191 on 30 September, the post will not be retained for the remainder of the year.
Class sizes in schools are affected by a variety of factors including enrolment fluctuations and available accommodation. Schools are best placed to determine the appropriate numbers in any class and so the configuration of classes and the deployment of classroom teachers are done at local school level. The Department's guidance to schools is that the number of pupils in any class is kept as low as possible taking all relevant contextual factors into account.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment when the January 2027 minimum annual remuneration thresholds will be confirmed; whether an impact assessment and engagement with an organisation (details supplied) will take place; and whether deferral will be considered given the implications for Fair Deal funding negotiations.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 627, 642, 655, 656 and 660 together.
The employment permits system is grounded in legislation that sets clear and objective criteria for minimum annual remuneration (MAR) thresholds, qualifications, and the eligibility of occupations. The MAR represents the minimum salary that must be paid to a non-EEA national for an employment permit to be issued or renewed.
The Employment Permits: Minimum Annual Remuneration – Outcome of the Roadmap Review 2025 published at the end of last year sets out the policy rationale, evidence basis and revised (phased) roadmap for implementation of the thresholds applicable across the employment permits system.
The review was informed by a public consultation process and undertaken in response to a range of structural changes in the labour market since MAR thresholds were last comprehensively updated. This included consideration of issues such as sustained inflationary pressures, increases in average earnings, rising costs of living, and changing labour market dynamics. Under this roadmap, the first increases took effect on 1 March 2026.
I can confirm that increases to MAR thresholds for 2027 will not be implemented in January 2027. In line with the approach taken for the 2026 increases, changes to the thresholds will be implemented with sufficient lead-in to allow sectors time to prepare for the changes.

reply:
The employment permits system is designed to address clearly evidenced labour and skills shortages that cannot be met from within the domestic or wider EEA labour market.

This review involves public and stakeholder consultation providing an opportunity to present sector-specific evidence of skills and labour shortages or surpluses.

question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will review the operation of the work permit system in relation to employers proving that they have made efforts to recruit from within the EU.
reply:
The employment permits system is designed to address clearly evidenced labour and skills shortages that cannot be met from within the domestic or wider EEA labour market. It aims to ensure that employment opportunities arising in Ireland are, in the first instance, made available to suitably qualified Irish and other EEA nationals.
Ireland’s economic migration regime focuses on key sectors and skills shortages, particularly in economically strategic enterprises with the potential for employment growth, and facilitates the recruitment of non-EEA nationals to address identified skills and labour shortages in the short to medium term. In developing policy in this area, consideration is also given to a range of wider measures available to address skills shortages across the economy.
The employment permits system is not intended to replace the critical work of developing and upskilling the domestic workforce to meet future labour market needs. One of the key objectives underpinning the framework is to ensure that it does not provide a mechanism which encourages the importation of low-cost labour.
A key mechanism supporting these objectives is the Labour Market Needs Test (LMNT), which requires employers seeking to recruit a non-EEA national under certain permit types to demonstrate that genuine efforts have been made to recruit from within Ireland and the wider EEA before an employment permit application can be considered.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the position regarding the Co-operative Societies Bill 2022; and whether it will include a review of the requirements as set out in the Irish Collective Asset-management Vehicles Act 2015.
reply:
The Co-operative Societies Bill provides for the most far-reaching reform of the legislation governing co-operatives in the history of the State. The Bill will introduce a modern legal framework which will place the co-operative model on a more favourable and clearer legal basis. It will create a level playing field with the situation applying to companies and encourage the consideration of the co-operative model as an attractive formation option for entrepreneurs and also for social and community activities.
This is a large and complex Bill running to over 490 sections. Work is ongoing within my Department and in the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel to complete a quality assurance exercise on the drafted Bill and with a view to producing a stamped copy in the coming weeks. The Bill will then be brought to Government seeking permission to publish and I look forward to progressing the Bill through the Oireachtas as soon as possible thereafter.
Matters relating to the Irish Collective Asset-management Vehicles Act 2015 come within the responsibility of my colleague the Minister for Finance. I understand that the Department of Finance's Ireland for Finance: Vision 2030 – Renewed and Refocussed for a Digital Age identifies a review of the Irish Collective Asset-management Vehicles Act 2015 as a key policy action.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment his views on whether Section 27C of the new Short Term Letting and Tourism Bill 2026 complies with the EU Court of Justice Smartflats judgment and EU Regulation 2024/1028.
reply:
The recent judgment of the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) in the Smartflats case (Case C-813/24), delivered on 22 October 2026, provides important clarity regarding the regulation of short-term tourist accommodation within the European Union.
The Court confirmed that Member States may impose authorisation and planning requirements on short-term letting activity where such measures pursue legitimate public policy objectives, including the protection of housing supply, the preservation of the urban environment, and consumer protection. Significantly, the Court rejected any suggestion that planning controls on tourist accommodation are inherently incompatible with EU law. Instead, it recognised that national, regional and local authorities retain the ability to regulate the sector where justified by objectives of public interest.
At the same time, the Court emphasised that any authorisation or planning regime must comply with the requirements of the EU Services Directive. In particular, restrictions must be necessary, proportionate and evidence-based. The Court also highlighted the importance of transparent procedures, objective criteria, clear decision-making processes, and appropriate rights of appeal for affected operators.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment his Department's assessment of the main barriers facing SMEs in adopting artificial intelligence technologies, including cost, skills shortages and access to technical expertise; and the actions being taken to address those barriers.
reply:
My Department actively monitors AI adoption across the enterprise base. Ireland’s performance on enterprise digitalisation remains strong. The European Commission’s Digital Decade Country Report 2026 shows that Ireland ranks ninth in the EU for SME adoption of AI, cloud computing and data analytics, with 70.95% of SMEs using these technologies compared with an EU average of 62.32%. SME AI adoption stands at 18.34%, broadly in line with the EU average of 18.9%.
Despite growing adoption, SMEs continue to face barriers to implementing and scaling AI. Research undertaken through a joint programme between my Department and the ESRI found that knowledge-related barriers are a key factor affecting AI uptake, while access to finance, security concerns and skills shortages also influence investment decisions.
Recognising that adoption pathways differ across sectors, my Department is developing a sector-specific strategy on AI in enterprise, initially focused on manufacturing, ICT services, tourism and construction, which together represent a significant share of Ireland’s businesses and employment. To inform the development of the strategy, my Department commissioned a study to examine AI opportunities, adoption pathways, barriers and requirements across these sectors.
The study found that enterprises face common challenges relating to awareness and readiness, skills and organisational capacity, data and digital foundations, and trust, governance and security.

Ireland operates a managed employment permits system, which seeks to maximise the benefits of economic migration while minimising disruption to Ireland’s labour market. The system is designed to facilitate the entry of appropriately skilled non-EEA nationals to fill skills and labour shortages required to develop and support enterprise for the benefit of our economy
The General Employment Permit application referenced by the Deputy is currently under review. The Employment Permits Section has requested additional information from the applicant, which is required to progress consideration of the application.
A decision will issue as soon as the requested information has been received and assessed.
Current employment permit processing dates are published and updated regularly on my Department’s website - enterprise.gov.ie/en/what-we-do/workplace-and-skills/employment-permits/current-application-processing-dates/.
