question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether contracts recorded in his Department's internal contract register can be linked to their corresponding contract award notices published on eTenders, where applicable; whether his Department records the relevant eTenders notice reference, URL or other identifier; and if not, the reasons that prevent this information from being recorded.
reply:
My Department’s internal contract register is not currently configured to systematically record or report e-Tenders contract award notices, URLs or specific e-Tenders reference numbers as a standard data field for all contracts. However, my Department manually records all awarded contracts, including those awarded through the e-Tenders system with their Tender number for reference, in the contract register.
While relevant information may be available within procurement documentation and contract records, there is no automated linkage between the contract register and e-Tenders due to the Registers current format. It is also important to note that contract records may originate from a variety of procurement routes, not all of which result in a standalone contract award notice on e-Tenders.
The Department keeps its contract management and record-keeping arrangements under review to ensure they continue to meet governance, transparency and operational requirements. In this regard, my Department is currently exploring the feasibility of updating the contract register to provide integrated solutions to improve data accuracy, reporting capabilities, operational efficiency and automatic prompts for expiring contracts. Linkages with contract award notices published on e-Tenders, e-Tenders notice references to include URLs or other such identifiers will be considered as part of this process.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the current rights of retired workers to representation, and to access the Workplace Relations Commission and the Labour Court, in disputes concerning their occupational pension entitlements; whether the provision introduced by the Industrial Relations (Amendment) Act 2015, permitting access for six months after retirement in respect of matters arising before retirement, remains the only such route; the number of referrals made under that provision in each year since 2015.
reply:
Retired workers have the ability to enforce their pension rights through various legal avenues, including the Pensions Act, the Pensions Authority, the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman (FSPO), and the courts. Where a pension scheme has an internal dispute resolution (IDR) procedure, this provides for a formal structure through which beneficiaries or potential beneficiaries can raise complaints or disputes and engage directly with the pension provider concerned. If an individual is dissatisfied with the outcome of an IDR process, they may advance a complaint to the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman, who is an independent and impartial statutory officer responsible for investigating and ruling on complaints from active members, deferred members and beneficiaries of occupational pension schemes.
In addition, Section 45 of the Industrial Relations (Amendment) Act 2015 inserted section 26A into the Industrial Relations Act 1990. It allows for a retired person access to the IR bodies in a period of 6 month post-retirement for matters arising pre-retirement. This 6 months is either from the date of retirement or the date from when it became known or should have been known, the time frame in which to make a complaint for matters arising post-retirement. That period may be extended by up to a further six months where reasonable cause for the delay is shown. question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether purchase orders issued by his Department under procurement contracts can be linked to the corresponding contracts held in its internal contract register; whether a contract reference or other unique identifier is maintained to enable this linkage; and if not, the way his Department monitors cumulative expenditure against the approved value of each contract.
reply:
My Department does not operate a purchase order system. Expenditure is processed and recorded through the Department’s financial management system, which captures transactions against suppliers using unique supplier identifiers.
The Department maintains an internal contract register containing key details of procurement contracts. The specific datasets recorded on the Register include contract reference numbers, contract award date and end date, supplier ID number, address and categorisation, contract scope and duration and contract value and expenditure.
Expenditure is recorded through my Departments Oracle Financial Management system, where each supplier is assigned a unique supplier number to support the recording and monitoring of spend. As my Department operates a devolved procurement model at Business Unit level responsibility for monitoring expenditure against approved contract values rests with the relevant business areas of the Department. This includes the day-to-day administration of contracts, including monitoring performance and expenditure, expenditure against approved budgets and ensures funds are available before contractual commitments are made. These arrangements enable the Department to track expenditure with suppliers and monitor spend against approved contract values, supporting compliance with contractual and procurement requirements.

question: Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the minimum annual remuneration threshold increase set for introduction in January 2027; and the exact timeline for its implementation.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 627, 642, 655, 656 and 660 together.
The employment permits system is grounded in legislation that sets clear and objective criteria for minimum annual remuneration (MAR) thresholds, qualifications, and the eligibility of occupations. The MAR represents the minimum salary that must be paid to a non-EEA national for an employment permit to be issued or renewed.
The Employment Permits: Minimum Annual Remuneration – Outcome of the Roadmap Review 2025 published at the end of last year sets out the policy rationale, evidence basis and revised (phased) roadmap for implementation of the thresholds applicable across the employment permits system.
The review was informed by a public consultation process and undertaken in response to a range of structural changes in the labour market since MAR thresholds were last comprehensively updated. This included consideration of issues such as sustained inflationary pressures, increases in average earnings, rising costs of living, and changing labour market dynamics. Under this roadmap, the first increases took effect on 1 March 2026.
I can confirm that increases to MAR thresholds for 2027 will not be implemented in January 2027. In line with the approach taken for the 2026 increases, changes to the thresholds will be implemented with sufficient lead-in to allow sectors time to prepare for the changes.

question: Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the KPI’s or performance targets that have been set for the National Artificial Intelligence Office to deliver over its first 12 months.
reply:

The annual Oversight and Performance Delivery Agreement (OPDA) to be agreed between the AI Office of Ireland and my Department will separately provide for appropriate performance, service-level and resource accountability, without conferring on me or my Department approval, veto or direction over the exercise of the Office’s statutory functions. question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if there are any legislative provisions entitling a person to the right to repair for a product or legislative provisions which mandate companies to ensure that there are available supplies of replacement parts for the original product for a certain period of time (details supplied).
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 628 and 637 together.
Irish consumer law contains provisions relating to the availability of spare parts and after-sales service in certain circumstances.
For vehicles purchased before 29 November 2022, the relevant provisions are contained in the Sale of Goods and Supply of Services Act 1980. For vehicles purchased on or after that date, the Consumer Rights Act 2022 applies.
Under these provisions, where a seller has represented that spare parts or after-sales service will be available, whether in an offer, description or advertisement, the seller is required to honour those commitments. These obligations arise in the context of the contractual relationship between the consumer and the seller.
Irish consumer law does not require motor vehicle manufacturers to maintain replacement parts for a specified period of time.
In addition, the EU Right to Repair framework, which aims to encourage the repair of certain consumer products and improve access to repair services and spare parts, does not currently apply to motor vehicles.
Accordingly, consumers may have rights in relation to the availability of spare parts and after-sales service where commitments have been made by the seller. However, there is currently no specific statutory requirement that such parts be maintained or supplied for motor vehicles for a prescribed period.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the current legislative timeline for the full implementation of the Short-Term Letting and Tourism Bill 2025 and the establishment of the short-term letting register; and the specific measures being taken to ensure local authorities are adequately resourced to enforce the associated planning regulations.
reply:
In April of last year, I obtained Government approval for the general scheme of the Short-Term Letting and Tourism Bill. Upon enactment, the Short-Term Letting and Tourism Bill will provide, for the first time, a comprehensive statutory framework governing the short-term letting sector in Ireland, including the establishment of a national register. On 6 October the Government approved the publication of the Short-Term Letting and Tourism Bill 2026 (STLT). The Bill was published on 23 October and is available to view at www.oireachtas.ie/en/bills/bill/2026/101/. This represents a significant step towards a more transparent and effectively regulated sector. The Bill will proceed to Second Stage in Dáil Éireann shortly.
This register, which has been broadly welcomed by the tourism sector, will be implemented and managed by Fáilte Ireland. The register will launch on 1 December 2026, with a legal obligation on all operators to register by 31 December 2026. The register will operate in compliance with the EU Short-Term Rental Regulation (EU) 2024/1028, which came into effect on 20 May 2026.
The planning policy framework for short-term letting activity, and all matters relating to planning and local authority resources, fall within the remit of the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage. My Department is, however, working closely with all stakeholders to support the implementation of the wider short-term letting regulatory framework.

reply:
The Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) is an independent statutory body under the aegis of my Department, established on 1 October 2015 under the Workplace Relations Act 2015. The WRC’s functions include promoting and securing compliance with employment law through inspections, providing information on employment rights and obligations, and delivering mediation, adjudication, conciliation, and advisory services.
The attached table presents data from the WRC insofar as adjudication and inspection complaints are concerned. In this regard, it should be noted that an adjudication complaint application may contain one or more individual complaints, and outcome figures relate to individual complaints closed during the relevant reporting period. reply:

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if his Department and each agency and public body under its aegis maintain a supplier register or equivalent electronic record in which suppliers are assigned unique identifier; the identifier types held by each body, including CRO registration numbers, VAT numbers and internally generated supplier IDs; whether these identifiers are recorded against individual purchase orders, contracts and payments; and, where no such identifier is maintained; and the way in which suppliers are uniquely identified within the body's financial and procurement systems, in tabular form.
reply:
My Department does not operate a purchase order system. In respect of the Department and its Offices expenditure is processed and recorded through the Department’s financial management system, which captures transactions against suppliers using unique supplier identifiers.
All suppliers are set up and maintained within Oracle financials. The Oracle supplier reference provides the basis for identifying suppliers within the Department's financial management system. A supplier report can be generated from the system to provide a listing of registered suppliers. Suppliers are assigned an individual supplier reference within Oracle, which facilitates their identification and the recording of associated financial transactions.
VAT registration details are maintained by the relevant business section, validated by Payables Section using ROS (Revenue Online Service) and recorded against the supplier's Oracle record. Supplier records are established when a supplier is initially required to be processed through the financial management system. Where no payments have been made to a supplier over a two-year period, the supplier record is made inactive. However, the record is retained within Oracle in order to maintain an audit trail.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the position regarding any review the employment-permit classifications applicable to specialist traditional circus workers, with a view to including these occupations on the critical skills occupations list, given the lack of these highly specialised skills within the Irish labour market.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 623, 624 and 625 together.
Ireland’s economic migration policy is designed to address verified and ongoing skills shortages across the economy. The system is vacancy?led and is managed through the Critical Skills Occupations List (CSOL) and the Ineligible Occupations List, both of which are reviewed on a regular basis by my Department.
The Employment Permits Act 2024 requires that, in order for an employment permit to be granted, at least 50% of the employees of an employer are Irish/EEA/UK/Swiss nationals. The mandatory application of the 50:50 rule underpins the Government's employment creation strategy by requiring employers in the State to hire in a balanced manner from domestic and EEA labour markets. Under this rule, an employment permit will not issue unless, at the time of application, at least 50% of the employees of the employer are EEA, UK or Swiss nationals.
Officials of my Department recently concluded a review of Ireland's use of the 50:50 rule, the outcome of which recommended amending the Employment Permits Act 2024 to address critical recruitment difficulties in key health and social care services sectors through the creation of new sector-specific and sector-wide regulation-making powers. I have not been made aware of such issues arising in the above sector.
The immediate focus is now progressing the amendments as set out in the General Scheme, and working with the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel to draft the Bill.

question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to outline the avenues available to a qualified teacher from a non-EEA country who wishes to work as a teacher in Ireland.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 614 and 616 together.
Ireland operates a managed employment permits system, which seeks to maximise the benefits of economic migration while minimising disruption to Ireland's labour market. The system is designed to facilitate the entry of appropriately skilled non-EEA nationals to fill skills and/or labour shortages required to develop and support enterprise for the benefit of our economy.
Where a non-EEA national has secured an offer of employment as a teacher, an application for an employment permit may be made to the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment by either the employer or the employee. All applications are considered having regard to the relevant statutory criteria and conditions.
A Labour Market Needs Test is required in respect of General Employment Permit applications. This requires the employer to advertise the vacancy in the prescribed manner before an application for an employment permit can be made.
Non-EEA nationals must also comply with the relevant immigration requirements, including obtaining an entry visa where required.
A person wishing to work as a teacher in a recognised school in Ireland must be registered with the Teaching Council. Further information regarding registration and qualification recognition is a matter for the Teaching Council and the Department of Education.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to provide a direct email address for correspondence with the AI Office of Ireland, aioffice.gov.ie, noting that its website currently provides a contact form but no published email address; to confirm whether the AI Office of Ireland is a public body subject to the Freedom of Information Act 2014; if so, to provide the designated email address for submitting FOI requests directly to the office.
reply:
The AI Office of Ireland invites persons raising queries concerning the EU AI Act and its implementation to engage through the Service Desk in the first instance.
The email address for correspondence with the Office for other matters (including FoI requests) is info@aioffice.gov.ie.
Pursuant to section 139 of the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Act 2026, amending the Freedom of Information Act 2014, the AI Office of Ireland is a ‘partially included agency’ included in Part 1 of Schedule 1 of the 2014 Act. This means that the AI Office is not a public body within the meaning of section 6 of the Act where records concerning the performance of its records would be disclosed. Instead, it is only in circumstances ‘as it relates to records concerning the general administration of those functions’ which records are disclosable.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if his Department will consider reviewing the Employment (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2018, particularly the current banded-hours arrangements for part-time workers, including reducing the reference period from 12 to six months and removing the two lowest weekly working-hour bands.
reply:
The Employment (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2018 introduced a number of important measures aimed at providing greater certainty and predictability of working arrangements for employees.
Among these measures were the banded-hours provisions, which provide employees whose contractual hours do not reflect the hours they regularly work with a statutory right to request placement in a band of weekly working hours that more accurately reflects their working pattern. Employers must respond within 4 weeks and can only refuse under specific conditions.
The legislation determines the appropriate band by reference to an employee’s average weekly hours worked over a 12 month reference period.
The current framework was designed to strike an appropriate balance between providing employees with greater certainty regarding their working hours and earnings while also recognising the operational requirements of employers.
The banded-hours provisions provide for eight bands of weekly working hours, ranging from 3 hours to less than 6 hours per week at the lowest end to 36 hours and over at the highest. The range of bands reflects the variety of working arrangements that exist across the labour market and ensures that employees working lower numbers of regular hours may also avail of the protections provided by the legislation.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will consider introducing measures requiring employers to offer increased contracted hours to part-time employees who consistently work beyond their contractual hours, and to give existing employees priority when additional working hours become available, particularly in the retail sector.

Clause 5.3 of Council Directive 97/81/EC concerning the Framework Agreement on part-time work states that employers should, as far as possible, consider requests from employees to transfer between full-time and part-time work.
Ireland addressed this by implementing a Code of Practice on Access to Part Time Work, prepared by the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC), in consultation with social partners. This Code of Practice has been recently revised by the WRC and was signed into law in January this year. The Code is admissible in evidence in any proceedings before a Court, the Labour Court, or a Workplace Relations Commission Officer.
The Code states that, as far as possible, employers should give consideration to requests by employees to transfer from full-time to part-time work; and requests by employees to transfer from part-time to full-time work-or to increase their working time should the opportunity arise.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether his attention or the attention of his officials has been drawn to the problem of forever chemicals and PFAS associated with data centres.
reply:
My department and I are aware of concerns regarding per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), commonly known as ‘forever chemicals’, including their potential use in data centre infrastructure.
PFAS are a group of man-made chemicals used in various industrial applications. They are highly persistent in the environment and raise concerns regarding potential impacts on human health and the environment. Depending on the technologies used, PFAS may be present in certain cooling systems, electrical components and other data centre equipment.
At EU level, the Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability aims to phase out PFAS unless their use is essential. A broad restriction proposal submitted by authorities in Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden to the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) in 2023 is at an advanced stage of assessment, including assessments following two public consultations, with a final opinion expected by the end of 2026 and a European Commission proposal anticipated in 2027. The EU proposal will not be available for EU Member States such as Ireland to assess and comment on until the ECHA and EU process is concluded.

question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to ensure that the megalithic tomb at Knockmaree Dolmen in the Phoenix Park is properly preserved and not subjected to further antisocial behaviour which has previously damaged the tomb.
reply:
The tomb referred to by the Deputy has many names. It is sometimes called the Knockmaree or Knockmary dolmen or cyst, the Knockmaree Linkardstown grave or simply the Linkardstown tomb. It is about 5,000 years old, with a capstone measuring around 2 m in length and 1 m in width that is supported by four slabs. It has a modern concrete pillar for stability. The underground chamber has a floor of compacted clay.
The cromlech was discovered in 1838 by workmen who were employed by the then commissioners of woods and forests to remove an ancient tumulus. When discovered, there were two almost complete male skeletons in the crouched position found inside the chamber. The artifacts found in the burial, which include a flint knife and a shell necklace, can now be found in the National Museum of Ireland.
Located close to the Chapelizod pedestrian entrance of the Phoenix Park, the tomb is cared for by the Office of Public Works, through their management of the Phoenix Park.
Unfortunately, the cromlech has been damaged a number of times over the course of its history. There are photographs from the 1970s that show the cromlech in pieces on the ground. It was extensively repaired with dowels at this time.
The Office of Public Works is committed to the repair and protection of the historically important cromlech, and has a monitoring programme in place to help ensure its protection. The cromlech is protected by the National Monuments Acts 1930 to 2014 and is a recorded monument RMP DU18 -

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the number of applications within the civil service mobility scheme that were impacted by the Human Resources Management System IT flaw which misrecorded departmental cancellations under the status "Employee Cancelled"; the steps the National Shared Services Office has taken to correct the historical records of the affected civil servants; the specific date on which the system modification agreed with the Department’s Mobility Policy section was fully implemented; and the total financial cost incurred to deliver this software patch and system upgrade.
reply:
I am informed by the NSSO that previously the system functionality for employee mobility requests only contained one reason for cancellation, namely, “employee cancelled”.
I understand that one NSSO customer questioned the cancellation reason which did not reflect their individual circumstances. Following development and testing, the functionality of the system was changed on 11 June, 2026 to provide more specific options when recording reasons for cancellation to include cancellations by Departmental administrators as well as employees.
I am informed that the costs were covered within the NSSO budget for IT development work for 2026 which provides for patching and upgrading of the Human Resources Management System as required throughout the year.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the number of mobility transfer offers within the civil service mobility scheme that were withdrawn or blocked due to alleged conflict of interest from 2024 to date in 2026; the specific criteria and guidelines utilised by departments to define and verify conflicts; the reason an independent, comprehensive general appeals mechanism does not exist to allow civil servants to formally contest these specific decisions; if he will act to eliminate this administrative deficit by establishing an independent appeals process to ensure transparency and protect staff from arbitrary or unverified refusals.
reply:
The Civil Service Mobility Scheme offers civil servants an opportunity to apply for Mobility (i.e. transfer) through an open and transparent system in the Civil Service only. Mobility opportunities are currently available for all general service staff members (Clerical Officer, Executive Officer, Higher Executive Officer, Administration Officer, Assistant Principal Officer, Principal Officer).
The Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation is responsible for setting overarching mobility policy in the Civil Service. The National Shared Service Office are the lead administrators of the scheme. Local Human Resources units are considered the lead administrators of the scheme where an offer is under consideration or has been made.
As per the Civil Service Mobility Scheme, a formal offer of mobility may be withdrawn in exceptional circumstances, as determined by the Local HR Unit. Such cases are considered on an individual basis. Where an offer has been withdrawn, the matter is managed by the relevant Local HR Unit. Records of these decisions are not held centrally by the Mobility Policy Unit.
As per the Civil Service Mobility Scheme, an applicant only has a right to lodge an appeal to the relevant HR unit if the applicant is deemed unsuitable on the grounds of attendance. This provision formed part of the agreed arrangement when the scheme was introduced in 2018. There are currently no plans to renew or amend these appeal provisions.

reply:

The Government recognises the risks associated with climate change and that increases in sea levels and storm surges will result in increased frequency of coastal erosion. In response to these challenges, the recommendations outlined in the Report of the Interdepartmental Group on National Coastal Change Management Strategy are being implemented.
The OPW has been designated by Government as the national lead coordinating body for the assessment of coastal change hazards and risks and the assessment of technical options and constraints. These assessments will build upon indicative assessment work previously undertaken by the OPW under the Irish Coastal Protection Strategy Study.
To implement the recommendations of the Coastal Change Management Strategy, the OPW is nearing the completion of a LiDAR survey of the entire national coastline that will produce high-resolution elevation data (digital elevation models) and imagery of the coastal zone and has commissioned an oblique imagery survey of the entire national coastline, that will produce high-resolution side-on images of the coast line around the country. The OPW has also developed and is populating a coastal asset defence database that identifies and collates data on the coastal frontage, such as man-made defences and natural features, dunes systems, etc.
All of these data will inform the National Coastal Erosion Hazard Mapping project that is currently being procured b

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation whether contracts recorded in his Department's internal contract register can be linked to their corresponding contract award notices published on eTenders, where applicable; whether his Department records the relevant eTenders notice reference, URL or other identifier; and if not, the reasons that prevent this information from being recorded.
reply:

All purchase orders raised on the system require a contract to be in place, to be in date and to have sufficient remaining funds available to fulfil the purchase order value in full.

question: Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if his Department has liaised with the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration on the number of gardaí who have returned to work in the force since 2013 after a break from service; and if his Department has costed whether a uniform service exemption to section 10 of the public service pension would be possible.
reply:
The Single Public Service Pension Scheme is a statutory Public Service Career-Average Defined Benefit Pension Scheme. It was established under the Public Service Pensions (Single Scheme and Other Provisions) Act 2012.
The provisions of the Single Scheme are clearly set out in law. All new-entrant public servants hired after 1 January 2013 are members of the Single Scheme. This includes uniformed members in An Garda Síochána, the Defence Forces, full-time Firefighters and Prison Officers.
Section 10 of the Public Service Pensions (Single Scheme and Other Provisions) Act 2012 sets out who membership of the Single Scheme applies to and any derogations applicable. For example, Section 10(5)(b) sets out that, where an individual was a member of a pre-existing public service pension scheme, left the public service and then returned to pensionable public service within 26 weeks of the last day of the previous employment, that individual has a right to remain in the relevant pre-existing public service pension scheme in their new role. Where the gap is greater than 26 weeks, the individual must be placed in the Single Scheme. This derogation applies across all cohorts of pensionable public service employees.
The introduction of the Single Scheme is central to ensuring the long?term sustainability of public service pensions, particularly in the context of improved life expectancy and rising public service employee numbers.
There are no planned changes to the derogations in Section 10

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the legislative basis for transferring to An Post the payment of pensions to civil servants who resigned or retired from the former Department of Posts & Telegraphs and who never worked in An Post; and the arrangements put in place for the calculation and payment of increases in these pensions.
reply:
Section 46 of the Postal and Telecommunications Services Act 1983, as amended by section 11 of the Telecommunications (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1996 and section 5 of the Postal and Telecommunications Services (Amendment) Act 1999, provides that a superannuation scheme prepared by An Post may include persons who were members of the staff of the former Department of Posts and Telegraphs and who retired or died before vesting day, 1 January 1984.
The legislation also provides for contributions by the Minister for Finance, as specified in schemes made pursuant to the 1983 Act, towards pensions, gratuities and other allowances related to reckonable service prior to 1 January 1984 in respect of this group.
An Post administers and pays the pensions concerned to those individuals or their dependants. Pension increases for individuals in this group are awarded in accordance with the relevant scheme rules applicable to former staff of the Department who retired or died before vesting day, having regard to the relevant departmental directions on civil service pension increases.
Following a request from the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport, I provided my concurrence on 28 September 2026 to the application of a series of pension increases for this group. reply:

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if a hardship mechanism exists in respect of recovery of overpayments from civil servants; the position regarding ensuring that repayment plans or deductions can be arranged in a manner that takes account of hardship of an individual employee in exceptional circumstances; and the discretion and safeguards that can or will be provided to civil service human resources and salaries departments in respect of same.
reply:
Circular 07/2018 Recovery of Salary, Allowances, and Expenses Overpayments made to Staff Members/Former Staff Members/Pensioners outlines the provisions for the recovery of salary, allowances and expenses overpayments in the Civil Service. The Circular includes provisions to address cases where the standard recovery arrangements would cause undue hardship and provides a mechanism for the consideration of exceptional circumstances.
Where a staff member considers that a proposed repayment arrangement would result in undue hardship, they may apply for a review of their case. Such applications are considered by a person designated by the relevant HR Manager and are assessed on the basis of the information and supporting documentation provided by the applicant.
In considering a request, account may be taken of the financial hardship arising from the proposed recovery arrangements and, where relevant, other circumstances associated with the overpayment. Any exceptional or hardship arrangement may also be reviewed periodically to ensure that it remains appropriate.
The Circular provides a structured mechanism for dealing with exceptional hardship circumstances, enabling Civil Service HR functions to exercise appropriate discretion, supported by defined review and assessment processes, while ensuring the proper recovery of monies due to the Exchequer.

reply:
The Infrastructure Division in my Department has been significantly expanded in the past year and a half to deliver on the Government's Accelerating Infrastructure agenda, which is vital to achieve the Government’s wider climate action objectives. The Accelerating Infrastructure Action Plan is already speeding up the approval of key projects which will have positive climate and environmental impacts. This defence-in-depth security strategy includes the implementation of an extensive Information Security Management System (ISMS) comprising of security policies and controls, aligned and certified to the international security standard ISO 27001:2022 to address risks from cyber security attacks. This framework underpins our overall approach for managing and mitigating cyber risks. Core capabilities such as threat analysis, vulnerability management, and cyber infrastructure support are delivered through an appropriate combination of resources and skillsets.

question: Deputy Johnny Mythen asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation with the ever-continuing digitalisation of public services, the measures that are in place to ensure that there can be no disadvantages to older people, people with disabilities or those with limited digital literacy; and the way in which access to in-person and telephone services will be maintained where needed.
reply:
A core element of the successful implementation of digital public services is ensuring that individuals needs and preferences are factored in to the design of these digital-first, but not digital-only, services, to avoid excluding people from participating fully with these services.
Work to develop the Life Events model for Irish public services so far has included engagement across a range of users with amplified needs when engaging with public services. This has included research with older adults and adults with intellectual disabilities to understand their preferences, challenges and needs when engaging digitally with the State. Understanding the experience of such users is the primary starting point for building out public services, recognising that access is dependent on having the requisite skills, and knowledge, and also the availability of material resources and connectivity.
This approach has allowed the work to move beyond merely increasing digitisation and toward a more holistic set of digitally enabled services that can be accessed across multiple channels, including over the telephone and are centered on the needs of the user, proactively mitigating exclusion.
Through the process of design the human journey of using a service is mapped out end to end based on real insight helping to highlight shared challenges and opportunities for improvement. question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to outline the work of the Accelerating Infrastructure Taskforce; and to set out its achievements to date.
reply:
I established the Accelerating Infrastructure Taskforce in May 2025 to advise and support my Department’s work to remove barriers to infrastructure delivery.
I chair the non-statutory Taskforce, which comprises six independent experts with experience in infrastructure delivery and eight ex-officio members from commercial semi-State bodies and the local government sector.
The Taskforce contributed to the development of the Accelerating Infrastructure Report and Action Plan, which the Government published in December 2025, by considering the key barriers to delivery and potential measures to address them.

Responsibility for implementation of each action remains with the Departments, agencies and other bodies assigned to lead them.
Its contribution is reflected in the matters considered at its meetings. Minutes are published on Gov.ie, providing a transparent record of its work: Accelerating Infrastructure Taskforce (www.gov.ie/en/department-of-public-expenditure-infrastructure-public-service-reform-and-digitalisation/collections/accelerating-infrastructure-taskforce-meetings/#relevant-links)

question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation for an update in relation to the Thomastown flood relief scheme.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 559, 560, 561 and 562 together.
To establish those communities that are at risk from significant flood events, the OPW completed the largest study of flood risk ever undertaken by the State in 2018. The OPW Catchment-based Flood Risk Assessment and Management (CFRAM) Programme was undertaken by engineering consultants on behalf of the OPW, working in partnership with local authorities. The CFRAM Programme studied 80% of Ireland’s primary flood risk and identified solutions that can protect over 95% of that risk.
The Government has committed €1.3 billion to the delivery of flood relief schemes over the lifetime of the National Development Plan to protect approximately 23,000 properties in communities that are under threat from river and coastal flood risk.
Since 2018, as part of a phased approach to scheme delivery, funding under the National Development Plan has allowed the OPW to treble work on flood relief schemes, through partnership with local authorities. Consequently, some 100 flood relief schemes are at design, planning or construction at this time.

In 2025, over €100m was spent on delivering flood relief schemes. This is a record high annual expenditure and is reflective of progress in delivering flood relief schemes nationally

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to provide an update on the review of a communications network (details supplied) for emergency services following Storm Eowyn which he stated was to be undertaken to avoid any repeated issues during future extreme weather events of the scale of Storm Eowyn; and if engagement has taken place with organisations.
reply:
Since Storm Éowyn officials in my Department have reviewed policies and procedures with Tetra Ireland due to the disruption caused by the extreme weather. Tetra Ireland has since implemented a number of improvements in the availability of equipment and new operational procedures.
Tetra Ireland has obtained additional generator units that can be deployed in the event of another sustained power outage to maintain service. A number of base station sites in the West and Northwest have also been upgraded to allow for additional battery and generator capacity.
Additionally, the 2026/2027 winter preventative maintenance inspection programme has been completed at all Tetra base station sites which included verification that battery backup units are performing as designed.

In recent weeks, officials from my Department have attended pre-winter preparedness check meetings with Tetra Ireland ESB networks to confirm that all parties are prepared for future storm events.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation whether any further progress has been made by the OPW in identifying a future usage for the Debtors Prison on Halston Street, given the new measures being brought in to tackle vacancy and dereliction in urban areas what steps will the OPW take to bring it into full use.
reply:
The Debtors’ Prison, Green Street, Dublin, originally known as the Sherriff’s Prison, was built in 1794 and ceased to function as a prison in the mid-nineteenth century. In the late 1860s, the property transferred to the Commissioners of Public Works in Ireland (CPW) to manage and was converted into a barracks for the Dublin Metropolitan Police and subsequently became a Garda station. An Garda Síochána vacated the property in 1962.
It was subsequently leased to Dublin Corporation and was used by them for the provision of emergency housing until 1987. In 1992 a lease was granted to the Green Street Trust however, due to difficulties with funding the lease was surrendered in 2006.
The OPW has over the years consulted with several agencies including Dublin City Council, to examine possible future uses for the property. A variety of uses have been explored, however as the property would require extensive refurbishment works, including fire safety works to comply with current regulations, and given the development limitations due to the property’s protected structure status, the level of substantial investment required has prevented its redevelopment.
The Debtors Prison is the last of the original debtor’s prisons in Dublin and is significant from an architectural and heritage point of view. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation further to Parliamentary Question No. 282 of 7 July 2026, whether the Department has undertaken any assessment of risks to reporting persons arising from administrative practices or interpretations currently subject to statutory or European review; the dates, findings and recommendations of any such assessment; whether any additional interim guidance or safeguards have been issued to public bodies; and if no assessment or additional guidance has been provided, the reasons for that decision.
reply:
The protections afforded to reporting persons under the Protected Disclosures Act 2014, as amended, continue to have full force and effect. The operation of the statutory framework is neither suspended nor qualified by the conduct of legislative or policy reviews.
The Act imposes clear and enforceable obligations on employers and public bodies in relation to the establishment, operation and resourcing of internal and external reporting channels. It also provides for specialised reporting channels in respect of disclosures relating to law enforcement, security, defence, international relations, and intelligence matters.
The legislation provides a suite of protections for reporting persons. It expressly prohibits penalisation, or the threat of penalisation, arising from the making of a protected disclosure. Penalisation is construed broadly and includes unfair dismissal, suspension, demotion, loss of pay or prospects, adverse changes to working conditions or hours, disciplinary action, reassignment of duties, coercion, intimidation, and harassment.
Statutory protection from penalisation is provided primarily through the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC), which may make orders for reinstatement, re-engagement, or compensation of up to five years' remuneration. Decisions of the WRC may be appealed to the Labour Court.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the assessment that has been undertaken of the practical accessibility and effectiveness of protection and remedies available to former public-sector employees who allege continuing penalisation following protected disclosures, including persons engaged in prolonged litigation or experiencing serious financial hardship; whether additional interim support measures have been considered.
reply:
Section 2A of the Protected Disclosures Act 2014, which was substantively amended in 2022, provides for a statutory review as follows:
“The Minister shall -
(a) not later than the end of the period of 5 years beginning on the passing of the Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 2022, commence a review of the operation of this Act, and
(b) not more than 12 months after the end of the period referred to in paragraph (a), make a report to each House of the Oireachtas of the findings made on the review and the conclusions drawn from those findings.”
This section of the Act ensures that a review is commenced in July 2027 at the latest, however, as the Deputy will be aware, the review of the legislation is due to commence in advance of 2027 with a public consultation expected to launch by the end of this year.
All aspects of the operation of the Act may be examined as part of this review and any recommendations to amend the legislation emanating from this engagement will be considered in full.
Full details of the public consultation are expected to be published on my Department's website in the coming weeks and the Deputy is encouraged to make proposals in that regard.

reply:

• An assessment of the completeness of the measures, i.e. if all the requirements of the Directive have been transposed and,
• an assessment of the conformity of the measures with the requirements of the Directive.
Two infringements were opened against Ireland in January 2022, both of which concerned the first type of assessment i.e. failure to notify measures transposing and failure to transpose the EU Directive 2019/1937. question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will consider introducing measures to ensure that persons with lifelong disabilities who inherit assets from their parents or guardians for the purpose of their future care and wellbeing are not disadvantaged through inheritance tax liabilities.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 532, 538 and 549 together.
The Capital Acquisitions Tax Consolidation Act 2003 (CATCA 2003) contains a number of exemptions from Capital Acquisitions Tax (CAT) for gifts and inheritances taken by individuals who are incapacitated by reason of physical or mental infirmity. The principal exemptions relevant to such individuals are outlined below.
Section 84 CATCA 2003 provides a specific exemption from CAT for a gift or inheritance taken exclusively to cover the “qualifying expenses” of an individual who is permanently incapacitated by reason of mental or physical infirmity. “Qualifying expenses” are expenses relating to medical care, including hospital charges, doctors’ fees, medicines and other pharmaceutical costs, together with the cost of maintenance relating to medical care. For the exemption to apply, the individual must be permanently incapacitated by reason of mental or physical infirmity, the benefit must be provided exclusively to meet qualifying expenses, and there must be clear evidence from the disponer (the person making the gift or bequest), whether by will or otherwise, that the benefit is provided solely for these purposes. Further information on this exemption is available in Capital Acquisitions Tax Manual Part 22, which can be found on the Revenue website at: www.revenue.ie/en/tax-professionals/tdm/capital-acquisitions-tax/cat-manual/part-09-exemptions/section-84-exemption-relating-to-qualifying-expenses-of-incapacitated-ind

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether his Department has assessed estimates of the lifetime net fiscal impact of migrants entering Ireland at different ages, taking account of tax contributions and public expenditure over their lifetime; if so, the methodology and findings; and if not, whether the Department considers such modelling necessary for evidence-based migration and public expenditure planning.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 545, 546, 547 and 548 together.
As part of the Department's mission to manage the public finances and to play a central role in the achievement of the Government’s economic and social goals, it undertakes research and analysis across a wide range of policy areas, in order to consider and assess their potential impacts on Ireland’s economy and public finances.
The Department's Future Forty: Ireland's Demographic Outlook, published in September 2025, undertook novel analysis to develop long-term migration projections for various migrant groups in Ireland.
The Department's subsequent publication, Future Forty: A Fiscal and Economic Outlook to 2065, which was published in November 2025, underlined the important role that net inward migration will continue to play in sustaining Ireland's long-term labour market development. The analysis also highlights the importance of demographics, including (net) inward migration, for fiscal sustainability into the future.
Analysing the net fiscal contribution of specific migrant groups in Ireland is not a straightforward exercise - data limitations and the challenges associated with fully attributing fiscal contributions and costs for various migrant groups, given variance in age and income distributions, are to the fore.
To date, therefore, the Department has not commissioned, completed or published any specific research or analysis regarding the net fiscal impacts of specific migrant groups in Ireland.
Howeve

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance for an update on progress towards delivering the Funds Sector 2030 commitment to abolish the eight-year deemed disposal requirement for Irish-domiciled investment funds; the way this commitment will be progressed in the context of the levers identified in the Roadmap for the Taxation of Retail Investment, including reducing tax rates and simplifying the taxation and administration of retail investments; whether he will confirm that the necessary measures will be progressed in advance of Budget 2028.
reply:

The main focus of the roadmap, and the Government’s action in this area in this year’s Budget, is the introduction of the new investment account, which will provide a simpler and more accessible investment option for retail investors. Investments held in these accounts will not be subject to the existing deemed disposal regime and will only be liable for tax when the account exceeds a value of €50,000.
However, the roadmap also identified three policy levers to be considered as part of the reform of the existing regime for taxation of retail investment. These are changes to the rate of taxation, reviewing the deemed disposal rule and administrative simplification.
In line with this, at Budget 2027 I announced a reduction in the rate of tax applying to Irish and equivalent offshore investment funds, as well as Irish and certain life assurance policies, from 38% to 35% taking effect from 1 January 2027. I also announced that the legislation underpinning the taxation of investment funds the units of which are held in a recognised clearing system, including Irish domiciled exchange-traded funds (ETFs), will be amended to bring greater clarity and certainty for investors.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance for an update on the drawdown of the €1.1 billion in funding from outbound payments defensive measures, including the amount drawn down to date; and whether progress on this funding will inform consideration of amending or abolishing the outbound payment restriction.
reply:
I thank the Deputy for her question. I am taking the €1.1 billion referred to in the question as being the total funding expected to be received under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF). Ireland’s RRF allocation is €1.15 billion, including REPowerEU.
The RRF is a performance-based instrument with payment contingent on evidenced completion of agreed milestones and targets. The Outbound Payments Defensive Measures (OPDM) is just one reform milestone included as part of Ireland’s recovery and resilience plan which includes 19 investment streams and 11 reforms in total. RRF projects are pre-funded through the Estimates processes and the National Development Plan, with the RRF allocated funding being recouped from the EU after the milestones and targets have been achieved.
Outbound Payments Defensive Measures
The Outbound Payments Defensive Measures (OPDM) were introduced in Finance (No.2) Act 2023. The purpose of these measures is to tackle aggressive tax planning and prevent double non-taxation and to meet a specific milestone under the Recovery and Resilience Plan. The measures operate by applying withholding taxes on outbound payments of interest, royalties and distributions (such as dividends) made by Irish resident companies, or by Irish branches of non-resident companies, to associated entities who are resident, or situated, in specified territories.

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the current position regarding investments held by the Ireland Strategic Investment Fund (ISIF) in companies listed on the United Nations database of businesses involved in activities relating to Israeli settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, and whether any investments in such companies have been sold or are under review.
reply:
The Government has made it clear that it opposes illegal Israeli settlements, which are contrary to international law and damaging to the pursuit of peace in the Middle East. Ireland has not been found wanting in its support of the Palestinian people and has taken practical steps at national, EU and international levels. We have been a clear and leading voice on this. Ireland has provided significant financial support to the people in Palestine since January 2023.
It is important to say from the outset that ISIF, has complete independence in implementing its investment strategy under the NTMA Acts through an investment committee that reports to the NTMA's board.
ISIF has, to date, completed several divestment programmes and excluded investments from the Fund, consistent with legislative changes enacted by the Oireachtas. Exclusion is used on a limited basis, reflecting exclusions mandated by legislation including the Fossil Fuel Divestment Act 2018 and the Cluster Munitions and Anti-Personnel Mines Act 2008 and exclusions on sustainable investment grounds including tobacco, nuclear weapons and certain companies on the UN Database.
ISIF has taken an investment decision to divest from six companies, all of which remain on the updated UN Database, with a total value at the time of the divestment decision of approximately €2.95m. question: Deputy Ged Nash asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the number of PAYE taxpayer units who may have either underpayments or overpayments for the 2024 and 2025 tax years respectively; the average value of underpayments; the average value of overpayments for each year concerned; and the number of PAYE units who have not yet submitted a tax return for each year.
reply:
At the end of every year, Revenue makes a Preliminary End of Year Statement (PEOYS) available to employees. The PEOYS sets out a provisional tax position based on the information available on Revenue records. It shows whether an employee has paid the correct amount of Income Tax and Universal Social Charge (USC) for the year.
I am advised by Revenue that the final position for PAYE taxpayers can only be determined when taxpayers submit their tax returns at the end of the year and where appropriate, claim any additional credits or reliefs that may be due or declare any additional income they may have received.
To assist taxpayers in regularising their position, Revenue issues letters to taxpayers who according to their PEOYS, may have either overpaid or underpaid tax in a particular tax year. These letters advise recipients to submit a PAYE Income Tax return to claim any additional tax credits or reliefs that may be due and/or to declare any additional income they may have received. These letters also remind taxpayers of a four-year statutory time limit in respect of submitting such claims.
Revenue has further advised me that over 894,000 PAYE taxpayer units, who have paid or are liable to pay tax, have yet to file an Income Tax return for 2024 and approximately 1.3 million have yet to file for 2025. question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether the Central Bank of Ireland has assessed the effectiveness of current safeguards operated by banks and online savings platforms in preventing customers from transferring substantial sums to fraudulent accounts.
reply:
The Central Bank of Ireland supports the integrity of the financial system to ensure it operates in a clean, transparent and accountable way.
Within that context, the Central Bank supervises regulated firms’ systems and controls for anti-money laundering, countering the financing of terrorism and fraud. This includes inspections, targeted and thematic reviews, and financial crime review meetings to assess the adequacy and effectiveness of firms’ risk management frameworks.
The Central Bank has recently completed a detailed thematic review of authorised push payment fraud in the banking and payments sector and expects to communicate the outcomes to relevant firms and sectors in due course, including both good practices the Central Bank has seen and where material gaps exist that require remediation.

question: Deputy John McGuinness asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance To ask the Minister for Finance whether the main banks, and other consumer lenders, should provide publicly accessible online calculators for personal loans (details supplied).
reply:
It is extremely important that consumers are supported and feel confident making financial decisions, particularly when taking out credit.
Under the Central Bank of Ireland's Consumer Protection Code, while it is not required that firms must provide online calculators, firms are required to inform their customers effectively by:
- ensuring that information is provided to a customer in such a way that the material features of the product or service in question can reasonably be understood by the customer;
- ensuring that all information provided to a customer is clear, accurate, up to date, and written in plain and accessible language, avoiding the unnecessary use of technical terms; and
- providing information to customers on a timely basis and bringing key information to the attention of customers.
Firms should consider how best to inform their customers through the use of various formats and delivery channels to meet the needs of their customer base taking account of factors including levels of financial literacy and knowledge and experience.
In relation to financial literacy, my Department is overseeing the rollout of Ireland’s National Financial Literacy Strategy which was published in February last year. This strategy has among its objectives that of supporting consumers in understanding credit and managing debt.

question: Deputy Michael Collins asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will review the vehicle registration tax regime, in light of concerns that it significantly inflates the cost of second-hand vehicles in Ireland compared with equivalent vehicles available in the UK and elsewhere in Europe, increases motoring costs for families, distorts the used car market, and unfairly taxes imported vehicles on a Revenue-assessed open market selling price rather than the actual purchase price paid.
reply:
Under Irish law, vehicles in Ireland are required to be registered, and excise, in the form of Vehicle Registration Tax (VRT), is assessed and payable at the time of registration. The Finance Act 1992 (as amended), sets out the statutory framework for vehicle registration and for VRT.
For passenger cars, the VRT charge is based on the vehicle’s value in Ireland – expressed as it’s ‘open market selling price’ (OMSP) – and on its emissions. This approach to calculating the VRT charge applies to both new and used vehicles when brought into the State. The VRT charge is not affected by the place of origin of a vehicle nor, in the case of a used imported vehicle, on the place of origin where it was previously registered.
Section 133 of the Finance Act 1992 provides that the OMSP of an imported used vehicle is the price, inclusive of all taxes and duties, which, in the opinion of the Commissioners, the vehicle might reasonably be expected to fetch on a first arm’s length sale thereof in the State by retail. When a used car, which has been brought into the State, is presented for registration, Revenue determines its OMSP on a case-by-case basis, having regard to a range of factors, including real-time data from domestic dealer price guides, market advertisements, and the specific vehicle’s age, condition, and mileage.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether contracts recorded in his Department's internal contract register can be linked to their corresponding contract award notices published on eTenders, where applicable; whether his Department records the relevant eTenders notice reference, URL or other identifier; and if not, the reasons that prevent this information from being recorded.
reply:
My Department maintains an internal contract register for contract management and oversight purposes. The contract register is maintained separately from the eTenders platform and is not electronically linked to individual contract award notices published on eTenders.
Information relating to contract award notices is available on the eTenders platform in accordance with applicable public procurement requirements. The Department's contract register serves a separate contract management function and does not currently incorporate links to information published on eTenders
As the contract register and eTenders operate as separate systems, establishing and maintaining automated links between individual contract register entries and corresponding contract award notices would require additional administrative processes and system functionality which are not currently in place, and would be complex to implement.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether purchase orders issued by his Department under procurement contracts can be linked to the corresponding contracts held in its internal contract register; whether a contract reference or other unique identifier is maintained to enable this linkage; and if not, the way his Department monitors cumulative expenditure against the approved value of each contract.
reply:
My Department uses the Financial Management Shared Service (FMSS), operated by the National Shared Services Office (NSSO), to support its accounting and financial management processes.
Contracts entered into by the Department are recorded in FMSS and a unique contract identifier is maintained within the system. Purchase orders associated with procurement expenditure are processed through FMSS and may be linked to the relevant contract records held within the system.
FMSS incorporates a range of financial and procurement controls designed to support contract management and expenditure oversight. These include controls which facilitate the monitoring of expenditure against approved contract values and which prevent expenditure in excess of approved contract limits without the appropriate authorisation.
My Department is therefore able to monitor expenditure incurred under contracts through the financial controls and reporting functionality available within FMSS and through oversight arrangements operated by the relevant business areas and finance functions. My Department maintains its contract register separately from the FMSS system.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the extent to which his Department is engaging with an organisation (details supplied) and industry stakeholders regarding the Section 481 film tax credit; and if he will introduce a permanent 8% regional uplift for audio-visual productions based outside the Dublin metropolitan area and Ashford (DMAA) corridor to address the 10% to 12% additional cost burden faced by regional producers, protect local creative talent, and expand production capacity nationwide.
reply:
Finance Act 2018 introduced a short-term, tapered regional uplift under the Section 481 Film tax credit for productions being made in areas designated under the State aid regional guidelines (among other criteria).
As the regional uplift was an approved State aid, any restoration of the uplift would require approval from the European Commission. It is worth noting that the Section 481 Film tax credit is explicitly linked to the promotion of Irish or European culture.
While the uplift was not a Regional Aid measure, it operated by reference to the regional aid map in force at the time it was introduced. A new regional aid map, covering a significantly smaller geographic area, came into effect in April 2021; consequently, it is not expected that such an approach would be viable for a future relief to support activities outside the main Dublin production hub.
Since the expiration of the Regional Uplift, Government supports for audio-visual productions have been considerably enhanced and broadened. There are no geographic restrictions on the availability of these supports, so they are available to projects taking place in all regions of the State.
For example, the Scéal Uplift was introduced as part of Finance Act 2024 to provide for an uplift of 8 per cent to the existing Film Tax Credit rate of 32 per cent for small-to-medium sized productions with a maximum qualifying expenditure of €20 million where certain additional cultural criteria are also met. question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will review the current double taxation arrangements between Ireland and Jordan, including whether a bilateral double taxation agreement could be introduced to prevent individuals and businesses from being taxed on the same income in both jurisdictions.
reply:
Ireland's long-standing policy has been to expand, maintain, and enhance Ireland's tax treaty network to remove barriers and facilitate trade. Ireland has signed 78 comprehensive tax treaties, of which 75 are currently in effect. Ireland remains open to assess all options to develop its tax treaty network further in that context.
Ireland published a Tax Treaty Policy Statement (https://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/irelands-tax-treaty-policy-statement.pdf) in 2022 and the statement formalises the policy of maintaining and enhancing the network of double tax agreements to provide for continued economic prosperity. The statement also provides the criteria for the creation of a priority list of potential partners.
Priority A jurisdictions for Ireland are the members of the G20. Priority B is to have tax treaties in place with all current OECD member countries and accession countries, as well as EU accession countries. Priority C is to modernise Ireland’s older tax treaties which may not be fully in line with recent treaties and current international norms.
These are the criteria which assist in identifying and prioritising future tax treaty negotiations generally but does not preclude any discussions beyond this where an economic justification for such an engagement can be evidenced.

question: Deputy Niamh Smyth asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance further to Parliamentary Question No. 72042/26, if he will review the correspondence; whether he will consider introducing a transitional arrangement for first-time buyers who received the previous maximum help-to-buy relief of €30,000 shortly before the increase to €35,000 announced in Budget 2027 and whose homes remain under construction; and if any alternative remedy is available.
reply:
I refer the Deputy to my reply to Parliamentary Question No. 188 of 13 October 2026.
As set out in that reply, as part of Budget 2027, I announced that the maximum amount of the relief, which can be claimed by a first time purchaser or self builder, would increase by €5,000, to €35,000. The change was implemented by way of a Budget night Financial Resolution which took effect from 7 October 2026.
Accordingly, the increased maximum amount of relief (€35,000) applies to HTB claimants who enter into a contract for the purchase of a new build home, or, in the case of a self-build home, who draw down the first tranche of their mortgage, on or after 7 October 2026.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the rationale for the €42,500 VAT threshold for businesses supplying services.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 524 and 525 together.
I am advised by Revenue that VAT registration thresholds are subject to the requirements of EU VAT law, with which Irish VAT law is obliged to comply. In general, the EU VAT Directive requires that all businesses supplying taxable goods and services are registered for VAT, charge VAT on those supplies to their customers, file returns and remit the VAT to the relevant national tax authority. However, the EU VAT Directive also permits a Member State to operate arrangements — within certain parameters — to allow small businesses to remain outside this system entirely, provided their turnover remains below a set level.
Ireland has operated VAT registration thresholds for goods and for services for many years. Following increases applied in Finance Act 2024, the levels are now €85,000 for supplies of goods and €42,500 for supplies of services. A business whose turnover is below the relevant threshold is not obliged to register for VAT and can supply its customers without charging and accounting for VAT, thereby avoiding entirely the administrative burden of VAT registration, record-keeping, and the filing of periodic VAT returns. The benefit of remaining below the threshold is therefore significant: such businesses have no VAT reporting obligations. Businesses whose turnover is below the relevant threshold are also entitled to elect to register should they so wish.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the rationale for the exclusion from relevant rent-related tax reliefs and supports of tenants renting a property from a closely related family member, even where the tenancy is a bona fide arrangement, the tenancy is registered with the Residential Tenancies Board market rent is being paid, and all tax obligations are being complied with; if he will review the current provisions to determine whether such tenants are being unfairly disadvantaged; and if he will consider amending the eligibility criteria to allow renters in genuine registered family tenancies to qualify.
reply:
The Rent Tax Credit (RTC) was introduced by the Finance Act 2022 and may be claimed by taxpayer units in respect of qualifying rent paid in 2022 and subsequent years to end-2028.
The credit is available in the following circumstances:
- where the claimant makes a qualifying payment in respect of a residential property which he or she uses as his or her principal private residence,
- where the claimant makes a qualifying payment in respect of a residential property which he or she uses to facilitate his or her attendance at or participation in his or her employment, office holding, trade, profession or an approved course, and
- where the claimant makes a qualifying payment in respect of a residential property which his or her child uses to facilitate his or her child’s attendance at or participation in an approved course.
The value of the credit for 2022 and 2023 was €500 for a singly assessed individual and €1,000 for a jointly assessed couple. For later years, the value of the credit increased to €1,000 for a singly assessed individual and €2,000 for a jointly assessed couple. Budget 2027 provided for the value of the credit to increase to €1,150 for a singly assessed individual and €2,300 for a jointly assessed couple.
Where the relationship between the claimant and the landlord is that of parent and child, or vice versa, the credit will not be available.
