question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the measures currently in place that will allow credit unions to finance the development of homes by approved housing bodies; and if restrictions are placed on any types of AHBs and moves to expand opportunities in this space.
reply:
Investment in Approved Housing Bodies (AHBs) is permitted under credit union regulations, introduced by the Central Bank of Ireland in March 2018. Under Regulation 25(1)(f) of the Credit Union Act 1997 (Regulatory Requirements) Regulations 2016, credit unions may invest through regulated investment vehicles where the underlying investments of the regulated investment vehicle are investments in permitted Approved Housing Bodies, as defined in the Regulations.
One Credit Union AHB Fund has been established under these Regulations. This is a Fund that all credit unions can invest their members’ savings in, subject to the limits as set out under the Regulations. Further information on the Fund, including its prospectus and updates on its investments, is available on the Credit Union AHB Fund website.
It is important to note that the Credit Union AHB Fund is independently established and governed, and neither I nor the Minister of State is involved in its operation. Furthermore, investment in the Credit Union AHB Fund is an independent decision for each individual credit union and their respective board of directors.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the way in which his Department is building cyber resilience; and the strategy in place to address cyber attacks.
reply:
I wish to advise the Deputy that the majority of ICT systems and associated services for my Department are provided by the Office of the Government Chief Information Officer (OGCIO), a division of the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation. OGCIO continuously enhances and strengthens ICT security measures to mitigate against emerging threats, risks, vulnerabilities and cybersecurity attacks.
My Department works closely with OGCIO and the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which monitors, detects and responds to cybersecurity incidents in the State, and builds resilience in IT systems with particular emphasis on critical infrastructure and Government.
For reasons of operational security, the Department does not disclose details of systems, tools, or processes in use to counter cyber attacks. However, I can assure the Deputy that my Department is committed to maintaining a robust and resilient cybersecurity posture.
Cybersecurity risks are assessed and managed as part of the Department's overall risk management framework. All staff are kept up to date on emerging cybersecurity threats and are required to complete annual cybersecurity awareness training.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if families who require a larger vehicle due to the disability related needs of their children may qualify for relief under the disabled drivers and disabled passengers scheme; the circumstances in which such relief may apply.
reply:
The Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme (DDS) provides relief from VRT and VAT on an adapted car, as well as an exemption from motor tax and an annual fuel grant.
The Scheme is open to severely and permanently disabled persons, as defined, as a driver or as a passenger and also to certain charitable organisations. In order to qualify for relief, the applicant must hold a Primary Medical Certificate issued by the relevant Principal Medical Officer (PMO) or a Board Medical Certificate issued by the Disabled Driver Medical Board of Appeal. Certain other qualifying criteria apply in relation to the vehicle, in particular that it must be specially constructed or adapted for use by the applicant.
The DDS rules do not impose any restrictions in terms of the dimensions of a vehicle but relief is restricted to a vehicle which has an engine capacity up to 6,000cc (except for organisations under specific conditions). By way of comparison, most passenger cars have an engine capacity of between 1,000cc and 2,000cc.
There are four categories of relief which determines the maximum relief allowable to DDS recipients. This includes a fourth category of relief of up to €48,000 for disabled drivers, for in-vehicle wheelchair accessible adaptations, and up to €32,000 for disabled passengers, for in-vehicle wheelchair accessible adaptations.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will give consideration to a refundable tax credit for qualifying tourism infrastructure, modelled on Ireland’s existing film and digital games tax credits, to support investment in major visitor attractions (details supplied).

As part of this, the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment (DETE) has allocated €400 million for support of the tourism sector, also aligning with broader national objectives, including climate action and sustainable growth.
Any consideration of a new tax-based incentive for tourism infrastructure would require more detail on the proposed design of the measure, including for example the nature of qualifying expenditure, categories of eligible claimants and other terms and conditions.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether restrictions are in place, proposed, or under consideration that would prevent persons resident in the State from purchasing kerosene or home-heating oil in the North of Ireland; and if discussions have taken place with revenue or other agencies regarding the cross-border purchase of heating fuels.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 512 and 514 together.
Council Directive 2003/96/EC of 27 October 2003, commonly known as the Energy Tax Directive (ETD), governs the application of excise duty to fuels and electricity. In accordance with the ETD, Finance Act 1999 provides for an excise duty in the form of Mineral Oil Tax (MOT) to apply to liquid fuels used for motor or heating purposes. In response to the ongoing fuel crisis, I brought forward a Financial Resolution on Budget Night to cut the MOT rate on heating kerosene from €160.81 to €122.83 per 1,000 litres effective from 14 October 2026. This reverts the MOT rate to the rate in place in 2023 and gives a VAT inclusive reduction of just over 4.3 cents per litre, providing a saving of almost €40 on a 900-litre fill.
The movement of excisable liquid fuels between Member States is governed by an EU-wide control and movement regime. Heating kerosene brought into the State from other Member States, including Northern Ireland, is generally moved under duty suspension to a tax warehouse and the MOT liability is deferred until release. reply:

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if his Department is aware that as Ireland has one of the lowest tax rates at 23% VAT in Europe on online slot machines, that this low tax rate on highly addictive online slot machines incentivises international gambling companies to entice gamblers from traditional forms of sports betting to the much more addictive and harmful high speed online slot machines, taking into account that addiction service have reported increased problem gambling especially from online slot machines.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 503 and 504 together.
Far from having one of the lowest standard VAT rates in Europe, as set out in this years VAT Tax Strategy Group Paper, Ireland has the joint fourth highest standard rate of VAT in the EU, at 23%, also having a higher standard VAT rate than the UK.
Betting duty law is set out in Chapter 1 of Part 2 of Finance Act 2002, as amended. The tax operates as an excise duty and applies to bets placed by persons in the State with a licenced bookmaker (either in-person or by remote means) and on commissions earned by licenced remote betting intermediaries in the State. Section 64 of Finance Act 2002 defines a ‘bet’ as
“…a transaction involving 2 or more persons, where–
(a) the parties hold differing views regarding the outcome of an event,
(b) the parties agree that depending on the outcome of the event, one or more parties shall pay to the other or others a sum, and
(c) the event upon the outcome of which the transaction depends shall not be the outcome of a game within the meaning of this Act;”
Betting duty is payable on all bets placed within the State with a licensed bookmaker and is charged at 2% of total betting turnover.
Activities such as online cash games in online casinos do not come within the definition of a bet and, therefore, they are outside the scope of excise duty. However, general online casino gaming services (such as virtual slot machines and table games) are subject to VAT at the standard rate of 23%.

question: Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance If he will detail in full the taxation procedures around fellowships, bursaries and other academic scholarships whether for undergraduate students, postgraduate students or post-doctoral researchers.
reply:
Income arising from a scholarship held by an individual receiving full-time instruction at a university, college, school or other educational establishment is exempt from income tax, Universal Social Charge (USC) and PRSI where the conditions for the relief in accordance with Section 193 of the Taxes Consolidation Act (TCA) 1997 are met.
I am advised by Revenue that, in order to qualify for the exemption, one of the key requirements is that the individual in receipt of the scholarship income must be in full-time instruction at an educational establishment. Section 193 TCA 1997 states that a scholarship includes an exhibition, bursary or other similar education endowment. In addition, the object of the scholarship must be the promotion of the education of the holder rather than the promotion of research through the holder. For the scholarship exemption to apply, there must be no element of service (directly or indirectly) between the sponsor and the student, and the award must not arise from an office or employment (directly or indirectly) with the sponsor.
Revenue also advises that fellowships are generally regarded as being distinct from a scholarship. Students, for example post-doctoral students, who have a salaried position in order to provide research services are not considered to be under full-time instruction.
In such cases where the scholarship exemption does not apply, the payment is subject to income tax, USC and PRSI and must be calculated in the normal way.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether it is his intention, under proposed new arrangements for the collection and enforcement of the derelict sites levy/derelict property tax by the Revenue Commissioners, for all monies collected to be transferred to the relevant local authorities in whose administrative areas the liable properties are located; and the mechanism by which such funds will be distributed.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 494 and 496 together.
The Derelict Property Tax (DPT) is intended to encourage the activation of derelict properties. The tax will be collected by the Revenue Commissioners and will be based on registers of derelict properties that are compiled and maintained by local authorities.
DPT will be legislated for as part of Finance (No. 2) Bill 2026. This allows for the tax to be brought in quickly and without delay. It also provides an annual opportunity to amend the tax, if required, following its introduction. For these reasons, it is my view that the Finance Bill is the most appropriate vehicle to introduce DPT. As with the majority of taxes, the proceeds of the tax must accrue to the Central Fund. This is also in line with other, similar taxes introduced in recent years, including the Vacant Homes Tax and the Residential Zoned Land Tax.

question: Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Transport the opening dates for the road transporters support scheme; if the scheme was reopened after the closing date; the criteria to be able to apply during this period; and to outline the appeal process for applicants who missed the deadline.
reply:
Thank you for your question in relation to the Road Transporters Support Scheme (RTSS). The Scheme opened at 12 noon on Wednesday 20 May and closed at 12 noon Friday 12 June 2026. During this window, my Department received over 4,400 applications in respect of approximately 31,500 vehicles.
Despite the large number of applications received, my Department was aware that situations could arise where eligible operators were unable to apply for the Scheme due to reasons outside of their reasonable control. Therefore, a second ‘request to submit a late application window’ was opened at 12 noon Monday 20 July and closed at 12 noon Friday 24 July 2026.
All applicants who submitted a request were asked to provide supporting evidence outlining the reason why they were unable to apply during the original application window. Situations that were considered included serious illness or injury of the applicant or an immediate family member, technical failure of the Scheme’s application system, natural disaster or major emergency event.
An appeals portal opened on 21 October 2026 and will close at noon on Wednesday 04 November. The purpose of the appeals process is to allow applicants to appeal a decision taken on the eligibility of one or more vehicles included on their application. It cannot be used by operators that did not submit an application during the original application window or late request window to apply for support under the Scheme.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Transport to clarify an apparent inconsistency raised by cross-Border student commuters whereby discounted fares are available on Expressway Route 64 between Letterkenny and Derry but equivalent discounts are unavailable on services between Letterkenny and Belfast; and the reasons for any difference.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. The National Transport Authority has responsibility for the regulation of fares charged to passengers in respect of public transport services provided under public service obligation (PSO) contracts.
Cross borders students who reside in the state who attend third-level institutions in Northern Ireland are eligible for a student or young adult TFI Leap card. To further clarify, third level students travelling from the South to third level institutions in Northern Ireland can avail of the 50% student/YAC reduction on the proportion of the journey carried out in the South. This means, for example, if 90% of the journey is through the South and the remaining 10% is through Northern Ireland, then the 50% discount will just apply to the 90% of the journey that is carried out within the State. The discount does not apply to the element of the journey that is carried out outside of the State.
The Young Adult Card initiative is an opt-in Scheme, meaning that while the discount is available on all PSO services, it is only available on those commercial bus operators that have decided to participate in the Scheme.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Transport if he is aware of the concerns expressed in correspondence (details supplied); if he will commit to reviewing the disproportionate fare stages on the Tralee, Killorglin and Killarney corridor; if he will consider introducing a flat fare structure that respects the reality of minimum wage earners in Kerry.
reply:

In this regard on 3 September 2026, the National Transport Authority (NTA) announced changes to the national fare structure for PSO services, effective from January 2027. These changes are the first major revision since 2018 forming part of the NTA’s National Fare Strategy published in 2023. They also represent an important step towards standardising fares nationwide, and support the continued expansion and improvement of public transport, while maintaining affordability.
Public transport requires ongoing investment to maintain, improve and expand services to meet growing demand. Keeping fares affordable is important, but so too is ensuring that we can continue to introduce new routes, increase frequencies, improve reliability and connect more communities to public transport. question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Taoiseach when the Cabinet Committee on Water Quality will meet next.
reply:

The Cabinet Committee met most recently in July and the next meeting will be scheduled shortly.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Transport the reason the 65 new battery electric carriages for the Dublin-Drogheda line has been delayed again until the end of 2027.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Transport to provide a time frame for the implementation of European Directive (EU) 2025/2205 which provides for an increase in in the weight of campervan which can be driven on a standard Irish driving licence Article 6 of the directive specifically states that a motor caravan with a maximum authorised mass exceeding 3500kg but not exceeding 4250kg, including in combination with a trailer, if the maximum authorised mass of the combination does not exceed 5000kg, may be driven on a category B licence.
reply:
Under the current provisions of Regulation 6 of the Road Traffic (Licensing of Drivers) Regulations 2006 (SI 537 of 2006), a category B driving licence permits the holder to drive vehicles with a maximum authorised mass not exceeding 3,500 kg. Such vehicles may be combined with a trailer not exceeding 750 kg, provided that the mass of the combination does not exceed 3,500 kg.
The Regulations also provide for category B licence holders to drive alternatively fuelled vehicles used for the transport of goods, without a trailer, with a mass exceeding 3,500 kg but not exceeding 4,250 kg, provided that the licence was issued at least two years previously and the excess mass is attributable exclusively to the propulsion system.
Article 6 of the Driving Licence Directive 2205/2025 provides that Member States may, after requiring the completion of a training course and/or a passing of a test of skills and behaviour, allow drivers with a category B licence to drive vehicles in combination with a trailer with a maximum combined mass not exceeding 5,000 kg. This may include a motor caravan and trailer, a power-driven emergency vehicle used for maintaining public safety and order, including for immediate assistance during emergencies, such as police vehicles, ambulances, civil protection and rescue or fire brigade vehicles or an alternatively fuelled motor vehicle.

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Transport if he or officials from his Department have met with the Irish Aviation Authority to discuss the potential transfer of responsibility for alcohol and psychoactive substance testing of aviation personnel from State authorities to individual airlines or other private entities; and the date of this meeting.
reply:
The Irish Aviation Authority (IAA) commenced a public consultation on the future regulatory approach to drug and alcohol testing in the Irish aviation sector on the 29th September, with a deadline for submissions on the 31st October. The consultation sought the views of aviation stakeholders, employees, industry representative bodies, public authorities and members of the public on the most appropriate means of introducing a comprehensive framework to manage the safety risks associated with impairment arising from alcohol and other psychoactive substances.
While the IAA sought views on a proposed Employer-Led Testing Framework with IAA Oversight, no decision has been taken yet on state policy in this area. The purpose of the consultation was to gather evidence, perspectives and views of all relevant stakeholders to inform future policy development.
My Department will be engaging with the IAA following the completion its review and consideration of submissions received.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Transport to provide an update on the progress of the BusConnects Dublin Road-Galway route.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. The National Transport Authority (NTA) has responsibility for the planning and development of public transport infrastructure, including the implementation of the BusConnects Galway programme.
Noting the NTA's responsibility in the matter, I have referred the Deputy's question to the NTA for a direct reply. Please contact my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 working days.
The major infrastructure component of the BusConnects Galway programme is the construction of Sustainable Transport Corridors. The NTA is advancing work on the Sustainable Transport Corridors, the Cross-City Link scheme and the Dublin Road scheme, which will improve travel times on the bus network and improve connections for pedestrians and cyclists.
The Dublin Road scheme will deliver 4km of high-quality pedestrian, cyclist and public transport infrastructure along this key transport corridor on the east of the city. I am advised the project is now moving into land acquisition and procurement to progress the next phases of development.
The NDP Sectoral Investment Plan, which was published by my Department in November last year, has allocated funding to progress BusConnects across the cities. The NTA will publish a more detailed plan later this year of what elements of the programme will be advanced within the funding available up to 2030.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Transport further to Parliamentary Question No. 40986/26, whether the protected disclosures policies and procedures of his Department require the prescribed person, under the Protected Disclosures Act 2014, to issue a written determination on prima facie evidence submitted by a reporting person; and if his Department’s procedures comply with the feedback obligations imposed by EU Directive 2019/1937 Article 11 as transposed into Irish law.
reply:
The Department of Transport's Protected Disclosures Policies and Procedures (October 2024) state that the Department will:
• acknowledge reports within 7 calendar days;
• diligently follow up;
• provide feedback within three months of acknowledgement; and
• provide further feedback at three-month intervals on written request.
Where no prima facie evidence is found in a submitted report, section 6.2 of the Policies and Procedures requires the Designated Person within the Department to notify the reporting person in writing of the decision and the reasons for it.
Where prima facie evidence is found in a submitted report or otherwise, section 6.2 of the policies and procedures says “appropriate action will be taken to address the wrongdoing”, which may include deciding whether and how it should be investigated.
The Designated Person will maintain communication with the reporting person and may, if required, make contact with the reporting person, in confidence, to seek further information or clarification regarding the matter(s) reported.
Insofar as possible, feedback will include information on the action taken or envisaged to be taken as follow-up to that report and also the reasons for such follow-up. Feedback will not include any information that could prejudice the outcome of an investigation or any other action that may follow.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Transport to urgently introduce a sustainability payment similar to the Code of Best Practice Payment (Part A) for all landowners living adjacent to the South Kerry Greenway.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and exchequer funding in relation to Greenways. To date, there has been a significant amount of investment for Greenway schemes in County Kerry, with €9,950,000 allocated in 2026 alone.
The Code of Practice for National and Regional Greenways includes information on the acquisition of private lands for developing Greenways and eligibility criteria for sustainability payments. The Code acknowledges the important role of farmers and landowners in the process. It outlines the procedures to ensure that they are treated fairly and equitably. TII are tasked with maintaining the Code of Best Practice for National and Regional Greenways.
Landowners on some greenway schemes are not eligible for Early Sign-on Payment part A of the Greenway Sustainability as the statutory consents granted preceded the introduction of the Code in January 2022. Additional proposals have been brought forward (by some landowners, farming organisations, and elected members) regarding providing a financial support similar to the ‘Early Sign-On Payment’ to these landowners.
While these fall outside the current Code of Best Practice, I am positively disposed to examining them further. Any such consideration will require careful assessment, and my Departmental Officials and TII colleagues have already begun this work and a decision will be made in the very near future.

reply:

question: Deputy Marie Sherlock asked the Minister for Transport the way in which the new learner permit rules apply to learners who already hold a valid permit when the changes come into effect; the action that will be needed if a learner fails a test shortly before their permit expires and the next available test is after the expiry date; whether EDT completed very recently will have to be repeated; and the way in which RSA cancelled tests are taken into account in these circumstances.
reply:
My Department is committed, under Action 7B of the Road Safety Strategy Phase 2 Action Plan, to addressing the issue of learner drivers holding multiple successive learner permits, particularly those who have never undertaken a practical driving test.
The Road Traffic (Licensing of Drivers) (Amendment) (No. 2) Regulations 2025 (SI 527/2025), which come into effect on 1 November 2026, introduce measures to address this issue.
Under the new arrangements, learner permit holders who have held a permit for four years or more must provide evidence of having undertaken a practical driving test before they can renew their permit. Where this requirement is not met, they must start the learner permit application process again in order to continue learning to drive. For category B (car) applicants, this means they will have to complete a driver theory test, obtain a learner permit, take 12 Essential Driver Training lessons and pass a practical driving test.
After seven years of holding a learner permit, any renewal application will be treated as a first application. Such applicants, if they wish to continue learning to drive, will also have to recommence the learning to drive process.
A learner permit is not a licence to drive. The learning to drive process is designed to ensure that learners, accompanied by a driving instructor or qualified driver, acquire the knowledge, skills and competencies required to drive safely and that they progress to becoming fully qualified drivers. question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Transport the current legal limit for cannabis found in a driver's system; and the legal ramifications this limit could potentially have on an individual who has consumed cannabis days before operation of a vehicle.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I wish to inform the Deputy that the legal limit for cannabis and driving is set out in Section 8 of the Road Traffic Act 2016. The limits are:
• 9-Tetrahydrocannabinol (Cannabis) 1ng/ml
• 11-nor-9-carboxy-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (Cannabis) 5ng/ml
Cannabis is an impairing substance which greatly increases the risk of dangerous driving. If a driver is convicted of exceeding the legal limit, they may be disqualified for at least one year for a first offence, and at least 2 years for a second or subsequent offence. On summary conviction, there is a fine of up to €5,000 and/or up to 6 months imprisonment.
The legal ramifications for a person who has consumed cannabis before operating a vehicle are dependent on blood concentration. Impairment can continue for significant periods and there is no residual use defence in statute. I have no intention of changing the current position.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Transport whether contracts recorded in his Department's internal contract register can be linked to their corresponding contract award notices published on eTenders, where applicable; whether his Department records the relevant eTenders notice reference, URL or other identifier; and if not, the reasons that prevent this information from being recorded.
reply:

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Transport whether purchase orders issued by his Department under procurement contracts can be linked to the corresponding contracts held in its internal contract register; whether a contract reference or other unique identifier is maintained to enable this linkage; and if not, the way his Department monitors cumulative expenditure against the approved value of each contract.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 393 and 436 together.
I wish to advise the Deputy that the Department uses Oracle, an electronic, centralised and standardised financial shared service operated by the National Shared Services Office (NSSO). Oracle contains the relevant details of each supplier including unique supplier ID number and VAT/Tax Registration number. These identifiers are recorded against individual purchase orders, contracts and payments.
Expenditure made via purchase order must be linked to a contract. All contracts set up on Oracle are assigned a unique contract number and this number is used when raising a requisition and is subsequently linked to the purchase order. Encumbered funds on a contract can be monitored via a purchasing contracts register report which is available to run from Oracle.
With regards to the agencies and public bodies under my remit this is a matter for the agencies and public bodies themselves, I will forward the Deputy's question to them for direct reply. If their reply is not received within 10 working days please contact my private office.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Transport the reason the registration-validation and pre-clamping payment checks in the NTA's 2019 Code of Practice were omitted from the 2022 Code; the evidence that informed that change; if he will introduce regulations requiring operators to search paid sessions before clamping and prohibiting release charges where a paid session with a minor registration error is verified; the number of second-stage appeals allowed on the paid parking ground in 2024 and 2025, by operator; the number many received; and the reason the powers in sections 26 and 28 of the Vehicle Clamping Act2015 have never been used.
reply:
Under the Vehicle Clamping & Signage Regulations 2017 (SI 421 of 2017), made under the Vehicle Clamping Act 2015 (No.13 of 2015), other than on public roads a vehicle may not be clamped for non-payment, or on expiry of a paid period, until at least 10 minutes after detection (Regulation 5); the operator must photograph the vehicle's full registration number when clamping (Regulation 10); and clamping operators must keep all payment records, including electronic records, for three years (Regulation 18).
Where an appeal is allowed at either stage, charges paid must be refunded (Sections 20(6) & 22(5) of the 2015 Act).
The remaining matters raised are matters for the National Transport Authority (NTA). These are the 2022 changes to the Code of Practice, the appeals data requested and the exercise of the NTA's enforcement powers. I have therefore referred those parts of the Deputy's question to the NTA for direct reply.

Fundamental to this project is a transition to an 'Account Based Ticketing' scheme incorporating mobile and card-based payments. question: Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Transport to provide an update in relation to the implementation of the vehicle adaptation scheme (VAS); to outline the criteria for the scheme; when the scheme will open for applications.
reply:
The Department of Transport has been tasked with developing a new Vehicle Adaptation Scheme (VAS) to provide financial assistance towards the cost of adapting vehicles for people with disabilities.
Over the past twelve months, the Department has made significant progress towards the implementation of the VAS. In line with the proposals set out by the Transport Working Group of the National Disability Inclusion Strategy and the Senior Officials Group on Disability, as well as further engagement and consultation, the core principles and parameters of the Scheme have been established. This, in turn, has enabled the Department to develop a high-level framework for its operation.
In line with the social model of disability, the VAS will be based on an individual's needs, not characteristics. Accordingly, eligibility will extend to drivers and passengers who require assistance to enter, exit, or operate a vehicle, rather than being linked to any particular medical condition or disability.
Subject to timely Government approval and the completion of the necessary preparatory work, it is possible that the VAS will open for applications in Q1 2027.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Transport in light of recent EU and planning decisions which had delayed the process now being completed, if the review of flight paths at Dublin Airport will now proceed, and if he will outline the method/approach to be taken and a timeline for completion.
reply:
I would like to begin by clarifying that the 15 October 2026 CJEU ruling is not relevant to the independent assessment of flight paths at Dublin Airport.
As I have previously advised the House, I have committed to ensuring that an independent assessment of flight paths at Dublin Airport will be undertaken at the appropriate time.
The most suitable point for this work remains unchanged and will most likely be when a final decision is made regarding the North Runway Relevant Action. This timing will ensure that the assessment is based on the most accurate and current operational data, incorporating the latest noise modelling methodologies, and can support the identification of appropriate solutions.
At this juncture, it would be pre-emptive to prescribe a methodology and timeline to the work.

question: Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh asked the Minister for Transport to clarify the changes in the law that now require applicants for or renewals of open driving insurance policies to hold a driving licence and furnish their driving licence number; if he is aware of the impact this change has on people whose disabilities prohibit them from obtaining a driving licence and who employ personal assistants to drive their insured adapted vehicles; and the provision being made to ensure they remain able to secure insurance.
reply:
I wish to clarify that Irish road traffic legislation does not require a vehicle owner to hold a driving licence to obtain motor insurance. Section 56A(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 1961, as inserted by the Road Traffic and Roads Act 2023, requires a person seeking to obtain a policy of motor insurance to provide their name and address.
The legislative changes to which you refer are set out in Section 56A(1)(d)(ii) of the Road Traffic Act 1961 (as inserted by the Road Traffic and Roads Act 2023). The legislation provides that only those named in Particular 6 of the Certificate of Insurance are required to provide their driver number.
In relation to open driving policies, it is the Department’s understanding that a driver number is not required where a driver is not specifically named in Particular 6 of the Certificate of Insurance. The precise approach adopted in respect of open driving policies is a matter for the insurer concerned. However, such policies typically provide cover for drivers aged between 25 and 70 who hold a full driving licence and have the policyholder’s consent.
Department officials will raise this matter with industry representatives as a matter of priority to ensure that no unintended operational issues arise in the implementation of the legislation.

reply:

Oracle contains the relevant details of each supplier including unique supplier ID number and VAT/Tax Registration number. Expenditure made via purchase order must be linked to a contract. Encumbered funds on a contract can be monitored via a purchasing contracts register report which is available to run from Oracle.

reply:

I have no role in the day-to-day operations of the SPSV sector.

question: Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Transport the timeline for his Department to publish its congestion action plan for Dublin.
reply:
Recognising the cost of congestion for commuters and wider society, I convened a Congestion Forum earlier this year bringing transport agencies, operators, local authorities and departmental officials together to collectively consider options for alleviating congestion in the Greater Dublin Area. A Congestion Action Plan has been developed which I will be bringing to Government shortly with publication to follow. The Plan represents a strong collective effort to identify impactful measures across the board, with lead owners in agreement on the approach required.
The Congestion Action Plan for the GDA will include a wide range of measures targeting Bus, Luas and Heavy Rail measures, M50 and National Road measures, Park & Ride, Park & Share, freight measures, traffic management measures, regulatory measures and active travel measures. It is intended that the Congestion Action Plan measures focus initially on the Greater Dublin Area, with a view to testing actions that can be replicated elsewhere.

reply:

question: Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Transport if his Department has conducted any feasibility studies into the introduction of a requirement for businesses to provide parent and child parking at premises that operate their own car park; and if not, if he would consider such an option.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I can confirm that my Department has not conducted studies on the introduction of parent and child parking bays in private car parks.
Currently, there is no statutory basis for such parking bays. Parent and child parking bays are considered courtesy designations and cannot be enforced by An Garda Síochána or traffic wardens. The Deputy may also note that parking regulations, as with most areas of road traffic legislation, can only be enforced for public roads and car parks. Parking enforcement in private car parks, such as those attached to shopping centres and other commercial premises, is the responsibility of the car park's owner. It is not within the power of An Garda Síochána or local authority traffic wardens to issue penalties in these private areas and it is not within the scope of road traffic legislation to grant such powers.
I can confirm that my Department has no current plans to introduce a statutory basis for parent and child parking.

question: Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Transport if disabled parking pass eligibility can be extended to those with Alzheimer’s disease.
reply:
As Minister for Transport I wish to advise that, in 2010, the Department conducted a review of the Disabled Parking Scheme, in consultation with various stakeholders. One of the issues examined was eligibility. Disability groups in particular were unhappy that some permits were issued for medical conditions, rather than mobility impairment. The Scheme was revised so that permits are now given on the basis of mobility impairment, rather than the diagnosis of a particular condition or illness. This is in line with the original intention of the scheme.
I and my Department appreciate that everyday life with a condition such as Alzheimer's can be challenging. I must emphasise, however, that issuing a large number of extra permits by extending the eligibility criteria would put the existing scheme under significant additional pressure and, crucially, compromise the availability of disabled parking spaces for those who need them the most.
The Deputy may note that my Department is currently undertaking a review of the Scheme, including eligibility criteria.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Transport whether recipients of State funding for electric vehicle charging infrastructure are required to provide data on charger uptime, reliability, fault rates or availability.
reply:
The Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR), which has applied directly across the European Union since 13 April 2024, lays down detailed rules and data specifications that will improve the user experience for EV drivers and ensure greater transparency, interoperability, and accessibility of recharging.
Under AFIR, operators of publicly accessible charging infrastructure are required to provide ad hoc charging and payment options, allowing EV drivers to charge their vehicles without entering into a contract with a particular charge point operator. This is intended to reduce reliance on multiple operator-specific applications and make public charging more convenient and accessible for consumers.
The Regulation also includes requirements for operators of publicly accessible charging infrastructure (who require payment for the recharging service) to set up an Application Programme Interface (API) that provides free and unrestricted access to both static and dynamic charging data, in order for the data to be made accessible on an open and non-discriminatory basis to all data users through national access points (in accordance with the relevant provisions related to such data). This will support the development of consumer applications that can provide information across multiple charging networks. A number of third-party apps are currently available and providing this data to the public that are not limited to any one charging operator.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Transport whether funding agreements entered into by his Department, Zero Emission Vehicles Ireland, or any agency under the aegis of his Department require publicly funded electric vehicle charging infrastructure to meet minimum operational or uptime standards.
reply:
Funding agreements entered into under ZEVI-supported charging schemes include a range of operational and performance requirements for publicly funded EV charging infrastructure. Under the ZEVI EV Charging Infrastructure Light-Duty Vehicles (LDV) National Road Grant Scheme, funded charging infrastructure must be publicly accessible on a 24/7 basis. The scheme also sets minimum technical and operational requirements relating to charger numbers and power output at each site, with infrastructure ranging from a minimum of one 100kW charging point to four 150kW charging points capable of operating simultaneously, depending on the phase of delivery.
In relation to the Shared Island Sports Club EV Charging Scheme, funding agreements include minimum operational standards for publicly funded charging infrastructure. CPOs are responsible for the provision and maintenance of the charging infrastructure and are required to maintain charge point uptime above 95% for the duration of the licence agreement. In addition, CPOs must provide 24-hour telephone customer support for users of the charging infrastructure.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Transport whether his Department intends to begin collecting information on the operational status, reliability and availability of publicly funded electric vehicle charging infrastructure; and the timeline for any such proposals.
reply:
Information on the operational status and availability of publicly accessible EV recharging infrastructure is already collected by the data office in Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII).
Under the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR) (Regulation (EU) 2023/1804), all Charge Point Operators (CPOs), including those operating publicly funded charging infrastructure, are required to share specified charge point data with the national Data Exchange Platform (DXP). This includes both static and dynamic data relating to publicly accessible recharging points.
The data shared includes information on the operational status of charge points, with status categories such as "Operational" and "Out of Order". Analysis of this data enables an assessment of the availability and reliability of the public charging network and provides data users with an indicative view of charger performance and uptime.
Accordingly, the information sought is already gathered through existing regulatory reporting arrangements and is available to TII for monitoring and analysis purposes.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport the number of fleet owners, motor traders and brokers who have failed to register their vehicles and named drivers insured on their policy, on the National Fleet Database (NFD), under the Road Traffic and Roads Act 2023; the number of fleet and motor trader policy holders who failed to upload driver information for all named drivers covered under their insurance policy to the NFD, managed by the Motor Insurers' Bureau of Ireland (MIBI), since 31 March 2025 when the law came into effect.
reply:
Under section 78A of the Road Traffic Act 1961, as amended, the Motor Insurers’ Bureau of Ireland (MIBI) is responsible for maintaining the Irish Motor Insurance Database (IMID). The data in the IMID is provided by motor insurers, brokers, fleet owners and motor traders, and includes policy holder details and vehicle registration numbers.
Within the IMID, the National Fleet Database (NFD) contains motor insurance details for motor vehicles operating under fleet and motor trade insurance policies in Ireland. The types of vehicle typically covered by fleet policies include buses and coaches, vehicles being sold in garages, construction vehicles, delivery vans, transport and logistical operations, hire cars, utility vehicles and service vehicles, as well as those operated by retailers, service providers, food and takeaway delivery operations, semi-state organisations and more. Following the commencement, in November 2023, of the relevant sub-sections of the Road Traffic and Roads Act 2023, it is a legal requirement that the insurance details for these vehicles are uploaded to the NFD.
According to data supplied by MIBI, currently there are 440,500 vehicles listed on the NFD. In addition, there are 9,851 fleet or motor trader policies which are yet to provide vehicle details for the NFD. question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Transport if a monthly cap on M50 toll charges has been considered for commuters, such as those in Dublin Mid-West, who cannot avoid using the M50 to access their place of work and who face high costs as a consequence.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and funding in relation to the national roads programme. Under the Roads Acts 1993-2015, the operation and management of individual national roads is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned.
Therefore, matters relating to the day to day operations regarding national roads, including toll roads are within the remit of TII. More specifically, the statutory power to levy tolls, to make toll bye-laws and to enter into agreements with private investors are vested in TII under Part V of the Roads Act 1993 (as amended). Moreover, the contracts for the privately-operated toll schemes are commercial agreements between TII and the Public Private Partnership (PPP) concessionaires concerned.
At present I have no plans to review tolling policy towards any particular group of road users. It must be borne in mind also that toll revenue is a key income stream for funding for protection and renewal of our road network, and accordingly any reduction in toll revenue would require additional funding to be raised elsewhere to maintain the current level of investment.

question: Deputy Aisling Dempsey asked the Minister for Transport to provide an update on the N3 M50 to Clonee bus priority and active travel scheme.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and exchequer funding in relation to the National Roads Programme. This is also subject to the Infrastructure Guidelines and the necessary statutory approvals. In this context, TII is best placed to advise you on the status of this project.
I can confirm that €500,000 has been allocated for the N3 M50 to Clonee bus priority and active travel scheme in 2026.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Transport if his Department, in conjunction with the Road Safety Authority, will run a public awareness campaign to highlight that pedestrians should wait for vehicles to stop before crossing at a designated pedestrian crossing.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 341 and 400 together.
Under the Road Safety Authority Act 2006, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) has responsibility for the promotion of public awareness of road safety and of measures, including the advancement of education, relating to the promotion of the safe use of roads. In order to inform these road safety measures, the RSA receives both coronial and collision data from An Garda Síochána.
Given the RSA's responsibility in this matter, I have referred the Deputies' questions to the RSA for direct reply. I would ask the Deputies to contact my office if a response has not been received within ten days.
Pending this response, the Deputies may wish to note that Budget 2027 increased funding to €20 million for road safety awareness, education and campaigns aimed at all road users, including vulnerable road users. The RSA website also includes specific safety advice aimed at pedestrians.
In addition, the recent October bank holiday Road Safety Appeal jointly launched by An Garda Síochána and the Road Safety Authority focused on ensuring the safety of pedestrians.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Transport which departmental budget shall provide the €600 million the Irish Government has committed to for the construction of the proposed upgrade of the A5 corridor between Aughnacloy and Strabane.
reply:
The planning and implementation of the A5 upgrade project is the responsibility of the authorities in Northern Ireland.
The funding arrangements in relation to the A5 were governed by the 2014 Stormont House Agreement and Implementation Plan - A Fresh Start, and under this Agreement the Government had previously committed to provide funding of £75 million towards the cost of the A5 upgrade scheme once the statutory planning process in Northern Ireland was concluded. It was announced on February 20th 2024 that as part of Government funding commitments for Shared Island projects, €600 million was being committed for the progression of the A5 project.
The planning and implementation of the A5 upgrade project is the responsibility of the authorities in Northern Ireland. A formal legal challenge to the project, brought by the Alternative A5 Alliance (AA5A), was heard through the High Court over a period of 5 days, concluding on 2 April 2025. On 23 June 2025, the High Court in Belfast ruled in favour of the legal challenge and quashed the decision to commence construction of the previously approved section from Ballygawley to south of Strabane. On October 6th 2026 the Court of Appeal overturned the decision of the High Court, thereby allowing the project to proceed.
The Department of Transport is currently engaging with the Department for Infrastructure in Northern Ireland regarding the next steps. This includes the provision of an updated timing and funding profile for the project

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Transport the reason the TFI live application has not received any improvements in three years; and his Department's plans to update and improve the application for passengers.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. However, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of public transport. The National Transport Authority (NTA) has responsibility for securing the provision of public passenger transport services provided under public service obligation (PSO) contracts including technology projects such as provision for the TFI live application.
The NTA is responsible for several mobile applications, including TFI Leap Top Up, the TFI Go mobile ticketing app, TFI Anseo Demand Responsive Application, and the TFI Live mobile application, which is used for journey planning and for the provision of real-time information to customers. In all cases, the NTA works extensively with the supplier to deliver the best possible result.
While the TFI Live application does function and does present journey planning and real-time data to customers, the NTA is currently investigating options to expedite improvements to the application to improve the customer experience.
One project that will produce improved quality journey data to the TFI Live app is Next Generation Automatic Vehicle Location, which replaces five old Automatic Vehicle Location systems with a new centralised solution, to provide higher quality and consistent data outputs to the TFI Live mobile app. This project went into pilot in March 2026, with full roll-out expected in 2027.

question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Transport if the upcoming review of the TaxSaver scheme will consider the inclusion of bike share and car share.
reply:
In line with the announcement made as part of Budget 2027 by the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance, Simon Harris. T.D., my Department will initiate a comprehensive review of the TaxSaver Scheme over the coming year, in close cooperation with the Department of Finance.
The TaxSaver Scheme is an important element of the Government's wider approach to supporting sustainable travel. The forthcoming Review will provide an opportunity to build on the success of the existing Scheme and to consider how it can continue to best support commuters into the future.
Commuting habits have evolved significantly in recent years, especially in light of an increase in hybrid working as well as more flexible and multimodal travel patterns. It is important that our supports keep pace with these changes and continue to enable people to make sustainable transport choices for their daily journeys.
While the scope of the Review has not yet been finalised, I am keen that it considers all opportunities to support greater sustainable transport choice. The contribution that shared mobility can make in expanding transport options will be an important consideration, subject to the agreed terms of reference for the Review.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Defence whether the decision taken in 2025 by the then Minister for Finance that Ireland should not apply for loans under the EU Security Action for Europe (SAFE) Regulation remains Government policy; whether any expression of interest, application or negotiation has since taken place, including for any second round of SAFE lending; and whether any approved EU defence loan or financing facility is unavailable for drawdown pending changes to Irish legislation.
reply:
Following an assessment by officials of the Department of Defence, in consultation with the Department of Finance and the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, the European Commission was informed in August 2025 that Ireland was not seeking financing under the EU Security Action for Europe (SAFE) loan instrument at that time, and that remains the current position. However, the Department keeps ongoing developments in EU defence and funding initiatives such as SAFE, under review.
As such, no application for SAFE loans has been submitted by Ireland and, accordingly, no negotiations are under way in respect of SAFE borrowing. While Ireland is not availing of the SAFE loan facility, the Department continues to examine opportunities for participation in collaborative procurement initiatives under the SAFE framework where these align with national capability priorities.
A second SAFE call, announced by the European Commission on 29 October 2026, makes available €21.3 billion in remaining SAFE funding. Member States have been invited to submit a non-binding Expression of Interest to the European Commission by 26 November 2026. Any future decision to access SAFE loans would require consideration and agreement with the Department of Finance and the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation. Such considerations would form part of the broader assessment of Ireland’s future defence inve

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Defence further to comments made in the media (details supplied), to clarify her position on Irish troops participating in peace enforcement activities in Lebanon, given the mandate for this mission derives from UN Security Council Resolution 1701 (2006), a traditional Chapter VI-style monitoring and support mission, rather than a Chapter VII enforcement mission.
reply:
Ireland’s contingent in UNIFIL operates under the authority of UN Security Council Resolution 1701 (2006) and subsequent mandate renewals. UNIFIL is a United Nations peacekeeping operation whose primary functions include monitoring the cessation of hostilities, supporting the deployment of the Lebanese Armed Forces in south Lebanon, assisting in ensuring humanitarian access, and helping to create the conditions for a permanent ceasefire.
Having just returned from a visit to our troops serving in UNIFIL, the situation there is extremely volatile and unpredictable. In 2026, seven international peacekeepers have lost their lives which is not consistent with a traditional Chapter VI type mission.
My comments on RTÉ's This Week programme were made in the context of discussion regarding proposals for a new EU mission in Lebanon and the broader range of overseas missions in which members of the Defence Forces have participated in, and may participate in the future.
The proposed EU mission under discussion would have a different mandate and operational tasks from those assigned to UNIFIL, and is envisaged as a non-executive Training Mission similar to the EU's Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine, which members of the Defence Forces currently participate in. As I have consistently stated, any proposal for Irish participation in an overseas mission, including the proposed EU Mission, will be considered on its individual merits, including its mandate, legal basis, operatio

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Defence to provide details of the 27 pre-legislative scrutiny recommendations of the Joint Committee on Defence and National Security that have been included in the Defence (Amendment) Bill 2026.
reply:
In line with normal practice, the general scheme of the Defence (Amendment) Bill was referred to the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Defence and National Security for consideration under the Pre-Legislative (PLS) process.
At the end of July 2025, the Joint Oireachtas Committee published its report on the PLS of the draft legislation and put forward 27 recommendations. I wish to thank the Committee for the constructive manner in which it carried out its work.
A wide range of views were expressed. I listened carefully to those views and to the stakeholders who participated in the PLS process, and I have carefully considered the recommendations contained in the Committee’s report.
While, in common with any piece of legislation, it is not always possible to accommodate every view that is put forward by stakeholders. A number of the recommendations, while well intended were not compatible with this legislation.
I have responded by including changes to the Bill as published.
The Bill before the House reflects that process of consultation and includes refinements and modifications to the General Scheme.
In particular, the legislation provides that:
• The Minister will make an annual report on all overseas deployments available to the Oireachtas and the matters that will be required to be covered by the annual report will be set out in legislation;
• Written notification will be provided to the relevant Joint Oireachtas Committee where a contingent of 50 personnel, or fewer, are deploy

question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Defence to outline discussions and consideration her Department is currently undertaking regarding increasing the retirement age for members of the Defence Forces from 62 years-of age up to 64 years-of-age.
reply:
As the Deputy is aware, prior to 29 March 2024, many Defence Forces personnel had a mandatory retirement age of less than 60. The age varied depending on rank. The initial increase in the mandatory retirement age to 60 provided an opportunity for personnel to extend their careers in the Defence Forces. They may also continue to retire at their original mandatory retirement age without any impact on their pensions. The Deputy will also be aware that the mandatory retirement age for Defence Force members further increased from 60 to 62 on 19 August 2024.
This is, but one of a number of very positive retention measures which have been introduced in recent years for members of the Defence Forces.
Data provided by the Defence Forces indicates that turnover rates have reduced over the last two years with a turnover rate of approximately 7.6% in 2025. This is significantly less than the turnover rate of 9% recorded for 2024 and is a very positive turnover rate when compared with militaries internationally where annual attrition rates of 8 to 12 per cent are typical.
While the reduction in the numbers leaving is due to a multitude of factors, the increased mandatory retirement age would appear to be a contributory factor.
There are no immediate plans for a review of retirement ages as there is merit in allowing the recent changes to bed down and provide for sufficient data to inform further consideration of the matter in the future. Any such consideration in the future would be invar

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Defence to confirm whether the Defence Forces Tribunal has appointed persons specifically to act as independent investigators, separate from its counsel and solicitors; if so, the number appointed, their professional qualifications, terms of appointment and functions; if none have been appointed, whether the Tribunal’s investigative work is being conducted solely through its legal team, presently comprising three senior counsel, three junior counsel and its solicitor or solicitors; whether she has sought or received any assessment of the adequacy of that investigative model (details supplied).
reply:
The Defence Forces Tribunal of Inquiry (‘Tribunal’) was established by Statutory Instrument on 20 June 2024 (S.I. 304 of 2024) to examine the effectiveness of the complaints processes in the Defence Forces concerning workplace issues relating to discrimination, bullying, harassment, sexual harassment and sexual misconduct. The Tribunal also has the power to investigate the response to complaints made regarding the use of hazardous chemicals within Air Corps’ headquarters at Casement Aerodrome, Baldonnel. The Tribunal is entirely independent in its functions.
In line with the Tribunal’s ‘Procedures of the Tribunal’ published on the Tribunal’s website at the following URL: www.toidf.ie/app/uploads/2024/06/Procedures-of-the-Defence-Forces-Tribunal.pdf, ‘the Tribunal will, insofar as practicable, consistent with its duties under the Tribunals of Inquiry (Evidence) Acts 1921 to 2011, conduct its investigation by seeking and facilitating the voluntary cooperation of any person who is or may be in possession of relevant information, knowledge or material relating to the Terms of Reference'.
In addition, and in accordance with section 6 of the Tribunals of Inquiry (Evidence) (Amendment) Act 2002, the Tribunal has requested the appointment of investigators. The request is presently under review as part of the applicable statutory process.[]

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Defence whether Ireland has applied for, entered negotiations on, or secured any loan under the EU Security Action for Europe (SAFE) Regulation or any other EU financing facility in respect of the acquisition order signed with the French Direction Générale de l'Armement on 18 September 2026 for radar systems (details supplied), the Armoured Fleet Programme, or any other procurement from the French State or a French company; and if she will set out how each such procurement is being financed, including the amount, source and repayment terms of any borrowing.
reply:
I can confirm that Ireland has not sought any loan under the EU SAFE Regulation, or any other EU financing facility, in respect of the Acquisition Order signed in September for long-range radars, or any other procurement programme.
All procurement activities are financed from Exchequer funding, provided nationally as part of the annual Estimates process, which includes Capital allocations under the multi-annual National Development Plan.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Defence whether any acquisition order, framework agreement, MoU or other agreement entered into with the French Government, the Direction Générale de l'Armement, a French company or an EU institution, including the France Ireland Joint Strategic Framework 2026- 2030, contains any term, condition, commitment, express or implied, relating to the Defence (Amendment) Bill 2026 or to the arrangements for Government and Dáil approval of overseas deployments of the Defence Forces; and whether delivery, payment or drawdown under any such agreement depends in any way on the enactment of that Bill.
reply: I can confirm that there are no terms, commitments, or obligations of any kind, expressed or implied, included in any orders, frameworks, MoUs or other arrangements entered into with French or EU authorities, or any companies, relating to the Defence (Amendment) Bill 2026 or arrangements for overseas deployments of Defence Forces personnel.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Defence the estimated total cost of the acquisition order signed with the French Direction Générale de l'Armement on 18 September 2026 for five radar systems (details supplied); the payment schedule and budget subhead from which it will be met; and whether any provisions of the EU SAFE Regulation, including the VAT exemption for common procurement, are being applied to this or any other procurement from France.
reply:
Due to the confidentiality requirements of the joint procurement process undertaken, which involves a number of other Member States, and also the commercial sensitivity arising, I am not in a position to disclose the payment terms associated with the acquisition of the radar systems referred to.
However, I can confirm that the five long-range radars that are being acquired will be funded entirely from the Defence Vote, and specifically from Capital allocations provided under the multi-annual National Development Plan.
While Ireland has not sought a loan under the EU SAFE Regulation, the application of the VAT exemption provisions will be examined on a case by case basis for all joint procurement initiatives undertaken.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Defence whether contracts recorded in her Department's internal contract register can be linked to their corresponding contract award notices published on eTenders, where applicable; whether her Department records the relevant eTenders notice reference, URL or other identifier; and if not, the reasons that prevents this information from being recorded.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 323 and 325 together.
The Contracts Register for the Department of Defence and the Defence Forces records details of all procurement contracts awarded over €25,000 (excluding VAT) on an annual basis. This register, which is examined by the Comptroller & Auditor General during its annual audit also includes contract reference numbers, purchase order details, contract value and contract spend.
Subhead Managers are responsible for the monitoring of expenditure on contracts across the Defence Organisation in line with the Infrastructure Guidelines/Public Spending Code published by the Department of Public Expenditure Infrastructure Public Service Reform and Digitalisation which sets out the obligations applying to each department in spending public money. This includes obligations at all stages of the expenditure lifecycle, from initial appraisal, through management and monitoring, to post-expenditure review and evaluation, and applies to both capital and current spending.
It is currently not possible for technical reasons to link the Defence Organisation Contracts Register and the eTenders system which is provided by the Office of Government Procurement.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Defence if her Department or public bodies under the aegis of her Department have tested their ability to transfer essential data and services from their principal cloud-service provider to an alternative provider or State-controlled infrastructure; the number possessing a fully costed and tested cloud exit plan; the number of critical public services that could not presently be migrated within six months; whether vendor-concentration risk is recorded centrally; and if she will publish an anonymised aggregate assessment of that risk.
reply:
My Department adopts a risk-based approach to the use of cloud services and the management of associated dependencies. All cloud services are hosted in the EU, are fully GDPR compliant, and are supported by resilient, high-availability infrastructure. Physically separate data centres provide additional protection against localised disruptions and service outages.
My Department does not operate any public-facing ICT systems or services cloud services. Existing cloud services are used to support internal business operations.
The Department's cloud-hosted applications are designed and developed using technologies and architectures that facilitate portability and support migration to alternative cloud service providers, where required. This approach minimises the risk of vendor lock-in and provides flexibility in responding to future business and operational requirements.
For operational security reasons, it is not appropriate to disclose details on specific cyber security and resilience measures.

question: Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh asked the Minister for Defence further to the decision of the Workplace Relations Commission in 2025 upholding a complaint under the Payment of Wages Act 1991 by a member of the Reserve Defence Force, whether her Department has since reviewed its compliance with employment legislation in respect of members of the Reserve Defence Force; and if so, the outcome of that review.
reply:

The adjudicator noted that a central purpose of the 1991 Act is the protection of wages, and the right to receive wages when they fall due. Compensation was duly paid.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Defence the number of cars, vans and other non-specialist vehicles owned or leased by her Department and public bodies under the aegis of her Department; and the total costs involved with respect to purchase and leasing of same.
reply:
The total number of non-specialist vehicles owned by the Department of Defence and the Defence Forces during the period from 2025 to date is 1,416.
Total expenditure on the purchase and leasing of non-specialist vehicles during the same period amounted to €6,785,041.96, comprising:
• €6,590,294.17 for the purchase of 138 new vehicles; and
• €194,747.79 in vehicle leasing costs.
For the purposes of this response, the non-specialist vehicle fleet includes all operational support vehicles including FFR (Fitted for Radio) Land Cruisers, which are configured to support military communications and operational tasks and articulated trucks, which are classified as operational support vehicles.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Defence the total budget allocated to the be emergency ready campaign; and the estimated final cost of the campaign and booklet distribution.
reply:
The Be Emergency Ready campaign was launched on 28 August 2026 to support household and community preparedness ahead of the winter season.
The campaign includes the nationwide distribution of a preparedness booklet to every household in the State, a dedicated information platform on gov.ie, a national communications campaign and engagement with local authorities to support preparedness initiatives.
Expenditure of €1,241,342.73 has been incurred to date.
To date, approximately 2.28 million booklets have been distributed to households nationwide within the planned delivery timeframe.
The allocation of €1.35 million was provided in 2026 for resilience and Critical Entities resilience activities, including the implementation of the Be Emergency Ready campaign. I am advised that the overall campaign outturn will be well within this allocation. The campaign continues to deliver strong levels of public engagement and awareness and has provided preparedness information to households across the State.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Defence further to Parliamentary Question No. 57271/26, if she will provide an update on the Irish Defence Force’s army force design process; when it will be completed; and when will the results be published.
reply:
As the Deputy is aware, the Commission on the Defence Forces recommended "The Chief of Defence to initiate an immediate force design process assisted by external experts with access to international military expertise, and to include a detailed force design process".
In response to this recommendation, the Defence Forces established three Force Design Teams across the Army, Naval Service and Air Corps, together with an overarching Strategic Force Design Office. The force design process is ongoing, with all teams working collaboratively to develop a coherent and integrated future force structure for the Defence Forces as a whole.
This work is nearing completion and I expect to receive a Force Design report for my consideration from the Chief of Staff in the near future.
This is challenging and important work, and it must be undertaken carefully to ensure we deliver a modern fit-for-purpose Defence Forces for the future. A key priority for me, as Minister, is that the force design process incorporate a phased transition plan, outlining clear steps from current force levels towards the Commission's recommended strength of 11,500 personnel.
As you will appreciate, the scale and complexity of this work should not be underestimated and its successful delivery will depend on the sustained engagement of all involved.

question: Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Defence the number of members of the Reserve Defence Force affected by the omission of technical pay from their payments since July 2026; the total amount of arrears subsequently paid and the date of payment; the reason for the omission; the way in which it was identified; whether affected members were notified; and the steps being taken to prevent a recurrence.
reply:
The Reserve Defence Force rates are directly linked to the Permanent Defence Force pay scales, adjusted proportionally for the days or training periods served with their technical pay based on a percentage of the daily training rate. The pay codes on the payroll system are set-up to apply the percentage applicable for technical pay to their appropriate rank.
In June 2026 improvements were made to pay categories on the Reserve Defence Force payroll with the introduction of the following descriptions – training domestic, training overseas, supplemental military service domestic and supplemental military service overseas.
The Pay Administration section in the Department of Defence received a technical pay query in September 2026 which prompted a review. In conjunction with our payroll provider, the National Shared Services Office (NSSO), it was discovered the new pay codes effective from 01 June 2026 were not linked to the technical pay percentage codes in error.
A full review was undertaken to identify those affected. Thirty-seven individuals were identified. The total amount of arrears due was €1,160; this equates to an average of €31 per person ranging from a minimum of €1.50 to a maximum of €180.
The error was rectified on the payroll system immediately and arrears were processed in pay period 202640 on 02 October 2026. Those affected were not contacted individually given the low levels of arrears involved. The relevant pay teams have been briefed on the issue and additional

question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the position regarding individuals that previously availed of the solar PV scheme for medically vulnerable customers through their provider, the additional support that is available for appropriate battery storage, compatible equipment and the electrical arrangements required to supply essential medical equipment safely during a power cut.
reply:

These homes have a dependence on electrically powered equipment, including medical equipment, life protecting devices and assistive technologies such as dialysis machines and respirators. As such, these households may have a higher energy demand than the average user and this scheme is designed to go some way towards helping to reduce those energy costs.

The scheme is kept under ongoing review by my Department and the SEAI, with the SEAI meeting regularly with the energy suppliers, with a focus on continuous improvement of the scheme.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he has received the NEAT action; when it will be published; and to provide a timeline for the implementation of measures contained within the report.
reply:
Addressing energy affordability is a priority for this Government. That is why in June of last year, I established the National Energy Affordability Taskforce, the NEAT, to identify, assess and implement measures that will enhance energy affordability for households and businesses while delivering key renewables commitments, and protecting security of supply and economic stability.
The first report of the Taskforce, which included measures for consideration in Budget 2026, was published last November.
The work of the Taskforce has also informed measures announced in Budget 2027. reply:
I note the news article supplied by the Deputy and the comments in the article attributed to the Head of Digital Infrastructure Ireland.
The Government position on Data Centres is clear and set out in the Programme for Government.
