question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he is aware of recent comments by Wopke Hoekstra, the EU Climate Commissioner, and EU commissioner Dan Jørgensen who have confirmed that member states can take measures to tackle windfall profits of energy companies; if he will reintroduce the cap on market revenues; if not, the reasons.
reply:
The major disruption to global energy supply, due to the situation in Iran and the Middle East, is reflected in extremely volatile commodity prices over the past number of months. Officials in my Department, along with other relevant Government Departments, continue to closely monitor these developments to assess their impacts on the Irish economy and society, as well as develop appropriate responses.
It is the Government’s view that tackling the energy crisis in a coordinated way between EU Member States is preferable, given the interconnectedness of EU energy markets, and that a State-by-State approach would risk fragmenting or unbalancing the level-playing-field for the single market for electricity.
Government has taken significant action to help households and businesses with the cost of fuel and energy by introducing one of the most comprehensive support packages in the EU. The National Energy Affordability Taskforce (NEAT) will identify, assess and implement additional measures that will enhance energy affordability for households and businesses while delivering key renewable commitments and protecting security of supply and economic stability. This Taskforce has noted a wide array of interventions, some of which in a previous form were based on EU-wide regulations and decisions. The Taskforce is due to submit an Action Plan to Government in the coming weeks.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the protections in place for a domestic energy customer who disputes a bill on the basis that an actual meter reading is incorrect, including whether the disputed amount is held while the reading is investigated and whether the customer is protected from collection action or disconnection in that period; if he will engage with the Commission for Regulation of Utilities on strengthening these protections.
reply:
The Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) is Ireland’s independent energy regulator, with statutory responsibility for protecting the interests of energy customers. As Minister, I have no role in individual billing disputes.
Where a customer believes an actual meter reading is incorrect, including an inflated reading from a smart meter, they should contact their supplier as soon as possible, submit the correct reading and make a complaint. The customer can ask for their next direct debit to be withheld while the issue is resolved.
Once a complaint about a bill has been registered, the supplier must pause collection activity on the disputed amount, and the customer cannot be disconnected for non-payment of that amount. If the customer remains unhappy after completing the supplier’s complaints process, they can refer the matter to the CRU’s dispute resolution service. Collection of the disputed amount must remain paused during that investigation. Customers must continue to pay any charges unrelated to the dispute.
Where a correction results in a large catch-up bill, the supplier can agree a suitable repayment plan. Under the CRU’s Electricity and Gas Suppliers’ Handbook, a supplier must make at least four attempts to contact a customer, including two in writing. It must also give the network operator at least ten working days’ notice before any disconnection can be requested.
I am satisfied that robust protections are in place. My Department engages regularly with the CR

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will request Gas Networks Ireland to provide the number of domestic gas meter readings recorded as actual readings in 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026 which were subsequently found to be incorrect and were corrected or cancelled following a query or complaint from a customer or supplier; the main causes identified, including misreads and readings recorded against the wrong meter, in tabular form.
reply:
Gas Networks Ireland (GNI) is responsible for the operation of the national gas network, including the reading of gas meters. This is an operational matter for GNI, which is regulated by the Commission for Regulation of Utilities. However, to assist the Deputy, I have asked GNI for the information requested, and I am advised as follows.
There are approximately 720,000 homes and businesses connected to the gas network, of which 691,000 are domestic customers. In 2025, 1.75 million actual meter readings were issued to gas suppliers.

GNI has advised that in every case where an actual reading was amended, the cause was human error by the meter reader, who recorded an incorrect digit. No cases of readings recorded against the wrong meter were identified.
A customer who believes a reading is incorrect can raise it with their supplier or directly with GNI. GNI will investigate the matter under its complaint handling procedure.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the number of planned actual meter readings per year a domestic gas customer is entitled to expect from Gas Networks Ireland, given that the network operator states four readings a year while at least one supplier tells its customers there are three planned readings a year; the number of actual readings per domestic meter achieved on average in 2024 and 2025; the performance targets that apply to meter reading.
reply:
Gas Networks Ireland (GNI) is responsible for the operation of the national gas network, including the reading of gas meters. This is an operational matter for GNI, which is regulated by the Commission for Regulation of Utilities. However, to assist the Deputy, I have asked GNI for the information requested, and I am advised as follows.
GNI aims to take four actual readings a year from each domestic meter. Meter reading levels fell significantly during 2020 and 2021 because of COVID-19 restrictions, and GNI has not yet returned to a full four-reading cycle. This is mainly due to difficulties gaining access to customers’ premises, along with a reduction in the number of meter readers available since 2020/21. GNI, therefore, targeted three actual readings a year in 2024 and 2025, and returned to a target of four readings a year in 2026.
GNI’s performance targets for 2024 and 2025 were an access level of at least 80% - meaning the share of visits where a reading is successfully taken - and an average of at least 2.4 actual readings per domestic meter. It exceeded both targets.

question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the current status of the regulations and compensation scheme promised under the Electricity (Supply) (Amendment) Act 2025; and when he expects to publish them.
reply:
The Electricity (Supply) (Amendment) Bill 2026 has recently been approved by Government and referred for Pre-Legislative Scrutiny. The Bill provides for a statutory compensation framework and regulation-making powers to support the implementation of the proposed Forestry Corridor and electricity network resilience measures.
As the legislation has not yet completed the Oireachtas process, the detailed compensation arrangements and associated regulations have not yet been finalised or published. Work is currently underway with the Office of Parliamentary Counsel on the drafting of the Bill, while officials are also continuing to develop the policy framework that will underpin compensation methodologies, administrative procedures and related implementation arrangements.
The proposed legislation provides for the establishment of the statutory principles governing compensation, while more detailed matters, including compensation methodologies, procedures and evidential requirements, are intended to be provided for through secondary legislation. This approach will allow the framework to be refined following stakeholder engagement, Pre-Legislative Scrutiny and the enactment of the primary legislation.

reply: My Department does not record eTenders notice references. The Department's internal contract register is not linked to the eTenders tendering platform and there is no way to automatically update it with eTenders contract award notices.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether purchase orders issued by his Department under procurement contracts can be linked to the corresponding contracts held in its internal contract register; whether a contract reference or other unique identifier is maintained to enable this linkage; and if not, the way his Department monitors cumulative expenditure against the approved value of each contract.
reply:
Since 2021, my Department has implemented a financial management system requirement whereby a categorisation code is required for each contract prior to raising a purchase order. Contracts are managed by contract owners within each business unit to ensure each contract delivers the required service on time and within budget.
As an additional measure, details of all contracts including total expenditure to date is issued on a quarterly bases to all relevant business units for monitoring and control purposes. This includes identification of contracts close to their end date or those nearing the full value of the contract.

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether he or his Department has issued guidance to the public on locations to bring discarded nitrous oxide canisters; whether an environmental impact assessment of the discarding of cannisters has been undertaken; and whether there has been consideration of designated collection points to safely dispose of such products.
reply:
Under EU waste legislation, discarded pressurised containers of nitrous oxide should be classified and treated as hazardous waste and as such used nitrous oxide canisters should not be placed in the residual waste bin or the recycling bin and require a specialist hazardous waste disposal service for collection and appropriate treatment.
The Department has continued to engage with the local authority sector and other relevant stakeholders, under the auspices of the National Hazardous Waste Management Plan, to prioritise the development of a system which will assist local authorities in managing discarded nitrous oxide canisters as a matter of urgency.
Arising from this process of engagement, a Working Group has been established, chaired by the Regional Waste Management Planning Offices, to address the issue. Membership of the Working Group consists of representatives of the local authority sector, the Environmental Protection Agency and officials from the Department. It will prioritise the development of guidance and procedures to assist all local authorities in appropriately managing this material via the civic amenity site network.
In addition, the Working Group is committed to developing appropriate awareness raising measures to ensure that the public are fully informed about how to properly dispose of this material. question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the measures being taken to ensure that salmon remain on the River Slaney; and if he is concerned at depleting numbers in recent years.
reply:
Ireland operates a science-based salmon management regime, where individual river stocks are assessed annually against their conservation limits. This scientific advice informs the application of annual conservation measures which can include restrictions on harvesting, catch-and-release requirements and fishery closures where necessary. In the case of the Slaney, specific restrictions are in place to protect its salmon stock including a prohibition on harvesting and restrictions on the angling season.
In relation to fisheries management, Inland Fisheries Ireland (IFI) undertake a range of activities to support the protection and conservation of salmon stocks. In the River Slaney catchment specifically:
• IFI is progressing 16 projects under its Barrier Mitigation Programme across the Slaney catchment, including 10 on the River Slaney itself. This includes a pilot project at Clonmahon to examine options for improving fish passage at an existing hydroelectric scheme.
• A number of habitat restoration projects are also planned across the catchment to improve/create salmon spawning and nursery habitats and improve climate resilience. Further river rehabilitation projects may also be eligible for conservation funding under IFI's Salmon and Sea Trout Rehabilitation, Conservation and Protection Fund.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the actions being taken to increase the maximum level of renewable electricity that can be accommodated on the grid, given the high levels of dispatch down in 2026.
reply:
The Government recognises that renewable dispatch down is an increasingly important issue as Ireland continues to increase levels of renewable electricity generation and works towards its climate and energy objectives.
At present, my focus is on delivering a holistic and enduring approach to addressing dispatch down and facilitating greater levels of dispatchable demand across the electricity system. A comprehensive strategic and operational assessment document is currently being prepared which will set out the full range of measures being progressed across Government, regulators, network operators and industry to address renewable dispatch down and maximise the utilisation of renewable electricity generation. This work encompasses a wide range of measures including demand response, storage, network reinforcement, smart technologies and other flexibility solutions, and is being progressed through established policy, regulatory and system planning processes.
By improving the efficiency with which renewable energy is utilised, these measures aim to support lower system costs, reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels and contribute to a more affordable energy transition, delivering benefits for all consumers, including households vulnerable to energy poverty.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the current status of the Celtic Interconnector; and whether the project remains on schedule for completion in the fourth quarter of 2028.
reply:
The Celtic Interconnector is a strategically important energy infrastructure project that will establish the first direct electricity connection between Ireland and continental Europe through France. With a capacity of 700 MW, the project comprises approximately 575 km of subsea and underground cable, including 500 km of subsea infrastructure, and will provide enough electricity to supply up to 450,000 homes. Construction commenced in December 2023 and substantial progress continues to be made across all elements of the project. I am advised that significant advancement has been achieved on both converter station construction and cable installation activities. Irish terrestrial works has seen all onshore cables installed with completion of the converter station currently scheduled for completion by the end of 2026.
Marine cable installation commenced in 2025, and a second offshore installation campaign is now well advanced in 2026, with approximately 100 km of cable laid to date.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to outline the measures being taken to achieve the target of 5GW of offshore wind generation by 2030; and the timeline for delivery.
reply:
Five Phase 1 offshore wind projects are in development off our east coast, with a planned capacity of 3.8 gigawatts (GW). All are advanced in the planning system with An Coimisiún Pleanála. An Coimisiún Pleanála is expected to make the first determinations on these planning applications in the first half of 2027. Subject to planning consent, I anticipate that projects will be in construction over the next few years and operational in the early 2030s.
The Phase 2 Tonn Nua project off the coast of Waterford is progressing well since approval in 2025 and will add a further 900 megawatts of capacity, making a total 4.7 GW of planned capacity in development. Tonn Nua was the first of four sites to be brought to auction from the South Coast DMAP.
Building on the 4.7 gigawatts of projects already in development, planning is underway for Ireland’s next offshore wind auction for the Lí Ban site, located off the coast of Waterford in the South Coast DMAP. Site surveys are underway to inform auction participants and work on planning a connection to the onshore grid is nearing completion.
Looking beyond the 5 GW target, my Department has been preparing a National DMAP over the past year. The National DMAP will designate sufficient additional renewable development areas around our coast to facilitate achievement of the longer term 20 GW offshore wind target. A draft of the National DMAP will be published for consultation in the first quarter of 2027.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment for details of any programme being developed to assess the extension of operating licences for older wind farms approaching the end of their planning life.
reply:
Ireland is a world leader in onshore wind with over 5GW of installed capacity. The continued operation of Ireland's fleet of onshore wind farms is critical to ensuring a secure and affordable energy supply to 2030 and beyond. Repowering of existing wind farms has the potential to deliver an increase in energy generation, usually by replacing older, less efficient turbines with newer models with higher capacities, with limited additional environmental impact. Extension of lifetime of existing windfarms also has a key role to play in ensuring a secure, renewable electricity supply.
The Programme for Government 2025 highlights the role that repowering of existing wind farms can play in ensuring a secure and affordable energy supply.
The Renewable Energy Directive requires Member States to introduce accelerated and simplified permitting procedures for the repowering of renewable energy projects.
As Minister, I have no function in overseeing the operating licenses of Wind Farm developments. However, my Department engaged consultants to conduct an independent analysis on the repowering and life extension of Ireland’s current installed onshore wind energy projects. This analysis will help to inform the requirement for any necessary future policy framework that supports repowering of onshore wind farms.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to provide the estimated cost of upgrading portions of the national electricity grid most vulnerable to weather-related outages; and the funding allocated for such works over the next five years.
reply:
The Commission for Regulation of Utilities' (CRU) Price Review 6 (PR6) provides for investment of up to €18.9 billion in Ireland's electricity networks over the five-year period 2026-2030, including a baseline investment allowance of €13.8 billion.
Of particular relevance to weather-related outages, PR6 provides for approximately €990 million in storm resilience investment targeted at those areas of the electricity network most vulnerable to severe weather. This investment supports a broad range of resilience measures including network reinforcement, flood protection, enhanced vegetation management, storm preparedness, restoration capability, vulnerable customer supports, operational resilience and customer communications. It also supports the continued development of measures to address vegetation and forestry-related risks to electricity infrastructure.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the measures in place to ensure that the €18.9 billion investment programme for electricity transmission and distribution infrastructure as part of PR6 is delivered on schedule and within budget.
reply:

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if his Department and each agency and public body under its aegis maintain a supplier register or equivalent electronic record in which suppliers are assigned unique identifiers; the identifier types held by each body, including CRO registration numbers, VAT numbers and internally generated supplier IDs, in tabular form; whether these identifiers are recorded against individual purchase orders, contracts and payments; and, where no such identifier is maintained, the way in which suppliers are uniquely identified within the body's financial and procurement systems.
reply:
A supplier register is maintained on my Department’s financial management system to enable payments to be made. Each supplier is assigned a supplier ID(s) which is unique to that supplier. reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 227 and 251 together.
While plug-in solar is an emerging low-carbon technology that has seen rapid adoption in countries such as Germany and was recently permitted in the UK, it is not yet permitted in Northern Ireland. It is the Government’s intention that we accelerate the introduction of plug-in solar in Ireland. Once enabled, it could present a cost-effective and accessible option for customers to become more active participants in our energy transition, potentially seeing benefits such as electricity bill reductions, greater demand flexibility and supporting our renewable energy and climate ambitions.
At my request, ESB Networks established a plug-in solar working group in May of this year. Its purpose is to identify and assess potential pathways to enable the safe, standardised and scalable deployment of plug-in solar in Ireland. The working group has convened nine times to date.
The working group recently submitted an options report for my Department’s consideration including recommendations on the proposed installation approach, product specification pathway, customer guidance and more. My Department is also working alongside the other stakeholders in the working group to accelerate aspects of the regulatory framework in the meantime. Next steps include conducting an Ireland-specific safety study, a wider legislative review, development of customer guidance and an online product registration portal.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to provide details of all engagements between senior officials in his Department and the European Commission in respect of Ireland's ETS2 derogation in light of changes to carbon tax rates announced in budget 2027.
reply:
ETS2 extends emissions trading to sectors of the economy that are currently covered by Ireland’s domestic carbon tax. My Department, therefore, at the request of the Department of Finance notified the European Commission of the derogation on 19 December 2023 under article 30e.3 of Directive (EU) 2023/959, which allows for a Member State with a carbon tax equivalent or higher than the average ETS2 auction rate, to be exempted from the obligation on regulated entities to surrender ETS2 allowances for each of the years 2028 to 2030.
In June 2026, the European Commission confirmed to my Department that they had no further observations on Ireland’s derogation.
Before Budget 2027, officials from the Department of Finance and my Department informed the Commission of the Government’s intention to amend its national carbon tax. Ireland is required under Article 30e.3(a) of Directive (EU) 2023/959 to notify the European Commission of changes made to the national carbon tax outlined in Budget 2027. Upon the enactment of the Finance Bill 2026, Ireland will formally outline changes made to the Commission, and the Commission will have three months under Article 30e.3(e) of Directive (EU) 2023/959 to raise any objections to Irelands derogation application.

question: Deputy Johnny Guirke asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to provide details of the fuel reserves held by Ireland.
reply:
Ireland maintains strategic oil stocks through the National Oil Reserves Agency (NORA) in accordance with national legislation, EU requirements and Ireland's obligations as a member of the International Energy Agency (IEA).
As of 22 October 2026, NORA holds approximately 1.56m tonnes of strategic oil stocks, equivalent to 85 days of Ireland's stockholding obligation. These stocks comprise a mix of refined petroleum products, including diesel, jet fuel/kerosene and petrol, together with a small volume of crude oil.
NORA has completed its obligations under the International Energy Agency (IEA) collective action agreed in March, under which IEA member countries were requested to release a total of 400m barrels of oil as part of a coordinated global response to international supply concerns. Any further release of Ireland's strategic oil stocks would be at the Minister’s discretion, having regard to prevailing market conditions and security of supply considerations. However, NORA does not anticipate that any further releases of strategic stocks will be required at this time.
Ireland's strategic stockholding position remains robust and NORA remains ready and able to release strategic stocks, if required, in the event of future supply disruptions or emergency situations affecting security of fuel supply.

By improving the efficiency with which renewable energy is utilised, these measures aim to support lower system costs, reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels and contribute to a more affordable energy transition, delivering benefits for all consumers, including households vulnerable to energy poverty.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the key milestones, by year between now and 2040, for Ireland to meet our current energy generation targets, specifically onshore and offshore.
reply:
Accelerating the deployment of renewable electricity generation is fundamental to our transition to a renewables-led system. Government support schemes are driving the onshore renewable electricity uptake in Ireland. The Programme for Government commits to holding at least one auction per annum under the Renewable Electricity Support Scheme (RESS), Ireland’s flagship policy to deliver onshore renewable electricity at scale. Three non-competitive support schemes – the Small-Scale Renewable Electricity Support Scheme (SRESS), the Microgeneration Support Scheme (MSS), and the Targeted Agriculture Modernisation Schemes (TAMS) – offer homes, communities, farmers, and businesses the opportunity to take an active role in the energy transition, while reducing their electricity costs.
As well as this, the Offshore Renewable Electricity Support Scheme (ORESS) has resulted in five Phase One projects currently progressing through the planning process which will deliver 3.8 GW of offshore wind capacity with a further 900 MW auctioned so far in Phase Two. question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to provide an update on the progress of the Electricity (Supply) (Amendment) Bill 2025 and to set out the measures it contains to enhance Ireland's storm preparedness; when it will be read at second stage in the Dáil.
reply:
The Electricity (Supply) (Amendment) Bill 2026 has progressed significantly since Government first approved the development of legislation in July 2025. Following extensive engagement with ESB Networks, the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine, the Office of the Attorney General, Coillte and other stakeholders, Government recently approved revised Heads of the Bill and approved their referral for Pre-Legislative Scrutiny.
The Bill is intended to strengthen the resilience of Ireland's electricity network in response to the lessons learned from Storm Éowyn and the increasing risks posed by severe weather events. Since Storm Éowyn, ESB Networks has delivered a €74.5 million Winter Resilience Programme, undertaken detailed assessments of approximately 3,782km of electricity infrastructure located within forestry areas, engaged with more than 1,800 forestry owners, completed works on more than 12,000 damaged and diseased hedgerow trees and progressed

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to provide an update on the timeline and the projected capacity of the Celtic Interconnector with France.
reply:
The Celtic Interconnector is a strategically important energy infrastructure project that will establish the first direct electricity connection between Ireland and continental Europe through France. With a capacity of 700 MW, the project comprises approximately 575 km of subsea and underground cable, including 500 km of subsea infrastructure, and will provide enough electricity to supply up to 450,000 homes. Jointly developed by EirGrid and its French counterpart, Réseau de Transport d’Électricité (RTE), the interconnector will strengthen Ireland's energy security, enhance market integration, support the transition to renewable energy, and facilitate greater electricity trading between Ireland and Europe.
Construction commenced in December 2023 and substantial progress continues to be made across all elements of the project. I am advised that significant advancement has been achieved on both converter station construction and cable installation activities. Irish terrestrial works has seen all onshore cables installed with the converter station currently scheduled for completion by the end of 2026.
Marine cable installation commenced in 2025, and a second offshore installation campaign is now well advanced in 2026, with approximately 100 km of cable laid to date.
While project timelines have been revised in line with the updated work programme, EirGrid advise that the project remains on track for commercial operations by the end of 2028.

SEAI also offers community groups free access to specialist technical advisor support for grid connection, planning permission applications, feasibility studies and community formation.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to outline Ireland's long-term electricity storage policy and progress toward achieving adequate levels of energy storage.
reply:
In line with the Electricity Storage Policy Framework for Ireland and the 10 Government actions contained within it, my Department is focused on removing the barriers to the development of electricity storage projects and their incorporation to the Irish grid system.
Action 6 of the Policy Framework supports the immediate procurement of 1GW of demand flexibility and long duration electricity storage to meet specific network needs on the distribution and transmissions systems respectively.
In line with action 6, ESB Networks have completed the first iteration of their route to market to deliver 500 MW of Demand Flexibility Products on to the Distribution system. First contracts for 42 MW were awarded in Q2 2026.
Likewise, EirGrid, in conjunction with the CRU, are developing a route to market for Long Duration Energy Storage (LDES). The first LDES contracts are expected to be signed in 2028.
Actions 7 and 8, as well as Actions 9 and 10 (if required), of the Policy Framework will provide a glidepath for electricity storage out to 2040.
Action 7 initiates a quantitative consultation to identify the minimum storage requirements between 2030 and 2040 for the electricity grid. Development of Action 7 is underway in my Department and outputs are expected by the end of 2028.

reply:
The Community Centre Investment Fund (CCIF) was introduced to provide high-quality community facilities that are available to all groups in both urban and rural communities. Through the CCIF, almost €112 million has been allocated for the enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres and the construction of new centres where such a need has been identified.
Earlier this year, I was delighted to launch the latest round of funding for enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres. The funding under CCIF 2026 is being delivered across two categories, with maximum funding levels of €25,000 and €100,000 respectively. A minimum of 5% of the total project budget was required by the applicant as match funding under Category 1 applications and a minimum of 10% of the total project budget was required by the applicant as match funding under Category 2 applications. My department supports successful applicants through phased payments and ongoing engagement through the project delivery period. Indeed, 90% of the funding is provided in advance for projects approved under category 1.
As part of CCIF 2026, a number of online information events and check-in clinics were held during April to July 2026. These events were held in order to provide guidance and supports in relation to the application process. A total of 5 information events were held in addition to 29 check-in clinics where applicants could ask questions in respect of their application.

question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht to clarify the regulatory framework for the operation of crematoriums in Ireland.
reply:
My Department has responsibility for policy and legislation in relation to local authority burial grounds while the actual operation of burial grounds is the responsibility of the local authority concerned.
Under the Local Government (Sanitary Services) Acts, 1878 to 2001, local authorities are deemed to be burial boards for their respective functional areas. Acting in their capacity as burial boards, local authorities are responsible for the management, regulation and control of burial grounds in their functional areas.
Regulations are currently in place regarding burials and burial grounds, namely Part III of the Public Health (Ireland) Act, 1878, as amended in Part VI of the Local Government (Sanitary Services) Act, 1948 and more recently, the Local Government Acts, 1994 and 2001, and also in the Rules and Regulations for the Regulation of Burial Grounds 1888 and amendments thereto. Local authorities also have powers to make bye-laws in relation to burial grounds.
In relation to the Deputy's specific query, in the context of Crematoria, I understand there are professional bodies for these activities with their own codes and standards, but my Department has no role in this regard.
In general, with regard to Crematoria, the establishment and operation of any such activity is subject, where applicable, to the provisions of legislation dealing with planning and development, environmental protection and air pollution.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht whether purchase orders issued by his Department under procurement contracts can be linked to the corresponding contracts held in its internal contract register; whether a contract reference or other unique identifier is maintained to enable this linkage; if not, the way in which his Department monitors cumulative expenditure against the approved value of each contract.
reply:
Since September 2025, all payments made by my Department are processed using the Financial Shared Service System provided by the National Shared Service Office. Invoices processed through this system require a corresponding Purchase Requisition and Purchase Order in order to be paid.
To raise a Purchase Order on the Financial Shared Service System, the supplier needs to be active on the system, and a contract must be generated and linked to the payment. Each contract contains a unique identifying number which enables linkage between payments and contracts in place, and ongoing monitoring of cumulative expenditure against the approved value of each contract.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 2382 and 2383 together.
The new SÍOL programme was launched on 8 July 2026, in line with the Programme for Government commitment to deliver funding for projects and initiatives in urban areas with the highest concentration of disadvantage. SÍOL means ‘Seed’ in English and SÍOL stands for Scéim Infheistíochta ag Obair Le Chéile, which translates to ‘Working Together Investment Scheme’. Capital funding of €31.5 million has been secured up to 2030 in the National Development Plan to support the new programme. Funding of €5m has been allocated to the programme for 2026 and Budget 2027 allocated an additional €1m for next year's programme.
The programme targets small areas of disadvantage in our towns and cities, providing funding for infrastructure to improve the areas and the lives of the communities. Priority is being given to those Small Areas with the highest population of extreme disadvantage, and the scheme is designed to provide similar supports to these areas that is given to rural areas through schemes such as CLÁR.
The new programme is focussed initially on 15 areas that have been designated as SÍOL areas. The programme takes into consideration the areas in Ireland already covered by the CLÁR programme, to ensure geographical complementarity.

question: Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht to extend the Pobal administered senior alert scheme to include grant funding for video doorbells (details supplied) to enhance the safety and security of older people, particularly those living alone.
reply:
My Department is responsible for the Seniors Alert Scheme which encourages community support for vulnerable older people in our communities through the provision of personal monitored alarms to enable them to live securely in their homes with confidence, independence and peace of mind. Funding is available under the scheme towards the purchase by a registered community-based organisation of a personal alarm or pendant and one year of monitoring.
Expenditure to date in 2026 under the SAS initiative has been €4.28 million. As it is a demand led scheme, it is kept under continuous review to ensure funding can be made available to meet the requirements of all qualifying applicants.
Officials in my department continue to work with stakeholders, agencies and other Government Departments in the assessment of new and developing technologies as part of the ongoing review of the scheme. However, there are no plans to provide funding for the provision of video doorbells at present.
The Department of Housing Local Government and Heritage provides funding for security additions through the Housing Adaptation Grants for Older People and Disabled People, which are administered by local authorities.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to outline the work of the Accelerating Renewable Electricity Taskforce; and to set out its achievements to date.
reply:
The Accelerating Renewable Electricity Taskforce (‘ARE Taskforce’) was established to identify, coordinate, and prioritise the policies required to fast-track and increase deployment of onshore renewable electricity generation and supporting infrastructure, including storage, ensuring that barriers are removed or minimised to the greatest extent possible.
The work being carried out under the aegis of the ARE Taskforce is supporting the deployment and integration of renewables in our power system, bolstering energy supply security and reducing the impact of imported fossils fuels on energy costs for homes and businesses.
Ireland currently has over 8.9 GW of installed renewable generation capacity, representing an approximate 4 GW of additional renewable generation capacity installed since 2020. Figures contained in the SEAI’s Energy in Ireland Report 2026, published in October, show that in 2025 we saw an increase in electricity supply from multiple renewable sources, including solar, onshore wind, and biomass, while also seeing a decrease in supply from fossil fuel sources, including natural gas, oil, and coal. This resulted in Ireland seeing our lowest level of electricity being met by fossil fuels on record (41.9%). Renewables accounted for 41% of our electricity grid demand in 2025, which doesn’t take into account the electricity demand reduction being seen due to the impact of domestic and other sources of embedded solar.

question: Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht when a decision will be made on application received under the Community Centre Investment Fund 2026.
reply:
The Community Centre Investment Fund (CCIF) was introduced to provide high quality community facilities that are available to community groups in both urban and rural communities. Through the CCIF, some €112 million has been allocated for the enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres and the construction of new centres where such a need has been identified.
I launched the latest round of funding under CCIF 2026 on the 26th of March for enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres. The fund will be delivered across 2 categories with maximum funding levels of €25,000 and €100,000 respectively. The closing date for the CCIF 2026 has now passed.
Applications are currently being assessed and I look forward to announcing the successful projects under category 1, which provides funding of up to €25,000, shortly. Approvals under category 2, which provides funding of up to €100,000, will be announced before year-end.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht for an update on matters raised in correspondence (details supplied).
reply:
The aim of the Community Development Pilot Programme (CDP) is to trial community development initiatives that address poverty, social exclusion and inequality, and promote human rights by providing supports to the most severely marginalised.
The CDP was launched on 4th March 2021 with seven projects. Additional funding was made available in 2023 for the expansion of the programme. Following a closed call for applications in 2023, three additional projects were approved under the programme for 3 years.

All schemes operated by my department including the CDP are reviewed on a regular basis, to ensure the funding available is put to best use in terms of supporting communities throughout the country.
The funding allocations for the CDP beyond 2026 are currently under consideration by my department.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the way in which his Department is building cyber resilience; and the strategy in place to address cyber attacks.

Maintaining strong governance, security controls, and risk management procedures.
Threat detection through monitoring, intelligence sharing, and vulnerability management.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to outline the work of the Offshore Wind Delivery Taskforce; and to set out its achievements to date.
reply:
The cross-departmental Offshore Wind Delivery Taskforce (OWDT) was established in 2022 to advance Ireland’s offshore wind energy objectives and to capture potential associated economic and social benefits. With membership drawn from senior officials from across government, the Taskforce has served as a primary policy vehicle for advancing Offshore Renewable Energy (ORE) policy.
Since June 2025, representatives from Wind Energy Ireland (WEI) and Marine Renewables Industry Association (MRIA) have also been invited to participate in Taskforce meetings.
A key output of the Taskforce is the Offshore Wind Energy Programme (OWEP), which brings together work ongoing across government into one system-wide plan. The OWEP consists of a range of workstreams grouped thematically into ‘pillars’ with clear objectives and actions.
An annual review including key actions for delivery in the coming year is also undertaken. The 2025 annual review with key actions for 2026 was published on the OWDT webpage in May 2026.

For example, the OWDT supported development of the following policy documents - 'Powering Prosperity' (DETE) and Ireland's Offshore Wind Skills Action Plan (DFHERIS).

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science his plans for the reform of the CAO admissions system.
reply:
The CAO admissions system is one route to higher education, but it is important to consider the overall transition of students to tertiary education and, ultimately, graduate outcomes. Officials in my Department are exploring policy options for reform to improve the experience of learners, both in their transition to higher education, and as they progress through it. A number of interrelated issues are being considered as part of this work including opportunities for a broader education; more transdisciplinary learning and the development of transversal skills.
This work is being considered alongside related policy areas, including progression to higher education from further education and training, with a view to expanding the prevalence and ease of this pathway. Improved access to guidance and greater transparency of information for learners are also important in supporting better decision-making.
My Department is also continuing to expand alternative pathways into higher education. There are 78 tertiary programmes available for the 2026/27 academic year across 24 counties, an increase of 70% on last year. These include a new pathway into primary teaching, opening the profession to a more diverse group of future teachers. question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science If he will review the SUSI grant eligibility criteria in the case of a person (details supplied).
reply:
The main support available to students is the statutory based Student Grant Scheme where students are studying for the first time or are progressing to study at a higher level. The decision on eligibility for a student grant is a matter, in the first instance, for the centralised student grant awarding authority SUSI (Student Universal Support Ireland) to determine.
For student grant purposes, students are categorised according to their circumstances either as students dependent on parents or a legal guardian, or as independent mature students.
The conditions for dependent and independent status are prescribed in the Student Grant Scheme. The scheme sets out that a student may be assessed as an independent mature student if:
• The student has attained the age of 23 on the 1st of January of the year of first entry to an approved course or of re-entry following a break in studies of at least three years and;
• is not ordinarily resident with their parents from the previous October.
Otherwise, they are assessed as a dependent student i.e. assessed with reference to parental income.
Applicants who do not meet the criteria to be assessed as an independent student for grant purposes, or who cannot supply the necessary documentation to establish independent living for the required period, may still apply to SUSI to have their grant eligibility assessed as a dependent student. The relevant information, including details of parental income, would be required by SUSI to determine grant

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science his plan to ensure each HEI has implemented the existing HEA national policy framework on generative AI.
reply:
The Higher Education Authority launched its Generative AI in Higher Education Teaching & Learning: Policy Framework in 2025 and are currently supporting its implementation in higher education institutions.
The Framework provides a national reference point to guide the adoption of generative artificial intelligence in teaching, learning and assessment. It sets out five core principles covering academic integrity, transparency and accountability; equity and inclusion; critical engagement, human oversight and AI literacy; privacy and data governance; and sustainable pedagogy.
Irish higher education institutions are statutorily independent, autonomous bodies, with responsibility for their own academic and administrative affairs, including the development and implementation of policies. As such, it is not within the remit of myself as the Minister, the department, or the HEA to determine or enforce institutional policy on the use of generative AI.
The Framework is therefore intended to support a consistent national approach while allowing institutions to independently take account of their individual contexts. The HEA has also made available guidance and resources to support institutions in applying the Framework's principles.
In 2027, the HEA - supported by my department - plans to undertake a follow-up review and prepare a report which will assess progress in implementing the Framework across the sector. This will examine how its principles have been reflected in institutional p

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if he is aware that the United States War Department has designated certain Institutes as a threat to national security (details supplied); and if he has any such concerns about the Institute located here.
reply:
I am aware of the designation given to Confucius Institutes by the United States Department of War.
Confucius Institutes are an initiative of the Chinese Government intended to promote and contribute to cultural and educational exchanges. There are three such institutions in the Republic of Ireland; in UCD, UCC and the University of Galway.
Within the meaning of the Universities Act 1997, Ireland's universities are autonomous institutions and as such, are responsible for the management of their international partnerships, in line with their individual institutional governance arrangements and associated policies.
It is a matter for each individual HEI therefore to consider the added value of the presence of a Confucius Institute on their campus, while ensuring that other considerations such as academic integrity and independence, are also maintained and supported.
The diverse international links maintained by our HEIs not only enrich the experience of students in Ireland, but also strengthen research collaboration, support knowledge exchange, broaden academic perspectives, and enhance the global reputation and competitiveness of the Irish higher education system.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science whether purchase orders issued by his Department under procurement contracts can be linked to the corresponding contracts held in its internal contract register; whether a contract reference or other unique identifier is maintained to enable this linkage; and if not, the way in which his Department monitors cumulative expenditure against the approved value of each contract.

The Department's financial and procurement controls provide oversight of cumulative expenditure over the lifetime of a contract and support audit and governance requirements.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if the application for a waiver of capping under mitigating circumstances is available to students in technological universities.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 2359 and 2360 together.
Higher Education Institutions, including universities and technological universities, are autonomous bodies within the meaning of the Universities Act 1997 and the Technological Universities Act 2018. Under this legislation, they are academically and administratively independent and entitled to regulate their own academic affairs and administrative processes.
Matters relating to mitigating circumstances, repeat examinations and the capping of marks are therefore matters for the institution concerned in accordance with its own academic regulations and procedures.
Neither my Department nor I have a role in reviewing or intervening in individual cases. Accordingly, I am not in a position to determine whether the student concerned may apply for, or be granted, a waiver of capping.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the reason the Owenriff (Barna) River System (No. 140) in County Galway has never been listed in any annual Conservation of Salmon and Sea Trout Bye-Laws, considering that Atlantic salmon have been harvested from the system in the years 2005, 2010, 2011, 2014, 2017, 2018 and 2023 as catalogued in the yearly Wild Salmon and Sea Trout Statistic Reports as published by the Central Fisheries Board/Inland Fisheries Ireland.
reply:
As set out to the Deputy in my replies to Questions No. 143 of 7 July 2026 and No. 246 of 12 May 2026, the Owenriff (Barna) is not a designated salmon river. Only designated rivers are subject to scientific assessment and catch advice from the Technical Expert Group on Salmon (TEGOS), as part of the annual salmon management framework.
As the Owenriff (Barna) river is not among the designated rivers assessed under this framework, it is not individually listed in the annual conservation regulations or associated bye-laws.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science further to Parliamentary Question No. PQ75135/26, given that the vast majority of English language education providers do not fall under his Department's Inspectorate, to outline the inspection, oversight and enforcement regime applying to such providers, including the number of inspections, compliance audits and complaints recorded since 2022.
reply:
Private English language schools do not come under the aegis of the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science.
However, inclusion on the Interim List of Eligible Programmes (ILEP) is necessary for a Higher Education or English language education provider to be eligible to recruit learners from non-EEA countries on Stamp 2 immigration permissions. The ILEP is administered by the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in conjunction with the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science.
The ILEP was introduced in 2015, as an interim measure, and is a restrictive list of education programmes eligible for international student immigration purposes. The list is used as a reference point for the immigration function of the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in considering visa and residency applications from non-EEA applicants wishing to study on a full-time basis in Ireland.
Providers must remain in compliance with the relevant criteria to retain a listing on the ILEP. Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) monitors compliance and any education provider may be subject to unannounced inspections, on-line monitoring, or random spot checks to ensure its compliance with ILEP criteria, and this includes the maintenance of records and reports. These may be requested by ISD at any time and failure to do so can result in the removal of a provider from the ILEP.

question: Deputy Martin Kenny asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the way the upcoming pay transparency Bill and equality Bill will protect grant-capped, community-sector education workers from systemic pay discrimination; and if the revised LTI guidelines will introduce formal incremental salary scales aligned with mainstream ETB roles.
reply:
I recognise the valuable contribution made by community-sector education workers, including those involved in the delivery of Local Training Initiative (LTI) programmes, in providing accessible education and training opportunities, particularly for individuals experiencing educational and socio-economic disadvantage.
The EU Pay Transparency Directive (EU) 2023/970 aims to strengthen the principle of equal pay for equal work, or work of equal value, between men and women through pay transparency and enforcement mechanisms. The Directive aims to increase transparency around pay and gender pay gaps and to strengthen the measures available to address instances of pay discrimination. The Directive does not provide for automatic pay parity between employees of different employers or organisations. Rather, it seeks to support the enforcement of existing equal pay rights between men and women performing the same work, or work of equal value. Accordingly, it does not create an automatic entitlement to pay equivalence between LTI staff and staff directly employed by Education and Training Boards (ETBs).
The new operational guidelines for third-party providers, which ETBI are developing in collaboration with the sector, and which will be published by SOLAS, will manage the operational relationship between ETBs and third-party providers, in line with the requirements of DPER Circular 13/2014 governing the administration and accountability of Exchequer-funded grants. question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science whether contracts recorded in his Department's internal contract register can be linked to their corresponding contract award notices published on eTenders, where applicable; whether his Department records the relevant eTenders notice reference, URL or other identifier; and if not, the reasons that prevent this information from being recorded.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science his views on reports of fourth year craft apprentice drop-outs; the number of persons who did not complete their apprenticeship in each of the years 2021 to 2025 and to date in 2026, per training institution, in tabular form; the number of persons who did not complete their apprenticeship in each of the years 2021 to 2025 and to date in 2026, by phase of apprenticeship, in tabular form; if he will legislate for a minimum wage for all apprentices; and if he will make a statement specifically on drops in pay for apprentices in their fourth year.
reply:
The most recent National Survey of Apprentices found that 87% of apprentices reported enjoying their apprenticeship experience and 94% believed their apprenticeship would lead to good employment opportunities. This positive experience is reflected in SOLAS data which shows that, on average, between 90% and 92% of first-year apprentices progress to their second year, comparing favourably with other tertiary education pathways.
Craft apprenticeships operate on a continuous intake basis, meaning apprentices complete their training at different times during the year. As a result, there is no single cohort expected to complete in any given year and, therefore, no definitive measure of the number who did not complete during a particular year. In light of these factors, SOLAS advise that it is not possible to provide completion data per institution and year. Apprentices may take longer to complete for a range of reasons, including deferred training, repeated assessments, employment changes or other personal circumstances.
Apprentices are employees, and all apprenticeship programmes are undertaken under a contract of employment. Responsibility for minimum wage legislation rests with the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment. Neither my Department nor SOLAS has a role in setting apprentice wages.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment his views on whether authorisations granted under section 59 of the Inland Fisheries Act 2010 are valid as substitute Ministerial Consents under the ‘Activities Requiring Consent’ (ARC) process as provided for under the European Communities (Birds and Natural Habitats) Regulations - S.I. No. 477 of 2011.
reply:
The Activities Requiring Consent (ARC) regime under European Communities (Birds and Natural Habitats) Regulations 2011 comes under the remit of the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage. It would not be appropriate for me to comment on or make determinations in relation to the application of that regime.
Section 59 of the Inland Fisheries Act 2010 does not establish a Ministerial consent or authorisation regime. Instead, this Section confers powers on Inland Fisheries Ireland (IFI) to carry out specified activities in exercise of its statutory functions including powers to take fish from a fishery, implement measures intended to alter or regulate fish stocks, monitor water quality and undertake certain fisheries improvement works.
IFI is an independent, statutory body. In exercising its statutory functions, IFI is responsible for ensuring that its activities comply with applicable environmental and nature conservation legislation including, where required, the Regulations referred to in the Question. Compliance with such requirements falls within IFI's operational responsibilities and neither I nor the Department have any function in relation to operational matters.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science his views on the need for standardised curricula for phase 2 craft apprenticeship courses.
reply:
The Phase 2 craft apprenticeship curricula is already delivered through a nationally standardised curriculum and assessment framework.
Craft apprenticeships are national programmes and already operate on the basis of a standardised curriculum and assessment structure for each individual craft. The curriculum for each apprenticeship is based on a uniform, pre-specified occupational profile determined and agreed with industry and is structured around defined national learning outcomes.
Phase 2 is an off-the-job component of the national craft apprenticeship programme and is delivered in accordance with the relevant national curriculum. This ensures that apprentices undertaking the same craft programme are working towards the same learning outcomes and assessment requirements, irrespective of the location in which their Phase 2 training is delivered. The national model is underpinned by common assessments and a quality assurance framework.
Craft apprenticeship programmes are reviewed and revalidated periodically to ensure that curricula remain current, industry-relevant and responsive to the needs of learners and the economy.
This national standardised approach supports consistency of training and assessment nationwide while ensuring apprentices develop the knowledge, skills and competencies required by employers and industry.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Health if she will consider the loss of means tested supports for persons with lifelong disabilities who inherit assets from their parents or guardians and medical card eligibility.
reply:
Medical Card provision is primarily based on financial assessment. In accordance with the Health Act 1970 (as amended), eligibility for a medical card is determined by the HSE, which assesses each application on a qualifying financial threshold.
The issue of granting medical cards on the basis of illness or a disability was previously examined in 2014 by the HSE Expert Panel on Medical Need and Medical Card Eligibility. question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Health her Department's policy on the development of cultured meat.
reply:
Dear Deputy Byrne,
"Cultured meat", also referred to as cell culture-derived food, falls within the scope of Regulation (EU) 2015/2283 on novel foods. Such products are considered novel foods because they were not consumed to a significant degree within the European Union before 15 May 1997 and fall within the category of foods consisting of, isolated from, or produced from cell or tissue cultures derived from animals, plants, micro-organisms, fungi or algae.
Under the EU novel foods framework, only products that have undergone a comprehensive safety assessment and have been authorised at EU level may be placed on the market. Any authorised product is subject to specific conditions of use and labelling requirements set out in the relevant authorisation.
To date, no cell culture-derived meat products have been authorised for sale within the European Union.
Two applications for cell culture-derived foods of animal origin are currently progressing through the EU authorisation process:
• Duck cells from cell culture, submitted in 2024, which is currently undergoing a safety assessment by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA).
• Cell-cultured bovine fat biomass derived from the species of cow or domesticated cattle (Bos taurus): The novel food application was submitted in 2024 and is under European Commission’s validation.
The assessment and authorisation of these products will proceed in accordance with the procedures set out in Articles 10 - 13 of Regulation (EU) 2015/2283.

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the total number of operational data centres in Ireland, by size; the number which are single developments or co-located; their total energy consumption over the previous 12 months; the total IT power demand installed, the total data centre water input; the weighted average power usage effectiveness, water usage effectiveness, renewable energy factor and energy reuse factor across all data centres operating in Ireland, by single development or co-located unit, in tabular form.
reply:
Publicly available information indicates there are in the order of 72 to 90 data centres in Ireland, depending on the metrics used, with the vast majority in the Greater Dublin Area.
Article 12 of the Energy Efficiency Directive 2023/1791 (‘EED’) provides for an obligation for Member States to require that owners and operators of certain sized data centres monitor and make publicly available, subject to Union and national law protecting trade and business secrets and confidentiality, information on key metrics on their energy and sustainability performance. The required indicators relate to energy consumption, cooling, waste heat utilisation, water usage and renewable energy use, among others. Reporting of this information by data centres in Ireland to this database is ongoing and the Commission is responsible for making it publicly available in an aggregated manner.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Health the way in which her Department reconciles the position that prioritising medical conditions for medical card eligibility is not ethically justifiable with the long-term illness scheme, which provides entitlements based on specific diagnoses; and if this inconsistency will be reviewed.
reply:
The Long-Term Illness (LTI) Scheme was established under Section 59(3) of the Health Act 1970 (as amended). Regulations were made in 1971, 1973 and 1975, prescribing 16 conditions to be covered by the Scheme. Further information, including the list of conditions, can be found at:
www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/lti/about/.
Under the LTI Scheme, patients receive drugs, medicines, and medical and surgical appliances directly related to the treatment of their illness, free of charge.
Under the Health Act 1970, eligibility for a medical card is based primarily on means. The Act obliges the HSE to assess whether a person is unable, without undue hardship, to arrange general practitioner, medical and surgical services for himself or herself and his or her family, having regard to his or her overall financial position and reasonable expenditure. In doing this, the HSE assesses each medical card application on a qualifying financial threshold.
Medical card holders can access a range of services including general practitioner services, prescribed drugs and medicines, all public in-patient services including consultant services in public hospitals, all public out-patient services including consultant services in public hospitals, home nursing, dental, ophthalmic, and aural services and appliances. Apart from prescribed drugs and medicines, which are subject to a prescription charge, public health services are provided free of charge to medical card holders.

reply:
The Government recognises the importance of timely access for patients to new medicines.
Under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013 the HSE has sole statutory responsibility for decisions on pricing and reimbursement of medicines. There are formal processes which govern applications for the pricing and reimbursement of medicines, and new uses of existing medicines, to be funded and / or reimbursed.
In line with the 2013 Act and the national framework agreed with industry, a company must submit an application to the HSE to have a new medicine added to the reimbursement list and continue to engage at all stages of the process with the HSE to progress applications. Reimbursement is for licenced indications which have been granted market authorisation by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) or the Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA).

question: Deputy Johnny Mythen asked the Minister for Health the initiatives she is taking to improve children's dental services in County Wexford.
reply:
At present, the HSE Oral Healthcare Service aims to provide an oral examination and necessary treatment for children at up to three intervals, targeting ages approximating to second and sixth class and, in some cases, fourth class. Emergency care is provided for children of all ages up to 16. The Dental Treatment Services Scheme provides dental care, free of charge, to medical card holders aged 16 and over. The HSE Orthodontic Service provides treatment to those children with the most severe and complex orthodontic treatment needs.
I am determined to ease the pressure that people are facing nationally, including in Co. Wexford, in accessing oral healthcare. In practical terms, that means improving access through the public oral healthcare system—especially for children and medical card holders. My Department and the HSE are finalising a focused two-year action plan to deliver real improvements on the ground.
The plan will be driven by a dedicated governance group, with progress monitored closely and aligned to wider HSE and Department priorities. It responds to sustained service pressures and long waiting lists—particularly for children and for people with additional needs.
It will focus on a number of clear priorities:
• Cutting waiting lists in the School Dental Programme and orthodontics
• Expanding the access programme for people with additional needs.

question: Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Health the restrictions she is considering to ensure young people are not vaping.
reply:
Significant legislation has been enacted to reduce young people's use of vapes and nicotine products. The Public Health (Tobacco Products and Nicotine Inhaling Products) Act 2023 introduced domestic regulation of nicotine inhaling products such as vapes, including:
A minimum age of sale of 18.
• Further advertising restrictions in cinemas, on public transport and near schools.
• A prohibition on the sale of nicotine inhaling products by self-service, at events aimed at children, and from temporary or moveable premises such as those at festivals.
A significant provision in the Act was the licensing system for the retail sale of tobacco products and nicotine inhaling products, which became operational for all retailers on 2 August 2026. Previously, there was a once-off registration system for tobacco retailers, and no register for retailers of nicotine inhaling products.
Those who wish to sell these products must now apply for a licence, pay the required fee and renew that licence annually. The licensing system will give the Health Service Executive's (HSE's) National Environmental Health Service robust oversight of who is selling nicotine inhaling products. The legislation allows for increased penalties for offences such as selling to minors, including minimum suspension periods and licence revocation.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Health if her Department has developed a policy or framework on the use of predictive diagnostics in healthcare; and to provide details of the areas it is being trialled or used.
reply:
The Minister for Health launched AI for Care – The Artificial Intelligence Strategy for Healthcare in Ireland 2026–2030 on 11 March 2026. While the Department has not developed a separate policy specifically described as a “predictive diagnostics” framework, AI for Care provides the overarching national policy framework for the safe, responsible and effective use of AI in health and social care. It sets out how AI can improve care across four key areas: clinical care, operations, research and innovation, and public health.
This is supported by guidance developed by HIQA on the safe and responsible use of AI and, at implementation level, by the HSE AI Implementation Framework. These provide the wider strategic, governance and implementation context within which AI applications in healthcare can be developed and used, including compliance with relevant legislation such as the EU AI Act.
AI for Care recognises the potential for AI to support faster diagnosis and improved clinical decision-making. AI tools can assist healthcare professionals by identifying patterns in health data, supporting the identification of health risks and informing treatment decisions. AI applications are intended to support rather than replace healthcare professionals, with clinical judgement and human oversight remaining central to their use. The Strategy is underpinned by principles including person-centred care, transparency and trustworthiness, governance and safety, and proven benefit.

question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will consider allowing plug in solar panels in Ireland, which are permitted in many other European countries.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 227 and 251 together.
While plug-in solar is an emerging low-carbon technology that has seen rapid adoption in countries such as Germany and was recently permitted in the UK, it is not yet permitted in Northern Ireland. It is the Government’s intention that we accelerate the introduction of plug-in solar in Ireland. Once enabled, it could present a cost-effective and accessible option for customers to become more active participants in our energy transition, potentially seeing benefits such as electricity bill reductions, greater demand flexibility and supporting our renewable energy and climate ambitions.
At my request, ESB Networks established a plug-in solar working group in May of this year. Its purpose is to identify and assess potential pathways to enable the safe, standardised and scalable deployment of plug-in solar in Ireland. The working group has convened nine times to date.
The working group recently submitted an options report for my Department’s consideration including recommendations on the proposed installation approach, product specification pathway, customer guidance and more. My Department is also working alongside the other stakeholders in the working group to accelerate aspects of the regulatory framework in the meantime. Next steps include conducting an Ireland-specific safety study, a wider legislative review, development of customer guidance and an online product registration portal.

reply:
GPs are private practitioners, most of whom hold a GMS contract with the HSE for the provision of GP services without charge to medical card and GP visit card holders.
Under the terms of the GMS contract, GPs are required to provide eligible patients with ''all proper and necessary treatment of a kind usually undertaken by a general practitioner and not requiring special skill or experience of a degree or kind which general practitioners cannot reasonably be expected to possess". Persons who hold a medical card or a GP visit card are not subject to any co-payments or other charges in respect of such services.
The issue of GPs charging GMS patients for phlebotomy services is complex given the numerous reasons and circumstances under which blood tests are taken. Clinical determinations as to whether a blood test should be taken to either assist in the diagnosis of illness or the treatment of a condition are made by the GP concerned. There is no provision under the GMS GP contract for persons who hold a medical card or a GP visit card to be charged for clinically necessary blood tests.
The HSE has previously communicated to GMS GPs on this matter. However, the relevant GP representative body, the IMO, does not agree with my Department’s and the HSE’s position regarding the provision of routine blood tests under the GMS contract. I am advised that the principal potential health impact attributed to wind energy developments is the possible effect from wind turbine noise. The Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment (DCEE) has primary responsibility for environmental noise matters. DHLGH is working in conjunction with DCEE, in the context of its environmental noise policy remit, to finalise the guidance on the noise aspect of the Review. As part of this work, which is now substantially complete, DCEE appointed noise consultants in May 2023 to inform any amendments to the noise aspect of the National Planning Statement. This is being considered in the context of Ireland's target to supply 80% of electricity demand from renewable energy and related energy security and affordability benefits, whilst having appropriate regard to the impacts of wind energy developments, including noise impacts.
The Review is addressing a number of other aspects of the Guidelines. My Department remains available to engage with DHLGH on the new National Planning Statement on Wind Energy.
