question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Health if she will review the income thresholds for eligibility for the over 70s medical card; whether consideration is being given to increasing these thresholds, which have remained unchanged for a number of years; and if she is aware of concerns that annual increases in the State Pension may result in older persons losing entitlement to an over 70s medical card and facing higher healthcare and prescription costs, thereby leaving them financially worse off.
reply:
Medical Card provision is primarily based on financial assessment. In accordance with the Health Act 1970 (as amended), eligibility for a medical card is determined by the HSE, which assesses each application on a qualifying financial threshold. This is the amount of money that an individual can earn a week and still qualify for a card. It is specific to the individual’s own financial circumstances.Persons aged 69 and under are assessed under the general means tested medical card thresholds which are based on an applicant’s household income after tax and the deduction of PRSI and the Universal Social Charge. Certain expenses are also taken into account. Detailed guidelines are available at: www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/medical-cards/applying/assessment/.
Persons aged 70 or older are assessed under medical card income thresholds which are based on gross income. However, it should be noted that those aged over 70 can also be assessed under the general means tested scheme where there are particularly high medical costs. Details are available at: www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/medical-cards/other-types-of-medical-card/over-70s/.
Every effort is made by the HSE, within the framework of the legislation, to support applicants in applying for a medical card and, in particular, to take full account of the difficult circumstances in the case of applicants who may be in excess of the income guidelines. question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Health if she is aware that a drug (details supplied) is available to patients in the State privately on payment of a substantial fee per session while remaining unavailable to public patients; her views on the equity implications of a licensed cancer therapy being accessible only to those who can pay for it.
reply:
The State recognises the importance of timely access to innovative medicines for patients in Ireland.
Under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013, the Health Service Executive (HSE), through its Senior Leadership Team has statutory responsibility for decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines and medical devices.
The Minister for Health has no role in this statutory process.
The Health Insurance Act 1994 (Minimum Benefit) Regulations 1996 require insurers to provide a minimum level of cover to every insured person, regardless of what insurance policy has been purchased. Private health insurance providers act as commercial entities in a competitive private health insurance market. Beyond this, the Minister does not have a role in the commercial decision making of any private health insurer. The Minister is not in a position to direct any insurer to provide cover for any particular procedure or service, or direct how that cover is to be provided.

I propose to take Questions Nos. 1885, 1886, 1889, 1890, 1891, 1938, 1993, 2035, 2060, 2149, 2176, 2239, 2325, 2327, 2330, 2331 and 2337 together.
The Deputy will be aware that the Health (Assisted Human Reproduction) Act 2004 – including Part 12, which has the heading “Past Domestic and International Surrogacy” – was enacted, having passed all stages in both Houses of the Oireachtas and then signed into law by the President, in July 2024.

The AHR Amendment Bill is a very substantive piece of legislation. question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Health if her Department plans on undertaking a review of the drugs payment scheme (DPS) to reduce the financial and administrative burden on patients who must pay upfront for essential ongoing treatment, with lengthy reimbursement timeframes.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1963 and 2229 together.
The Drugs Payment Scheme (DPS) provides for the refund of the amount by which expenditure on approved prescribed medicines or medical and surgical appliances exceeds a named threshold in any calendar month. The DPS is not means tested and is available to anyone ordinarily resident in Ireland.
Currently, under the DPS, no individual or family pays more than €80 a month towards the cost of approved prescribed medicines or medical and surgical appliances. Further information can be found at: https://www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/drugs-payment-scheme/card/.
Patients registered under the DPS can apply for a refund where they opted to use more than one pharmacy to supply their family medicines needs or where they received items from their community pharmacy, and have paid in excess of the DPS threshold.
The HSE is committed to continuously improving its services and recognises that the provision of digital services offers significant advantages both for patients and the HSE. The HSE is developing an easy-to-use online refund application with upload capabilities to support the delivery of refunds by electronic fund transfer. This is one of several ICT initiatives that the HSE is working on developing during 2026.

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the reason Article 12 of the Energy Efficiency Directive has not yet been transposed and implemented in Ireland.
reply:
Article 12 of the Energy Efficiency Directive establishes the legislative framework for the annual monitoring, reporting and publication of information on key metrics on energy and sustainability performance of data centres above a specified size threshold. My Department has advanced to near finalisation the secondary legislation to effect the transposition of the relevant provisions which includes assignment of compliance oversight to the SEAI, confidentiality safeguards, and penalties for non-compliance.
While Article 12 must be transposed by Member States, that framework is supplemented and implemented by the directly applicable Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364. The Delegated Regulation operationalises the reporting regime established under the EED by detailing the information, key performance indicators (KPIs) and reporting methodology required for compliance with Article 12, including the public disclosure of and reporting of that information to the European database for data centres established and operated by the European Commission.
Data centres in Ireland are actively reporting to this European database, as overseen by my Department, with publication of the data by the Commission in an aggregated manner in accordance with the Delegated Regulation.

question: Deputy Marie Sherlock asked the Minister for Health the statutory basis for the requirements introduced in June and July 2026 that HSE invoices above €10,000, and non-clinical invoices above €5,000, be approved by the HSE CEO; and whether those requirements were laid before the Houses of the Oireachtas.
reply:
Public expenditure is subject to both an approved budget and expenditure sanction. Under the Ministers and Secretaries (Amendment) Act 2013, the Government sets the overall spending limit and Ministerial expenditure ceilings. On the Government’s proposal, Dáil Éireann approves funding each year through the Estimates process, with voted expenditure subsequently given statutory effect through the Appropriation Act.
Each Minister, supported by their Department and Accounting Officer, is responsible for managing expenditure and delivering public services within the resources approved by Dáil Éireann. In addition to those statutory arrangements, expenditure is managed through the system of sanction and delegated authority set out in the Public Financial Procedures. Formal sanction from the Minister for Public Expenditure is an essential element of the management and control of voted expenditure, and sanction may be delegated subject to conditions or requirements appropriate to the expenditure concerned.
The letter of delegated sanction for current expenditure for the Health Vote in 2026 issued on 28 May 2026. It reflected the provisions of Department of Public Expenditure Circular 21/2026, Expenditure Control and Escalation Process, which provides a framework for addressing expenditure pressures, including through additional expenditure oversight and control measures where required.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Health her plans to operationalise the Register for Advance Healthcare Directives; her views on section 84(12) of the Assisted Decision Making (Capacity) Act 2015 in respect of the powers it confers on her to make regulations regarding advance healthcare directives including requiring the director to establish and maintain a register of advance healthcare directives that are notified to him or her; the reason no such regulation has been made; and to report on progress with the establishment of an independent cross-sectoral national body with responsibility for adult safeguarding.
reply:
Advance Healthcare Directives
Part 8 of the Assisted Decision Making (Capacity) Act 2015 provides the legislative framework for Advance Healthcare Directives (AHDs).
The Act provides that a Register of Advance Healthcare Directives, to be maintained by the Decision Support Service may be established. This will provide an additional means by which a person’s AHD is available to healthcare professionals where the circumstances arise.
Further consideration and discussion is required in relation to the technical infrastructure required for such a Register. Work is still ongoing in this regard and the Department will continue to engage with stakeholders.
The registration of an AHD however is not linked to its validity. It was not considered legally necessary for such a Register to be established prior to commencement of Part 8 of the Act. An AHD made by any person in any form is considered valid if it is in writing, and has been appropriately signed and witnessed, thus ensuring its accessibility in a wide range of circumstances.
To support those who wish to make an AHD, an approved template form which may be used or adapted is available on the websites of the Decision Support Service, the HSE and from Citizens Information sources. Guidance and further information on the making of a valid directive is also available.

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Health when the shingles vaccination programme for adults aged 65 years and over will be implemented; and whether there are plans to extend eligibility to persons under 65 years, particularly those who are immunocompromised or otherwise at increased risk of shingles.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1767, 1850, 2068 and 2193 together.
Ireland’s immunisation programme is informed by the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). NIAC considers the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland as well as international best practice in relation to immunisation when developing its advice.
The current NIAC guidelines state that the shingles vaccine may be considered for those aged 65 years and older, due to the greater burden and severity of disease in this age group and in those aged 18 years and older at increased risk of shingles.
I can confirm that I have approved the introduction of a Shingles Vaccination Programme, in line with NIAC advice, to be implemented on a phased basis over 5 years, for immunocompromised groups and persons aged 65 and over.
The programme is expected to commence in 2027, initially offering shingles vaccines to immunocompromised groups. This will be followed by the 80 years and older cohort. The programme will conclude with the 65–69 year-old cohort.
It is expected that the vaccine will be administered in the main by GPs and Pharmacists. Further programme details will become available in due course.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Health if she will provide an update on any review of the motor travel rates applicable to HSE home support staff who use their privately owned vehicles in the course of their duties; and if consideration is being given to the increased costs associated with fuel, vehicle maintenance, insurance and depreciation since the rates were last revised in September 2022.
reply:
Thank you for your email regarding mileage rates for HSE home support staff.
The Department of Health recognises the important role community nurses play in delivering services, particularly in rural areas where significant travel is often required.
However, responsibility for determining and reviewing official public service mileage, travel and subsistence rates rests with the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation (DPER). These rates apply across the public service and are set by DPER through the relevant circulars.
Accordingly, the Department of Health does not have a role in setting or reviewing these rates.

The current processing time for FBR applications is approximately 12 months from receipt of all required supporting documentation. Applications that are incomplete or incorrect will take longer.
Prior to the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020, the processing time for FBR applications stood at 18 months due to an unprecedented surge in applications as a result of Brexit and the rigorous processing that applies to citizenship applications.
During the pandemic, Passport Service staff were reassigned to the HSE for essential contact tracing, to the Department of Social Protection for the processing of PUP payments and to support the Department of Health with quarantine issues. This resulted in a pause in overall FBR processing.
FBR processing recommenced in November 2021. Throughout 2022, processing time was in excess of two years, due to the backlog of applications on hand. The processing time reduced throughout 2023 and now stands at 12 months.
The information requested in relation to the number of children born to people whose applications to the Foreign Births Register were still pending for over 12 months when the child was born in the years 2020 to 2023 is not available to the Department.

question: Deputy Marie Sherlock asked the Minister for Health the statutory provision under which the revised recruitment, replacement and promotion sanction process for HSE regions was put in place; whether it was issued as a direction under section 10(1) of the Health Act 2004 and, if so, under which paragraph; the date of issue; the date on which it was or will be laid before the Houses under section 10(6).
reply:
The revised recruitment, replacement and promotion sanction process for HSE regions is an administrative and operational process implemented by the HSE in the context of workforce management, pay and numbers controls, and the delivery of approved service plans.
The process was not established by means of a direction issued by the Minister under section 10(1) of the Health Act 2004. Accordingly, the requirements relating to the laying of Ministerial directions before the Houses of the Oireachtas under section 10(6) of that Act do not arise in this case.
The Department of Health and the HSE continue to engage on workforce planning and recruitment arrangements to ensure that staffing resources are aligned with service priorities, approved funding and Government policy. The recruitment sanction process forms part of these wider governance and accountability arrangements.

reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the Public Only Consultant Contract was introduced in March 2023 as a key step towards a universal, single-tier health service in which access to care is based on clinical need rather than ability to pay.
The POCC is applicable to all specialities, not just to maternity care. The transition to POCC will take place progressively as consultants are recruited to, or move to, the new contract. Consultants choosing that contract cannot continue to provide private practice in public hospitals after 31 December 2025. Consultants who remain on earlier contracts may continue to provide private care in public hospitals in accordance with their contractual arrangements. Accordingly, the change does not involve an immediate cessation of private maternity care. Private maternity care in public hospitals will therefore reduce gradually over time.
I recognise that this change may cause concern for some private patients. However, this reform supports equitable access to care based on clinical need.
Women with complex pregnancies will continue to receive appropriate consultant-led care.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if Ireland will oppose the nomination of Lana Nusseibeh for the role of United Nations Secretary General given her role in providing political cover for the relationship between the United Arab Emirates and the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan.
reply:
Ireland believes that we need a United Nations Secretary-General firmly committed to the UN Charter and focused on preventing and resolving conflicts, rebuilding trust in multilateralism, bridging divides, mobilising collective action, delivering tangible results, and accelerating system-wide UN reforms.
The Secretary-General of the United Nations is appointed by the General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council. Ireland has been supportive of efforts to increase the transparency of the selection process, particularly the interactive dialogues with each candidate, chaired by the President of the General Assembly with the participation of all Member States and civil society representatives. The Government remains deeply concerned by the conflict in Sudan, which has created the world’s worst humanitarian, displacement and protection crisis. Ireland has been very clear that harmful external interference in Sudan must end, and that States and external actors must cease arming, financing and otherwise enabling the war in Sudan.
Ireland calls on all parties to the conflict in Sudan to de-escalate, and to reach agreement on a sustained cessation of hostilities, followed by an inclusive Sudanese-led transition to civilian rule.

question: Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Health further to the Programme for Government commitment to expand free GP services to children up to at least 12 years-of-age, the age she expects to increase it to in this years budget.
reply:
The Programme for Government includes a commitment to 'expand free GP services to children up to at least 12 years, and keep its further extension under review'. The delivery of GP services without charges can be achieved through the expansion of the GP visit card eligibility.
Following the expansion of GP visit card eligibility in 2023, all children under 8 years of age are currently eligible for a GP visit card. As set out in the Programme for Government, it is our intention within the life-time of this Government to expand GP care without charges to all children up to the age of at least 12 years. This will be done in a planned way, in cooperation with GPs to ensure that there is adequate capacity in place. The outcome of the Strategic Review of General Practice, which is underway, will also be a key factor in enabling the expansion of GP care without charges.

reply:

International experience and the specific context of the Irish public health service were considered in the review. The HSE paused the recruitment of Physician Assistants pending the outcome of the review.
An extensive consultation process formed part of the review, including surveys, focus groups, written submissions, verbal input and face-to-face meetings. Stakeholders consulted as part of the review included patient and service user representatives, HSE leadership and management, clinical leaders, professional system regulatory bodies, educational and professional institutions, trade unions and representative bodies. The HSE has moved to an implementation phase focused on strengthening governance, role clarity and national consistency. Implementation of the review’s recommendations is a matter for the HSE.

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health the status of the proposal to deliver a Stem Cell Tissue Establishment and Advanced Cellular Therapies Unit at Cork University Hospital; the next steps in the planning and approval process; the estimated cost of this project; if funding will be provided; and the expected timeline for delivering this project.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 2118 and 2121 together.
The Government is committed to improving cancer care, ensuring better prevention, maintaining improvements in cancer survival rates, and facilitating timely access to treatments. This includes through the increased provision of access to advanced cellular therapies. Advanced cellular therapies are highly specialised treatments used in the management off a range of malignant and non-malignant diseases. These therapies require specialist multidisciplinary teams, dedicated laboratory facilities, tissue establishment infrastructure, specialised inpatient facilities and robust regulatory and accreditation arrangements.
Cellular therapies currently available to patients in Ireland include autologous stem cell transplantation, allogeneic stem cell transplantation and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. Adult Autologous Stem cell transplantation services are currently provided in St James's Hospital, University Hospital Galway and St Vincent's University Hospital. Adult allogeneic stem cell transplantation is currently provided through St James's Hospital.
The Government continues to progress the expansion of advanced cellular therapies nationally. In 2026, Beaumont Hospital was designated as an additional autologous stem cell transplantation and CAR-T Centre, working towards commencement of services in 2027.

question: Deputy Martin Daly asked the Minister for Health the arrangements in place to co-ordinate the development of adult safeguarding legislation across Government departments, particularly in relation to protecting adults at risk of abuse, neglect and exploitation outside health and social care settings.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 2020, 2022, 2024, 2026, 2028 and 2097 together.
Safeguarding at-risk adults against abuse is of paramount importance and is taken very seriously by the Government. The Programme for Government includes a commitment to publish a national policy on adult safeguarding for the health and social care sector.
Following this commitment, Ireland’s first ever National Policy Framework for Adult Safeguarding in the Health and Social Care sector was published in December 2025. The national policy framework will extend across all public, private and voluntary health and social care services. Included are a range of both legislative and non-legislative measures that will significantly expand and strengthen existing supports and protections for adults at risk of harm across the health and social care sector. The national policy framework was developed by the Department of Health, in liaison with the Department of Children, Disability and Equality.

- The Health Service Executive (HSE) will have responsibility for leading and co-ordinating adult safeguarding across the sector and will have statutory functions, duties, and powers to underpin this role.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the steps the Government is currently taking to support undocumented Irish citizens living in the US particularly given the increased focus on immigration enforcement; and if she will provide the most up to date figures on the number of undocumented Irish citizens who have been deported or returned to Ireland from the US over the past two years.
reply:
Addressing issues impacting on Irish communities in the U.S., including relating to immigration, is a consistent priority in our engagements with the U.S., at political and official levels. Efforts to advance the situation of undocumented Irish emigrants have been made with successive U.S. administrations.
Ireland’s diplomatic network in the U.S. works in close partnership with Irish community organisations and immigration centres. So far this year, the Government has allocated more than €4.7 million to such organisations, including those providing trusted information, legal advice and practical assistance to individuals seeking to regularise their immigration status.
Our embassy and consulates also provide direct consular assistance to Irish citizens, including those impacted by deportation. Irish citizens requiring support in relation to immigration matters can contact the Embassy in Washington, D.C., or any of Ireland’s consulates throughout the United States.
In 2025, 65 Irish citizens requested assistance from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade in relation to deportation from the United States of America. To date in 2026 this figure is 24.
The Deputy should note that these figures only relate to cases where a citizen or their family has requested consular assistance and do not necessarily reflect all deportations to Ireland.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Health further to her closing response during statements on Children’s Health Ireland on 22 October 2026 (details supplied), the way this will be reflected in the proposed Commission of Investigation’s terms of reference, whether the commission will be empowered to investigate relevant pre-2019 surgical practices, clinical governance and management responses, as distinct from receiving accounts of families’ experiences; and whether the hip dysplasia module will cover the full January 2010 to March 2025 period.
reply:

I published the independent report of the Children's Health Ireland Inquiry into Spina Bifida and Complex Scoliosis Scoping Exercise on 28 September following engagement with patients and families. The first would be a personal/family statement module and the second would be a module in relation to the response of CHI management to waiting list issues. reply:
Section 22(4) of the Health Act 2004 provides that the HSE shall obtain the consent of the Minister for Health for the creation of certain grades of employee where required.
The revised HSE recruitment sanction process is an administrative and financial assurance mechanism designed to strengthen expenditure control and support compliance with the HSE's pay budget. The process applies particularly to Regions that are significantly over their pay allocation and requires additional HSE prioritisation and approval before recruitment requests are submitted to the Department.
To date, the Minister has not been required to provide consent under section 22(4) of the Health Act 2004 in respect of the revised recruitment sanction process itself. question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Health with regards to the new shingles vaccine programme recently announced, if the criteria have yet been established; the expected timeline for roll out; and if a person over 65, with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, COPD, and a heart condition would qualify.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1767, 1850, 2068 and 2193 together.
Ireland’s immunisation programme is informed by the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). NIAC considers the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland as well as international best practice in relation to immunisation when developing its advice.
The current NIAC guidelines state that the shingles vaccine may be considered for those aged 65 years and older, due to the greater burden and severity of disease in this age group and in those aged 18 years and older at increased risk of shingles.
I can confirm that I have approved the introduction of a Shingles Vaccination Programme, in line with NIAC advice, to be implemented on a phased basis over 5 years, for immunocompromised groups and persons aged 65 and over.
The programme is expected to commence in 2027, initially offering shingles vaccines to immunocompromised groups. This will be followed by the 80 years and older cohort. The programme will conclude with the 65–69 year-old cohort.
It is expected that the vaccine will be administered in the main by GPs and Pharmacists. Further programme details will become available in due course.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade in light of Ireland’s intended ratification of the CETA without any reservation referable to S.25A3 (new) of the Arbitration Act, 2010, if the EU, Canada, or any EU Member State raised an objection with the Government to this qualification of the obligation under Article 54(1) of the Washington/ICSIO Convention made applicable to determinations of the CETA Tribunal.
reply:
The ratification of the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement between Canada and the EU (‘CETA’) is a priority for Government. The 2025 Programme for Government contains a specific commitment to ratify this important free trade agreement.
Ratifying CETA is a priority for the Government against the background of today’s volatile international trading environment. Such agreements are vital for Ireland’s credibility as a trading nation and as a favourable destination for foreign investment, supporting the growth of Irish businesses including small and medium-sized businesses, and creating jobs. The ratification of CETA is also a key priority for Canada, which has been repeatedly raised with Ireland by Canadian partners.

reply:
Medical Card provision is primarily based on financial assessment. In accordance with the Health Act 1970 (as amended), eligibility for a medical card is determined by the HSE, which assesses each application on a qualifying financial threshold. This is the amount of money that an individual can earn a week and still qualify for a card. It is specific to the individual’s own financial circumstances.
Persons aged 69 and under are assessed under the general means tested medical card thresholds which are based on an applicant’s household income after tax and the deduction of PRSI and the Universal Social Charge. Certain expenses are also taken into account. Detailed guidelines are available at:www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/medical-cards/applying/assessment/.
Persons aged 70 or older are assessed under medical card income thresholds which are based on gross income. However, it should be noted that those aged over 70 can also be assessed under the general means tested scheme where there are particularly high medical costs. Details are available at: www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/medical-cards/other-types-of-medical-card/over-70s/.
In response to the Deputy’s query regarding the impact of State pension payment increase on medical card eligibility, it is important to note that where a person's sole household income is derived from a social protection payment, he/she will be awarded a medical card.

question: Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Health if she will consider the provision of training for all professionals in contact with children, including mental health professionals, to raise awareness of the issues of parental problem alcohol use.
reply:
The HSE in partnership with Tusla have developed training in this area. The 'Hidden Harm - Impact of Parental Alcohol and Other Drug Use' training programme is for staff who work with parents, children, young people, or families who may be affected by problem alcohol and drug use. The training is open to staff in the HSE, Tusla, community and voluntary sectors.
The training aims to help staff become more aware of and respond to Hidden Harm (experiences of children who live with and are affected by parental problem alcohol and drug use). It aims to encourage services and stakeholders to work together to support families.
The training includes guidance from parents and professionals from voluntary and community sectors, the HSE and Tusla. It is based on the HSE and TUSLA Hidden Harm Practice Guide (2019). Topics include:
- impact of Hidden Harm
- the parents' voice
- working together
- Hidden Harm in practice
The training equips professionals to recognise the impact of Hidden Harm on children and young people, to provide support to parents to limit the impact of problem alcohol and other drug use on children or young people, and to work in partnership with parents and other services to meet the needs of the child or young person. Details on the training are available via https://healthservice.hse.ie/staff/training-and-development/national-social-inclusion-office-training-programmes/hidden-harm-impact-of-parental-alcohol-and-other-drug-use-training/

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Health to reconsider going forward with the commission of investigation into scoliosis and spina bifida care scandals at Children's Health Ireland and instead proceed with a tribunal of inquiry as has been requested by parents and advocacy groups.
reply:
I published the independent report of the Children's Health Ireland Inquiry into Spina Bifida and Complex Scoliosis Scoping Exercise on 28 September following engagement with patients and families. Mr Farrell, the independent facilitator of the scoping exercise, recommended a Commission of Investigation covering four defined modules; waiting lists, spinal surgery, hip dysplasia and the cohort of children who were not transferred to Temple Street post 2008.
Mr Farrell’s recommendation for a Commission of Investigation was based on the view that a Commission can deliver the same core statutory powers as a Tribunal while being better suited to the specific subject matter of the inquiry, namely the medical treatment of children. A Commission can compel witnesses and the production of documents and would publish a final report. Mr Farrell is of the view that as the issues deal with the personal and medical information of children who have specific legal protections and given the relatively finite number of children, there is a significant risk that children may be identifiable.
A Commission, by default is conducted in private which alleviates those concerns compared to a Tribunal which by default is conducted in private. I am aware that there is a view among some parents that it should be entirely in public. A Commission has a more flexible framework which could allow an element of the proceedings to occur in public.

question: Deputy Denise Mitchell asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if the Government will seek the continuation of UN Peacekeeping deployments in Lebanon (UNIFIL) via a United Nations General Assembly vote under the Uniting for Peace mechanism in order to bypass the deadlock at the UN Security Council.
reply:
Ireland is immensely proud of its long-standing commitment to UNIFIL and believes that the peacekeeping mission has made an essential contribution to the safety and security of Lebanon and the wider region. Ireland’s participation in UNIFIL over many decades is a highly visible and concrete sign of our commitment to UN peacekeeping.
Our peacekeepers in Lebanon continue to operate in an extremely difficult environment against the backdrop of conflict and instability. Yet, despite these challenges, they carry out their duties with the utmost professionalism and courage. I witnessed this first hand during my recent visit to Lebanon, where I had the honour of presenting medals to Defence Forces personnel at Camp Shamrock. I wish to reiterate my deep appreciation to our peacekeepers and their families for their exceptional service.
As the Deputy will be aware, in August 2025, the UN Security Council renewed the UNIFIL mandate until 31 December 2026, to be followed by a period of drawdown and withdrawal through 2027.
In a letter to the Security Council earlier this year, the UN Secretary-General outlined a range of proposals for the future implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1701 following UNIFIL’s withdrawal. Consultations on Lebanon are continuing at the UN Security Council and Ireland remains fully engaged on this matter, in close consultation with our partners and with the Lebanese authorities.

question: Deputy Martin Daly asked the Minister for Health whether a lead Government Department has been designated to oversee the development of an independent national adult safeguarding body and coordinate its establishment across relevant sectors.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 2020, 2022, 2024, 2026, 2028 and 2097 together.
Safeguarding at-risk adults against abuse is of paramount importance and is taken very seriously by the Government. The Programme for Government includes a commitment to publish a national policy on adult safeguarding for the health and social care sector.
Following this commitment, Ireland’s first ever National Policy Framework for Adult Safeguarding in the Health and Social Care sector was published in December 2025. The national policy framework will extend across all public, private and voluntary health and social care services. Included are a range of both legislative and non-legislative measures that will significantly expand and strengthen existing supports and protections for adults at risk of harm across the health and social care sector. The national policy framework was developed by the Department of Health, in liaison with the Department of Children, Disability and Equality.

- The Health Service Executive (HSE) will have responsibility for leading and co-ordinating adult safeguarding across the sector and will have statutory functions, duties, and powers to underpin this role.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the actions she is taking to try and encourage other EU countries to accept the Irish passport card in European airports, specifically at the automated travel/immigration entry terminals linked to the entry/exit system, where it is often only possible to use the passport book.
reply:
The passport card was launched in October 2015 and offers Irish citizens the convenience of travel, with a credit card sized travel document, to all EU Member States, the members of the EEA (Iceland, Liechtenstein, and Norway), Switzerland and the United Kingdom. The Passport Card is fully compliant with International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) regulations concerning requirements for passports in card format.
In June 2026, I launched a next-generation passport book and card featuring world-first security technologies. In conjunction with the launch of the new book and card, the Passport Service engaged with national government border control and immigration authorities worldwide to advise them of the updates to Ireland's secure travel documents.
Individual national government border control and immigration authorities are responsible for machine-readable zone (MRZ) scanners and automated e-gates at their airports. Government agencies maintain border sovereignty, deploy the scanning hardware, and run the security database checks. It is up to each country to ensure it keeps up with the advancement in passport design and enhancements. It was ensured, via the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, that all e-gates at Dublin airport received this update prior to the launch of the new passport book and card.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Health if her attention has been drawn to the call for a fully funded DEXA screening programme for women over 50 years-of-age; if she supports such an initiative; and to outline the work being undertaken to help protect women’s bone health.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1854, 1967, 2016 and 2067 together.
As Minister for Health, I am dedicated to enhancing Ireland’s population screening programmes, which are a vital component of our health services. They enable early treatment and care for many people, thereby enhancing the overall health of our community.
I would note that consideration of any proposed changes to Ireland’s screening programmes will be facilitated through established evidence-driven protocols.
The National Screening Advisory Committee (NSAC) is the expert group that considers proposed changes to Ireland’s screening programmes. NSAC assesses the evidence in a robust and transparent manner and against internationally accepted criteria, before making recommendations to myself as Minister.
It is important that we have rigorous processes in place to ensure our screening programmes are effective, quality assured, validated and operating to safe standards, and that the benefits of screening outweigh the harms.
NSAC holds annual Calls for Submissions, which invite all stakeholders, including members of the public, HSE and other medical professionals, to propose changes to Ireland’s screening programmes. question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Health if she will initiate an enhanced influenza vaccine tender process to provide a high-dose vaccine and deliver a positive impact on hospitalisations for flu this winter.
reply:
The National Immunisation Programme in Ireland, which includes the influenza immunisation programme, is based on the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). The committee's recommendations are based on the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland and international best practice in relation to immunisation. NIAC make recommendations on vaccination policy to the Department of Health.
The National Influenza Vaccination Programme ensures that those most vulnerable to the effects of influenza have access to the flu vaccine, free of charge. By providing vaccination to those most at risk, and those most likely to require admission to hospital should they contract influenza, the programme aims to prevent, as far as possible, the need for influenza-related hospital admissions, as well as to reduce the overall spread of influenza in the community.
The seasonal Flu Vaccination Programme for 2026/2027 commenced in early October 2026.
This flu season, the flu vaccine will be offered to the following eligible groups:
• Adults aged 60 years and over.
• Individuals in specified health related at-risk groups.
• Children aged 2 to 17 years.
• Healthcare workers.
The flu vaccine is available free of charge to individuals in these specified eligible groups from local GPs or pharmacies throughout the flu season, which runs until April.

question: Deputy Pat the Cope Gallagher asked the Minister for Health further to Parliamentary Question No. 60997/26, and the subsequent response from Letterkenny University Hospital dated 14 September 2026, which did not specify a timetable for national consideration, an implementation deadline or accountable delivery arrangements for the Letterkenny University Hospital Model 3 Clinical Care Plan 2026, if she will outline the actions taken to secure its publication and a formal national response; specifically, whether she and her Department have received the full report and recommendations; and if she can make a statement on the matter.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1996 to 1999, inclusive, and 2005 together.
In 2023, Professor Brian Kinirons launched the National Doctors in Training and Planning (NDTP) Model 3 Hospitals Report. This report was developed by the NDTP Unit, a division of the Health Service Executive (HSE). This report involved an analysis of the recruitment and retention of Consultants in Model 3 Hospitals throughout Ireland.
Letterkenny University Hospital was chosen by the NDTP as one of the 3 pilot sites to implement the suite of recommendations from the Model 3 Hospitals Report.
As part of this pilot, Saolta recruited a Clinical Director to lead out on the Pilot Programme for LUH. Mr Michael Sugrue was selected following a competitive recruitment process to fulfil this role. One of the objectives of this role was the development of the Model 3 Clinical Care Plan for LUH, amongst a range of other measures to implement the recommendations of the NDTP's Model 3 Hospitals Report.
It is understood that the draft plan is currently undergoing consideration in line with standard internal HSE processes.

Reducing these waits and improving patients’ experience of urgent and emergency care remain priorities for my Department and the Health Service Executive (HSE).
The 2026 Urgent and Emergency Care Operational Plan takes a whole-system approach across hospital avoidance, emergency department operations, in-hospital care and discharge management. Measures include enhanced senior clinical decision-making, progressing seven-day working, improving access to diagnostics and strengthening discharge planning and coordination between hospital and community services. Daily performance monitoring and regular oversight meetings support the identification of emerging pressures and the escalation of issues requiring intervention. question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if there any situations in which Irish citizens in prisons abroad may have been unlawfully imprisoned.
reply:
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, through the Consular Assistance Unit in Dublin and our Embassies and Consulates overseas, provides assistance to citizens who are arrested abroad, as well as to prisoners in detention abroad.
Under Article 36 of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, authorities must inform a detained foreign national without delay of their right to have their Embassy or Consulate notified of their detention. However, some citizens choose not to notify their Embassy or Consulate of this information and do not request consular assistance.
This means that the number of Irish citizens detained abroad and receiving consular assistance is likely to be less than the total number of Irish prisoners abroad. As such, the Department does not have access to information relating to all Irish citizens in prison overseas.
To date this year, my Department has been informed of 252 new arrest cases overseas, though not every person who is arrested becomes a prisoner. My Department is also providing ongoing consular assistance in longer-running prisoner cases around the world.
My Department is not aware of any cases where an Irish citizen currently in prison abroad has raised concerns with us that they consider themselves to be unlawfully imprisoned.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the actions taken in 2026 to further highlight ongoing human rights abuses in Belarus and to support the recognition of democracy in that country.
reply:
The Government remains deeply concerned by the continuing erosion of human rights and democracy in Belarus, including the ongoing incarceration of political prisoners.
The Lukashenka regime’s relentless repression of human rights, restrictions on political participation, and restrictions on access to independent media are intended to stifle opposition voices and entrench authoritarian rule.
Ireland’s response to the situation in Belarus has focused on working directly; through the European Union; and in multilateral fora to support civil society and the democratic opposition in exile, while highlighting concerns regarding the Lukashenka regime’s violations of human rights.

We reiterated our call for the release of all those arbitrarily detained in Belarus for peacefully exercising their human rights, an end to transnational repression, and accountability for violations.
Ireland is strongly committed to supporting the Belarusian democratic movement in its pursuit of a democratic future for all Belarusians.

question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Health her views on whether it is in the interest of Irish citizens to allow the large-scale acquisition of GP practices in Ireland; and her views on whether this could make the implementation of Sláintecare, including the provision of universal free access to GP care, more difficult.

A contract for service is essentially a commercial arrangement with an independent contractor working in private practice as opposed to a contract of service which is more typically defined as a contract of employment.

Ireland considers the Court to be the cornerstone of the international criminal justice system and an essential institution in the global fight against impunity. The Government has expressed profound regret regarding the recent decision of the United States to impose sanctions on the ICC as an institution, as well as sanctions on its officials and those who cooperate with the Court.
The Government has been consistent in calling for all measures against the ICC to be withdrawn. I reiterated this message when I welcomed ICC President, Judge Tomoko Akane, to Dublin for the opening of the Irish Judicial Year on 5 October. The Taoiseach also emphasised Ireland’s continued support for the ICC in Ireland's national statement to the United Nations General Assembly during High Level Week in September.
In its role as President of the Council of the European Union, Ireland has been actively engaged in efforts to ensure that the Court can continue to carry out its mandate independently, impartially and free from external interference. Ireland has convened a series of additional meetings of the relevant EU Council Working Party to discuss the implications of the sanctions and the range of options available to support and protect the Court.

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Health whether there are minimum training or certification requirements for healthcare professionals reporting DXA scans in Ireland and if so, to outline those requirements.
reply:
Medical exposures to ionising radiation including DXA scans are regulated under Council Directive 2013/59/EURATOM which lays down the basic safety standards for protection against the dangers arising from exposure to ionising radiation. This Directive, insofar as it relates to medical exposures, was transposed into national law in the European Union (Basic Safety Standards for Protection Against Dangers Arising from Medical Exposure to Ionising Radiation) Regulations 2018 (S.I. No. 256 of 2018) (‘the Regulations’).
Reporting on DXA scans relates to the clinical evaluation of the image and falls within the meaning of clinical responsibility. Under Regulation 10 of the Regulations, all medical exposures must take place under the clinical responsibility of a practitioner. One of the following health professionals, acting as a practitioner, can take clinical responsibility for an individual medical exposure -
(a) a registered dentist within the meaning of the Dentists Act 1985 (No. 9 of 1985),
(b) a registered medical practitioner within the meaning of the Medical Practitioners Act 2007 (No. 25 of 2007), or
(c) a person whose name is entered in the register established and maintained by the Radiographers Registration Board pursuant to Section 36 of the Health and Social Care Professionals Act 2005 (No. 27 of 2005).

These indicators measure the time from registration to admission or discharge, rather than solely the time waiting to be seen by a clinician. They provide an important measure of access and patient flow, but do not, on their own, capture the full experience of children and families.

Hospital staff, the HSE and the DOH continue to work to find improvement in these figures at what is a stressful time for patients and their families.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she intends to send a legal observer to a trial (details supplied), given the concerns expressed that their trial is falling short of normal European standards.
reply:
I wish to assure the Deputy that I am following this case very closely and will continue to do so. At the heart of this, there is a citizen and their family who are going through a very difficult experience. My Department’s focus, as it is for all Irish prisoners abroad, is on providing compassionate, non-judgemental consular assistance to ensure the wellbeing of the citizen.
Our Consulate General in Munich, supported by our Embassy in Berlin and Consular Assistance Unit in Dublin, has been providing consular assistance to the citizen since September 2025. A dedicated consular officer in Munich is assigned to the case, and Consulate staff, including the Consul General, have visited the citizen in prison on eight separate occasions, most recently on 5 October. question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Health to consider providing direct financial support to patients who require access to CPAP equipment.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1939 and 2217 together.
The Drugs Payment Scheme (DPS) provides for the refund of the amount by which expenditure on approved prescribed medicines or medical and surgical appliances exceeds a named threshold in any calendar month. The DPS is not means tested and is available to anyone ordinarily resident in Ireland.
Under the DPS, no individual or family pays more than €80 a month towards the cost of approved prescribed medicines and medical appliances. The DPS is not means tested and is available to anyone ordinarily resident in Ireland. Further information can be found at: https://www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/drugs-payment-scheme/card/.
The rental costs for a continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) machines are included under the DPS. Further information, including how to claim, can be found at: https://www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/drugs-payment-scheme/refunds/.
There are currently no plans to refund the purchase cost of CPAP machines under the Drug Payment Scheme.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Taoiseach to outline the way in which his Department measures 'Youth Unemployment'.
reply:
Referred to CSO for answer
The Labour Force Survey (LFS) is a quarterly household survey carried out by the Central Statistics Office and is the official source of estimates of unemployment in the State. The official labour market classification of respondents to the survey is based on International Labour Organisation concepts and definitions.
To meet the definition of unemployment, the respondent must:
Have not worked in the week before the survey for one hour or more for payment or profit, including work on the family farm or business and all persons who were away from work during the reference week but had a job to which they could return to
Be available to start work within the next two weeks
Have taken specific steps in the previous four weeks to find work
Youth unemployment refers to persons aged 15 to 24 years who meet the definition of unemployment.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Taoiseach for an update on plans for Seanad reform; and the actions to be taken arising from the Seanad reform implementation plan published in 2018.
reply:
The Government recognises the important role of Seanad Éireann in our constitutional framework and our parliamentary democracy, including the valuable contribution its Members make to the development of legislation.
A significant reform of the process for electing Seanad University Members has been put in place with the enactment of the Seanad Electoral (University Members) (Amendment) Act 2024. The Act provides for the establishment of a new, single six-seat Higher Education constituency, significantly extending the franchise for electing the six Higher Education members to the Seanad beyond the traditional National University of Ireland and University of Dublin constituencies. The Act also provides for the establishment of the National University of Ireland as the new Central Registration Authority, responsible for maintaining the Register of Electors.
A number of other measures have been put in place to give effect to the non-electoral recommendations arising from the 2018 reports on Seanad reform. These include the establishment of the Seanad Select Committee on the Scrutiny of Draft EU Statutory Instruments, revision to Seanad Standing Orders to change the way in which the reports of Joint Committees are debated and increased engagement with Ireland’s MEPs.
There are currently no immediate plans to bring forward further proposals in this regard.

question: Deputy Martin Daly asked the Minister for Health whether consideration has been given to using any savings arising from lower-than-projected uptake of GP visit cards to increase the income eligibility thresholds for full medical cards.
reply:
Medical Card provision is primarily based on financial assessment. In accordance with the Health Act 1970 (as amended), eligibility for a medical card is determined by the HSE, which assesses each application on a qualifying financial threshold. This is the amount of money that an individual can earn a week and still qualify for a card. It is specific to the individual’s own financial circumstances.
The 2023 GMS GP Agreement provided for the expansion in 2023 of GP visit card eligibility to all children under 8 years of age and to all those earning up to the median household income. As of the start of October, there are 820,106 GP visit card holders, nearly 300,000 more than as of 2023 prior to the expansion of eligibility under the Agreement.
Several measures have been taken to support GP visit card uptake. A bespoke online application process was developed for the median income expansion, and commencement of the expansions were accompanied by a media campaign, with subsequent annual campaigns, to promote GP visit card uptake. In 2024, the HSE commissioned research to better understand why potentially eligible individuals may not have applied for a GP visit card, the findings of this research have been used to refine the subsequent public information campaigns.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Health if she will ensure that an independent mediator agreed with patient advocacy groups and family representatives is appointed to discuss the terms of reference of the statutory inquiry into spina bifida and complex scoliosis services will be as agreed at a meeting on 12 November 2025.
reply:
I published the independent report of the Children's Health Ireland Inquiry into Spina Bifida and Complex Scoliosis Scoping Exercise on 28 September following engagement with patients and families. Mr Farrell, the independent facilitator of the scoping exercise, recommended a Commission of Investigation covering four defined modules; waiting lists, spinal surgery, hip dysplasia and the cohort of children who were not transferred to Temple Street post 2008.
Government has accepted the report's recommendations and have agreed to the initiation of drafting the Terms of Reference (ToR) for the proposed Commission of Investigation. Officials in my Department will work in close consultation with the Office of the Attorney General on drafting the Terms of Reference. There will be a call for input from advocacy groups on the ToR.
The final ToR will be submitted to Government for approval.

question: Deputy Martin Daly asked the Minister for Health the current status of the Strategic Review of General Practice announced in 2023; when the final report and recommendations will be published; the reasons for any delay in publication.
reply:
The Programme for Government includes a commitment to publish the Strategic Review of General Practice, and bring forward a new, modern GP contract.
My Department, with support from the HSE, is currently undertaking a Strategic Review of General Practice. The review is a comprehensive examination of issues affecting general practice, focusing on GP training, GP capacity, Out of Hours services reform, the eHealth Agenda, and the financial support model for general practice. Significant progress has been made under the review, and the review is to be completed this year.
When completed, a report will be presented to me outlining the findings of the review and setting out recommended actions necessary to improve the current system of GP care as part of a primary care focused health service. The report will be published subsequently.

question: Deputy Joe Neville asked the Taoiseach the amount Ireland is paying oil companies each year in fossil fuel subsidies.
reply:
Referred to CSO for answer
The CSO publishes an annual release on fossil fuel subsidies available on the CSO’s website at www.cso.ie/en/releasesandpublications/ep/p-ffes/fossilfuelsubsidies2024/ The most recent release was published in September 2025 and relates to 2024 data. The next iteration of the release for 2025 data is expected to be published in December 2026.
Fossil fuel subsidies were €4.67 billion in 2024, down 6% from €4.98 billion in 2023. Subsidies are divided into two categories – direct and indirect. In that context, no direct subsidies to oil companies were identified in 2024.
Two earlier schemes aimed at promoting hydrocarbon exploration and development activities have been terminated with no further payments identified. The Petroleum Exploration and Production Promotion and Support (PEPPS) scheme provided €0.9 million in 2021, and SFI funding of €0.2 million was provided for fossil fuel R&D in 2020. Together, these direct subsidies accounted for 0.8% of total direct fossil fuel subsidies in 2020.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health the current operational status of the Assisted Human Reproduction Regulatory Authority; if a chief executive officer has been appointed; the number of staff in post; the number of board vacancies; the funding allocated to the authority in 2026 and 2027; the date on which the authority is expected to commence performing its statutory functions.
reply:
The Deputy will be aware that the Health (Assisted Human Reproduction) Act was enacted, having passed all stages in both Houses of the Oireachtas and been signed into law by the President, in July 2024.
The establishment of the Assisted Human Reproduction Regulatory Authority (AHRRA), as provided for in the legislation, is a vital component in the effective regulation of the assisted human reproduction (AHR) sector. It is a new independent regulatory authority tasked with protecting, promoting, and ensuring the health and wellbeing of children born through AHR, individuals undergoing treatment, and intending parents.
I signed orders to formally establish the AHRRA, and appointed a Chair, Ms. Deirdre Madden, and a Board, with effect from 13 October 2025. The Board has been meeting on a monthly basis since. It appointed Mr. Colm O’Leary as the AHRRA’s inaugural Chief Executive Officer (CEO) to lead the AHRRA following a comprehensive and rigorous recruitment process conducted by the Public Appointments Service and he took up the post in April 2026.
The AHRRA recently published its first Strategic Business Plan, outlining a comprehensive roadmap to build Ireland’s new fertility treatment and surrogacy regulatory framework. Covering the period from 1 July 2026 to 31 December 2027, the Plan focuses on building essential operational capacity, recruiting skilled staff, and securing the necessary digital infrastructure ahead of commencing its extensive statutory functions. question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Health if there is sufficient independent oversight of the fairness of settlement offers for south Kerry CAMHS, particularly where claimants are psychologically vulnerable or have experienced substantial educational and developmental harm.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1878, 1879, 1880, 1881, 1882 and 1883 together.
As the Deputy will be aware, the Maskey Report, published in 2022, examined the files of everyone who received care from South Kerry Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS) between 1 July 2016 and 19 April 2021. The review identified that 240 young people did not receive the standard of care they should have from CAMHS.
The HSE issued an apology to the affected young people and their families as determined through the Maskey Report. Importantly, HSE officials and clinicians offered meetings to each of the 240 young people who did not receive the care they should have. During these individual Open Disclosure meetings, the HSE outlined the review findings and sincerely apologised to the young person in question and their family.
Following publication of the Maskey Report, the Government introduced a non-adversarial route for children and their families to seek compensation for the shortfall in care received. This resulted in the development and delivery of the South Kerry CAMHS Compensation Scheme, which is managed by the State Claims Agency on behalf of the HSE.
The scheme operates in a fair, transparent and compassionate manner for those affected and provides for full compensation, in accordance with established principles of compensatory damages, and agreed clinical supports to persons who suffered injury or harm as identified through the Maskey Report and whom have been notified by

question: Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Health if her Department plans to bring in new safety measures to improve the way in which the risks of suicidal thoughts and behaviours and persistent sexual dysfunction are communicated to patients taking antidepressant medications, similar that introduced in Britain recently (details supplied).
reply:
The Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA) is Ireland's state agency responsible for regulating medicines, health products, and devices and I understand they are aware of the measures recently communicated by the UK's Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) concerning antidepressant medicines.
Ireland operates as part of the European Union medicines regulatory network. The HPRA, as the national competent authority for medicines in Ireland, works with the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and other EU medicines regulators to monitor and assess the safety of medicines.
The relevant authorised product information, including the package leaflet provided with the antidepressant medicines for patients, provides advice should an individual experience suicidal thoughts and behaviours, and sexual dysfunction. This includes contacting their doctor or going to a hospital straight away if a person has thoughts of harming themselves or suicide.
The safety of all medicines, including antidepressant medicines, remains subject to ongoing review through the European medicines regulatory system. Where new evidence emerges, the need for regulatory action, including changes to product information or additional risk communication measures, can be considered through the appropriate European regulatory processes.
I am advised that the HPRA will continue to monitor the evidence and relevant regulatory developments and contribute to any consideration of these matters at European

The Long-Term Illness (LTI) Scheme was established under Section 59(3) of the Health Act 1970 (as amended). Regulations were made in 1971, 1973 and 1975, prescribing 16 conditions to be covered by the Scheme. Further information, including the list of conditions, can be found at:
https://www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/lti/about/.
Under the LTI Scheme, patients receive drugs, medicines, and medical and surgical appliances directly related to the treatment of their illness, free of charge. While there are currently no plans to extend the list of conditions, it is important to remember that the LTI Scheme exists within a wider eligibility framework.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Health if she and her Department have engaged with HSE West/North West in relation to the approval of contracts for newly graduated nurses and midwives.
reply:
The recruitment and retention of newly qualified nurses and midwives is critical to ensuring a sustainable workforce and the continued delivery of high-quality patient care.
The HSE is aware of the number of nurses and midwives expected to graduate each year and must align its recruitment planning accordingly. Retaining newly qualified graduates is critical to the long-term sustainability of the health service and remains a key priority. HSE recruitment must also be strategic to ensure graduates are placed in locations of greatest service need, while balancing workforce requirements and being aware of the overall pay bill.
The most recent information provided by the HSE indicates that, nationally, there are 1,375 graduate nurses and midwives, of whom 1,145 have been offered positions to date and more than 1,000 have accepted.
There is no recruitment embargo in the HSE, and recruitment activity continues. Strengthened controls are in place in four Regions to ensure that appointments are affordable, properly prioritised and directed to areas of greatest patient and service demand.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Health the regulations in place to ensure mental health treatments and practices are safe and evidence based.
reply:
The Government recognises the importance of ensuring all mental health services, both inpatient and community, and both adult and child and adolescent, are fully registered, regulated, and inspected by the Mental Health Commission in its role as the independent regulator of mental health services.
Under the current Mental Health Act 2001, the Mental Health Commission regulates all inpatient mental health services, known as 'approved centres'. This includes reporting on compliance with the provisions of Part 4 of the Act, which relate to the consent and provision of mental health treatment in approved centres, as well as on Rules and Codes of Practice in relation to restrictive practices (seclusion, mechanical restraint and physical restraint). Therefore, any administration of mental health treatment or use of a restrictive practice must be done in accordance with the Mental Health Act 2001.

question: Deputy Eamon Scanlon asked the Minister for Health if she has plans for an Independent inquiry into endometriosis care in Ireland; if it will examine the experiences of women who have navigated endometriosis care in Ireland and the way in which our current situation developed; to examine access to diagnosis, appropriately trained specialists, multidisciplinary care, surgery, pain management and mental-health support, as well as the implementation and impact of the National Endometriosis Framework; and to examine the changes needed to ensure women across Ireland can access timely, appropriate and equitable endometriosis care.
reply:
Last October I launched the National Framework for the Management of Endometriosis. Developed by the HSE's National Women and Infants Health Programme (NWIHP), the Framework reflects the voices of patient advocates and aims to transform how endometriosis is recognised and treated across the country. Central to the Model of Care is the principle of presumed diagnosis, acknowledging that women are always the most reliable narrators of their own symptoms and pain.
The Framework marks the first step in developing a more holistic and comprehensive approach to care for women with endometriosis in Ireland.
Regional Specialist Centres for moderate cases have been established in the Rotunda Hospital, the Coombe Hospital, and University Hospital Limerick, with clinics under further development in University Hospital Galway and the National Maternity Hospital.
Two supra-regional specialist centres, in Tallaght University Hospital and Cork University Maternity Hospital, have been established for the management of complex cases.
In conjunction with the publication of the National Endometriosis Framework, I also mandated an immediate action plan to accelerate development of our endometriosis services.

question: Deputy Johnny Mythen asked the Minister for Health to provide an update on plans to make the shingles vaccine free for people aged over 65.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1767, 1850, 2068 and 2193 together.
Ireland’s immunisation programme is informed by the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). NIAC considers the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland as well as international best practice in relation to immunisation when developing its advice.
The current NIAC guidelines state that the shingles vaccine may be considered for those aged 65 years and older, due to the greater burden and severity of disease in this age group and in those aged 18 years and older at increased risk of shingles.
I can confirm that I have approved the introduction of a Shingles Vaccination Programme, in line with NIAC advice, to be implemented on a phased basis over 5 years, for immunocompromised groups and persons aged 65 and over.
The programme is expected to commence in 2027, initially offering shingles vaccines to immunocompromised groups. This will be followed by the 80 years and older cohort. The programme will conclude with the 65–69 year-old cohort.
It is expected that the vaccine will be administered in the main by GPs and Pharmacists. Further programme details will become available in due course.

question: Deputy Brian Stanley asked the Minister for Defence to review the decision of the Board of Assessors regarding the rewarding of 1916 service medals to Laois volunteers who were on active service during Easter week 1916, under the direction of Padraic Pearse and who were not awarded a service medal.
reply:
The 1916 Medal was awarded to persons who were awarded 1916 service under the Military Service Pensions Acts or to those who did not apply for a pension but who satisfied the Minister that they would have been awarded 1916 service if they had applied under the Acts.
The Military Service Certificate under the 1924 Act, which formed the basis for the award of a pension, is also the basis for the award of a 1916 medal. Section 3(6) of the Military Service Pensions Act 1924 provided that the Board of Assessors could at any time re-open their findings at the request of the Minister on the ground that evidence not previously available had subsequently become available.
The power given to the Board of Assessors to reopen findings was removed by the Military Services Pensions Act 1949. Therefore, there is now no statutory provision available to re-open the findings of the Board. The process by which applications and petitions or appeals under the Military Service Pensions Acts were made, investigated and verified was wound up in 1958 and there is no statutory or other mechanism available now by which service can be investigated or verified.
The Deputy refers to a group of Laois volunteers who participated in the relevant Easter Rising events, of whom six received 1916 medals on foot of awards under the relevant Military Service Pensions Acts, while others did not.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Defence to report on the meeting of the Minister of State with the NATO Supreme Allied Commander in Europe in August 2026.
reply:
As the House knows the Government is committed to broadening and deepening Ireland's international security engagement with key partners, including through the EU, UN and NATO, while fully maintaining Ireland's established policy of military neutrality.
Minister of State at the Department of Defence, Thomas Byrne TD, met with General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR) in Dublin on 12th August last. The meeting focused on Ireland’s engagement with NATO through the Partnership for Peace programme, which has been in place since 1999 and covered a range of international security and defence issues.
Partnership for Peace provides valuable opportunities for Defence Forces personnel to access military training, education and best practice. This helps ensure that the Defence Forces can operate effectively alongside international partners on peacekeeping and peace-support missions.
The engagement was open and productive. General Grynkewich praised the Irish Defence Forces’ long history of peacekeeping contributions with UNIFIL in Lebanon, as well as with KFOR in Kosovo.
During the meeting, Minister Byrne and General Grynkewich discussed Ireland's EU Presidency and Irish priorities for that term, as well as national defence capability development projects. reply:

Following the recent announcement of a total health allocation of €29.1 billion for 2027, the Department of Health and HSE have been engaging in budgetary processes to determine overall allocation of funding for next year. These processes are ongoing, and the HSE will produce its National Service Plan (NSP) for next year in the coming weeks.
It will be for the HSE Mid West Health Region to determine how best to resource the Surgical Hub, taking into account the staffing requirements of the Hub as well as those of the wider health service across the region.
In line with other Surgical Hubs which have opened over the course of 2025 and 2026, the Surgical Hub in Limerick will open on a phased basis. A further two theatres are also expected to open at the Hub next year which will further increase elective care capacity. The HSE is therefore aiming to have all four theatres and 6-day working progressed over the course of 2027.

reply:

The Government has committed to measures to safeguard undersea critical infrastructure and the Department of Defence and the Defence Forces have a body of work underway in that regard.
The Defence Equipment Development Plan manages requirements for the immediate term and recognises the need to maintain and upgrade military capabilities having regard to emerging priorities, operational requirements and changes in technology. There is a body of work currently underway to ensure that the Defence Forces have the required capabilities, with equipment projects in various stages of the project lifecycle.
One of the key programmes underway that will contribute to monitoring and protecting undersea cables relates to subsea domain awareness. The investment in sonar capability, announced in 2025 is the first project within that programme of work which will see the Naval Service acquire sonar capability which will be used to detect objects near cables and pipelines in Irish territorial waters and the EEZ. This new acquisition will enhance awareness below the surface, contributing to the overall maritime picture available to Naval Service and the wider Defence Forces.
