question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Health if she has made representations to the HPRA in respect of the need to make available 2mg and 1mg doses of a mediction (details supplied) for treating anaphylaxis, approved in August 2025 and March 2026, respectively.
reply:
The Health Product Regulatory Authority (HPRA) is the competent authority for the regulation of medicines in Ireland. Medicines placed on the Irish market must be authorised by the HPRA or, in the case of centrally authorised products, by the European Commission.
Epinephrine (Eurneffy®) is an authorised medicinal product in Ireland. The Marketing Authorisation Holder (MAH) has confirmed to the HPRA that Epinephrine (Eurneffy®) 2mg nasal spray solution is currently available for supply to Irish patients, and no shortages are anticipated or ongoing. The MAH has also confirmed to the HPRA that Epinephrine (Eurneffy®) 1mg nasal spray solution is to be made available for supply to Irish patients from November 2026 onwards. As of 21st October 2026, only the 2mg presentation (pack sizes available have not been specified) has been marketed.
The HPRA cannot require companies to market medicinal products in Ireland, and they also have no role in relation to pricing and reimbursement. The HPRA remains willing at any stage to engage with and to provide regulatory guidance to any company who wishes to make medicinal products available in Ireland.

question: Deputy Marie Sherlock asked the Minister for Health when the review of vaginal mesh surgery was completed and sent for consideration to her Department.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1793 and 1794 together.
In 2018, the Chief Medical Officer produced a report, ‘The Use of Uro-Gynaecological Mesh in Surgical Procedures, 2018’, which made several recommendations in this area. Following this, a pause on the use of mesh for urinary stress incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse surgeries in Irish public hospitals was introduced.
In 2023 the HSE established a National Vaginal Mesh Implant Oversight Group. The focus of this group was to review and assess implementation of the CMO’s recommendations and assess the appropriateness of resuming uro-gynaecological mesh procedures. My Department received an updated report from the group in February 2025.
The report is currently under consideration by officials in my Department. In parallel, the HSE is working closely with my Department to determine whether the findings of the CMO report could be adopted into an evidence-based actionable framework for potentially reintroducing uro-gynaecological Mesh for the treatment of Stress Urinary Incontinence. This work is ongoing.
We acknowledge the impact the pause on the use of uro-gynaecological mesh can have women who wish to avail of this surgery. This is an extremely complex and sensitive issue which requires a safety-first approach; therefore, it is not possible to give a timeline for decision at this moment.

question: Deputy Máire Devine asked the Minister for Health the immediate steps being taken to stabilise the supply of Lenzetto transdermal spray HRT medication in pharmacies; and the protocols being introduced to ensure that when critical shortages occur, alternative options such as imported stocks are fully available and accessible without compromising patient care.
reply:
The Department is aware of the stress that medicine shortages can cause for patients and healthcare professionals. Managing and mitigating medicine shortages is a priority for the Department of Health and is the subject of several workstreams across the Department and the wider health service.
Under European and national medicines legislation, pharmaceutical companies and wholesalers are required to ensure an appropriate and continuous supply of the medicines they place on the market. Companies are also required to notify the Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA) of actual or anticipated shortages affecting the Irish market. The HPRA maintains a publicly available list of current and resolved medicine shortages and works closely with suppliers to minimise the duration and impact of shortages on patients.
All shortages, including persistent shortages, are managed via the national Medicines Shortages Framework (MSF), which is coordinated by the HPRA. The MSF involves a multi-stakeholder approach to handling shortages of human medicinal products. Where required, the HPRA engages with all relevant stakeholders to support continuity of care until sufficient supply of the medicinal product is available to meet demand.

question: Deputy Rose Conway-Walsh asked the Minister for Defence to define a “relevant international force”; the criteria that will be used by the Irish Government to determine whether a force meets that definition; and the legal basis under international law for authorising Irish Defence Forces participation in such a force in the absence of a UN mandate.
reply:
Thank you Deputy for the question.
As I have previously advised the House, the Defence (Amendment) Bill 2026 is currently progressing through the Houses of the Oireachtas. The Bill proposes a number of reforms to the legislative framework governing overseas deployments by members of the Defence Forces, including replacing the current requirement relating to an "international United Nations force" with the broader concept of a "relevant international force".
The purpose of this reform is to provide Ireland with greater flexibility to consider participation in a wider range of international peace support, humanitarian, monitoring and crisis-management missions, while continuing to operate in accordance with the principles of the UN Charter and international law.
A "relevant international force" is intended to encompass international missions and operations established by, or operating under, recognised international organisations or international arrangements that have a legitimate legal basis and whose activities are consistent with international law and the maintenance of international peace and security. This may include missions conducted under the auspices of the United Nations, the European Union, the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe, or other recognised international frameworks.

reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, CORU’s role is to protect the public by regulating the health and social care professions designated under the Health and Social Care Professionals Act 2005 (as amended).
CORU is a hugely experienced regulator responsible for the registration of over 40,000 health and social care professionals.
The recognition of international applicants is a critical part of CORU’s role in protecting the public, ensuring that professionals who qualified outside Ireland have the right qualifications, skills and standards before they can join a CORU register and work under a protected professional title.
I wish to inform the Deputy that Pinnacle Consulting conducted the audit referred to. The audit report was finalised in January 2026. There were four findings with a ‘housekeeping’ grading, with no findings of ‘significant’ or ‘important’ grading. Housekeeping findings in an audit are of low risk. They do not indicate serious non-compliance and are corrected easily in a timely manner through management action. The findings were addressed by the end of Q2 2026.
The audit was presented to CORU’s Audit and Risk Committee and to CORU’s Council. The audit report was not presented to the Professional Regulation Unit in my Department or published publicly.
The chair of Council is responsible for reporting to me and no issues in relation to CORU’s recognition processes have been brought to my attention through any of the established governance oversight mechanisms in place

question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Health the details of the shingles vaccination programme announced in budget 2027.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1767, 1850, 2068 and 2193 together.
Ireland’s immunisation programme is informed by the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). NIAC considers the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland as well as international best practice in relation to immunisation when developing its advice.
The current NIAC guidelines state that the shingles vaccine may be considered for those aged 65 years and older, due to the greater burden and severity of disease in this age group and in those aged 18 years and older at increased risk of shingles.
I can confirm that I have approved the introduction of a Shingles Vaccination Programme, in line with NIAC advice, to be implemented on a phased basis over 5 years, for immunocompromised groups and persons aged 65 and over.
The programme is expected to commence in 2027, initially offering shingles vaccines to immunocompromised groups. This will be followed by the 80 years and older cohort. The programme will conclude with the 65–69 year-old cohort.
It is expected that the vaccine will be administered in the main by GPs and Pharmacists. Further programme details will become available in due course.

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Defence the way in which it is envisaged that the United Nations would still be part of the structure of the Defence (Amendment) Bill 2026.
reply:
The Defence (Amendment) Bill 2026 retains an important role for the United Nations in the deployment of members of the Defence Forces overseas.
The purpose of the Bill is not to remove the United Nations from Ireland's approach to overseas deployments, but rather to modernise the legislative framework governing such deployments and to ensure that Ireland can continue to contribute effectively to international peace and security operations alongside our international partners.
Under the Bill, the Government remains committed to overseas missions that are conducted in accordance with international law and the principles of the United Nations Charter. United Nations mandates, resolutions and authorisations will continue to be an important consideration in the assessment of overseas missions in which Ireland may participate.
The Bill recognises the reality that many contemporary international peace operations are undertaken not only by the United Nations itself, but also by regional organisations acting with the support, endorsement or authorisation of the United Nations. This includes operations undertaken by organisations such as the European Union and other international organisations.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Defence to clarify the difference between peace keeping and peace enforcement missions that will apply to the despatch of members of the Defence Forces.
reply:
I would like to thank the Deputy for raising this issue. There has recently been a great deal of mischaracterisation of this matter and I am happy to provide clarity that participation in peace enforcement missions is not a new departure for our Defence Forces. Indeed, the Defence Forces have been despatched on a range of peace enforcement missions over the years.
Since 1990, the majority of overseas deployments by members of the Defence Forces have been peacekeeping (i.e. Chapter 6) missions, including service with UNIFIL in Lebanon, UNDOF in the Golan Heights and UNTSO in the Middle East.
However, Irish personnel have also served in a number of UN missions operating under more robust authorisations for the use of force (Chapter 7). Examples include the United Nations Mission in Liberia (UNMIL), the United Nations Stabilisation Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), the United Nations Multidimensional Integrated Stabilisation Mission in Mali (MINUSMA) and East Timor. Irish personnel have also served in UN-authorised and underpinned missions such as KFOR, in Kosovo, ISAF in Afghanistan and EUFOR Tchad/RCA in Chad, all of which operated under robust international mandates.
It may be useful in this regard for me to outline the distinctions between peacekeeping and peace enforcement to the House.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Defence if she will consider a referendum before removing Ireland's Triple Lock.
reply:
There have been a number of calls for a referendum or public plebiscite on the Government’s proposed changes to the Triple Lock, either to enshrine neutrality in the Constitution or to vote directly on the legislative amendments. Many of these calls incorrectly conflate an amendment to legislation, which the Defence Amendment Bill proposes, with an amendment to the Constitution.
The Triple Lock is not a constitutional provision. Ireland was a militarily neutral country before the introduction of the Triple Lock, and it will remain a militarily neutral country after the legislation is passed. Our military neutrality remains grounded in Ireland’s long-standing policy of non-participation in military alliances.
The proposed amendments do not alter this traditional position of military neutrality, despite the repeated and disingenuous accusations from certain quarters. Any overseas deployment of Defence Forces personnel will continue to be based on the principles of the UN Charter and international law, and will require the approval of Ireland’s democratically elected representatives.
It is important to emphasise most strongly again that the Bill does not remove the United Nations from Ireland's framework for overseas deployments. Nor does it diminish Ireland's longstanding commitment to the United Nations, to UN peacekeeping, or to the principles of the UN Charter. question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Health if funding for the Understanding and Managing Adult ADHD Programme has been secured; and when it will be confirmed.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1679, 1681, 1709, 1710, 1728 and 1729 together.
The development of Specialist Mental Health Services, including for adults with ADHD, has been a priority since my appointment as Minister for Mental Health in 2020. As Minister, I'm proud to have launched the Model of Care for Adult ADHD and to have resourced the establishment of the teams envisioned by the Model of Care. Prior to this, there were no publicly funded ADHD services for Adults in Ireland.
The National Clinical Programme for ADHD in Adults is being implemented on a phased basis. Since the introduction of a Model of Care for the programme in 2021, over €5 million has been made available for funding ADHD posts from Programme for Government funding. This has enabled the establishment of 8 fully operational ADHD teams with 3 community-based teams currently in development.
The HSE have stated that nationwide demand for Adult ADHD services has been significantly higher than originally projected. The HSE is progressing service development on a phased basis, supported by approved funding and workforce availability.
In parallel, the National Clinical Programme for ADHD in Adults has developed a draft amended Model of Care, incorporating a stepped-care approach, informed by engagement with service users, families, clinicians and ADHD Ireland. This revised Model of Care is currently being trialled in a number of ADHD teams and will guide the next phase of service development nationally.

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health if the stem cell tissue establishment and advanced cellular therapies unit project for Cork University Hospital will be considered for inclusion in the next National Cancer Strategy.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, work is progressing on the development of Ireland's next National Cancer Strategy. The Strategy will provide a comprehensive national framework for cancer control, encompassing prevention, early diagnosis, treatment, survivorship, research and service development. Subject to the completion of the necessary approvals, it is intended that a National Cancer Strategy Development Steering Group will be appointed in the coming weeks. The Steering Group will oversee the development of the successor to the National Cancer Strategy 2017–2026. It is currently expected to bring together expertise from across the health service, clinical care, research, patient experience, and related areas.
The Steering Group is expected to commence its work shortly after appointments have been finalised. The Steering Group will be informed by independent evaluation of the current Strategy along with best available evidence and international practice, and engagement with patients, clinicians and other stakeholders.
As this body of work is ongoing, I trust the Deputy will understand that it would be inappropriate to anticipate the outcome of the evaluation, the work of the Steering Group, or any recommendations of the successor strategy, by commenting on specifics at this time.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Health to provide details of the regions that currently have access to an operations specialist adult ADHD team.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1679, 1681, 1709, 1710, 1728 and 1729 together.
The development of Specialist Mental Health Services, including for adults with ADHD, has been a priority since my appointment as Minister for Mental Health in 2020. As Minister, I'm proud to have launched the Model of Care for Adult ADHD and to have resourced the establishment of the teams envisioned by the Model of Care. Prior to this, there were no publicly funded ADHD services for Adults in Ireland.
The National Clinical Programme for ADHD in Adults is being implemented on a phased basis. Since the introduction of a Model of Care for the programme in 2021, over €5 million has been made available for funding ADHD posts from Programme for Government funding. This has enabled the establishment of 8 fully operational ADHD teams with 3 community-based teams currently in development.
The HSE have stated that nationwide demand for Adult ADHD services has been significantly higher than originally projected. The HSE is progressing service development on a phased basis, supported by approved funding and workforce availability.
In parallel, the National Clinical Programme for ADHD in Adults has developed a draft amended Model of Care, incorporating a stepped-care approach, informed by engagement with service users, families, clinicians and ADHD Ireland. This revised Model of Care is currently being trialled in a number of ADHD teams and will guide the next phase of service development nationally.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1708, 1741, 1743 and 1745 together.
Under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013 the HSE has sole statutory responsibility for decisions on pricing and reimbursement of medicines. The HSE must assess applications for pricing and reimbursement to make sure that it can stretch available resources as far as possible and to deliver the best value in relation to each medicine and ultimately more medicines to people living in Ireland.
HSE decisions on which medicines are reimbursed by the taxpayer are made on objective, scientific and economic grounds. There are formal processes which govern applications for the pricing and reimbursement of medicines, and new uses of existing medicines, to be funded and / or reimbursed.
In line with the 2013 Act and the national framework agreed with industry, a company must submit an application to the HSE to have a new medicine added to the reimbursement list and continue to engage at all stages of the process with the HSE to progress applications. Reimbursement is for licenced indications which have been granted market authorisation by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) or the Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA).

Recruitment decisions are managed by the HSE in accordance with approved workforce plans, recruitment controls and available funding.

question: Deputy Aisling Dempsey asked the Minister for Defence if she will report on the work of the new Defence Attachés in London, Paris and Washington.
reply:
In March 2026, Government approval was secured for the establishment of a Defence Attaché Network on a pilot basis, to be initially established in Ireland's Embassies in Paris, London and Washington D.C. These locations were selected in recognition of their strategic importance and Ireland's defence and security relationships with key international partners.
The establishment of the Defence Attaché Network represents a significant milestone in the implementation of the recommendations of the Commission on the Defence Forces and forms part of the Government's broader programme to strengthen Ireland's defence capabilities and international defence engagement.
The Defence Attachés who will shortly take up their roles, will play an important role in advancing Ireland's defence diplomacy and international engagement. Their responsibilities will include representing Ireland on defence matters, supporting bilateral defence and security cooperation, facilitating military-to-military engagement, promoting strategic dialogue with key partners, and acting as representatives of the Defence Forces within their assigned regions. They will also support information exchange and engagement with relevant international organisations, as appropriate.

question: Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Health the reason there is no dedicated stem-cell transplantation unit in Cork or elsewhere in the south.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1670, 1686, 1687 and 1688 together.
As the Deputy will be aware, haematopoietic stem cell transplantation and cellular therapies are highly specialised treatments used in the management of a range of malignant and non-malignant diseases.
As such, these therapies require specialist multidisciplinary teams, dedicated laboratory facilities, tissue establishment infrastructure, specialised inpatient facilities, and robust regulatory and accreditation arrangements.
Cellular therapies currently available in Ireland include autologous stem cell transplantation, allogeneic stem cell transplantation and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. The provision of these services has increased nationally in recent years. Adult autologous stem cell transplantation is currently provided in St. James's Hospital, University Hospital Galway, and St. Vincent's University Hospital. Additionally, adult allogeneic is currently provided through St. James's Hospital.
This year, Beaumont Hospital was designated as an additional stem cell transplantation centre and is working towards commencement of services in 2027.
It is within this national context that HSE South West is considering proposals for a Stem Cell Tissue Establishment and Advanced Cellular Therapies Unit at Cork University Hospital (CUH), which upon completion would support the further expansion of advanced cellular therapies nationally.
A Strategic Healthcare Investment Framework (SHIF) proposal

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Health the amount of Adult ADHD referrals from 2021-2026 broken down by region and year, in tabular form.

I propose to take Questions Nos. 1679, 1681, 1709, 1710, 1728 and 1729 together.
The development of Specialist Mental Health Services, including for adults with ADHD, has been a priority since my appointment as Minister for Mental Health in 2020. As Minister, I'm proud to have launched the Model of Care for Adult ADHD and to have resourced the establishment of the teams envisioned by the Model of Care. Prior to this, there were no publicly funded ADHD services for Adults in Ireland.
The National Clinical Programme for ADHD in Adults is being implemented on a phased basis. Since the introduction of a Model of Care for the programme in 2021, over €5 million has been made available for funding ADHD posts from Programme for Government funding. This revised Model of Care is currently being trialled in a number of ADHD teams and will guide the next phase of service development nationally.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Defence to report on her recent visit to Lebanon.
reply:
During my recent visit to Lebanon, last week, I had a series of engagements with Irish Defence Forces personnel serving with the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), with Lebanese Government representatives, with senior United Nations officials, and with international partners.
A key focus of the visit was to meet members of the 128th Infantry Battalion at Camp Shamrock in South Lebanon. I was pleased to have the opportunity to thank our personnel personally for their professionalism, resilience and dedication in representing Ireland overseas particularly at the current time given the unpredictability and volatility in the mission area. I also attended a medal presentation ceremony recognising their service during what has been a particularly demanding deployment.
I also met senior UNIFIL leadership to discuss the security situation in southern Lebanon, the implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1701, and preparations for the conclusion of Ireland's military contribution to UNIFIL following almost five decades of continuous service.
During my visit, I also met with President Joseph Aoun, Minister for Foreign Affairs and Emigrants Youssef Rajji and Minister of Justice Adel Nassar. Discussions focused on Ireland's long-standing friendship with Lebanon, regional developments, support for peace and stability, and the importance of continued international engagement in supporting Lebanon through a challenging period.

question: Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Health the stem-cell transplantation and related services that are currently available to patients in the South of Ireland.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1670, 1686, 1687 and 1688 together.
As the Deputy will be aware, haematopoietic stem cell transplantation and cellular therapies are highly specialised treatments used in the management of a range of malignant and non-malignant diseases.
As such, these therapies require specialist multidisciplinary teams, dedicated laboratory facilities, tissue establishment infrastructure, specialised inpatient facilities, and robust regulatory and accreditation arrangements.
Cellular therapies currently available in Ireland include autologous stem cell transplantation, allogeneic stem cell transplantation and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. The provision of these services has increased nationally in recent years. Adult autologous stem cell transplantation is currently provided in St. James's Hospital, University Hospital Galway, and St. Vincent's University Hospital. Additionally, adult allogeneic is currently provided through St. James's Hospital.
This year, Beaumont Hospital was designated as an additional stem cell transplantation centre and is working towards commencement of services in 2027.
It is within this national context that HSE South West is considering proposals for a Stem Cell Tissue Establishment and Advanced Cellular Therapies Unit at Cork University Hospital (CUH), which upon completion would support the further expansion of advanced cellular therapies nationally.
A Strategic Healthcare Investment Framework (SHIF) proposal

question: Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Defence if employment protections, such as the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977, will be extended to members of the Reserve Defence Forces.
reply:
The modernisation of our Defence Forces and revitalising our Reserve Defence Force is a vital part of that transformation process.

The launch of Supplemental Military Service on 1st June, includes support military service both within or outside the State and is remunerated. Members of the RDF deployed on Supplemental Military Service are entitled to the benefits of the Working Time Directive, where appropriate, as well as allowances and subsistence.
The issue of Employment Protection is complex and involves input from many stakeholders. Finalised proposals will be brought forward to me for consideration by end Q2 2027.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether she will support the establishment of an independent public inquiry into historical child sexual abuse connected to St John Ambulance; including an examination of whether opportunities to investigate allegations and intervene to protect children or hold individuals to account were missed.
reply:
St John Ambulance Ireland is not a body under the aegis of the Department. It is an independent registered charity, and the Department has no role in the governance or oversight of the organisation. The Department has no contractual relationship with the organisation.
Having said that, like all independent similar organisations, St John Ambulance Ireland is required to abide by relevant statutory legislation i.e. the Children First Act, 2015 in relation to safeguarding and mandated reporting. The Children First Act 2015, provides for a number of key child protection measures, including raising awareness of child abuse and neglect, providing for mandated reporting of child protection concerns and improving child protection arrangements in organisations providing services to children.
The Dr Geoffrey Shannon Report —officially titled the "Independent Review of the Handling of Past Complaints of Abuse in St John Ambulance Ireland", was commissioned by the Board of St. John Ambulance Ireland, in 2021, to investigate the management of historical child sexual abuse allegations within the organisation and evaluate its ongoing child safeguarding practices. The Review was initially recommended by Tusla and this Department following a number of complaints of historic child sexual abuse against a former volunteer at St. John Ambulance Ireland. Dr. Shannon’s Review was published in March, 2023.

question: Deputy Gillian Toole asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality when the National Oversight and Governance Framework with equivalent statutory protections will be developed for all children in State funded residential care.
reply:
The Child Care Act 1991 is the statutory framework for child welfare and protection in Ireland. The legislation places a statutory duty on Tusla to promote the welfare of children who are not receiving adequate care and protection. It sets the legislative provisions in relation to taking children into care, and the responsibilities of the State in that regard, which aim to improve outcomes for looked after children.
The placement of children in Residential Care is governed by the National Standards for Children’s Residential Centres 2018, and underpinned by the Child Care (Placement in Residential Care) Regulation 1995, and the Child Care (Standards in Children’s Residential Centres) 1996. The placement of children in Special Care is governed by the National Standards for Special Care Units 2014, as well as the Health Act 2007 (Care and Welfare of Children in Special Care Units) Regulations 2017, Health Act 2007 (Care and Welfare of Children in Special Care Units) (Amendment) Regulations 2018, and the Health Act 2007 (Registration of Designated Centres) (Special Care Units) Regulations 2017.
Tusla has also advised that private residential providers can only be awarded a contract following a successful application via the tender process, which outlines in detail the minimum requirements and standards that must be met and sets the funding level applicable for the service type.

question: Deputy Gillian Toole asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the findings of the personal assistance review of the HSE funded personal assistant services; and when will the definition of a personal assistant be finalised.
reply:
In 2023, the HSE established a Personal Assistance (PA) Review Group initially to advise on operational matters concerning eligibility and funding allocations. The group subsequently set out a programme of work, including matters relating to service definition, scope, access and governance.
At an early stage of the Group's work, a working definition of PA was developed. While the definition sought to articulate the distinct nature of the service, challenges emerged in applying it in a manner that would clearly and consistently distinguish PA from other comparable forms of support for the purposes of the Department's policy and legislative development.
Since 2023, the policy context within which PA is being considered has continued to evolve such that policy considerations in relation to the service are now being progressed by the Department within a broader system-level perspective through the development of a Policy Framework on Supports for Community Living.
The Framework is examining the future structure and delivery of home support, PA and related support arrangements, with a particular focus on clarifying the range of support options available to individuals, the differing levels of choice, control, autonomy and self-direction associated with those options, and the role that personalised budgets may play within that framework.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if she will expand the definition of "qualifying person" in the Birth Information and Tracing Act 2022 to include grandchildren to ensure that they are not continued to be locked out of information about their grandparent and denied access to such significant information in cases where the direct generation is deceased or unwilling to apply for such information.
reply:
A statutory review of the operation of the Birth Information and Tracing Act 2022 is currently underway. An independent research organisation has been appointed to carry out the review, and a Service User Advisory Group has been established, following a public expression of interest process, to play a key role in developing the methodology for the review, communications and recommendations.
Work on the review to date has included an online survey of 579 individuals with experience of the operation of the birth information and tracing services introduced under the Act and one-to-one interviews with 64 individuals. Focus groups and additional interviews are ongoing.
This question will be considered as part of the review process. The review, which will be completed by the end of Q1 2027, will be published and will include recommendations for improving birth information and tracing services.

This strategy is now being developed, provisionally entitled Equal Lives, and it will become the flagship reform strategy for disability services for the coming years. It will act as a successor to the Action Plan for Disability Services 2024–2026. Equal Lives will also focus on deeper systemic reform of the model of service delivery to ensure services continue to become more human rights based and more sustainable into the future.
Significant work has been undertaken throughout 2026, including extensive engagement with stakeholders, including Disabled Persons’ Organisations, people who access disability services, relevant subject matter experts, service provider umbrella bodies and wider advocacy organisations. A dedicated expert Advisory Council has also informed the development of policy options.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if she will provide details of the way in which the 212 new residential placements funded in Budget 2027 will be allocated by HSE region; the criteria for prioritisation; and the number of people under 65 living in nursing homes who will move to community settings in 2027.
reply:
Increasing funding provided to the HSE has supported the creation of over 1,000 new specialist disability residential places since 2020 including 182 new places from January to September 2026.
Budget 2027 delivers significant progress for disabled children and adults, bringing the budget for Disability Services to over €4billion for the first time. While continuing to fund existing placements, this Budget will provide additional investment of €108.4million for residential services, which includes the full year cost of 2026 service delivery and a further expansion of services in 2027.
This additional investment includes €62.4million for new developments. This will support a range of residential measures including new placements as well as enhancements for existing residential places where individual needs have become more complex. Subject to finalisation of the HSE’s 2027 National Service Plan, this is expected to support 212 newly created placements (including approximately 100 planned and 112 placements to respond to urgent need), the majority of whom will move from their family home.
In addition to the 212 placements, this funding will also support a number of new placements into existing vacant places with necessary enhancements as well as continuing to support the transition of disabled people under the age of 65 living in nursing homes to more appropriate homes in the community while also supporting further transitions from congregated settings into community-based place

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality for an update on the implementation progress of strand 2 of equal start stand D and E (details supplied).
reply:
Equal Start is a funding model and a set of associated universal and targeted measures to support access and participation in early learning and care (ELC) and school-age childcare (SAC) for children and their families who experience disadvantage.
Strand 2 of Equal Start focuses on child-targeted measures that provide additional supports for children. Child-targeted measures are designed to support children and families from Equal Start priority groups, regardless of what service they attend. This includes a commitment to reducing practical barriers to children's participation in early learning and childcare (Equal Start measure D) and to co-create tailored responses that address other barriers for children from priority groups (Equal Start measure E).
The Back-to-School Clothing and Footwear Allowance (BTSCFA) was extended to children in pre-school, starting from September 2026. The BTSCFA is a means-tested allowance for pre-school children that was introduced to support Equal Start measure D, by reducing practical barriers for families to engage in early learning and childcare. Providing funding directly to families ensures that each child will receive the specific supports they need to participate more equitably.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the current steps she is taking to ensure that the recommended 1,900 additional residential places as recommended by 2021 Disability Capacity Review are made available by 2032.
reply:
A key focus of this Government and the HSE, is an increased emphasis on longer term planning for residential placements and measures continue to be implemented this year and into next year to move towards strengthened operational processes.
The Department of Health’s 2021 Disability Capacity Review projected a need for a minimum of an additional 1,900 residential places by 2032 under a minimum projection.
Increased funding provided to the HSE has supported the creation of over 1,000 new specialist disability residential places since 2020 including 182 new places from January to September 2026.
In recognition of the high demand for these services, approximately €3.9 billion of funding has been allocated to Specialist Disability Services in 2026. Specialist disability residential services make up the largest part of the Disability funding disbursed by the HSE, almost 60% (€2.2bn) of the total budget.
€65m has been allocated to Disability Residential Services in 2026 for new developments, which includes €40m of funding that will provide in the region of 199 new residential responses. This includes 152 newly created residential placements consisting of 72 planned placements and 80 (Priority 1) new placements to meet urgent need, as outlined in the HSE’s National Service Plan for 2026. Funding will also support new residents in existing placements that have become vacant and require enhancement and in limited circumstances, placements in nursing home settings.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Defence if she will commit to holding a referendum on any changes that the Government are making to the triple lock.
reply:
There have been a number of calls for a referendum or public plebiscite on the Government’s proposed changes to the Triple Lock, either to enshrine neutrality in the Constitution or to vote directly on the legislative amendments. Many of these calls incorrectly conflate an amendment to legislation, which the Defence Amendment Bill proposes, with an amendment to the Constitution.
The Triple Lock is not a constitutional provision. Ireland was a militarily neutral country before the introduction of the Triple Lock, and it will remain a militarily neutral country after the legislation is passed. Our military neutrality remains grounded in Ireland’s long-standing policy of non-participation in military alliances.
The proposed amendments do not alter this traditional position of military neutrality, despite the repeated and disingenuous accusations from certain quarters. Any overseas deployment of Defence Forces personnel will continue to be based on the principles of the UN Charter and international law, and will require the approval of Ireland’s democratically elected representatives.
It is important to emphasise most strongly again that the Bill does not remove the United Nations from Ireland's framework for overseas deployments. Nor does it diminish Ireland's longstanding commitment to the United Nations, to UN peacekeeping, or to the principles of the UN Charter. They are also engaging with officials from the Department of Social Protection as the Minister for Social Protection has responsibility for the payment of any associated benefits.

question: Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to provide an update on the building blocks extension grant scheme; and whether she intends to provide further funding under the scheme.
reply:
The Building Blocks Extension Scheme Phase 2, which will fund projects in 2027 to deliver additional capacity, recently closed for applications.
Under the scheme, community providers could apply for a capital grant of between €100,000 and €530,000 to extend their existing premises, while private providers could apply for a capital grant of between €50,000 and €265,000. Match funding was a requirement for private providers. Up to €10 million has been set aside for the scheme.
Applications under Phase 2 were appraised by the Department with input from the Office of Public Works. Services will be notified of the outcome of this appraisal process in the coming weeks.
There are currently no plans to open a further Building Blocks scheme although subject to sufficient funding, additional rounds of Building Blocks will be considered in the coming years, and criteria for any future rounds will be the subject of further consideration.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1622 and 1655 together.
Special Care units are secure residential facilities for children in care aged between 11 and 17 years who are detained under a High Court care order for a short-term period of stabilisation when their behaviour poses a real and substantial risk of harm to their life, health, safety, development or welfare. Tusla has statutory responsibility for the operation of Special Care and the provision of Special Care beds.
Tusla has indicated that difficulties in the recruitment and retention of staff are the primary factors limiting the operation of Special Care beds. Tusla has advised that, as of 22 October 2026, there are 13 beds in operation across three Special Care centres.
A range of measures has been introduced by Tusla to support recruitment and retention and to increase operational capacity within Special Care services.
A new grade and pay scale for Special Care was sanctioned in 2024 in an effort to increase staff numbers. The new grade represents a promotional opportunity, with a higher salary scale for both Social Care Workers and Social Care Leaders. As of June 2026, the new Tusla Special Care Worker grade offers approximately 20.3% higher pay at the top of the scale compared with the Social Care Worker grade, and 3.6% higher pay compared with the Social Care Leader grade.

The NCS attendance rules are designed to provide significant flexibility for families. With respect to the Deputy's latter question, the Scheme is designed to support the agreed childcare arrangement and hours of care actually provided to the child. While subsidies are based on agreed hours, the attendance rules are in place to allow flexibility for normal fluctuations while helping to ensure that public funding continues to reflect genuine childcare usage.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether her Department and Tusla have reviewed Children First national guidance and safeguarding training materials following the abolition of exemptions permitting marriage under 18 from 1 January 2019; whether she is aware of safeguarding training continuing to advise that a person aged 16 or 17 may marry with parental permission and consequently cease to be considered a child; and the steps that will be taken to clarify the current position for training providers, mandated persons and voluntary organisations.
reply:
Section 31(1)(a) of the Family Law Act 1995 confirms that a marriage between persons, either of whom is under the age of 18 years is not valid in law. A previous exemption to this provision provided for in section 33 of the Act was repealed on commencement of section 45(e) of the Domestic Violence Act 2018.
Currently, the definition of a child for the purposes of the Child Care Act 1991 reflects the position prior to the repeal of section 33. Section 2 of the Child Care Act 1991 provides that a child means a person under the age of 18 years other than a person who is or has been married.
In practice, Tusla assesses referrals concerning all children and young people under 18 having regard to their welfare and protection needs and works to ensure that appropriate supports and interventions are available.
The Deputy may wish to note that the Child Care (Amendment) Bill 2025 includes provisions to amend the definition of child in both the Child Care Act 1991 and the Child and Family Agency Act 2013 by removing the wording that excludes persons who are, or have been, married from the definition of a child. The amendment to the definition in the Child Care Act 1991 will also apply to the Children First Act 2015 upon commencement. The purpose of these amendments is to ensure that all persons under the age of 18 are included within the statutory definition of a child for the purposes of those Acts.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Defence whether her Department has plans to seek a UN mandate for Irish overseas missions, either via the Security Council or the General Assembly, once the triple lock is removed.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the Defence (Amendment) Bill is currently progressing through the Houses of the Oireachtas. Following debate on 21 October 2026, it passed Second Stage in Dáil Éireann.
It is important to address some of the claims that have been made regarding the purpose and effect of the proposed reforms. Much of the criticism advanced during the Second Stage debate has been based on a mischaracterisation of the legislation, and an exaggerated portrayal of its practical consequences.
The Bill does not impact Ireland's long-standing policy of military neutrality or provide for unrestricted overseas deployments of Defence Forces personnel. No provision of the Bill provides for this.
The central reform contained in the Bill is set out in section 4, which replaces the existing concept of an "International United Nations Force" with the term "relevant international force". This is the substantive change proposed by the legislation.

question: Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to address issues with the operation of the national childcare scheme (details supplied).
reply:
The NCS is designed to be flexible, recognising that early learning and childcare needs are different for each family. Under the NCS, subsidies are awarded as an hourly rate, up to a maximum number of 45 hours a week for which the subsidy applies.
The hours-based nature of the NCS is designed to fit around the needs of families and ensure that the effectiveness of funding is maximised for all. The NCS enables families to agree the number of hours to be used with their service provider within overall scheme limits. The number of hours can be altered week to week so, for example the subsidy can be increased during a school midterm where a parent requires more hours of care.
The Department designed the NCS to also be flexible around children’s attendance, recognising that children’s attendance may vary from week to week. If a child is occasionally picked up early or misses an occasional day, this will not impact on a family’s subsidy. The NCS subsidy will only be impacted if a child consistently under attends for 8 consecutive weeks.
This combination of flexibility and accountability provides an appropriate balance of supporting parents and providers while also ensuring the efficient use of Exchequer funding.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if the State's commemorative programme includes a date for the commemoration of those who died in Industrial and Reformatory School Institutions, Magdalene Laundries, and Mother and Baby Homes and County Home Institutions.
reply:
In March 2022, Government approved plans for a national memorial – the National Centre for Research and Remembrance - to be located in Seán MacDermott Street, Dublin 1.
The National Centre will stand as a site of conscience to honour equally all those who spent time in Industrial Schools, Magdalen Laundries, Mother and Baby and County Home Institutions, Reformatories, and related institutions, and all those who have lived experience of Ireland’s historical adoption and boarded out systems.
The National Centre will stand as part of our national institutions and will comprise:
• a museum and exhibition space, the development of which is being led by the National Museum of Ireland;
• a research centre and repository of records related to institutional trauma in the 20th century, which will form part of the National Archives; and
• a garden space for reflection and remembrance.
A Steering Group, whose membership includes representatives of the relevant state bodies, the Special Advocate for Survivors and survivor members, is driving the overall coordinated development of the National Centre campus.
In February 2025, planning permission for the development of the National Centre was granted by Dublin City Council. Detailed restoration works on the historic structures are now underway at the site, as well as archaeological works and other essential enabling works.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to review the exclusion of children who spent less than 180 days in institutions for the mother and baby institutional redress scheme.
reply:
The Mother and Baby Institutions Payment Scheme acknowledges circumstances experienced while resident in a Mother and Baby institution and the associated conditions, shame and stigma endured over a period of time. Using time spent as the deciding factor is intended to support a non-adversarial approach which avoids the need for applicants to have to bring forward evidence or prove abuse or harm. This non-adversarial approach ensures that those who spent longer periods of time in these institutions, and endured the harshest conditions, receive the highest level of support.
The six-month eligibility criterion was initially referenced in the Commission of Investigation report and was subsequently included in the report of the interdepartmental working group which was asked to scope out the Scheme.
It is acknowledged that some survivors are not eligible for the Scheme and are disappointed by this. However, it should be noted that the Payment Scheme is just one of a large suite of actions being undertaken to respond to the legacy of these institutions under the Action Plan for Survivors and Former Residents of Mother and Baby and County Home Institutions.
For those who spent shorter periods of time in institutions as young children, the overwhelming priority need which has been expressed by survivors has been access to records. To date, under the Birth Information and Tracing Act, the Adoption Authority of Ireland and Tusla have completed over 18,700 applications for information.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the basis on which Tusla released the annual cost of each individual out of State residential placement in reply to Parliamentary Question No. 66232/26, but declined in reply to Parliamentary Question No. 71219/26 to state the category of each provider or the general reasons for the variation in cost, on the grounds that this could identify a child; whether Tusla's Data Protection Officer was consulted on either reply.
reply:
As the Deputy will appreciate, due to the very small number of children and young people who are placed in out-of-state placements, publishing information regarding the specialised types of placements may inadvertently risk identification of the children and young people involved. In this regard, the names of specific companies or centres are understandably more likely to lead to identification of individual children and young people than anonymised costings.
Tusla is statutorily independent in the performance of its functions under Section 8(11) of the Child and Family Agency Act 2013. It is a matter for the Agency whether its Data Protection Officer is consulted in regards to replies to Parliamentary Questions.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the number of cases in which the Child and Family Agency, acting in respect of a child in its care, expressed a view to An Garda Síochána or the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions that a prosecution should not proceed or should be discontinued, on welfare grounds or otherwise, in each of the years 2023 to 2025 and to date in 2026; the policy governing such representations.
reply: Noting that decisions on whether or not to proceed with a prosecution are solely a matter for An Garda Síochana and the Director of Public Prosecutions, the Department has contacted Tusla in relation to the Deputy's question. Tusla has said it may give an opinion on the likely impact of prosecution on a child's welfare if such an opinion were requested by either of those bodies. question: Deputy Denise Mitchell asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality for an update on the issues of bed capacity at special-care units operated by Tusla; if she will clarify the number of beds that are operational; and the action being taken to increase capacity.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1622 and 1655 together.
Special Care units are secure residential facilities for children in care aged between 11 and 17 years who are detained under a High Court care order for a short-term period of stabilisation when their behaviour poses a real and substantial risk of harm to their life, health, safety, development or welfare. Tusla has statutory responsibility for the operation of Special Care and the provision of Special Care beds.
Tusla has indicated that difficulties in the recruitment and retention of staff are the primary factors limiting the operation of Special Care beds. Tusla has advised that, as of 22 October 2026, there are 13 beds in operation across three Special Care centres.
A range of measures has been introduced by Tusla to support recruitment and retention and to increase operational capacity within Special Care services.
A new grade and pay scale for Special Care was sanctioned in 2024 in an effort to increase staff numbers. The new grade represents a promotional opportunity, with a higher salary scale for both Social Care Workers and Social Care Leaders. As of June 2026, the new Tusla Special Care Worker grade offers approximately 20.3% higher pay at the top of the scale compared with the Social Care Worker grade, and 3.6% higher pay compared with the Social Care Leader grade.
Tusla continues to prioritise recruitment initiatives for special care with a number of targeted campaigns and through a variety of media outlet

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Defence for an update on recruitment in the permanent Defence Forces in 2026.
reply:
As Minister for Defence, I am fully committed to increasing and strengthening recruitment and supporting retention in the Permanent Defence Force.
The Military Authorities advise that the strength of the Permanent Defence Force (PDF) stood at 8,034 personnel on the 30 September 2026, the latest date for which this figure is available
Last year saw a growth in the overall strength of nearly 200, with a total of 790 inductions achieved- the highest in twenty years - while the number of personnel who discharged was at its lowest level in more than five years. I am determined to build on the increase in the strength achieved since 2024 have set a target of 850 inductions to year end.
Interest in a career in the Defence Forces remains notably strong with over 15,700 applications received to the end of September of this year. The challenge now for the Defence Forces is to convert this high level of applications to inductions. A draft Strategic Workforce Plan, prepared by the Defence Forces remains the subject of active consideration. As the Deputy will be aware, the aim of this process is to provide a pathway to the achievement of an overall strength of 11,500, inclusive of civilian personnel, commensurate with Level of Ambition 2.

question: Deputy Keira Keogh asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality for an update on the potential extension of paternity leave beyond two weeks currently legislated for.
reply:
There have been significant developments in entitlements for parents of working families in recent years. The Government is committed to supporting workers, including by extending paid leave for parents to allow them to spend more time with their child during their earliest years.
The Paternity Leave and Benefit Act 2016 provides the relevant parent (other than the mother of the child) with 2 weeks paid Paternity Leave. Ireland's statutory Paternity Leave arrangements are fully aligned with the requirements of the EU Work-Life Balance Directive, which introduced a minimum standard for Paternity Leave across EU Member States.
Under the Parent’s Leave and Benefit Act 2019, working parents are also entitled to nine weeks of paid Parent's Leave for each relevant parent, to be taken in the first two years after the birth or adoptive placement of a child. Parent's Leave is an individual separate entitlement and is non-transferable between parents.
Under the Parental Leave (Amendment) Act 2019, an employee who is a relevant parent in respect of a child under the age 12 is entitled to 26 weeks’ unpaid Parental Leave for each child. Where a child has a disability or long-term illness, the entitlement can continue until the child is 16. A relevant parent is a parent, an adoptive parent, or a person acting in ‘loco parentis’. Both parents have an equal, separate entitlement to Parental Leave.

question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether she will review the age eligibility criteria for the early childhood care and education programme to address circumstances where children born close to the eligibility cutoff can access only one year of the scheme before their intended primary school starting date.
reply:
The ECCE programme provides up to two years of pre-school free of charge to families and is based on the National Practice Frameworks - Aistear and Síolta. Currently, children are eligible for ECCE starting at 2 years and 8 months to an upper age limit of 5 years and 6 months. The current ECCE eligibility criteria were set based on a number of considerations, including national experience and a review of international practice. The lower age range is informed by Tusla regulations for minimum adult-to-child ratios for children in early learning and childcare settings. These regulations take account of the needs and developmental stages of children such as toilet training and sleeping arrangements. The current arrangements also ensure that all children have the same eligibility for 2 years of ECCE.
The age eligibility criteria for ECCE have evolved significantly over the lifetime of the programme. When first introduced in 2010, eligibility was limited to children aged between 3 years and 2 months and 4 years and 7 months and provided one year of pre-school. In 2016, the eligibility criteria for the Programme changed with children eligible to enrol in the Programme at age three and remain in Programme until they transitioned to primary school. question: Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if she will consider the provision of direct services for children impacted by parental problem alcohol use, regardless of whether a parent is in treatment or not.
reply:
The Department of Health leads Government policy on substance misuse. The recently-published National Drugs Strategy 2026-2030, along with the Action Plan 2026-2028, outline a whole-of-Government response which aims to minimise the harms of drug and alcohol use and to ensure that people can access high quality, person-centred, integrated and compassionate health and social care where and when they need it.
I am aware that Action 1.4 of the strategy is to “Enhance services to address hidden harm for children, young people and families impacted by parental and familial drug and alcohol use.” The adverse experience of children affected by parental substance misuse is often referred to as ‘Hidden Harm’ because these children are often unknown to services and yet they suffer harm due to compromised parenting. While the Department of Health has policy responsibility in this area, I am aware that Tusla is committed to keeping the needs of children affected by parental substance misuse visible in the professional community, ensuring they are identified and supported.
For its part Tusla has advised that it supports families dealing with addiction by bridging the gap between adult addiction services and child welfare to implement early intervention, community-based care, and family-preservation strategies. Tusla focuses on stabilising the home environment, protective monitoring, and mitigating the impact of substance misuse on children as well as liaising with the HSE, An Garda Síochán

reply:

The current ECCE eligibility criteria were set based on a number of considerations, including national experience and a review of international practice. The lower age range is informed by Tusla regulations for minimum adult-to-child ratios for children in early learning and childcare settings. These regulations take account of the needs and developmental stages of children such as toilet training and sleeping arrangements. The current arrangements also ensure that all children have the same eligibility for 2 years of ECCE.
The Department recognises that the use of age limits in programmes such as ECCE can result in some children narrowly falling outside the eligibility range in a given year. However, in the interest of fairness and consistency, the Department must apply a clear and fixed age threshold, and cannot make exceptions. question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality for a breakdown of available aftercare spaces for children in the care of Tusla, by area, in tabular form.
reply:
Young people who have had a care history with Tusla are entitled to an aftercare service based on their eligibility and assessed needs. This assessment considers a number of factors including the young person’s educational and accommodation needs.
Upon reaching the age of 18, a young person is deemed to have left State care. All eligible care leavers are supported through aftercare services provided by Tusla. Aftercare is a demand-led service. Care leavers, depending on need, may be allocated an aftercare worker. All care leavers, without exception or age limit, can attend drop-in services organised by the Tusla aftercare service.
The Child Care Act 1991, as amended, sets out that where Tusla is providing assistance to a person in accordance with an aftercare plan by arranging for the completion of education and by contributing to maintenance while completing education, and that person attains the age of 21 years, Tusla may continue to provide that assistance until the completion of the course of education or the end of the academic year during which the person attains the age of 23, whichever is the earlier.
Tusla provides financial support to eligible care leavers who are engaged in a qualifying educational course or training programme. question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the number of children who accessed AIM Level 7 in early years settings in Cork City and County in the 2025/2026 programme year; and will she make a statement on the matter.
reply:
The Access and Inclusion Model (AIM) is a model of supports designed to ensure that children with a disability or additional needs can access the Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) Programme. The goal of AIM is to empower Early Learning and Care (ELC) providers to deliver an inclusive preschool experience, ensuring that every eligible child can meaningfully participate in the ECCE Programme and reap the benefits of high-quality early learning and care through universal and targeted supports.
AIM Level 7 support provides additional funding to ELC providers for a child who requires extra support in an ECCE service. AIM Level 7 funding acts to either reduce the child-to-adult ratio in the room or to fund an extra staff member as a shared resource with other children in the setting. In September of 2024, Level 7 funding was expanded to include an additional 3 hours per day during term time, or 6 hours per day during non-term time.

reply:
Pay is one of a number of challenges impacting the early learning and care and school-age childcare workforce. The level of pay for early years educators and school-age childcare practitioners does not reflect the value of their work for children, families, society and the economy.
Currently the costs of staff wages are supported through the Government's Core Funding scheme and through other Government schemes such as AIM, Equal Start and Community Employment Schemes.
Although h the Government is the primary funder of the sector, it is not the employer and cannot directly set wages or conditions for any staff in the sector.
The Joint Labour Committee (JLC) is the formal mechanism established by which employer and employee representatives can negotiate minimum pay rates, which are set down in Employment Regulation Orders (EROs), and is independent in its functions.
The State currently supports service providers with staff costs through the Government’s Core Funding scheme. For programme year 2026/2027, Core Funding has increased by 23% to €480 million. An additional €45 million has also been ringfenced from September 2026 to support services in meeting the potential costs of increasing rates of pay, contingent upon new ERO’s being enacted following successful negotiations by the independent JLC.

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to provide a comprehensive update on the mediation process currently underway between Cork City Council and the owners of the Bessborough lands (details supplied).
reply:
I am very conscious of the hurt felt by survivors and family members of people who died in Bessborough. One of the most tragic aspects of what happened is the uncertainty regarding the burial place of many children who were resident there.
I understand that the application to build on lands at Bessborough, the granting of planning permission and the upholding of this decision by An Coimisiún Pleanála, has been traumatic for some survivors. The decision to uphold planning permission was an independent decision of An Coimisiún Pleanála. I understand that a stakeholder group has filed for a judicial review of this decision.
In the meantime, the Taoiseach has asked Cork City Council to engage with the landowners at Bessborough with a view to exploring all options for the future of the site. I understand that mediators have now been appointed to negotiate between Cork City Council and the two landowners. This process is ongoing and it is important to allow it time and space to proceed. The Department has no role in the mediation and can, therefore, provide no further information on the process.

question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the way in which the commitment to reduce parental fees to €200 per month will apply to families whose providers remain outside core funding; and the measures will ensure that these families will see benefits.
reply:
Shaping the Future: The Early Years Action Plan, Phase 1 report (published last December) sets out measures to achieve key Programme for Government commitments on the affordability, quality, and accessibility of early learning and care (ELC) and school-age childcare (SAC). One of the main objectives of Shaping the Future is to reduce parental fees to a maximum of €200 per month over the lifetime of the Government.
The Action Plan adopts a phased approach that enables action to be taken in 2026 while allowing adequate time for a broad public consultation and analysis on longer-term actions.
The consultation process, which has taken place throughout this year, has had a number of channels designed to facilitate the participation of a wide range of stakeholders. The final stage (a national forum that took place on 23rd September) built on insights from surveys, local consultation events, and stakeholder engagement. Results of this consultation, and additional analysis, will inform Phase 2 of Shaping the Future.
Core Funding is a supply-side grant to ELC and SAC providers towards their operating costs. It is designed to promote affordability for parents and sustainability for providers through increased funding to the sector, paid on a consistent and equitable basis.

question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if her Department are currently reviewing the supports in place for foster families; if she will commit to increasing the weekly allowance per child; if foster parents are to be considered for pension contributions through their work as foster parents; her views on whether the current cost of living issues are having a profound effect on foster families given the limited rate of the allowance which is in place.
reply:
Foster carers play a vital and valued role in the care of the most vulnerable children in our society. Foster carers provide a safe, secure and stable home environment for these vulnerable children and young people.
This Department has overseen record investment in foster carers, including a 21% increase to the foster care allowance over the past two years, resulting in the current weekly allowance for children in foster care of €400 per week for children aged under 12, and €425 per week for those over 12.
Additionally, in 2025 a bonus payment at the start of each initial foster care placement was introduced. This payment aims to alleviate the substantial out-of-pocket expenses that can be incurred by foster carers during the initial period after a child is placed in their care.
A revised Mileage Payment Scheme for foster carers also came into effect in April 2025. This broadens the categories of journeys which may be considered eligible for payment under the Foster Care Travel Payments Scheme. Additionally, the cumulative weekly travel distance to qualify for these payments has been reduced from 300km to 250km.
However, it is recognised that we must do more to support children in care and the foster carers who do so much for them. The Programme for Government 2025 introduced a number of commitments relating to foster care. This included commitments to examine and develop a pension solution for foster carers, in recognition of the enormous contribution they make to vulnerable

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Defence to outline her interactions with the Lebanese authorities during her recent trip to Lebanon about the death of a UN soldier (details supplied).
reply:
Early last week, I visited Lebanon as part of a programme of engagements with Irish Defence Forces personnel serving with UNIFIL, senior Lebanese Government representatives, United Nations officials and international partners.
During the visit, I met with President Joseph Aoun, Minister for Foreign Affairs and Emigrants Youssef Rajji and Minister of Justice Adel Nassar. In each of these engagements, I raised matters relating to the death of Private Seán Rooney and reiterated the importance Ireland attaches to securing accountability and justice in this case.
I informed the Lebanese authorities of the deep concern that continues to be felt the Government and by the family of Private Rooney regarding the progress of the judicial process. I took the opportunity to again emphasise Ireland's expectation that all available legal avenues should continue to be pursued to ensure accountability for those responsible.
I have also recently been advised that the Lebanese State's appeal on the leniency of sentences of those found guilty before the Military Court of Cassation has been rejected. This is a deeply disappointing development. The Department's Lebanese legal representative is currently examining the judgment and considering what further legal options may be available to seek a review of the decision or to pursue the matter further through the Lebanese legal system.

question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality when the building blocks scheme will re-open for new applications.
reply:
The Building Blocks Extension Scheme Phase 2, which will fund projects in 2027 to deliver additional capacity, recently closed for applications.
Under the scheme, community providers could apply for a capital grant of between €100,000 and €530,000 to extend their existing premises, while private providers could apply for a capital grant of between €50,000 and €265,000. Match funding was a requirement for private providers. Up to €10 million has been set aside for the scheme.
Applications under Phase 2 were appraised by the Department with input from the Office of Public Works. Services will be notified of the outcome of this appraisal process in the coming weeks.
There are currently no plans to open a further Building Blocks scheme although subject to sufficient funding, additional rounds of Building Blocks will be considered in the coming years, and criteria for any future rounds will be the subject of further consideration.

question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality for a breakdown of the supports being provided to small and sessional childcare providers.
reply:
The Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) programme and the National Childcare Scheme (NCS) are currently available to parents regardless of whether or not the early learning and childcare service their child is attending is participating in Core Funding.
ECCE is a universal programme which provides 2 years of free preschool to children in the eligible age range of 2 years and 8 months to 5 years and 6 months. Over 70% of families on low-income report that they would not be able to send their child to pre-school without this Programme.
The Department funds private early learning and care service providers to provide the ECCE programme at a standard rate of €69 per week per child attending the ECCE programme.
Core Funding is a supply-side grant to early learning and childcare providers towards their operating costs. It is designed to promote affordability for parents and sustainability for providers through increased funding to the sector, paid on a consistent and equitable basis.
When Core Funding was introduced in 2022, services previously in receipt of ECCE standard capitation saw an increase to their capitations through a combination of their ECCE and Core Funding allocation. For the current programme year, with ECCE and Core Funding combined, services receive a minimum of €81.75 per child per week, owing to increases in the Core Funding allocation.

question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality for a breakdown of the number of providers participating in core funding who have chosen not to renew their agreements this year, by area, in tabular form.
reply:
Core Funding, which began in September 2022, is now worth over €480 million in full year costs for the fifth year of the scheme to build the partnership for the public good between the State and providers. Its primary purpose is to improve pay and conditions in the sector as a whole and improve affordability for parents as well as ensuring a stable income to providers. Payments are made on the staffed capacity of the services, meaning the number of children the providers can accommodate according to the staffing levels; it does not matter whether the places offered are subsequently occupied or vacant. However, a minimum of one child availing of NCS and/or ECCE must be registered for each hour of each staffed session in order to attract funding and the number of children the staff can accommodate must also satisfy the minimum staff to child ratios as set in the Regulations.
While the Department cannot mandate providers to participate in the Scheme, every effort has been made to carefully design Core Funding to meet the policy objectives including to achieve high levels of participation by providers.
Under the Core Funding Partner Service Funding Agreement, Partner Services must comply with the rules of the Core Funding scheme, such as the associated fee management measures and minimum notice periods.
