question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if her Department and each agency and public body under its aegis maintain a supplier register or equivalent electronic record in which suppliers are assigned unique identifiers; the identifier types held by each body, including CRO registration numbers, VAT numbers and internally generated supplier IDs; whether these identifiers are recorded against individual purchase orders, contracts and payments; and, where no such identifier is maintained, the way in which suppliers are uniquely identified within the body's financial and procurement systems, in tabular form.
reply:
Supplier accounts are stored on the Department’s Financial Management System (FMS). Each supplier account has an internally generated supplier code (unique identifier or ID) assigned to it.
The Finance Unit records suppliers’ VAT numbers on FMS and matches against invoices as a control.
FMS does not provide a field for either CRO numbers or Registered Charity Numbers (RCNs) to be captured, and for this reason reports cannot be generated on the FMS system on the basis of either category of unique identifier.
Standard FMS spend reports rely on our supplier codes as unique identifiers on the system rather than VAT numbers. Every transaction in our spend reports - including payroll transactions and grants to aegis bodies- is associated with a unique transaction ID that FMS generates automatically.
Separately, contract details are stored on the Department’s Contract Management System and linked to suppliers through FMS supplier codes. Purchase orders and payments are then recorded against each contract, with a running total spend to date tracked against the maximum value of the contract.
The Department's aegis bodies have been contacted and responses will issue directly.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the way in which her Department is building cyber resilience; and the strategy in place to address cyber attacks.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether she intends to make a decision on amending the lower age eligibility criteria for the Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) programme before the commencement of the September 2027 programme year; the specific timeline for completing the evaluation committed to in the Programme for Government.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1584, 1585, 1586 and 1587 together.
The ECCE programme provides up to two years of pre-school free of charge to families and is based on the National Practice Frameworks - Aistear and Síolta. Currently, children are eligible for ECCE starting at 2 years and 8 months to an upper age limit of 5 years and 6 months.
In line with the Programme for Government commitment to “evaluate options to amend the ECCE eligibility criteria”, Department officials are considering potential changes in the context of Shaping the Future. Shaping the Future, Early Years Action Plan Phase 1 Report published in December 2025, notes that the potential to extend the ECCE free pre-school programme and amend the age-eligibility criteria will be included in consultations and analysis under Phase 2 of the Action Plan. Phase 2 actions, which will be undertaken from 2027 through to the end of 2029, will be published in Q4 2026. It is not possible to provide further information on Phase 2 of the Action Plan until after its publication.
The age eligibility criteria for ECCE have evolved significantly over the lifetime of the programme. When first introduced in 2010, eligibility was limited to children aged between 3 years and 2 months and 4 years and 7 months and provided one year of pre-school. In 2016, the eligibility criteria for the Programme changed with children eligible to enrol in the Programme at age three and remain in the Programme until they transitioned to primary

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Defence the position regarding Ireland’s preparedness for a significant cyber attack on her Departments offices and institutions.
reply:

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), an operational arm of the Department, is the State’s primary authority for cyber security and is supported by An Garda Síochána and the Defence Forces in the security domain.
The NCSC leads the management of major cyber incidents across Government, provides guidance to citizens, businesses and the public sector, and supports international cooperation and information sharing.
I can inform the Deputy that myself and my Department place a high priority on cyber security and the Department operates in line with NCSC guidance. The Department participates in the Government Cyber Security Coordination & Response (GovCORE) network to support information sharing and best practice across the public sector.
Core IT infrastructure in my Department is delivered by the Office of the Government Chief Information Officer (OGCIO) under the ‘Build to Share Managed Desktop’ shared service. In partnership with the OGCIO, the Department applies a defence in depth approach to cyber security, combining people, processes and technology. This includes an Information Security Management System aligned with ISO 27001:2022 to ensure a consistent and effective approach to managing cyber risks.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Defence to outline the expected functions and duties of Defence Forces personnel should they be part of the new EU mission in Lebanon.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 135 and 157 together.
International support for the Government of Lebanon, and the Lebanese Armed Forces more broadly, is an important priority for Ireland.
Our participation in UNIFIL, alongside many of our EU colleagues, over many decades is a highly visible and concrete sign of our commitment and has made an essential contribution to the safety and security of Lebanon and the wider region.
On 12 October, the Council of the European Union adopted a decision establishing a new European Union Support Mission in Lebanon (EUSM Lebanon) under the Common Security and Defence Policy (CSDP). This is a training mission. and advisory mission. Operational planning is now taking place at EU-level and the Council will adopt a separate decision launching the new mission once operational planning has been completed.
The ending of the UNIFIL operation at the end of this year will leave a massive gap in Lebanon's security. While the CSDP training mission is not a replacement for UNIFIL, it will provide an important EU presence in Lebanon.
Recent commentary on EU Support Mission, Lebanon has unfortunately generated a degree of confusion by conflating a non-executive training and advisory mission with peace enforcement or other operations.

question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality her plans to ensure that staff in the childcare sector receive better pay and conditions for the essential role they provide.
reply:
Those working with babies, young children and their families are at the heart of the early
childhood system. They are central to delivering high-quality services, and play a crucial role
in bringing about the changes necessary to realising the vision for early childhood.
Pay is one of a number of challenges impacting the early learning and care and school-age childcare workforce. The level of pay for early years educators and school-age childcare practitioners does not reflect the value of their work for children, families, society and the economy.
Although the Government is the primary funder of the sector, it is not the employer and cannot directly set wages or conditions for any staff in the sector.
The Joint Labour Committee (JLC) is the formal mechanism established by which employer and employee representatives can negotiate minimum pay rates, which are set down in Employment Regulation Orders (EROs), and is independent in its functions.
Pay and conditions are improving. Through the work of the JLC and successive EROs, minimum pay rates have now risen three times in four years, delivering an average 15% increase in minimum rates of pay. This marks significant progress in professionalising the workforce. The latest ERO came into effect in October 2025 which saw an increase in minimum pay rates of, on average, 10% and is estimated to have increased pay for over 67% of staff in the sector.

question: Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality when statutory neonatal care leave and pay is due to be introduced.
reply:
There have been significant developments in entitlements for parents of working families in recent years, and the Government remains committed to supporting parents, in particular for those who are dealing with pre-mature babies.
It is important to note that the Maternity Protection Act 1994 provides for an extension to Maternity Leave where a child is born pre-maturely. Under Section 13 of the Act as amended, the mother's 26-week maternity leave is extended by the exact number of weeks between the actual birth date and the planned start of the maternity leave.
The Work Life Balance and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2023 was enacted on 4th April 2023, and introduces important entitlements for workers, including 5 days leave for medical care purposes for parents of children under 12, and the right to request flexible working for parents and carers.
The Paternity Leave and Benefit Act 2016 provides the relevant parent (other than the mother of the child) with 2 weeks paid Paternity Leave. Under the Parent’s Leave and Benefit Act 2019, working parents are also entitled to nine weeks of paid Parent's Leave for each relevant parent, to be taken in the first two years after the birth or adoptive placement of a child. Parent's Leave is an individual separate entitlement and is non-transferable between parents.

question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Defence the strength of the permanent Defence Forces as of 31 October 2026 or latest date available; and the way in which this compares to the end of 2025.
reply:
As Minister for Defence, I am fully committed to increasing and strengthening recruitment and supporting retention in the Permanent Defence Force.
The Military Authorities advise that the strength of the Permanent Defence Force (PDF) stood at 8,034 personnel on the 30 September 2026, the latest date for which this figure is available. This compares to a strength of 7,756 personnel as on the 31 December 2025.
Last year saw a growth in the overall strength of nearly 200, with a total of 790 inductions achieved- the highest in twenty years - while the number of personnel who discharged was at its lowest level in more than five years. I am determined to build on the increase in the strength achieved since 2024 have set a target of 850 inductions to year end. The signs in this regard for the year to date are positive with 729 inductions achieved to the end of September, while the number of personnel who have discharged stood at 441.
Interest in a career in the Defence Forces remains notably strong with over 15,700 applications received to the end of September of this year. The challenge now for the Defence Forces is to convert this high level of applications to inductions. A draft Strategic Workforce Plan, prepared by the Defence Forces remains the subject of active consideration. As the Deputy will be aware, the aim of this process is to provide a pathway to the achievement of an overall strength of 11,500, inclusive of civilian personnel, commensurate with Level of Ambition 2.

question: Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether an exceptional extension of eligibility under the ECCE programme can be granted to a five-year-old child (details supplied) who commenced junior infants in September 2026; whether provision exists for children who have already commenced primary education to re-enter the ECCE programme in such circumstances; and the appeals or exceptional review mechanisms available to parents.
reply:
The Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) Programme is a universal free programme available to all children within the eligible age range of 2 years and 8 months to 5 years and 6 months. It provides children with their first formal experience of early learning prior to commencing primary school.
The upper age limit of 5 years and 6 months for ECCE was set in consultation with the Department of Education and ensures that children transition into primary school with their peers. In a limited number of circumstances, it is possible to apply for an exemption to the ECCE upper age limit of 5 years 6 months where a child has additional needs.
As the child referred to has previously commenced primary school, there is no provision to grant an overage exemption under the ECCE programme to facilitate them reverting to a preschool setting. In the interest of fairness and consistency, the Department cannot make exceptions to this rule.
Primary school education comes under the responsibility of the Department of Education and Youth.
Supports are available for school-aged children through the National Council for Special Education (NCSE), affiliated to the Department of Education and Youth, to support a child in a primary school setting. The Department in this instance would advise the child's parents to contact their local Special Education Needs Organiser (SENO) for further assistance at https://ncse.ie/.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if any child has been placed outside the State since 2023 in an institution in which the majority of children are being treated for acute illnesses, or in an institution for children with physical or intellectual disabilities, either of which is excluded from the definition of a residential centre in Article 3 of the Regulations (details supplied); if so, the number of such placements and the regulations that govern them.
reply:
Tusla has stated that it seeks to place all children within a placement in Ireland where possible. However, in a small number of cases, this may not be in the best interests of the child, generally where the child is placed with relatives who happen to live outside this jurisdiction. Another reason for placement abroad is for those children requiring specialised care not currently available in Ireland, such as specialist secure forensic mental health services, or therapeutic residential services addressing specific needs identified in the child's care plan and in the best interests of the child.
As the Deputy will appreciate, due to the very small number of children and young people who are placed in out-of-state placements, publishing information regarding the specialised types of placements may inadvertently risk identification of the children and young people involved. For this reason, it is not possible to provide the specific information sought by the Deputy.
Further information on children and young people in out-of-state placements is published in Tusla's annual Review of Adequacy reports, available on Tusla's website at: https://www.tusla.ie/publications/review-of-adequacy-reports/.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality further to Parliamentary Question No. 71087/26, which stated both that children placed abroad have court appointed Guardians ad Litem and that the courts are not typically involved in out of State foster care placements, the number of children currently in out of State placements who do not have a Guardian ad Litem; the person or body responsible for representing the views and wishes of those children in decisions about their placement.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, Guardians ad litem (GALs) are appointed by the court for children who are the subject of care proceedings under the Child Care Act 1991. The role of the GAL is to inform the court of any views which the child wishes to express and to advise the court on what, in his or her professional opinion, is in the child’s best interests. Where a GAL is not appointed, it is a requirement under the Act and set out in associated Regulations and Standards, that Tusla give due consideration to the wishes and best interests of the child insofar as it is practicable.
While Tusla has stated that the courts are not typically involved in out-of-State foster placements, it has also noted in its reply of October 20th 2026 that, all children placed abroad remain in the care of the State, have an allocated social worker who visits them in their placement, and have a care plan which is reviewed within the statutory framework. It should also be noted that to remain in the care of State requires that a court has overseen the care application under the Act in respect of that child or young person.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the process by which it is ensured that data for all relevant people is recorded through the National Ability Supports System (NASS) each year; the way the Health Research Board (HRB) ensures that data is collected annually; and the way the HRB measures the data that may be missing.
reply:
The National Ability Supports System (NASS) includes data pertaining to people with intellectual, physical, sensory, or autism-related disabilities who are in receipt of or require HSE funded specialised disability services. People with borderline or mild ID may be in receipt of services through primary care, data collection pertaining to these services are not under the remit of NASS. It is ensured that data for the relevant people specified above is recorded on the NASS by making it a condition within the Service Level Agreement (SLA) between the HSE and service providers to provide data to NASS.
The Health Research Board (HRB) manages the system and ensures that data is collected annually through a range of measures. The HRB issues progress reports on status of reviews to all stakeholders/service providers on monthly basis from March to August and then every two weeks, moving to weekly from September to the deadline for ‘closing’ of annual datasets.
Training is provided by the HRB on an ongoing basis to service providers to ensure standards are maintained and to all staff members who enter data onto NASS. The HRB NASS staff and HSE NASS personnel have a close working relationship to ensure coverage and completeness of the data.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the number of children currently in care who do not have an allocated social worker, by county; and the length of time that the children have been waiting on a social worker.
reply:
At the end of August 2026, there were 5,851 children in Tusla care. 98% (5,717) had an allocated case worker, with 2% (134) awaiting allocation. Of the children with an allocated case worker, 89% (5,098) were allocated to a social worker. 11% (619) were allocated to other professionals.
The Service for Separated Children Seeking International Protection had 161 children in care at the end of August 2026. All children were allocated.
Allocation to professionals other than to social workers reflects a changing environment in Tusla, with social care workers and other professionals becoming integrated into social work teams, working alongside social workers. Social workers retain oversight of all cases, and all cases awaiting allocation are reviewed and monitored on an ongoing basis, and prioritised accordingly.
Of the 134 children awaiting allocation to a case worker, 31% (42) were waiting for under 1 month, 25% (33) were waiting between 1 and 3 months, and 44% (59) had been waiting for 3 months and over.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the target publication date for the Equality (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill; the specific legislative measures included to ensure the transposition of the EU Pay Transparency Directive that applies to disabled workers; and if these provisions will incorporate the Joint Committee's Pre-Legislative Scrutiny recommendations to explicitly prohibit sub-minimum wage practices and differential pay rates for disabled people.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1533 and 1534 together.
The Equality (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill has been given Priority Drafting on the Autumn Legislative Programme, which was published on 16 September. The proposed Bill includes a number of legislative provisions arising from a comprehensive review of Ireland’s equality legislation.
A drafter has been appointed and work is underway. It is hoped that the Bill will be ready for publication in the first half of 2027.
The Joint Oireachtas Committee on Children and Equality undertook pre-legislative scrutiny of the General Scheme of the Bill last year. Officials in the Department are considering the Committee’s report as part of ongoing work.
The General Scheme includes a proposal to remove an existing provision that allows differential pay rates to be paid to disabled persons. This proposal is strongly supported by stakeholders and was welcomed by the Joint Oireachtas Committee. It is intended that this be included in the Bill.
The Department is also exploring options for strengthening the reasonable accommodation provisions in the Equal Status Acts, having regard to the State’s obligations under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD). The Department is giving consideration to the Joint Committee’s recommendation and agrees that a stronger, wide-ranging reasonable accommodation requirement would promote equality and the accessibility of goods and services that are available to the

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the position regarding the Government commitment to reduce childcare fees to €200 per month; and if this plan is to include band F childcare centres at the same price point.
reply:
Shaping the Future: The Early Years Action Plan, Phase 1 report (published last December) sets out measures to achieve key Programme for Government commitments on the affordability, quality, and accessibility of early learning and care (ELC) and school-age childcare (SAC). One of the main objectives of Shaping the Future is to reduce parental fees to a maximum of €200 per month over the lifetime of the Government.
The Action Plan adopts a phased approach that enables action to be taken in 2026 while allowing adequate time for a broad public consultation and analysis on longer-term actions.
The consultation process, which has taken place throughout this year, has had a number of channels designed to facilitate the participation of a wide range of stakeholders. The final stage (a national forum that took place on 23rd September) built on insights from surveys, local consultation events, and stakeholder engagement. Results of this consultation, and additional analysis, will inform Phase 2 of Shaping the Future.
Phase 2, which will be published later this year, will set out actions to be undertaken from 2027 through to the end of 2029 to achieve key Programme for Government commitments on the affordability, quality, and accessibility of ELC and SAC.
A number of steps have already been taken in 2025 and 2026 to reduce the costs of ELC and SAC for parents, with further measures announced in Budget 2027.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality for an overview of the discretionary financial supports or emergency allowances available through Tusla for a relative who assumes full-time care of multiple dependent children with complex special needs following a sudden parental bereavement; if the acceptance of voluntary community fundraising affects Tusla's assessment for financial assistance.
reply:
I understand the Deputy is referring to informal kinship care which refers to arrangements where children live with and are cared for by a relative or close family friend when a parent is unable to care for them.
A Private Family Arrangement (PFA) is a type of informal kinship care that Tusla has helped to arrange, but where the child is not in the care of the State. These are voluntary arrangements, made within the child’s family, with support from Tusla.
The current definition of a PFA as set out in Tusla’s Policy and Procedures for Governance and Financial Supports for Tusla Private Arrangements is:
A private arrangement is where a person, other than a parent or guardian, is:
1. Caring for a child(ren) on an ongoing basis
a. Where the child is not in care, and
b. Is not being cared for by a legal guardian; and
2. The arrangement was established in consultation with and the support of Tusla and therefore must be part of an ongoing Tusla Child Protection, Safety plan, or Meitheal plan, which is supported and reviewed by Tusla; and
These arrangements may involve recurring financial support from Tusla.
Financial support is not an automatic entitlement of a Tusla PFA. Tusla provide financial support to families in a PFA on a case by case basis, which is assessed by the Tusla Social Worker, as per their Financial Policy.

question: Deputy Rose Conway-Walsh asked the Minister for Defence to clarify the distinction between 'peacekeeping' and 'peace enforcement' for the overseas deployment of Irish Defence Forces troops once the triple lock is removed.
reply:
I thank the Deputy for raising this issue, as there has been a considerable degree of misunderstanding regarding the distinction between peacekeeping and peace enforcement, particularly in the context of the proposed reforms to the Triple Lock.
At the outset, I want to be clear that participation in missions operating under more robust mandates is not a new departure for the Defence Forces. Since 1990, the majority of overseas deployments by members of the Defence Forces have been traditional peacekeeping missions, including service with UNIFIL in Lebanon, UNDOF in the Golan Heights and UNTSO in the Middle East.
However, Irish personnel have also served for a considerable number of years in a number of missions operating under Chapter VII of the UN Charter , where the use of force was authorised in certain circumstances. These included missions in Liberia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Mali and East Timor. Irish personnel have also served in UN-authorised operations such as KFOR in Kosovo, ISAF in Afghanistan and EUFOR Tchad/RCA in Chad.
In simple terms, peacekeeping involves helping to maintain a peace that already exists. Peacekeepers monitor ceasefires, support political agreements, protect civilians and help create the conditions for long-term stability. Traditionally, these operations are associated with Chapter VI of the UN Charter.
Peace enforcement is different. It involves the use, or threatened use, of force to restore peace and security where violence is on

question: Deputy Marie Sherlock asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the number of the 1,000 disability residential beds (details supplied) that were used for closing down beds due to the decongregation policy, moving adults back out of for-profit residences into state run settings and moving adults out of inappropriate nursing home placements.

question: Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to outline the financial reporting and accounting requirements imposed on early learning and childcare providers participating in core funding; the reason providers are required to submit additional financial returns where annual accounts are already prepared; whether her Department has assessed the financial burden these requirements place on smaller ECCE-only services; whether consideration will be given to simplifying the reporting requirements for such providers.
reply:
Core Funding is a grant to Early Learning and Care (ELC) and/or School Age Childcare (SAC) Partner Services towards their operating costs and is funding directly to Partner Services.
I am required to ensure all exchequer funding is managed in a clear and transparent manner. This includes a requirement to ensure robust and transparent Financial Reporting structures are in place. As a condition of receiving the Core Funding grant, Partner Services are required to submit comprehensive and validated financial. Information is provided directly by a Partner Service and their nominated accountant. The Department does not require Partner Services to provide their Companies Registration Office Annual Financial Statements (AFS) as part of this process.
In March 2026, Partner Services were required to submit Financial Reports for Year 3 (2024/25 programme year) of Core Funding. A full Trial Balance underpinned by sector-specific nominal codes contained in the Core Funding Chart of Accounts was required. The Financial Reporting is structured in such a way that more complex business structures had more complex reporting whereas smaller businesses such as ECCE only services have a smaller report to submit, for example, the number of income nominal codes for ECCE is likely to be only one - ECCE income.
The portal for Trial Balance submissions opened on 27 February 2026 with a published deadline for submissions of 31 March 2026 at midnight.

question: Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether she intends to review the current ECCE capitation rate of €69 per child per week, which has remained unchanged since 2018, in light of increased staffing costs, inflation, insurance, rent and other operational expenses; whether her Department has assessed the adequacy of this funding for ECCE-only providers.
reply:
The Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) Programme scheme is a universal scheme which provides 2 years of free preschool to children in the eligible age range of 2 years and 8 months to 5 years and 6 months. The Department funds private early learning and care service providers to provide the ECCE programme at a standard rate of €69 per week per child attending the ECCE programme. The ECCE programme is delivered over 3 hours per day, 15 hours per week and 38 weeks of the year. There is no charge to parents for the ECCE programme. ECCE capitation is paid to providers in respect of each eligible child enrolled.
In 2010, when the ECCE Programme was first introduced, the standard capitation was €64.50, the higher capitation rate (for services with graduate room leaders) was €75 and the adult child ratio was 1:10. This equated to a maximum weekly income to providers of €645 (with standard capitation) and €750 (with higher capitation) for every 10 children to one adult.
In 2012, as part of austerity measures, the standard capitation was reduced to €62.50 and the higher capitation rate was reduced to €73. To offset this, the adult child ratio increased from 1:10 to 1:11. This equated to a maximum weekly income to providers of €687.50 (with standard capitation) and €803 (with higher capitation) for every 11 children to one adult.

Additional Core Funding is available to services delivering the ECCE programme through Graduate Premiums, Targeted Measures and the Staff Funding Additional Contributions.

Core Funding operates alongside all other early learning and childcare programmes and constitutes additional income to services on top of these programmes (and parental fees) towards their operating costs.

question: Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the emergency financial supports are currently available to ECCE-only providers experiencing serious financial difficulties; whether such supports are available to services participating in core funding; the number of providers who have received sustainability assistance in 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026, broken down by county.
reply:
Sustainability funding is not accessed through a direct application process. The Department oversees a case management process, through which local City and County Childcare Committee (CCCs) and Pobal work together to assess and provide support to all Core Funding Partner Services experiencing difficulties, and through which Sustainability Funding may be granted should the need arise.
Under the direction of the Department, Pobal co-ordinate the overall case management process with the CCC administering on-the-ground case management assistance. This can include help for services with completing and interpreting analysis of staff ratios and cash flow, as well as more specialised advice and support appropriate to individual circumstances.
In some instances, financial supports through Sustainability Funding may be appropriate, in tandem with this case management process. Pobal undertake a detailed financial review of any service wishing to access sustainability funding to assess their financial eligibility and need for funding. At the conclusion of this process, Pobal decide based on the funding criteria and the information gathered whether to recommend sustainability funding. These recommendations come to the Department for decision.
Once a service engages with their local CCC they will be able to avail of sustainability supports through the case management process.

question: Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether her Department has assessed the impact of increased wage costs arising from Employment Regulation Orders on ECCE-only preschool providers; whether increases in core funding have been sufficient to cover these additional staffing costs; whether particular consideration has been given to providers operating for three hours per day during the ECCE programme year.
reply:
Pay is one of a number of challenges impacting the early learning and care and school-age childcare workforce.
Although the Government is the primary funder of the sector, it is not the employer and cannot directly set wages or conditions for any staff in the sector.
The Joint Labour Committee (JLC) is the formal mechanism established by which employer and employee representatives can negotiate minimum pay rates, which are set down in Employment Regulation Orders (EROs). In line with the provisions of the Industrial Relations Acts, the JLC is independent in its functions and neither I nor the Department have a statutory role in its processes of setting minimum rates.
The Department's approach to Core Funding is informed by consideration of the full range of operating costs associated with the delivery of Early Learning and Care and School-Age Childcare services, including both pay and non-pay costs. A number of targeted supports for small and sessional services were introduced to Core Funding in order to improve sustainability of small-medium services. These measures currently included a flat rate top up of €5,000 for sessional-only services, and a minimum base rate allocation of €14,400. This allocation supports smaller Partner Services with their operating costs, particularly those in rural areas, who are more vulnerable to fluctuations in income to cover costs.

question: Deputy Noel McCarthy asked the Minister for Defence the current fleet strength of the Naval Service; and her Department’s plans, if any, for the further upgrade of the existing fleet.
reply:
The Naval Service is the State's principal sea-going agency, responsible for a broad range of defence and security functions. Its principal operational task is the enforcement of fisheries protection obligations arising from Ireland's membership of the European Union. To fulfil this role, the Naval Service conducts regular patrols throughout Irish waters, from the coastline to the outer limits of the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). These patrols are carried out on a regular and frequent basis and are directed to all areas of Irish waters, as necessary.
The Naval Service currently has a fleet of eight commissioned vessels. These eight vessels consist of two P50 class large patrol vessels, four P60 class offshore patrol vessels, and two P70 inshore patrol vessels.
I am advised by the military authorities that there are four vessels available for operations and regularly deployed on Maritime Defence and Security Operations on a rotation basis. The operational availability of Naval Service vessels is managed through a strategic rotation which takes account of maintenance, crew training, and rest periods. This approach ensures a continuous and sustainable naval presence in Irish waters.
I would like to reassure the Deputy that the regeneration of the Naval Service is one of my key priorities as Minister for Defence. So too is it a priority for the Defence Forces. question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will establish a central animal cruelty register, to track persons with animal cruelty convictions and-or who are banned from keeping or owning animals, in order to prevent breaches of such bans and to prevent anyone with a cruelty conviction from working with animals.
reply:
My Department takes the matter of animal welfare most seriously and is committed to the enforcement of the Animal Health and Welfare Act, 2013. Prosecutions under the Act are pursued following investigations by authorised officers who investigate matters relating to animal cruelty and neglect. Offences under the Act may be prosecuted in the District Court by the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine, local authorities and members of An Garda Síochána. Matters tried on indictment are the remit of the Director of Public Prosecutions in the normal manner.
Since the Animal Health and Welfare Act 2013 came into operation in March 2014, 230 cases have been successfully prosecuted by my Department and the National Society for Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (formerly ISPCA and DSPCA). My Department does not hold records on prosecutions taken by An Garda Síochána and local authorities.
Repeat offenders are identified from their previous offences, as adjudicated by the courts. My Department does not maintain a central register to identify repeat offenders and currently there are no plans to introduce such a mechanism.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the measures Ireland has in place to prevent the arrival of migratory pests and to highlight their impact on agriculture.
reply:
My Department’s Plant Health and Biosecurity Strategy sets out a vision for plant health and biosecurity in Ireland for the period 2026-2030. This vision is to protect Ireland’s agriculture, horticulture and forestry sectors and the wider environment from plant pests and diseases thereby safeguarding food security, facilitating safe trade and protecting the environment. The Strategy sets out three strategic goals-Risk Anticipation, Risk Surveillance and Management; and Risk Awareness and Communication.
Furthermore, my Department is the Competent Authority for plant health under the EU Official Controls Regulation 2017/625 and has responsibility for verifying compliance with the EU Plant Health Regulation 2016/2031. These regulations together set out a framework of protective measures and controls to prevent the introduction of pests and diseases harmful to plants and plant products.
My Department has put in place a series of measures to prevent the arrival of harmful pests and diseases including-
• international horizon scanning for new and emerging pests;
• a living Plant Pest Risk Register which supports enhanced risk-based surveillance operations; and
• the provision of modern border control posts, including investment in IT and human resources to inspect imports of plants and plant products entering Ireland.
Communication and stakeholder involvement are critical elements of the overall plant health effort. In this regard, my Department has taken a number of initiatives to

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine his views on the way in which artificial intelligence is transforming and will transform the farm sector; and the action his Department is making to support farmers in that transition.
reply:
My Department supports research into the application of AI in agriculture through competitive research funding programmes and projects. This includes the use of AI to support precision nitrogen management, improve the monitoring of greenhouse gas emissions and strengthen the early detection of animal diseases. These projects aim to develop practical tools and generate evidence to support their application within the sector. On completion, the findings of these projects will help inform future policy development and provide the evidence- base for policy to support farmers in understanding and adopting these emerging technologies, while promoting more sustainable and productive farming.
Operationally my Department's approach is to embrace AI responsibly: leveraging innovation to improve outcomes, supporting staff and our customers with modern digital tools, and maintaining strong governance to ensure AI is deployed safely, ethically, and in the public interest.
My Department is advancing its AI Strategy to build an AI-enabled workforce and enhance customer services through the effective use of data, automation, and artificial intelligence. AI is already delivering value across a range of operational and policy functions, with current applications largely focused on machine learning and predictive analytics rather than generative AI.
My Department has also completed a number of AI proof-of-concept and research initiatives to explore new opportunities for improving service delive

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the way in which his Department is supporting the roll-out of digital agriculture systems to farmers to enable them to improve efficiency, productivity and sustainability.
reply:
My Department has published a Digital Strategy (2023-2026) which sets out a vision to digitise at least 90% of customer-facing paper processes by 2030. All key Department business applications, for farmers, are already online-only, allowing for improved automation, speed and efficiency of processing. The Department complements these with integrated AI services such as Area Monitoring System and mobile device applications such as AgriSnap.
The modernised “MyAgfood” portal has been codesigned with farmers and stakeholders to enhance customer access to, and experience of, our IT systems, with functions such as an easy-to-use Nitrates Planner to assist with farm management activities. We provide investment supports through the Targeted Agricultural Modernisation Scheme (TAMS) that can assist precision farming and improved sustainability measures.
Our stated Digital Principles also include data-driven decision making and improving access to information. My Department has established an Open Data portal which provides access to land use, forestry, climate, and animal health data (among others) for farmers, researchers and the agri-tech industry. Additionally, my Department directly funds agricultural research and innovation projects that further explore precision farming objectives, environmental monitoring and climate-smart farming practices.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to outline moves towards automation and the potential role of agricultural robots in future farming and food production.
reply:
Automation, including robotics, currently play a significant role in the agri-food sector and this is likely to grow into the future. Mission Four of Food Vision 2030 identifies automation as an important component of addressing and reshaping the way we produce, distribute, and consume food.
My Department has funded research in this area. For example, the HOLOSEU project developed automation and digital integration of real-time soil and climate data to improve land use planning and decision-making. The VisioBot project developed a robotic platform for the accurate rehydration of infant milk formula powders.
In addition, significant work has taken place in the Enterprise Ireland (EI) supported Meat Technology Ireland centre and the Dairy Processing Technology Centre on robotics and automation in these sectors.
EI also supports the innovation and commercialisation of automation and robotics, through discovery grants, innovation vouchers, commercialisation funds and dedicated initiatives.
The Disruptive Technologies Innovation Fund, administered by EI, offers support for research & development including in areas of robotics and automation. The 8th call for proposals opened on October 1st and will close on February 3rd 2027. It has a budget of €40million available and I would encourage relevant stakeholders in the agri-food sector to consider this opportunity.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to provide an update on the national tillage strategy.
reply:
This Government recognises the importance of the tillage sector and the challenges it has faced in recent years including reduced grain prices, higher input costs and the impacts of adverse weather. It is Government ambition to grow the area in tillage in the years ahead.
The report of the Food Vision Tillage Group sets out the roadmap for the sustainable growth and development of the sector. Implementation of the recommendations is ongoing, with progress reviewed regularly by the Food Vision Tillage Group.
Considerable work has been undertaken across many of the key themes identified in Food Vision Tillage Report, and in particular to achieve greater recognition of the sustainability of Irish grain, along with securing new and expanded value-added opportunities. Additionally, significant funding has been provided for research focusing on areas such as the sustainability of protein production, new added-value opportunities to support the expansion of plant protein production, and the feasibility of organic feed milling and oilseed processing in Ireland.
My Department will continue to work closely with stakeholders to advance implementation of the report's recommendations, recognising that their successful delivery requires ongoing collaboration and commitment from many stakeholders across the sector.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine his Department's approach to the use of gene-editing in order to reduce crop disease.
reply:
On 17 June 2026, the European Parliament and the Council adopted Regulation (EU) 2026/1388 on plants obtained by certain new genomic techniques and their products, based on a Commission proposal from 2023. The new rules entered into force on 16 July 2026 and will apply from 17 July 2028.
Ireland supported the adoption of the Regulation. There is a need to adopt such innovation and technology to help address current challenges in the agri-food system such as food security, climate change and biodiversity reduction. NGTs have the potential to address these challenges and can deliver benefits to farmers, consumers and the environment.
The European Commission has published an implementation strategy that sets out actions at Union and Member State level that are necessary for the effective and consistent application of the NGT Regulation throughout the Union.
Plant applications of NGTs have developed rapidly and are continuing to do so on a global scale. There is ongoing public and private research using NGTs on a variety of crops and traits including crops with higher yields, improved tolerance or resistance to pests and diseases, improved tolerance to environmental and climate change effects, improved nutrient use efficiency and improved quality and nutritional characteristics.
It is anticipated that the first NGT varieties could enter national variety evaluation trials in 2029. However, this will depend on how quickly breeding companies and research institutions accelerate thei

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the assessments that have been carried out on the potential longterm implications of climate change on land use in Ireland.
reply:
Several assessments have examined the longer-term impacts of climate on land use in Ireland. The Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Ireland’s Climate Change Assessment (2024) and National Climate Change Risk assessment (2025) examine projected changes in temperature precipitation, drought, Flooding and extreme weather events and their implications for agriculture, forestry soils, and ecosystem through to 2050 and 2100.
More targeted research, including the EPA’s ClimAg project (2024) and Teagasc’s extensive climate adaptation and modelling research, has assessed potential changes in grassland productivity, growing seasons, fodder availability and agricultural vulnerability.
Whilst uncertainties remain, the long-term climate risks for land use in Ireland include increased flooding and waterlogging, increased drought and heat stress, higher occurrence of storm damage, pests and diseases and the degradation of soils peatlands and ecosystems.
To address these challenges, I published an updated adaptation plan, Agriculture, Forestry and Seafood Climate Change Sectoral Adaptation Plan 2025, marking a significant step in strengthening Ireland’s preparedness for the impacts of climate change.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Defence the specific retention measures being put in place for personnel returning from UNIFIL, in view of the expected rise in discharges once the mission ends.
reply:
The Defence Forces have an incredibly proud tradition in the area of international peace-keeping. I am aware that once the UNIFIL mission is wound down next year, the number of defence personnel overseas would be expected to fall from over 400 to 90, with those members working in office roles. However, on my instruction both my Department and the Defence Forces are looking at options for future overseas missions.

question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the steps Coillte is taking to solve the deer problem in Ireland.
reply:
Coillte was established as a commercial state company with private limited status under the Forestry Act, 1988, to become custodian and manager of the national forest estate. The company manages 440,000 hectares of land (7% of the total area of Ireland). Its day-to-day operations, such as the management of deer on the Coillte estate are a matter for the company.
Regarding deer management at a national level, the Irish Deer Management Strategy Group (IDMSG) was established in 2022 by the Minister for Agriculture Food & the Marine to develop initiatives to ensure sustainable deer numbers while achieving the objectives of landowners ranging from biodiversity, forestry, agriculture, animal health and road safety. The IDMSG includes representatives of my Department, the NPWS and Coillte.
The current deer management programme is an outcome of the work of this group and is being delivered by Farm Relief Services (FRS). At present 15 Deer Management Areas (DMAs) have been set up around the country and are managed by a dedicated team of co-ordinators. Where required, Coillte work actively with many of the these co-ordinators to ensure the ongoing contribution to the deer management effort.

question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the reason we have not found a way to vaccinate against bovine TB in cattle.
reply:
In September 2025, my Department launched the Bovine TB Action Plan Addressing Bovine TB in Ireland, the action plan is based on scientific research and veterinary expertise and includes five measures which are underpinned by 30 actions.
As we continue to focus on these immediate actions, I am closely monitoring the developments around the potential vaccination of bovines against TB, particularly in the UK where much of this research is being carried out. I will continue to monitor the progress of research and development of cattle TB vaccines and will be guided by research and scientific guidelines.
It should be noted that if the research is successful, a significant number of legal and international trade obstacles remain to be surmounted before a vaccine for tuberculosis in bovine animals can be used as part of our bovine TB eradication programme.

question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the reason it is not mandatory that all deer are tagged when shot; and the reason it is not mandatory that all deer are not being sampled and tested for TB.
reply:
The terms and conditions for the licensing of the shooting of deer is a matter for the National Parks and Wildlife Service.
My Department does however offer a free post mortem service for any deer samples presented to any of the various Regional Veterinary Laboratories located throughout the country.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if an ownership/responsibility issue can be examined in regard to Kilkeaveragh Pier, Portmagee, County Kerry, given Trinity College records seem to be at odds with those of his Department; and if he will request his Department to liaise with the college.
reply:
The Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine’s records indicate that the pier at Kilkeveragh Pier, Portmagee, Co. Kerry was built and owned by Trinity College Dublin as part of the Iveragh Estate. These records further indicate that, while the Trinity College Dublin estates, including the Barony of Iveragh, were transferred to the Congested Districts Board in 1913, Kilkeveragh Pier was specifically excluded from that transfer. Based on these records, which were shared with Trinity College Dublin in June of this year, it appears that Trinity College Dublin retained ownership of the pier following the 1913 transfer.
I must reiterate this Department, nor its predecessors in title, has any ownership interest in Kilkeveragh Pier. To date the Department has not been made aware of any records at variance with this position. However the Department remains willing to engage with Trinity College Dublin should their records indicate otherwise.

question: Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Defence the implications for Ireland’s participation in overseas peace support missions following Ireland’s withdrawal from Operation IRINI.
reply:
Ireland's withdrawal from Operation IRINI does not diminish Ireland's commitment to peacekeeping and international peace and security more generally. Ireland continues to make significant contributions through the deployment of Defence Forces personnel on missions under United Nations, European Union and other international frameworks.
The experience of Operation IRINI does however underpin the need for the change to the Triple Lock. When the United Nations Security Council mandate underpinning the operation was not renewed, Ireland was required to withdraw its personnel, despite the fact that the operation itself continued and other participating states remained engaged. Because of Ireland's legislative requirement for a UN mandate as part of the Triple Lock, Ireland was the only participating state obliged to cease its participation in those circumstances. This demonstrated how the current framework can, in certain cases, prevent Ireland from continuing to contribute alongside our international partners.
The Government's proposed reforms are intended to address that issue while maintaining robust safeguards, including legal scrutiny, military advice, adherence to international law, Government decision-making and Dáil oversight where required. Ireland remains committed to being an active and credible contributor to international peace and security.
In terms of any future deployments, as this House is aware, overseas deployments are considered on a case-by-case basis. Any pro

reply:

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether he will remove the requirement that applicants to the women farmer capital investment scheme be under 67 years of age, particularly in recognition of women who take over farms later in life through inheritance, succession or bereavement and continue actively farming.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1497 and 1498 together.
The Targeted Agriculture Modernisation Scheme (TAMS 3) provides grants to farmers to build and/or improve a specified range of farm buildings and equipment on their holdings. The Women Farmer Capital Investment Scheme (WFCIS) is a measure under TAMS 3 which was introduced to address the issues of both generational renewal and gender balance in farming.
Eligible applicants under the WFCIS are entitled to an enhanced grant aid of 60% compared to the standard rate of 40%. The eligibility criteria include:
• Aged 18 years of age and under 67 when she applies for support.
• Meet the conditions for being head and having control of the holding.
• Meets the requirements for the appropriate training and/or skills required at the time of applications.
The eligibility criteria of this measure in respect of the upper age limit has a strong legal basis as it provides an enhanced payment for the target category, while continuing to provide grant access to other sectors. Applicants who do not meet the criteria above, similar to all farmers, regardless of their gender and age, will remain eligible to apply under the general TAMS 3 schemes at the standard rate of 40%.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether proposals to support working animal harness and agricultural equipment and to remove the upper age limit under the women farmer capital investment scheme will be examined as part of the call for evidence on on-farm capital investments; the timeframe for publishing the findings and responding to submissions; and the way in which these findings will inform investment supports after 2027.
reply:
The call for evidence, inviting observations and comments regarding both current investments under TAMS 3 and potential new innovative investments will be open until Friday, 27 November 2026. All proposals submitted during this call will form part of the wider discussions and consultations on the post 2027 CAP programming period. The decisions on appropriate supports for inclusion in any future on farm investment scheme post 2027 will be targeted at investments which deliver the optimal animal welfare, environmental and economical benefits on farm.
The current CAP places a particular focus on generational renewal and on promoting the participation of women in the social and economic development of rural areas, with special attention to farming.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether his Department has assessed the animal welfare benefits of modern harness and low-draught agricultural equipment for working animals; the way in which these benefits are considered when determining eligible investments under TAMS; and whether he will review the provision of support for such equipment in light of relevant Irish and EU animal welfare obligations.
reply:
The Targeted Agriculture Modernisation Scheme (TAMS 3) provides grants to farmers to build and/or improve a specified range of farm buildings and equipment on their holdings.
Farmers using a traditional working horse are eligible for TAMS funding for stables and all other equine investments that are included in TAMS 3. However, support for horse powered farming equipment is outside the scope of scheme.
TAMS 3 is a demand led scheme with a defined allocated budget. Taking into consideration the huge number of applications already received and the budget available, it is not possible to consider adding additional items to the current TAMS 3
However, I announced a call for evidence, inviting observations and comments regarding current investments under TAMS 3, which will be open until Friday, 27 November 2026. This call also seeks submissions and potential new innovative investments which could be considered in the future to support the transition to more sustainable systems of production.

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to outline his plans to minimise the export of seaweed from Ireland and maximise the job creation potential at Irish based production plants, in a sustainable and environmentally friendly approach.
reply:
Since the establishment of MARA, applicants may apply to the Regulator for a licence to harvest seaweed, in accordance with Schedule 7 of the Maritime Area Planning Act 2021, which provides for Maritime Usages that may be undertaken pursuant to the granting of a Licence.
A key research project, led by the Marine Institute, entitled ‘A Socio-Economic Study of Seaweed Harvesting in Ireland’, provides baseline socio-economic information regarding seaweed harvesting activity and product usage in Ireland. The report is available at the following link:
Socioeconomic Study of Seaweed Harvesting in Ireland.pdf (www.emff.marine.ie/sites/default/files/bluegrowth/PDFs/Socioeconomic%20Study%20of%20Seaweed%20Harvesting%20in%20Ireland.pdf).
The report also sets out a number of recommendations for consideration by industry and policy makers, including the development of a sustainable seaweed harvesting policy.
The development of a seaweed harvesting policy, led by the most appropriate Government Department, will require significant inter-Departmental engagement and stakeholder consultation given the range of factors (social, economic and environmental) that would need to be considered.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether contracts recorded in his Department's internal contract register can be linked to their corresponding contract award notices published on eTenders, where applicable; whether his Department records the relevant eTenders notice reference, URL or other identifier; and if not, the reasons that prevent this information from being recorded.
reply:
My Department does not record details of the contract award notices published on eTenders on the Department’s internal contract register. Payment Divisions are required to record such information on their contract files and be able to provide it if requested.
My Department is not currently required to keep a centralised register of eTender notice references or URL links. Amending the Department's internal contract register to include those details, or creating a new register that can be linked to it would be a lengthy process and difficult to apply retrospectively.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether purchase orders issued by his Department under procurement contracts can be linked to the corresponding contracts held in its internal contract register; whether a contract reference or other unique identifier is maintained to enable this linkage; and if not, the way his Department monitors cumulative expenditure against the approved value of each contract.
reply:
My Department is proactive in monitoring expenditure under procurement contracts.
Purchase Orders (POs) are linked to the number assigned to a contract on the Department’s internal contract register when the PO is being created.
Payment Divisions are required to monitor the expenditure under a contract and ensure that it remains compliant with the terms of the contract. The Central Procurement Unit run reports three times a year examining expenditure under contracts to ensure compliance and assists Payment Divisions by providing them with reports on the status of their contracts.

question: Deputy Brian Stanley asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to ensure that every effort is made during the Irish Presidency of the EU not to allow the proposed cut to the CAP budget and that a better deal is got for Irish agriculture.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1481, 1489 and 1490 together.
In discussing the budget for the post-2027 Common Agricultural Policy, it should be borne in mind that this funding forms part of the broader EU budget (Multiannual Financial Framework), which is negotiated by Finance Ministers, and ultimately agreed by Heads of State.
Following the October European Council, where the Irish Presidency’s Negotiating Box was discussed, the negotiations on the MFF are now continuing under the President of the European Council, António Costa, with a view to resolving outstanding issues for all Member States and reaching agreement at Head of State level.
In parallel, in my role as President of the AgriFish Council during Ireland’s EU Presidency, I was pleased to secure unanimous support for a Partial General Approach on the CAP Regulation at the AgriFish Council of Ministers meeting on 26th October. This establishes the Council’s position and provides a basis for the next stage of negotiations between the European Council, the European Commission and the European Parliament.
I have consistently emphasised that the future CAP must be adequately funded to support viable farm incomes, food security, generational renewal, environmental sustainability and vibrant rural communities across the EU and in Ireland in particular.
Over the coming months, I will continue to work closely with my Government colleagues and to engage constructively with Member State counterparts to help secure an outco

question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine his plans to make anaesthesia and analgesia mandatory for disbudding and castration of bovines; and if he is required to do so under EU law.
reply:
Animal welfare is a key priority for me as Minister and for the Government. My Department has lead policy responsibility within government for animal welfare, which is protected by legislation and takes the matter of animal welfare most seriously.
The welfare of calves is covered by EU and Irish national legislation. The EU legislation is Council Directive 2008/119/EC which lays down minimum standards for the protection of calves as well as Directive 98/58/EC concerning the protection of animals kept for farming purposes. This legislation is transposed into Irish legislation by Statutory Instrument No. 311 of 2010 (welfare of farmed animals) Regulations 2010.
Regarding procedures such as castration and disbudding of bovine animals, specific additional national provisions apply, namely Statutory Instrument No. 127 of 2014, Animal Health and Welfare (Operations and Procedures) (No. 2) Regulations 2014 and Statutory Instrument No. 107 of 2014, Animal Health and Welfare (Section 17) Regulations 2014. These regulations set out a number of specific requirements for carrying out these procedures including the age at which calves may be castrated or disbudded, the permitted methods that can be used for both procedures and whether local anaesthesia and analgesia is required.
My Department keeps all policy in relation to animal welfare, particularly in light of new information and/or developments at EU level, under review on an ongoing basis.

question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will consider lifting the 100 tonne cap limit in relation to the fertiliser scheme to enable farmers who are above this usage to benefit.
reply:
The Fertiliser Exceptional Aid Scheme that I launched on 13 October 2026, set the minimum tonnage of chemical fertiliser eligible for payment under the scheme at 2.5 tonnes and the maximum tonnage for which support will be granted will be up to 100 tonnes. The rate per tonne will be €40/tonne and the minimum payment under the Scheme will be €100.
It is important to note that in developing the Scheme eligibility thresholds I have had to take into account that there is an absolute maximum level of funding available for the Scheme, €46.2m, and the need to target support in the most meaningful manner to the widest possible group farmers exposed to higher input costs.
These levels of tonnage and the rate per tonne were arrived at to ensure that the funding of €46.2 million allocated to the Scheme can be distributed to support the maximum number of farmers in the most meaningful and efficient manner possible.
I extended by a week, to 30 October, the period for farmers to check the fertiliser purchased entered for them on the National Fertiliser Database for the 2025 Fertiliser year. My Department is now analysing the total eligible tonnage in order to determine eligible farmers and calculate payments in accordance with the Terms and Conditions of the Fertiliser Exceptional Aid Scheme.

question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will revisit the fuel rebate scheme and allow for applications which were below the €100 threshold for the first application tranche, but would qualify now with the additional months secured.
reply:
My Department has introduced the Fuel Income Support Scheme as a targeted income support to assist farmers and agricultural or forestry contractors facing unprecedented increases in fuel costs.
Separate schemes have been put in place to support fishers and specialist horticultural growers.
As announced in the Budget, I am pleased to have secured agreement on the extension to the end of this year of the important fuel supports schemes provided for farmers and agricultural contractors, fishermen and women and horticulture producers impacted by higher fuel prices. The allocation of €31.2 million to cover the five months August to December 2026 for these supports will be rapidly implemented by my Department.
The scheme has a minimum payment threshold of €100, which originally equated to a claim of 1,200 litres or more. Applicants that applied under the Fuel Income support Scheme and claimed a fuel usage between 600 litres and 1,199 litres of Marked Gas Oil are now eligible for payment under the scheme as with the second round of payments those in excess of 600 litres are now above the €100 minimum. Applicants do not need to reapply. Payment will automatically issue to eligible applicants when the second tranche of payments commence.

question: Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will verify that a co-operative satisfies the conditions for the derogation in Article 148(5)(a) of Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013, as revised by Regulation (EU) 2026/1739, before that derogation is relied upon from 19 August 2028.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1466, 1469 and 1470 together.
Article 148(5)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2026/1739, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1739, sets out the legal conditions under which deliveries of milk by members to their cooperative are exempt from the requirement for written contracts.
Article 148(5)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2026/1739, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1739, sets out very clearly the specific legal conditions and criteria a cooperative must satisfy in order to avail of the derogation set down under Article 148(5)(a).
The eligibility for the exemption is dependent on compliance with the conditions set out clearly in the Regulation.
The Regulation does not confer the power on the Minister to designate bodies as cooperatives for the purpose of availing of the exemption.
As noted in the recitals to the adopted Amendment to the Regulation "in order for operators to adapt their contractual relations to the new rules on written contracts and for producer organisations in the milk sector to adjust their statutes, the application of those rules should be deferred until two years after the date of entry into force of this Regulation."
My Department is currently considering the implementation of the new Amendment, which does not enter into force until 19 August 2028.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Defence to report on the meeting of Defence ministers at the recent Foreign Affairs EU Council.
reply:
On 28 September last, I participated in the latest formal meeting of EU Defence Ministers in Brussels, which followed the Informal meeting of the Council on 1st September last in Wicklow under the Irish Presidency of the Council of the European Union.
This meeting, which took place at the mid-point of the Presidency , saw Defence Ministers convene against the backdrop of an evolving and increasingly complex security environment. In particular, it was a key moment for EU Member States to reaffirm their steadfast solidarity with, and support for, Ukraine.
The main topic on the agenda was EU Support to Ukraine and Ministers were joined for this session by Minister of Defence of Ukraine, Evgeniy Khmara, via VTC for an informal exchange.
Ministers discussed latest developments, with a particular focus on how to increase air defence support, the implementation of the Ukraine Support Loan, the future of the EU's Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine (EUMAM Ukraine) and efforts to counter the Russian shadow fleet.
Ministers also agreed the first step of the strategic review of EUMAM Ukraine, extending the mission's mandate for another two years, and welcomed the recent unblocking of €6.6 billion in European Peace Facility (EPF) support for Ukraine.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to provide the number of calls made by members of the public to his Department's animal welfare helpline; and the number of emails from members of the public reporting suspected cases of animal abuse or mistreatment to his Departments animalwelfare@agriculture.gov.ie address from 2025 to date in 2026.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1452, 1454 and 1464 together.
My Department has lead policy responsibility within Government for animal welfare and takes the matter of animal welfare most seriously. I am committed to the policy that animal welfare standards are vigorously applied in a fair and even-handed manner.
All reports of alleged animal cruelty or neglect received by my Department are investigated. My Department and authorised officers appointed under the Animal Health and Welfare Act 2013, including An Garda Síochána, Customs agents, local authorities, and the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (NSPCA), undertake appropriate enforcement action, where breaches or shortcomings are identified.
My Department keeps the Act under review in light of key developments in the areas of animal welfare, the law and having regard to the practical lessons learnt from its operation.
Since the introduction of the Act, approximately 1,000 staff within my Department have been designated as authorised officers under the Act. A large number of these authorised officers are based in my Department’s network of Regional Veterinary Offices throughout the country, providing nationwide coverage. A feature of the enforcement of the Act is my Department can work alongside An Garda Síochána and the Local Authority on certain enforcement matters, resulting in a very effective and efficient use of resources.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to address matters raised in correspondence (details supplied) given the tourism impact of such developments in tourist and scenic areas.
reply:
My Department considers all applications for aquaculture and foreshore licences in accordance with the provisions of the Fisheries (Amendment) Act 1997 as amended, the Foreshore Act 1933 (as amended) and applicable national and EU legislation. The licensing process involves consultation with a wide range of scientific and technical advisers as well as various Statutory Consultees. The legislation also provides for a period of public consultation.
As the Competent Authority for aquaculture licencing, my Department is responsible for ensuring all applications are appropriately assessed in the context of the EU Birds and Habitats Directives. The Marine Institute, as my Department’s scientific advisor, is requested to undertake these Appropriate Assessments.
The visual impact of operations proposed in all marine aquaculture applications is assessed by my Department’s Marine Engineers in accordance with the ‘Guidelines for Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment of Marine Aquaculture’ 2001, and additionally, all marine finfish aquaculture applications (other than for trial or research purposes where the output would not exceed fifty tonnes) undergo an Environmental Impact Assessment in accordance with the applicable legislation, which includes consideration of potential impacts on tourism, where relevant, and the likely significant effects of the proposed project on the landscape. question: Deputy Pat the Cope Gallagher asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the steps taken by Ireland to obtain a blue fin tuna quota (details supplied).
reply:
The Bluefin Tuna quota available to the EU is allocated each year to Member States based on relative stability, as established in the late 1990s. At that time, Ireland did not have a record of commercial fishing for Bluefin Tuna and, accordingly, did not receive a quota allocation.
A small Bluefin Tuna by-catch quota is available to Ireland, primarily for use in our important Northern Albacore Tuna fishery and Celtic Sea Herring fishery, where there can be Bluefin Tuna by-catch.
In 2018, Ireland was successful in securing, for the first time, an agreement that allowed Ireland to set up a catch-tag-release fishery to contribute to the collection of scientific data for the Bluefin Tuna stock. A catch-tag-release science-based fishery for authorised recreational angling vessels has been in place since 2019 and supports the collection of valuable data on the migratory patterns of Bluefin Tuna in Irish waters. This fishery is most beneficial to Ireland as it increases our knowledge of the behaviour and abundance of Bluefin Tuna in northwestern waters, while also providing a small but valuable tourism benefit to peripheral coastal communities.
Ireland has made clear to EU Member States and the European Commission that it considers that there is a case for an allocation of Bluefin Tuna quota to be made available to Ireland for a targeted fishery. The case is supported by the data collected in the catch-tag-release science-based fishery for authorised recreational angling vessels.
