question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Defence the plans for further investment in Aiken Barracks.
reply:
I am pleased to advise the Deputy that I had the pleasure of officially opening the new Dining Facility at Aikens Barracks earlier this year. This project was completed at a cost of €5.7m. This has replaced the catering infrastructure currently used by Defence Forces military and civilian staff and includes a kitchen, front of house dining facilities and co-located ration storage. In addition, a central heating upgrade and the installation of New Electric Vehicle (EV) Charging points have been delivered to Aiken Barracks.
Currently in construction, at a cost of €0.8m is the refurbishment of Ablution facilities and insulation works to a three-storey accommodation block in the barracks. This work is expected to be completed in the middle of next year.

question: Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if, given that lobsters are sentient creatures capable of suffering, he will ban the practice of boiling lobsters alive which causes excruciating pain.
reply:
My Department has lead policy responsibility within Government for animal welfare and takes the matter of animal welfare most seriously. I am committed to the policy that animal welfare standards are vigorously applied in a fair and even-handed manner.
Animal welfare is a topic of increasing importance to society and to consumers, in Ireland and internationally. question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the Government's strategy for ensuring that Ireland's long standing right to invoke the Hague Preferences at the EU Fisheries Council, is not blocked by a minority of Member States again in 2026; and the discussions that have taken place with his European counterparts about this breach of faith since December 2025.
reply:
The share allocation of stocks between Member States was established as a principle of the first Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) in 1983 and was based on the average catch of each Member State over a period of reference years (track record). The only exception to this relates to the Hague Preferences, on the basis of a special recognition agreement of the underdeveloped nature of the Irish fleet and the heavy control responsibility arising when Ireland joined the EU. The Hague Preferences are additional amounts of quota that Ireland claims for a number of key stocks when the Total Allowable Catches (TACs) fall below specified levels.
The Hague Preferences are negotiated annually and over the years, many Member States have objected strenuously to their application as the additional quota for Ireland comes off their allocations.
These objections have been intensifying in recent times arising from reductions in quota due to both the quota transfers under the EU-UK Trade & Cooperation Agreement and to scientific advice.
Regrettably, during the December 2025 Fisheries Council a group of Member States chose to block the invocation of Ireland’s Hague Preferences for 2026 and the Danish Presidency did not include the Hagues in the final Presidency Compromise on the Fishing Opportunities Regulation. This unfortunately resulted in reduced fishing opportunities for Irish fishermen and women in 2026.

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the steps he is taking to strengthen transparency laws on the beneficial ownership of fishing vessels at EU level to ensure that quota remains a public resource in practice as well as policy.
reply:
European beneficial ownership laws apply across economic sectors, including the seafood sector. For instance a package of new EU anti-money laundering rules, including rules in relation to beneficial ownership, was adopted in 2024. The Common Fisheries Policy Basic Regulation does not specify requirements regarding ownership of vessels, other than providing that a Union fishing vessel is one flying the flag of a Member State and registered in the Union. The Irish Register of Fishing Boats is publicly available on my Department's website.
As regards quota allocation, the CFP provides that it is a matter for each Member State to decide how its fishing opportunities, which are not subject to a system of transferrable fishing concessions, are allocated to the vessels in its fleet. In allocating fishing opportunities, the CFP requires Member States to apply transparent and objective criteria, such as the contribution to the local economy.
A system of transferrable fishing concessions allows for a Member State's quota to be allocated to an individual fisher or group of fishers which is available to them to transfer, lease or sell to other vessel owners. This is commonly known as an Individual Transferable Quota (ITQ) system.
The last reform of the CFP set out the option for Member States to introduce ITQ systems for their fleets. The European Commission had proposed that such a system be mandatory for all Member States. Ireland was successful in strongly opposing a mandatory ITQ sy

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the reason his Department did not submit an action plan in relation to the assessment of balance between fishing capacity and fishing opportunities; and the reason his Department does not consider any of the Irish fishing fleet segments to have a structural imbalance.
reply:
Article 22(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1380/2013 of the European Parliament and the Council of 11 December 2013 on the Common Fisheries Policy (“the CFP Basic Regulation") provides that Member States shall put in place measures to adjust the fishing capacity of their fleet to their fishing opportunities over time with the objective of achieving a stable and enduring balance between them.
Article 22(2) provides that in order to achieve this objective, Member States shall send to the Commission an annual report on the balance between the fishing capacity of their fleets and their fishing opportunities.
The annual fleet capacity reports for Member States, including Ireland, for 2025 have been published by the Commission and are available at the following link: https://oceans-and-fisheries.ec.europa.eu/fisheries-management/fishing-fleet-capacities/fleet-capacity-reports-2025_en
The annual fleet capacity report provides a description of the Irish fishing fleet including, for example, information on compliance with the capacity entry/exit regime and national fleet management measures. The report also includes an assessment of the fleet based on biological and economic parameters with the Marine Institute and BIM providing the necessary analysis in this regard.

question: Deputy Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire asked the Minister for Defence her views on the purchase of additional medium lift helicopters as recommended under the CODF.
reply:
The rolling Equipment Development Plan (EDP) encompasses a programme of sustained equipment procurement/acquisition across the Air Corps, Army, and Naval Service as identified and prioritised in the Strategic Framework and the recently updated Detailed Implementation Plan for the Report of the Commission on the Defence Forces.
This is part of the ambitious programme of work to move to Level of Ambition 2 (LOA2) and will ensure that the Air Corps and the wider Defence Forces have the major equipment platforms, ancillary equipment and force protection equipment required to carry out their important roles both at home and overseas.
Capital funding of €1.7 billion has been allocated to Defence under the National Development Plan for the period 2026-2030. The funding represents an increase of €600 million or 55% on the previous baseline figure of €1.1 billion.
The Commission on the Defence Forces (CoDF) Report recommended that, within the scope of LOA2, two additional medium lift rotary wing aircraft (AW139) should be acquired, increasing the current medium lift fleet to eight helicopters. However, the Commission also stated that:
“in making these recommendations the Commission acknowledges that future defence planners may, in their detailed analysis, assess that the same effect can be delivered by different methods and as such the specific equipment recommendations outlined are intended to be indicative rather than prescriptive once the recommended capability requirement is met.”

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to urgently provide clarity on when a seed fishery will open (details supplied).
reply:
I wish to fully assure the Deputy that I understand the importance of the Irish Sea mussel seed fishery and of wild mussel seed as a raw material for the bottom grown mussel aquaculture sector. These primary producers, in turn, supply the downstream indigenous seafood processing and export industries and help to sustain the livelihoods of coastal communities. The importance of these primary and secondary seafood production activities is reflected in the Food Vision 2030 strategy.
I wish to inform the Deputy that a number of matters must be finalised before a decision on an opening can be made. Every effort is being made by my Department and its agencies to conclude this work as quickly as possible.
Given the all-island nature of the fishery, my Department remains in close contact with the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs in Northern Ireland, and I note its decision to open a mussel seed fishery at Skullmartin from 15 to 20 November 2026.
My Department will continue to keep industry updated through the Bottom Grown Mussel Consultative Forum (BGMCF).

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine further to Parliamentary Question No. PQ2607/26, the number of the estimated 81 full-time jobs listed for Dundalk Stadium relate exclusively to greyhound racing, given that this venue also hosts horse racing (details supplied); and he will provide a breakdown of the employment roles covered.
reply:
Rásaíocht Con Éireann (RCÉ) is a commercial state body established under the Greyhound Industry Act 1958 chiefly to control greyhound racing and to improve and develop the greyhound industry. RCÉ is a body corporate and a separate legal entity to the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine.
The question raised by the Deputy is an operational matter for RCÉ and, therefore, the question has been referred to that body for direct reply.

question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of members of his Department that are responsible for processing and reviewing requests for priority in relation to visa application and appeals in each of the years 2024 and 2025.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1365 to 1367, inclusive, 1390, 1396, 1438 to 1440, inclusive, and 1443 to 1447, inclusive, together.
I can advise the Deputy that, in order to ensure fairness to all applicants, visa applications and appeals are generally processed in the order in which they are received and are not routinely expedited.
While the Department acknowledges that applicants may experience difficult personal circumstances, prioritisation is generally confined to rare and exceptional time-sensitive situations, such as where a family member has been hospitalised, is in a life-threatening situation, or in the unfortunate event of a bereavement.
Priority may also be considered in other exceptional circumstances specific to an individual applicant. However, in order to maintain a fair, equitable and coherent processing system, circumstances affecting a country, region or population generally, however serious, cannot in themselves justify the prioritisation of an individual application. While I recognise the impact that conflict, humanitarian crises and other challenging circumstances may have on individuals and communities, requests for priority consideration must be assessed on the basis of the particular circumstances of the individual applicant.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Defence to outline the process for the awarding of historical IRA medals to families of volunteers.
reply:
The Government decided in January 1941 that two Medals should be struck in respect of service during the 1916-1921 period, one for service during Easter Week 1916 and the second for subsequent service up to the Truce of the 11 July 1921. In May 1942 the Government further decided that the second Medal, the Service (1917-1921) Medal, should be issued as follows:
• Medal with Bar to persons who are in possession of a military service certificate entitling them to a pension under the Military Service Pensions Acts in respect of the period subsequent to 1916 and prior to 11 July 1921 and to those persons not in possession of a certificate who satisfy the Minister for Defence that had they applied for a pension, their service was such as would have merited the award of a pension;
• Medal without Bar to persons who were enrolled in the Irish Republican Army, Fianna Éireann, Cumann na mBan and the Irish Citizen Army not less than three months prior to 11 July 1921, but who did not qualify for a pension.
In certain exceptional situations a medal can be posthumously awarded if no medal was previously issued. However, in order not to diminish the intrinsic value of such medals, this is only done in exceptional cases and only where there is incontrovertible verified evidence available that the criteria for the award of a medal have been met. question: Deputy Seán Crowe asked the Minister for Defence the number of motor technician fitters in the Irish army; and the number of additional motor technician fitters that the Defence Forces have advised will be required to service and maintain the new armoured vehicle fleet.
reply:
With regard to the first part of your question, seeking the number of motor technician fitters in the Irish Army, I can confirm that the number of same currently stands at 113 out of an establishment of 172.
I can further confirm that the overall strength across all three services stands at 120, out of an overall establishment of 186, with an additional 34 personnel currently in training.
With regard to the second part of your question pertaining to the future needs of the Armoured Vehicle Fleet I must clarify that, as the programme remains in the assessment phase, specifications as to the role, fleet size, timelines, costs, training arrangements and support requirements remain subject to ongoing negotiations and the necessary approval processes.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the procedures that apply where an international protection, resettlement or family-reunification application raises concerns about a child's welfare, including suspected abuse, exploitation or uncertainty about parentage; which agencies are consulted; the way in which referrals to Tusla are managed; and the way in which the child's best interests are considered in decisions.

Refugees considered for resettlement to Ireland under the Irish Refugee Protection Programme (IRPP) are generally referred to Ireland by the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR). Information concerning the individual and family, including relevant vulnerabilities and family circumstances, is provided as part of the referral and is further considered during the Irish selection process.
The referral process provides personal and family-composition information and supporting UNHCR documentation. As part of the Irish assessment process, IRPP also gathers and reviews relevant identity and family documentation and applicants are interviewed during selection missions.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to state the current oversight mechanism used to scrutinise the impartiality of members of the International Protection Appeals Tribunal.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1391, 1392, 1393, 1394, 1416, 1417 and 1421 together.
The International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) is a statutorily independent body and exercises a quasi-judicial function under the International Protection Act 2015.
The Tribunal consists of a Chairperson, two Deputy Chairpersons, and ordinary members appointed on either a whole-time or part-time capacity.
All Tribunal members are either barristers or solicitors with a minimum of two years’ professional experience and are appointed by the Minister for Justice following an open competition run by the Public Appointments Service (PAS) in accordance with section 62(4) of the International Protection Act 2015.
Members are appointed for fixed terms and may only be reappointed in accordance with the Act.
Tribunal decisions are subject to challenge through the courts by way of judicial review.
Information on the Tribunal’s practices and procedures, including Chairpersons Guidelines (www.protectionappeals.ie/chairpersons-guidelines/), the Administrative Practice Note - IPAT (www.protectionappeals.ie/administrative-practice-note/) and the Other Practices and Procedures - IPAT (/www.protectionappeals.ie/other-practices-and-procedures/) are available on www.protectionappeals.ie

question: Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Defence whether in view of the lack of an army barracks in the central Border area, if further consideration will be given to the re-opening of Dún Uí Néill Cavan.
reply:
As the Deputy is aware, the Commission on the Defence Forces recommended "The Chief of Defence to initiate an immediate force design process assisted by external experts with access to international military expertise, and to include a detailed force design process".
In response to this recommendation, the Defence Forces established three Force Design Teams across the Army, Naval Service and Air Corps, together with an overarching Strategic Force Design Office. The force design process is ongoing, with all teams working collaboratively to develop a coherent and integrated future force structure for the Defence Forces as a whole.
No decisions on the future disposition or locations of Defence Forces formations, installations and personnel, including the central Border area, have been made at this time. Currently there are no plans to consider reopening Dún Uí Néill site in Cavan, it is currently being used by Cavan and Monaghan Education and Training Board.
This work is nearing completion and I expect to receive a Force Design report for my consideration from the Chief of Staff in the near future.
This is challenging and important work, and it must be undertaken carefully to ensure we deliver a modern fit-for-purpose Defence Forces for the future. question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Defence the international organisations that the Defence Forces will engage with in deployments abroad should the 'triple lock' be removed.
reply:
Thank you Deputy for the question.
At the outset, it is important to clarify that the Defence (Amendment) Bill 2026 does not remove all of the existing safeguards that apply to overseas deployments. Rather, it proposes to remove the requirement for a specific mandate from the United Nations Security Council while retaining the requirements for Government approval and Dáil approval, where appropriate. Deployments would also continue to be conducted in accordance with the principles of the UN Charter and international law.
The purpose of the reforms is to provide Ireland with greater flexibility to participate in international peace support, crisis-management and humanitarian operations where a UN Security Council mandate may not be obtainable due to the use, or threatened use, of a veto by one of its permanent members.
The Bill does not identify or predetermine specific missions in which Ireland will participate. Rather, it establishes a framework that would allow the Government and Dáil Éireann to consider participation in operations conducted by what the legislation describes as a "relevant international force".
This could include missions organised by the United Nations, the European Union, the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), or other international organisations that we are already members of, operating in accordance with international law and the principles of the UN Charter.
Any proposal for participation in an overseas mission would continue

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1395 and 1397 together.
It is a central priority for me that Ireland's immigration system is robust and rules based. Effective enforcement of our immigration laws, including the implementation of deportation orders, is essential to maintaining confidence in the integrity of the system and ensuring that our legislation is applied consistently.
Deportations are often costly and complex to carry out. Consequently, voluntary return is the preferred option wherever possible. My Department operates a voluntary return programme to assist individuals who wish to leave the State before a deportation order is issued. As access to this programme is only available prior to the making of a deportation order, I have increased the resources available to support those who choose to return voluntarily at an earlier stage.

Where a person does not leave the State following the issuance of a deportation order, enforcement action may be required. In recent years, my Department has taken significant steps to strengthen immigration enforcement and increase the number of removals carried out.

While the Department acknowledges that applicants may experience difficult personal circumstances, prioritisation is generally confined to rare and exceptional time-sensitive situations, such as where a family member has been hospitalised, is in a life-threatening situation, or in the unfortunate event of a bereavement.

question: Deputy Holly Cairns asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide detail on the membership of the International Protection Appeals Tribunal; their qualifications for membership of the tribunal; and the process for the appointment, oversight, and accountability of IPAT members.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1391, 1392, 1393, 1394, 1416, 1417 and 1421 together.
The International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) is a statutorily independent body and exercises a quasi-judicial function under the International Protection Act 2015.
The Tribunal consists of a Chairperson, two Deputy Chairpersons, and ordinary members appointed on either a whole-time or part-time capacity.
All Tribunal members are either barristers or solicitors with a minimum of two years’ professional experience and are appointed by the Minister for Justice following an open competition run by the Public Appointments Service (PAS) in accordance with section 62(4) of the International Protection Act 2015.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Defence the role mental health and wellbeing supports play in the retention of Defence Forces personnel; and the measures that have been introduced in recent years in relation to same.

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will review the decision to deport a family (details supplied) who have established employment and community connections in Ireland, and who face significant danger if returned to their home country.
reply:
It is a central priority for me as Minister that our immigration laws are robust and enforced.
As the Deputy may be aware, my Department is unable to publish any information that would identify any person as being an international protection applicant. This is a separate matter to the law dealing with data protection matters more generally.
My officials and I are legally obliged, under Section 26 of the International Protection Act 2015, to ensure that the identity of any person who applies for international protection is kept confidential. Section 26(1) sets out that:
“the Minister and the Tribunal and their respective officers shall take all practicable steps to ensure that the identity of applicants is kept confidential”.
As I am sure you will appreciate, these confidentiality requirements are especially important for an asylum-seeker, whose claim inherently supposes a fear of persecution by the authorities of their home country and whose situation, or that of their family or friends still living in the country from which they have sought protection, can be jeopardised if the protection of their personal information is not ensured.
More generally, where an applicant has been refused and has exhausted all appeal avenues for international protection, they have the option of voluntary return, which if not accepted will in the normal course lead to the making of a deportation order. question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding work ongoing within his Department to address concerns related to the use of smart glasses in public spaces at a legislative level.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1384 to 1386, inclusive, together.
Across Europe, concerns have been raised regarding the privacy implications of smart glasses and similar wearable technologies. These concerns include issues relating to transparency, awareness of when recording is taking place, and the collection and processing of personal data relating to third parties.
Functionalities vary between smart glasses on the market. The most common include listening to music, making or receiving a phone call, taking photos/videos, accessing real-time translation services, and live streaming. The use of smart glasses and other wearable technologies capable of capturing images, video and audio create new opportunities for communication, assistance and innovation including for persons who are blind or visually impaired. question: Deputy Holly Cairns asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an update on work conducted within his Department on the proposed removal of daylight savings time, as voted upon by the European Parliament in 2021; and to detail any discussions held on a European level or with the Northern Ireland Executive on the matter.
reply:
EU Directive 2000/84/EC sets out the obligation on all EU Member States to switch to summer time on the last Sunday of March and to switch back to their standard time (winter time) on the last Sunday of October each year. Following a resolution of the European Parliament in 2018, the European Commission proposed a change to this arrangement whereby Members States would remain free to choose their standard time, on the condition that they give 18 months’ notice to the Commission.
Ireland’s consistent position at the EU Transport, Telecommunications and Energy (TTE) Council has been that it will not support the proposal. A major consideration is the possibility that the proposal could lead to the imposition of two time zones on the island of Ireland, and that the proposal could reduce synchronicity resulting in a ‘patchwork’ of time zones across the EU.
Discussions with Member States on the proposal are ongoing via the TTE Council.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether the process for forwarding a visa application to the relevant department, embassy or consulate, varies based on the nationality of the applicant; and if so to outline the way in which the process may vary.
reply:

These are important screening processes, designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel. Verifying an application is an important part of our immigration system.
I can advise the Deputy that a visa-required national who wishes to enter the State and remain for up to 90 days must obtain a Type C (Short Stay) visa. A visa-required national who intends to reside in the State for more than 90 days must obtain a Type D (Long Stay) visa.
Visa applications are made online through the Automated Visa Application and Tracking System (AVATS), available at www.visas.inis.gov.ie. Applicants are generally required to apply from their country of nationality or from a country in which they are lawfully resident.

The summary form contains details of the application and provides instructions on the next steps required to lodge supporting documentation. question: Deputy George Lawlor asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of fines issued at a static speed camera (details supplied) from 1 to 30 September 2026 inclusive.
reply:
Whether it is fixed cameras, average speed cameras or GoSafe vans, the use of technology is a vital component of reducing speeding on our roads.
Road safety cameras are intended to be, first and foremost, a tool to support safety, prevention and behavioural change across the road network. The aim of road safety cameras across Ireland is to encourage safer driving practices, reduce collisions and protect road users by promoting compliance with speed limits.
Nine static speed safety cameras are in operation across the country since 2024. The locations of these cameras were selected based on fatal and serious injury collision data and speed data, as well as feedback from stakeholders.
I am informed by the Garda Authorities for the month of September 2026 there were 2,714 speed detections issued for the static spot camera at the N25, Ballynamona, Co. Kilkenny. This data is based upon operational data from the Fixed Charge Processing System as was available on the 29th October 2026 and is liable to change.

question: Deputy Seán Crowe asked the Minister for Defence to provide clarity on her publicly stated preference for Ireland to be involved in a peace enforcement mission in Lebanon; and the mission parameters that she envisages.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 135 and 157 together.
International support for the Government of Lebanon, and the Lebanese Armed Forces more broadly, is an important priority for Ireland.
Our participation in UNIFIL, alongside many of our EU colleagues, over many decades is a highly visible and concrete sign of our commitment and has made an essential contribution to the safety and security of Lebanon and the wider region.
On 12 October, the Council of the European Union adopted a decision establishing a new European Union Support Mission in Lebanon (EUSM Lebanon) under the Common Security and Defence Policy (CSDP). This is a training mission. and advisory mission. Operational planning is now taking place at EU-level and the Council will adopt a separate decision launching the new mission once operational planning has been completed.
The ending of the UNIFIL operation at the end of this year will leave a massive gap in Lebanon's security. While the CSDP training mission is not a replacement for UNIFIL, it will provide an important EU presence in Lebanon.
Recent commentary on EU Support Mission, Lebanon has unfortunately generated a degree of confusion by conflating a non-executive training and advisory mission with peace enforcement or other operations.
At the outset, it is important to define what this new mission is and what it is not. As a non-executive training mission, EUSM Lebanon is not a peace enforcement mission and is mandated only to provide training and advisory

question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update in relation to a single Garda vetting card.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1349 and 1405 together.
The primary purpose of vetting carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau is to ensure the safety of children and vulnerable adults. Clearly, this requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust.
The Government is aware of ongoing concerns regarding certain aspects of the vetting process and I have listened carefully to the views of affected sectors. I believe that the vetting system should be updated to ensure that the burden of seeking vetting disclosures, particularly on volunteers and organisations working in their communities, is minimised to the greatest extent possible, while maintaining the high standards that are necessary.
Further to the work carried out by the Garda Vetting Review Group, steps are now being taken to implement a number of key changes to the process that will ensure it remains robust and effective while improving the service to customers.
In practice, and subject to a general requirement that vetting be renewed every three years, it is envisaged that this will mean that when a person is vetted for the work they will be or are likely to be involved in as part of their employment or volunteering within identified risk categories, the person would not be required to repeat the process if they were to move to another role within the same risk category.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of persons who were the subject of a deportation order and who were residing in International Protection Accommodation Service accommodation at the end of each quarter of 2025 and to date in 2026; the average time such persons remained in that accommodation after the order was signed.
reply:
The number of people resident in the International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centres who have been refused permission to remain in the State is a small proportion of our total resident population of nearly 32,000 people.
Currently, there are over 900 people subject to deportation orders residing in IPAS accommodation. This number fluctuates regularly as people leave Ireland under the relevant return pathways, and as new orders are made, and data is not routinely collated on the duration of their stay after a deportation order being issued. The breakdown of data requested for 2025 has not been collated for publication, and is therefore not available.
Some people subject to deportation orders may have the enforcement of their order suspended due to legal proceedings or due to personal circumstances such as health grounds. Others will be in the process of arranging to leave the State as directed.
My Department works closely with the Garda National Immigration Bureau to arrange for the removal of persons subject to deportation orders.
The enforcement of deportation orders is an operational matter for the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB), and my Department works closely with the GNIB to progress arrangements for the removal of people subject to deportation orders. If a person issued with a deportation order does not leave the State independently then they are required to present to the GNIB in accordance with the conditions of their deportation order.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Defence if her Department has conducted any public consultation regarding the triple lock and Irish neutrality.
reply:
The Consultative Forum on International Security Policy, chaired by Professor Dame Louise Richardson, was held in 2023, convened to launch a national conversation on Irish foreign, defence, and security policy in light of the changing geopolitical environment and the emergence of new and emerging threats to the nation’s security.
It involved a consultative discussion with a wide range of stakeholders, with participation from civilian and military experts and practitioners representing a breadth of experience and views. This Forum was open to, and attended by, many academics, current and former members of the Defence Forces as well as representatives from international institutions and members of the public.
It had 80 panellists and moderators, approximately 1,000 attendees in person, with discussions live-streamed, with over 10,000 online views. In addition, over 850 written submissions were also received as part of this process.
The Forum took place in three different locations across four days in June 2023: 22 June at University College Cork 23 June at the University of Galway 26 and 27 June at Dublin Castle.
On the Triple Lock, the prevailing view was that it should be reconsidered and Government undertook to legislate on that basis.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of IPAS accommodation contracts audited or reviewed for value for money by or on behalf of his Department since 1 January 2019; the findings of those audits or reviews; the amounts recovered from providers as a result; whether the reports will be published.
reply:

Since May 2025, the Department measures value for money within the International Protection accommodation portfolio across a number of indicators, with a view to strengthening budgetary oversight and driving continuous value for money.
Implementation of a rate-card for all new and renewing contracts, aligned with this value for money drive, has resulted in over €162 million in projected savings of contract values per annum, across 259 contracts.
The budget allocation for 2027 for this service is reduced by over €250 million compared to the 2026 allocation. Through increased inspections and application of the rate-card to contracts, costs have been reduced on renewed and new contracts, and 46 contracts have terminated since 2025.

All expenditure on international protection accommodation is subject to review by the Comptroller and Auditor General.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department has assessed whether the payment basis of IPAS accommodation contracts, including payment per person per night or payment for contracted rather than occupied beds, gives providers a financial incentive to maintain or increase the number of persons accommodated; the payment basis used in current contracts.
reply:
Providing reception conditions to people who are applying for international protection is part of EU and Irish law, and people are entitled to accommodation for the duration of their application process.
The State is currently accommodating nearly 32,000 people seeking international protection in 293 International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centres around the country.
With respect to the allocation of accommodation placements to applicants, this is not managed by the accommodation providers, it is managed by IPAS on behalf of the Department under Section 76 of the International Protection Act 2026. Accommodation providers do not determine how many applicants are allocated accommodation at a centre.
The Department seeks to maximise occupancy levels across our accommodation portfolio to ensure value and effective use of public funds. In addition to this, since 2025, a comprehensive programme of contract reviews and improved governance arrangements has been progressed across the accommodation system. A new rate-card process has been employed at contract renewal stage, leading to cost reductions across over 259 contracts.
The Department treats details of contractual arrangements and individual contracts as confidential and commercially sensitive, as to disclose details of contractual arrangements would limit the State's ability to achieve continued improvement in value for money in this sector.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to clarify when sections 143, 145, 146, 147, 148, 149, 151, 157 and 159 of the Gambling Regulation Bill will commence which include marketing, advertising and sponsorship, taking into account the huge rise in gambling addiction, especially due to the marketing of 24 hour Online slot machines.
reply:
The Gambling Regulation Act 2024 (the Act) establishes a comprehensive framework for the licensing and regulation of betting, gaming, and certain lotteries, including activities provided online to persons in the State. It also establishes a new, independent statutory body, the Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland (GRAI). Last year, I signed orders to commence the first provisions of the Act and to establish the GRAI from 5 March 2025.
At its core, the Act is a public health measure aimed at protecting citizens from gambling harm, particularly children, young people, and those in our communities who are more vulnerable. It provides for a number of safeguards to protect people, most notably children and vulnerable persons, from the harms associated with gambling, with a particular focus on online activities.
The provisions referenced by the Deputy relate to the regulation of gambling marketing, advertising, and sponsorship, and confer significant regulation-making powers on the GRAI, including a suite of enforcement measures where a licensee is in breach of same. My Department is currently working with the Office of the Attorney General to commence these provisions.
The protections and safeguards provided for in the Act are contingent on the providers in the sector being licensed and regulated by the GRAI. In collaboration with the GRAI, officials in my Department are continuing to progress the further commencement of the Act's remaining provisions as quickly as possible.

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to outline the enforcement that can be taken where large nitrous oxide canisters are marketed for recreational use or alternative means beyond their intended use.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1311, 1332, 1333 and 1335 together.
The misuse of nitrous oxide is currently addressed under the Criminal Justice (Psychoactive Substances) Act 2010.
This Act aims to prevent of the misuse of dangerous or otherwise harmful psychoactive substances and provides for offences relating to the sale, importation, exportation or advertisement of those substances. The Act provides that a person who sells, or who imports or exports, a psychoactive substance knowing, or being reckless as to whether that substance is being acquired or supplied for human consumption, shall be guilty of an offence.
That legislation also provides An Garda Síochána with powers in relation to the issuing of prohibition notices to a person engaged in selling, importing, exporting, or advertising nitrous oxide, or any psychoactive substance, for human consumption. The 2010 Act also provides a member of An Garda Síochána with powers of entry, search, seizure and detention, powers to search persons and vehicles and powers of arrest for obstruction where, with reasonable cause, they suspect a person of committing an offence under the Act.
Nitrous oxide has a number of legitimate uses, particularly in the medical and catering industries. I am informed that it is for this reason that it is not listed under the Misuse of Drugs Acts, nor is it the intention to classify it as a substance under those Acts. question: Deputy Aisling Dempsey asked the Minister for Defence for an overview of the Budget 2027 measures in Defence.
reply:
Budget 2027 provides a significant increase in funding for Defence, with an allocation of just over €1.6 billion for the Defence Vote Group, comprising of €1.283 billion for the Defence Vote and €324 million for the Army Pensions Vote. The Army Pensions Vote, which is demand-led and non-discretionary, will increase by €7 million, while the Defence Vote will increase by €122 million, or 10.5%, compared with 2026.
As Minister for Defence, I am committed to ensuring that our Defence Forces are appropriately resourced and equipped to meet the challenges of an increasingly complex and volatile security environment.
Investment in our people is essential. Budget 2027 provides funding for a net increase of 400 Permanent Defence Force (PDF) personnel, including specialist roles, bringing the overall PDF strength up to 8,300 personnel by the end of 2027. Funding is also provided for up to 100 civilian and civil service posts to support capability development and organisational capacity. Additional funding will support recruitment campaigns, healthcare supports for Defence Forces personnel and implementation of the Reserve Defence Force Regeneration Plan, including the expansion of the Naval Service Reserve and the establishment of the Air Corps Reserve.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if the current bail system needs to be reformed.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1294, 1295, 1298, 1299 and 1327 together.
It is important to recognise that restricting a person’s liberty is a serious issue, given the Constitutional presumption that a person is deemed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law. Applications for bail are made to a judge, who is independent in the exercise of their judicial functions, and the decision to grant bail in a particular case is solely a matter for the court.
Last year, I appointed Senior Counsel Lorcan Staines to undertake an assessment of the current operation of bail in Ireland, both legal and practical. The report completed by Mr Staines, ‘An Assessment of the Efficacy of Bail Laws in Ireland’, was published by my Department in November 2025. A number of Mr Staines’ recommendations are under consideration, in progress or have been implemented.
My Department is leading a cross-agency project to introduce electronic monitoring for specific categories of individuals, as committed to in the Programme for Government, and in line with existing legal provisions. €2.1m of funding was secured in Budget 2026 and €1.5m in Budget 2027 for the project to allow for staffing, procurement, and other set up costs.

Verifying an application is an important part of our immigration system.
I can inform the Deputy that the visa application referred to has been reviewed by a Visa Appeals Officer. In conducting this review, the Appeals Officer considered all of the information and documentation submitted with both the original application and the subsequent appeal.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the way in which the changes that are due to come into effect in March 2027 affect a person (details supplied).
reply:
Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection hold temporary permission to remain in Ireland, renewable annually for as long as the Directive remains in force.
On 30 July 2026, the Justice and Home Affairs Council extended the application of the Temporary Protection in respect of the war in Ukraine from March 2027 until March 2028. This provides certainty for beneficiaries who can continue to avail of the protection that the Directive provides. Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection in Ireland, such as the person to whom the Deputy refers, will continue to have access to the labour market, access to education and training, and access to medical care in the State in the same manner and to the same extent as an Irish citizen.

question: Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of naturalisation applications in which the applicant has been asked for further information or documents, in each of the last three years; whether an application retains its place in the queue once that information is submitted; the average time taken to resume processing and reach a decision after the information is received; and the steps he is taking to ensure all required documents are requested at the earliest stage so that applicants are not delayed.
reply:
I wish to clarify to the Deputy that, during the registration process, the Citizenship Division of my Department is not seeking additional information from applicants but rather ensuring that all required supporting documentation has been submitted and correctly certified.
Prior to submitting an application, applicants should ensure that they are in possession of all required supporting documentation and that any documents requiring certification have been properly certified.
I can inform the Deputy that my Department does not record the number of applications returned due to missing supporting documentation. Accordingly, the information requested is not available and could only be obtained through the manual examination of thousands of individual applications.
Where a naturalisation application is found to be missing required documentation, or where there is an issue with documentation that has been submitted, the application is returned to the applicant with a request to provide the outstanding documentation within 28 days. A reminder issues after 18 days where the requested documentation has not yet been received.
The application is removed from the registration queue and will only re-enter the queue once the required documentation has been submitted by the applicant. Any resubmitted application re-enters the queue based on the date of resubmission rather than the date of the original application.
My Department does not maintain statistics on the average time taken to resu

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if there are plans to introduce an independent enforcement mechanism for child maintenance payments; given the onus remains on the receiving parent to seek enforcement through the courts in circumstances of non-payment.
reply:
It is important to note that the management of the courts and the conduct of court proceedings are a matter entirely for the Judiciary and the Courts Service. The courts are, subject only to the Constitution and the law, independent in the exercise of their judicial functions.
The Programme for Government commits to enhancing the enforcement mechanisms for child maintenance orders to ensure that children receive the financial support they need from both parents. My Department’s Review of the Enforcement of Child Maintenance Orders put forward 26 recommendations focused on generating maximum compliance with child maintenance orders, to ensure security and stability for children, and to aid poverty prevention. The key recommendations include:

reply:
My Department currently uses an Oracle-based Financial Management System (FMS). The FMS holds individual supplier information, which includes a unique supplier ID generated by the system. Any purchase order and payment is recorded against an individual supplier. This financial management system is separate to the national tendering system (eTenders), it is also separate to the management information system my Department uses to record contract details.
A unique contract reference number is mandatory for invoice approvals over €25,000, with all payments made by my Department required to be authorised by a designated officer in strict adherence with internal financial authorisation limits. These limits relate to the approval of invoices, entering the Department into any commitments through any means including authorising invoices for payment, and entering into contracts and funding / grant agreements.
I can assure the Deputy that the benefits of linking expenditure with the procurement process through having greater connections between data from the tendering (pre-award) and the expenditure (post-award) stages of public procurement transactions are recognised, and my Department has begun a process to identify a suitable replacement solution for our current management information system used to record contract details.

question: Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to outline Governments plans to combat the growing misuse of nitrous oxide in Ireland.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1311, 1332, 1333 and 1335 together.
The misuse of nitrous oxide is currently addressed under the Criminal Justice (Psychoactive Substances) Act 2010.
This Act aims to prevent of the misuse of dangerous or otherwise harmful psychoactive substances and provides for offences relating to the sale, importation, exportation or advertisement of those substances. The Act provides that a person who sells, or who imports or exports, a psychoactive substance knowing, or being reckless as to whether that substance is being acquired or supplied for human consumption, shall be guilty of an offence.
That legislation also provides An Garda Síochána with powers in relation to the issuing of prohibition notices to a person engaged in selling, importing, exporting, or advertising nitrous oxide, or any psychoactive substance, for human consumption. The 2010 Act also provides a member of An Garda Síochána with powers of entry, search, seizure and detention, powers to search persons and vehicles and powers of arrest for obstruction where, with reasonable cause, they suspect a person of committing an offence under the Act.
Nitrous oxide has a number of legitimate uses, particularly in the medical and catering industries. I am informed that it is for this reason that it is not listed under the Misuse of Drugs Acts, nor is it the intention to classify it as a substance under those Acts. question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if consideration has been given to offering a formal State apology to the family of a person (details supplied) in recognition of failures in the Garda investigation into their killing.
reply:
The bombing of Dublin Airport on 29 November 1975, which was carried out without warning, was a callous attack that killed one person and left eight others injured. It is deeply regrettable that, to date, no person has been brought to justice for this crime.
The Garda Authorities have assured me that their investigation remains open and that any new evidence that may come to light, from whatever source, will be pursued by An Garda Síochána. I understand that the family of the deceased has engaged directly with the Garda Commissioner in relation to the investigation. The Deputy will appreciate that, as Minister, I have no role in relation to the conduct of Garda investigations.
The Deputy may also be aware that the bombing formed part of Operation Denton, an analytical review by the independent Kenova Investigation Team in the UK into the activities of the so called 'Glenanne Gang' in Northern Ireland. The final report of Operation Denton has yet to be published pending the resolution of a legal challenge.
I met with a family member of the deceased in the bombing on 19 January 2026 and understand that the family was briefed on Operation Denton’s conclusions in relation to the bombing last year. I can assure the Deputy, as I did the family member concerned, that the Government is committed to seeking out the truth behind this appalling event.

question: Deputy Brian Stanley asked the Minister for Defence to consider using a statutory instrument/secondary legislation to re-open the findings of the Board of Assessors decisions regarding the awarding of 1916 service medals to Laois volunteers who were on active service during Easter week.
reply:
The 1916 Medal was awarded to persons who were awarded 1916 service under the Military Service Pensions Acts or to those who did not apply for a pension but who satisfied the Minister that they would have been awarded 1916 service if they had applied under the Acts.
The Military Service Certificate under the 1924 Act, which formed the basis for the award of a pension, is also the basis for the award of a 1916 medal. Section 3(6) of the Military Service Pensions Act 1924 provided that the Board of Assessors could at any time re-open their findings at the request of the Minister on the ground that evidence not previously available had subsequently become available.
The power given to the Board of Assessors to reopen findings was removed by the Military Services Pensions Act 1949. Therefore, there is now no statutory provision available to re-open the findings of the Board. The process by which applications and petitions or appeals under the Military Service Pensions Acts were made, investigated and verified was wound up in 1958 and there is no statutory or other mechanism available now by which service can be investigated or verified.
The Deputy refers to a group of Laois volunteers who participated in the relevant Easter Rising events, of whom six received 1916 medals on foot of awards under the relevant Military Service Pensions Acts, while others did not.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1294, 1295, 1298, 1299 and 1327 together.
It is important to recognise that restricting a person’s liberty is a serious issue, given the Constitutional presumption that a person is deemed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law. Applications for bail are made to a judge, who is independent in the exercise of their judicial functions, and the decision to grant bail in a particular case is solely a matter for the court.
Last year, I appointed Senior Counsel Lorcan Staines to undertake an assessment of the current operation of bail in Ireland, both legal and practical. The report completed by Mr Staines, ‘An Assessment of the Efficacy of Bail Laws in Ireland’, was published by my Department in November 2025. A number of Mr Staines’ recommendations are under consideration, in progress or have been implemented.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of the Government’s consideration of the recommendations contained in the review of Ireland’s bail laws; which recommendations it intends to implement; and the expected timeline for their implementation.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1294, 1295, 1298, 1299 and 1327 together.
It is important to recognise that restricting a person’s liberty is a serious issue, given the Constitutional presumption that a person is deemed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law. Applications for bail are made to a judge, who is independent in the exercise of their judicial functions, and the decision to grant bail in a particular case is solely a matter for the court.
Last year, I appointed Senior Counsel Lorcan Staines to undertake an assessment of the current operation of bail in Ireland, both legal and practical. The report completed by Mr Staines, ‘An Assessment of the Efficacy of Bail Laws in Ireland’, was published by my Department in November 2025. A number of Mr Staines’ recommendations are under consideration, in progress or have been implemented.

question: Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Defence the number of Naval Service vessels currently operational and available for deployment; the number not operational, including the principal reasons; and the level of personnel required to crew the full Naval Service fleet.
reply:
The Naval Service is the State's principal sea-going agency, responsible for a broad range of defence and security functions. Its principal operational task is the enforcement of fisheries protection obligations arising from Ireland's membership of the European Union. To fulfil this role, the Naval Service conducts regular patrols throughout Irish waters, from the coastline to the outer limits of the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). These patrols are carried out on a regular and frequent basis and are directed to all areas of Irish waters, as necessary.
The Naval Service currently has a fleet of eight commissioned vessels. These eight vessels consist of two P50 class large patrol vessels, four P60 class offshore patrol vessels, and two P70 inshore patrol vessels.
I am advised by the military authorities that there are four vessels available for operations and regularly deployed on Maritime Defence and Security Operations on a rotation basis. The operational availability of Naval Service vessels is managed through a strategic rotation which takes account of maintenance, crew training, and rest periods. This approach ensures a continuous and sustainable naval presence in Irish waters.
The strength of the Naval Service, as at 30 September 2026 was 894 personnel out of an establishment of 1,094 personnel. The Military Authorities have advised that the total number of personnel currently required to crew all vessels is 294.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to review a renewal application for a person (details supplied), in view of the fact that the application has exceeded the processing timeline and their employment will be affected.
reply:
I can advise the Deputy that the Turkish Association Agreement (TURA) application cited continues to be processed by my Department.
The processing of TURA applications was paused earlier this year pending the resolution of legal proceedings. I can further advise that applications resumed processing in July 2026 and my Department is currently examining TURA applications submitted in April 2026.
While my Department endeavours to process applications as quickly as possible, processing times may vary due to a number of factors, such as the number of applications on hand, individual circumstances, the complexity of applications and whether further information is required.
While applicants await the outcome of their TURA application, they can continue to renew their stamp 1 immigration permission provided that they are still working for the same employer to which the permission was originally granted.
All nationwide applications for renewal of immigration permissions are submitted using the Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) online renewal portal. Further information on the renewal process as well as the list of documents required for each stamp type are available on the ISD website at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-register-your-immigration-permission-for-the-first-time/required-documents/.
The Registration Office also provide a live application processing date broken down by stamp category, which is updated every Monday,

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1286, 1313 and 1326 together.
Visa and preclearance applications provide legal avenues for people moving to Ireland and to facilitate visitors who wish to travel for business and/or tourism. These are important screening processes, designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel. Verifying an application is an important part of our immigration system.
I can inform the Deputy that the visa application referred to has been reviewed by a Visa Appeals Officer. In conducting this review, the Appeals Officer considered all of the information and documentation submitted with both the original application and the subsequent appeal.
Following this review, the appeal was unsuccessful and the original decision to refuse the visa application has been upheld. The reasons for this decision were set out in the refusal letter issued on 9 October 2026.
I appreciate that this decision is disappointing for the applicant. Guidelines in this regard are posted on our website. Applicants that follow these guidelines have an improved prospect of receiving a positive decision.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the way in which his Department is building cyber resilience; and the strategy in place to address cyber attacks.
reply:
My Department employs a range of policies and practices to ensure the integrity, confidentiality and availability of the Department’s data and IT services and to protect it from all potential threats, both external and internal. In these efforts, my Department utilises expert support from specialist resources.
In addition, my Department also liaises with the National Cyber Security Centre. The National Cyber Security Centre issues general cyber security updates on a regular basis and issues continuous alerts to my Department in relation to specific potential cyber security breaches, including advice on appropriate actions to mitigate such threats.
My Department manages data breaches in line with Data Protection legislation and liaises with the Data Protection Commission as required. My Department does not disclose details of cyber security protocols, as it could potentially reduce their effectiveness and increase the risk of breaches.

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of fines issued by An Garda in respect of non-compliance with new e-scooter rules since their introduction (details supplied); and if he will provide a breakdown by offence and fines issued.
reply:
Our road safety strategy takes a whole of government approach and is a shared responsibility. Development and implementation of road traffic legislation and policy falls within the remit of my colleague, the Minister for Transport, and the vital role of enforcing road traffic laws is carried out by An Garda Síochána.
Gardaí have significant legislative powers to combat the antisocial and dangerous misuse of e-scooters and other such vehicles and I am assured that An Garda Síochána continues to adopt a proactive approach in addressing this issue.
Road traffic legislation is enforced as part of the day-to-day duties of members of An Garda Síochána, as well as through a programme of high-visibility road safety and enforcement operations carried out in partnership with other state agencies, in order to make our roads safer for all.
I am informed by An Garda Síochána there have been 2,055 FCNs issued in respect of non-compliance with e-scooter regulations between 1 January 2025 and 30 September 2026, inclusive. These are grouped together in the offence categories listed below.
All information is based upon operational data from the FCPS system, as was available on 23 October 2026 and is liable to change. Data in respect of revised regulations introduced in early October 2026 are not available.

question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 586 of 29 September 2026, if he has received the necessary information from Garda authorities to answer the PQ.
reply:
I refer to Parliamentary Question No. 586 of 29 September 2026 where you sought: “ the percentage of the Garda motorcycle fleet that also have off-road capabilities".
I am informed by the Garda Authorities that the Garda motorcycle fleet does not have off-road capabilities.
The purchase and allocation of vehicles by An Garda Síochána is made on the basis of identified operational demands, the availability of resources and is reviewed on a continual basis.
Under section 33 of the Policing Security and Community Safety Act 2025, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the administration and management of An Garda Síochána, including the allocation and deployment of all resources available to him such as the Garda fleet. The Commissioner is independent in his functions under Section 34 of the Act.

reply:

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his Department provides exceptional visa processing flexibility or dedicated case coordination to enable family members specifically including spouses and young dependent children to leave Gaza together; to clarify the exact administrative or humanitarian pathways available; and the way his Department coordinates this with the Department of Foreign Affairs.
reply:
I am acutely aware of the grave humanitarian crisis in Gaza, and my Department continues to work closely with our colleagues in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade to ensure a coordinated national response to this situation.
My Department is very limited in the assistance it can provide to those who wish to resettle in Ireland. In common with the position for all non-EU nationals, entry of Palestinian nationals is undertaken through the existing legal immigration pathways available. Palestinian nationals are visa required and must have a valid Irish visa before they seek to enter Ireland. Palestinian nationals can apply for a visa and for permission to remain in Ireland based on a variety of different reasons, including employment, education or to join a family member in the State. Details of these legal pathways can be found on my Department's Immigration Service website: www.irishimmigration.ie/.
It is important to note that visa applications are part of a screening process, designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel, and all such applications undergo this process. There are no special arrangements for Palestinian nationals in place. question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current status of the intoxicating liquor Bill listed in the Government Legislation Programme for Autumn 2026 as a condensed Bill to introduce certain key reforms from the general scheme of the Sale of Alcohol Bill 2022; when he expects the Bill to be published and enacted.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1273, 1274 and 1277 together.
Neither the Sale of Alcohol Bill 2022 nor the Intoxicating Liquor Bill 2024 progressed in the lifetime of the last Government. The Programme for Government commits to updating our licensing laws.
The Autumn Legislative Programme, published on 16 September, sets out the 32 Bills that have been prioritised for publication, and a further 32 Bills that have been prioritised for drafting in the current Dáil session.
Other legislative projects, including work on updating liquor legislation, will be taken forward in subsequent iterations of the legislative programme, to be determined by Government in due course.
The points raised in respect of obtaining new licences will be considered.

reply:
Coroners are independent office holders, whose core function is to investigate sudden and unexplained deaths so that a death certificate can be issued. As they are independent office holders, my Department has no role in directing any coroner’s work during their investigation of any death. I am advised that a coronial death investigation can take a number of months, depending on whether a post mortem is required and, thereafter, if an inquest is to be held into the death.
The Department does not collate the data requested. However, under Section 55 of the Coroners Act, 1962 – 2024, coroners make annual returns to my Department on completed cases in their districts. Details of which can be found here: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/collections/coroners-annual-returns-2018-2025/. The inquest data contained in these returns relates to completed inquests, where a death certificate can issue. The 2026 data will be requested from coroners in early 2027 for future publication.

As part of this work, my Department is examining ways to increase efficiencies and minimise the impact of the death investigation process on bereaved people. question: Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Defence the peace enforcement missions Ireland has been involved in since 1990.
reply:
Since 1990, the majority of overseas deployments by members of the Defence Forces have been peacekeeping (i.e. Chapter 6) missions, including service with UNIFIL in Lebanon, UNDOF in the Golan Heights and UNTSO in the Middle East.
However, Irish personnel have also served in a number of UN missions operating under more robust authorisations for the use of force (Chapter 7). Examples include the United Nations Mission in Liberia (UNMIL), the United Nations Stabilisation Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), the United Nations Multidimensional Integrated Stabilisation Mission in Mali (MINUSMA) and East Timor. Irish personnel have also served in UN-authorised and underpinned missions such as KFOR, in Kosovo, ISAF in Afghanistan and EUFOR Tchad/RCA in Chad, all of which operated under robust international mandates.
It may be useful in this regard for me to outline the distinctions between peacekeeping and peace enforcement to the House.
In simple terms, peacekeeping involves helping to maintain a peace that already exists. Peacekeepers monitor ceasefires, support political agreements, protect civilians and help create the conditions for long-term stability. Such operations are generally associated with the principles set out under Chapter 6 of the United Nations Charter.
Peace enforcement, on the other hand, involves the use, or threatened use, of force to restore peace and security where violence is ongoing or where parties have not agreed to stop fighting.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Defence to outline the safeguards and approval mechanisms that will continue to apply to the deployment of Irish Defence Forces personnel overseas under the Defence (Amendment) Bill 2026; to clarify the role of Dáil Éireann in approving such deployments; the way in which the legislation will ensure that Ireland continues to act in accordance with the UN Charter and international law:.
reply:
I wish to emphasise to the Deputy that the purpose of this piece of legislation is not to remove safeguards or approval mechanisms governing overseas deployments. Rather, it is to modernise the legislative framework while preserving democratic oversight, accountability and adherence to the principles of the UN Charter and international law.
I want to be very clear with the House that the Bill does not remove the United Nations from Ireland's framework for overseas deployments. Nor does it diminish Ireland's longstanding commitment to the United Nations, to UN peacekeeping, or to the principles and values of the UN Charter. Likewise, the Bill does not alter Ireland's policy of military neutrality or the constitutional protections relating to participation in any common defence arrangement.
The central reform proposed by the Bill is the replacement of the current requirement relating to an "international United Nations force" with the broader concept of a "relevant international force". This will allow Ireland to consider participation in a wider range of international peace support, humanitarian, monitoring and crisis-management missions where such participation is consistent with international law and supports international peace and security.
Importantly, the United Nations will continue to play a central role in that framework. Ireland will remain fully able to participate in UN-led and UN-mandated peacekeeping operations, and future deployments will continue to be assessed

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 72359/26, the evidence, data or analysis, beyond the number of persons granted family reunification permission, relied upon by the Department in deciding to change the family reunification provisions in the International Protection Act 2026, including any analysis of reliance on State supports; and whether this will be published.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1257 and 1259 together.
In preparation for the drafting of the International Protection Act 2026, my Department undertook a review of family reunification policies across EU Member States. This review examined a range of measures, including self-sufficiency, accommodation and social welfare requirements, as well as any waiting periods that apply before a sponsor may seek family reunification.
My Department also considered relevant case law to inform the legislative drafting process, including recent judgments concerning Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for private and family life and the home.
As outlined in my previous response to the Deputy, I consulted with the Attorney General during the development of the legislation. It is longstanding practice not to publish legal advice provided by the Attorney General, nor details relating to such advice. No further external consultations were undertaken by my Department.
However, a number of representations were received during the drafting process. My Department routinely receives submissions from a variety of stakeholders on legislative and policy proposals. These submissions are considered as part of the policy development process but are not routinely published.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 72353/26, whether an equality, human rights or regulatory impact assessment was carried out in respect of the policy decision, effective from 8 December 2025, to increase the reckonable residence requirement for refugees from three to five years; the date on which that decision was made; whether it was approved by Government; and whether any assessment will be published.
reply:
The standard requirement for naturalisation based on residency in the State under section 15 of the Irish Naturalisation and Citizenship Act 1956 is that the applicant has had a period of one year's continuous residence in the State immediately before the date of the application and, during the eight years immediately preceding that period, has had a total residence in the State amounting to four years - cumulatively a five-year residence requirement.
Up until 8 December 2025 Ministerial discretion was exercised in accordance with s 16 to allow for beneficiaries of international protection to be granted certificates of naturalisation where the five-year residence condition in section 15 was not met, instead they were allowed to naturalise after three years' residence.
As the policy change was one entirely within the Minister's discretion and did not involve amendments to legislation a separate, formal, Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) was not required and was not undertaken, nor was a separate, formal equality impact assessment or human rights impact assessment conducted in relation to this policy change. However, it is important to note that the fundamental rights of beneficiaries of international protection, and the Minister's obligations under the Constitution and the 1956 Act were considered in the decision to change the policy.

reply:

Character and conduct checks are also carried out before applicants can be granted any permission to remain in the State. An Garda Síochána notifies my Department of any matters that may be relevant to its considerations.
Since the introduction of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum in June of this year, all international protection applicants have been subject to a screening procedure that includes checks for security and criminality concerns, as well as identity verification. Information is shared, where appropriate, with all relevant authorities.
In addition to checks carried out on those applying for international protection, every person arriving at a port of entry in the State is subject to a Schengen Information System (SIS) check. In this regard, Ireland sends and receives SIS information, known as "alerts", relating to persons and objects. These include, for example, persons wanted by Member States for criminal purposes, missing persons, and objects that have been stolen or are sought as evidence for judicial proceedings.
