question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 72357/26, whether Chapter 3 of Part 2 of the Gambling Regulation Act 2024 has been commenced; if not, the date on which it will be commenced; and on which the National Gambling Exclusion Register will be fully operational.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1250, 1251 and 1254 together.
The regulation of the gambling sector is being overhauled through the phased commencement of the Gambling Regulation Act 2024 (the ‘2024 Act’). The 2024 Act establishes an independent agency to regulate the gambling sector, the Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland (GRAI), and ensures that the GRAI can respond appropriately to ongoing and future developments in the gambling sector.
The provisions relating to the various gambling sectors are being commenced on a phased basis to enable the development of the necessary regulatory, licensing, and compliance framework, including guidance and codes of practice where appropriate. Once commenced, Chapter 3, Part 2 of the 2024 Act provides that the GRAI shall establish and maintain a National Gambling Exclusion Register. The Register, which represents an important public health protection measure, will allow individuals to request exclusion from remote gambling indefinitely and will prevent all such Business to Consumer licensees from:
- providing gambling services to persons entered in the Register;
- accepting payments from them; and
- communicating with them in a manner that invites (or has the effect of inviting) them to participate in a relevant gambling activity.

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the reason he will not meet with the family of a person (details supplied).
reply:
I can confirm that my office has received correspondence from the family mentioned and officials from my Department have been in contact with the family directly on this matter.
Without disclosing any personal information, in some cases, a meeting with myself or my officials would likely not be of benefit - this applies particularly in the case of operational matters for organisations like An Garda Síochána or Fiosrú. I am unable to overturn or review a decision made in such cases.
The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of all Garda operational matters. Under Section 34 of the Policing Security and Community Safety Act 2024, he is independent in his functions. As a result, as Minister, I cannot intervene in or direct him in relation to any individual case.
Further, Fiosrú is the independent body responsible for receiving complaints from the public concerning members of An Garda Síochána. Neither I, as Minister, nor my Department have any role in overseeing Fiosrú's operations or investigative decisions, or in reviewing complaints.

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Defence the way in which the proposed reforms to the Triple Lock mechanism contained in the Defence (Amendment) Bill 2026 will strengthen Ireland’s capacity to participate in international peacekeeping and humanitarian missions.
reply:
Thank you Deputy for the question.
The purpose of the proposed reforms contained in the Defence (Amendment) Bill 2026 is to strengthen Ireland's capacity to contribute to international peacekeeping, peace support and humanitarian operations in an increasingly complex international security environment.
At the outset, I want to emphasise that the reforms are not intended to reduce Ireland's commitment to the United Nations or to international peacekeeping. On the contrary, Ireland remains fully committed to the principles of the UN Charter, to multilateralism, and to the important role of peacekeeping in supporting international peace and security.
Ireland has a proud record of service overseas. Since 1958, members of the Defence Forces have served with distinction on UN and UN-mandated missions across the globe, including in Lebanon, the Congo, Liberia, Chad, Mali and the Golan Heights. The Government is committed to ensuring that Ireland can continue to make meaningful contributions to such missions into the future.
The challenge with the current Triple Lock arrangements is that larger overseas deployments require not only Government approval and Dáil approval, but also a mandate from the United Nations Security Council. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 72363/26 of 13 October 2026, under the existing provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, which social welfare payments and State supports are currently taken into account in assessing an application for naturalisation; and whether internal guidance on this exists and will be published.
reply:
Under the existing provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended, there is no statutory requirement for an applicant for naturalisation to demonstrate financial self-sufficiency. Naturalisation applications are assessed on a case-by-case basis in accordance with the requirements of the 1956 Act.
Accordingly, there is no prescribed list of social welfare payments or State supports which are taken into account in assessing eligibility for naturalisation under the current legislative framework.
The Deputy will be aware that the General Scheme of the Irish Naturalisation and Citizenship (Amendment) Bill includes provisions relating to self-sufficiency and reliance on certain social protection payments. Until the new Bill is passed by Oireachtas, signed into law by the President and then enacted, all applications for a certificate of naturalisation continue to be assessed individually based on the existing provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended.

As Presidency, we are working closely with EU partners to navigate our complex and evolving threat environment, including in response to the events of recent weeks and months.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of prisoners currently accommodated otherwise than in a cell or room certified under Rule 18 of the Prison Rules 2007.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1232 and 1233 together.
As Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, I must formally certify that all cells or rooms intended for prisoner accommodation are suitable in terms of size, lighting, heating, ventilation, and available fittings in accordance with Rule 18 of the Prison Rules 2007. Rule 18 allows me to set an Operational Bed Capacity for each prison and to certify specific areas, such as special observation cells, which are strictly designated for managing prisoners who pose immediate risks of harm.
I am informed by the Irish Prison Service that no prisoners are currently accommodated somewhere other than a cell or room certified under Rule 18 of the Prison Rules 2007.
Rule 19 of the Prison Rules 2007 allows the Governor of a prison to temporarily house a prisoner outside of a certified cell or room if reasonable grounds show that exceptional circumstances exist. The Governor must notify me if this temporary placement lasts for more than 24 hours.
The Irish Prison Service have informed me that no such notifications under Rule 19(2) of the Prison Rules 2007 were issued to my office from 1 January 2023 to date.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current number of prisoners subject to rule 63; the number of such prisoners who are in single accommodation; and the number of such prisoners sharing accommodation with one or more other prisoners.
reply:
I can advise the Deputy that the Irish Prison Service has confirmed that statistics available regarding prisoners on a restricted regime are collated by the Irish Prison Service Statistics Unit and published on a quarterly basis on its website (www.irishprisons.ie). This information can be found in the Information Centre under Statistics & Information, Census Reports.
Rule 63 of the Prison Rules, 2007 provides that a prisoner may, either at their own request or when the Governor considers it necessary, in so far as is practicable and subject to the maintenance and good order and safe and secure custody, be kept separate from other prisoners who are reasonably likely to cause significant harm to them. The Governor may also seek to place a prisoner on Rule 63 if information from An Garda Síochána or other intelligence sources indicate concerns about safety.
The number of prisoners on Rule 63 fluctuates daily and the length of time spent on Rule 63 varies greatly as the level of threat and perceived threat changes. Prisoners on Rule 63 may be permitted to mix with other prisoners on Rule 63 in different risk groups.
The Irish Prison Service has advised that on 14 July 2026, the number of Rule 63 prisoners in single cell accommodation was 221 and the number of Rule 63 prisoners sharing accommodation with one or more similar prisoners was 654. This information was compiled from the July 2026 restricted regime census data, the latest validated information available.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection whether his Department has identified cases in which economically inactive EEA nationals may not satisfy the applicable conditions of residence under Directive 2004/38/EC; the number of cases that were referred to the relevant immigration authorities, in each of the years 2016 to 2025 and to date in 2026; and whether his Department receives information on any subsequent residence decisions or removals.
reply:
EU nationals have the right to move to and reside in any other EU Member State, the EEA countries (Iceland, Liechtenstein, and Norway), and Switzerland under Directive 2004/38/EC (Free Movement Directive) and the European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015 (S.I. 548 of 2015).
Nationals of Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway acquire equivalent rights through their participation in the European Economic Area (EEA) and the incorporation of Directive 2004/38/EC into the EEA Agreement. Accordingly, EEA nationals generally benefit from the same free movement and residence rights as EU nationals and are not required to obtain permission to reside in Ireland from the Department of Justice.
My department’s role is to determine eligibility for social welfare schemes in accordance with the relevant legislation and as such does not have any role in identifying economically inactive EEA nationals who may not satisfy the residence conditions provided for under Directive 2004/38/EC. Where questions arise regarding a person's entitlement to reside in the State, in the context of an application for a social welfare payment, these matters may be referred to the appropriate immigration authorities as necessary. My department does not maintain statistics on such referrals and accordingly, the information requested is not available.
Responsibility for decisions relating to residence permissions or removal from the State rests with the relevant immigration authority.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection the procedures that apply when an economically inactive EEA national claims social assistance and questions arise about their right of residence under Directive 2004/38/EC; the way in which his Department liaises with immigration authorities in such cases; and the number of cases that have resulted in a referral to immigration authorities, in each of the years 2016 to 2025 and to date in 2026.
reply:
EU nationals have the right to move to and reside in any other EU Member State, the EEA countries (Iceland, Liechtenstein, and Norway), and Switzerland under Directive 2004/38/EC (Free Movement Directive) and the European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015 (S.I. 548 of 2015).
Nationals of Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway acquire equivalent rights through their States’ participation in the European Economic Area (EEA) and the incorporation of Directive 2004/38/EC into the EEA Agreement. Accordingly, EEA nationals generally benefit from the same free movement and residence rights as EU nationals and they are not required to obtain a residency permit or permission to reside in Ireland from the Department of Justice to exercise those rights.
Where an EEA national applies for certain social assistance payments they must satisfy the Habitual Residence Condition (HRC). The HRC assessment consists of two parts, both of which must be satisfied and requires a person to (1) have a right to reside in Ireland and (2) show that they are habitually resident using the five factors outlined in legislation. Where the HRC is a qualifying condition for entitlement to a scheme, an EU/EEA citizen’s right to reside is the first factor considered as part of the HRC assessment.
Where questions arise regarding an applicant's right of residence, Department officials will examine all relevant facts and documentation available to them and, where necessary, may engage with the Immigr

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will review the eligibility criteria for the €500 cost of disability lump sum payment announced in Budget 2027, to ensure that persons with disabilities who have transitioned from invalidity pension or other disability payments to the State Pension upon reaching 66 years-of-age are not excluded from the payment solely on the basis of age.
reply:

I recognise that disabled people of any age can incur additional costs. The Budget package includes a range of measures to support people in receipt of a State Pension as well as disabled people.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will consider a request from a person (details supplied) regarding back payment of pension.
reply:

reply:

The payment is made for 28 weeks over the winter season - usually from late September to early April. The current weekly rate is €38.00 or, if preferred, by way of two instalments - one of €532.00 in late September/early October and one in January.
In line with Budget 2027, the Fuel Allowance rate is increasing by €5.00 per week to €43.00, effective from week commencing 4th January 2027. Fuel Allowance is administered across many qualifying social welfare schemes, ranging from jobseeker's payments, to disability related payments and pensions. All officers deciding Fuel Allowance applications undergo training to ensure that decisions are made in accordance with the scheme guidelines. In addition, quality checking of decisions made is also conducted.
Where errors are identified, steps are taken to correct the error as soon as possible, including providing additional training, where appropriate.

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Social Protection the status of the carer's allowance claim for a person (details supplied) now that the person requiring care has returned home from hospital.
reply:
Carer's allowance (CA) is a means-tested social assistance payment made to a person who is habitually resident in the State and who is providing full-time care and attention to a child or an adult who has such a disability that, as a result, they require that level of care.
I can confirm the person concerned is in receipt of CA since 15 May 2025.
A carer may continue to be regarded as providing full-time care and attention to a person while the person being cared for is undergoing medical or other treatment in a hospital or other institution for a period not longer than 13 weeks.
Following receipt of the requested documents, CA has been reinstated. Payment will issue to the nominated bank account of the person concerned on 05 November 2026. Any arrears due will issue shortly.
The person concerned was notified of this decision in writing on 29 October 2026.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will review a case (details supplied) of a person who had made Class A PRSI contributions to ensure they are provided the corresponding pension.
reply:
As the person concerned has not yet reached pension age, it is not possible at this stage to determine whether they will qualify for a State Pension (contributory), or the rate that may be payable. Entitlement to State Pension (contributory) is not based solely on having paid Class A PRSI contributions. Qualification depends on satisfying the statutory conditions in force when pension age is reached, including the relevant social insurance contribution requirements, with entitlement assessed based on the person's full social insurance record.
A decision was made by Scope Section in 2023 that the persons employment from 01 January 2018 to 07 April 2022 was covered by the subsidiary employment regulations of S.I. 312 of 1996 was insurable for occupational injury benefit only at PRSI Class J for their subsidiary employment.
Both the person concerned and their employer were notified of Scope’s decision.
As the person paid a Class AO which was converted to a Class J , based on their subsidiary employment, there was no refund due to the individual as Class J contributions are not liable for employee PRSI.
The person concerned can check their social insurance record by requesting a statement through MyWelfare.ie. This statement will provide a summary of their PRSI contributions and credits up to the end of the last tax year. It should be noted that the statement is not a forecast of the State Pension.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Defence to outline the implications of the winding down of UNIFIL for Ireland's longstanding peacekeeping contribution in Lebanon; to explain the opportunities for continued Irish participation in international peace support operations, including any future EU mission; and to clarify the way in which the existing triple lock requirements could affect Ireland's ability to participate.
reply:
Deputy, Ireland's contribution to the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, UNIFIL, represents one of the most significant commitments in the history of the Defence Forces. Since 1978, more than 30,000 members of the Defence Forces have served in Lebanon in pursuit of peace and stability, and their professionalism, courage and sacrifice have earned Ireland an international reputation as a respected peacekeeping nation.
As the House will be aware, the mandate of UNIFIL is currently due to conclude on 31 December 2026, with a drawdown and withdrawal phase planned during 2027. Earlier this year, the Government approved the continued participation of the Defence Forces in the mission through its final operational phase and into the withdrawal period, ensuring that Ireland will continue to play its full part in supporting a safe, orderly and coordinated conclusion to the mission. Ireland currently maintains approximately 350 personnel in theatre, including an infantry battalion and personnel serving in headquarters appointments.
While the planned conclusion of UNIFIL will bring to a close almost five decades of continuous Irish service in Lebanon, it does not mark the end of Ireland's commitment to international peacekeeping. Ireland's commitment has always been to the principles of peacekeeping rather than to any single mission, and we remain committed to playing a meaningful role in international efforts to maintain peace and stability.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection if his Department has assessed the number of retired CIÉ pensioners and former public servants who are living alone and are excluded from the living alone increase solely because they are in receipt of an occupational pension rather than a qualifying social welfare payment; and whether he will consider extending eligibility to this cohort.
reply:
My Department does not hold data on the number of retired CIÉ pensioners or former public servants living alone who are not in receipt of a qualifying primary social welfare payment and, consequently, do not qualify for the Living Alone Increase.
There are currently no plans to extend eligibility for the Living Alone Increase to people living alone who are not in receipt of a qualifying primary social welfare payment. Any proposal to do so would have significant policy and cost implications and would need to be considered in the wider budgetary and policy context.

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Social Protection the evidence on which reserve service in the Defence Forces is designated as subsidiary employment under Schedule C, paragraph 4 of S.I. 312 of 1996; when that designation was last reviewed; and the way in which it is consistent with the statement of the Minister for Defence that each case is determined on its own facts.
reply:
Determining the correct PRSI class is the responsibility of the employer or, for self-employed individuals, themselves. For members of the Reserve Defence Forces, the Department of Defence is responsible for determining whether their employment qualifies as subsidiary under Schedule C, paragraph 4 of S.I. No. 312/1996.
Statutory Instrument 26 of 1970 provided for the exception from insurance under the Social Welfare Acts of employment for short periods as members of An Fórsa Cosanta Áitiúil or An Slua Muirí, now the Reserve Defence Force.
It is my understanding that the Reserve Defence Force is a part-time, volunteer organisation. Members are free to determine their own level of participation in Reserve activities and may resign from the Reserve at any time. Their service is provided entirely on a voluntary basis with no compulsion to attend.
Consequently, service as a member of the Reserve Defence Force for a period not exceeding 21 consecutive days is not considered insurable employment for social insurance purposes as this employment is considered to be subsidiary employment only and not the principal means of livelihood. PRSI Class M applies in these cases and therefore no PRSI is liable. PRSI Class M does not provide entitlement to any social insurance benefits.
For those who undertake more than 21 consecutive days service, they are liable to pay PRSI under Class H. Class H contributions can be used to qualify for most of the social insurance benefits available.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Social Protection to review the decision to disallow entitlement to the State pension or a disability allowance payment when a person inherits shares in an organisation (details supplied) and ensure that they are at least entitled to a reduced payment on a weekly basis.
reply:
Social welfare legislation provides that means tests take account of the income and assets of the person (and their spouse or partner) applying for the relevant scheme. The means assessment includes income from sources such as employment, self-employment, and occupational pensions. It also includes property owned, other than the family home, and capital such as savings, shares, and other investments.
In the case of any shares, including in this case Kerry Group shares, it is the market value of the shares that is taken into account, and a formula that is set out in legislation is applied to determine how the value of the shares is incorporated into the means test.
In the means assessment for a personal rate of the State Pension (Non-Contributory), for example, the first €20,000 (or €40,000 for a couple) of capital an applicant holds is fully disregarded; the next €10,000 is assessed at €1 per thousand; the next €10,000 is assessed at €2 per thousand, with the remainder assessed at €4 per thousand. Under this system people with capital assets of up to €111,000 - excluding the value of their family home - can still receive a partial pension payment.
The assessment of capital reflects an expectation that people with reasonable amounts of capital and property are in a position to use that capital to support themselves without having to rely solely on a means-tested welfare payment. question: Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Social Protection the COAP amount a person will receive who starts work as a nurse at 36 years-of-age in 2006 and they retire on 1 January 2036 at 66 years-of-age with 30 years of stamps (1,560 in total).

It is advisable that the person concerned maintains their social insurance record by continuing to pay PRSI while in insurable employment or self-employment. Periods covered by credited contributions during unemployment, illness, or certain caring responsibilities, can also help to maintain this record.
In addition, Long-Term Carer's Contributions may be awarded to a person who has provided care for an incapacitated person for 20 years or more. These contributions are treated in the same way as paid contributions for the purposes of state pension contribu

question: Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Social Protection the OAP amount (not COAP) a person with no stamps having not worked, would receive who is 66 on 1 January 2036.
reply:
State Pension (non-contributory) is a means tested scheme. Items which count as means include cash income, including foreign pensions, the value of any property (excluding a person’s own home) and the value of any savings and investments which a person or their spouse, civil partner or cohabitant may have. In order to qualify for the State Pension (non-contributory) a person must be habitually resident in the State.
It is not possible to confirm the rate of payment that may be payable in 2036 at this stage. Any entitlement and corresponding rate of payment will be assessed based on the legislation, qualifying conditions, and payment rates applicable in 2036.
Currently, if a person satisfies the qualifying criteria for state pension non-contributory, the rate of payment ranges from €3.00 per week up to the maximum rate of €288.00 per week.
In January 2024, a new Long-Term Carers Contribution scheme was introduced. Under the scheme, a person who has been a full-time carer for an incapacitated dependent for at least 20 years (1,040 weeks), can get Long-Term Carers Contributions which can help them qualify for the State Pension Contributory.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Social Protection further to Parliamentary Question No. 55066/25, whether purchase orders raised by his Department under procurement contracts can be linked to the relevant contract recorded in its internal contract register; whether a common contract reference or other identifier is maintained to enable this linkage; if not, the way in which his Department reconciles expenditure against individual contracts and monitors cumulative payments against their approved values.
reply:
My Department has robust governance arrangements in place to support effective procurement and contract management. A central register of all awarded contracts is maintained by the Project Office and Procurement Policy Unit.
A contract reference number, where applicable, is recorded on the contract register and is also included on associated purchase orders and within the Department's financial management system, enabling expenditure to be linked to the relevant contract.
The Department operates a range of controls to monitor expenditure against contractual commitments. These include regular monitoring of payments and purchase orders, with all purchase orders in excess of €20,000 subject to quarterly review to ensure compliance with public procurement procedures and internal governance requirements. These measures support the reconciliation of expenditure against individual contracts and facilitate ongoing oversight of cumulative spend relative to the approved contract values.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Social Protection further to Parliamentary Question No. 661 of 14 October 2025 (55066/25), whether contracts recorded in his Department's contract register include the eTenders contract award notice reference or URL where available; if not, whether another identifier is maintained to link contracts with published award notices; whether such information could be included in the Department's purchase-order reports without integrating financial systems with eTenders; and, if not, to outline the specific technical or operational barriers to doing so.
reply:
My Department has a robust governance process in place to assure the proper control of projects and expenditure, which has ensured delivery in accordance with the approved budgets and agreed timeframes.
A central register of all awarded contracts is maintained by the Project Office and Procurement Policy Unit. Once a tender competition has concluded and a contract has been awarded, expenditure is managed through the Department's internal financial management system. This system is separate from the national eTenders platform and also operates independently of the Department's internal contract register, which is used to record contract management information.
The contract register does not currently record a link or reference to the associated contract award notice published on eTenders. Rather, it records key contract information, including details of the procurement process used.
As the Department's financial management system, contract register and the eTenders system operate as separate platforms, information relating to eTenders award notices is not captured as a standard data field within purchase order records or related expenditure reports. However, the contract register number is captured on the purchase orders and the financial management system. The inclusion of the contract register number assists the monitoring of expenditure.
The inclusion of the award notice published on eTenders would not enhance this process and would require a reengineering of existing robus

reply: In accordance with Circular 25/2025 requirements for Appropriation Account 2025, the €568 million published in the Department's 2025 account Statement on internal financial control represents the total procurement expenditure by the Department in 2025.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Social Protection whether a dedicated paid benefit for parents of children born through surrogacy will be introduced; and the proposed timeframe for same.
reply:
The Programme for Government includes a commitment to the introduction of paid surrogacy leave. My colleague the Minister for Health has responsibility for the Health (Assisted Human Reproduction) Act 2024, which was signed into law in July 2024. This complex and far-reaching legislation encompasses the regulation for the first time of a wide range of practices undertaken in this jurisdiction, including domestic altruistic surrogacy, but also provides for the regulation of future surrogacy arrangements undertaken by Irish residents in other jurisdictions.
In addition, the legislation allows for the recognition of parentage arising from past domestic and international surrogacy arrangements.
The implementation of this legislation is a prerequisite for the introduction of surrogacy leave and the payment by my Department of an associated benefit.

question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of people in receipt of a State pension, both contributory and non, who have had their fuel allowance withdrawn from them because there is a non-qualifying person living in the house with them, in each of the past three years, in tabular form.
reply:
The Fuel Allowance scheme is a means-tested payment designed to assist pensioners and other long-term social welfare dependent households with their winter heating costs. The allowance is intended as a contribution towards heating expenses and is not designed to meet these costs in full. I was pleased to announce, as part of Budget 2027, that Fuel Allowance will increase to €43 per week from January 2027.
Due to the way Fuel Allowance operates as an additional payment on top of an underlying qualifying scheme, this involves multiple different operational systems. Fuel Allowance processing statistics, including refusals, are collected on an annual, rather than monthly, basis due to the complexity involved, and are subsequently published in the Departments Annual Statistics Report, available from gov.ie/dsp/statistics.
I am conscious that there may be exceptional circumstances where a person does not qualify for Fuel Allowance but nonetheless requires financial support. In such cases, assistance may be available through the Additional Needs Payment scheme, which forms part of the Supplementary Welfare Allowance system. Additional Needs Payments are intended to assist with essential expenses that a person cannot meet from their weekly income or other personal and household resources. Any person who considers they may have an entitlement is encouraged to phone Lo-call 0818 607080 to find their local Community Welfare Office or apply online through their MyWelfare account.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will consider introducing measures to ensure that persons with lifelong disabilities who inherit assets from their parents or guardians for the purpose of their future care and well-being are not disadvantaged through inheritance tax liabilities or the loss of means-tested supports, including disability allowance and medical card eligibility.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1201 and 1206 together.
Disability Allowance is my Department’s primary disability-related social assistance scheme. It is a means-tested payment for people with a disability aged between 16 and 66. To qualify, a person must have a disability that has continued, or is expected to continue, for at least one year and, as a result of that disability, be substantially restricted in undertaking work that would otherwise be suitable having regard to their age, experience and qualifications. Eligibility is also subject to satisfying the habitual residence condition.
Social welfare legislation provides that, for means-tested social assistance schemes, all income and assets belonging to the claimant, and their spouse or partner, where applicable, is assessable. This recognises the fact that couples operate as a single household and can share living expenses in a manner not available to a single person. The means test takes account of the income a person or couple has in terms of cash, property – other than the family home – and capital.
Where an adult with a disability resides with their parents or other family members, the income of their parents or other family members is not assessed when applying for Disability Allowance, only income and assets belonging to the claimant are assessed.
The purpose of a means test is to ensure that scarce resources are directed to those with the greatest need and it supports an economically sustainable and socially eq

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Social Protection whether he will consider reviewing and increasing the fuel allowance income threshold for single and widowed pensioners to reflect the cost of heating a home, given the disparity between the income limits for single people and couples.
reply:
Fuel Allowance eligibility encompasses 22 qualifying schemes, demonstrating the comprehensive nature of the support available to eligible households. In addition to these qualifying schemes, people over 66 do not need to be in receipt of a payment from this Department to qualify for Fuel Allowance, subject to satisfying a means test. According to the latest CSO data, there are just over 1.8 million households in Ireland. Of these, 466,723 households are eligible for the Fuel Allowance scheme, representing approximately 26% of all households nationwide.
In Budget 2027, I announced a Social Protection Budget package worth over €30 billion, an increase of €2 billion on 2026. This included a package of targeted measures to protect pensioners, support carers, lift more children out of poverty, and help disabled people with the cost of disability.
These targeted measures include that from January 2027 the weekly allowable means of a single person aged 66 or over for Fuel Allowance purposes will increase from €534 to €653. This is a 20% increase in the allowable means and will allow more single pensioners to qualify for the Fuel Allowance payment.
Any decision to further increase the weekly allowable means of a single person aged 66 or over would have to be considered in the context of scheme policy and future budgetary negotiations.
Budget 2027 also provides for a €10 across the board increase to scheme payments including the State Pension and the Bereaved Partners Pension, as well

question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Social Protection if there are free travel entitlements for cancer patients to travel to and from hospital appointments.
reply:
The Free Travel scheme permits travel on most CIE public transport services as well as Luas, Local Link and some 71 private operators. Free travel is also available on cross border journeys to and from Northern Ireland, and for those over age 66, within Northern Ireland. The Free Travel Scheme is available to all persons aged over 66 who are living legally and permanently in the State.
It is important to note that, in general, access to a free travel pass for those aged under 66 is a secondary benefit linked to a person being in receipt of certain primary Social Protection payments.
However, individuals who have never been medically fit to drive due to a disability or are medically certified as unfit to drive for a period of at least 12 months can qualify for the Free Travel Scheme. There is no requirement that a person must be in receipt of a Social Welfare payment or any means limits in order to qualify for a Free Travel Pass on these medical grounds, provided the other qualifying criteria are met.
As many illnesses or physical conditions have an impact ranging from mild to severe, entitlement to these social welfare schemes is not provided on the basis of a diagnosis but on the basis of the impact of that diagnosis on the individual concerned. question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Social Protection his current plans to address issues with parents who are transgender not being recognised as the parents of their children.
reply:
The legislation governing the registering of a birth is set out in the Civil Registration Act (2004). The required particulars of the parent(s) of a child to be recorded in the birth registration include the sex of the parent.
Where the gender of the person who gives birth to the child is female, that person can select "mother" or "parent" as their label on the child's birth certificate.
Where the gender of the person who gives birth to the child is male, that person can only select "parent" as their label on the child's birth certificate.
Where the gender of the other parent is female, that person can only select "parent" as their label on the child's birth certificate.
Where the gender of the other parent is male, that person can select "father" or "parent" as their label on the child's birth certificate.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection whether retired members of occupational defined benefit pension schemes have any statutory right to nominate or be represented on the trustee boards of their schemes under the Pensions Act 1990 and associated regulations; whether the Pensions Authority holds data on the number of schemes with a pensioner trustee; whether he will consider legislating to provide for at least one retired member representative on such boards.
reply:
Under section 62 of the Pensions Act 1990, as amended, members (active and pensioner) of relevant schemes have a statutory right to participate in member trustee selection procedures, where the scheme is subject to the member participation provisions of Part VI of that Act and the regulations made thereunder, namely, the Occupational Pension Schemes (Member Participation in the Selection of Persons for Appointment as Trustees) Regulations 1996. Those regulations define 'relevant scheme' as meaning occupational pension schemes established under trust with a total of 50 or more qualified members and certain smaller schemes.
The Act does not provide a statutory right to guaranteed representation for pensioner members or active members on trustee boards rather it provides an opportunity for membership from each cohort and such members may avail of the opportunity to become scheme trustees or nominate others to act on their behalf.
The Pensions Authority does not hold data on the number of schemes with a pensioner trustee.
Pension scheme trustees have duties and responsibilities under the Pension Act 1990, as amended, under trust law and under other relevant legislation. The duties of pension scheme trustees include administering the scheme in accordance with the law and the terms of the trust deed and scheme rules as well as ensuring compliance with the requirements that apply to these schemes. Trustees must act in the best financial interests of all scheme members, whether activ

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will review the impact of inheritance and means-testing rules on persons with lifelong disabilities who inherit assets from their parents; and if he will consider exempting such inheritances from assessments affecting entitlement to disability allowance, medical cards and related supports.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1201 and 1206 together.
Disability Allowance is my Department’s primary disability-related social assistance scheme. It is a means-tested payment for people with a disability aged between 16 and 66. To qualify, a person must have a disability that has continued, or is expected to continue, for at least one year and, as a result of that disability, be substantially restricted in undertaking work that would otherwise be suitable having regard to their age, experience and qualifications. Eligibility is also subject to satisfying the habitual residence condition.
Social welfare legislation provides that, for means-tested social assistance schemes, all income and assets belonging to the claimant, and their spouse or partner, where applicable, is assessable. This recognises the fact that couples operate as a single household and can share living expenses in a manner not available to a single person. The means test takes account of the income a person or couple has in terms of cash, property – other than the family home – and capital.
Where an adult with a disability resides with their parents or other family members, the income of their parents or other family members is not assessed when applying for Disability Allowance, only income and assets belonging to the claimant are assessed.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Defence if she will provide an update on the implementation of the Defence Forces Cyber Defence Strategy 2024-2027; the progress made to date; the key milestones outstanding; and the timeline for their delivery.
reply:

The implementation of the strategy is primarily a matter for the Defence Forces. question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Social Protection if a review will be carried out on a person's (details supplied) State pension (contributory) rate.
reply:
The person concerned reached pension age on 31 October 2018. The state pension contributory was awarded from their 66th birthday.
Following the award of Pension Caring Supports, their entitlement was reviewed. A revised decision issued on 18 November 2025 advising that there was no change to the rate of pension in payment.
The records held by my Department show that the person concerned has 591 paid contributions and 701 credited contributions from their entry into insurable employment on 6 April 1979 to the date they reached pension age on 31 October 2018. In addition, they were awarded the Homemaker's Scheme from 6 April 1994 to 26 July 2000 and HomeCaring Periods from 13 July 1983 to 26 July 2000.
Their entitlement to State Pension Contributory was assessed under both the Yearly Average method and the Total Contributions Approach (TCA). The Yearly Average calculation gave the person concerned a rate of 89.9% of the maximum personal rate, while the TCA calculation gave a rate of 78.41%.
As the Yearly Average method was financially more beneficial to the person concerned, they were awarded state pension contributory based on this calculation method.
I note that the case is currently under appeal with the Social Welfare Appeals Office. The appeal is being considered, and a decision will issue in due course.
I trust this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Social Protection his views on whether fair and due process has occurred regarding a social welfare appeal for a person (details supplied) that was submitted over seven years ago in 2019, with the appeal to now be heard and adjudicated on.
reply:
The person concerned received a revised decision under Section 302 (a) of the Social Welfare Consolidation Act in relation to his Jobseeker’s Allowance. The revised decision stated that he had not shown that his weekly means were less than the rate of Jobseeker’s Allowance that would be paid to a person of his family size and circumstances under Section 141 (1) (c) off the Act.
The person concerned submitted an appeal against the decision he received. An oral hearing was scheduled to take palace in August 2020 but not all parties were available to attend. There was correspondence and activity on the appeal up to that point and this continued into 2021 but the oral hearing wasn't rescheduled.
The information that the Social Welfare Appeals Office has on this appeal is on a legacy appeal system. Given that there was no recent activity when data on appeals was transferred to a new system in 2023, this appeal wasn't moved to the new system.
In order to finalise the appeal and give the appellant an opportunity to provide any relevant evidence and outline his grounds of appeal in person, an Appeals Officer has written to the appellant to arrange an oral hearing on a date in November.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Defence to clarify if the Government are considering taking out a loan under the EU’s Security Action For Europe Programme.
reply:
The Security Action for Europe (SAFE) instrument entered into force on 29 May 2025 and provides EU Member States with access to up to €150 billion in EU-backed loans to support defence investment.
Following consultation with the Department of Finance and the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, a decision was taken in August 2025 that Ireland would not seek to avail of the SAFE loan mechanism at that time. However, Ireland remains fully engaged with SAFE and is committed to participating in joint procurement opportunities where these align with defence capability requirements and represent value for money.
The SAFE Regulation offers Member States a mechanism to enhance defence capabilities through collaborative procurement. The Department of Defence will continue to examine opportunities under the Regulation where these support the delivery of identified capability requirements. Joint procurement can provide greater purchasing power, improved access to defence equipment and potential cost efficiencies when compared with individual national procurement.
A second SAFE call, announced by the European Commission on 29 October 2026, makes available €21.3 billion in remaining SAFE funding. question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Social Protection the plans his Department has to reform the working family payment.
reply:
The Working Family Payment is a tax-free income support designed to prevent in-work poverty for low paid employees with children, and to offer a financial incentive to take-up employment.
As of September 2026, there were 58,010 families in receipt of Working Family Payment.
The Government has demonstrated its commitment to supporting low-income working families through significant increases to the Working Family Payment thresholds in recent budgets. Since 2020, the threshold for a one-child household has increased by over 40%, from €531 to €765. In this year’s budget I announced a further increase to all thresholds of €30. In addition, entitlement to Fuel Allowance was extended to recipients of Working Family Payment from the start of 2026.
My Department is currently undertaking broader policy work on the future design of working-age and child income supports. The Programme for Government includes commitments to introduce a new Working Age Payment and to explore a Targeted Child Payment. These represent potentially significant reforms of the existing system of income supports.
The Working Age Payment is being examined as a more flexible payment for people of working age, whether unemployed or on a low income. A key objective is to reduce the cliff edges which can arise under the current system and ensure that people see a financial benefit when they take up additional work.

Employees between 16 and pensionable age, currently 66 years of age, and those born on or after 1 January 1958 aged between 66 and 70 years who have not been awarded the State Pension (Contributory) are liable for Pay Related Social Insurance (PRSI). The class and rate of contribution payable is determined by the nature of the employment and the persons weekly earnings.
If the wrong PRSI rate has been deducted from a person’s wages or income, they can apply to my department for a refund. Applications for the last 4 complete tax years can be made online at MyWelfare. If a person cannot access the online system, the application form ‘Employee Refund of PRSI contributions (PRSI REF1)’ can be download from Gov.ie and posted to the Department of Social Protection, Gandon House, Amiens Street, Dublin 1, D01 A361.
A PRSI REF1 has issued to the person concerned on 22/10/2026 and on receipt of the completed form, it will be submitted to Scope Section of the Department for a decision on the insurability of all the employments of the person concerned.
The person concerned can also check their social insurance record by requesting a statement through MyWelfare.ie. This statement will provide a summary of their PRSI contributions and credits up to the end of the last tax year.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Defence to put their proposals to remove the triple lock neutrality protection before the Irish people via referendum.
reply:
There have been a number of calls for a referendum or public plebiscite on the Government’s proposed changes to the Triple Lock, either to enshrine neutrality in the Constitution or to vote directly on the legislative amendments. Many of these calls incorrectly conflate an amendment to legislation, which the Defence Amendment Bill proposes, with an amendment to the Constitution.
The Triple Lock is not a constitutional provision. Ireland was a militarily neutral country before the introduction of the Triple Lock, and it will remain a militarily neutral country after the legislation is passed. Our military neutrality remains grounded in Ireland’s long-standing policy of non-participation in military alliances.
The proposed amendments do not alter this traditional position of military neutrality, despite the repeated and misinformed claims from certain quarters. Any overseas deployment of Defence Forces personnel will continue to be based on the principles of the UN Charter and international law, and will require the approval of Ireland’s democratically elected representatives.
It is important to emphasise most strongly again that the Bill does not remove the United Nations from Ireland's framework for overseas deployments. Nor does it diminish Ireland's longstanding commitment to the United Nations, to UN peacekeeping, or to the principles of the UN Charter. question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will provide an update on the review of the household package which is a commitment in the Programme for Government.
reply:
The Programme for Government includes a commitment to examine key ancillary benefits such as the fuel allowance, household benefits package and living alone allowance to support vulnerable groups. This is an ongoing activity as part of the Department's budget planning each year.
Given the many competing demands for the limited funding available to the Department, Budget 2027, provided for increases to primary Social Welfare payments as well as increases to targeted payments, such as Fuel Allowance and the Living Alone Increase.
From January 2027, Budget 2027 has provided for a €5 weekly increase to the Fuel Allowance payment. Over the last two budgets the weekly rate of Fuel Allowance payable has increased by 30%.
Furthermore, the weekly allowable means of a single person aged 66 or over will be increased from €534 to €653. This is a 20% increase in the allowable means and will allow more single pensioners to qualify for the Fuel Allowance payment.
Fuel Allowance eligibility encompasses 22 qualifying schemes, demonstrating the comprehensive nature of the support available to eligible households. In addition to these qualifying schemes, people over 66 do not need to be in receipt of a payment from this Department to qualify for Fuel Allowance, subject to satisfying a means test. According to the latest CSO data, there are just over 1.8 million households in Ireland. question: Deputy Holly Cairns asked the Minister for Social Protection to outline the reasoning for a disparity by which people on job initiative (JI) schemes must retire at 68 years-of-age on the basic State pension, with no option to extend, while supervisors of these schemes are permitted to extend their working lives up to 70 years-of-age; and if this disparity will be addressed.
reply:
Job Initiative (JI) is an employment support scheme which was designed to provide eligible long-term unemployed people and other disadvantaged persons with an opportunity to engage in useful work within their communities. Recruitment onto the scheme ceased from November 2004, while existing participants can have their annual contracts renewed until they reach 66 years of age.
In response to the recommendations from the Commission on Pensions, a set of new pension measures were approved by Cabinet in September 2022. The set of reforms agreed included maintaining the State pension age at 66 and introducing a new flexible pension model, which came into effect from January 2024, whereby people have the option to continue working up until the age of 70 in return for a higher pension.
The new measures are specifically for people in standard employment situations and do not apply to State supported schemes like JI, where the participant qualifies due to having been on a specific social welfare payment in advance of their placement on the scheme.
Accordingly, the position regarding funding for participants on employment support schemes, including the JI scheme, remains the same. Funding for participants will continue to be available to State Pension Age, which is currently 66.
Should participants wish to continue to work after they reach 66, it is open to them to apply for positions that are not state funded.

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Social Protection if he has considered providing a full carer's payment for those on a State pension (contributory).
reply:
The Government recognises the invaluable contribution made by our family carers, often over many years and into pension age.
Generally under the single payment per person rule, where a person qualifies for more than one social welfare payment, they receive the higher payment.
However, in recognition of the important contribution made by carers, an exception applies where a person who is receiving a primary social welfare payment and who is also providing full-time care and attention may receive a half-rate Carer's Allowance in addition to their main payment. This arrangement applies to almost all weekly social welfare payments, including the State pension.
There are currently more than 112,000 people receiving Carer’s Allowance, at an estimated cost of more than €1.4 billion in 2026. Of these, 52,377 are receiving their full primary social welfare payment together with a half-rate Carer's Allowance payment.
Currently, eligible Carer’s Allowance recipients who qualify for the full State Pension (Contributory) see the amount they receive each week increase from €270 to €453.30 at age 66, an increase of €183.30 per week. Following Budget 2027, from next January the weekly payment will further increase from €453.30 to €468.30, an increase of €15 per week.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Social Protection if written instructions have been issued to deciding officers or other social welfare staff concerning applications submitted before January 2027 by applicants who will now qualify under the revised fuel allowance income thresholds; if existing applications awaiting a decision be will reassessed automatically, or if applicants must contact the Department or submit a new application; the arrangements being made to process the expected increase in applications; if there is a timeframe for decisions; and if eligible applicants will retain their original application date for payment purposes.
reply:
The Fuel Allowance scheme is a means-tested payment to assist pensioners and other long-term social welfare dependent householders with their winter heating costs. The payment is made for 28 weeks over the winter season - usually from late September to early April. The current weekly rate is €38.00 or, if preferred, by way of two instalments - one of €532.00 in late September/early October and one in January.
In line with Budget 2027, the Fuel Allowance rate is increasing by €5.00 per week to €43.00, effective from week commencing 4th January 2027. For those who opt to receive the allowance by two instalment payments, the January instalment payment will amount to €602.00. Only one Fuel Allowance is payable per household. Those who qualify for the allowance do not need to reapply annually.
Fuel Allowance applications currently being received are initially being assessed based on the 2026 means assessment. If the customer doesn’t satisfy the 2026 means assessment, their entitlement to Fuel Allowance under the 2027 means assessment is also being considered and they are being informed of the outcome. Customers will not need to contact the department or to re-apply.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Social Protection the value of social-welfare payments issued after the recorded date of a recipient’s death in each of the years from 2022 to 2025 and to date in 2026; the amount recovered, written off or remaining outstanding; the average interval between notification of death and termination of payment; the number of estates contacted for repayment; and whether delays in data transmission between the Civil Registration Service and his Department contributed to any such payments.
reply:
The Department recognises the need for a transition period during which people can grieve following the death of a family member. Within the social welfare system, there are a number of supports for those in receipt of a pension who suffer a bereavement. In particular, there is an arrangement known as the six-weeks payment after death which allows for certain payments to continue to be made after a person dies.
Where a deceased person has been in receipt of a social welfare payment the next of kin or personal representatives should notify my Department of the death directly, by telephone or in writing, pending issuance of the death certificate. The person’s payment can thus be suspended for review of the pension claim, not only to minimise potential overpayments of pension, but also to ascertain if further payments are due to the next of kin, where there may be uncollected payments at date of death or where there may be an entitlement to six weeks' payment after death to a surviving spouse, civil partner or cohabitant.
The Civil Registration Act 2004 also places a legal obligation on the relatives, and other named parties in the absence of a relative, to register the death of a person and to do this within three months of the person dying. Once a death is registered, the Department of Social Protection is automatically informed of the death and any social welfare entitlements in payment will be stopped. This also minimises the potential for any overpayment to occur.

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Social Protection if he is aware of an anomaly in PRSI contributions (details supplied).
reply:
The Treatment Benefit scheme provides dental, optical, aural services and hair replacement products to insured workers, the self-employed, retired people and their dependent spouse or partner who have the required number of social insurance contributions. Government has provided €190 million for the scheme in 2026.
Contributions made under social insurance (PRSI) Classes A, E, P, H or S count towards eligibility for Treatment Benefit. The amount of social insurance contributions required depends on the person's age, taking into account their opportunity to have accumulated contributions.
To qualify for Treatment Benefit, a person under 21 years of age is only required to have paid at least 39 qualifying contributions at any time.
To qualify for Treatment Benefit at age 21-28 a person needs to demonstrate a stronger attachment to the workforce and have at least 39 PRSI contributions paid and have at least 39 paid or credited contributions in the governing contribution year (2024 is the governing contribution year for claims made in 2026) or 26 paid contributions in each of the second and third last contribution years (for claims made in 2026, the second last contribution year is 2024 and the third last contribution year is 2023).
I am advised that the person referred to by Deputy will have an entitlement to the scheme in January 2027.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Social Protection whether all roles within his Department are covered by a current safety statement and risk assessment in accordance with health and safety legislation; and whether these documents are available to staff on request.
reply:
The Department takes its obligations under the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 very seriously. This commitment is supported by a dedicated Health and Safety Unit, which provides advice, support, and training to staff on health and safety matters and ensures compliance with all relevant health and safety legislation.
All roles within the Department of Social Protection are covered by current Safety Statements and Risk Assessments in accordance with legislative requirements.
The Department uses standard Safety Statement and Risk Assessment templates across both Head Office and Regional Office locations. These documents are completed, reviewed, and maintained locally to ensure they reflect the specific hazards, activities, and working environments of each office. In addition, the Department has five Regional Safety Advisors who conduct inspections of Department buildings to help ensure compliance with the Act.
Safety Statements and Risk Assessments are available to all staff and can be accessed through internal SharePoint sites, displayed on staff notice boards, or provided upon request.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of protected disclosures made by staff of his Department in each of the past five years; the measures in place to protect reporting persons from penalisation; and whether any review has been undertaken of the effectiveness of those protections.
reply:
The Protected Disclosures Act 2014, as amended by the Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 2022, provides a framework for workers to report relevant wrongdoing and protects them from penalisation for doing so. My Department is committed to providing a clear, accessible and confidential process through which workers can raise concerns, and to ensuring that reports received are assessed and followed up in a fair, proportionate and timely manner and in accordance with the law. The Department has in place policies and procedures for the making of protected disclosures and is committed to protecting workers against penalisation for having reported concerns about wrongdoing in the workplace, and will take any necessary action where reports of penalisation are made. These policies and procedures have been developed in line with the Act, and agreed by the Department’s Management Board. The operation of the procedures is reported on an ongoing basis to the Department's Management Board and Audit and Risk Committee. The assessment and management of reports is assigned to a group of nominated senior managers within the Department. All reports received under the Act are assessed. Following assessment, it may be determined that the matters raised do not meet the legislative criteria of a Protected Disclosure, or that the report refers to matters under the remit of the Department which require follow-up action.

question: Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Defence the measures the Department is taking to support the mental health and wellbeing of serving members of the Defence Forces; and the supports that are currently available to personnel.
reply:
Thank you Deputy for raising this important issue. I can assure the Deputy that the health and wellbeing of the men and women of the Defence Forces is something I care deeply about as Minister for Defence. Medical mental health services available to personnel include access to clinical psychology and psychiatry services. The psychology service assesses, diagnoses, treats and advises on strategies to prevent mental health disorders, while psychiatry services specialise in the assessment, diagnosis and treatment of mental illness.
In addition to these clinical supports, non-medical mental health services are provided by the Defence Forces Personnel Support Service (PSS). The PSS provides a welfare, information, psycho-social support and referral service to serving members of the Defence Forces and their families. The service is also available to civilian employees, and in a limited role to retired personnel. This service sustains and enhances the individual well-being of personnel, and promotes a safe and positive work culture, in order to support the effectiveness of the Defence Forces.
The service is delivered through a network of military PSS Officers and civilian Occupational Social Workers across the Defence Forces. This network of professionals is prepared to provide immediate help to service personnel and their families in a routine environment or at a time of crisis. question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Social Protection if he is aware of the food safety order against a company (details supplied); and if it directly impacts the hot school meals programme in schools who have this company as a provider.
reply:
All suppliers participating in the School Meals Programme are registered food business operators and, like all food businesses in Ireland, are required to comply with food safety legislation.
Responsibility for producing and supplying safe food rests with the food business operator, while the Food Safety Authority of Ireland, as Ireland's independent regulator and central competent authority for food safety, oversees compliance with food safety legislation. School Meals suppliers are subject to the same high standards, inspection regimes and enforcement measures as all other registered food businesses.
The Department of Health advised my Department on 24 September 2026 that a Closure Order has been served by the HSE National Environmental Health Service on a food business operator in Timahoe GAA, Páirc Mochua, Cremorgan, Timahoe, Portlaoise, Co. Laois.
The premises operated as a distribution hub and at the time of inspection, my Department was advised no food was stored at the premises.
Officials from my Department contacted the supplier who advised only one school was being served from the affected premises and that food provision for this school has been moved to a neighboring Heating hub.
Closure Orders and Improvement Orders remain listed in the enforcement reports on the Food Safety Authority website for a period of three months from the date of when a premises is adjudged to have corrected its food safety issue.

reply:

SWA payments are administered by Community Welfare Officers (CWOs) in the Community Welfare Service (CWS), considering the requirements of the legislation and all the relevant circumstances of the case. All ANP applications are considered on a case-by-case basis based on the need presenting.
According to the records of the Department, the person concerned applied for an ANP to assist with the cost of car repairs. This claim was disallowed on the basis that it is normally considered to be an individual’s own responsibility to ensure that they can meet all costs associated with owning a car. At the person’s request, a Review Officer reviewed her claim and considering the circumstances of the case, upheld the original decision of the CWO on the basis that car ownership inherently includes the responsibility to cover maintenance and repair costs, and the level of repairs required could not reasonably be considered within the circumstances.
Upon completion of the Department’s review process, the person concerned referred the case to the Office of the Ombudsman to review who did not uphold her case.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection further to Parliamentary Question No. 72304/26 of 13 October 2026, the date on which the review of means testing will be submitted to him and published; whether the review examines the treatment of inherited capital for people with lifelong disabilities; and whether his Department will engage with the Department of Finance on aligning the tax and means test treatment of such inheritances.
reply:
The Programme for Government commits to carrying out a comprehensive review of means tests across the social welfare system, taking into account the Report on Means Testing by the Oireachtas Joint Committee on Social Protection, Community and Rural Development, and the Islands.
My Department is conducting a review of means testing within the social protection system. The aim is to examine various means-tested schemes and identify any issues related to their respective means tests. With over 140 schemes and services, many of which are means-tested, this is a complex and detailed task.
It is my intention that the review's findings will inform decisions regarding potential changes to means testing in future Budgets. The review is currently with senior management of the Department for review and I expect that it will be submitted to me shortly.
Due to the complexity of the review, I will carefully and thoroughly evaluate it to determine the best way to utilise its findings and identify those that may warrant further consideration. However, any prospective changes to means-testing arrangements will need to be evaluated and considered within the overall policy and budgetary context.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection further to Parliamentary Question No. 71927/26 of 13 October 2026, whether his Department receives information from the Irish Prison Service on committals for the purpose of suspending or terminating payments; and if so, the number of payments suspended or terminated on foot of such information in each of the years 2023, 2024 and 2025.
reply:
My Department receives information from the Irish Prison Service for people who are committed to prison. Payments will be suspended as soon as possible after the person is imprisoned to minimise overpayments. A Deciding Officer, on review of the information may subsequently terminate the payment depending on the individual circumstances of the case. Overpayments are assessed for periods of ineligibility and the recovery of same is followed up by the relevant section of the Department.
Statistics on suspension or termination of welfare payments due to imprisonment are not available.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Social Protection if the receipt of voluntary community donations or localised fundraising proceeds can negatively impact a child's eligibility for domiciliary care allowance or the guardian's payment (contributory/non-contributory) following the death of a parent; the guidelines his Department issues on how these funds should be legally structured to protect family entitlements.
reply:
Domiciliary Care Allowance is a monthly payment for a child, aged under 16 with a severe disability who requires ongoing care and attention, substantially over and above the care and attention usually required by a child of the same age and where the child is likely to require full-time care and attention for at least 12 months. There are no Pay Related Social Insurance conditions, and it is not means tested. As such, any voluntary community donations or localised fundraising proceeds do not impact eligibility.
Guardian’s Payment (Contributory) is a social insurance-based payment made in respect of a child who satisfies the definition of “orphan” under Irish social welfare law. Guardian’s Payment (Contributory) is payable in respect of an orphan, where either a parent or step-parent of the orphan has paid at least 26 qualifying social insurance contributions. Guardian’s Payment (Contributory) is not a means-tested payment and, as such, any voluntary community donations or localised fundraising proceeds do not impact eligibility.
Guardian’s Payment (Non-Contributory) is a means-tested payment and is based on the child's means. Means include any income belonging to the child and any property or an asset that could provide them with an income. The means of the guardian are not assessed when establishing entitlement.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Social Protection if funds raised via a community fundraiser or crowdfunding platform for a full-time family carer are treated as capital or income during a means assessment for carer's allowance; if he will clarify the distinct assessment rules if such funds are placed in a restricted trust account exclusively for the benefit of orphaned or dependent children.
reply:
Social welfare legislation provides that means tests take account of the income and assets of the person (and their spouse or partner, if applicable) applying for the relevant scheme. The conditions attached to payment of Carer’s Allowance are consistent with the overall conditions that apply to social assistance payments generally. This system of social assistance supports provides payments based on an income need with the means test playing the critical role in determining whether or not an income need arises as a consequence of a particular contingency, be that illness, disability, unemployment or caring.
Means assessments can include income from employment, self-employment and occupational pensions depending on particular rules of the scheme concerned. Property owned, other than the family home, and capital such as savings, shares, and other investments are also considered.
The means assessment for Carer's Allowance are calculated in accordance with Part 5 of the Third Schedule to the Social Welfare (Consolidation) Act 2005 (as amended). A qualifying condition for Carer’s Allowance is that a person’s weekly means must be below a certain amount. Income and capital are assessed, with any relevant deductions applied, and the assessable means are added together. The Carer's Allowance weekly disregard is then applied to determine the net weekly means. The current weekly disregard for Carer's Allowance is €1,000 for a single person and €2,000 for a couple.
