question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Social Protection the current status of a carer’s benefit application for a person (details supplied); the timeframe for a decision to be reached; and if serious consideration will be given to the application due to the circumstances involved.
reply:
Carer's Benefit is a social insurance payment payable to insured individuals who leave the workforce, or reduce their working hours, in order to provide full-time care and attention to a child or adult who requires such care.
To qualify for Carer's Benefit, an applicant must satisfy the relevant social insurance and employment conditions and meet the scheme's care requirements.
An application for Carer's Benefit was received from the person concerned on 14 October 2026.
I am advised that the application has been examined by a Deciding Officer, who determined that further information is required before a decision can be made. A request for this information issued to the applicant on 20 October 2026.
Once the requested information has been received and considered, a Deciding Officer will make a formal decision on the application. The person concerned will be notified directly of the outcome.
If the person concerned is experiencing financial hardship while awaiting a decision on their claim, they may wish to contact their local Community Welfare Officer to enquire about possible eligibility for Supplementary Welfare Allowance.

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Social Protection to carry out a review of the social welfare entitlement of a person (details supplied), who was recently refused jobseekers allowance.
reply:
The person concerned applied for Jobseekers Allowance (JA) on the 07/09/2026. Their claim was disallowed on 06/10/2026 as their means were assessed as being in excess of that allowed for their family circumstances.
A review of this decision was completed on the 22/10/2026 and although the means on their assessment did reduce, the means are still in excess of their family rate payable for Jobseekers Allowance. A review letter and the revised means assessment have issued to the person concerned.
The person concerned has been advised by phone that if they have a change in circumstances in relation to their household finances they should reapply for Jobseekers Allowance.
If the person concerned is not satisfied with this revised decision the option to appeal to the Social Welfare Appeals Office is open to them. An appeal can be made in the following manner:
Online: Submit their appeal on MyWelfare (https://services.mywelfare.ie/en/topics/appeals/make-an-appeal/) using a verified MyGovID account or,
By Post: Download and complete the Notice of Appeal SWAO1 Form (https://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/20250425_Appeal_Notice_Form_SWAO1_Apr_2025_.pdf), attach a copy of the decision letter and supporting documents, and post them to:
Social Welfare Appeals Office.
D'Olier House, D'Olier Street.
Dublin 2, D02 XY31.
The deadline for submitting an appeal is within 60 days of the date on the decision letter.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Social Protection when An Cheathrú Rua ceased to have a community welfare officer; and if there are plans in place to reinstate such a role.
reply:
The delivery of locally based Community Welfare Services (CWS) to meet the challenges and the needs of people across the country, including Co. Galway, is a priority for me and for my Department.
Arrangements for Community Welfare Service clinics which were provided in Health Service Executive (HSE) facilities changed with the transition of the service from the HSE into my Department in 2012. The CWS clinic in An Cheathrú Rua permanently ceased in 2013. The CWS continues to provide a flexible service to meet the different needs of people, who may find themselves in a financially difficult or vulnerable situation. The service remains easily accessible and responsive to our client’s needs.
While local face-to-face engagement with people continues to be a cornerstone of the Community Welfare Service, it is important to mention that a person now has multiple access options for the service. Clients who either do not wish or who are unable to travel for any reason do not need to meet with a CWO to make an application. Any person who needs to access the CWS can now call the National CWS freephone number at 0818 60 70 80 to make an enquiry, to get a claim application form, to ask about a claim already made, to make an appointment to see a CWO either in the office or at home. It is also possible for a person to speak directly to a CWO. question: Deputy Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire asked the Minister for Defence to provide an update on the publication of the Command and Control Bill.
reply:
As Minister for Defence, I am deeply committed to the transformation of the Defence Forces into a modern fit for purpose organisation to defend the State and meet the challenges not only of today, but also the future.
The Commission on the Defence Forces recommended significant changes for the Defence Forces and Defence provision in Ireland. It covers high level Defence Forces structures, defence capabilities, organisation, culture and human resources, the Reserve Defence Force and funding.
The Commission on the Defence Forces made significant recommendations around command and control of the Defence Forces (C2) including command being delegated from the Minister to the head of the Military to be titled Chief of Defence (CHOD). Currently, military command is delegated from the Minister for Defence (on behalf of the Government) to five separate high ranking military Officers commanding Army Brigade units, the Naval Service and Air Corps (all Brigadier General rank).
This work is on-going, significant, complex and sensitive involving a fundamental review of the current regulatory framework governing the relationship between the Minister for Defence, the Defence Forces and the Department of Defence.
Following approval by Government, work is progressing on the legislative requirements for high level C2. A Bill to include provision for new high-level Command and Control arrangements is being progressed by my Department with a General Scheme to be completed in the near future.

question: Deputy Johnny Guirke asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if his Department will publish national guidance for planning authorities and conservation officers on the assessment of solar installations on protected structures and in architectural conservation areas, in order that decisions are consistent across local authorities.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1045, 1048, 1049, 1051, 1052, 1053, 1147, 1148 and 1149 together.
My Department introduced new planning regulations in October 2022 that significantly enhanced existing provisions regarding planning exemptions for rooftop solar installations.
There is now no rooftop limit on houses and new exemptions were also introduced for the erection of solar panels on apartments and certain non-domestic structures including hospitals, libraries and places of worship, subject to certain conditions and limitations.
These provisions are considered to be an effective measure which have significantly assisted with the roll out of rooftop solar, particularly on the domestic level, and meeting climate targets in this regard.
The matter of solar exempted development and the potential impact on protected structures and Architectural Conservation Areas (ACAs) was a primary consideration of the Department in the development of these regulations. It remains the case that a development is not considered exempted development if it would materially affect the character of a protected structure or a building in an Architectural Conservation Area.
With regards to any future changes, there has been significant progress on the review of Exempted Development Regulations.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage his opinion of the recent European Court of Justice SmartFlats Ruling (details supplied); and whether it will impact Government plans for regulation of the short term letting sector.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1113, 1114, 1116 and 1146 together.
In line with the introduction of the Short -term Letting and Tourism Bill, all short-term letting accommodation providers will be required to register with Fáilte Ireland. As part of the registration process, accommodation providers will need to confirm that they are planning compliant.
The Planning Acts provide that the short-term letting of a residential property is a material change of use of the property concerned, thereby requiring planning permission, unless otherwise specifically exempted.
The National Planning Statement on Short-term Letting sets out a threshold-based approach to consenting by planning authorities that generally precludes new planning permissions for short-term lets in larger towns and cities with a population in excess of 20,000 (twenty five at the most recent Census of Population). In all other locations, i.e. outside the largest towns and cities, policy is more amenable to granting short-term letting permission and accommodation providers will be able to avail of an extended period to meet planning compliance requirements.
Furthermore, in line with existing established rights, where it can be proven that a residential property has been operated by a short-term letting accommodation provider for at least seven years and no enforcement action has been taken by the planning authority, planning permission for retention may be sought to regularise an established but unauthorised use.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether his Department has sought information from local authorities regarding State-funded homeless accommodation that lacked required fire-safety certification or compliance since 2020; when the Department was notified, what records of inspections and risk assessments are held, and the steps that were taken to address any identified risks.
reply:
My Department's role in relation to homelessness involves the provision of a national framework of policy, legislation and funding to underpin the role of housing authorities in addressing homelessness at local level. Statutory responsibility in relation to the provision of homeless services rests with individual housing authorities. The administration of homeless services is organised on a regional basis with a lead local authority in each of the nine regions.
My Department does not fund any homeless service directly but provides funding to housing authorities towards the operational costs of homeless accommodation and related services under Section 10 of the Housing Act, 1988. A homelessness consultative forum has been established in each region in accordance with Chapter 6 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 2009. It is a matter for the management group of the consultative forum, in the first instance, to determine the type and range of homeless services including emergency accommodation, and the funding required to address homelessness in each region. Any contractual or operational matters in relation to these services are also matter for the individual local authority in consultation with the relevant homeless consultative forum.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of applications received nationally under each domestic wastewater treatment systems grant scheme in 2025 and to date in 2026; the number approved, refused, withdrawn and awaiting a decision; the number of grants actually paid and the total value of those payments in each period, distinguishing payments relating to applications from earlier years; and if he will provide a breakdown by local authority and scheme, in tabular form.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1129, 1131 to 1133, inclusive, and 1144 together.
Under the Water Services Act 2007, as amended, and the associated Regulations, owners of domestic wastewater treatment systems have a statutory responsibility to ensure that their systems are properly maintained and renewed. Regulation 2(3) specifically requires owners to ensure that the parts and components of their systems are fit for purpose, operational where appropriate and kept in good order and repair so as to prevent a risk to human health or the environment. This responsibility includes meeting the associated costs of maintenance, repair and renewal.
Notwithstanding this statutory requirement, the Domestic Wastewater Treatment Systems (DWWTS) Grant Scheme is a targeted support measure designed to assist eligible homeowners in exceptional circumstances where there is a public health or environmental need for intervention. The scheme provides financial assistance for the remediation of defective systems where the work delivers wider public benefits. It is not intended as a general grant for the replacement or upgrade of all septic tanks.
The DWWTS Grant Scheme provides support under the National Inspection Plan (NIP), Areas for Action, and High Status Objective Catchment Areas. Recent regulatory amendments have extended eligibility to Areas for Action identified in the River Basin Management Plan 2022–2027.
Most grants are awarded under the NIP stream, which requires an initial inspectio

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the progress that has been made on the development of successor schemes for communities affected by restrictions on turf cutting on protected bogs; whether new compensation, restoration or stewardship schemes are planned; the income supports that will be available for local bog stewards engaged under these schemes.
reply:
The Cessation of Turf Cutting Compensation Scheme (CTCCS) was established following engagement with stakeholders in 2011 for active domestic turf cutters arising from the restrictions on turf cutting on 53 raised bog special areas of conservation (SAC) and was extended in 2014 to include 36 raised bog natural heritage areas (NHA).
This scheme has compensated those impacted by restrictions on turf-cutting on protected sites, and over its 15-year term has helped to ensure the conservation of important peatland sites of unique ecological value.
My Department has now concluded its review of its options to follow the Cessation of Turf Cutting Compensation Scheme and are now advancing initiatives on these sites to support their conservation and the NPWS Raised Bog Restoration Programme:
• Offering the (voluntary) purchase of land or turbary rights on any protected raised bog.
• Revision and expansion of the Protected Raised Bog Restoration Incentive Scheme to include other eligible property holders. My Department intends to contact qualifying CTCCS beneficiaries with further information on incentives now available to them under this scheme.
• Development of a pilot initiative to support landowners, local networks and community groups who may take on a stewardship role for designated nature sites. These initiatives would support training of local stakeholders and community groups who wish to take part in the conservation of designated nature sites and provide valuable information on

question: Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if his Department will implement safeguards for property owners currently living in pyrite homes that do not reach the criteria for the remediation scheme currently but the property may do so in the future, past the cut off date of the scheme.
reply:
The Pyrite Remediation Scheme was launched in February 2014 and has been running for over 12 years. It is expected that a total of 3,017 homes will have had remediation completed by the end of this year, at a cost in excess of €205million.
In November 2025 the government approved a significant expansion to the damage eligibility criteria under the Pyrite Remediation Scheme to ensure that additional homes within affected areas could be remediated as the Scheme enters its final phase.
Under this widening of eligibility, the Pyrite Resolution Board (PRB) will evaluate each eligible application using strict qualification criteria. Applicants approved will follow the existing eight stages of pyrite remediation, with an additional assessment step. The Scheme engineer will revisit the property within a defined period to reassess whether any current progression has occurred as determined by the PRB. The Housing Agency will oversee assessment and testing on behalf of the PRB.
The Scheme will close to applications on 30 November 2026. The works programme will continue up to the end of 2029 when it is expected that all dwellings that have been significantly damaged as a result of pyritic heave will be remediated.
I have approved the establishment of a Working Group to assist the PRB in the wind-down process of the Scheme, including technical aspects associated with the potential for additional pyrite cases into the future, following the Scheme closing for applications.

question: Deputy Gillian Toole asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if all local authorities have housing and disability steering groups; the reports to they produce; and when will groups and reports be reviewed by the Department to ensure timely and consistent outcomes for persons with disabilities.
reply:
My Department jointly published the National Housing Strategy for Disabled People (NHSDP) 2022-2027 and Implementation Plan with the Department of Health and the Department of Children, Disability, and Equality. The Strategy and Implementation Plan may be accessed on my Department’s website at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/publication/60d76-national-housing-strategy-for-disabled-people-2022-2027/

The Plan aims to deliver 300,000 new homes by the end of 2030, including 72,000 social homes and 90,000 affordable housing supports by the end of 2030.
Local authorities play a key role in the planning and provision of social housing in their areas, and decide on the number and types of dwellings to provide, based on identified need including disabled people.
All local authorities have Housing and Disability Steering Groups (HDSGs) whose role is to put in place strategic plans for housing for disabled people and to monitor activity under these plans. The HDSGs are representative of disabled people as well as the Health Services Executive, the local authority and Approved Housing Bodies and are a key driver of the provision of housing for disabled people at local level. question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Defence the strength of the Naval Service in each of the years 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026; and her target for the overall number of personnel in the Naval Service.
reply:
As Minister for Defence, I am fully committed to supporting recruitment and retention in the Naval Service and across the Defence Forces as a whole.
It is very positive to see the growth in Naval Service numbers achieved over the past three years. Figures provided to me by the military authorities indicate that the strength of the Naval Service, as at 30 September 2026, stood at 894 personnel or 81% of an establishment of 1,094. This constitutes a significant upturn in the overall strength from a totals of 807 and 719 recorded at the end of 2025 and 2024 respectively. Building on the 97 inductions achieved in 2024, last year saw a total of 162 inductions to the Naval Service which included a notably high expansion in Direct Entry specialist recruitment. A further 146 inductions have been achieved to the end of September of this year. By contrast, the number of departures has been steadily decreasing each year, falling from over 100 in 2021 and 2022, to 47 in 2025 and 34 to the end September of this year.
There has been a significant surge in interest in a career in the Naval Service as reflected in a substantial year on year increase in the number of applications received with 3,265 applications received as of the 30 September, 39% more than the 2,357 received by the end of September 2025. The growth in application numbers for Direct Entry specialist competitions is particularly noteworthy, with 762 applications received to the end of September compared to 457 for the same pe

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether he accepts that the European Communities Environmental Objectives (Freshwater Pearl Mussel) Regulations 2009 require the preparation of a sub-basin management plan for the Dawros catchment in Co Galway; if such a plan has not yet been prepared, the reasons for this; the agencies and bodies that will be involved in its development; the timeframe he expects the process to commence; and the proposed date of completion of any such plan.
reply:

The protection and restoration of freshwater pearl mussel populations require an integrated catchment management approach, particularly in relation to water quality, sediment management, hydromorphological conditions and the maintenance of suitable aquatic habitats.
The third River Basin Management Plan (RBMP), the Water Action Plan 2024, published in September 2024, provides the national framework for implementing measures to protect and restore water quality during the period 2022–2027.
The Dawros catchment has been subject to targeted assessment and management activities under successive River Basin Management Plans. It was identified as a Priority Area for Action under the second RBMP and subsequently incorporated into the Blue Dot Catchments Programme under the third RBMP.
Between 2020 and September 2024, the River Basin Management Service undertook detailed local catchment assessments within the Dawros Blue Dot Priority Area for Action. These investigations identified potential pressures on water quality, and the relevant findings were referred to the appropriate implementing authorities for follow-up action.

The third River Basin Management Plan, the Water Action Plan 2024, provides the framework for the implementation of measures to protect and improve water quality during the period 2022–2027. These investigations identified potential pressures on water quality, including agricultural activities and a licensed discharge. The relevant findings were communicated to the appropriate implementing authorities, including Galway County Council, through established referral processes.

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the reason demolition, even if required under the defective concrete blocks grant scheme (Option 1), is not listed as a permitted ground for terminating a tenancy during the six-year TMD for small landlords, nor at any time for large landlords, except at the end of the TMD for small landlords under the ground of substantial refurbishment or renovation; and if he will seek a resolution.
reply:
The Remediation of Dwellings Damaged by the Use of Defective Concrete Blocks Act 2022 (the Act of 2022) provides for the payment of grants for the remediation of certain dwellings damaged by the use of defective concrete blocks in their construction.
Section 9(3)(b) of the Act of 2022 provides for the grant for a vacant former rental property provided a tenancy of that dwelling stood registered with the Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) on or before 1 November 2021.
The precise timing of the carrying out of the necessary works to avail of the grant is a matter for any landlord, within the confines of the Act of 2022.
The Residential Tenancies Acts 2004 to 2026 (the RTA) regulate the landlord-tenant relationship in the rented residential sector and set out the rights and obligations of landlords and tenants.
From 1 March 2026, the Residential Tenancies (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 provides for a national rent control which allows the resetting of rents for new tenancies to market rent, subject to certain conditions, and significantly strengthens security of tenure for tenants.
It is lawful under the RTA for a landlord of a tenancy that commenced before 1 March 2026 to terminate the tenancy on the ground of substantial refurbishment or renovation, including a relevant dwelling under the Defective Concrete Blocks Grant Scheme that was subject to a tenancy on 1 November 2021 and stood registered with the RTB on that date.

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage his plans to assist in the transfer of responsibility for the Multi-Unit Developments (MUD) Act 2011 from the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to his Department.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1081, 1125 and 1136 together.
Responsibility for the oversight of Owner Management Companies (OMCs) and related legislation including the Multi-Unit Developments Act, 2011 (the "MUDs Act") currently sits with the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration.
Arising from a Programme for Government commitment, responsibility for the MUDs Act is intended to transfer to my Department. Transfer was contingent on the resolution of a legal matter which was dealt with in the recent Criminal Law, Civil Law and Defence (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 2026.
As legal matters are resolved, a formal Transfer of Functions process will be undertaken and this is led by the Transferring Department. While no formal meetings have taken place there has been pro-active engagement on matters such as financing, staffing, records management and other such relevant matters.
A Transfer Order will be prepared and a Memo to Government advanced by the Transferring Department. It is anticipated that this will be finalised over the coming weeks.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will address a matter regarding a toilet in a national park (details supplied).
reply:
Officials in the National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) have confirmed that they have recently installed temporary toilets, including a universally accessible toilet, to complement existing toilet facilities in the Park. This is in response to the significant increase in demand for these facilities.
These toilets are designed to be self-contained and do not discharge locally – the waste water from these temporary toilets is collected in two tanks that are installed underground adjacent to the toilets. The tanks are emptied regularly and the waste is taken to the nearby Waste Water Treatment Plant for appropriate treatment.
Last week due to exceptional rainfall arising from storms Austen and Boelo, ground water levels in the area were raised significantly. Arising from this, one of the empty waste storage tanks rose above ground level and, because both tanks are connected, the second tank also rose slightly. There was absolutely no contamination of adjacent ground or surface water bodies. In response to this event, it is planned that engineering works will take place when water levels recede to 'pin' the tanks to their foundations, which will help to avoid the issue happening again.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the implementation status of changes extending the geographical eligibility of domestic wastewater treatment systems grants under the River Basin Management Plan 2022–2027; the date on which each local authority was notified and began accepting applications under the revised criteria; whether all relevant public maps and Eircode search tools have been updated and where these can be accessed; and whether previously refused applicants whose properties are now within eligible areas will be notified and invited to reapply.
reply:

Under the Water Services Act 2007, as amended, and the associated Regulations, owners of domestic wastewater treatment systems have a statutory responsibility to ensure that their systems are properly maintained and renewed. Regulation 2(3) specifically requires owners to ensure that the parts and components of their systems are fit for purpose, operational where appropriate and kept in good order and repair so as to prevent a risk to human health or the environment. The DWWTS Grant Scheme provides support under the National Inspection Plan (NIP), Areas for Action, and High Status Objective Catchment Areas. Recent regulatory amendments have extended eligibility to Areas for Action identified in the River Basin Management Plan 2022–2027.

question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage given that applications to the apartment and duplex defects remediation scheme must be made by an owners' management company, the provisions that will apply to affected duplexes and apartment developments where no owners' management company exists or is operational; the way in which homeowners in such developments can access the scheme; and the steps being taken to ensure that the absence of an owners' management company does not exclude otherwise eligible homeowners from redress.
reply:
Drafting of the Apartment and Duplex Defects Remediation Scheme Bill is at an advanced stage and it is listed for publication this session. The statutory scheme will be in place as soon as possible following its passage through the Dáil.
The scheme is based on a whole-of-building approach. Applications will be made by the Owner Management Company (OMC), as the persons having control of the buildings. OMCs have existing legal responsibilities and obligations to their members under the Multi-Unit Developments Act 2011 which must be met in ensuring the on-going repair, maintenance and management of the buildings.
It is recognised that a small number of developments may not have a functioning OMC and consideration has been given to whether and how the Bill may provide for such situations. It is expected that the Bill will be published shortly.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to provide an update on talks between his Department and Galway Country Council in order to secure the necessary funding to bring Dunguaire Castle back into public use.
reply:
My Department has been working to progress the acquisition of Dunguaire Castle from the Shannon Group on the basis of its exceptional heritage value. The conveyancing process is ongoing, and it is not possible to determine when this complex legal process will be completed.

question: Deputy Gillian Toole asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage when the national guidelines for the assessment and allocation process, for social housing provision for people with a disability, will be reviewed by his Department and the Housing Agency.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1027 and 1126 together.
Decisions on the qualification of households for support, the awarding of medical priority, and the allocation of that support, are a matter solely for the local authority concerned, in accordance with their allocation schemes made under section 22 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2009 and associated Regulations.
Updated National Guidelines for the Assessment and Allocation Process for Social Housing Provision for People with a Disability were published in 2017 under section 5 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2009. The purpose of the National Guidelines for the Assessment and Allocation Process for Social Housing Provision for People with a Disability is to drive consistency in streamlining the management of the social housing assessment and allocation process for disabled people across all local authorities. The Guidelines support housing authorities in carrying out assessments of social housing need for disabled people within a planned and structured framework to ensure that their needs can be assessed as effectively as possible in a timely manner including disabled people transitioning to community independent living from residential/institutional/congregated/hospital care setting or long-term residential care settings.
The Guidelines are available on my Department’s website at the following link:
www.gov.ie/en/department-of-housing-local-government-and-heritage/publications/national-guideli

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the reason for the delay in transfer to his Department of responsibility of the Multi-Unit Developments Act 2011 and amendments to same; when the transfer will be complete; the number of staff assigned to the transfer; if there have been substantive meetings between his officials and their counterparts in the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration and; and if so, the number of meetings that took place and the issues discussed.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1081, 1125 and 1136 together.
Responsibility for the oversight of Owner Management Companies (OMCs) and related legislation including the Multi-Unit Developments Act, 2011 (the "MUDs Act") currently sits with the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration.
Arising from a Programme for Government commitment, responsibility for the MUDs Act is intended to transfer to my Department. Transfer was contingent on the resolution of a legal matter which was dealt with in the recent Criminal Law, Civil Law and Defence (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 2026.
As legal matters are resolved, a formal Transfer of Functions process will be undertaken and this is led by the Transferring Department. While no formal meetings have taken place there has been pro-active engagement on matters such as financing, staffing, records management and other such relevant matters.
A Transfer Order will be prepared and a Memo to Government advanced by the Transferring Department. It is anticipated that this will be finalised over the coming weeks.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the treatment will be applied to auto-enrolment pension contributions under My Future Fund when calculating differential rents for local authority tenants; and whether such contributions will be included in the assessment of reckonable income for rent purposes.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1118 and 1123 together.
Local authorities set and collect rents on their dwellings in accordance with section 58 of the Housing Act 1966. The making or amending of such differential rent schemes is a matter for local authorities within broad principles set out by my Department, including that rent levels should be based on income and reflect tenants’ ability to pay.
Local discretion and flexibility are inherent in the devolved administration of differential rent schemes and different approaches are taken to rent setting across local authorities. Accordingly, decisions regarding the sources of income included and disregarded for rent assessment purposes are matters solely for individual local authorities.
The Housing Plan Delivering Homes, Building Communities, commits to reviewing rents paid by local authority and AHB social housing tenants with a view to introducing a national framework that provides a consistent and equitable system of rents and protects vulnerable households.
My Department is progressing, with the assistance of the Housing Agency, detailed analysis of existing rents schemes in order to explore the range of reform options that may be available. It is essential that any potential options place sufficient emphasis on achieving the best blend of equity, progressivity and sustainability, and critically, protect those on lowest incomes and at greater risk of poverty.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of people homeless in Dublin south central over the past five years, in tabular form.
reply:
My Department’s role in relation to homelessness involves the provision of a national framework of policy, legislation and funding to underpin the role of local authorities in addressing homelessness at local level. Statutory responsibility in relation to the provision of accommodation and related services for homeless persons rests with individual local authorities.
While responsibility for the provision of homeless accommodation and related services rests with individual housing authorities, the administration of homeless services is organised on a regional basis with a lead authority in place for each region. The Dublin region includes Dublin City Council, Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council, Fingal County Council and South Dublin County Council, for the purposes of homeless administration, with Dublin City Council as lead authority.
My Department gathers and publishes data on a monthly basis on the number of homeless persons accommodated in homeless emergency accommodation funded and overseen by local authorities. These reports are based on data provided by local authorities, produced through the Pathway Accommodation & Support System (PASS).
The monthly homelessness report includes details of individuals, families and the dependants of these families who accessed emergency accommodation during the relevant count week of the month in question. question: Deputy Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire asked the Minister for Defence the number of PC 12 helicopters currently available for operations; the number that are currently grounded as unserviceable due to their being no technicians available to do corrosion checks.
reply:
I would like to thank the Deputy for the question. The Air Corps operates a range of rotary and fixed wing aircraft within existing organisational structures. Their principal aim is to ensure that the Air Corps can continue to undertake the required military operations and to deliver a broad range of air supports to other government departments and agencies in line with Memorandum of Understandings and Service Level Agreements. Typical operations include Inshore & Offshore Maritime Patrol, Garda Air Support, Air Ambulance, Military transport, the Ministerial Air Transport Service and Inland Search & Rescue.
The Air Corps fleet consists of both Fixed Wing and Rotary craft. Four (4) Pilatus PC-12 fixed wing aircraft entered service in 2020. Their primary function is Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR), they also function in air ambulance and transport roles as required.
In line with best practices, The Air Corps carries out scheduled maintenance on the PC-12 fleet at intervals prescribed by the aircraft manufacturer, all scheduled through a Maintenance Information System. All maintenance is carried out by appropriately qualified and approved maintenance personnel in accordance with manufacturer requirements.

question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if his Department has assessed the extent to which the grant available under the enhanced defective concrete blocks grant scheme covers the actual cost of completing approved qualifying remediation works, including associated professional fees; the number of cases which the cost of approved qualifying works exceeds the grant amount available; if an assessment has been undertaken of the financial shortfalls faced by affected homeowners; and if so, if he will publish the findings of any such assessment.
reply:
The Remediation of Dwellings Damaged by the use of Defective Concrete Blocks Act 2022 as amended by the Act of 2025 sets out the framework under which the Grant Scheme which provides grant funding to cover 100% of approved remediation costs to people whose homes have been affected by Defective Concrete Blocks (DCB).
As the Deputy is aware, a number of amendments contained in the 2025 Act came into operation on 25 February 2026 and more recently further provisions commenced on 27 May 2026.
Following updated cost reports from the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland (SCSI) and advice from the Expert Group established to consider the matter, increases in the grant scheme remediation rates were provided for over and above the original amounts contained upon commencement of the current grant scheme in 2023. Along with the rates the overall Scheme Cap increased by 10% from €420,000 to €462,000.
It should be noted that homeowners eligible for works under the DCB grant scheme may also apply for energy upgrade grants administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) similar to other homeowners.
The exact final costs of remediation are ultimately a matter for the homeowner applicant and/or their professionals. Therefore, details relating to applications where the cost of approved works may have exceeded their determined grant amount are not available to my Department.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to consider the European Court of Justice ruling in the SmartFlats case, and to review his Departments proposed planning restrictions on STLs considering the ruling.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1113, 1114, 1116 and 1146 together.
In line with the introduction of the Short -term Letting and Tourism Bill, all short-term letting accommodation providers will be required to register with Fáilte Ireland. As part of the registration process, accommodation providers will need to confirm that they are planning compliant.
The Planning Acts provide that the short-term letting of a residential property is a material change of use of the property concerned, thereby requiring planning permission, unless otherwise specifically exempted.
The National Planning Statement on Short-term Letting sets out a threshold-based approach to consenting by planning authorities that generally precludes new planning permissions for short-term lets in larger towns and cities with a population in excess of 20,000 (twenty five at the most recent Census of Population). In all other locations, i.e. outside the largest towns and cities, policy is more amenable to granting short-term letting permission and accommodation providers will be able to avail of an extended period to meet planning compliance requirements.
Furthermore, in line with existing established rights, where it can be proven that a residential property has been operated by a short-term letting accommodation provider for at least seven years and no enforcement action has been taken by the planning authority, planning permission for retention may be sought to regularise an established but unauthorised use.

In line with the introduction of the Short -term Letting and Tourism Bill, all short-term letting accommodation providers will be required to register with Fáilte Ireland. As part of the registration process, accommodation providers will need to confirm that they are planning compliant.
The Planning Acts provide that the short-term letting of a residential property is a material change of use of the property concerned, thereby requiring planning permission, unless otherwise specifically exempted.
The National Planning Statement on Short-term Letting sets out a threshold-based approach to consenting by planning authorities that generally precludes new planning permissions for short-term lets in larger towns and cities with a population in excess of 20,000 (twenty five at the most recent Census of Population). In all other locations, i.e. outside the largest towns and cities, policy is more amenable to granting short-term letting permission and accommodation providers will be able to avail of an extended period to meet planning compliance requirements.
Furthermore, in line with existing established rights, where it can be proven that a residential property has been operated by a short-term letting accommodation provider for at least seven years and no enforcement action has been taken by the planning authority, planning permission for retention may be sought to regularise an established but unauthorised use.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1107, 1108, 1109, 1110, 1111 and 1112 together.

Engaging the services of a suitably qualified professional will assist in informing owners of the works required, building and statutory requirements to be met and indicative costs for undertaking such projects. There is no obligation on the owner to a make a grant application after receiving the Expert Advice Grant.

question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether his Department has directed Limerick City and County Council to require applicants under the enhanced defective concrete blocks grant scheme to provide proof of funding available to complete their build where the total project cost, including professional fees, exceeds the grant amount offered; and the statutory, regulatory or administrative basis for this requirement.
reply:

The Remediation of Dwellings Damaged by the use of Defective Concrete Blocks Act 2022 as amended by the Act of 2025 sets out the framework under which the Grant Scheme which provides grant funding to people whose homes have been affected by Defective Concrete Blocks (DCB) operates.
A number of amendments contained in the 2025 Act came into operation on 25 February 2026 and, more recently, further provisions commenced on 27 May 2026.
The detailed operation of the Scheme is a matter for the designated local authorities in the first instance and their role is set out clearly in the 2022 Act.
Local authorities have responsibility for the administration of the scheme. This includes the initial validation of applications, notifying homeowners of the Housing Agency's determinations on damage threshold, the appropriate remediation option and grant amount, determination of the grant payable for alternative accommodation and storage costs and immediate repair works and the subsequent payment of grants to successful applicants.
My Department engages regularly with the local authority teams responsible for the operation and administration of the Scheme. Representatives from the designated local authorities attend meetings of the Implementation Steering Group, which provides a forum for the ongoing monitoring of the operation and implementation of the Defective Concrete Blocks Grant Scheme.

reply:

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the reason there is no nationally agreed protocol, based on the updated I.S. 465: 2026, for houses being bought and sold in areas affected by defective concrete blocks; if his attention has been drawn to the fact that the absence of such a protocol has a profound effect on the housing market in those areas with devastating impacts on some homeowners that cannot sell their homes.
reply:
The Remediation of Dwellings Damaged by the use of Defective Concrete Blocks Act 2022 as amended by the Act of 2025 sets out the framework under which the Grant Scheme which provides grant funding to people whose homes have been affected by Defective Concrete Blocks (DCB) operates.
As the Deputy is aware, a number of amendments contained in the 2025 Act came into operation on 25 February 2026 and more recently further provisions commenced on 27 May 2026.
My Department keeps the operation of the scheme under continuous review. An Implementation Steering Group for the DCB Grant Scheme which has been in place since 2023. In addition, a sub-group of this Steering Group was established to consider and discuss financial aspects of the scheme.
Through this group, my Department has had a number of engagements with the Banking and Payments Federation (BPFI) on specific issues raised by DCB homeowners. As part of these discussions the BPFI has confirmed to my Department that, from their perspective, once a home has been certified as remediated under the DCB Scheme it will be treated by them in a similar manner to other properties.
My Department maintains regular contact with the BPFI providing updates on the grant scheme and addressing any queries they may have relating to statistical information or the operation of the scheme.
Matters relating to conveyancing fall outside the scope of the Defective Concrete Blocks (DCB) Grant Scheme.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether purchase orders issued by his Department under procurement contracts can be linked to the corresponding contracts held in its internal contract register; whether a contract reference or other unique identifier is maintained to enable this linkage; if not, the way his Department monitors cumulative expenditure against the approved value of each contract.
reply: My Department's financial management system and its internal contracts register are not linked, meaning that purchase orders cannot be automatically matched to corresponding contracts through those systems. Monitoring expenditure against approved contract values is therefore the responsibility of the relevant business unit managing the contract. My Department's internal contracts register provides a unique identifier for each contract awarded with a value equal to or exceeding €25,000, excluding VAT.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether contracts recorded in his Department's internal contract register can be linked to their corresponding contract award notices published on eTenders, where applicable; whether his Department records the relevant eTenders notice reference, URL or other identifier; and if not, what prevents this information from being recorded.
reply: My Department's internal contracts register includes a field for recording the relevant eTenders resource ID number where a procurement competition has been conducted through the eTenders platform. This enables the Department to link contracts recorded in the register with the corresponding procurement competition and contract award notice published on eTenders.

question: Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Defence for an update on the actions her Department is taking to increase retention and recruitment in the Defence Forces.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 110, 132 and 154 together.
As Minister for Defence, I am fully committed to increasing and strengthening recruitment and supporting retention in the Permanent Defence Force.
The Military Authorities advise that the strength of the Permanent Defence Force (PDF) stood at 8,034 personnel, of which 627 were female, as at the 30 September 2026.
Last year saw a growth in the overall strength of nearly 200 personnel, with a total of 790 inductions achieved- the highest in twenty years - while the number of personnel who discharged was at its lowest level in more than five years. This trend has continued with a total of 729 inductions achieved to the end of September, while the number of personnel who discharged stood at 441. I am determined to build on the increase in overall PDF strength achieved since 2024 have set a target of 850 inductions to year end.
Furthermore 73 women were inducted to the PDF at end of September, which already exceeds the 70 inductions recorded in total for 2025.
Interest in a career in the Defence Forces remains notably strong with over 15,700 applications received to the end of September of this year, of which 2,394 were from females. The challenge now for the Defence Forces is to convert this high level of applications to inductions. question: Deputy John McGuinness asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if in the implementation of the European Union drinking water regulations 2023 SI 99, in respect of small private water supplies, SPS, a tiered pricing structure for the cost of water testing and monitoring will be put in place to reflect the size of the commercial establishment and its turnover, in order that the costs of the tests will not have a negative impact on the smaller businesses in the sector, particularly family-run businesses; if all local authorities throughout the country will have a common approach and pricing structure.
reply:
Small Private Supplies (SPS) provide drinking water through commercial or public activities such as schools, crèches, nursing homes, self-catering accommodation and hotels. These often rely on private wells for their water supply. There are over 1,600 SPS registered with local authorities, who regulate the SPS in compliance with the Drinking Water standards. The SPS are required to meet the requirement of the Drinking Water Directive transposed into national legislation through European Union (Drinking Water Regulations 2023 (SI 99 of 2023) as amended. The general obligation on water suppliers including SPS is to ensure that all water intended for human consumption is wholesome and clean, does not present a risk to human health and meets the requirements of the Regulations.
I have no specific plans in relation to a pricing structure for testing of SPS but I am conscious of the challenges relating to small private supplies in meeting the drinking water standards and my Department is considering how best to achieve improvements in compliance.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the timeframe for the commencement and operation of Sections 13 and 14 of the Planning and Development Act 2024, whether these provisions will require a public notification and consultation process in respect of applications for licences relating to telecommunications masts and associated infrastructure.
reply:
The Planning and Development Act 2024 (Act of 2024) was signed into law on 17 October 2024. Since June 2025, a phased commencement of the Act of 2024 has been underway, in accordance with the corresponding Implementation Plan published in March 2025, to facilitate the transition from the legislative framework established under the Planning and Development Act 2000 (Act of 2000) to that provided for under the new legislation.
It is anticipated that almost all of the remaining provisions in the Act of 2024 (approximately 390 sections) that have yet to be commenced will be brought into operation shortly, including sections 13 and 14 of that Act. The repeal of the corresponding provisions of the Act of 2000 will be carried out simultaneously.
There are no public notice or consultation obligations required under section 13 of the Act of 2024. The matters to which a planning authority must have regard to when considering a licence application are set out under subsection (7) of section 13 and any person may appeal a decision of a planning authority under that section to An Coimisiún Pleanála. Subsection (4) of section 13 also provides a power to prescribe a class or classes of appliance, apparatus or structure for which an applicant for a licence under section 13 shall give public notice of their application in the prescribed manner and form. question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the supports that are in place to help a family (details supplied) whose land is being destroyed by a badger.
reply:
Section 42 of the Wildlife Act, 1976 (as amended) provides, that where protected wild animals or birds are causing serious damage, persons affected may, on application to the Minister, seek a permission to take appropriate steps to mitigate the damage.
Applications are investigated by local National Parks and Wildlife (NPWS) staff to determine if serious damage is being caused and, if so, the most practical method of controlling the problem. Consideration of the license applications made under Section 42 includes reference to any conservation issues facing the protected species in question.

question: Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if his Department plans to review regulations that allow owner management companies to prevent home owners from having pets in the apartments they own within a residential building.
reply:
At present, the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration and his Department continues to have responsibility for the oversight of Owner Management Companies (OMCs) and related legislation including the Multi-Unit Developments Act, 2011.
The Programme for Government committed to moving the responsibility for the MUDs Act to my Department to streamline support for OMCs and improve oversight and it is expected to transfer in due course. I set out my priority with regard to a review of the MUDs Act to strengthen the operation of management companies in the 2025 National Housing Plan, "Delivering Homes, Building Communities 2025-2030". The proposed review will commence, once responsibility has moved to my Department.
Separately, my Department is examining the issue of pet ownership in social housing tenancies through the ongoing review of the CCMA Code of Practice - Approved Housing Body (AHB) Allocation Process (the Code). A dedicated Working Group comprising representatives of local authorities and Approved Housing Bodies has been established to consider the operation and implementation of the Code.
As part of its work, the Working Group is examining how the Code can better support social housing tenants, whether housed by local authorities or Approved Housing Bodies, to keep domestic pets, while having regard to the rights and responsibilities of landlords, residents, and the management arrangements governing individual developments.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the total number of homes delivered, approved, or drawing down funding within County Mayo for the full year of 2025 under the first home scheme, shared equity completions; the local authority affordable purchase scheme; the local authority home loan, approved and drawn down; the help to buy scheme, claims approved and paid out by Revenue; the tenant (incremental) purchase scheme; the ready to build scheme, serviced sites allocated.
reply:
Affordability and the chance to own a home is at the heart of the Government’s housing policy, as embodied within the housing action plan Delivering Homes, Building Communities 2025 - 2030. This action plan reinforces the range of existing measures being implemented by the Government to tackle the issues of supply and affordability, thereby supporting the increased provision of new homes to purchase and rent.
Over 252 starter home supports have been delivered in Mayo to the end of Q1 2026, with 122 starter home supports being delivered in 2025, through the Starter Home Purchase scheme, the First Home scheme, the Vacant Properties Refurbishment Grant, and the Cost Rental Tenant in Situ scheme.
Mayo County Council has received funding approval to deliver 40 new homes for purchase across 2 schemes, supported by the Affordable Housing Fund, to end 2027. By the end of Q1 2026, 5 of these homes had already been delivered. To further drive the delivery of Starter Homes under the new action plan, local authorities, including Mayo County Council, have commenced the preparation of new Housing Delivery Action Plans (HDAPs) for review by my department, setting out how the Starter Homes Programme will be implemented within their area. These plans are progressing at local authority level and are expected to be published by local authorities

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the timeframe for the planning policy statement on short-term letting to be published; and whether the Oireachtas Committee on Housing, Local Government and Heritage will have an opportunity to scrutinise the draft statement before it is approved by Cabinet.
reply:
To ensure that there is a clear view, both at national level and local authority level, as to the overall policy approach to determining planning applications for short-term lets, a National Planning Statement (NPS) on Short-Term Letting has been developed.
Development of the NPS was informed by a Working Group (comprising my Department, the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment and the County and City Management Association) and engagement with relevant stakeholders.
As part of the process pre-legislative scrutiny of the Short Term Letting and Tourism (STLT) Bill, the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Enterprise Tourism and Employment held two separate sessions solely focused on planning and housing related considerations.
The NPS is expected to be approved by Government imminently.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the review of the HAP payment limits.
reply:
The HAP scheme plays a vital role in housing eligible families and individuals. At the end of Q1 2026, over 133,100 HAP tenancies had been set up since the scheme commenced, of which there were 48,355 households actively in receipt of HAP support nationally.
Maximum rent limits for HAP were set for each housing authority area in 2016 in conjunction with the Department of Social Protection. Since 11 July 2022, each local authority has statutory discretion to agree to a HAP payment up to 35% above the prescribed maximum rent limit. Discretion can be increased up to 50% above the prescribed maximum rent limits for Homeless HAP tenancies in Dublin. Local authorities also have additional flexibility to apply a couple HAP rate to single-person households.
I gave my approval for a review of the current HAP rent limits to be undertaken to ensure there is sufficient support under the HAP scheme to assist eligible households in accessing accommodation in the private rental sector.
As part of this review, the Housing Agency carried out an analysis of the rental market and produced a report. This has helped inform my Department’s review of the HAP rent limits, which has now concluded. I am currently considering its findings before setting out the next steps.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the review of the social housing income eligibility thresholds.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1069 and 1091 together.
My Department has been examining the existing social housing income limits in the context of current market and household income conditions, including the suitability or otherwise of the current framework having regard to the significantly changed landscape since the standardised income limits were introduced. This includes examining the findings of research commissioned by my Department and this work is ongoing.
I expect that the analysis will be concluded shortly to facilitate a final determination on next steps. I am also keen to put in place a more structured and frequent process for the review of these limits going forward.

Existing beneficiaries will continue to have access to the rights associated with Temporary Protection, including access to employment and education, for the duration of the protection.
Council Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/1912 also introduced a new eligibility requirement for Temporary Protection. Article 2 of the Decision provides that, without prejudice to Union law and fundamental rights, Temporary Protection shall only be granted to persons who satisfy their military obligations in Ukraine, upon presenting proof where applicable.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage If he is aware that homeowners who suspect defects in their domestic waste water treatment system (DWWTS) require an inspection report to support an application for a DWWTS remediation grant but cannot directly request an inspection from their local authority; the reason for this restriction; and if he will consider introducing a mechanism whereby householders can request such inspections.
reply:
The Domestic Wastewater Treatment Systems (DWWTS) Grant Scheme is a targeted support measure designed to assist eligible homeowners in exceptional circumstances where there is a public health or environmental need for intervention. The scheme provides financial assistance for the remediation of defective systems where the work delivers wider public benefits. It is not intended as a general grant for the replacement or upgrade of all septic tanks.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether the Government intends to require community, sports and recreational facilities to be included as part of the design and planning process for large residential developments.
reply:
The local authority development plan is the principal planning policy tool for planning authorities to set out their objectives in relation to the planning and sustainable development of their functional area.
Part 3, Chapter 5 ‘Development Plans’ of the Planning and Development Act 2024 commenced on 31st December 2025. When preparing a new development plan under the Act of 2024, planning authorities are required to prepare a strategy relating to creation, improvement and preservation of sustainable places and communities. This includes objectives for ‘the provision, or the facilitation of the provision, improvement, extension and preservation of amenities, facilities and services to meet the social, community, recreational and cultural requirements of the functional area’. The plan-making process is subject to independent oversight by the Office of the Planning Regulator in the performance of its statutory plans evaluation and assessment function.

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to provide details of the latest guidelines issued to local authorities in relation to implementation of Section 39 (2)(e) of the miscellaneous Provisions Act 2014 which relates to “Good Faith” HAP tenancies.
reply:
The Housing Assistance Payment (HAP) Scheme is deemed to be a social housing support under the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2014. As a long term housing support, an assessment of housing need must be completed in order for a household to qualify for HAP. Any household with an identified housing need is eligible for HAP.
In order for housing assistance to be provided under the Act the housing authority must be satisfied that the tenancy concerned is or would be a tenancy in good faith. Where there is a family relationship between the tenant and the landlord, the housing authority may seek evidence of a previous landlord and tenant relationship in respect of the property. This evidence may include:
• Proof of rent payments;
• A lease or tenancy agreement for the property; and
• Registration of the tenancy with the Residential Tenancies Board.
In order for a housing authority to be satisfied that a tenancy is or would be in good faith; the onus is on the applicant and landlord to prove that what is being proposed is a bona fide tenancy.
The Housing Agency, on behalf of my Department, issued an Information Note to all local authorities in December 2025 to help decision-makers in local authorities when the issue arises of whether a HAP tenancy is in ‘good faith’. The guidance provides information about the legal concept of good faith and how it may apply to scenarios that arise in the administration of the HAP scheme.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the status of the older persons housing financial contribution scheme; the reason for the curtailment or discontinuation of the scheme, if applicable; whether a review of the scheme has been undertaken; and if he will consider reinstating or expanding the scheme in view of its role in supporting older people to rightsize into more suitable accommodation while increasing the availability of housing stock for local authorities.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1043 and 1082 together.
The Government is committed to increasing housing available to older people to facilitate ageing in place with dignity and independence and to supporting rightsizing on a voluntary basis. Delivering Homes, Building Communities includes measures to increase delivery of social housing for older people, increase delivery of more suitable homes and choice for older people in private housing, and increase choice to support voluntary rightsizing.
I understand that existing financial contribution schemes in place in some local authorities are non-statutory and therefore a matter for the individual local authorities. Details on the operation of these schemes and the number of households accessing the schemes may be available from the individual local authorities. In line with a commitment in Delivering Homes, Building Communities to review the operation of existing local authority financial contribution schemes, work is already underway with the Housing Agency in advancing this review and this review will inform policy considerations.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of meetings that have taken place and the dates of these meetings, between his officials and the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration regarding the transfer of responsibility for the Multi-Unit Developments Act 2011 and related functions from the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to his Department; the additional resources required by his Department to facilitate the transfer of these functions; when further meetings are due to take place; and the steps he is taking to resolve this matter.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1081, 1125 and 1136 together.
Responsibility for the oversight of Owner Management Companies (OMCs) and related legislation including the Multi-Unit Developments Act, 2011 (the "MUDs Act") currently sits with the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration.
Arising from a Programme for Government commitment, responsibility for the MUDs Act is intended to transfer to my Department. Transfer was contingent on the resolution of a legal matter which was dealt with in the recent Criminal Law, Civil Law and Defence (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 2026.
As legal matters are resolved, a formal Transfer of Functions process will be undertaken and this is led by the Transferring Department. While no formal meetings have taken place there has been pro-active engagement on matters such as financing, staffing, records management and other such relevant matters.
A Transfer Order will be prepared and a Memo to Government advanced by the Transferring Department. It is anticipated that this will be finalised over the coming weeks.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage when the proposed revised national planning statement is expected to be brought before Government for approval; the current stage of its preparation; and if a target date has been set for its publication and implementation.

Until they are replaced by any final National Planning Statement, the 2005 Sustainable Rural Housing Guidelines for Planning Authorities, 2005 remain in effect.

reply:

Digital transformation and the better use of data are central to the ongoing modernisation of the Defence Forces. The implementation of the Defence Forces Digital Transformation Strategy is designed to continuously modernise and secure a unified Defence Forces digital backbone, enabling an agile, adaptive and resilient force. By integrating people, processes, data and technology, they give the women and men of Óglaigh na hÉireann real time access to mission critical data, operational support systems, career development tools and support data centric decision making.
In tandem with this transformation, the implementation of the Defence Forces Data Strategy requires coordinated effort across all Formations and Functions to elevate current practices, embed a data-driven approach, and foster a culture that values the use of centralised, standardised data in everyday decision-making. This collective commitment will enable the Defence Forces to fully harness the power of data in support of mission effectiveness.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the current status of the apartment defects remediation scheme; the number of developments and residential units that have applied for, been approved for or received support; the measures being taken to protect apartment owners from remediation costs; whether changes to the scheme are under consideration; the role of engineers, surveyors and other construction professionals in assessing and certifying defects and remedial works; the challenges identified in implementing the scheme.
reply:
Drafting of the Apartment and Duplex Defects Remediation Scheme Bill is at an advanced stage and it is listed for publication this session. The statutory scheme will be in place as soon as possible following its passage through the Dáil.
The General Scheme of the Bill completed pre-legislative scrutiny in December 2025 and the recommendations of the Joint Committee on Housing, Local Government and Heritage's report have been considered in the context of the drafting of the Bill.
The statutory scheme will provide supports for the remediation of relevant fire safety, structural safety and water ingress defects in purpose-built apartment buildings, including duplexes, constructed between 1991 and 2013. In light of their existing legal responsibilities and ownership of common areas, Owners' Management Companies (OMC) will be funded to carry out the necessary remediation works.
The statutory scheme will provide for a form of certification in relation to the works completed under the scheme. This is important for a range of stakeholders and processes.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether his Department will introduce quarterly reporting and publication of actual expenditure incurred by each of the nine homelessness regions, broken down by expenditure category, including emergency accommodation and homelessness prevention, tenancy sustainment and resettlement supports; whether the relevant lead local authorities currently record this expenditure on a quarterly basis; whether the existing annual reporting arrangements could be amended to provide quarterly returns; and if not, the specific legal, technical or administrative reasons preventing this.
reply:
My Department’s role in relation to homelessness involves the provision of a national framework of policy, legislation and funding to underpin the role of housing authorities in addressing homelessness at local level. Statutory responsibility in relation to the provision of homeless services rests with individual housing authorities. The administration of homeless services is organised on a regional basis with a lead local authority in each region.
My Department does not fund any homeless service directly but provides funding to housing authorities towards the operational costs of homeless accommodation and related services under Section 10 of the Housing Act, 1988. Under Exchequer funding arrangements, housing authorities must provide at least 10% of the cost of services from their own resources. Furthermore, housing authorities may also incur additional expenditure on homeless related services outside of the Exchequer funding arrangements provided by my Department. Therefore, the exact amounts spent by housing authorities on homeless services are a matter for individual housing authorities in consultation with the Management Group of the relevant regional joint Homelessness Consultative Forum.
Section 10 funding is recouped to housing authorities under an annual delegated funding grant agreement. This grant agreement sets out the principles and objectives of the funding, reporting requirements, and details the responsibilities of housing authorities under DPER Circular 13/2

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of houses constructed in the 1930s that have received funding under the Historic Structures Fund in each of the past five years; whether a dwelling built in the 1930s that is not included on a Record of Protected Structures is eligible for assistance under the scheme; and whether he plans to extend eligibility to historically and architecturally significant properties of this period that are currently excluded from support.
reply:
Under the Historic Structures Fund (HSF), a total of 2 houses constructed in the 1930s have received funding over the past five years. The HSF provides capital funding for works to buildings listed on the Record of Protected Structures (RPS) of each Local Authority; to structures or works within Architectural Conservation Areas (ACAs) or within the amenity of a National Monument; and/or to structures eligible for or proposed for inclusion in the RPS but which have not yet been formally approved for inclusion.
Structures within the latter category must meet the criteria for inclusion in the RPS by the Local Authority, i.e. they must be of special interest from an architectural, historical, archaeological, artistic, cultural, scientific, social or technical point of view. It is important to note that this reference to "special interest" is not therefore solely dependent on the age of a building or the date of its original construction.
Each year the HSF application process is exceptionally competitive and is always extremely oversubscribed with applications for proposed projects that meet the eligibility criteria as set out above. As such, I have no plans at present to broaden the eligibility criteria for qualifying structures.

question: Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the scheme to allow victims and survivors of domestic violence to transfer to a different local authority housing list and keep their time; and if people on HAP transfer lists will also be considered for same.
reply:
The Protocol to allow victims and survivors of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV) to transfer their time on the social housing waiting list between different local authorities was published in July of this year by my Department and has been implemented by the local authorities.
The Protocol gives effect to a commitment contained in Delivering Homes, Building Communities, which recognised that fleeing domestic violence continues to be a significant factor in presentations to homeless services and committed to removing barriers faced by victims and survivors.
The Protocol allows victims and survivors of DSGBV assessed as qualified for social housing support, and who satisfy the necessary evidential requirements, to apply to another local authority and, subject to meeting the receiving authority's eligibility criteria, retain their original qualification date for waiting-list purposes. An important feature of the Protocol is that it will be actively monitored as it is rolled out, this monitoring will help ensure that the Protocol is meeting the needs of victims and survivors and will allow any concerns to be identified and addressed quickly should they arise.
Local authorities also assist victims and survivors with both their emergency and long-term housing needs under the Department's "Policy and Procedural Guidance for Housing Authorities in Relation to Assisting Victims of Domestic Violence with Emergency and Long-Term Accommodation Needs" , first published i
