question: Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the review of HAP rates; and if changes are forthcoming this year to the rates and discretion levels.
reply:
The HAP scheme plays a vital role in housing eligible families and individuals. At the end of Q1 2026, over 133,100 HAP tenancies had been set up since the scheme commenced, of which there were 48,355 households actively in receipt of HAP support nationally.
Maximum rent limits for HAP were set for each housing authority area in 2016 in conjunction with the Department of Social Protection. Since 11 July 2022, each local authority has statutory discretion to agree to a HAP payment up to 35% above the prescribed maximum rent limit. Discretion can be increased up to 50% above the prescribed maximum rent limits for Homeless HAP tenancies in Dublin. Local authorities also have additional flexibility to apply a couple HAP rate to single-person households.
I gave my approval for a review of the current HAP rent limits to be undertaken to ensure there is sufficient support under the HAP scheme to assist eligible households in accessing accommodation in the private rental sector.
As part of this review, the Housing Agency carried out an analysis of the rental market and produced a report. This has helped inform my Department’s review of the HAP rent limits, which has now concluded. I am currently considering its findings before setting out the next steps.

question: Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage his plans to address the worsening homelessness crisis; and the recent engagement he has had with local authorities in this regard.
reply:
Supporting individuals and families experiencing or at risk of experiencing homelessness is a priority for my Department and Government.
Our housing plan, ‘Delivering Homes, Building Communities: An Action Plan on Housing Supply and Targeting Homelessness’ is an integrated housing and homelessness plan. The plan is based on two key pillars: activating the supply of 300,000 more homes; and supporting people to have a home of their own.
Increased supply is key to addressing homelessness. Government is focused on making sure that everyone has access to good quality, affordable and secure homes that suit their needs. Over €9 billion in capital funding will be made available for housing in 2026.
Prevention of homelessness in the first instance is an absolute priority. There are many preventions initiatives already underway in my own Department and across Government. This includes the provision of social and affordable housing, HAP and homeless HAP, and our strong tenancy protection legislation. In order to ensure a fully aligned all-of-Government approach under the Plan, we are committing to develop a national Homelessness Prevention Framework within which homelessness can be prevented in a structured and planned way with tailored prevention measures for each potential at risk cohort. This Framework will be in place in 2026.
Addressing family homelessness is a key priority for Government. Our housing plan commits to the development of a Child and Family Homelessness Action Plan. T

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Defence her views on whether the current policy to loosen the Triple Lock on overseas military engagement works and that it has complete popular legitimacy (details supplied); and if she will acknowledge Ireland's achievements under the Triple Lock and set out a policy to strengthen rather than to undermine it.
reply:
As Minister of State for Defence, I want to acknowledge and pay tribute to the outstanding achievements of Irish peacekeepers. For almost seven decades, members of the Defence Forces have served with distinction on UN missions across the globe, including in the Congo, Lebanon, Liberia, Chad, Mali and the Golan Heights.
Nothing in the Defence (Amendment) Bill 2026 will diminish Ireland's ability to participate in current, or future, UN led or UN mandated missions. The rationale for the proposed reforms proposed by the Defence Amendment Bill is straightforward. The international security environment has evolved significantly and the current requirement for a UN Security Council mandate can restrict Ireland's ability to participate in international missions due to the use, or threatened use, of a veto by a permanent member of the Security Council.
The Government believes that decisions on the deployment of Irish Defence Forces personnel should be a sovereign decision, made by Ireland's democratic institutions rather than being dependent on factors outside the State's control.
The Bill does not alter Ireland's policy of military neutrality and our constitutional expressly prohibits participation in a common European defence.
The advice of the Attorney General, and Government, and Dáil approval where appropriate, will continue to be required on the deployment of Irish Defence Forces personnel. The Bill also strengthens transparency through enhanced reporting and oversight arrangem

question: Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the review of the social housing income eligibility thresholds.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1069 and 1091 together.
My Department has been examining the existing social housing income limits in the context of current market and household income conditions, including the suitability or otherwise of the current framework having regard to the significantly changed landscape since the standardised income limits were introduced. This includes examining the findings of research commissioned by my Department and this work is ongoing.
I expect that the analysis will be concluded shortly to facilitate a final determination on next steps. I am also keen to put in place a more structured and frequent process for the review of these limits going forward.

question: Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage If he intends to further fund Louth County Council with more resources to keep up with the growing demand for Housing Adaptation Grants which has resulted in the local authority having to close the schemes for applications due to funding constraints.
reply:
My Department provides funding under the suite of Housing Adaptation Grants for Older People and Disabled People, to assist those in private houses to make their accommodation more suitable for their needs. The suite of grants, which include the Housing Adaptation Grant for Disabled People, the Mobility Aids Grant and the Housing Aid for Older People Grant, are funded by my Department with a contribution from the local authority. The detailed administration of the scheme including assessment, approval, prioritisation and apportionment is the responsibility of local authorities.
The Exchequer funding available for these grants in 2026 increased substantially by €30 million to €129.5 million, or over €152 million when accounting for the local authority contribution, continuing the year on year increases since 2014.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to provide the number of hectares of forest removed already or to be removed in 2027 and in subsequent years in the Slieve Bloom mountains SPA to support conservation of the endangered hen harrier; and to provide details on the number of hectares of forestry to be removed in the Slieve Aughty mountains SPA, Mullaghanish to Musheramore SPA, Slieve Beagh SPA, Slievefelim to Silvermines mountains SPA, and the Stack's to Mullaghereirk mountains, West Limerick hills and Mount Eagle SPA to support hen harrier conservation.
reply: My Department is working closely with other Departments and Coillte on the implementation of the Hen Harrier Threat Response Plan. As part of the Plan delivery, NPWS and Coillte have commenced a pilot project in the Slieve Bloom Mountains SPA, involving the felling of trees in order to improve the habitat for use by breeding hen harrier and to reduce associated threats and pressures. The final number of hectares to be removed is yet to be confirmed and is subject to the approval that is required through Department of Agriculture Food and Marine’s licensing process. The learnings from this pilot project will be used to inform the development of next steps in terms of further delivery of the Threat Response Plan in this and the other five breeding hen harrier SPAs.

question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the capital funding available to local authorities to install, upgrade and maintain gates and access control systems in local authority flat complexes; whether such works are eligible under existing refurbishment or estate regeneration programmes; the amount drawn down by Dublin City Council for such works in each of the years 2024 to 2026; and if he will consider a dedicated funding stream to improve security for local authority tenants affected by anti-social behaviour.
reply:
While such measures are not precluded from support as part of a broader flat complex regeneration supported through my Department's local authority estate regeneration programme, local authorities are ultimately responsible for such matters as part of the management and maintenance of their social housing stock. To this end, local authority officials and elected members are obliged to ensure adequate funding is made available for these purposes through their respective annual budgetary processes.
There are no plans to introduce a dedicated Exchequer supported funding stream for gates or access control systems for local authority owned flat complexes. That said, my Department continues to provide significant funding to local authorities under the Planned Maintenance and Voids Programme to support local authorities in the management and maintenance of their housing stock, including measures that contribute to the safety and wellbeing of tenants and communities.
My Department does not collect data on expenditure by local authorities on gates and access control systems. Accordingly, details of the amounts expended on such works in any given year should be sought directly from Dublin City Council.

question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage If his Department will consider the introduction of a rent to buy scheme for households who have previously been accommodated through the tenant in situ and are paying rent to a local authority.
reply:

The programme is an option to be used when no other solution is available. Households accommodated through the Social Housing Second-Hand Acquisitions Programme become local authority tenants and are afforded the same tenancy rights and responsibilities as other local authority tenants.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Defence the reasons she is opposed to giving the people a say on abolishing the Triple Lock.
reply:
Thank you Deputy for the question. There have been a number of calls for a referendum or public plebiscite on the Government’s proposed changes to the Triple Lock, either to enshrine neutrality in the Constitution or to vote directly on the legislative amendments. Many of these calls incorrectly conflate an amendment to legislation, which the Defence Amendment Bill proposes, with an amendment to the Constitution.
The Triple Lock is not a constitutional provision. Ireland was a militarily neutral country before the introduction of the Triple Lock, and it will remain a militarily neutral country after the legislation is passed. Our military neutrality remains grounded in Ireland’s long-standing policy of non-participation in military alliances.
The proposed amendments do not alter this traditional position of military neutrality, despite the repeated and disingenuous accusations from certain quarters. Any overseas deployment of Defence Forces personnel will continue to be based on the principles of the UN Charter and international law, and will require the approval of Ireland’s democratically elected representatives.
It is important to emphasise most strongly again that the Bill does not remove the United Nations from Ireland's framework for overseas deployments. question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether his Department has issued guidance to designated local authorities administering the defective concrete blocks grant scheme regarding cases where competent building professionals fail or refuse to provide the final invoices, certificates or other documentation required to facilitate the release of grant payments; and whether a formal procedure exists for escalating complaints concerning such professionals.
reply:
The Remediation of Dwellings Damaged by the use of Defective Concrete Blocks Act 2022 as amended by the Act of 2025 sets out the framework under which the Grant Scheme which provides grant funding to people whose homes have been affected by Defective Concrete Blocks (DCB) operates.
A number of amendments contained in the 2025 Act came into operation on 25 February 2026 and more recently further provisions commenced on 27 May 2026.
Under the terms of the scheme, a homeowner must engage a Competent Building Professional (CBP) to design the remediation works approved or being carried out and prepare a remedial works plan in that regard.
The homeowner is required to retain the services of their CBP throughout the project and they will inspect the works as they progress, prepare interim valuation certificates to allow for stage payment requests to be lodged with the relevant local authority and sign off on the Certificate of Remediation on completion of the remediation works.
Any issue that may arise between a homeowner and their CBP in relation to the provision of final invoices, certifications, or other documentation required to facilitate the payment of grant assistance is a matter for the parties concerned to resolve. Accordingly, my Department has no role in the matter.

question: Deputy Martin Kenny asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if the payments listed by the Department of Social Protection under the Social Welfare Acts (Part4. Income that is not assessable) on the Government household means policy should be disregarded in all cases when calculating local authority and social housing schemes rent.
reply:
Local authorities set and collect rents on their dwellings in accordance with section 58 of the Housing Act 1966. The making or amending of such differential rent schemes is a matter for local authorities within broad principles set out by my Department, including that rent levels should be based on income and reflect tenants’ ability to pay.
Local discretion and flexibility are inherent in the devolved administration of differential rent schemes and different approaches are taken to rent setting across local authorities. Accordingly, decisions regarding the sources of income included and disregarded for rent assessment purposes are matters solely for individual local authorities.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the current heritage and ownership status of a location (details supplied); whether his Department has a record of the site transferring from public to private ownership; if so, when; whether his Department has information identifying the current landowner; and the protections in place for the site.
reply:
St. Fintan’s Well is not a national monument in Ministerial ownership. It is a recorded monument, and as such, St. Fintan’s Well is protected under section 12(3) of the National Monuments (Amendment) Act 1994 Act.
The Act provides that where the owner or occupier of a monument or place included in the Record, or any person, proposes to carry out, or to cause or permit the carrying out of any work at or in relation to such monument or place, he or she shall give notice, in writing, of the proposal to the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage and shall not, except in the case of urgent necessity and with the consent of the Minister, commence the work for a period of two months after having given the notice.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of appeals to An Bord Pleanála relating to solar installations on protected structures or within ACAs since October 2022; and the outcome of those appeals.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1045, 1048, 1049, 1051, 1052, 1053, 1147, 1148 and 1149 together.
My Department introduced new planning regulations in October 2022 that significantly enhanced existing provisions regarding planning exemptions for rooftop solar installations.
There is now no rooftop limit on houses and new exemptions were also introduced for the erection of solar panels on apartments and certain non-domestic structures including hospitals, libraries and places of worship, subject to certain conditions and limitations.
These provisions are considered to be an effective measure which have significantly assisted with the roll out of rooftop solar, particularly on the domestic level, and meeting climate targets in this regard.
The matter of solar exempted development and the potential impact on protected structures and Architectural Conservation Areas (ACAs) was a primary consideration of the Department in the development of these regulations. It remains the case that a development is not considered exempted development if it would materially affect the character of a protected structure or a building in an Architectural Conservation Area.
With regards to any future changes, there has been significant progress on the review of Exempted Development Regulations.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of local-authority posts sanctioned by his Department in each year from 2022 to 2025 and to date in 2026 that remain unfilled, broken down by local authority, functional area and year of sanction; the median time between departmental sanction and appointment; and the number of sanctioned posts subsequently withdrawn or allowed to lapse.
reply:
Following the issue of any required sanction by my Department for a new or replacement post, responsibility for progressing the appointment rests with the Chief Executive who, under Section 159 of the Local Government Act 2001, is responsible for the staffing and organisational arrangements necessary to carry out the functions of the local authority for which he or she is responsible. Recruitment in the local government sector is undertaken by a local authority directly or by publicjobs on their behalf depending on the grade and tenure of the post concerned.
My Department does not have a recruitment role and therefore does not hold data on the filling of posts following the issuing of sanctions, or on the functional areas to which new staff may be assigned. This is a matter for the Chief Executive and such information would, therefore, be available from each local authority.

I propose to take Questions Nos. 1044, 1046, 1047 and 1055 together.
The Local Government Act 2019 (the Act) was enacted on 31 January 2019 to provide for the transfer of part of the administrative area of Cork County Council to the administrative area of Cork City and this took place when the new Councils took office after the local elections in late May 2019.
Section 18 of the Act provided for the establishment of the statutory Cork Boundary Alteration Implementation Oversight Committee to oversee arrangements for the alteration of the boundary in accordance with the statutory implementation plan.
Work on finalising the transfer of functions was completed in late 2020 and both local authorities have confirmed that all the actions contained in the statutory implementation plan have been discharged with new service delivery models now in place in both authorities. While the Oversight Committee has not been active since the transfer was concluded, it has not been dissolved.
Section 31(2)(b) of the Act provides that where, before the transfer day for the Cork boundary alteration, Cork County Council had performed any function under Part VIII of the Planning and Development Act 2000 in relation to a contravention in the area transferred to Cork City Council, all functions under that Part in relation to that contravention shall, from the transfer day, be performable by the county council after consultation with the city council.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if his Department has instructed local authorities to suspend financial contribution schemes for age friendly rightsizing due to an ongoing review by the Department.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1043 and 1082 together.
The Government is committed to increasing housing available to older people to facilitate ageing in place with dignity and independence and to supporting rightsizing on a voluntary basis. Delivering Homes, Building Communities includes measures to increase delivery of social housing for older people, increase delivery of more suitable homes and choice for older people in private housing, and increase choice to support voluntary rightsizing.
I understand that existing financial contribution schemes in place in some local authorities are non-statutory and therefore a matter for the individual local authorities. Details on the operation of these schemes and the number of households accessing the schemes may be available from the individual local authorities. In line with a commitment in Delivering Homes, Building Communities to review the operation of existing local authority financial contribution schemes, work is already underway with the Housing Agency in advancing this review and this review will inform policy considerations.

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage his plans to assist Kildare County Council in dealing with the backlog of unauthorised development cases in County Kildare.
reply:
The powers of planning authorities to enforce planning control and deal with breaches of planning law are currently provided for under the Planning and Development Act 2000, which obliges all planning authorities to investigate and follow through on any complaint of unauthorised development. Enforcement powers include issuing warning letters, enforcement notices and taking legal action against unauthorised development. The key objectives of planning enforcement are to bring unauthorised development under control, remedy its impacts and take legal action where necessary.
While responsibility for investigating and taking enforcement action in relation to unauthorised development rests with individual planning authorities in the exercise of their statutory functions, the Department supports the effective operation of the planning system through a range of measures aimed at strengthening capacity, capability and performance across the local authority planning sector. These measures are intended to assist planning authorities in carrying out their planning responsibilities, including those relating to planning enforcement.
The Department has taken steps to strengthen staffing capacity across the local authority planning sector. The Ministerial Action Plan on Planning Resources sets out a coordinated programme of measures addressing recruitment, education, retention and the longer-term supply of planning expertise. My Department operates a number of funding programmes that assist local authorities to work in partnership with Approved Housing Bodies (AHBs) to construct and purchase new homes and make them available for social housing. The main funding programme that AHBs progress Social Housing projects through is the Capital Advance Leasing Facility (CALF).
CALF funding is capital support provided to Approved Housing Bodies (AHBs) by local authorities which fund the construction or purchase of new build social housing units. This loan facility can support between 25% and 30% of the eligible capital cost of the housing project, with the remaining finance sourced by the AHBs from private lenders (usually the Housing Finance Agency (HFA).

Accelerated CALF must be outlined in the initial application and provided for in the CALF approval letter. McGuinness asked the Minister for Defence for an update on the acquisition of the modular towed array sonar system and the implementation of Phase 2 sonobuoy technology under the Equipment Development Plan; the specific milestones achieved in personnel training for subsea domain awareness; the exact origin of the equipment currently being procured; and the updated delivery timescales for these systems to achieve initial and full operational capability.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 104 and 138 together.
The Government has committed to measures to strengthening Ireland’s maritime security framework particularly in response to threats to critical undersea infrastructure, increased geopolitical tensions, and the need for enhanced maritime domain awareness. This requires a multifaceted and a whole of Government approach encompassing strategic policy initiatives, national capability development programmes and participation in collaborative EU projects.
Firstly, I am fully committed to the implementation of our first National Maritime Security Strategy which I published in February this year. This whole of Government approach sets out a 5 year roadmap (2026 -2030) to protect the State's maritime domain, safeguard critical infrastructure and strengthen national security.
In terms of capability projects the Towed Sonar and Sonobuoys are two projects within a broader programme of work, initiated in 2023, to enhance monitoring and surveillance of the subsea domain.
Following a period of market research, planning and evaluation in line with the Infrastructure Guidelines, a contract for Towed Sonar was awarded to Thales DMS France in Q2 2025. This project will see the Naval Service acquire sonar capability which will be used to detect objects near cables and pipelines in Irish territorial waters and the EEZ. question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will provide an update on the timelines for the rural planning guidelines to be published by his Department; and if he will outline whether his Department is considering changing guidelines around ribbon development.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1036 and 1080 together.

In accordance with Section 26(4) of the Planning and Development Act 2024, the draft NPS and the associated environmental documentation will be published for public consultation, and submissions will be invited before the Statement is finalised.
Under Section 25 of the 2024 Planning and Development Act, draft National Planning Statements are subject to approval by Government prior to issue by the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the legacy defects support scheme.
reply:
Drafting of the Apartment and Duplex Defects Remediation Scheme Bill is at an advanced stage and it is listed for publication this session. The statutory scheme will be in place as soon as possible following its passage through the Dáil.
The scheme will provide supports for the remediation of relevant fire safety, structural safety and water ingress defects in purpose-built apartment buildings, including duplexes, constructed between 1991 and 2013. It is envisaged that 100% of eligible remediation costs will be funded.
It is expected that applicants to the current Interim Remediation Scheme will transfer seamlessly over to the new statutory scheme, which will be managed by the Housing Agency. My Department and the Housing Agency will work to ensure that applications under the statutory scheme are progressed as quickly as possible.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if provision exists within the vacant property refurbishment grant scheme for discretion or exceptional arrangements where a homeowner has complied with all scheme requirements, including verifying and submitting a contractor's valid tax clearance certificate prior to the commencement of works, but is subsequently unable to obtain an updated tax clearance certificate because the contractor has become uncontactable (details supplied).
reply:
Addressing vacancy and dereliction is a key priority for this Government, as reflected in the Housing Plan, Delivering Homes, Building Communities. The Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant, funded under the Croí Cónaithe Towns Fund, has been a key measure in addressing vacancy and dereliction across the country.
The Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant provides a grant of up to €50,000 to support the refurbishment of vacant properties for occupation as a principal private residence and for properties which will be made available for rent. A top-up grant of up to €20,000 is available where the property is confirmed to be derelict, bringing the total grant available for a derelict property up to a maximum of €70,000.
The Vacant Homes Unit in my Department offers support and guidance to local authorities in their administration of the scheme. While the Department issues guidance on the scheme, it has no direct role in deciding on individual applications. The grant is administered and managed by local authorities, who process and decide on applications and issue grant payments on completion of approved refurbishment works.
The grant application process involves the local authority receiving and reviewing applications to ensure that the grant conditions are met and arranging for a qualified person to visit the property to check the refurbishment work being applied for and to assess the proposed cost.

question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether his Department is developing a relocation scheme for the nine households at Elm Park, Buncrana, County Donegal, whose homes are affected by defective concrete and flood risk, following previous ministerial statements regarding agreement in principle to relocation; if so, when its terms are expected to be finalised; and if no such scheme is currently being developed, whether the proposal has been abandoned or deferred.
reply:
The Remediation of Dwellings Damaged by the use of Defective Concrete Blocks Act 2022 as amended by the Act of 2025 underpins the Grant Scheme which provides grant funding to people whose homes have been affected by Defective Concrete Blocks.
I visited Donegal last year where I met many of the residents affected and I understand the flood issue pertaining to Elm Park in Buncrana, where nine homeowners are particularly affected.
The majority of homeowners impacted are eligible to avail of the Defective Concrete Block Scheme which is funded by my Department. They are understandably worried about availing of the scheme and remediating their homes without the flood risk having been addressed. I know that the Office of Public Works has a plan to undertake flood relief works in the coming period in that area which will address the flood risk.
The residents however, are concerned about the length of time before those flood works would be completed and have asked that consideration be given to relocation options.
I appreciate the genuine concerns of the residents based on their own personal experiences in recent years.
Legal advice from the Attorney General’s office regarding a scheme to assist these homeowners is being considered by my Department who are working with officials in the OPW.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage further to Parliamentary Question No. 71213/26, the date on which the lawful residency and habitual residency provisions of the Housing and Residential Tenancies (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 will be commenced; the date on which guidance for local authorities and applicants will be published; and whether the new criteria will apply to households already qualified for social housing support on the date of commencement.
reply:
Preparations are underway for the commencement of Part 3 of the Housing and Residential Tenancies (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026, which provides for lawful residency and habitual residency as eligibility criteria for social housing support. Although a commencement date has not been set, I expect this part of the legislation will be commenced in the coming weeks.
These new statutory arrangements will include detailed guidance on how housing authorities should assess lawful and habitual residency requirements. My Department has been working closely with the Housing Agency to create this guidance, alongside a series of training resources, which will be made available to housing authorities prior to commencement. Furthermore, detailed guidance documents aimed at the general public will also be published prior to commencement.
Applications for social housing support are assessed by the relevant local authority, in accordance with the eligibility and need criteria set down in section 20 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2009 and the associated Social Housing Assessment Regulations 2011, as amended. Regulations 27 to 29 of the 2011 Regulations provide for a review of social housing assessments. A review involves a fresh determination of whether a household continues to qualify for social housing support. reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1027 and 1126 together.

Updated National Guidelines for the Assessment and Allocation Process for Social Housing Provision for People with a Disability were published in 2017 under section 5 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2009. The purpose of the National Guidelines for the Assessment and Allocation Process for Social Housing Provision for People with a Disability is to drive consistency in streamlining the management of the social housing assessment and allocation process for disabled people across all local authorities. The Guidelines support housing authorities in carrying out assessments of social housing need for disabled people within a planned and structured framework to ensure that their needs can be assessed as effectively as possible in a timely manner including disabled people transitioning to community independent living from residential/institutional/congregated/hospital care setting or long-term residential care settings.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage further to Parliamentary Question No. 430, to state clearly whether any assessment has been undertaken by the Department of the extent to which increases in local property tax receipts since 2021 have resulted in additional local authority services rather than maintaining existing service levels; if so, whether it will be published; and if not, whether one will be undertaken.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1025 and 1026 together.
The overall amount of Local Property Tax (LPT) for a local authority’s own discretionary use, i.e. excluding any self- funding amounts, has increased by 48% in the last five years from €422m in 2021 up to €623.4m in 2026. As well as assisting local authorities in meeting the costs of providing essential services, increases in LPT funding enables a level of flexibility and discretion for each authority to address priority and additional resource demands arising.
My Department has not undertaken, and has no plans to undertake, an assessment of whether increased LPT receipts have resulted in additional local authority services or have primarily supported the maintenance of existing service levels. Local authorities are independent corporate entities with full responsibility in law for the performance of their functions and the discharge of their governance responsibilities. Elected members have direct responsibility for reserved functions, including the adoption of the annual budget. Accordingly, it is a matter for each local authority to determine its own spending priorities through the budgetary process, having regard to local needs and available resources. In that context, decisions regarding the allocation of discretionary LPT funding within a local authority area are matters for the local authority concerned and are determined in line with local budgetary priorities; my Department has no role. question: Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the Government’s September 2026 commitment to exempt ECCE-only preschool services from commercial rates; when the exemption will take effect; whether commercial rates bills already issued to providers will be withdrawn or refunded; whether local authorities will be instructed to suspend collection pending implementation.
reply:
Tailte Éireann is an independent Government agency and provides a property registration system, property valuation service, and national mapping and surveying infrastructure for the State. Tailte Éireann is independent in the exercise of its valuation functions under the Valuation Act 2001, as amended (the Act), and I, as the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage, have no function in decisions in this regard.
Tailte Éireann has overall responsibility under the Act, for the maintenance of all Valuation Lists used by Local Authorities in the calculation of rates liability. Under the Act, all property is rateable unless it falls into one of the exempt categories listed in Schedule 4 of the Act. There is a very specific range of exemptions that can be applied, and Tailte Éireann has no discretionary latitude to grant exemptions not covered by Schedule 4. In general, the Act, maintains the long-standing position that all properties of occupiers that operate with the intention of making a profit are rateable.

reply:

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage when he intends to request An Coimisiún Toghcháin to prepare a report on amendments to local electoral area boundaries as recommended by the local democracy task force.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1022 and 1119 together.
Section 23 of the Local Government Act 2001 empowers the Minister to divide a local authority administrative area into local electoral areas by order and to determine the municipal districts within the administrative area by order. Each municipal district must consist of one or more than one local electoral area. The section also empowers the Minister to amend those orders. In advance of deciding to make an order under section 23 of the 2001 Act, the Minister must, in accordance with section 32(2) of the Local Government Act 1991, request An Coimisiún Toghcháin to prepare a report having regard to such matters as may be specified by the Minister.
Before making a request to An Coimisiún, section 61 of the Electoral Reform Act 2022 provides that the Minister shall lay a draft of the request before each House of the Oireachtas for approval by resolution by each House. Following the completion of a review, the Minister must publish the report of An Coimisiún and must have regard to the report in deciding whether to make an order in relation to any amendment to local electoral area boundaries or municipal districts.

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the current status of notifications under the basic income for the arts pilot scheme: the number of successful applicants notified to date; the number of successful applicants yet to be notified; and if he will provide a clear timetable for the issuance of all remaining notifications.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 961, 978, 1007, 1017 and 1021 together.
In February 2026, the successor scheme to the Basic Income for the Arts Pilot scheme was announced. The main objective of the Basic Income for the Arts scheme is to support professional artists whose creative practice is based in Ireland. This is a major milestone for the arts in Ireland and research conducted by the Department of Culture provided Government with a clear evidence base upon which to make that decision.
The Department's allocation in Budget 2027, has provided for the full year cost of Basic Income for the Arts of €34.4m to ensure that all commitments under scheme to fund 2,000 artists could be met.
The Department commenced communication to 780 applicants invited to participate in the scheme on Thursday 15 October. Further successful applicants will be notified in future tranches in the coming weeks once assessments are finalised.
As an appeals process is necessary for those deemed ineligible the full cohort of 2,000 cannot be informed until the appeals process concludes. Once the full 2,000 cohort of successful applicants has been finalised those who were unsuccessful will be informed, that may take a number of weeks as the assessments and appeal processes are ongoing.
The Department is processing the applications as promptly as possible and all successful candidates will receive the full allocation of €325 per week for three years.

question: Deputy Rose Conway-Walsh asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the assurances he will provide to rural and isolated households, who currently rely on copper telecommunication lines, that their telephone and communications services will not be disrupted when these lines are decommissioned and that alternatives will be in place before they are phased out.
reply:
The Government remains supportive of an orderly transition to fibre-based networks, while ensuring that any copper switch-off is carried out in a proportionate manner and in the best interests of consumers and the wider telecommunications market.
The first step in the migration from legacy copper-based infrastructure to modern fibre infrastructure will be the approval by the Commission for Communications Regulation (ComReg) of a Switch-Off Proposal submitted by eir. Once approved, copper switch-off will be implemented on an exchange-area-by-exchange-area basis in accordance with the requirements set out in ComReg Decision D09/23.
ComReg published guidance for retail service providers on customer migrations during copper switch-off (ComReg 24/76) in September 2024. Further public information on the copper switch-off process will be made available as this work progresses.
Customers will not be required to migrate off copper services until alternative communications services are available to them. Any copper switch-off programme approved by ComReg will include migration arrangements designed to ensure continuity of service and minimise disruption to consumers, including those in rural and isolated areas.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to provide, for each department, the expenditure levy amount applied from 2027; the specific measures submitted and approved to meet it; the posts to be supressed, programmes reduced and grants to State agencies reduced; the amount classified as efficiencies versus reductions in services; and if proposals by any department were rejected or remain unagreed.

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he will give assurances that 100% of revenue collected through the carbon tax will be ringfenced for climate action measures to facilitate a just transition, and that all unspent carbon tax revenue will be carried over to the following year rather than returned to the Exchequer.
reply:
In Budget 2027, and as set out in the Budget Publication "The Use of Carbon Tax Funds", a total of €1,114 million from carbon tax revenue is being allocated to programmes which support climate measures and ensure the most vulnerable are protected from unintended impacts of the tax.
The Programme for Government 2025 – Securing Ireland’s Future commits to using the carbon tax as a key tool to encourage a shift away from fossil fuels and to invest in a sustainable future. It also commits to continue to use carbon tax revenues to fund social welfare measures, agri- environmental schemes and retrofitting.
Between Budget 2020 and Budget 2026, additional carbon tax revenues have been allocated incrementally each year to programmes to insulate the most vulnerable from increases in the carbon tax and to support decarbonisation and energy efficiency programmes across buildings, agriculture and transport.
More recently, in light of the deviation from the previously scheduled increases to the carbon tax rates, carbon tax allocations will remain in line with those made in Budget 2026. While there is no increase in the amount allocated from the carbon tax in 2026, Government is committed to prioritising those key measures which promote a just transition and is increasing the overall expenditure allocations to these measures through wider State funds.

question: Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he will commit to meaningful public sector pay talks with the unions representing public sector workers.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 50, 55, 64 and 82 together.
I have always been, and remain, committed to meaningful engagement with public service unions and staff associations in relation to a successor Public Service Pay Agreement.
I am very pleased that, following intensive engagement in recent days, industrial action scheduled for 21 October 2026 has been averted.
In this regard, I am appreciative of the efforts of Mr Kevin Foley, as chair, as well as Mr Owen Reidy and Ms Oonagh Buckley in engaging with both parties to identify a pathway back to formal negotiations.
The first formal engagement between the parties took place in the Workplace Relations Commission on 19 October 2026. This represents a constructive step forward and will support efforts to secure a new agreement. There is now a genuine opportunity to make progress through constructive engagement and a shared commitment to dialogue.
I recognise the significant contribution made by public service workers to our society and our country. They are the backbone of our healthcare, social care, education, policing and many other essential services. The Government is committed to negotiating a pay agreement that is fair, affordable and sustainable. However, given the confidential nature of the process, I am not in a position to comment further on the substance of the ongoing discussions or the terms of any potential agreement.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the measures being taken to ensure that the continued digitalisation of public services does not disadvantage older people, people with disabilities or those with limited digital literacy; and the way in which access to in-person and telephone services will be maintained where needed.
reply:
The strategic goal to digitalise public services carries with it a risk of excluding people from participating fully with these services, if their individual needs and preferences are not factored in to the design of these digital-first, but not digital-only, services.
Work to develop the Life Events model for Irish public services so far has included engagement across a range of users with amplified needs when engaging with public services. This has included research with older adults and adults with intellectual disabilities to understand their preferences, challenges and needs when engaging digitally with the State. Understanding the experience of such users is the primary starting point for building out public services, recognising that access is dependent on having the requisite skills, and knowledge, and also the availability of material resources and connectivity.
This approach has allowed the work to move beyond merely increasing digitisation and toward a more holistic set of digitally enabled services that can be accessed across multiple channels, including over the telephone and are centered on the needs of the user, proactively mitigating exclusion.
Through the process of design the human journey of using a service is mapped out end to end based on real insight helping to highlight shared challenges and opportunities for improvement. question: Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the basis on which it was decided to award excessive salary increases to the CEOs of many State bodies.
reply:
On 27 June 2023, the Minister for Public Expenditure National Development Plan Delivery and Reform published the final review of the Report of the Independent Review Panel on Senior Public Service Recruitment and Pay Processes. The Panel made a range of findings and 38 recommendations. Among these recommendations was the establishment of a Review Body on Higher Remuneration to advise the Minister on total remuneration arrangements for senior posts in the Public Service and for Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) of CSBs. It further recommended that the CEOs of CSBs be prioritised for review by the recommended Body arising from the lack of an agreed mechanism to review rates and their exclusion from national pay agreements.
The Government subsequently established the Senior Post Remuneration Committee (SPRC) in March 2024 on an administrative footing and, as per the recommendations of the Report of the Independent Review Panel, the first task of the Committee was to perform a review of the remuneration arrangements for the CEOs of CSBs. In doing so Government was conscious of the scale, complexity and commercial responsibilities associated with leading major State companies, and their role in the management of critical national infrastructure and the delivery of significant investment programmes.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he will provide an update on plans to develop flood mitigating measures in the vicinity of Shannon town and Shannon Airport in County Clare.
reply:
Shannon Town and its Environs are at risk of flooding from both coastal and fluvial (stream/river) sources. The main sources of coastal flooding risk are wave water overtopping of the embankment crest driven by strong winds during high tide periods and also through any potential breaches of the embankments. The main sources of fluvial flooding risk are the inadequate capacities of the existing drainage systems (surface water channels/culverts and pumping systems) and limited outflow capacities of the tidally affected outfall systems
The design options for the Shannon Town & Environs Flood Relief works are being progressed to protect 1,400 properties, including 1,237 residential and 163 commercial properties. A Value Engineering Review Workshop was held in January 2026 to consider all potential options for the Scheme. Meetings with the National Parks and Wildlife Services are also informing the potential options.
An additional Public Consultation Day took place in Q3 2026 where the emerging preferred Option was presented to the public, prior to the submission of a planning application.
On completion of the review and the feedback from the public consultation day, an emerging preferred option will be agreed by the project Steering Group, with the final report expected at the end of 2026. An Environmental Impact Assessment Report for the Scheme is projected to be completed by Q2 2027.

reply:

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the measures he has introduced to ensure value-for-money in respect of public capital projects.
reply:
My Department is responsible for the Infrastructure Guidelines. These set the value for money requirements and guidance for evaluating, planning and managing Exchequer-funded capital projects to ensure that vital infrastructure projects will be delivered on time and in a manner that ensures value for money through detailed evaluation, appraisal and planning. Management and delivery of investment projects and public services within allocation and the national frameworks, including the Infrastructure Guidelines, is a key responsibility of every Department, Accounting Officer and Minister.
Under the Accelerating Infrastructure Action Plan, a number of reforms to the Infrastructure Guidelines have been progressed and implemented under Action 23. In February, the following changes were implemented:
• In relation to Major Projects, the threshold will increase from €200m to €500m for sectors with a well established track record of delivery (Transport, Energy and Water)
• For all sectors, the External Assurance Process (EAP) will be replaced with a streamlined and time-bound internal review by the relevant Vote section in DPER; and
• Major projects at Approval Gate 2 will no longer need Ministerial approval and may now be approved solely by the Accounting Officer of the Government Department that is funding the proposed project.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation whether the Government plans to move beyond annual capital investment targets and introduce a strategic framework, as recommended in the Future Forty report, with medium and long-term goals for infrastructure provision across housing, transport, energy and water services.
reply:
The Government is fully committed to providing financial certainty for infrastructure projects needed to transform our housing, energy, water, transport, and health infrastructure over the next 10 years to ensure we meet the needs of our growing population.
The Review of the National Development Plan (NDP), published in July 2025, set out a €275 billion public capital investment programme to 2035, the largest in the history of the State. The plan set out Exchequer funded sectoral capital allocations of €102.4 billion for the years 2026 to 2030; and a further €100 billion for the period 2030 to 2035. In addition, an estimated total of €63 billion in non-Exchequer funding by commercial semi-state bodies, will be invested in capital expenditure. A further €10 billion, equity funding, has also been provided for the period 2026 to 2030 to support the delivery of large projects, such as electricity grid capacity, water and transport infrastructure.
The review increased overall allocations by an additional €34 billion relative to the previous 2021-2030 NDP.
This is the largest ever capital investment plan in the history of the State and will enable the delivery of thousands of new homes, increase Ireland's competitiveness, improve transport services, provide more childcare and school places, invest in children’s disability services and ensure better healthcare for all.

reply:

Clifden has a long history of flooding including in 2020 and more recently in November 2024.

The OPW engaged with Galway County Council (GCC) and confirmed that the OPW would fund the costs of developing and implementing a scheme to alleviate flooding in Clifden, through the Government’s €1.3bn investment in flood measures under the National Development Plan.
Galway County Council, is the lead authority for the Clifden Flood Relief Scheme, with funding from the OPW, for one full time Engineer. The Council appointed Engineering and environmental consultants to design a scheme for Clifden in 2021.
The final Options Report for a viable flood relief scheme to manage the flood risk within Clifden for some 24 properties has been delivered by the appointed consultant and is being discussed with Galway County Council.

question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the way in which he will enhance public trust in how the public sector uses AI.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 54 and 73 together.
My Department is taking a proactive and coordinated approach to enabling the responsible and effective adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) across the Public Service, both to improve service delivery and to maintain public trust, in line with the policy objectives and targets set out in the Better Public Services Strategy, the Digital Public Services Plan, and the National Digital and AI Strategy.
My Department is ensuring the roll out generic AI capability across Government over 2027 to ensure that all public service bodies can avail of shared, trusted AI digital building blocks. This will provide interoperable AI platforms and services that will include tools for virtual assistants, summarisation and analysis of documents, as well as translation, transcription and efficient knowledge management. These technical tools will be supported by an AI Advisory Unit that will provide advice and expertise to guide effective deployment.

This funding is in addition to ongoing investment of €9 million in Government digital infrastructure to support the transformation of public services to ensure the delivery of Better Public Services.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the position regarding the work he is doing to ensure that all OPW owned buildings, structures and monuments are fully accessible.
reply:
The Office of Public Works endeavours to prioiritise accessibilty across its owned buildings, structures and monuments a) as far as is practicable in the case of protected structures and b) in compliance with the Technical Guidance Documents of the Building Regulations in circumstances relating to accessibility of the modern estate.
New government department office buildings, garda stations, coast guard stations, cultural facilities and visitor centres are designed to Part M of the current building regulations across the OPW portfolio unless exemptions are in place.
In addition, existing buildings are modified on a phased basis in accordance with the terms set out in the OPW Universal Access Programme. This Programme targets access solutions for all OPW owned sites or leased buildings and facilities. Schedules of works typically involve site specific solutions which can consist of adjustments to entrance areas, easing of circulation routes by automation of doors, alterations to sanitary facilities and customer services areas. Access audits are undertaken by qualified personnel and lead to a solution informed by the end users and clients of the facility or service. Compliance with the Disability Act 2005 forms the basis of accessibility where a service is provided to the public. reply:

Achieving value for money in public expenditure is a key Government priority. Over the past two years, a number of initiatives have been introduced to strengthen the focus on value for money and drive efficiencies across the public service.

question: Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation his plans for the Corlea Trackway; the timeline of implementation; the funding available; and to confirm a start date for the project.
reply:
Corlea Trackway is an Iron Age roadway, or togher, located near Keenagh in County Longford and dating from approximately 148 BC. It is one of the most significant surviving examples of an Iron Age wooden trackway in Europe, with an 18-metre section of the original structure preserved and displayed at the Visitor Centre. This National Monument is cared for and managed by the Office of Public Works. The Visitor Centre provides an important opportunity for the public to experience and learn about this exceptional archaeological monument. It opens seasonally each year from March to November and welcomed 19,537 visitors in 2024, and 22,082 visitors in 2025, an increase of 13% on the previous year.
In 2024, the Office of Public Works made an application under the European Union Just Transition Fund programme for funding to develop potential options for the future development of Corlea Trackway and Visitor Centre. Grant funding of up to €262,500 was subsequently awarded under the Fund to support a feasibility assessment exploring options for the future development of the site and its interaction with the wider destination. question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation his plans to review capital expenditure allocation; and whether consideration is being given to increasing the level of capital funding available to the Department of Education and the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science.
reply:

This leads to a total public capital investment of €275.4 billion over the period to 2035. This comprises €202.4 billion in Exchequer Voted capital expenditure from 2026 to 2035.
Of this, €102.4 billion is being allocated for the next five years – an additional €23.9 billion on what was previously allocated in the NDP. A further €10 billion in equity and fund releases is being provided for megaprojects in water, energy and transport. This brings the total additional capital investment to €33.9 billion for the period to 2030.
The agreement of five-year annual sectoral allocations provides multi-year certainty to departments as to their level of capital funding over the next five years. This multi-year certainty has enabled Departments to plan for the delivery of their capital investment priorities through to 2030. It also provides visibility on the investment pipeline to enable construction firms to scale capacity and prepare commercial bids to deliver on the planned investment.
The Department of Education have been allocated a capital budget of €7.5 billion over the period 2026 to 2030, which represents a significant increase of 73% over their 2021 to 2025 NDP allocation of just under €4.4 billion.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if his Department has been involved in any discussions in relation to the future of Dunguaire Castle, Kinvara, County Galway; and if OPW staff have assessed the condition of the castle.
reply:
The Office of Public Works is responsible for the conservation, maintenance and presentation of over 780 National Monuments and 33 Historic Properties nationwide.
Dunguaire Castle was built around 1520, it is believed to have been built on the site of the Dún (or fort) of Guaire, a 6th century King of Aidhne. This gives the castle its name, Dún Guaire. The 16th-century castle is thought to have been a seat of the Ó hEidhin (O’Hyne) family, who were the regional rulers.
By the early 17th century, the castle was owned by the Martyn family, one of the wealthy and famous merchant ‘Tribes’ of Galway. The family owned the castle up until the 20th century.
In 1924, Dunguaire was bought and repaired by Oliver St. John Gogarty, the famous surgeon and literary figure and in 1954 the castle was acquired by Christobel, Lady Ampthill who completed the restoration started by Oliver St. John Gogarty.
Subsequently the castle became the property of the Shannon Development Company and it was an important feature of its tourism offering, giving an insight into the lifestyle of the people who lived from 1520 to modern times.
As the Deputy is already aware, the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage is responsible for the designation of National Monuments and the decision as to what properties come into care. Since its introduction in 2009, some €70 million has been approved under the Scheme for 930 local authority led projects that are delivering flood mitigation and coastal protection for some 8,000 properties.

The revisions include an increase in the upper threshold in funding for projects from €750,000 to €2 million and an increase in the OPW contribution from 90% to 95% for approved funding above €300,000. I have also expanded the Scheme to include interim flood mitigation measures for communities where a major flood relief scheme is planned, but not complete. Further revisions include the relaxing of some economic criteria.

reply:

reply:

question: Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the up-to-date position on advancing the Crookstown flood relief scheme; if the local authority has contacted the OPW in relation to securing the additional funding required for this project.
reply:
The River Bride overtops its banks both upstream and downstream of Crookstown Bridge during flood events, affecting residential properties and local and regional roads. The 2014 Lee Catchment Flood Risk Assessment and Management (CFRAM) Programme examined the flood risk at Crookstown but did not identify a viable major flood relief scheme.
In 2021, the OPW approved funding of €295,027 to Cork County Council under the Minor Flood Mitigation Works and Coastal Protection Scheme for interim mitigation works at Crookstown. These works included drainage improvements, a storm water pumping station and associated works, and were intended to mitigate flood damage pending consideration of further options.
Cork County Council has advised that it was engaging with its consultants to develop further works at Crookstown. While the OPW has not received a request from Cork County Council for additional funding in relation to the proposed further works, any future application would be considered in accordance with the revised criteria for this Scheme, that I announced in May this year. The revised criteria has relaxed some of the previous qualifying criteria, including economic benefits and has increased the funding thresholds to €2m and OPW’s contribution to 95% for funding amounts greater than €300,000.

question: Deputy Noel McCarthy asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to provide an update on the rollout of the east Cork individual property protection scheme to date.
reply:
In October 2024, the OPW approved €5.8m in funding for Cork County Council to make Individual Property Protection (IPP) (i.e. flood barriers/gates) available free of charge to an estimated 923 home and business owners who were so badly impacted by Storm Babet in Midleton (749) and East Cork (174), including Castlemartyr, Mogeely, Killeagh, Rathcormac and Youghal.
The scheme opened for applications on 7th October 2024 to all households and businesses in the affected areas. Applications for the scheme were accepted until 18th November 2024. Cork County Council received a total of 721 valid applications.
Cork County Council arranged for an independent assessment by engineering consultants of the suitability of the properties for IPP and subsequently the type of IPP products required (e.g. expandable flood gates, slot in flood gates, etc.). These property surveys were completed for all properties deemed eligible for inclusion in the scheme early in 2025.
Delivery of flood gates to suitable properties began in mid-April 2025. Ancillary building works have been carried out by contractors working on behalf of Cork County Council since June 2025. This is the largest such scheme ever delivered in Ireland. The delivery programme has experienced some scheduling challenges arising from procurement and supply chain factors. Cork County Council continues to work closely with contractors and suppliers to progress the scheme and maintain momentum towards completion.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if there are any proposals under consideration to review, revise or expand the current statutory Gaeltacht boundaries; whether any assessment has been undertaken of communities located immediately adjacent to existing Gaeltacht areas which have significant Irish-speaking populations or strong Irish-language educational provision.
reply:
Both my Department and its agencies, Foras na Gaeilge and Údarás na Gaeltachta, remain committed to promoting and strengthening the Irish language both within and outside designated Gaeltacht areas through a range of policies and initiatives aimed at supporting the use of the language.
In accordance with the provisions of the Gaeltacht Act 2012, the Gaeltacht is now divided into 26 Language Planning Areas. In addition, the Act provides for the recognition of towns serving Gaeltacht communities as Gaeltacht Service Towns. Sixteen of these towns have been identified following a public consultation process, 2 of which are situated within the Gaeltacht boundaries with the remaining 14 situated outside the Gaeltacht. In addition, there are currently 3 statutory Irish Language Networks recognised under the Act with a further 2 recognised under a non-statutory scheme administered by Foras na Gaeilge north of the border. The Deputy should be aware that I recently approved a proposal by Foras na Gaeilge to seek expressions of interest from a further 3 language communities for recognition as statutory Irish Language Networks.
I can confirm that I, as Minister, do not have the authority, under the Act, to extend the boundaries of the Gaeltacht.

question: Deputy Liam Quaide asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the number of vacant or derelict buildings have been acquired and brought back into productive community use through the town and village renewal scheme and Rural Regeneration and Development Fund since 2022, broken down by county and year; the number of acquired buildings that remain vacant or awaiting redevelopment; and the additional funding being provided in 2027 to accelerate their redevelopment.
reply:

question: Deputy Liam Quaide asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the assessment that has been undertaken of the effectiveness of the Social Inclusion and Community Activation Programme (SICAP) in reaching people experiencing poverty, social isolation and disadvantage in rural communities; the proportion of the programme funding has been allocated to rural areas in each of the past three years, broken down by county; and the additional measures and resources planned for 2027 to address rural disadvantage.
reply:
The Social Inclusion and Community Activation Programme (SICAP), is our country’s primary social inclusion intervention.
SICAP has 2 programme goals. Goal one is supporting communities, which involves supporting local community groups representing disadvantaged communities and target groups. Goal two involves supporting individuals who have been identified as being in need, to improve their life through lifelong learning and training, labour market supports to improve work readiness, or working with people in broader and more holistic ways so that they can improve their quality of life and general well-being.
Under each of these goals, Programme Implementers (PIs) and their relevant Local Community Development Committees (LCDCs) are required to set and meet Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) based on indicative Department data on an annual basis. Information on KPI outputs as well as beneficiary progress and results are captured through the Integrated Reporting and Information System (IRIS).
The 2025 SICAP Annual Report highlights the significant impact of the programme, which has a renewed focus on targeting those who are most disadvantaged in Irish society. By the end of 2025, KPIs for the programme were exceeded by 22%, indicating strong programme reach among marginalised individuals and communities.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the reasons for the exclusion of Darndale/Priorswood from the SÍOL programme despite its recognised levels of deprivation; the specific criteria and weighting used to select eligible areas; whether the decision to exclude Darndale/Priorswood will be reviewed; and whether additional areas will be considered for inclusion in 2027.

question: Deputy Gillian Toole asked the Minister for Health if the HPRA (Health Product Regulatory Authority) warning system will be inspected and upgraded in light of findings from the Food and Drug Administration in the United States where warnings about adverse events relating to Messenger RNA Covid vaccines were not on alerts.
reply:
The Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA) is the national competent authority responsible for monitoring the safety of medicines, including vaccines, in Ireland.
In Ireland, the HPRA participated in vaccine safety surveillance through the European Medicines Regulatory Network.
The safety of COVID-19 vaccines authorised for use in Ireland was monitored through this European network, which brought together the national competent authorities (NCAs) of European Member States under the coordination of the European Medicines Agency (EMA). Coordinated action ensured that COVID-19 vaccines and treatments were closely monitored and used as safely as possible.
This work began with preparations for intensified safety monitoring of COVID-19 vaccines prior to the commencement of immunisation campaigns. reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the Public Only Consultant Contract was introduced in March 2023 as a key step towards a universal, single-tier health service in which access to care is based on clinical need rather than ability to pay.
The POCC is applicable to all specialities, not just to maternity care. The transition to POCC will take place progressively as consultants are recruited to, or move to, the new contract. Consultants choosing that contract cannot continue to provide private practice in public hospitals after 31 December 2025. Consultants who remain on earlier contracts may continue to provide private care in public hospitals in accordance with their contractual arrangements. Accordingly, the change does not involve an immediate cessation of private maternity care. Private maternity care in public hospitals will therefore reduce gradually over time.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he will provide an update on plans to remediate the defective concrete blocks in the structure of Shannon Garda, Station, County Clare.
reply:

The outcome of this monitoring and preliminary testing determined that a detailed assessment (desktop study, inspections, testing, analysis) and design would be necessary to enable potential remedial solutions to be determined.
In September 2025 the Office of Public Works prepared a public tender for the services of a consultant structural engineer to undertake the necessary detailed assessment, design and provide remedial options, to enable the Office of Public Works to evaluate and determine the optimum remedial solution.
In November 2025 a consulting structural engineer was appointed by the Office of Public Works.
The consultant has advised the Office of Public Works that their inspections do not raise any structural concerns at present and that they do not anticipate the need for structural remedial works within the next five years.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Health to address the gaps in the assisted human reproduction legislative framework that continue to affect LGBTQ+ families, including the lack of recognition for international surrogacy arrangements, the exclusion of some same-sex female couples from parental recognition pathways, the limited routes available to gay men seeking to become parents, and the absence of definitions that reflect the lived realities of transgender parents.
reply:
The Health (Assisted Human Reproduction) Act 2024 was signed into law by the President in July 2024, having passed all stages in both Houses of the Oireachtas.
The primary purpose of this complex and far-reaching legislation is to regulate fertility clinics providing treatment and ensure that assisted human reproduction (AHR) practices and related areas of research are conducted in a more consistent and standardised way and with the necessary oversight. The 2024 Act encompasses the regulation of a wide range of practices undertaken in Ireland, including: the use and donation of gametes and embryos for AHR and research; pre-implantation genetic testing of embryos; and embryo and stem cell research. The establishment of the Assisted Human Reproduction Regulatory Authority (AHRRA), as provided for in the legislation, is a vital component for the effective regulation of this sector.
Prior to this, the Children and Family Relationships Act 2015 introduced a regulatory framework for the legal parentage for children born in Ireland as a result of a donor-assisted human reproduction (DAHR) procedure which takes place in an authorised Irish DAHR facility. This allows for the birth of a donor conceived child to be registered as such by an tArd-Chláraitheoir (the Chief Registrar). This applies equally to single women, same-sex female couples and heterosexual couples, when they have undertaken a DAHR procedure in full accordance with the 2015 Act.

Through the governance structures established under the National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People, Departments and agencies are accountable for delivering actions that improve access, inclusion, autonomy and participation for disabled people.

reply:
The National Childcare Scheme (NCS) provides financial support to help families with their early learning and childcare costs. The families of almost 247,000 children availed of National Childcare Scheme (NCS) subsidies in 2025 to help offset the costs of early learning and childcare. Up to 277,000 children are expected to avail of the Scheme this year.
The NCS is designed to be flexible, recognising that childcare needs are different for each family. Under the NCS, subsidies are awarded as an hourly rate, up to a maximum number of 45 hours a week for which the subsidy applies.
The Department designed the NCS to also be flexible around children’s attendance, recognising that children’s attendance may vary from week to week. If a child is occasionally picked up early or misses an occasional day, this will not impact on a family’s subsidy. This is outlined in Section 8.3.2 of the NCS policy guidelines under “Occasional under-attendance”, which is the section highlighted by the Deputy in their question.
Section 8.3.2 also states that ‘If a child is not using the hours registered on a consistent basis the under-attendance rules will apply.
