question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to examine the current age eligibility rules for the Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) scheme; and if she accepts that children born in January are at a distinct educational disadvantage as they will not be 2 years and 8 months old by the time September comes around.
reply:
The ECCE programme provides up to two years of pre-school free of charge to families and is based on the National Practice Frameworks - Aistear and Síolta. Currently, children are eligible for ECCE starting at 2 years and 8 months to an upper age limit of 5 years and 6 months. The current ECCE eligibility criteria were set based on a number of considerations, including national experience and a review of international practice. The lower age range is informed by Tusla regulations for minimum adult-to-child ratios for children in early learning and childcare settings. These regulations take account of the needs and developmental stages of children such as toilet training and sleeping arrangements. The current arrangements also ensure that all children have the same eligibility for 2 years of ECCE.
The Department recognises that the use of age limits in programmes such as ECCE can result in some children narrowly falling outside the eligibility range in a given year. However, in the interest of fairness and consistency, the Department must apply a clear and fixed age threshold, and cannot make exceptions. The current arrangements ensure that all children have the same entitlement of 2 years of ECCE regardless of their birth date. Some parents may prefer for their children to start school at age 4 rather than 5 years. These parents may therefore choose to avail of 1 year of ECCE only. question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the reason the Disability (Amendment) bill 2025 is continuing its passage through the Oireachtas given that a review of the parent act, the Disability Act 2005, is currently underway.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 391 and 392 together.
The National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People 2025-2030 commits to a broad legislative programme that recognises the need to review and update existing disability legislation, and to consider where a need for new legislation may exist, particularly following Ireland’s ratification of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD). The Programme for Government also commits to reform of the Disability Act 2005 in consultation with stakeholders. The Department's review of the Disability Act is in line with these commitments.
The Disability Act is a wide-ranging piece of legislation that relates to the definition of disability, the Assessment of Need process, accessible public buildings, universal design, the use of genetic data, public sector employment and more.
However, improvements to the Assessment of Need process are required as soon as possible; this cannot wait for the review of the Act as a whole. Accordingly, the Disability (Amendment) Bill 2026 is now progressing through the Oireachtas. The Bill makes specific and targeted changes to Part 2 of the Disability Act 2005 which sets out the Assessment of Need process. These targeted changes aim to make the Assessment of Need process more efficient and effective for children and their families.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to outline the regulations for deer hunting licenses issued by Coillte; the way in which license holders are required to engage with privately owned land and neighbouring landowners; the steps that Coillte takes in the event that these regulations are breached by license holders; and if there is a mechanism for landowners to complain to Coillte regarding the behaviour of deer hunting license holders.
reply:
Coillte was established as a commercial state company with private limited status under the Forestry Act, 1988, to become custodian and manager of the national forest estate. question: Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the steps being taken by his Department to ensure equine chip and pin legislation is enforced.
reply:
The rules relating to equine traceability are set down in EU Regulation 2016/429 and its delegated and implementing acts, known collectively as the Animal Health Law.
I have invested significantly in improving equine traceability, with a particular focus on maximising the potential of digital technology to keep our equine traceability system accurate. A new Central Equine Database was launched in October 2025, linking horses to the premises where they are kept and to a responsible operator. This represents a significant step forward and strengthens accountability across the sector.
My Department has designed the new equine traceability system so that enforcement with traceability rules is built into the day-to-day operation of the industry. The database is now supported by nine key traceability checkpoints at which an active equine premises number or database check is required, helping to ensure compliance and that records are kept up to date. These include registrations, accessing veterinary medicines, registration updates, access to grant aid, export checks, inspections, entering sales catalogues, the census and death notification. This systematic enforcement makes it more difficult for operators to operate outside of the rules and prompts engagement and compliance.

question: Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine for an update on the online portal launched in July 2023 which allows members of the public to check whether an equine is recorded on the central equine database.
reply:
The online equine chip checker can be found at: https://equine-chipcheck.apps.services.agriculture.gov.ie/ and is an important tool in strengthening equine identification, traceability and transparency across the sector.
This portal allows members of the public to check whether an equine UELN (passport number) or an equine microchip number is valid and listed on the central equine database, empowering horse owners, purchasers and others involved in the industry to satisfy themselves that an animal is appropriately identified and registered.
Since July of this year, the portal has been further enhanced to allow users to verify the validity of an equine premises registration number (EPRN), which is mandatory for premises keeping equines in Ireland, or an Equine Establishment Number (EEN) which is mandatory for premises in Northern Ireland. This new functionality represents an important step forward in promoting greater transparency and accountability, enabling individuals to verify not only the registration status of an animal but also that of the premises where it is being kept or traded from.
The growing use of the portal is encouraging with over 92,000 hits on the website up to the end of September this year, representing a 41% increase on the corresponding period in 2025. question: Deputy Tony McCormack asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the way in which he is facilitating SMEs to participate in public procurement processes.
reply:
The Programme for Government includes a commitment to review the public procurement process to make it more transparent and to ensure greater participation from SMEs. As part of this review, my Department engaged extensively with the broad spectrum of Irish enterprise through a public consultation process, stakeholder meetings, a dedicated supplier webinar and three regional roadshows. This culminated in the publication of Procuring for our Future: National Public Procurement Strategy 2026-2030, which sets out a clear ambition to optimise the use of public procurement as an investment mechanism while making it easier for SMEs, particularly micro-enterprises, start-ups and social enterprises, to participate in public procurement. In doing so, the Strategy aims to enhance competition, deliver better value for money and support better public services.
Reflecting this ambition, the Strategy includes a dedicated pillar, Investing in our Enterprise Base, which contains a range of actions designed to reduce barriers for SMEs, improve awareness of public procurement opportunities, strengthen buyer-supplier engagement, enhance access to procurement information, and support a diverse and competitive supplier base. question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 72780/26, the precise reasons the regulations and contribution model as laid down in the relevant Statutory Instrument have never been implemented before now; if this was a political or policy decision by his Department or by Cabinet; and if implementation of the S.I. has been objected to by any advocacy group in the migration or asylum space.
reply:
IPAS Accommodation is provided for in EU regulations and transposed into Irish law. Statutory Instrument No 230/2018, European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018, provides that all IP applicants are entitled to Material Reception Conditions.
The Regulations further provide that where a resident is in receipt of an income above a certain level, they may be required to make a contribution to the cost of providing reception condition services. The contribution rates are set out in a Schedule to the Regulations and are proportionate to the amount that people earn.
The 2025 Programme for Government included a commitment to introducing a contribution model for people in international protection accommodation.
Recommendations for Government on a contribution model for people in international protection accommodation were originally developed by the then Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration, and Youth (DCEDIY) in 2024.
A proposal for working international protection applicants to contribute to the cost of their IPAS accommodation was then considered by Government in November 2025 and is now being progressed by the Department of Justice, Home Affairs, and Migration.
The Department and I are not in receipt of any formal objections to the implementation of this contribution model since its announcement in November 2025, as outlined in the Deputy's question.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department is aware of any investigations undertaken since 2023 into suspected breaches of the gaming and lotteries Acts by online lottery, prize draw and competition operators or of any prosecutions initiated or convictions secured; if he has received any reports relating to commercial operators offering houses, vehicles, cash and other prizes exceeding the statutory limits applicable to lottery permits; the measures being taken to ensure compliance with existing legislation.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 371, 372 and 373 together.
Lotteries and raffles are currently licensed under the Gaming and Lotteries Act 1956, as amended, with permits issued by An Garda Síochána and the licences by the District Court. A lottery with a prize value in excess of €360,000 is not permitted under the current legislation. Therefore, any alleged or suspected breach of the provisions of the 1956 Act is currently a matter for An Garda Síochána to investigate, and, if necessary, to prosecute those in breach of the current legislation.
The regulation of the gambling sector, including certain lotteries, is being overhauled through the phased commencement of the Gambling Regulation Act 2024 (the ‘2024 Act’). The Act establishes an independent agency to regulate the gambling sector, the Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland (GRAI), and ensures that the GRAI can respond appropriately to ongoing and future developments in the gambling sector. The provisions relating to the various gambling sectors are being commenced on a phased basis to enable the development of the necessary regulatory, licensing and compliance framework, including guidance and codes of practice where appropriate.
The 2024 Act, once the relevant provisions are commenced, will repeal the 1956 Act. The 2024 Act provides for a licence to allow once-off lotteries (to be operated once every 12 months) with prizes of up to €360,000 for both commercial and charitable/philanthropic purposes.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 371, 372 and 373 together.
Lotteries and raffles are currently licensed under the Gaming and Lotteries Act 1956, as amended, with permits issued by An Garda Síochána and the licences by the District Court. A lottery with a prize value in excess of €360,000 is not permitted under the current legislation. Therefore, any alleged or suspected breach of the provisions of the 1956 Act is currently a matter for An Garda Síochána to investigate, and, if necessary, to prosecute those in breach of the current legislation.
The regulation of the gambling sector, including certain lotteries, is being overhauled through the phased commencement of the Gambling Regulation Act 2024 (the ‘2024 Act’). The Act establishes an independent agency to regulate the gambling sector, the Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland (GRAI), and ensures that the GRAI can respond appropriately to ongoing and future developments in the gambling sector. The provisions relating to the various gambling sectors are being commenced on a phased basis to enable the development of the necessary regulatory, licensing and compliance framework, including guidance and codes of practice where appropriate.
The 2024 Act, once the relevant provisions are commenced, will repeal the 1956 Act. The 2024 Act provides for a licence to allow once-off lotteries (to be operated once every 12 months) with prizes of up to €360,000 for both commercial and charitable/philanthropic purposes.

reply:
Minor Flood Mitigation Works and Coastal Protection Scheme
Localised flooding issues are a matter, in the first instance, for each Local Authority to investigate and address, and a Local Authority may carry out flood mitigation works using its own resources. Local Authorities may apply to the OPW for funding for flood mitigation and coastal protection works under the OPW Minor Flood Mitigation Works and Coastal Protection Scheme.
In May this year, I was pleased to announce that the revised criteria for the Minor Flood Mitigation Works and Coastal Protection Scheme are available and greatly increase the scope of the Scheme. The revised scheme provides local authorities with a greater opportunity to address localised flooding and coastal erosion risk within their administrative areas. The revisions include an increase in the upper threshold in funding for projects from €750,000 to €2 million and an increase in the OPW contribution from 90% to 95% for approved funding above €300,000. question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will clarify whether planning applicants for strategic-scale developments such as large data centres must disclose existing put and call options, or agreements for sale, under which the applicant company or the land will pass to another party once permission is granted; and whether he will consider making such disclosure mandatory.

Any party who wishes to carry out the development approved by the grant of permission must comply with the terms of the permission itself, including any conditions imposed by the planning authority.

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will clarify whether sectoral nominees to local authority Strategic Policy Committees must make declarations of interest under Part 15 of the Local Government Act 2001; and whether those declarations must cover directorships of companies that hold or are pursuing an interest in land being zoned in a local area plan the committee considers.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 312, 313 and 314 together.
The ethical framework that applies to members of committees of a local authority is provided for under Part 15 of the Local Government Act 2001, as amended, and the Code of Conduct published under that Act. The Code of Conduct gives guidance in relation to the standards of conduct required of members of a committee of a local authority. External members of SPCs should abide by the provisions of Part 15 of the 2001 Act, where relevant and the principles of the Code. In particular, they should avoid any conflict of interest and are subject to the disclosure requirements concerning pecuniary and other beneficial interests. Legal responsibility for compliance with these requirements rests with each individual member.
Where a possible contravention of the ethical framework by a member of a committee arises, this should be brought to the attention of the local authority’s Ethics Registrar. When the Ethics Registrar becomes aware of a possible contravention of the ethical framework by a member, he or she has a duty to bring this to the attention of the Chief Executive. Following this, the Chief Executive must consider what action should be taken. That action may include, among other things, investigative or disciplinary procedures which may be exercised within the legal framework, including referral of the matter to the Standards in Public Office Commission (SIPO) for further investigation.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if, in the case of a member of the local government superannuation scheme who entered local authority service prior to 1 April 2004, who is entitled to professional added years under the local government superannuation scheme and who retires on certified permanent ill-health grounds after attaining the age of 60 years but before normal retirement age, such retirement is regarded as an ill-health retirement or as a standard age-related retirement for the purposes of pension calculation; and if any distinction arises in the treatment of professional added years in such circumstances.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 306, 307, 308, 310 and 311 together.
Under section 159 of the Local Government Act 2001, each Chief Executive is responsible for the staffing and organisational arrangements necessary for carrying out the functions of the local authority for which they are responsible. Local authorities are entirely independent corporate entities having full responsibility under law for the performance of their functions and responsibilities, including that of employers.
My Department does not hold employment records for local authority employees and as such, I have no role in this regard. Any queries regarding an individual’s pension arrangements should be directed to the pension administrator of the local authority concerned. Local HR will deal with any complaint through their own internal complaint handling process, called internal dispute resolution (IDR). If the person is still unhappy having completed the IDR process, they may bring their complaint to the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman.

Local HR will deal with any complaint through their own internal complaint handling process, called internal dispute resolution (IDR). question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage which body has ultimate authority for interpreting the provisions of the local government superannuation scheme in relation to ill-health retirement and professional added years, namely the Department, local authorities, MyPay, or another body; and the appeals or review mechanisms available where conflicting advice is issued.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 306, 307, 308, 310 and 311 together.
Under section 159 of the Local Government Act 2001, each Chief Executive is responsible for the staffing and organisational arrangements necessary for carrying out the functions of the local authority for which they are responsible. Local authorities are entirely independent corporate entities having full responsibility under law for the performance of their functions and responsibilities, including that of employers.
My Department does not hold employment records for local authority employees and as such, I have no role in this regard. Any queries regarding an individual’s pension arrangements should be directed to the pension administrator of the local authority concerned. Where a person is unhappy with any benefits calculated under the provisions of the Local Government Superannuation Scheme (LGSS), they must seek a review by their local HR. Local HR will deal with any complaint through their own internal complaint handling process, called internal dispute resolution (IDR). If the person is still unhappy having completed the IDR process, they may bring their complaint to the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman.

reply:
When a sports club seeks a deed of discharge (whether full or partial) in respect of a grant from the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF), my Department requires supporting documentation from the club before it can then instruct the Chief State Solicitor’s Office.
The club referred to by the Deputy supplied the necessary documentation to my Department on 20 October and my officials have now referred the file to the Chief State Solicitor’s Office to progress the legal formalities associated with the deed of partial discharge.

question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport whether he has met, or plans to meet, the newly appointed chair of the Steering Group on Integration of organisations (details supplied); the priorities he will raise regarding progress towards integration; and whether he has received an updated roadmap for integration.
reply:
Gender equality across sport is a Government priority and, while not directly involved in the process, the Government is very supportive of the integration of the Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA), the Ladies Gaelic Football Association (LGFA) and the Camogie Association into a single unified structure for Gaelic Games.
Minister O'Donovan and I met with the three associations in September 2026 to discuss progress towards integration. During these meetings, each of the three bodies reaffirmed their commitment to achieving integration and confirmed that this process is ongoing.
All parties recognised the need for greater transparency and clear communications on how the integration process is happening, both within their own organisations and more widely. In this regard, I expect that a clear overall timetable for integration will be set out by the steering group in the coming months and we have asked that quarterly progress updates be provided to the Department.
I welcome the appointment of former GAA President John Horan as the new Chair of the Steering Group on Integration. My Department and Sport Ireland remain available to offer any support and advice needed to support this process and I look forward to further engagement on this in due course.

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport further to Parliamentary Question No. 71116/26, the reason pension increases for retired An Post workers must be approved by New Era before Ministerial sign off.
reply:
Under section 46 of the Postal and Telecommunications Services Act 1983, the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport with the concurrence of the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, approves any superannuation schemes submitted by An Post. The operation of the schemes is a matter between the management of An Post, staff representatives and the trustees of the schemes.
In accordance with the Act and the relevant Code of Practice for the Governance of State Bodies, An Post must seek Ministerial approval from both Ministers to increase pensions and deferred pensions for members of the An Post superannuation scheme. Section 2.13 of the Code of Practice for Governance of State Bodies Superannuation and Remuneration annex sets out that NewERA advice should be sought in respect of pension amendment proposals, as is appropriate in their role as commercial and financial advisors to the Ministers.

reply:

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Education and Youth to clarify if English language schools for foreign nationals are subject to inspection by her Department.
reply:
The function of the Inspectorate as set out in the Education Act 1998 is to support and advise recognised schools, centres for education and teachers on matters relating to the provision of education.
The Inspectorate evaluates a range of educational settings. These include state-funded early learning and care (ELC) settings, recognised primary, post-primary and special schools, centres for education, agricultural colleges and other educational settings. A Memorandum of Understanding between the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science (DFHERIS) and Department of Education and Youth provides inspectors with the authority to carry out inspections in state-funded centres of education currently operating under the remit of DFHERIS.
The provision of English language education in Ireland is a broad and diverse sector with the vast majority of activity undertaken by privately owned education providers. These providers do not fall under the remit of the Department of Education and Youth’s Inspectorate.

reply:

This includes recruitment, learning and development, succession planning, talent management and other workforce measures.
In line with objectives of the Better Public Services Transformation 2030 Strategy, my Department has taken steps to accelerate initiatives across workforce skills and capabilities requirements. The vision of the Strategy is to deliver inclusive, high quality and integrated public services that meet the needs and improve the lives of the people of Ireland, framed around the three pillars of Digital and Innovation at Scale, Workforce and Organisation of the future, and Evidence-Informed Policy and Services Designed for and with Our Public.
The development of the Institute of Public Administration (IPA) as a Centre of Excellence for learning and development in the Public Service is a flagship initiative. The IPA works in collaboration with my Department to ensure learning and development is aligned to Government priorities and skills requirements. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to Parliamentary Question No. 331 of 13 October 2026, if she will confirm whether any provision of the Education Act 1998, or of any other enactment, confers on a principal, board of management or patron the power to suspend or dissolve a parents' association established under section 26 of the Act; and if such a power exists, to state the specific section.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 258, 259, 261, 262, 263, 273, 274, 275, 276, 277, 280 and 281 together.
Section 26 of the Education Act 1998 provides for the establishment and operation of parents' associations. The Act does not contain any provision conferring on a principal, board of management or patron the power to suspend or dissolve a parents' association established under that section. The Act does, however, require boards of management to facilitate and give all reasonable assistance to parents who wish to establish a parents' association and to a parents' association when it is established. The Act does not provide for a specific complaints mechanism, nor does it designate a particular body or office to which a parents' association may bring a complaint alleging non-compliance with section 26(3). The department does not hold a record of complaints in relation to Section 26(3).
Any organisation wishing to seek recognition as a national association of parents under the Education Act 1998, should ensure that it meets the criteria set out in Section 2 of the Education Act and engage directly with the Department. The department has no record of receiving a request for such recognition since 2016.

question: Deputy Tony McCormack asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation for a report on the implementation of the Accelerating Infrastructure Action Plan.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 27 and 58 together.
The Programme for Government established a clear priority for the National Development Plan Review: to maximise investment in the strategic infrastructure required to support Ireland’s future development. This includes the energy, water and transport networks that underpin housing delivery, economic growth and regional development. These sectors were subsequently identified as critical infrastructure in the Accelerating Infrastructure Actions Report and Action Plan.
The Plan sets out 30 targeted actions across four pillars of reform. Measures include increasing exemption thresholds for critical infrastructure projects, streamlining processes involving agencies and regulators, advocating for reforms at EU level, and establishing a duty on State bodies to cooperate in making land available for nationally significant projects.
Implementation continues to maintain strong momentum, with delivery on track across all 30 actions and major reforms progressing from policy development into implementation. question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her Department will review the decision to remove a mainstream teaching post from a school (details supplied) from 31 October 2026, which would result in a class of 35 pupils, many of whom have additional educational needs; and if she will consider retaining the teaching post given the class size and level of support required.
reply:
The key factor for determining the level of staffing resources provided at individual school level is the staffing schedule for the relevant school year and pupil enrolments on the previous 30 September. The staffing schedule operates in a clear and transparent manner and treats all similar types of schools equally.
The staffing arrangements include a provision whereby schools experiencing rapid increases in enrolment can apply for additional permanent mainstream posts, using projected enrolment. The school referred to by the Deputy has been allocated a post on this basis, having advised of an expected enrolment of 207 pupils. The school was advised that to retain the post, an enrolment of 199 was required on 30 September. To date, the school has not provided its census return to the Department.
Class sizes in schools are affected by a variety of factors including enrolment fluctuations and available accommodation. Schools are best placed to determine the appropriate numbers in any class and so the configuration of classes and the deployment of classroom teachers are done at local school level. The Department's guidance to schools is that the number of pupils in any class is kept as low as possible taking all relevant contextual factors into account.

question: Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Education and Youth if eligible teaching staff are entitled to apply for a scheme (details supplied); if she can confirm that doing so will not impact on their maternity leave benefits.
reply:
The terms and conditions of the Maternity leave scheme for teachers are contained in the department’s Circular Letter 0054/2019 (Chapter 2). The Maternity Leave Scheme is regulated by the Maternity Protection Act, 1994 as amended.
A teacher absent on Maternity Leave may not engage in any type of teaching or other paid employment. However, there is provision that a person in receipt of Maternity Benefit can engage in public representative work and therefore a teacher who is also a councillor can continue in a public representative role during the period they are in receipt of maternity benefit and maternity leave.
Under the Department of Social Protection regulations, Maternity Benefit may be terminated if a teacher engages in paid employment while on Maternity Leave. It is the Maternity Benefit Section of the Department of Social Protection that administers the provisions of the Maternity Benefit scheme and we would advise any teacher to engage with the Maternity Benefit Section of that Department of Social Protection to confirm that they are continuing in the councillor role during their Maternity Leave and provide any information that may be required by the Department of Social Protection to ensure their maternity benefit does not get stopped.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Education and Youth her current plans to upgrade school buildings to improve indoor air quality to reduce airborne illnesses such as Covid-19 and influenza.
reply:
In relation to School Buildings, the Planning and Building Unit (PBU) of the Department of Education and Youth publish technical design guidance on requirements for indoor air quality and ventilation in new school buildings. This guidance is included across several documents available on the Department’s website on gov.ie.
The guidance emphasises the importance of good indoor air quality and ventilation as critical to the functioning of a teaching space. This includes guidance on the requirements for ventilation of all internal spaces in schools based on Part F of the Building Regulations as well as specific requirements for natural ventilation in schools. Since Covid, teaching spaces are fitted with Carbon Dioxide (CO2) monitors that include a LED display with a Traffic Light Display Indicator Range based on an Optimum Range <1500CO2 ppm (parts per million).
School Design Guidance Document SDG 03-TN01 published in March 2025 by the PBU with development support from the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) under the Schools Pathfinder Programme, provides design and technical guidance relating to the installation of Mechanical Ventilation Heat Recovery (MVHR) in new and retrofit school building projects. Since 2018, and working with Local Authorities, the OPW has trebled, to some 100, the number of Flood Relief Schemes at design and construction. The OPW is funding 1.5 staff members in Cavan County Council to lead the delivery of Flood Projects across the County and the Council is working in partnership with the OPW.
Cavan County Council is leading the delivery of Cavan Town Flood Relief Scheme to protect 110 properties. Engineering and Environmental Consultants were appointed to the Scheme in May 2022. The development of Cavan Town Flood Relief Scheme is overseen by a Project Steering Group that meets monthly with representatives from the OPW and Cavan County Council.
Emerging Options for the Scheme are expected at the end of 2026, with a next Public Consultation Day scheduled for Q1 2027. The preferred Option is due to be presented to the public at the end of 2027 and then submitted for planning in 2028. The design of the scheme has taken longer than originally planned, due to delays with surveys from demand in the market and the consultant's challenges with modelling of this complex scheme.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 258, 259, 261, 262, 263, 273, 274, 275, 276, 277, 280 and 281 together.
Section 26 of the Education Act 1998 provides for the establishment and operation of parents' associations. The Act does not contain any provision conferring on a principal, board of management or patron the power to suspend or dissolve a parents' association established under that section. The Act does, however, require boards of management to facilitate and give all reasonable assistance to parents who wish to establish a parents' association and to a parents' association when it is established. The Act does not provide for a specific complaints mechanism, nor does it designate a particular body or office to which a parents' association may bring a complaint alleging non-compliance with section 26(3). The department does not hold a record of complaints in relation to Section 26(3).

question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to a meeting with representatives of a school (details supplied), if she will outline the follow-up undertaken by her Department; whether the school’s circumstances and needs have since been reviewed; what additional targeted resources, staffing or funding are available to schools demonstrating significant disadvantage but which do not meet the current DEIS criteria; and whether a mechanism exists for such schools to have their circumstances individually reviewed.
reply:
Addressing educational disadvantage in all schools remains a key priority for me as Minister for Education and Youth.
The DEIS Strategy to 2035, published in March this year, is the first long-term, whole-system approach to addressing educational disadvantage. This strategy recognises education as central to breaking cycles of disadvantage, expanding opportunity, and ensuring long-term security. It sets out a more flexible model of support, so that resources are aligned with each school’s level of need as it changes over time. The strategy also acknowledges that students at risk of educational disadvantage are present in all schools. It therefore focuses on improving outcomes, encouraging innovation, and ensuring schools can access the right supports when needed.
The DEIS Strategy implementation plan 2026-2028, under the strategic objective 2.2, sets out to develop an agile resource allocation model to support children and young people at risk of educational disadvantage in all primary and post-primary schools. These actions focus on the continued enhancement of the data available to measure school level disadvantage and for the development of a more flexible resource allocation model that can react to change in school needs and provide the right resources at the right time.

reply:

Due to a national shortage of suitably qualified educational psychologists not all schools have an assigned educational psychologist. For those schools without an assigned educational psychologist, the school will be supported by NEPS through the Advisory Support Service. All schools continue to have support in the event of a critical incident through the local NEPS office and has access to training and support from NEPS for school staff.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether he is aware of concerns regarding the practical operation of banded-hour arrangements in the retail sector, including where such arrangements are governed by collective agreements; the protections that apply to employees where their weekly hours are spread across multiple short shifts; and whether he will engage with representative trade unions, including unions (details supplied), and retail employers to examine these concerns.
reply:
Ireland has a comprehensive set of employment rights. The Protection of Employees (Part-Time Work) Act 2001 and the Employment (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2018 provide important provisions to improve job security and working conditions for part-time workers and for employees in precarious or variable-hour roles.
The Protection of Employees (Part-Time Work) Act 2001 is accompanied by a recently revised Workplace Relations Commission Code of Practice on Access to Part-Time Work which states that, as far as possible, employers should give consideration to requests by employees to transfer from full-time to part-time work; and requests by employees to transfer from part-time to full-time work-or to increase their working time should the opportunity arise.
The Employment (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2018 represented a major step forward in strengthening employment protections for workers, particularly those in precarious forms of employment or with variable working hours.
The 2018 Act inserted banded hours provisions into the Organisation of Working Time Act 1997. Under the legislation, employees whose actual hours differ from their contract can request to be placed in a band of weekly hours that reflects their average over the previous 12 months. Employers must respond within 4 weeks and can only refuse under specific conditions.
Employees have recourse to the Workplace Relations Commission if they feel their rights have been contravened.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if the Health and Safety Authority received a notification of, or carried out an inspection or investigation into, an incident in June 2020 in which a member of An Garda Síochána was injured on duty outside an embassy in Dublin by the discharge of a firearm; and whether the authority has engaged with An Garda Síochána on the safety of issue holsters.
reply:
The Health and Safety Authority (HSA) is the national body in Ireland with responsibility for ensuring workers and those affected by a work activity are protected from work related injury and ill health. This responsibility arises from the functions of the Authority as set out in the occupational Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005.
The Health and Safety Authority (HSA) carries out its statutory functions including investigations, completely independently of the Minister. The Minister has no role or influence in any investigation being carried out and does not interfere in any way.
Officials in my Department contacted the HSA regarding this particular matter and it advised that under the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work (General Application) Regulations 2016 all employers and self-employed persons are legally obliged to report the injury of an employee as a result of an accident while at work. Injuries must be reported if an employee is unable to carry out their normal work for more than three consecutive days, excluding the day of the accident.
The HSA is prohibited from disclosing any information on individual employers and therefore cannot comment on this particular matter.

reply:

(b) the cumulative value of the transaction (and other related transactions between the parties) is equal to or greater than €2,000,000 in the 12 months prior to the date of the transaction

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the progress that has been made under the Government’s Accelerating Infrastructure Action Plan in reducing delays to major public infrastructure projects, particularly in the areas of housing, water treatment and transport.
reply:
The Programme for Government established a clear priority for the National Development Plan Review: to maximise investment in the strategic infrastructure required to support Ireland’s future development. This includes the energy, water and transport networks that underpin housing delivery, economic growth and regional development. These sectors were subsequently identified as critical infrastructure in the Accelerating Infrastructure Actions Report and Action Plan.
The Plan sets out 30 targeted actions across four pillars of reform. Measures include increasing exemption thresholds for critical infrastructure projects, streamlining processes involving agencies and regulators, advocating for reforms at EU level, and establishing a duty on State bodies to cooperate in making land available for nationally significant projects.

As of the end of Q3 2026, two-thirds of the full Action Plan has been implemented, with 85% of commitments due by end-Q3 completed.
In the water sector, progress is already evident. reply:

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the assessments the State makes of the ultimate beneficial owners, creditors and lien-holders of foreign entities that acquire Irish data-centre projects after permission is granted.
reply:
My Department is the National Competent Authority with responsibility for inward investment screening. The Screening of Third Country Transactions Act, 2023, commenced on the 6th of January 2025, provides for the implementation of Ireland’s inward investment screening mechanism.
The mechanism provides for assessment, investigation, authorisation, mitigation or prohibition of foreign investments based on a range of security criteria.
Transactions, that meet the criteria under the Act to be mandatorily notified, are assessed according to the factors set out in Section 13 of the Act, including consideration of the parties to the transaction.
My officials conduct a rigorous assessment of the transaction that includes examining the ownership structure of the parties to determine whether or not the transaction affects, or would be likely to affect, the security or public order of the State. As part of this assessment, my officials consult with colleagues across Government, including those appointed to the advisory panel under the Act. Officials also consult with the EU Commission and relevant member states depending on the details of the transaction.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the way in which the Government is balancing its engagement with multinational AI companies (details supplied) with public concerns regarding the development of artificial superintelligence; the safeguards and oversight measures being considered; and the steps that have been taken to date to address these concerns.
reply:
Artificial superintelligence is a term being used to refer to a hypothetical future form of AI that would exceed human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks. While such systems do not currently exist, rapid advances in AI capability have intensified international discussion regarding the governance and oversight of increasingly capable AI systems and the potential societal implications of future developments.
The Government engages with a broad range of stakeholders on AI policy, including multinational technology companies, researchers, civil society organisations, regulators and international partners. This engagement helps to inform Ireland's approach to AI governance and ensures that innovation is balanced with the need for appropriate safeguards, oversight and public trust.
Many of the technologies and models that are considered potential stepping stones towards artificial superintelligence are among the most advanced AI models currently in development. These models are increasingly being applied to scientific research, including areas such as healthcare, life sciences and materials science.
The EU AI Act provides what is often referred to as the world's first comprehensive legal framework for artificial intelligence. question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment for an update on the Short-Term Letting and Tourism Bill.
reply:
In April of last year, I obtained Government approval for the general scheme of the Short-Term Letting and Tourism Bill. Upon enactment, the Short-Term Letting and Tourism Bill will provide, for the first time, a comprehensive statutory framework governing the short-term letting sector in Ireland, including the establishment of a national register. The Government approved the Bill for publication on 6 October, representing a significant step towards a more transparent and effectively regulated sector. The Department, in conjunction with the relevant parliamentary offices, is finalising the necessary arrangements for publication of the Bill this week. Once published the Bill will proceed to Second Stage in Dáil Éireann.
This register, which has been broadly welcomed by the tourism sector, will be implemented and managed by Fáilte Ireland. The register will launch on 1 December 2026, with a legal obligation on all operators to register by 31 December 2026. The register will operate in compliance with the EU Short-Term Rental Regulation (EU) 2024/1028, which came into effect on 20 May 2026.
The planning policy framework for short-term letting activity, and all matters relating to planning and local authority resources, fall within the remit of the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the value-for-money reports published by his Department in the years 2023 to date in 2026.
reply:
Securing value for money is an ongoing priority for my Department. Policy analysis is a core component of the public expenditure management and value for money frameworks. A wide range of policy and expenditure analysis is undertaken and published by Government Departments annually.
Under the public expenditure framework, Departments operate on the basis of delegated sanction, whereby authority is granted to spend within agreed allocations, subject to conditions and oversight set out by my Department. This also places clear responsibilities on each Department to ensure adherence to value-for-money principles and to monitor and control spending.
In this context, individual Departments are responsible for conducting detailed policy analysis and expenditure evaluations within their own sectors, including assessing the efficiency and impact of programmes under their remit, and for contributing sector-specific insights and evidence to the policy making process.
The format and scope of their analysis have broadened in recent years, with a shift away from a focus on single-issue analysis papers to a wider variety of analytical output. This is reflected in the wide variety of publications including Staff Papers, Focused Policy Assessments, Spending Reviews, and Analytical Notes among others. All of this work feeds directly into key Government strategies, policies and spending decisions.

question: Deputy John McGuinness asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation further to previous PQs regarding the restoration of pay parity relative to medical scientists and biochemists, the reason he has not sanctioned the increase due to retired employees (details supplied); the reason he continues to ignore these facts and instead is describing the circumstances as an upgrade.
reply:
The pay adjustments arising from the Medical Scientist Grades Assessment were implemented following a 2023 Labour Court recommendation, which provides for their application no later than 1 January 2024 and subsequently formed part of the Public Service Agreement 2024-2026.
The revised rates introduced under Circular 2/2024 represented a regrading and movement to a new salary scale for Medical Scientist grades, effective from 1 January 2024. It is established practice that in such cases, the changes are not passed on to those who retired before its implementation.
The application of the new Medical Scientist Grade is in line with Public Service Pension Policy in this regard, i.e. where a post is upgraded, the terms of the upgrade apply from the date of the sanctioned upgrade. Terms do not apply retrospectively to previous post-holders, either employees who formerly held the post or retirees who previously held the post. This pertains across all grades of staff across the public service. This policy position has been subsequently supported by the Labour Court.
Accordingly, the exclusion of Medical Scientists who retired before 1 January 2024 from these specific adjustments is consistent with long-standing practice across the public service and with the operation of pension parity arrangement.

It is the responsibility of Individual Accounting Officers to ensure that their public procurement functions are discharged in line with the standard accounting and procurement rules and procedures and are publicly accountable for expenditure incurred. Individual contracting authorities are responsible for establishing arrangements for ensuring the proper conduct of their affairs, including conformance to standards of good governance and accountability regarding procurement.

Information on procurement opportunities and contract award notices is published through the eTenders platform, which provides transparency in public procurement activity.
Following contract award, responsibility for monitoring compliance with procurement requirements and contractual obligations rests primarily with the contracting authority concerned. Additional oversight may arise through internal audit by the office of the Comptroller and Auditor General.

Individual contracting authorities are responsible for contract management and may maintain supplier performance records for their own operational, governance and procurement purposes. question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation whether any public body conducts systemic analysis of procurement data for the purposes of identifying corruption risks, bid-rigging indicators or supplier concentration risks.
reply:
As a division of my Department, the Policy, Service Delivery, eProcurement, Data, Analytics and Systems Division (OGP) is responsible for national public procurement policy, eProcurement, the national eTendering platform, service delivery, and data. The OGP engages on an ongoing basis with a wide range of stakeholders, including the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC).
The CCPC is the statutory body with responsibility for promoting compliance with, and enforcing, competition and consumer protection law in Ireland, including in relation to the detection and prevention of bid rigging.
At present, there is no formal automated mechanism in place to systematically identify or manage potential collusion between suppliers. Contracting authorities are responsible for conducting their own procurement processes in accordance with national and EU public procurement rules. In practice, buyers compare bids manually to identify any indications of collusive behaviour.
My Department assists buyers through the OGP’s Public Procurement Guidelines for Goods and Services, directing them to the CCPC Business Guide for Detecting Bid Rigging. Where a contracting authority suspects bid-rigging or collusive tendering, such activities represent serious infringements of competition law and should be brought to the attention of the CCPC. In these instances, buyers are advised to report findings promptly to the CCPC.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation whether a review process is automatically triggered where only one compliant tender is received in a procurement competition above a specified value.
reply:
There is no general requirement under public procurement law or national procurement policy that an automatic review process would be triggered where only one compliant tender is received in a procurement competition above a specified value.
The eTenders system does not display the number of tenders received until the Tender Box has been opened by the contracting authority. Once the Tender Box is opened, the contracting authority gains access to the submitted tenders and can see the number of responses received. The contracting authority then assesses the submissions against the selection and exclusion criteria to determine whether tenderers qualify to proceed to the evaluation stage. Following this validation process, compliant tenders are evaluated in accordance with the award criteria set out in the competition documentation.
Where only one compliant tender is received, the contracting authority must satisfy itself that the competition was conducted appropriately, that the tender meets the requirements of the competition, and that the proposed award represents value for money.
Responsibility for conducting procurement procedures rests with the individual contracting authority, which must ensure that all procurement processes are carried out in accordance with the principles of transparency, equal treatment, non-discrimination and proportionality.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to provide an update on the impact of increased AI use within the public service, as encouraged through his Department's publication, Guidelines for the Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence in the public service, will impact public sector jobs.
reply:

Our objective is to ensure that public servants have the skills, confidence and organisational support required to use AI effectively.
This approach is central to Better Public Services 2030, particularly its priorities of Digital and Innovation at Scale, a Workforce and Organisation of the Future, and Evidence-Informed Policies and Services Designed for and with our Public. AI adoption should strengthen the capacity of the public-service workforce, by reducing the administrative burden of repetitive processes and free up more time for higher order work involving complex cases, professional judgement, policy analysis and engagement with the public.

They are intended to equip Public Service Bodies and their staff with the skills needed to assess when AI is appropriate, manage its risks and retain meaningful human involvement in decisions and service delivery.

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the procedures in place for the OPW that helps ensure no conflicts of interest in the subcontracting of work.
reply:
The Office of Public Works (OPW) is a scheduled office of Government, and its staff are bound by the statutory obligations set out under the Ethics in Public Office Acts 1995 and 2001, as well as the Civil Service Code of Standards and Behaviour. The OPW operates under a comprehensive Corporate Governance Framework which mandates strict adherence to the Capital Works Management Framework (CWMF) guidelines to ensure absolute transparency and the elimination of conflicts of interest across all stages of procurement, including subcontracting.
As a public body, the OPW is required to comply with all relevant public procurement requirements and the applicable ethical, governance and conflict of interest provisions. These include measures designed to ensure that procurement processes are conducted in a fair, transparent and accountable manner. Under Office of Government Procurement Guidelines, any form of interest which may impinge, or might reasonably be deemed by others to impinge on impartiality should be disclosed in writing to line management. Conflict checks continue throughout the procurement process including at tender evaluation and selection stages. The OPW has formal procedures in place to prevent, identify, manage and record conflicts of interest in procurement and subcontracting-related activity.
Under the OPW Conflict of Interest Policy and Guidelines staff are required to disclose any actual or perceived conflict of interest in writing to the Chair of the Evaluation

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the policies in place for the disclosure of gifts in the OPW.
reply:
The Office of Public Works (OPW) is a scheduled office of Government, and its staff are bound by the statutory obligations set out under the Ethics in Public Office Acts 1995 and 2001, as well as the Civil Service Code of Standards and Behaviour.
Under the Civil Service Code of Standards and Behaviour, civil servants are prohibited from soliciting or accepting gifts, hospitality, or benefits of any kind that could reasonably be seen to compromise their personal judgment, integrity, or the official impartiality of the State. These standards are highlighted to all staff on an annual basis.
Individuals occupying designated positions of employment within the OPW are required to submit annual Statements of Interest to the Standards in Public Office Commission (SIPO), www.sipo.ie/en/ which explicitly mandates the declaration of reportable gifts and material interests.
The OPW continuously monitors compliance with these frameworks to maintain the highest standards of transparency and ethical conduct across its public services.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation whether he will bring forward amendments to the Protected Disclosures Act 2014 to prohibit the transmission of a report, or of information capable of identifying the reporting person, to the organisation or persons the report concerns.
reply:
Section 2A of the Protected Disclosures Act 2014, which was substantively amended in 2022, provides for a statutory review as follows:
The Minister shall -
(a) not later than the end of the period of 5 years beginning on the passing of the Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 2022, commence a review of the operation of this Act, and
(b) not more than 12 months after the end of the period referred to in paragraph (a), make a report to each House of the Oireachtas of the findings made on the review and the conclusions drawn from those findings.
This section of the Act ensures that a review is commenced in July 2027 at the latest, however, as the Deputy will be aware, the review of the legislation is due to commence in advance of 2027 with a public consultation expected to launch by the end of this year.
All aspects of the operation of the Act may be examined as part of this review and any recommendations to amend the legislation emanating from this engagement will be considered in full.
Full details of the public consultation are expected to be published on my Department's website in the coming weeks and the Deputy is encouraged to make proposals in that regard.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the arrangements in place where a report made or transmitted to his Department under the Protected Disclosures Act 2014, as amended, concerns his Department's own functions under that Act, including the statutory guidance issued by him; whether a conflict of interest assessment is carried out on receipt of such a report; whether such reports may be referred to another suitable person or to the Office of the Protected Disclosures Commissioner.
reply:

Section 6A(1)(a), in respect of internal reporting channels, states that:

Section 6A(1)(c) goes on to state that:
"the designation of an impartial person or persons who are competent to follow-up on reports (who may be the same person or persons as the recipient of the report) (in this section referred to as a "designated person") who will maintain communication with the reporting person and, where necessary, request further information from, and provide feedback to, that reporting person".
Section 10.3 of the Protected Disclosures Statutory Guidance refers to the form that follow-up action could take. It states:
"the precise form of follow-up that is appropriate to each individual report will vary depending on the content and nature of the report. For example while some cases may require substantial investigation to establish the facts, others may not merit such detailed follow-up as the facts are clear and uncontroversial. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation whether his Department's internal protected disclosures policy and procedures are published on its website; if not, the reason; whether the statutory guidance encourages public bodies to publish their internal procedures.
reply:
For the purpose of clarity, I will refer directly to the legislation in answering the Deputy's question.
Section 6(3) of the Protected Disclosures Act 2014 (as amended) requires employers with 50 or more employees to establish, maintain and operate internal reporting channels and procedures for the making of reports and for follow-up.
Section 6A(1)(g), with regard to those internal reporting channels, requires the provision to workers of clear and easily accessible information, in such form and manner as the employer considers appropriate.
Section 7(2A) of the Act requires prescribed persons and the Protected Disclosures Commissioner to establish, maintain and operate independent and autonomous external reporting channels and procedures for receiving and handling reports made to them.
Section 7A(10), with regard to those external reporting channels, requires prescribed persons to publish on a website maintained by or on their behalf, in a separate, easily identifiable and accessible section, a range of procedural information.
In line with both the legislation and the Statutory Guidance on same, I can confirm that the relevant procedural information in respect of internal protected disclosures is made accessible on my Department's intranet and procedural information in respect of external reports is published on my Department’s website.
I trust this answers the Deputy's question.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if his Department has carried out or commissioned any assessment of the effect of euro area monetary policy since 2015, including the ECB's asset purchase programmes and the subsequent tightening of interest rates, on Irish house prices, rents and the general cost-of-living; if so, the findings of such assessment; if not, the reason.
reply:
My Department publishes forecasts twice annually, which are explicitly conditioned on a number of external assumptions. These inputs include the implied path for monetary policy based on market futures prevailing at the time of the forecasts. As such, each of these forecasts incorporate inter alia the expected impact of interest rate changes on the Irish economy, including rental inflation and prices more generally.
These forecasts are independently endorsed by the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council and published on my Department’s website.
As part of the Budget 2024 Economic and Fiscal Outlook, my Department also published additional scenario analysis conditioned on the ECB’s main refinancing rate rising from 4.5 per cent to 5.5 per cent. This analysis found that the impact of such a tightening of monetary policy was to reduce the level of Modified Domestic Demand by around 1 per cent over the medium term.
The results of this exercise were broadly similar to separate analysis carried out by the ESRI in 2023 and funded by my Department under its Joint Research Programme. This research assessed the impact of tighter monetary policy on the Irish economy, finding that domestic activity and house prices were lower in higher interest rate scenarios relative to baseline. This analysis is available at the link below.
www.gov.ie/en/department-of-finance/publications/interest-rate-snapback-and-the-impacts-on-the-irish-economy-august-2023.

The first tranche of designated projects, covering the energy, transport and water sectors, was approved by Government in July 2026 and the relevant designation Orders have been laid before the Oireachtas. Specifically, the following nine projects have been designated by Government:
• MetroLink.
• Cork Area Commuter Rail Programme.
• Galway City Ring Road.
• Water Supply Project for the Eastern and Midlands Region.
• Greater Dublin Drainage Project.
• Limerick (Bunlicky) Wastewater Treatment Plant Upgrade and Bioresource Centre.
• North South 400 kV Interconnector.
• Moneypoint 400 kV Series Capacitor Project.
• Letterkenny 110 kV Redevelopment Project.
As I have said previously, my priority is to ensure that this legislation delivers practical improvements in how we deliver critical infrastructure. Designation in itself is not the objective. The objective is to accelerate delivery and improve coordination across the State system where delays arise.

question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will consider developing a whole-of-Government strategy to combat the illicit tobacco trade, in line with the approach adopted by the UK government (details supplied).
reply:
As the national tax and customs administration, Revenue is responsible for implementing tax and duty legislation and applying customs controls. Revenue robustly targets the illicit tobacco trade using a range of measures to identify and target the smuggling, supply or sale of illicit tobacco products in the State and, where possible, prosecuting those involved. Revenue monitors trends in the illicit tobacco trade on an ongoing basis and adjusts its actions and redeploys its resources on an agile, risk-focused basis.
There are over 900 Revenue staff assigned across the ports, airports and mail centres as well as national profiling and risk assessment units and inland teams, dedicated to the enforcement of and ensuring the protection and integrity of customs controls in relation to all excisable products including tobacco products. In addition, at present, Revenue utilises 24 detector dog teams deployed at airports, ports, mail centres nationwide and in freight forwarding premises. Revenue’s detector dogs assist in screening passengers or postal packages, searching warehouses, commercial and private premises, all manner of vehicles, freight consignments, and air or sea passenger baggage. They also provide regular support for nationally coordinated operations, many of which are carried out on a joint multi-agency basis. reply:
The Central Bank of Ireland is the independent statutory body responsible for the regulation and supervision of regulated financial service providers. Questions concerning compliance with regulatory requirements by such firms fall within its remit. The Central Bank does not generally adjudicate on individual disputes or determine compensation claims between consumers and financial service providers. Further information on investment risks and investor protections is available through the Central Bank’s Consumer Hub, including its guidance on investing.
The extent of any regulatory protections available to an investor will depend on the nature of the investment concerned, the services provided by the intermediary, and whether the relevant activities were regulated activities under applicable legislation.
In certain limited circumstances, protection may also be available through the Investor Compensation Company DAC (ICCL), which operates the statutory investor compensation scheme for eligible clients of authorised investment firms. Eligibility for compensation depends on the specific facts of a case and the statutory criteria governing the scheme.
It is important to note that the investor compensation scheme does not protect against losses arising from poor investment performance or market movements. It applies only in specific circumstances where an authorised investment firm fails or is unable to meet its obligations to investors.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the environmental impact assessments that are planned for the development of the Floating Storage and Regasification Unit; and the impact the disapplication of the Habitats Directive by the Development (Strategic Gas Reserve) Act 2026 has on the required environmental impact assessments.
reply:

The delivery of a strategic gas reserve is critical to Ireland's energy security as we transition to indigenous, clean renewable energy. Crucially, the strategic gas emergency reserve will also ensure compliance with EU standards and regulations.
The State-led, transitional nature of the reserve ensures that the risk of stranded fossil fuel assets is reduced, that the reserve will be used for emergency use only, and that it does not support increased gas demand with a view to minimising impacts on greenhouse gas emissions.
The Development (Strategic Gas Reserve) Act 2026 requires an application for development consent to be subject to an Environmental Impact Assessment and an Appropriate Assessment under bespoke processes set out within the Act.
Chapter 2 of Part 4 of the Act outlines the Appropriate Assessment process that will apply to an application for designated development, in accordance with the requirements of the Habitats Directive.
Chapter 3 of Part 4 of the Act outlines the Environmental Impact Assessment process that will apply to an application for designated development, in accordance with the requirements of the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to outline the consequences of the disapplication of Section 15 of the Climate Action and Low Carbon Development Act 2015 by the Development (Strategic Gas Reserve) Act 2026 are for the development of the Floating Storage and Regasification Unit.
reply:
In March 2025, I received Government approval to develop a State-led strategic gas emergency reserve. The delivery of a strategic gas reserve is critical to Ireland's energy security as we transition to indigenous, clean renewable energy. Crucially, the strategic gas emergency reserve will also ensure compliance with EU standards and regulations.
The State-led, transitional nature of the reserve ensures that the risk of stranded fossil fuel assets is reduced, that the reserve will be used for emergency use only, and that it does not support increased gas demand with a view to minimising impacts on greenhouse gas emissions.
The section in question disapplies the duties imposed under Section 15 of the Climate Action and Low Carbon Development Act 2015 on certain public and prescribed bodies in the performance of their functions under the Development (Strategic Gas Reserve) Act 2026, as well as from the Commission for Regulation of Utilities in the performance of its functions under section 39A of Gas Act 1976 in relation to the construction of a pipeline approved by the Minister.
The purpose of the legislation is to provide for an expedited planning consenting pathway to allow the next stage of delivery of the strategic gas emergency reserve project, which is critical to Ireland’s energy security during Ireland's transition to indigenous, clean renewable energy.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to respond to the open letter (details supplied) to you signed by over 1000 people and approximately 40 environmental groups calling for a ban on LNG terminals.
reply:
In March 2025, I received Government approval to develop a State-led Strategic Gas Emergency Reserve. The delivery of this gas reserve is critical to Ireland’s energy security during Ireland's transition to indigenous, clean renewable energy. Crucially, the Strategic Gas Emergency Reserve will also ensure compliance with EU standards and regulations.
In 2025, my Department published an updated analysis of security of energy supply in Ireland beyond 2030 which considered the ability of increased interconnection and battery storage to secure Ireland's energy system. This analysis informed the Government's decision to proceed with a Strategic Gas Emergency Reserve as the best option to secure Ireland's energy systems as a transitionary measure which will be divested when no longer required.
This Government remains committed to taking decisive action to radically reduce our reliance on fossil fuels and has greatly boosted the share of renewables in our increasingly electrified energy system. Ireland has recently reached 8GW of renewable electricity capacity and almost 50% of electricity came from renewable sources in February and in March of this year.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether the CRU monitors supplier margins; if it has the powers it needs to make sure prices come down when wholesale costs do.
reply:
The role and remit of the Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU), underpinned by the Electricity Regulation Act 1999 (the ERA) as amended, is to ensure an open market with effective competition within both wholesale and retail markets. The CRU is also required to monitor the evolution of grid tariffs and levies, including examining their underlying charges and costs. The CRU is permitted to intervene or take corrective action should market failings be identified. The Electricity Market Design Directive (EU 2024/1711), is currently being transposed into national legislation by my officials and includes strong oversight measures for national regulatory authorities to oversee suppliers and ensure they are hedging responsibly.
Additionally, the CRU published an Interim Report on Competition Assessment and Retail Price Drivers in the Energy Market on 12 May 2026 to provide input into the work of the National Energy Affordability Taskforce (NEAT). Within the report, it is noted that initial assessment of supplier profit margins does not suggest excess profitability or that suppliers have been able to sustain materially elevated returns.
Section 9(1)(da)(x) of the ERA outlines the CRU's responsibility for monitoring the relationship between retail and wholesale prices. The Interim Report shows that retail prices track with movements in wholesale market prices. However, it also highlights a delay in the pass-through of wholesale cost changes to retail prices. This lag reflects

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she is aware that a 23-year-old woman (details supplied) has been sentenced to death in Iran; and if she will engage with her European counterparts to condemn this death sentence.
reply:
I am deeply concerned by the passing of a death sentence on a young woman in Iran on a charge of blasphemy.
This is part of a worrying trend in Iran, where there has been a drastic year-on-year increase in the number of executions since the 2022 ‘Women, Life, Freedom’ protests. It regrettably does appear that the conditions of the current war have emboldened the authorities to carry out further executions of political prisoners, protestors and human rights activists.
Ireland's position on the death penalty is consistent and clear: we are opposed to it in all cases and in all circumstances.
Ireland raises our concerns about Iran’s human rights abuses both bilaterally and in multilateral fora; such as the United Nations Human Rights Council and the UN Third Committee on Human Rights. At the 2025 Universal Periodic Review of Iran at the UN Human Rights Council, Ireland raised the death penalty and highlighted Iran’s use of the death penalty against human rights defenders, especially women. We called for the end of all executions in Iran. Ireland was also instrumental in the establishment by the Human Rights Council of an ongoing special procedure to investigate human rights abuses in Iran following the protests in 2022, and the violent suppression of protests earlier this year by the Iranian authorities.
Along with our EU partners, we make these points directly to the Iranian authorities at every opportunity, both in Dublin and in Tehran. Department officials met with the Irania

Ní mór do gach tionscadal tógála scoile, de réir mar a théann siad ar aghaidh tríd an bpróiseas, dul faoin dícheall cuí riachtanach atá leagtha amach sna Treoirlínte Bonneagair agus sa Chreat Bainistíochta Oibreacha Caipitil.
