question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether she will instruct her officials to modify the new build currently underway for a school (details supplied) to include permanent SEN rooms rather than the prefabs that are currently proposed.
reply:
Modular accommodation is one of the delivery mechanisms used by the department to provide permanent accommodation in schools. Today’s modular buildings represent a major advancement from earlier prefabricated forms, meet very high standards of energy efficiency and sustainability and provide a very comfortable environment for teaching and learning. The department consistently receives positive feedback from schools that have new modular accommodation.
Having assessed the position regarding additional capacity for special classes, the department has determined that modular accommodation represents the most cost-effective method for provision of additional permanent accommodation for the school referred to by the Deputy. The alternative of a traditional build extension has been explored but does not represent value for money in this specific context. The department has to take account of special education needs requirements not just in this one school but across the country and value for money is therefore a key priority.
The accommodation proposed for the school in question is extensive and includes four classrooms, four quiet spaces, four toilets, and two multi-purpose rooms measuring 479 square metres in total.
The department will be meeting with the patron and school authority shortly to provide clarity and as much practical assistance as possible on this important project for the local community.

question: Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Education and Youth her plans to increase the numbers of DEIS+ schools in Limerick.
reply:
Addressing educational disadvantage and ensuring that every child and young person can reach their full potential is a key priority for me as Minister for Education and Youth and for the Government. Overall, approximately €230 million is invested in the DEIS programme. This includes the additional €48 million secured under Budget 2026 to support the implementation of the DEIS Strategy to 2035 and the introduction of the DEIS Plus scheme. Budget 2027 provides a further €6 million to support the expansion of DEIS Plus.
DEIS Plus is designed to provide enhanced, evidence-based supports to a small cohort of schools with the highest concentrations of children and young people at risk of educational disadvantage. Schools in the scheme will receive strengthened, research-informed supports across wellbeing, attendance, engagement, guidance, leadership capacity, community partnerships and access to services, including a new positive mental health and wellbeing initiative to support a whole-school approach to student wellbeing.
Schools were identified for inclusion in DEIS Plus through a nationally consistent, evidence-based identification model which drew on a range of indicators associated with persistent and intergenerational disadvantage. The model was applied uniformly across all eligible schools to ensure a fair and objective process.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which she is responding to the recent spate of threatening emails to schools which have resulted in some cases to forced school closures.
reply:
The Department of Education and Youth was made aware on Wednesday 14 October, that a number of schools across the country received a threatening email. In line with standard practice, my department consulted with An Garda Síochána regarding this matter. An Garda Síochána advised that any school that had received this email should ring 999 and report the threat to An Garda Síochána and cooperate fully with any Garda instructions. My department communicated this message to school management bodies and directly to schools.
I understand that this type of threat is concerning for school communities. My department always follows the advice given from An Garda Síochána in these circumstances, in the best interests of school communities and the staff and students concerned.
My department is currently examining the lessons learned from recent incidents. Officials in my department are reviewing the protocols in place to deal with incidents such as this and wider emergency planning measures as a whole.
As part of this, my officials will continue engage with principal response agencies and relevant education stakeholders.
We will continue to work with school authorities and stakeholders if and when these issues arise and appreciate schools’ assistance in co-operating with advice given in such circumstances.

question: Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Education and Youth for an update on the pilot expansion of the home school community liaison scheme to high-need non-DEIS schools; whether consideration is being given to making the scheme permanent and extending it to further schools.
reply:
Addressing educational disadvantage in all schools remains a key priority for me as Minister for Education and Youth.
The HSCL scheme is a core element of the DEIS programme and forms part of the wider Tusla Education Support Service (TESS). HSCL coordinators are teachers assigned to work directly with parents, guardians, school staff and community services to strengthen engagement between home, school and community. The overarching aim of HSCL is to improve attendance, participation and retention, particularly for children and young people experiencing educational disadvantage.
Under the DEIS Strategy to 2035, a pilot project was introduced to extend Home-School-Community-Liaison (HSCL) provision to 130 schools that are in the DEIS Rural band and outside the DEIS programme. This pilot provides an important opportunity to trial the extension of this support to additional schools and to inform future policy development in relation to the scheme.
Budget 2027 provides an additional €3 million from September 2027, rising to €9 million on a full-year basis from September 2028, to support a targeted expansion of the HSCL scheme for children and young people at risk of educational disadvantage. A detailed approach on the targeting of this additional funding is currently being developed.
The implementation and outcomes of the HSCL pilot project will continue to be monitored and evaluated to inform future planning. Any future allocation of resources, including any potential further ex

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Education and Youth her proposals to ensure the effective running of the school transport scheme.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
The scheme is made up of three separate schemes, the school transport scheme for primary, post primary and for children with special educational needs.
The scheme has expanded significantly over the past six years. In that time, the numbers of children and young people using the service have grown from under 120,000 pupils in 2018 to over 180,000 pupils in 2025, which equates to an increase of close to 50%.
The purpose of my Department's School Transport Scheme is, having regard to available resources, to support the transport to and from school of children who reside remote from their nearest school.
Children are eligible for school transport at primary level where they reside not less than 3.2 kilometres from and are attending their nearest national school, and at post primary level where they reside not less than 4.8 kilometres from and are attending their nearest post primary school/education centre, as determined by the department/Bus Éireann, having regard to ethos and language.
A minimum number of 10 eligible children residing in a distinct locality, as determined by Bus Éireann, are required before consideration may be given to the establishment of school transport services, provided this can be done within reasonable cost limits.

question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her Department has examined the reason many students complete primary and post-primary education with limited confidence in speaking Gaeilge; and the specific measures being considered to improve oral fluency and everyday use of the language in schools.
reply:
Factors affecting primary and post-primary students’ confidence in speaking Irish have been examined extensively in research and consultation with stakeholders during the development of policy initiatives and new curricula for Irish.
This includes research and consultation that have informed the development of the Action Plan for Irish in English-Medium Schools and the Policy for Irish-Medium Education outside of the Gaeltacht, published in November 2025. It also includes research and consultation that have informed the development of curriculum specifications for Irish at primary level, junior cycle and senior cycle, and ongoing research being carried out by An Chomhairle um Oideachas Gaeltachta agus Gaelscolaíochta (COGG) on Irish in English-medium and Irish-medium schools. Reports on the findings of this research are available on the websites of my department, the National Council for Curriculum and Assessment, and COGG.
This research indicates that the learning of Irish as a second language is complex and that there are many reasons affecting students’ confidence in speaking it. These include attitudes, motivation, exposure to the language, opportunity to use it, the teaching methodologies used, and the language and pedagogical skill of the teacher.
One of my priorities is to build greater confidence in spoken Irish among students, and to ensure that they experience Irish as a living language at school.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Education and Youth the steps being taken to guarantee that children in rural communities, particularly in County Galway, can access school transport given many children have been left without transportation under the existing scheme.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
All eligible children have been facilitated with mainstream transport services where there is a service and capacity to do so, and where families have applied and paid/entered medical card details on or before 08 May 2026.
Under the current terms of the School Transport Schemes, children are eligible for transport at primary level where they reside not less than 3.2 kilometres from and are attending their nearest national school, and at post primary level where they reside not less than 4.8 kilometres from and are attending their nearest post primary school/education centre as determined by the department/Bus Éireann, having regard to ethos and language.
The School Transport 2030 report was published in early 2024 following a comprehensive analysis and review of the scheme as it currently operates. It was outlined at the time the Review was published that the proposed changes to the eligibility criteria would further increase demand for the scheme. Therefore, it was considered prudent to implement the changes on a phased basis.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of children who applied and paid on time for school transport for 2026-2027 who have not been offered a place, by concessionary/eligible and, by county.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
Under the current terms of the mainstream school transport scheme, children are eligible for transport at post primary level where they reside not less than 4.8 kilometres from and are attending their nearest post primary school/education centre as determined by the department/Bus Éireann, having regard to ethos and language.
Where a child is eligible for transport and the application and payment process has been completed on time, they will get a seat on a school bus service, where a service is available.
Children who are not eligible, but who apply for school transport are considered for spare seats that may exist after eligible children have been facilitated; previously known as concessionary seats.
Because of the nature of transport for non-eligible children and the priority of providing places for eligible children, there may be an excess of demand over supply for non-eligible pupils. In these cases, Bus Éireann will allocate tickets for spare seats using an agreed selection process.
The information requested by the Deputy is being collated by Bus Éireann and will be issued to the Deputy directly.

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Education and Youth her views on early intervention for ASD classes in Waterford.
reply:
The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) is the statutory body responsible for the provision of special education and allocating supports for students with special educational needs.
The Access and Inclusion Model (AIM) under the Department of Children, Disability and Equality, facilitates the full inclusion and meaningful participation of children with disabilities/additional needs in the Early Childhood Care & Education Scheme (ECCE) programme. Its goal is to create a more inclusive environment in pre-schools, so all children availing of preschool, regardless of ability, can benefit from high-quality early learning and care. There has been a significant increase in resources and supports provided to children with additional needs accessing the AIM programme over recent years.
It is important to note that a diagnosis is not required in order to access AIM supports and that while some children require additional supports at preschool level, many will transition into mainstream classes thereafter.
Early intervention classes are available in mainstream and special school settings for children aged 3 -5 years old with a diagnosis of autism. There is also a small number dedicated to children who are deaf/hard of hearing. These classes are intended to provide early support to children before they start school and can aid their transition to junior infants.

question: Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Education and Youth for an update on the AI Schools Advisory Taskforce.
reply:
The AI in Education External Advisory Taskforce has been established to support the Department in developing a coherent national approach to the safe, responsible and effective use of AI across the school system at primary and post-primary level. Two AI Taskforce meetings have been held to date, 14 May and 21 September.
Meetings are attended by teacher unions, management bodies and other stakeholders such as teachers, parents and student representative groups and research bodies and other relevant agencies. Its membership ensures a broad range of perspectives and expertise are brought to the discussion.
To support its work the Taskforce has established two working groups. The first is focused on assessment, including both summative and State-certified assessment, with the second Working Group focusing on teaching, learning and formative assessment.
The current phase of the taskforce is expected to operate over an initial 18-24 month period with outputs delivered on a rolling basis. The first quarterly report will be published on gov.ie in the coming weeks. The quarterly report publications will provide greater transparency regarding the Taskforce's work programme and priorities.
The taskforce will help ensure that the department’s response is informed by practical experience, ongoing work across the education system, and emerging national and international developments.

reply:

There are 15,200 special education teachers allocated to primary and post-primary schools to enable them to support children with special educational needs.
It is important to note that the majority of students with literacy difficulties currently receive additional teaching support from a special education teacher in a mainstream class. Furthermore, there are four schools dedicated to supporting students with specific learning disability (SLD). There are also fourteen SLD classes in eleven mainstream primary schools located across the country, in counties Dublin, Clare, Louth, Galway, Kerry and Wexford.
However, I recognise that more needs to be done. I am happy to advise that my officials in conjunction with the NCSE are currently at an advanced stage in developing a pilot programme to test best practice and support policy formulation going forward.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Education and Youth the process for a school to appeal a negative decision in relation to applications for DEIS status.
reply:
Addressing educational disadvantage in all schools remains a key priority for me as Minister for Education and Youth. The DEIS programme is targeted at schools with the highest levels of concentrated disadvantage. Schools that were included in the most recent expansion of the programme in 2022 were those with the highest levels of concentrated disadvantage as identified through the refined DEIS identification model. Schools were not required to apply for inclusion in the DEIS programme, and the model was applied fairly and equally to all schools. A detailed paper on the refined DEIS identification model is available on gov.ie.
All schools that were not satisfied with the outcome following the application of the DEIS identification model to their enrolment data, were provided with the opportunity to make an appeal at the time. Circular 0019/2022 outlined the details of the DEIS appeals process.
The DEIS Strategy to 2035, launched in March, sets out a long-term plan to address educational disadvantage in all schools and work to ensure that any child or young person experiencing educational disadvantage is supported through their education journey. It sets out a more flexible model of support so that resources are aligned with each school’s level of need as it changes over time.

question: Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Education and Youth if an assessment of need is required for children to apply for either a special class place in a mainstream school or a special school place.
reply:
This government is fully committed to supporting students with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this objective.
The Department of Education and Youth is committed to an education-based, needs-led approach to accessing education services. Children and young people in the education system have never required an Assessment of Need (AON) in order to access education supports. Since 2017, children and young people in mainstream schools have not required a diagnosis to access supports from the 15,000 special education teachers in our school system. The department has also removed the need for health-related information for special education teaching allocations, transitions between primary and post-primary special classes, assistive technology supports, and additional SNA requirements. A diagnosis is currently still required for access to a special school or class place.
Looking ahead, the department is examining how best to ensure equitable and appropriate access to educational provision and supports for children and young people with special educational needs. This work remains at an early stage of development. Any proposals that may emerge will be informed by extensive engagement with education stakeholders, advocacy organisations and disabled persons organisations to ensure that a broad range of perspectives is considered before decisions are made. This includes the additional €48 million secured under Budget 2026 to support the implementation of the DEIS Strategy to 2035 and the introduction of the DEIS Plus scheme. Budget 2027 provides a further €6 million to support the expansion of DEIS Plus.

question: Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide an update on the provision of a school bus route (details supplied).
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
Under the terms of the Post Primary School Transport Scheme, children are eligible for transport where they reside not less than 4.8 kms from their nearest post primary school/centre as determined by the Department/Bus Éireann, having regard to ethos and language.
Where a child is eligible for transport and the application and payment process has been completed on time, they will get a seat on a school bus service, where a service is available.
Children who are not eligible, but who apply for school transport are considered for spare seats that may exist after eligible children have been facilitated; previously known as concessionary seats.
Because of the nature of transport for non-eligible children and the priority of providing places for eligible children, there may be an excess of demand over supply for non-eligible pupils. In these cases, Bus Éireann will allocate tickets for spare seats using an agreed selection process.
Further to the Deputy's request for information on a school bus route for Calverstown, Bus Éireann has advised that at present, one route currently operates through Calverstown to St Kevin’s Community College. This service commences at Suncroft and stops in Calverstown on its route to St. Kevin’s Community College.

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Education and Youth the measures in place to ensure that children awaiting an assessment of need or formal diagnosis are not disadvantaged when seeking access to special education supports or placements; and if her Department intends to review the eligibility criteria for special classes.
reply:
This government is fully committed to supporting students with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this objective.
The Department of Education and Youth is committed to an education-based, needs-led approach to accessing education services. Children and young people in the education system have never required an Assessment of Need (AON) in order to access education supports. Since 2017, children and young people in mainstream schools have not required a diagnosis to access supports from the 15,000 special education teachers in our school system. The department has also removed the need for health-related information for special education teaching allocations, transitions between primary and post-primary special classes, assistive technology supports, and additional SNA requirements. A diagnosis is currently still required for access to a special school or class place.
Looking ahead, the department is examining how best to ensure equitable and appropriate access to educational provision and supports for children and young people with special educational needs. This work remains at an early stage of development. Any proposals that may emerge will be informed by extensive engagement with education stakeholders, advocacy organisations and disabled persons organisations to ensure that a broad range of perspectives is considered before decisions are made. question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether she will review the assistive technology scheme under Circular 0010/2013, which excludes communication devices that have a general application outside school, so that pupils who need augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) devices to access the curriculum are no longer referred between her Department and the HSE; and whether she will agree a joint protocol with the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to provide a single pathway for these pupils.
reply:
Under the Assistive Technology Scheme, as set out in my Department’s Circular 0010/2013, funding is provided to schools towards the cost of computers and specialist equipment, which are required for educational purposes.
The Assistive Technology Scheme is provided by my department to supplement the overall funding approach for digital technology and equipment to support children for education purposes. All equipment provided under this scheme supports children who require essential specialist equipment to access the school curriculum. For children with more complex disabilities who require such equipment to access the school curriculum, which they do not already have or which cannot be provided for them through the schools' existing provisions, schools can apply for this equipment under the terms of the Assistive Technology Scheme.
As per the terms of the current scheme, communication devices and medical or therapy-related equipment which are not specific educational interventions, or equipment specifically required as essential for school educational access, are not eligible for support. This includes those devices that have a general application outside the school setting that would normally be provided by the Health Service Executive (HSE) to children with disabilities. Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) devices fall into this category and so they would not be provided under my department's Assistive Technology Scheme.

reply:
Addressing educational disadvantage in all schools remains a key priority for me as Minister for Education and Youth.
The HSCL scheme is a core element of the DEIS programme and forms part of the wider Tusla Education Support Service (TESS). While HSCL Coordinator posts are full-time positions, not all posts are assigned exclusively to a single school. In some cases, a HSCL Coordinator is allocated on a shared basis across a cluster of schools, including arrangements that may span both primary and post-primary sectors. This approach allows HSCL resources to be targeted across schools based on identified need and the overall allocation model.
The DEIS Strategy to 2035 sets out a long-term vision to address educational disadvantage in all schools. Under Strategic Objective 2.2 the strategy sets out actions to develop an agile resource allocation model to support children and young people at risk of educational disadvantage in all primary and post-primary schools. These actions focus on the continued enhancement of the data available to measure school level disadvantage and for the development of a more flexible resource allocation model that can react to change in school needs and provide the right resources at the right time.

reply:

reply:

Under the current schemes, children are eligible for transport at primary level where they reside not less than 3.2 kilometres from, and are attending, their nearest national school. At post primary level, young people are eligible where they reside not less than 4.8 kilometres from, and are attending, their nearest post primary school/education centre as determined by the Department/Bus Éireann, having regard to ethos and language.
Temporary Alleviation Measures (TAMS) at post-primary level, have been in place since 2019. Under these measures, transport is provided where there is a route in operation and where capacity exists for post-primary pupils who are eligible for transport to their nearest school but are attending their second nearest school.
In relation to the question raised by the Deputy, the School Transport 2030 report, recommended changes to the future operation of the schemes including expansion of the current eligibility criteria. question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth the position regarding any review or reassessment available for four schools in the Dún Laoghaire constituency in relation to their allocation under the Home School Community Liaison Programme; and her views on whether their current assessment is acceptable in the context of significant increases in school population and a shift in demographics since this allocation was last assessed.
reply:
Addressing educational disadvantage in all schools is a key priority for the Department of Education and Youth.
The HSCL scheme is a core element of the DEIS programme and forms part of the wider Tusla Education Support Service (TESS). HSCL coordinators work directly with parents/guardians, school staff and relevant community services to strengthen engagement between home, school and the wider community, with the aim of improving attendance, participation and retention for children and young people at risk of educational disadvantage.
As part of the development of the DEIS Strategy to 2035, all schools qualifying for HSCL support were recently reassessed using the most up-to-date data available to the department. This reassessment informed HSCL allocations for the 2026/27 school year.
The DEIS Strategy to 2035, under Strategic Objective 2.2, sets out actions to develop an agile resource allocation model to support children and young people at risk of educational disadvantage in all primary and post-primary schools. These actions focus on the continued enhancement of the data available to measure school level disadvantage and for the development of a more flexible resource allocation model that can react to change in school needs and provide the right resources at the right time.
Budget 2027 provides an additional €3 million from September 2027, rising to €9 million on a full-year basis from September 2028, to support a targeted expansion of the HSCL scheme for children and yo

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Education and Youth the proportion of the additional school building and capital investment funding announced in Budget 2027 is expected to support school accommodation projects in rapidly growing constituencies such as Kildare north.
reply:
The capital allocation available to the Department of Education and Youth in 2027 is €1.6 billion, representing a very significant level of investment in the school estate.
This will support the delivery of many important projects in County Kildare, an area of demographic growth, and across the country.
There has already been a significant level of investment in school infrastructure in County Kildare with investment since 2020 alone totalling €261 million in North Kildare and €203 million in South Kildare.
Eight projects are currently on site across Kildare North, including the construction of new school buildings for Gaelscoil Ruairí, Maynooth, and Coláiste Naomh Mhuire, Naas. In addition, a project at Scoil Uí Riada, Kilcock, has progressed to the tender stage.
There are also 7 projects on site in Kildare South including new school buildings for Patrician Secondary School and Curragh Community College. In addition, a project at Scoil Naomh Cill Daingin, has progressed to the tender stage.
Furthermore, 33 large-scale and additional accommodation projects are progressing through the design pipeline in County Kildare: 7 at Preliminary Design (Stage 1), 15 at Developed Design (Stage 2a), 11 at Detailed Design (Stage 2b).
Two of the Stage 2b projects, the new school buildings for St. Farnan’s, Prosperous and St. Anne's Special School, Ballymany Cross have been included in the priority tranche of projects published in January as part of NDP Rollout.

question: Deputy Keira Keogh asked the Minister for Education and Youth the steps being taken to improve the school transport scheme for families in rural counties such as Mayo, particularly where pupils have experienced difficulties accessing school bus services; and ask that she make a statement on the matter.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
The scheme has expanded significantly over the past six years. In that time, the numbers of children and young people using the service increased by close to 50%.
In the 2025/26 school year over 181,000 children were transported daily in over 8,500 vehicles across over 11,000 routes to primary, post-primary and special schools throughout the country.
It is recognised that the School Transport Scheme is vital to families and its benefits extend to support parents and guardians who are accessing employment. It continues to support pupils living in rural and remote areas, children and young people with additional needs, as well as assisting towards national sustainability and climate goals.
The scheme is demand-led based on the number of eligible children who apply and pay on time.
As of the 29 September 2026, 6,399 pupils are travelling on mainstream services in Mayo.
Of this figure, 914 eligible and 1,075 non-eligible pupils travel to primary schools and 3,360 eligible and 1,050 non-eligible pupils travel to post primary schools.
59 families in Mayo have also availed of the Remote Area Grant for the 2025/26 school year. This grant is paid to families of children who are eligible for school transport but for whom no service is available, towards the cost of making private transport arrangements. The Remote Area Grant is also payable for eligible chil

It is expected that the next tranche of projects to proceed to tender under the National Development Plan will be published in 2027.
Prioritisation will continue over the coming months to identify this next tranche of projects.
This will be informed by latest available demographic and capacity data, the department’s energy and condition inventory (the validation of which is due to be completed by early 2027), opportunities for phased development to prioritise the most urgent accommodation needs and consultation with school patrons and management bodies.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage when the adopt a monument scheme will open to new applicants.
reply:
The Adopt a Monument Scheme is operated by the Heritage Council and aims to help communities become actively involved in the conservation and interpretation of their local archaeological and cultural heritage sites.
The Heritage Council is a statutory body established by the Heritage Act 1995. The Council is a body under the aegis of this Department but is independent in the performance of its functions. As such, details of its schemes should be sought, in the first instance, from the Council directly.
Arrangements have been put in place by all bodies under the aegis of my Department to facilitate the provision of information directly to members of the Oireachtas. This provides a speedy, efficient and cost effective system to address queries directly to the relevant bodies. The contact email address for the Heritage Council is oireachtas@heritagecouncil.ie.

question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the position regarding the development of the child and family homelessness action plan.
reply:
The Government's national housing plan, ‘Delivering Homes, Building Communities: An Action Plan on Housing Supply and Targeting Homelessness’ is an integrated housing and homelessness plan. The Plan is based on two key pillars: activating the supply of 300,000 more homes; and supporting people to have a home of their own.
Our housing plan recognises that homelessness is the single most pressing social issue that we face and introduces a number of key measures to address homelessness. Increased supply is key to addressing homelessness. Government is focused on making sure that everyone has access to good quality, affordable and secure homes that suit their needs. Over €9 billion in capital funding will be made available for housing in 2026.
Addressing child and family homelessness is a key priority for Government. Our housing plan commits to the development of a Child and Family Homelessness Action Plan. Development of the Plan brought together key stakeholders to drive the continued focus on preventing children and families entering emergency accommodation, providing enhanced supports for children experiencing homelessness, as well as measures to accelerate exits and reduce the time spent by children and their families in homeless emergency accommodation. It is anticipated that the Child and Family Homelessness Action Plan will be published this year.

question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether apartment owners in pyrite-affected multi-unit developments can access State remediation supports; will they be treated equitably with homeowners in traditional housing developments affected by similar defects; and will he explore the establishment of further remediation schemes where existing arrangements do not adequately address apartment developments.
reply:
Drafting of the Apartment and Duplex Defects Remediation Scheme Bill is at an advanced stage and it is listed for publication this session. The statutory scheme will be in place as soon as possible following its passage through the Dáil.
The scheme will provide supports for the remediation of relevant fire safety, structural safety and water ingress defects in purpose-built apartment buildings, including duplexes, constructed between 1991 and 2013.
Only defects that are attributable to defective design, defective or faulty workmanship, defective materials (or any combination of these) and were in contravention of the relevant Parts of the Building Regulations applicable at the time of construction will be eligible for inclusion in the statutory scheme.
Apartment and duplex buildings with deleterious material will be covered for remediation funding under the scheme, which will take a whole of building approach. Applications will be made by Owner Management Companies, as the persons having control of the buildings. Eligibility will be determined by reference to the scope of the scheme as approved by Government.
It is envisaged that 100% of eligible remediation costs will be funded.
The Pyrite Remediation Scheme and the Defective Concrete Blocks Grant Scheme are both underpinned by legislation. The forthcoming Apartment and Duplex Defects Remediation Scheme will complete a comprehensive suite of measures in place to support homeowners, including providing considerable financial

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to provide an update on the interim fire safety scheme, the fire detection and alarm safety scheme and the retrospective payments scheme for people living with defects including applicant numbers, approval numbers, funding allocations, drawdowns and number of homes that have completed each of these schemes.
reply:
As of the end of September 2026, 302 applications to the Interim Remediation Scheme have been validated, having met the required eligibility criteria. These applications represent 26,724 residential units, with circa 73% in the Dublin region.
Approximately €9.3 million has been paid by the Housing Agency to the four pathfinder OMCs to date, representing 595 residential units. Remediation works have commenced in three locations.
In February 2026, the Government announced some significant amendments to the Interim Remediation Scheme in order to simplify procurement and cut through administrative hurdles. This has allowed works relating to fire detection and alarm systems to be completed more quickly, while ensuring residents can remain safely in their homes until full building remediation is finished.
Ten OMCs were invited to participate representing 1,945 residential units. The Housing Agency has received four tender submissions to date. Letters of advice from the Local Authority Fire Services have issued to nine of the OMCs. Funding has been allocated for this initiative and will be disbursed as claims arise.
As per its decision of January 2023, the Government is committed to consideration of remediation costs already incurred.
A Retrospective Costs Pathfinder project using a representative sample of eight OMCs was established to identify an appropriate process to address retrospective issues more broadly. The Retrospective Costs Pathfinder Exercise is now complete.
A Memoran

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of residential properties purchased in the State by persons who were not ordinarily resident in Ireland in each of the past five years, by county; the number of such purchases that were made by purchasers whose principal residence was outside the State; and the proportion these purchases represented of all residential property transactions in each year.
reply:
My Department does not hold the data sought. The Central Statistics Office collects and publishes data in relation to residential dwelling property transactions disaggregated by dwelling status and buyer type and can be found on the CSO website at: https://data.cso.ie/table/HPM02.
Data show some 51,415 homes were purchased by households in the 12-months ending August 2026, an increase of 3% year on year and up 4% on the same period in 2022. At the same time, first time buyers purchased 8,564 new homes in the year to August 2026, an increase of 24% year-on-year [6,914]. While the number of new homes purchased by all household purchasers in the 12 months to August 2026 increased 19% year on year, from 11,235 to 13,378.

question: Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the remediation scheme to fix defects in apartments and duplexes; when he expects to bring legislation before the house.
reply:
Drafting of the Apartment and Duplex Defects Remediation Scheme Bill is at an advanced stage and it is listed for publication this session. The statutory scheme will be in place as soon as possible following its passage through the Dáil.
The scheme will provide supports for the remediation of relevant fire safety, structural safety and water ingress defects in purpose-built apartment buildings, including duplexes, constructed between 1991 and 2013.
Only defects that are attributable to defective design, defective or faulty workmanship, defective materials (or any combination of these) and were in contravention of the relevant Parts of the Building Regulations applicable at the time of construction will be eligible for inclusion in the statutory scheme.
It is envisaged that 100% of eligible remediation costs will be funded.
The Interim Remediation Scheme ('the Scheme') has been in place since December 2023, to provide an acceptable level of fire safety in buildings pending introduction of the Statutory Scheme and completion of the full remedial works. The Scheme is for the funding of emergency fire safety defect works in apartments and duplexes constructed between 1991 and 2013. The Scheme is administered by the Housing Agency. Applications can be made via the Housing Agency’s website at www.housingagency.ie.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she can detail any step that has been taken by Ireland in its position of EU Presidency to try to facilitate peace between Ukraine and Russia.
reply:
Ireland remains steadfast in our support for Ukraine. We all want to see peace in Ukraine.
However, Russia’s aggression continues, and while a deadly stalemate is maintained on the frontline, there has been a clear escalation in Russia's wider missile and drone attacks on Ukraine's towns and cities and on its energy infrastructure. These have targeted civilians and have caused extensive damage to Ukraine’s critical infrastructure and Ukraine's economic capacity. Attacks on Ukraine's Black Sea grain facilities are having an impact not only on Ukraine, but are contributing to a wider crisis on food security.
Russia’s illegal war in Ukraine is deadlier today for civilians than at any point since the start of the full-scale invasion. In the first eight months of 2026, more civilians were killed and injured in Ukraine than during the whole of 2025.
Russia can halt its brutal attacks any time, yet it refuses to do.
We maintain our call for a ceasefire and for Russia to cease its illegal aggression and engage in meaningful negotiations.
Ireland and EU Member States remain united in our resolve to support the people of Ukraine in the face of Russia's continuing aggression. Along with our EU partners, Ireland welcomes efforts to achieve a just, lasting and comprehensive peace agreement. It is crucial that any agreement that might be reached upholds the fundamental principle that borders cannot be changed by force.
Ukraine is a horizontal priority for our EU Presidency; we are pursuing

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to provide an update on the progress of a review of HAP limits.
reply:
The HAP scheme plays a vital role in housing eligible families and individuals. At the end of Q1 2026, over 133,100 HAP tenancies had been set up since the scheme commenced, of which there were 48,355 households actively in receipt of HAP support nationally.
Maximum rent limits for HAP were set for each housing authority area in 2016 in conjunction with the Department of Social Protection. Since 11 July 2022, each local authority has statutory discretion to agree to a HAP payment up to 35% above the prescribed maximum rent limit. Discretion can be increased up to 50% above the prescribed maximum rent limits for Homeless HAP tenancies in Dublin. Local authorities also have additional flexibility to apply a couple HAP rate to single-person households.
I gave my approval for a review of the current HAP rent limits to be undertaken to ensure there is sufficient support under the HAP scheme to assist eligible households in accessing accommodation in the private rental sector.
As part of this review, the Housing Agency carried out an analysis of the rental market and submitted its report to my Department on 16 July. This helped inform my Department’s review of the HAP rent limits, which has now concluded. I am currently considering its findings before setting out the next steps.

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport for an update on his engagement with Coimisiún na Meán regarding the broadcasting levy on independent radio stations.
reply:
There is a long-standing principle that costs of regulation are met by regulated sectors themselves, and therefore, the Broadcasting Act provides for the imposition by Coimisiún na Meán of levies to meet the costs of its full range of statutory functions and duties.
Furthermore, the Act vests authority and responsibility for such a levy in Coimisiún na Meán, and as such as Minister, I have no role in approving the proposed income or expenditure of Coimisiún na Meán, or importantly in the setting of the annual levy for any category of regulated entities, including that of sound broadcasting.
I have, however, met Coimisiún na Meán in order to seek clarity regarding their approach to implementing their statutory responsibilities in this regard. It was also an opportunity for me to impress upon them the need to take the opportunity to more clearly communicate such matters to their stakeholders and the wider public, and also consider how the levy can in future be formulated to avoid placing an unnecessary burden on the sector.
In formulating its annual levies, Coimisiún na Meán is required to ensure that the levies are such an amount so as to meet all expenses properly incurred in the period, and is also required to ensure proportionality in attribution of expenses and application of levies across relevant categories of regulated service providers or entities. An Coimisiún must also have regard to a number of factors in setting the levy including the financing of a service provide

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport whether consideration will be given to establishing a formal funding pathway for Irish athletes competing at international level in codes outside those traditionally supported through Sport Ireland.
reply:
Sport Ireland, which is funded by my Department, is the statutory body with responsibility for the development of sport, increasing participation at all levels and raising standards, including the allocation of funding across its various programmes.
Accordingly, I have referred the Deputy's question to Sport Ireland for direct reply. I would ask the Deputy to inform my office if a reply is not received within 10 days.

question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport whether security and transport costs are included in the €14.275 million operational budget for hosting an event (details supplied); and when a full, updated estimate of the total cost to the State will be published.
reply:
Major international sporting events can play a key role in increasing sporting participation, boosting domestic and international tourism and promoting Ireland as a destination for education and business opportunities. They present a wonderful opportunity to showcase the island of Ireland and our world-class tourism and sport offering to Europe and the world.
When the Government took the decision in 2019 to proceed with hosting this event, it agreed to an allocation of €14.275 million for the operational budget to support the event's staging. These costs included transport, security, local authority costs, ceremonies and fanzones.
The operational budget for the event was estimated in 2019 prior to COVID-19 and recent international conflicts that have led to global supply chain pressures and significant cost of living increases. It is therefore reasonable to presume that the costs associated with the operational budget would have increased, in line with the potential benefits from hosting the event. A continuous review of the operational budget (transport, security, local authority costs, etc) is taking place in parallel with the strategic planning to host the event which is governed by the Government Steering Group.
A full economic analysis/assessment will be conducted post-event to evaluate the total economic impact of this event once it has concluded.

question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport when applicants can expect to be notified of the outcome of the selection process for the basic income for arts scheme; when the first payments are expected to actually reach successful applicants.
reply:
In February this year I announced that the Government had approved a permanent successor to the Basic Income for the Arts pilot scheme and that 2,000 artists would be provided with funding of €325 per week for three years. This is a major milestone for the arts in Ireland and I am particularly pleased that the research my Department conducted provided Government with a clear evidence base upon which to make that decision.
The deadline for application to the Basic Income for the Arts 2026 - 2029 was 5pm on Tuesday 12th May, with over 10,000 applications received by the deadline.
I appreciate that applicants are eager to know the outcome, however, in order to protect the integrity of the scheme the assessment process is by necessity very intensive and time consuming. No two professional arts practices are the same and therefore the proofs supplied vary considerably. The Department has commenced communication to applicants invited to participate in the scheme on Thursday 15 October. Due to the volume involved, successful applicants will be notified in tranches as assessments are completed.
My Department is processing the applications as promptly as possible and I anticipate that payments will commence shortly. All successful candidates will receive the full allocation of €325 per week for three years.

question: Deputy Pat the Cope Gallagher asked the Minister for Education and Youth when she expects her Department to conclude its assessment of the accommodation requirements at a school (details supplied) given that students and staff continue to work in prefabricated accommodation dating back to the 1980s which has been described as damp, mould-ridden and unsuitable for a modern educational environment; if she will outline a timeline for the delivery of a permanent accommodation solution.
reply:
I can confirm that my department is in receipt of an application, under the Additional School Accommodation (ASA) scheme, from the school referred to by the Deputy. In 2022 the department approved Modular accommodation for a classroom for students with special educational needs and a further application was submitted for reconfiguration to create additional special educational needs accommodation.
A department-led prioritisation process will continue over the course of 2026 and 2027 to assess and evaluate the progression of individual projects through the design pipeline having regard to the continual need to maximise existing capacity and determine the prioritised needs going forward. This process will involve engagement with key stakeholders and individual schools and will ultimately inform the next tranches of programme rollout to tender. The Department led Energy and Condition Survey of the school estate, which will be finalised later in 2026, will provide an additional evidence base for assessing priorities and will give a good picture of the nature of accommodation at all schools. This will facilitate good strategic overview and decision-making on relative priorities between schools for further investment in the existing school estate. A decision on this application will be communicated to the school authority in due course based on this information.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will review the circumstances of a staffing appeal submitted by a school (details supplied); and if consideration will be given to retaining the teaching post concerned for the remainder of the 2026/2027 academic year.
reply:
The key factor for determining the level of staffing resources provided at individual school level is the staffing schedule for the relevant school year and pupil enrolments on the previous 30 September. The staffing schedule operates in a clear and transparent manner and treats all similar types of schools equally.
The staffing process also contains an appeals mechanism for schools to submit a staffing appeal to an independent Primary Staffing Appeals Board. The school referred to by the Deputy has submitted an appeal which will be considered by the Appeals Board at their meeting this week. The Primary Staffing Appeals Board operates independently of the Department and its decision is final.

question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether there is Government funding, grant assistance or a transport subsidy available to small rural schools that are forced to travel significant distances, including across the border, to access swimming facilities.
reply:
The purpose of my Department's School Transport Scheme is, having regard to available resources, to support the transport to and from school of children who reside remote from their nearest school.
Children are eligible for school transport where they satisfy the distance criterion and are attending their nearest national school or post primary education centre, having regard to ethos and language.
In accordance with the terms of my Department's School Transport Scheme, school transport services operate during the standard school year and facilitate a child's attendance during normal school opening and closing times. Transport to extracurricular activities is outside the remit of the scheme.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Education and Youth the steps she is taking to facilitate school patronage change on foot of the national parents’ survey.
reply:
The Primary School Survey gathered the views of both parents of children currently attending primary school and parents of children yet to enter the school system. It explored preferences regarding school patronage/ethos, language (education through Irish or English) and single-sex or co-educational school provision.
In early June, my department issued primary schools with their school-specific results and explanatory information.
Boards of Management have been asked to share their survey results and explanatory information with their school communities, to review their survey results and to engage with their communities (including parents), and the local community (including parents with children not yet in school), before deciding on their next steps.
The future direction of primary schools arising from the Primary School Survey work should be led by school communities themselves, who should then engage with their patron and my department. It is important that schools are given the time and space to reflect carefully on their results and to engage fully with parents and their wider school communities.
My department has published all school-level reports, survey results, guidance documents and supporting materials on www.gov.ie/PrimarySchoolSurvey. These resources are designed to support Boards of Management in sharing results and engaging openly with parents, staff, patrons and the wider school community. My department will continue to support and engage with schools as the

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth when schools will be notified of and receive payment under the minor works grant scheme and the ICT infrastructure grant scheme for the 2027-2028 school year; and if her Department remains committed to the December/January payment schedule announced in December 2025.
reply:
As part of the NDP Sectoral Plan published in January 2026, and in line with Programme for Government commitments, clarity and certainty has been provided for school system on annual grant payment timeline which is now set at December/January each year.
The next payment of Minor Works Grant for school year 2027/2028 will issue in either December 2026 or January 2027. Since 2020, close to €340 million in Minor Works Grants and Enhanced Minor Works Grants, have been allocated to schools. This includes the payment of Minor Works Grants totalling almost €30 million for the school year 2026/2027 which has issued in December 2025.
Primary and special schools need not apply for Minor Works Grant aid. Under the scheme, funding is made available to all primary and special schools on the following basis:
€5,500 basic grant plus €18.50 per mainstream pupil and €74 per special needs pupil enrolled in the school on the 30th of September of the year prior to the issue of the grant. The €74 rate applies to a special needs pupil attending a special school or attending a special class attached to a mainstream school.
The Digital Strategy for Schools to 2027 and its associated implementation plan is underpinned by funding of €200m over the course of the strategy, committed to under Ireland’s National Development Plan. question: Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the pathways that exist for students at relevant third level courses in Ireland to secure an internship with her Department or related agency in order to gain experience in diplomacy, international relations and Irish foreign policy; the positions are advertised and where, if there is an email address or a point of contact to make applications.
reply:
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has a number of established paid graduate internship programmes which run from 6 to 22 months depending on the role. These internships are in the areas of human rights, conflict resolution, legal affairs, communications and development. Recruitment to these internship opportunities is carried out by means of a competitive selection process which usually attracts strong interest from well qualified applicants.
All graduate internships in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade are advertised on our career page on www.gov.ie.
The Department also facilitates the placement of four University of Limerick students under the University's Cooperative Education Programme each year. These placements run for 6 months and recruitment is carried out by a competitive selection process in conjunction with the university.

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Education and Youth for an update on the additional school accommodation project for a school (details supplied), including details of any recent review and the current status of the project.
reply:
The school referred to by the Deputy was approved to enter the Department’s pipeline of school buildings under the Additional School Accommodation Scheme for a project providing one special educational needs classroom and one central activities space. This project is devolved to the school authority for delivery.
The Stage 2b (post planning) report was submitted to my Department. Following a review, Department officials requested clarifications and these were recently received. This project remains under review from a technical and cost perspective. It is expected that the next tranche of projects to proceed to tender will be published in 2027. Prioritisation will continue over the coming months to identify this next tranche of projects. question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Education and Youth for an update on the recent application for a modular build for a school (details supplied).
reply:
The school to which the deputy refers was approved to enter the Department’s pipeline under the SEN Repurposing scheme for a project providing one SEN classroom.
The school has been sanctioned to open a special class for 2026/2027 by the National Council for Special Education (NCSE). The school received the €30,000 Start Up Grant and was advised additional funding was available if required.
The school submitted an application for additional funding under the SEN Repurposing Small Scale Works Scheme. The application was reviewed by the Department’s Professional & Technical Unit and based on the information provided the application was approved for €70,000. The project has now been devolved to the school authority for delivery.
Officials at my Department will continue to engage with the school to provide practical assistance for the delivery of this project.
There is no modular build application noted for this school.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide the annual performance targets, service-level agreements and outcome reports required from the National Parents Council for each year from 2021 to 2026, including the number of parents and parents' associations supported, training delivered, and the results achieved against each target.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 73, 74, 75, 76 and 77 together.

Under the Education Act, parents’ associations affiliated with the NPC must conduct their affairs in accordance with the following guidelines: Working Effectively as a Parent Association.
The NPC serves as an important channel of communication between parents and my department. It represents parents’ views on education policy, curriculum reform and educational resources, ensuring that parental perspectives are reflected in policy development, implementation and decision-making.
In addition to the provision of training and supports for parents’ associations in schools, the NPC has developed anti-bullying training for parents, as well as training to support parents as their children transition from primary to post-primary school.
Partnership Schools Ireland (PSI) is a joint initiative of the National Parents Council, the Irish Primary Principals' Network and the Department of Education and Youth that promotes collaboration between families, schools and communities.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether her Department has conducted a value-for-money review of funding provided to the National Parents Council since 2021, including an assessment of administrative costs, direct services, measurable outcomes and alternative methods of delivering parent support; and if she will publish the findings.

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of school capital projects completed in 2021 to 2025 inclusive and to date in 2026, where the final design team fees exceeded the original contracted fees; the average percentage increase in such cases; and the total additional expenditure incurred, broken down by reason for these increases, in tabular form.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 70 and 71 together.
Since 2021 my department has invested over €6.8 billion in our schools throughout the country under the National Development Plan. This has facilitated the completion of over 1,500 school building projects, along with over 4,100 small-scale improvement works to meet priority maintenance needs and advance energy efficiency and climate goals.
Design Team appointments are governed by the Department's published Design Team Procedures and associated conditions of engagement. Any increase in Design Team fees are done in accordance with contractual provisions and conditions of engagement and typically arise due to factors such as where the nature of the project evolves to cater for example for additional accommodation requirements for mainstream or special education needs or where additional works arise due to planning conditions, site specific issues, decarbonisation etc.
Given the volume of projects delivered under the school building programme, mainly on a devolved basis and across all the different delivery mechanisms, the department does not maintain a central record of the type of detailed data requested by the Deputy. If the Deputy wishes to provide details of a specific project, my Department will examine further and provide the information available.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the measures her Department is taking, through its foreign policy and Irish aid programme, to respond to the growing influence of anti-rights movements globally, particularly those seeking to undermine gender equality and women's rights; and whether additional policy or funding measures are being considered to support women's rights organisations and movements responding to these threats.
reply:
The Government remains firmly committed to advancing gender equality and protecting human rights internationally. We recognise gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls as a fundamental human right and a strategic imperative.
The global pushback against gender equality poses a significant challenge to strengthening gender perspectives and women’s empowerment globally. It threatens an unacceptable rollback of core values and progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals, while making it increasingly difficult to advance a rights-based approach in external action.
As human rights and gender equality face serious levels of opposition globally, leadership is needed now more than ever in defending and promoting fundamental human rights, including gender equality, women’s and girls’ empowerment, and sexual and reproductive health and rights. Ireland is deeply concerned by growing global challenges in these areas and continues to advocate internationally for them.
Reductions in international development budgets risk undermining progress on gender equality. We believe it is important to protect resources for gender equality, including support for women-led and women's rights organisations at the frontline of humanitarian and development responses. In line with the Government's international development policy, A Better World, we provide direct funding for gender equality programmes to ensure integration of gender and women’s rights across all interventions.

reply:
Under the Education Act 1998, the School Board of Management (BOM), appointed by the school’s patron, is the body charged with the direct governance of a school and the principal manages the school on a day-to-day basis. Each school has the autonomy to design its own timetables and decide which subjects and programmes to offer based on the educational needs and interests of its students as well as considerations such as classroom space, staffing, time limitations etc.
The study of Modern Foreign Languages is optional at Junior and Senior Cycle. However, it should be noted that schools may have their own rules in relation to the study of a foreign language and higher educational institutions may require a foreign language to be studied for matriculation purposes.
The Deputy may wish to note that Languages Connect, Ireland’s Strategy for Foreign Languages in Education 2017 – 2026 aims to increase and diversify the teaching and learning of foreign languages at all levels. A key action of the policy is to promote the importance of foreign language learning and to provide supports to schools and teachers in this regard.
A significant development under the Strategy is that, under the new Primary Curriculum Framework, Modern Foreign Languages (MFL) are being introduced on a phased basis from September 2026, Learning outcomes will focus on Language Awareness in 3rd and 4th class and Language Competence at 5th and 6th class. question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of NEPS posts currently filled and unfilled, respectively.
reply:
The National Educational Psychological Service (NEPS) provides educational psychological support to all schools. Due to a national shortage of suitably qualified educational psychologists not all schools have an assigned educational psychologist. For those schools without an assigned educational psychologist, the school will be supported by NEPS through the Advisory Support Service. All schools continue to have support in the event of a critical incident through the local NEPS office and has access to training and support from NEPS for school staff.
Through the NEPS Advisory Support Service, schools have an opportunity to access responsive support and advice from a NEPS psychologist. The educational psychologist can provide advice and support and where the need is established can sanction an assessment through the Scheme for the Commissioning of Psychological Assessments (SCPA). Schools can contact the service as needed throughout the school year.
There are currently 242 educational psychologists employed in NEPS with 56 maingrade vacancies. The Department is making every effort to recruit additional educational psychologists to address the shortage. Public Jobs recently concluded a recruitment campaign for the recruitment of educational psychologists and educational psychologists from that panel will join NEPS over the coming months.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which she plans to address the ongoing costly issue of school uniforms.
reply:
Ultimately, decisions on school uniforms are a matter for individual schools and Boards of Management. Under the Education Act 1998, all recognised schools are managed by school Boards of Management. Individual school authorities are responsible for the drawing up of a school policy in relation to the wearing of uniforms. Decisions on changes to school uniform polices are a matter for schools at local level. Schools are advised to consult with parents and students when drafting a policy on uniforms.
My department’s Circular 0032/2017 is currently being reviewed. In addition to a focus on reducing costs for parents, the review is looking at the comfort and sustainability of school uniforms. My officials will continue to engage with the education partners, including the National Parents Council, as we progress this important work.
The Education (Charter and Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2019 includes provisions to enhance financial transparency within school communities and support greater awareness of school-related costs. The Bill provides that charter guidelines may require schools to make available information on school finances, including details of income and expenditure, and extend this transparency to funds raised and spent by parents’ associations. The amendments also provide that such information may be made available to teachers and other school staff, in addition to parents and students.

reply:

In respect of pay and allowances, the Government is committed to the delivery of quality public services and continues to approach public service pay in a balanced way that is reasonable and fair to both public servants and to the taxpayer. reply:
The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) is the statutory body responsible for the provision of special education and allocating supports for students with special educational needs.
My department and the NCSE identify the need for special educational provision with consideration to demographical and statistical data and in regard to an areas existing school provision and future capability. In addition, part of the forward planning process as to where new classes, schools or expansion is required looks at how far students are travelling to access an education that meets their needs. This is an important factor which has been incorporated into the decision-making process. Consideration is also given to the information the NCSE hold at local level on the number of children and young people seeking a special school place in a region.
The information held on the department's Geographical Information System (GIS), particularly in relation to student demographics, is a key component when forecasting the need for additional special class and special school places. My department and the NCSE have undertaken analysis of the trends in special class and special school provision over recent years by county and local school planning area. In total there are 314 local school planning areas.

Since September 2025, for the first time, all children and young people enrolled in primary, special and post-primary schools in the Free Education Scheme have been provided with schoolbooks and core classroom resources. This was the final step in the delivery of a key programme for government commitment to provide free schoolbooks and to support parents by reducing back to school costs. Approximately 940,000 children and young people and their parents have benefit from this scheme.

The guidance contains information highlighting that schools should adopt a cost-conscious and environment-conscious approach to the selection and purchasing of items under the scheme and provides schools with advice and support on how the scheme should be implemented at a local level. Schoolbooks are defined in the guidance and can include eBooks where they are used alongside or in place of physical books.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will intervene in the case of a constituent (details supplied) facing an unfair duplicate €440 registration fee from the Teaching Council due to protracted administrative delays; if the council has the power to issue manual fee waivers in such instances.
reply:
The Teaching Council is the body with the statutory authority and responsibility for the regulation of the teaching profession in Ireland including the registration of teachers in the State.
The Teaching Council register teachers under the Teaching Council Act 2001-2015 and in line with the Teaching Council Registration Regulations 2025. Per the legislation, my department has no role in the registration of individual teachers.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Education and Youth the work her Department is doing to ensure that school pupils in single-sex schools have access to a range of subject choices, and that subject choices available to pupils are not influenced by gender-stereotypes.
reply:
My Department is committed to providing an education system that is inclusive, equitable, and empowering for all. Every learner deserves the opportunity to thrive. Our focus is on high standards, inclusive practices, and strong supports to ensure no one is left behind.
My Department’s work in this area includes the STEM Education Policy Statement 2017–2026, which aims to improve STEM experiences and outcomes for all learners, from early learning and care through to post-primary level. It acknowledges that there is a need to increase the uptake of STEM subjects and to enhance STEM learning for learners of all backgrounds, abilities and gender, with a particular focus on uptake by females
In addition, I announced the publication of subject and career information leaflets in September this year supports learners at the key transition to post-primary schools with information on subject choices, including STEM.
The range of subjects offered depends on each school’s resources, staffing, and student needs. Each school retains autonomy to design timetables and determine which programmes and subjects to provide. Schools aim to balance available resources with student demand. Any issues arising on the matter of subject provision and subject choice should be addressed to the principal of the school in question in the first instance.

question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will provide an update on the application for additional accommodation by a primary school (details supplied) in Cork.
reply:
I can confirm that the department has received an application for capital funding under the Additional School Accommodation (ASA) scheme from the school referred to in September 2026. The application relates to a request for accommodation for a special education classroom and is currently under assessment.
My department is prioritising applications which relate to essential mainstream and special education accommodation. In assessing ASA applications, my department consider whether some or all of the requirements presented can be met within the school’s existing accommodation or accommodation available at other schools in the area. The team also review demographic and enrolment projections to consider the impact on accommodation requirements – for example, accommodation becoming available in the medium term due to decreasing enrolments.
I can confirm that an official acknowledged receipt of the school's application in September and a decision will issue to the school directly upon completion of the assessment process.

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the reason incremental credit has been refused to a person (details supplied); and if officials from her Department can meet with the applicant to resolve the issue.
reply:

The Appeals Committee subsequently considered the case in October 2019 and upheld the Department's original decision. The Committee found that the service being claimed constituted self-employed service.
