question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will urgently review the exclusion of HGV driving schools from the diesel rebate scheme in view of the substantial fuel costs incurred by these businesses, the essential service they provide in training HGV and bus drivers, and the potential impact on driver supply to the transport industry.
reply:
The Diesel Rebate Scheme (DRS) is a State aid that operates under Article 7(2) of Council Directive 2003/96/EC (Energy Tax Directive/ETD).
Article 7(2) explicitly allows EU Member States to apply a differentiated rate of excise duty to gas oil (auto diesel) used for commercial purposes, provided that the EU minimum levels of taxation are respected.
The ETD limits the scope of "commercial gas oil" to auto diesel used by specific segments of road transport. In line with this, the scope of Ireland’s DRS is defined by reference to road transport licensing criteria and includes licensed road haulage (goods transport) and passenger transport operators (such as bus and coach services).

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether the Department has assessed the share of new build homes purchased in each of the years 2023 to 2025 by first-time buyers who had been resident in the State for fewer than five years; whether any such analysis has informed the Department's position on the extension and increase of the help to buy scheme.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 389 and 406 together.
The Help to Buy (HTB) incentive, is a tax-based scheme to assist first-time purchasers with the deposit they need to buy or build a new house or apartment. It also aims to encourage additional supply of new houses by supporting demand.
Based on the latest available data (30 September 2026), the scheme has supported over 70,000 individuals or couples to buy or build their own home.
The level of support available to first time buyers under the HTB scheme, is whichever is the lesser of:
€35,000 (from 07 October 2026); or
10 per cent of the purchase price of the new property; or
the amount of Income Tax and DIRT paid in the four years before application for the relief.
For a property to qualify for the HTB scheme, it must be new or converted for use as a dwelling, having not previously been used as a dwelling. Additionally, the purchase value/approved valuation of the property must not exceed €500,000.
HTB provides a refund of Income Tax and Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) paid in Ireland over the previous four years, subject to limits outlined in the legislation. Consideration of the matters raised in the Deputy's questions did not form part of the Budget 2027 process, nor has it formed part of TSG or other Department of Finance analyses, in relation to HTB.

reply:

The Government is taking a comprehensive and proactive approach to improving the affordability and availability of flood insurance in the Irish insurance market with the implementation of refoms under the Action Plan for Insurance Reform 2025-2029.
The decision on whether to offer home insurance, level of premiums charged, and the policy terms applied are matters for individual insurers based on an actuarial assessment of the risks they are willing to accept. The Solvency II Directive restricts Member States in terms of intervening in insurers’ pricing or underwriting decisions. Insurers rely on their own claims’ histories, risk assessments, and cost projections when deciding whether to provide cover. Factors such as inflation in building materials and labour are also influencing premium levels across the sector.
In terms of flood insurance, the Central Bank of Ireland has undertaken extensive research into the nature and scale of the flood insurance protection gap in Ireland. Neither my Department nor the Central Bank of Ireland hold data on the refusal of home insurance or flood insurance.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether an insurer is required to tell a customer the basis on which their property has been classified as at risk of flooding; whether any process exists for a homeowner with no recorded flood history to have that classification reviewed; and, if not, whether he will consider requiring one.
reply:
The Government remains committed to protecting Ireland’s present and future generations by investing in climate adaptation measures to manage the impacts of extreme weather. Accordingly, €1.3 billion has been committed to the delivery of flood relief schemes over the lifetime of the National Development Plan (NDP) to 2030. This will protect approximately 23,000 properties across various communities from river and coastal flood risk.
In terms of flood insurance, the Central Bank of Ireland has undertaken extensive research into the nature and scale of the flood insurance protection gap in Ireland. They found that 1 in 20 buildings (approximately 5%) have limited access to flood insurance; and that 54% of this gap is concentrated in Dublin, Cork, Louth, Clare, and Kildare.
In terms of assessing flood risk, insurers use a variety of different flood data models (both internally developed models and flood models procured from third party vendors). Insurers will generally utilise (i) flood risk maps licenced from a third-party consultancy; (ii) bespoke flood maps based on individual historical claims experience/risk surveys undertaken of locations, and (iii) other information such as the flood defence benefit area data provided to Insurance Ireland by the OPW under the terms of the MOU, if applicable.
Insurance undertakings are bound by the provisions of the Central Bank’s Consumer Protection Code (the Code) in their dealings with consumers for the provision of financial services.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether he has considered increasing the VAT registration threshold for service providers; whether his Department has assessed the extent to which the threshold acts as a disincentive for small businesses and agricultural contractors seeking to expand their turnover; and whether any review of the threshold is planned.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 385, 386 and 401 together.
As the Deputy will be aware, no change was made to the VAT registration thresholds in Budget 2027.
VAT registration thresholds are subject to the requirements of EU VAT law, with which Irish VAT law is obliged to comply. In general, the EU VAT Directive requires that all businesses supplying taxable goods and services are registered for VAT, charge VAT on those supplies to their customers, and file returns and remit the VAT to the relevant national tax authority.
Within the framework of the Directive, Ireland has operated VAT registration thresholds for goods and for services for many years. Following increases applied in Finance Act 2024, the levels are now €85,000 for supplies of goods and €42,500 for supplies of services. Generally, a business whose turnover is below the relevant threshold is not obliged to register for VAT and can supply its customers exempt from VAT; when its turnover reaches the threshold, the business is obliged to register for and operate VAT in accordance with normal rules. Businesses whose turnover is below the threshold are entitled to elect to register should they so wish. Separate to the turnover rules, as required under EU law, there are also other circumstances where businesses are required to register for VAT, for example, when making intra-community acquisitions or when accounting for VAT under the reverse charge mechanism because of receiving taxable services from a supplier outside

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether his Department has assessed Poland's decision to apply an 8% VAT rate to petrol and diesel from 3 October 2026; whether such a measure is compatible with the EU VAT Directive; whether he has sought greater flexibility on fuel VAT at EU level; and the estimated cost to the Exchequer of each one percentage point reduction in VAT on petrol and diesel.
reply:
The EU VAT Directive which Irish VAT law is obliged to comply, generally holds that all goods and service are liable for VAT at the standard rate which Member States must set at a minimum of 15%. Ireland currently charges a standard rate of 23%.
If a good or service is included in a list of goods and services under Annex III of the Directive, a reduced rate of VAT or exemption may be applied. Member States are permitted to apply up to two reduced rates at a minimum of 5%. Ireland currently has two reduced rates of VAT of 13.5% and 9%. Member States may also avail of a derogation under the terms of the Directive that allows for a reduced rate of VAT be applied to specific goods and services that have historically been charged below the standard rate and not included under Annex III. Reduced rates applied because of a derogation cannot be moved lower than 12%.
As auto fuels are not included under Annex III there is no legal basis to apply a VAT rate below 15%. As such the standard rate of VAT, currently 23%, applies to auto fuels. This rate can be reduced as low as 15% but would require all goods and services at 23% to be moved to 15%. The estimated cost of a 1% reduction in the standard rate of VAT is €707m. The full year cost of the standard rate of VAT being reduced from 23% to 15% is estimated to be €5.7 billion.
It should be noted that any VAT reduction may not be passed to consumers.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he is aware of the excessive and disproportionate customs charges and administrative fees being imposed on everyday purchases and deliveries, which are adding to the cost-of-living burden on ordinary families; and whether any review or engagement with relevant bodies is planned to address this situation.
reply:
Revenue, as Ireland’s Tax and Customs administration, is responsible for managing the importation of goods in accordance with EU Customs. It is a legal requirement across the EU that electronic customs import declarations are required for all parcels / packages coming from non-EU countries including those coming through the postal system regardless of the value of the goods being sent. VAT and Customs Duty are also payable unless there are reliefs available.
In certain circumstances, Gift Relief may apply meaning that Customs Duty and VAT on importation is not payable. However, this only applies where the value of the gift is €45 or less. Where the gift is valued in excess of €45, then VAT and Customs Duty apply on the full value of the gift. In the instance referenced by the Deputy, the value of the gift was €48 which is greater than the gift threshold and as a result, tax and duties apply.
The fees charged by An Post for completing the Customs declaration and collecting the tax and duty owed, is a contractual arrangement between An Post and its customers. Revenue has no role in relation to the fees charged.
Customs rules are standard across the EU and Ireland cannot unilaterally change these rules and this includes the thresholds for Gift Relief.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to provide an update on the corporate taxation matters currently under discussion at European Union level, including those being considered by the Economic and Financial Affairs Council, ECOFIN, during Ireland's Presidency of the Council of the European Union; to identify the relevant legislative and non-legislative proposals, including proposals concerning corporate tax transparency, taxation of multinational enterprises and implementation of the EU Minimum Tax Directive; to outline the position of the Irish Government on each of these matters.
reply:
At European Union (EU) level, discussions on corporate taxation are currently focused on a number of legislative and non-legislative initiatives, primarily aimed at simplifying the EU corporate tax framework and improving tax transparency standards.
As part of Ireland's Presidency of the Council of the EU, my officials are focused on progressing the European Commission's Tax Simplification Package, published on 24 June 2026, through Council. This package comprises two principal legislative proposals: a Tax Omnibus and a recast of the Directive on Administrative Cooperation (DAC).
The Tax Omnibus proposal seeks to amend a number of existing corporate tax directives, including the Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive (ATAD), the Parent-Subsidiary Directive (PSD), the Interest and Royalties Directive (IRD), the Tax Merger Directive (TMD), the Tax Dispute Resolution Mechanism Directive (DRM) and the FASTER Directive, with the stated objective of simplifying rules, reducing administrative and compliance burdens and strengthening competitiveness of companies operating in the EU.
The DAC Recast proposal seeks to consolidate the existing DAC framework into a single instrument, streamline administrative cooperation between tax authorities and reduce reporting obligations where these are no longer considered necessary or proportionate.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether he will review the current VAT registration threshold of €42,500 for persons only supplying services and consider increasing it to €50,000 (details supplied).
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 385, 386 and 401 together.
As the Deputy will be aware, no change was made to the VAT registration thresholds in Budget 2027.
VAT registration thresholds are subject to the requirements of EU VAT law, with which Irish VAT law is obliged to comply. In general, the EU VAT Directive requires that all businesses supplying taxable goods and services are registered for VAT, charge VAT on those supplies to their customers, and file returns and remit the VAT to the relevant national tax authority.
Within the framework of the Directive, Ireland has operated VAT registration thresholds for goods and for services for many years. Following increases applied in Finance Act 2024, the levels are now €85,000 for supplies of goods and €42,500 for supplies of services. Generally, a business whose turnover is below the relevant threshold is not obliged to register for VAT and can supply its customers exempt from VAT; when its turnover reaches the threshold, the business is obliged to register for and operate VAT in accordance with normal rules. Businesses whose turnover is below the threshold are entitled to elect to register should they so wish. As the Deputy will be aware, each of these long-term savings’ funds were established to help offset future spending pressures, to provide for counter-cyclical expenditure in economic downturns, and to address climate and nature goals.
The Future Ireland Fund is the longer-term fund, designed to support in a consistent and sustainable manner, State expenditure in 2041 or any year thereafter. Decisions in relation to that expenditure will be a matter for the Government of the day and the Act does not limit the areas to which drawn down funding may be allocated.

Achievement of conservation objectives or the improvement of habitats.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to provide the methodology, calculations, datasets and assumptions used in determining the reduction of the farmer VAT flat-rate addition to 4.5%.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 380 to 382, inclusive, together.
The VAT treatment of goods and services is subject to the requirements of EU VAT law with which Irish VAT law is obliged to comply. In accordance with the EU VAT Directive, farmers can elect to register for VAT or can remain unregistered.
Under VAT law, unregistered farmers can avail of the Flat-rate Farmers Scheme, an administrative simplification arrangement unique to the farming sector, which allows farmers to remain unregistered for VAT – thereby remaining outside the VAT system and avoiding the burden of registration and filing – and yet be compensated on an overall basis for the VAT incurred by such farmers in the course of their business. As is normal for VAT-unregistered businesses, unregistered farmers are not entitled to reclaim VAT incurred on the various individual inputs used in their farming business. The flat-rate addition is not tax; it is an amount that unregistered farmers availing of the flat-rate scheme are permitted to charge on top of their selling price and to retain.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the estimated revenue foregone if the VAT rate for electricity was set at 0%, in each of the years 2020 to date; the estimated revenue foregone if the VAT rate for gas was set at 0%, in each of the years 2020 to date; the estimated revenue foregone if the VAT rate for electricity was set at 0% for domestic customers only, in each of the years 2020 to date; and the estimated revenue foregone if the VAT rate for gas was set at 0% for domestic customers only, in each of the years 2020 to date, in tabular form.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 367 to 372, inclusive, together.
I am advised by Revenue that traders are not required to provide a breakdown of their supplies by product type or customer category on either their VAT returns, their electricity tax returns, or their natural gas carbon tax returns. It is therefore not possible from Revenue's tax returns to identify the VAT generated on supplies of gas or electricity by fuel type, by customer type, or on a monthly basis as requested.
The Deputy should note that VAT-registered businesses, which include the majority of large energy users and non-domestic consumers, are entitled to reclaim VAT incurred on their energy costs as an input credit. As such, the net Exchequer yield from VAT on energy relates primarily to non-VAT-registered consumers.
I am further advised by Revenue that the VAT Directive provides that all goods and services are liable to VAT at the standard rate unless they are exempt from VAT or fall within Annex III of the Directive, in which case lower VAT rates may apply subject to certain rules. On this basis, Ireland applies the second reduced rate, 9%, to the supply of gas for domestic or industrial heating or lighting and electricity since 1 May 2022 and this is currently due to run until 31 December 2030. Prior to 1 May 2022, the second reduced rate of 13.5% applied to these supplies. It is not possible, under the Directive, to apply the zero rate of VAT to the supply of gas or electricity.
I am advised by Reve

question: Deputy Grace Boland asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether, in the context of the carbon tax measures announced in Budget 2027, consideration was given to extending to liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), the treatment applied to natural gas and kerosene; and whether representations have been received regarding the tax treatment of LPG users.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 357 and 366 together.
As per the most recent CSO Energy Use Survey (2024), around three in every five households use home natural gas or heating oil (kerosene) as their main home heating fuel. Around 1 per cent of households identified as using Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) as their main heating fuel according to this survey.
The Natural Gas Carbon Tax and the carbon component of Mineral Oil Tax on kerosene used other than as a propellant has been reduced to €48.50 per tonne of CO2 emitted.
These reductions were targeted to provide a cost reduction on the two predominate home heating fuels in the country, taking into account the extraordinary, market driven, price increases to kerosene since March and an anticipated increase in natural gas price inflation arising from recent increases in unit rates by major suppliers. Reductions were not extended across all fuels.
LPG used other than as a propellant does not attract the non-carbon component of Mineral Oil Tax. Only the carbon component of Mineral Oil Tax (i.e. carbon tax) applies.
The carbon tax on LPG used other than as a propellant is currently paused at €63.50 per tonne of CO2 emitted. This is the same rate that has applied since 1 May 2025.
Finally, LPG used other than as a propellant also attracts a 9 per cent VAT rate.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will review the eligibility criteria for the help-to-buy incentive scheme to accommodate returning Irish citizens who do not meet the full four-year tax look-back window; and if he will consider expanding the window to account for a broader historical Irish tax record or, alternatively, factoring in verified future Irish income tax commitments.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 359 and 365 together.
The Help to Buy (HTB) incentive, is a tax-based scheme to assist first-time purchasers with the deposit they need to buy or build a new house or apartment. It also aims to encourage additional supply of new houses by supporting demand.
HTB provides a refund of Income Tax and Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) paid in Ireland over the previous four years, subject to limits outlined in the legislation.
The level of support available to first time buyers under the HTB scheme, is whichever is the lesser of:
• €35,000 (from 07 October 2026); or
• 10 per cent of the purchase price of the new property; or
• the amount of Income Tax and DIRT paid in the four years before application for the relief.
For a property to qualify for the HTB scheme, it must be new or converted for use as a dwelling, having not previously been used as a dwelling. Additionally, the purchase value/approved valuation of the property must not exceed €500,000.
Based on the latest available data (30 September 2026), the scheme has supported over 70,000 individuals or couples to buy or build their own home.
In relation to the Deputies' proposals, the design of the scheme aligns with Revenue’s standard operational four-year look-back period. reply:

There was a total of 112 certificates issued in 2025 for all Section 481 projects (including the 22 Scéal projects). To date in 2026, 98 Section 481 certificates (including the 23 Scéal projects) have been issued.

While the uplift was not a Regional Aid measure, it operated by reference to the regional aid map in force at the time it was introduced. question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if there is a standard, predictable approach to calculating VRT for vehicles taken in from the North of Ireland; the criteria that apply; and if this approach is consistent between makes, models and engine types and sizes.
reply:
Vehicles used in the State are generally required to be registered here, and Vehicle Registration Tax (VRT) is assessed and paid at the time of registration. The calculation of VRT is governed by Section 132 of the Finance Act 1992, as amended.
Under the law, the method for calculating VRT on a vehicle is based on the Category of vehicle involved. Within a Category, the calculation method is consistent across all makes, models, engine types and sizes. Furthermore, the VRT calculation method does not differ according to whether a vehicle is new or used at the time of registration, nor does it depend on where the vehicle has come from. Accordingly, the fact that a vehicle has come into the State from Northern Ireland does not impact on how its VRT is calculated.
VRT on Category A vehicles (passenger cars and certain light commercial vehicles) is calculated based on the vehicle’s value and its emissions level, with the level of the tax increasing in line with both factors. There are two components of the VRT charge for Category A vehicles, relating to their carbon dioxide (CO2) and nitrogen oxide (NOX) emissions.
The CO2 component of the VRT charge is calculated by multiplying the value of the vehicle (its Open Market Selling Price - OMSP) by a percentage from a 20-band table, with the vehicle’s CO2 emissions level determining which band applies. reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the Future Ireland Fund (FIF) and the Infrastructure, Climate and Nature Fund (ICNF), were established in 2024 following the commencement of the Future Ireland Fund and Infrastructure, Climate and Nature Fund Act 2024 (‘the Act’).
Transfers to each of the funds are governed by the Act. Subject to an annual fiscal and economic assessment process, €2bn will transfer to the ICNF each year from 2025 – 2030, while 0.8% of GDP shall transfer to the FIF in each year from 2024 – 2035. In addition, each fund received an initial transfer from the National Reserve Fund (NRF) in 2024.
Management and investment of the FIF and ICNF rests with the National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA), who invest each fund in accordance with their respective long-term investment strategies.
The financial accounts of the FIF and ICNF are published in the NTMA’s annual report each year, which are available on the NTMA’s website. A detailed schedule of investments held by the funds as at 31 December 2025, is published in the NTMA’s 2025 Annual Report.
I am advised by the NTMA that the value of the FIF as at 31 December 2025 was €12.7bn, and that the value of the ICNF on the same date was €4.1bn.
Transfers of €4.5bn to the FIF and €2bn to the ICNF occurred in 2026.

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Transport the extent to which he and or his officials have engaged with the Department of Infrastructure in Northern Ireland in respect of a reciprocal arrangement for smaller passenger vans (details supplied) and so on, to operate in each other's jurisdictions; if he has consulted with Tourism Ireland in respect of same; and if he has engaged with the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment regarding same.
reply:
As the Deputy is aware, the regulation of the small public service vehicle (SPSV) industry is a matter for the independent transport regulator, the National Transport Authority (NTA), under the provisions of the Consolidated Taxi Regulation Acts 2013 and 2016. Under section 6(2) of this Act, An Garda Síochána is responsible for the granting of SPSV driver licences. I have no role in the day-to-day operations of the SPSV sector.
Under the provisions of the Taxi Regulation Act 2013, operators are required to hold an SPSV licence and an SPSV driver licence to carry persons for hire or reward in the State. The 2013 Act and its requirements only apply to services provided in the State - it does not provide for services across a border. The legislative position in Northern Ireland is similar. Thus, under current legislation, a taxi operator wishing to operate cross-border services, would have to apply for and obtain SPSV licences on each side of the border. Unlike other areas of transport - such as bus and road haulage operations - taxi services are not subject to EU harmonisation, so arrangements for regulating taxi services remain a matter for the relevant authorities in each EU Member State, in respect of services that operate in their jurisdiction.

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Transport for an update on the progress made towards giving effect to the changes agreed between CIÉ and the Trade Union Group representing staff with regards to CIÉ pension schemes; and a timeline for final implementation.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. As a commercial semi-state body, Córas Iompair Éireann (CIÉ) are responsible for the provision of pension schemes for their employees.
Following on from the constructive and collaborative approach of the Trade Union Group and CIÉ management in reaching agreement on a pathway forward as of May 2025, my Department is progressing the agreement of bringing CIÉ pensions onto a more stable footing for the benefit of active, and retired scheme members, including review of the relevant draft Statutory Instruments, and the matter of increases to pension payments.
Under the Transport Act, 1950, a Statutory Consultation process is required regarding amendments to CIÉ Pension Schemes, which took place over the early summer, and representations from interested parties required review.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Transport for an update on the proposed development of a Road Safety Commissioner as part of reforms to strengthen road safety governance and oversight; and to outline the progress made in considering the role, functions and statutory basis of such a Commissioner. .
reply:
Parliamentary Question No. 253 of 1 October sets out the position on this matter, which remains unchanged: www.oireachtas.ie/en/debates/question/2026-10-01/253/#pq_253
The current framework for road safety governance is set out in the Government’s Road Safety Strategy 2021–2030 and its Phase 2 Action Plan 2025–2027. The Strategy follows the internationally recognised Safe System approach, under which responsibility is shared across the relevant road safety bodies working in partnership.
My Department coordinates implementation of the Strategy. Oversight is provided by the Road Safety Leadership Group, which I chair and which includes the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration and senior representatives of the principal road safety partners. The Group reviews delivery and progress on a quarterly basis.
Within that framework, no decision has been taken to establish a Road Safety Commissioner and detailed proposals on the role, functions or statutory basis of such an office have not been developed. I am not aware of any EU country that follows the model of a Road Safety Commissioner and, as I have noted above, to do so would go against the partnership model which is the central tenant of the Safe System approach that is best practice in the EU.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Transport for an update on the ongoing expansion of average-speed and static safety cameras on the national road network; the number of additional cameras planned; their expected deployment timeframe; and the consideration being given to further expansion on high-risk routes.
reply:
Enforcement of road traffic offences is primarily the responsibility of An Garda Síochána and to assist with this work, my Department published the National Safety Camera Strategy in April of this year. The Strategy aligns with Programme for Government commitments to expand the use of safety cameras across the road network and also delivers on part one of Action 6 of the Government’s Road Safety Strategy Phase 2 Action Plan 2025 - 2027.
The Strategy provides the framework for the increased deployment of cameras across the network, in both urban and rural locations, to assist with the enforcement of a wide range of road traffic offences. It focuses on speeding, red light running, and bus lane infringements, with flexibility for the enforcement of other types of offence in future.
A Camera Enforcement Oversight Group has been established to deliver the Strategy, chaired by the CEO of the National Transport Authority (NTA) and comprising senior leaders from An Garda Síochána, NTA, Transport Infrastructure Ireland, the Road Safety Authority, the Courts Service and the Local Authority sector. The Oversight Group has met twice, on 16 June and 5 August, and I expect a progress update to be presented at the next Road Safety Leadership Group meeting in November.

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Transport if his Department will consider correspondence in relation to the Transport RTSS scheme (details supplied).
reply:
The Road Transporters Support Scheme (RTSS) supports the road transport sector in recognition of its essential role in Ireland’s supply chains and in providing essential connectivity across both urban and rural communities.
The RTSS provides financial support to licenced hauliers, the own account sector, and commercial coach operators to help meet the challenges posed by increased fuel costs arising from the war in the Middle East. The Scheme is designed to support operators transporting goods and passengers across the country. Certain categories of vehicle, including those that do not primarily transport goods or passengers, are excluded from support under the RTSS.
Where an application has been refused, or support not provided for one or more vehicles on an application, applicants may submit an appeal through the dedicated online portal. Only applicants that have a valid RTSS Application ID are permitted to submit an appeal. Submitting an appeal does not guarantee that it will be successful, and each appeal will be assessed on its own merits and in accordance with the appeals eligibility criteria. The appeals portal is accessible via the RTSS webpage: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-transport/campaigns/road-transporters-support-scheme/

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding the National EV Charging Infrastructure Strategy; the Regional and Local EV Charging Network Plan and the measures to ensure affordability for charging EVs; and the engagements between his Department and the ESB to ensure rates for charging EVs remain affordable.
reply:
The Government is fully committed to supporting a significant expansion of the EV charging network by 2030.
In order to achieve Ireland’s EU targets under the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR) and depending on level of power supplied at charging points, it is expected that there will be 3,200 – 6,210 public chargers required nationally by 2030. . Based on currently reported charge-point data and the current fleet of BEV and PHEVs on the road, Ireland has achieved 92% of the AFIR fleet based target.
The National EV Charging Infrastructure Strategy 2026-2028 is due to be published in the coming weeks and outlines the requirements for publicly accessible charging and installing EV Infrastructure that is capable of meeting future demand and user needs.
The Regional and Local EV Charging Network Plan, which focuses on neighbourhood and destination charging locations, will be led by Local Authorities in partnership with both public and private sectors.
Local authorities are being supported by ZEVI to develop regional and local EV charging network strategies and implementation plans. This work will identify charging requirements at local level, including neighbourhood charging solutions for residents without access to private off-street parking.

reply:

The Road Traffic (Licensing of Drivers) (Amendment) (No. 2) Regulations 2025 (SI 527/2025), which come into effect on 1 November 2026, introduce measures to address this issue. Under the new arrangements, learner permit holders who have held a permit for four years or more must provide evidence of having undertaken a practical driving test before they can renew their permit. Where this requirement is not met, they must start the learner permit application process again in order to continue learning to drive.

For category B (car) applicants, this involves completing a driver theory test, obtaining a learner permit, undertaking 12 Essential Driver Training lessons and passing a practical driving test.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding progress in legislation to enable the National Transport Authority to apply for planning permission for delivery of the BusConnects programme of sustainable transport corridors in Cork; his Department’s view on Cork City Council bringing forward the necessary planning permissions directly if this legislation is further delayed.
reply:
The General Scheme of the Dublin Transport Authority (Amendment) Bill was originally given approval by Government on 17 September 2025. The Bill passed second stage in the Dail on 26 May 2026 and Committee Stage on 24 June 2026. I anticipate a date to be set for Report Stage in the Dail shortly.
The purpose of the Bill is to provide a clear legislative framework to extend the National Transport Authority’s (NTA) remit under section 44 of the Dublin Transport Authority Act 2008 (Act of 2008), to enable the NTA to undertake the construction of public transport infrastructure projects, such as BusConnects, in the State, as it currently does in the Greater Dublin Area (GDA).
For large scale projects it is important to have a National Authority who can provide public transport infrastructure outside of the Greater Dublin Area. The NTA has the capacity and experience in progressing megaprojects, having successfully secured planning consents for all 12 of its Core Bus Corridor schemes in Dublin as of 2025.
The provisions of the Bill will ensure Government’s ambition in megaproject delivery is complemented by a robust and appropriate legislative framework and will allow the NTA to submit planning applications to An Coimisiún Pleanála in respect of the infrastructure elements of BusConnects Cork.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Transport further to Parliamentary Question No. 93 of 13 October 2026, the details of the re-examination of policy; the process envisaged as part of engagement with the National Transport Authority and Dublin City Council in coming weeks to determine the most appropriate next steps; the intended steps to be proposed by his Department; if those steps include legislation; the powers An Garda Síochána possesses to act against motorised rickshaws carrying passengers for reward; and the adequacy of same.
reply:
Further to Parliamentary Question No. 93 of 13 October 2026, I have written to both the National Transport Authority (NTA) and Dublin City Council outlining that I intend to hold a meeting with them in the coming weeks to discuss how regulation for rickshaws is best achieved.
The drivers of all vehicles used on public roads, including rickshaws, are required to comply with road traffic legislation and to behave in a safe manner, paying due care to other road users. The enforcement of such road traffic legislation is a matter for An Garda Síochána. If a rickshaw is fitted with a small engine or electric motor of any kind, it is essentially considered to be a mechanically propelled vehicle (MPV). Under road traffic law, if an MPV is used in a public place it is subject to all of the regulatory controls that apply to other vehicles, i.e., it must be roadworthy, registered, taxed and comply with road traffic regulations.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Transport the position Ireland intends to adopt on the joint proposal from the Governments of Germany and France to reduce the EU's mandatory CO emissions cut for new cars by 2035 from 100% to 80%, compared with 2021 levels at the EU Council meeting on 15 of October 2026.
reply:
The European Commission's December 2025 Automotive Package proposal moved away from the existing 100% tailpipe emissions reduction requirement for new cars from 2035 by proposing a 90% CO2 reduction target, with the remaining 10% addressed through a system of credits linked to low-carbon fuels and materials.
As of 16 October 2026, it is understood that France and Germany have reached political agreement on a common position on the Automotive Package. One element of their position is a 90% CO2 reduction target from 2035 without an offset requirement to be compensated by manufacturers through the use of low carbon steel or fuel credits.
The position put forward by France and Germany will need to be considered carefully by Member States through the normal Council legislative process. No agreement has yet been reached at Council level on this matter.
In its role as Presidency of the Council of the European Union, Ireland will continue to act as an honest broker, facilitating discussions among Member States and seeking progress on the file while ensuring that all views are fully reflected in the negotiations.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Transport to outline his position on a joint proposal from the Governments of Germany and France to reduce the EU's mandatory CO emissions cut for new cars by 2035 from 100% to 80%, compared with 2021 levels.
reply:
The European Commission's December 2025 Automotive Package proposal moved away from the existing 100% tailpipe emissions reduction requirement for new cars from 2035 by proposing a 90% CO2 reduction target, with the remaining 10% addressed through a system of credits linked to low-carbon fuels and materials.
As of 16 October 2026, it is understood that France and Germany have reached political agreement on a common position on the Automotive Package. One element of their position is a 90% CO2 reduction target from 2035 without an offset requirement to be compensated by manufacturers through the use of low carbon steel or fuel credits.
The position put forward by France and Germany will need to be considered carefully by Member States through the normal Council legislative process. No agreement has yet been reached at Council level on this matter.
In its role as Presidency of the Council of the European Union, Ireland will continue to act as an honest broker, facilitating discussions among Member States and seeking progress on the file while ensuring that all views are fully reflected in the negotiations.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Transport if he will provide an update on the current status of the Statutory Instrument required to implement the agreed reforms to the CIÉ pension scheme; when he expects the Statutory Instrument to be signed and commenced; the reason for the delay in completing the process; and when approximately 2,000 affected CIÉ pensioners can expect to receive the pension increases approved under the 2025 agreement.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 266 to 268, inclusive, together.
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. As a commercial semi-state body, Córas Iompair Éireann (CIÉ) are responsible for the provision of pension schemes for their employees.
Following on from the constructive and collaborative approach of the Trade Union Group and CIÉ management in reaching agreement on a pathway forward as of May 2025, my Department is progressing the agreement of bringing CIÉ pensions onto a more stable footing for the benefit of active, and retired scheme members, including finalisation of the relevant draft Statutory Instruments, and the matter of increases to pension payments.
Under the Transport Act, 1950, a Statutory Consultation process is required regarding amendments to CIÉ Pension Schemes, which took place over the early summer, and representations from interested parties required review.
This process has now been completed and the S.I. text has been approved. My Department is progressing with the printing of the S.I.s and I expect to sign the orders imminently.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Transport the action being undertaken by his Department for the provision of a specific electric vehicle (EV) charging point app which would include all EV charging providers, in order to provide a more streamlined and user-friendly service, in view that at present each provider has their own individual downloadable app.
reply:
The Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR), which has applied directly across the European Union since 13 April 2024, aims to improve the user experience for electric vehicle drivers by ensuring that publicly accessible charge points can be used without the need for a subscription or a specific mobile application.
Under AFIR, operators of publicly accessible charging infrastructure are required to provide ad hoc charging and payment options, allowing EV drivers to charge their vehicles without entering into a contract with a particular charge point operator. This is intended to reduce reliance on multiple operator-specific applications and make public charging more convenient and accessible for consumers.
The Regulation also includes requirements for operators of publicly accessible charging infrastructure (who require payment for the recharging service) to set up an Application Programme Interface (API) that provides free and unrestricted access to both static and dynamic charging data, in order for the data to be made accessible on an open and non-discriminatory basis to all data users through national access points (in accordance with the relevant provisions related to such data). This will support the development of consumer applications that can provide information across multiple charging networks. A number of third-party apps are currently available and providing this data to the public that are not limited to any one charging operator.

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Transport if he supports the transfer of responsibility for alcohol and psychoactive substance testing of aviation personnel from State authorities to individual airlines or other private entities; if the constitutional, employment-law, licensing, criminal-law, privacy, data-protection and fair-procedure implications of such a transfer have been fully examined; and whether consideration has been given to retaining testing as an independent State function while providing the IAA and/or An Garda Síochána with the resources necessary to operate an effective testing regime.
reply:
On 29 September the Irish Aviation Authority (IAA) commenced a public consultation on the future regulatory approach to drug and alcohol testing in the Irish aviation sector. The consultation seeks the views of aviation stakeholders, employees, industry representative bodies, public authorities and members of the public on the most appropriate means of introducing a comprehensive framework to manage the safety risks associated with impairment arising from alcohol and other psychoactive substances. The deadline for submissions is 31 October 2026.
While the IAA is seeking views on a proposed Employer-Led Testing Framework with IAA Oversight, no decision has been taken yet on state policy in this area. The purpose of the consultation is to gather evidence, perspectives and views of all relevant stakeholders to inform future policy development.
My department will be engaging with the IAA following completion of the consultation process.

reply:

It is also the case that serving public servants who are successful in their application to join the Defence Forces, may be in a position to transfer existing pensionable entitlements to the Defence Forces subject to meeting the agreed terms and conditions.

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he has considered a retrospective Sustainable Energy Agency of Ireland, SEAI, solar PV grant for homeowners who installed solar panels in or before June 2026, shortly before the recent changes to grant eligibility.
reply:
My Department funds a number of grant schemes, administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI), to support homeowners to improve the energy efficiency of their existing properties.
These schemes have terms and conditions in place to ensure the transparent administration of public funds. These terms and conditions must be adhered to consistently by the SEAI to ensure fairness as well as value for money for the Exchequer.
Grant assistance for residential retrofitting measures provided by Government through these schemes is intended to incentivise future behaviour. Homeowners who have not applied and been approved for grant support through the SEAI prior to commencing works on their properties are not entitled to retrospective awarding of SEAI grants. While my Department, in partnership with the SEAI, continues to ensure that grant schemes terms and conditions, eligibility criteria, and rates are kept under review, taking account of demand, research, innovation, evolving technology and other relevant factors, there are no plans to change the eligibility criteria in terms of retrospectively providing grant support as set out by the Deputy.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the timeline for transposing the EU directive on energy sharing, EU Directive 2024/17111, published in 2024, into Irish law, given that a Commission for Regulation of Utilities, CRU, consultation on the topic was completed in April 2026, and that the Community Energy Federation of Ireland, CEFI, have outlined how energy sharing can support households and communities investing in and benefiting from renewables to lower energy bills (details supplied).
reply:
The Electricity Market Design Directive aims to put the consumer at the centre of the clean energy transition, enabling active participation, with a strong framework for consumer protection. The Directive includes measures addressing concerns over exposure to volatile short-term fossil fuel prices by improving the design of the electricity market and emphasising long-term instruments, alongside the boosting of renewable energy investments, protecting and empowering EU consumers and enhancing the competitiveness of the European electricity market. The rules also enable more flexibility to accommodate the increasing share of renewable energy on the grid.
Significant progress in transposition was made recently with the publication in July 2026 of Statutory Instrument (SI) 319/2026. This SI transposes most of the provisions in the Directive. Article 15a (energy sharing) is of a more complex nature and requires additional time and consultation to ensure appropriate transposition in the Irish electricity market. Officials from my Department are currently working with officials from the Commission for the Regulation of Utilities and ESB Networks to facilitate transposition of these two articles. It is expected that this work on transposition will continue into 2027.

question: Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment when his Department last reviewed its policies, operations and handling of protected disclosures under all relevant protected disclosures legislation.
reply:
I can confirm that my Department's Protected Disclosures Policy was reviewed in 2025, including internal and external legal review, with the updated Policy circulated to all staff and published in November 2025.
I can assure the Deputy that all reports of wrongdoing submitted to my Department are formally processed in accordance with the published Protected Disclosures Policy which aligns with the Protected Disclosures Act 2014 as amended.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the Government giggawatt, GW, targets for roof-top solar, including residential and commercial; the agricultural and utility scale solar provided on land including privately owned land and State/State-agency owned land, by category; and the way in which these targets have been selected and categorised.
reply:
The Climate Action Plan sets out Ireland's Solar Strategy to deliver a target of 8 GW of solar energy by 2030.
The National Planning Framework establishes regional renewable electricity capacity allocations for solar and onshore wind which are to be incorporated into revised Regional Spatial and Economic Strategies (RSES) and Regional Renewable Energy Strategies (RRES).
National Policy Objective 75 of the National Planning Framework provides that local authorities shall plan for the delivery of Target Power Capacity (MW) allocations consistent with the relevant Regional Spatial and Economic Strategy, through their City and County Development Plans.
Utility-scale solar is now Ireland's third largest source of indigenous electricity generation, while embedded solar is having a significant impact on reducing grid demand during periods of high solar generation.
Ireland currently has approximately 3.2 GW Solar generation capacity installed (both utility-scale & rooftop).

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the extent to which the solar capacity of roof space, including but not limited to residential, commercial and agricultural, has been assessed as viable for solar; the potential available capacity identified; and the efforts made to realise that potential.
reply:
My Department is aware of one national study that has assessed the potential for rooftop solar photovoltaic (PV) deployment across Ireland, namely Quantifying the Potential for Rooftop Solar Photovoltaic in Ireland, published by the Irish Solar Energy Association and MaREI (Foundation Ireland Research Centre for Energy, Climate and Marine). The study estimated that Ireland's rooftops could theoretically accommodate up to 13 GW of installed solar PV on potentially 1 million to 1.3 million homes.
The study focused on rooftop solar potential and included analysis of residential buildings. My Department is not aware of any comparable national assessment that quantifies rooftop solar potential across the residential, commercial and agricultural sectors on a consistent national basis. It should be noted that any assessment of rooftop solar potential is subject to data limitations and methodological assumptions regarding building suitability, roof characteristics, shading and other site-specific factors. Accordingly, estimates of national rooftop solar capacity should be considered indicative rather than definitive.
While no comprehensive assessment of rooftop solar potential across all building categories has been undertaken by my Department, a range of measures are in place to support the deployment of rooftop solar generation where viable. These include grant support through the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI), such as the Microgeneration Support Scheme (MSS) for d

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the details of the land use strategy in relation to the use of land for solar energy; and the way in which this will inform Government policy.
reply:
Solar energy, through rooftops and utility scale solar farms, is rapidly increasingly in importance in terms of supplying growing energy demand and reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels, both in Ireland and globally. Last month, I announced that Ireland reached a record 3 gigawatts (GW) of solar generation capacity, with utility scale solar meeting over a third of national electricity demand on the grid at one point.
Government policy is focused on maintaining this momentum and harnessing our indigenous solar energy as a part of a renewable, secure and affordable energy system.
Under the Government’s Accelerating Renewable Electricity Taskforce, officials from my Department will continue to liaise and work closely with the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage on the ongoing planning reforms, including the alignment of local development plans and regional spatial and economic strategies with national targets and regional allocations for solar and wind in the National Planning Framework.
The ESB has indicated that Ireland could expect the 8GW target for solar in Ireland by 2030 to require an area equal to 0.26% of all agricultural land, based on a similar study in the UK.
The final report of Phase 2 of the Land Use Review, entitled 'A Living Land', and associated supporting reports / documents were published by the three responsible Ministers on 2 July 2026.

reply:

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if there is a retrospective element available, or being considered, in relation to the solar grant scheme for people in receipt of certain payments from the Department of Social Protection.
reply:
As part of Budget 2027, the Government announced a package of enhanced renewable energy and retrofit grants designed to help households and businesses reduce energy costs, lower dependence on fossil fuels and strengthen Ireland’s energy security.
A particular focus of the package of measures is on ensuring that households most exposed to high energy costs can also benefit from the energy transition. Enhanced supports for households at risk of energy poverty, medically vulnerable customers, lower-income homeowners and renters will help ensure that those who need support most can access the benefits of lower energy bills.
Included in these measures was the addition of solar PV and battery storage under the Warmer Homes Scheme (WHS) and the introduction of a new enhanced grant, of up to €9,000, for solar PV and battery storage for households in receipt of certain Department of Social Protection (DSP) payments. This grant is set at 100% of the median cost for the installation of these systems. Importantly this grant is available for homeowners in homes built prior to 2025, while the WHS applies to homes built prior to 2006.
Where a homeowner has previously received an upgrade under the WHS they are also now eligible for the enhanced grant of up to €9,000 for solar PV and battery storage via the main Solar PV Scheme. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he is aware that price comparison websites accredited by the Commission for Regulation of Utilities, CRU, calculate the cost of smart day-night-peak tariffs using a fixed assumed split of household usage rather than the customer's actual consumption; if his Department has assessed the extent to which this may lead households to choose a tariff that costs them more than an alternative.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 225 and 226 together.
The Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) introduced its Price Comparison Website (PCW) Accreditation Framework in 2011 and since then has required accredited websites to provide customers with clear, independent and accurate information. These websites help customers compare available offers and identify the price plan and energy supplier that best suits their needs to assist in making an informed decision about whether to switch.
The CRU has recently updated the framework to bring it in line with developments in the energy market, including smart meters, microgeneration and new types of tariffs. Under the updated framework, customers can still rely on accredited PCWs for independent and impartial comparisons of all available offers. They can now also:
• upload their smart meter data to receive a personalised comparison based on how they actually use electricity, helping them identify the tariff that may suit them best;
• if they have microgeneration through solar panels, exported energy can now be factored into the comparison. As a result, more than 200,000 customers with microgeneration can see what the best tariff is for them; and
• if a customer is interested in dynamic electricity tariffs, they can compare supplier offers.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the number of domestic electricity customers on smart time of use tariffs; the number of customers who have downloaded their smart meter data file (HDF) from ESB Networks, in each of the years 2024, 2025 and 2026 to date, in tabular form.
reply:
The assessment of retail market arrangements, including the uptake of smart tariffs and use of smart meter data by suppliers and third-party service providers, falls primarily within the remit of the Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU). Additionally, the National Smart Metering Programme is overseen by the CRU while ESB Networks is delivering the electricity smart meter rollout and the smart meter data portal. These are not matters in which I, as Minister, have a function.
The CRU publishes information from time to time on the number of customers on smart time of use tariffs so the first part of this Question should be directed to the CRU. The CRU's Interim Review of the Electricity and Gas Retail Markets shows that over 2.1 million smart meters have been installed to date, representing 85% of domestic customers. Of the customers with smart meters, over 20% are availing of Time-of-Use tariffs as of February 2026, a trend that is increasing. Questions around the number of smart meter data downloads should be directed to ESB Networks. The CRU and ESB Networks have contact e-mail addresses for Deputies should they wish to raise matters of concern or seek updates on the National Smart Metering Programme: oireachtas@cru.ie and oireachtas@esb.ie.

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether a homeowner may avail of the one-stop shop scheme for the installation of a heat pump without other fabric upgrades; and the minimum building energy rating or energy improvement that applies to such a project.
reply:

This scheme is delivered through the SEAI’s registered One Stop Shop (OSS) model which provides a complete start-to-finish service for the homeowner. With grants of up to €14,500 for heat pump systems now available, the OSSs pass on the grant savings as an upfront discount on the works, meaning the homeowner only has to fund the balance themselves. Homeowners can apply through one of the participating OSSs or Energy Partner which are listed on the SEAI website at: www.seai.ie/grants/find-a-registered-professional/energy-partners
For a heat pump to perform efficiently, the building fabric must meet a specified minimum performance standard. question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the details of the SEAI pilot on high-temperature heat pumps; its start date; the number and type of dwellings involved; and when its findings will be published.
reply:
In February, under the new National Residential Retrofit Plan 2026, a High Temperature Heat Pump (HTHP) Pilot was launched to evaluate the performance of these heat pumps in Irish homes.
A HTHP works in the same way as any other heat pump but delivers heat at a higher temperature that can be used in existing central heating systems. HTHPs can operate at temperatures similar to traditional boilers which means that many homes may be able to keep their existing radiator systems, subject to advice.
The pilot is particularly focused on homes with higher heat loss that may not currently qualify for existing heat pump grants and older homes where high temperature operation could reduce the need for extensive upgrades. Data from the UK Electrification of Heat Study shows that HTHPs installed in homes built up to 1980 achieved an average performance of 303%, demonstrating strong efficiency even in older homes.
The pilot aims to collect data on system performance, energy use, indoor comfort levels and heating patterns. This data will help assess the overall efficiency, running costs and performance of HTHPs for different home types. If the data demonstrates high efficiencies at higher levels of heat loss or lower levels of insulation, this will inform policy on the operational direction of the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland's retrofit delivery programme that could facilitate an acceleration of the uptake of heat pumps in Ireland. question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment further to the flexibility introduced by SEAI in July 2026 on the heat loss indicator requirement for the one-stop shop, community energy grant and warmer homes schemes, the mechanism under consideration to extend that flexibility to the better energy homes scheme; and the timeline for its introduction.
reply:
My Department funds a number of schemes administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) to maximise emissions reductions and deliver energy savings for the widest range of homeowners possible.
Heat pump heating systems are most efficient when they operate in homes with a low level of heat loss. Therefore, to qualify for the heat pump grant, the building fabric must meet a specified minimum performance standard. Since the launch of the heat pump grant in 2018, the SEAI has used the Heat Loss Indicator (HLI) as the first step in determining heat pump grant eligibility. To date, this metric has guided the market to focus on reducing heat demand through fabric improvements to optimise heat pump performance.
According to the SEAI, recent analysis of on-site heat pump performance data has shown that heat loss is not the only factor affecting overall heat pump performance in a home. Other factors such as the sizing and system design, installation, commissioning, the control strategy, maintenance and the occupant’s understanding and use of the system also impact heat pump performance and system efficiency. Interim findings from the SEAI HLI Research Pilot also indicate a trend where the correct design, installation, commissioning and control strategy are critical factors to ensure optimal heat pump system performance.

question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will clarify aspects of the battery storage grant through the SEAI, the rate of the grant is currently €600, however an updated BER rating is required to avail of the grant which costs €300; the reason a BER report would be needed to supply battery storage; if he is satisfied that a BER cert is necessary; and if he can commit to increasing the grant to incorporate the cost of same.

Effective from 6 October 2026, the package of measures includes a new grant for battery storage and expanded eligibility for solar PV and solar thermal grants. In addition, among the tax measures in Budget 2027 is an increase to the income tax disregard for micro-generation income received under the Clean Export Guarantee by households who sell electricity back to the grid from €400 to €600.

A post-works BER is not required when a standalone battery is installed without a solar PV system. This is because there is no uplift in the BER in this case. question: Deputy Paul Donnelly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment If he had a bilateral meeting with his Canadian counterpart during the recent UN High Level Week.
reply:
I attended the United Nations General Assembly High-level Week in September. While in attendance, I attended a number of events and held bilateral meetings with several of my international counterparts. As you can imagine, the High-Level week is an extremely busy time for those in attendance. Unfortunately, I was unable to meet with my Canadian counterpart as we were unable to align our schedules.
However, I was able to meet with the Canadian Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Claude Guay, when he attended the Informal Meeting of Energy Ministers which I chaired in Dublin Castle the following week. I am please to report we had an excellent discussion on how Ireland and the EU can bolster relations with Canada. It was an honour, as Chair, to be able to invite Canada for the first time to attend an EU meeting of Energy Ministers.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment when regulations to allow domestic microgeneration will be put in place; and the way in which microgeneration will be incentivised.
reply:
The regulatory framework to enable domestic microgeneration has been in place since 2018, before being put on a statutory footing in 2022. The Renewable Energy Regulations 2022 (S.I. No. 76 of 2022) transposed key provisions of the EU Recast Renewable Energy Directive, introducing an obligation on electricity suppliers to provide a Clean Export Guarantee (CEG) tariff to qualifying micro and small-scale generators, ensuring that households and businesses can receive payment for excess renewable electricity exported to the grid reflective of the market value.
The Commission for Regulation of Utilities has statutory responsibility for regulating the electricity market. In line with long standing policy on deregulation, price setting by electricity suppliers, including remuneration for microgeneration for householders and businesses, is a commercial and operational matter for the companies concerned.
While exporting electricity to the grid can provide an additional income stream, self-consumption of the electricity generated generally offers the greatest financial benefit. The introduction of Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) battery storage supports in the run-up to Budget 2027 is intended to help households retain electricity generated on site for their own use, if it is more favourable for them to do so, and ensure that those who install solar panels can maximise the benefit they get from the electricity they generate.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will put regulations in place to allow the use of microinverters in domestic energy generation.
reply:
Microinverters are already permitted for use in domestic solar PV installations and are eligible under the existing Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland Solar PV Grant Scheme. The choice of whether to install microinverters or other technologies is a matter for the designer and installer of the system, having regard to the specific characteristics of the property and the requirements of the customer.
Accordingly, there are no plans at present to introduce specific regulations to allow the use of microinverters, as their use is already accommodated within the current regulatory and grant framework. Contractors assess the suitability and necessity of microinverters as part of the design and installation of solar PV systems, including systems incorporating battery storage.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether a vulnerable domestic electricity customer who is in arrears but making regular repayments can be prevented from switching electricity supplier; the arrears thresholds and time limits that apply; and the measures available to ensure such customers can access more affordable tariffs.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 214 and 215 together.
The Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) Supplier Handbook sets out the minimum service requirements, including customer protection measures for all domestic households, including renters, that energy suppliers must adhere to. These rules are in place to ensure that customers experience a high standard of protection when interacting with energy suppliers. A Code of Practice on Vulnerable Customers is also in place.
The definition of Vulnerable Customers is set out in Regulation 2 of Statutory Instrument No. 463 of 2011. Under this Regulation, energy suppliers must establish and maintain:
• a Priority Services Register of customers critically dependent on electrically powered equipment, which shall include but is not limited to life protecting devices; assistive technologies to support independent living; and medical equipment; and
• a Special Services Register of customers particularly vulnerable to disconnection during Winter months for reasons of advanced age or physical, sensory, intellectual or mental health challenges.
Current best practice as conducted by suppliers allows customers to self-register as ‘priority vulnerable’ (those customers dependent on life protective equipment), or ‘special-services vulnerable’ (those customers who require additional protection from being unduly affected during the Winter months). question: Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if the proposed direct lines/private wires legislation will permit a renewable electricity generator to supply electricity directly to a neighbouring premises rather than exporting that electricity to the national grid.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 209 to 212, inclusive, together.
The intention of the upcoming legislation to provide for privately owned electricity wires which will support the development of Ireland's electricity network by providing an alternative and complementary route for connection, investment, and grid development. In certain circumstances, it may alleviate demand pressures on the national electricity grid by facilitating dedicated private connections.
Government recognises the vital importance of transitioning to a climate neutral and environmentally sustainable economy and that this transition must be contextualised within Ireland’s broader energy security priorities. It is envisaged that privately owned electricity wires will contribute to these climate and energy goals.
My Department has been engaging with the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel to finalise drafting of the legislation and this is a priority for the Government. It is intended that the Bill will be published this year and will complete its passage through the Oireachtas as soon as possible thereafter.
The regulatory regime will be developed in line with the legislation and this will set out in detail the approvals and requirements that will apply to a privately owned electricity wire between a generator and a customer.

question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if his Department will examine changes in relation to SRESS-2 and look to open-ended European templates such as Germany’s "combination premiums", Italy’s 15-year availability capacity contracts, or simple time-of-use peak tariff windows that satisfy commercial lenders.
reply:
The Programme for Government commits to promoting the Small-Scale Renewable Electricity Support Scheme (SRESS) to simplify market access for community, SME and farmer-owned solar and wind projects.
The SRESS export tariff is designed for community, SME and farmer export only projects above 50kW to 6MW. SRESS offers a simple route to market for those groups, with fixed tariffs for solar and wind. All other export projects up to 1MW can also apply to SRESS, and need not be community, SME or farmer owned projects.
In February 2026, my Department commenced a review of the SRESS tariffs to ensure tariff levels remain effective and that the scheme provides appropriate support and value for money to consumers. The initial SRESS design process examined a range of supports offered across Europe. This helped inform the design of the scheme. This review process also considered support offered to similar types of projects in Europe.
Furthermore, the SRESS review is considering changes to the scheme, such as the creation of a distinct farmer-specific tariff, as well as potential partnerships between communities and developers, by reviewing the existing 100% community ownership requirement.
The current tariff rates continue to apply while this work is underway, with completion expected later this year.

reply:
The Programme for Government included a commitment to bring some of the high-level meetings of the EU Presidency to cities and counties across Ireland, ensuring the entire country benefits from the profile the Presidency brings. In addition to a range of official level meetings taking place across the country, it was decided by Government that 6 of the 22 informal Ministerial meetings would take place outside of Dublin as follows:

In all of these cases, the Office of Public Works, as official provider of conference services for the EU Presidency, conducted a detailed assessment to determine the most suitable available venue in the relevant area taking into account the specific delivery requirements of the particular meeting. In the case of the FAC Defence and Gymnich meetings, Druids Glen emerged from the assessment process as the most suitable venue available in Wicklow to host both meetings which are traditionally held back to back at the end of August.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade which of the 23 commitments in Ireland's Diaspora Strategy 2026 to 2030 relate to access to housing for Irish citizens returning to the State; if the Department or the Minister of State for international development and the diaspora has engaged with the Department of Finance or the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage on a housing or tax support for returning emigrants; if so, the outcome of any such engagement.
reply:
Ireland’s Diaspora Strategy 2026-2030 sets out 23 commitments across five interconnected threads: wellbeing and advocacy; identity and culture; connection and contribution; departure and return; and sharing our experience. The drafting of the strategy followed a year-long consultation of the Irish abroad, with 27 meetings in 17 countries, which were complemented by the first ever online survey of our diaspora, the Global Irish Survey, which received almost 10,000 responses.
The Strategy recognises that many returning emigrants can face practical challenges on their return to the State and, in line with the Programme for Government, commits to facilitating their return including through addressing administrative challenges and improving access to information and supports.
I am conscious that issues relating to housing can impact on someone's decision to return to Ireland. In responding to those who raised this with me directly during the consultations, I noted that housing, among other matters, are not just of concern to the diaspora but also affect people living in Ireland. Addressing them is a key priority for the Government and this work will go on outside of the diaspora strategy. This approach is reflected in the Diaspora Strategy (on page 6 and page 12).
I have not had any discussion with the Department of Finance or the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage on a housing or tax support for returning emigrants.
