question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for an update on the interstate case against the British Government regarding the Legacy and Reconciliation Act.
reply:
I can confirm that the interstate case in respect of the 2023 Legacy Act remains in place. If the Joint Framework is faithfully translated into amending legislation, including the removal of immunity and the restoration of civil cases, we would expect to be in a position to revisit the status of the case.
I have been in regular contact with the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland, Chris Bryant, since his appointment in July. These engagements have been positive, with the Secretary of State expressing agreement around the need to progress implementation of the commitments in the Joint Framework on the Legacy of the Troubles, including by advancing the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill in Westminster.
I have strongly emphasised to the Secretary of State the importance of implementing legislation, in both jurisdictions, that is faithful to the Joint Framework. This is the best route to legacy mechanisms that are compliant with the European Convention on Human Rights and can secure the confidence of victims and survivors of the Troubles.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the position regarding the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill progressing through Westminster; and in particular, if it is the position that measures requiring consent of the Advocate General in Northern Ireland to prosecute for Troubles related crimes amounts to political interference.
reply:
UK Government amendments to the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill were laid before the House of Commons on 12 October. On 13 October, the Commons voted in favour of the carry-over extension of the Bill with 304 votes in favour and 179 against. The amendments have been scheduled for debate at Committee Stage (Committee of the whole House) on 19 and 20 October. The progress of the Bill to this stage marks an important milestone. Last year’s Joint Framework was a momentous step forward, and what is needed now is full and faithful implementation of what was agreed.
The Taoiseach has discussed the implementation of the Joint Framework on Legacy with PM Burnham and both governments have expressed a shared commitment to implementing the agreement as soon as possible.
I have been in regular contact with the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland, Chris Bryant, since his appointment in July. We discussed the implementation of the Joint Framework in detail during his first visit to Dublin in his new role on 24 August and again at our next in person meeting at the British Irish Association Conference in Oxford on 4 September. I had further constructive engagements with the Secretary of State in Belfast in recent weeks as his team worked to progressing the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill’s progress to Committee Stage at Westminster.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the position regarding the total number of Irish passport cards issued since their launch in 2015, broken down by year.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 186, 187 and 192 together.
The passport card was launched in October 2015 and offers Irish citizens the convenience of travel, with a credit card sized travel document, to all EU Member States, the members of the EEA (Iceland, Liechtenstein, and Norway), Switzerland and the United Kingdom. The Passport Card is fully compliant with International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) regulations concerning requirements for passports in card format.
In June 2026, I launched a next-generation passport book and card featuring world-first security technologies. In conjunction with the launch of the new book and card, the Passport Service engaged with national government border control and immigration authorities worldwide to advise them of the updates to Ireland's secure travel documents.
Each individual national government border control and immigration authorities are responsible for machine-readable zone (MRZ) scanners and automated e-gates at their airports. Government agencies maintain border sovereignty, deploy the scanning hardware, and run the security database checks. It is up to each country to ensure it keeps up with the advancement in passport design and enhancements. It was ensured, via the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, that all e-gates at Dublin airport received this update prior to the launch of the new passport book and card.
The Passport Service engages directly with over half a million citizens annually through it

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the status of negotiations with the British Government to reinstate access for Irish fishermen to their traditional fishing grounds at Rockall; the engagements between her office and the UK authorities over the last number of years; the number of instances it was raised by the Irish government; and if she will go to international mediation or arbitration to resolve this long running injustice, that has cost the fleet millions of euro each year.
reply:
The consistent position of successive Irish Governments is that Ireland does not recognise Britain’s claim of sovereignty over Rockall. Accordingly, Ireland does not accept that a 12 nautical mile (22km) territorial sea exists around Rockall. We understand that the UK takes a different view.
Reaching an agreement on issues relating to Rockall continues to be important for the Government and discussions are ongoing at both political and senior official level with our UK government and Scottish government counterparts.
The matter has been raised with the First Minister of Scotland and the former Cabinet Secretary for the Constitution, External Affairs and Culture with agreement that we would continue to work together to seek a resolution.
The issue is also discussed regularly at official level, and it was most recently raised in a meeting between senior officials in my department and their Scottish counterparts in September 2026.
I will continue to work closely with the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine, Martin Heydon TD, and the Minister of State with responsibility for Fisheries and the Marine, Timmy Dooley TD, on this issue.

question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Taoiseach the number of people in employment in County Laois in 2022; and the current estimate level of employment in 2026.
reply:
The exact information requested by the Deputy is not available.
The Labour Force Survey (LFS) is the official source of estimates of employment in the State. The most recent figures available are for Q2 2026.
Due to the methodology and sample size of the survey it is not possible to produce reliable county estimates from the LFS.
Regional estimates of employment are produced by NUTS 3 level. NUTS are the geocode standard developed and regulated by Eurostat. The NUTS 3 Midland region includes counties Laois, Longford, Offaly and Westmeath.
According to the LFS, there were 159,600 people in employment in the Midlands in Q2 2022. This has since increased to 166,700 in Q2 2026.
While the information at county level is not provided by the LFS, administrative data sources of employment estimates, which are available on an annual basis, may provide further insight on employments.
Earnings Analysis using Administrative Data Sources (EAADS) outputs contain employment figures on an annual basis, based on Revenue Commissioner’s employee tax data. It should be noted that EAADS estimates are for employees only, and do not include persons who are self-employed. Please also note that the estimate provided by EAADS relate to the number of employments, rather than number of employees. The annual employment estimates from the EAADS dataset are restricted to employments which were active during the month of October, in line with Eurostat requirements relating to Structure of Earnings Statistics

question: Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he will provide an update in respect of the new National Sports Policy; and the way in which it will deliver more playing pitches in Dublin.
reply:
The National Sports Policy 2018–2027, which runs to the end of 2027, established Ireland's first national framework for sport, setting out objectives to increase participation, strengthen governance, enhance high-performance sport and increase investment across the sector. The implementation of the policy has been delivered by two action plans, the current one running from 2024-2027.
Development of the successor National Sports Policy is being progressed through a phased approach.
Phase 1 (Initiation) has been completed and the Department is now undertaking Phase 2 (Planning and Development), within which a sectoral consultation represents the primary evidence-gathering activity.
The development of the National Sports Policy 2028–2037 provides an opportunity to take stock of progress under the current policy and identify where future policy interventions can have the greatest impact.
Through a programme of evaluation, sectoral consultation, international best practice review, stakeholder engagement and policy mapping, the Department is undertaking a comprehensive evidence-gathering process to inform the successor policy.
This work is examining the effectiveness of existing policy measures and implementation structures, identifying areas where policy approaches may require strengthening, and assessing future priorities for investment and action.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport his plans to invest in new public swimming pools.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 144, 169 and 178 together.
Ireland’s first-ever National Swimming Strategy was published in 2024 and it sets out a vision to provide everyone in our country with an opportunity to swim. It includes an Action Plan containing over fifty actions across five thematic strands, focusing on providing improved facilities, increasing access for people with disabilities, improving the culture of inclusion, better coaching supports, increasing safety awareness and providing a pathway that allows for the nurturing and development of potential high performers.
In support of the National Swimming Strategy, my Department provided additional funding of €500,000 to Swim Ireland in 2024 and 2025 for the deployment of swimming activators to work within local authority areas, focusing on increasing participation amongst under-represented groups and improving coaching supports and facilities. This additional funding is being continued in 2026, delivering a total investment of €1.5 million over three years. The impact of local activation is already being felt on the ground as evidenced by the number of participation programmes and partnerships initiated.
While government support for new swimming pools or the refurbishment of existing pools is now directed via the Large-Scale Sport Infrastructure Fund (LSSIF), it was previously provided through the Local Authority Swimming Pool Programme (LASPP).

reply:

In May 2024, over €26 million was allocated to 900 sporting organisations that applied for equipment only category. question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the measures his Department is taking to support community-based arts festivals and cultural events that promote participation in the arts and preserve local culture and heritage; whether additional funding streams are being considered for long-running festivals and events that have demonstrated significant community engagement; and if he will provide information on this with regard to festivals and events held throughout Galway City and County Galway.

The Arts Council also provides financial support to a range of festivals, large and small, both single art form and multidisciplinary arts festivals. The Regional Festival Scheme, which they also support, is available to local community festivals and is administered by the local authorities. Each local authority manages their own application and grant process.
Complementing these supports, my Department has a Small Scale Local Festivals and Summer Schools Scheme. question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport whether his Department has plans to expand the number of spaces on the basic income for the arts scheme; and if his Department will provide further support to the arts in 2027.
reply:
In February 2026, a successor scheme to the Basic Income for the Arts Pilot scheme was annouced. The main objective of the Basic Income for the Arts scheme is to support professional artists whose creative practice is based in Ireland. Guidelines for the new scheme were published on 1 April and the deadline for applications was Tuesday 12 May. Just over 10,000 applications were received. reply:

With regard to a future round of the LSSIF, I am committed to ensuring sustained investment in sports facilities to meet our ambitious goals for sports participation nationwide. question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the actions he is taking to progress the ban on social media use by under 16s in Ireland.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 141 and 171 together.
The European Commission published a Proposal for the EU KIDS Act on 17 September. The Proposal, which is aimed at strengthening the protection of children online with a common EU framework, includes new obligations on social media, video sharing platforms, online games, and AI chatbots and companions.
These obligations are intended to ensure that services that are available to minors are designed to be safe for children and young people.
My Department will conduct a public consultation on the Proposal with all stakeholders, including with any services, such as game companies and AI providers that will be in scope of that Proposal. The outcome of those consultations will inform the Irish position in the EU negotiations. Prior to the publication of this Proposal, and in the context of the Presidency, I hosted a two-day high-level Presidency Conference on Online Safety for children and young people on 10 and 11 September. The conference featured cross-sector representation, including from industry, and I met with representatives from Google. The Department has also been meeting with a number of services regarding age verification and the Digital Wallet
With respect to age restrictions for access to social media, the Government’s preference is for an EU wide measure. As digital services are provided across borders, a coherent EU approach makes compliance more straightforward and cooperation on enforcement more effective.

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if support will be available to the sports organisations affected by the liquidation of a company (details supplied) who have an approved Sports Capital Grant being processed.
reply:
I am aware of media reports that the company referred to by the Deputy has ceased trading and is due to enter liquidation. It is regrettable that this development is likely to impact on a range of sports clubs and organisations.
While any contractual arrangements, and disputes arising, between clubs or organisations and the company referred to are outside of my Department's remit and are civil matters between the parties, my Department will be as flexible as possible in working with grant recipients under the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF) that have been impacted by this liquidation.
In line with established procedures, the Department will allow any organisation that received formal approval for works to be carried out for this company, and have not commenced works, to change to another supplier. Additionally, in cases where works were commenced by the company referred to by the Deputy, my Department will allow clubs to employ a different supplier to complete the works.
If any club or organisation has queries in relation to this matter, it can contact my Department and officials will engage with them in relation to their CSFF allocation.

question: Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the reforms to the TV licence he is proposing to introduce; and if the reforms are based on the Report of the Future of Media Commission recommendations or any other previously published report.
reply:
On consideration of the Report of the Future of Media Commission, Government decided not to accept the Commission's recommendation of Exchequer based funding for all public service media. Instead, an interdepartmental Technical Working Group (TWG) was established to examine measures to reform and enhance the TV licence system. In March 2023, the TWG submitted its report to the then Minister for Tourism, Culture, Arts, Gaeltacht, Sport and Media.
Following the revelations regarding payments in RTÉ, consideration of the report was paused until completion of the work of the independent examination of RTÉ. As part of the July 2024 decision on the funding of RTÉ and wider public service media and content, the Government decided to retain the television licence system, underpinned by new measures designed to improve collection and compliance in order to maximise revenue generation.
On this basis, the TWG was reconvened to examine potential administrative and legislative measures to enhance compliance and maximise revenue generation. The Report of the TWG was finalised before the Summer Recess and will be brought to Government shortly. As the Deputy will appreciate, it would not be appropriate to discuss any potential measures prior to the report being brought to and considered by Government.

question: Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the number of homes across the country benefitting from the national broadband plan; and if his Department plan to go back into areas a second time to further improve connectivity for more homes not included in the first round.
reply:
Ireland's Digital Connectivity Strategy published in December 2022, sets out a number of targets including that all Irish households and businesses will be covered by a Gigabit network no later than 2028.
The National Broadband Plan (NBP) is the Government initiative to deliver high speed broadband to all premises in Ireland. The Government identified a need to deliver broadband services where commercial operators would not operate. As part of the NBP, the Government appointed National Broadband Ireland (NBI) to deliver wholesale broadband services to those parts of the country, not served by commercial operators. The Department defines high-speed broadband as a connection with minimum speeds of 30Mbps download and 6Mbps upload.
Currently, the NBP deployment is expected to be delivered on time and on budget with the main infrastructure build scheduled to be completed by end of 2026.
I am advised by NBI that of the over 564,000 premises currently in the Intervention Area (IA) across the State, design work has been completed for 100% of these and 531,977 premises have now been passed by the fibre rollout, 94% of the premises in the IA. NBI also advise that 549,951 premises, across all counties in mainly rural areas, can now order or pre-order broadband and 194,596 premises have already been connected.

reply:
On 2 October, my Department published the Information Guide for the 2026 round of the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF).
The 2016 round will be administered on a new grant management system, SPRAOI, which opened for registrations on 28 September. SPRAOI opened for applications yesterday, Monday 19 October 2026, and will remain open until Friday 26 February 2027.

question: Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the Bills his department may be working on with the help of Coimisiún na Meán and the Garda to address the issue of antisocial behaviour being recorded and posted online on social media by mainly teenagers.
reply:
The Online Safety Framework comprises legislation and codes such as the Online Safety and Media Regulation Act 2022, the Online Safety Code and the EU Digital Services Act.
Under that Framework, there are provisions relating to illegal content online.
For example, platforms must act promptly to remove illegal content as soon as they become aware of it. They also have an obligation to report to An Garda Síochána if they become aware of any information that gives rise to a suspicion that a criminal offence involving a threat to the life or safety of someone has taken place, is taking place, or is likely to take place. Platforms are obliged to have an easy way for people to report content that they think may be illegal.
The Online Safety Code also places restrictions on the dissemination to minors of content that glorifies violence or dangerous challenges.
Very Large Online Platforms have additional obligations, such as the obligation to assess and mitigate risks. This includes the risk of dissemination of illegal content and the risk of negative effects on public health, public security or the protection of children.
Coimisiún na Meán and the European Commission are responsible for the supervision and enforcement of these provisions and there are some investigations underway. Coimisiún na Meán is independent in the exercise of its functions.

question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the steps he will take to address the lack of a full-sized sports pitch in Dublin 1.
reply:
The provision of land for recreational purposes including sports facilities is primarily a matter for local authorities in accordance with their functions under the Planning and Development Act.
Once lands are acquired for sporting purposes, applications for capital investment (including equipment) on those lands can be supported via the Community Sports Facilities Fund (CSFF) or the Large Scale Sports Facilities Fund.
On 2 October, my Department published the Information Guide for the 2026 round of the CSFF. The 2026 round introduces increased maximum grant amounts, allowing local project applications to apply for up to €250,000 and regional Tier 1 projects to apply for up to €550,000.
The 2026 CSFF also introduces, on a pilot basis, a new Regional Tier 2 Grant category with a maximum funding amount of €750,000 with either a local authority or National Governing Body of Sport (NGB) as the project development lead. It is intended that this category will encourage a particular focus on the development of full-sized multisport all-weather pitches.

question: Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport to detail the supports for independent radio broadcasters included in budget 2027.
reply:
Commercial and independent radio broadcasters are eligible to apply for funding under a number of schemes operated by Coimisiún na Meán which support the capacity of the media sector to produce and distribute high quality, independent and trustworthy public service content.
Total support for broadcast and media funding schemes is being maintained in Budget 2027. €5M will be made available for the News Reporting Scheme, with €3M ringfenced for independent radio. Independent radio will also be able to seek funding under the Digital Transformation Scheme (to which €4M is being allocated) and Local Democracy and Courts Reporting Schemes (to which €6M is being allocated), which are administered by Coimisiún na Meán on a platform neutral basis. In addition, 7% of net TV Licence Fee receipts will be allocated to Coimisiún na Meán's longstanding Sound and Vision Scheme under which independent radio can also lodge applications for funding. In 2026, over €7M was awarded by Coimisiún na Meán through the various media funding schemes to support the commercial radio sector, at a local, regional and national level.
I am aware of the challenges facing our independent radio stations in the current climate in an increasingly competitive market. The independent radio sector plays an important role in providing valuable public service content to the Irish public, contributing to diversity and a plurality of voices.

The organisation to which the Deputy refers has benefited from both current and capital funding provided by my Department. The relevant Local Authority applied on their behalf for capital works, drawing down €72,929 in 2023 under the Cultural Capital Scheme 2019-2022. Under the Creative Communities partnership, the organisation has since 2023 received €6,350 from the relevant local authority from the allocation provided by my Department.
My Department provides capital grants as a contribution towards the development and maintenance of the nationwide network of cultural infrastructure throughout the country. Much of the existing cultural infrastructure of venues, arts centres and museums were initiated and funded by local authorities, in accordance with their functions under the Planning and Development Acts. Annual support, including programming and revenue supports, is provided to this arts and culture infrastructure by local authorities and the Arts Council.
I have asked the Arts Council to make direct contact with the Deputy in relation to supports available to the facility referred to. Please contact my private office if you do not hear from the Council within the next ten working days.
I recently launched the new Arts Capital Investment Fund to support arts and culture facilities across the country to purchase equipment and undertake refurbishment works to their premises. This scheme is open until 18 December 2026 at which point applications will be assessed.

question: Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport where the €5 million cut in capital funding for arts and culture in his Department will come from in budget 2027.
reply: The change in capital allocations relates principally to Shared Island allocations which will be addressed in the Revised Estimates Volume. I anticipate that final capital allocations for 2027 will be broadly in line with the 2026 allocation.

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport further to the recent announcement of the Arts Capital Investment Fund (details supplied), his plans to expand the scheme to allow for the development of facilities where there are none in place.
reply:
My Department provides capital grants towards maintaining and enhancing existing arts and culture infrastructure but does not provide funding for the purchase of buildings or land. In accordance with their functions under the Planning and Development Acts, the local authorities prepare county and city development plans which incorporate plans for cultural infrastructure at a local level. Accordingly, proposals for the development of new arts and culture facilities are a matter in the first instance for the local authority.
The Arts Capital Investment Fund will support arts and culture facilities across the country to purchase equipment and undertake refurbishment works, including climate action upgrades, health and safety upgrades and works to provide universal access. It will also support community and voluntary groups with funding for equipment to increase participation in arts and culture.
If I may also draw the Deputy's attention to my Department's €6 million Artist Workspaces Scheme. Local authorities outside Dublin City Council are invited to propose projects which enable them to provide additional artist workspaces in their regions on a sustainable basis and produce fit for purpose workspaces. Funding of up to €300,000 is available for densely populated local authority areas and €150,000 for other local authorities. question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the measures he is taking to protect children and young people from the negative effects of frequent AI use, harmful content in online spaces and platforms designed to be addictive.
reply:
Ireland's Online Safety Framework comprises the Online Safety and Media Regulation Act 2022, the EU Digital Services Act, the EU AI Act, and the Online Safety Code.
With respect to protecting minors from the uses of AI, the EU AI Act was recently amended to add new prohibited practices. One of the new prohibited practices is the placing on the market of systems that can generate child sexual abuse material. Another new prohibited practice is the generation of non-consensual sexually explicit or intimate content, such as “nudification apps”.
These provisions will take effect on 2 December 2026. The implementation of the EU AI Act is within the remit of the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment.
More recently, the European Commission published a Proposal for the new EU KIDS Act. That Proposal includes provisions on AI chatbots and companions in the context of protecting children and young people online.
The Proposal provides that AI companions and chatbots that are accessible to minors may not use designs that simulate human relationships in ways likely to create emotional dependency. They will not be able to carry a child’s conversations into later ones, by default. They must be tested for risks to children before being launched onto the market and monitored for harm afterwards. Children under 13 can only use them through parental control tools. Where an AI chatbot is built into a platform or game, it must not switch on automatically, may not be promoted to children

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport whether his Department has engaged with an organisation (details supplied) regarding its current examinership, governance arrangements and relationship with its affiliated organisations; whether he is satisfied that appropriate structures are in place to ensure meaningful engagement with affiliates and stakeholders across the equestrian sector; and whether he will consider measures to support the long-term sustainability, transparency and effective governance of the organisation.
reply:
While the organisation in question, Horse Sport Ireland, has written to me to provide an update on the examinership process, I have not had direct formal engagement with it on the matter.
HSI is the Sport Ireland recognised NGB for equestrian sport in Ireland and is recognised for the purpose of international sporting competitions by the Fédération Équestre Internationale. It provides breeding services and studbook services to the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine (DAFM) under contract, and it also leads the development of the sports side of the sport horse sector. Sport Ireland, as the statutory body with responsibility for the development of sport, increasing participation at all levels and raising standards, allocates annual funding under its various programmes to HSI.
My officials, and Sport Ireland, are in contact with colleagues in DAFM regarding the ongoing examinership process, and the outcome of that process is awaited with keen interest. While Sport Ireland plays an important role in promoting, supporting, and strengthening good governance practices across the sector, all NGBs, including HSI, are independent, autonomous bodies and are responsible for their own governance procedures.
It is understood that the protection provided by the examinership process will allow a period during which the finances, operations and future structure of the company can be objectively considered with the aim of securing the organisation’s longer-term viability.
My Departm

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the way in which the Community Sport Facilities Fund is being used to advance the Government's objectives under the Sports Action Plan 2024–2027 in relation to equality, inclusion and participation in sport; the steps being taken to encourage projects that specifically support girls' and women's sport and improve access for people with disabilities.
reply:
Female participation in sport is an important element of both the National Sports Policy 2018-2027 and its associated Sports Action Plan 2024-2027 and represents a core priority for me and my Department.
The Government is committed to a "Sport for All" approach aimed at ensuring that all persons can partake equally in sport and physical activity, regardless of gender. This commitment is reaffirmed in the Programme for Government and is also reflected in Sport Ireland's Women in Sport Policy. The Women In Sport (WIS) funding programme, administered by Sport Ireland, was first established in 2005 and since then over €30 million has been invested through the National Governing Bodies of Sport and the Local Sports Partnerships.
My Department operates two capital funding programmes for sport, namely the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF) and the Large-Scale Sport Infrastructure Fund (LSSIF). All CSFF grantees, including GAA clubs, must sign a declaration that, from the date of the grant, they will not deny anybody access to any facility or part of a facility for which they received a grant on the grounds of gender, civil status, family status, age, disability, race, sexual orientation, religious belief, or membership of the Traveller or Roma community without just, reasonable and proper cause.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport whether he will withdraw or amend legislation which proposes that 25% of RTÉ's budget should be redirected to the independent sector, and provide that any policy of support for the latter sector should come from dedicated funding streams, rather than from the budgetary allocation for RTÉ as proposed.
reply:
Section 116 of the Broadcasting Act 2009 currently provides that RTÉ shall pay a fixed index-linked sum into the RTÉ independent programme account for the purpose of commissioning programmes from the independent sector.
The Future of Media Commission examined the independent programme account and highlighted that RTÉ’s investment in new programming plays a vital role in supporting the wider creative economy in Ireland. The Commission recommended (Recommendation 5 – 10) the funding level of RTÉ’s Independent Programme Account should be increased to 25% of RTÉ’s public funding, and in the longer-term to a proportion to be recommended by Coimisiún na Meán.
Section 46 of the Broadcasting (Amendment) Bill gives effect to this recommendation by providing that RTÉ’s annual contribution to the independent programme account shall be a minimum of 25% of public funding and that Coimisiún na Meán may increase this minimum percentage, subject to the approval of the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport for an update on the relevant projects under the Sport Ireland campus master plan vision; and the way in which the campus development will coincide with Dunsink City Quarter.
reply:
The Sport Ireland Campus Masterplan provides an ambitious blueprint setting out a vision and framework for the growth of the Sport Ireland Campus over the next 15 to 20 years. Significant progress has been made in recent years, with the National Velodrome and Badminton Centre (NVBC) and the National Cricket Centre (NCC) now under construction since earlier this year. Both projects are progressing well and it is anticipated that they will be delivered on time and within budget.
The NVBC project will deliver a 250-metre cycling track, 12 badminton courts, seating for 1,000 spectators and ancillary facilities.
Phase 1 of the National Cricket Centre will deliver the main field of play, 4,240 spectator seats, a high-performance centre and a player and match officials' building. This is being managed in two distinct construction contracts to ensure that the playing surface will be adequately prepared in time for the 2030 T20 World Cup tournament, which Ireland will co-host.
Other projects being planned at the Campus under the Masterplan include the expansion of the Sport Ireland Institute and the redevelopment of Abbotstown House and Gardens. Future potential projects of benefit to national governing bodies of sport are also under consideration.

reply:

The recommendations in the Report have been reviewed and an extension of the pilots has been approved until June 2027. I understand that the Department has written to all nine pilot locations to inform the relevant local authorities that funding for the posts has been extended until June 2027.
Discussions have now commenced between officials in the Department and local government in relation to the outcomes of the review, and the potential future expansion of the project, with all partners working towards mapping out a pathway forward for a more permanent structure for this valuable initiative.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the reason TG4 was not allocated additional funding in budget 2027; and the engagement his Department has had with the broadcaster since the budget announcements.
reply:
The Budget 2027 allocation for the Department is set out in the Expenditure Report published by the Department of Public Expenditure, along with the allocations at a programme level.
Further details were set out by Minister O’Donovan and myself at our press conference on Wednesday 7th October, and in the Department's press release which was published on its website.
The allocations to each subhead, public body or initiative as part of the budget process were based on total available funding in the context of the competing demands across the Department.
Minister O'Donovan and I are fully aware of TG4’s priorities, their important role in not just the media sector but across Irish society, and Government remains committed to ensuring that TG4 is funded appropriately.

reply:

My Department will conduct a public consultation on the Proposal with all stakeholders, including with any services, such as game companies and AI providers that will be in scope of that Proposal. The Department has also been meeting with a number of services regarding age verification and the Digital Wallet

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the measures being considered by his Department to recognise the 50th anniversary of the first Galway Arts Festival; and his plans to support the organisation of special commemorative events as part of the festival in 2027.
reply:
My Department has not been contacted by Galway Arts Festival with any request for assistance or support to mark its 50th anniversary. However, the Arts Council, which is funded by my Department, has provided significant support to Galway Arts Festival over many years and I would expect that that would continue to be the case.
More generally, the State's approach to Commemorations recognises that organisations are best placed to lead and develop their own commemorative paths with appropriate State support if required.
The Commemorations Advisory Committee, which is Chaired by Bryan Dobson, was established in 2025 to provide independent and expert advice to the State and key stakeholders on commemorative matters. The Committee consists of experts from a broad range of fields including academia, politics and the National Cultural Institutions.
One of the roles of the committee is to identify key historic anniversaries and events that the State could mark nationally or at local level using a partnership approach with the local authorities.
Each year I make a funding allocation available for the development and delivery of local or community-led Commemorations.
The fund is administered by the local authority who are recognised as being best placed to identify significant local anniversaries and events to commemorate their locality. The Commemorations Coordinators within each local authority are listed on the commemorations webpage on gov.ie.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport to provide an update on his Department's plans to ensure a more proactive approach to online safety, particularly regarding the use of recommender systems and their impact on social media users.
reply:
It is a Government priority to ensure a robust framework for online safety, in particular for children and young people.
The recent Proposal for a new EU KIDS Act includes new provisions on recommender systems that are specifically designed to protect minors. For example, social media services will have to prioritise the clearly expressed preferences of children instead of implicit ones that are inferred from the behaviour of a child online. Personalisation based on tracking must be off by default. Social media will have to prominently display tools that enable minors to modify or control elements of a recommender system, including making it easy to delete previous preferences. At least one option of a system not based on profiling must be easily available. There are also measures to avoid the “rabbit hole” effect of recommending similar content repeatedly, where the cumulative effect can be harmful.
The EU KIDS Act has other provisions intended to make safer the overall design of social media and other digital services available to minors. These include provisions addressing addictive design, such as infinite scroll, and safeguards against contact from strangers.
As online safety, especially for children and young people, is a key theme of Ireland’s EU Presidency, we are giving priority to the negotiations on the EU KIDS Act and those discussions are advancing.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the progress made to date in implementing Ireland's International Sports Diplomacy Strategy 2026-2030, launched in February 2026; the actions completed; and those currently underway.
reply:
The International Sports Diplomacy Strategy 2026-2030, which was published earlier this year by my Department and the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, seeks to enhance the many related activities already underway to maximise the value of significant government investment in both Ireland’s international footprint and in sports at every level, to support stronger coordination among key stakeholders and to identify and support new international sports diplomacy initiatives in line with the goals of this Strategy.
The four goals of the strategy include promoting Ireland as a Sporting Nation; using Sport including Gaelic Games to deepen our diaspora’s connection to Ireland; supporting international sporting partnerships and cooperation in line with Ireland’s values and interests and maximising the economic value of international sports diplomacy and engagement in major sporting events.
An implementation group, jointly chaired by my Department and the Department of Foreign Affairs has recently been established, and it is anticipated that proposals to establish the first round of the International Sports Diplomacy Fund will brought forward soon. This fund, will have an annual budget of €200,000, jointly funded by both Departments. Once established, a targeted call for applications will be published and I look forward to publishing more information in this regard in due course.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the further measures he intends to take to strengthen the protection of children and young people using social media and online platforms; and the way in which the Government intends to progress age restrictions and effective age-assurance measures.
reply:
The protection of children and young people online is a whole of Government priority.
The Online Safety Framework, which includes the Online Safety and Media Regulation Act 2022, the Online Safety Code, the EU Digital Services Act, and the EU AI Act, already provides protections for minors online.
With respect to age restrictions, the Government supports an EU wide approach to support compliance and effective enforcement. Therefore, we welcome the recently published Proposal for a new EU KIDS Act, which provides new age thresholds for access to social media and video sharing platforms. The Proposal takes a graduated approach, starting with measures to prohibit under 13 year olds from having accounts on those services. Children aged between 13 and 15 will be able to have limited accounts, opened and managed by parents, while those over 15 may open their own accounts provided they are on services that are safe for minors.
As part of Ireland’s EU Presidency, we have given priority to the negotiations on this Proposal, to advance the discussions in the Council as efficiently as possible.
Effective enforcement of obligations on digital services is another important aspect of protecting children online. The Broadcasting (Amendment) Bill 2026 provides a new binding information gathering power for Coimisiún na Meán to use as regulator for the Online Safety Framework.

reply:
The Night-Time Economy pilots were established in nine locations in support of Action 19 in the Report of the Night-Time Economy Taskforce. My Department has written to all nine pilot locations to inform the local authorities of this and that funding has been guaranteed until then.

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the number of meetings he has held with an organisation (details supplied) on the funding plan for integration of codes.
reply:
Minister O'Donovan and I, since taking office in February 2025, have jointly and separately met the Gaelic Games associations on a number of occasions to discuss a range of matters, including the integration process.
Gender equality across sport is a Government priority and, while not directly involved in the process, the Government is very supportive of the integration of the Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA), the Ladies Gaelic Football Association (LGFA) and the Camogie Association into a single unified structure for Gaelic Games.
Most recently, Minister O'Donovan and I met with the three associations in September 2026 to discuss progress towards integration. During these meetings, each of the three bodies reaffirmed their commitment to achieving integration and confirmed that this process is ongoing.

reply:

This is a major milestone for the arts in Ireland and research conducted by the Department of Culture provided Government with a clear evidence base upon which to make that decision.

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if an application (details supplied) has been assessed as part of the dormant accounts funded sustaining social enterprise scheme 2026/2027; and when the applicant will be informed of the decision.
reply:
Objective Two of Trading for Impact, the National Social Enterprise Policy 2024-2027, is to help social enterprises grow and become more sustainable. reply:

reply:

SÍOL means ‘Seed’ in English and SÍOL stands for Scéim Infheistíochta ag Obair Le Chéile, which translates to ‘Working Together Investment Scheme’.
Capital funding of €31.5 million has been secured up to 2030 in the National Development Plan to support SÍOL. Funding of €5m has been allocated to the programme for 2026 and annual funding is expected to reach €7m by 2030. SÍOL funding will increase from €5m in 2026 to €6m next year.

question: Deputy Eamon Scanlon asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht further to Parliamentary Question No. 1590 of 20 March 2024, if the BDO report commissioned by his Department in 2023 on the cost and availability of public liability insurance for the community and voluntary sector has been finalised; when the final report was received, if applicable; if outstanding, the reason for the delay and expected completion date; whether the report has been or will be published; and if so, when and where it may be accessed.
reply:
Action 23 of the National Volunteering Strategy 2021-2025 was to “Represent the views of the sector in relation to the impact of the cost and availability of public liability insurance on volunteering through engagement with the Insurance Reform Sub-group of the Cabinet Committee on Economic Recovery and Investment, which was established to implement the Government’s insurance reform agenda”.
In furtherance of this action, independent research was commissioned to investigate the impact of insurance costs and liability on the Community and Voluntary Sector in Ireland. Undertaken following a competitive tendering process, the purpose of the research project was to understand and represent the views of the national and international Community and Voluntary sectors in relation to the impacts of the cost and availability of public liability insurance.
The final report was presented by the researchers to the National Volunteering Strategy Implementation Group in March 2024. While the report was not published, it is available from the Department on request.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science whether the AIReady.ie course content addresses the energy use and carbon emissions associated with AI services, and the guidance, if any, given to learners; and whether any assessment of the environmental impact of the programme was carried out or considered.
reply:
The current AI Ready courses focus on foundational AI literacy, practical every day and workplace use, online safety and scams, career support, and the safe and responsible use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)
As part of the responsible-use content, learners are introduced to the environmental considerations associated with AI. The courses explain that the data centres used to provide AI services consume electricity and require resources for cooling, including water, and that the use of generative AI services therefore has an associated environmental footprint. The material also provides practical guidance on using AI thoughtfully and responsibly.
A standalone environmental impact assessment of the AI Ready programme was not considered necessary as the programme is delivered online through short, self-paced courses and does not itself develop, host or operate AI models or the computing infrastructure on which commercial AI services run.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the measures, if any, taken or planned to offset or mitigate the additional energy use and emissions arising from the AIReady.ie target of upskilling one million people; and how the programme is consistent with the Government’s legally binding climate targets.
reply:
AIReady.ie is an upskilling and awareness initiative designed to demystify artificial intelligence (AI). The platform is focused on building AI skills and capability and does not involve the development, provision or operation of digital infrastructure.
AIReady.ie does not have responsibility for energy consumption, emissions or climate policy. Measures to manage, mitigate or offset energy use and emissions arising from digital infrastructure do not form part of the programme and are generally matters for the relevant Departments, agencies and regulatory bodies within their respective remits.
More broadly, the Government's wider approach to ensuring that digitalisation and decarbonisation progress together is reflected in the Government Statement on the Role of Data Centres in Ireland's Enterprise Strategy (2022). This sets out the Government's policy principles for the sustainable development of data centre infrastructure in the context of Ireland's climate and energy objectives.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science whether the AI Ready courses direct learners to specific commercial AI products (details supplied), without referring to alternative providers; the criteria by which any such products were selected; and whether he considers this consistent with neutrality between competing providers.
reply:
The AI Ready courses are introductory AI literacy courses intended to help learners understand and make practical use of commonly available artificial intelligence tools. The course materials refer to ChatGPT and Google Gemini as practical examples of generative AI tools. These examples were selected because they are widely recognised, readily accessible through free versions, and suitable for demonstrating the relevant learning outcomes to beginners.
Learners are not required to purchase software or premium subscriptions, nor are they required to use these tools. Learners may simply follow the examples provided, and the skills and principles taught can be applied to alternative AI tools.
The inclusion of named products is therefore illustrative and does not constitute an endorsement of the providers concerned. The content-development approach focuses on the purpose and use of AI tools rather than on the companies providing them, and no commercial consideration formed part of the selection of the examples.
The programme is designed to teach transferable skills, including understanding AI, writing effective prompts, critically assessing AI-generated material, protecting personal information, and using AI safely and responsibly. The use of recognisable examples to support introductory learning is considered consistent with provider neutrality, as the material does not promote or recommend one commercial provider over another and the learning is applicable across different AI to

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science whether SOLAS, his Department, or the National Skills Council has any commercial, sponsorship or data-sharing arrangement with any AI provider in connection with AI Ready; whether any AI provider contributed to the course content; and whether a procurement process was held for its content or tools.
reply:
My Department, SOLAS or the National Skills Council have no commercial, sponsorship or data sharing arrangement with any AI-product provider in connection with the AI Ready courses.
Learners are not required to purchase an AI product, and AI Ready does not sell learner data or share learner data with advertisers, AI providers or other third parties.
The course content was developed with reference to the European Digital Competence Framework (DigComp), with individual course learning outcomes mapped against relevant DigComp 3.0 competence areas, including information and data literacy, communication and collaboration, digital content creation, safety and problem solving.
Pre-existing SOLAS frameworks for online learning services including content development, platform and technical services were used and were subject to the applicable public procurement and financial governance requirements.
No commercial AI tool was procured for use by learners. Where commercial AI products are referenced in learning activities, they are used as illustrative examples and learners can follow the activities without purchasing or subscribing to those products.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science whether he is concerned that it appears Irish universities have spent hundreds of thousands of euros on animal testing outside the jurisdiction (details supplied).
reply:
The Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA), a state body under the aegis of the Department of Health, is the competent authority in respect of the use of animals for scientific purposes within Ireland. Any project on animals conducted in Ireland must be evaluated by the HPRA in accordance with Directive 2010/63/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes. The latter Directive seeks to replace the use of live animals for scientific and educational purposes as soon as it is possible to do so. This legislation applies throughout the European Union and is transposed into Irish law by the European Union (Protection of Animals used for Scientific Purposes) Regulations 2012 (S.I. No. 543 of 2012). Projects must be justified from a scientific point of view or required by law, and must be conducted in the most humane and environmentally sensitive manner possible.
Further information in relation to this Directive, and concerning the scope and remit of the HPRA, can be obtained via the Department of Health. In terms of research institutions which are responsible for ensuring the planning and implementation of research which may involve the use of animals, these are individually liable for ensuring all such research is in accordance with all relevant regulations and legislation.

question: Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Health the measures her Department is taking to ensure that private health insurance products are presented to consumers in a clear, transparent and easily comparable manner.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1104 to 1106, inclusive, together.
As Minister for Health, I am responsible for the legal framework governing the health insurance market in Ireland. This is a voluntary market that operates under the principles of community rating, open enrolment, lifetime cover and minimum benefits. These protections are designed to support fairness and keep health insurance as affordable as possible for all consumers.
The Health Insurance Act 1994 (Minimum Benefit) Regulations 1996 require insurers to provide a minimum level of cover to every insured person, regardless of what insurance policy has been purchased. Private health insurers operate as commercial entities within a competitive market, and where a procedure or service is not designated as a minimum benefit under the Regulations, insurers may determine themselves whether to include it on particular plans.
Beyond the scope of this legislation, I do not have a role in the commercial decision making of any private health insurer and therefore cannot direct any insurer to provide cover for any particular procedure or service, or direct how that cover is to be provided.
The statutory framework governing private health insurance provides for a number of independent oversight and consumer protection mechanisms to ensure that consumers are treated fairly and in accordance with the relevant legislation and regulatory requirements.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Health the progress made to date on the refurbishment of the maternity unit, paediatric unit and diagnostic services, together with improvements to transport routes, at University Hospital Galway; the forthcoming stages of the project; the expected timelines for delivery; the estimated cost range associated with the works.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1059, 1064, 1067, 1081 and 1097 together.
A number of proposals of significant scale have been proposed on the University Hospital Galway (UHG) campus. A Development Control Plan (DCP) for the campus has been completed to provide a clear plan for the sequencing and phased delivery of the new capacity and facilities. This sequencing has been led and informed by the clinical priorities for the region and the need to deliver new and replacement capacity in a phased manner to minimise disruption to ongoing service delivery on a live hospital campus.
The immediate priority identified in the master planning is the delivery of significant additional inpatient bed capacity to mitigate the pressures on, and support delivery of, a range of services on the campus.
The first three priority phases of the DCP are as follows:

Phase 2: Laboratory building, ambulatory cancer centre

A critical enabler for campus development is construction of a new, fit-for-purpose helipad. The existing helipad greatly constrains development to the west of the existing hospital buildings, primarily due to the constraints imposed by the flight paths into it. The new location for the helipad will unlock the UHG campus and enable the next development phases of major capital projects to move ahead.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Health the progress made to date on the delivery of the new surgical hub at Merlin Park University Hospital under the Elective Care Programme; the forthcoming stages of the project; the expected timelines for those stages; when the surgical hub will become operational; the estimated cost range attributable to the project.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1093 and 1096 together.
The Government’s Elective Care Programme is being delivered in two phases: a national network of Surgical Hubs in the first instance to meet medium term demand and capacity, and then a national network of Elective Treatment Centres (Elective Hospitals) in Cork, Galway and Dublin.
The new elective facilities enable the separation of scheduled (elective) from unscheduled care. This will mean fewer cancellations and fewer delays for elective care caused by seasonal surges, localised outbreaks, and surges in emergency attendances. Reducing waiting times for elective cases can help to avoid patient conditions from deteriorating further while waiting for treatment. Providing additional elective care capacity will therefore lead to better health outcomes and improved quality of life for those individuals being treated and for their families. Developing increased elective care capacity will also release capacity in existing hospitals, allowing them to focus on non-elective, acute and other inpatient activity.
All efforts are being made to ensure the swift and safe delivery of the new Surgical Hub in Galway. Once fully operational the new Surgical Hub will provide significant additional elective care capacity, including more than 8,100-day case procedures and 5,700 minor ops procedures every year.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Health when the final report of the Alcohol Act Technical Evaluation Group, AATEG, will be published; and the key recommendations arising from its work.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1094 and 1095 together.
In November 2024, the Alcohol Act Technical Evaluation Group (AATEG) was established to evaluate the effectiveness of the measures in the Public Health (Alcohol) Act 2018, including MUP. The Group submitted an interim report earlier this year which is being considered for publication and will submit its final report in 2027.
The rate at which the minimum unit price is set is considered on an ongoing basis as provided for in the Public Health (Alcohol) Act. It is worth noting that the recent increase to the level of MUP in Wales, and the earlier increase in Scotland, brought these on to a similar level to the current Irish rate.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Health to outline Ireland’s position on proposed EU maximum permitted levels for vitamins and minerals in food supplements; which bodies represent Ireland in the relevant PAFF Committee discussions; and the timetable for consideration and adoption of these measures.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1079 and 1080 together.
I am aware of the ongoing work of the European Commission on the possible establishment of harmonised maximum amounts for vitamins and minerals in food supplements and fortified foods.
It is important to note that the European Commission has not yet presented final proposals and no binding limits have been agreed at EU level. The Commission is continuing its preparatory work and has indicated that stakeholders will have opportunities to provide evidence and feedback through forthcoming consultation processes.
As the Commission has not yet published proposed maximum levels, a comprehensive assessment of the impact on consumer access to individual food supplements currently available in Ireland has not been completed. However, the Department is actively monitoring the process and will carefully consider any future proposals, including their potential implications for consumers, public health and access to appropriate food supplements in Ireland.
The Department will closely be monitoring developments and engaging with the European Commission, the FSAI and relevant stakeholders. The Department has not yet finalised a national position on this matter. Any position taken by Ireland will be informed by the scientific evidence provided by EFSA and other expert bodies, consideration of consumer safety, the views of stakeholders, and the need to ensure that consumers continue to have access to safe and appropriately regulated foo

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health whether the Pharmaceutical Society of Ireland and the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Ireland collect data on registrants whose qualifications were obtained outside the State and on fitness to practise complaints concerning them; and, if so, the most recent figures for each.
reply:
I thank the Deputy for his question.
My department have engaged with both the Pharmaceutical Society of Ireland (PSI) and the Nursing & Midwifery Board of Ireland (NMBI) who have provided the following information
The Pharmaceutical Society of Ireland (PSI) collects information on the country in which a pharmacist obtained their qualification as part of the qualification recognition and registration process.
As of 15 October 2026, there are 7,997 pharmacists registered in Ireland. Of these, 4,032 (50.4%) presented a pharmacist qualification obtained outside Ireland during the registration process.
The PSI also manages fitness to practise complaints relating to registered pharmacists. However, complaint data is not routinely categorised or reported by the country in which a pharmacist obtained their qualification.
The Nursing & Midwifery Board of Ireland (NMBI) have said there are approximately 92,000 nurses and midwives on the NMBI Register, of whom 51% obtained their qualifications outside the state.
In 2024, NMBI received 109 complaints about the fitness to practise of a registered nurse or midwife. This represents 0.12% of the total number on the Register. Of the 109 complaints received, 57 registrants obtained their qualifications outside the state (including the United Kingdom).
The NMBI annual State of Complaints report gives an overview of the fitness to practise process and is published on their website.

question: Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Health the plan or pathway under consideration to enable clinical embryologists to obtain CORU registration; whether she is aware that the current eligibility criteria for andrology posts in the HSE Regional Fertility Hubs exclude experienced clinical embryologists from applying.
reply:
Work is ongoing in my department to develop a framework to guide policy on the regulation of health and social care professionals into the future. The framework will modernise our approach to professional regulation both in terms of how decisions are made regarding professional regulation and the ways in which we regulate professions. The framework will be informed by an evidence and risk-based approach to regulation in line with requirements set out in the EU Proportionality Test Directive.
The issues to be considered regarding the proportionate degree of regulatory force required to protect the public are complex and this is therefore a significant project requiring considerable research and engagement with relevant stakeholders.
It should be noted that statutory regulation forms a part of a system of assurance that the Department utilises to mitigate risk posed to the public by the practise of health and social care professions. Many professions employed in the health service, including in the HSE and the publicly funded sector, are not subject to statutory regulation. For example, audiologists, clinical measurement physiologists, medical physicists, play therapists and play specialists, and perfusionists are among the non-regulated groups which are currently employed by the HSE.

ADHD Ireland has confirmed that it will receive the same level of HSE funding for UMAAP in 2026 as it has received in previous years. question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Health to provide an update on the implementation of the recommendations outlined in the Diabetes Policy and Services Review: A Strategy for Better Care, in particular the increased access to continuous glucose monitors in cases where there is a clinical indication outside of patients with T1D.
reply:
The Diabetes Policy and Services Review: A Strategy for Better Care (www.assets.gov.ie/static/documents/a41e7d5d/Diabetes_Policy_and_Services_Review_-_A_Strategy_for_Better_Care.pdf) was launched on the 21st of May.
This is Ireland’s first national strategy for diabetes, marking a major milestone in diabetes care in Ireland. It provides a detailed assessment of our current diabetes services and sets out series of recommendations and actions to improve diabetes care delivery. This includes access to diabetes technology based on clinical need, such as continuous glucose monitoring.
The recommendations cover four key themes:
• Service Development
• Affordability and Access to care
• Better support for people living with diabetes
• Digital Healthcare
The recommendations are marked in the strategy as either short, medium or long-term goals. Short-term refers to recommendations which can be implemented within three years. Medium term recommendations can be implemented within five years, and long-term recommendations are those that will take longer than five years to fully implement.
The HSE is currently working to develop an implementation plan to ensure that the recommendations are followed through at national level and throughout the Health Regions.

question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Health her plans to implement a shingles vaccination programme for those who are immunocompromised and those aged 65+ as announced in Budget 2027; and the expected timeline for the programme to commence.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 882 and 1039 together.
Ireland’s immunisation programme is informed by the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). NIAC considers the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland as well as international best practice in relation to immunisation when developing its advice.
The current NIAC guidelines state that the shingles vaccine may be considered for those aged 65 years and older, due to the greater burden and severity of disease in this age group and in those aged 18 years and older at increased risk of shingles.
I can confirm that I have approved the introduction of a Shingles Vaccination Programme, in line with NIAC advice, to be implemented on a phased basis over 5 years, for immuno-compromised groups and persons aged 65 and over.
The programme is expected to commence in 2027, initially offering shingles vaccines to immuno-compromised groups. This will be followed by the 80 years and older cohort. The programme will conclude with the 65–69-year-old cohort.
It is expected that the vaccine will be administered in the main by GPs and Pharmacists. Further programme details will become available in due course.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Health if legislation to provide a legislative underpinning for adult safeguarding in the health and social care sector will be published this quarter; and if preparations are underway to give effect to proposed legislative commitment, including ensuring that safeguarding structures within the HSE are independent.
reply:
A National Policy Framework for Adult Safeguarding in the Health and Social Care sector was published in December 2025, in line with the commitment in the Programme for Government. The policy framework will extend across all public, private and voluntary health and social care services.
Included are a range of both legislative and non-legislative measures that will significantly expand and strengthen existing supports and protections for adults at risk of harm across the health and social care sector. The Government has also approved the development of legislation to underpin these commitments. Key legislative commitments include:
• The Health Service Executive (HSE) will have responsibility for leading and coordinating adult safeguarding across the sector and will have statutory functions, duties, and powers to underpin this role.
• Current safeguarding structures within the HSE will be strengthened and legislation will provide that they will operate independently in the performance of their functions.
• New powers of entry for safeguarding and protection teams and powers to obtain court protection orders.
• The Health Information Quality Authority's (HIQA’s) remit will be extended to include independent oversight and monitoring of adult safeguarding services for the Health and Social care sector delivered by the HSE.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Health the measures that have been taken to provide nursing home support for survivors of Industrial and Reformatory Schools under the agreement concluded on 10 November 2025; the number of survivors who have benefited from such measures to date.
reply:
The Department of Education and Youth’s Supports for Survivors of Residential Institutional Abuse Act 2025 was signed into law in July 2025. The Act makes available - amongst other supports - the provision of health services without charge to survivors of residential institutional abuse, in the form of a medical card administered by the HSE.
The health supports to be provided under the 2025 Act are similar to those under the standard medical card but with some additional benefits. The supports include, a general practitioner service, approved prescribed drugs, medicines, medical and surgical appliances, home nursing, home support services, dental, aural, ophthalmic and chiropody services. In addition, the survivors’ medical card will be for life and will not be subject to review or means-testing. Holders of this medical card will not be required to pay prescription charges and will also have improved access to counselling and physiotherapy services. The HSE will also appoint dedicated liaison officers for survivors.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Health whether her Department supports the key recommendations in the European Commission’s recent proposals for a council recommendation on health checks for cardiovascular diseases, including the screening actions for specific age groups, blood pressure and blood glucose assessments and vaccination status assessments.
reply:
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) encompasses a range of conditions including heart attack and stroke, remains one of the most significant public health challenges facing Europe. It is the leading cause of death across the EU, claiming approximately 1.7 million lives each year, while in Ireland it accounts for around 10,000 deaths annually and remains a major contributor to ill health and hospitalisation.
Although substantial progress has been made in reducing mortality, more people are living longer with cardiovascular disease and require ongoing care and support. Cardiovascular disease also places a significant economic burden on society.
As up to 80% of cardiovascular disease are preventable, there is a strong focus in both Ireland and the EU on prevention, early identification and timely intervention to reduce avoidable illness, improve outcomes and lessen its health, social and economic impact.
Last December, I welcomed the publication of the EU Cardiovascular Health Plan, known as the Safe Hearts Plan. The plan aims to support Member States in reducing the burden of cardiovascular disease by strengthening national policies across prevention, health promotion, early detection and screening, and treatment, while also driving innovation.
One of the Plan's ten flagship initiatives is the proposed Council Recommendation on cardiovascular health checks, which was published on 28 September to coincide with the EU's first Screening Week.

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health the funding provided to implement the National Maternity Strategy in Budget 2027; and to provide a detailed breakdown of this allocation.
reply:
The National Maternity Strategy is in its final year. The Strategy has delivered significant reform since 2016, with the majority of actions now completed or well underway. Work is ongoing to ensure completion of the remaining actions of the Strategy in 2026.
Since 2016, €28 million in development funding has been invested through the Strategy, supporting the recruitment of more than 567 additional whole-time equivalent staff, including 44 consultants and over 390 nurses and midwives.
Over €130 million of capital investment has been directed into maternity services over the lifetime of the strategy. This has modernised facilities, delivering refurbishments to wards, and home-from-home birthing rooms across the country.
More than €20 million capital funding has also advanced our information sharing infrastructure, with the Maternal and Neonatal Clinical Management System now live in Cork, Kerry, Limerick, the Rotunda, the National Maternity Hospital, and the Coombe.
Budget 2027 provides a significant increase of €1.6 billion (6.2%) in current funding and €160 million (10.3%) in capital funding for the health service in 2027.
While there is no specific ringfenced allocation for the National Maternity Strategy arising from the Budget, the overall additional funding will support the continued delivery and development of services across hospital and community care settings.
