Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health if an issue with glass on the new National Children’s Hospital has been identified; to outline, in detail, the nature of this issue; the date at which it became known; the amount of glass involved; the delay incurred; the cost of remedial works; and the name of the supplier.
reply:
Opening the National Children’s Hospital Ireland (NCHI) is a Government priority. Everything possible is being done to ensure this world-class hospital will open as quickly as possible, on behalf of children, young people, and their families.
I have been clear that the responsibility for committing to, resourcing, and delivering this project sits squarely with the project’s main contractor, BAM Ireland. The State will not reduce the pressure or dilute that accountability.
BAM is responsible for the supply and installation of the glass in the NCHI. I am aware that there are a small number of glass panes that have yet to meet the required compliance standards. BAM is also responsible for rectifying all defects, and this defect will be rectified to the required standard by substantial completion.
Over the last 18 months, significant rework has impacted BAM’s progress. BAM has closed c.200,000 defects, with c.1,900 outstanding. Defects continue to be identified and closed through the ongoing inspection process, including the panes of glass in question. These defects are the responsibility of the contractor BAM.
The National Paediatric Hospital Development Board (NPHDB), on behalf of the State, will only accept completed work that meets contractual standards. Normal room inspection on projects such as this is sampling 10-20%, whereas the Design Team is inspecting 100% of rooms to ensure standards are met. In some instances, the Design Team has had to re-inspect some rooms 6 times.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Health whether she will review the income thresholds that apply as part of the medical card scheme especially in the context of planned increases to the minimum wage.
reply:
Medical Card provision is primarily based on financial assessment. In accordance with the Health Act 1970 (as amended), eligibility for a medical card is determined by the HSE, which assesses each application on a qualifying financial threshold. This is the amount of money that an individual can earn a week and still qualify for a card. It is specific to the individual's own financial circumstances.
Every effort is made by the HSE, within the framework of the legislation, to support applicants in applying for a medical card - in particular, to take full account of difficult circumstances in the case of applicants who may be in excess of the income guidelines. In such circumstances, the HSE may exercise discretion and grant a medical card, for example:
• Discretionary medical cards issued to patients with significant medical expenses, but who do not satisfy the means test.
• Emergency medical cards are issued to patients that are terminally ill, or are seriously ill, and in urgent need of medical care that they cannot afford.
I can assure the Deputy that, in order to ensure the medical card system is responsive and sensitive to people's needs, my Department keeps medical card issues under review and any proposals are considered in the context of any potential broader implications for Government policy, the annual budgetary estimates process and legislative requirements arising.

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh den Aire Forbartha Tuaithe agus Pobail, agus Gaeltachta cé mhéad go sonrach atá le baint ó bhuiséad caipitil na nOileán agus cé mhéad atá le baint ó bhuiséad caipitil na Gaeltachta sa chiorrú atá leagtha amach sa Bhuiséad ar airgead caipitil na Gaeltachta agus na nOileán ó €55,362,000 in 2026 go €50,362,000 in 2027.

Tá leithdháileadh iomlán de €628 milliún faighte ag mo Roinn i gCáinaisnéis 2027, lena n-áirítear leithdháileadh caiptil de €273 milliún. Foilseofar leithdháileadh mionsonraithe de réir fomhír san Imleabhar Meastachán Athbhreithnithe (REV) roimh dheireadh na bliana.
Tá pleananna fíor-uaillmhianacha ag mo Roinn d'fhorbairtí caipitil chun tacú le pobail Ghaeltachta, pobal na Gaeilge agus pobail na n-oileán araon. Maoinítear na forbairtí seo as Clár C de bhuiséad na Roinne - An Ghaeltacht, an Ghaeilge agus na hOileáin. Is fiú a mheabhrú gur tháinig ardú ar an mbuiséad caipitil do Chlár C ó €30 milliún in 2025 go beagnach €55 milliún in 2026. Bhain cuid mhaith den ardú sin le trí phríomhthionscadal infreastruchtúir:

Rinneadh gealltanas i leith na dtionscadal seo sa Phlean Forbartha Náisiúnta, agus is cúis áthais dom an maoiniú a fháil chun iad a thabhairt i gcrích anois. reply:

The fund is administered locally on behalf of the Department by Local Community Development Committees (LCDCs) across the country, with support from their local authority.
The Local Enhancement Programme (LEP) for 2026 provided €7 million in capital supports. Each LCDC decided the projects that were funded under LEP 2026. The closing date for community groups to submit applications for LEP 2026 was 27 February 2026 and the list of successful projects was announced on 2 July 2026. Therefore, the 2026 programme is now closed.
I was delighted to secure current funding of €2 million for the LEP in Budget 2027 to assist community organisations in easing the pressure of rising operating costs. This is in addition to €5 million in capital funding that is available for LEP 2027. My Department is currently considering the detailed design of the LEP for 2027 and I hope to announce the new programme before the end of this year.

question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the level of funding remaining under the LEADER Programme 2023-2027; and the measures being taken to ensure that funding is fully utilised.
reply:
The LEADER Programme is co-funded by the European Union and is delivered through Local Action Groups (LAGs) across rural Ireland. A feature of the LEADER programme is that it is based on a community-led, bottom-up approach to rural development.
The 2023-2027 LEADER programme has total funding of €180 million, with 75% or €135 million available to support projects being completed by rural groups and businesses.
The funding is allocated in advance to LAGs to provide them with greater flexibility to manage their budgets over the programming period. Funding is then paid out by my Department as costs are incurred and claims for payment are submitted.
Using this allocation, LEADER LAGs have approved funding of over €76.8 million for some 1,537 LEADER projects countrywide. This means that c. 57% of the overall project allocation is committed, with some €58 million or 43% remaining. Of these, 551 projects have been completed to date, with the remainder due to be completed over the coming months and years. There are an additional 172 projects progressing through the approval stages across all sub-regional areas.
The €180 million also includes €45 million (or 25%) which is available to support the administration and animation costs of the LAGs involved in running the programme. Of this, €20.1 million has been drawn down to date, with some €24.9 million remaining. question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the funding allocated to the Social Inclusion and Community Action Programme (SICAP) for 2027.
reply: The Social Inclusion and Community Activation Programme (SICAP) is Ireland's primary social inclusion programme, which aims to reduce poverty and promote social inclusion and equality by supporting disadvantaged individuals and communities across the country. The programme works with individuals and local community groups to address barriers to participation and strengthen community capacity. I am pleased to have secured almost €74 million for SICAP and other social inclusion supports in Budget 2027. Just under €65 million of that allocation is for SICAP providing greater long-term funding stability for the programme and enabling the continuation of important work across the country. It should be noted that the final estimated allocations for each area will be confirmed in the Revised Estimates Volume which will be published in December, and considered by the relevant select committees. A particularly welcome development is the provision of long-term funding certainty, with previously temporary funding for new arrivals made a permanent part of the core SICAP allocation. This represents an important step towards ensuring that community integration supports can be delivered on a more sustainable, long-term basis. This provides greater certainty for those planning and delivering services and helps sustain integration supports in communities. question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to give a breakdown of how the €150m unlocked from the NTF in the Budget will be spent over the next three years.
reply:
Budget 2027 provides for a multiannual investment of €150 million from the National Training Fund over the next three years, with €50 million to be provided in 2027.
The investment is intended to strengthen Ireland's capacity to anticipate and respond to emerging skills needs arising from technological, economic and labour market change, including the impact of artificial intelligence and the transition to a low-carbon economy.
The package responds directly to recommendations of the National Skills Council and will strengthen Ireland’s capacity to anticipate and respond to these changes. Funding will support curriculum renewal, educator capability, specialist and emerging skills needs, technology adoption, and expanded opportunities for upskilling, reskilling and lifelong learning.

Meeting future skills needs is essential to ensuring people can access quality employment, and businesses can continue to innovate and grow. This investment package will strengthen Ireland’s skills infrastructure, support labour market participation, help address skills shortages, and enhance productivity and competitiveness.

This package will support curriculum renewal, educator capability, specialist and emerging skills needs, technology adoption, and lifelong learning opportunities across the economy. My officials are currently working through the details of the package.
This additional NTF funding will be delivered through existing NTF-supported programmes and mechanisms. It is important to note that the NTF is not a direct grant mechanism for businesses. question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if a person (details supplied) in County Kildare can resume a chosen career given the previous issues that forced them to withdraw from the apprenticeship that they had commenced.
reply:
The apprenticeship system supports individuals in developing the skills, knowledge and qualifications required to build a successful career in their chosen field.
Where a registered apprentice has previously withdrawn from an apprenticeship due to personal or other circumstances, this does not necessarily prevent them from resuming their apprenticeship or pursuing a career in that occupation.
In general, a person who has withdrawn from an apprenticeship may be able to resume their apprenticeship, subject to meeting the relevant requirements, including securing an approved employer.
The options available will depend on the individual's specific circumstances, including the stage they had reached in their apprenticeship and the time elapsed since withdrawal.
The person concerned may wish to contact their Training Advisor to discuss their circumstances and the pathways available to re-engage with apprenticeship training. My Department and SOLAS are committed to supporting participation in apprenticeship and ensuring that individuals have access to appropriate information and guidance on available options.
The Apprenticeship Code of Practice for Employers and Apprentices sets out the rights and responsibilities of apprentices, employers and training providers, including arrangements relating to training, mentoring, progression and supports. The Code provides a framework for addressing issues and supporting engagement with the apprenticeship system.

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health to provide a detailed breakdown of the additional funding provided for in Budget 2027 in relation to the cost of maintaining existing levels of service, demographic growth and inflation; and separately, funding for new services, expanded services and reform.
reply:
Budget 2027 provides an additional €1.6 billion in current funding for health services. Of this increase, €155 million additional pay funding is being provided for workforce growth, equivalent to approximately 2.2% growth in staffing over the course of 2027, while €94 million additional non-pay funding is being allocated to support new and expanded services, reform initiatives and other Ministerial priorities.
The remaining €1.351 billion is being provided primarily to maintain existing levels of service and to meet underlying demand and cost pressures, including demographic growth, inflation, the full-year cost of existing commitments and pay-related costs.
The impact of demographic growth and inflation varies across different service areas. For example, demographic pressures are generally higher in areas such as Older Persons Services, reflecting population growth and ageing.
Similarly, inflationary pressures vary across care groups depending on the particular mix of non-pay expenditure. Funding requirements are therefore assessed on a service-by-service basis, taking account of the particular cost and demand drivers affecting each care group, rather than applying a single demographic or inflation assumption across the health system.
Detailed allocations by Health Region and care group will be set out in the Department's Letter of Determination and the HSE National Service Plan for 2027.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Health when a comprehensive endometriosis national service and strategy will be established.
reply:
Last October I launched the National Framework for the Management of Endometriosis. Developed by the HSE's National Women and Infants Health Programme (NWIHP), the Framework reflects the voices of patient advocates and aims to transform how endometriosis is recognised and treated across the country. Central to the Model of Care is the principle of presumed diagnosis, acknowledging that women are always the most reliable narrators of their own symptoms and pain.
The Framework marks the first step in developing a more holistic and comprehensive approach to care for women with endometriosis in Ireland.
Regional Specialist Centres for moderate cases have been established in the Rotunda Hospital, the Coombe Hospital, and University Hospital Limerick, with clinics under further development in University Hospital Galway and the National Maternity Hospital.
Two supra-regional specialist centres, in Tallaght University Hospital and Cork University Maternity Hospital, have been established for the management of complex cases.
In conjunction with the publication of the National Endometriosis Framework, I also mandated an immediate action plan to accelerate development of our endometriosis services.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the funding available for the LEADER Programme under Budget 2027.
reply:
The LEADER programme is delivered by LEADER Local Action Groups in rural areas across the country.
For the 2023-2027 LEADER programme, €180 million was allocated in advance to these Local Action Groups to provide them with greater flexibility to manage their budgets over the programming period. Funding is then paid out by my Department as costs are incurred and claims for payment are submitted.
Given the structure of the programme, expenditure is not evenly spread over each year. For example, in certain years expenditure can be lower as Local Action Groups focus on engaging with applicants to develop and progress project applications. In other years, expenditure can be higher as projects are delivered and costs are incurred.
To ensure there is sufficient funding available to deliver the 2023-2027 LEADER programme, Budget 2027 provides for funding of €43 million for LEADER for 2027, an increase of €11 million relative to the 2026 allocation.
I am committed to ensuring that the LEADER programme continues to be well funded into the future.

question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Health the reason reimbursement applications under the HSE Cross Border Directive dating back to November 2025 remain outstanding (details supplied); the number of applicants waiting six months or longer for reimbursement; whether sufficient funding has been allocated to clear the current backlog; the reason applicants are receiving conflicting information regarding the status of their claims; the urgent measures being implemented to support patients experiencing financial hardship as a result of prolonged delays; and if sufficient funding has been secured for future reimbursement demand.
reply:
The Cross Border Directive (CBD) allows public patients to access necessary healthcare, which they would have been entitled to access in the public healthcare service in Ireland, in another EU or EEA country. The patient pays upfront for the treatment and is reimbursed upon return to Ireland.
The HSE is responsible for the operation of the Cross Border Directive and has a dedicated office for that purpose.
The continued growth in use of the scheme has placed additional demands on the HSE CBD office and given rise to a build-up of applications. The increased activity is evidenced by the number of treatments reimbursed increasing by approx. 75% between 2020 and 2024.
It is important that this service operates in a responsive way and that reimbursement applications are processed within a reasonable timeframe. The HSE advises it usually aims to repay patients within 30 working days of receipt of all completed documents. The HSE advise the CBD office is currently processing applications received in early April 2026. A 6-month delay for reimbursement is clearly unacceptable. To address this the HSE has advised my Department that additional resources are being assigned to manage this increase in demand with the aim of restoring processing times to expected levels. I have set the HSE a specific target of getting back to the 30-day target by the end of 2026.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health the number of inspections, market surveillance checks and product sampling exercises carried out by the Health Products Regulatory Authority on cosmetic products used in nail salons and nail bars, including acrylic monomer liquids and gel nail products, in each of the years 2023 to 2025 and to date in 2026; the number of products found to contain substances prohibited or restricted under the EU Cosmetics Regulation; the enforcement action taken in each case.
reply:
The Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA) is the competent authority in Ireland for the regulation of medicines, medical devices, and other health products such as cosmetic products. The HPRA’s role includes helping ensure cosmetic products on the Irish market are safe for consumers and meet the requirements of the primary cosmetics legislation, as amended (‘the Cosmetics Regulation’). Each cosmetic product placed on the European market must have a designated responsible person (RP) established in the European Economic Area (EEA) or Northern Ireland.
Article 22 of the Cosmetics Regulation requires the HPRA to monitor compliance with the Regulation through in-market controls. The HPRA carries out market surveillance in collaboration with the National Environmental Health Service (NEHS), which is a part of the Health Service Executive (HSE). The NEHS’ role involves the sampling of products at retail/salon level as a part of the annual market surveillance plan.
Increased surveillance activity in late 2025 and 2026 was undertaken following the prohibition of trimethylbenzoyl diphenylphosphine oxide (TPO) in cosmetic products from 01 September 2025 under amended cosmetics legislation. This resulted in an increased number of non-compliant nail products being identified during targeted market surveillance activities.

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health to provide further details regarding her plans for the €7 million allocation for general practice reform in Budget 2027; and if the Strategic Review of General Practice will conclude by year end.
reply:
The Programme for Government includes a commitment to publish the Strategic Review of General Practice, and bring forward a new, modern GP contract.
The review is a comprehensive examination of issues affecting general practice, focusing on GP training, GP capacity, Out of Hours services reform, the eHealth Agenda, and the financial support model for general practice. Significant progress has been made under the review, and the review is to be completed this year.
The review will identify the arrangements necessary to improve the current system of GP care as part of a primary care-focused health service and when completed will make recommendations for a more sustainable general practice into the future.
Budget 2027 provides for €7 million for the reform of GP services, ensuring funding is available for appropriate recommendations to be progressed early after the review is completed. It is expected the focus of the funding will be the reform of GP out of hours services, for better and more equality of access for patients.
The implementation of the recommendations from the review will build on the progress already made under the 2019 and 2023 GP Agreements in improving and better supporting our GP services, as well the progress in increasing GP training places in recent years and in recruitment of GPs from abroad, to improve GP capacity and access to GP services.

reply:
The Department of Health recognises the important role HSE home support staff play in delivering services, particularly in rural areas where significant travel is often required.
However, responsibility for determining and reviewing official public service mileage, travel and subsistence rates rests with the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation (DPER). These rates apply across the public service and are set by DPER through the relevant circulars.
Accordingly, the Department of Health does not have a role in setting or reviewing these rates.

question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if he will commit to expanding the local improvement scheme, given the benefits to rural Ireland.
reply:
The Local Improvement Scheme (LIS) funds the upgrade of non-public rural roads and laneways, which are not usually maintained by local authorities. My department reinstated the Scheme in 2017, and it is a central element of the overall Rural Development Investment Programme. Since 2017, over €201 million has been allocated to local authorities, resulting in the improvement of over 5,500 roads.
Eligible road projects include works on non-public roads which provide access:
• to parcels of land, of which, two or more are owned/occupied by different persons, one of which must be for agricultural purposes, or
• for harvesting purposes (including turf/seaweed) for two or more persons, or
• to at least one parcel of land owned/occupied by a person engaged in agricultural activities and which separately provides access for harvesting purposes (including turf/seaweed) for at least one other person
In addition, works can be carried out on amenity roads, which are non-public roads leading to important community amenities such as graveyards, beaches and piers.
The scheme’s provision were last expanded in 2024, when the requirement for 2 landowners/occupiers to be involved in separate agricultural activities was reduced to one, and has resulted in an increase in applicants applying for works under the scheme.

question: Deputy George Lawlor asked the Minister for Health when publicly funded donor assisted reproduction services, including donor sperm IUI and IVF will be made available to same sex female couples or others who require donor gametes, if the Government has a specific timeline for the provision of this service including programmes of donor assisted treatment including sperm donation and if funding for this service have been provided for in the 2027 Estimates for her Department.
reply:
The Model of Care for Fertility was developed by the Department of Health in conjunction with the Health Service Executive (HSE) National Women and Infants Health Programme to ensure that fertility-related issues are addressed through the public health system at the lowest level of clinical intervention necessary.
The Model of Care comprises three stages of care. These begin in primary care (GPs), progress to secondary care through the six HSE-run Regional Fertility Hubs located across the country, and, where clinically indicated, advance to tertiary care.
Referrals for publicly-funded, privately-provided assisted human reproduction (AHR) treatment – including IVF (in-vitro fertilisation), ICSI (intra-cytoplasmic sperm injection) and IUI (intrauterine insemination) – commenced in September 2023, subject to patients meeting the criteria agreed by my Department and the HSE. The access criteria were developed by a multidisciplinary group, with reproductive medicine expertise and followed consultation with experts in the field along with a review of the international evidence. These criteria are in keeping with those applied in other jurisdictions.
The terms of the publicly-funded AHR treatment initiative are underpinned by the primary policy principle of supporting couples experiencing fertility issues and, most specifically, those who have been trying unsuccessfully to conceive naturally at the time in question.

The State Claims Agency (SCA) does not record information in respect of these claims in a manner which allows a response to the question, in a readily extractable format.
The SCA has been notified of 78 claims involving Members of the Public or Service Users relating to the National Ambulance Service between 01/01/2022 & 01/10/2026, as recorded on the National Incident Management System (NIMS). These claims are recorded under a variety of hazard categories on NIMS, including Crash/Collision (motor), Clinical Care, Exposure to Physical Hazards, Exposure to Psychological Hazards, and Exposure to Biological Hazards.
Of the 78 claims, 31 are finalised and 47 remain active as at 01/10/2026. A total of €1.775m has been paid out on the 31 finalised claims in the period.

The Local Improvement Scheme (LIS) funds the upgrade of non-public rural roads and laneways, which are not usually maintained by local authorities. Since 2017, over €201 million has been allocated to local authorities, resulting in the improvement of over 5,500 roads.
The 2026 scheme was launched in February with subhead funding of €17 million. While the Department provides LIS funding, local authorities administer the scheme and are responsible for managing waiting lists, selecting and prioritising roads and managing works undertaken. I thank the Deputy for their question.
Attracting and retaining newly qualified nurses and midwives is central to building a sustainable health workforce and supporting the delivery of high-quality patient care. The HSE is aware of the expected number of graduates each year and plans recruitment accordingly, matching graduates to services and locations where need is greatest.
The latest information provided by the HSE indicates that 974 graduate nurses and midwives have confirmed start dates. Of these, approximately 834 are expected to commence employment before the end of this year, with a further 140 due to commence from January onwards.
To be clear, there is no recruitment embargo in the HSE and recruitment has not ceased. Enhanced controls are currently in place in four Health Regions to ensure appointments are affordable, appropriately prioritised and aligned with areas of greatest patient and service need. Essential posts continue to be filled.
An important element of this approach is the recruitment of permanent staff to fill vacancies currently met through agency staffing. This can provide additional opportunities for graduates, support a more stable workforce, strengthen continuity of care and deliver better value for the taxpayer.

question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Health the actions are being taken to compensate the children who were affected by the delays in surgery for scoliosis and spina bifida; and if a public inquiry into the matter is being considered.
reply:
I published the independent report of the Children's Health Ireland Inquiry into Spina Bifida and Complex Scoliosis Scoping Exercise on 28 September following engagement with patients and families. Mr Farrell, the independent facilitator of the scoping exercise, recommended a Commission of Investigation covering four defined modules; waiting lists, spinal surgery, hip dysplasia and the cohort of children who were not transferred to Temple Street post 2008.

question: Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the reason no additional funding has been allocated to SICAP in Budget 2027, despite rising demand for its services; and the assessment that has been made of the impact on community organisations and the people they support.
reply:
The Social Inclusion and Community Activation Programme (SICAP) is Ireland’s primary social inclusion programme, which aims to reduce poverty and promote social inclusion and equality by supporting disadvantaged individuals and communities.
SICAP is a national programme delivered in both rural and urban areas by Local Development Companies (LDCs), providing targeted supports to those experiencing poverty, disadvantage and social exclusion.
I am pleased to have secured almost €74 million for SICAP and other social inclusion supports in Budget 2027. Just under €65 million of that allocation is for SICAP providing greater long-term funding stability for the programme and enabling the continuation of important work across the country. It should be noted that the final estimated allocations for each area will be confirmed in the Revised Estimates Volume which will be published in December, and considered by the relevant select committees.
A particularly welcome development is the provision of long-term funding certainty, with previously temporary funding for new arrivals made a permanent part of the core SICAP allocation. While this does not increase the overall SICAP allocation for 2027, it represents an important step towards ensuring that community integration supports can be delivered on a more sustainable basis. question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht for an update on the development of a new rural development policy.

I propose to take Questions Nos. 62, 73 and 83 together.
Since its launch in 2021, Our Rural Future has delivered vital investment and supports, strengthened local economies, and improved quality of life across rural Ireland.

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh den Aire Forbartha Tuaithe agus Pobail, agus Gaeltachta cárb as a dtiocfaidh an laghdú ar bhuiséad caipitil na Gaeltachta i mBuiséad 2027, agus cad é an buiséad caipitil go sonrach a bheidh ag Údarás na Gaeltachta in 2027 i gcomparáid le 2026; agus an ndéanfaidh sé ráiteas ina thaobh.
reply:
Tá leithdháileadh iomlán de €628 milliún faighte ag mo Roinn i gCáinaisnéis 2027, lena n-áirítear leithdháileadh caiptil de €273 milliún. Foilseofar leithdháileadh mionsonraithe de réir fomhír san Imleabhar Meastachán Athbhreithnithe (REV) roimh dheireadh na bliana.
Tá pleananna fíor-uaillmhianacha ag mo Roinn d'fhorbairtí caipitil chun tacú le pobail Ghaeltachta, pobal na Gaeilge agus pobail na n-oileán araon. Maoinítear na forbairtí seo as Clár C de bhuiséad na Roinne - An Ghaeltacht, an Ghaeilge agus na hOileáin. Is fiú a mheabhrú gur tháinig ardú ar an mbuiséad caipitil do Chlár C ó €30 milliún in 2025 go beagnach €55 milliún in 2026. Bhain cuid mhaith den ardú sin le trí phríomhthionscadal infreastruchtúir:
• Cé Inis Oírr,
• An tIonad Gaeilge agus Cultúir ar Shráid Fhearchair, agus
• athfhorbairt shuíomh Choláiste Lurgan in Indreabhán mar Ionad Oideachais agus Óige do Ghaeltacht Chonamara.
Rinneadh gealltanas i leith na dtionscadal seo sa Phlean Forbartha Náisiúnta, agus is cúis áthais dom an maoiniú a fháil chun iad a thabhairt i gcrích anois. Táim den tuairim mheáite go mbeidh an t-allúntas caipitil atá faighte ag mo Roinn leordhóthanach le freastal ar riachtanais chlár na Gaeltachta, na Gaeilge agus na nOileán, lena n-áirítear Údarás na Gaeltachta, i 2027 agus sna blianta ina dhiaidh sin.

question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Health the number of newly qualified nurses and midwives who have been offered jobs in hospitals on completion of their studies in 2026; the number of newly qualified nurses and midwives who have not been offered roles due to the HSE hiring freeze; if there are vacancies in hospitals not being filled due to the hiring freeze; and her plans to ensure that these newly qualified medical professionals are offered jobs in Irish hospitals.
reply:
Attracting and retaining newly qualified nurses and midwives is vital to building a sustainable workforce and supporting high-quality patient care.
I have been clear that the HSE must make every effort to offer employment opportunities to nursing and midwifery graduates and support their transition into the public health service.
Since the beginning of 2021, the number of nurses and midwives employed in the health service has increased by 9,924, an increase of almost 25%.
At the same time, the HSE must manage recruitment within available funding and ensure that new appointments are properly prioritised. Strengthened controls have been introduced, but these do not amount to a blanket recruitment embargo. Essential and patient-facing posts continue to be filled, taking account of clinical need, patient safety, patient benefit and available funding.
The latest information provided by the HSE indicates that 974 graduate nurses and midwives have confirmed start dates. Of these, approximately 834 are expected to commence before the end of this year, with a further 140 due to commence from January onwards.
The HSE continues to make offers where vacancies exist, including in areas with workforce pressures and high agency usage. Retaining newly qualified nurses and midwives within the public health service remains a priority for Government.

question: Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if he will report on his engagements regarding the LEADER programme under the next EU budgetary cycle.
reply:

To facilitate the on-going negotiation process for the post 2027 period, the Department of Agriculture Food and the Marine established a CAP Consultative Committee, which includes representation from my department and other rural stakeholders.
I acknowledge that the proposed consolidation of the main EU funding programmes within a single National and Regional Partnership Plan for each Member State, financed through one overarching fund, is leading to uncertainty. However it is important to note that the draft regulations include the continuation of the LEADER programme as a mandatory measure.
Furthermore, the current draft regulations also proposed a 10% rural target in recognition of the valuable support provided to rural communities. I will continue to work to ensure that this provision can serve to provide adequate funding for LEADER in the next programming period.
My department continues to input into these draft EU regulations, to ensure continued prioritisation of LEADER in Ireland, and has consistently emphasised the importance of a ringfenced allocation for LEADER, to ensure the post-2027 programme can continue its vital role.

question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to provide an update on the national policy statement on outdoor learning and play in ELC.
reply:
The Department of Children, Disability and Equality, mission is to enhance the lives of children, young people, adults, families and communities, recognising diversity and promoting equality of opportunity.
The key strategy delivering this mission in early learning and care is the First 5: Whole-of-Government Strategy for Babies, Young Children and their Families 2019-2028. This strategy recognises the importance of outdoor learning and play in young children’s lives.
Outdoor play is a core component of Aistear: the Early Childhood Curriculum Framework, recently updated by the NCCA, and the Síolta, the National Quality Framework for Early Childhood Education in Ireland.
'When the Roof is the Sky', is Tusla, Early Years Inspectorate’s guidance for Early Learning and Care and School-Age Childcare services operating fully or mostly outdoors, promoting safe, enriching outdoor play and learning for children. This guidance published in 2023, encourages all services to reflect on how they use their outdoor space, and to take measures to ensure children have increased opportunities to spend time outdoors.
A policy statement on Outdoor Play and Learning in Early Learning and Care and School Age Childcare, including Childminding Settings, in Ireland, is currently under development. Once finalised later this year, it will be published in draft form, welcoming consultation from the sector.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the measures being taken to increase childcare capacity in the Kilshanroe, Johnstownbridge, Carbury and Enfield areas of county Kildare; and whether an assessment has been carried out of childcare demand and available capacity in these rapidly growing communities.
reply:

Early learning and childcare capacity is increasing. Data from the Annual Early Years Sector Profile 2024/25 shows that the estimated number of enrolments increased by approximately 25% from the 2021/22 programme year.
The most recent published capacity data for the 2024/25 programme year estimated that there were 12,087 children enrolled in ELC and SAC services in County Kildare. This data also indicated that 43% of service providers in County Kildare had at least one vacant place and 52% had a waiting list.
However, it appears that demand for early learning and childcare remains higher than available supply in certain parts of the country, particularly for younger children.
The Department of Children, Disability and Equality is supporting the development of early learning and childcare capacity nationally through Core Funding which was introduced in 2022.

The Government is also supporting the expansion of capacity through capital funding. question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to provide an update on the public consultation on the development of an induction process, as committed to under Nurturing Skills.
reply:
The Department continues to roll out ‘Nurturing Skills: The Workforce Plan for Early Learning and Care and School-Age Childcare, 2022-2028’. It aims to strengthen the ongoing process of professionalisation for those working in the sector. It contains a range of commitments to raise the profile of careers in the sector and to support recruitment, retention and diversity in the workforce.
Nurturing Skills recognises the importance of an induction process for new entrants beginning their first job in the profession, to help them adjust to their new professional role with the support of experienced colleagues. The need for an induction process reflects on the responsibilities that are open to a student on a practice placement.
Nurturing Skills states that work will begin during the lifetime of the plan (2022-2028) on developing and incrementally introducing an induction process, through research, consultation, piloting and review, along with actions to develop services’ capacity and external supports for induction. This process will support movement towards a future requirement for all entrants into the profession (other than childminders) at all qualification levels to complete a supported induction period.

question: Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if he will provide an update on plans to expand Líonra Gaeilge scheme to new towns.
reply:
Irish Language Networks may be recognised under the Gaeltacht Act 2012 provided that language plans have been agreed with the communities in the various networks in accordance with prescribed language planning criteria. Foras na Gaeilge is responsible under the Gaeltacht Act, 2012 for supporting organisations in the preparation and implementation of language plans in Irish Language Networks.
Three Irish Language Networks have been approved to date under the Gaeltacht Act: Inis, Baile Locha Riach and Cluain Dolcáin. In addition, two further networks in the north – Carn Tóchair and Iarthar Bhéal Feirste – have been approved under a non-statutory process administered by Foras na Gaeilge.
In 2020, Foras na Gaeilge reviewed the organisation's Irish Language Community Scheme and, as a successor, the Irish Language Network Development Scheme was launched. Among the aims of this scheme is that current grantees place a particular emphasis on working towards recognition as an Irish Language Network. Through the scheme, groups are being empowered to come forward and enter the next round of both the statutory application process in operation in the southern jurisdiction and the non-statutory process in the north.
Officials from my Department are currently engaging with their counterparts in Foras na Gaeilge regarding the potential expansion of the number of Networks. An announcement in this regard will be made in due course.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to provide an update on the mid-point review of Nurturing Skills, which was due out by 2025, given that the mid-point review and revised implementation plan are scheduled to be completed in early Q2 2026.
reply:
The Department continues to implement Nurturing Skills: The Workforce Plan for Early Learning and Care and School-Age Childcare 2022-2028, which sets out a long-term plan to support a well-qualified, skilled, diverse and valued professional workforce that is centred on children’s rights, needs and potential and that provides quality experiences for children in partnership with families, and which continues to advance its professional development within a coherent and competent system.
The midpoint review, originally due in 2025, was postponed to allow key evidence to inform the review process, including findings from the OECD TALIS Starting Strong Survey, the CSO Early Learning and Care Graduate Outcomes report, and the publication of Shaping the Future: Early Years Action Plan.
The review has now been completed and draws on a comprehensive evidence base, including national and international research, administrative and sectoral data, and extensive stakeholder engagement. Consultation undertaken as part of the review included stakeholder engagement sessions, focus groups with early years educators and school-age childcare practitioners, and survey responses from the workforce.
The review assesses progress made across all five pillars of Nurturing Skills and includes a revised implementation plan covering the period 2026-2028. It identifies key achievements to date, considers ongoing challenges, and sets out priority actions for the remainder of the plan's lifetime.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to provide details of the proposed extension to the deadline for registration of childminders with Tusla as required under the National Action Plan for Childminding 2021-2028.
reply:
The National Action Plan for Childminding 2021-2028 (NAPC) committed to a review of the initial implementation of the regulations before 2028. Acting on feedback received from childminders and childminding representative organisations, I have brought the review forward, to ensure there is sufficient time to implement any changes arising from the review, before the end of the transition period.
The review which is being managed by an external research company commenced on the 19 June. Preliminary findings were delivered at the end of September, with the final report due at the end of October. As indicated in my Budget 2027 speech, these preliminary findings from the consultation suggest childminders want more time before mandatory registration. I will be making an announcement on this in the near future, looking to ensure childminders have the time and space they need. Following conclusion of this review and receipt of the final report, I will give consideration to the appropriate next steps.

question: Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the status of plans to provide a community centre-community facility in the Garryowen area of Limerick.
reply:
The Community Centre Investment Fund (CCIF) was introduced to provide high quality, accessible community spaces that are available to communities in both rural and urban areas. Since 2022, some €112 million has been allocated for the enhancement and refurbishment of existing facilities and the construction of new centres where such a need has been identified.
Earlier this year, I launched the latest round of CCIF for enhancement and refurbishment of existing centres. The closing date has now passed and I look forward to announcing successful projects before year-end.
I understand from Limerick City & County Council that they are working with relevant stakeholders for the development of a community centre for the Garryowen area, albeit that discussions are at an early stage.
I am committed to delivering further iterations of the CCIF in the coming years in line with the commitment in the Programme for Government for this to become a permanent rolling fund. I have indicated previously that the 2027 scheme will focus on new build centres and the eligibility criteria and funding limits that will apply will be announced when that scheme is launched next year. In the meantime, communities planning to develop a new community centre should be engaging with their local authority to advance the preparatory work required to be in a position to apply for funding.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if funding is available for the maintenance or repair of damage to playgrounds in disadvantaged rural towns following damage due to anti-social behaviour or wear and tear.
reply:
The Department of Children, Disability and Equality provides funding to local authorities through the annual Capital Grant Scheme for Play and Recreation, which supports the development of new play and recreation facilities as well as the refurbishment and upgrading of existing facilities. The scheme can support improvements to playgrounds, including the replacement or upgrading of equipment that has deteriorated through normal wear and tear.
The Capital Grant Scheme for Play and Recreation has operated annually since 2013 and continues to support local authorities in improving the quality, accessibility and inclusivity of play facilities for children and young people throughout the country, including in rural communities.
Under the scheme, local authorities may apply for funding for projects aimed at refurbishing existing play and recreation facilities or developing new facilities. In 2026, funding of up to €22,000 per project was available, with each local authority required to provide matching funding of at least 25% of the grant awarded.
Responsibility for the day-to-day management, maintenance and repair of public playgrounds rests primarily with the relevant local authority. As such, there is no dedicated scheme within the Department specifically for repairing damage arising from anti-social behaviour.
However, local authorities may consider applying under the Capital Grant Scheme for eligible refurbishment and upgrade works, subject to the terms and conditions of the s

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if her Department will encourage and support more registered childminders in rural and growing communities to meet growing demand for childcare.
reply:
Childminders are a hugely important part of early learning and care and school-age childcare provision, and they continue to be the option of choice for many families.
All paid, non-relative childminders who work in their own homes can now register with Tusla and access the National Childcare Scheme.
The National Action Plan for Childminding 2021-2028 set out a pathway for the extension of regulation to childminders. A key objective of the National Action Plan for Childminding is to enable parents who use childminders to also benefit from State subsidies through the National Childcare Scheme. The Childcare Support Act 2018, which provides a statutory basis for the National Childcare Scheme, specifies that only Tusla-registered childminders are eligible to participate in the Scheme. The limitation of public funding schemes to Tusla-registered childcare providers helps to ensure that public funding is provided where there is assurance of the quality of provision.
As a result of the commencement of the relevant parts of the Child Care (Amendment) Act 2024 and the Childminding Services Regulations, which came into effect on 30 September 2024, childminders are now able to apply to register with Tusla. The 2024 Act, under which the timeframes are established, provides for a transition period, in which childminders are being encouraged and supported to register, but registration is not yet mandatory. This phased approach aims to facilitate the largest possible number of childminders

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality her plans for increasing capacity and funding for additional early childhood care and education spaces in Kildare.
reply:
Improving access to quality and affordable early learning and childcare is a key priority of Government.
Early learning and childcare capacity is increasing. Data from the Annual Early Years Sector Profile 2024/25 shows that the estimated number of enrolments increased by approximately 25% from the 2021/22 programme year.
However, it appears that demand for early learning and childcare remains higher than available supply in certain parts of the country, particularly for younger children.
The Department of Children, Disability and Equality is supporting the development of early learning and childcare capacity nationally through Core Funding which was introduced in 2022.
This provides stability to services, and reduces the risk associated with opening a new service or expanding an already existing service.
The Government is also supporting the expansion of capacity through capital funding. The Building Blocks Extension Grant Scheme, which is currently operating, is designed to increase capacity in the 1–3-year-old, pre–Early Childhood Care and Education, age range for full day care. Core Funding Partner Services could apply for capital funding to physically extend their premises or to construct or purchase new premises. Two services from Kildare are working closely with the Department to deliver quality, affordable places.
Separately, the State-led early learning and childcare capital programme will invest €135 million in buildings in the coming five years to support the expan

question: Deputy Denise Mitchell asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the steps being taken to encourage and incentivise childcare providers that have previously left the core funding scheme to rejoin.
reply:
I am aware that a small number of providers are regrettably considering withdrawing from the Core Funding scheme.
The Department, through the local Childcare Committees, engages directly with any such service to highlight the benefits of staying in Core Funding, not only for their services but also for the families who avail of them. I am hopeful that the providers may reconsider their decision.
As Core Funding is an optional scheme, service providers have the autonomy and business freedom to withdraw from or choose not to participate in Core Funding, even though this will result in the loss of the significant financial support it offers them and the substantial benefits and certainty it brings to families.
While the State cannot mandate providers to participate in the scheme, Core Funding has been designed with maximum participation of providers in mind as reflected in the year-on-year growth of investment in the Scheme (rising from €259 million in year 1 to over €482 million in year 5). This represents an increase of 86% in Core Funding in four years.
I was delighted to announce further investment in Core Funding in Budget 2027. The additional funding being made available in 2027 will see the projected allocation for Core Funding in the next programme year, which begins in September 2027, increase to over €650 million. Such an increase would represent an additional €170 million on the current allocation, or a 35% increase.
The continued investment in Core Funding will suppo

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if she will provide a schedule of external communications and or public relations services provided to her Department and bodies under her aegis, by the costs incurred, the service provider name, nature and or summary of services provided; and if any of the service providers engaged are contracted to her Department or to the body under her aegis, in each of the years 2023 to date in 2026.
reply: The Department is currently collating the information requested and a reply will issue directly to the Deputy on this matter as soon as possible.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the way in which Budget 2027 will support community centres.
reply:
The Community Centre Investment Fund (CCIF) was introduced to provide high quality community facilities that are available to community groups in both urban and rural communities. Through the CCIF, some €112 million has been allocated for the enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres and the construction of new centres where such a need has been identified.
I launched the latest round of funding under CCIF 2026 on the 26th of March for enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres. The fund will be delivered across 2 categories with maximum funding levels of €25,000 and €100,000 respectively. The closing date for the CCIF 2026 has now passed.
Applications are currently being assessed and I look forward to announcing the successful projects under category 1 which provides funding of up to €25,000 in the coming weeks with approvals under category 2 providing funding of up to €100,000 being announced before year-end.
I am committed to delivering further iterations of the scheme in the coming years in line with the commitment in the Programme for Government for this to become a permanent rolling fund. I have indicated previously that the 2027 scheme will focus on new build centres and the eligibility criteria and funding limits that will apply will be announced when that scheme is launched next year.
My Department secured funding of €628 million in Budget 2027. This funding will work to ensure that community centres across the country continue to b

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the reason for the delay in developing a national policy statement on the use of digital technologies and digital learning in Early Learning and Care, building on OECD (2023) Empowering Young Children in the Digital Age; and the status of this work.
reply:
The Department of Children, Disability and Equality, mission is to enhance the lives of children, young people, adults, families and communities, recognising diversity and promoting equality of opportunity.
As identified in ‘Ireland’s Literacy, Numeracy and Digital Literacy Strategy 2024-2033: Every Learner from Birth to Young Adulthood’, the meaning of digital literacy and the use of digital technologies are complex, particularly in the birth to three age cohort. Parents, early years educators and childminders are often presented with conflicting information. Given the need for greater clarity in this area, a commitment was made by the department to develop a policy statement on the use of digital technologies in ELC.
While Aistear, the early childhood curriculum framework does not set specific expectations for digital literacy, it does suggest possible opportunities for parents, early years educators and childminders to integrate digital technologies into children’s learning experiences. Through active, playful and enquiry led engagement, young children are supported to acquire the foundations for digital learning that are deepened and refined as they move through the education system.
A policy statement on the use of Digital Technologies in Early Learning and Care and School Age Childcare, including Childminding Settings, in Ireland, is currently under development. This policy sets out a national policy to guide the safe, ethical and developmentally appropriate use of digi

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the reason the consultation process on terminology relating to the ELC and SAC sector, committed to under First Five, has been put under review.
reply:
First 5 is a whole-of-government strategy to improve the lives of babies, young children and their families. It is a ten-year plan to help make sure all children have positive early experiences and get a great start in life. Under action D.1.A.8. there is a commitment to undertake a consultation process on terminology relating to the Early Learning and Care (ELC) and School Age Childcare (SAC) sector.
In this context, in 2024 the Department of Children, Disability, and Equality (DCDE) completed a review and frequency analysis of the terminology currently in use across a range of relevant sources. This work examined terminology as it appears in registered service names, media content, and approved academic qualification titles, and also involved engagement with international colleagues, with a view to establishing current prevalence of terms used across the sector nationally and internationally.
Timelines for a wider consultation process on terminology are currently under review while the Department focuses its engagement with the sector on the development of Shaping the Future, the Early Years Action Plan, and the National Conversation on Education. As part of the National Conversation on Education: the First 5 years and School-Age Childcare, DCDE undertook a public consultation process on the future of ELC and SAC including childminding. Full details of the consultation process are available on gov.ie. The feedback gathered through the consultation process is currently being

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the reason for the delay in a real-time finder of regulated ELC and SAC settings, which has been pushed to phase 3 of the First Five Implementation Plan.
reply:
First 5 is a whole-of-government strategy to improve the lives of babies, young children and their families. It is a ten-year plan to help make sure all children have positive early experiences and get a great start in life.
Under action C.8.2.9, First 5 commits to explore the potential to develop a real-time finder of regulated early learning and childcare places with links to inspection reports and other relevant information.
This action needs to be considered within the context of the current prioritisation of work under way to replace the platform for early learning and childcare schemes and programmes. A multiphase programme of work was tendered for in late 2025 to:
a) review options for a long-term digital system for early learning and childcare, including the option of modernising the existing system or developing a new system and
b) carry out a detailed analysis of the proposed long-term-digital system identified to include functional and non-functional specifications.
Following conclusion of this procurement, Deloitte were appointed in late March 2026. They will also carry out detailed requirements gathering and provide the necessary technical documentation to enable a call for tender for the design and build and implementation of such a system. This work will conclude in the coming weeks.

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if she will clarify a matter (details supplied).
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 652, 653, 654, 655 and 656 together.
The Deputy has asked a number of related questions about the Assessment of Need process and the possibility of duplication of effort within the process. The process is briefly outlined below including certain key aspects which should address those questions.
Under the Disability Act 2005, an Assessment of Need is a specific assessment process carried out by the HSE to determine whether a child or young person has a disability as defined within the Act, and if they do, to identify the health and education needs (if any) arising from that disability.
A person may apply for an Assessment of Need if they think they or their child has a disability as defined under the Disability Act. The definition of disability is very specific in the Act. It is defined as a substantial restriction in the person’s capacity i.e. that a person has a significant difficulty with communication, learning, mobility or significantly disordered cognitive processes. In addition, this restriction should be permanent or likely to be permanent and require the continued provision of services to meet the person’s needs.
An application for an assessment is need is made by the applicant, if they are an adult born on or after 1 June 2002, or on behalf of the applicant where they are a child or are not in a position to apply on their own behalf.

question: Deputy Martin Kenny asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the number of hectares of land currently under afforestation in Ireland.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 650 and 651 together.
There are over 800,000 hectares of forests in Ireland. This represents just under 12% of the total area of the State. For the last hundred years we have been creating new forests in Ireland, and we keep building on this legacy. Ireland is a success story, as going from 1% forest cover to 12% today, we have reversed centuries of deforestation.
There are 84,013 hectares of afforested lands currently eligible to receive premia payments.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht when a decision will be made on RRDF applications.
reply:
The Rural Regeneration and Development Fund (RRDF) is a major capital investment programme, which seeks to support large-scale, ambitious projects that can achieve sustainable economic and social development in rural areas. The focus of the RRDF is on rural towns and villages with a population of less than 10,000 people.
To date, the RRDF has awarded over €611 million for 271 projects across Ireland. The assessment process for the RRDF applications received under this 6th Call for Proposals, which is undertaken on a competitive basis, is ongoing. Following the assessment of applications, it is anticipated an announcement of successful projects will be made before the end of this year.
I am committed to ensuring that the RRDF can continue to support high quality and transformational projects across rural Ireland in line with the objectives of Our Rural Future and the Town Centre First policy.

question: Deputy Martin Kenny asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine for a breakdown on where the recent cases of bluetongue have been found; if they were found on farms or in meat processing plants / factories; and to clarify if they were ovine or bovine.
reply:
As of 10 October 2026, 28 confirmed bluetongue herd cases have been recorded during the current reporting period. These comprise of 26 bovine herd cases and 2 ovine cases.
The bovine herd cases were recorded in Cork(2), Dublin(1), Kildare(5), Longford(1), Louth(1), Monaghan(1), Roscommon(1) Waterford(2), Westmeath(1), Wexford(9) and Wicklow(2). The two ovine cases were recorded in Kildare and Wexford.
None of the recent confirmed cases were detected in meat processing plants. The cases were identified though clinical investigations, targeted screening or private sampling undertaken for other purposes such as trade.
Bluetongue is a notifiable disease in Ireland. Where a veterinary practitioner suspects the Bluetongue virus disease, the regional veterinary office should be contacted so that the case may be investigated. If the disease cannot be ruled out on clinical examination, Departmental Veterinary Inspectors will take samples for laboratory testing.
Additional information, including a regularly updated case-table can be found on the Government website at: www.gov.ie/bluetongue.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if his Department has formulated any contingency measures to support Irish farmers in the event of a highly reduced EU CAP budget.
reply:
Negotiations on the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) for 2028–2034, which will determine the overall EU budget available for the post-2027 Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), are ongoing, alongside negotiations on the future CAP regulations.
Once these negotiations have concluded at European Council level, Ireland’s overall CAP allocation and the national co-financing rates required under the agreed regulations will be clear.
My Department will then work on designing the CAP chapter of the new National and Regional Partnership Plan, taking account of the specific needs and circumstances of Irish farmers and the wider agricultural sector. The objective will be to develop a CAP chapter that supports viable farm incomes, food production and food security, environmental sustainability and the vitality of rural communities, while ensuring that the measures are practical and workable for farmers and the implementing authorities.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the cooperation or discussions undertaken with his northern Ireland counterpart with respect to the monitoring of bluetongue infection rates.
reply:
My Department engages with counterparts in Northern Ireland's Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs regarding bluetongue and other animal diseases of common concern. This engagement occurs on a regular basis and information regarding surveillance of Bluetongue is shared.
Further information on Bluetongue can be found at Bluetongue Virus (www.gov.ie/en/department-of-agriculture-food-and-the-marine/publications/bluetongue-virus/).

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he can confirm reports that a registered racing greyhound died during the week of 22 June 2026 while being transported in very high temperatures between Croom, County Limerick and County Carlow; and if he can confirm that the owner of the vehicle in which the dog was travelling did not hold valid type 1 transporter authorisation for this vehicle.
reply:
My Department strongly condemns any cruelty or mistreatment of animals. It is the policy of my Department to investigate all allegations of illegal or criminal behaviour and prepare files for prosecution where appropriate. My Department operates a confidential animal welfare helpline through which members of the public can report suspected cases of animal welfare breaches: The dedicated email address and helpline in place for reporting suspected cases of animal welfare are:
Helpline Phone No: 01 607 2379.
Email address - animalwelfare@agriculture.gov.ie
My Department’s helpline has received no report in relation to the report referenced by the Deputy.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the specific recommendations in respect of greyhound welfare and integrity as contained in a report (details supplied) are to be funded by the allocation of a further 2.9 million to the Horse and Greyhound Fund in Budget 2027.
reply:
Rásaíocht Con Éireann (RCÉ) is a commercial state body established under the Greyhound Industry Act 1958 chiefly to control greyhound racing and to improve and develop the greyhound industry. RCÉ is a body corporate and a separate legal entity to the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine.
As recommended by the Public Accounts Committee, my Department arranged for an external review of its governance of both the Horse and Greyhound Racing Fund (the Fund) and the bodies in receipt of the Fund in the context of the operating legislative and policy framework.
In respect of RCÉ, the review, conducted by Indecon, found that while RCÉ has made progress on the welfare agenda with a welfare programme being implemented, more work needs to be done. The review recommended that the share of the Fund ringfenced for welfare and integrity purposes for RCÉ should be increased over the medium term and communicated in the annual parameters letter to the body and that my Department should agree stretch targets with RCÉ in respect of its care and welfare programme and review these on a regular basis.
My Department will continue to work with RCÉ on greyhound welfare and integrity both in the context of the new Animal Welfare Strategy which I will launch shortly and the implementation of the Indecon Report findings and recommendations.
I expect the outcome of this deliberative process to be in place in the first half of next year and that it will involve new stretch targets and performance

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he has received reports that veterinary personnel at Greyhound Racing Ireland licensed greyhound tracks are under instruction not to euthanise injured dogs; that greyhound owners are being advised to attend their own vets should their dog be so seriously injured as to require euthanasia, and that this is being done to minimise the number of track deaths being recorded and reported.
reply:
Rásaíocht Con Éireann (RCÉ) is a commercial state body established under the Greyhound Industry Act 1958 chiefly to control greyhound racing and to improve and develop the greyhound industry. RCÉ is a body corporate and a separate legal entity to the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine.
The question raised by the Deputy is an operational matter for RCÉ and, therefore, the question has been referred to that body for direct reply.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the reasons his Department rejected an offer of the planting of a forest in Adare, County Limerick to offset the carbon footprint for the hosting of a sporting event (details supplied); the reason they refused to meet with and engaged with the project promoters; and the measures being put in place to support carbon offsetting for this event.
reply:
I very much welcome and support progress being made by those seeking to establish new forests to help offset the carbon footprint associated with the hosting of an event in Adare. My Department has met with anyone who sought a meeting in this regard.
My Department provides a range of supports for the establishment of new forests. The establishment of new forests can provide a lasting environmental legacy beyond the event itself, delivering long-term benefits including carbon sequestration, biodiversity enhancement and an increase in Ireland’s overall forest cover.
My Department engaged in a Pre-Application Discussion (PAD) relating to seven potential planting areas at Adare in January 2026 and four of the areas were considered potentially capable of progressing subject the relevant licensing and environmental assessment processes. For archaeological reasons, three were deemed to be unsuitable at pre application discussion stage. My Department has not yet received any formal application related to any of the potential planting areas referred to above.
Two afforestation applications, not associated with the seven sites above, have been submitted to my Department in respect of lands owned by a public authority. These applications relate to carbon offsetting for the event.
My Department remains available to provide information and guidance on the forestry supports available and to assist those seeking to progress applications.

question: Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to consider purchasing a ship to be used by his Department to transport cattle from Ireland to international markets.
reply:
The intra community trade and export of live animals to third countries from Ireland is a private commercial activity which is regulated by my Department in accordance with EU and National Regulations. As such my Department is not considering the purchase of a ship to be used to transport cattle to international markets.
In order for Roll on Roll off vessel (RoRo/Ferry ) to be allowed carry vehicles containing livestock out of Ireland it must be approved by my Department in accordance with the provisions of Statutory Instrument (S.I.) No. 580/2007 - Diseases of Animals (Animal Transport) (Roll-on Roll-off Vessels) Order 2007.
In order for a dedicated livestock vessel to be allowed load and transport livestock out of Ireland it must be approved by my Department under the provisions of Statutory Instrument (S.I.) . No. 356/2016 - Carriage of Livestock by Sea Regulations 2016.
While this trade is a private commercial activity my Department is available to assess and approve vessels under the above Regulations to facilitate the transport of livestock out of Ireland.

question: Deputy Rose Conway-Walsh asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht his assessment of the future impact on rural and community development in eastern Mayo and Sligo if the proposed Sligo greenway is installed on the disused Western Rail Corridor railway line.
reply:
The Government’s rural development policy, Our Rural Future, recognises the important role that investment in outdoor recreation infrastructure can play in supporting the economic and social development of rural communities. My department is supporting the development of the outdoor recreation sector through the delivery of “Embracing Ireland’s Outdoors”, Ireland’s national outdoor recreation strategy.
Greenway projects can support tourism, stimulate local enterprise and create opportunities for employment and economic activity in towns and villages. In addition to their economic contribution, amenities such as greenways provide valuable opportunities for recreation, physical activity, and social interaction, enhancing the quality of life of local residents and making rural communities more attractive places to live, work and visit.
There is a commitment within the Programme for Government to ‘develop a connected network of greenways and cycle routes across Ireland’ signalling Government’s commitment to progress Greenway routes. This is supported by the NDP Transport Sectoral Plan, published in November 2025, which committed €360m per annum for active travel and Greenways until 2030.
My colleague the Minister for Transport holds responsibility for the overall policy and exchequer funding in relation to national and regional greenways. The planning design and construction of individual greenways is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland in conjunction with the relevant

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he is considering the introduction of a dedicated farm succession scheme to support the transfer of farms to younger generations.
reply:
Supporting young farmers and facilitating generational renewal is a priority of mine and critical to ensure a bright future for the agri-food sector.
There are currently a range of supports in place. Ireland’s CAP Strategic Plan 2023-2027 provides substantial resources focused on generational renewal. There are also strong national taxation measures to facilitate succession and assist land mobility. In addition, my Department continue to work with the Strategic Banking Corporation Of Ireland (SBCI) on the funding requirements for young farmers.
