question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the measures he will put in place to offset the carbon footprint of an event (details supplied); and the way in which sustainability will be promoted at the event.
reply:
The event in question is expected to be one of the largest sporting events ever held in Ireland. It is intended that a key sustainability initiative for this event will be a major planting scheme of native Irish trees (within Adare and across the county of Limerick) which will significantly offset the carbon footprint generated by the hosting of the event.
My Department is currently engaging with an Irish philanthropist and with the Department of Agriculture in relation to this initiative and both the local authority and the host venue have identified suitable lands for tree planting. It is envisaged that up to 100 acres in total could be planted using a combination of conventional planting methodologies and a pilot planting scheme using the Miyawaki method, a dense planting approach. With a view to making this event a more sustainable one, I intend to allocate up to €500,000 towards this tree planting initiative, once an agreed approach has been reached with all relevant stakeholders.
It is the ambition of government that this event will be the most sustainable edition in its long history, supported by green initiatives, government funding, and corporate partnerships. In this regard, the event organisers are currently preparing a sustainability plan for the event.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport whether any consideration was given to expanding the basic income for the arts scheme in Budget 2027.
reply: The introduction of the Basic Income for the Arts scheme on a permanent basis is a major milestone for the arts in Ireland and has been a priority for me as Minister since taking office. Under this scheme, 2,000 artists will be provided with funding of €325 per week for three years. My priority in the context of Budget 2027 was to secure the necessary substantial resources to fund the full year cost of the scheme which was announced earlier this year.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht his views on the results of the Social Inclusion and Community Activation Programme (SICAP) Annual Report 2025.
reply:
The Social Inclusion and Community Activation Programme (SICAP) is Ireland’s primary social inclusion programme, which aims to reduce poverty and promote social inclusion and equality by supporting disadvantaged individuals and communities.
SICAP is a national programme delivered in both rural and urban areas by Local Development Companies (LDCs), providing targeted supports to those experiencing poverty, disadvantage and social exclusion.
I was very happy to launch the SICAP Annual Report 2025 in September with my colleague Minister Chambers. The Report provides a comprehensive overview of programme delivery, detailed analysis of programme beneficiaries, supports provided and progress achieved in 2025.
The 2025 report highlights the impact of the current programme, which has a renewed focus on targeting those who are most disadvantaged in Irish society. To support this objective, resources are targeted locally based on local needs and local knowledge. By the end of 2025, key performance indicators (KPIs) for the programme were exceeded by 22%, indicating strong programme reach among marginalised individuals and communities.
In 2025, 3,097 Local Community Groups and 33,714 individuals were supported by the programme, with significant levels of new participation. The report also acknowledges the important role of the Local Community Development Committees (LCDCs), the Local Development Companies (LDCs), local community groups and volunteers who support the delivery of the Prog

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport whether, under the multi-annual funding arrangement for RTÉ agreed in 2024, the amount paid to RTÉ under section 123(3) of the Broadcasting Act 2009 is calculated as the difference between a fixed total funding figure and television licence fee receipts; if so, whether any increase in licence fee receipts arising from improved compliance would reduce the Exchequer contribution rather than increase total funding to RTÉ.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 474, 475 and 476 together.
The Revised Estimates 2025 and 2026 set out the total public funding allocated to RTÉ in each of those years, split between funding allocated through TV licence receipts and through direct Exchequer funding. question: Deputy Holly Cairns asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her attention has been drawn to shortfalls at a school (details supplied) resulting in graduates being unable to have their diplomas recognised by an organisation; if this issue has been satisfactorily resolved; and if not, if a process has been put in place to allow graduates of this course to gain recognition.
reply:
The Teaching Council is the body with the statutory authority and responsibility for the regulation of the teaching profession in Ireland including the registration of teachers in the State.
The Teaching Council register teachers under the Teaching Council Act 2001-2015 and in line with the Teaching Council Registration Regulations 2025. As set out in the Schedule of the Regulations, the Council registers teachers under five routes of registration: Route 1 - Primary, Route 2 - Post-primary, Route 3 - Further Education, Route 4 - Other and Route 5 - Student Teacher. The qualification requirements for each route are set out in the Schedule of the Regulations. Per the legislation, my department has no role in the registration of individual teachers.
As the independent regulator of the teaching profession in Ireland, the Teaching Council’s role is to protect the public by promoting and regulating professional standards in teaching. This is carried out through the statutory registration of teachers, ensuring a highly qualified teaching profession whose members meet and uphold high standards of professional competence and conduct.
The qualification requirements for Route 2 (post-primary) can be summarised as follows:
Completion of an undergraduate degree in teacher education, accredited by the Teaching Council which satisfies the requirements for at least one curricular subject:
or
Completion of a post-primary programme of teacher education (ITE) accredited by the Teaching Council

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth the changes to school transport fees planned for 2027-2028 arising from budget 2027.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is now larger than ever, with 181,000 children and young people using school transport to get to and from school every day.
In line with the Programme for Government commitment to ensure the financial sustainability of the scheme, the school transport fees will be restored to the original 2021 rates for the 2027/28 school year.
This means €100 per primary level pupil, which equates to 55 cent per school day. There is a family cap of €220 per year for primary school.
While at post primary, it will be €350 per pupil, or €2.11 per school day, with an overall family cap of €650.
€3.92 is the maximum daily cost to a family, no matter how many children per family use the service.
Based on an estimated transport cost of between €1,400 and €1,500 per pupil, the State funds the vast majority of the cost of school transport. For primary pupils, where families contribute €100, the State subsidy is over 92%. For post-primary pupils, where families contribute €350, the State subsidy is over 75%.
Importantly, school transport remains free for the 46,000 pupils with specialised transport needs and medical card holders.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth the impact the additional teachers provided for in budget 2027 will have on class sizes and the pupil-teacher ratio.
reply:
Budget 2027 provides for a record investment of €14.435 billion in our school-level education. This is an increase of €5.3 billion (58%) since 2021.
Funding for approximately 1,600 new teachers has been provided for in Budget 2027. This brings the total number of teachers in our school system to circa. 82,000. Of these 1,600 new teachers, 1,353?are special education teachers working in special classes, special schools and mainstream, to further support children with special educational needs. Additional Home School Community Liaison coordinators are being provided for in our DEIS Plus schools. Increased school leadership supports are also being provided, increasing the number of deputy principals in our schools. These additional teachers will improve the primary pupil teacher ratio which, in 2025/26, stood at 12.6:1, comparing favourably with the OECD average of 14:1.
The primary staffing schedule has improved from an average allocation ratio of 26:1 five years ago to 23:1 for the current school year, the lowest ever at primary level. More favourable staffing arrangements apply in DEIS Urban Band 1 and DEIS Plus schools. Average class sizes have fallen from 24.1 to 21.9 pupils in that time.

question: Deputy Johnny Mythen asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the total capital funding allocated in Budget 2027 for Gaeltacht development, Irish-language infrastructure and Irish-language organisations, compared with 2026; the reasons for any reduction in capital expenditure; and the way in which his Department intends to ensure that investment is sufficient to support the sustainability of Gaeltacht communities and the objectives of the Government's Irish-language policy.
reply:
My Department has received a total allocation of €628 million in Budget 2027, including a capital allocation of €273 million. A breakdown by sub-head of the allocation will be published in the Revised Estimates Volume (REV) before the end of the year.
My Department has very ambitious plans for capital developments to support Gaeltacht communities, the Irish language community and island communities alike. These developments are funded under Programme C of the Department’s budget – The Gaeltacht, the Irish Language and the Islands. It is worth noting that the capital budget for Programme C increased from €30 million in 2025 to almost €55 million in 2026. A significant portion of that increase related to three key infrastructure projects:
• Inis Oírr Pier,
• The redevelopment of the Conradh na Gaeilge headquarters on Harcourt Street as a language and cultural hub, and
• The redevelopment of the Coláiste Lurgan site in Indreabhán as an Education and Youth Hub for the Connemara Gaeltacht.
A commitment regarding these projects was made in the National Development Plan, and I am pleased to have secured the necessary funding to bring them to completion. It is my considered view that the capital allocation secured by my Department will be sufficient to meet the requirements of the Gaeltacht, the Irish Language, and the Islands programme in 2027 and beyond.

reply:

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide a detailed breakdown of the €687 million allocated to the school transport scheme in budget 2027; the amount allocated to existing school transport services, service expansion, fleet investment; the new initiatives or pilots to help operators meet increased bus contractor running costs.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 465 and 466 together.
The expenditure on the scheme has more than doubled over a six-year period from over €200 million in 2018 to €537 million in 2025 (included a cost-of-living advancement for 2025 of €58m). The allocation in 2026 is estimated at €641m.
The increasing cost of the scheme over the past number of years is due to increased pupil numbers, COVID cleaning and increased distance measures, cost of living measures, provision of transport for children from Ukraine and increased contractor rates for operators under contract to Bus Éireann for the provision of services.
Transport for pupils with special educational needs continues to represent the largest area of expenditure within the scheme, accounting for just under 60% of the total spend in 2025, while serving approximately 13% of the total overall pupils on transport.
School Transport budget will increase to €687 million in 2027. This equates to over €3.7 million on school transport alone per school day. Extra funding will provide for the additional demand for specialised transport and increased transport running costs.

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh den Aire Oideachais agus Óige cad iad a pleananna chun an liúntais do mhúineadh trí Ghaeilge a thabhairt ar ais do mhúinteoirí meánscoile chun aitheantas a thabhairt do na dúshláin a bhaineann leis an obair sin.
reply:
Foráiltear le Comhaontú na Seirbhíse Poiblí 2024 – 2026 go bhféadfaidh fostóirí agus ceardchumainn/comhlachais athruithe breise ar rátaí pá agus/nó ar choinníollacha fostaíochta a idirbheartú suas go 1% ar a mhéad den chostas bunphá, lena n-áirítear liúntais de chineál pá, a bhaineann leis an ngrád, leis an ngrúpa nó leis an gcatagóir fostaí ar leith nó leis an aonad margála ar leith. Féadfaidh go n-áireofar leis sin tograí a bhfuil athruithe ar struchtúir, ar chleachtais oibre nó ar choinníollacha eile seirbhíse i gceist leo.
Roghnaigh Cumann Múinteoirí Éireann (INTO) an Ciste Margála Áitiúla a úsáid chun roinnt éileamh a shocrú de réir théarmaí an Chiste agus laistigh den teorainn cistiúcháin Státchiste atá i bhfeidhm. Leagtar amach i gCiorclán 54/2026 an toradh a comhaontaíodh le INTO i ndáil le roinnt éileamh atá á socrú don earnáil bunscoile.
Ós rud é go bhfuil roinnt ceardchumann ag déanamh ionadaíocht do mhúinteoirí, is faoi gach eagraíocht ionadaíoch atá sé idirbheartú thar ceann a comhaltaí féin.
Ní fhéadfar leasuithe breise ar Théarmaí agus Coinníollacha múinteoirí, lena n-áirítear pá agus liúntais, a bhaint amach ach amháin trí idirchaidreamh agus comhaontuithe cómhargála idir an Rialtas agus na ceardchumainn Seirbhíse Poiblí. Ní fhéadfar athruithe den sórt sin a dhéanamh ach amháin faoi na próisis sin, agus ba ghá don Roinn, don Roinn Caiteachais Phoiblí agus Athchóirithe agus do na ceardchumainn iomchuí mionbhreithniú a dhéanamh ar aon tograí dá leithéid.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether her Department has the authority to direct a primary school Board of Management to review or remove a designated liaison person (details supplied) where concerns have been formally substantiated; and the procedures in place to address such matters while ensuring fair procedures for all involved.
reply:
Tusla is the agency of the State with the statutory responsibility to assess all reports of child welfare and protection concerns and as such my Department does not have powers to investigate child protection concerns.
My Department has no role in employer/employee matters. The Education Act, 1998 sets out the legal framework for schools and their patrons. The act provides that the board of management is the body charged with the direct governance of a school on behalf of the patron and is the employer of school staff. In the case of schools established or maintained by an ETB the ETB in the employer of school staff. Any actions in relation to the school employee, in relation to employment matters, are exclusively a matter for the employer.
My Department's Child Protection Procedures for Schools set out the reporting requirements for school personnel, including the Designated Liaison Person. Where any member of school personnel fails to report a matter to Tusla where advised by Tusla to do so, or otherwise fails to comply with the procedures, this is to be reported to and dealt with separately by the employer in accordance with the relevant disciplinary procedures. The procedures are available on the gov.ie website: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-education/policy-information/child-protection-procedures-in-schools/.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Education and Youth the mandatory items that must be on every agenda of a Board of Management meeting for primary schools in Ireland as required by law and under the School Governance Manual 2023-2027.
reply:
The Education Act, 1998 sets out the legal framework for schools and their patrons. The act provides that the board of management is the body charged with the direct governance of a school on behalf of the patron.
The agreed procedures for the appointment of boards of management of primary schools and the rules under which these boards operate are set out in the department’s publication ‘Governance Manual for Primary Schools 2023-2027’.
Boards of management are required to comply with the provisions of the Education Act 1998, and all other relevant legislation and department circulars relating to the operation of boards.
A primary school board of management must hold a minimum of one meeting per school term and not less than five meetings in any school year.
The agenda for every board of management meeting should include the following, the minutes of the previous board meeting, matters arising from the minutes, correspondence, treasurer’s report, principal’s report, principal’s child protection oversight report, health and safety, and the agreed report. The agreed report is the decision reached at the end of each board meeting on the information to be disclosed to the school community and on the manner in which this information is to be communicated. The agreed report shall not include details of any issues which must remain confidential to board members.

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide an update on the commitment in the DEIS plus scheme to increase funding for youth services (details supplied) near post primary schools.
reply:
The Department of Education and Youth (DEY) is dedicated to enhancing the delivery and development of youth work services and opportunities for young people across the country.
UBU Your Place Your Space (UBU) is the largest youth services scheme funded by the department. The scheme targets young people aged between 10 to 24 who are identified as marginalised, vulnerable and at risk of not flourishing, providing funding to 258 (in 2026) targeted youth services across the 16 education and training board (ETB) areas.
Over €54 million has been allocated to the UBU scheme in 2026.??This year’s allocation builds on an increase of over €10 million or 24% over the period 2021 to 2025.
Earlier this year the department asked ETBs to provide details on waiting lists for UBU projects in their functional areas. The request for this information forms part of the department's broader work to support the implementation of the new DEIS Plus Scheme, as part of which, funding has been provided to expand UBU provision near DEIS Plus schools.
The information gathered through this exercise, which will be completed this year, will help to inform this targeted expansion of youth services in communities where demand is greatest and where additional supports can contribute to improved outcomes for disadvantaged young people, focusing on youth services in areas with post-primary DEIS Plus schools in the first instance.

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Education and Youth the educational campaigns that are being implemented in schools to inform teenagers about the harms of recreational nitrous oxide use.
reply:

Substance misuse prevention is a key focus within the new Primary Wellbeing specification and is addressed in an age and stage appropriate way, where children develop knowledge and skills to understand the potential impacts and risks associated with substance misuse, follow safety rules and make informed and responsible decision to keep them safe.
At Junior Cycle, the SPHE strand on Making Healthy Choices has an explicit focus on learning about drugs, alcohol and other addictive behaviours and substances. These resources include those in relation to substance misuse. At Junior Cycle, for example, the NCCA’s toolkit includes a range of up-to-date materials created by the HSE in conjunction with the Department of Education and Youth. question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if he plans to introduce additional financial supports for community and voluntary organisations in County Louth experiencing increased insurance, energy, maintenance and staffing costs; and if he has considered providing recurring operational funding rather than capital grants alone.
reply:

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether her Department has undertaken an assessment of the actual average cost incurred by families providing private transport under the special transport grant or exceptional no service interim grant compared with the grant amounts paid.
reply:

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Education and Youth the total number of reps submitted to Bus Éireann school transport via the designated public representatives line, broken down by year, from 2023 to date in 2026.
reply:

reply:
Funding for the Local Youth Club Grant Scheme (LYCGS), a key universal support for volunteer?led youth work has increased by 32% from €2.1 million in 2020 to over €2.8 million in 2026.
The majority of youth funding is administered by the 16 Education and Training Boards (ETBs) on behalf of the department, supporting youth clubs, local youth services, and ETB-led functions within each ETB’s functional area rather than on a county-by-county basis. This includes the LYCGS which is administered at a local level by the sixteen ETBs. Funding for 2026 has been allocated to all ETBs and the application and award of grants to clubs is currently in process. As the 2026 application and award process is not yet complete in all 16 ETBs it is not possible at this stage to provide comprehensive data on the scheme for 2026.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide an update on the work of the AI in Schools External Advisory Taskforce; to list its membership; the number of meetings to date; and to indicate when it expects to report.
reply:
The AI in Education External Advisory Taskforce has been established to support the Department in developing a coherent national approach to the safe, responsible and effective use of AI across the school system at primary and post-primary level. Two AI Taskforce meetings have been held to date, 14 May and 21 September. The list of members will be published on gov.ie in the coming weeks.
Meetings are attended by teacher unions, management bodies and other stakeholders such as teachers, parents and students representative groups and research bodies and other relevant agencies. Its membership ensures a broad range of perspectives and expertise are brought to the discussion.
To support its work the Taskforce has established two working groups. The first is focused on assessment, including both summative and State-certified assessment, with the second Working Group focusing on teaching, learning and formative assessment.
The current phase of the taskforce is expected to operate over an initial 18-24 month period with outputs delivered on a rolling basis. Quarterly reports will be published on gov.ie in due course. These publications will provide greater transparency regarding the Taskforce's work programme and priorities.
The taskforce will help ensure that the department’s response is informed by practical experience, ongoing work across the education system, and emerging national and international developments.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of children in Ireland who are home-educated; and the measures in place to assess the quality of that education.
reply:
The Constitution of Ireland acknowledges the family as the primary and natural educator of the child and sets out the rights and duties of the State in the matter of education. The Constitution makes explicit that the State does not oblige parents to send their children to any particular type of school. Parents are free to provide education in their homes, in private schools, or in schools recognised or established by the State.
Tusla’s Alternative Education Assessment and Registration Service (AEARS) is under the remit of my department. AEARS is responsible for the regulation of provision for education in places other than recognised schools, including children who are home schooled or who are enrolled in a non-recognised independent school.
Parents who wish to educate their child in a place other than a recognised school are required to make an application to AEARS to have their child included on the Section 14 Statutory Register. AEARS will then carry out an assessment of the educational provision to determine if the child is eligible to be placed on the register. Assessments are carried out by an authorised person in line with the ‘Guidelines on the Assessment of Education in Places other than a recognised School’, issued by my department and which is available to view at the following link: Guidelines on the Assessment of Education in Places Other Than Recognised Schools (File Format PDF 1.3MB). www.tusla.ie/uploads/content/Guidelines_on_Assessment_of_Education.pdf

My department and the NCSE have sanctioned 587 new special classes for the school year 2026/27, including 70 inclusive special classes. This is one of many ways my department is actively engaging to meet the increased demand.
My department and the NCSE are committed to ensuring that all students can access the required supports to enable them to achieve their educational goals. At the heart of this are the special education teachers and special needs assistants (SNAs) dedicated to ensuring each child is valued and is actively supported and nurtured to reach their full potential.
Supporting this is the variety of differentiated teaching approaches encouraged by my department to accommodate the varying levels of ability in classrooms. This facilitates the inclusion of all learners to access the school curriculum in a meaningful way.

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy David Cullinane den Aire Forbartha Tuaithe agus Pobail, agus Gaeltachta an mbeidh an méadú €1 milliún ar mhaoiniú Fhoras na Gaeilge i mBuiséad 2027 leordhóthanach chun coinneáil suas le boilsciú agus le hardú ar chostais reatha; agus cén tionchar a bheidh aige seo ar chumas an Fhorais tacú le heagraíochtaí agus tionscnaimh Ghaeilge ar fud an oileáin.
reply:
Is í an Chomhairle Aireachta Thuaidh-Theas a cheadaíonn buiséid bhliantúla na gComhlachtaí Forfheidhmithe Thuaidh Theas, an Foras Teanga san áireamh. Cuireann Rialtas na hÉireann 75% de bhuiséad Fhoras na Gaeilge ar fáil agus tagann an 25% eile ó Fheidhmeannas Thuaisceart Éireann, de réir an chóimheas maoinithe a aontaíodh nuair a bunaíodh an Foras Teanga.
Cuireadh maoiniú comhaontaithe de €20 milliún ar fáil d'Fhoras na Gaeilge agus do Ghníomhaireacht na hUltaise i mbliana. Ardaíodh maoiniú Chlár na Leabhar Gaeilge go €2 milliún in 2026, an leibhéal is airde riamh. Chomh maith leis sin, chuir mo Roinn maoiniú breise os cionn €2 milliún ar fáil do chláir agus do ghníomhaíochtaí eile Fhoras na Gaeilge in 2026.
Fógraíodh maoiniú breise de €1 mhilliún i mBuiséad 2027 an tseachtain seo caite, chun tacú le hobair an Fhorais Teanga. Tá na pleananna gnó agus buiséid an Fhorais Teanga do 2027 fós á bplé ag na Ranna sa dá dhlínse agus beidh siad á gcur faoi bhráid na Comhairle Aireachta Thuaidh Theas roimh dheireadh na bliana.
Tabharfaidh an maoiniú breise seo cinnteacht don bhForas Teanga agus do na heagraíochta agus grúpaí pobail ar fud an oileáin a bhaineann tairbhe as na scéimeanna tacaíochta agus maoinithe a chuirtear ar fáil.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth if the design team has submitted the tender report in relation to the new school building project for a school (details supplied) to her Department; and if construction is still due to commence in Q4 2026.
reply:
The large-scale capital project for the school referred to by the Deputy is for the provision of a new 600 pupil school building including all associated ancillary accommodation, with the inclusion of additional classrooms for children with Special Educational Needs configured within the existing layout.
The invitation to tender issued in late Q4 2025. The Design Team recently submitted the tender report to my Department and a detailed review is currently ongoing. It is envisaged that construction will commence in the coming months.
I would like to advise the Deputy, since 2020, the Department of Education has provided over €2 billion in capital funding for Dublin schools. Over this period, a total of 300 schools have been upgraded through provision of either a new school building, extension, modular accommodation or climate pathfinder projects. 20 school projects to go to tender or construction in 2026 and 2027 were included in the NDP Implementation Plan including Gaelcholaiste Reachrann.
There are currently 47 large-scale, extension, modular or climate pathfinder projects in Dublin under construction.
There are also 53 projects underway through the Climate Action Summer Works Scheme.
In addition, since 2020 a total of 541 special classes have been sanctioned in Dublin, of which 140 were sanctioned for September 2026.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which the proposed common enrolment system will operate where linked schools have different patrons; whether parents will have an opportunity to vote on a specific proposal; the way in which the transition will accommodate pupils already enrolled; and the options that will be available to schools that do not join the initial group by 31 October 2026.
reply:
As a first step towards implementing a commitment in the Programme for Government for a nationwide common applications system, my department launched the Apply to School pilot scheme in October 2025 and this scheme was expanded for the 2026/2027 admissions cycle. The expanded pilot covers 22 post-primary schools in ten school planning areas and represents a significant step towards improving the school admissions system. It provided families with a single online application process for first year places and introduced synchronised and streamlined timelines for schools to manage admissions and issue offers. Participating schools retain full control of their own individual admissions policies and associated legal responsibilities under the Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018. Under the pilot arrangements, parents submit one application through a central portal and may apply to multiple participating schools, with applications processed in accordance with the admissions criteria of each school concerned. Where schools in the same area have different patrons, the operation of the Apply to School system will not alter the patronage or ethos of any participating school. Each school will continue to apply its own admissions policy, approved by its board of management and patron, and any arrangements between schools will be implemented in a manner that respects the governance and patronage structures of the schools concerned.

question: Deputy Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire asked the Minister for Education and Youth the process for applying for a new Gaelcholáiste; to outline such a process; and if applications for new Gaelcholáistí will be considered other than if it this is the outcome of the public voting process which has been in place in various locations in recent years.
reply:
New schools are established in areas of demographic growth, as the resources available for school infrastructure have to be prioritised to ensure that every child has a school place.
Demographic requirements in an area determine the need or otherwise for establishing new schools and while there are no Irish medium or English medium schools planned currently (other than new special schools) this position is kept under constant review by my department.
The Programme for Government 2025, Securing Ireland’s Future, includes a commitment to establish Gaelscoileanna and Gaelcholáistí where there is demand and support parents choosing Irish-medium education for their children.
In November 2025 my department published a ‘Policy for Irish-medium Education outside of the Gaeltacht’ and established a Taskforce on Models of Provision for Irish-medium Education.
The role of the taskforce is to provide a platform for collaboration between my department and key stakeholders to develop a pathway to increase provision of Irish-medium education nationally. The taskforce's work is expected to be completed by the end of the year. It will make recommendations to my department on areas such as the criteria for Irish-medium education provision, how to support schools transitioning to Irish-medium and mechanisms to facilitate expansion of provision.

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will review the criteria governing the recognition of overseas teaching service for incremental credit and pensionable service purposes; the number of years of overseas teaching service that may currently be recognised; and whether consideration is being given to recognising all teaching service completed abroad where it can be verified.
reply:
The criteria for the award of incremental credit are set out in the Department of Education & Youth’s Circulars 10/2001, for primary teachers, and 29/2007 and 29/2010, for post-primary teachers. These circulars provide for the award of incremental credit in respect of prior teaching service, including overseas teaching service, both within and outside the EU.
There is no separate scheme in the Department to recognise overseas teaching service for pensionable service purposes alone and under the Department Pension schemes, service given in countries outside Ireland does not constitute pensionable service.
Teaching service given outside the Republic of Ireland by a qualified teacher in a school or college must be deemed to be equivalent to teaching service given in a primary or post primary school in the Republic of Ireland. This includes teaching service given in a public or private primary or secondary school abroad.
Criteria such as whether the school is subject to state funding, which can be of relevance when examining claims relating to private teaching schools, and the length of time the school has been in existence, must be satisfied for service at that school to be recognised for incremental credit. Where a school satisfies the criteria set out in the circulars to have service at that school recognised for incremental credit, an award of incremental credit can be made.

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to Parliamentary Question No. 65501/26, for an update on the implementation of the SC L1\L2 programmes for special schools.
reply:
As the Deputy will know, Senior Cycle Level 1 and Level 2 Learning Programmes (SCL1/SCL2 LPs) were introduced to special and post-primary schools in September 2024 as follow-on programmes for students following Level 1 and Level 2 at Junior Cycle. In August 2026, I approved the final suite of elective modules for the SCL1/SCL2 LPs, marking the culmination of the work of the Post-Primary Special Educational Needs Development Group on these programmes. Schools can now offer a full programme of diverse modules and curriculum areas that ensure that every student can access a Senior Cycle experience that is appropriate to their individual needs.
Since its initial introduction in 2024, there has been strong uptake of the programmes across both mainstream and special schools. Following a programme of work, SCL1/SCL2 LPs have now been integrated on the Post-Primary Online Database (PPOD) and the Primary Online Database (POD), allowing students in mainstream and special schools to have their programmes registered for the 2026/27 school year as part of the annual October Returns process. Separately, students register with the State Examinations Commission (SEC) via their assessment portal to obtain certification.

reply:

In early June, my department issued primary schools with their school-specific results and explanatory information.
Boards of Management have been asked to share their survey results and explanatory information with their school communities, to review their survey results and to engage with their communities (including parents), and the local community (including parents with children not yet in school), before deciding on their next steps.

It is important that schools are given the time and space to reflect carefully on their results and to engage fully with parents and the wider school communities before making decisions.
My department has published all school-level reports, survey results, guidance documents and supporting materials on www.gov.ie/PrimarySchoolSurvey. question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth to examine the vetting process for staff in special schools; and to outline the process that takes place if it has been established that there is a recorded TUSLA finding of concern against a particular candidate.
reply:
This government is fully committed to supporting students with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this objective.
My department takes child protection very seriously and considers that the protection and welfare of children is a fundamental responsibility of all involved in the care and education of children.
Under the Education Act 1998, every school is managed by its board of management on behalf of the patron. The board employs the school’s teachers and other staff, except in Education and Training Board schools, where the ETB is the employer. Decisions on employing or engaging staff are therefore a matter for the school authority as employer, and my department has no role in employer–employee matters.
The vetting of persons undertaking relevant work or activities with children or vulnerable persons is governed by the National Vetting Bureau (Children and Vulnerable Persons) Acts 2012 to 2016 (the Vetting Act), which are the responsibility of the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration. Vetting is carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau. Tusla – the Child and Family Agency has statutory responsibility for assessing child welfare and protection concerns and determines whether an allegation of abuse is founded or unfounded. question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht for an update on CLÁR applications for Carlow and Kilkenny.
reply:
The CLÁR programme provides funding under several measures for small-scale infrastructure projects in designated rural areas. Last year, I approved over €14 million for 238 projects covering community facilities and amenities, community vehicles, and specific support for island communities. Since 2020 almost €68 million has been allocated to over 1,500 projects including over €800,000 for 22 projects in Carlow and over €1.4 million for 35 projects in Kilkenny.
The 2026 CLÁR programme was launched on 10th March with the following measures:
Measure 1: Developing Community Facilities & Amenities
Measure 2: Mobility, Cancer Care, First Responder and Meals on Wheels Transport
Measure 3: Our Living Islands
The closing date for applications under all measures has now passed. Earlier this month I was delighted to announce over €2.5 million for 44 projects under measure 2 of the CLÁR programme. My officials are currently evaluating applications under measures 1 and 3 of the 2026 programme, including those from Carlow and Kilkenny under measure 1. I expect to announce the successful projects before the end of the year.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 438 and 439 together.
Under the Education Act 1998, the School Board of Management (BOM), appointed by the school’s patron, is the body charged with the direct governance of a school and the principal manages the school on a day-to-day basis. Each school has the autonomy to design its own timetables and decide which subjects and programmes to offer based on the educational needs and interests of its students as well as considerations such as classroom space, staffing, time limitations etc.
The study of Modern Foreign Languages is optional at Junior and Senior Cycle. However, it should be noted that schools may have their own rules in relation to the study of a foreign language and higher educational institutions may require a foreign language to be studied for matriculation purposes.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her Department has issued guidance to post-primary schools on the position of students with dyslexia who hold an exemption from Irish and experience significant difficulty learning a modern foreign language; if not, if she will issue guidance clarifying that, while an Irish exemption does not automatically extend to a foreign language, such students should have their individual educational needs considered and should be informed of available alternative arrangements.
reply:
While individual schools may have their own rules in relation to the study of a foreign language, the Department of Education and Youth does not require students to study these subjects and therefore no exemption system exists.
Where an exemption from the study of Irish is granted, it should not be interpreted as an exemption from the study of other languages.
Any decision not to study a language should be made carefully and following detailed discussion with the student, their teachers and school principal. A student may commence the study of a language (including the study of Irish) at an appropriate level after the granting of an exemption from the study of Irish. The reasons for this will vary from student to student and may include having a background in language, that the subject is being studied at an ab initio level and/or that they have experienced an improvement in their ability to engage in language learning.
When making a decision it is important to remember that the study of foreign languages is a common entry requirement for many 3rd level courses and students/parents are advised to contact the school’s guidance teacher and seek advice on how best to proceed. 3rd level institutions may set their own rules for the entry requirements for the courses they offer, therefore a language exemption at 3rd level is a matter for the individual University. question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the qualifications a person requires to become a SENO, given that they will be dealing with schools and children's needs; if they require experience teaching additional needs children and working as an SNA in a school setting; and if not, if she will consider introducing such a requirement.
reply:
The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) is the statutory body responsible for the provision of special education and allocating supports for students with special educational needs.
The NCSE is, in the first instance, the primary body responsible for the matter the Deputy has raised. I will arrange for your query to be forwarded to the NCSE for their attention and direct reply. Deputies are also welcome to raise such queries with the NCSE directly through their dedicated Oireachtas email address.
My department and the NCSE are committed to delivering an education system that is of the highest quality and where every child and young person feels valued and is actively supported and nurtured to achieve their full potential.

question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Education and Youth to list those countries in the OECD which have school principals who also teach classes and those which have principals who only work as administrators; the reason this State has teacher principals; and if she will consider introducing administrator principals.
reply:
I recognise the key role school leadership in improving educational outcomes by creating a positive school climate and environment as well as motivating and empowering educators and learners within their school communities. The appointment of Administrative Principals and Deputy Principals is determined on an enrolment basis, with the relevant thresholds outlined in Appendix B of Circular 0025/2026.
Recent improvements in relation to school management and leadership structures include:
• all primary schools with a teaching principal have a minimum of 37 Principal Release Days, that is, one administrative day per week. Schools with one special class have 4 additional release days, a total of 41 in the school year. • schools with two special classes have administrative principal status regardless of enrolment
• the Administrative Principal pupil threshold has been reduced from an enrolment of 178 to 169, with the Deputy Admin Principal threshold reduced from an enrolment of 655 to 550.
• Budget 2024 removed the threshold for the appointment of an Administrative Deputy Principal in Special Schools.
• the second teacher in two-teacher schools have Deputy Principal status as opposed to holding Assistant Principal II posts.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her attention has been drawn to a school (details supplied) that has not had an assigned NEPS psychologist for the past two years and that to date none have been assigned for the 2026/27 school year; will she comment on the fact that a major residential hub with 14 primary schools serving the Blackrock area has been completely without this service across multiple school years; will she agree that the structural freeze on educational assessments means that vulnerable children across every one of these schools are missing out and being left behind by the system.
reply:
The National Educational Psychological Service (NEPS) provides educational psychological support to all schools. Due to a national shortage of suitably qualified educational psychologists not all schools have an assigned educational psychologist. For those schools without an assigned educational psychologist, the school will be supported by NEPS through the Advisory Support Service. All schools continue to have support in the event of a critical incident through the local NEPS office and has access to training and support from NEPS for school staff.
Through the NEPS Advisory Support Service, schools have an opportunity to access responsive support and advice from a NEPS psychologist. reply:
The Convention on Education was established to deliver on a Programme for Government commitment to hold a Convention on Education, bringing together all stakeholders in Education. The Convention on Education is the largest exercise in deliberative democracy in the state to date, with 150 people taking part. The 150 person membership comprises 30 parents and guardians, 30 school employees and early years educators, 60 education stakeholders and for the first time ever, 30 children and young people between the ages of 8 and 24 will be full members.
To ensure that all citizens had an opportunity to add their voice and perspectives to this important exercise in deliberative democracy, I launched a National Conversation in January 2026, in which over 42,000 people participated. I expect to receive the final report from the Convention in early 2027.
While Citizens’ Assemblies are a mechanism used by the Oireachtas to involve members of the general public in helping it respond to important constitutional, legal or policy questions, the Convention on Education has been designed by the Government to provide a deliberative perspective on the future of the Irish school system.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht to consider allowing supports for the development and protection of beaches under the town and village renewal funds, which would specifically help coastal towns and villages.
reply:

The Scheme also supports the development of public realm works, recreational amenities, and town and village centre plazas with funding ranging from €50,000 to €500,000.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 425 and 426 together.
Addressing educational disadvantage in all schools remains a key priority for me as Minister for Education and Youth. The DEIS programme is targeted at schools with the highest levels of concentrated disadvantage. Schools that were included in the most recent expansion of the programme in 2022 were those with the highest levels of concentrated disadvantage as identified through the refined DEIS identification model. Schools were not required to apply for inclusion in the DEIS programme, and the model was applied fairly and equally to all schools. A detailed paper on the refined DEIS identification model is available on gov.ie.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if his attention has been drawn to the concerns of an organisation (details supplied) in relation to the requirement for their industry to have least half of their workforce to be EEA, UK, or Swiss nationals; and if any flexibility or derogation can be considered.
reply:
The Employment Permits Act 2024 requires that, in order for an employment permit to be granted, at least 50% of the employees of an employer are Irish/EEA/UK/Swiss nationals. This policy fulfils Ireland's obligations under the Union Preference principles of membership of the EU. The mandatory application of the 50:50 rule underpins the Government's employment creation strategy by requiring employers in the State to hire in a balanced manner from domestic and EEA labour markets.
Under this rule, an employment permit will not issue unless, at the time of application, at least 50% of the employees of the employer are EEA, UK or Swiss nationals. The Employment Permits Act does provide waivers to the application of the 50:50 rule : where the employer applying for the employment permit has been registered with Revenue Commissioners within the last two years and the application is supported by either Enterprise Ireland or IDA Ireland; or where the employer has no employees and the foreign national concerned will be the sole employee of the employer.
Officials of my Department recently concluded a review of Ireland's use of the 50:50 rule, the outcome of which recommended amending the Employment Permits Act 2024 to address critical recruitment difficulties in the health and social care sector through the creation of new sector-specific and sector-wide regulation-making powers.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if his previous commitment to make a decision to abolish subminimum pay rates for young workers in 2029 still stands.
reply:
As the Deputy is aware, the National Minimum Wage Acts allow for lower, or sub-minimum rates of the minimum wage for those employees aged under 20 years of age. Those aged less than 18 years can be paid 70 per cent of the full minimum wage rate, while those aged 18 years and 19 years can be paid 80 and 90 per cent of the full rate, respectively.
Since the current system of youth rates is based on a percentage of the full minimum wage; when the minimum wage increases, these sub-minimum youth rates also increase, with young people in receipt of these rates seeing a commensurate increase in their wages.
As part of Budget 2027 Government agreed to accept the recommendation of the independent Low Pay Commission to increase the National Minimum Wage by 79 cent, or 5.6%, from 1st January 2027.
Sub-minimum youth rates will also increase by 5.6% on that date.
If we include the planned 2027 increase, the National Minimum Wage has increased by 46% since 2021 - well ahead of consumer price inflation.
In April 2025, as part of measures designed to bolster business resilience and support competitiveness, the Government agreed to defer a decision on the future use of sub-minimum youth rates until 2029.
This decision should be considered in the context of the significant increases in the minimum wage and wider improvements in statutory employment measures.
The Government will continue to closely monitor the use of subminimum youth rates to ensure they do not undermine fair pay or progression

This provides greater certainty for those planning and delivering services and helps sustain integration supports in communities.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment for an update on the progress of the Government’s life sciences strategy; the expected date for publication of the strategy.
reply:
The Life Sciences sector is one of the strongest drivers of our economy, fuelling both growth and exports. It combines a thriving indigenous enterprise base with some of the world's largest multinational companies, underpinned by a continually advancing world-class research ecosystem. question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the methodology and criteria used to determine the number of employment permits made available under occupational quotas; the basis on which the numerical quota for each occupation currently subject to a quota was calculated; the labour shortages identified in each such occupation; and the number of permits sought by relevant sectoral representatives during the most recent review compared with the quota ultimately approved.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 404 and 408 together.
Ireland's employment permits system is designed to support employers in addressing identified labour and skills shortages while maintaining a clear policy preference for recruitment from within Ireland and the wider EEA.
Ireland's economic migration framework focuses on addressing skills and labour shortages, particularly in sectors of strategic economic importance, while facilitating the recruitment of non-EEA nationals where labour needs cannot be met from within Ireland or the EEA.
A number of policy areas, including employment, migration and education, intersect in addressing skills and labour shortages. In recent years, my Department has used the employment permits system to support an integrated response to these challenges and to help establish a sustainable domestic pipeline of labour for future vacancies. This has included the use of employment permit quotas together with additional conditions such as training and upskilling measures, where lower-skilled occupations have been removed from the Ineligible Occupations List.
To ensure the appropriate use of the employment permits system in respect of lower-skilled occupations, an occupation may be removed from the Ineligible Occupations List subject to a quota restriction on the number of General Employment Permits that may be granted, alongside initiatives designed to develop a domestic supply of labour.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether the availability and capacity of housing, healthcare, education, childcare, transport and other public services are taken into account when determining the number of employment permits made available generally or under individual occupational quotas; if so, the methodology used to assess these factors; and the Departments, agencies and other bodies consulted in this regard.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 405 and 407 together.
Ireland’s economic migration policy is designed to address verified and ongoing skills shortages across the economy. The system is vacancy led and is managed through the Critical Skills Occupations List (CSOL) and the Ineligible Occupations List, both of which are reviewed on a regular basis by my Department.
My Department works in close cooperation with other key government departments to ensure that the employment permits system is aligned with the national objective of meeting skills and labour demands. This engagement is focused on evaluating that demand and the availability in the domestic labour force, while identifying alternative pathways aimed at contributing domestically to addressing shortages of skilled candidates in key sectors.
In considering changes to the occupation lists, my Department assesses not only labour market evidence but also wider whole of Government factors. These include the potential impact of inward migration on housing demand, transport capacity, healthcare, and other public services.
The Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, Department of Health, Department of Education and Youth and other relevant Government Departments are formally consulted before recommendations are submitted for my consideration regarding eligibility for permits, renewal or amendment of employment permit quotas. This consultation takes place through the Interdepartmental Group on Economic Migration Pol

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether regulations have been made pursuant to section 47(12)(a) of the Employment Permits Act 2024 specifying accommodation to be provided to a foreign national as a condition of the grant of a general employment permit or seasonal employment permit; if so, to set out the employments and categories of employment to which such regulations apply; and if not, whether consideration is being given to making such regulations, particularly in respect of occupations subject to employment permit quotas.
reply:
The overarching objective for the State’s national economic migration and employment permit system is that the State’s employment permit system should help meet, in the short to medium term, the demand for skills and labour in the Irish economy without disrupting the Irish labour market.
The 2024 Employment Permits Act provides for a regulation making power under section 47(12) that allows the Minister to specify conditions for the grant of a General Employment Permit or a Seasonal Employment Permit in particular roles.
The Act allows that conditions may be set around accommodation, training, or expenses provided to the employment permit holder in question. These conditions may also cover measures taken by the employer to increase the skills knowledge, qualifications or experience within the sector, including employing trainees or apprentices. It also covers measures taken by the employer to reduce their reliance on the permit system, including through technical changes to work processes.
The Department is committed to keeping pace with rapid labour market changes and to proactively support sectors and addressing shortages as they arise. Active policy consideration is being given to the development of new regulations under these powers, in line with the national economic migration, and general migration policy.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to provide an update on his Department's work on the transposition of the Platform Work Directive.
reply:
The Improving Working Conditions in Platform Work Directive entered into force on 1 December 2024 and EU Member States have until 2 December 2026 to transpose the Directive into national law.
The Directive is significant, technically complex and wide-ranging, legislating for numerous areas. It seeks to ensure that people working through digital labour platforms have the correct legal employment status that corresponds to their actual working arrangements, enabling them to benefit from the employment rights to which they are entitled.
The Directive also aims to regulate the use of algorithms by digital labour platforms. It will make the use of algorithms in human resources management in platform work more transparent, ensuring that automated systems are monitored by qualified staff, and that workers have the right to contest automated decisions. The Directive also imposes substantial limitations on the processing of personal data by these systems.
My Department has undertaken extensive consultation with relevant Government Departments, agencies and stakeholders, and has also undertaken a public consultation process to inform the transposition of the Directive. Officials have also engaged with the European Commission's work on implementation of the Directive. The views received through these engagements have informed the development of the legislative measures required for transposition. question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment If there is a process through which his Department receives employment related complaints from persons granted work permits; if so, the number of such complaints received in each year from 2022 to date in 2026.
reply: The Workplace Relations Commission provides an e-Complaint Portal to facilitate the lodging of all complaints. Relevant information for submitting a complaint is available on the e-Complaint Portal home screen on the WRC website where a step-by-step guide is available. The portal does not specifically track the employment status of people submitting complaints. Furthermore, I can confirm that persons employed through a Work Permit enjoy the full range of employment rights entitlements and protections.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment his Departments definition of "data sovereignty" and its policy approach to current geopolitical discussions on data sovereignty, residency and localisation.
reply:
My Department does not currently apply a single statutory definition of “data sovereignty”. Ireland is a signatory, along with all EU Member States, to the Declaration for European Digital Sovereignty, which describes digital sovereignty as the ability of the EU and its Member States to make their own choices about digital technologies and services while remaining open to cooperation with international partners. The Declaration also recognises data sovereignty as an important element of this broader objective and highlights the need to ensure appropriate protection for sensitive European data.
Our approach is also guided by and aligned with the EU framework governing data protection, data sharing, cybersecurity and digital resilience, including the GDPR and the wider Digital Decade agenda. The Government supports the secure and trusted flow of data across borders and an open, rules-based digital economy, while maintaining high standards of privacy, security and resilience.
In line with the Declaration, Ireland views digital and data sovereignty not as a basis for protectionism or broad data localisation requirements, but as a means of strengthening Europe’s ability to act independently where necessary, reducing strategic dependencies, and protecting its interests, values and security in the digital sphere.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if his Department considered the ability of civil servants to adequately support EU presidency work requirements in digital and AI policy units of his Department prior to appointing external consultants to digital policy teams; whether criteria for specific expertise were laid out.
reply:
My Department considered the resourcing requirements associated with Ireland's EU Presidency and identified and redeployed several civil servants to support Presidency-related work in the Digital and AI policy areas. Given the exceptional workload associated with the Presidency, including the advancement of key policy priorities and the delivery of major events such as the AI Summit, the Department also sought to supplement internal capacity through temporary secondments from external organisations.
Specific criteria were established for these opportunities. The Department sought experienced professionals with strong analytical, research and communication skills, and expertise relevant to digital, AI, technical, legal and policy issues, including familiarity with EU legislative and policy processes where appropriate.
These temporary secondments are designed to provide additional specialist capacity during the Presidency period and to complement the work of existing civil servants. All secondees complete the Department's onboarding and security requirements and they are subject to the Civil Service Code of Standards and Behaviour, as well as strict ethics, confidentiality, security and conflict of interest requirements., including declarations under the Official Secrets Act. Secondees serve as temporary members of staff under the direction and management of the Department.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the safeguards being put in place regarding the use of AI helpdesks and AI-tools to screen queries and complaints from the public within his Department and within bodies under its aegis.
reply:
There are currently no use cases, either deployed or in development, in which generative AI-based automation is embedded in processing or decision-making (including systems to manage helpdesks and/or complaints from the public).
My Department first issued a policy document on the use of Generative AI to all staff in July 2023. That policy highlighted some of the potential areas where Generative AI can deliver efficiencies, but it also set out the risks of using such technologies and the mitigations that staff in the Department must adopt to avoid those risks. This was based on contemporaneous guidance received from the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC).
The Department's original Generative AI Policy was reviewed again and updated in 2025. The revised policy position encourages and fosters greater use of Generative AI while also emphasising governance and accountability where AI tools have been used. General use cases include conducting research, creating initial drafts or layouts for documents, and supporting decision-making.
Department staff have been advised that they must make their own value judgements and be transparent and vigilant about any significant use of Generative AI. Staff remain 100% responsible for all outputs, and they must ensure that these are fit for use and factually correct. question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether the Government will consider legislation to provide enforceable workplace access rights for trade union representatives if agreement cannot be reached between organisations (details supplied); when a decision on this matter is expected; and whether such a decision will be made before the scheduled 2028 mid-term review of the Action Plan to Promote Collective Bargaining.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 391 and 392 together.
Where an employer does not engage in collective bargaining, a trade union may use the voluntary dispute-resolution procedures provided through the Workplace Relations Commission. The Code of Practice on Voluntary Dispute Resolution provides for the appointment of an Advisory Officer to assist the parties, with defined timeframes for engagement. Where the process does not resolve the dispute, the matter may, subject to the relevant statutory conditions, be referred to the Labour Court under the Industrial Relations (Amendment) Acts 2001 to 2015.
Employees are also protected against victimisation arising from trade union membership or legitimate trade union activity. The Code of Practice on Victimisation identifies adverse or unfavourable treatment arising from union membership or activity as victimisation and provides that a complaint may be presented to the Workplace Relations Commission. Separately, dismissal because of trade union membership or legitimate trade union activity is protected under the Unfair Dismissals Acts.
While I acknowledge that the existing arrangements do not amount to a statutory right to trade union recognition or a general enforceable right of access for external union representatives, the question of both physical and digital access was considered during the development of Ireland’s Action Plan to Promote Collective Bargaining 2026–2030. question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to outline any plans that he may introduce for compulsory safety reporting and monitoring of frontier artificial intelligence.
reply:
Frontier AI refers to some of the most advanced AI models currently in development. These models are increasingly being applied to scientific research, including areas such as healthcare, life sciences and materials science.
The rapid pace of technological progress has intensified international discussion regarding the governance of frontier AI, particularly in relation to model evaluation, safety testing, risk management, cybersecurity, access to computing infrastructure, and the development of common technical standards.
The EU AI Act provides what is often referred to as the world's first comprehensive legal framework for artificial intelligence. While the term "frontier AI" is not specifically defined in the Act, the most advanced AI models are addressed through the Act's framework for general-purpose AI models, including those designated as posing systemic risk. These models are subject to enhanced requirements relating to risk management, model evaluation, incident reporting and cybersecurity. The European Commission AI Office has primary responsibility for the supervision of these obligations and plays a central role in the governance of advanced AI models within the European Union. In addition to its supervisory functions, it supports coordination among Member States and contributes to wider discussions on AI governance and safety.
The broader European approach combines regulation, technical standards, codes of practice, market oversight and international cooperation

reply:

The review was undertaken in response to a range of structural changes in the labour market since MAR thresholds were last comprehensively updated including sustained inflationary pressures, increases in average earnings, rising costs of living, and changing labour market dynamics. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether his Department has assessed the position where the minimum annual remuneration for healthcare assistants and home carers, equivalent to €16.12 an hour on a 39 hour week, exceeds the national minimum wage of €14.15 an hour, such that Irish and EEA workers in the same roles may legally be paid less than permit holders.
reply:
National Minimum Wage (NMW) sets the out the minimum pay terms permitted to employ someone in Ireland. Minimum annual remuneration (MAR) thresholds set the minimum salary to recruit someone, from anywhere in the world, to work in Ireland and therefore regulates access to the labour market, shaping the composition of economic migration.
The Government's objective in establishing MAR thresholds within the employment permits system is to support fair remuneration, facilitate the attraction and retention of essential skills, ensure that employment permit holders have access to quality employment opportunities, can contribute positively to the Irish economy and have the financial capacity to support a reasonable standard of living for themselves and, where applicable, their families, without undue recourse to State supports.
In addition, aligning employment permit remuneration thresholds with broader earnings growth helps to mitigate the risk of disruption or displacement within the domestic labour market, including potential wage suppression. It also supports the objective of ensuring that the employment permit system complements, rather than substitutes for, investment in workforce development, innovation, productivity improvements, and skills enhancement. Maintaining appropriate remuneration thresholds helps to ensure that Ireland's employment permits framework remains balanced, sustainable and responsive to the needs of both workers and employers.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment in relation to the general employment permit application, if websites (details supplied) are acceptable online platforms for the second job advertisement required for the Labour Market Needs Test.
reply:
The employment permits system is grounded in legislation that sets clear and objective criteria applied to the grant of an employment permit including minimum salary thresholds, availability of skills in the domestic labour market, and the eligibility of occupations. These criteria ensure that permits are issued only where there is a demonstrable shortage and that the system remains fair, transparent, and responsive to Ireland’s labour market needs.
The labour market needs test (LMNT) is a core safeguard within the system. It ensures that job vacancies are first made available to Irish and EEA nationals before an employer may recruit a non EEA national.
Where an LMNT is required, including for General Employment Permit applications, employers must advertise the vacancy through the Department of Social Protection’s JobsIreland and EURES online employment services, and on at least one additional online platform jointly for at least 28 days (continuously and unaltered). Suitable platforms for the additional advertisements should be accessible to the general public, the principal purpose of which is to publish offers of employment including for example online newspaper publications and employment websites.

reply:
Fáilte Ireland is aware of Carrigglas Manor and Demesne, which is a privately owned property. There has been no engagement between Fáilte Ireland and the owners, or Longford County Council, in relation to any proposed redevelopment of the property.
Fáilte Ireland offers a range of supports that can be useful to promoters seeking to start or develop tourism businesses in Ireland, with details and contact information available on their website.
In line with A New Era for Irish Tourism, the national tourism policy statement, and Fáilte Ireland’s recently published corporate strategy, the organisation is currently developing a new capital investment plan. As these schemes are still under development, it is not possible to comment on the provide detail on the eligibility of individual projects at this stage.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to provide clarity on the refusal of an employment permit (details supplied); and what is required in order to remedy this.
reply:
The Employment Permits Acts provide a statutory process for the consideration of employment permit applications, including review and appeal mechanisms. Where an application is refused, the reasons for refusal are set out in the decision letter issued to the applicant together with information on the options available to seek a review of the decision.
Information on employment permit requirements and the relevant application processes is available on the Department's website. The Department also provides assistance through its general queries mailbox, and a dedicated mailbox is available to Members of the Oireachtas making representations on behalf of constituents.
In this case, the application was assessed in accordance with the statutory criteria set out in the Employment Permits Acts and Regulations and was refused because those criteria were not met. The reasons for refusal were set out in the decision letter issued to the applicant, together with details of the statutory review process available.

The decision on whether to offer flood insurance, the level of premiums charged and the policy terms applied are matters for individual insurers. Insurance companies make commercial decisions on the provision of insurance cover based on their assessment of the risks they would be accepting on a case-by-case basis. The Government cannot interfere in the provision or pricing of insurance products, as reinforced by the EU framework for insurance (Solvency II Directive).

In this regard, the OPW has a Memorandum of Understanding with Insurance Ireland, the representative body of the insurance industry. This Memorandum sets out principles of how the two organisations work together to ensure that appropriate and relevant information on these completed schemes is provided to insurers to facilitate, to the greatest extent possible, the availability to the public of insurance against the risk of flooding. While the Memorandum does not guarantee the availability of flood insurance, Insurance Ireland members have committed to take into account all information provided by the OPW when assessing exposure to flood risk within the protected areas.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he will provide an update on capital infrastructure allocations under the national development plan specifically earmarked for Cavan and Monaghan; to ensure that the specific economic vulnerabilities of rural border towns are weighted heavily in upcoming mid-term budgetary reviews.
reply:
As Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, I am responsible for setting the overall capital allocations across Departments and for monitoring expenditure at Departmental level.
The National Development Plan (NDP) Review 2025 was published in July 2025 and set out overall Government capital expenditure ceilings to 2035 alongside annual sectoral capital expenditure ceilings for the period 2026 to 2030.
Following the agreement of annual sectoral capital allocations for the period out 2030, each Department developed a Sectoral Investment Plan. These Plans were published throughout November and December 2025 outlining the specific capital projects and programmes to be prioritised and delivered within their five-year allocation.
The responsibility for the management and delivery of individual projects within these Sectoral Investment Plans rests with the individual sponsoring Department in each case. Each Minister is responsible for deciding on the priority programmes and projects that will be delivered under their remit within the NDP. Expenditure is therefore allocated and monitored on a Departmental basis.
A key priority for this Government is the achievement of balanced regional development. This goal is at the heart of Project Ireland 2040, which includes the National Planning Framework (NPF) setting out Government’s overarching spatial strategy for the next twenty years, alongside the NDP.
