question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to address a pension related matter (details supplied).
reply:
I am advised that the National Shared Services Office (NSSO) has examined the case referred to by the Deputy.
The person concerned served in the former Department of Posts and Telegraphs between 1969 and 1975. However, a distinction must be made between total period of employment and reckonable service for superannuation purposes.
Records indicate that the period from 14 July 1969 to 3 June 1973 was served in a non-pensionable capacity and, the service, therefore is not reckonable for pension purposes. The individual's pensionable service ran from 4 June 1973 to 12 May 1975 and amounted to 1 year and 344 days of reckonable service.
Under the superannuation arrangements applicable at the time, an officer was required to have a minimum of five years' qualifying pensionable service in order to be entitled to preserved pension benefits on leaving the public service. While the individual's overall period of employment exceeded five years, only reckonable pensionable service may be counted in determining entitlement to superannuation benefits. As the individual had less than five years' qualifying pensionable service, the individual concerned did not meet this statutory qualifying requirement and therefore there is no entitlement to a preserved pension under the terms of the applicable scheme.
The NSSO has reviewed the case and confirmed that the position is consistent with the relevant superannuation provisions. Pension benefits can only be awarded where the conditions prescribed

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to provide the necessary funding to address tidal flooding where family homes have been flooded at Cromane Lower, Killorglin, County Kerry.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 376 and 377 together.
Minor Flood Mitigation Works and Coastal Protection Scheme.
Localised flooding issues are a matter, in the first instance, for each Local Authority to investigate and address, and a Local Authority may carry out flood mitigation works using its own resources. Local Authorities may apply to the OPW for funding for flood mitigation and coastal protection works under the OPW Minor Flood Mitigation Works and Coastal Protection Scheme. Since its introduction in 2009, some €70 million has been approved under the Scheme for 930 local authority led projects that are delivering flood mitigation and coastal protection for some 8,000 properties.
In May this year, I was pleased to announce that the revised criteria for the Minor Flood Mitigation Works and Coastal Protection Scheme (Minor Works Scheme) are available and greatly increase the scope of the Scheme and provides local authorities with a greater opportunity to address localised flooding and coastal erosion risk within their administrative areas. The revisions include an increase in the upper threshold in funding for projects from €750,000 to €2 million and an increase in the OPW contribution from 90% to 95% for approved funding above €300,000. I have also expanded the Scheme to include interim flood mitigation measures for communities where a major flood relief scheme is planned, but not complete. Further revisions include the relaxing of some economic criteria.
Cromane

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to consider decentralising Government departments to Iveragh and south Kerry to boost economic growth in these areas.
reply:
Decentralisation was announced in 2003 to support the relocation of jobs and organisational functions across the Civil Service from Dublin to towns and cities throughout Ireland. From 2003 to 2011, the economic development programme for rural towns was supported through a number of interlinked policies and funding streams, including a programme of decentralisation in line with commitments in the National Spatial Strategy (2002 - 2020) to balance regional growth in Ireland.
On 17th November 2011, the Government announced the cancellation of the programme in light of substantial changes in the national budgetary and workforce environment. This decision was also influenced by the need to focus on programmes and projects that would best support economic recovery and identify significant expenditure savings and efficiencies. There are currently no plans to reintroduce this programme.
The Civil Service Mobility Scheme was introduced in 2018 to facilitate the structured movement of Civil Servants between Departments and locations across Ireland. The Scheme supports skills development, career progression and increased workforce flexibility and also allows civil servants to avail of transfers to posts located nationwide, including outside the Dublin area.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the estimated capital and current expenditure associated with implementing the European Digital Identity Wallet; the projected annual operating cost; and the source of funding for same.
reply:
Since 2024, my Department has invested a total of €4,628,866 in capital funding in the national Government digital wallet initiative. This initiative is being delivered on a phased basis, with funding provided over multiple years to support its design, development, testing, and rollout.
The implementation leverages a suite of technical building blocks and digital public infrastructure components to ensure the efficient and effective use of public investment. This approach supports the development of Ireland's national digital wallet, providing the foundation for Ireland's EU-compliant digital wallet under the European Digital Identity Framework Regulation.
As the solution remains under development and has not yet entered full operational service, separate estimates of ongoing annual operating costs have not yet been finalised. Operational requirements, including hosting, support, maintenance, certification and service management arrangements, will continue to be assessed as implementation progresses and the operating model is finalised.
Funding for this initiative to date has been provided through the Department's Digital Transformation Fund (DTF). Future operational costs associated with the national digital wallet will be met from Exchequer resources through the annual estimates process, in line with funding arrangements that apply to other national digital public services.

As announced in Budget 2027, a holistic assessment of Ireland’s enterprise support regime including grant schemes and tax incentives available to businesses will be undertaken. Further detail on this review will be announced in due course.

reply:

question: Deputy Holly Cairns asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the safeguards in place to ensure that Revenue enforcement and sheriff procedures adequately provide for exceptional circumstances when dealing with small, family operated businesses; and whether additional discretion should be available in cases where hardship, bereavement or serious family illness can be clearly evidenced.
reply:
I am advised that Revenue only refers outstanding tax liabilities to its enforcement agents, including sheriffs, as a last resort. Revenue’s strong preference is to engage constructively with taxpayers who are experiencing temporary cash-flow difficulties, and, where possible, to agree mutually acceptable payment solutions, including Phased Payment Arrangements (PPA) where appropriate, rather than resorting to debt collection or enforcement measures.
I am further advised that Revenue’s debt collection and enforcement framework incorporates a range of safeguards including constructive engagement with taxpayers in difficulty, a graduated series of contacts before any enforcement is initiated, and case by case discretion to take account of hardship and exceptional circumstances.
As part of Revenue’s standard debt collection procedure, where taxes become overdue in accordance with the statutory due date, a request for payment will issue with details of the tax(es) due, requesting payment within a set timeframe. This request outlines the consequences of continued non-payment and affords the taxpayer up to 10 days to engage. In the absence of payment or meaningful engagement, a final demand issues allowing a further 7 days for the customer to engage. It is only where there is continued lack of engagement from the customer in response to these notices that the case is escalated for enforcement action, which may include referral to the Sheriff.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the number of communities in Galway east that became newly eligible for CLÁR funding, following the recent review of the scheme; and if he will consider further expanding eligibility to rural communities experiencing population growth but which continue to face significant deficits in community infrastructure and services.
reply:

The 2025 Programme for Government made a commitment to carry out a comprehensive review of the eligible CLÁR areas. This review has now been completed, and an additional 110 electoral divisions (EDs) have been designated as eligible under the CLÁR programme.
The review was completed by the All-Island Research Observatory in Maynooth University utilising two nationally recognised datasets, based on the results from Census 2022. As a result of the review, the ED of Crumpaun was newly designated in Galway and almost 70% of Galway is now designated for CLÁR.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if the Flood Insurance Protection Gap Working Group has met yet; if so, the matters discussed; the frequency with which it is due to meet; the schedule of options it will discuss; the manner in which its recommendations will be published and considered; and a timeline for same.
reply:

Accordingly, €1.3 billion has been committed to the delivery of flood relief schemes over the lifetime of the National Development Plan (NDP) to 2030. This will protect approximately 23,000 properties across various communities from river and coastal flood risk.
In terms of flood insurance, the Central Bank of Ireland has undertaken extensive research into the nature and scale of the flood insurance protection gap in Ireland. They found that 1 in 20 buildings (approximately 5%) have limited access to flood insurance; and that 54% of this gap is concentrated in Dublin, Cork, Louth, Clare, and Kildare.

reply:

• the amount of Income Tax and DIRT paid in the four years before application for the relief.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to outline the CPI projections that underpin the Budget 2027 rather than the HICP.
reply:
Under Regulation (EU) No 473/2013, my Department is required to send the macroeconomic and fiscal forecasts produced for Budget 2027 to the European Commission in the Draft Budgetary Plan (DBP) by October 15th. In line with guidelines from the Commission, my Department uses the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) as the measure of inflation used in its forecasts.
As the Deputy will be aware, my Department’s forecasts are independently endorsed by the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council. A memorandum of understanding (MOU) between my Department and the Fiscal Council details the key elements of the endorsement process including the variables the Department is required to provide to the Fiscal Council. This MOU specifies that my Department forecast inflation on a HICP basis. As such, my Department projects inflation, as measured by the HICP rather than on the basis of the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the position regarding any review of the requirement under the Irish Collective Asset-management Vehicles (ICAV) Act 2015 for the central bank to maintain a publicly accessible database of company directors that includes their name, date of birth, personal residential address and a copy of their signature; and if he is concerned about the implications on their privacy as a result of this requirement.
reply:
As you may be aware, the Department recently published a refreshed Ireland for Finance Strategy, ‘Vision 2030 - Renewed and Refocussed for a Digital Age’.
In the Strategy, the Department also highlights its intention to review the Irish Collective Asset-Management Vehicles Act 2015 (ICAV Act) and has identified this as a key policy action.
Section 11 of the ICAV Act 2015 requires the Central Bank to maintain an ICAV’s register of directors and secretaries, and Section 65(2) specifies the information that must be included in an ICAV's register of directors including certain personal data relating to directors. The requirement reflects long-standing corporate governance provisions that also apply under the Companies Act 2014.
The purpose of these requirements is to support transparency, accountability and effective regulatory oversight of ICAVs and their directors. In the context of investment funds, such information assists the Central Bank of Ireland in the discharge of its statutory supervisory functions and helps ensure appropriate governance standards are maintained.
Your concerns raised regarding the privacy concerns of directors is duly noted.
The Department will consider them for further analysis and review in the context of the wider review of this legislation.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if his Department has conducted a costing of the proposal to align the substantial shareholding exemption with the dividend participation exemption; and, if so, to outline the costs involved.
reply:
The Participation Exemption for Foreign Dividends regime was introduced in Finance Act 2024. The exemption, which applies simplifies the double tax relief system and enhances Ireland’s attractiveness for multinational businesses. The exemption is available, subject to conditions, in respect of distributions received from qualifying subsidiaries in EEA and treaty partner jurisdictions and jurisdictions that have imposed a non-refundable withholding tax on the distribution.
Section 626B TCA 1997, Substantial Shareholding Exemption, introduced in 2004, provides for an exemption from capital gains tax on certain disposals of subsidiary shareholdings, subject to conditions including shareholding, residence and trading requirements.
In relation to the costing of the proposal to align the aspects of Substantial Shareholding Exemption regime with the Dividend Participation Exemption, I am advised by Revenue that the data required to provide an estimated cost is not available on its statistical records.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will consider expanding or adjusting the Small Benefit Exemption framework to explicitly incentivise and favour locally administered town or chamber gift card schemes; if he will assess the way in which such a mechanism can prevent economic leakage and sustain local retail sectors in rural border towns.
reply:
Section 112B Taxes Consolidation Act 1997 (TCA) provides that an employer may give non-cash rewards (such as a voucher) to an employee without giving rise to a charge to tax where certain conditions are met. This is referred to as the Small-Benefit-Exemption (SBE).
The principle of the SBE has existed for over 20 years. When BIK was broadly introduced, in 2004, an issue arose as the provision of vouchers, gifts etc., from employers to employees in recognition of life events, or performance, became taxable events. In acknowledgement of this, Revenue applied an administrative concession to the provision of one benefit/gift, to the maximum value of €100. This concession was subsequently increased to €250.
Section 11 of the Finance Act 2015 introduced it to the Statute Books, providing for a tax-free threshold of €500, which could apply to the provision of one benefit/gift. In 2022, this increased to a tax-free threshold of €1,000, which could be provided via no more than two benefits/gifts. On 1 January 2025 this increased to a tax-free threshold of €1,500, to be provided via no more than five benefits/gifts.
The policy objective is to allow employers provide some form of recognition to employees that is not subject to tax in a manner that is straightforward and easy to implement. The provision is broad – a benefit is defined as ‘a tangible asset other than cash’. As such, it is not restricted to the issuance of vouchers. question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the regulatory protections available to investors where an investment vehicle has entered liquidation and the regulated intermediary that advised on or serviced that investment has also entered liquidation (details supplied); the responsibilities that a regulated intermediary retains for advice provided prior to liquidation.
reply:
The Central Bank of Ireland is the independent regulator for financial services and it determines what measures or actions need to be taken in relation to any potential, or actual, wrongdoing by regulated financial service providers.
European and Irish legislation requires the regulation of financial services firms providing investment services in relation to investment products. The law lists the various types of regulated investment services and investment. Regulated firms may also sell investment products which are not specifically mentioned in the law (i.e. unregulated products). Where they do so, certain investor protections, which apply to regulated activities do not apply.

Firms are also required to take appropriate steps to mitigate the risk that a customer will understand an activity to be, or to carry the protections of, a regulated activity where this is not the case. question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if his Department has engaged with the Central Bank and an organisation (details supplied) on the credit risk posed by uninsured flood-exposed homes; and if he has considered the proposal by another organisation in August 2026 for mortgage top-up lending to fund property-level flood resilience works.
reply:
The availability of flood protection insurance is an important factor in protecting the financial resilience of property owners and in turn credit risk of properties in flood risk areas.
My Department and the Central Bank of Ireland are members of the Flood Insurance Protection Gap Working Group. This group will progress long term sustainable solutions to the protection gap, as set out in the Action Plan for Insurance Reform. Proposals, such as that outlined by the Deputy, may be considered by this group as part of their work.
There are channels in which flood risk and flood events can impact on credit risk in Ireland. A flood event damages buildings, fixtures, fittings and contents, and the lack of flood insurance could worsen the borrower's financial position, with potential consequences for probability of default. There is also a potential collateral channel, as buildings with higher flood risk, all else being equal, would be worth less.
Central Bank analytics have advanced significantly to support understanding how flood risk interact with the financial sector. Published research available on the Central Bank website includes:
• Flood Protection Gap Report: www.centralbank.ie/news/article/press-release-central-bank-publishes-flood-protection-gap-report-14-oct-2024.
• Flood Exposure in Business Lending: www.centralbank.ie/statistics/statistical-publications/behind-the-data/measuring-flood-risk-in-business-lending.
• Flood Exposure and Credit Conditions: www.centralbank.ie/

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the Government's position on a request (details supplied) that the Government endorse a national flood framework and establish a sustainable flood insurance fund and flood agency through enabling legislation, with collection of a flood insurance protection contribution to begin in 2027 and the fund to begin taking on risk by 2028; the date by which the Flood Insurance Protection Gap Working Group is due to report; and whether the 2027 timeline is considered achievable.
reply:

Accordingly, €1.3 billion has been committed to the delivery of flood relief schemes over the lifetime of the National Development Plan (NDP) to 2030. This will protect approximately 23,000 properties across various communities from river and coastal flood risk.
In terms of flood insurance, the Central Bank of Ireland has undertaken extensive research into the nature and scale of the Flood Protection Gap in Ireland. They found that 1 in 20 buildings (approximately 5%) have limited access to flood insurance; and that 54% of this gap is concentrated in Dublin, Cork, Louth, Clare, and Kildare.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht to provide an update on his plans to support regeneration in towns and villages across Galway East.
reply:
The Town Centre First (TCF) Policy is a major government initiative that supports the regeneration of Irish towns to ensure that they are vibrant, viable and attractive places to live, work, visit and invest in.

They are a key link between local authorities and their communities. They work closely across multi-disciplinary town regeneration teams, including dedicated Capital Delivery Teams made up of technical and administrative staff, also funded by my department.
My department provides a range of capital funding to support delivery on TCF objectives. question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if his Department has assessed the potential financial and economic implications for Ireland of the European Commission’s proposed new own resource based on non-collected waste electrical and electronic equipment, including the potential cost to the Exchequer and impacts on businesses and consumers.
reply:
The European Commission published its proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), to cover the years 2028-2034, in July and September 2025, including a package of amended and new own resources - i.e. revenue sources for the EU budget. The nine existing, amended and new own resources under the Commission's proposal include, for example, customs duties, contributions based on the Emissions Trading System, and an own resource based on non-collected waste electrical and electronic equipment (e-waste).
Member States' contributions to the EU budget are composed of the different own resources, and a Member State's share of each own resource will vary according to the nature of that own resource. If during negotiations an own resource is removed from the package, Member States would contribute that level of revenue according to the GNI-based own resource instead. For Ireland, the Department's analysis suggests our EU budget contribution would be marginally lower under the e-waste own resource compared to GNI.
With regard to potential impacts on businesses and consumers, the Commission's proposal stated that while Member States would contribute to the EU budget an amount proportional to €2 per kilogram of non-collected e-waste, it should be left to the discretion of the Member States as to whether to take any related domestic policy actions, in line with the principle of subsidiarity.

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he has considered reviewing the income thresholds that apply for the purposes of the Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) exemption for persons aged 65 years and over; his views on whether the current thresholds continue to reflect increases in the State Pension and other income supports in recent years; whether his Department has undertaken any analysis of the number of older persons who may no longer qualify for the exemption as a result of such increases.
reply:
The Deputy will be aware that Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) is a withholding tax that is deducted by Irish financial institutions on deposit interest paid or credited on the deposits of Irish residents.
Since 1 January 2020, the DIRT rate is 33%. DIRT is a final liability tax. This means that an individual has no further tax liability in respect of the deposit interest earned.
Deposit interest is specifically excluded from the Universal Social Charge. Individuals may however have a liability to Pay Related Social Insurance (PRSI) in certain circumstances.
Interest may be received without paying DIRT in certain circumstances. Where an individual, or their spouse/civil partner, is aged over 65 and their total income, including gross deposit interest does not exceed the annual exemption limit, as provided for in section 188 Taxes Consolidation Act (TCA) 1997, their deposit interest earnings are exempt from DIRT.
As the Deputy is aware, the current exemption limit is €18,000 in the case of a single person and €36,000 in the case of a married couple or civil partners. The relevant income thresholds may be increased further if the individual has a qualifying child. Additionally, marginal relief may be available where the individual’s or couple’s income exceeds the relevant exemption limit but is less than twice that amount. These exemption limits were considered as part of the Review of the Personal Tax System carried out by my Department in 2023. This review is available o

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance for and updated timeline for the completion of a review (details supplied).
reply:
The Central Bank of Ireland has provided me with the following information on the matter.
The Central Bank has commissioned an independent review of its enforcement activities.
The review is not focused on a specific case rather will evaluate the effectiveness of the Central Bank's enforcement activities and the role of enforcement within the wider supervisory framework. It will examine structures and processes for enforcement activity and decision-making; case-selection criteria and processes; timeliness; and transparency for the public, firms and individuals who may be impacted. It will have regard to best practice by regulators performing similar functions domestically and internationally and applicable international standards and principles.
The review is underway and as per the Terms of Reference (www.centralbank.ie/docs/default-source/news-and-media/press-releases/terms-of-reference---july-2026.pdf?sfvrsn=eb8711a_1) a report will be provided to the Governor by 31 January 2027 and published in due course.

The rule was introduced to protect the Exchequer from indefinite deferral of tax, and as the Funds Review final report states, any move to remove it requires the simultaneous implementation of appropriate guardrails which require further consideration. question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he has considered introducing income tax relief on overtime earnings, particularly for workers maintaining essential public services and infrastructure; whether any such relief could be restricted to overtime verified through employer records or other auditable systems; and the estimated annual Exchequer cost of exempting the first €2,500, €5,000 and €10,000 of overtime earnings per worker.
reply:
It is a general principle of taxation that, as far as possible, income from all sources should be subject to taxation.
Ireland has a progressive income tax system which is structured such that the more income you earn, the more tax you pay. As a person’s income increases, they move up through the various rates and bands and, as a result, while the levels of take-home pay increase overall, the amount of tax they pay also increases.
The ‘Programme for Government 2025: Securing Ireland’s Future’, contains specific undertakings with regard to personal taxation, it commits to “implementing progressive changes in taxation if the economy remains strong, including indexing credits and bands to prevent an increase in the real burden of Income Tax while in the event of an economic downturn and unexpected deterioration in the public finances we would postpone changes to Income Tax credits or bands, as we did in Budget 2021”.
In Budget 2027 I introduced a significant personal income tax package with an estimated full year cost of €1.5 billion. This personal income tax package has been carefully designed to support workers.
The entry point to the higher rate of income tax for all earners is being increased by €2,500 for the 2027 tax year and subsequent years of assessment. question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will consider extending the 9% VAT rate to qualifying beauty, aesthetic and nail-care services, which already applies to hairdressing services as part of the Finance Bill 2027 (details supplied). whether he acknowledges that extending the 9% rate would provide a fairer and more consistent VAT framework for the wider personal-care sector.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the VAT rating of goods and services is subject to the requirements of the EU VAT Directive with which Irish VAT law is obliged to comply. In general, the EU VAT Directive provides that all goods and services are liable to VAT at the standard rate, unless they are exempt from VAT or fall within the categories of goods and services listed in Annex III of the EU VAT Directive, to which Member States are permitted to apply lower VAT rates subject to certain rules.
Beauticians are not included in the categories of goods and services on which the EU Directive allows a lower rate of VAT, and therefore they would fall to be taxed by Member States at their standard rate of VAT – which in Ireland is currently 23%. However, the Directive allows that a Member State may retain certain long-standing VAT arrangements that they had in place, subject to strict conditions including that the terms of the historic arrangement cannot be extended.
On this basis, Ireland is permitted to retain its long-standing application of its reduced VAT rate – which is currently 13.5% – to services related to the care of the human body, which includes beautician services. In accordance with the Directive this arrangement is treated as a ‘parked’ rate, which means that it cannot be reduced below 12%. If Ireland were to cease the application of the parked rate to these supplies, then under the terms of the Directive these services would have to be subject to the standard rate of VAT

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht for an update on the forthcoming review of the CLÁR programme; the timeframe for its commencement and completion; and if the eligibility of footpath construction in rural towns and villages forms part of the review.
reply:
The CLÁR programme provides funding under a number of different measures for small-scale infrastructural projects in designated rural areas. Last year over €14 million was approved for 238 projects under the programme, with funding being provided for community facilities and amenities, community vehicles and specific support for island communities. The 2026 CLÁR programme was launched on March 10th.
In line with a commitment in the Programme for Government, a comprehensive review of eligible CLÁR areas was completed in advance of launching the 2026 programme. On completion of the review, an additional 110 electoral divisions (EDs) were included as newly eligible areas, including one additional area in County Galway.
In addition to this review, I consider the measures to be funded in advance of the launch of the CLÁR programme each year, including the eligibility criteria to be applied. I will again examine the measures being funded in advance of the launch of the 2027 programme. I have no specific plans to fund footpaths at this time given the focus on community facilities and amenities, and community vehicles and the existence of other funding streams across Government. However, I will keep the position under consideration.

question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Transport the status of plans to re-open the Mullingar to Athlone rail line; and if this is a priority for public transport in the region.
reply:

question: Deputy Johnny Guirke asked the Minister for Transport the extent of bilateral agreements currently in place between the Road Safety Authority (RSA) / National Driver Licence Service (NDLS) and non-EU jurisdictions for the reciprocal recognition and exchange of driving licences; the specific criteria, technical assessments, and verification processes, used to evaluate foreign driving standards prior to entering into such agreements; whether these assessments evaluate driver comprehension of Irish road signs and traffic legislation.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 341 to 346, inclusive, together.
Irish driver licensing operates within a framework of EU law, which sets out the driver licensing legislation with which all Member States must comply. Licence formats, vehicle categories and driving test standards are all set at EU level. As all Member States test drivers to the same standards, there can be mutual recognition of driving licences.
Ireland and other member states may also have bilateral driving licence exchange agreements with other jurisdictions. The main purpose of licence exchange agreements with non-EU jurisdictions is to ensure that anyone from those jurisdictions who obtains an Irish driving licence by exchange has been tested at an equivalent standard to drivers who passed a test in Ireland.
Reaching an agreement is not a matter of political will. The core principle is to ensure the continued safety of Irish road users in alignment with government and EU commitments to reduce road deaths and injuries by 2050 (Vision Zero). The RSA is responsible for undertaking a technical and independent review, to ascertain that the other licensing and testing regime is comparable with that in Ireland.
An agreement also allows for the verification of licences produced for exchange, to confirm whether the licence is valid and that the applicant is the licence holder. question: Deputy Johnny Guirke asked the Minister for Transport his plans to reduce toll costs in Meath.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and funding in relation to the national roads programme. Under the Roads Acts 1993-2015, the operation and management of individual national roads is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned.
Therefore, matters relating to the day to day operations regarding national roads, including toll roads are within the remit of TII. More specifically, the statutory power to levy tolls, to make toll bye-laws and to enter into agreements with private investors are vested in TII under Part V of the Roads Act 1993 (as amended). Moreover, the contracts for the privately-operated toll schemes are commercial agreements between TII and the Public Private Partnership (PPP) concessionaires concerned.
Noting the above position, I have referred the question regarding tolls to TII for a direct reply. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 working days.

question: Deputy Tony McCormack asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the initiatives being developed to combat social isolation in rural communities, particularly among older people and those living alone; and whether additional investment in community meeting places and local voluntary organisations is planned.
reply:
Loneliness and social isolation are complex issues that can arise from a range of social, economic, and demographic factors and, therefore, relate to policy areas across many departments. Issues such as access to transport, economic disadvantage or social exclusion can all contribute to isolation in rural areas. My department works closely with colleagues across Government to ensure that rural communities in particular are not left behind in the provision of public services.
With regard to my own department, ‘Our Rural Future’ recognises the importance of addressing loneliness and isolation, particularly for older people and those living alone. The next iteration of the policy, which is due to be published later this month will continue to focus on this important issue which impacts both rural and urban communities.
One of the values underpinning the new five-year government strategy in support of the community and voluntary sector, ‘Ar Scath a Cheile’, which was launched earlier this week, is a commitment to social inclusion, prioritising the needs of communities experiencing social or economic exclusion.
There are schemes and programmes operated by my department which directly help to address this issue. Of particular importance with regard to capital funding are the Community Centre Investment Fund, LEADER, CLÁR and the Local Enhancement Programme. reply:

question: Deputy David Maxwell asked the Minister for Transport to substantially increase the funding available to local authorities under the low-cost safety improvement works scheme, recognising the significant number of towns, villages and settlements across the country where additional traffic-calming and road-safety measures are required.
reply:
For 2027, grant allocations to be provided through the Regional and Local Roads Grant Programme are under consideration and will be finalised after the publication of the Revised Estimates Volume.
Applications for Low-Cost Safety Improvement Works are sought each year from local authorities for consideration for funding in the subsequent year. The schemes for inclusion in these applications are decided by the local authorities themselves and submitted in order of priority.
This year, funding of €14 million was allocated towards over 300 Low-Cost Safety Improvement Works, targeting remedial measures to improve road safety for vulnerable road users and vehicular traffic. This is an increase of 8% from 2025 and follows an increase of 23% in 2025, upholding the Programme for Government commitment in road safety.

reply:

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Transport regarding the proposed change to the regulatory framework governing alcohol and psychoactive substance testing of pilots and other safety-sensitive aviation personnel in Ireland, whether his Department supports the transfer of responsibility for alcohol and psychoactive substance testing from State authorities to individual airlines or other private entities; whether the constitutional, employment-law, licensing, criminal-law, privacy, data-protection and fair-procedure implications of such a transfer have been fully examined.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 292, 293, 294, 295, 323 and 324 together.
On 29 September the Irish Aviation Authority (IAA) commenced a public consultation on the future regulatory approach to drug and alcohol testing in the Irish aviation sector. The consultation seeks the views of aviation stakeholders, employees, industry representative bodies, public authorities and members of the public on the most appropriate means of introducing a comprehensive framework to manage the safety risks associated with impairment arising from alcohol and other psychoactive substances. The deadline for submissions is 31 October 2026.
While the IAA is seeking views on a proposed Employer-Led Testing Framework with IAA Oversight, no decision has been taken yet on state policy in this area. The purpose of the consultation is to gather evidence, perspectives and views of all relevant stakeholders to inform future policy development.
My department will be engaging with the IAA following completion of the consultation process.

question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht for an update on CCIF applications for Carlow and Kilkenny.
reply:
The Community Centre Investment Fund (CCIF) was introduced to provide high quality, accessible, community spaces that are available to all groups in all communities in both rural and urban areas. Some €112 million has been allocated since 2022 for the enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres and the construction of new centres where such a need has been identified.
Since 2022, I am pleased to confirm that 15 projects in County Carlow have been approved for funding under the CCIF representing a total investment of over €5.1 million. This includes an allocation of over €4.1 million under CCIF 2023 towards the development of a new community centre at Tullow Road, Carlow. County Kilkenny has received over €2.5 million for 35 projects under the CCIF.
I was delighted to launch the latest round of funding under CCIF 2026 on the 26th of March for enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres. The fund will be delivered across two categories with maximum funding levels of €25,000 and €100,000 respectively. The closing date for the CCIF 2026 has now passed.
Applications are currently being assessed, including those received in respect of centres in Carlow and Kilkenny. I look forward to announcing the successful projects under category 1, which provides funding of up to €25,000, in the coming weeks. The successful projects under category 2, which provides funding of up to €100,000, will be announced before year-end.

question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Transport the eligibility criteria for a disabled person parking permit for a person (details supplied) in county Kildare.
reply:
As Minister of State for International & Road Transport, Logistics, Rail & Ports, I wish to advise that the Road Traffic (Traffic & Parking) Regulations 1997, as amended, sets out the statutory foundations for the Disabled Parking Scheme.
Disabled parking permits are available to an individual with permanent conditions or disabilities that severely restrict their ability to walk. Eligibility is thus defined on the basis of mobility impairment rather than on the basis of a specific medical condition. An individual who is certified as blind may also qualify for a permit.
The websites of the issuing bodies, the Irish Wheelchair Association and the Disabled Drivers Association of Ireland, which issue disabled parking permits on behalf of the State, have details of the application process and eligibility criteria (www.iwa.ie and www.ddai.ie).
The Deputy may also wish to note that neither I, nor my Department, can intervene in any individual Disabled Parking Scheme application or appeals process.

question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Transport if there are plans to increase the fine for persons parking in disabled persons parking bays; and if so, what are his plans to remodel the scheme.
reply:
As Minister of State for International & Road Transport, Logistics, Rail & Ports, I wish to advise that officials from my Department are currently undertaking a review of the Disabled Parking Scheme. Any potential changes to this scheme, through legislative amendment, would be done in conjunction with the transposition of EU Directive (EU) 2024/2841, which introduces measures to strengthen the mutual recognition of disability entitlements, including the European parking card.
My Department has no current plans to increase the current fixed charge notice (FCN) penalties for disabled parking offences. These values are amongst some of the highest FCNs that can be issued by An Garda Síochána or traffic wardens, highlighting the seriousness of these offences.
FCNs are issued by members of An Garda Síochána and local authority traffic wardens, and my Department does not hold the information requested.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport the status of the B-Spine rollout following Budget 2027.

The National Transport Authority (NTA) has responsibility for the planning and development of public transport infrastructure in the Greater Dublin Area, including the BusConnects Dublin programme.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Transport if he has considered amending the Railway Safety Bill 2026 to strengthen the preventative role of the Railway Accident Investigation Unit (RAIU); if the reporting, recording and investigation of near miss incidents, including incidents at level crossings, will form part of the statutory framework under the Bill; if the RAIU will have powers to make recommendations on emerging safety risks before serious accidents occur; and if annual reports on railway safety recommendations and trends will be submitted to the Minister and laid before the Houses of the Oireachtas.
reply:
The statutory powers of the Railway Accident Investigation Unit (RAIU) for reporting and investigations are set out under the European Union (Railway Safety) (Reporting and Investigation of Serious Accidents, Accidents and incidents) Regulations 2020 (SI No. 430 of 2020). These Regulations of 2020 which are based on the EU Railway Safety Directive apply to the Iarnród Éireann network. The equivalent provisions will be provided for other railways in Part 2 of the Railway Safety Bill 2026.
The legislation already has a preventative goal. The Regulations of 2020 state that the objective of an investigation is to improve, where possible, railway safety and the prevention of accidents. The purpose of RAIU investigations is to make safety recommendations in order to prevent accidents and incidents in the future and improve railway safety. During an investigation, if the RAIU make some early findings on safety issues that require immediate attention, the RAIU will issue a Safety Advice Notice (SAN) or an Urgent Safety Advice Notice) (USAN) outlining the associated safety recommendations.
I can confirm that the reporting of accidents and incidents at present to the RAIU includes near miss incidents and incidents at level crossings. In that regard, the Regulations of 2020 state that in addition to the investigation of a serious accident, the RAIU may also investigate those accidents and incidents which under slightly different conditions might have led to serious accidents.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Transport if he will introduce legislation to extend existing requirements for priority seating on public transport to explicitly include elderly and vulnerable passengers; and if he will consider creating a legal requirement for passengers who do not require priority seating to vacate such seats when they are needed by an elderly, disabled or vulnerable passenger.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Transport if his Department has been informed of the specific economic baseline and calculations used by the National Transport Authority to justify fare increases of up to 30% on regional bus routes servicing Cavan and Monaghan.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport; however, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of public transport.
As the statutory body responsible for regulating fares across services operated under PSO contracts, the National Transport Authority (NTA), is central to shaping a public transport system that is fair, efficient, and accessible. In April 2023, the NTA published its National Fares Strategy and through its management of fare strategies, they help to ensure that pricing structures support social inclusion and modal shift, while also underpinning the financial viability and resilience of the network.
As the next phase of the Strategy, the NTA made the decision to publish a new Fares Determination on 3 September 2026, with the revised fares taking effect from January 2027. question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Transport further to Parliamentary Question No. 71158/26 when the appeals portal for the road transporters support scheme (RTSS) will open; whether his Department will provide a helpline or other mechanism to assist applicants through the process.
reply:
My Department received over 4,400 applications, in respect of approximately 31,500 vehicles, for the Road Transporters Support Scheme (RTSS). As of 06 October 2026, all applications received during the original application window have been assessed and approved for payment.

Officials in my Department are engaging with trade representative bodies to ensure the portal and information documents relating to appeals are clear and comprehensive to support applicants in completing the appeals process. question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Transport if the disabled parking permit scheme provides any mechanism for exceptional cases to be assessed according to the child's actual functional ability, mobility requirements and safety risks, including the need for a special-needs buggy, rather than physical walking ability alone.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 300 and 302 together.
As Minister of State for International & Road Transport, Logistics, Rail & Ports, I wish to advise that neither I, nor officials within my Department, can intervene in any individual application or appeals process for a disabled parking permit.
The day to day responsibility of the Disabled Parking Scheme, including issuance and refusal of permits, falls under the remit of the issuing bodies, the Irish Wheelchair Association and the Disabled Driver's Association of Ireland.
Disabled parking permits are available to an individual with permanent conditions or disabilities that severely restrict their ability to walk. Eligibility is therefore defined on the basis of mobility impairment, rather than a specific medical condition. An individual who is certified as blind may also qualify for a permit.
The Deputy may wish to note, however, that my Department is currently undertaking a review of the Disabled Parking Scheme, including the eligibility criteria.

question: Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the up-to-date position regarding funding for the Community Services Programme.
reply:
My Department's Community Services Programme (CSP) currently supports the delivery of 453 services nationally via 434 community organisations to provide local social, economic, and environmental services through a social enterprise model, with a budget of €59.4m in 2026.
The CSP Programme provides an annual co-funding contribution towards each full-time equivalent (FTE) position being supported and, where warranted, towards the cost of employing a manager. The Programme currently provides funding towards the employment of over 1,723 FTE positions and 354 manager posts.
In line with a Programme for Government commitment, nine organisations that had been waitlisted following the 2023 Open call, joined the CSP Programme in April this year. Additionally, an Open Call for organisations join the Programme was launched on 30 March. The closing date for receipt of preliminary applications was 08 May and the review process is ongoing. Further details of the Open Call can be found on Pobal's web-site www.pobal.ie, under the community services programme link.
I am delighted that Minister Calleary and I have secured a further €5 million increase for the CSP Programme in Budget 2027, bringing the total CSP funding allocation to circa €64.4 million in 2027. question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport if he supports the transfer of responsibility for alcohol and psychoactive substance testing from State authorities to individual airlines or other private entities under the Irish Aviation Authority's proposed Employer-Led Drug and Alcohol Testing Framework; and whether his Department will make a submission to the IAA's ongoing consultation regarding the proposed framework.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 292, 293, 294, 295, 323 and 324 together.
On 29 September the Irish Aviation Authority (IAA) commenced a public consultation on the future regulatory approach to drug and alcohol testing in the Irish aviation sector. The consultation seeks the views of aviation stakeholders, employees, industry representative bodies, public authorities and members of the public on the most appropriate means of introducing a comprehensive framework to manage the safety risks associated with impairment arising from alcohol and other psychoactive substances. The deadline for submissions is 31 October 2026.
While the IAA is seeking views on a proposed Employer-Led Testing Framework with IAA Oversight, no decision has been taken yet on state policy in this area. The purpose of the consultation is to gather evidence, perspectives and views of all relevant stakeholders to inform future policy development.
My department will be engaging with the IAA following completion of the consultation process.

While the IAA is seeking views on a proposed Employer-Led Testing Framework with IAA Oversight, no decision has been taken yet on state policy in this area. The purpose of the consultation is to gather evidence, perspectives and views of all relevant stakeholders to inform future policy development.
My department will be engaging with the IAA following completion of the consultation process.

question: Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Transport if a new bus will be considered to travel through the Fonthill Road, onto the N4 road toward the city centre; if existing routes can be rerouted to serve this path; and to outline the process of route determination.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport; however, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of public transport. The National Transport Authority (NTA) has statutory responsibility for securing the provision of public passenger transport services nationally and for the scheduling and timetabling of these services in conjunction with the relevant transport operators.
The NTA are managing the current 2026 allocation by focusing on maintaining and strengthening the existing network after several years of reliance on significant supplementary funding. This ensures that high-demand public transport services can continue to operate effectively, while supporting longer-term reforms to enhance capacity, accessibility, and efficiency across the system. Enhancements within the allocation are prioritised, some changes are cost-neutral, while others require additional resources, and all are subject to funding, readiness, and capacity.
Looking to 2027, €1.042 billion is being allocated to PSO services across the bus, light rail and heavy rail networks. This is a record investment in the PSO funding allocation and supports the continued expansion and enhancement of our public transport network, with approximately 140 new and enhanced services in the planning pipeline for 2027 across flagship programmes such as Connecting Ireland, BusConnects, and New Town Services.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport whether the ICE2EV scrappage scheme has been fully exhausted; and whether his Department plans to launch a second round of funding.
reply:
The ICE2EV Pilot Scrappage Scheme was designed and launched as a capped pilot initiative. The full €17 million allocated from the Climate Action Fund has been committed, comprising €10 million for the scrappage grant and €7 million for the associated EV purchase grant.
The strong level of interest in the scheme is encouraging and highlights increasing consumer engagement with the transition to electric vehicles. This positive response aligns with Ireland’s broader Climate Action objectives, including the ambition to increase the uptake of electric vehicles to 30% of the national car fleet by 2030.
The policy purpose of the capped initiative was to test the effectiveness of scrappage as a tool to stimulate EV uptake among those who may not otherwise transition in the near term, with the ultimate goal of delivering additional emissions reductions necessary for our climate targets.
While the pilot scheme has closed for new applications, validation and payment processing remains ongoing. A post-completion evaluation of the scheme will be undertaken to assess its effectiveness, emissions impact and overall value for money, and to inform future policy decisions in this area. The evaluation will consider a range of factors, including the drawdown of available funding, participation across different geographic areas, the characteristics of vehicles being scrapped, and the types of electric vehicles supported under the scheme.

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Seán Kyne den Aire Forbartha Tuaithe agus Pobail, agus Gaeltachta cén teagmháil a bhí ag a Roinn le Comhairle Contae na Gaillimhe agus le hÚdarás na Gaeltachta maidir le tithíocht a sholáthar i bpobail Ghaeltachta i gConamara agus cén bearta sonracha atá á mbreithniú chun tacú le seachadadh tithe do mhuintir na háite agus do phobal na Gaeilge.
reply:
Is fiú nótáil gurb í an Roinn Tithíochta, Rialtais Áitiúil agus Oidhreachta, faoin Acht Pleanála agus Forbartha 2000, atá freagrach go príomha as pleanáil agus tithíocht i gceantair Ghaeltachta. É sin ráite, bhí teagmháil rialta ag mo Roinn féin leis Roinn Tithíochta, Rialtais Áitiúil agus Oidhreachta maidir le cúrsaí pleanála sa Ghaeltacht agus na moltaí atá sa dréacht Ráiteas Náisiúnta Pleanála á n-ullmhú. Bhí teagmháil ag mo Roinn leis na hÚdaráis Áitiúla ábhartha, Comhairle Chontae na Gaillimhe ina measc, agus Údarás na Gaeltachta freisin agus an obair sin ar bun. Tá i gceist go gcinnteoidh an Ráiteas seo go mbeidh nósmhaireacht comhsheasmhach i bhfeidhm mar a bhaineann sé le pleanáil i ngach contae ina bhfuil ceantair Ghaeltachta lonnaithe.
Tuigim go bhfuil Údarás na Gaeltachta i mbun plé gníomhach le húdaráis áitiúla chun feasacht a chothú faoi na deontais atá ar fáil d'úinéirí tí le haghaidh tithe folmha. Chuige sin, tá ceardlanna á reáchtáil ar fud na Gaeltachta i gcomhair le Comhordaitheoir Tithe Folmha na Gaeltachta - post atá maoinithe ag an Údarás i gComhairle Contae Mhaigh Eo ach ag freastal ar an nGaeltacht ar fad.
Is fiú a lua go ndéanann mo Roinn aighneachtaí ar iarratais phleanála sa Ghaeltacht, Contae na Gaillimhe ina measc, nuair atá iarratais phleanála ábhartha faoi bhráid na gcomhairlí. Déantar seo chun a chinntiú go dtógfar stádas na Gaeilge sa Ghaeltacht san áireamh agus iarratais phleanála á meas agus go gcuirfear coinníollacha teanga oiriúnacha i bhfe

question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Transport the total value of contractual claims, variations and disputed payments currently outstanding between Iarnród Éireann and a company (details supplied); the extent to which these represent potential additional liabilities for Iarnród Éireann; and whether financial provisions have been made for such liabilities.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 286, 287, 289, 297 and 298 together.
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. The National Transport Authority (NTA) has responsibility for the planning and development of public transport infrastructure.
Iarnród Éireann have contracts with Alstom for a number of projects currently, including the purchase of new DART+ electric and battery-electric carriages, the installation of recharging infrastructure to charge new battery-electric carriages at Drogheda station, and the upgrade of signalling, electrical and telecommunications infrastructure on the Glounthaune to Midleton line as part of the Cork Area Commuter Rail Programme.
The National Transport Authority (NTA) is the day-to-day Approving Authority for these projects and, together with Iarnród Éireann, responsible for their delivery. It is also assisted by JASPERS, an advisory service under the European Investment Bank.

question: Deputy Frankie Feighan asked the Minister for Transport if there is an appeal process under the fuel support scheme.
reply:
My Department received over 4,400 applications, in respect of approximately 31,500 vehicles, for the Road Transporters Support Scheme (RTSS). As of 06 October 2026, all applications received during the original application window have been assessed and approved for payment.
The appeals portal is being finalised and will open shortly. Officials in my Department are engaging with trade representative bodies to ensure the portal and information documents relating to appeals are clear and comprehensive to support applicants in completing the appeals process. Information will be published on the Department’s website once this feedback has been received.
Once the appeals portal launches, all applicants will be contacted directly by the Department with instructions on how to submit an appeal. Please note, only applicants who have a valid RTSS application ID will be permitted to submit an appeal.
Queries that are not answered by the website material can be sent to rtss.appeals@transport.gov.ie.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Defence further to Parliamentary Question No. 70836/26, the number of protected disclosures made by members and staff of the Defence Forces (details supplied), either directly to her Department or through internal Defence Forces channels, in each of the years 2023, 2024, 2025; the number of which returned by the Office of the Protected Disclosures Commissioner for examination; and the status or action taken regarding such by category, such as referred to a separate body or closed.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Defence the number of permanent members of the Defence Force, broken down per year from 2016 to date, in tabular form.
reply:
As Minister for Defence, I am fully committed to increasing and strengthening recruitment and supporting retention in the Permanent Defence Force.
The Military Authorities advise that the whole time equivalent (WTE) strength of the Permanent Defence Force (PDF) stood at 7,815 personnel on the 31 August 2026, the latest date for which this figure is available. The table below indicates the year end WTE strength for the PDF from 2016 to 2025.

Last year saw a growth in the overall strength of nearly 200, with a total of 790 inductions achieved- the highest in twenty years - while the number of personnel who discharged was at its lowest level in more than five years. I am determined to build on this and have set a target of more than 800 inductions for 2026.
Interest in a career in the Defence Forces remains robust with a total of 16,510 applications received in 2025 and over 14,000 applications received to the end of August of this year. The challenge now for the Defence Forces is to convert this high level of applications to inductions. A draft Strategic Workforce Plan prepared by the Defence Forces is being considered by a Civilian/ Military Working Group. As the Deputy will be aware, the aim of this process is to provide a pathway to the achievement of an overall strength of 11,500, inclusive of civilian personnel, commensurate with Level of Ambition 2.
Recruitment to the Defence Forces remain open and ongoing via a diverse range of competitions including general service rec

question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Defence the up-to-date position on her plans for the curragh plains in County Kildare; the most recent meetings held about these plans; the timeframe involved in the action on the curragh plains.
reply: The Conservation Plan for the Curragh recommended the transferring of the Curragh Plains to the agency that is best suited to managing this historic landscape and it is intended to implement the recommendations, as called for in the Programme for Government. My officials are continuing to engage with the National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS), who undertook several visits on the Plains during the summer. A formal assessment from the NPWS is awaited within my Department and on receipt of same, I will consider the matter further.

reply:

question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Defence the updated position regarding the use of her Department's swimming pool for public use; the times allocated; if classes are available for the public.
reply:
I am advised that while the swimming pool in the Defence Forces Training Centre, Curragh Camp is primarily for the training and exercise of Defence Forces personnel, my Department positively engages with local schools and community groups in allowing the use of this facility. Permission for the use of the pool is subject at all times to Defence Forces requirements and signed conditions, which includes the requirement for the schools and organisations to have appropriate insurance.

reply:

In respect of the 14 consecutive day ‘limit’ on reserve service mentioned, this is an internal control mechanism for RDF training activity.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if his Department will consider providing Gaeltacht funding to Omeath.
reply:
My Department provides funding to Foras na Gaeilge to fund and deliver various programmes to help develop and promote the Irish Language across the island.
My Department is not aware of any Irish language groups in Omeath. However, I am advised that two groups located in the wider area currently receive funding under Foras na Gaeilge's Irish Language Networks Development Scheme, namely Gaeláras Mhic Ardghail in Newry and Craobh Pheadair Ó Dhubhda in Dundalk.
The scheme aims to promote, protect and engrain the Irish language in particular areas with an emphasis on the development and implementation of comprehensive language plans.
Other supports are available to groups outside of the Irish Language Networks Development Scheme. Glór na nGael, nominated by Foras na Gaeilge as its lead organisation for community development, offer many practical supports in enabling and empowering local community groups to encourage the use of the Irish language.
I would recommend to the Deputy that any groups interested in promoting the use of the language in Omeath contact Foras na Gaeilge, in the first instance, to discuss the various supports available both from the agency itself and from its lead organisations.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Defence further to Parliamentary Question No. 69615/26, if she will address the specific matters raised in further correspondence (details supplied), including the rationale for the withdrawal of a proposed property sale, apparent inconsistencies in correspondence issued by her Department regarding occupancy of the property, and the application of current disposal policies in light of previous sales of similar properties in the same estate.
reply:
With regard to the specific property referred to by the Deputy, officials in my Department have, over the years since the original offer was made, engaged with the parties subject to the original sale offer and the current occupant on this matter. In that regard, the Department advised on the 24 October 2005, that if the then Contract for Sale was not received within a specified period of time then the Department will be obliged to consider the offer withdrawn. In addition, the Department also went on to advise that it would also be obliged to apply current market values should there be any future offers of sale. Subsequently, I am advised that, the current occupant was advised on the 13 March 2022 that the Department could not proceed with the sale. This remains the case.
The Deputy may wish to note that it has been a long-standing policy that long term residential married quarters are no longer provided. There is no immediate plan to reverse this long-standing policy, which was introduced in the early 1990’s and was implemented on a gradual basis in recognition of the sensitivities involved for military personnel and their families then occupying Department properties. In this particular instance, the offer of a licence to the occupant to regularise their occupation of the premises remains open.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he has evaluated the concerns of the liquid fuel sector that the proposed obligation rates in the forthcoming renewable heat obligation scheme are too low to provide any additional renewable fuel and will consequently have no impact in reducing carbon emissions.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 265 and 267 together.
Decisions made in relation to the Renewable Heat Obligation (RHO) scheme design, including initial obligation rates and level increases as the scheme progresses, were based on a full examination of the scale of obligation required to meet Ireland’s renewable heat targets, and encompassed extensive engagement with key industry stakeholders, including the liquid fuel sector. The scheme is considered appropriate and effective to support market participation and achievement of our energy and climate targets.
Priority drafting of the RHO Bill is now at an advanced stage and nearing completion. Once finalised, I intend to submit the final scheme to Government seeking approval to publish.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment when the NORA levy will be reapplied to relevant fuels.
reply: The NORA levy is a charge of 2 cent per litre applied to most petroleum products sold in the market, for the purpose of funding the operations of NORA and the Climate Action Fund (CAF). The levy has been reduced to a nominal amount, with the reduction coming into effect from 1 April 2026. In Budget 2027, it was announced that the levy reduction, which was due to expire on 31 October 2026, will be extended until 31 December 2026.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment when his Department will bring forward legislation to fully implement the Energy Efficiency Directive.
reply:
The Recast Energy Efficiency Directive (EU) 2023/1791 (EED) is a wide-ranging European directive that seeks to enhance energy efficiency across all EU Member States and forms a key component of the EU's Fit for 55 package. The Recast EED replaces the 2012 EED, as amended in 2018, which Ireland has previously fully transposed and implemented.
The new Directive entered into force in October 2023, with a transposition deadline of 11 October 2025, and contains a range of new measures aimed at further improving energy efficiency across society. The Government has an ambitious programme in place to enhance energy efficiency across all sectors as a key part of its efforts to decarbonise the economy and achieve national climate targets. The Government remains fully committed to implementing the EED and recognises the significant benefits arising from increased energy efficiency, including reduced energy costs for households, businesses and the Exchequer; enhanced competitiveness and job creation; reduced fossil fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions; reduced energy poverty; improved health outcomes; and greater energy security.
The Government has invested significantly in promoting energy efficiency across all sectors. This includes residential energy efficiency grant schemes administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI), investment in transport measures that support greater use of public transport, active travel and electric vehicles, and a range of initi

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment further to Parliamentary Questions Nos. 70575/26 and 70577/26, whether the feasibility study on transitioning household waste collection to a franchise model, described in those replies as recently completed, will be published; the date of publication; whether the National Waste Collection Permit Office study on incentivised charging structures will also be published.
reply:
It is the Department’s intention to publish the report titled, Study to Explore the Feasibility of Transitioning Ireland’s Waste Collection Market from its Current Side-by-Side Licensing System to a Franchise Tendering System, in the coming weeks. The report is intended to inform policy development and stakeholder engagement. It should be noted that its findings and recommendations remain under consideration by the Department and publication should not be interpreted as indicating any final decision on future policy direction.
The National Waste Collection Permit Office Report on Incentivised Charging will also be published in due course. Together, these reports represent important evidence-based inputs to the development of the next iteration of the Waste Action Plan for a Circular Economy. Their development reflects the Department’s commitment to ensuring that future waste policy is informed by robust analysis, stakeholder perspectives, and international best practice.

question: Deputy John McGuinness asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the policy changes if any he is considering to provide greater transparency and oversight relative to the deposit return scheme for plastic bottles and cans; if the unclaimed cash can be estimated with a view to the State taking control of part of the sum for use in the public interest.
reply:
Re-turn is a producer-led and owned, not-for-profit company established by beverage producers to meet their obligations under the Separate Collection (Deposit Return Scheme) Regulations 2024 (S.I. No. 33 of 2024).
The framework for governance and oversight of the scheme is set out in the Regulations, the Ministerial Approval issued under those Regulations, and the Code of Corporate Governance for Compliance Schemes. While Re-turn is responsible for the operational and financial management of the scheme, officials from the Department closely monitor its performance through monthly meetings with Re-turn, supported by quarterly engagements on strategic priorities and governance matters. I have also met with representatives of the company on a number of occasions.
Under Regulation 4(3) of the Separate Collection (Deposit Return Scheme) Regulations 2024 (S.I. No. 33 of 2024), unredeemed deposits are one of the sources of funding for operation of the scheme. These funds generated must be re-invested in its operation. question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the projected increased cost of the Dublin District Heating Project; if his Department has met with Dublin City Council since the cost projected was revised upwards; if the council has sought further grants from his Department to fund the development; and his views on the need for sustainable district heating options in urban centres, and Dublin in particular.
reply:

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to outline the legal and site specific measures that were taken in respect of Dunsink dump-landfill following the decision of the European Court of Justice in Case C-494/01; which of these measures are still being implemented; and can he confirm whether the European Commission continues to monitor the measures Ireland is taking with respect to the Dunsink dump-landfill.
