question: Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Health if she will amend the criteria for the nursing homes support scheme to ensure that payment under the fair deal scheme is effective from the date the application is submitted on behalf of the patient.
reply:
The Nursing Homes Support Scheme (NHSS – or Fair Deal) is a procedure encompassing the gathering of detailed clinical and financial information, and its administration is governed by the 2009 Act. As set out in the Act, an applicant’s contribution to the cost of their care is calculated based on the financial assessment of their income and assets on the date they first make an application under the Nursing Homes Support Scheme. In addition, transferred assets and income, defined as assets or income transferred to another person up to five years before a person's first application to the scheme, are also assessed.
The programme for Government includes commitments to including increased funding for the Fair Deal Scheme to ensure that the wait for funding does not exceed four weeks after approval. Applicants who transfer from acute settings to a nursing home can, under certain circumstances, avail of Transitional Care Funding provided by the HSE.
The Department of Health consistently seeks to identify improvements and introduce enhancements to the scheme, where feasible, which aims to ensure that long-term nursing home care remains sustainable, accessible and affordable for everyone and that people continue to be cared for in the most appropriate settings. Given the size, complexity and cost of the NHSS, implementation is complex and any changes in policy direction need to be carefully assessed and kept under review. There are currently no plans to amend the application process.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Health if a 24 hour rapid response vehicle will be introduced at Tuam ambulance base; and if an analysis of calls to Tuam ambulance base will be undertaken.
reply:
I thank the Deputy for this question, and I am aware that this matter has been raised by the Deputy on a number of occasions including earlier this year.
I am informed by the National Ambulance Service that while there are no plans at present for a Rapid Response Vehicle for Tuam in 2026, demands across all ambulance bases and health regions are continuously monitored and assessed to inform future decision making around resourcing and National Service Plans.
County Galway currently has two RRVs operating on a 24/7 basis located at Merlin Park Hospital, Galway and in Recess. These are deployed to incidents across the HSE West and North-West region, including Tuam. A third RRV based in Co Roscommon provides cover to Co Galway on a dynamic deployment basis.
The Government is committed to further resourcing the National Ambulance Service. Investment has seen NAS staffing increase by 30% since 2020 in order to meet increasing demand for services.
This year, the West and North West health region will benefit from a new NAS Helicopter Emergency Medical Service. This service has been operational on a test basis from Sligo Airport as of July and will enhance service delivery to critically ill and injured patients across the region, particularly in rural and isolated areas. In addition, a new Emergency Ambulance operating from Recess, is due to be added by the end of the year.

question: Deputy Martin Daly asked the Minister for Health the measures being taken to improve access to dental services for children and adults with additional needs living in rural communities, particularly in counties Roscommon and Galway, including access to specialist dental care and treatment under general anaesthetic.
reply:
The Government recognises that significant challenges continue to affect the delivery of public dental services.
In particular, children and adults with additional needs can face delays in accessing specialist dental care and treatment under general anaesthetic. The response to this is multi-faceted and requires a mix of shorter-term interventions and meaningful strategic reform.
To address the immediate access challenges and to underpin longer term reforms, my Department and the HSE are finalising a focused two-year action plan to deliver real improvements on the ground.
The Oral Health Action Plan responds to sustained service pressures and long waiting lists—particularly for children and for people with additional needs.
It will focus on a small number of clear priorities:
• Tackling waiting lists in the School Dental Programme and Orthodontics.
• Improvement and expansion of the access programme to oral healthcare for people who have additional needs including those with disabilities.
• Commencing a reform of the Dental Treatment Services Scheme.
• Supporting recruitment, education and training.
• Supporting innovation and new ways of delivering care.
Over the next two years, the aim is to stabilise services, reduce waiting times, and make access measurably better for patients—while laying the groundwork for longer-term reform. The plan will be overseen by a dedicated governance group, with progress monitored closely and aligned to wider Department and HSE priorities

question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Health for an urgent update on the continuing lack of adequate community ophthalmology services in South Tipperary; the measures now being taken to address the significant waiting list, particularly for children; when the proposed waiting-list initiative and additional clinics will commence; and the progress that has been made in securing a sustainable long-term service for the area.

question: Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Health her plans to increase virtual care capacity.
reply:
Virtual Care is clinically led, digitally-enabled care, that allows patients to receive safe, high-quality care in their homes or communities. It supports more effective use of healthcare resources and reduces pressure on hospital services.
Significant progress has already been made through the rollout of Virtual Wards focused on earlier discharge. These enable patients who would otherwise require a hospital bed to recover at home, helping reduce occupancy and improve patient flow. There are currently 147 Virtual Ward beds of this kind available. While we have yet to reach 100% occupancy of these beds, I would like to acknowledge the significant progress made to date, with particular increases in occupancy across sites in Cork and Drogheda recently. To date, over 5,100 patients have been admitted to Virtual Wards, delivering over 47,000 bed days.
In 2027 we will continue to expand capacity. Each Region will work towards providing an additional virtual care option, enabling services to reach people earlier and help avoid Emergency Department attendances or hospital admissions.
My Department is also progressing a National Virtual Care Policy, which will launch in coming weeks. This will support additional virtual pathways in each region, increased telehealth and remote-monitoring initiatives, and enhanced workforce capability.
Through these measures, we are ensuring that more patients receive appropriate care in the right place, at the right time.

question: Deputy Rose Conway-Walsh asked the Minister for Health the reason for the continued delays, in some cases extending over months and years, in transitioning agency staff to permanent positions within the Health Service Executive.
reply:
Agency staff have long played an important role in keeping health services running safely, covering vacancies and absences, and helping services respond to short-term increases in demand. However, what should be a flexible support has become too significant a feature of the workforce. The health service remains overly reliant on agency staffing, which is more costly and provides less continuity and workforce stability than direct employment. With agency expenditure expected to exceed €800 million in 2026, this level of reliance is not sustainable.
It has always been my clear direction to the HSE that they need to reduce agency use while supporting direct recruitment into approved and funded posts. Direct employment offers better value for the health service, greater job security, improved continuity of care for patients and a more stable workforce, while retaining skills and experience within the public system rather than repeatedly purchasing the same capacity through external agencies.
A national Agency Conversion Framework has been in place in the HSE since 2024 with over 900 posts converted from agency between 2024 and 2025. Efforts have ramped up in 2026 and to date this year a further 1,492 agency staff have already converted to direct employment, representing 57.8% of the HSE’s 2026 target of 2,581 conversions. reply:

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 98 and 100 together.
MetroLink is Ireland's largest public transport infrastructure project and a key National Development Plan priority, delivering long-term benefits for economic growth, housing competitiveness and climate action. MetroLink will provide a high-capacity, fully automated metro connection Dublin airport with key destinations across the city, including a reliable 25-minute journey to the city centre.
Over the last year, significant progress has been made in moving MetroLink from planning and design and into procurement and construction.
As the Deputy will be aware, An Coimisiún Pleanála published its decision to grant the MetroLink Railway Order, or planning permission, in October 2025. Following the resolution of a subsequent legal challenge, MetroLink secured an Operative Railway Order in January 2026. This enabled Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII) to commence the shortlisting process for major MetroLink contracts.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Transport the independent oversight arrangements that will be in place throughout the delivery of MetroLink; whether external audits will be conducted during the construction phase; and if the findings will be published.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 89, 97 and 99 together.
As the Deputy may be aware, significant progress has been made recently in moving MetroLink towards the construction phase. There has been, and will continue to be, appropriate oversight arrangements in place as part of this development.
Under the Infrastructure Guidelines, the Government provided "Approval Gate 2" consent for MetroLink on 16th September 2026. MetroLink may now proceed to the detailed procurement phase for the key contracts, with the main tender packs expected to issue to the market in the first half of next year and heavy construction anticipated to commence in 2028. Before MetroLink may commence these heavy construction works, the Government's approval will be required at Approval Gate 3 of the Infrastructure Guidelines.
Furthermore, on 16th June 2026, the Government approved the drafting of the MetroLink Bill 2026, in line with the General Scheme which I presented to Cabinet. This Bill will establish the Statutory Delivery Body charged with overseeing MetroLink through construction. The Statutory Delivery Body will be responsible for delivering MetroLink on budget and on time, and its Board and CEO will be fully accountable to the Minister for Transport and to the Oireachtas. The Body is expected to be subject to audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General, which publishes reports on its findings. question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Transport if he will provide an update on the development of legislative changes to the Taxi Regulation Act 2013 with respect to cross-Border taxi services.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 92 and 96 together.
The regulation of the small public service vehicle (SPSV) industry is a matter for the independent transport regulator, the National Transport Authority (NTA), under the provisions of the Consolidated Taxi Regulation Acts 2013 and 2016. Under section 6(2) of this Act, An Garda Síochána is responsible for the granting of SPSV driver licences. I have no role in the day-to-day operations of the SPSV sector.
Under the provisions of the Taxi Regulation Act 2013, operators are required to hold an SPSV licence and an SPSV driver licence to carry persons for hire or reward in the State. The 2013 Act and its requirements only apply to services provided in the State - it does not provide for services across a border. The legislative position in Northern Ireland is similar. Thus, under current legislation, a taxi operator wishing to operate cross-border services, would have to apply for and obtain SPSV licences on each side of the border. Unlike other areas of transport - such as bus and road haulage operations - taxi services are not subject to EU harmonisation, so arrangements for regulating taxi services remain a matter for the relevant authorities in each EU Member State, in respect of services that operate in their jurisdiction.

reply:

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Transport when an RTSS scheme payment will be made to a haulier (details supplied).
reply:
My Department received over 4,400 applications, in respect of approximately 31,500 vehicles. As of 06 October 2026, all applications received during the original application window have been assessed and approved for payment.
The applicant whose details you have shared with me provided the incorrect email address on their application. An official from my Department made contact with the applicant by phone and gathered corrected contact information for the applicant.
The applicant was advised that other information provided on their application was invalid and was provided a link to the application portal to correct their application. Unfortunately, the applicant did not provide the updated information necessary to process their application. As a result, the applicant will need to submit an appeal under the appeals process.
If the applicant provides the necessary information required to accurately and fairly assess their application during the appeals process, officials in my Department can then process their application.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding so-called rickshaw vehicles carrying passengers for monetary reward; the adequacy of measures to enforce a ban on motorised rickshaws announced in 2018; the number of enforcements taken against operators of mechanically propelled rickshaws carrying passengers for reward under existing SPSV legislation in each year since 2016, in tabular form; his plans to further review guidance to An Garda Síochána or new legislation, following recent road traffic incidents involving rickshaws.
reply:
For the Deputy's information, if a rickshaw is fitted with a small engine or electric motor of any kind, it is considered to be a mechanically propelled vehicle (MPV). Under road traffic law, if an MPV is used in a public place it is subject to all of the regulatory controls that apply to other vehicles i.e., it must be roadworthy, registered, taxed and comply with the following regulations:
• SI 190 of 1963 – Road Traffic Construction, Equipment and Use of Vehicles Regulations 1963.
• SI 189 of 1963 – Road Traffic Lighting of Vehicles Regulations 1963.
• SI 5 of 2003 – Road Traffic Construction and Use of Vehicles Regulations 2003.
The drivers of all vehicles on public roads, including motorised rickshaws, are required to comply with road traffic legislation and to behave in a safe manner paying due care to other road users. The enforcement of such road traffic legislation is a matter for An Garda Síochána. Therefore, statistics on the number of enforcement actions taken against operators of mechanically propelled rickshaws, would be a matter for An Garda Síochána.
A provision was contained in section 31 of the Road Traffic Act 2016, which was aimed at amending section 20 of the Taxi Regulation Act 2013, to allow the National Transport Authority (NTA) to make regulations for “non-motorised passenger transport” in towns and cities which includes rickshaws propelled by pedal cycle. It is important to note that the section 31 provision does not allow for the regulation of ricks

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht when decisions on applications under the Community Centre Investment Fund be made.
reply:
The Community Centre Investment Fund (CCIF) was introduced to provide high quality community facilities that are available to community groups in both urban and rural communities. Through the CCIF, some €112 million has been allocated for the enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres and the construction of new centres where such a need has been identified.
I launched the latest round of funding under CCIF 2026 on the 26th March for enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres. The fund will be delivered across 2 categories with maximum funding levels of €25,000 and €100,000 respectively. The closing date for the CCIF 2026 has now passed.
Applications are currently being assessed and I look forward to announcing the successful projects later in the year.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht when decisions on recent CLAR applications be announced.
reply:
The CLAR programme provides funding under a number of different measures for small-scale infrastructural projects in designated rural areas. Last year I approved over €14m million for 238 projects under the programme, with funding being provided under a number if measures for community facilities and amenities, community vehicles and specific support for island communities.
On the 10th of March I launched the 2026 CLAR programme with 3 funding measures that were broadly similar to last year. On 1 October 2026 I was delighted to announce funding of €2.5 million for 44 vehicles nationwide under measure 2 of the 2026 CLAR programme.
My officials are currently assessing applications under measures 1 and 3 of the 2026 CLAR programme and I expect to announce the successful projects in the coming months.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if a further allocation for the local improvement scheme will be made to Local Authorities before the end of 2026.
reply:
The Local Improvement Scheme funds the upgrade of non-public rural roads and laneways, which are not usually maintained by local authorities. My department reinstated the Scheme in 2017, and it is a central element of the overall Rural Development Investment Programme. Since 2017, over €201 million has been allocated to local authorities, resulting in the improvement of over 5,500 roads.
The 2026 scheme was launched in February with voted funding of €17m million. This represents an increase on base funding allocated to the scheme in previous years. Kerry County Council received an allocation of €1.133 million.
While the Department provides funding for the Scheme, it is administered by each local authority, who retain responsibility for the selection and prioritisation of roads and management of waiting lists. It should be noted that the ability of local authorities to meet demand under the scheme is not purely a function of available funding, as other factors such as weather conditions, rising costs and the availability of contractors and labour are also relevant.
Local authorities are in the process of preparing their funding drawdown requests for works completed this year. My department officials will monitor this process closely and work with each local authority to ensure funds are fully utilised and that as many roads as possible are completed under the scheme.
The next round of funding that will be made available to local authorities has been secured as part of Budget 2

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if funding has been secured to reopen the scéim na mBóithre áise scheme in 2027.
reply:
The current Programme for Government includes a commitment to restoring Scéim na mBóithre Áise during this Government's term. The mechanism and approach related to reintroducing this scheme are currently being examined by officials in my Department.
In the meantime, funding is available through my department under the Local Improvement Scheme (LIS) to assist local authorities in carrying out improvement works on private roads and on roads that are not normally publicly maintained.
The 2027 Local Improvement Scheme has a budget of €17 million for repairs and improvement works on non-public rural roads and laneways.
Further information on the Local Improvement Scheme (LIS) is available on my Departments website.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the additional supports he intends to provide for community infrastructure and recreational facilities in rapidly growing rural towns and villages; and the way in which his Department will ensure that investment in community facilities keeps pace with population growth in areas such as Galway east.
reply:
The Town Centre First Policy (TCF) is a major government initiative supporting the regeneration of Irish towns and villages, intended to help ensure they can become vibrant, viable and attractive places to live, work, visit and invest in. To help deliver on the objectives of TCF at local level, my Department provides funding to local authorities, including Galway County Council, for dedicated Town Regeneration Officers who work closely with communities and multi-disciplinary regeneration teams.
In addition, over €7m in dedicated TCF support funding has been provided nationally. This has included funding for the development of 52 TCF Town Plans nationally, including in Gort and Athenry and funding to support the establishment of over 100 Town Teams nationwide, including in Headford, An Cheathrú Rua, and Oranmore. These initiatives aim to support local communities in identifying and addressing the key issues in their own towns and communities.
Separately, a range of capital funding streams is available across my department to support delivery on TCF objectives. Calls for Proposals under these funds are structured to allow local authorities prioritise needs using a place based local development approach and to themselves select the priority areas for applications.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the projects funded under the town and village renewal scheme in Limerick in 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form.
reply:
The Town and Village Renewal Scheme (TVRS) was introduced in 2016 and is one of a number of measures designed to rejuvenate rural towns and villages throughout Ireland. Since the launch of the scheme over €217 million has been allocated to almost 2,000 projects across the country and of this, over €9.2 million has been allocated to 78 projects in County Limerick.
This scheme places particular emphasis on projects which support sustainable employment creation, town centre resilience and regeneration, enhance streetscapes, and bringing derelict and vacant buildings and sites back into use as multi-purpose community spaces.
A TVRS Call for Proposals was issued to local authorities on 16 September 2026. There are two funding streams available under this Call: The Main Scheme and the Project Development Measure and further details are available on my department's website. The closing date for the submission of applications is 22 January 2027.
A separate Call for Proposals under the TVRS ‘Building and Land Acquisition Measure’ (BLAM) issued earlier this year. Under BLAM, local authorities can apply for funding of up to €500,000, which can be used to purchase up to three buildings or sites to re-develop into multi-purpose community facilities or infrastructure. question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if his Department can provide clarity on the recruitment panel which has been put in place to serve on the board of Pobal; and the length of time the panel will remain in place to fill any upcoming positions on the board.
reply:
Pobal works on behalf of Government to support communities and local agencies in their work to achieve social inclusion and support community development. Pobal operates under the aegis of the Department of Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht.
Pobal is governed by a voluntary Board of Directors. Members of the Board are appointed by Government, on the nomination of the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht, in line with the Guidelines for Appointments to State Boards. The Minister requests the Government to appoint Directors to the Board of Pobal to fill vacancies arising from the ordinary rotation of the Board, and, when required, to fill casual vacancies arising.
Where upcoming vacancies on the board of Pobal are identified, my Department initiates the State Boards appointments process at least six months before the current member’s term of office expires. The process is managed by the Public Appointments Service (PAS).
The PAS public jobs website is the portal through which all State Board vacancies are advertised, and information is provided there on the appointments process. When expressions of interest are received, an assessment panel is convened by PAS to consider the applications received. A shortlist of suitable candidates is put forward for the Minister's consideration. The Minister then nominates the chosen candidate(s) for appointment by Government.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the funding streams for local authorities such as Fingal Country Council to progress an upgrade to Howth library.
reply:
The provision of library services, including the upgrading of library buildings and services, is primarily a matter for local authorities in their capacity as library authorities under the Local Government Act 2001.
As the Deputy will be aware, the Libraries Capital Programme for the period 2023-2027 was announced in April 2024. I am advised that no application was received from Fingal County Council for a library project in Howth at that time and the programme is now fully committed. My Department will be developing a successor Libraries Capital Programme to the 2023-2027 programme, setting out the terms and conditions including eligibility, and all Local Authorities will be invited to submit applications in due course.
On 26 June 2026, under the Libraries Capital Programme, Minister Calleary and I announced €3m in funding for targeted Small-scale Capital Investment in public libraries. This funding will provide sensory equipment, accessibility infrastructure, ICT hardware upgrades to increase broadband speed, and modern furniture and operational equipment for public libraries across the country. Fingal County Council was awarded €147,505 under this fund.
These strategic investments and targeted initiatives demonstrate my Department’s commitment to ensuring public libraries remain accessible, inclusive and dynamic spaces that empower individuals and communities alike.

question: Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if the Charities Regulator has been notified of any changes in the trusteeship, senior management or governance structure of a registered charity (details supplied) since 2020; whether all changes requiring notification were notified within the appropriate timeframe.

Any concerns, complaints and correspondence relating to financial or governance matters in specific charities are a matter for the Charities Regulator to manage. question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Transport whether he plans to review the vehicle price ceiling under the SEAI electric vehicle purchase grant scheme; whether a tapered reduction in grant assistance above the ceiling has been assessed as an alternative to the immediate loss of eligibility.
reply:
The Government is fully committed to supporting the transition to zero-emission and the ambitious target to have 30% of private car fleet switched to electric by 2030.
Regarding the EV Purchase Grant, the maximum eligible vehicle price threshold for the grant will now be €50,000, rather than €60,000. This change has been made to target funding for EV transition towards lower price bracket cars and enables a greater proportion of the funding available within the National Development Plan to support the roll-out of charging infrastructure. The amended price threshold came into place for new applications received after 31 July 2026, and will be kept under review in 2027.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science for an update on the provision of a borrowing framework for the technological universities.
reply:
The National Student Accommodation Strategy 2026-2035 recognises the important role that higher education institutions, including Technological Universities, can play in increasing student accommodation capacity.
Building on the Programme for Government commitment, my Department is working with the Higher Education Authority and the sector to examine the financing arrangements required to support future student accommodation projects.
As Minister, I am committed to ensuring that Technological Universities have the tools to support strategic investment and expand accommodation provision. One model which is widely used internationally is a nomination agreement. These provide institutions with guaranteed beds for their students while giving developers the occupancy certainty needed to secure finance and deliver new accommodation.
At present, Technological Universities do not have approval to enter into nomination agreements. My Department is working with the Departments of Finance, Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, and the Higher Education Authority, to develop an appropriate mechanism, with the necessary safeguards and controls, to allow Technological Universities to enter into such agreements on a strictly limited basis. As part of this work, NewERA has agreed to undertake a financial assessment.
I will continue to advance this work to support the delivery of student accommodation while protecting institutional and Exchequer finances

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if there has been consideration given to enhancing graduate entry medicine tuition support or a state-backed finance scheme; and the future plans for same.
reply:
I am committed to ensuring that financial circumstances do not present an undue barrier to participation in higher education and tertiary education. This is particularly important in disciplines where Ireland faces significant skills shortages, including healthcare professions.
In Budget 2027, the Government further strengthened these supports through a €34 million student support package, including increases in SUSI maintenance grants, enhanced student contribution grant supports for families with multiple students in tertiary education, expanded eligibility for certain supports, and measures to assist students with the cost of attending college.
The question of introducing an interest-free student loan scheme has been considered in a variety of policy contexts over the years. Any proposal of this nature would require careful consideration of its affordability, overall cost to the Exchequer, administrative arrangements, repayment mechanisms, impact on student participation and interaction with the existing student support framework. It would also need to be assessed in the context of wider Government priorities and value-for-money considerations.
There may, however, be circumstances where alternative financing models could assist students who face significant education costs but who are not eligible for existing grant supports. question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if annual targets have been established for each county or region for 2026 to 2030 regarding the Government target of 12,500 apprenticeship registrations annually by 2030, in tabular form; and, if not, the way in which the geographic distribution of the additional apprenticeship places required to meet the national target is being planned.
reply:

Apprenticeships are national programmes delivered through a network of Education and Training Boards, higher education institutions and other training providers across the country. Many apprenticeship programmes, such as the electrical apprenticeship, are delivered in multiple locations. Programmes with lower demand may be delivered in a more limited number of locations.
Decisions on the local provision and capacity of individual programmes are matters for the relevant ETB, higher education institution or training provider. My priority as Minister is to ensure that apprenticeship continues to provide quality and accessible options for learners across the country, while responding effectively to the skills needs of employers and the wider economy.
Minister Harkin and I intend to publish the successor to the current Action Plan for Apprenticeship later this year. question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the appeal process available for third level students in relation to free fee's for Irish students in circumstances (details supplied).
reply:
The State pays tuition fees, under the Free Fees Initiative, exclusive of the student contribution, on behalf of eligible students attending approved full-time undergraduate courses. To qualify for funding under the Department's Free Fees Initiative, students must meet the criteria of the scheme including the residency requirements in their own right.
To meet the residency criteria a student must have been ordinarily resident in an EU/EEA/Swiss/UK state for at least three of the five years preceding their entry to an approved third level course.
All students are required to meet the residency criteria of the scheme preceding their entry to an approved third level course. Under EU law, nationals of other EU jurisdictions are entitled to access education on the same basis as Irish citizens. Therefore, it would not be feasible to provide an exemption for persons of Irish nationality only.
The three out of five-year rule takes cognisance of students who wish to take time out to travel or work abroad. Such students can still meet the residency requirement if they have not been outside the countries referenced above for more than two of the previous five years. Similar, and in some cases more restrictive residency criteria apply in other countries. For example, in the UK, a student must be resident for the three years immediately preceding his/her commencement in college.

question: Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the projected increase of student enrolments over the next five years; and the anticipated additional funding that will be required to meet this demand.
reply:
In June, my Department published “Projections of Demand for Higher Education 2025–2045”, highlighting strong expected growth in demand for full-time higher education places over the coming years.
The report shows that overall student numbers are projected to rise significantly over the next five years, increasing by up to 18% from current levels, from 211,540 in the 2024/25 academic year to between 243,750 and 250,260 in the 2031/32 academic year, depending on the scenario considered.
The main drivers of this growth are a projected increase in undergraduate enrolment demand from Irish school leavers (demographic increase) and growth in postgraduate enrolment demand, with continued growth in non-EU postgraduate enrolment
Ireland experienced high annual births of over 70,000 between 2007 and 2012 (provisional number of births in 2025 was 54,125) – these individuals, who have been going through primary and secondary education, are now reaching higher education age. These trends have potential implications for funding for the higher education sector and will inform policy development and investment planning over the coming decade.
I am committed to supporting the higher education sector to meet this increasing demographic demand. The total allocation to higher education in Budget 2027 is €2.85 billion.

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the reasons ICOT have been removed from the Interim List of Eligible Programs.
reply:
The Department does not comment on individual cases.
Inclusion on the Interim List of Eligible Programmes (ILEP) is necessary for a Higher Education or English language education provider to be eligible to recruit learners from non-EEA countries on Stamp 2 immigration permissions. The ILEP is administered by the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in conjunction with the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science.
To have its programmes listed for this purpose, a provider must meet the relevant ILEP criteria on an ongoing basis. Where issues of non-compliance are identified and brought to the attention of the ILEP, these issues are reviewed and considered by a Committee comprised of officials from both Departments. Subject to its deliberations, this Committee may decide that the provider and its programmes are to be removed from the ILEP given the nature of non-compliance with established criteria. When such a decision is made and communicated, the provider may appeal within five working days and this shall be considered by the ILEP appeals committee.
It should be noted that the ILEP is in the process of being superseded by the TrustEd Ireland statutory quality mark. question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if he will address the concerns raised in correspondence (details supplied) regarding a university student who has been refused progression to fourth year.
reply:
I am sorry to learn of the difficulties experienced by the student concerned.
Higher education institutions are statutorily independent and autonomous bodies with responsibility for the management of their own academic and administrative affairs. Decisions concerning a student’s academic progression are therefore matters for the institution concerned, and neither I nor my Department has a role in reviewing or intervening in individual cases.
A student who wishes to challenge such a decision should, in the first instance, engage with the institution and avail of any relevant internal review, appeal or complaints procedures. Information on these procedures should be available directly from the institution.
Publicly funded higher education institutions come within the remit of the Office of the Ombudsman. Where a student has exhausted the institution’s internal procedures and remains dissatisfied, it is open to them to contact the Ombudsman. The Ombudsman may examine complaints concerning administrative actions or procedures, including alleged unfair treatment, a failure to provide clear reasons for a decision, undue delay or a failure to deal properly with a complaint. However, the Ombudsman cannot examine matters involving academic judgement.
Further information on making a complaint is available at www.ombudsman.ie or by contacting the Office of the Ombudsman at 6 Earlsfort Terrace, Dublin 2, D02 W773, or on 01 636 5600.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Transport if he will address the concerns raised in correspondence (details supplied) regarding the driver testing system, including matters relating to testing standards, consistency and the appeals process.
reply:
Under the Road Safety Authority Act 2006, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) has statutory responsibility for the National Driver Testing Service, including all operational matters. The RSA conducts the driving test to a standard that complies with the EU Driving Licence Directive. Given the RSA's responsibility in this matter, I have referred the Deputy's question to the Authority for direct response. Please contact my office if a reply is not received within ten days.
Pending this response, the RSA provides an appeals process whereby, if an applicant is unhappy with how a driving test was conducted or they believe they were unfairly treated, they can appeal the decision or raise a complaint.
Under section 33(6)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 1961, a person aggrieved by a test decision may also appeal to the District Court. The court will then examine whether or not the test was conducted properly. If the court determines that the tester did not conduct the test in accordance with procedures, a further test would be offered to the applicant free of charge.

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Transport if he has examined correspondence received by the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht regarding speed signage in Gaeltacht areas that continue to display speed limits in English only; and the steps he will take to overturn the rules laid out by his Department on the matter.
reply:
My Department received correspondence from the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht on the 16 February 2026. I issued a reply to the Minister on 25 May 2026.
The Official Languages Act 2003 at (Section 9) Regulations 2008 (SI 391/2008) at Section 3.3 exempts road signage from the requirement under the Act. However, the Traffic Signs Manual at Section 1.1.52 states:
It is a statutory requirement that place names on information signs be in both Irish and English, except:
For names of destinations in Gaeltacht areas where there is a direction by statute that only the Irish language version of the placename shall be used; and where the spelling of a place name is similar in both languages, in which case only the Irish form of the name should be shown.
I wish to assure you that at all times, especially within Gaeltacht areas, roads authorities are aware of their obligations under the provisions of the Traffic Signs Manual. It must be noted that a significant amount of traffic signage has the same display in both Irish and English. In addition, speed limit signs in the Republic of Ireland are language independent; hence no Irish or English text is used with them. They display a number along with the abbreviation km/h. Abbreviations such as ‘m’, ‘km’ and ‘km/h’ are Système International units and, as such, are not in any particular language. The abbreviation km/h is used because on the Island of Ireland the speed limits in the Republic are set in kilometres

The Government has also supported the growth of specialist services through sustained investment in maternity, neonatal and women's health services, including specialist midwifery and perinatal mental health posts.

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Health for an update with regard to the regulation of vapes; and if she plans to restrict retail vaping outlets.
reply:
The focus of policy and legislation regarding nicotine inhaling products is on reducing youth use.
The Public Health (Tobacco Products and Nicotine Inhaling Products) Act 2023 introduced domestic regulation of nicotine inhaling products including:
• A minimum age of sale of 18
• Further advertising restrictions in cinemas, on public transport and near schools
• Prohibition on the sale of nicotine inhaling products by self-service, at events aimed at children, and from temporary or moveable premises.
A significant provision in the Act was the licensing system for the retail sale of tobacco products and nicotine inhaling products, which became operational for all retailers on 2 August 2026. Previously, there was a once-off registration system for tobacco retailers, and no register for retailers of nicotine inhaling products.
Those who wish to sell these products must now apply for a licence, pay the required fee and renew that licence annually. The licensing system will give the HSE's National Environmental Health Service robust oversight of who is selling nicotine inhaling products. The legislation allows for increased penalties for offences such as selling to minors, including revocation of a licence. In addition, licences will not be granted to temporary or moveable premises such as those at festivals, and the sale of these products at events aimed at children is also prohibited.

question: Deputy Pat the Cope Gallagher asked the Minister for Transport the reason 16, 17 and 18-year-olds are required to pay full adult public transport fares while providing a 50% discount to 19 to 25-year-olds, including adults earning a full-time income; the reason a 16-year-old secondary school student with no income can therefore face a fare twice that paid by a 15-year-old travelling on the same service (details supplied).
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. However, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of public transport. The National Transport Authority (NTA) has responsibility for the regulation of fares charged to passengers in respect of public transport services provided under public service obligation (PSO) contracts.
The Young Adult Card (YAC) provides individuals aged 19 to 25 with 50% off adult fares across the entire Transport for Ireland (TFI) network and for participating commercial operators. This discount is applied irrespective of employment or educational status. To clarify in relation to the specific matter raised, those in full-time education aged 16-18 or 26 and above may access an equivalent discount through the Student Leap Card.
The Government remains fully committed to improving the affordability and accessibility of public transport. The current discounted fare initiatives are designed to help with the cost of living for young people, students and children, encouraging them to start using public transport from an early age, by offering them more affordable and flexible travel options.
Any further enhancement to these initiatives would need to be considered, taking account of competing funding demands and wider public transport priorities.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Transport if he is aware of the reduced public bus services operating between Claremorris/Ballina and Galway following the withdrawal of Expressway Route 52; the actions being taken to ensure adequate public transport capacity on this corridor.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport; however, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of public transport.
I am aware that Bus Éireann announced the withdrawal of some services which operated under its Expressway service, which included the Route 52. This decision was taken following a financial and operational review carried out by Bus Éireann with regard Expressway performance over recent years, which sought to ensure the long-term financial sustainability of the company as a whole.
As is the case with any such commercial route withdrawals, the withdrawal of these routes triggered the NTA’s PSO Determination process, the outcome of which has been published on the NTA's website. I have been advised that a commercial operator is currently operating along the corridor, which does not fall under the purview of the PSO network.
The NTA as the statutory authority responsible for securing the provision of public transport services nationally keep the network under review, and would be best placed to advise the Deputy of public transport capacity and provision in the region.
For further information I have forwarded your query to the NTA for their consideration and direct reply. Please notify my office if you have not received a reply within 10 working days.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the number of Irish election observers to be deployed to Serbia for the upcoming OSCE/ODIHR election observation mission; the number who have previous election observation experience; and if she will consider increasing the size of the Irish contingent and the proportion of experienced observers.
reply:
The Government is committed to supporting democratisation, human rights, and the rule of law, as a key element of our foreign policy. Support to election observation is central to this commitment and Ireland has contributed observers to international election observation missions since the 1990s.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade maintains and administers a roster enabling Ireland to respond to calls to participate in election observation missions coordinated by the OSCE and the EU. The current five-year Roster commenced on 1 January 2024 and has 169 members.
In response to OSCE calls for nominations for positions on an Election Observation Mission to the Serbian Parliamentary Elections scheduled for 25 October 2026, one Irish Roster member has been selected and deployed as a Long-Term Observer. Ten further Roster members will shortly fill Short-Term Observer positions, all of whom have previous election observation mission experience.
The window for nominations to this mission is closed, with logistical planning for arrival of Short-Term Observers underway. The participation of 11 Irish observers is consistent with the level of participation in other OSCE missions in 2026.

question: Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Health the number of psychiatry training places that are available under the HSE’s postgraduate schemes; and whether Budget 2027 provides for an expansion of these to meet projected service demand.
reply:
The HSE, through National Doctors Training and Planning (NDTP), funds postgraduate specialist training in Psychiatry delivered by the College of Psychiatrists of Ireland at both Basic Specialist Training (BST) and Higher Specialist Training (HST) level.
For the 2026/2027 training year, 80 doctors commenced Basic specialty training (BST) and a further 47 commenced higher speciality training (HST) within Psychiatry. Planning for the July 2027 intake is continuing with the College of Psychiatrists of Ireland and the final HST intake will depend on the training posts and associated WTE/funding available.
Psychiatry operates a streamlined training pathway, whereby trainees who successfully complete BST and meet the College’s requirements for progression can progress to Higher Specialist Training. To support this progression, additional Psychiatry Senior training posts are being considered as part of plans to continue expansion of Postgraduate Medical Specialty Training Posts in 2027.
There has been significant expansion in postgraduate medical training capacity over the last five years, with the number of doctors enrolled in postgraduate medical training increasing by 21% over that period (HSE National Doctors Training and Planning (NDTP) Medical Workforce Report 2025–2026). This includes expansion in Psychiatry training posts in recent years, with BST intake in Psychiatry having increased by approximately 30% since 2021 and this increased cohort now progressing through to HST.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Health whether she is aware of delays in accessing a drug (details supplied) for Friedreich’s ataxia due to capacity constraints at the Combined Ataxia Clinic, Tallaght University Hospital; the timeframe for all eligible patients to commence treatment; whether additional resources will be provided; the current clinic waiting times; and measures to ensure timely specialist review and annual multidisciplinary assessment.
reply:
Under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013 the Health Service Executive (HSE) has statutory responsibility for decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines and medical devices.
Following extensive engagement between the HSE and Biogen, the HSE’s Senior Management Team (SMT) approved the reimbursement of Skyclarys for patients over 16 years of age with Friedreich’s Ataxia.
From the 1st October 2026, omaveloxolone (Skyclarys®) is approved to be added to the list of reimbursable items under the High-Tech Drug Arrangements for the treatment of Friedreich’s ataxia in adults and adolescents aged 16 years and older. Prescribing of omaveloxolone (Skyclarys®) is through the High-Tech Hub and will be restricted to designated approved consultants.
The National Ataxia Clinic at Tallaght University Hospital has put in place additional clinics to assess suitability for treatment with Skyclarys.
For the small number of patients who attend other hospitals, assessment will be managed locally by the responsible clinical teams and treating physicians.
A number of patients attending Tallaght University Hospital, Cork University Hospital, and University Hospital Galway have received approved prescriptions for Skyclarys.
In relation to the operational matters raised, I have asked the Health Service Executive to respond to the Deputy directly.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Health the reason the allocation to the National Treatment Purchase Fund in the Estimates for Public Services has been reduced from €230 million in 2025 to €200 million in 2026 and to €150.4 million in 2027; the number of patients treated through NTPF-funded activity in 2025 and to date in 2026; the number expected in 2027; and whether the minimum waiting time for eligibility for NTPF-funded treatment will remain at nine months in 2027.
reply:
The Government is focused on having a public health service in which everyone has timely access to high-quality scheduled care, where and when they need it.
The only sustainable solution to addressing waiting times in acute hospitals is by increasing core activity within the public health service through improved productivity and efficiencies and through ongoing reform and leveraging enabling supports.
Measures to do this are underway, such as continuing the implementation of POCC contract, 5/7 working and implementation of Seven Day Services; Increasing the level and volume of services that will be available earlier in the day, in the evening and at weekends in acute hospitals.
Other ongoing developments to enhance regional capacity are in the Surgical Hubs. These are already making a difference. Four Hubs are now operational at Tallaght, Mt Carmel, Swords and Cork.
In 2027, we will deliver more, with the addition of new Surgical Hubs, we expect to see approximately 85,000 patients – making a real difference to people’s lives.
Other productivity measures such as OPD optimisation through the OPD toolkit is increasing activity levels where it is operational and through the theatre utilisation programme, which aims to increase theatre effectiveness and patient throughput to help reduce surgical waiting lists.
Funding for the National Treatment Purchase Fund (NTPF) is to supplement this increased activity and provide targeted measures to address specific areas of concern.

Significant progress has been made under this approach in reducing the length of time patients are waiting.
With the 2026 plan, we will continue to build upon the progress delivered to date under the multi annual action plan approach, moving towards the ultimate vision of a public healthcare service in which everyone has timely access to high-quality scheduled care, where and when they need it.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Health the reason lung transplant patients are not reimbursed for vaccinations they must have before undergoing transplant surgery (details supplied); and if consideration will be given to extending reimbursement to this cohort given the significant cost of the vaccinations required.
reply:
Prior to solid organ transplantation, including lung transplantation, it is important that patients remain up to date with their vaccinations. This can be done through their local medical practitioner or local hospital service.
While some vaccinations may be required in advance of transplantation, others may be recommended.
I have been informed by the Mater Misericordiae University Hospital that Shingles, RSV, and HPV vaccines are recommended but not mandatory prior to lung transplantation. The Hospital has advised that not having these vaccines does not preclude a patient from being listed or transplanted.
Where a patient has queries about vaccinations in advance of transplantation, these should be discussed with their transplant team, who can provide specific advice.
Regarding reimbursement, I am advised that the HSE Primary Care Reimbursement Service does not supply vaccines or provide reimbursement support for vaccines through community pharmacies under the Statutory Drug Schemes.
When the public health imperative to support particular vaccines to defined cohorts becomes national policy, vaccines are directly procured by the HSE and supplied through the national vaccine distribution arrangements to GPs and pharmacies for eligible cohorts.
The Shingles, RSV or the HPV vaccines are not reimbursed under Community Drug Schemes including both the General Medical Services and Drugs Payment Scheme.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Health the supports she plans to put in place for pregnant women who go to accident and emergency departments and face long wait times.
reply:
The Government is committed to ensuring that pregnant women who require urgent or emergency care receive safe, timely and appropriate assessment. All patients presenting to an emergency department are triaged and seen according to clinical urgency. Any woman whose condition requires immediate attention will therefore be prioritised accordingly.
Where clinically appropriate and local arrangements allow, pregnant women are directed to dedicated maternity emergency and assessment services, including Emergency and Assessment Units or maternity emergency rooms within maternity networks.
The HSE continues to work with hospital groups and maternity services to support clear referral pathways, appropriate escalation and coordination between emergency departments and specialist obstetric teams. These arrangements are intended to ensure that pregnant women are assessed in the most appropriate clinical setting and that any deterioration or additional risk is identified and managed promptly.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Health her plans to reduce accident and emergency wait times.
reply:
I recognise that long waits in emergency departments can place additional burden on patients and their families. Patients attending the ED are prioritised according to clinical need so that those requiring the most urgent treatment are seen first. Reducing waiting times and ensuring that patients receive safe and timely care remains a priority for me and for this Government.
The HSE’s 2026 Urgent and Emergency Care Operational Plan provides the framework for improving performance across the full patient pathway. It focuses on strengthening operational management, enabling people to avail of appropriate care and supports outside of acute hospital settings, improving emergency department and in-hospital processes, and supporting timely discharge. The Department continues to work closely with the HSE to support delivery of the Plan and ongoing improvements in urgent and emergency care.
A central element of the Plan is to provide more appropriate alternatives to emergency department attendance. This includes expanding and promoting Injury Units, strengthening GP out-of-hours services, increasing access to community diagnostics and specialist ambulatory pathways, and using virtual wards and enhanced community care to treat suitable patients closer to home.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Health for an update on the new National Maternity Hospital, the scheduled opening date, the expenditure to date and the projected expenditure.
reply:
Government is committed to the development of the new National Maternity Hospital (NMH) at the St Vincent’s University Hospital (SVUH), Elm Park.
It is a major infrastructural investment by the State for women’s health, providing much needed facilities for women and babies for generations to come. The extra capacity to be provided at the new NMH will help safeguard national neonatal, maternity and gynaecology service provision.
The procurement and tender process for the main works contract concluded in 2025, and the outcomes were incorporated into a Final Business Case. This Final Business Case has been submitted for review to officials in the Department of Health and is being finalised in line with the requirements of the Infrastructure Guidelines.
Concurrently, the successful tenderers entered a non-binding pre-construction services agreement (PCSA) with the HSE. This PCSA process brings contractors and suppliers together to agree detailed delivery programmes, de?risk sequencing, and mobilise supply chains.
This approach, drawn from lessons in other large projects, seeks to ensure greater programme certainty before entering into the contract. The PCSA process has now concluded and, together with the final business case, will inform a Memorandum for Government, which I hope to bring to Government in the coming weeks, seeking approval for the HSE to proceed to sign main works contracts and commence full construction.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Health for an update on the National Children's Hospital, the scheduled opening date, the expenditure to date and the projected expenditure.
reply:
Opening the National Children’s Hospital Ireland (NCHI) is a Government priority. Everything possible is being done to ensure this world-class hospital will open as quickly as possible, on behalf of children, young people, and their families.
I have been clear that the responsibility for committing to, resourcing, and delivering this project sits squarely with the project’s main contractor, BAM Ireland. The State will not reduce the pressure or dilute that accountability.
Ultimately, realising substantial completion is dependent on BAM’s execution and delivery of its own programme. BAM has shifted its Substantial Completion date 20 times over the last 6 years. On 13 July, BAM issued an updated programme to the Employer’s Representative (ER- independent third party responsible for administering the contract). The ER subsequently wrote to BAM for further detail to inform that review. That updated programme is still awaited from BAM.
In June, Children’s Health Ireland (CHI) gained early access to Level 1 where the critical care beds are, and this is welcome. However, access to Level 2, remains outstanding due to BAM’s repeated failure to deliver as committed. Achieving substantial completion is essentially a ‘volume exercise,’ to complete over 5,728 rooms. There has been a continued reduction in resources on site and while 5,079 of the 5,728 (88%) rooms have been delivered to the contractual standard, this is still falling behind BAM’s own completion targets.

question: Deputy Johnny Guirke asked the Minister for Transport the measures he is taking to ensure that the shortage and availability challenges in rural Ireland at peak times for small public service vehicles is dealt with.
reply:
The regulation of the small public service vehicle (SPSV) industry, including the local area hackney licence, is a matter for the independent transport regulator, the National Transport Authority (NTA), under the provisions of the Consolidated Taxi Regulation Acts 2013 and 2016. I have no role in the day-to-day operations of the SPSV sector.
The local area hackney (LAH) licence is a special, limited hackney licence that supports rural community transport through a locally operated hackney service. As of 31 August 2026, there are 23 licensed LAH drivers and 28 licensed vehicles.
In April 2026, the NTA introduced a series of enhancements to the local area hackney (LAH) licence intended to increase uptake. Under the new approach, where a local community gives support to an LAH licence applicant, the applicant will receive a licence offer from the NTA. This removes the requirement for additional assessments that were previously required.
To increase service availability, up to five local area hackney licensed drivers may now operate a single local area hackney vehicle. These may include friends or family members where the service is privately operated, or staff of a local business where the business owner provides the community service. This marks a significant change from the previous requirement, which allowed only one driver permitted to operate the hackney. question: Deputy Michael Collins asked the Minister for Health if guidance will be issued (details supplied) to pharmacies to allow patients who depend on essential prescribed medicines, including pregabalin, to obtain a limited emergency supply for use during prolonged power outages, evacuations or other disruptions.
reply:
Provision is made under Regulation 8 of the Medicinal Products (Prescription and Control of Supply) Regulations 2003 (as amended) to permit pharmacists, in emergency circumstances, to supply certain prescription only medicines without a prescription. Emergency supply can be carried out at the request of a patient or at the request of a prescriber. Pregabalin is not currently classified as a controlled drug under Ireland's Misuse of Drugs legislation and therefore may be dispensed under these ‘emergency supply’ provisions, as appropriate. Additionally, registered pharmacists must, at all times, act in accordance with a statutory Code of Conduct.
The Pharmaceutical Society of Ireland – the pharmacy regulator has issued advice on its website on emergency supply provisions and on its statutory Code of Conduct for pharmacists, which are accessible at www.psi.ie.
My Department does not currently intend to issue any supplementary guidance on this matter.

question: Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Health the steps she has taken to ensure that eligible patients will have access to a medication (details supplied) since its approval for reimbursement without avoidable capacity delays; whether regional services will be developed to assist in access and ongoing care; if she will outline the way in which patients will be identified and assessed; the way prescriptions will be issued; the way in which monitoring will be organised; and the way in which the medicine will be supplied through community pharmacies.
reply:
Under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013 the Health Service Executive (HSE) has statutory responsibility for decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines and medical devices.
Following extensive engagement between the HSE and Biogen, the HSE’s Senior Management Team (SMT) approved the reimbursement of Skyclarys for patients over 16 years of age with Friedreich’s Ataxia.
From the 1st October 2026, omaveloxolone (Skyclarys®) is approved to be added to the list of reimbursable items under the High-Tech Drug Arrangements for the treatment of Friedreich’s ataxia in adults and adolescents aged 16 years and older. Prescribing of omaveloxolone (Skyclarys®) is through the High-Tech Hub and will be restricted to designated approved consultants.
The National Ataxia Clinic at Tallaght University Hospital has put in place additional clinics to assess suitability for treatment with Skyclarys.
For the small number of patients who attend other hospitals, assessment will be managed locally by the responsible clinical teams and treating physicians.
A number of patients attending Tallaght University Hospital, Cork University Hospital, and University Hospital Galway have received approved prescriptions for Skyclarys®.
In relation to the operational matters raised, I have asked the Health Service Executive to respond to the Deputy directly.

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Health the average distance travelled by patients attending specialist menopause clinics; and whether consideration is being given to establishing additional regional services.
reply:
The delivery of menopause care is primarily based in the community and most women can access appropriate assessment, advice and treatment through their GP.
For women who require complex specialist menopause care that cannot be suitably managed within primary care, there are six specialist menopause clinics in operation nationally, one in each maternity network.
I am not aware of data being collected on the average distance travelled by patients attending specialist menopause clinics. However, these services are organised on a maternity network basis, with clinics located in the National Maternity Hospital, the Rotunda Hospital, the Coombe Hospital, Nenagh Hospital, Galway University Hospital and Cork University Maternity Hospital.
These clinics accept referrals from GPs within their respective catchment areas.
At present, there are no plans to establish additional regional specialist menopause clinics, though funding was provided to expand the existing service last year. The current model is designed to provide specialist menopause care, where needed, through the six maternity networks. The majority of menopause care is delivered as close to home as possible through primary care services, ensuring minimal travel to services.

question: Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Health the arrangements in place for the follow-up care, monitoring and management of patients who undergo surgical procedures abroad under the cross-border directive; the supports available to patients who subsequently develop complications following their return to Ireland; the person or body responsible for co-ordinating their ongoing care; whether data is collected on complications and adverse outcomes arising from procedures undertaken under the directive.
reply:
Under the terms of the EU Cross Border Directive (CBD), where a patient has received healthcare abroad, in another EU/EEA country under the provisions of the CBD, and medical follow-up proves necessary the home country (in this case Ireland) is obliged to provide the patient with the same follow-up treatment it would have provided had the treatment taken place on its territory.

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Health the measures in place to ensure that claims to private health insurers in respect of private patients treated in public hospitals are completed and submitted within the required period; whether recovery of this money is monitored as part of hospital performance management; and the steps being taken to recover claims reported as unpaid over the past three years.
reply:
The billing and collection of private health insurance income is an operational matter for the HSE.
The Department expects that all valid income due to the public health service is identified, billed and collected promptly. The Department has raised this matter directly with the HSE and monitors progress through its ongoing financial oversight and engagement arrangements.
The latest information provided by the HSE indicates a material improvement in the position, with outstanding private health insurer debt reducing by approximately €40 million, or 20%, from €200 million to €160 million. Claims awaiting action and sign-off by consultants also reduced by approximately €13 million, or 23%, from €55 million to €42 million. It is important to distinguish between outstanding debt and debt written off. Outstanding debt includes claims at various stages of processing and collection, whereas the HSE reported that €3.4 million was written off in 2025 due to claims not being submitted within the relevant time limits.
As the matters raised by the Deputy regarding the processes in place for the submission of claims, the monitoring of income recovery as part of hospital performance management, and the recovery of unpaid claims are operational matters for the HSE, I have asked the HSE to respond directly to the Deputy with the most up-to-date information available.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport whether he will reconsider the current arrangements whereby a person returning to Ireland, whose Irish driving licence has expired for more than ten years but who has continued to hold a valid driving licence and driving entitlement in another jurisdiction, may be required to recommence the driver licensing process; and if he will consider permitting such persons to renew their previous Irish driving entitlement subject to appropriate verification and road-safety safeguards.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 68, 69 and 70 together.
Irish driver licensing operates within a framework of EU law, which sets out the driver licensing legislation with which all member states must comply. Licence formats, vehicle categories and driving test standards are all set at EU level. Therefore, EU/EEA licences are recognised in all member states.
Under section 38 of the Road Traffic Act 1961, as amended, it is an offence to drive a vehicle in a public place without a valid driving licence. Irish driving licences may be renewed at any point up to ten years after expiry. This gives the holder twenty years from the award of the licence to ensure it is renewed.
After ten years without a valid licence, the holder is no longer considered a qualified driver and may not renew that licence. This provision is set out in Regulation SI 537/2006 - the Road Traffic (Licensing of Drivers) Regulations 2006, made under the 1961 Act.
Where a driver, who is resident in Ireland, holds a valid exchangeable licence, such as an EU/EEA licence obtained by passing a test in the EU/EEA or a licence for which Ireland has an exchange agreement, it may be exchanged for an Irish licence on application to the National Driver Licence Service.

reply:

Following extensive engagement between the HSE and Biogen, the HSE’s Senior Management Team (SMT) approved the reimbursement of Skyclarys for patients over 16 years of age with Friedreich’s Ataxia.
From the 1st October 2026, omaveloxolone (Skyclarys®) is approved to be added to the list of reimbursable items under the High-Tech Drug Arrangements for the treatment of Friedreich’s ataxia in adults and adolescents aged 16 years and older. Prescribing of omaveloxolone (Skyclarys®) is through the High-Tech Hub and will be restricted to designated approved consultants.
The National Ataxia Clinic at Tallaght University Hospital has put in place additional clinics to assess suitability for treatment with Skyclarys.
For the small number of patients who attend other hospitals, assessment will be managed locally by the responsible clinical teams and treating physicians.
A number of patients attending Tallaght University Hospital, Cork University Hospital, and University Hospital Galway have received approved prescriptions for Skyclarys®.
In relation to the operational matters raised, I have asked the Health Service Executive to respond to the Deputy directly.

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh den Aire Leanaí, Míchumais agus Comhionannais if consideration has been given by her Department to screening for dyslexia as part of the AON process.
reply:
Under the Disability Act 2005, an Assessment of Need is a specific assessment process carried out by the HSE to determine whether a child or young person has a disability as defined within the Act, and if they do, to identify the health and education needs (if any) arising from that disability.
A person can apply for an Assessment of Need if they think they or their child has a disability, as defined by the Disability Act. The definition of disability is very specific in the Act. It means a substantial restriction in the person’s capacity i.e. that a person has a significant difficulty with communication, learning, mobility or significantly disordered cognitive processes. In addition, this restriction should be permanent or likely to be permanent and require the continued provision of services to meet the person’s needs.
If a determination of disability is made, the applicant’s health and/or education needs are identified as well as the health services required to meet those needs. Although the Assessment of Need process can include the identification of a child’s education needs, the identification of the education services that they may require is not part of the process.
The Assessment of Need process is not designed to screen for particular conditions. Any clinical assessment undertaken as part of an assessment of need is focused on identifying the person's needs arising from their disability and informing the identification of supports. reply:
