question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Transport the way in which he has allocated the €2 billion allocated to his Department under the ICNF; the amount that has been spent to date; the amount that has been allocated to date; and the amount that has yet to be allocated, in tabular form.
reply:
As the Deputy may be aware, the Government has committed over €10 billion in funding to support the delivery of major public transport infrastructure projects over the period 2026 to 2030 in the National Development Plan (NDP) Review 2025, published in July last year, with an additional €2 billion committed from the Infrastructure, Nature and Climate and Fund (ICNF) to support MetroLink.
MetroLink is the only project under the remit of my Department which has been designated funding from the ICNF. This allocation will assist in moving MetroLink into construction. For 2026, MetroLink has been funded solely from Vote 31 and none of the €2 billion allocation has yet been drawn down from the ICNF.
Government consented to "Approval Gate 2" for MetroLink on 16th September, marking a significant milestone. With Government's approval, MetroLink will now be able to proceed to the detailed procurement phase, with the main tender packs expected to issue to market in the first half of 2027 and heavy construction works anticipated to commence in 2028.
I also warmly welcome the additional €6 billion earmarked for the construction of MetroLink to 2030, as provided for under "Budget 2027".

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality in the context of the review of the Right to Request Flexible Working provisions as outlined in her previous reply, if the review will examine the increasing level of congestion facing commuters and the knock on impact on their wellbeing.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 666, 667, 668 and 669 together.
Under the Work Life Balance and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2023, there is a provision for a review of the Right to Request Flexible Working provisions. As noted in my previous response this review is currently being scoped and is due to be undertaken in the coming months.
It is important to note that the review is a Statutory review and is to be focused on how the provisions for requesting flexible working operate, with an additional element to review as to whether the right should be extended to all workers rather than just carers and parents as is currently legislated for.
As part of the National Strategy for Women and Girls 2025-2030 and its associated first Action Plan, the review will also focus on what additional flexibilities may be introduced to workplaces to support parents and carers.

reply:

Acting on feedback received from childminders and childminding representative organisations, I have brought the review forward, to ensure there is sufficient time to implement any changes arising from the review, before the end of the transition period.
The review aims to evaluate the initial implementation of the childminding specific regulations and assess whether the regulatory model is appropriate, proportionate and aligned with the realities of childminding practice in a home-based setting.
The scope of the review is broader than initially outlined in the National Action Plan for Childminding and now also examines the effectiveness of supports made available to assist with the registration of childminders, as well as examining the barriers to registration and regulatory compliance, including financial and information barriers.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the position regarding families with children in childcare centres that are not part of the core funding scheme; if they will benefit from the €550 cap per month as announced in Budget 2027.
reply:
Core Funding is a supply-side grant to ELC and SAC providers towards their operating costs. It is designed to promote affordability for parents and sustainability for providers through increased funding to the sector, paid on a consistent and equitable basis.
A key condition of receiving the significant State funding that is available through the Scheme requires that a Partner Service adhere to the Core Funding fee management system, which includes a freeze on fees at 2021 levels and fee caps. This is to ensure that the State’s significant investment through the Scheme is not absorbed by unnecessary fee increases.
These fee management conditions of the Core Funding Scheme apply exclusively to Partner Services who have signed a Core Funding Agreement. These regulations are not applied to services which remain outside of the Core Funding scheme.
It is a matter for providers to decide whether they wish to sign up to Core Funding and benefit from the significant financial supports it offers to providers and the certainty it gives to parents through the associated fee management measures. It should be noted that services that provide the Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) programme and/or the National Childcare Scheme (NCS) are not required to take part in Core Funding, reducing the impact of the NCS as some families are not benefiting from the fee-control measures (fee-freeze and fee caps) or additional funding for quality provision that is provided by Core Funding. reply:

The Department has had extensive engagement with the legal profession, through the Law Society of Ireland, in respect of the EPA application process. The Department met with the Law Society and the Decision Support Service in September 2025 to discuss any issues of concern in respect of the 2015 Act, particularly as it relates to the role of the legal profession in the EPA application process, to provide any required clarification on the application process and how the legal profession can, and are, engaging, and to agree next steps.
In that regard, in October 2025 the Decision Support Service hosted a workshop for the Law Society of Ireland in order to identify the specific functionality sought by the Law Society in respect of a solicitors portal. The Department awaits feedback from the Law Society following that workshop in order to progress a resolution to any remaining concerns.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the percentage of staff turnover, by county within the early years sector in 2025, in tabular form.
reply:

question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to provide details of the funding being made available in 2027 for the assessment of need targeted waiting list initiative, commonly referred to as Cara’s Fund; the total allocation in 2027 and how this compares with the allocation in 2026; the number of children whose assessments are expected to be completed through the initiative in 2027; the criteria that will apply in identifying and prioritising children for assessment; whether private providers will continue to be commissioned to provide assessments under the initiative; and the number of children awaiting an AON nationally.
reply:
The Department and the HSE are working intensively to address delays in the provision of Assessments of Need to children and young people and their families.
It is important to emphasise that the provision of an Assessment of Need and the delivery of services are separate issues. Children do not need an Assessment of Need report to access health or education supports, and having an Assessment of Need does not speed up access to services. Support continues to be provided through HSE Primary Care, Children’s Disability Services Teams, and CAMHs. Families can access and apply for services directly through the HSE.
Nevertheless, the Disability Act 2005 makes provision for a statutory assessment of need where a person thinks they or their child may have a disability. The Assessment of Need process determines whether an applicant has a disability as defined under the Disability Act, and if so, identifies the health and education needs resulting from this disability (if any), as well as the health services and supports required to meet those needs. Assessment of Need applications are processed in the date order in which they are received within the relevant area. There is no prioritisation of applications.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the timeline for the publication of the national childcare scheme review; the reason the publication of the review has been delayed from the original scheduled time of Q3 2026.
reply:
The independent evaluation of the National Childcare Scheme (NCS) commenced in March 2026 following a procurement tendering process which launched in late 2025. It is expected that the evaluation run for approximately 18 months with a final report expected to be published in Q3 2027. This evaluation aims to assess the performance of the NCS to date and its operation within the wider early learning and childcare funding and policy environment.
The evaluation will examine whether the NCS, as part of the wider funding model, is making high-quality early learning and childcare more accessible and affordable, particularly for families in the lowest income groups and the most disadvantaged households. It will also identify any improvements that could be made to enhance accessibility and affordability and to ensure that the NCS is working for as many families as possible.
The evaluation will include consultation and engagement with parents, educators, practitioners, providers and representative organisations. Any changes to the NCS will be carefully considered in light of the findings of this evaluation.

question: Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality when she expects to publish the findings of her Departments review of the mother and baby institutions payment scheme.
reply:
The Mother and Baby Institutions Payment Scheme opened for applications in March 2024.
The underpinning legislation for the Scheme provides for a number of reports and reviews to be produced. Section 48 of the Mother and Baby Institutions Payment Scheme Act provides for two reviews of the operation of the Scheme, the first of which is to take place around the Scheme's mid-point.
The scope of the review is prescribed in the Act. It is focused on administrative and operational aspects of the Scheme. It will consider issues such as the level of uptake of the Scheme, the experience of applicants, the extent to which payments have been made and if the Scheme is achieving its purpose as set out by the Oireachtas. The Act does not provide for a revisiting of Scheme scope or eligibility criteria, matters already decided on by the Oireachtas during the legislative process.
Department officials have been undertaking preparatory work for the review over the last number of months and I approved the overall approach and authorised the review to commence on 16th of September. The review will include statistical assessment, business processes analysis and a survey of applicant experience, overseen by a Steering Group and independently quality assured.
I do not wish to estimate timeframes at this juncture but I will ensure the review report will be laid before the Houses of the Oireachtas when completed.

question: Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the recourse an adopted person has when their adoption file reveals serious concerns about the circumstances in which their adoption took place.
reply:
The Adoption Act 2010, which came into effect on 1 November 2010, was introduced to ensure high standards in both domestic and intercountry adoption.
An adopted person who has concerns about the circumstances of their adoption has a number of options available to them.
If their concern relates to the Child and Family Agency, Tusla, an adopted person can make a complaint to that body through the complaints process set out on the Tusla website. If the concern relates to the Adoption Authority of Ireland, they can make a complaint in accordance with the complaints procedure set out on the Authority’s website. Complaints concerning registered social workers can be made to CORU, the health and social care regulator, under its Fitness to Practice process.
In addition, an adopted person has the right to complain to the Office of the Ombudsman or the Ombudsman for Children. An adopted person may also wish to seek independent legal advice and, depending on the circumstances, may wish to pursue a personal injuries claim through the Injuries Resolution Board, bring judicial review proceedings or seek other appropriate reliefs through the courts.

question: Deputy Aisling Dempsey asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality her plans to increase the statutory two week paternity leave.
reply:
There have been significant developments in entitlements for parents of working families in recent years. The Government is committed to supporting workers, including by extending paid leave for parents to allow them to spend more time with their child during their earliest years.
The Paternity Leave and Benefit Act 2016 provides the relevant parent (other than the mother of the child) with 2 weeks paid Paternity Leave. Ireland's statutory Paternity Leave arrangements are fully aligned with the requirements of the EU Work-Life Balance Directive, which introduced a minimum standard for Paternity Leave across EU Member States.
Under the Parent’s Leave and Benefit Act 2019, working parents are also entitled to nine weeks of paid Parent's Leave for each relevant parent, to be taken in the first two years after the birth or adoptive placement of a child. Parent's Leave is an individual separate entitlement and is non-transferable between parents.
Under the Parental Leave (Amendment) Act 2019, an employee who is a relevant parent in respect of a child under the age 12 is entitled to 26 weeks’ unpaid Parental Leave for each child. Where a child has a disability or long-term illness, the entitlement can continue until the child is 16. A relevant parent is a parent, an adoptive parent, or a person acting in ‘loco parentis’. Both parents have an equal, separate entitlement to Parental Leave.

question: Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Defence if her Department has adopted or is developing initiatives to encourage former members of the Defence Forces to re-join.
reply:
Encouraging talented former personnel to re join the Defence Forces continues to be a priority for me as part of the overall recruitment and retention initiatives within the Defence Forces.
There are two methods by which a person can ‘re-join’ the Permanent Defence Force (PDF) – re-enlistment and re-commissioning.
In April 2020, a scheme was launched to re-enlist former PDF enlisted personnel. The focus of the scheme is on those former PDF personnel with particular skillsets identified by the Chief of Staff which are not available within the Defence Forces. Applicants can initially re-enlist for a minimum term of six months to a maximum term of three years. There was an amendment made to the Defence Act in 2024 to allow members to apply for further terms.
The Re-Commissioning of Former Officers of the Permanent Defence Forces Scheme facilitates the re-entry of former officers, where vacancies exist, and where there are particular skillsets that are not available in the PDF at the time of the application, to be re-commissioned.
Recommissioned officers are offered a short service commission for a period of three years. Subject to vacancies, the recommissioned officers may be offered a substantive appointment after three years if the requirement for the particular skill set still exists.

One of the main objectives of Shaping the Future is to reduce parental fees to a maximum of €200 per month over the lifetime of the Government.
The Action Plan adopts a phased approach that enables action to be taken in 2026 while allowing adequate time for a broad public consultation and analysis on longer-term actions.
The consultation process, which has taken place throughout this year, has had a number of channels designed to facilitate the participation of a wide range of stakeholders. The final stage (a national forum that took place on 23rd September) built on insights from surveys, local consultation events, and stakeholder engagement and will help inform future policy direction. Results of this consultation, and additional analysis, will inform Phase 2 of Shaping the Future.
Phase 2, which will be published later this year, will set out actions to be undertaken from 2027 through to the end of 2029.
A number of steps have already been taken in 2025 and 2026 to reduce the costs of ELC and SAC for parents, with further measures announced in Budget 2027.

question: Deputy John McGuinness asked the Minister for Defence the intended purpose for providing the “complaints processes” in S.I. No. 304 of 2024 “to include, but is not limited to” the listed processes; which additional complaint or reporting pathways were envisaged, including routes used where no formal process was accessible; the assessment her Department records of the intended interaction between that non-exhaustive definition, and the definitions of “abuse” and “complaints of abuse”.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 55, 56, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61 and 62 together.
The report of the Independent Review Group established to examine dignity and equality issues in the Defence Forces was published on 28 March 2023. The Deputy will be aware that the Government agreed to progress the recommendations contained in the Report, which included the establishment of a Statutory Inquiry to identify systemic failures, if any, in the complaints system, in order to ensure accountability and transparency.
Draft Terms of Reference for this Statutory Inquiry were prepared in consultation with the Attorney General and shared with a broad range of stakeholders and interested parties including the Defence Forces' Representative Associations and Defence Forces' Veteran Associations prior to being finalised.

The Defence Forces Tribunal of Inquiry (‘Tribunal’) was then formally established by Statutory Instrument on 20 June 2024, (S.I. 304 of 2024). The Tribunal's role is to examine the effectiveness of the complaints processes in the Defence Forces concerning workplace issues relating to discrimination, bullying, harassment, sexual harassment and sexual misconduct. The Tribunal also has the power to investigate the response to complaints made regarding the use of hazardous chemicals within the Air Corps’ headquarters at Casement Aer

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the number of children in County Mayo awaiting completion of an assessment of need; the number waiting less than six months, six to 12 months, one to two years and more than two years; the number of assessment of needs completed in County Mayo in each of the past five years and to date in 2026.
reply:
The Department and the HSE are working intensively to address delays in the provision of Assessments of Need to children and their families.
There has been significant increase in demand for Assessment of Need in recent years. Applications for Assessment of Need have risen from 4,700 in 2020 to over 13,000 in 2025, with some 7,100 applications received in the first six months of this year. This reflects both the increase in population and the number of families exploring all options to access services for their child. This increase can be seen in the number of applications received within the Mayo Local Health Office area with applications rising from 65 in 2022 to 310 in 2025, an almost fivefold increase.
Unfortunately, demand has outpaced the capacity of the system to respond. The HSE reports that at the end of June, 23,282 applications were overdue for completion within the statutory timeframe set out in the Disability Act 2005.
Nevertheless, there has been progress over the past two years with a noticeable increase nationally in the number of completed applications, albeit with some regional variations. Over 5,900 AON reports were completed in 2025 – a 43% increase compared to 2024, with 3,043 assessment reports have been completed in the first six months of 2026. This improvement must continue.

reply:
During Ireland’s Presidency of the Council of the European Union, more than 280 Government-hosted events are scheduled to take place in Ireland. This is in addition to the extensive programme of meetings of the Council and its preparatory bodies taking place in Brussels and Luxembourg, led by the Irish Presidency.
The Department of Children, Disability and Equality is hosting 10 events in Ireland, with nine events taking place in Dublin and an Informal Meeting of Equality Ministers in Kerry. The Department is working the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and the Office of Public Works on all of these events. The details of these events are as follows:
The Deputy may wish to note that the core programme of Presidency meetings and events is published on the official Presidency website at eire2026.eu and ireland2026.eu, and includes the name, date, location and lead Department for relevant meetings.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the actions she is taking to engage with a childcare centre (details supplied) in relation to their withdrawal from the core funding model; and the actions she will take to support parents with the knock-on price increase.
reply:
I am aware that The Magic Roundabout Crèche and Montessori, registered as Beautiful Minds Crèche and Montessori Ltd, has not participated in the Core Funding scheme since the 2023/2024 programme year.
Core Funding is a supply-side grant to early learning and childcare providers towards their operating costs. It is designed to promote affordability for parents and sustainability for providers through increased funding to the sector, paid on a consistent and equitable basis.
As Core Funding is an optional scheme, service providers have the autonomy and business freedom to withdraw from or choose not to participate in Core Funding, even though this will result in the loss of the significant financial support it offers them and the substantial benefits and certainty it brings to families.
If a Partner Services wishes to withdraw from the Core Funding Programme, they must provide 3 months’ notice to the Scheme Administrator. This must be done by submitting a Service Request on the Early Years Early Years Hive outlining the withdrawal date and the reason for the withdrawal.
However, if an existing Partner Service decides not to enter a contract for the new programme year starting on 1 September, they, as private businesses, would no longer be subject to the provisions of the Core Funding Agreement and, by extension, the required minimum notice period to parents. They are also not required to provide a reason for choosing not to reapply for Core Funding to the Scheme Administrator.

question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the plans to expand paid surrogacy leave to parents of new-born children born through surrogacy, either within Ireland or abroad.
reply:
I wish to acknowledge the difficulties faced by couples pursuing surrogacy arrangements and reaffirm Government's commitment to recognising and supporting Irish families in all their diversity.
The Programme for Government 2025 - Securing Ireland's Future commits to introducing paid surrogacy leave and department officials are examining how best to implement this commitment. They are also engaging with officials from the Department of Social Protection as the Minister for Social Protection has responsibility for the payment of any associated benefits.
The Minister for Health leads on the Health (Assisted Human Reproduction) Act 2024, which includes provisions in relation to surrogacy which have implications for the introduction of surrogacy leave, while policy on parentage is a matter for the Minister for Justice. It is not possible to finalise provisions in relation to surrogacy leave in advance of the commencement of that Act as it will determine who is to be recognised as a parent when a child is born through a surrogacy arrangement.
Decisions on the date of commencement of the 2024 Act are matters for the Minister for Health. I can assure the Deputy that this Department will work closely with relevant Departments, once the 2024 Act has commenced, to progress proposals for surrogacy leave.
While it is not as comprehensive as paid surrogacy leave, the Deputy may be interested to note that under the Parent’s Leave and Benefit Act 2019 (as amended), working parents are entitl

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the rationale for increasing State funding to the greyhound racing industry in Budget 2027.
reply:
Rásaíocht Con Éireann (RCÉ) is a commercial state body established under the Greyhound Industry Act 1958 chiefly to control greyhound racing and to improve and develop the greyhound industry. RCÉ is a body corporate and a separate legal entity to the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine.
The horse and greyhound racing industries, via Horse Racing Ireland (HRI) and RCÉ, receive financial support from the State through the Horse and Greyhound Racing Fund. The Programme for Government commits that the Government will continue to support the Horse and Greyhound Fund, considering the vital economic and social contribution generated by these sectors in rural areas.
In Budget 2027, €102m has been allocated to the Fund of which €81.6m will be allocated to HRI and €20.4m to RCÉ. The allocation is subject to Oireachtas approval and is split 80/20 between HRI and RCÉ respectively in line with the relevant legislation.
The proposed increase in the Fund will be linked to the implementation of the recommendations contained in the Indecon Review, in respect of equine and greyhound welfare and integrity. This will form part of my Department’s overall animal welfare package and is in line with the Programme for Government commitments on equine and greyhound welfare and with the strategic plans of both RCÉ and HRI.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will consider reopening the fuel support scheme for a short period of time for new applicants.
reply:
My Department has introduced the Fuel Income Support Scheme as a targeted income support to assist farmers and agricultural or forestry contractors facing unprecedented increases in fuel costs.
Separate schemes have been put in place to support fishers and specialist horticultural growers.
As announced in the Budget, I am pleased to have secured agreement on the extension to the end of this year of the important fuel supports schemes provided for farmers and agricultural contractors, fishermen and women and horticulture producers impacted by higher fuel prices. The allocation of €31.2 million to cover the five months August to December 2026 for these supports will be rapidly implemented by my Department.
Final details are being worked on at present, but it is not envisaged that a second application will be required, nor will the scheme open for new applicants. A second payment will be made to all those who applied for the original Fuel Income Support Scheme and who met the eligibility criteria of the scheme as set out in the Terms and Conditions.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the reason for the decrease in current expenditure in the farm safety budget from €3 million to €2.3 million for 2027.
reply:
The safety, health and wellbeing of our farmers is a priority for this Government. The Programme for Government has prioritised farm safety, health and wellbeing and places a specific focus on farmer mental health and well-being, recognising the unique challenges faced by the sector.
I secured an allocation of €2.3 million of current funding for 2027. An additional €500,000 in capital funding is being made available for farm safety projects in 2027 from within existing capital allocations. This combined funding is in line with expenditure for 2026. This funding allocation will facilitate a significant focus on this important area in 2027 and will allow my Department to continue to support existing initiatives and to introduce new initiatives.
Farm safety is also a feature of our TAMS schemes, with all TAMS applicants required to complete a half-day farm safety training. The TAMS3 Farm Safety Capital Investment Scheme (FSCIS) attracts a higher rate of payment of 60% for farm safety related investments.
In addition, I have secured the renewal of the Accelerated Capital Allowance for Farm Safety Equipment for another three years, until 31 December 2029 and significantly extended the list of eligible farm safety equipment. This will enable farmers to improve their own safety and that of their farm and underlines our commitment in delivering on the priority afforded to the issue of farm safety in the Programme for Government.

question: Deputy Keira Keogh asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether engine replacement or re-engineering projects are currently eligible for grant aid under any BIM-administered EMFAF scheme; if not, the reason they are not eligible; whether consideration is being given to introducing a dedicated support scheme to assist fishers in upgrading to more fuel-efficient engines.
reply:
Ireland’s €258 million Seafood Development Programme 2021-2027, which is co-funded by the Government and the EU Commission under the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF) is the primary source of funding for the Irish commercial seafood sector including the inshore sector.
EMFAF fisheries grant aid schemes are designed to provide maximum value for money and to Ireland and the EU.
While re-engining projects are not currently eligible under BIM EMFAF schemes, equipment that improves fuel (energy)efficiency of engines is eligible under the BIM Sustainable Fisheries Scheme.
Items such as
• Fuel/energy monitoring systems,
• Generators for producing electricity (harbour set type)/shaft generators/PTOs
• Towed gear monitoring equipment (trawleye or equivalent type sensors)
are all eligible under the scheme.

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the date on which the report of the independent chair of the Food Vision Seafood Sector Group was received by his Department; whether the report has been circulated to the member organisations of the group; the date on which it will be published.
reply:
In February this year, Minister Heydon and I established a working group under the auspices of Food Vision 2030 - the Food Vision Seafood Sector Group - to consider the challenges facing all three components of the Irish seafood sector (catch fisheries, aquaculture and seafood processing).
The Group’s overarching objective was to identify and develop a framework of measures to respond to these current challenges. I engaged Mr. Michael Berkery to chair the Group and to submit an independent report to me by June 2026.
I received Mr. Berkery's interim report on 31 July, and final report on 30 September. I am currently considering the report and will make a decision on its circulation and publication in due course.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the total allocation for the bovine TB eradication programme in 2027 compared with 2026, given that the Budget 2026 expenditure report provided over €157 million and the Budget 2027 expenditure report lists €142.4 million; the cost of increasing reactor compensation ceilings by €500.
reply:
Budget 2026 provided an increased budget for the bTB programme with €157 million allocated for 2026. This was to allow the bTB programme to focus on driving down disease through the implementation of the measures laid out in the bTB Action Plan which I launched in September 2025.
The primary driver of the cost of the bTB programme is disease levels and there has been encouraging progress in recent months in reducing bTB levels. The latest statistics for 2026 indicate 5,372 herds have suffered a bTB breakdown in the last 12 months which is down 10.9% compared to this time last year with a herd incidence now of 5.42% compared to 6.03% this time last year. This is due to the combined efforts of all stakeholders in engaging with farmers to reduce the risk bTB poses to Irish herds and rural communities.
I am confident that the changes I have introduced in the bTB Action Plan will help drive down disease levels further. To continue this progress I have secured a further allocation of €142.4 million for bTB measures in 2027.
The On Farm Market Valuation Scheme (OFMV) is the principal compensation measure available to Herdowners whose herds are affected by a bovine TB breakdown in their herd. The Scheme aims to compensate farmers up to the open market value of an animal as if they were not affected by disease, subject to ceilings. question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether Budget 2027 includes a dedicated support for farmers facing fodder deficits following the 2026 drought, including a fodder transport support scheme, further to the Tánaiste's indication on 24 September 2026 that Budget 2027 would include fodder support; and the amount allocated.
reply:
I am very aware of the pressures that farmers experienced due to the prolonged dry spell of weather this summer, including impacts on fodder supplies. Following regular rainfall since the end of August, grass growth has recovered significantly. Teagasc is continuing to advise farmers to reassess fodder stocks and complete updated fodder budgets, and a further advisor-led fodder survey is planned following the maize harvest.
At my request, the National Fodder and Food Security Committee has met twice to assess the position and coordinate the response. The Committee will meet again later this week to review the latest information on fodder availability and grass growth.
In response to the ongoing challenges, I announced increases in advance payment rates under the 2026 Basic Income Support for Sustainability (BISS), the Complementary Redistributive Income Support for Sustainability Scheme (CRISS) and the ECO Scheme, along with flexibilities on requirements associated with certain actions in the Agri-Climate Rural Environment Scheme (ACRES) and the Scheme of Investment Aid for the Development of the Commercial Horticulture Sector.
Minister Browne and I granted a one-week extension to the slurry spreading period extending it to the 7 October 2026. Horse Racing Ireland (HRI) is a commercial state body established under the Horse and Greyhound Racing Act, 2001, and is responsible for the overall administration, promotion and development of the horse racing industry.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the timeline for the publication of the new Animal Welfare Strategy, the consultation for which closed in January 2026; the reason it has not been published.
reply:
The term of Ireland’s first ever Animal Welfare Strategy 2021-2025 - Working Together for Animal Welfare reached a conclusion at the end of 2025.
In 2025, a process was initiated to develop a new animal welfare strategy, which will act as a framework for engagement and collaboration to direct future activities with the aim of benefiting both animals and Irish society.
Development of the strategy is now approaching completion following a broad stakeholder engagement including a non-statutory public consultation that was launched on November 19th and ran to January 2nd. In excess of 1750 individual submissions were received as part of that process.
The new strategy will continue to adopt a ‘One Health, One Welfare’ approach, acknowledging and valuing the inter-dependencies between human, animal and environmental health, and taking an evidence-led approach to policy making, target-setting, monitoring and evaluation.
I anticipate that the new strategy will be published in the near term.

question: Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the written scientific criteria applied by his Department in determining when detection of Salmonella Typhimurium in an environmental sample at a duck premises is sufficient to conclude for enforcement purposes that animals or animal products may be affected; when direct faecal, cloacal, egg or other confirmatory testing is required; and whether the criteria was applied in the County Wicklow case that resulted in the Section 42 notice of 15 March 2024.
reply: Environmental sampling is a standard method used in the detection of Salmonella spp. to assist in the control of this zoonosis as prescribed by EU Regulation 2160/2003. The value and sensitivity of environmental sampling in identifying Salmonella serovars infection in the birds kept within that environment is well established in the veterinary literature. My Department will not be commenting on the specific case referenced as it is subject to court proceedings.

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the consideration he has given to the impact of the recent High Court ruling on the application of commercial rates to agricultural buildings used for essential crop storage and handling; whether he recognises the additional financial burden this could place on growers and other farmers already facing significant input and production costs; and the supports or exemptions are available to affected growers.
reply:
Tailte Éireann provides a property registration system, property valuation service, and national mapping and surveying infrastructure for the State. It is independent in the exercise of its valuation functions under the Valuation Act 2001.
My Department has no responsibility in this regard.
However, I am aware of the recent High Court Judgement and my Department is considering the potential implications for the sector. While the Act provides an exemption from rates for certain farm buildings, it specifically excludes from this exemption: “buildings, parts of buildings, or other structures, used for the processing or sale of agricultural, horticultural or forestry goods (whether produced on the land attached to such buildings or structures or not)”.

question: Deputy Denise Mitchell asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine further to Parliamentary Question No. 64947/26, the plans in place in the event of a significant disruption of trade flows affecting the approximately 4.5 million tonnes of animal feed which the State imports annually.
reply:
Whilst 80% of animal feed in Ireland is derived from grazed grass/preserved forage, about 6.5 million tonnes (2025) of compound feed is manufactured in Ireland. Approximately 2.2 million tonnes of home-grown cereals are produced – barley, wheat and oats (includes human consumption) and some 5.1 million tonnes (2025), imported.
In the case of pigs and poultry, virtually all their nutrition is derived from compound feeds. The main commodities imported are maize and maize by-products, soyabean meal and hulls, rapeseed meal, vegetable oils and fats, minerals and vitamins. Imports from the EU make up approximately 25% of imported feed, with the balance sourced from third countries, mainly Argentina, USA, Canada and Brazil.
The issue of feed supply is linked to the overall principles of European food security. The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), in supporting farm incomes and sustainable food production, plays a fundamental role in ensuring European food security. At the Informal meeting of EU Agriculture Ministers which I hosted in Dublin and Kildare in September, discussions focused on the European Commission’s new Livestock Strategy and Protein Action Plan, including the need to strengthen European protein production.
With regards to Irish feed importers, these companies have well established commercial relationships and have significant knowledge and experience in dealing with trade and climate disruptions as well as logistical difficulties.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if the criteria for health testing are different when only contract rearing for one farmer than that of multiple contract rearing for multiple farmers.
reply:
The Bovine TB Action Plan, Addressing Bovine TB (bTB) in Ireland outlines changes to bTB testing requirements for contract rearing as follows
• All animals returning from a contract rearer will require a 30-day pre-movement test.
• If a contract rearer is rearing animals from more than one herd, then all animals over 42 days will require a 30-day pre-movement test before they can enter the contract rearing herd.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the action his Department is taking in view of the fact that tropilaelaps, a parasite mite originating from Asia, is now present in Europe and spreading west; if they are monitoring the progression of this pest, in view of the fact that this pest is a severe threat to the Irish Honey Bee, and once established, eradication is not achievable and permanent costly control measures are required.
reply:
My Department is very aware of the increasing threat posed to the Irish beekeeping sector by Tropilaelaps spp., and the Animal Health Risk Assessment Unit in my Department is currently carrying out an assessment of the risks posed to bees from these pests.
My Department operates the Sentinel Apiary Programme (SAP) the aim of which is to ensure the early detection of two exotic pests, Tropilaelaps spp. and the Small Hive Beetle. The 2026 programme is ongoing with 12 volunteer beekeepers participating. For anyone who might be interested in participating in the programme for 2027 they can contact [Beekeeping@agriculture.gov.ie] for further information.
Furthermore, my Department engages with the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs in Northern Ireland on issues such as Tropilaelaps spp. including a bee health contingency test exercise held in February 2024.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of persons granted international protection status, that is, refugee status, subsidiary protection or permission to remain, in each of the past ten years, who were nationals of countries designated as safe countries of origin at the time of their application; the countries concerned; and the number granted status from each such country in each year, in tabular form.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, International Protection applications from the previous ten years involve two separate pieces of legislation, namely the International Protection Act 2015, which applies to applications made before 12 June 2026, and the International Protection Act 2026, which applies to applications made on or after that date.
Under Section 215 of the International Protection Act 2026, the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration is empowered to make an order designating a country as a safe country of origin. A country may only be designated as a safe country of origin only if I am satisfied that, on the basis of the legal situation, the application of the law within a democratic system and the general political circumstances, it can be shown that there is no persecution and no real risk of serious harm. These provisions are similar to those in the previous applicable legislation, section 72 of the International Protection Act 2015.
If an applicant for international protection is from a country designated as a safe country of origin, their application will still receive a full consideration on its merits. However, if you are from a designated safe country, you will be dealt with through an accelerated process or the border procedure.
My Department does not publish statistics on the number of people who were granted international protection status, by nationality.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on the construction of a new courthouse in Tralee, County Kerry.
reply:
Management of the courts and operational matters are the responsibility of the Courts Service, which is independent in the exercising of its functions under the Courts Service Act 1998 and given separation of powers in the Constitution. Matters pertaining to court buildings are a responsibility of the Courts Service.
The existing courthouse on Ashe Street in Tralee currently comprises two courtrooms. The Courts Service project for a courthouse in Tralee will include four courtrooms and related facilities which are necessary to meet future requirements.
The Courts Service has received an initial funding allocation under the revised National Development Plan to advance this project. This funding will support the preparatory work required to develop a robust business case for a new courthouse and to progress the project through the early stages of the Infrastructure Guidelines. I am advised that a Design Team has been appointed to undertake the Strategic Assessment and Preliminary Business Case for the proposed development. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of appeals pending before the International Protection Appeals Tribunal as of the latest date for which figures are available; the number pending for more than 12 months and more than 24 months, respectively; the current median time from lodgment of an appeal to decision.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 577, 584 and 585 together.
It is a central priority for me that Ireland's immigration system is robust and rules-based.
The number of international protection applications had been rising over recent years, reaching 18,500 in 2024. In 2025, application numbers fell by approximately one-third. Applications received up to the end of September 2026 show a further reduction compared with the same period in 2025.
Over the same period, there has been a significant increase in investment in the international protection system which has facilitated a major increase in processing capacity and demonstrates a strong commitment to reducing the number of cases on hand.
This investment has already demonstrated results.
In 2025, the International Protection Office (IPO) delivered over 20,200 first instance decisions compared to approximately 14,100 in 2024: a 44% increase. The International Protection Appeal Tribunal (IPAT) more than doubled the number of appeals closed from 3,100 in 2024 to nearly 6,300 in 2025. This year, as of 1 October 2026, IPAT had already closed 6,902 appeals, exceeding the total number of appeals completed during the whole of 2025.
The increased resourcing of the international protection system has been particularly evident at IPAT in recent years, with the Tribunal's budget increasing by 95% between 2023 and 2025. Administrative staffing at IPAT has increased from 37 at the beginning of 2023 to 92 currently.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current status of the national gambling exclusion register established under the Gambling Regulation Act 2024; the date on which it became or will become fully operational; the number of persons registered to date; and whether all licensed remote operators are currently connected to the register.

reply:

Citizenship represents the fullest expression of membership of Irish society, and it is important that the legislative framework governing access to citizenship is robust, fair and sustainable.
The Programme for Government contains a commitment to continue to implement a firmer and more sustainable migration system which protects the integrity of the State's immigration framework. In that context, the General Scheme of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Bill 2026 proposes a number of reforms to the citizenship process.
The General Scheme is available on the Departmental pages of the Gov.ie website here:
https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/publications/general-scheme-of-the-irish-nationality-and-citizenship-amendment-bill-2026
While the proposals may affect the timeframe within which some individuals become eligible to apply for citizenship, they do not affect a person's entitlement to reside, work, study, establish a business or establish a life in Ireland in accordance with the terms of their immigration permission.
I can also advise the Deputy that these proposals will be subject to detailed scrutiny through the legislative process in the Oireachtas.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of protected disclosures within An Garda Síochána that remained at initial assessment stage at the end of each of the years 2023, 2024 and 2025; and the longest period any such disclosure has remained at that stage.
reply:
In An Garda Síochána, a Garda member or a staff member has a number of options if he or she wishes to make a protected disclosure. They can report concerns directly to the Protected Disclosure Unit within An Garda Síochána; they can go directly to Fiosrú; they can go directly to the Office of Protected Disclosures Commissioner, or they can report their disclosure to a Minister.
The legislation places reporting obligations on all public bodies concerning the number of disclosures made in each year. These reports are published by my Department, An Garda Síochána and Fiosrú - the Office of the Police Ombudsman.
Details of the disclosures for the relevant years are available in the relevant Garda Annual Report under Section 22 of the Protected Disclosures Act 2014 (as amended). These are available at: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/publications/annual%20reports/an-garda-siochana-annual-reports/

Section 9.7 also outlines the file closure process for disclosures.

question: Deputy Paul Donnelly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in relation to join family applications, the reason decisions are issued in such uneven bursts; and whether a daily, steady processing target for join family can be introduced.
reply:
Visa and preclearance applications provide legal avenues for people moving to Ireland for employment, study and family reasons, as well as for visitors travelling for business or tourism. These are important screening processes designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel. Verifying an application is an important part of our immigration system, and each visa application is assessed on its own merits, taking all relevant information into consideration at that time.
I am acutely aware that Join Family applications are of significant importance to the individuals and families concerned. I understand that people are eager to have their families join them in Ireland. While every effort is made to process applications as quickly as possible, applications can vary considerably in complexity and in the level of examination required. Consequently, decisions are issued once an application has been fully assessed, rather than according to a fixed daily processing pattern.
My Department continually reviews processing arrangements with a view to improving efficiency and reducing waiting times for applicants. reply:
The primary purpose of vetting carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau is to ensure the safety of children and vulnerable adults. Clearly, this requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust.
The Government is aware of ongoing concerns regarding certain aspects of the vetting process and I have listened carefully to the views of affected sectors. I believe that the vetting system should be updated to ensure that the burden of seeking vetting disclosures, particularly on volunteers and organisations working in their communities, is minimised to the greatest extent possible, while maintaining the high standards that are necessary.
Further to the work carried out by the Garda Vetting Review Group, steps are now being taken to implement a number of key changes to the process that will ensure it remains robust and effective while improving the service to customers.
In practice, and subject to a general requirement that vetting be renewed every three years, it is envisaged that this will mean that when a person is vetted for the work they will be or are likely to be involved in as part of their employment or volunteering within identified risk categories, the person would not be required to repeat the process if they were to move to another role within the same risk category.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration given the increasing use of certified copies of passports and other identity and residency documents in citizenship and immigration applications, the guidance provided to peace commissioners on verifying documents presented to them; whether peace commissioners are expected to establish the authenticity of an original document or solely that the copy corresponds with the document presented; the protections which apply where a peace commissioner certifies a copy in good faith but the document subsequently proves fraudulent.
reply:

The office of Peace Commissioner was created in accordance with section 88 of the Courts of Justice Act 1924. The original intention underlying the office of Peace Commissioner was to provide a service of use to the public that was free, local and easily accessible. The powers and duties of Peace Commissioners consist primarily of:
• taking statutory declarations;
• witnessing signatures on documents if required by various authorities;
• signing certificates and orders under various Acts.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for a breakdown of the additional €5.3 million provided in Budget 2027 for domestic, sexual and gender-based violence initiatives and for Cuan, by initiative, compared with the additional €11.5 million for DSGBV initiatives and €0.7 million for Cuan provided in Budget 2026.

Combatting all forms of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence (DSGBV) remains a key priority for me and for this Government, as demonstrated by the significant investment being made through Cuan.
Cuan’s total budget for 2026 is €79.17 million, representing an increase of €12.25 million, or 18%, compared with 2025. The table below sets out the breakdown of the additional €11.5 million provided for DSGBV initiatives and the additional €0.7 million provided to Cuan in 2026. This funding supports a range of measures, including core service funding, the domestic violence accommodation programme, education and awareness initiatives, and other measures supporting implementation of the Third National Strategy.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether an international protection applicant residing in IPAS accommodation who receives a custodial sentence retains their allocated accommodation for the duration of their imprisonment; whether their daily expenses allowance continues during imprisonment; whether the accommodation is available to them automatically on release; and if not, the criteria that determine whether accommodation and the allowance are restored.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 541 and 542 together.
Under the European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018, International Protection Applicants are provided with material reception conditions, including housing, food, clothing and a Daily Expenses Allowance (DEA).
When people seeking international protection take up an offer of accommodation at an IPAS accommodation centre, they are provided with the ‘IPAS House Rules’ which explains the rules and procedures that are designed to make reception and accommodation centres safe and effective. This document which includes information on absence policy is issued to all residents on arrival.
In line with Section 76 of the International Protection Act 2026, accommodation is offered to applicants on the understanding that they will be living in their allocated accommodation centre on a daily basis. It is the responsibility of IPAS to ensure that accommodation is available to all international protection applicants without sufficient means and that all allocated beds are used on a continuous basis. Attendance in centres is monitored by centre managers and by IPAS.
If an applicant is in custody and therefore not living in allocated accommodation on a daily basis, this accommodation is withdrawn by IPAS and the applicant may reapply for accommodation upon their release. They are not eligible for the Daily Expense Allowance during the time spent outside of IPAS accommodation.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration notwithstanding operational security considerations, whether there is a formal mechanism whereby information indicating that an applicant for international protection has links to a prescribed terrorist organisation is communicated to the authority responsible for determining or reviewing their protection status; and whether such information is considered in an application for naturalisation.
reply:
It is a central priority of this Government that our immigration laws are robust and effectively enforced. Since taking office, I have worked to ensure the integrity, efficiency and public confidence of our migration system.
When processing international protection applications, criminal convictions are always taken into consideration. Character and conduct checks are also carried out before applicants can be granted any permission to remain in the State. An Garda Síochána notifies my Department of any matters that may be relevant to its considerations.
Where a person has applied for citizenship, further checks are carried out as part of the good character assessment. An Garda Síochána is requested to make enquiries into the applicant’s background; the detail and extent of which is a matter for An Garda Síochána. For sound security and operational reasons, it is not the practice to comment on the enquiries that may be conducted.
Since the introduction of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum in June of this year, all international protection applicants have been subject to a screening procedure that includes checks for security and criminality concerns, as well as identity verification. Information is shared, where appropriate, with all relevant authorities.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Defence the strength of the permanent Defence Force at the end of 2025 and at the latest date in 2026; the projected strength at the end of 2026 and the end of 2027; and how the recruitment of 400 additional Permanent Defence Force members and almost 100 civilian and civil service roles announced in Budget 2027 relates to the increase in the Defence staffing figure from 9,140 to 9,370 in the Budget 2027 expenditure report.
reply:

The Military Authorities advise that the strength of the Permanent Defence Force (PDF) stood at 7,815 personnel on the 31 August 2026 or 80% of an agreed establishment of 9,739, the latest date for which this figure is available. The strength of the PDF stood at 7,756 personnel on the 31 December 2025.
Last year saw a growth in the overall strength of nearly 200, with a total of 790 inductions achieved- the highest in twenty years - while the number of personnel who discharged was at its lowest level in more than five years. I am determined to build on this and have set a target of more than 800 inductions for 2026.

The challenge now for the Defence Forces is to convert this high level of applications to inductions. A draft Strategic Workforce Plan was prepared by the Defence Forces and submitted earlier this year. It remains the subject of active consideration. question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if engagement has taken place with his Australian counterparts to learn from and understand the cyber breach of Australian government websites by rogue AI agents (details supplied) in June; and the measures in place here to prevent such an attack.
reply:
My Department continuously evaluates and adapts its strategies to deal with the evolving cyber security threat landscape. Frontier AI models are creating unprecedented opportunities for cyber security; conversely however, they have the capabilities to create novel and heightened security risks. The National Cyber Risk Assessment, which I published in December 2025, highlighted how AI drives systemic risk by increasing the speed, scale and sophistication of cyberattacks.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), is an operational arm of my Department and holds the lead role in the management of major cyber security incidents across government. The NCSC also specifically monitors developments in AI-enabled cyber capabilities on a continuous basis and collaborates with our international partners in the EU and more broadly on this issue. The Deputy will appreciate that the National Cyber Security Centre does not comment on arrangements for the sharing of cyber security intelligence.
In June 2026, the NCSC published “Securing AI Adoption in the Public Sector” which provides new guidance to help public sector bodies adopt artificial intelligence securely. These guidelines are part of a wider package of government support for AI adoption and deliver on a commitment in “Digital Ireland – Connecting our People, Securing our Future”, the National Digital and AI Strategy published by the Government in February 2026.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an update on the implementation of the NIS2 directive.
reply:
The National Cyber Security Bill will transpose the Revised Network and Information Systems Directive (NIS2) into Irish law. This legislation represents a significant step in strengthening the State’s cyber security and resilience. It will enhance cyber security risk management in Ireland bringing with it significant improvements in our capacity to protect against, recover from and respond to major incidents.
In anticipation of having the legislation in place and to ensure that Ireland is ready to fully implement the directive, we have taken significant steps to ensure that various implementing measures are in place. This includes a robust approach to sectoral regulation for the Directive with the designation of National Competent Authorities to carry out enforcement and supervision. National Competent Authorities are already undertaking significant preparations to take on these new functions.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) is engaging with its constituents and stakeholders to ensure the requirements of the Bill are communicated ahead of time and has produced resources and guidance for entities that fall within the scope of NIS2. The NCSC has also prepared a media campaign for launch when the Bill is enacted.

question: Deputy George Lawlor asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of fines issued at a static speed camera (details supplied) from the 1 August 2026 to the 31 August 2026 and the 1 September 2026 to the 30 September 2026.
reply:
Whether it is fixed cameras, average speed cameras or GoSafe vans, the use of technology is a vital component of reducing speeding on our roads.
Road safety cameras are intended to be, first and foremost, a tool to support safety, prevention and behavioural change across the road network. The aim of road safety cameras across Ireland is to encourage safer driving practices, reduce collisions and protect road users by promoting compliance with speed limits.
Nine static speed safety cameras are in operation across the country since 2024. The locations of these cameras were selected based on fatal and serious injury collision data and speed data, as well as feedback from stakeholders.
I am informed by the Garda Authorities that there were 4,067 fixed charge notices issued for speed detections at the static speed camera on the N25 for the period from 01/08/2026 to 31/08/2026.
Figures are based on incidents which occurred from 01/08/2026 to 31/08/2026, inclusive. All information contained in this report is based upon operational data from the Fixed Charge Processing System as was available on 05/10/2026 and is liable to change.
The Garda authorities are currently only in a position to provide FCN statistics up to the end of August. As the processing of FCNs involves a reporting lag, September figures are not yet available.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the rationale for setting the minimum annual income requirement under the temporary protection transition scheme at €29,432; if he will consider providing flexibility or individual assessment for applicants who fall below the threshold due to variable working hours, caring responsibilities, disability or other circumstances, but who have a sustained record of employment and PRSI contributions in the State; and if a review of the operation of the income threshold is planned following the commencement of the scheme.
reply:
The Temporary Protection Transition Scheme opened for applications on 30 September 2026.
An applicant must demonstrate that they have been in employment or self-employment for at least six months immediately prior to the opening date of the Scheme, with average gross earnings of €29,432, and must continue to be in employment both at the date of application and at the date a decision is made on their application. This rate is set to reflect full-time minimum wage employment.
It is important to note that the Temporary Protection Transition Scheme is not intended to replace Temporary Protection, but to provide an additional pathway for those who are eligible and who wish to remain in Ireland on an independent basis. Persons who do not satisfy the eligibility criteria will continue to benefit from Temporary Protection and its associated rights and entitlements while the Temporary Protection Directive remains in effect. Temporary Protection is currently in place across the EU until March 2028. People in Ireland will continue to have access to the associated rights of the Directive for the duration of Temporary Protection to include the right to reside in Ireland and the right to access to social welfare, education, and employment.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will provide an update on a family reunification application (details supplied).
reply:
I can advise the Deputy that the Join Family visa application referred to was created on 4 July 2025. Supporting documentation was received in the Abu Dhabi Visa Office on 4 August 2025 where it awaits examination and processing.
My Department's business target for join family visa applications is 12 months. It must be made clear that these are business targets for the immigration service and some applications can take longer than others. The business target reflects the detailed and often complex assessment that is required to be carried out in relation to applications for family reunification.

question: Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an update on an application (details supplied); if correspondence has issued to the applicant since the acknowledgement of 20 March 2024; and when a decision on the application will be made.
reply:
The naturalisation application referred to by the Deputy continues to be processed by my Department.
This application is based on Section 16 'Irish Association', which can take longer to process than applications based upon residency.
Section 15 of the Act sets out the statutory conditions that must be fulfilled for a certificate of naturalisation to be granted. Section 16 of the Act gives discretion to waive the statutory conditions (including the 5 year residency requirement) in certain circumstances. This includes where the applicant is a direct descendant of someone who is or was an Irish citizen (for example, a grandparent), has a family connection to an Irish citizen (including by blood, adoption, or civil partnership), or is related by affinity, meaning a close relationship through a spouse’s family.
Last year my Department published new guidelines for applications on the basis of Irish Associations under Section 16(1)(a) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. They set out the factors that may be considered when deciding whether to waive the statutory conditions in certain circumstances, including where the applicant is of Irish descent or Irish associations. Details of the guidelines are available on my Department’s website at the following link:
https://www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-an-irish-citizen-guide/

reply:
I am advised that while the swimming pool in the Defence Forces Training Centre, Curragh Camp is primarily for the training and exercise of Defence Forces personnel, my Department positively engages with local schools and community groups in allowing the use of this facility. Taking into account Defence Forces usage, the limited availability that remains has now been allocated to local National Schools and a community group located in the immediate vicinity of the camp.

question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current processing time for applications to the National Garda Vetting Bureau.
reply:
The primary focus of the Garda National Vetting Bureau is to safeguard children and vulnerable adults across the country. This requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust.
The Garda National Vetting Bureau (GNVB) is responsible for the Garda Vetting system under the general superintendence of the Garda Commissioner, under the National Vetting Bureau (Children and Vulnerable Persons) Acts. As Minister, I have no role in the Garda Vetting system, nor in individual applications.
I am advised by the Garda authorities that vetting applications are processed on a first-come, first served basis in chronological order from the date of receipt. The current average turnaround time for vetting applications is approximately seven business days from the date the application is received at the GNVB, for 85% of applications received.
Detailed statistics related to the work of the GNVB are updated monthly and are available at:
https://www.garda.ie/en/about-us/organised-serious-crime/garda-national-vetting-bureau-gnvb-/garda-vetting-statistics.html

reply:
The Free Travel Scheme is available to everyone who is 66 or over, and to certain people who are under 66 in receipt of qualifying payments or who meet the medical conditions for Blind Pension and legally living permanently in the State.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Social Protection his views on whether existing State financial supports for people with a disability are sufficient in the context of Article 28 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities that guarantees the right to an adequate standard of living and social protection without discrimination; and if this is being considered in relation discussions around the Cost of Disability payment as set out by the Disability Federation of Ireland.
reply:
The Government recognises the additional costs that disabled people can face in their daily lives and is committed improving outcomes for disabled people by introducing permanent measures. That is why the Programme for Government includes a commitment to introduce a permanent annual cost of disability payment.
Last year, the Government published the National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People 2025-2030. The strategy was developed with significant input from disability groups and advocates. It is a whole-of-Government framework for the implementation of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.
The strategy, includes a commitment to a Strategic Focus Network Summit on the Cost of Disability, emphasising the cross-government nature of the issue. In advance of the Summit, I launched an extensive consultation process on the cost of disability including bilateral meetings with disability representative groups and DPOs, and a public consultation which received more than 1,100 submissions. I hosted the Strategic Focus Network Summit on May 13th attended by over 300 people, in person or online.
The submissions to the consultation process, the output of the Strategic Focus Network and the engagements I attended such as the Pre-Budget Forum and the National Economic Dialogue have all informed the approach that we, across Government, have taken in Budget 2027 towards addressing the cost of disability.
As a result of Budget 2027, over €30 billion wi

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection the way in which an inheritance received by a recipient of disability allowance is assessed under the means test; the amount of capital that may be held before any reduction in payment applies; the amount at which the payment ceases entirely; if consideration has been given to disregarding, in whole or in part, an inheritance received from a parent by a person with a lifelong disability.
reply:
Disability Allowance (DA) is my Department's primary disability related social assistance scheme. DA is a weekly payment for people aged 16 to 66 with a disability expected to last at least one year. Eligibility is subject to medical assessment, means test and habitual residence conditions. Applicants must demonstrate that they are substantially restricted in undertaking work that would otherwise be suitable given their age, experience, and qualifications, as a result of their condition.
Social welfare legislation provides that, for means-tested social assistance schemes, all income and assets belonging to the claimant, and their spouse or partner, where applicable, is assessable. This recognises the fact that couples operate as a single household and can share living expenses in a manner not available to a single person.
The purpose of a means test is to ensure that scarce resources are directed to those with the greatest need and it supports an economically sustainable and socially equitable allocation of scarce resources.
Inheritance is treated as capital and is thus assessable under Social Welfare legislation.
DA has one of the highest capital disregards operated by my Department. A recipient can have up to €50,000 in savings and still receive the full rate of payment. This is compared to a €20,000 disregard for most social welfare payments. reply:
The Department does not collect or maintain detailed data on individual sources of assets and so it is not possible to provide a breakdown of the number of recipients whose payment was reduced or ceased due to inherited capital nor those who lost entitlement to the free travel pass in each of the years 2020 to 2025 and to date in 2026, as requested by the Deputy.

Any changes to means testing could only be considered in the context of the budgetary process.
I trust this clarifies the issue for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Niamh Smyth asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will clarify the eligibility criteria for the household benefits package and fuel allowance in the case of an Irish citizen (details supplied), who is in receipt of a disablement pension but resides in Northern Ireland; if residence outside the State automatically disqualifies a person from the household benefits package; and if the same residency requirement applies to the fuel allowance.
reply:
The Household Benefits Package comprises of an electricity or gas allowance, and a Free Television Licence. Only one Household Benefits Package is payable per household. The Household Benefit Package is generally available to applicants aged 66 years or over, who are in receipt of a social welfare type payment, or who satisfy a means test. The package is also available to applicants under age 66 who are in receipt of certain social welfare payments. For applicants aged 70 or over, there is no requirement to be in receipt of a qualifying payment or to satisfy a means test.
Fuel Allowance is a means-tested payment to assist pensioners and other long-term social welfare dependent householders with their winter heating costs. The payment is made over the winter season - from September to April or, if preferred, by way of two lump sum instalments - one at the start of the Fuel Allowance season (usually late September) and one in January. Only one Fuel Allowance is payable per household. For those aged 66 years or over, the applicant must satisfy a means test and be living alone or only with other qualified people. For those aged under 66 years, the applicant must be in receipt of certain social welfare payments and be living alone or only with other qualified people.
Both Household Benefits Package and Fuel Allowance are assistance-based payments and, as such, to qualify for either of these payments, the applicant must be legally resident in the State.

However, in recognition of the important contribution made by carers, an exception applies where a person who is receiving a primary social welfare payment and who is also providing full-time care and attention may receive a half-rate Carer's Allowance in addition to their main payment. This arrangement applies to almost all weekly social welfare payments, including the State pension.
There are currently more than 112,000 people in receipt of Carer’s Allowance at an estimated cost of more than €1.4 billion in 2026. Of that total, 52,377 are receiving their full primary social welfare payment together with a half-rate Carer's Allowance payment.

Following Budget 2027, from next January the weekly payment in this case will increase from €453.30 to €468.30, an increase of €15.00.
