question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if Government employment or job-creation projections and targets for 2026 to 2030 have been disaggregated by region; to provide by region and year; and to provide the equivalent regional projections or targets underpinning the national planning framework for comparison, in tabular form.
reply:

Separately, my Department has undertaken a statistical analysis to examine how projected national employment growth is likely to be distributed regionally. The analysis is anchored to the central scenario in the Department of Finance’s Future Forty framework and extends to 2040. It provides a baseline projection of how regional employment might develop if historical relationships between national and regional employment continue. However, these projections are not Government employment or job-creation targets.
The analysis indicates that employment would grow across all regions, with some concentration in Dublin and the wider eastern region, reflecting the existing scale of these labour markets as well as their projected growth rates. At the same time, most regions exhibit broadly similar growth rates over the projection horizon, and are projected to grow at rates broadly in line with the national average. Differences in the number of additional people employed largely reflect the existing distribution of employment across the regions.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether he is considering measures to ban a product associated with ineradicable and significant occupational safety risks (details supplied) with regard to his responsibility for workplace safety legislation and in line with a proposal under consideration in California.
reply:
The safety, health and welfare of workers is a priority for my department. There are existing legal obligations under the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 and associated regulations requiring employers to identify, assess and control risks arising from exposure to respirable crystalline silica dust.
In particular, work involving exposure to respirable crystalline silica dust generated by a work process is classified as carcinogenic under the Carcinogens, Mutagens and Reprotoxic Substances (CMRS) Regulations. These Regulations require employers to reduce the use of carcinogenic substances in the workplace, in particular by replacing them, insofar as is technically possible, with a substance, mixture or process which, under its conditions of use, is not dangerous or is less dangerous to employees’ health or safety. Employers are also required to ensure that the level of exposure of employees is reduced to a level as low as technically possible, representing a high duty of care.
The existing framework therefore places significant obligations on employers to prevent or minimise exposure to respirable crystalline silica dust. These include conducting risk assessments, implementing appropriate engineering controls and safe systems of work, using dust suppression techniques such as wet cutting, providing suitable respiratory protective equipment and undertaking health surveillance where appropriate.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment for an update on matters raised in correspondence (details supplied).
reply:
The Companies Registration Office (CRO) has advised that it has no statutory power under the Registration of Business Names Act 1963 to remove a person from the register of business names, nor does it have a power to remove or suppress a residential address that has been properly registered under that Act.
Unlike the Companies Act 2014, which contains provisions allowing for the non-disclosure of a company officer's residential address in certain exceptional circumstances, no equivalent provision exists in the Registration of Business Names Act 1963.
Accordingly, there is currently no statutory mechanism available to the Registrar to remove, redact or suppress a residential address from the business names register, including in circumstances where personal safety concerns have been raised. Similarly, the fact that a person who has made a registration of a business name, and who subsequently determines that that registration was not required, does not provide a legal basis for the removal of the registration or the associated address from the register.
My Department is currently developing legislation to repeal and replace the Registration of Business Names Act 1963.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment his views on whether the right-to-request model is sufficient in the context where an employee's request to work remotely is refused but the WRC cannot examine whether the refusal itself was reasonable.
reply:
Under Part 3 of the Work Life Balance Act 2023, employees are able to refer a dispute to the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) where an employer fails to fulfil their obligations under the Act. The WRC and the Labour Court can direct employers to comply with the requirements of the Act however, neither the WRC nor the Labour Courts are empowered to assess the merits of the employer’s decision, nor are they empowered to overturn a refusal of remote working. The obligation on the employer is to comply with the procedures set out in the Act.
It is not the Government’s role, nor the role of the Workplace Relations Commission, to effectively assess and direct when employees can or cannot work remotely. Providing a right to request strikes the right balance between flexibility and the need for businesses to remain competitive, profitable and viable.
The Department completed a statutory review of the right to request remote working provisions of the Work Life Balance Act 2023 in March 2024. The report is available on the Department’s website and has been laid before the Houses of the Oireachtas. The review found that, when used, the legislation is operating effectively in practice with the majority of requests to work remotely being either fully or partially approved. While the number of requests made under the legislation is currently low, when employees do avail of their right, the legislation works well. On this basis, amendments to the primary Act are not proposed at this tim

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the current wait time for applicants to the SEAI warmer home scheme to receive an initial assessment.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 25, 31 and 42 together.
The Warmer Homes Scheme (WHS) aims to improve the energy efficiency and warmth of homes owned by people at risk of energy poverty by providing fully funded retrofits. The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) on behalf of my Department and is funded through carbon tax revenues and the European Regional Development Fund.
The scheme targets support to those on the lowest incomes who are living in the least efficient homes so that the resources available can have the greatest impact in addressing energy poverty. Over 8,100 homes were upgraded last year, 109% of the annual target.
Applications to the scheme are assessed on the basis of when they first apply to the SEAI. Homes with the worst Building Energy Ratings also known as BER (E, F or G) are then prioritised for works. No other prioritisation takes place under the scheme.
Under the WHS, a pre-works BER is an obligation mandated for EU funding via the ERDF. The BER rating enables the SEAI to prioritise the worst performing homes and it is also key in determining the increase in energy efficiency as a result of the works upon completion.
Over 8,060 upgrades were completed under the scheme to end September 2026, an increase of 34.5% on the same period last year. At the same time, 11,823 applications have been received to the WHS to end September compared to 7,905 in the same time window last year, an increase of 49.6%.

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he is examining whether consumers should have a statutory right to speak with a human customer service representative, rather than being required to deal exclusively with artificial intelligence or automated systems, when engaging with telecommunications, utility and other essential service providers.
reply:
With the exception of financial products or services, there is currently no general provision in Irish consumer protection law requiring traders to provide consumers with access to a human customer service representative or preventing the use of artificial intelligence, chatbots or other automated systems for customer interactions. The way a trader provides customer service is a commercial decision for the trader.
However, under Part 5 of the Consumer Rights Act 2022, there is certain information which traders must provide to consumers before they enter a contract. This includes information which will allow consumers to contact traders and direct complaints, such as the geographical address at which the trader is established, the trader’s telephone number and the trader’s email address. Where applicable, traders must also provide consumers with information as to their complaint handling policy.
Where a consumer is seeking to exercise their rights under consumer protection law, such as seeking a remedy for a non-conformity with a good or service, they must be able to contact the trader in order to do so. Where a trader fails to facilitate consumers in exercising their statutory rights, this may give rise to issues under consumer protection legislation, depending on the circumstances.
Certain regulated sectors, including telecommunications, energy and financial services, are subject to sector-specific requirements in relation to customer service and complaints handling. These i

question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if his Department will provide an update on an application for a work permit (details supplied).
reply:
The Employment Permits System is governed by the provisions of the Employment Permits Act 2024. All applications are assessed in line with the legislative criteria in force at the time a decision is made, ensuring that the system operates in a fair, transparent and consistent manner across all cases.
An application for a Sports & Cultural Employment Permit in respect of the individual concerned was received by my Department and was subsequently refused following assessment.
The decision was made in accordance with the relevant section of the Employment Permits Act 2024, which provides that an employment permit shall not be granted where the relevant requirements outlined in the legislation and regulations have not been met.
The applicant has been informed of the outcome of the review process and the reasons for the refusal. If the applicant is not satisfied with the decision, a request for a review under section 35 of the Employment Permits Act 2024 must be submitted within 28 days of the date of the refusal decision.

reply:

The current guidance was published in November 2023 following enactment of the Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 2022.

reply:

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the specific savings and efficiency measures each Department will implement in 2027 to meet the expenditure levy totalling €446 million set out in the Budget 2027 Expenditure Report, in tabular form, by Department; and the reason the Department of Education and Youth is not subject to the levy.
reply:
The achievement of value for money in public expenditure is a Government priority, with an agenda for reform and efficiencies established over the past year. Public expenditure must be managed to maximise value for money for the taxpayer and support the delivery of Government priorities within the voted allocation, as outlined in Circular 18/2025 (Value for Money Obligations).
Earlier this year, the Government agreed that additional funding of €646 million would be provided to the Department of Education and Youth in 2026. To accommodate this reprioritisation and deliver on the 2027 ceiling agreed under the Medium Term Fiscal Plan, an Expenditure Levy of €446 million has been reflected in all Budget 2027 funding allocations, with the exception the Department of Education and Youth.
In April, my Department wrote to all other Departments highlighting the Government decision to apply an Expenditure Levy for 2027 and emphasising the need to achieve savings. Given that the levy was applied to offset a permanent increase in the funding allocation for the Department of Education and Youth, no levy was applied to that Department.
In September 2026, I wrote to all Ministers, asking them to identify efficiencies and reforms in the context of the Estimates process for Budget 2027. Reforms and efficiencies were published and are set out in tabular form for each Vote or Vote Group in Part II of the 2027 Expenditure Report, which can be accessed at the following link: assets.gov.ie/static/

reply:
The Infrastructure Guidelines and the Capital Works Management Framework (CWMF) set down the procedures that public bodies who are charged with the delivery of public infrastructure and building projects must follow.

Delivering value for money is about securing the efficient and effective use of public resources in the pursuit of better public services, living standards and infrastructure for the people of Ireland. It is not solely concerned with costs and price levels – it also involves the consideration of quality, specialist expertise, and social and environmental impacts.
Under the Infrastructure Guidelines and the CWMF, public works contracts are structured so that risks are allocated to the party best placed to manage and mitigate them.
The CWMF provides a comprehensive suite of standard public works contracts. These contracts clearly define the circumstances in which contractors may be entitled to additional payment and the risks that remain the responsibility of the contractor. Compensation events are limited and are explicitly identified in the contract documentation.

reply:

Local Property Tax (LPT) was legislated for in 2012 in the Finance (Local Property Tax) Act 2012. On the introduction of the LPT, the Government decided that a liability to the tax should apply to all owners of residential properties based on the market value of the property and with a limited number of reliefs available. This ensures that liable taxpayers are not charged more to account for a shortfall driven by reductions in LPT charges based on other factors, including household composition.
The design of LPT was considered by an interdepartmental group chaired by Dr. Don Thornhill in 2012. In 2019, the tax was subject to a review by an interdepartmental group chaired by the Department of Finance. The distributional impact of LPT according to household composition or property ownership was not examined as part of these reports.
The 2019 review group conducted a distributional impact analysis according to income using the ESRI SWITCH (Simulating Welfare and Income Tax Changes) tax and benefit micro-simulation model. This model was used to compare the impact that different reform scenarios for LPT would have on household incomes relative to a benchmark position where the property value increases but there is no change in the structure of LPT. The results indicate that all scenarios were progressive rather than regressive to varying degrees.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 188 and 217 together.

HTB provides a refund of Income Tax and Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) paid in Ireland over the previous four years, subject to limits outlined in the legislation.
Based on the latest available data (30 September 2026), the scheme has supported over 70,000 individuals or couples to buy or build their own home.
For a property to qualify for the HTB scheme, it must be new or converted for use as a dwelling, having not previously been used as a dwelling. Additionally, the purchase value/approved valuation of the property must not exceed €500,000. • €30,000; or
• 10 per cent of the purchase price of the new property; or
• the amount of Income Tax and DIRT paid in the four years before application for the relief.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance that RZL tax should not be applicable to local authorities; and if he will examine this issue (details supplied).
reply:
Finance Act 2021 introduced Part 22A Residential Zoned Land Tax (RZLT) into the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997. RZLT is designed to prompt residential development by owners of land that satisfies the relevant criteria for the tax, that being that the land is zoned for residential or mixed-use (including residential) purposes and that is serviced.
RZLT is an annual tax, calculated at a rate of 3% of the market value of the land within its scope. The tax is due and payable from 2025 onwards in respect of land which satisfied the relevant criteria on 1 January 2022, or in the course of 2022, as where land satisfies the relevant criteria after 1 January 2022, RZLT will be first due in the third year after the year in which it satisfies the relevant criteria. RZLT first arose on 1 February 2025 and the 2026 liability was payable by 23 May 2026, subject to certain exceptions.
The legislation underpinning RZLT provides for a number of exemptions, deferrals and abatements subject to the relevant criteria being met. The legislation does not provide for a specific exemption for local authorities. Local authorities that own land meeting the criteria for RZLT are subject to the tax. It is important to note that, to come within the scope of RZLT, land must be both zoned by the local authority for residential use and serviced. The intention of RZLT is to activate development of this residentially zoned and serviced land to meet critical housing needs.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if the increase in rent a room relief is universal or solely for multi-room lets; and the assessment or analysis carried out on the likely impact this will have on rents charged.
reply:
Rent a Room relief was introduced in 2001 as an incentive to encourage individuals to let rooms in their sole or main residence as residential accommodation in order to bring about an increase in the availability of rental accommodation.
To qualify for the exemption, it is necessary for the residential premises to be situated in the State and occupied by the individual as his or her sole or main residence during the tax year. The relief only applies to individuals. It does not apply to companies or partnerships. Nor does it apply to income from the carrying on of a trade, such as the trade of operating a B&B.
Currently, the scheme provides an exemption from Income Tax, PRSI and USC on rent received where a person rents out a room or rooms in his or her principal private residence and the rent received does not exceed €14,000 per year. This figure includes payments for utilities (such as gas and electricity) and any other charges.
The Rent a Room rental income ceiling was last increased in Budget 2017 from €12,000 to €14,000.
Budget 2027 announced an increase in the maximum rental income which can qualify for the relief from €14,000 to €16,000. This revised ceiling will apply to the 2027 year of assessment and subsequent years.
The increased rental income ceiling of €16,000 will apply to all claimants regardless of the number of rooms let or the number of tenants accommodated.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if the estimated cost of the CGT changes outlined in budget 2027 of 46.5million first year and 186 million full year are based on CGT for individuals and some corporates in respect of gains on development land solely or if it also includes chargeable gains for corporates; in the case of the former provide a full estimated cost including all chargeable gains for corporates.
reply:
I am advised by Revenue that, in general, capital gains tax (CGT) is chargeable on a gain arising on the disposal of an asset, at the rate of 31% for disposals made on or after 7 October 2026. The chargeable gain is generally the difference between the cost of acquisition of the asset and sales proceeds realised on the disposal of the asset.
Chargeable gains may arise to individuals, non-corporate persons and companies. With the exception of chargeable gains arising on the disposal of development land, companies pay corporation tax on chargeable gains, rather than CGT. As the rates of corporation tax and CGT are different, a chargeable gain which arises to a company is adjusted, such that when the relevant corporation tax rate is applied to the adjusted amount, the result is the same as if the chargeable gain was subject to the relevant CGT rate.
I am further advised by Revenue that the €186 million full year cost outlined in Budget 2027 includes the chargeable gains for corporates. As outlined above, this is payable as corporation tax but is included in the overall estimated CGT costing.

reply:
As part of the Fit for 55 package, the European Commission published a proposal to revise the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) Directive. The revised proposal was agreed in May 2023 when the EU adopted Directive 2023/959. This Directive strengthened rules in relation to the existing EU ETS and made provision for the introduction of a separate but adjacent system for the Buildings, Road Transport and Additional Sectors (ETS2).
Directive 2023/959 provides for Member States who operate a national carbon tax in buildings, road transport and additional sectors to apply for a derogation from obligations under the EU ETS2 once certain criteria are met. The derogation allows a Member State with a national carbon tax rate equivalent or higher than the average ETS2 auction price, in a given reference year, to exempt regulated entities from the obligation to surrender ETS2 allowances between 2027 and 2030.
In December 2023, Ireland requested a derogation under Article 30 (e)(3) of the ETS Directive. Following engagement with the Commission, amendments were made to carbon tax legislation in Finance Act 2025 to align the scope of Ireland's Carbon Tax with the ETS2 Directive.
Subsequently, Ireland secured a derogation which is subject to ongoing review. In order to retain this derogation, Ireland is required to ensure its carbon tax rate is higher than the average auction clearing price in the ETS2 system for each reference year. question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to outline the level of funds currently held in the Climate and Nature Fund.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the Infrastructure, Climate and Nature Fund (ICNF) was established in 2024 alongside the Future Ireland Fund (FIF), following the commencement of the Future Ireland Fund and Infrastructure, Climate and Nature Fund Act, 2024.
The Act sets out that annual contributions of €2bn occur each year between 2025 and 2030, subject to the results of an annual fiscal and economic assessment process carried out by the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council and my Department.
Given these annual contributions, and an initial transfer of €2bn from the National Reserve Fund (NRF) in 2024, the Act provides for resourcing of the ICNF of up to €14bn.
Management and investment of the ICNF rests with the National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA), who invest according to the long-term investment strategy. The financial accounts of the ICNF are published in the NTMA’s annual report each year, which are available on the NTMA’s website. A detailed schedule of investments held by the ICNF as at 31 December 2025, is published in the NTMA’s 2025 Annual Report
The NTMA has informed me that the ICNF was valued at approximately €4.1 billion as of 31 December 2025. So far this year an additional €1.5bn has been transferred to the ICNF, with a further €500m to transfer before year end.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the number of businesses currently authorised under section 56 of the Value-Added Tax Consolidation Act 2010; the estimated annual value of VAT zero-rated under the scheme; the estimated cash-flow and Exchequer impact arising from the operation of the scheme.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 203, 204, 205 and 206 together.
The VAT treatment of goods and services is subject to EU VAT law, with which Irish VAT law is required to comply. VAT is a tax on consumption of goods and services within the EU, and each Member State is obliged to operate its own VAT system in accordance with a common framework of principles and rules that are designed to support coherent application of the tax across the EU, protection of the tax base, and facilitation of trade.
The EU VAT Directive provides that VAT is not charged on goods exported from the Union. The Directive also provides that VAT does not apply on the supply of goods cross-border within the EU between VAT-registered businesses; in those cases, it is the business who receives the goods who is obliged to account for VAT on them in its own Member States, and not the supplier. The Directive further provides that a Member State may, subject to certain procedures and limitations, relieve from VAT the inputs of a business that is exporting or making intra-Community supplies.
In accordance with the Directive Ireland applies its zero rate of VAT to exports outside the EU and to intra-Community supplies of goods. This means that businesses predominantly engaged in making such supplies outside the State would be in a permanent repayment position for VAT. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the estimated number of existing investors who will remain subject to deemed disposal following the introduction of the personal investment account announced in Budget 2027; the number facing a deemed disposal charge in 2027; the estimated cost to the Exchequer of extending equivalent treatment to these existing investors.
reply:
The information available to Revenue does not allow them to isolate the tax returned due to the deemed disposal rule from other chargeable events which give rise to a tax liability. Chargeable events include:
• the making of relevant payments;
• the redemption of the investment;
• the transfer by an investor of their investment; and
• the ending of an eight-year period following the acquisition of the investment and then every eight years thereafter (deemed disposal).
Therefore, it is not possible to directly identify the tax revenue arising from the application of the deemed disposal rule. This is because investment funds and life companies are not obliged to report the category of chargeable event that the exit tax relates to at the time of making payment to Revenue. Nor do they specify the number of investors or policyholders to whom the Investment Undertaking Tax (IUT) or Life Assurance Exit Tax (LAET) paid by the investment fund or life company relates.
Similarly, as respects investments in certain Irish domiciled funds and offshore funds in respect of which investors are required to self-assess tax due, taxpayers are not required to separately report data for each category of chargeable event when filing their tax return.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he has considered amending section 626B of the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997 to align the Substantial Shareholding Exemption with the Dividend Participation Exemption introduced in Finance Act 2024; the estimated cost of such an amendment; the reason it was not included in Budget 2027.
reply:

The Participation Exemption for Foreign Dividends regime was introduced in Finance Act 2024. The exemption, which applies simplifies the double tax relief system and enhances Ireland’s attractiveness for multinational businesses. This strong uptake demonstrates that householders continue to recognise the benefits of investing in solar PV.
In the run-up to Budget 2027 (and as part of the broader work of the National Energy Affordability Task Force), I delivered a suite of enhanced SEAI energy upgrade grants to help households and businesses reduce energy costs and move away from volatile, imported fossil fuels. The package of measures includes a new grant for battery storage systems and expanded eligibility for solar PV and solar thermal grants. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the number of discretionary trusts claiming exemption from initial and annual discretionary trust tax on the basis that the principal objects include a permanently incapacitated individual, in each of the years 2020 to 2025; the number of trusts claiming relief under section 189A of the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997 in the same period; if the Department has reviewed whether these reliefs adequately protect adult children with lifelong disabilities who inherit from their parents.
reply:
Sections 17 and 22 of the Capital Acquisitions Tax Consolidation Act (CATCA) 2003 provide for a number of exemptions from the initial and annual charges to discretionary trust tax (DTT) for trusts that are established for certain specified purposes. The discretionary trusts within the scope of these exemptions include trusts that are established exclusively for the benefit of one or more named individuals, and for the reason that the individual(s) is, or are because of age, improvidence, physical, mental or legal incapacity, incapable of managing their affairs.
A discretionary trust established for the benefit of a permanently incapacitated person could come within the scope of this exemption but only to the extent that the trust is established exclusively for the benefit of the incapacitated person(s). Where the trust is established for other purposes the exemptions from Discretionary Trust Tax do not apply.

question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the timeline for the application of the derelict property tax; and when the digitally accessible online register will be activated.
reply:
The introduction of a new Derelict Property Tax (DPT) forms part of the ‘Delivering Homes, Building Communities 2025-2030’ housing plan. The tax will be collected by the Revenue Commissioners and will be based on registers of derelict properties that are compiled and maintained by local authorities.
In its first year of operation, the tax will apply to towns and cities which were recorded as having populations of 4,000 or greater in Census 2022. In the second year of operation, the tax will expand to towns with populations of 2,000 or greater.
DPT will be legislated for as part of Finance (No. 2) Bill 2026. Local authorities will conduct visual surveys of the designated towns and cities under the tax and place derelict properties that they identify on a derelict property register. They key timelines for the first liability year for DPT are as follows:

• 1 September 2027: Preliminary registers of derelict properties are published.
• 1 September 2027 to 30 November 2027: Property owners can seek review of inclusion on register.
• 1 September 2027 to 29 February 2028: Local authorities decide on reviews.
• 28 February 2028: Final registers of derelict properties published and Revenue pay and file window opens.
• 23 June 2028: First pay and file deadline.

reply:

www.revenue.ie/en/corporate/information-about-revenue/statistics/tax-expenditures/cost/index.aspx.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will progress the aligning of the substantial shareholding exemption with the existing dividend participation exemption as part of the upcoming Finance Bill.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 191 and 201 together.
Ireland’s corporation tax approach has been consistent for many years – a low rate on a broad base, providing stability and certainty for businesses. This approach has provided businesses with a clear and reliable framework within which to plan and invest, contributing to Ireland’s success in attracting multinational enterprises. Ireland remains committed to a tax system that is both competitive and internationally respected.
The Participation Exemption for Foreign Dividends regime was introduced in Finance Act 2024. The exemption, which applies simplifies the double tax relief system and enhances Ireland’s attractiveness for multinational businesses. The exemption is available, subject to conditions, in respect of distributions received from qualifying subsidiaries in EEA and treaty partner jurisdictions and jurisdictions that have imposed a non-refundable withholding tax on the distribution.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether as part of the Government’s planned holistic review of enterprise taxation in 2027, he will include a review of the taxation of residential landlords, with a view to recognising landlords as businesses for taxation purposes.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 190 and 219 together.
As announced Budget 2027, a holistic assessment of Ireland’s enterprise support regime including grant schemes and tax incentives available to businesses will be undertaken. Further detail on this review will be announced in due course.
I expect that the assessment will examine the full range of enterprise supports, including grant schemes, tax incentives and business development programmes currently available.
It is not intended to include the taxation of the residential rental market in this assessment. The taxation of rental income was considered by my Department as part of the 2022 Tax Strategy Group process. (Further details set out in chapter 7 of the "Property-Related Tax Issues Tax Strategy Group – 22/04 July 2022" paper, available at the following link: https://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/tsg-22-04-property-related-tax-issues-4b78c888-4c5a-4642-9f8b-5a28c181ee1a.pdf).
My Department continues to monitor all aspects of the property market, and I will continue to work with my colleagues in Government to ensure that any further interventions in the housing market are appropriately calibrated, represent the best use of public resources and boost the supply of housing in both the public and private sectors.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether he is aware of concerns among medically vulnerable electricity customers regarding solar panel supports where their electricity supplier is not participating; whether customers must change supplier to qualify; how those in fixed-term contracts will be accommodated; why customers can no longer apply directly; the timeframe for contacting eligible households; whether installing solar panels independently could affect future eligibility for the medically vulnerable scheme; and if he will review the arrangements to ensure households are not disadvantaged due to their electricity supplier.
reply:
The Solar PV for the Medically Vulnerable Scheme is a targeted scheme for the installation of solar photovoltaic (PV) panels for customers/households who are registered on the life support category of the Priority Services Register. These homes have a dependence on electrically powered equipment, including medical equipment, life protecting devices and assistive technologies such as dialysis machines and respirators. As such, these households may have a higher energy demand than the average user and this scheme is designed to go some way towards helping to reduce those energy costs.
The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) in conjunction with energy suppliers and is open to all suppliers who wish to participate, with each energy supplier contacting their own eligible customers directly, in line with the work plans for their solar PV installers.
The scheme is energy supplier-led, meaning each energy supplier is responsible for contacting their own eligible customers directly. Government, through the SEAI, funds each energy supplier for the installations they provide to their eligible customers.
It is important to note that suppliers, who manage the administrative aspects of the scheme under the SEAI, issue offers to eligible homeowners. Each participating supplier received an allocated amount of funding under their Memorandum of Understanding with the SEAI and contacts eligible households in batches, based on operational capacity.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if there are planned changes to the disabled drivers and disabled passengers scheme in 2027, following the publication of Budget 2027.
reply:
My Department and I share concerns that the Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme or DDS is no longer fit-for-purpose. The Government has now agreed to commence from early 2027 the Department of Transport’s Vehicle Adaptation Scheme (VAS). The VAS will provide direct financial assistance to all individuals with qualifying vehicle adaptation needs to meet the costs of those adaptations. The VAS will improve individuals’ functional mobility that in turn can contribute to better social and economic opportunities.
The Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme (DDS) remains with the Department of Finance and will be kept under review. Learning from the commencement and initial operation of the VAS will further inform reform options for the DDS.
As the Deputy will be aware, when this government took office, we committed to a step change in the delivery of supports and services for people with disability and their families.
Budget 2027 delivers significant progress for disabled children and adults, bringing the budget to over €4 billion for the first time.
This funding will be vital in delivering the National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People. The commitment to develop a new scheme by the Department of Transport, and in this context review the Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme, are strong commitments in this strategy.

question: Deputy Denise Mitchell asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the regulatory or other protections which apply to investors where the underlying investment company has entered liquidation and the firm that advised or serviced the investment has also entered liquidation.
reply:
The Central Bank of Ireland is the independent regulator for financial services and it determines what measures or actions need to be taken in relation to any potential, or actual, wrongdoing by regulated financial service providers.
European and Irish legislation requires the regulation of financial services firms providing investment services in relation to investment products. The law lists the various types of regulated investment services and investment. Regulated firms may also sell investment products which are not specifically mentioned in the law (i.e. unregulated products). Where they do so, certain investor protections, which apply to regulated activities do not apply.
The Central Bank recently reviewed the Consumer Protection Code (CPC) and this included a review of the rules around the sale of unregulated products by regulated entities. As part of the review, the Central Bank held a public consultation, and changes came into effect in March 2026.
Under the Code’s Standards for Business, firms are required to ensure that all information they provide to customers is presented in a way that seeks to effectively inform the customer.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if his Department has assessed the distributional impact of LPT according to household composition, including households with dependent children and households without dependent children; and if consideration has been given to incorporating household composition or ability to pay into the calculation of LPT liability.
reply:

On the introduction of the LPT, the Government decided that a liability to the tax should apply to all owners of residential properties based on the market value of the property and with a limited number of reliefs available. This ensures that liable taxpayers are not charged more to account for a shortfall driven by reductions in LPT charges based on other factors, including household composition.
The design of LPT was considered by an interdepartmental group chaired by Dr. Don Thornhill in 2012. In 2019, the tax was subject to a review by an interdepartmental group chaired by the Department of Finance. This model was used to compare the impact that different reform scenarios for LPT would have on household incomes relative to a benchmark position where the property value increases but there is no change in the structure of LPT. The results indicate that all scenarios were progressive rather than regressive to varying degrees.

question: Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the total amount of interest on late payment of tax charged and collected by the Revenue Commissioners, broken down by tax head, in each of the past five years in tabular form; if his Department or the Revenue Commissioners have undertaken research or analysis into the reasons taxpayers fail to discharge their tax liabilities by the relevant payment deadlines; and if so, if he will provide the findings of any such research.
reply:

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether his Department has assessed the introduction of an electric vehicle salary sacrifice scheme, similar to that operating in the United Kingdom; the findings of any such assessment, including the implications for benefit-in-kind taxation and the Exchequer; whether he plans to introduce such a scheme.
reply:
Section 121 of the Taxes Consolidation Act (TCA) 1997 provides that where a car is made available for the private use of an employee then the employee is chargeable to BIK. Where such a benefit is provided for an employee by his or her employer, the employer is required to include that notional payment as part of the employee’s emoluments and to deduct tax via the PAYE system accordingly.
A CO2-based BIK regime for employer provided vehicles became effective from 1 January 2023. From that date the taxable BIK amount is based on the car’s original market value (OMV) and the annual business kilometres driven, with new CO2 emissions-based bands determining whether a standard, discounted, or surcharged rate applies. The number of mileage bands was also reduced from five to four.
Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs) and plug in hybrids benefit from a preferential rate of BIK, while fossil-fuel vehicles are subject to higher BIK rates. This new structure with CO2-based discounts and surcharges is designed to incentivise employers to provide employees with low-emission cars. This brought the taxation of employer provided cars into step with other CO2-based motor taxes as well as with the long-established CO2-based vehicle BIK regimes in other EU Member States.
Furthermore, there is a BIK exemption on the installation of an EV charging facility by an employer at the home of a director or employee, subject to certain conditions.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether his Department has assessed the combined impact of income tax, USC, PRSI and the withdrawal of income-related supports on the financial benefit to working households of additional earnings; whether measures to address abrupt eligibility thresholds are being considered with the relevant Departments.
reply:
As part of the Budgetary process, officials in my Department conduct a distributional analysis of all the changes made to the welfare and tax system. This analysis is carried out using the ESRI’s SWITCH model, which accounts for the interaction between policy changes, and the impact that these have on households. The results of this assessment are published each year in the Beyond GDP document.
The Department of Finance also works closely with other Departments to ensure that budgetary measures do not create unintended interactions that discourage individuals from taking on additional work. For example, the Tax Policy Changes Book, produced by Department officials, examines how changes to selected Department of Social Protection payments affect the effective marginal tax rates faced by workers across different income levels.
These considerations are also reflected in policy. Budget 2027, for instance, raised the 2 per cent threshold for USC to account for the increase in the minimum wage. This was done to ensure that part-time workers on minimum wage continue to face a low marginal tax rate on any additional hours worked. Similarly, the Working Family Payment thresholds were also increased, allowing low-income families to work additional hours while continuing to receive income support from the state.

The tracking of chemical usages falls under the remit of the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment. question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will ensure that online retailers within the European Union apply the appropriate VAT rate when selling products to Irish consumers, including the 0% VAT rate that applies to certain items such as children’s clothes.
reply:
I am advised by Revenue that the VAT rating of goods and services is subject to EU VAT law, with which Irish VAT law is obliged to comply. In general, the EU VAT Directive provides that all goods and services are liable to VAT at the standard rate, unless they are exempt from VAT or fall within the categories of goods and services listed in Annex III of the EU VAT Directive, to which Member States are permitted to apply lower VAT rates subject to certain rules.
The EU VAT Directive allows that a Member State may be permitted to maintain a historic VAT treatment, subject to strict conditions, including that the scope of its historic treatment is not expanded. question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the position regarding the review of the Local Property Tax system that would allow for a reduction for people on a State pension or other social welfare payment.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 166 and 167 together.
On the introduction of the Local Property Tax (LPT), the Government decided that a liability to the tax should apply to all owners of residential properties with a limited number of reliefs. Limiting the exemptions or reductions available allows the rate to be kept low for property owners who do not qualify for such relief. There is no specific provision for a reduction in LPT for those in receipt of the State pension or other social welfare payments under the Finance (Local Property Tax) Act 2012 (as amended). However, homeowners in receipt of social welfare payments may be entitled to an exemption or deferral subject to meeting the qualifying conditions.
The LPT legislation provides for the possibility of deferring the charge to LPT in certain circumstances to assist individuals who may have difficulty paying the tax. A qualifying person may opt to defer, or partially defer, payment of the tax. Where a person qualifies for a full deferral, 100% of the liability can be deferred. Where a person qualifies for partial deferral, then 50% of the liability can be deferred. The balance of 50% of the tax must be paid. The deferred tax remains as a charge on the property and must be paid before a sale or transfer can be completed. Interest is charged at 3% per annum on the deferred amount.

reply:
The rotating Presidency of the Council of the European Union is a core institutional requirement of EU membership. Assuming responsibility for organising ministerial and official-level meetings facilitates negotiations between Member States and supports the effective functioning of the Council’s legislative and policy agenda. On this basis, the Government committed in the Programme for Government to resource and deliver a successful EU Presidency. Significant planning and inter-departmental engagement have taken place to ensure costs are managed across all expenditure headings. Prudent financial planning will continue to ensure value for money.
The Revised Estimates for 2026, published in December 2025, included allocations to individual Government Departments for the requirements of the EU Presidency. This included an allocation of €4,083,000 for the Department of Finance. The overall estimated pay costs of €3,438,000 cover the additional temporary staffing need in Brussels and in Ireland to deliver on the Council’s legislative and policy agenda and to support policy and operational planning. The overall estimated non-pay costs of €645,000 are being used for costs associated with organising Presidency-related events in Ireland and to cover the costs of Presidency associated official travel.
At all times value for money is pursued.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the position regarding any research specifically carried out by his Department into the removal of the deemed disposal rule in the context of investment funds.
reply:
The final report of the Funds 2030 Review, Funds Sector 2030: A Framework for Open, Resilient and Developing Markets Final Report, made recommendations regarding the taxation of investments. It noted that changes to the deemed disposal rule require guardrails to protect the Exchequer and ensure that appropriate tax is paid.
Developing such guardrails requires careful consideration to ensure that any changes strike a balance between supporting retail investment while retaining necessary anti-avoidance protections and considering changes in the investment landscape since its introduction in Finance Bill 2006.
In addition, for every Budget, the cost to the Exchequer of different polices must be considered in the context of the agreed Budget package, and there is an immediate Exchequer impact from removing deemed disposal, notwithstanding the potential for more tax to be paid at a future date.
As outlined in the Roadmap for the Taxation of Retail Investment, published 31 August, measures of this nature are considered as part of the annual budgetary process and any decision has to consider the Budget ceilings agreed by Government, and the range of options across the entire tax system.

reply:

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Transport further to Budget 2027, the funding available for regional and local road allocations to local authorities.
reply:

The focus of the Regional and Local Roads Grant Programme is protection and renewal. As such, allocations to local authorities, in the main grant categories, are determined on as equitable a basis as possible, taking the length of their regional and local roads network into account.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Transport his views on concerns regarding roaming deer on road safety issues; and the steps he will take to address the matter.
reply:
The safety of all road users is a priority for me and my Department. I am aware of concerns regarding the risk posed by stray deer, particularly on rural roads and during periods when deer are more active, however management measures in relation to deer do not come under the remit of my Department or agencies.
The Irish Deer Management Strategy Group (IDMSG) was set up in 2023 with representatives from the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine (DAFM), National Parks & Wildlife Service (NPWS) and Coillte.
The role of the IDMSG was to develop initiatives to ensure sustainable deer numbers while achieving the objectives of landowners ranging from biodiversity, forestry, agriculture, animal health and road safety.
I would encourage the Deputy to contact these bodies directly for further information.
In relation to road safety, appropriate road signage including hazard warning signs regarding deer or other wild animals is the responsibility of the local authorities.
The Road Safety Authority (RSA) advises motorists to stay alert and reduce speed when driving in areas with known deer populations and particularly where deer warning signs are in place. I have referred the Deputy's question to the RSA and requested that they advise if there is any further relevant information they can provide in relation to this matter.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Transport whether National Transport Authority contracts or public bus service licences contain requirements concerning unnecessary engine idling and vehicle emissions; the way in which any such requirements are monitored; and whether consistent engine-off guidance will be introduced for extended layovers at bus stops and termini.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport; however, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of public transport. The National Transport Authority (NTA) has statutory responsibility for securing the provision of public passenger transport services nationally.
PSO services support a wide range of Government policy objectives, including climate action, sustainable mobility, regional development, social inclusion, compact growth, economic competitiveness, as well as the accommodation of population growth.
Under Bus Connects we are transitioning to a Zero Emissions Bus Fleet, which will see the procurement of zero emission electric buses. There are now over 100 electric buses in operation in Dublin and circa 30 in Limerick, with more to come.
In light of the NTA’s responsibility in this area, I have forwarded the Deputy's question to the NTA for direct reply. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a response within ten working days.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Transport the statutory provisions, governing prolonged stationary engine idling by buses and coaches on public roads and at bus stops; the authorities responsible for enforcement and the sanctions available; whether these provisions address vehicles left running unattended; and whether he will consider specific measures to restrict unnecessary idling, subject to defined safety and operational exceptions.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I am aware of the impact that vehicular emissions arising from engine idling can have on air quality and public health. Engine idling can contribute to both carbon emissions and local air pollution, particularly in built-up areas and public spaces such as outside schools. From a regulatory perspective, under current traffic legislation, notably S.I. No. 190/1963, Road Traffic (Construction, Equipment and Use of Vehicles) Regulations 1963, Article 87(1)(a)), it is already an offence to leave a vehicle unattended while its engine is running. This provision is intended to address vehicle safety and security concerns primarily.
To address and mitigate transport-related air pollution more broadly, a broad range of national measures are currently in place. These include multi-stakeholder working groups such as UTRAP - the Urban Transport-Related Air Pollution (UTRAP) Working Group which is co-chaired by the Department of the Environment, Climate and Communications and the Department of Transport, and consists of representation from a range of key government departments, agencies and local authorities. The group was established among other things to address rising concerns about the level of transport-generated ambient air pollution in certain areas.

reply:

No. 477 of 2006), the Road Safety Authority (RSA) is the body with statutory responsibility for the operation and oversight of Commercial Vehicle Roadworthiness Testing (CVRT), including the authorisation of CVR test centres. question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport further to Parliamentary Question No. 261 of 29 September 2026, if he is aware that the Road Safety Authority already has a Road Safety Advocate Programme (details supplied); the difference between his proposed new Road Safety Ambassadors Programme and the RSA's Road Safety Advocate Programme which already exists and has carried out numerous activities; and the cost of his proposed new Road Safety Ambassadors Programme.
reply: As the Deputy is aware, the Government approved proposals on 29 July to further reform the Road Safety Authority (RSA) while maintaining the one organisation. One of the key reform proposals is the introduction of a new Road Safety Ambassadors Programme this year which will see the appointment of road safety advocates to work with the RSA to target different audiences with road safety messaging. This new programme will enhance and expand existing road safety advocacy programmes. My Department is engaging with the RSA on the implementation of the reform proposals including the Road Safety Ambassadors programme. The RSA is largely self-funded and income from customer services, such as driver testing, driver licencing and the NCT service, is used to fund public interest work. As part of Budget 2027, the RSA has been directed to ringfence €20m for investment in road safety public awareness and promotional campaigns. This is an increase of €2m on the 2025 and 2026 investment in this important area.

Through its management of fare strategies, they help to ensure that pricing structures support social inclusion and modal shift, while also underpinning the financial viability and resilience of the PSO network.
Fare revenue currently covers approximately 38% of the cost of operating the PSO services nationally. Any overall increase in revenue generated from the NTA’s recent fare determination announcement will be reinvested directly into public transport services, delivering better connectivity, capacity and reliability for passengers and commuters across the network. question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding the ICE2EV scrappage scheme; and if it is proposed to be extended beyond the initial pilot.
reply:
The ICE2EV Pilot Scrappage Scheme was designed and launched as a capped pilot initiative, supported by €17 million in funding from the Climate Action Fund, comprising of €10 million for the scrappage grant and €7 million for the EV purchase grant.
The strong level of interest in the scheme is encouraging and highlights increasing consumer engagement with the transition to electric vehicles. This positive response aligns with Ireland’s broader Climate Action objectives, including the ambition to increase the uptake of electric vehicles to 30% of the national car fleet by 2030.
The policy purpose of the capped initiative was to test the effectiveness of scrappage as a tool to stimulate EV uptake among those who may not otherwise transition in the near term, with the ultimate goal of delivering additional emissions reductions necessary for our climate targets.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport if the planned review of the TaxSaver scheme announced in Budget 2027 will include consideration of extension to the scheme to include shared mobility services.
reply:
In line with the announcement made as part of Budget 2027 by the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance, Simon Harris. T.D., my Department will initiate a comprehensive review of the TaxSaver Scheme over the coming year, in close cooperation with the Department of Finance.
The TaxSaver Scheme is an important element of the Government's wider approach to supporting sustainable travel. The forthcoming Review will provide an opportunity to build on the success of the existing Scheme and to consider how it can continue to best support commuters into the future.
Commuting habits have evolved significantly in recent years, especially in light of an increase in hybrid working as well as more flexible and multimodal travel patterns. It is important that our supports keep pace with these changes and continue to enable people to make sustainable transport choices for their daily journeys.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the position Ireland has taken in discussions on the European Commission’s proposed new own resource based on non-collected waste electrical and electronic equipment; and the way in which this proposal fits with Ireland’s wider priorities for the 2028–2034 Multiannual Financial Framework.
reply:
Pursuing agreement on the next EU long-term budget, the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), is an overarching priority for the Irish Presidency. At the European Council in June, the President of the European Council, Antonio Costa, tasked the Irish Presidency with advancing work on new Own Resources.
On 10 October, the Presidency published our revised compromise proposal, or Negotiating Box. This is an important milestone in MFF negotiations and includes carefully considered adjustments on a range of issues, including on the Commission’s proposal for new Own Resources.
The Presidency’s Negotiating Box is based on strong evidence gathered through an extensive programme of engagement including bilateral meetings with all Member States, and several discussions at EU negotiating fora. In assessing proposals for new Own Resources, the Presidency has been guided by the principle that a significant package of new Own Resources will be essential, while also needing to be capable of generating sufficient new revenue, securing agreement by all Member States, and being implementable by 2028.
The Negotiating Box therefore sets out a package of new Own Resources, which includes a proposed new Own Resource on e-Waste.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport following the publication of Budget 2027, to provide the rationale for the €26 million cut within Programme E: Maritime Transport and Safety section of his Department's budget when compared to 2026; and the initiatives or schemes which had funding cut or removed as part of this budget decrease.
reply:
In his capacity as Minister of State for International & Road Transport, Logistics, Rail & Ports, my colleague Seán Canney T.D, has responsibility for the Irish Coast Guard and the SAR Aviation Contract.
It should be noted that Programme E: Maritime Transport and Safety encompasses a range of services and bodies, including the Irish Coast Guard, the Commissioners of Irish Lights and related departmental administration costs. Consequently, changes in the overall Programme E allocation cannot be attributed solely to Coast Guard expenditure or to any single programme within the Vote.
The reduction in the 2027 allocation for Programme E: Maritime Transport and Safety, from €162.5 million in 2026 to €136.6 million in 2027, is primarily attributable to the non-recurring nature of certain expenditure incurred in 2026 and the impact of expenditure control measures applied across Government.
A significant element of the 2026 provision related to one-off costs associated with the transition to the new Irish Coast Guard Search and Rescue (SAR) Aviation Service contract. In addition, the 2027 provision reflects the application of the Government's expenditure levy and associated expenditure management measures.
The Irish Coast Guard will continue to provide its statutory maritime search and rescue, maritime safety and emergency response functions.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport following the publication of Budget 2027, to provide a breakdown of funding that will be provided to road safety initiatives in 2027.
reply:
Under the Road Safety Authority Act 2006, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) has responsibility for the promotion of public awareness of road safety and of measures, including the advancement of education, relating to the safe use of roads.
The RSA is largely self-funded and income from customer services, such as driver testing, driver licencing and the NCT service, is used to fund public interest work.
As part of Budget 2027, the RSA has been directed to ringfence €20m for investment in road safety public awareness and promotional campaigns. There will be a focus on broadening and enhancing educational programmes to make our roads safer for all road users. This is an increase of €2m on the 2025 and 2026 investment in this important area and ensuring that one-off expenditure increases in 2023 and 2024 are now embedded in budgeting and business planning.
The Deputy may also wish to note that €718 million was initially allocated for 2026 under the Regional and Local Roads Grant Programme for the improvement and maintenance of regional and local roads, with approximately 90% of this funding allocated to road maintenance and renewal.
Under this programme, my Department provides supplemental funding to local authorities under several different grant categories. Approximately €14 million was provided for low-cost safety improvements in 2026, which funded over 300 projects. question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport to provide an update on the progress to establish a PSO flight service between Dublin and Derry.
reply:
This Government is fully committed to establishing a new Public Service Obligation (PSO) air service between Dublin Airport and City of Derry Airport. This will deliver the Programme for Government commitment to establish air connectivity between the two cities.
As City of Derry Airport is outside of the European Union, the PSO air service will operate outside of Regulation (EC) 1008/2008, which provides for the common rules for the operation of air services in the Community. My Department has had extensive engagement with the Chief State Solicitors Office (CSSO) and the Office of the Attorney General in recent months, in relation to the appropriate legal framework to underpin the procurement. Detailed work is being undertaken to ensure that the Request for Tenders (RfT) is compliant with the appropriate Regulations as well as EU State aid rules.
My Department anticipates being in a position to publish the RfT very shortly, with a view to a contract being awarded this year and services commencing on the route as soon as operationally feasible by the successful operator.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport following the publication of Budget 2027, to provide an update on his Department's planned vehicle adaptation scheme; when applications will open; and the criteria that will be imposed as part of the scheme.
reply:
As Minister of State for International and Road Transport, Logistics, Rail and Ports, I can confirm that in recent months my officials have made significant progress in the development of the Vehicle Adaptation Scheme (VAS). Guided by the proposals set out by the Transport Working Group of the National Disability Inclusion Strategy and the Senior Officials Group on Disability, as well as further engagement and consultation, the Department has established the key principles and parameters underpinning the Scheme. This has facilitated the development of a high-level framework for its operation, further details of which are available on Gov.ie (www.gov.ie/en/department-of-transport/press-releases/minister-canney-announces-framework-for-new-vehicle-adaptation-scheme/).
In line with the social model of disability, the VAS will be based on an individual's needs, not characteristics. Accordingly, eligibility will extend to drivers and passengers who require assistance to enter, exit, or operate a vehicle, rather than being linked to any particular medical condition or disability. The Scheme will be simple to access, use, and receive payments through. It will not be means tested and applicants needing adaptations will not be required to pay upfront themselves.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport whether the road transporters support scheme will operate in 2027, following the publication of Budget 2027.
reply:
My Department received over 4,400 applications in respect of approximately 31,500 vehicles during the original application window. As of 06 October, all applications have been assessed and approved for payment.
The Scheme was introduced to provide support to eligible road transporter operators with rising fuel costs. The Scheme provided payments for the months of March, April and May as the average cost of a litre of diesel exceeded €1.90 as measured by the CSO. An allocation of €120 million was provided for this initial period.
The RTSS will receive an additional €73 million in 2026, enabling payments to be made for a further two months to assist haulage and passenger operators with the high price of diesel.
Since the beginning of the fuel crisis, both I and officials from the Department of Transport have engaged with representative bodies from the road transport sector. The Scheme’s additional allocation reflects both the immediate need for financial support and the ongoing commitment of Government to work with the sector to support Ireland’s essential trade and strategic supply chains.
This Government will continue to engage with representatives from the road transport sector and monitor the situation.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her plans to open a new Irish Consulate General Office in Doha Qatar in 2027.
reply:

Ireland enjoys strong bilateral relations with Qatar. I had the opportunity to travel to Doha in July this year, where I had a positive meeting with Qatar’s Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs. We already have strong trade, investment and people-to-people links, and we are committed to deepening these.
Our Embassy team in Abu Dhabi regularly visits Qatar in support of our broad policy objectives, including the development of political and trade relations, and supporting the needs of Irish businesses and the wider Irish community.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Transport if the NTA will fund the installation of additional shelter seating area on platform 2 of Athy Train Station.
reply:
As Minister of Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding of public transport. The operation, maintenance and renewal of the rail network and stations on the network, including any proposed works at Athy , is a matter for Iarnród Éireann in the first instance.
Noting Iarnród Éireann's (IÉ) responsibility in the matter, I have referred the Deputy's question to IÉ for a direct reply on the specific matter raised. Please contact my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 days.

question: Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Transport the regulations that apply to rickshaws; the authority or department responsible for checking safety; and if this will be reviewed in the lifetime of this Government.
reply:
For the Deputy's information, if a rickshaw is fitted with a small engine or electric motor of any kind, it is considered to be a mechanically propelled vehicle (MPV). Under road traffic law, if an MPV is used in a public place it is subject to all of the regulatory controls that apply to other vehicles i.e., it must be roadworthy, registered, taxed and comply with the following regulations:
• SI 190 of 1963 – Road Traffic Construction, Equipment and Use of Vehicles Regulations 1963.
• SI 189 of 1963 – Road Traffic Lighting of Vehicles Regulations 1963.
• SI 5 of 2003 – Road Traffic Construction and Use of Vehicles Regulations 2003.
The drivers of all vehicles on public roads, including motorised rickshaws, are required to comply with road traffic legislation and to behave in a safe manner paying due care to other road users. The enforcement of such road traffic legislation is a matter for An Garda Síochána.
A provision was contained in section 31 of the Road Traffic Act 2016, which was aimed at amending section 20 of the Taxi Regulation Act 2013, to allow the National Transport Authority (NTA) to make regulations for “non-motorised passenger transport” in towns and cities which includes rickshaws propelled by pedal cycle. It is important to note that the section 31 provision does not allow for the regulation of rickshaws with an electric motor, only non-motorised rickshaws. Section 31 was subsequently found not to be legally permissible and could not be commenced.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Transport the breakdown of the estimated €6 billion project cost, by major expenditure category, including tunnelling, stations, rolling stock, land acquisition and consultancy fees for the MetroLink project.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 98 and 100 together.
MetroLink is Ireland's largest public transport infrastructure project and a key National Development Plan priority, delivering long-term benefits for economic growth, housing competitiveness and climate action. MetroLink will provide a high-capacity, fully automated metro connection Dublin airport with key destinations across the city, including a reliable 25-minute journey to the city centre.
Over the last year, significant progress has been made in moving MetroLink from planning and design and into procurement and construction.

Following the resolution of a subsequent legal challenge, MetroLink secured an Operative Railway Order in January 2026. This enabled Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII) to commence the shortlisting process for major MetroLink contracts.
In February, TII published the contract notice and Pre-Qualification Questionnaires (PQQ) for the two heavy civil works contracts, M401 and M402. The maximum combined contract value stated in the contract notice for these PQQs is €7.9 billion, excluding VAT.
