question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade to clarify whether ODA funding as outlined in Budget 2027 is more or less than the funding provided for ODA in 2026.
reply:
The Programme for Government commits to annual increases in Official Development Assistance (ODA), working towards the UN target of providing 0.7% of Gross National Income.
I am very pleased that Budget 2027 has provided an increased allocation of €855 million for the international development programme, Irish Aid, managed by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. This is a €14 million increase on the Budget 2026 allocation.
At a time of great uncertainty internationally, when some other countries are cutting their international development budgets, this is an important demonstration of the Government's commitment to Ireland's work on long term development and life-saving humanitarian assistance, with a focus on reaching the furthest behind first. The Government has increased the allocation for the Irish Aid programme every year since 2020.

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Taoiseach the amount, in totals over €20,000, spent by his Department and agencies under its aegis to third parties in connection with a sporting event (details supplied) in 2025 and to date in 2026.
reply: Neither the Department of the Taoiseach nor the National Economic and Social Development Office – the only body under the aegis of the Department – has made payments to any third party in connection with the sporting event in question in the period specified.

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine for an update on the progress of payments under the fuel income support scheme.
reply:
My Department has introduced the Fuel Income Support Scheme as a targeted income support to assist farmers and agricultural/forestry contractors facing unprecedented increases in fuel costs.
Separate schemes have been put in place to support fishers and specialist horticultural growers.
Applications under the scheme closed on June 2nd and payments commenced on July 22nd. To date 31,025 applicants have received payments totalling €26.52 million. It is expected that the total final payments under this scheme will be approximately €27 million.
Incomplete payments are due to a number of issues. For certain cases my Department is waiting on further information from applicants to allow them to be set-up on payment systems or a request has been made for further evidence, for example fuel receipts. As information is supplied cases are being cleared and payments will continue to be made on a weekly basis.
As announced in the Budget, I am pleased to have secured agreement on the extension to the end of this year of the important fuel supports schemes provided for farmers and agricultural contractors, fishermen and women and horticulture producers impacted by higher fuel prices. The allocation of €31.2 million to cover the five months August to December 2026 for these supports will be rapidly implemented by my Department.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will outline the framework set out under the National Bioeconomy Strategy 2026–2030.
reply:
At the outset, I wish to highlight that the new National Bioeconomy Strategy 2026-2030 has not yet been published. This will occur on the occasion of the Global Bioeconomy Summit which the Government, in conjunction with the International Advisory Council for the Global Bioeconomy, will host here in Dublin on October 20th and 21st. The Taoiseach, Minister O'Brien and I look forward to presenting the Strategy to the national and international audience that will gather for that important Summit.
Notwithstanding this, I can refer the Deputy to the framework of the Strategy that was set out in the draft that was issued for public consultation in July. The Strategy’s Vision is that by 2030, Ireland’s bioeconomy is a core driver of economic prosperity, climate action, and rural regeneration. It is characterised by the sustainable and circular use of biological resources, innovative high-value industries, and thriving local communities.
The Strategy focuses on five strategic objectives and contains targeted actions for each of these. They are:
• Scaling Infrastructure, Technology and Investment.
• Strengthening Market Demand and Development.
• Leveraging Innovation, Knowledge and Skills.
• Bioeconomy as a tool for Climate Action and Circularity.
• Improving Governance, Cooperation and Partnerships.
The Strategy also provides for focused development across five priority sectors where Ireland has strong potential to expand sustainable biobased activity. They include the Agri-Bioeconom

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will consider adding a cap on the number of breeding females permitted within a dog breeding establishment to the legislation proposed in this area.
reply:
In order to bring a coherent approach to dog control, policy and legislative responsibility under both the Control of Dogs Act 1986 and the Dog Breeding Establishments Act 2010 transferred to my Department last year. In both cases, local authorities retain responsibility for all operational and enforcement matters.
On 19th May 2026, my Department published draft legislation, the Dog Breeding Establishments Bill 2026 to update the existing regulatory framework for dog breeding establishments in Ireland across three key areas - welfare and breeding, sales and record keeping, and administration and enforcement.
The Bill was approved for priority drafting and is currently undergoing pre-legislative scrutiny with the Oireachtas Joint Committee on Agriculture.
The Bill has seventeen Heads and addresses three broad areas: welfare and breeding standards, sales and record-keeping, and administration and enforcement.
It seeks to address concerns about excessive numbers through a mandatory staffing ratio of 1:20 which creates an indirect but real constraint on establishment size. The strengthened improvement notice regime will explicitly empower authorised persons to require a reduction in the number of dogs on premises where welfare concerns arise.
Local authorities also retain the ability to set conditions on the number of breeding females as part of the registration process, and this avenue remains open to them, particularly in respect of new applications.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine when the updated Land Use Strategy will be published; and to provide an update on same.
reply:
The Land Use Review Phase 2 titled “A Living Land” was published in July of this year. It provides an evidence base to inform and support landholders and policymakers in their future decisions for land-use, in the context of achieving Ireland’s agricultural, socio-economic, climate and environmental objectives.
The report is not an articulation of government policy or a strategy in relation to land use, given that there are many economic, environmental, and social elements to be balanced in considering land use. Rather, this report will help to inform and support future considerations in this complex area. For example, the role of State-owned lands in leading the way to achieve integrated land use objectives.
To consider fully the recommendations of the Phase 2 of the Land Use Review, my Department has committed to co-chair with DCEE, a Land Use Taskforce, with members to include DHLGH and other relevant Departments and bodies.
Establishment of a Land Use Taskforce is the next step to examine how the State can encourage optimal use of land to meet a variety of societal needs including socio-economic, restoring nature, improving water quality, enhancing climate adaptation and mitigation.

question: Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the number and value of TAMS solar applications approved and not approved to date in 2026; if he will approve additional funding to meet the demand.
reply:
The Targeted Agriculture Modernisation Scheme (TAMS) is a demand-led scheme with a defined budgetary allocation. The budgetary allocation for TAMS 3 is spread across all eleven sub schemes therefore it is not possible to allocate a budget to each of the eleven schemes individually.
TAMS 3 has been hugely successful to date, with over €195 million issuing to farmers since payments commenced in June 2024. Over the first eight tranches of the scheme, all valid applications received were approved.
However, to ensure the available budget for TAMS 3 is distributed fairly over the remainder of the current CAP programming period, it was necessary to limit the number of approved applications per tranche from Tranche 9 onwards by applying ranking and selection criteria to manage the budget to the end of 2027.
Specifically in respect of the Solar Capital Investment Scheme (SCIS) the number of applications and the level of funding provided to date has also well exceeded expectations, to the extent that more than 20% of the TAMS budget is being spent on SCIS.
A total of 7,331 applications have been received under the SCIS with approvals of 3,787 issuing to farmers allowing them to proceed with their investments. The average payment under SCIS is €18,777 per application with an estimated value of the overall approved applications in excess of €71m. Payments amounting to €39.5m have issued to 2,107 farmers since payments commenced in June 2024.

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine when he will publish the report from the Food Vision Seafood Sector Group (details supplied).
reply:
In February this year, Minister Heydon and I established a working group under the auspices of Food Vision 2030 - the Food Vision Seafood Sector Group - to consider the challenges facing all three components of the Irish seafood sector (catch fisheries, aquaculture and seafood processing).
The Group’s overarching objective was to identify and develop a framework of measures to respond to these current challenges. I engaged Mr. Michael Berkery to Chair the Group and to submit an independent report to me by June 2026.
I am currently considering Mr. Berkery's report and will make a decision on its publication in due course.

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine when the Dog Control Stakeholder Group Report will be published.
reply:
I have recently received the report of the Dog Control Stakeholder Group which was established in 2024, which I am considering, including any recommendations in relation to dog control legislation.
My Department is considering avenues of implementation, in particular the forthcoming Animal Welfare Strategy, scheduled for publication in the near term. I also hope to publish the Dog Control Stakeholder Group report shortly.
The insights and recommendations arising from the Group’s work will make an important contribution to the ongoing development of policy in relation to dog control, responsible dog ownership, public safety and animal welfare.
I am deeply grateful for the time and effort devoted by the group to this important area of public policy.

question: Deputy Keira Keogh asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the urgent measures he and his Department is taking to address the backlog in aquaculture licence renewals, reviews and new applications in County Mayo; whether additional resources or personnel will be allocated to the Aquaculture and Foreshore Management Division to tackle the significant backlog, in view of the fact that some licences have expired and some applications submitted remain undetermined due to delays.
reply:
Applications for aquaculture and foreshore licences are considered by my Department in accordance with the provisions of the Fisheries (Amendment) Act 1997, the Foreshore Act 1933 (as amended) and applicable national and EU legislation. The licensing process is complex and involves consultation with a wide range of scientific and technical advisors, in addition to various Statutory Consultees. The legislation also provides for a period of public consultation.
The length of time taken to process an aquaculture licence application varies depending on a number of factors including location, species, scale and intensity of production, statutory status of sites and potential visual impact. My Department also takes full account of all scientific and technical advice, in addition to all issues identified during the public and statutory consultation phases.
Further factors that can impact the time taken to process an application can include; the requirement for an Appropriate Assessment and whether the application is required to be accompanied by an Environmental Impact Assessment Report; the need for additional underwater or archaeological assessments, etc. Decisions in respect of aquaculture licence applications are only taken following the fullest consideration of all consultations and public interest elements of each application, including environmental considerations.

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the measures he is taking to enable farmers to participate directly in Ireland's renewable energy transition; and the opportunity he foresees for renewable energy to provide an income stream for farms.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware overall national energy policy formation is the direct responsibility of my colleague the Minister for Climate Energy and the Environment. My Department works closely with the Department of Climate Energy and the Environment on energy related matters from an agricultural perspective, as well as with a wide range of industry and other stakeholder groups.
Solar and Biomethane are renewable energy options available to farmers which can improve their financial resilience through the diversification of their income stream. Both Solar and Biomethane have received significant support from my Department.
My Department co-led the development of the National Biomethane Strategy, with the Department of Climate Energy and the Environment, which was published in 2024. This was Ireland’s first major policy statement on Biomethane. A key outcome of the Strategy was the Biomethane Capital Grant Scheme, which was run by my Department. The scheme recently concluded with funding of approximately €19 million issued to 7 projects. Not only will these projects contribute to the achievement of Ireland’s Biomethane target set out in the Climate Action Plan, but they also represent an opportunity for farmers to provide feedstock for biomethane generation, thus providing a new income stream for farmers. question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will support a ban on surgical artificial insemination of greyhounds.
reply:
The Veterinary Council of Ireland (VCI) in April 2024 updated its Code of Professional Conduct for Veterinary Practitioners to prohibit veterinarians from carrying out surgical artificial insemination in dogs due to ethical and welfare considerations. However, this new prohibition does not apply to greyhounds, as the practice is provided for in legislation under the Artificial Insemination of Greyhound Regulations 2005.
The report of the Working Group on Control of Dogs, which was approved by Government in March 2023, and has been published online at: www.gov.ie/en/publication/0d6d7-working-group-on-control-of-dogs/#report-of-the-working-group-on-the-control-of-dogs, includes a recommendation that surgical artificial insemination in canines be prohibited, where the word canine encompasses all breeds of dogs.
In 2024, my Department held a public consultation on whether the practice of carrying out surgical artificial insemination in greyhounds should be banned or not and the results of the public consultation are now available on: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-agriculture-food-and-the-marine/publications/animal-welfare/#surgical-artificial-insemination-in-greyhounds.
In compliance of section 5 of the Greyhound Racing Act, S.I. question: Deputy Martin Kenny asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the supports his Department is providing to Irish farmers to deal with rising input costs in the agriculture sector.
reply:
The agri-food sector has demonstrated its ongoing adaptability and resilience despite numerous uncertainties and economic pressure in recent years. The Government continues to provide strong support to farmers via Ireland’s €10.3 billion CAP Strategic Plan, as well as other national sectoral schemes. This results in payments to support farmers of over €2 billion annually.
I am conscious of the exceptional cost pressures family farms are facing at present. I introduced the Fuel Income Support Scheme as a targeted income support, alongside the fuel excise and levy reductions and delay of Carbon Tax increases introduced by Government. To date total payments of €26.52m have been made under the Fuel Income Support Scheme, with over 31,000 farmers and contractors paid.
I acknowledge that the impact of prolonged dry weather this year has increased the challenges family farmers face this year. The dry conditions resulted in significant supplementary feeding on affected farms and the use of silage and other fodder conserved for winter feeding. This has increased costs while also reducing the quantity of fodder available for the coming winter. Responding to the ongoing challenges, I have also availed of the flexibility to increase the rate of advance payments under the BISS, CRISS and Eco-scheme from 70% to 75%, helping to put more money in farmers pockets as early as possible in the year.
Flexibilities have also been provided on requirements associated with certain actions under the A

question: Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the measures his Department has taken to introduce additional resources for enforcement of animal welfare legislation.
reply:
My Department has lead policy responsibility within government for animal welfare, which is protected by legislation. I am committed to ensuring that animal welfare standards are vigorously applied in a fair and even-handed manner. All reports of alleged animal neglect or cruelty received by my Department are investigated and appropriate action is taken.
My Department and authorised officers appointed under the Animal Health and Welfare Act 2013, including An Garda Síochána, Customs agents, local authorities and the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (NSPCA), undertake appropriate enforcement action, where breaches or shortcomings are identified. Since the Act came into operation in March 2014, 230 cases have been successfully prosecuted by my Department and the NSPCA.
My Department has policy and legislative responsibility for the Control of Horses Act 1996. However, Local Authorities are responsible for operation of the Act, and they may take a range of actions in relation to equines, including prohibiting horses in certain areas, issuing licences and seizing horses. These powers can be used in respect of straying horses, including horses put on land without owner’s permission, including public land. Local authorities may also prosecute offenders.
I support sustainable initiatives in line with the Programme for Government and our current Animal Welfare Strategy, including nationwide urban horse projects. Working with local authorities, charities and c

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the position regarding work ongoing to address animal cruelty concerns related to the export of live animals; and if he has engaged with animal welfare organisations in this regard.
reply:
The intra community trade and export of live animals to third countries is a private commercial activity which is regulated by my Department in accordance with EU and National Regulations. Relevant Regulations for this sector include Council Regulation (EC) No. 1/2005 on the protection of animals during transport and related operations which is given effect at national level by S.I. No. 675/2006 European Communities (Animal Transport and Control Post) Regulations 2006. S.I. No. 580/2007 - Diseases of Animals (Animal Transport) (Roll-on Roll-off Vessels) Order 2007 and S.I. No. 356/2016 - Carriage of Livestock by Sea Regulations 2016.
My Department demands the highest standards of animal welfare at every stage of the animal’s life, including during transport. My Department has continuously reinforced its practical, administrative and legislative measures to protect the welfare of animals during transport, often going beyond the minimum requirements of EU law, for example in terms of extra space for calves, more frequent driver retraining and temperature control.
Ireland is a major livestock trading country. Based on data collected by my Department, from 1 January to 20 September 2026, some 278,000 bovines were the subject of intra-community trade, or exports to third countries, from Ireland; 203,000 of these bovines were un-weaned calves. These calves are highly valued by other Member States with long established veal industries. There is very limited demand for veal in Irelan

question: Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the number of bluetongue cases notified to his Department; if he is satisfied that the measures being put in place are adequate to control the disease.
reply:
As of 2nd October 2026, there have been 21 cases of bluetongue serotype three (BTV-3) across the country notified to my Department since mid-July 2026. Recent detections of bluetongue highlight the importance of submitting carcases of livestock suffering from unexplained mortalities and samples from animals with suspected clinical signs for veterinary investigation
Vaccination is the best tool we have to mitigate the losses which can be caused by BTV-3. To that end, I included bluetongue vaccination as an option in the 2026 beef and sheep welfare schemes. With the recent detections in both cattle and sheep herds of BTV-3, the majority with clinical signs, farmers that have not vaccinated their stock yet should talk to their private veterinary practitioner as to whether vaccination is appropriate for their flock or herd.
My Department undertakes extensive surveillance in relation to bluetongue to inform on farm decision making around vaccination. I encourage farmers who carried out vaccination in 2026 to consult their veterinary practitioner in relation to the need for a booster vaccination in 2027.
Additional information on BTV-3, including the latest figures on cases detected, can be found on the Government Website at: www.gov.ie/bluetongue.

question: Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the issues discussed at the recent meeting of Agriculture Ministers held in Ireland. .
reply:
I had the pleasure of hosting the Informal Meeting of EU Agriculture Ministers in Dublin and Kildare from 6 to 8 September, as part of Ireland’s Presidency of the Council of the EU. The plenary session was held at Dublin Castle on 8 September.
Plenary discussions centred on the Commission’s Livestock Strategy and Protein Action Plan, and particularly on how research and innovation can strengthen the competitiveness, sustainability and resilience of European livestock farming.
Ministers considered how to support farmers, particularly smaller farms, in adopting new technologies and practices through investment, advice and knowledge transfer. Key considerations included food security, farm incomes, support for rural communities, the need to strengthen European protein production, and the need to accommodate diverse farming systems, including Ireland’s grass-based model.
The discussion included contributions from representatives of European farmers, co-operatives and young farmers, and the European Parliament. The European Economic and Social Committee also presented its opinion on the Livestock Strategy. In addition, Commissioner Hansen provided an update on drought conditions affecting European farmers, which have created significant pressures on fodder production, water availability and livestock management.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether he intends to introduce a dedicated farm succession or retirement scheme to support generational renewal in agriculture; and the measures being considered to address barriers faced by young farmers in accessing land and taking over family farms.
reply:
The Programme for Government prioritises “supporting inter-generational farm succession”. Supporting young farmers and facilitating generational renewal is a priority of mine and critical to ensure a bright future for the agri-food sector.
There are currently a range of supports in place. Ireland’s CAP Strategic Plan 2023-2027 provides substantial resources focused on generational renewal. There are also strong national taxation measures to facilitate succession and assist land mobility. In addition, my Department continue to work with the Strategic Banking Corporation Of Ireland (SBCI) on the funding requirements for young farmers. Teagasc education and knowledge activities focus on equipping young farmers with necessary education, training and advice to build long and successful careers in farming. As stated in the Commission on Generational Renewal in Farming Report, the total financial support to generational renewal in Ireland was some €428.6m in 2024.
However, farm succession is a complex issue and there are many factors that impact farmers’ decisions. That is why the Commission on Generational Renewal in Farming was established, to consider whether the existing supports are having the desired effect, and how supports might best be configured for the future. The Commission produced a thorough analysis and made 31 recommendations across a wide range of areas including CAP Supports; Pensions; Taxation; Access to Finance; Access to Land; Collaborative Arrangements; Advisor

question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the steps his Department is taking to amend the policy to allow farm vehicles registered in the UK, brought in through Northern Ireland and purchased by Irish farmers without a phytosanitary certificate to be registered with Customs in Ireland.
reply:
Under EU plant health law second hand agricultural vehicles and machinery originating from a third country are regulated and subject to import controls. This is to prevent the spread of plant pest and diseases associated with soil and plant debris contamination attached to such machines. This means a phytosanitary certificate is required on entry into the EU for all second hand agricultural vehicles and machinery. Ireland is therefore required to comply with these EU wide requirements.
Under the Windsor Framework the movement of second hand agricultural machinery from Great Britain (GB) to Northern Ireland (NI) can happen without a phytosanitary certificate only if it is going to a person and entity in NI and such machines must stay in NI. In these cases it must travel with a UK/NI plant passport and such imports must be notified to NI authorities. For agricultural machines purchased in GB by an Irish importer and imported through NI such imports must be pre notified to the NI plant health authorities in DAERA and the importer is required to present the consignment and the necessary phytosanitary certification on import.
Where the custom procedure has not been complied with and a second hand agricultural vehicle has come through Northern Ireland without the necessary phytosanitary certification, my Department will refer importers to contact NI authorities on their situation. My Department will collaborate with NI plant health colleagues on such cases and is guided by the dire

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the progress made to date in implementing the Programme for Government commitment on intergenerational farm succession; if he plans to review the effectiveness of existing succession schemes and supports; and the further actions he plans to take to encourage younger people to enter farming and to support the sustainable transfer of family farms to the next generation.
reply:
The challenge of generational renewal in farming is widely recognised at both national and EU level. It is important that we have skilled, innovative young farmers coming into the sector to secure a viable and sustainable future for Irish farming.
Ireland’s CAP Strategic Plan 2023-2027 provides substantial resources to achieving generational renewal and measures including the Complementary Income Support for Young Farmers; the National Reserve Scheme, which prioritises young farmers; and a higher grant rate of 60% for qualified young farmers under the TAMS capital investment measure. A Collaborative Farming Grant Scheme provides financial support to encourage farmers to form partnerships with young, trained farmers and the Succession Planning Advice Grant provides financial support towards the costs incurred for independent legal and financial advice for older farmers about succession planning.
Nationally, there are strong taxation measures to facilitate succession and assist land mobility. For succession, Agricultural Relief is the key measure, along with 100% Stamp Duty Relief and Consanguinity Stamp Duty Relief. Long-term leasing income tax relief support access to land for young farmers and provides a route to retirement for older farmers.

reply:
Generational Renewal is one of my big priorities to ensure the long-term sustainability and competitiveness of Irish agriculture. A range of supports are in place to encourage timely succession, facilitate generational renewal and assist young farmers in establishing viable farm businesses.
Ireland’s CAP Strategic Plan 2023-2027 provides substantial resources to achieving generational renewal and measures include the Complementary Income Support for Young Farmers (CIS-YF); the National Reserve Scheme, which prioritises young farmers; and a higher grant rate of 60% for qualified young farmers under the TAMS capital investment measure. A Collaborative Farming Grant Scheme provides financial support to encourage farmers to form partnerships with young, trained farmers and the Succession Planning Advice Grant provides financial support towards the costs incurred for independent legal and financial advice for older farmers about succession planning.

For succession, Agricultural Relief is the key measure, which along with 100% Stamp Duty Relief and Consanguinity Stamp Duty Relief, and Long-term leasing income tax relief support access to land for young farmers and provides a route to retirement for older farmers.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the actions he will take to support farmers with the rising cost of fuel.
reply:
The Government recognises the exceptional pressure that rising fuel costs are placing on our farmers and agricultural contractors.
A substantial support package for agricultural or green diesel (MGO) has been put in place, with the full removal of all non-carbon excise on green diesel of 7.4c/l, and a further payment worth up to 20c/l through the Fuel Income Support Scheme.
The Fuel Income Support Scheme was introduced as a targeted income support, alongside the excise and levy reduction. The payment of 20c/l covered the months of March up to the end of July 2026, which coincides with peak fuel usage on farms. These supports, totalling 27.5c/l, exceed by almost 6c/l the entirety of excise (carbon and non-carbon) charged on green or agricultural diesel prior to the conflict in the Middle East.
To date total payments of €26.52m have been made under the Fuel Income Support Scheme, with over 31,000 farmers and contractors paid.
As part of Budget 2027, I secured agreement on the extension to the end of this year of the important fuel supports schemes provided for farmers and agricultural contractors, fishermen and women and horticulture producers impacted by higher fuel prices. The allocation of €31.2 million to cover the five months August to December 2026 for these supports will be rapidly implemented by my Department.
Taxation policy is the responsibility of my colleague the Minister for Finance, while energy policy is the responsibility of my colleague the Minister for Climate

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine for an update on the progress of the Bovine TB Action Plan.
reply:
In recent years there has been a significant increase in bovine TB levels nationally. I am very aware of the emotional and financial challenge for Irish farmers, their families and rural communities of a bovine TB breakdown.
To address these high disease levels, I have undertaken extensive engagement with stakeholders and farming organisations to agree measures to tackle disease levels. I launched the ‘Bovine TB Action Plan:Addressing Bovine TB in Ireland’ in September 2025 it includes 5 measures and 30 actions underpinned by scientific research, evidence and veterinary expertise. The aim of the Action Plan is to reset the TB programme by putting in place measures necessary to tackle the current disease situation.
On 13 April 2026 a number of changes were introduced to animal testing and animal movement requirements to the bTB programme to reduce the transmission of bTB from cattle to cattle including:

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the status of negotiations with the British government to reinstate access for Irish fishermen to their traditional fishing grounds at Rockall; and if he will seek international mediation or arbitration to resolve this long running injustice, that has cost our fleet millions of euro each year.
reply:
Rockall is a small, uninhabitable rock located approximately 160 nautical miles west of the Scottish islands of St. Kilda, and 230 nautical miles to the north-west of Donegal.
As the Deputy is aware, Ireland has not sought to claim sovereignty over Rockall. The UK claimed sovereignty over Rockall in 1955 and sought to formally annex it as part of Scotland under its 1972 Island of Rockall Act. The consistent position of successive Irish Governments is that Ireland does not recognise Britain’s claim of sovereignty over Rockall.
Accordingly, Ireland does not accept that a 12 nautical mile (22km) territorial sea exists around Rockall. Ireland’s long-held view is that a rock incapable of sustaining human habitation does not allow for the creation of a territorial sea. Therefore, the agreement under the TCA relating to access to the UK 12-200 mile zone should apply inside the 12nm zone around Rockall.
We understand that the UK takes a different view.
Irish vessels have traditionally fished for haddock, which is subject to a quota limit, and squid, which is not subject to a quota limit, in the waters around Rockall. Haddock may be caught both within and outside 12 nautical miles of Rockall, but squid is caught within 6 nautical miles of Rockall. Other stocks caught in the waters around Rockall, both within the 12 miles area and outside, are monkfish and megrim.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to outline his views on the Protection of the Native Irish Honey Bee Bill 2021.
reply:
The Protection of the Native Irish Honey Bee Bill 2021, a Private Members Bill, which seeks to ban the importation of non-native honey bees is currently before Dáil Éireann, Second Stage.
Following legal advice from the Office of the Attorney General in relation to the Protection of the Native Irish Honey Bee Bill 2021, my Department procured independent scientific evidence and in October 2023, a contract was signed with the National University of Ireland, Galway for the provision of research services on the native Irish honey bee (Apis mellifera mellifera).
The research work concluded, and the research report was subsequently evaluated by an external expert. Following the completion of the evaluation, the research service provider was afforded the opportunity to respond to the evaluator’s comments and these comments were received in September 2025. My Department is currently finalising the overall response to the report and I will publish same in due course.

question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the status of the work of the interdepartmental working group established to examine the racing of horse-drawn vehicles on public roads; the progress made to address the serious animal welfare concerns associated with the practice; whether the group is examining the measures required to prohibit racing of all horse drawn vehicles on public roads; and when recommendations are expected.
reply:
Animal welfare is a key priority for me as Minister and for the Government.
The welfare of equines is protected by legislation and there is a commitment in the Programme for Government to build on existing inspectorate supports across the country, ensuring a consistent approach to dealing with horse welfare. However, it must be emphasised that primary responsibility for the health and welfare of equines lies with the owner or keeper.
The use of horse-drawn vehicles, as with all vehicles on public roads, is governed by the relevant provisions of the Roads and Road Traffic Acts, which is under the remit of the Minister for Transport. The drivers of such vehicles are required to comply with road traffic legislation, with the enforcement of this legislation falling under the remits of my colleagues the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration and the Minister for Transport.

An initial meeting of this group has taken place, and I understand that further meetings are planned in order to progress this complex issue.

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to outline the funding available for TAMS under budget 2027.
reply:
The Targeted Agriculture Modernisation Scheme (TAMS) is a demand-led scheme, that has been hugely successful to date, with payments of over €195 million issuing to farmers since payments commenced in June 2024.
The TAMS on-farm capital investment scheme continues to be one of my key priorities over the lifetime of this Government. In Budget 2027 I have secured an increase in the 2027 TAMS allocation to €93.35 million, the largest ever annual budget allocation in on-farm investment scheme by my Department.
This underlines the Government's renewed commitment to supporting competitiveness on Irish farms, generational renewal, and crucially, will fund farmers to invest in additional slurry storage, a critical component in supporting Ireland’s Nitrates Derogation.

In respect of the TAMS 3 Solar Capital Investment scheme (SCIS) this measure was launched on 22 February 2023. It is supporting farmers to transition to renewable energy sources, reducing dependence on fossil fuel based energy.

question: Deputy Brian Stanley asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the additional financial or structural incentives the Government is introducing to encourage older farmers to step back earlier, given the aging demographic in farming, in order to facilitate a more timely handover to younger successors.
reply:
The challenge of generational renewal in farming is widely recognised at both national and EU level. The Programme for Government prioritises supporting inter-generational farm succession. Specifically in relation to older framers, a Collaborative Farming Grant Scheme provides financial support to encourage farmers to form partnerships with young, trained farmers. Teagasc also provide succession advice and provide annual “Transferring the Family Farm” clinics to guide farmers.
Farmers can access a suite of strong taxation measures to facilitate succession and assist land mobility. Framers who are 55 years of age or older can claim Retirement Relief, a relief on Capital Gains Tax (CGT) when disposing of any part of business or farming assets. question: Deputy Keira Keogh asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he recognises the importance of the aquaculture industry in Clew Bay, which produced approximately 5,400 tonnes of finfish and shellfish in 2025 with a first-sale value of almost €30 million; the steps he is taking to support its continued growth.
reply:

This strategy was developed in the context of the EU’s strategic guidelines for aquaculture, and reflects these guidelines.
It sets out a framework to support a sustainable, profitable, competitive, and market-focused aquaculture industry in Ireland, while optimising environmental performance and supporting the natural capital upon which aquaculture production depends.
The NSPSA, which was developed in conjunction with broad range of stakeholders, is structured around four key objectives, those being:
1. Building resilience and competitiveness.
2. Participating in the green transition.
3. Ensuring social acceptance and consumer information.
4. Increasing knowledge and innovation.
The Plan has 58 actions. The lead agencies for the implementation of the actions are my Department, BIM, the Marine Institute, and Bord Bia. Included among the actions are the rollout of a user-friendly online aquaculture licensing and information system, increased focus on fish welfare, support for innovation in aquaculture and the development of a human capacity plan to promote the sector as an attractive career option.

question: Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the current average processing time for foreshore licence applications; the way in which this compares with previous years; and the principal causes of delays in the system.

question: Deputy Joe Cooney asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether his Department has undertaken an assessment of risks to Ireland's food security arising from climate change related risks, such as drought, flooding, biodiversity loss and disruption to global food supply chains; and whether he will consider establishing a cross-departmental review of Ireland's food security resilience in view of growing climate-related risks.
reply:

Furthermore, the most recent Teagasc Sustainability Report finds that Irish dairy, cattle, tillage and sheep farms produce protein sufficient to meet the requirements of over 36 million people (or 30 million people on a net basis).
Nonetheless, recent extreme weather events challenge established assumptions on food security. My Department's Climate Change Sectoral Adaptation Plan (2025 to 2030) provides the strategic framework for strengthening resilience across the agriculture, forestry and seafood sectors. The current plan represents the most comprehensive climate adaptation assessment undertaken to date of climate risks affecting the sectors under the Department's remit and reflects the findings of Ireland's National Climate Change Risk Assessment (NCCRA). These risks span a wide range of issues including flooding, prolonged wet periods, drought, water availability, animal health and welfare, soil degradation, infrastructure resilience, biosecurity, forestry impacts, coastal change, supply chain disruption and food system resilience.

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the measures he is taking at EU level to secure increased fishing opportunities and quota allocations for the Irish fishing fleet.
reply:
The share allocation of stocks between Member States was established as a principle of the first Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) in 1983 and was based on the average catch of each Member State over a period of reference years (track record).
Any change to the existing system of quota allocations would require a majority of Member States to agree under the qualified majority voting system. This would require other Member States to give up existing quota shares, and therefore poses particular challenges in a qualified majority voting context.
Notwithstanding these challenges, I have frequently raised the matter of Ireland's fishing opportunities at the AgriFish Council, and will continue to seek additional opportunities for Ireland at every available opportunity.
Ireland has consistently called for the European Commission to fully analyse and report on the impacts of Brexit on the CFP, and in particular, the impact on the EU and Member States’ fishing opportunities as a result of quota transfers under the EU-UK Trade & Cooperation Agreement (TCA). I have emphasised to the Commissioner of Fisheries and Oceans, Costas Kadis, the need to address the impacts of Brexit on our fishing sector when Ireland carried a disproportionate burden of the quota transfers to the UK under the TCA.

reply:

Approved actions may then be implemented by the participants, and the details can then be submitted to the NPI claims system.
It is important to note that there is no obligation on a participant to carry out an approved action, and the claim serves as confirmation from the participant that the action has been implemented. Once a claim is submitted, NPI payment may then issue.

Ireland is strongly committed to improving animal welfare standards during transport and supports the revision of the EU Regulation for this sector.
Ireland demands the highest standards of animal welfare at every stage of the animal’s life, including during transport. Ireland has continuously reinforced its practical, administrative, and legislative measures to protect the welfare of animals during transport, often going beyond the minimum requirements of EU law, for example in terms of extra space for calves, more frequent driver retraining and stricter policies on temperature conditions during transport.
Ireland is currently chairing the EU Council Working Party on this proposal as part of its Presidency of the EU Council from 1 July to 31 December 2026. In this context Ireland is working to reach a consensus on this proposal on behalf all Member States.
Ireland has chaired three EU Council Working Party meetings on this proposal since our tenure commenced. The Irish Presidency team is treating this file as a matter of priority.

question: Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will consider extending any existing or future fuel support schemes to include hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO), noting that while reliefs have been provided in respect of petrol and diesel, many tractors and agricultural machinery are capable of operating on HVO; whether he has examined the potential environmental and economic benefits of supporting the use of HVO in the agricultural sector.
reply:
My Department has introduced the Fuel Income Support Scheme as a targeted income support to assist farmers and agricultural/forestry contractors facing unprecedented increases in fuel costs.
Separate schemes have been put in place to support fishers and specialist horticultural growers.
The fuel income support is targeted towards farmers and agricultural/forestry contractors who have and will continue to use Marked Gas Oil (MGO), which is the predominant fuel used in the agricultural and forestry sectors at present.
As announced in the Budget, I am pleased to have secured agreement on the extension to the end of this year of the important fuel supports schemes provided for farmers and agricultural contractors, fishermen and women and horticulture producers impacted by higher fuel prices. The allocation of €31.2 million to cover the five months August to December 2026 for these supports will be rapidly implemented by my Department.

I have no plans no plans to amend the eligibility criteria for the scheme at this point to include Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil (HVO).

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether he will consider a report (details supplied) as regards the relationship between State procurement and agricultural emissions, and develop similar proposals.
reply:
The report referenced by the Deputy refers to School Meals. My Department has responsibility for implementing the EU School Scheme in Ireland. The EU School Scheme is implemented in Ireland through the Food Dudes Programme and the School Milk Scheme. The main objective of the Scheme is to increase fruit, vegetables and milk consumption amongst schoolchildren in recognition of the fact that across all Member States children are consuming less than the recommended amounts as per the WHO guidelines.
The EU Commission published proposals in July 2025 to amend Council Regulation (EU) No 1308 of 2013 which provides the basis for the EU School Scheme (School Fruit & Vegetables and Milk). Any future schemes under this Regulation will be informed by the outcome of these discussions.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to outline Ireland's strategy to play a significant role in the development of robotics; and the plans to increase the number of graduates operating in this space.
reply:
The development and adoption of robotics across the economy is a cross-Government matter involving enterprise, innovation and industrial policy. Demand for robotics-related skills is closely linked to broader trends in digitalisation, automation and advanced manufacturing. Research undertaken through the skills forecasting system, including work by the Skills and Labour Market Research Unit and Future Skills Ireland, consistently highlights growing demand for high-level engineering, automation, digital and artificial intelligence (AI) skills across the economy. Recent analysis also points to increasing demand for AI and advanced technology capabilities, reflecting the continuing transformation of industry and workplaces.
Ireland's tertiary education system provides a strong range of programmes relevant to robotics. At undergraduate level, disciplines such as mechatronic engineering, automation engineering, robotics and automation, electronic engineering, computer engineering and related STEM fields are delivered across a number of higher education institutions and technological universities. In addition, specialised postgraduate programmes, including robotics and intelligent manufacturing, support the development of advanced technical expertise. Further Education and Training provision, including through apprenticeships, micro-credentials and upskilling programmes, also contributes to meeting emerging skills needs in this area.

reply:
The Cross Border Directive (CBD) allows public patients to access necessary healthcare, which they would have been entitled to access in the public healthcare service in Ireland, in another EU or EEA country. The patient pays upfront for the treatment and is reimbursed upon return to Ireland.
The HSE is responsible for the operation of the Cross Border Directive and has a dedicated office for that purpose.
The continued growth in use of the scheme has placed additional demands on the HSE CBD office and given rise to a build-up of applications. The increased activity is evidenced by the number of treatments reimbursed increasing by approx. 75% between 2020 and 2024.
It is important that this service operates in a responsive way and that reimbursement applications are processed within a reasonable timeframe. The HSE advises it usually aims to repay patients within 30 working days of receipt of all completed documents. To address this the HSE has advised my Department that additional resources are being assigned to manage this increase in demand with the aim of restoring processing times to expected levels. I have set the HSE a specific target of getting back to the 30-day target by the end of 2026.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to provide an update on efforts being made to support farmers install solar panels.
reply:
The Targeted Agriculture Modernisation Scheme (TAMS) is a demand-led scheme with a defined budgetary allocation and is key scheme in Ireland's CAP Strategic Plan supporting farmers in developing their farm businesses in a sustainable manner.
The budgetary allocation for TAMS 3 is spread across all eleven sub schemes and it is therefore not possible to allocate a budget to each of the eleven schemes individually.
In respect of the TAMS 3 Solar Capital Investment scheme (SCIS) this measure was launched on 22 February 2023. It is supporting farmers to transition to renewable energy sources, reducing dependence on fossil fuel based energy.
The solar scheme is ring fenced with its own investment ceiling of €90,000, and grant aided at the enhanced rate of 60%.
The TAMS Solar Capital Investment Scheme (SCIS) has proved to be very successful with the number of applications and the level of funding provided to date exceeding expectations. To date more than 20% of the total TAMS budget across the eleven TAMS measures is being spent on SCIS.
A total of 3,787 SCIS applications have received approval to proceed with their investment while payments amounting to €39.5 million have already issued to 2,107 farmers.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the work his Department is undertaking to protect Ireland’s native and solitary bee populations; whether it is supporting or engaging with online platforms and citizen-science initiatives that allow the public to record, monitor and support native bee populations; and whether further support for such initiatives is being considered.
reply:
My Department is committed to protecting Ireland’s native bees, including solitary bees, through support for habitat improvement, scientific monitoring and public participation.
A central element of this work is our support for the All-Ireland Pollinator Plan, delivered in partnership with the National Biodiversity Data Centre (NBDC) and other bodies. The new Plan, covering 2026 to 2030, was launched in July. My Department is funding two Farmland Pollinator Officers throughout this period to help farmers implement practical, evidence-based measures. These will contribute to the Plan’s ambition to provide food and shelter for pollinators every 200 meters, particularly benefiting solitary bees with limited foraging ranges.
My Department also supports pollinator habitats through the CAP Strategic Plan. ACRES actions, including planting new hedgerows, establishing grass margins and planting traditional orchards, help provide food and habitats for native bees. Such actions not only support the National Pollinator plan but will contribute to delivery on Ireland Nature Restoration plan.
We have funded the Protecting Farmland Pollinators European Innovation Partnership and the Great Yellow Bumblebee Project. These projects have supported practical conservation on farms and helped develop approaches to improving pollinator habitats.

question: Deputy Noel McCarthy asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to outline the changes, if any, he is considering to the eligibility criteria to the TAMS Scheme.
reply:
The Targeted Agricultural Modernisation Scheme (TAMS 3) is part of Ireland's current CAP Strategic Plan. The scheme provides grants to farmers who wish to invest in building and/or improving a specified range of farm buildings and equipment on their holdings. question: Deputy Martin Kenny asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if his Department has put forward a proposal on the definition of an active farmer as part of the CAP negotiations; and if he will give an update on discussions around the active farmer definition.
reply:
The Irish Presidency has proposed a definition of an “active farmer” as part of the negotiations on the post-2027 Common Agricultural Policy (CAP). The proposal was developed following consultation with each Member State and with the European Commission.
The proposed definition is intended to provide for continuity and consistency with the current approach, allowing Member States flexibility to take account of different farming structures and circumstances.
There has been broad support from Member States for the proposed definition. There are still some issues to be resolved, including in relation to which interventions the definition should apply to, and whether its application should be mandatory or voluntary for Member States.
The Irish Presidency will continue to work with Member States and the European Commission over the coming weeks to resolve these remaining issues, and to develop a definition that will gain the required support among Member States.
In the meantime, negotiations on all aspects of the proposed CAP Regulation are continuing in accordance with the principle that nothing is agreed until everythig is agreed.

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the measures his Department is taking to increase food security in Ireland in view of the huge impact that changes to weather patterns have.
reply:
Ireland is one of the most food secure countries in the world, ranking second of 113 countries assessed for food security in the Global Food Security Index. Furthermore, the most recent Teagasc Sustainability Report finds that Irish dairy, cattle, tillage and sheep farms produce protein sufficient to meet the requirements of over 36 million people (or 30 million people on a net basis).
Nonetheless, recent extreme weather events challenge established assumptions on food security. My Department's Climate Change Sectoral Adaptation Plan (2025 to 2030) provides the strategic framework for strengthening resilience across the agriculture, forestry and seafood sectors. The current plan represents the most comprehensive climate adaptation assessment undertaken to date of climate risks affecting the sectors under the Department's remit and reflects the findings of Ireland's National Climate Change Risk Assessment (NCCRA).
These risks span a wide range of issues including flooding, prolonged wet periods, drought, water availability, animal health and welfare, soil degradation, infrastructure resilience, biosecurity, forestry impacts, coastal change, supply chain disruption and food system resilience.

question: Deputy Danny Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine for updates on the fuel subsidy support schemes.
reply:
My Department has introduced the Fuel Income Support Scheme as a targeted income support to assist farmers and agricultural/forestry contractors facing unprecedented increases in fuel costs.
Separate schemes have been put in place to support fishers and specialist horticultural growers.
Applications under the scheme closed on June 2nd and payments commenced on July 22nd. To date 31,025 applicants have received payments totalling €26.52 million. It is expected that the total final payments under this scheme will be approximately €27 million.
Incomplete payments are due to a number of issues. For certain cases my Department is waiting on further information from applicants to allow them to be set-up on payment systems or a request has been made for further evidence, for example fuel receipts. As information is supplied cases are being cleared and payments will continue to be made on a weekly basis.
As announced in the Budget, I am pleased to have secured agreement on the extension to the end of this year of the important fuel supports schemes provided for farmers and agricultural contractors, fishermen and women and horticulture producers impacted by higher fuel prices. The allocation of €31.2 million to cover the five months August to December 2026 for these supports will be rapidly implemented by my Department.

question: Deputy Tony McCormack asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the progress that has been made in reducing the administrative and regulatory burden on farmers; the further simplification measures that are being considered at national and EU level; and the timeframe for their implementation.
reply:
As President of the AGRIFISH Council during Ireland’s Presidency of the Council of the European Union, I continue to engage actively and constructively in negotiations concerning CAP post-2027 to ensure that the agri-food sector in Ireland and Europe continues to benefit from an ambitious, workable and adequately funded CAP that balances economic, social, and environmental sustainability and underpins food security.
While it is my Department's responsibility to ensure that funding provided by European taxpayers is properly administered, it is also the case that the regulation associated with farming has become increasingly complex and there is scope for simplification of the Common Agricultural Policy.
Farmers need rules that are clear, proportionate and capable of being implemented effectively on the ground. In recent years, simplification of the Common Agricultural Policy has been a key focus for my Department and significant progress has been made on reducing the burden for farmers to-date:
• In 2024, the European Commission introduced changes to the CAP regulations to reduce the administrative burden for farmers. These changes included an exemption from controls and penalties under the CAP conditionality for the 20,000 farmers in Ireland farming on less than ten hectares.

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the measures his Department is taking to address the expected increase in grocery prices towards the end of 2026, given warnings (details supplied) that continued inflation of over 3% will put pressure on food prices.
reply:
As Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine, I have no role in determining or intervening in prices for agri-food commodities at farm gate or retail level.
Ireland's participation in the EU Single Market and Common Agricultural Policy remains the key instrument to ensure the EU’s food security and to support a food system which is economically, socially and environmentally sustainable.
While market prices are a matter between suppliers and buyers, my Department continues to administer support payments via Ireland's CAP Strategic Plan and other supports as required, and continues to monitor developments in agricultural input and output prices on an ongoing basis.
We have also provided signficant supports as part of Budget 2027 to help support critical parts of the food supply chain with increased costs experienced in recent months.
The Central Statistics Office (CSO) reports monthly on the Agricultural Output Price Index, which tracks the prices paid to farmers for their produce, and the Agricultural Input Price Index, which tracks the prices paid by farmers for purchases of goods and services. These prices are sensitive to geopolitical and global economic trends and shocks and have experienced considerable volatility in recent years.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to provide an update on the Protection of the Native Irish Honey Bee Bill 2021; and when the scientific research report issued to his Department in December 2024 will be published.
reply:
The Protection of the Native Irish Honey Bee Bill 2021, a Private Members Bill, which seeks to ban the importation of non-native honey bees is currently before Dáil Éireann, Second Stage. Progression of the Bill through Dáil Éireann is subject to the procedures of the Oireachtas.
Following legal advice in relation to the Protection of the Native Irish Honey Bee Bill 2021, my Department procured independent scientific evidence and in October 2023, a contract was signed with the National University of Ireland, Galway for the provision of research services on the native Irish honey bee (Apis mellifera mellifera).

My Department is currently finalising the overall response to the report and I intend to bring this evaluation to the attention of Government in the near future.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will confirm if fox cub hunting is prohibited under animal welfare regulations; and if he will support a ban on the practice.
reply:
Animal welfare is a key priority for me as Minister and for the Government. My Department has lead policy responsibility within government for animal welfare and takes this matter most seriously.
I am committed to the policy that animal welfare standards are vigorously applied in a fair and even-handed manner and remain committed to the continued robust enforcement of the Animal Health and Welfare Act 2013, which provides a modern framework for regulating and applying standards in the area of animal health and welfare.
On the general matter of hunting, a detailed debate was held during the passage of the Animal Health and Welfare Act 2013 and the Dáil decided to allow the continuation of fox hunting in accordance with an appropriate code of conduct. On 28th May 2025, a Private Members Bill to ban fox hunting was introduced. It proceeded to a second stage reading on 17th December 2025, where it was opposed.
Section 25 of the Animal Health & Welfare Act 2013 allows for the establishment of codes of practice and for the adoption of codes published by other persons for the purposes of providing practical guidance relating to any aspect of the Act, including fox hunting. Voluntary codes of practice have been established by the Hunting Association of Ireland which detail the conduct to be adhered to in respect of the hunting of foxes and the treatment of the animal during the hunt. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 68776/26 of 29 September 2026, which did not address the matters, the date on which officials were asked to examine the confidentiality provisions of the International Protection Acts 2015 and 2026; whether terms of reference were set; whether any paper or submission has been prepared; whether the Attorney General has been consulted; the target date for proposals; and whether the outcome will be published.
reply:
As set out in my replies of 16 September 2026 and 29 September 2026, the principle of confidentiality is a fundamental element of asylum law and is reflected both in the Asylum Procedures Regulation and in domestic legislation, namely the International Protection Act 2015, which applies to applications made before 12 June 2026, and the International Protection Act 2026, which applies to applications made on or after that date.
I have asked my officials to examine this matter with a view to determining whether the provisions of those Acts relating to the publication of information that is likely to lead members of the public to identify a person as an applicant for international protection, without that person's consent, can be amended or clarified to provide greater flexibility regarding what may be reported in the media, particularly in the context of reporting on a person of interest in a criminal investigation.
This examination is ongoing within my Department, with a view to developing a legislative proposal that complies with the Asylum Procedures Regulation, which is binding on Ireland as a matter of EU law, as well as with other international instruments in the field of asylum law to which Ireland is a party.
As regards timing, I have asked my officials to bring forward proposals at an early date.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of the proposal to demolish the old Cork prison on Rathmore Road, Cork; whether a decision has been made following the 84 submissions received by 3 July 2026; whether any alternative sites have been assessed for the proposed expansion of Cork Prison; and he will make a statement on the matter.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 241, 243 and 244 together.
Government has allocated funding for a significant building programme across the prison estate. As part of this, I have secured a record capital investment of €67.9 million for 2026, as part of a total investment of €528 million from 2026 to 2030, of which €495 million is being invested in building projects to increase prison capacity. This reflects the Government’s commitment to increase prison capacity and modernise the estate in line with population growth, with an overall target of delivering over 1,500 spaces by 2031.
The Cork Prison extension is an important element of the prison building programme. The project aims to redevelop the site of the former Cork Prison and provide approximately 330 additional prison spaces, including accommodation for around 100 women and 230 men.
There is a critical need for additional prison accommodation in Cork for people from the county. As of 7 October, 57 prisoners from Cork were being accommodated on mattresses on the floor in Cork Prison. In addition, on 17 June, 16 female prisoners with Cork city/county addresses were being accommodated in Limerick Prison, while a further 34 male prisoners were accommodated in other prisons due to capacity constraints at Cork Prison. The final capacity to be delivered through the project will be determined through the detailed design process, with overall project costs to be confirmed following completion of the construction tender process.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 68475/26 of 29 September 2026, the current ownership of lands at Kilworth, County Cork, transferred from the Department of Defence to his Department in 2006 for the purpose of a new prison; if the lands were transferred back to the Department of Defence or another body, the date and reason; if the lands remain held by his Department or the Irish Prison Service; the reason they were not included in the reply to Parliamentary Question No. 68475/26.
reply:
I am informed by the Irish Prison Service that, between 2006 and 2010, consideration was given to the development of a new prison facility at Kilworth, Co. Cork, on a portion of a larger site owned by the Department of Defence.
As part of this process, the Irish Prison Service commissioned a preliminary assessment of the suitability of the site. This work included a range of surveys and assessments, including in respect of archaeology, flora and fauna, roads and infrastructure, and topography. I am informed that expenditure of approximately €64,000 was incurred in respect of these assessments during 2007 and 2008.
While agreement in principle had been reached regarding the transfer of a portion of the site to the Irish Prison Service, the transfer did not ultimately proceed and the proposed development at Kilworth was not progressed.
Accordingly, no site at Kilworth was transferred to the Irish Prison Service or my Department for the purposes of the proposed prison development, and the project did not proceed.
As the lands were not owned or otherwise held by my Department or by any body and agency under the aegis of my Department, they were not included in the response to Parliamentary Question No. 68475/26.

question: Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if his Department has considered the use of native rare cattle breeds, such as Dexter cattle, for conservation grazing on upland and mountainous areas, including Slievenamon, as a means of reducing excessive vegetation growth and mitigating wildfire risk; and if grants or support schemes are available, or are being considered, to assist farmers and landowners in undertaking such conservation grazing projects.
reply:
My Department recognises the potential role of appropriately managed conservation grazing in maintaining upland habitats, supporting biodiversity and controlling vegetation growth. Appropriate livestock grazing can also reduce the accumulation of combustible vegetation and contribute to mitigating wildfire risk as part of wider land management.
Native rare breeds are an important part of Ireland’s agricultural heritage and a valuable genetic resource. My Department recognises Dexter, Droimeann, Irish Moiled and Kerry cattle as native rare bovine breeds. Each is supported by an approved breeding programme operated by its recognised breed society in accordance with EU Animal Breeding Regulations.
My Department provides annual grants to eligible organisations to assist in conserving Irish rare breed farm animals. These grants support activities such as DNA analysis, promotion and equipment purchase. Funding is also available to organisations under the Genetic Resources Grant Aid Scheme for projects supporting the conservation and sustainable use of genetic resources for food and agriculture.
Hardy, smaller cattle breeds, such as Dexter cattle, may be suitable for conservation grazing where their characteristics match the terrain, vegetation and habitat management objectives. For upland and mountainous areas, including Slievenamon, suitability would need to be assessed locally. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his Department or the Garda National Immigration Bureau operates mechanism to verify that persons subject to a deportation order who state they will leave voluntarily have in fact left the State; if not, the basis on which such departures are recorded.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 236 and 239 together.
It is a central priority for me that Ireland's immigration system is robust and rules-based. Effective enforcement of our immigration laws, including the implementation of deportation orders, is essential to maintaining confidence in the integrity of the system and ensuring that our legislation is applied consistently.
Deportations are often costly and complex to carry out. Consequently, voluntary return is the preferred option wherever possible. My Department operates a voluntary return programme to assist individuals who wish to leave the State before a deportation order is issued. As access to this programme is only available prior to the making of a deportation order, I have increased the resources available to support those who choose to return voluntarily at an earlier stage.
Where a person does not leave the State following the issuance of a deportation order, enforcement action may be required. In recent years, my Department has taken significant steps to strengthen immigration enforcement and increase the number of removals carried out.
The number of deportation orders signed in 2024 (2,403) represented an increase of 180% compared with 2023 (857). In 2025, a total of 4,700 deportation orders were signed, a further increase of 96% on the 2024 figure. As of 2 October 2026, 3,538 deportation orders had been signed.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of addiction counsellors employed by the Irish Prison Service, by institution and by year, from 2020 to date in 2026.
reply:
It is estimated that up to 70% of the prisoner population have addiction issues. To support rehabilitation, reduce reoffending and facilitate successful reintegration into society, people in custody have access to a broad range of clinical and rehabilitative interventions associated with addition need.
A multi-disciplinary, multi-layered approach includes opioid substitution treatment, counselling, harm reduction initiatives, peer-support programmes, psychoeducational services delivered through prison education units, and podcasts provided through the prison television channel. Assessment and intervention is provided by nurses, general practitioners, pharmacists, and psychologists, supported by in-reach addiction counselling services delivered by Merchants Quay Ireland (MQI), Recovery College, and AA and NA meetings.
The treatment and management of addiction is guided by the High-Level Taskforce on Mental Health and Addiction Challenges of Persons Interacting with the Criminal Justice System, the Health Needs Analysis and more recently by a Rapid Evidence Assessment of addiction treatment in prisons internationally. Collectively, these reports and reviews identify opportunities to continue to enhance treatment and support for individuals experiencing addiction difficulties within the criminal justice system improve outcomes for the prison population.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when the Government will ratify and implement OPCAT.
reply:
Ireland ratified the UN Convention against Torture in 2002 and signed the Optional Protocol to the convention (OPCAT) in 2007. The OPCAT obliges signatory states to establish a system of inspections of all places where persons can be detained, to be carried out by inspection bodies to be known as National Preventive Mechanisms.
The Inspection of Places of Detention Bill will provide the legislation necessary for Ireland to ratify the OPCAT. The Bill is on the priority for publication list and my Department is working with the Office of Parliamentary Counsel towards publication in 2026.
The legislation will provide for the designation of a single National Preventive Mechanism (NPM) to visit and inspect all places of detention in the Justice Sector and for Government Ministers in other sectors to appoint appropriate NPMs for any places of detention that may lie within their remit.
The existing post of Inspector of Prisons will be replaced by a new post of Chief Inspector of Places of Detention to take on the role of NPM for the Justice sector to include prisons, Garda stations, the courts and vehicles used for the transport of prisoners by the Irish Prison Service and Gardaí. The new Chief Inspector will have a mandate to monitor a person’s entire journey through detention, from being placed in a Garda vehicle, through their time in a custody (Garda and court), on remand and, if sentenced, into a term of imprisonment.
