reply:
The contract for an Electronic Monitoring pilot was awarded to Allied Universal Electronic Monitoring (AUEM), a company registered in the United Kingdom. They provide electronic tagging and monitoring services across the world and have a number of subsidiary companies.
AUEM were selected through an open procurement competition carried out in accordance with Irish and EU public procurement rules. The company was assessed against the published selection, mandatory and award criteria and was found to be compliant with all mandatory requirements.
My Department is required to conduct procurements in accordance with the principles of equal treatment, transparency, proportionality and non-discrimination, and all tenderers were assessed on the same basis. The contract award decision was made following completion of the evaluation process, including compliance checks and operational product testing of the proposed solution.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he plans to lobby members of the European Parliament prior to a final vote on the Mercosur deal which is expected in 2027.
reply:
The Government has highlighted Ireland’s concerns in relation to the EU-Mercosur Agreement over a number of years, particularly in relation to its potential impact on the beef sector, the strength of its climate and sustainability commitments, and the food safety and environmental standards enforced by Mercosur countries.
The EU-Mercosur Trade Agreement has been applied on a provisional basis since 1st May 2026. While the Council of the EU voted by Qualified Majority Voting to grant authority to the Commission to apply the agreement on a provisional basis, Ireland did not support that vote.
Earlier this year, the European Parliament approved a motion to refer the EU-Mercosur Agreement to the Court of Justice of the European Union. This is now a matter for the Court to consider and, ultimately, to deliver its opinion on whether the EU-Mercosur Interim Trade Agreement and Partnership Agreement comply with EU law.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of confidential reports made to his Department by members of the public for each year from 2020 to date in 2026 with respect to suspected cases of possibly fraudulent or illegitimate claims for social protection payments; and to provide a breakdown of report numbers by payment type for each of the above years.
reply:
Reports from members of the public on their suspicions of social welfare fraud or wrongdoing are an important element in my Department’s overall efforts to prevent and detect fraudulent activity. Suspected fraud can be reported in a variety of ways. The Department provides a dedicated service on its website to enable reports to be made. A concerned member of the public can also write to the Department or telephone with information.
All reports are received on an anonymous and confidential basis. The report received provides a ‘trigger’ for the instigation of a review of a specific entitlement and further investigation may occur if it is considered to be warranted. A payment is not suspended or stopped on the basis of the report received – instead this happens when evidence of wrong-doing has been ascertained by the appropriate scheme area.
The Department is not able to make use of all the information it receives, for example where insufficient information is provided to identify a person or the person might not be in receipt of a social welfare payment. In addition, there are many situations where the information provided about a person may not constitute fraud and may already be known or may be permitted under the terms of a particular scheme.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Social Protection to consider increasing the fuel allowance payable to persons who qualify for it by 30 euro given the increase in fuel prices.
reply:

Also from January 2027, the weekly allowable means of a single person aged 66 or over will be increased from €534 to €653. This is a 20% increase in the allowable means and will allow up to 10,000 single pensioners to qualify for the Fuel Allowance payment.
Fuel Allowance eligibility encompasses 22 qualifying schemes, demonstrating the comprehensive nature of the support available to eligible households. In addition to these qualifying schemes, people over 66 do not need to be in receipt of a payment from this Department to qualify for Fuel Allowance, subject to satisfying the means test through the National Fuel Scheme. Of these, 463,910 households are eligible for the Fuel Allowance scheme, representing approximately 26% of all households nationwide.

question: Deputy George Lawlor asked the Minister for Social Protection the reason an application for an additional needs payment in respect of a child (details supplied) has been rejected by his Department on the basis that the supports urgently needed should be supplied by the HSE; when the child aged five years and four months have been left waiting for some of these services for four years; his views that the benefits of therapy is time sensitive; and if there is any other means available for this child to access these services.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Social Protection whether his Department has plans to review the current means assessment for the working family payment including whether any income from the child support payment should be included in the means assessment.
reply:
The Child Support Payment is a supplement paid on a primary payment to support with the cost of raising children. It is currently paid at a rate of €58 for children under 12 and €78 for children aged 12 and over. Most weekly social welfare payments include a Child Support Payment in respect of each qualified child up to the age of 18, which is extended to encompass older children to age 22 under certain circumstances.
The Working Family Payment is a weekly, tax-free payment available to employees with children. It gives extra financial support to families with children with rates depending on their incomes and family size. The rate of Working Family Payment is determined as 60% of the difference between the household income and the threshold for that family size. A Child Support Payment is not paid as a supplement to the Working Family Payment.
In cases where a family on Working Family Payment is also in receipt of another social welfare payment, the amount of the payment, including any Child Support Payment, is included in the means assessments for Working Family Payment. This ensures that the full household income is considered when determining the rate of Working Family Payment.
The Programme for Government commits to carry out a comprehensive review of means tests across the social welfare system taking into account the Report on Means Testing by the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Social Protection. In line with this commitment, my Department is conducting a review of mean

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Social Protection whether he is able to offer any discretion regarding the allowable time spent in education or training for carers every week, to account for situations such as an individual (details supplied).
reply:
The main income supports for family carers provided by my Department are Carer’s Allowance, Carer’s Benefit, Domiciliary Care Allowance and the Carer’s Support Grant. Spending on these payments is expected to amount to over €2.2 billion in 2026.
To qualify for Carer's Allowance, Carer's Benefit or the Carer's Support Grant, the carer must provide full-time care and attention. A carer is considered to be providing full-time care and attention to a relevant person, where the number of hours providing such care is not less than 35 hours in a period of seven consecutive days, and care is provided on any five days, whether consecutive or not, within a period of seven consecutive days.
While these payments are based on the provision of full-time care and attention by the carer, the statutory qualifying conditions allow carers to engage in work, training or education up to 18.5 hours per week.
The 18.5 hour threshold was increased from 15 hours as part of Budget 2020 following feedback from carers and carer's organisations who found the 15 hours too restrictive. In effect, this allows carers to participate in these activities for half of a full-time working week. During this time, adequate provision must be made for the care of the relevant person.
There are no plans to amend this condition at this time. In setting the relevant threshold, it is essential to balance the needs of the carer and the needs of the person receiving care. The 18.5-hour rule represents a reasonable balance b

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the measures he is taking to simplify systems for making applications to agricultural schemes making them more user friendly for the farmers involved; and his plans to ensure that payments are issued swiftly and without delay.
reply:
Delivery of payments is a key priority for my Department and I fully understand how important they are for every farmer in Ireland.

The Charter not only agrees the dates for payments, but also agrees minimum number of applicants to be paid at commencement of payments. I am pleased to be able to report that so far this year, all targets have been met or exceeded.
Payments under the ANC scheme commenced on the 16th of September and so far this year have paid out €188m to over 88,000 farmers and payments continue on a weekly basis.
Advance payments under the BISS, CRISS and Eco-scheme will issue this year on the 16th of October as agreed at the higher rate of 75% compared to last year following implementation of flexibilities agreed with the EU Commission earlier this year. Balancing payments under these schemes, and payments under other schemes operated by my Department are on schedule for delivery in line with the Farmers’ Charter.
My Department has a culture of continuous improvement when it comes to providing schemes to support farmers, and the systems used to access them.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Social Protection to ensure the substantial rise in the income disregarded for the means testing of carers allowance in 2026, and all subsequent years is abolished.
reply:
Carer’s Allowance is the main income support for carers, with 112,000 people receiving the payment at an estimated cost of over €1.4 billion this year. The primary objective of the payment is to provide an income support to people whose earning capacity is substantially reduced because they cannot work full-time due to their caring responsibilities.
The Programme for Government commits to significantly increasing the income disregards for Carer’s Allowance, with a view to phasing out the means test during the lifetime of this Government.
We are well on our way to achieve this commitment and the changes announced as part of Budget 2027 shows the Government's determination to further deliver to carers.
Budget 2026 is the Government's second Budget, and during that period we have increased the income disregard for single carers by €525 and by €1,050 for carers who part of a couple, an increase of 84%. Since June 2022, changes to the disregards have resulted in cumulative increases of almost 246%.
From July 2026, we increased the weekly income disregard by 60% from €625 to €1,000 for a single person, and from €1,250 to €2,000 for carers who are part of a couple. These disregards are now by far the highest in the social welfare system.
These changes mean that a carer in a two-adult household with an income of €110,000 can retain their full Carer’s Allowance payment and receive a partial payment with a household income up to €139,000. Some 2,700 carers received an increase in their

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Social Protection the financial supports, grants, or exceptional needs payments are available to families caring for an 18-year-old who is terminally ill.
reply:
Families caring for a person who is terminally ill face significant challenges. The Department of Social Protection provides a range of income supports that may be available to support them.
Depending on the individual circumstances of the case, a family caring for an 18-year-old who is terminally ill may qualify for supports including Carer's Allowance, Carer's Benefit and/or the Carer's Support Grant. Expenditure on caring income supports in 2026 is estimated at over €2.2 billion.
Carer's Allowance is a weekly social welfare payment for people who provide full-time care and attention to someone who needs support due to age, disability, or a physical or mental illness. There are currently over 112,000 carers receiving this payment. As part of Budget 2027, the maximum weekly rate of Carer's Allowance will increase by €10 from January 2027. In addition, the weekly income disregards for Carer's Allowance will increase to €1,150 for a single person and €2,300 for a couple, allowing carers to earn more while retaining entitlement to the payment. Under current arrangements, a carer in a two-adult household with an income of €110,000 can retain their full Carer’s Allowance payment and receive a partial payment with a household income up to €139,000. The income thresholds will increase further from July 2027.

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of protected disclosures received by his Department in each of the years 2019 to date in 2026, in tabular form; if an external contractor has been engaged regarding a protected disclosure over that time period; if so, the cost of same; and the number of protected disclosures that were rejected, accepted and that remain under review for the time period in question.
reply:
Details on the number and status of protected disclosures received by my Department in each year from 2019 to 2025 is published in the Department's Protected Disclosures Annual Reports, which are available on my Department's website here: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-housing-local-government-and-heritage/collections/protected-disclosures-annual-reports/.
My Department is fully compliant with the requirements of the Protected Disclosures Act 2014, as amended by the Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 2022. My Department has a protected disclosures policy in place which aims to foster a working environment where employees feel safe and comfortable in raising concerns relating to potential wrongdoing within the department and to provide the necessary supports for those that raise genuine concerns.
The number of Protected Disclosures received by my Department for 2026 to date is three.
In relation to the engagement of external contractors, one external contractor, was engaged in 2022 to review a protected disclosure that had been received in 2021. The total cost incurred by my Department in respect of this review was €2,518.42.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the measures currently in place for the process of local authorities taking in charge housing estates or roads that are not currently in public ownership; and the actions that have been or are being taken in 2026 to address this challenge.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 214 and 216 together.
The legislative process for the taking in charge of housing estates by local authorities is set out in section 180 of the Planning and Development Act 2000. The prescribed process applies to residential developments consisting of two or more dwellings that have been granted planning permission under section 34 of the Act.
Under section 180 (1) of the Act of 2000, the planning authority is obliged to initiate the taking in charge process where requested by either the developer or the majority of owners of the dwellings in the estate in question. This is subject to the development being completed to the satisfaction of the authority and in accordance with the permission and any conditions attached thereto.
To conclude the taking in charge process, where the development has been deemed to have been satisfactorily completed, a local authority is required to make a declaration under section 11 of the Roads Act following a proposal by the executive. The making of such a declaration, which effectively confirms that the authority is prepared to take over responsibility for the ongoing maintenance of the public works elements of the estate, is a reserved function of the elected members of a local authority.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage further to Parliamentary Question No. 65798/26 of 1 October 2026, which stated that a Child Rights Impact Assessment was undertaken in developing the Child and Family Homelessness Action Plan, whether the assessment will be published; if not, the reason.
reply:
Addressing child and family homelessness is a key priority for Government. I recognise that the experience of homelessness for a child goes beyond housing alone and requires a response across Government. Our housing Plan, Delivering Homes, Building Communities, commits to the development of a Child and Family Homelessness Action Plan.
Development of the Plan has brought together key stakeholders to drive the continued focus on preventing children and families entering emergency accommodation, providing enhanced supports for children experiencing homelessness, as well as measures to accelerate exits and reduce the time spent by children and their families in homeless emergency accommodation. As part of its development, a Child Rights Impact Assessment was undertaken to ensure that consideration of children's rights was embedded in the Plan. The Assessment will be published shortly following publication of the Plan.

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to share the link for the national online GIS platform that his Department has developed to map the locations and relevant details of community support centres across the country.
reply:
Following Storm Éowyn, my Department, through the National Directorate for Fire & Emergency Management, undertook a review of the National Emergency Coordination Group (NECG) response. The review was circulated to the Government Task Force on Emergency Planning, chaired by the Department of Defence, and subsequently submitted to Government. The review has since been published and is available on my Department's website.
A key recommendation arising from the review, and a priority for my Department, was the further development of Community Hubs, now known as Community Support Centres (CSCs). In collaboration with the Local Government sector, guidance has been developed to support the identification of suitable premises and the activation of CSCs where required during emergency events.
This approach has already proven effective in practice. Community Support Centres were successfully activated in Donegal following Storm Amy and in Aughrim and Enniscorthy following Storm Chandra, providing practical assistance and support to affected communities.
Community Support Centres serve as an important focal point during emergencies, providing access to essential supports such as phone charging facilities, refreshments, welfare assistance, and reliable, up-to-date information and advice for the public.
To support this initiative nationally, 572 locations have been identified to date as potential Community Support Centres. My Department has developed a national GIS-based platform to map C

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will consider introducing a grace period or flexibility mechanism for self-builders under the temporary development contribution waiver scheme whose homes are currently under construction and well-advanced but face missing the 31 December 2026 completion deadline due to documented trade and construction delays.
reply:
In the first instance, the management and delivery of the development contribution scheme waiver is a matter for the local authorities concerned, and Local Authority officials will determine locally if a waiver applicant has complied with the terms and conditions of the scheme.
On foot of requests received from the Local Government Sector, my Department recently issued guidance to assist with the cessation of the Development Contribution Levy Scheme waiver. For most developments, the submission of a valid Certificate of Compliance on Completion under the Building Control Regulations will provide an indication of dwelling completion but the local authority can also determine an appropriate standard of completion.
The guidance also states that the deadline for the lodgement of a Certificate of Compliance on Completion on the Building Control Management System (BCMS) to comply with the terms and conditions of the waiver scheme will be the 31 December 2026. There is provision for the Building Control Authority to allow for follow-up queries and clarification.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the position regarding any proposals to provide multiannual funding for animal welfare organisations to allow for longer term planning; and his views on whether these organisations are sufficiently funded to deal with their work loads.
reply:
Animal welfare is a key priority for me as Minister and for the Government.
Considerable funding is provided to support, eligible, animal welfare charities, nationwide, through the annual Animal Welfare Grant Programme, which is administered by my Department.
Each year my Department invites eligible animal welfare charities to submit a funding application, under the Animal Welfare Grants Programme. To qualify, applicants must meet specified requirements, which are clearly set out in the application process.
This application process is robust and comprehensive. Applicants are asked to provide information on their activities, including reporting specific data and metrics, with successful applicants allocated funding on the basis of objective criteria which are reviewed on an annual basis.
The awards support a wide range of criteria and can include the numbers of animals assisted, re-homing figures, the provision of education and knowledge sharing to the public on animal welfare and responsible pet ownership, helping to raise animal welfare standards. Veterinary inspection results are also taken into consideration when grant amounts are determined.
In December 2025, I provided funding of almost €6.5 million to 94 animal welfare charities throughout the country, this figure represents the highest allocation of funding awarded under the Animal Welfare grants programme, greatly exceeding the Programme for Government commitment to double the €2.4 million of funding available to anim

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the reason section 28 of the Water Services (No. 2) Act 2013, which provides that pension benefits for ex-local authority staff transferred to Uisce Éireann will be no more and no less favourable than those that would have applied had the employee remained in local authority employment, diverges significantly from the provision for “not less favourable conditions” (details supplied).
reply:
I refer to my reply to Dáil Question No. 74 of 23 September 2026 which sets out the position as it relates to employees who transferred to Uisce Éireann from local authorities.
I have no function in relation to the pension arrangements of the other bodies referred to in the Question.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he plans to extend the first home scheme to second-hand houses.
reply:
The First Home Scheme is a shared equity scheme designed to help bridge the gap between a purchaser’s deposit and mortgage, and the price of their new home, within price ceilings established across the country. First time buyers, Fresh Start applicants and those who wish to build their first home are eligible to apply.
The First Home Scheme Designated Activity Company (DAC) is responsible for the operation and management of the First Home Scheme on behalf of its shareholders - the State, Allied Irish Bank, Bank of Ireland and Permanent TSB.
In relation to the use of the Scheme for second hand homes, the DAC introduced the Tenant Home Purchase Product in April 2023. This Product allows tenants to purchase their current rental property where they have received a Notice of Termination because the landlord is selling the property.

question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the average waiting time currently experienced by applicants under the defective concrete blocks grant scheme for the scheduling and completion of core testing, broken down by local authority area; and if homeowners participating in the defective concrete blocks grant scheme who miss a scheduled core testing appointment are placed at the bottom of the waiting list for testing; if not, the procedures that apply where an appointment is missed, cancelled or requires rescheduling; and whether discretion is exercised in cases involving illness, family emergencies or other exceptional circumstances.
reply:
The Remediation of Dwellings Damaged by the use of Defective Concrete Blocks Act 2022 as amended by the Act of 2025 sets out the framework under which the Grant Scheme which provides grant funding to people whose homes have been affected by Defective Concrete Blocks (DCB) operates.
Under the terms of the Scheme the Housing Agency acts as agent on behalf of the local authorities. Once a home has met the damage threshold for entry to the Scheme, the Housing Agency works with Chartered Engineers from an approved framework to help assess applications. This assessment includes surveys, sampling, testing and the categorisation of dwellings under the Scheme. Based on these evaluations, the Housing Agency then determines the appropriate remediation option and grant amount.
For further information regarding waiting times for core testing and the operational procedures that apply, the Deputy may wish to contact the Housing Agency directly at the specific email address established to deal with queries from public representatives: publicreps@housingagency.ie.

question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage when he expects to introduce the regulations necessary to operationalise the application for review of approved remediation option provided for under section 23 of the Defective Concrete Blocks (Amendment) Act 2025; the reasons for the delay in commencing these provisions; whether a draft of the proposed regulations has been prepared; and the anticipated application process for homeowners seeking a review.
reply:
The Remediation of Dwellings Damaged by the use of Defective Concrete Blocks Act 2022 as amended by the Act of 2025 sets out the framework under which the Grant Scheme which provides grant funding to people whose homes have been affected by Defective Concrete Blocks (DCB) operates.
A number of amendments contained in the Amendment Act of 2025 came into operation on 25 February 2026 and further provisions commenced on 27 May 2026.
Upon commencement of Section 17 of the Act of 2025, homeowners who received a determination under the previous standard (I.S. 465:2018) that is not the demolition of the relevant dwelling and either have not started works or paused works as of 6 November 2024 will be able to apply for a review of the approved remediation option.
Work is ongoing on the drafting of these regulations that will contain the process for homeowners. A commencement date for these provisions will be determined as soon as possible, following which homeowners will be able to submit an application through their designated local authority.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage his views that there should be a moratorium on new solar developments pending the publication of solar farm guidelines.
reply:
In line with commitments in the Programme for Government 2025, my Department is working with the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment (DCEE), which holds policy responsibility for renewable energy matters, in respect of the introduction of a number of National Planning Statements related to Ireland's Climate Action Plan target to increase the share of electricity generated from renewable sources up to 80% in 2030. This includes the preparation of a National Planning Statement for solar energy development.
Further to the commencement of Chapter 3 of Part 3 of the Planning and Development Act 2024 on 2 October 2025, provisions for National Planning Statements have been introduced to replace the provisions for Ministerial guidelines issued under section 28 of the Planning and Development Act 2000. All existing Section 28 guidelines will, over time, be revoked and replaced with new National Planning Statements. Any current section 28 guidelines will however remain in force until revoked or replaced by a corresponding National Planning Statement. The timing of the issuing of National Planning Statements will be based on Government priorities.
In respect of sectoral national planning statements in particular there is also an important role for the relevant policy Department in collaborating with my Department on the development of these National Planning Statements. In that context, my Department is working closely with the DCEE as the Department with policy responsibi

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the reason the national standard operating procedure for the Irish Fire Service is that the fire service do not routinely call An Garda Síochána to every report of a fire they receive.
reply:
The provision of a fire service within its functional area, including the establishment and maintenance of a fire brigade, the assessment of fire cover needs and the provision of fire station infrastructure, is a statutory responsibility of each individual local authority under the Fire Services Acts 1981 & 2003. My Department supports fire authorities through the development of national policy and legislation, the provision of a central training programme, the issuance of operational guidance and support on related matters, and through capital funding for equipment and priority infrastructure projects.
Local authority fire services do not routinely notify or request the attendance of An Garda Síochána for every emergency call received. Garda involvement is generally required only where specific circumstances arise. The attendance of An Garda Síochána is determined in accordance with inter-agency arrangements and based on the operational assessment and professional judgement of the fire service Incident Commander at the scene of an emergency. Such circumstances may include incidents requiring the establishment of safety cordons, the protection of emergency personnel, multi-agency emergency coordination, incidents involving fatalities or serious injuries, suspected criminal activity, or any situation where evidence may need to be preserved.
The Incident Commander has responsibility for assessing conditions at an incident and determining what additional resources may be require

question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the estimated cost of repair works cost in relation to bonfires in each local authority area, in the past 12 months.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 199 and 200 together.
The provision of a fire service in its functional area, including the establishment and maintenance of a fire brigade, the assessment of fire cover needs and the provision of fire station premises, is a statutory function of individual fire authorities under the Fire Services Acts, 1981 & 2003. My Department supports fire authorities through setting general policy, providing a central training programme, issuing guidance on operational and other related matters, and by providing capital funding support for equipment and priority infrastructural projects.
My Department does not receive reports on incidents involving bonfires specifically. However, it does collect annual fire statistics from fire authorities, including information on the locations and causes of fires. These records are published annually as part of the Department's fire and emergency incident statistics and can be accessed at: www.fireireland.ie/fire-safety/fire-statistics/.
The National Directorate for Fire & Emergency Management (NDFEM), within my Department, does not maintain records relating to damage arising from bonfires, associated remediation works, or the costs incurred in undertaking such works. Responsibility for recording any such damage, remediation measures or related expenditure rests with the relevant local authority or other agency with responsibility for the affected area, as appropriate.

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the measures his Department is taking to insulate households from the expected increase in grocery prices towards the end of 2026 and start of 2027, in view of warnings (details supplied) that inflation will put pressure on food prices.
reply:
As Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine, I have no role in determining or intervening in prices for agri-food commodities at farm gate or retail level.
Ireland's participation in the EU Single Market and Common Agricultural Policy remains the key instrument to ensure the EU’s food security and to support a food system which is economically, socially and environmentally sustainable.
While market prices are a matter between suppliers and buyers, my Department continues to administer support payments via Ireland's CAP Strategic Plan and other supports as required, and continues to monitor developments in agricultural input and output prices on an ongoing basis.
We have also provided signficant supports as part of Budget 2027 to help support critical parts of the food supply chain with increased costs experienced in recent months.
The Central Statistics Office (CSO) reports monthly on the Agricultural Output Price Index, which tracks the prices paid to farmers for their produce, and the Agricultural Input Price Index, which tracks the prices paid by farmers for purchases of goods and services. These prices are sensitive to geopolitical and global economic trends and shocks and have experienced considerable volatility in recent years.
I acknowledge the exceptional pressures our primary producers and food business face due to cost increases and moderations in prices received in recent months, while at the same time many consumers are facing higher grocery bills.

These records are published annually as part of the Department's fire and emergency incident statistics and can be accessed at: www.fireireland.ie/fire-safety/fire-statistics/.

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine his views on whether the current forestry programme has been a success; and if he will detail the metrics to support his position, in tabular form.
reply:
The Forestry Programme 2023-2027 is ambitious and was designed to incentivise landowners to engage with tree-planting as part of a diverse landholding enterprise and to support forest owners to manage their forests sustainably.
The 8,000 hectare afforestation target is an ambitious one and I am aware that it has not been reached. However, as the table attached shows, almost 7,000ha of new forests have been created since 2023 and I am confident that these would not have been planted without the afforestation supports offered through the current Forestry Programme.
The Forest Road Scheme has provided grants to forest owners to facilitate the construction of over 215 kilometres of forest roads. The Scheme provides opportunities for forest owners to create and improve access to forests to facilitate maintenance, recreation, harvesting and the monitoring and protection of forests.
Sustainable Forest Management schemes such as the Woodland Improvement and Native Woodland Conservation Schemes continue to offer assistance to existing forest owners.
The Programme also provides a mechanism to support forest owners with the restoration of their forests after adverse events such as disease or storms. Since 2023, site clearance grants have been paid for over 3,200 hectares of forests impacted by ash dieback. reply:

reply:

The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) has advised that the local special educational needs organiser (SENO) is working closely with the student’s family regarding options for school placements and other special education supports for the coming school year.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will intervene in the case of a child (details supplied) without a primary school place following the disallowance of a Section 29 appeal, resulting in significant transport and financial difficulties for the family; and the actions she is taking to secure a suitable school place locally or within a reasonable distance of the family home.
reply:
My department’s main responsibility is to ensure that schools in an area can, between them, cater for all pupils seeking school places in the area.
Parents have the right to choose which school to apply to and where the school has places available for the relevant year, the student should be admitted. However, in schools where there are more applicants than places available, a selection process will be necessary. This selection process and the enrolment policy on which it is based must be non-discriminatory and must be applied fairly in respect of all applicants. However, this may result in some students not obtaining a place in the school of their first choice.
Tusla Education Support Service (TESS) is the agency which can assist parents who are experiencing difficulty in securing a school place for their child. TESS advise the parents to make applications to both local schools and schools outside of their locality.
TESS have advised that the parents may contact the local regional office directly, and they can assist this parent with a referral to the service, from which support will be given regarding same. The contact details for this area are 01 5252166 or by email tess.dml@tusla.ie.

reply:

Under the current terms of the School Transport Schemes, children are eligible for transport at primary level where they reside not less than 3.2 kilometres from and are attending their nearest national school, and at post primary level where they reside not less than 4.8 kilometres from and are attending their nearest post primary school/education centre as determined by the department/Bus Éireann, having regard to ethos and language.
Where a child is eligible for transport and the application and payment process has been completed on time, they will get a seat on a school bus service, where a service is available.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Education and Youth if emergency capital funding will be fast-tracked for a school in County Cavan (details supplied); and if the ongoing plumbing and electrical deterioration caused by severe overcrowding will be addressed.
reply:
The purpose of the Emergency Works Scheme (EWS) is to provide funding specifically for unforeseen emergencies. It does so by ensuring the availability of funding for urgent works to those schools that are in need of resources as a result of an emergency situation.
An emergency is deemed to be a situation which poses an immediate risk to health, life, property, or the environment, which is sudden, unforeseen and requires immediate action, and in the case of a school, if not corrected would prevent the school or part thereof from opening.
The EWS operates on the basis of the minimal scope of works required to remedy an emergency situation. The EWS usually provides an interim solution until such time as a comprehensive solution can be provided under the Summer Works Scheme (SWS).
The purpose of the Climate Action Summer Works Scheme (CASWS) is to enable individual school authorities to undertake small-scale building works on a devolved basis that, ideally, can be carried out during the summer months or at other times that avoid disrupting the operation of the school. The CASWS operates on a multi-annual basis across a number of categories of works.
It is envisaged that approvals in any given year will involve a spread of categories rather than the traditional single category at a time. This is aimed at managing market capacity and maximising value for money opportunities for school authorities.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to provide an update on the implementation of the recommendations contained within the report of the Commission on Generational Renewal in Farming.
reply:
Supporting young farmers and facilitating generational renewal is a priority of mine and critical to ensure a bright future for the agri-food sector. The challenge of generational renewal in farming is widely recognised at both national and EU level. It is important that we have skilled, innovative young farmers coming into the sector to secure a viable and sustainable future for Irish farming. We recognised the need to consider whether existing supports are having the desired effect, and how supports might best be configured for the future. Farm succession is a complex issue and there are many factors that impact farmers’ decisions and that is why the Commission on Generational Renewal in Farming was established.
The Commission adopted an objective, evidence-based approach to examining all the factors involved and engaged closely with stakeholders. They have produced a thorough analysis and have made 31 recommendations across a wide range of areas including CAP Supports; Pensions; Taxation; Access to Finance; Access to Land; Collaborative Arrangements; Advisory Services; Education and Training; Gender Balance; and the Overall Attractiveness of the Sector.

reply:

My Department’s ‘Felling and Reforestation Policy’ document sets out numerous reforestation objectives supported by my Department ranging from Conifer Forest for Wood Production to Reforestation for Biodiversity and Water Protection. Depending on site suitability, a landowner may select the objective which best suits their own management objective. The document also states that permanent forest removal may be considered where there is an over-riding environmental consideration such as protecting habitats and species listed as qualifying interests within Special areas of Conservation or Special Protection Areas.

Action 43 of the Forest Strategy Implementation Plan supports “habitat restoration measures for forests on peatlands based on the best available science”.

reply:
Supporting Irish SMEs to scale and grow remains a key priority for the Government and is a core theme of the Government’s Action Plan on Competitiveness and Productivity.
Scaling SMEs continue to face a structural disadvantage arising from persistent gaps in access to venture capital, scale?up financing and public market liquidity. In 2025, my Department published an economic analysis report titled: Market Demand for and Supply of Scaling Finance in Ireland. That report identified a €1.1 billion funding gap for deals from €3 million and for Series A and later?stage rounds over the next three to four years. The report also highlighted that the small size of equity funds operating in Ireland is the main driver of this gap. This gap contributes to founders selling early or seeking overseas investment, with the risk of businesses relocating and the associated loss of jobs and expertise to the State.

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the number of protected disclosures received by his Department in each of the years 2019 to 2026 to date, in tabular form; if an external contractor has been engaged regarding a protected disclosure over that time period; if so, the cost of same; and the number of protected disclosures that were rejected, accepted and that remain under review for the time period in question.
reply:
The Protected Disclosures Act 2014, www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2014/act/14/enacted/en/html, as amended by the Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 2022, www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2022/act/27/enacted/en/index.html, provides a framework for workers to report relevant wrongdoing and protects them from penalisation for doing so. My Department is committed to providing a clear, accessible and confidential process through which workers can raise concerns, and to ensuring that reports received are assessed and followed up in a fair, proportionate and timely manner and in accordance with the law.
Every report of potential wrongdoing received in the manner prescribed under the Act is considered in line with the provisions of the Act, the Department’s own Policy on Protected Disclosures and the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation’s Statutory Guidelines for public bodies and prescribed persons. Following assessment, reports may be closed, referred to another relevant procedure , or they may require further follow-up or investigation.
Section 22(5) of the Protected Disclosures Act 2014 requires public bodies to provide an annual summary of the number of protected disclosures received during the preceding year, and any actions taken, if any, as a result of those disclosures. All of the reports for the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment are available online at www.enterprise.gov.ie/en/publications/protected-disclosure

reply:

My Department complies with the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation's guidelines for engagements of consultants by the civil service. Contracting authorities must require tenderers to declare that neither their organisation, proposed staff, nor relevant relatives have any actual or potential conflict of interest relating to the contract. question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he intends to advance legislation to afford protection to the native Irish honey bee.
reply:

question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the measures being taken under the Action Plan to Promote Collective Bargaining to address circumstances where workers have chosen trade union representation but an employer declines to engage in collective bargaining or recognise that representation; if he is satisfied that the voluntary framework is sufficient to deliver a meaningful increase in collective bargaining coverage; if specific criteria or benchmarks have been established for assessing the effectiveness of that approach; and if legislation will be considered where voluntary engagement does not deliver progress.
reply:
Under Irish law, workers are free to join and participate in trade unions, and existing industrial relations legislation provides a range of mechanisms, through the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) and the Labour Court, to address disputes where collective bargaining does not take place. Moreover, while employers are not legally required to recognise trade unions for collective bargaining purposes, employees may avail themselves of the statutory industrial relations machinery in circumstances where collective bargaining arrangements are not in place, including the services of the Workplace Relations Commission and the Labour Court.
The agreed Action Plan on Collective Bargaining seeks to address barriers to collective bargaining through a combination of measures rather than through any single mechanism. These include improving the capacity of trade unions and employer representative bodies to engage effectively; promoting awareness and good practice; examining workplace access; reviewing relevant legal protections for workers and trade union representatives; and strengthening the evidence base on collective bargaining coverage. The combined measures in the Action Plan, supported by close engagement with ICTU and Ibec to identify and understand the most significant barriers, have the potential to deliver meaningful and lasting progress. question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if, in the context of the Action Plan to Promote Collective Bargaining 2026–2030, he intends to introduce measures to provide trade unions with reasonable access to workplaces for the purposes of communicating with and representing workers; the current status of discussions with ICTU and Ibec on this matter; the timeframe for their conclusion; and if he will consider legislation should agreement not be reached.
reply:
Ireland's Action Plan to Promote Collective Bargaining, developed through the Labour Employer Economic Forum (LEEF) Technical Sub-Group comprising Department officials, ICTU and Ibec, seeks to strengthen the environment for collective bargaining through a range of practical measures, including ongoing engagement with the social partners on issues relevant to collective bargaining and workplace dialogue.
As part of the implementation process, the issue of workplace access is being considered by the Sub-Group alongside other priority matters under the Plan and those discussions are ongoing. Importantly, the existing Code of Practice on the Duties and Responsibilities of Employee Representatives provides that employee representatives should be granted reasonable access to workplaces where they represent trade union members and where access is necessary to enable them to carry out their representative functions. Consideration of workplace access under the Action Plan will have regard to this existing framework.
Since the launch of the Action Plan, six dedicated meetings have taken place between Department officials, ICTU and Ibec to oversee implementation and consider proposals and actions to support collective bargaining. Engagement on a number of issues remains ongoing and no final position has yet been reached on all measures under consideration.
Implementation of the Action Plan, which runs from 2026 to 2030, is being progressed on a phased basis and is subject to ongoing mon

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he has received representations or data from the CCPC on consumer complaints relating to shelf price labelling where the displayed price applies only to loyalty app members; and whether current price display rules require such conditions to be clearly shown on shelf labels.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 152, 153 and 154 together.
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) is the independent statutory body responsible for enforcing competition and consumer protection law under the remit of my Department. I have consulted the CCPC in relation to the issues raised.
The CCPC is aware of concerns regarding app-based and loyalty scheme pricing models, particularly where some consumers may not have regular access to the internet or do not wish to participate in a loyalty programme.
In general, businesses in Ireland are free to set the prices they charge and may offer discounts to members of loyalty schemes as part of their commercial strategy. There is currently no requirement under competition or consumer protection law for retailers to charge members and non-members of loyalty schemes the same price.
The CCPC notes that some grocery retailers provide a range of options for consumers to participate in loyalty schemes, including smartphone applications and physical loyalty cards.
Retailers must, however, comply with consumer protection law, including requirements to display prices and discounts clearly and accurately. Consumers must be provided with clear and unambiguous pricing information so that they can make informed purchasing decisions, including where a discounted price is conditional on membership of a loyalty scheme.
The CCPC actively monitors compliance with these requirements and takes enforcement action where breaches are

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether there are sufficient protections, safeguards or expectations around how employment permit sponsorship is communicated to migrant workers on time-limited immigration permissions, particularly where a worker may reasonably believe for several months that an application is progressing and is only informed close to the expiry of their permission that the employer will not proceed.
reply:
The employment permits legislation governs the making and assessment of employment permit applications submitted to the Department. Where an employer indicates to an individual that they may support or submit an employment permit application but subsequently decides not to proceed before an application is made, that decision does not fall within the scope of the employment permits legislation.
The circumstances outlined in the question appear to relate to a person who is already present in the State on a time-limited immigration permission which is approaching expiry. The granting, renewal of immigration permissions are matters for the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration. Individuals who have concerns regarding their immigration status should engage with that Department at the earliest opportunity.

reply:

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the timeline for completion of the Whitechurch flood alleviation scheme; if he is aware that some residents have just completed works on their homes almost nine months after the flooding and some are just returning to their homes following the flooding (details supplied).
reply:
The Whitechurch Stream Flood Alleviation Scheme (Whitechurch Stream FAS) is being progressed by South Dublin County Council with funding provided by the Office of Public Works (OPW), as part of the Government's commitment to support the delivery of flood relief schemes under the National Development Plan. The Scheme consists of river bank improvements, flood defence walls, increasing wall heights, the removal or replacement of low-level bridges, and the provision of trash screens. The Scheme is expected to provide flood protection from the Whitechurch Stream for some 52 residential and commercial properties when complete.
The construction of the Whitechurch Stream FAS is being undertaken by the OPW's direct labour force, with approximately 77% of the linear meters of flood defences completed to date. The substantial completion date for the Whitechurch Stream FAS is programmed for the end of 2026. Temporary flood defences will remain in place for the remaining duration of the construction phase, and will be rechecked for effectiveness ahead of all forecast flood events.
South Dublin County Council, that has responsibility for flood emergency response and planning, has advised that it will provide sandbags to local residents for flood mitigation, in advance of any future forecast flood events pending the scheme's completion.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation his views on the use of a system (details supplied) in public procurement; to detail the advantages and challenges; and if he envisions its use in the near future.
reply:
My Department does not currently use agentic AI in public procurement. However, we recognise the potential of AI to improve public service delivery, including procurement processes.
In May 2025, my Department published the Guidelines for the Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Public Service, which support the adoption of AI while emphasising transparency, safety, data protection, and human oversight. Also in May 2025, the Office of Government Procurement, a Division within my Department, updated the Cloud Services Procurement Guidance Note, to include references and high-level guidance relevant to the procurement of AI solutions, solely in the context of cloud services.
The Office of Government Procurement is currently assessing the feasibility of providing AI-specific procurement supports and has completed a pre-market consultation with the AI market as the first step in this process.
The consultation has provided clarity on the market’s position on procuring AI technologies across the public sector, which would, by default, include process supporting AI which could potentially be used in the procurement function.
There is evidence to show that the potential benefits of agentic AI include greater efficiency, reduced administrative burden, improved analysis of data, enhanced process consistency, and better-informed decision-making. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the total legal costs, including solicitors' and counsel fees, incurred by Government Departments and public bodies in defending complaints and proceedings under the Protected Disclosures Acts 2014 to 2022, at the Workplace Relations Commission, the Labour Court and the superior courts, from 2014 to date, by year and by body, in tabular form; if this information is collated centrally; and if not, the reason therefor.
reply:
I thank the Deputy for the question.
The information requested is not held or collated centrally by my Department.
The Protected Disclosures Act 2014, as amended, requires public bodies to report annually on specified information relating to protected disclosures. Information published by public bodies in relation to protected disclosures is available through their annual reporting arrangements and on their respective websites.
The Act does not require the central collection or publication of information on any legal costs, including solicitors' and counsel fees, incurred in defending complaints or proceedings under the Protected Disclosures Act before the Workplace Relations Commission, the Labour Court, or the courts.
Decisions relating to the management of litigation, including whether to defend complaints or proceedings under the Protected Disclosures Act and any associated legal costs are matters for the individual Government Department or public body concerned, having regard to the particular circumstances of each case.

reply:
Section 50 consent under the Arterial Drainage Act 1945, as amended is required from the Commissioners of Public Works in Ireland by bodies proposing to carry out construction or alteration works on bridges and culverts.
A Section 50 application for a proposed project at Ballyhooly Primary Care Centre was received on behalf of Horganlynch Consulting Engineers by the OPW in November 2025. question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to ensure that CAP is adequately funded and that leader is included and adequately funded.
reply:
Discussions on the overall EU budget for the post-2027 CAP form part of negotiations on the broader Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), or EU budget, for 2028–2034. The MFF is negotiated by Finance Ministers and will ultimately be agreed by Heads of State and Government at the European Council.

Member State Agriculture Ministers have been clear that the future CAP must be adequately funded if it is to continue to support viable farm incomes, food production and food security, to contribute to the development of rural areas, and to enable farmers to contribute to environmental and climate objectives.

The CAP budget must be considered in the context of the wider negotiations on the next EU Multiannual Financial Framework. Heads of State and Government must ultimately agree on a balanced outcome across all EU budgetary headings that will support the delivery of CAP and other EU objectives.

LEADER is provided for as a mandatory intervention in the proposed CAP Regulation. This means that Member States will be required to provide support for LEADER under their future plans. Funding for LEADER will be provided from the general National and Regional Partnership Plan (NRPP) allocation, outside the amount ring-fenced for CAP. The level of funding will be determined through the wider funding negotiations during the development of Member State NRP plans.

Ireland's current approach is to build upon the State's existing electronic identification infrastructure comprising SAFE registration and a verified MyGovID account. question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation further to Parliamentary Question No. 352 of 21 October 2025, whether, when his Department commissioned the "Review of MyGovID on eIDAS Level of Assurance" in 2024, it was aware that the firm engaged had worked on the design, delivery and operation of MyGovID; the way in which the independence of the review was assured; and whether any re-evaluation recommended by that review has since been carried out.
reply:
The Office of the Government Chief Information Officer (OGCIO) within my Department commissioned a review of MyGovID's alignment with eIDAS Levels of Assurance following a competitive procurement process conducted in 2023. Four companies were invited to submit quotations for the review.
None of the four companies invited to participate in the procurement process had been involved in the design, delivery or operation of MyGovID. Following an evaluation of the responses received against the criteria established for the competition, Deloitte Belgium was selected to undertake the review.
While MyGovID was originally developed by Deloitte Ireland, Deloitte Belgium had no involvement in the design, delivery or operation of the MyGovID service. The independence of the review was assured through the competitive procurement process and the evaluation of tender submissions against the requirements established for the competition.
The review examined the alignment of MyGovID with the eIDAS framework and made a number of observations and recommendations. The findings of the review have informed the Department's broader consideration of matters relating to digital transformation, digital public services and developments in the area of digital identity.
No separate re-evaluation of the type conducted in 2024 has been commissioned since the completion of that review.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if consideration will be given to including second hand properties as part of the help to buy scheme.
reply:
The Help to Buy (HTB) incentive, is a tax-based scheme to assist first-time purchasers with the deposit they need to buy or build a new house or apartment. It also aims to encourage additional supply of new houses by supporting demand.
HTB provides a refund of Income Tax and Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) paid in Ireland over the previous four years, subject to limits outlined in the legislation.
The level of support available to first time buyers under the HTB scheme, is whichever is the lesser of:
• €35,000 (from Budget 2027); or
• 10 per cent of the purchase price of the new property; or
• the amount of Income Tax and DIRT paid in the four years before application for the relief.
For a property to qualify for the HTB scheme, it must be new or converted for use as a dwelling, having not previously been used as a dwelling. Additionally, the purchase value/approved valuation of the property must not exceed €500,000.
Based on the latest available data (31 August 2026), the scheme has supported over 69,000 individuals or couples to buy or build their own home.
In relation to second-hand properties, an increase in the supply of new housing remains a priority aim of Government policy. The HTB scheme is specifically designed to support the demand for affordable new build homes so as to encourage the construction of an additional supply of such properties.

reply:
Agentic AI is understood as AI systems capable of autonomous multi-step decision-making and action without human intervention at each stage. Revenue has implemented several AI-assisted tools to improve operational efficiency, including services to classify and route taxpayer queries, to simplify access to Tax and Duty Manuals, and to extract key data from documents. All these systems operate under human supervision at every decision point. They assist professional judgment rather than replace it.
Revenue IT systems follow strictly defined business rules underpinned by the appropriate legislative and operational requirements. Revenue has advised me that these systems are designed, developed, tested, scaled, and deployed to match those criteria. AI systems will likely have a role to play in these business processes and if appropriate will be built into business workflows and tested accordingly.
Any such deployment in Revenue collection would constitute a high-risk AI system under the EU Artificial Intelligence Act and would require conformity assessment, human oversight architecture, transparency obligations, and fundamental rights impact assessment.
Revenue continues to monitor international developments in AI capability, including agentic systems, and engages with EU and OECD working groups on responsible AI deployment in tax administration. question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the reason early years educators and school-age childcare practitioners are excluded from Revenue’s flat rate expense allowance registry; the details of any recent reviews conducted by his Department or Revenue into Section 114 of the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997 regarding modernising this registry for low-paid sectors; and if he intends to update the tax code to include early years professionals.
reply:
The flat rate expense (“FRE”) regime is operated by Revenue on an administrative basis where both a specific commonality of expenditure exists across an employment category and the statutory requirement for the tax deduction as set out in section 114 of the TCA 1997 is satisfied, namely, that the expenses are wholly, exclusively and necessarily incurred in the performance of the duties of the office or employment by the employee concerned and that such expenses are not reimbursed by his or her employer.
The FRE regime was established to apply a uniformity of approach to tax deductibility for expenses of large groups of employees and to facilitate ease of administration for both Revenue and employees. The expense should apply to all employees in that category and not be discretionary.
I am informed by Revenue that the FRE regime and individual FREs are kept under review to ensure they remain justified, appropriate to current employment practices and consistent with the statutory requirements for deductibility.
In addition, Revenue advised that it considers FRE applications where a large number of employees incur broadly identical qualifying expenses which are not reimbursed by their employer. Applications are only accepted once they are made by the representative bodies in the employment sectors concerned and are based on the specific commonality of expenses within the employment category and compliance with the strictly applied statutory requirement for a tax deduction.

question: Deputy Denise Mitchell asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will consider the introduction of an 8% Section 481 uplift for all productions filming outside the main production hub within the Dublin Metropolitan Area incorporating Ashford.
reply:
Finance Act 2018 introduced a short-term, tapered regional uplift under the Section 481 Film tax credit for productions being made in areas designated under the State aid regional guidelines (among other criteria).
As the regional uplift was an approved State aid, any restoration of the uplift would require approval from the European Commission. It is worth noting that the Section 481 Film tax credit is explicitly linked to the promotion of Irish or European culture.
While the uplift was not a Regional Aid measure, it operated by reference to the regional aid map in force at the time it was introduced. A new regional aid map, covering a significantly smaller geographic area, came into effect in April 2021; consequently, it is not expected that such an approach would be viable for a future relief to support activities outside the main Dublin production hub.
Since the expiration of the Regional Uplift, Government supports for audio-visual productions have been considerably enhanced and broadened. There are no geographic restrictions on the availability of these supports, so they are available to projects taking place in all regions of the State.
For example, the Scéal Uplift was introduced as part of Finance Act 2024 to provide for an uplift of 8 per cent to the existing Film Tax Credit rate of 32 per cent for small-to-medium sized productions with a maximum qualifying expenditure of €20 million where certain additional cultural criteria are also met. Ireland supports the objectives of the Clean Corporate Vehicles proposal, recognising the significant role that corporate vehicles play in accelerating the uptake of zero emission vehicles and in driving wider market transformation.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of persons held in prison pending deportation in 2025 and 2026 to date; and the median length of that detention.
reply:
A deportation order is a legal order to leave the State. If a person does not remove themselves from the State following the issuance of a deportation order, they will be removed. The enforcement of deportation orders is an operational matter for the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB).
If a person has not complied with their requirement to present to GNIB or has not left the State, they may be detained under Section 5 of the Immigration Act 1999 for up to 56 days for the purpose of ensuring their deportation from the State. An application to extend this period of detention must be made to the District Court. Alternatives to detention are widely used where they are deemed appropriate.
Under the European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015, which transposes the Free Movement Directive (Directive 2004/38/EC) into Irish law, orders can be made for both the removal and exclusion of citizens of the European Union, European Economic Area and Switzerland.
Such orders are made after a full assessment of a person’s individual circumstances and can be made on the grounds of public policy, public security or public health; legally, such orders must not be disproportionate and an individual assessment of factors such as length of residence in the country, integration (e.g. work history), age, health etc. must be carried out.
This year, 3,538 deportation orders have been signed up to 2 October, while 1,809 people have had their departure from the State confirmed.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on Ireland's operation and implementation of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact.
reply:
The International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and came into effect on 12 June 2026.
The Pact provides for a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through greater convergence in asylum practices across the EU, including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for a standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures, and two months for inadmissible cases.
The Department undertook significant preparation prior to commencement, developing and resourcing new processes and procedures to ensure readiness for the new timelines required under the Pact. The new system has been in place for almost four months and is operating as intended.
At the front end of the process, screening, registration and pathway allocation are functioning effectively, with statutory timelines being met and cases successfully channelled into the appropriate procedural pathways. Early data also suggests that screening under the new framework is being successfully operationalised at scale, with 2,427 applicants for international protection commencing screening and 2,113 completing screening between 12 June and 23 September 2026.
The Pact has strengthened our ability to establish identity and assess vulnerabilities at an early stage. Enhanced screening measures, improved document verification capabilities, and more effective use of electronic evidence are supporting more robust and informed decision-maki

question: Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when there will be a roll out of a new youth justice strategy; and the priorities his Department will focus on.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 44 and 75 together.
The Government’s approach to tackling youth offending is primarily through youth diversion and early intervention. The core exchequer and dormant account funding allocation for youth justice measures has almost doubled since 2020, standing at a record €43 million.
The Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027 emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It targets behavioural change so the cycle of offending by young people is broken. It follow operates a graduated response, ranging from diversion to detention. As offending increases in severity, so too does the criminal justice response to address youth crime.
The Government has fulfilled its commitment in the Youth Justice Strategy to ensure the availability of YDPs throughout the State. Every young person in Ireland now has access to a youth diversion service.
An evaluation of the YDPs was commissioned in 2022 and published in June 2023 concluding that YDPs are performing well in many areas that are known to impact positively on reducing crime and reoffending.
There has been an estimated 20% reduction in youth offences referred to An Garda Síochána between 2020 and 2025; with this decrease taking place during a period of population growth in the 12-17 cohort. question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when he expects to publish the draft National Migration and Integration Strategy; and if it will include consideration of an all-island approach to the management of migration.
reply:
The Programme for Government contains a commitment to publish a National Migration and Integration Strategy setting out how the Government intends to respond to the demands and opportunities facing Ireland's society and economy over the next decade.
My Department is currently working collaboratively with a wide range of Government Departments to develop this Strategy, with the aim of publishing Ireland's first overarching, whole-of-government National Migration and Integration Strategy in the coming months.
The scope of the Strategy will include issues such as social impacts, labour market needs, legal pathways, international education and planning for public service provision, including housing, among other migration-related issues. While the Strategy cannot extend beyond matters within the State's control, it will recognise the importance of Irish migration policy accounting for developments elsewhere, including in Northern Ireland and the Common Travel Area generally, as well as migration policy development within the European Union. This is particularly important in protecting the Common Travel Area and ensuring the free movement of citizens between Ireland and the United Kingdom.
To support this work, a Strategic Migration Policy Group (SMPG) was established in December 2024. The Group now comprises ten Government Departments meeting at senior official level.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the categories of harmful and violent material that will be covered by the forthcoming legislation criminalising the possession, production, and distribution of extreme pornography; and to provide an update on the proposed scope of the legislation.
reply:
In July, I secured Government approval to draft legislation to criminalise the possession, production and distribution of extreme or violent pornography, addressing a significant gap in Irish law. Such material is having a harmful impact, particularly on young people, and is distorting healthy sexual development and contributing to misogynistic attitudes.
The proposed offences will criminalise extreme or violent pornographic material, including depictions of rape or violence causing serious harm to a person and depictions of bestiality or necrophilia. It is intended to set out specific categories of such extreme or violent content, which will be defined during the drafting process.
In developing this proposal, my Department has considered a range of sources, including the Resolution 1835 (2011) of the Council of Europe Parliamentary Assembly on violent and extreme pornography and a review of approaches in other jurisdictions. All of these sources have informed development of the proposal to date. The specifics of the approach will be further examined, with the benefit of advice from the Office of the Attorney General. The timeline will depend on completion of drafting, the publication of the Bill and its subsequent passage through the Oireachtas.

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he is aware of work ongoing in the Cork Detention Barracks; the nature of the work; and the amount that has been spent in the past 12-months in the building.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 49 and 72 together.
I am acutely aware of the capacity constraints in our prisons and the challenges faced by those who work and live in our prisons as a result. Since 2024, 292 spaces have been constructed across the prison estate, with 126 delivered in 2024, 106 in 2025 and a further 60 so far in 2026. There are plans to build another 10 spaces in 2026 and 102 in 2027.
In addition, Government has allocated funding for a significant building programme across the prison estate. reply:

Since the commencement of the new system, and as of 2 October, almost 2,400 new certificates (invoices for payment) for legal aid have issued with an approximate total value of €1.25 million in the District Court alone.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the reason he overturned in excess of 500 deportation orders last year.
reply:
