question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether he is aware that local authorities are no longer continuing roles funded on pilot basis due to funding uncertainty.
reply:
Under Section 159 of the Local Government Act 2001, each Chief Executive is responsible for the staffing and organisational arrangements necessary for carrying out the functions of the local authority for which he or she is responsible. It is a matter for each local authority as an entirely independent corporate entity, having full responsibility under law for the performance of their functions and the discharge of their governance and other responsibilities, to determine its own spending priorities, having regard to both locally identified needs and available resources. They receive income from a variety of sources including grants from Central Government, Local Property Tax proceeds, commercial rates and other locally-raised charges.
Where a local authority is implementing a programme or project that is funded by another Government Department, State agency or other external funding body, certain associated delivery costs are ordinarily expected to be met from that funding source. Each public body that seeks to have services delivered through local government should engage directly with the sector to agree service delivery and funding arrangements.
My Department does not fund posts in local authorities unless they relate to programmes specifically under my Department's remit such as housing, planning, etc. The Exchequer provides support for the additional costs associated with public service pay agreements, but not pay support for loca government staff generally.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of referrals for housing first since its inception received by each local authority in the country, in tabular form; the number that were translated into housing allocations following referral; the number of local authorities that have ceased accepting housing first referrals; and the reasons for cessation.
reply:
The Housing First approach to addressing homelessness places direct access to housing first and foremost for vulnerable individuals using homeless services consistently or intermittently over long periods of time, and those unable or resistant to accessing homeless services and who may then become habitual rough sleepers. These individuals often have complex high support needs such as mental or physical health problems, addiction issues or dual diagnosis (the presence of mental ill health and a substance addiction).
Housing for All committed to the further expansion of Housing First. A new National Implementation Plan, which provides for a further 1,319 tenancies covering the period 2022-2026, was published in December 2021. These targets are based on an analysis of need, which involved all key stakeholders and was supported by The Housing Agency. The implementation of the Plan is a joint initiative of my Department, the Department of Health, the Health Service Executive (HSE), the criminal justice sector (the Probation Service and the Irish Prison Service) and Local Authorities, in conjunction with NGO partners. A key initiative under Delivering Homes, Building Communities is the further expansion of the Housing First programme to create 2,000 tenancies to help eliminate long term homelessness.

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether a households (details supplied) income after incapacitated tax credit is applied, is considered assessable income for social housing under the Housing Means Policy 2026.
reply:
Applications for social housing support are assessed by the relevant local authority, in accordance with the eligibility and need criteria set down in section 20 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2009 and the associated Social Housing Assessment Regulations 2011, as amended.
The 2011 Regulations prescribe maximum net income limits for each local authority, in different bands according to the area concerned, with income being defined and assessed according to a standard Household Means Policy. Under the Household Means Policy, the determination of whether a household meets the applicable income limits is based on its net income. Net income is defined as gross income less Income Tax, Universal Social Charge (USC), PRSI and, where applicable, the Additional Superannuation Contribution (ASC).
Accordingly, where a household benefits from an incapacitated tax credit, the effect of that credit is reflected in the calculation of the household's net income through the reduction in income tax liability. The resulting net income is assessed for social housing eligibility purposes under the Household Means Policy.
My Department has been examining the existing income limits in the context of current market and household income conditions, including the suitability or otherwise of the current framework having regard to the significantly changed landscape since the standardised income limits were introduced. question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage when updated guidance will be provided to local authorities on the provision of allotments and community gardens.
reply:
The planning and provision of allotments is supported via the Planning and Development Acts and the Local Government Act 2001 (as amended). These instruments enable local authorities to identify locations in development plans for allotment development, and to establish allotments as a part of local government’s role in promoting the interests of local communities.
Part 3, Chapter 5 ‘Development Plans’ of the Planning and Development Act 2024 commenced on 31 December 2025. When preparing a new development plan under the Act of 2024 planning authorities will be required to prepare a strategy relating to creation, improvement and preservation of sustainable places and communities within their development plans. This includes the reservation of land for use and cultivation as allotments and prescribed community gardens and the regulation, promotion, facilitation or control of the provision of land for that use. All development plans that are currently in place were made under the Planning and Development Act 2000 and planning authorities will, in due course, commence the preparation of new 10 year development plans under the Act of 2024.

question: Deputy David Maxwell asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the implementation of the Memorandum of Understanding between the NPWS and a national organisation (details supplied); to outline the meeting structures are in place to monitor progress; and when the next meeting is due to take place.
reply:
The National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) of my Department is currently undertaking a review of its MOUs as part of a broader assessment of commitments and resource allocation across the organisation and it is expected that this review will be completed by the end of the year.
Pending the outcome of that review, the NPWS continues to engage regularly with the organisation through a range of established channels and stakeholder fora, including the Sustainable Hunting of Wild Birds Stakeholder Forum, which met earlier this week and through the Midland's Mink Eradication Programme, which is a collaboration between the Breeding Waders EIP and the National Association of Regional Game Councils (NARGC) and is supported by the NPWS.

question: Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to review correspondence from a person (details supplied).
reply:

The Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) was established as a quasi-judicial, independent statutory body under the RTA to operate a national tenancy registration system and to facilitate the resolution of disputes between landlords and tenants.
The Residential Tenancies (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 came into effect on 1 March 2026, introducing a new national rent control for tenancies, which limits rent increases to inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI) up to a maximum of 2% per annum pro rata.
Under the RTA, rent reviews for private tenancies may take place every 12 months, or earlier in limited circumstances, with any rent increase restricted. question: Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport his views on a recent media report which suggested a Department of Culture, Communications and Sport proposal on telecoms broadband infrastructure for new homes could add almost €400 million to the cost of building these new homes over the next five years; if he has concerns about the risk of these additional costs impacting the affordability of new homes; if he has engaged with the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport on this proposal; and the measures he has undertaken to ensure that these costs do not materialise.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 168 and 173 together.
The matter referred to by the Deputy relates to the implementation of Article 10 of the EU Gigabit Infrastructure Act (GIA), which requires Member States to establish technical specifications for telecommunications in-building physical infrastructure, fibre wiring in new buildings and buildings undergoing major renovation. The objective of these provisions is to ensure that homes and businesses are "fibre-ready" and capable of accessing high-quality digital connectivity services in the future. This is a requirement arising from directly applicable EU legislation and forms part of wider efforts to reduce the overall cost and complexity of deploying gigabit-capable broadband networks.
My Department recently conducted a public consultation on proposed technical specifications to support the implementation of these requirements. The consultation was undertaken specifically to gather views and evidence from developers, telecommunications operators, planners, and other stakeholders before any final decisions are made. The proposals remain under consideration, and no final standards have been adopted at this stage.
As the consultation process is designed to elicit stakeholder feedback, including views on implementation costs and benefits, it would be premature to draw conclusions regarding the financial implications of any final measures. question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if, in Budget 2027, he will provide accessible and simple funding for public service content on independent radio, which would not involve disproportionate bureaucracy or a requirement to produce content that does not fit current radio schedules.
reply:

The independent radio sector plays an important role in providing valuable public service content to the Irish public, contributing to diversity and a plurality of voices.
So far in 2026, over €7m has been awarded by Coimisiún na Meán to support the commercial radio sector, at a local, regional and national level, through media funding schemes. This includes dedicated ring-fenced funding allocated to the commercial radio sector under the News Reporting scheme. The scheme was designed in consultation with the independent radio sector and provides accessible funding for the production of additional high-quality public service content. Total support for broadcast and media funding schemes is being maintained in Budget 2027.

This should provide the least amount of administrative burden as is practicable, while maintaining appropriate governance and accountability requirements.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he will consider steps to lessen the burden on independent radio due to recent increases in regulatory charges for radio compared to other media and will he make provision for this in Budget 2027.
reply:
There is a long-standing principle that costs of regulation are met by regulated sectors themselves. Therefore, the Broadcasting Act provides for the imposition by Coimisiún na Meán of levies to meet the costs of its full range of statutory functions and duties. Furthermore, the Act vests authority and responsibility for such a levy in Coimisiún na Meán.
As Minister, I do not have a role in approving the proposed income or expenditure of Coimisiún na Meán, or importantly in the setting of the annual levy for any category of regulated entities, including that of sound broadcasting.
I have, however, met Coimisiún na Meán in order to seek clarity regarding their approach to implementing their statutory responsibilities with regard to the levy. It was also an opportunity for me to impress upon them the need to take the opportunity to more clearly communicate such matters to their stakeholders and the wider public, and also consider how the levy can in future be formulated to avoid placing an unnecessary burden on the sector.
I do not intend to replace An Coimisiún’s existing levy income with direct Exchequer funding as I believe that this would run contrary to the long-standing principle that the costs of regulation are met by regulated sectors themselves.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport when applicants can expect to be notified of the outcome of the selection process on the new basic income for arts scheme; when the first payments are expected to reach successful candidates.

This is a major milestone for the arts in Ireland and I am particularly pleased that the research my Department conducted provided Government with a clear evidence base upon which to make that decision.
The deadline for application to the Basic Income for the Arts 2026 - 2029 was 5pm on Tuesday 12th May, with over 10,000 applications received by the deadline.

question: Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of persons diverted by An Garda Síochána to health services under the health diversion scheme since its commencement; the number of Garda members who received specific training on the operation of the scheme prior to its commencement and to date; and the number of occasions on which a person eligible for diversion was not referred.
reply:
The Health Referral Scheme is a health-led response for people who are found in possession of drugs for personal use for the first time. The scheme provides eligible adults with an opportunity to engage with health services at an early stage, receive advice and support and, where appropriate, be referred to further services.
The scheme is now live nationally and is supported by investment in HSE services across all health regions.
The scheme does not legalise drug use but has been introduced as a health-led pathway for eligible first-time personal possession cases, with a focus on early intervention, reducing harm and supporting people to access appropriate services.
All first-time drug offenders must be assessed for suitability for the scheme by the investigating Garda member, in consultation with their Superintendent or an Inspector acting in that capacity. Where a decision is made not to offer a health referral, the rationale for that decision must be clearly recorded and communicated to the person concerned.
It should be noted that the scheme is voluntary. If the person is eligible and consents to partake in the scheme they are referred to the HSE for support. Those referred will receive information and advice on reducing harm and if additional support is needed, the person may be referred to addiction or other health services.
As the scheme has only recently been implemented, the specific data on the numbers referred or partaking in the scheme are not available.

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the number of local authorities that have not continued the Night Time Economy Advisor pilot.
reply:
The Night-Time Economy is an important component in the development of towns and cities, playing a crucial role in economic growth, cultural vibrancy, social vitality, and urban regeneration. The Night-Time Economy pilots were established in nine locations in support of Action 19 in the Report of the Night-Time Economy Taskforce. The Night-Time Advisors are employed by the local authority in the selected locations (Dublin City, Cork City, Limerick City, Galway City, Kilkenny, Sligo, Drogheda, Longford Town and Buncrana). The pilot projects remain a key element in my Department's support for the Night-Time Economy nationwide.
In 2025, the Department commissioned Communiqué International to undertake an independent review of the nine Night-Time Economy pilots, to look critically at the structures involved in supporting the Advisors, the visibility and impact of each in their respective areas, the future roll-out and/or expansion of the pilots and whether a further roll-out is warranted and what needs to be put in place to make this model effective. I have reviewed the recommendations in the Report and recently approved an extension of the pilot until June 2027.
Discussions have now commenced between officials in my Department and local government in relation to the outcomes of the review, and the potential future expansion of the project, with all partners working towards mapping out a pathway forward for a more permanent structure for this valuable initiative.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the expected timeline to sign off and roll out the new Code of Behaviour guidelines for special schools.
reply:
Under section 23 of the Education (Welfare) Act 2000, the Board of Management of each school must prepare and make available a code of behaviour for its students. A code of behaviour specifies the standards of behaviour that shall be observed by each student. The current guidelines to schools on developing a code of behaviour issued from the National Educational Welfare Board in 2008.
The review and updating of the 2008 ‘Developing a code of behaviour guidelines for schools’ is an action in Cineáltas: Action Plan on Bullying. Tusla Education Support Service (TESS) are leading to update the code and to reflect current Department of Education and Youth policies and procedures for schools.
A steering group chaired by TESS was formed and its membership comprised of representatives from the management bodies, unions (teaching and student), parents’ representative body along with officials from my department. A structured systematic consultation processes took place which included children and young people. The updated Code of Behaviour guidelines are nearing finalisation. The rollout of the new Guidelines will be led by TESS and will include supports for schools to assist them in updating their current codes.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth to outline the work she is doing to provide full time behavioural therapists for a school (details supplied); and if work is being undertaken to provide multi-disciplinary teams, comprised of an occupational therapist, speech and language therapist, and psychologist for these schools.
reply:
My department is committed to strengthening access to therapy supports for children and young people with special educational needs through the Education Therapy Service (ETS), delivered by the National Council for Special Education (NCSE). The service provides access to Speech and Language Therapy (SLT) and Occupational Therapy (OT) within school settings, supporting students' communication, participation, independence and learning while also building the capacity of school staff to meet students' needs effectively.
My department recognises that access to therapeutic supports has been a longstanding challenge. Historically, therapy services were provided through the HSE and schools had limited direct access to dedicated educational therapy supports. Following the allocation of funding to establish the ETS, my department has begun building a new model of service delivery from the ground up, representing a significant development in the provision of supports for children with additional needs.
The ETS is currently focused on delivering SLT and OT directly within schools. The service will work closely with school communities, parents and children to maximise participation and engagement in learning and school activities.

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Education and Youth the supports available to young people aged 16 and over seeking a post primary school place, given that the educational welfare service does not support those aged 16 and over.
reply:
Under the Education (Welfare) Act, 2000 Educational Welfare Officers (EWOs) of the Child and Family Agency work with young people and their families who are experiencing difficulty with school attendance. The role of an EWO is to work with parents, children/young people and schools to support attendance at school.
The Education (Welfare) Act, 2000, covers a child who has reached the age of 6 years and who;
has not reached the age of 16 years, or
has not completed 3 years of post-primary education, whichever occurs later.
The Educational Welfare Service (EWS) is a statutory service covering approximately 4,000 schools nationally, both DEIS and non-DEIS, and both primary and post-primary.
The EWS will provide advice to the parents of a child over the age of 16 years who are seeking a post-primary school place. If a parent requires advice at any time, they can contact the local EWS regional office for their area. Contact details are available at the following link: www.tusla.ie/get-in-touch/education-and-welfare/.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether, in light of the Department's promotion of physical activity through the Active School Flag and ‘Run Around the EU’ Challenge, she will commit to instructing schools to discontinue formal school uniforms and adopt comfortable, practical and cost-effective alternatives, including tracksuits or suitable leisurewear, which facilitate physical activity and reduce costs for families.
reply:
As the Deputy is aware, Circular 0032/2017 is currently being reviewed. In addition to a focus on reducing costs for parents, the review is looking at the comfort and sustainability of school uniforms. My officials will continue to engage with the education partners, including the National Parents Council, as we progress this important work.
Ultimately, decisions on school uniforms are a matter for individual schools and Boards of Management. The decision whether to have a uniform in a school is entirely the prerogative of the individual school and my department has no input in this regard.

reply:

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth if consideration has been given to the development of a HIQA type section of the inspectorate in her Department.
reply:
Consideration has not been given to the development of a HIQA-type section in the Inspectorate of my Department. The Inspectorate operates predominantly as an educational evaluation and improvement service, working across Early Learning and Care settings, schools and other centres for education. It provides for quality assurance of the Irish education system experienced by children and young people from birth to eighteen years; and it fulfils an accountability remit and regulatory and compliance functions, as set out in the Education Act 1998 and in the published Inspection Policy (DEY, 2025).
HIQA functions as an independent regulator concerned with safety, statutory compliance and risk in health and social care services. The operational contexts of the two organisations are quite different, and they deliver on their statutory functions differently.
A key driver of quality and standards within the Inspectorate and across schools, settings and centres, is the Inspectorate’s Evaluation Support and Research Unit (ESRU). It designs and publishes the research procedures, standards, survey tools and quality criteria that underpin the Inspectorate’s evaluative and advisory work. This work is research-informed and evidence-based. ESRU draws on the expertise of inspectors in policy support roles to ensure that inspection procedures are based soundly on expert research and latest curriculum developments. question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Education and Youth if consideration could be given to the special circumstances surrounding a school transport issue (details supplied).
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
The National Council for Special Education acts in an advisory role to the Department on the suitability of placements for children with special educational needs. Under the terms of the School Transport Scheme for Children with Special Educational Needs, the Department will consider the report of the Special Education Needs Organiser (SENO). School transport is provided to children with special educational needs who are attending the nearest school to their place of residence that is or can be resourced to meet their educational needs, as identified by the SENO.
The Department and Bus Éireann are very conscious of the specialised nature of transport provision for children with special educational needs. This is reflected in the standard of dedicated service provided and the fact that these services are generally planned and timetabled to operate on a door-to-door basis. In certain cases, the Department also provides funding to schools for the employment of escorts to accompany children whose care and safety needs require this level of support while they travel to and from school.
Given the concerns regarding welfare of children with special educational needs, it is not always practical to make these services available to children who can travel on standard mainstream school transport services as to do so might diminish the level of care and safety

question: Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Education and Youth when a school transport ticket (details supplied) will issue for an eligible student.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
The closing date for on-time applications for the 2026/27 school year was 08 May 2026. While the pupil referred to by the Deputy is eligible for transport under the scheme and applied on time, no payment was received before the deadline. The service is now operating at capacity, and no additional capacity can be added to the route.

question: Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Education and Youth the intervention that is required where a student remains on a reduced timetable while awaiting a recommended special class placement; the way compliance with reduced school day guidelines is monitored; and the ways her Department ensures that a shortage of suitable placements does not result in prolonged loss of teaching time.
reply:
Enabling students with special educational needs to receive an education that meets their needs is a priority for this Government, my Department and the National Council for Special Education (NCSE). The vast majority of students with special educational needs are supported in mainstream schools, while special classes and special schools provide additional supports for students with more complex needs. This approach is guided by the principle of inclusion and supporting students to receive an education in the most appropriate setting for their needs.
The Department's position is that all students should attend school for the full school day wherever possible. Reduced School Days should only be used in exceptional, limited and time-bound circumstances and must not be used as a substitute for an appropriate placement or the supports required to meet a student's needs.
Where a student remains on a Reduced School Day while awaiting a special class placement, schools are encouraged to engage with the NCSE, the National Educational Psychology Service (NEPS) and the Tusla Educational Support Service (TESS) to identify supports that may facilitate full-time attendance. Through data-sharing arrangements between TESS and the NCSE, SENOs are notified when a student with special educational needs commences a Reduced School Day and can work with schools to identify additional supports and interventions.
Compliance with the Reduced School Day Guidelines is monitored through the TESS notifi

question: Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Education and Youth the pathway in place for children with rare genetic syndromes and intellectual disabilities to access appropriate specialist educational placements based on their assessed needs, including where they do not have an autism diagnosis; and whether she will review provision, eligibility criteria and training for schools, NEPS and the NCSE.
reply:
Enabling students with special educational needs to receive an education that meets their needs is a priority for this Government. It is also a key priority for me, my department and for the National Council for Special Education (NCSE).
The vast majority of students with special educational needs are supported to attend mainstream classes with their peers. Where students with more complex needs require additional supports, special class and special school places are provided. This is in keeping with policy on an inclusive education, which promotes that students will be supported to receive an education in the most inclusive setting possible.
My department and the NCSE have sanctioned 587 new special classes for the school year 2026/27, including 70 inclusive special classes. This brings the total number of special classes sanctioned to date to over 4,300. Forward planning has already commenced ahead of the 2027/28 school year.

This circular informs school management and patrons of measures introduced to support forward planning and reiterates the need for parents to inform the NCSE through the Parent Notify process that they are seeking a special educational placement for their child.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she can provide an update on the allocation of the €4 million capital allocation for Youth Affairs for her Department for 2026; if she can provide a timeline for the process including when the calls were issued and deadlines for applying; the number of applications made; and if the full allocation will be used.
reply:
The Department of Education and Youth is committed to supporting the delivery of high-quality youth work and non-formal developmental opportunities to young people.
In this regard, there has been a significant increase in dedicated capital funding for the youth sector which will be aligned with the National Development Plan (NDP) framework. Youth capital funding of €4 million will be available annually to support the youth sector from 2026 to 2030. This annual capital allocation represents a significant increase of €3.5 million on the 2025 allocation and an enhancement on the annual youth capital allocations of recent years.
The 2026 youth capital funding scheme was launched in July and notified to eligible youth organisations and youth services with clear guidance documentation on the operation of the scheme and application process provided. The application deadlines were in August and September, depending on the relevant funding stream.
The €4 million funding available in 2026 will be utilised to support the purchase of essential equipment, upgrades to youth facilities and digital infrastructure for youth organisations and youth services.
The first tranche of capital funding totalling over €1.6m was allocated last week to 158 UBU Your Place Your Space funded organisations to support minor works, equipment purchases and facility upgrades in youth services nationwide. question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which her Department intends to ensure that the NDP allocation for Youth Affairs to 2030 is rolled out in a way that ensures that youth spaces and places are provided, upgraded or expanded; and if she is confident that the funding scheme will be delivered in a way that is accessible to youth organisations in terms of the application process and deadlines to apply and spend the funds.
reply:
The department places a high value on both formal and non-formal education, recognising that youth work provides unique developmental, social and participative opportunities for young people that complement and enhance outcomes achieved through the formal education system.
Youth capital investment of €20 million over the period 2026 to 2030 will support development and sustainability and this funding represents a significant increase on the annual youth capital allocations of recent years.
The NDP Sectoral Investment Plan funding of €20 million for the youth sector was informed by the level and type of demand for capital expenditure within the sector over recent years and with a view to providing more capacity to continue targeted investment in essential upgrades to youth facilities, equipment, and digital infrastructure in a modern youth work environment.
The overarching vision is to ensure that young people have access to safe, inclusive, fit-for-purpose spaces that support meaningful engagement, development, and participation. This framework marks the first time that the youth sector has had clear visibility and certainty regarding capital funding over a multi year period.
Importantly, establishing a defined capital envelope under the NDP provides a predictable basis for planning, allowing the youth sector to prepare projects in a structured and strategic way. It also supports value for money and a coherent long term development of youth facilities nationally.

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Education and Youth the ways that the ETS and CDNT services are designed to work alongside one another in a complimentary fashion.
reply:
As you are aware, in line with the 2025 programme for Government, there is a commitment to introduce a national therapy service in education settings. The Education Plan 2025, which was announced on the 19th of June 2025, confirmed Government approval for the establishment of the Education Therapy Service (ETS).
The ETS is an additional support for children with special education need and has been established as a critical and important support for children and young people in their school environment. It is to supplement and not replace family centred supports provided by existing children’s health and disability services.
The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) ETS and Health services therapists have distinct but complementary roles and will work together, where appropriate, to provide coordinated support for children and young people.
NCSE ETS therapists focus on educationally relevant needs within the school context, while HSE and HSE-funded services continue to provide support within their established scopes of service, including the child and family context. A child or young person may receive support from both services where needs arise across different contexts.
Since the establishment of the ETS work has been ongoing with existing services to ensure alignment and integration with these services. A Health and Education Oversight Group has been established for the ETS. This group provides strategic leadership across both sectors.

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Education and Youth for an update in relation to progress on a new school building (details supplied).
reply:
The brief for the project referred to by the Deputy is to provide a new 16 classroom Special school including the demolition of some existing buildings. It also includes the retention of an extension completed in 2012.
The major building project for the school is currently at an advanced stage of architectural planning – Stage 2(b) Detailed Design, where the Design Team have secured all statutory approvals and are preparing the suite of tender documents.
My Department remains committed to progressing this matter and will make contact in the coming days to arrange a meeting with the School Principal and relevant stakeholders.
St Anne's is one of the 105 prioritised projects to progress to tender on a rolling basis over the course of 2026 and 2027 and within the context of NDP funding parameters. question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Education and Youth her plans to address the teacher shortage in a school (details supplied).
reply:
This Government is committed to ensuring that every child has a positive school experience, with access to qualified and engaged teachers who are dedicated to supporting their learning.
The school referred to by the Deputy is a five-teacher school. The school also has an administrative principal post, as a result of operating two special classes. The staffing arrangements include a provision whereby schools experiencing rapid increases in enrolment can apply for additional permanent mainstream posts, using projected enrolment. The school has been allocated a post on this basis and will retain the post, pending confirmation of enrolment of 141 pupils on 30 September. The staffing process also contains an appeals mechanism for schools to submit a staffing appeal to an independent Primary Staffing Appeals Board. Information and application forms are available in Circular 0025/2026.
Teaching is an attractive profession, and there are a significant number of newly qualified teachers graduating annually. Over 1,800 newly qualified primary teachers registered with the Teaching Council in 2025 and CAO data for 2026 shows a consistent demand for undergraduate ITE programmes. Salaries are competitive, starting at €45,833 and rising to €84,412 under the current pay deal. Few teachers resign, with less than 3% of the teaching workforce resigning or retiring annually from contracted teaching posts.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Education and Youth for an update on the progress of a schools additional special classroom accommodation (details supplied).
reply:
The school referred to by the Deputy was approved to enter the Department’s pipeline of school buildings under the Additional School Accommodation Scheme for a project providing a three-classroom special educational needs base. This project is devolved to the school authority for delivery.
The project is currently at Stage 2b, Detailed Design. During this stage, statutory approvals are obtained and the project design is further progressed to reflect any conditions of planning.
The project remains at Stage 2b. In order for the Department to assess the project's readiness to progress to tender, an updated cost plan is required reflecting any cost implications arising from the planning process and associated planning conditions.
Until this information has been submitted and reviewed by the Department, it is not possible to determine whether the project is ready to progress to tender and, consequently, it is not possible to provide a definitive timeline for the project's advancement. Any progression to the next phase will be subject to the satisfactory review of the required documentation and the project being considered in the context of the prioritisation framework under the National Development Plan.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to Parliamentary Question No. 66822/26, if she will provide a timeline for the establishment of the Workforce Advisory Group; and the timeline that exists for the Strategy to be developed.
reply:
Action 7 in Opportunities for Youth: National Strategy for Youth Work and Related Services 2024-2028 is to produce a Workforce Development Strategy in respect of the youth work sector. This strategy will include consideration of training needs and the requirement for high-quality, accessible and inclusive youth work services and opportunities. Support for youth workers emerged as a strong theme in the consultation with the youth work sector as part of the development for Opportunities for Youth.
In advance of the development of the strategy a consultation with the youth work sector was undertaken and included a survey of the workforce and an employer questionnaire which were followed by 11 in-person and online sector consultations.
It is proposed that the development of the Workforce Development Strategy, will be supported by a workforce advisory group. The exact makeup of this oversight structure is currently being advanced. Engagement with the National Youth Council of Ireland regarding the establishment of the workforce advisory group, including its membership, is underway.
It is proposed that this group, which will include representatives from across the sector, will work with the department to prepare the Workforce Development Strategy and support the implementation of the strategy over the coming years. It is intended that this group will be established and meet this year, at which point a timeline for development of the strategy will be agreed.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to Parliamentary Question No. 66820/26, if the comprehensive scoping exercise of the UBU scheme’s operating processes has been completed; and if the review will be published.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 137 and 138 together.
The UBU Your Place Your Space (UBU) scheme’s operating processes exercise is still ongoing, with further stakeholder suggested administrative improvements in progress. This exercise involves incremental improvements to administrative processes as they arise in the UBU cycle, taking into account feedback gathered, as opposed to a published report.

Engagement with key stakeholders will be an integral part of this work.

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her Department will conduct an audit of community special schools in light of the recent reports of substandard facilities and service.
reply:
This Government is fully committed to supporting students with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this important objective.
The Deputy will be aware that a key focus of the recently published National Development Plan (NDP) investment plan for the education and youth sector is the creation of additional places in special classes and special schools. It also emphasises the critical requirement to maximise the use of existing school accommodation.
The optimisation of existing school capacity is a key aspect of the department’s infrastructure strategy. This supports an inclusive approach, addresses climate objectives and ensures value for money, recognising the many competing demands across the programme. question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she is aware of cohorts of children who may effectively be on a reduced timetable but are not captured by the official data.
reply:
The Department's official Reduced School Day (RSD) data is based on notifications submitted by schools to the Tusla Education Support Service (TESS) in accordance with the Reduced School Day Guidelines.
The Department continues to engage with parents, advocacy groups and representative organisations, including organisations representing Traveller and Roma communities and families of children with special educational needs. Through these engagements, concerns have occasionally been raised regarding students who may not be attending for the full school day despite not appearing in the official Reduced School Day statistics.
For this reason, the Department has strengthened monitoring and reporting arrangements, including enhancements to the TESS reporting portal, engagement with schools, and ongoing collaboration with TESS, the NCSE and NEPS.
Information from inspections, parent questionnaires and engagement with parents and advocacy organisations can also highlight concerns regarding students who may not be accessing their full educational entitlement.
The Department remains particularly concerned where vulnerable students, including students with special educational needs, are not receiving their full educational provision. question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of home tuition applicants, by category of application.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 133 and 134 together.
The Home Tuition Grant Scheme provides funding towards the provision of a compensatory educational service for children who, for a number of specific reasons, are unable to attend school. By its nature, home tuition is intended to be a short-term intervention.
The purpose of the Home Tuition Grant Scheme (Special Education Component) is to provide funding towards the provision of a compensatory educational service for:
(a) Pre-school children with autism who meet the scheme's eligibility criteria;
(b) Children seeking a Special School or Special Class placement;
(c) Students enrolled in schools with a significant medical condition which has caused, and is likely to continue to cause, major disruption to their attendance at school; and
(d) Students enrolled in schools with school phobia and/or associated depression/anxiety which has caused, and is likely to continue to cause, major disruption to their attendance at school.

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will provide an update on a UBU Youth Project (details supplied).
reply:
The Department of Education and Youth is dedicated to enhancing the delivery and development of youth work services and opportunities for young people across the country.
UBU Your Place Your Space (UBU) is the largest youth services scheme funded by the department, targeting young people aged between 10 to 24 who are identified as marginalised, vulnerable and at risk of not flourishing.
The UBU scheme provides funding to 258 targeted youth services across the 16 education and training boards (ETBs) that coordinate delivery of funding to the services in their local ETB areas.
Over €54 million has been allocated to the UBU scheme in 2026.
In Budget 2025, €1.2 million was secured for the establishment of ten new UBU services to provide targeted youth worker-led support for up to an additional 1,000 young people.
Kildare and Wicklow ETB were one of the successful applicants, securing funding to establish a new UBU service in Newbridge Urban and Morristownbiller.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to address the minimum working hours for retail workers (details supplied).
reply:
While the facility to change the existing hours of work of employees is a matter which can be agreed between the employer and the employee, Ireland’s Protection of Employees (Part-Time Work) Act 2001 and the Employment (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2018 provide important provisions to improve job security and working conditions for part-time workers and for employees in precarious or variable-hour roles.
The Protection of Employees (Part-Time Work) Act 2001 is accompanied by a Workplace Relations Commission Code of Practice on Access to Part-Time Work which states that, as far as possible, employers should give consideration to requests by employees to transfer from full-time to part-time work; and requests by employees to transfer from part-time to full-time work-or to increase their working time should the opportunity arise.
The Employment (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2018 is a significant piece of Irish legislation aimed at improving job security and working conditions, particularly for employees in precarious or variable-hour roles. The 2018 Act inserted banded hours provisions into the Organisation of Working Time Act 1997. Under the legislation, employees whose actual hours differ from their contract can request to be placed in a band of weekly hours that reflects their average over the previous 12 months. Employers must respond within 4 weeks and can only refuse under specific conditions.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will consider a review of legislation to ensure there is a statutory right to a minimum bereavement leave.
reply:
There is currently no form of statutory bereavement leave in Ireland. Bereavement leave is normally addressed through employment contracts and can be negotiated between employers and employees when entering into contracts of employment. Employers may also grant bereavement leave at their discretion if their employees suffer the bereavement of close family members.
The introduction of any new form of broad-based employment rights or leave entitlements require careful consideration to ensure that the needs of employees are adequately met and to assess impacts for employers. There is currently no commitment in the Programme for Government to introduce bereavement leave for the loss of a family member.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the estimated annual cost to the Exchequer of reducing the VAT rate on agricultural diesel from 13.5% to 9%.
reply:
The VAT treatment of goods and services is subject to EU VAT law, with which Irish VAT law is obliged to comply. In general, the EU VAT Directive provides that all goods and services are liable to VAT at the standard rate, unless they fall within the categories of goods and services specified in Annex III of the VAT Directive, in respect of which Member States may apply a lower rate of VAT.
Motor fuels are not included in the categories of goods and services for which the EU Directive allows a lower rate of VAT, and so they are generally liable to VAT at the Member State’s standard rate, which in Ireland is currently 23%.
However, the Directive also allows that a Member State may retain a historic VAT treatment that it had in place, subject to certain strict conditions, and on this basis, Ireland continues to apply its reduced VAT rate, currently 13.5%, to the supply of marked gas oil (commonly known as ‘agricultural diesel’ or ‘green diesel’). Under the conditions imposed by the Directive, the rate is ‘parked’, which means that it cannot be reduced below 12%. If a good or service is removed from the parked rate arrangement, it can only be subject to VAT at the standard rate.
Therefore, Ireland does not have scope under EU law to apply its second reduced VAT rate of 9% to agricultural diesel, as proposed by the Deputy. Furthermore, the Directive limits a Member State to having no more than the two reduced rates we already operate, so it would not be possible for Ireland to ap

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if it is proposed to expedite the signing of a double taxation agreement between the Government of Ireland and the Government of Barbados.
reply:
Ireland's long-standing policy has been to expand, maintain, and enhance Ireland's tax treaty network to remove barriers and facilitate trade. Ireland has signed 78 comprehensive tax treaties, of which 75 are currently in effect. Ireland remains open to assess all options to develop its tax treaty network further in that context.
Ireland published a Tax Treaty Policy Statement (https://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/irelands-tax-treaty-policy-statement.pdf) in 2022 and the statement formalises the policy of maintaining and enhancing the network of double tax agreements to provide for continued economic prosperity. The statement also provides the criteria for the creation of a priority list of potential partners.
Priority A jurisdictions for Ireland are the members of the G20. Priority B is to have tax treaties in place with all current OECD member countries and accession countries, as well as EU accession countries. Priority C is to modernise Ireland’s older tax treaties which may not be fully in line with recent treaties and current international norms.
These criteria assist in identifying and prioritising future tax treaty negotiations generally. It is Irish policy that the status of any current or future double tax treaty negotiations remain strictly confidential. Therefore, I am unfortunately unable to update you on the specific status of any current negotiation, or the possible timeframe of any future negotiation.

reply:
The Central Credit Register (CCR) is a database operated by the Central Bank of Ireland under the Credit Reporting Act 2013.
It stores personal and credit information on loans of €500 or more and produces credit reports on request to lenders and borrowers.
Lenders are obliged to report information that is accurate, complete and up to date and the consent of the borrower is not required for this.
Credit information submitted by lenders in respect of loan agreements is held on the CCR for a period of a maximum of five years at any given time.
Where all of the liabilities under a loan agreement have been repaid, written off or discharged, credit information continues to be held on the CCR for a period of five years.
If a borrower defaults or ceases to make repayments and the loan has not been repaid, written off or discharged, then information in respect of that loan agreement may continue to be reported to the CCR.
However, during the COVID-19 pandemic, a range of measures were implemented to support borrowers experiencing payment difficulties.
Borrowers were offered flexible loan repayment arrangements, including payment breaks of up to six months on mortgages and other loans for personal borrowers impacted by COVID-19.
The Central Bank has advised that it worked to ensure that COVID-19-related payment breaks operated in borrowers' best interests and in line with regulatory requirements.

reply:

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether he intends to review the current Capital Acquisitions Tax rules, which provide for differing tax-free thresholds depending on the relationship between a beneficiary and the disponer; the policy rationale for retaining these distinctions; the estimated Exchequer cost of equalising the applicable thresholds; and whether options for reform are being examined as part of preparations for budget 2027.
reply:
Capital Acquisitions Tax (CAT) is a tax which applies to both gifts and inheritances and is charged at a rate of 33%. For CAT purposes, the relationship between the person giving a gift or inheritance and the person who receives it determines the maximum amount, known as the “Group threshold”, below which CAT does not arise. The group thresholds were most recently increased in Budget 2027.
The Group A threshold increased to €420,000 from €400,000. This threshold applies where the beneficiary is a child of the disponer. This includes adopted children, stepchildren and some foster children. Parents may also fall within this threshold where they take an inheritance from a child.
The Group B threshold increased to €44,000 from €44,000. This threshold applies where the beneficiary is a brother, sister, niece, nephew, or lineal ancestor or lineal descendant of the disponer. Following recent changes made to Capital Acquisitions Tax legislation, the Group B threshold also applies to persons who receive gifts and inheritances from the wider family of their foster parents, for example, from their foster siblings, uncles, aunts and grandparents.
The Group C threshold increased to €22,000 from €20,000 with this threshold applying to all other cases.
My Department produced a Tax Strategy Paper that sets out the policy rationale for retaining these distinctions and the estimated cost to of equalising the applicable threshold which is linked here:
https://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/01a7

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Transport whether students resident in the State who attend recognised third-level institutions in Northern Ireland are eligible for a student or young adult TFI Leap card; if not, the rationale for excluding such students, given that students resident in Northern Ireland attending third-level institutions in the State may avail of the scheme; and whether he considers this approach equitable.
reply:

The National Transport Authority has responsibility for the regulation of fares charged to passengers in respect of public transport services provided under public service obligation (PSO) contracts.
Third level students travelling from the South to third level institutions in Northern Ireland can avail of the 50% student/YAC reduction on the proportion of the journey carried out in the South. This means, for example, if 90% of the journey is through the South and the remaining 10% is through Northern Ireland, then the 50% discount will just apply to the 90% of the journey that is carried out within the State. It is also important to note the National Transport Authority (NTA) has statutory responsibility for the regulation and approval of fares on public transport services operated under Public Service Obligation (PSO) contracts, within Ireland only. This includes determining fare structures and available ticket products for eligible passengers, such as those using Student Leap Cards and Young Adult (YAC) Leap Cards, across PSO-funded services.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport if the European Union’s clean corporate vehicle proposal to set binding national targets for the number of electric vehicles in corporate fleets from 2030 is achievable; and if he believes that Ireland will be in the position to achieve the target set out in the European Union’s clean corporate vehicle proposal.
reply:
The proposal on Clean Corporate Vehicles forms part of the European Commission’s Automotive Package, published on 16 December 2025. It is designed to accelerate the transition to zero and low emission corporate fleets, reduce fossil fuel expenditure in road transport and accelerate the availability of zero emission vehicles on the second-hand market.
Ireland supports the objectives of the Clean Corporate Vehicles proposal, recognising the significant role that corporate vehicles play in accelerating the uptake of zero emission vehicles and in driving wider market transformation.
Many Member States, including Ireland, are relying heavily on a rapid transition to deliver on their decarbonisation plans. Ireland’s Climate Action Plan target is to have 30% of the national vehicle fleet be electric by 2030. This is Ireland’s single biggest transport mitigation action up to 2030.
The current Commission proposal includes a 58% minimum 2030 target for the share of zero-emission vehicles among large undertakings, while allowing Member States flexibility regarding the implementation pathway. It is important to note that the measure remains at proposal stage, with negotiations underway at EU level. The Regulation will not be finalised until agreement is reached between the Council and the European Parliament, a process that has not yet concluded.

Discussions have included the operational realities of the transition to electric vehicles and the charging infrastructure required to support the electrification of rental fleets.
The expansion of the charging network is being guided by the National EV Charging Infrastructure Strategy 2026-2028, which is due to be published in the coming weeks. The Strategy outlines the requirements for publicly accessible charging infrastructure capable of meeting user needs and ensuring that charging infrastructure continues to stay ahead of growing demand as more drivers, businesses and fleet operators make the switch to electric vehicles.
This work is supported by the Regional and Local EV Charging Network Plan, which focuses on the rollout of public, destination and neighbourhood charging. A range of infrastructure schemes has also been developed to strengthen the national charging network, including the LDV National Road Grant

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the position of the Government on the European Commission's Savings and Investments Union Strategy and associated proposals, including the Commission's recommendation on savings and investment accounts; whether Ireland has sought or secured an opt out from any element of those proposals.
reply:
Consideration of the proposed Investment Account is taking place in the context of the EU Savings and Investments Union project (SIU). The Savings and Investments Union (SIU) is a flagship project within EU financial services policy. It aims to deepen and further integrate Europe’s capital markets, support growth, and enhance the resilience of the financial system. SIU is the umbrella term for the Capital Market Union and the Banking Union, and it is initiative a key priority for this Commission’s legislative term.
The main aim of SIU is to help European citizens to invest more to ensure that they have better financial outcomes and are better provided for in the future. Furthermore, the project also seeks to deepen the pools of capital that can be made available for investment purposes to ultimately grow the European economy. In March 2025, the European Commission launched the SIU Strategy, which included discrete measures to advance the SIU project. From the outset, Ireland has been a strong supporter of the SIU and its objectives.
Since the publication of the SIU Strategy in March 2025, the European Commission has been active in bringing forward a number of legislative and non-legislative reforms that were announced in the Strategy, including reviews of the Securitisation Framework and the Supplementary Pensions Framework as well as the Market Integration and Supervision Package.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if consideration has been given to the policy of introducing a personal tax credit for people with a disability in employment.
reply:
The Government recognises the significant financial pressures experienced by households with disabilities, particularly amid the heightened cost?of?living conditions of recent years. In response, we have implemented targeted budget measures designed to support those most vulnerable.
When this Government took office, we committed to a step change in the delivery of supports and services for people with disability and their families, in line with our Programme for Government commitments.
There are currently a number of tax measures within the tax system that support people with disabilities and carers, this includes Tax Relief for Health Expenses which provides relief to individuals who have incurred costs in respect of qualifying health expenses and the Blind Person’s Tax Credit, which is available to a blind person or a person who has impaired vision.
There are more than 346,000 people with disabilities in Ireland who are already in work. They are contributing to our economy, supporting their families and communities, and making an enormous contribution to our country.
Recognising there is a significant gap in participation, over the course of the next year, the Government is committed to examining what further measures can be taken to recognise the contribution of those who are already working while doing more to remove the barriers faced by those who want to enter or remain in employment.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the number of individual taxpayers who have paid tax as a result of the so-called "deemed disposal" rule in relation to exchange traded funds in each year since it was introduced; and the total tax revenue generated in each year.
reply:
The information available to Revenue does not allow them to isolate the tax returned due to the deemed disposal rule from other chargeable events which give rise to a tax liability. Chargeable events include:
• the making of relevant payments;
• the redemption of the investment;
• the transfer by an investor of their investment; and
• the ending of an eight-year period following the acquisition of the investment and then every eight years thereafter (deemed disposal).
Therefore, it is not possible to directly identify the tax revenue arising from the application of the deemed disposal rule. This is because investment funds and life companies are not obliged to report the category of chargeable event that the exit tax relates to at the time of making payment to Revenue. Similarly, as respects investments in certain Irish domiciled funds and offshore funds in respect of which investors are required to self-assess tax due, taxpayers are not required to separately report data for each category of chargeable event when filing their tax return.
On the basis of the information available to Revenue work undertaken in the context of Budget 2026, and based on tax paid over the last eight years at the time it was examined, if it was assumed that 100% of tax paid by funds in respect of unit holders, tax paid by life companies in respect of policy holders, and income tax accounted for by individuals in respect of their investments in Irish domiciled funds, offshore funds and life products

reply:
Encouraging retail investment remains a key priority of mine. The Roadmap was published on 31 August.
A key aspect of the Roadmap is the inclusion of key parameters of the proposed new investment account, acknowledging the need for industry to understand how the account is intended to operate. This information is to facilitate the design and introduction of the necessary operational systems by providers, to allow accounts to be available in 2027, with the specific details of the investment account forming part of the normal budgetary process, in October 2026. The intention is to legislate for the account in 2026 and to allow accounts to be offered in 2027.
As mentioned in the Roadmap, the current taxation regime for retail investment, including the deemed disposal rule, will not apply to the new account.
The key features of the proposed investment account are as follows:

• No minimum contribution requirement.
• Maximum annual contribution limit.
• One account per person.
• Eligible investors are Irish resident i

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport If his attention has been drawn to the actions of the French government which has introduced a specific penalty of €100 per tonne for non-compliance with CORSIA offsetting obligations together with the possibility of an operating ban; whether the Government will introduce an equivalent national penalty for non-compliance with CORSIA that is consistent with the excess emissions penalty applicable under the EU ETS, in order to ensure that Irish airlines operate on a level playing field with competitors in other Member States and to support the integrity of multilateral climate action.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 92 and 93 together.
The Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) was adopted by ICAO in 2016 as a global market-based measure to address CO? emissions from international aviation. The scheme requires airlines to offset emissions above an agreed baseline and is being implemented in three phases: a Pilot Phase (2021-2023), Phase I (2024-2026) and Phase II (2027-2035). Participation is voluntary during the first two phases, while from 2027 the scheme will apply more broadly, subject to certain exemptions, including for Least Developed Countries, Small Island Developing States and Landlocked Developing Countries. Ireland, together with all EU Member States, has participated in CORSIA since its commencement. Participation has continued to expand, with 130 States participating in the scheme from 1 January 2026.
CORSIA enters Phase II from 1 January 2027 during which participation will be determined based on 2018 Revenue Tonne Kilometres (RTK) data. As a result, participation is anticipated to expand further to 134 States as Brazil, China, India and the Russian Federation will come into scope for participation.
Within the EU, both CORSIA and the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) are implemented through Directive 2003/87/EC. The EU ETS applies to intra-EEA aviation emissions, while CORSIA applies to eligible international flights between the EEA and participating third countries. The EU has also concluded agreement

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Transport the measures in place to ensure quicker recognition of driving licences of bus and truck drivers from outside the European economic area.
reply:
The exchange of non-EU driving licences is managed through the National Driver Licence Service, the provision of which is delegated under national legislation to the Road Safety Authority. The requirements of the licensing process, including licence exchange, are available on www.ndls.ie.
There are various factors which can affect the time it takes to process licence exchange applications. For example, the applicant may need to submit outstanding information, such as a medical or eyesight report, or the physical driving licence itself in the case of an online application.
The most common reason for delays is in verification of the driving licence by the other licensing authority. However, it is vital, to protect the safety of Irish road users and the integrity of the Irish licensing system, that the validity of a driving licence presented for exchange can be verified.
Neither I nor my officials have any role in the exchange application process. Therefore, I have therefore referred your query regarding the exchange of bus and truck licences to the Authority for direct reply. Please contact my office if a response is not provided within 10 working days.

question: Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Transport the immediate action can be taken to address the frequent lateness and occasional non-operation of the 8:10am service in Whitechurch, County Cork.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport; however, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of public transport. The National Transport Authority (NTA) has statutory responsibility for securing the provision of public passenger transport services nationally and for the scheduling and timetabling of these services in conjunction with the relevant transport operators, in this case, Bus Éireann.
The performance of all public transport operators is monitored by the NTA as part of the contractual arrangements in place between it and the operators. These contractual arrangements allow for not just the monitoring of performance by the NTA and the publication by it of annual performance reports, but importantly, the contracts also allow for the imposition of financial penalties where performance does not meet the required standard.
In light of the NTA and Bus Eireann's responsibility in this area, I have forwarded the Deputy's query to them both for direct reply. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a response within ten working days.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if the impact of these transport challenges on student participation, retention and educational opportunity has been assessed; the measures being considered to support affected students.
reply:

The Strategy highlights the need to address long and unsustainable student commutes through greater integration of accommodation, transport planning and sustainable mobility initiatives. It recognises that excessive commuting can create barriers to accessing and participating in higher education and sets out measures to better understand and address these challenges through improved data collection, coordinated planning and cross-sectoral collaboration.
In particular, the Strategy includes commitments to support higher education institutions (HEIs) in developing sustainable commuting policies, improving understanding of student travel behaviours and strengthening engagement with relevant transport stakeholders. HEIs are encouraged to use data-driven insights to assess student mobility needs and support more efficient and sustainable commuting, while participating in sustainable transport initiatives and promoting active travel and public transport options.

question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the progress that has been made in acquiring lands for a third level institution in Swords County Dublin; if a site has been identified and purchased; and the exact location.
reply:
Dublin and Dún Laoghaire ETB (DDLETB) are currently being supported by SOLAS in developing their Preliminary Business Case for their proposal under the FET College Major Capital Programme.
The site preference for this new college is Swords due to its population base and future growth projections. A site option was previously identified but unfortunately despite the best efforts of DDLETB, they were not able to complete the legal and site due diligence on the site due to a number of issues remaining outstanding including access and site boundaries.
I understand that DDLETB are currently working closely with the Local Authority towards the identification of other sites in the Swords area, suitable for this FET College. A meeting is being arranged this week between my officials, the Local Authority and DDLETB to progress this.
SOLAS and my department will endeavour to continue to support DDLETB in progressing this major capital project which will deliver key FET infrastructure to meet the needs of learners in Fingal and surrounding areas.

reply:

The Strategy notes that lessons were learned following a Short-Term Activation Programme, which provided Government funding to assist in the delivery of around 1,000 new PBSA beds., namely that the cost per bed under the programme indicated a funding level that would be untenable for the State, given the projected requirement of 42,000 addition student beds by 2035.

The programme will assist HEIs in securing additional Purpose-Built Student Accommodation (PBSA) capacity, through private development, delivering accommodation on or near campus via nomination agreements, licensed sites, and site servicing arrangements.

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if his attention has been drawn to the ongoing delays in registration of students at Technological University Dublin following on from issues with result delays earlier this year; and the action that has been taken to resolve this issue.
reply:
Thank you, Deputy, for your question.
I am aware of issues raised earlier this academic year regarding the publication of some examination results and the associated timing of registration for certain students at Technological University Dublin (TU Dublin). However, at this point in time I understand that those issues have been resolved.
As the Deputy will no doubt be aware, TU Dublin is an autonomous higher education institution under the Technological Universities Act 2018 and, as such, is responsible for the management of its academic and administrative affairs, including student registration and the administration of examinations.
Nevertheless, my officials have engaged with the HEA to seek updates from TU Dublin in relation to these matters.
As of 18th September, TU Dublin confirmed 93% of the overall student cohort had been issued an invitation to register (ITR). The University also clarified that students who have not yet received an ITR continue to have full access to the University’s facilities and resources while awaiting the completion of the relevant results and registration processes. Arrangements were also in place to facilitate access to learning materials for students awaiting registration.
My understanding is that registration processes are operating as planned and that students are being registered in line with normal University procedures.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the measures his Department is taking to address the growing affordability crisis facing students in third-level education, particularly in relation to the escalating cost of student accommodation; and the measures his Department intends to make to ensure that young people can access and fully participate in higher education regardless of their financial circumstances.
reply:

In March 2026, I published the National Student Accommodation Strategy 2026-2035, which sets out a pathway to improve access to higher education by addressing accommodation affordability and supply and viability.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science his plans to increase the support for dyslexic students in third level education.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 728, 729 and 730 together.
Under the National Access Plan (NAP) 2022-2028 inclusion and diversity in the student body in Higher Education is a key priority.
The Plan has identified a number of priority-groups who continue to be underrepresented in higher education including students with disabilities.
The Programme for Access to Higher Education (PATH) is the main funding stream that supports the implementation of the NAP. PATH is delivered through five strands that work together to widen participation and support student success, with PATH 4 targeting those with disabilities.
Targets in the NAP for new entrant students with a disability are set at 16% by 2028, and we have reached this at the midterm point of the plan with current figures at 16.3%.
The main source of funding for Students with disabilities is the Fund for Students with Disabilities (FSD) which allocates funding to HEIs for the provision of services and supports to full- and part-time students with disabilities. The FSD provides supports for students with dyslexia, autism and mild general learning difficulties among a wide range of disabilities which are supported by the fund.
The FSD aims to ensure that students with disabilities have the necessary supports and equipment to enable them to access, fully participate in and successfully complete their chosen course of study. In Budget 2026 I increased funding by €1m bringing the total annual fund in higher education to over €10.5m
