question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science his plans to increase the support for students with mild general learning difficulties in third level education.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 728, 729 and 730 together.
Under the National Access Plan (NAP) 2022-2028 inclusion and diversity in the student body in Higher Education is a key priority.
The Plan has identified a number of priority-groups who continue to be underrepresented in higher education including students with disabilities.
The Programme for Access to Higher Education (PATH) is the main funding stream that supports the implementation of the NAP. PATH is delivered through five strands that work together to widen participation and support student success, with PATH 4 targeting those with disabilities.
Targets in the NAP for new entrant students with a disability are set at 16% by 2028, and we have reached this at the midterm point of the plan with current figures at 16.3%.
The main source of funding for Students with disabilities is the Fund for Students with Disabilities (FSD) which allocates funding to HEIs for the provision of services and supports to full- and part-time students with disabilities. The FSD provides supports for students with dyslexia, autism and mild general learning difficulties among a wide range of disabilities which are supported by the fund.
The FSD aims to ensure that students with disabilities have the necessary supports and equipment to enable them to access, fully participate in and successfully complete their chosen course of study. In Budget 2026 I increased funding by €1m bringing the total annual fund in higher education to over €10.5m

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Health whether the free HRT scheme will be extended to cover hormone replacement therapy for patients with congenital or permanent endocrine conditions, including testosterone replacement for Klinefelter syndrome.
reply:
The HSE has statutory responsibility for decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines. This arises from the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013.
Reimbursement is for licenced indications which have been granted marketing authorisation by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) or the Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA). Pharmaceutical companies must apply to the HSE for reimbursement.
Under the Free Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) arrangement, which came into effect on 1 June 2025, where a woman has been prescribed a HRT product on the reimbursement list by her healthcare provider for the purpose of alleviating the symptoms associated with all stages of menopause, the cost of the HRT medications or products, and the dispensing fees will be met by the State.
This measure is intended to support the management of the symptoms of menopause and, therefore, relates to the provision of treatment for a specific medical condition/life stage i.e. menopause. HRT is the most commonly used treatment for managing symptoms of menopause and has shown to be the most effective intervention.
Menopause has been highlighted as a key priority area by the Women’s Health Taskforce. It is a key action in the Women’s Health Action Plans. A number of measures have been implemented in recent years to improve the experience of menopause for women in Ireland, including this HRT arrangement.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Health the action the HSE and HPRA are taking on the current supply shortage of budesonide orodispersible tablets in the State.
reply:
The Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA), as the competent authority in Ireland for coordinating the management of medicine shortages, has advised that it has received no notifications indicating a current supply interruption affecting Jorveza (budesonide orodispersible tablets).
Ireland has a multi-stakeholder Medicines Shortages Framework, operated by the HPRA, through which the Department of Health, the Health Service Executive (HSE), the HPRA and other stakeholders work together to help prevent and mitigate medicine shortages and minimise any impact on patients.
Marketing authorisation holders are required to report actual and anticipated medicine shortages to the HPRA. Where a shortage is reported, details are assessed by the HPRA and published on its publicly available medicines shortages database.
Patients who are experiencing difficulty obtaining their medication should consult their healthcare professional, such as their GP or pharmacist.

reply:
Opening the National Children’s Hospital Ireland (NCHI) is a top priority. Whilst waiting for construction to conclude, there is a significant ongoing programme of work to prepare for the opening of the hospital, involving preparation for operational commissioning, implementation of the EHR, and the integration of current service and staffing in advance of transition.
The National Oversight Group (NOG), chaired by the Secretary General with membership including the HSE CEO, oversees and monitors the progress of the NCHI Project and Programme. The NOG is supported by the HSE Lead Director, with responsibility for reporting on the oversight and co-ordination of the overall programme.
In 2024, the HSE Lead Director commissioned an assurance review of CHI’s operational readiness to commission and commence operations at the NCHI.
The external review contained 13 recommendations, with 45 actions identified by CHI in their Implementation plan in response. The HSE has advised that the majority of the actions contained within the plan have been completed and the remainder have transitioned and continue to be implemented and monitored as part of the ongoing work of the CHI's operational, commissioning, governance and clinical integration workstreams to open the new hospital.
I can assure the Deputy that I am regularly updated on the NCHI Project and Programme.
As this is an operational query I have referred this matter to the HSE.

question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Health the amount of funding allocated towards research into multiple sulfatase deficiency in each of the years of 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form.
reply:
My Department funds health research through the Health Research Board (HRB), the largest funder of health and social care research in the state. The HRB operates through a combination of project and programme grants, capacity building initiatives, collaborative research networks and infrastructure investment. The HRB does not typically issue calls restricted to specific disease conditions but considers submissions from the research community in any and all areas of clinical research, population health sciences and health services and policy research.
Since 2026, the HRB-Health Research Charities Ireland (HRCI) Joint Funding scheme has funded internationally competitive and innovative research in areas of strategic relevance to HRCI-registered research charities. This has proven to be an important funding avenue for rare disease research, with Government investment (via HRB) in this scheme of up to €1M per year. The HRB also facilitate Ireland’s formal participation in the European Rare Diseases Research Alliance, enabling researchers in Ireland to engage with Joint Transnational Calls focused on turning cutting-edge science into tangible benefits for the thirty million Europeans living with a rare disease.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health the steps being taken to protect and expand midwife led continuity of care services, including the Domino scheme and home birth service at Cork University Maternity Hospital, in line with the National Maternity Strategy.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 603 and 695 together.
Maternity care in Ireland is provided in line with the National Maternity Strategy and is built around the principle of woman-centred care.
Care is delivered through three pathways, tailored to the clinical needs and risk profile of each woman and her baby:
- The Supported Care Pathway – for normal-risk pregnancies, led by midwives within a multidisciplinary team.
- The Assisted Care Pathway – for medium-risk pregnancies, or normal-risk pregnancies where obstetric care is chosen.
- The Specialised Care Pathway – for high-risk pregnancies, led by a named consultant obstetrician with midwives and other specialists.
Women are offered a choice of pathways, with a focus on the normalisation of pregnancy and birth, continuity of care, and one-to-one support in labour.
While women’s choice is facilitated wherever possible as patient safety takes priority in the delivery of services.
The DOMINO Scheme is a highly valued scheme offering a midwifery-led model of care for women on the supported care pathway with uncomplicated pregnancies. The DOMINO Scheme at Cork University Maternity Hospital remains operational and available both to women currently using the service and to new patients who meet the eligibility criteria. I understand the concern arising from recent reports of changes to the operation of the Scheme in Cork. question: Deputy Mary Lou McDonald asked the Minister for Health the measures being taken to reduce waiting times for endometriosis assessment and specialist treatment in Ireland.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 686, 687 and 688 together.
On 18 October 2025, I launched the National Framework for the Management of Endometriosis. The Framework sets out for the first time in Ireland a defined clinical pathway for women with endometriosis, which spans primary to secondary care to specialist complex care in tertiary settings.
Developed by the HSE's National Women and Infants Health Programme (NWIHP), the Framework marks the first step in developing a more holistic and comprehensive approach to care for women with endometriosis in Ireland.
Central to the Model of Care is the principle of presumed diagnosis, acknowledging that women are always the most reliable narrators of their own symptoms and pain. The Framework reflects the voices of patient advocates and aims to transform how endometriosis is recognised and treated across the country.
Regional Specialist Centres for moderate cases have been established in the Rotunda Hospital, the Coombe Hospital, and University Hospital Limerick, with clinics under further development in University Hospital Galway and the National Maternity Hospital.
Two supra-regional specialist centres, in Tallaght University Hospital and Cork University Maternity Hospital, have been established for the management of complex cases.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Health if her Department is considering measures aimed at reducing the financial burden on coeliac sufferers who must abide by a gluten free diet.
reply:
The Health Service Executive (HSE) has statutory responsibility for decisions on pricing and reimbursement of medicines and medical items, in accordance with the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013.
In line with the 2013 Act and the national framework agreed with industry, a company must submit an application to the HSE to have a new medicine added to the formal Reimbursement list. In making a relevant reimbursement decision, the HSE is required under the Act to have regard to a number of criteria including efficacy, the health needs of the public, cost effectiveness and potential or actual budget impact.
Gluten-free products were removed from the list of reimbursable items under the General Medical Services (GMS) scheme, with several other products, in September 2012. The marketplace has evolved whereby such products are widely available in supermarkets at a more reasonable price than was historically costed to the State when they were available in pharmacies through the statutory schemes, and without incurring the further extra costs of a dispensing fee. There are currently no plans to reinstate these products on the list of reimbursable items under the GMS and other community drug schemes.
Patients can claim tax relief for certain food products if they have specific dietary requirements due to a medical condition. This applies to persons with coeliac disease where they require gluten free foods specifically manufactured to be gluten free.

question: Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Health the advice that she can provide to a person (details supplied) resident in Monaghan who has contacted every GP in the county and has been unable to register with a GP for them and their child.
reply:
GPs are private practitioners, most of whom hold a GMS contract with the HSE for the provision of GP services without charge to medical card and GP visit card holders. Eligibility for a medical card, or a GP visit card for those aged between 8 and 69 years of age, is primarily based on means testing. All children under 8 years of age and all those aged 70 years and over are eligible for a GP visit card.
Where a person that holds a medical card or GP visit card, or a person eligible for either card, experiences difficulty in finding a GP to accept them as a patient, the person concerned having unsuccessfully applied to at least three GPs in the area (or fewer if there are fewer GPs in the area) can apply to the HSE Eligibility Unit which has the power to assign a GMS patient to a GP's GMS patient list, in accordance with the GMS contract. Likewise, a parent on behalf of an eligible child who experiences difficulty in finding a GP that will accept their child as a patient can apply to the HSE Eligibility Unit also.
People who do not hold a medical card or GP visit card access GP services on a private basis and can make enquiries directly to any GP practice they wish to register with. As private practitioners, it is a matter for each individual GP to decide whether to accept additional private patients.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Health the total capital expenditure incurred by the HSE and her Department on the development of day-surgery centres and elective hospitals in each year from 2020 to date, by site; the estimated final project cost for each completed, active and planned facility; and the expected opening date of each facility.
reply:
Since its approval by Government in December 2021, the Elective Ambulatory Care Programme has been evolving to ensure that medium term demand and capacity for elective day-case care can be met through the delivery of a national network of nine Surgical Hubs in the first instance, while also planning for future elective care capacity requirements through a national network of Elective Treatment Centres (ETCs), also known as Elective Hospitals, in Cork, Galway and Dublin.
Four Surgical Hubs are now operational in Tallaght (the Reeves Centre), South Dublin (Mt Carmel), North Dublin (Swords) and Cork, with Hubs at Waterford, Limerick and Galway due to open in the coming months. Plans are also advancing for Surgical Hubs in Sligo and Letterkenny. Together these nine Hubs will provide significant additional elective care capacity across the country, including 30 day-case theatres, 16 minor operations theatres, and 38 outpatient diagnostic/treatment rooms, and will help drive down waiting times for elective day-case care.
The Elective Treatment Centres, also known as Elective Hospitals, are being developed to meet the longer term elective care needs of the country. Locations identified are in Cork (at St Stephen’s Hospital, Glanmire), Galway (Merlin Park) and Dublin (emerging preferred sites previously identified at Connolly Hospital in Blanchardstown and at Crumlin-Children’s Health Ireland). The HSE is continuing to progress the detailed design works for the ETCs in Cork and Galwa

Clinical and cost-effectiveness assessments are carried out after a company submits a pricing and reimbursement application to the HSE. As such no such assessment has been carried out.

On the 21st of May, The Diabetes Policy and Services Review: A Strategy for Better Care was launched by the Minister for Health.

The strategy marks a major milestone in diabetes care in Ireland, representing the development of a unified approach to the delivery of diabetes care.

question: Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Health if the MCAP review has commenced; if stakeholders have been appointed to the review group; and the length of time the review is expected to take once it begins.
reply:
On 1st April 2026, Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill formally appointed Professor Shane Allwright to chair the Review Group.
The Group will:
- Review the current operation of the Medical Cannabis Access Programme and the availability of Schedule 2 Cannabis products.
- Examine the appropriateness to expand the range of conditions covered by the programme, where sufficient evidence exists that cannabis may prove beneficial.
- Review the current access to Schedule 1 Cannabis products and the current operation of the ministerial licence.
- Develop a national policy on access to, and the administration of cannabis products that are subject to ministerial licence.
The Review Group is comprised of a wide range of medical specialists and experts including patient representatives.
The timeline for completing the “Review of Access to Cannabis for Medical Use” which also evaluates the Medical Cannabis Access Programme (MCAP) is anticipated to be in the region of 12 months from the date of the group's initial meeting which took place on 27th May 2026.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Health the way in which the suspension of the DOMINO scheme at Cork University Maternity Hospital is consistent with the supported care pathway under the National Maternity Strategy 2016–2026; and whether the successor to that strategy will commit to protecting and expanding midwife-led continuity of care schemes.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 603 and 695 together.
Maternity care in Ireland is provided in line with the National Maternity Strategy and is built around the principle of woman-centred care.
Care is delivered through three pathways, tailored to the clinical needs and risk profile of each woman and her baby:
- The Supported Care Pathway – for normal-risk pregnancies, led by midwives within a multidisciplinary team.
- The Assisted Care Pathway – for medium-risk pregnancies, or normal-risk pregnancies where obstetric care is chosen.
- The Specialised Care Pathway – for high-risk pregnancies, led by a named consultant obstetrician with midwives and other specialists.
Women are offered a choice of pathways, with a focus on the normalisation of pregnancy and birth, continuity of care, and one-to-one support in labour.
While women’s choice is facilitated wherever possible as patient safety takes priority in the delivery of services.
The DOMINO Scheme is a highly valued scheme offering a midwifery-led model of care for women on the supported care pathway with uncomplicated pregnancies. The DOMINO Scheme at Cork University Maternity Hospital remains operational and available both to women currently using the service and to new patients who meet the eligibility criteria. I understand the concern arising from recent reports of changes to the operation of the Scheme in Cork. reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 595 and 664 together.

Clinical and cost-effectiveness assessments are carried out after a company submits a pricing and reimbursement application to the HSE. As such no such assessment has been carried out.

question: Deputy Noel McCarthy asked the Minister for Health to outline the measures being taken to reduce delays in the repayment of applications under the Cross Border Directive.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 544 and 594 together.
The Cross Border Directive allows public patients to access necessary healthcare, which they would have been entitled to access in the public healthcare service in Ireland, in another EU or EEA country. The patient pays upfront for the treatment and is reimbursed upon return to Ireland.
The HSE is responsible for the operation of the cross-border directive and has a dedicated office for that purpose.
The continued growth in use of the scheme has placed additional demands on the HSE CBD office and given rise to a build-up of applications. The increased activity is evidenced by the number of treatments reimbursed increasing by approx. 75% between 2020 and 2024.
It is important that this service operates in a responsive way and that reimbursement applications are processed within a reasonable timeframe. The HSE advises it usually aims to repay patients within 30 working days of receipt of all completed documents. The HSE advise the CBD office is currently (as of 2 September 2026) processing applications received at the end of February 2026. A 6-month delay for reimbursement is clearly unacceptable. To address this the HSE has advised my Department that additional resources are being assigned to manage this increase in demand with the aim of restoring processing times to expected levels. I have set the HSE a specific target of getting back to the 30-day target by the end of 2026.

question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Health for an update on the proposed prohibition on the sale of high-caffeine energy drinks to children under 16 years of age.
reply:
Stimulant drinks, commonly known as energy drinks, are often marketed as products that improve energy, focus and performance. However, many contain high levels of caffeine and sugar and may have negative effects on health, particularly for children and young people.
In September 2026, Safefood published its report, A survey of energy drinks on the island of Ireland 2026. The report found high levels of energy drink consumption among young people, with more than half of 15 to 24-year-olds reporting that they consume energy drinks at least once a week. The report also found strong public support for restrictions on the sale of energy drinks to children, with more than three-quarters of adults supporting the introduction of a legal age restriction.
The Government recognises the public health concerns associated with the consumption of high-caffeine energy drinks by children and young people. The Department of Health is considering the findings of the Safefood report and other available evidence in relation to possible measures to reduce children's access to these products. This issue is also being considered in the context of the forthcoming Obesity Policy and Action Plan and its focus on creating healthier food environments and supporting healthier choices for children and young people.
Any proposal to introduce restrictions on the sale of high-caffeine energy drinks would require careful consideration of the public health benefits, regulatory implications and enforcement arran

question: Deputy Marie Sherlock asked the Minister for Health the current status of the Rotunda Maternity Hospital capital project; and the timeline for progressing this project.
reply:
This Government is committed to driving improvements across maternity services including continued investment in the Rotunda Hospital, Dublin.
The Minister for Health was deeply disappointed by the decision of An Coimisiún Pleanála (ACP) to overturn the position of Dublin City Council and refuse planning permission for the proposed Critical Care Wing at the Rotunda.
The planned development at Parnell Square West is necessary to provide essential upgrades to the Rotunda that are needed now and includes capital developments to manage the current and future needs of women and babies.
The Minister met with the Master of the Rotunda and agreed that a new planning application will be submitted by the Rotunda.
The application will also include critical care capacity for women, expanding on the earlier application, which was focused solely on infants, and will also include provision for an enhanced Sexual Assault Treatment Unit.
The Rotunda and HSE are preparing a pre-application submission which will facilitate the direct application of planning permission to ACP. This process is in line with the requirements of the Planning and Development Act 2000.
The Minister’s priority is to ensure the delivery of appropriate neonatal and critical care capacity for the Rotunda as quickly as possible.

question: Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Health to provide an update on plans to make the shingles vaccine free for people aged over 65.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 546 and 583 together.
The immunisation programme in Ireland is informed by the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). NIAC considers the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland as well as international best practice in relation to immunisation when developing its advice
The current NIAC guidelines state that the shingles vaccine may be considered for those aged 65 years and older, due to the greater burden and severity of disease in this age group and in those aged 18 years and older at increased risk of shingles.
The Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA) has carried out a Health Technology Assessment (HTA) on the herpes zoster vaccine which protects against shingles. A HTA is a multidisciplinary research process that collects and summarises information about a health technology. HIQA’s HTA examined the evidence on the clinical effectiveness and safety of shingles vaccines. The cost effectiveness and budget impact were also reviewed, along with the ethical, social and organisational implications of including the vaccine in the adult immunisation schedule.
HIQA published this HTA on 19 July 2024. The HTA found that adding the shingles vaccine to the routine immunisation schedule, at the vaccine price at the time, for all adults aged 65 years and over would not be cost effective and would be associated with a substantial budget impact.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Health if she is aware that the European Commission granted marketing authorisation on 15 July 2026 for jascayd (nerandomilast); if an application for reimbursement has been received by the HSE and/or the National Centre for Pharmacoeconomics (NCPE); the current status of any assessment, pricing negotiations or reimbursement consideration; the anticipated timeline for completion of these processes; and if she will consider measures to expedite access to this treatment for patients.
reply:
The Government is committed to investing in new medicines. Supported by €158 million of funding in Budgets 2021-2025, the State delivered access to 250 new medicines. 70 of these were for rare diseases. Budget 2026 allocated €217 million additional investment in medicines, including €30 million in funding for new medicines. This has, as of August 2026, delivered access to 30 new medicines, including 7 for rare diseases.
The Health Service Executive (HSE) has statutory responsibility for decisions on pricing and reimbursement of medicines, in accordance with the provisions of the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013. The Minister has no role in decisions on pricing and reimbursement.
The HSE robustly assesses applications for pricing and reimbursement to make sure that it can stretch available resources as far as possible and to deliver the best value in relation to each medicine and ultimately more medicines to Irish citizens and patients.
There are formal processes which govern applications for the pricing and reimbursement of medicines, and new uses of existing medicines, to be funded and / or reimbursed. HSE decisions on which medicines are reimbursed by the taxpayer are made on objective, scientific and economic grounds.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Health if the recruitment freeze in Galway University hospital will be lifted in order to fill the 23 vacant midwifery posts; and the way in which she plans to retain recently qualified midwives in Ireland while a recruitment ban is in place.
reply:
There is no recruitment embargo in place in the HSE. However, due to ongoing budgetary issues, several Regional Health Authorities (RHA) have been placed in a strengthened financial control framework. One of these is the West & North-West RHA, which includes Galway University Hospital.
In the period from 1 January 2026 to 31 August 2026, the West & North-West RHA incurred pay costs of €1,286 million against a budget of €1,254 million, equating to a deficit of €32 million (2.6%). To manage these costs, the HSE placed the West & North-West RHA in a strengthened financial control framework, one of whose measures is a requirement for HSE CEO approval of any proposed recruitment. A further requirement for Departmental sanction of any recruitment proposals was announced in recent weeks.
These controls are about ensuring that new recruitment is properly prioritised, affordable, evidenced and clearly linked to patient need. The HSE must show that the need and any patient-safety risk have been assessed, that alternatives such as redeployment, roster changes, skill-mix changes, staff banks, agency conversion, cross-site working or the use of vacancies have been considered, and that funding or a genuine recurring offset is available.
Any requests to recruit additional midwives to Galway University Hospital maternity services will be considered in this context.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Health her plans to increase education about HPV, and the vaccine in schools.
reply:
Increasing vaccination uptake rates in the routine HPV vaccination programme is vital in order for Ireland to achieve elimination of cervical cancer by its target date of 2040. The World Health Organisation has set a target for all countries to ensure that 90% of girls are vaccinated with the HPV vaccine by the age of 15 years.
The ages at which vaccines are recommended in the immunisation schedule are recommended by the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC), in order to give each child the best possible protection against vaccine preventable diseases. As the HPV vaccine is a preventative measure, it is intended to be administered, if possible, before a person becomes exposed to HPV infection. Therefore, the gender-neutral HPV vaccination programme targets all girls and boys in first year of secondary school.
The Laura Brennan HPV Catch-up Vaccination Programme offered HPV vaccination to 5th and 6th year students in secondary school for the 2025/2026 academic year, as a once off opportunity, for those who previously missed the HPV vaccine while in first year of secondary school.
The second phase of the programme launched on 3 September with HSE vaccination teams visiting post-primary schools across the country to offer the HPV vaccine to eligible students.
The programme is open to:
• All eligible boys and girls in 2nd to 5th year of post-primary (secondary) school.
• Home-educated young people born between 1 September 2008 and 31 August 2013.

question: Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Health her plans to make the shingles vaccine (shingrix) available through the HSE.

The immunisation programme in Ireland is informed by the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). NIAC considers the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland as well as international best practice in relation to immunisation when developing its advice
The current NIAC guidelines state that the shingles vaccine may be considered for those aged 65 years and older, due to the greater burden and severity of disease in this age group and in those aged 18 years and older at increased risk of shingles.
The Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA) has carried out a Health Technology Assessment (HTA) on the herpes zoster vaccine which protects against shingles. A HTA is a multidisciplinary research process that collects and summarises information about a health technology. HIQA’s HTA examined the evidence on the clinical effectiveness and safety of shingles vaccines. The cost effectiveness and budget impact were also reviewed, along with the ethical, social and organisational implications of including the vaccine in the adult immunisation schedule.
HIQA published this HTA on 19 July 2024. The HTA found that adding the shingles vaccine to the routine immunisation schedule, at the vaccine price at the time, for all adults aged 65 years and over would not be cost effective and would be associated with a substantial budget impact.

The Cross Border Directive allows public patients to access necessary healthcare, which they would have been entitled to access in the public healthcare service in Ireland, in another EU or EEA country. The patient pays upfront for the treatment and is reimbursed upon return to Ireland.

It is important that this service operates in a responsive way and that reimbursement applications are processed within a reasonable timeframe. The HSE advises it usually aims to repay patients within 30 working days of receipt of all completed documents. The HSE advise the CBD office is currently (as of 2 September 2026) processing applications received at the end of February 2026. A 6-month delay for reimbursement is clearly unacceptable. To address this the HSE has advised my Department that additional resources are being assigned to manage this increase in demand with the aim of restoring processing times to expected levels. I have set the HSE a specific target of getting back to the 30-day target by the end of 2026.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if she is familiar with the remit of the UK Office of Public Guardian; and which Irish statutory body performs the same or similar functions by investigating allegations of mistreatment of elderly people at the hands of family members who may have powers of attorney over their affairs.
reply:
In Ireland, under the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015 (2015 Act), the DSS has statutory responsibility for the review, registration and supervision of Enduring Powers of Attorney (EPA), including the investigation of complaints in relation to the execution of a person’s responsibilities as an attorney under the Act. Safeguarding of adults with decision-making difficulties is central to the EPA application and registration process under the 2015 Act.
As part of the registration process for an EPA, the DSS must review it with regard to the suitability of the attorney and its compliance with the 2015 Act. There are also notice periods set out in the 2015 Act which enable notice parties to object to the registration of the EPA on number of grounds, including, inter alia, that the donor did not have capacity, that fraud, coercion or undue influence was used to induce the donor to execute the instrument creating the EPA, or that the attorney is not a suitable person to carry out that role.
If non-compliance issues are identified but not addressed and/or objections are deemed to be well-founded, then the DSS will decline to register the EPA, a decision that may be appealed to the Circuit Court. These measures help to ensure that the attorney is suited to the role and will act in line with the person’s will and preferences.

reply:

The Pilot concluded in May 2025 and subsequently entered its evaluation phase, led by the National Disability Authority (NDA). The NDA has produced an evaluation report that is now nearing finalisation. The report sets out key findings from the Pilot, drawing on the experiences of participants, families and other stakeholders.

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether she will review HSE guidance and training for adult disability services on the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015, particularly how staff should assess and manage foreseeable safety risks when a person wishes to leave a service unaccompanied; how families’ views should be considered, consistent with the person’s rights; and whether she will issue clarification to providers.
reply:
The Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act (2015 Act), which commenced in 2023, marked a landmark reform of Ireland’s capacity laws, bringing the state into much closer alignment with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD). The commencement of the 2015 Act represented an important shift away from a ‘best interests’ approach to a rights-based approach, privileging a person’s will, preferences and autonomy.
The 2015 Act brought an end to wardship in the State for adults by repealing the outdated Lunacy Regulation (Ireland) Act 1871 and replacing it with a rights-based model of tiered decision support arrangements. This new suite of tiered decision support arrangements is designed to enable those with diminished decision-making capacity to retain as much control over their own lives as possible, and over the decisions that affect them.
The HSE has developed a range of training and resources for staff across the HSE and HSE-funded services, including disability services, to support the implementation of the 2015 Act in practice. This includes e-learning programmes on supporting decision-making in health and social care, as well as guidance for healthcare workers on applying the legislation in practice.

question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the circumstances in which sustainability funding may be provided to an early learning and childcare service required to relocate as a consequence of defective concrete; the categories of expenditure which may be supported under such funding; and whether the funding can contribute towards temporary relocation, long-term relocation or replacement accommodation.
reply:
The sustainability fund for service providers is a support mechanism introduced to ensure the stability and viability of early learning and childcare services for those participating in the Core Funding model. The fund is accessed through a collaborative process involving the service, their local City/County Childcare Committee (CCC), and Pobal, who assess financial eligibility and need.
A childcare service required to relocate due to defective concrete may be eligible for Sustainability Funding under the Emergency Relocation Supports strand. This strand provides community not-for-profit services facing financial difficulty with once-off funding to assist with rental and relocation costs while alternative long-term accommodation is secured.
Once a service engages with their local City/County Childcare Committee, they will be able to avail of supports through the case management process.
Contact details for all City and County Childcare Committees are available on the gov.ie website.

question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the policy measures in place to ensure that childcare capacity is maintained within communities where an existing early learning and childcare facility is affected by defective concrete; and the supports available to prevent the permanent loss of childcare places in such areas.
reply:
The defective concrete blocks issue is an ongoing wider government issue. Responsibility for defective concrete blocks remediation and capital reconstruction rests primarily with other government Departments and local authorities. The Department of Children, Disability and Equality does not have direct responsibility for structural remediation or compensation for defective concrete affected buildings.
However, the Department of Children, Disability and Equality works with Pobal and local Childcare Committees to offer Case Management Supports to services in difficulty. Through this, services may also access Sustainability Funding following an assessment of need. There are examples of sustainability funding for services who needed to relocate due to defective concrete.
Any service which is affected by defective concrete blocks should contact their local City/County Childcare Committee in the first instance.
The City/County Childcare Committee will assist the service in finding a suitable alternative location and will engage with Pobal and the Department regarding sustainability funding to facilitate the relocation of the service.
The local City/County Childcare Committees will also source suitable alternative places for children in attendance of these services to ensure minimal disruption to their learning and care should the service be unable to relocate.
Contact details for the CCCs can be found at City and County Childcare Committees.

question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the additional measures that can be introduced to prevent the illegal hunting of livestock by lurcher hounds in the Loop Head peninsula.
reply:

Legislative and policy responsibility for the Control of Dogs Acts transferred to my Department on 01 June 2025 and for the Dog Breeding Establishments Act on 01 August 2025. This fulfilled a Programme for Government commitment to centralise all legislation and policy in relation to the control of dogs, dog welfare and dog breeding establishments rests with my Department.

Funding of €2m was made available to Local Authorities by the Department of Rural and Community Development (DRCD) in 2025 to facilitate the hiring of additional wardens. This funding will not necessarily cover the full cost of hiring additional dog wardens but is meant as a contribution towards same. question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will designate Greencastle Harbour, County Donegal as a pelagic landing port for catches over ten tonnes, considering the safety concerns for those vessels that currently have to land at the next nearest designated harbour in Killybegs.
reply:
I am advised that a key component of Ireland's Control Plan, operated by the Sea Fisheries Protection Authority (SFPA), currently in force for pelagic landings is that of pre-transport, control-supervised weighing undertaken on publicly-owned weighbridges - which Greencastle port does not have at present.
In light of this, there are no current plans to designate Greencastle port in the manner suggested by the Deputy.
However, I would also like to assure the Deputy that the designation of ports for landings does not preclude vessels from coming into ports for force majeure reasons such as safe harbour.

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to detail the methodology which will be used to calculate grants and premiums rates for the next forestry program.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 485 and 491 together.
The Forestry Programme 2023–2027 was designed to incentivise landowners to engage in tree planting and to support forest owners to manage their forests sustainably, with grant rates reflecting the direct costs of these operations.

The purpose of State Aid is to facilitate changes in the behaviour of an undertaking, such as additional activity contributing to the development of the sector, where it would not have taken place without such aid or where in its absence the activity would have transpired in a restricted or different manner.
My Department, as the granting Authority in this instance, must ensure that any State Aid provided is therefore proportionate and does not subsidis

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to list the number of engagements between his Department and the European Commission in relation to the next forestry programme.
reply:
The Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) contains a general prohibition on the use of State aid to prevent distorting the internal market. However, the TFEU also provides for a number of specific policy objectives that may be supported through the use of State aid by a Member State.
Ireland’s next Forestry Programme will therefore require State Aid approval from the European Commission to implement. This requires submission of a formal application under the Guidelines for State aid in the agricultural and forestry sectors and in rural areas. My Department recognises the importance of engaging with the Commission ahead of any such formal process.

All efforts are directed towards building on the potential contained in our current Forestry Programme 2023-2027 for the post 2027 period, so that we can continue to deliver lasting benefits for climate change, biodiversity, wood production, economic development alongside quality of life.

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine given the importance of afforestation towards climate change mitigation, if his Department will conduct annual reviews when targets are constantly missed in order to address shortcomings, if changes are advised.
reply:
The 2024 Climate Action Plan recognises that afforestation is one of the largest land-based, long-term climate change mitigation measures available to Ireland and sets out the Government’s target of 8,000 hectares of new forestry per year.
The Forestry Programme 2023–2027 provides the implementation mechanism through financial incentives and a range of different forest types available to landowners for afforestation. The 8,000 hectare target is an ambitious one, as forestry remains demand led and is a complex land use choice which is not solely based on incentives. Progress towards this target is closely monitored and my Department are continually developing opportunities to increase the rate of planting.
Last year, my Department prepared a Forestry Opportunities Map which incorporates environmental considerations and associated mapping layers relevant to the Forestry Programme 2023–2027. The Forestry Opportunities Map fed into the Land Use Review (Phase 1 and 2) which forms part of the Programme for Government. The map identifies areas most suitable for planting, primarily based on environmental considerations and soil productivity.
Further, in March this year my Department published the results of a Mid-Term Review of the Forestry Programme 2023–2027. This included a comprehensive package of financial and administrative measures which provided for increases in grants and premia in key areas including forest roads, fencing and agroforestry. These additional supports were des

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine in the context of negotiations on revising the EU Animal Transport Regulation, increasingly frequent extreme heat events, the position Ireland is taking on proposed temperature requirements; and if Ireland supports species/category-specific temperature ranges based on EFSA evidence (details supplied).
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 484, 486 and 488 together.
In December 2023, the EU Commission published a legislative proposal for new rules on the protection of animals during transport, to replace the current EU Regulation (EC) No 1 of 2005 protection of animals during transport and related matters in the context of the EU’s Farm to Fork Strategy. Ireland is strongly committed to improving animal welfare standards during transport and supports the revision of the EU Regulation for this sector.
Ireland is currently chairing the EU Council Working Party on this proposal as part of its Presidency of the EU Council from 1 July to 31 December 2026. In this context Ireland is committed to act as the honest broker during its tenure and will work on behalf all Member States to reach a consensus on this proposal.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the projected allocation to Ireland under the Common Agricultural Policy in the European Commission's proposal for the Multiannual Financial Framework 2028 to 2034, compared with the allocation for 2021 to 2027, in tabular form; if CAP funding will remain ring fenced under the proposed single national and regional partnership plans.
reply:
In July 2025, the European Commission published its proposals for the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) as part of its wider proposals for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) for the period 2028–2034. These proposals represent a significant structural change to the current model of CAP delivery, as it is proposed that the CAP will form part of a broader National and Regional Partnership Plan (NRPP), which consolidates several EU funding streams under a single framework.
It is important to note that the funding for the CAP forms part of the broader EU budget negotiations, which is negotiated by Finance Ministers, and is ultimately agreed by Heads of State and Government.
Under the proposals, Ireland’s indicative ring-fenced CAP allocation is €8.162 billion, within a total NRPP allocation of €11.4 billion.
Over the current programming period of the Multiannual Financial Framework (2021-2027), Ireland receives approximately €10.7 billion in EU funding for the CAP.
Comparing the proposed allocation for Ireland’s CAP for the 2028-2034 period with the current CAP period is not a like-for-like comparison. Different interventions or schemes are included in the €8.162 billion ringfenced amount, compared to the €10.7 billion figure for 2021-2027.
In addition, the proposed framework is intended to allow Member States the possibility to supplement CAP interventions from the wider NRPP allocation, thereby offering flexibility to address national priorities.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 477, 478, 479, 480 and 482 together.
My Department demands the highest standards of animal welfare at every stage of the animal’s life, including during transport. My Department has continuously reinforced its practical, administrative and legislative measures to protect the welfare of animals during transport, often going beyond the minimum requirements of EU law, for example in terms of extra space for calves, more frequent driver retraining and temperature control.
The intra community trade and export of live animals to third countries is a private commercial activity that is regulated by my Department in accordance with EU and National Regulations. reply:

The UK remains by far the most important market for Irish agri-food exports, and we also have significant imports from the UK. question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if the National Standards on Accommodation offered to people in the International Protection process apply to all accommodation centres for international protection applicants, including those living in so called "emergency centres" and designated border facilities as proposed under the newly adopted International Protection Act 2026.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 468, 469, 470 and 474 together.
All IPAS accommodation centres are inspected each year, either by HIQA, by Department officials, or by external inspectors commissioned by the Department. The inspection regime, along with a range of other key quality and compliance actions, has been stepped up significantly over the last 18-24 months, as the Department works to improve standards and value for money across the IPAS system. In 2026 to date, 332 inspections have been completed, covering 261 separate properties. These inspections are fully transparent and available online on gov.ie.
The European Communities (Reception Conditions) (Amendment) Regulations 2023 commenced on 9 January 2024 and provide for the Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA) to conduct inspections of certain accommodation centres contracted by the Department.
The purpose of HIQA inspections is to ensure that IPAS accommodation centres within its remit are operating in compliance with the National Standards for accommodation offered to people in the international protection process, which were adopted in 2019 and have been in effect since the beginning of 2021.
A centre may no longer fall under HIQA’s remit for inspections following a change in contract. question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration can he provide an update on the drafting of National Cyber Security Bill; and when is it expected this Bill will be published.
reply:
The National Cyber Security Bill transposes the Network and Information Systems Directive (NIS2) into Irish law and will place the National Cyber Security Centre on a statutory footing. NIS2 significantly enhances the cyber security supervision and enforcement regime that is already in place in the State.
In anticipation of having the legislation in place and to ensure that Ireland is ready to fully implement the directive, we have taken significant steps to ensure that various implementing measures are in place. This includes a robust approach to sectoral regulation for the Directive with the designation of National Competent Authorities to carry out enforcement and supervision. National Competent Authorities are already undertaking significant preparations to take on these new functions.
The enactment of the National Cyber Security Bill is a priority for myself and the Government. Officials in my Department continue to work with the Office of Parliamentary Council on the drafting of the Bill, which is at a very advanced stage. I expect to be in a position to bring a Memo to Government shortly seeking approval to publish the Bill and to notify transposition of the NIS2 Directive by the end of 2026.

The C&AG report reviewed 14 IPAS accommodation contracts not proceeded with in 2025 as part of a range of measures to limit growth of the IPAS system overall, to reduce longer-term cost and support public safety concerns.
Proceedings were initiated against the Minister by five providers in relation to these contracts. The potential combined value of the related accommodation contracts exceeded €100 million.

The settlement amounts have been categorised as accrued expenses and come from within the €35 million of accrued expenses in the Justice vote.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if the forthcoming legislation on violent and extreme pornography will adopt the Council of Europe’s definition of such material, including depictions or simulations of violence, coercion, sexual assault, degradation and non-consensual conduct; and if the council will also criminalise content involving necrophilia and bestiality.
reply:

Such material is having a harmful impact, particularly on young people, and is distorting healthy sexual development and contributing to misogynistic attitudes.
The proposed offences will criminalise extreme or violent pornographic material, including depictions of rape or violence causing serious harm to a person and depictions of bestiality or necrophilia. It is intended to set out specific categories of such extreme or violent content, which will be defined during the drafting process.

The timeline will depend on completion of drafting, the publication of the Bill and its subsequent passage through the Oireachtas.

The Government’s approach to tackling youth offending is primarily through youth diversion and early intervention. This Department has, in recent years, significantly increased the funding for Youth Justice initiatives; the budget allocation for Youth Justice measures has almost doubled from 2020 to 2026, and the total allocation for youth justice measures is now €43 million.
The Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027 emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It targets behavioural change so the cycle of offending by young people is broken.
The Government operates a graduated response, ranging from diversion to detention. As offending increases in severity, so too does the criminal justice response to address youth crime.
Youth Diversion Projects (YDPs) are community-based, multi-agency youth crime prevention initiatives which primarily seek to divert young people who have been, or are at risk of becoming, involved in anti-social and/or criminal behaviour away from formal engagement with the Criminal Justice System. There are currently 92 YDPs and 4 Targeted Youth Diversion Projects in operation nationwide. reply:
The regulation of the small public service vehicle (SPSV), including the dispatch operator review and maximum fare reviews, is the responsibility of the independent transport regulator, the National Transport Authority (NTA), under the provisions of the Consolidated Taxi Regulation Acts 2013 and 2016. I have no role in the day-to-day operations of the SPSV sector.
From a legislative perspective, Section 24 of the Consolidated Taxi Regulation Acts 2013 & 2016 empowers the NTA Board to make a “Maximum Fares Order” fixing the maximum fare that may be charged by the driver of a taxi for any journey. The current maximum fares order took effect in December 2024, and a maximum fare review is carried out approximately every two years. Hackneys and limousines agree their fares in advance and do not use a meter. As set out in the legislation, charging more than this maximum fare can lead to a prosecution, however, charging below the maximum fare is permitted.
I wrote to the NTA in November 2025 to request clarification on the regulatory position on the Uber fixed price fare for the information of taxi operators and public representatives alike. In their response to my letter, the NTA advised me that the charging of a fixed fare is in accordance with the applicable regulations and that they continue to keep the regulatory model under review.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the timeline for introducing revised qualifying and eligibility criteria for individuals seeking access to both civil and criminal legal aid schemes; if his Department plans to amend the financial means-assessment thresholds to ensure greater access to justice; and the current progress of any draft regulations or legislation regarding these changes.
reply:
It is important to distinguish between the Civil Legal Aid Scheme, which is administered by the Legal Aid Board and provides legal aid and advice in civil matters subject to statutory eligibility criteria, and the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme, under which legal aid is granted by the courts through the judiciary in accordance with the Criminal Justice (Legal Aid) Act 1962.
The Legal Aid Board is the statutory, independent body responsible for the provision of civil legal aid and advice to qualifying individuals. The Civil Legal Aid Scheme has two parts: a legal advice element and a legal representation element. Eligibility for the scheme is determined by reference to a financial assessment and the merits of the case being taken. In accordance with the provisions of the Civil Legal Aid Act 1995 (as amended) and associated Regulations, the Legal Aid Board calculates financial eligibility with reference to the applicant’s disposable income and disposable assets after certain allowances are applied to both.
In June 2022, a Civil Legal Aid Review Group under the chairmanship of former Chief Justice Frank Clarke, SC, was established to review the current operation of the Civil Legal Aid Scheme. question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total value of Youth Diversion funding for each recipient organisation in each of the 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular from.
reply:
The Government has fulfilled its commitment in the Youth Justice Strategy to ensure the availability of Youth Diversion Projects (YDP) throughout the State. Every young person in Ireland now has access to a youth diversion service.
The Government’s approach to tackling youth offending is primarily through youth diversion and early intervention. This Department has, in recent years, significantly increased the funding for Youth Justice initiatives; the budget allocation for Youth Justice measures has almost doubled since 2020 and the total allocation for youth justice measures is now €43 million.
The Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027 emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It targets behavioural change so the cycle of offending by young people is broken.
The Government operates a graduated response, ranging from diversion to detention. As offending increases in severity, so too does the criminal justice response to address youth crime.
Youth Diversion Projects (YDPs) are community-based, multi-agency youth crime prevention initiatives which primarily seek to divert young people who have been, or are at risk of becoming, involved in anti-social and/or criminal behaviour away from formal engagement with the Criminal Justice System. There are currently 92 YDPs and 4 Targeted Youth Diversion Projects in operation nationwide.
The attached table sets out the funding provided to each recipient organisation in 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026.

question: Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number applicants under the AMMR strand of the International Protection Act 2026; the number of appeals under AMMR; the outcomes of those appeals; the number transferred to another member State under AMMR.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and came into effect on 12 June 2026.
The EU Migration and Asylum Pact has been designed to establish a common approach to migration and asylum that is based on the concepts of solidarity and responsibility amongst Member States.
The Asylum and Migration Management Regulation (AMMR) replaces the current “Dublin III Regulation” and improves the system for determining the Member State responsible for asylum applications by making it more efficient and stable, and preventing secondary movements. Key changes include:?
• Shorter deadlines for all procedures, thus contributing to a faster and more efficient process for determining the Member State responsible.
• Introducing the obligation to apply for protection in the Member State of first entry and remain there until the Member State responsible is determined. Lack of compliance with this obligation will lead to important consequences, like providing only for basic needs rather than the full reception conditions.
• Making the ‘take-back’ procedure for returning someone from one Member State to another more effective, in particular by introducing shorter time limits and no shift of responsibility in case the take-back notification is not sent on time.
• Reinforcing family criteria, among others by:
• Including families formed in transit before they arrive in the EU;
• Introducing the possibility to establish responsi

question: Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the legal basis for the issuing of a labour market access permit to an international protection applicant under the international protection act 2026.
reply:
Prior to 12th June 2026, Article 15 of the 2013 Reception Conditions Directive (Directive 2013/33/EU) formed the legal basis on which applicants for international protection were granted labour market access.
Article 15 of the 2013 Directive was transposed into Irish law by the European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018 (S.I. No. 230 of 2018) as amended by S.I. No. 436 of 2020, S.I. No. 52 of 2021, S.I. No. 178 of 2021, S.I. No. 31 of 2022, and S.I. No. 649 of 2023.
Under S.I. No. 230 of 2018 as amended, people are eligible to apply for labour market access permission if:
• They are an international protection applicant under the 2015 Act; and
• They have waited at least 5 months from their “Application Received” date for their first instance recommendation; and
• They are cooperating with the international protection process – delays in receiving a first instance recommendation within 6 months must not be attributed, or attributed in part, to the applicant
• They have not received a final decision on their application.
Following that, a person may be issued a permission for labour market access if, at 6 months, they have not yet received a first instance recommendation. This permission is valid for 12 months and may be renewed until a final decision is made on the person's international protection application.
As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 came into effect on 12 June 2026 and gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum P

question: Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of implicit withdrawals under the International Protection Act 2026; the reason for the decisions; the number of appeals; the outcomes of those appeals.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and came into effect on 12 June 2026.
An application for international protection may be deemed to have been implicitly withdrawn for a number of reasons relating to an applicant's failure to qualify for, comply with, or engage with the international protection process. The grounds on which an application may be considered implicitly withdrawn are set out in section 71 of the International Protection Act 2026 and include, among other matters, a failure to lodge an application, failure to attend a scheduled interview, failure to comply with reporting requirements, or failure to remain available to the competent authorities.
Since the commencement of the Act until , 179 implicit withdrawal decisions have been made by the International Protection Office.
The grounds on which those decisions were made are as follows:
• 143 decisions under section 71(1)(a);
• 30 decisions under section 71(1)(d); and
• 6 decisions under section 71(1)(f).
Of the 179 decisions made, two have been appealed to the Tribunal of Asylum and Return Appeals (TARA). Both appeals remain active.

question: Deputy Pat the Cope Gallagher asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when the District and Circuit Court will return to Donegal town courthouse.
reply:
Management of the courts and operational matters, including matters pertaining to the maintenance and use of court buildings, are the responsibility of the Courts Service, which is independent in the exercise of theses functions.
I am advised by the Courts Service that Donegal Courthouse was temporarily closed in September 2025 following significant health and safety concerns identified by the Office of Public Works (OPW). The most serious issues relate to the entrances for both the public and the judiciary, including a partial collapse of the ceiling in the public entrance porch. In the interests of public safety, all sittings scheduled for Donegal are being accommodated at Ballyshannon Courthouse on a temporary basis.
Since then, the Courts Service has been working closely with the OPW to determine the scope of remedial works and associated costs. I am advised that, following a request from the Courts Service, the OPW carried out a full building condition survey of Donegal Courthouse. The report was provided to the Courts Service in January of 2026 for their consideration.
I am further advised that at this stage, the building condition assessment is part of an ongoing process of technical evaluation and options development being undertaken. The findings are being used to inform decision making on potential remediation and investment options, and further information will be made available as the process progresses and key decisions are reached.

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of complaints or disclosures received by An Garda Síochána to date in 2026 relating to sex-for-rent arrangements following the enactment of the new legislation; the number of cases referred for investigation or prosecution for such incidents; and if he will provide a breakdown by Garda division where available.
reply:
Offering or advertising accommodation in exchange for sexual activity, or “sex for rent”, is a criminal offence. I secured the introduction of this measure through the Criminal Law, Civil Law and Defence (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 in July 2026. Part 15 of the Act, which addresses the issue of “sex for rent”, was commenced on 1 September 2026.
The Act introduces two specific criminal offences around ‘sex for rent’ – offering accommodation in exchange for sexual activity and the advertising of accommodation in exchange for sexual activity. The provisions encompass both rental agreements between landlords and tenants, and ‘rent-a-room’ situations. It is the offer or advertisement that is being criminalised - there is no requirement to prove that sexual activity occurred. The proposed penalty for these offences is a Class A fine of up to €5,000.
The legislation delivers on a specific Programme for Government commitment and forms part of broader efforts to address domestic, sexual and gender-based violence and abuse.
I have been advised by An Garda Síochána that work is currently underway to provide a structured mechanism which will allow for the recording of complaints, disclosures and incidents relating to sex-for-rent arrangements.

question: Deputy Gillian Toole asked the Minister for Social Protection if a comprehensive review of the social welfare system is to be carried out to ensure capacity for all requirements including migration reforms and to ensure fairness, equity and transparency.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 386 and 417 together.
The social protection system comprises of over 100 schemes administered by my Department that provide a wide range of income and employment supports.
Many of these schemes operate in line with specific legislation, eligibility criteria, income thresholds or means tests, and operating guidelines.
My Department regularly reviews its schemes and policies to ensure that they continue to provide effective support and respond to changing demographic, social and economic conditions.
In doing so, we consider submissions from our regular engagement with community and voluntary organisations, including through our bi-annual meetings with the Community and Voluntary Pillar, our annual flagship Social Inclusion Forum, the Carers, and Pre-Budget Forums, and our quarterly Disability Consultative Forum, as well as our public consultation processes.
We consider the engagement we have with other Government Departments, as well as data and research from, for example, my Department's Social Impact Assessments, the Central Statistics Office, the Vincentian MESL Research Centre's Minimum Essential Standard of Living which my Department funds, and international sources such as Eurostat and the OECD. In addition, the Department has a poverty research contract with the ESRI, and occasionally awards contracts to consultancy firms, such as Indecon who are currently researching low hours workers.
Customer feedback is also very important in reviewin

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Social Protection if it is possible to introduce a reduced rate of employers' PRSI for employees under the age of 24, to incentivise the employment of young people.
reply:
In general, the issue of targeted supports to incentivise the employment of young people is a matter for the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment. However, the following is the position with regards to employer PRSI.
The main finding of the latest Actuarial Review of the Social Insurance Fund was that the Fund will experience significant long term sustainability challenges. It is in this regard that the previous Government agreed to a series of annual incremental increases in all PRSI rates, including employer PRSI, up to and including 2028. A further evaluation of the position of the Fund will be held after the completion of the next Actuarial Review next year.
It is in this context that there are no proposals, nor has consideration has been given to reduce the employer PRSI rate for employees of any age group. However, in recognition of the pressures faced by businesses, the Government agreed, in Budget 2026, to increase the employer PRSI threshold from €527 to €552 per week, effective from 1 January 2026. This will ensure that employers with full time employees on the national minimum wage or employees with earnings under €552 per week will attract the lower employer PRSI rate of 9%.
Any further changes to the PRSI employer rates or threshold would have to be considered in a budgetary context, taking account of the economic circumstances and with a view to the sustainability of the Social Insurance Fund.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection whether consideration has been given to a waste collection support for State pensioners living alone, in view of annual minimum bin charges exceeding one week's pension.
reply:
The matter of waste collection charges is the responsibility of my colleague the Minister for the Environment, Climate and Communications. The waste management market in Ireland is now serviced by private companies, where prices charged are matters between those companies and their customers, subject to compliance with all applicable environmental and other relevant legislation, including contract and consumer legislation.
However, my Department does provide Additional Needs Payments as part of the Supplementary Welfare Allowance scheme for people who have essential expenses, which they cannot meet from their own resources.
The decision process involves consideration of the need presented and the ability of the person and their household to meet that need. This entails an assessment, as opposed to a specific means test, of an applicant’s weekly household income, their savings and investments, their outgoings and the type of assistance needed. Other State supports that may already be available to the person are also considered. This ensures that support is provided to people with the greatest financial need.
Any person who considers that they may have an entitlement to an Additional Needs Payment is encouraged to contact their local community welfare service. There is a National Community Welfare Contact Centre in place - 0818-607080 - which will direct callers to the appropriate office. In addition, applications can be made online via www.mywelfare.ie.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Social Protection when the comprehensive review of means testing within the social protection system commenced; the status of that review; when he expects the review to be completed and its finding published; and the reasons for the length of time taken to complete the review.
reply:
The Programme for Government commits to carry out a comprehensive review of means tests across the social welfare system taking into account the Report on Means Testing by the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Social Protection. My Department is conducting a review of means testing within the social protection system.
The aim is to examine various means-tested schemes and identify any issues related to their respective means tests. With over 140 schemes and services, many of which are means-tested, this is a complex and detailed task.
It is my intention that the review's findings will inform decisions regarding potential changes to means testing in future Budgets.
The review is currently with senior management of the Department for review and I expect that it will be submitted to me shortly.
Due to the complexity of the review, I will carefully and thoroughly evaluate it to determine the best way to utilise its findings and identify those that may warrant further consideration.
However, any prospective changes to means-testing arrangements will need to be evaluated and considered within the overall policy and budgetary context.

The person concerned was notified of this decision in writing on 26 June 2026 and afforded the right of review and/or appeal.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Social Protection further to Parliamentary Question No. 6110/26, to provide the actual outstanding social welfare overpayment debt balance owed to his Department at the end of each year from 2016 to 2025, inclusive; and the amount written off in each of those years.
reply:

The overall value of overpayments raised in any given year represent less than 0.5% of total expenditure.
A structured debt management policy in line with normal good practice in recovery of overpayments operates within my Department. Persons who have been overpaid social welfare have a liability to refund the overpayment as they have been in receipt of a payment to which they were not entitled.

In general, overpayments of deceased customers are only written off where there are not sufficient funds in the estate to repay the overpayment.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Social Protection the proportion of the total social welfare overpayments raised in each of the years 2016 to 2025 that was attributable to proven fraud, customer error and official or administrative error respectively; and the monetary value associated with each category.
reply:
The Department of Social Protection administers approximately 140 schemes and programmes, and while most payments are correct, overpayments can sometimes occur for a variety of reasons.
In general, the majority of overpayments are a result of customer error, where information that affects entitlement to payments is not provided in a timely manner resulting in small overpayments.
Debt holders are made aware that a social welfare debt will remain on their records until fully recovered. This will result in a reduction of all future entitlements up to, and including pension. Following the death of a customer owing a debt, the Department will have a claim on any estate remaining.

Following correspondence received on 23 July 2026, the case was reviewed. As a result of this review, it was established that the person was working fewer than 18.5 hours per week and CA was awarded from 16 July 2026.
